15650-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's weekly for boys and girls, for June 17, 1897, number 32 of volume one, cost five cents, with a yearly rate of two dollars fifty. William Beverley Harison published it from West 18th Street, New York. The front again pushes the bicycle premium, and a note announces a second bound volume of the paper, containing numbers 16 onward.

The bicycle offer repeats in full: any wheel in the market for one hundred regular subscriptions, sent in as fast as received. Six-month subscriptions count as one half, three-month as one quarter, and sample copies go at half price. The number shows the paper's business model in action: news for children, paid for by subscriptions, and subscriptions won by prizes. Its readers were also its sales force, town by town.
5935-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
Love games and government worries fill chapters forty-six through forty-eight of this Don Quixote portion. Chapter forty-six treats the terrible bell and cat fright Quixote got during the enamoured Altisidora's wooing, after music left him wrapped in reflections that clung like fleas. Chapter forty-seven continues the account of Sancho's government, and chapter forty-eight what befell Quixote with Dona Rodriguez, the duchess's duenna.

Readers watch the duke's household tease knight and governor alike, with Altisidora's songs and a duenna's grievances as weapons. The chapters favor bedroom farce and island administration in turn, letting comedy and responsibility alternate. This part suits readers deep in volume two, since its household pranks test Quixote's courtesy and Sancho's rule together.
arxiv-2412-00232:
Aishwarya Kumar, Fereshteh Rajabi, and Martin Houde analyse how travel effects distort fast radio bursts, in work from 2024. These bursts are brief, bright flashes of radio waves from deep space. Inside each burst, smaller sub-bursts drift in frequency over time in a pattern that follows a known slope law.

Two effects can bend that pattern. Scattering on the way spreads the pulse, while errors in correcting for dispersion shift it. Scattering keeps the basic inverse link between slope and width but scales it up. Dispersion errors act unevenly: too little correction flattens the slope, too much steepens it and can flip its sign. Very short bursts prove far more sensitive to both errors. The analysis gives observers practical diagnostics for reading burst structure.
arxiv-2412-00532:
The authors introduce ChemTEB, a benchmark built to test text embedding models on chemistry material. Embedding models turn text into numbers that machines can search and compare. General benchmarks exist, but chemistry has its own language and meaning traps, so models need a domain test. ChemTEB supplies a suite of tasks drawn from chemical literature and data.

The team runs 34 models, both open-source and commercial, through the benchmark. The results expose where current methods handle chemical text well and where they stumble. Generic models show uneven skill in this specialized setting. The benchmark ships with open code and data. The authors aim to give the community a standard yardstick that pushes embedding models toward greater precision and efficiency for chemistry work.
arxiv-2412-01132:
Joseph Raj Vishal, Divesh Basina, Aarya Choudhary, and Bharatesh Chakravarthi test video question answering models on traffic footage. Their twenty twenty-four study moves beyond standard benchmarks. Traffic staff need answers about counts, colours, and incidents over time. Synthetic and real traffic sequences supply the test material.

Questions ranged from basic detection to time-based reasoning. A large language model judged accuracy, relevance, and consistency of answers. One model led the field, especially on combined reasoning questions. Still, every model struggled with tracking many objects at once. Keeping a steady sense of time also proved hard. The authors map where current systems help traffic monitoring and where they still fail.
arxiv-2412-02132:
Ke-Tai Wu and six co-authors simulate black holes growing scalar hair in a 2024 paper. Their model mixes gravity, a scalar field, and a nonlinear version of electromagnetism, inside a universe with a boundary that acts like a box. Numerical runs found a surprising flip: the scalar field jumps between stable states as inputs vary. One flip appears when the starting push or coupling changes, and a double flip when the black hole's charge changes.

Near each jump, settling time grows with a clean logarithmic law. The flips trace back to an unstable black hole state sitting between phases. Strong nonlinearity in the field makes the hair vanish altogether.
arxiv-2412-02232:
Natalya Porayko and a large European Pulsar Timing Array collaboration searched in twenty twenty-four for ultra-light axion dark matter hiding in pulsar polarization data. If axion-like particles fill the galaxy, their oscillating field should slowly rotate the polarization plane of light passing through it. Millisecond pulsars are ideal probes: their radio beams are strongly linearly polarized and remarkably steady.

The team examined polarimetry measurements from the array's pulsar sample, looking for the monochromatic polarization wobble an axion field would imprint. The search turns an existing precision data set to a new purpose, complementing the array's famous gravitational wave hunting. Null or positive, such polarization searches constrain how strongly axion-like dark matter can couple to light across a mass range no laboratory experiment reaches.
arxiv-2412-02632:
Jiangtao Wang and six co-authors set out Grouped Spherical Quantization in twenty twenty-four. It is a way to tokenize images for generative models. Image tokenizers squeeze pictures into discrete codes. Past designs used old adversarial training recipes. Tests of them were not even, so scaling was hard to judge. Their method starts the codebook on a sphere. It holds lookups to codes on that sphere.

Their tokenizer beat the best rivals on reconstruction quality. It did so with fewer training iterations. Scaling studies then varied latent dimension, codebook size, and compression ratio. They showed new regimes at high and low spatial compression. The method restructures high-dimensional latents into compact spaces. That lets it scale with less waste. At sixteen-fold downsampling it hit a reconstruction score the authors call state of the art.
arxiv-2412-03832:
Akshay Prasadan and Matey Neykov study a hard problem in statistics, in two thousand twenty-four. They estimate a mean from data where a share of the points has been spoiled on purpose. The mean is also known to lie inside a star-shaped set, a shape defined around a center point.

The pair find the best rate any method can reach in this setting, up to a constant factor. Their rate rests on a local measure of how complex the set is at each scale. A form of their method also works when the noise type is known. When the noise type is unknown, they show the best rate slows a little.
arxiv-2412-04232:
Nanjangud Narendra and co-authors lay out a research agenda for intent-based scheduling in programmable networks, in this 2024 position paper. Fifth-generation and later networks must run themselves, with needs stated as formal intents that people can still read. Many schedulers will run at once across huge, spread-out networks. A meta-scheduler must coordinate them so the intents hold overall.

The authors build their agenda on active inference, a causal method that grants each scheduler some autonomy. The meta level then steers the whole toward the stated intents. They sketch a starter architecture for that design. A set of open research questions closes the paper, covering modeling, building, and fielding such meta-scheduling in practice.
arxiv-2412-04432:
Yuying Ge, Yizhuo Li, Yixiao Ge, and Ying Shan introduced Divot in twenty twenty-four, a video tokenizer powered by diffusion. Language models that both understand and generate video need a tokenizer capturing space and time, whose codes can be decoded back into realistic clips. Their insight inverts the usual training: let a video diffusion model do the judging.

If the diffusion model can denoise clips when conditioned on the tokenizer's features, those features must hold the video's spatial and temporal content. The same diffusion model then serves as the de-tokenizer. Wrapping Divot around a pretrained language model produced competitive results across comprehension and generation benchmarks. An instruction-tuned variant, Divot-Vicuna, handled video storytelling, interleaving narrative text with generated video segments.
arxiv-2412-05032:
Christoph Dalitz and Felix Lögler present a software paper from two thousand twenty-four on a bootstrap variant for the R language. The bootstrap estimates uncertainty by resampling data, but some estimators break its standard form. Resampling fewer points than the full sample, the m-out-of-n method, can rescue such cases under weaker conditions.

The catch is choosing the resample size and a scaling factor well, since coverage depends on both. Their package, called moonboot, computes these intervals and includes tools to estimate the needed parameters. Monte Carlo simulations in the paper test the methods against each other for several estimators. The work gives applied statisticians a ready implementation of a method that was largely theoretical.
arxiv-2412-06532: Nobuki Takeda proves a pullback formula for a class of modular forms on unitary groups, in work from 2024. Modular forms are highly symmetric functions at the heart of modern number theory. The forms here take values in vector spaces and live on groups tied to fields with complex conjugation. The formula describes what happens when such a form is restricted to a smaller group. Takeda also gives an exact condition for when a differential operator keeps the special symmetry properties of these forms.
arxiv-2412-07632:
Bartosz Kasza, Sebastian Borowka, Wojciech Wasilewski, and Michal Parniak tackle a theory problem for atomic radio receivers in a 2024 paper. Some receiver designs use atoms where several light paths interfere, which allows phase sensitive detection of radio waves. In such loop designs, the atoms never settle into a steady state, so standard theory cannot predict limits such as bandwidth or saturation.

The authors propose a method based on expanding the non steady state in a Fourier series. The method runs well on a computer and can predict edge cases such as saturation. As a worked example, they fully describe a receiver design based on highly excited atoms. Their results give practical limits for atomic sensing tools.
arxiv-2412-08232:
Bas van den Heuvel and Jorge Pérez give a gentle tour of recent work on deadlock freedom in asynchronous message-passing programs, in this 2024 arXiv overview paper. In session-based concurrency, types spell out the rules of a two-party conversation over a channel. Real systems send messages without waiting, though, and tangled networks of processes can jam.

The paper walks readers through three typed frameworks, building up step by step. Each framework uses types to promise that a network of processes cannot deadlock, even when messages are in flight at different speeds. The authors show how these ideas carry into a concurrent functional programming language with sessions. The overview is aimed at readers new to the field.
arxiv-2412-08732:
Zoltan Bajnok, Bercel Boldis, and Gregory P. Korchemsky study exact results in a class of quantum field theories. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. The theories are superconformal Yang-Mills theories in four dimensions. Many of their observables can be written as Fredholm determinants of Bessel operators. A single generating function ties these observables together.

The authors analyze that function across a wide range of values and coupling strengths. At weak coupling, its series expansion settles within a finite radius. At strong coupling, the terms grow too fast to stand alone. Extra corrections, tiny at strong coupling, must be added. They compute those corrections and note a strong likeness to the weak-coupling side. The work sharpens exact methods for these theories.
arxiv-2412-09132:
Nine researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four proposing a beam-dump experiment in China to hunt long-lived particles. Many theories beyond the standard model predict such particles, which travel far before decaying. The planned site is CiADS, a proton accelerator facility still being built.

The detector would sit in the beam's forward direction, where the particles' boost is strongest. The long run from dump to detector leaves room for shielding, keeping background events low. As a test case, the team studies the dark photon, seeking electron-positron pairs from its decay. Five years of running would probe untested ground for such particles.
arxiv-2412-10932:
Luis Rodríguez, Susana Lizano, Jorge Cantó, Ricardo González, and Mauricio Tapia wrote a study from 2024 on radio waves from a star named V2187 Cyg. The star is a hot, pulsing type found in the Cygnus region. The team used saved data from a large radio array in New Mexico. They looked at ten rounds of data taken at two radio bands.

The signal was too small to map, but its strength across the two bands gave clues about its source. One burst lasted about a month, which fits a shock inside the wind that blows off the star. A steady glow remained that a lit-up wind alone cannot explain. The team thinks the glow more likely comes from the star's magnetic field.
arxiv-2412-11232:
Calysta Tesiman and co-authors survey spin qubits that can be read with light, in work from 2024. Quantum tools promise faster, sharper work than classic tools, but sound and scalable hardware is still scarce. The review centers on spin-electronic materials, where electron or nuclear spins hold the quantum bits.

The authors walk through each family of light-read spin qubits and grade their promise side by side. Trends emerge in how qubit life spans depend on how the material is made. The spread and density of the bits, plus lab conditions, matter too. The survey aims to help readers spot which lines are most worth backing.
arxiv-2412-13332:
Matias Bundgaard-Nielsen and co-authors introduce a software framework for simulating waveguide quantum optics, in this 2024 paper. In this field, a small quantum system sits in a light guide and meets photons one time slice at a time. That collision picture is intuitive, and users of common quantum toolboxes can pick it up fast. The framework is written in the Julia language.

Despite its simple base, the tool handles rich cases: single and paired photon pulses scattering off emitters or cavities. It also covers memory effects, where reflected photons feed back into the system. Such non-Markovian behavior is hard for many solvers. The authors pitch the framework as an efficient, friendly route into a fast-growing research area.
arxiv-2412-13932:
El Hassan Saidi and Rajae Sammani rebuild the geometry of Narain conformal field theories out of Lie algebra data. Narain theories are a well-studied family whose moduli space carries the Zamolodchikov metric. The authors show that root and weight lattices of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra can encode the theories' momenta and partition functions.

In that algebraic frame, the Zamolodchikov metric is realized directly through the Cartan matrix and its inverse. The paper also derives properties concerning ensemble averaging of these theories and their holographic duals. Extensions to theories with unequal left and right central charges are discussed. Special features of particular partition functions receive attention as well.
arxiv-2412-14532:
Mendel Nguyen and Mithat Unsal study how confining tubes of flux split into fractions in three-dimensional theories. Their paper came out in 2024. Confinement means quarks are bound so tightly that the force between them grows into a tube, rather than fading with distance.

In the theories they study, clusters of magnetic particles generate that confinement. Each tube then splits into equal shares, one for each unit of the underlying symmetry. By curling one dimension into a small circle with a defect inserted, they preserve the vacuum structure. Even without electric charges in the basic equations, large loops of the field get screened by new charges that emerge at junctions. Those charges carry fractional values, and screening is complete or partial depending on whether the symmetry order is even or odd.
arxiv-2412-14632:
Wanda Hou, Molan Li, and Yi-Zhuang You teach machines to discover hidden symmetries of tidy mechanical systems. Conserved quantities reveal a system's deep order but are hard to spot by eye. Their framework fits candidate conserved amounts with neural networks. A closure rule on Poisson brackets forces the candidates into a true Lie algebra.

A soft penalty keeps the found quantities from collapsing into copies. Two classic systems test the method: the Kepler problem and the round harmonic oscillator. The known non-Abelian algebras, SO(4) and SU(3), came back up to basis change. Chaotic and mixed systems are named as the next frontier.
arxiv-2412-17132:
Jannis Kockläuner and Dorothea Golze wrote this physics and chemistry paper, published in 2024. It improves a method for predicting faint extra peaks in X-ray spectra of large molecules, peaks that show how a molecule's electrons react when a deep electron is knocked out.

The standard GW method predicts the main binding energies well but misses these shake-up satellite peaks. The authors extend a combined approach, GW plus cumulant, to cover them. They work out when the method can be trusted, and build a fast version that handles molecules with dozens of atoms. Checks on sixty-five spectra showed which math settings the peaks are sensitive to. For chain-like carbon molecules, the predicted main satellites landed close to measured values and helped explain what experiments see.
arxiv-2412-18032:
Edward Oughton and co-authors chain physics, engineering, and economics to price a giant geomagnetic storm. Space weather threatens power grids, but dollar losses were barely quantified. Their model runs from solar drivers to ground electric fields, then to transformer heating, then to lost output. The United States anchors the worked example.

A storm of the kind expected once in 250 years costs about 2.04 billion dollars per day. Roughly 5.7 million people and 150,000 businesses would lose power in that case. The count covers only heat damage to transformers. Voltage collapse, cascade failures, and repair bills would push losses higher. The frame ports to other countries as a planning template.
arxiv-2501-02132:
Tomer Jordi Chaffer, Dontrail Cotlage, and Justin Goldston study AI agents as cultural actors in online communities, in this 2025 paper. Their focus is the Web3 world on the platform X, where humans and AI agents post side by side. The cultural weight of these agents has drawn little academic study. The authors propose hybrid netnography, a method that treats both kinds of posters as co-participants.

They describe a hybrid marketplace of ideas, where human and machine content compete for attention. Case material shows agents generating, spreading, and engaging with ideas, acting as cultural agents in their own right. A memetics lens frames that role. The paper also flags strains for privacy, ownership of ideas, and governance when machines join public discourse.
arxiv-2501-02632:
Ahmed Abdalla, Stefano Antonini, Luca Iliesiu, and Adam Levine ask what gravity looks like from inside, in a 2025 physics paper. Quantum gravity theory often describes a universe from no one's point of view. The authors instead build their math around a real observer who lives in the spacetime.

They apply the idea to two cases: an observer in a closed universe and one falling into a black hole. In both, the space of possible states seen by the observer turns out far larger than outsider math suggests. A closed universe is no longer reduced to a single state. The team also computes what such an observer would measure. The work reframes deep puzzles about black holes around lived experience.
arxiv-2501-03032: Shuwen Chen and Fangyang Zheng verified a guess in complex geometry in 2025. The guess, due to Chen and Nie, concerns space forms for canonical metric links on compact Hermitian manifolds. The authors prove it for two special groups: complex nilmanifolds whose complex form is nilpotent, and non-balanced manifolds whose Bismut link has parallel torsion.
arxiv-2501-03332:
Tanay Agrawal and co-authors add plug in adapters that let transformer models learn across mixed video data sets, in work from twenty twenty-five. Data sets differ in setting and may lack some input types, and retraining big models is costly. Their frame, called CM3T, aims to bridge a general model and a specific task.

Two adapter types do the work: vision adapters for transfer and cross attention adapters for mixed inputs. The backbone stays frozen, so only a small share of weights trains. Tests on three action and interaction data sets matched or beat top methods with far fewer trained weights. The frame needs no special pretraining. Gains held across recording setups and tasks.
arxiv-2501-03432:
Donatella Genovese and a large team build an explainable AI in 2025 for spotting rare events in particle collisions. The Large Hadron Collider smashes particles and records huge data, where the most prized signals hide. Graph neural networks read collisions well but act as black boxes, which physicists distrust.

Their model mixes a graph transformer with mixture-of-experts layers, where different expert parts handle different patterns. Attention maps show which parts of an event swayed the call, and the experts' split lines up with known physics features. Tested on simulated ATLAS events, it separated rare supersymmetric signals from background with competitive accuracy. The authors argue that trust needs this built-in clarity.
arxiv-2501-04132:
Anibal Medina and five co-authors probe triple gauge couplings in anomalous gauge theories in two thousand twenty-five. Such theories break down as full theories but work as effective ones with a cutoff. Loops in them leave a trace in couplings among gauge bosons. The team takes a model with an extra Z prime boson as their case.

In the model, second generation leptons carry an axial charge. That charge seeds the anomalous couplings of interest. The team tests if colliders could see them past big backgrounds. The high luminosity LHC falls short in their study. A far stronger proton collider and lepton colliders fare better in set mass ranges.
arxiv-2501-04232:
Houari Benammar Ammar's 2025 paper tackles a central open question in the geometry of complex varieties, the non-vanishing conjecture. The conjecture predicts that a certain natural bundle on a variety always has sections, which is a key step toward classifying such spaces. Ammar works with pairs, a variety plus a boundary divisor, under mild singularity conditions.

The first result is a reduction. For irregular varieties, those with a rich structure of maps to tori, the conjecture follows if it holds in lower dimensions. The proof leans on a known splitting result for direct image sheaves. The second part extends a classic decomposition theorem to a broader singularity class. From that extension, sections of the key bundle appear in situations where they were not known before. The paper is short and technical, aimed at specialists in higher-dimensional geometry.
arxiv-2501-05032:
Ethem Yagiz Calik and Talha Ruzgar Akkus wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on making large language models respond in a more human-like way. They review and test routes that improve how well a model follows a conversation, grasps plain language, and reads emotion in what a user says.

The routes include fine-tuning on varied data sets, adding ideas from psychology, and shaping models to copy human reasoning more closely. The authors report that these steps improve how users experience the systems. They also widen where such systems can be used. They note that future work must deal with ethics and bias raised by human-like traits.
arxiv-2501-05132:
Xiang Zhang and six co-authors build a detector that compensates for its own delay in a 2025 paper. Real-time perception systems lose accuracy because sensing and computing take time, so the world has moved on by the time results arrive. Their method estimates timing cues at runtime and predicts where objects will be in future frames. It then outputs the prediction that matches the present moment in the real world.

Motion estimation and feature boosting sharpen the predictions. Across devices from a large server card to a modest gaming card, the system topped rivals on current, next, and multi-frame prediction. It also met real-time limits everywhere, which many rivals failed on weaker hardware.
arxiv-2501-05832:
François-Xavier Gauci and four co-authors watch air bubbles invade model leaves in twenty twenty-five. Plants move water under tension through the xylem. Bubbles that nucleate and spread there, called embolisms, block sap flow. Drought and warming make the threat worse, up to killing trees.

The team uses soft polymer leaves that mimic evaporation and transpiration. Earlier work showed a slender channel constriction produces intermittent embolism spread. Elasticity of the channel ceiling and capillary forces at the air-water boundary interact to cause it. This study focuses on how the channels deform during that spreading. Understanding the coupled mechanics may explain how real xylem fails, and how it sometimes resists. Readers get plant hydraulics studied in a leaf you can watch.
arxiv-2501-07132:
Halsne and Li work out how shore waves bend as they cross shifting flows and a changing sea floor in this twenty twenty-five paper. Bending is the main force that makes wave fields uneven near a coast. Depth shifts and flow shifts both bend waves, but how they mix was not well known.

Inside, the pair finds a clean rule for wave path curve that splits into a flow part and a depth part. Each part rests on how fast its own field shifts from place to place. Test cases show when the two parts add up and when they cancel out. The team also shows which part rules in each case, a help for coast wave forecasts.
arxiv-2501-07632:
Ruiyun Zhang, Martine Schut, and Anupam Mazumdar work out how shaky magnetic fields can spoil a delicate quantum setup, in a 2025 physics paper. The setup floats a tiny non-magnetic sphere, with the goal of placing it in two states at once to test basic physics. Heat-driven field noise can blur that state away.

Using a standard rule that links noise to energy loss, the authors derive a simple rate for that blurring. Their result looks much like the known case of a material in a noisy electric field, but the rate here is often smaller thanks to the sphere's own traits. The formula gives builders of such experiments a quick way to judge how much field noise they can allow.
arxiv-2501-07932:
Andrei Kulikovsky models fuel cell impedance in twenty twenty-five. Solid oxide fuel cells turn hydrogen into electric power, and the anode's impedance spectrum reveals its transport losses if read with care. He builds two models for a hydrogen-fed anode in a button cell: one analytical, for low currents, and one numerical, for high currents.

Both models rest on the dusty gas transport model for the binary mixture of hydrogen and steam. A warning emerges: if the pressure gradient is left out, the effective hydrogen diffusivity in the support layer comes out far too low. The analytical model is fitted to a printed spectrum by least squares, and the fit returns traits such as Knudsen diffusivity, permeability, and ionic conductivity. The paper also flags traps in the use of Warburg elements in stand-in circuits. The result is impedance analysis grounded in transport physics, not circuit guesswork.
arxiv-2501-08832:
Guixiang Hong, Xudong Lai, and Liang Wang prove a local smoothing estimate on two-dimensional quantum Euclidean space, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Their result is the noncommutative analogue of a known estimate by Mockenhaupt, Seeger, and Sogge. Work of this kind transfers classical harmonic analysis results into quantum settings. The generalized Moyal planes provide the underlying geometry.

As an application, and simultaneously a motivation, the authors obtain a noncommutative Bourgain circular maximal theorem. That resolves an open problem left by earlier work of Hong. Circular maximal theorems control averages over circles, a classical theme in analysis. Carrying them into noncommutative geometry requires the smoothing estimate proved here. The paper thus extends a circle of ideas from Euclidean harmonic analysis to quantum Euclidean spaces. Specialists in noncommutative analysis are its natural audience.
arxiv-2501-09832:
Hafiz Majid Hussain, Ashfaq Ahmad, and Pedro Nardelli present a 2025 study on managing local energy systems with software agents. Their work combines a crossover form of binary particle swarm optimization with a layered agent design for a setup connected to the main grid. One lead agent runs the planning while smaller agents report local conditions.

Inside, the lead agent works to cut energy buying costs, limit battery wear, and reduce delays in scheduling loads. The smaller agents send status updates and receive action plans in return. In simulations the authors report lower average system costs than the methods they compared against, while still meeting user demand and service quality.
arxiv-2501-09932:
Yoshihiko Nishikawa and co-authors improve swap algorithms that help glassy materials settle into stable states in computer models, in a paper from 2025. Swapping particle sizes lets a simulated glass relax far faster than normal motion. A recent method did this without rejection for hard spheres, but soft particles were not covered.

The team extends the method to soft particles that repel each other with smooth forces. One route uses a split form of the acceptance rule, but that split weakens the speed gains. They then propose a second method that keeps the standard rule and still breaks the usual balance. It relaxes soft glasses faster at low temperatures than the first method. The tools produce very stable glass states for study.
arxiv-2501-10532:
Shooting photons at a proton and watching a heavy particle called a J/psi come out can reveal how mass and pressure are spread inside the proton. Yuxun Guo, Feng Yuan, and Wenbin Zhao use fresh measurements of this near-threshold reaction from two experiments to pin down the proton's gravitational form factors, which encode that inner structure. They analyze the data with Bayesian methods inside a standard parton framework.

Their fits agree well with the best lattice calculations of the same quantities. In particular, the data strongly favor negative values for the quark and gluon parts of one key form factor. The authors argue that sharper experiments planned for the future could turn this reaction into a precise tool for mapping the forces that hold the proton together.
arxiv-2501-10632:
Jason Li and Thatchaphol Saranurak give a new flow algorithm in twenty twenty-five. Multi-commodity flow sends many goods through one network at once. Their algorithm is local, meaning it works from limited views rather than the whole graph. They apply it to expander graphs, networks that are very well connected.

On expanders, their method gives a near-exact approximation in time that breaks a long-standing barrier. All prior methods needed time tied to the product of commodities and edges, or settled for rough answers. Their trick localizes Sherman's algorithm inside a multiplicative weights frame. In each round, tiny weights are rounded to zero, so few large weights remain. The oracle call then runs in sublinear time. The insight may serve other problems too.
arxiv-2501-12532:
Eric Ching, Ryan Johnson, and Andrew Kercher wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about simulating compressible flows with several gases mixed together. Where gases meet, pressure and velocity should stay in balance if they start balanced. Many standard schemes quietly break the pressure balance, which seeds false waves at the interface.

The authors first derive when a standard discontinuous Galerkin scheme keeps each balance. They then build a variant that solves a pressure equation instead of the energy equation, with correction terms that restore energy conservation in a discrete sense. Small changes recover both balances at once, at some trade-offs they discuss. Tests on smooth interface flows in one, two, and three dimensions show the scheme behaving as designed.
arxiv-2501-14432:
Carlos Muñiz-Cuza, Matthias Boehm, and Torben Bach Pedersen wrote a paper from 2025 on shrinking time series data without spoiling later study. Sensors pour out long series that cost space to store and time to move. Lossy shrinking saves far more space than exact methods, at a small loss of precision. The catch is that no one knows in advance what the loss does to forecasts and other checks.

Their method, named CAMEO, promises to keep two key patterns of a series intact: how each point echoes the last, and the deeper form of that echo. It builds the shrunken series from line pieces and keeps running sums. On test sets, it shrank data twice as much as past methods on average. Forecast accuracy held, and at times grew. The frame can stretch to many series at once.
arxiv-2501-15732:
Jie Li, Qi Li, and Zi-Xiang Hu present a study from twenty twenty-five on the inner edge of a quantum Hall state laid on a cone. In a Hall state, the edge is pinned by the walls of the sample. The inner interface is free to move and may sag like a string. On a disk, its energy gains a term from its curve that scales with disk size.

A cone lets them tune the curve with one angle dial. They work out the interface energy in exact form on the cone. The curve term from the disk case checks out. The tip of the cone adds its own extra term to the energy. The result sharpens how shape feeds into Hall physics.
arxiv-2501-15832:
Vladislav Pokidkin solved a long-open algebra problem in a 2025 paper. A discriminant is a formula that tells when a system of equations has a repeated or special solution. For systems with as many equations as unknowns and free coefficients, experts long lacked a full picture of the discriminant's parts and sizes.

Pokidkin first maps where a related determinant stays impossible to factor. With that map he proves a named conjecture: for a basic nonlinear square system, the discriminant forms a single unfactorable surface. He then lists all parts, sizes, and degrees for three standard versions of the discriminant. A theory of matroid-like structures guides the proof throughout.
arxiv-2501-16332:
Maimon, Alus, and Kedar offer a way to cut clashes between wireless links that share one channel in twenty twenty-four. When links use the same frequency, their signals muddy each other and slow the network. New networks need to reuse each frequency as much as they can. The team's method leans on how much power each link uses.

They split time among links that share a frequency, so rivals do not talk at once. Power levels are set to keep each link clear of the rest. In their tests, the plan cut total clashes a lot. It also cut the count of frequencies the whole network needs. That frees scarce spectrum for other uses.
arxiv-2501-17432:
Gavrichkov, Polukeev, and Ovchinnikov present a 2025 paper on magnetic coupling across the diagonal of a copper oxide layer. Cuprate materials, famous for high-temperature superconductivity, are built from such layers. Many models make the diagonal coupling between next-nearest copper neighbors a key knob, so its true sign and size matter.

The authors study an idealized square layer. They show that extended hopping models represent the magnetism correctly only in that ideal case. There, symmetry forbids any ferromagnetic part, so the diagonal coupling is always antiferromagnetic. In real layers the same estimate can overshoot. The paper also discusses why these systems frustrate easily, and why their patchy spin patterns react so strongly when the square symmetry breaks.
arxiv-2501-18432:
Eneko Osaba and six co-authors solve drone routing with hybrid quantum computing in two thousand twenty-five. Their method is named Q4DR, short for Quantum for Drone Routing. It joins the two main styles of quantum machines. Gate based machines run one phase, and annealers run the other.

The first phase groups stops with a quantum approximation method. The second phase finds routes on D-Wave annealers. Code uses a known quantum language for the gate side. Three test cases of rising hardness prove the method. Real limits span uneven costs, banned paths, and charge stops on the route. The work shows quantum tools at work in logistics.
arxiv-2501-18732:
Zhao and co-authors present a 2025 study on how wind and solar farms should bid into power markets that settle twice, once a day ahead and once in real time. Poor coordination between the two stages raises costs. The authors propose benchmark bidding curves for renewable power. A two-level model tunes the curves. It foresees how the market clears under each weather outcome and aims for the lowest total expected cost.

They prove that a simple one-step curve with a zero price can reach the best total cost when renewable power costs nothing to produce. Tests on a model of the New York grid with 1,576 nodes beat the standard practice of bidding the plain forecast. The method came close to the ideal outcome that a fully uncertain market design would give.
arxiv-2502-00032:
Connor Shorten and co-authors test, in twenty twenty-five, how well large language models query databases via function calling. Function calling lets a model invoke tools in a set format. Database access is a top use, since it lets models reach private or fresh data. The authors define one tool that unifies search, filters, and result transforms such as sums and grouping. They built a test pipeline that makes synthetic database schemas and queries, adapted from a known framework.

Eight models from five families were tested. The best matched the true query call in about three quarters of cases. Models handled yes-or-no filters well. They struggled with text filters. Results are split by query part and by use case.
arxiv-2502-00132:
Way, a solo author writing under initials in the record, models a small planet around the nearby star TRAPPIST-1 in a 2025 paper. The planet sits near the border between a Venus like world and an Earth like one. Recent work on its sibling planets raised doubt that it holds any thick atmosphere at all.

Assuming it does keep an atmosphere, the author ran three dimensional climate models with a moving ocean. The planet could sit in the habitable zone, but only within a narrow range of conditions. It could equally be a hot Venus like world, a dead airless one, or in transition between states. Such modeling helps observers tell these cases apart with future data.
arxiv-2502-02132:
Matias Cattaneo and Boris Shigida wrote this optimization theory paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on the hidden effects of memory in training algorithms. Modern optimizers let each step depend on past steps, with old steps fading fast; momentum is the classic case.

The authors give a general recipe for building a memoryless stand-in for such an algorithm. Replace every past position in the update rule with the current one, then add a correction term that the memory leaves behind. That correction reads as a change to the loss itself, so memory quietly reshapes what the algorithm thinks it is minimizing. Applied to two popular optimizers, the theory shows one gains a harmful anti-regularizing push from memory while the other does not. That split matches the second one's better test scores reported in practice.
arxiv-2502-02432:
Tewodros Amdeberhan, Michael Griffin, and Ken Ono revisit three classic invariants of shapes in a 2025 math paper. The invariants, known as genera, sum up deep facts about a manifold in a single value. They carry names from their makers and from the classes of shapes they fit, and they have been studied for decades.

With a small tweak that uses a classical trick, the authors show two of the genera flow straight from a famous theta function. For each level they give exact formulas that write the genera as traces of partition-based series. Those forms convert back to the classic topological ones with ease. A surprise in the paper is that Ramanujan had already twisted one of these series in his lost notebook, long before the topology was built.
arxiv-2502-03132:
Sun and a team of colleagues at Carnegie Mellon introduced SPARK in twenty twenty-five, a safety toolkit for humanoid robots. Humanoids are powerful machines that move in complex spaces near people, so safety failures can hurt someone. Their body shape also makes general safety design harder.

SPARK packages leading safe control algorithms in a modular framework users can compose. Safety criteria and sensitivity can be tuned to balance caution against performance. Simulation benchmarks compare safety approaches across settings, tasks, and robot models. For real hardware, the kit works with an Apple Vision Pro or motion capture cameras for sensing, and accepts other sensors too. Demonstrations included a Unitree G1 humanoid in both simulation and case studies. The code is open source.
arxiv-2502-03832:
Xi Luo and colleagues studied a magnet whose spiral order talks back to its electrons in a 2025 paper. Certain rare-earth semimetals host Weyl fermions, exotic electrons with point-like band crossings, inside a crystal lacking mirror symmetry in its magnetic pattern. The magnetism itself is negotiated among a ferromagnetic pull, a twisting interaction, and the coupling to those Weyl electrons, and the authors map the outcome on a lattice model.

Both quantum and thermal transitions appear between plain ferromagnetism and a correlated helical state. Unlike a detached spiral, the correlated helix imprints a coupling-dependent nesting pattern on the electron bands, and it strongly suppresses a signature current from the chiral magnetic effect. That suppression could explain observations in the real material family.
arxiv-2502-06232:
Tobias Larsen, Claus Ekstrom, and Anne Petersen wrote this statistics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on learning cause-and-effect maps when time gives part of the answer. If some variables are known to come earlier, whole arrows in a causal graph can be ruled in or out at once.

Their algorithm, TGES, is a score-based search that bakes tiered time knowledge into its scoring rule. They prove it always returns a graph of a stated kind, maximally oriented within its class. In the large-sample limit, that graph contains the true causal map. Simulations show gains over a constraint-based rival method, with a better trade between hits and false alarms. A worked example on life-course health data shows the method in use. The paper supplies both the tool and the terms to talk about tiered causal search.
arxiv-2502-08432:
Daeyoung Roh and four co-authors improve learning on hypergraphs in a 2025 machine learning paper. A hypergraph links items in groups rather than in pairs, which fits real settings like group chats or shared tags. Contrastive learning teaches models by pulling like items together and pushing unlike ones apart, but it has barely been tried on hypergraphs.

Their method, HyFi, adds noise to node features instead of wrecking the group structure, as older augmentation tricks do. It also adds a middle category of weak positives, items that are somewhat alike, between true matches and true mismatches. Across ten data sets, HyFi beat both guided and unguided rivals while training fast and using little memory.
arxiv-2502-08732:
Danat Issa and four co-authors simulated collapsing massive stars in twenty twenty-five to see how black hole spin evolves when neutrino cooling is included. Collapsars power long gamma-ray bursts through jets from a spinning black hole wrapped in a magnetically arrested disk. Such disks spin their holes down to an equilibrium; without cooling, that equilibrium is so low the jets may be too weak to escape the star.

Their three-dimensional simulations add two-moment neutrino transport to general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics. Neutrino-cooled disks still spin the hole down fast, but equilibrium lands near zero point one three — two to four times the non-radiative value, matching gravitational-wave spin estimates. The resulting jets are four to sixteen times stronger, far more able to drill out of the star.
arxiv-2502-08832:
Tirmazi shows how foes can slow key-store reads by fooling their quick-pass screens in this twenty twenty-five paper. These stores stack writes in log form for speed and use chance screens to skip blank reads. A foe who knows the screen's weak spots can flood it with false hits.

Inside, tests show read waits can swell to nine times their fair grade under such floods. The author sets a foe model and a shield mark for what safe must mean here. Two big stores are then re-built with that shield baked in from the base. Runs on the re-built stores show the flood tax can be cut back hard. The work sets a bar for stores that must face foes.
arxiv-2502-09232:
Kalonji Kalala's 2025 thesis gives smart contracts a logical foundation in the situation calculus. Smart contracts automate agreements on blockchains across cyber-real systems, yet legal contracts are riddled with exceptions and nested subcontracts. Translating them truly into code is slow, error-prone work with no uniform formalism to check against. The situation calculus, a logic built for thinking about actions and how worlds change, supplies the missing specification language.

Kalala shows how contract actions, procedures, and effects can be specified and reasoned about in that logic. Aiming at a somewhat universal account of contract actions. Formal foundations would let lawyers and engineers verify that code enforces the agreement signed.
arxiv-2502-09532:
Biswas, Erlei, and Gadiraju test if tool flaws in one tongue sway use in a next. New write aides lean on tools that speak more than one tongue. Such tools vary in grade by tongue, by wide past proof. Users of more than one tongue thus face split tool grades. Men oft spread a tool's flaws cross lone tasks in past work. That spread breaks the choice-free rule in act terms.

Their task is a gift ad write job in two tongues. They ask if aide grade in tongue two bends use in tongue one. They also weigh how that bend shapes the ad's pull. Faith in tool use joins the weigh, as do gift picks. Finds show aides' users do break choice-free acts in the task. Grade in one tongue bent trust and use in the next.
arxiv-2502-11332:
Chen, Tokdar, and Groh estimate block shaped covariance matrices with a Bayesian ladder in twenty twenty-five. The work was spurred by brain data, where neurons fall into hidden groups. Within a group, ties share one pattern, and across groups another. Signs can flip between groups, unlike plain block diagonal forms.

Their method finds the hidden blocks and the full matrix together. Tests show the ladder and a shrink prior are both vital when blocks are many. The form cuts dimension for free and mimics factor models with no factor count to pick. Brains and markets both fit the frame, they note.
arxiv-2502-12832:
Sara Alfaro and a team of co-authors propose a new way to make exotic ions for precision measurement. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses antiproton annihilation: when an antiproton hits matter, it can leave behind a highly charged ion in an excited, long-lived state. Trapped, such ions could serve as fine probes.

The team looks at atoms made of one such isomer plus a single electron. In that setup, the hyperfine splitting of energy levels gives a light signal that can be measured. They pick out good cases among five elements, from yttrium to antimony. Their signals sit in the infrared, and the excited states live long enough for careful metrology.
arxiv-2502-12932:
Salsabila Zahirah Pranida, Rifo Ahmad Genadi, and Fajri Koto published this study in 2025. Commonsense stories rooted in local culture are scarce for low-resource languages, and hiring native writers is costly. The team worked with Javanese and Sundanese, two Indonesian languages. They compared three ways to build training stories: language-model stories prompted with cultural cues, machine translations of Indonesian tests, and stories written by native speakers. Human judges rated the outputs.

Model-written stories matched native ones on cultural fidelity, though they lagged in coherence and correctness. Models trained on the synthetic stories then performed better on a human-written test than models trained on translations. They also beat models trained on Indonesian human stories. The team released a benchmark of culturally grounded stories in both languages. Their results suggest synthetic data can support reasoning research where native annotation is hard to fund.
arxiv-2502-14132:
Nadav Borenstein and co-authors ask whether crowd-written community notes can replace professional fact-checkers, in a 2025 study. Community notes are short corrections that users add to posts on social media. The team used language models to tag a large set of notes from Twitter/X by topic, sources cited, and the claims they answer.

The analysis shows that notes lean heavily on fact-checking work. Notes cite fact-checking sources up to five times more often than earlier reports suggested. Notes that tackle broad false stories are twice as likely to cite such sources as other notes. The authors conclude that crowd moderation works because professional checking sits underneath it, not instead of it.
arxiv-2502-14432:
Sarvin Moradi and four co-authors build neural networks that hold the shape of a physics frame for systems with inputs, loss, and noise. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Networks built on the classic energy frame have shown much use. But real gear adds three hard facts: drives from outside, loss of energy, and noisy reads. The new frame, with an output-error noise part, builds all three in. Its shape lets it model complex gear from noisy data. The team also gives a way to fit such nets, drawn from a known encoder path. The aim is a physics-true model that works on real bench data.
arxiv-2502-14632:
Jennifer Haase published a 2025 study on how professional coaches actually use generative AI. Chatbots and large language models have slipped into coaching work quietly. The study surveyed 205 coaches about their habits, hopes, and worries. Adoption turned out to be wide: coaches use the tools for research, drafting content, and paperwork. The relational heart of coaching, reading a client and interpreting their story, stays human.

Two traits predicted who adopts the tools: AI know-how and a belief that AI will matter. Coaches who felt the tools worked used them more; fear of being replaced did not hold anyone back significantly. Ethics weighed heavily, especially openness with clients and data privacy. Frequent users, notably, showed the sharpest ethical awareness. The paper sketches a near future where AI handles the desk work of coaching while people keep the conversation. It also flags where norms and training must catch up.
arxiv-2502-14832: Lee and Moritoh present a math paper from twenty twenty-five on locating fine-scale singularities of functions. They define microlocal Sobolev singularities through a wavelet transform due to Pandey and Upadhyay. The new definition is then compared with Hörmander's classic microlocal notion. The aim is a wavelet-based lens on where and how functions misbehave.
arxiv-2502-14932:
Han Zhang, Langshi Zhou, and Hanfang Yang present a method that teaches a language model to reason over a knowledge graph with self-reflection, in a paper from 2025. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked nodes. Pairing them with language models can improve reasoning, but how models use the graph was not well understood.

Their framework lets the model control its own reasoning path. Special tokens signal when to fetch more facts and how to judge them. Judgments are graded on several aspects rather than a simple yes or no. The model is trained end to end, so fetching and checking improve together. The paths it produces can be read by humans, which aids study of its choices. On standard graph reasoning tasks, the model beat past baselines.
arxiv-2502-16132:
Craig Gidney and Thiago Bergamaschi wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on building a fault-tolerant quantum computer in the shape of a line. Their qubits, the basic units of the machine, sit in a row and link only to their nearest neighbors. A known limit had suggested that good error-correcting codes need a denser layout than a line allows.

The authors show by construction that the limit does not extend to full circuits. Their design keeps a coding rate above five percent, with time costs that grow slowly. It builds on a tower of Hamming codes and uses a variant of a known method to check the qubits.
arxiv-2502-17832:
Hyeonjeong Ha and colleagues show how little poison it takes to break a multimodal retrieval system. Retrieval-augmented models consult external knowledge to stay factual. Attackers who slip malicious content into that knowledge can steer the model. The team builds a framework to study such poisoning systematically, with two new attacks.

A localized attack plants query-specific misinformation and hit its target up to fifty-six percent of the time, even with restricted access. It transferred across four retrievers without re-tuning. A globalized attack needs just one untargeted injection to wreck generation across all queries, driving accuracy to zero. Existing defenses failed against both. The authors offer the framework as a foundation for securing retrieval systems. The results read as a warning: the knowledge base is now part of the attack surface.
arxiv-2502-18632:
Zhangqi Duan and co-workers automated the skill tagging of coding problems in a 2025 paper. Intelligent tutoring systems track student mastery of fine-grained knowledge parts, the skills a problem exercises. Experts must handcraft and tag those parts, a labor narrow point that keeps coding courses from scaling feedback. Their chain uses large text models to generate and tag knowledge parts for open-ended coding problems. Then feeds them into a text-model-based knowledge tracing setup, KCGen-KT, that predicts how well students do from submission histories.

On two real data sets of student code in unlike languages. The system beat current tracing methods and even human-written parts at predicting future responses. Learning curve analysis showed the machine-generated parts fit student actions better under a cognitive model, and course instructors judged the generated tags reasonably exact. The chain points toward tutoring that improves itself.
arxiv-2503-01332:
Cheng-Kuang Wu, Zhi Rui Tam, and colleagues study when a language model should answer, refuse, or guess in a 2025 study. Agents built on these models act step by step toward goals, and some wrong steps carry severe costs. An agent that never defers will eventually blunder; one that always defers is useless, and the right balance depends on how bad a mistake would be.

The authors investigate risk-aware decision making, where the tendency to hold back should scale with the stakes. Calibrated deference is a safety property that benchmarks rarely grade, yet every deployed agent depends on it.
arxiv-2503-01732:
Vito Mengers and Oliver Brock wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It solves chains of robot tasks with no plan at all, by letting a gradient descent controller reshape its own guiding field as feedback comes in.

The field is myopic, seeing only the next step, but it shifts with the task's built-in patterns, which hide the needed subgoals. The method clears the classic Blocks World test, a stacking puzzle that planners were made for, with no planner in sight. In a hundred real-world trials with drawers, it beat planning on sturdiness. Sensing and error recovery arose on their own from the descent. The authors link this style to how living things solve such tasks.
arxiv-2503-01832:
André Jonasson presents a 2025 study of strange large activations that show up in the attention layers of modern language models. These models locate words with rotary position encodings, which rotate queries and keys by their relative positions. Certain features in the rotated queries and keys, called rotary offset features, keep emerging with outsized values and are often read as outliers. Jonasson asks why they arise and where they live.

He derives bounds predicting which rotary frequencies spawn the features and how far apart the query-key angles must sit. Tests across models of many sizes and designs confirm the predictions. The features appear reliably across layers, heads, and architectures. The work gives model builders a principled account of an artifact they often just notice and work around.
arxiv-2503-06632:
Mingxiao Li, Tingyu Qu, Tinne Tuytelaars, and Marie-Francine Moens tackle two flaws in personalized image generation: models that copy their few training photos too closely, and scorekeeping that flatters them. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Personalization teaches a generator one subject from a handful of images. The aim is new scenes with the same subject, not replays.

Their training pipeline adds an attractor that filters distractions out of the training shots. The model can then focus on the subject itself. For fair grading, they built a fresh test set with varied, well-designed prompts. Past practice graded models on their own training images, which inflates scores. Human grading, the usual fallback, wobbles with bias. The new bench lets automatic scores be trusted again.
arxiv-2503-10432:
Can Zheng, Jiguang He, Guofa Cai, Zitong Yu, and Chung G Kang use camera images and large language models to aim millimeter-wave beams, in a 2025 paper. Such beams carry fast wireless data but are narrow, so finding the right direction costs time and training signals. Their framework watches the scene instead of probing the air.

A vision step pulls the position of the user's device from ordinary photos. A reprogramming step then translates those visual and time features into a form the language model can reason over. On a realistic vehicle-to-base-station test, the method picked the exact best beam about sixty-one percent of the time and landed in the top three nearly always, beating standard deep learning models. With very few examples, its scores slipped only modestly over time.
arxiv-2503-11032:
Lilin Zhang, Chengpei Wu, and Ning Yang harden image models against trick inputs when labeled data is scarce, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Standard hardening perturbs only some weak traits of an image, so false links to labels survive and the model learns the wrong traits. Full perturbation is hard when labels are few and traits are hard to tell apart.

Their method pairs contrastive learning with attack training over partly labeled data. Grounding in information theory guides full attack builds that break weak-trait links to labels. Broad tests on standard sets beat prior methods. Code is shared for reuse. Readers who guard vision systems get a stronger training recipe for scarce-label settings.
arxiv-2503-11832:
Yiwei Chen and five co-authors expose a safety mirage in twenty twenty-five. Vision-language models can produce harmful content when prompted badly. The standard defense is supervised safety fine-tuning on curated data. The authors argue this defense is shallower than it looks.

Fine-tuning, they show, reinforces spurious correlations between surface text patterns and safe responses. The model learns the look of a dangerous request, not the danger. A one-word substitution attack can then slip past the fine-tuned model. Changing a single word to a correlation-triggering alternative breaks the refusal behavior. Machine unlearning is proposed as a mitigation that removes the spurious links. Readers in AI safety get a named failure mode and a first remedy for multimodal alignment.
arxiv-2503-11932:
Dhruv Kudale and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a table-reading system that works across writing scripts, not just English. Reading table structure is key for search, rebuilding tables, and document understanding. Most top systems were trained on English, and building labeled data for other languages is slow and costly.

Their system treats the task as predicting the arrangement of cells, in a compact sequence code for table layout. Paired with a grid estimator, it raised structure scores even on non-English documents. On standard benchmarks it matched top models while running faster. On non-English tables it beat the leaders by a wide margin. The team also gives a converter to web table format and releases its code.
arxiv-2503-12432:
Shuwen Chen and Fangyang Zheng test a conjecture about complex spaces whose mixed curvature stays constant, in a paper from 2025. Hermitian manifolds carry both a metric and a twist that need not mesh. Tang had guessed that a compact such space with steady nonzero mixed curvature must mesh after all. He proved it for surfaces and for one broad class.

The pair confirm the guess for several fresh classes of spaces. Their list covers nilmanifolds, certain solvable groups, and nearly abelian groups. They also settle all compact balanced threefolds whose Bismut link has steady twist. Each case adds weight to the guess. The full claim stays open, but the net of proven cases widens. The paper is a step in complex geometry's map of curvature rules.
arxiv-2503-13332:
Nora Takacs, Csaba Kiss, Robert Szakats, and Andras Pal test what a space telescope can tell us about asteroids. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses TESS, a survey satellite, which caught many main belt asteroids from more than one angle. From how an asteroid's brightness shifts as it spins, we can guess its shape and spin axis.

The team fit simple ellipsoid shapes to forty-four asteroids and checked the results against a known database of shapes from ground data. Spin axes matched fairly well, and matched a second large survey even better. Their verdict is mixed: TESS data alone finds spin periods well, but shape and axis calls from it have clear limits.
arxiv-2503-13832:
Yun-Jie Wang and eight co-authors sharpen the rules for when error filtration can clean up a quantum memory. Their paper from twenty twenty-five studies QRAM, quantum random access memory, a key part for data lookup in superposition. It lacks fault tolerance, which blocks real use. Error filtration offers a leaner path than full correction, but its reach at mid-level noise was murky.

A new simulator for bucket-brigade QRAM makes the test possible. Sparse state coding plus a noise-aware pruning step let it scale far past past tools. Runs expose odd suppression failures at high noise or large address size. Post-selection odds cap the gains there. Folded into theory, this yields near-deterministic criteria for when filtration helps. Memory and time costs of the simulator are charted as well.
arxiv-2503-14032:
Hua, Mohammadi, Ngo, and Matthaiou add stacked intelligent surfaces to cell free networks that send power and data in twenty twenty-five. Future wireless systems may charge devices while communicating with them. Cell free massive MIMO spreads many access points around users. Stacked metasurfaces can shape radio waves in layers.

The team derived formulas for data rates and harvested energy. They then maximised total harvested energy while keeping each data user above a rate floor. Phase settings for the surfaces and power budgets were optimised together. A layer by layer method handles the surface settings. More layers gave almost seven fold energy gains in simulations. Their power scheme also raised the minimum data rate by up to forty percent.
arxiv-2503-14232:
Yuyang Xue and co-authors present a method for erasing concepts from text-to-image models without erasing look-alikes, in work from 2025. Erasure is needed when models can produce unwanted content, from private likenesses to protected characters. Past methods either leave traces of the target or wipe unrelated concepts that merely resemble it.

Their framework uses a large language model to list concepts related to the target, which should go too, and distinct concepts that must be kept. That semantic map guides a precise removal process. Tests cover objects, person identities, and abstract style traits tied to intellectual property. The method beat existing approaches across the tasks. The authors also built a dataset for this finer kind of erasure test.
arxiv-2503-14332:
Siyu Jiang and Fa Peng Huang explore a light particle as dark matter, born from primordial black holes, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The particle is a pseudo-Goldstone boson from a broken symmetry, and its weak links keep it out of early thermal balance. Black holes could still make it, by glowing or by spinning effects.

Light and heavy versions are tracked for still and spinning holes alike. Gravitational wave traces from wall collapse, density ripples, and hole glow are weighed. A recent ultra-high-energy neutrino event at a sea detector could fit the setup, the authors claim.
arxiv-2503-15232:
Ashley Willis and Michael Burin revisit a 60-year-old puzzle about rolls in rotating fluid flow, in a research paper from 2025. In Taylor-Couette flow, fluid spins between two cylinders. A classic 1965 study saw short-lived rolls aligned with the axis when the outer cylinder started and stopped fast, set across the usual Taylor rolls.

Guided by a newer lab sighting, the team found the same instability in simulations. It traces to a bend in the speed profile across the gap, and it appears while the flow slows down. The instability links to a known one in oscillating boundary layers. For narrower gaps than the classic setup used, standard rolls overrun it fast, which helps explain why it hid for so long.
arxiv-2503-19732:
Nenad Vukmirović simplifies in 2025 how physicists compute the way electrons lose energy to lattice vibrations in materials. Those losses set electrical resistance and device heat. Standard codes precompute couplings on dense grids of electron and vibration momenta, which is slow and memory-hungry.

His method skips the grid. It handles the energy-matching condition analytically and averages over vibration directions, then sums over a modest sample of electron states. Tests on a textbook model and on the real semiconductor zinc telluride gave accurate results with only about a hundred momenta of each kind. The count stays low whatever the carrier mass, promising faster materials screening.
arxiv-2503-20432:
Deniz Aybas and co-authors lay out, in twenty twenty-five, a European strategy to discover axions and other very weakly interacting particles. Axions are hypothetical light particles that could be dark matter. The class, called WISPs, covers slim particles lighter than one giga-electron-volt. Such particles appear in many extensions of the Standard Model. The last European strategy update already urged these searches, and the physics case has since grown. WISPs could explain dark matter and puzzling observations.

The document surveys current searches and the next decade's outlook, from theory to astrophysical signs to lab experiments. Europe runs a rich, diverse, low-cost program, they stress. A European network funded under the COST program coordinates the theory, astrophysics, and experiment efforts.
arxiv-2503-20632:
Christian Kuehn models, in a 2025 math paper, the race between fast cancer growth and the body's power to adapt its defense, a balance that immune therapy tries to tip. Two deliberately simple models capture that contest. The aim is insight into when outside help can let self-defense win, not a full picture of any one cancer.

The first model, a set of four linked equations, has three regimes set by the level of outside push. A mid-level push can leave only a cancer-free steady state, but a dangerous spike in cancer often comes first. A second, random micro-level model shows a sharp tipping point. Memory plus rare lucky adaptation events move that point to where therapy wants it.
arxiv-2503-21132:
Aleksis Koski, Jani Onninen, and Haiqing Xu characterize when a circle map extends to a Sobolev homeomorphism of the disk in this 2025 paper. Classical theorems say any boundary homeomorphism extends inside. Energy finite, one to one extensions are far more delicate. Internal distances inside the domain give the test used here.

The characterization covers all embeddings of the unit circle with such extensions. A corollary handles quasiconvex target domains in place of the disk. Any boundary map with a continuous finite energy extension then also has a homeomorphic one. Such results secure well posedness for variational problems. Nonlinear elasticity and geometric function theory both depend on them. Extension theory gains a complete Sobolev answer.
arxiv-2503-21232:
Ayush Bheemaiah and Seungyong Yang ask if a self-driving car can judge what a road block is made of. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Cars sense blocks with cameras and laser scans, but those tools say little about traits such as softness, weight, or stretch. Those traits shape whether a car should swerve, stop, or drive on.

They add a knowledge graph as a world model, which links each block to facts about its stuff. In the CARLA test world, the graph-equipped car dealt with blocks better than a plain car. It changed lanes for hard blocks and drove over soft bags. It also stopped more often when sensors clashed.
arxiv-2503-22332: Mahdi Anbarloei, a solo author, introduces a new algebraic concept in a 2025 paper. The work sits in the study of multiplicative hyperrings, a branch of abstract algebra. Its new objects are a special kind of hyperideal tied to square differences and factor absorption, along with a weaker version of the same idea. The evidence shown is brief, so readers mainly get a new definition framed for further study by specialists in this corner of algebra.
arxiv-2503-22732:
Mohamed Amine Ferrag, Norbert Tihanyi, and Merouane Debbah review the top language models of the past two years for how they reason, and name the open tasks. Their review is from two thousand twenty-five.

Fresh ways — more compute at ask time, reward learning, tuned training, and shrinking big models into small ones — have sharply lifted such models. The team reads twenty-seven top models and sorts their core new tricks and gains. They give a like read of models in many tongues, with ways to lift thought past the English-first base. The review maps a fast field and the gaps that still bar it.
arxiv-2503-22832:
Simeng Sun and co-authors test whether language models can run simple programs step by step without error, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Their bench, L0-Bench, grades full execution traces on made-up Python functions with plain steps. Made-up tasks let step count and other axes scale at will.

All tested models, closed and open, slipped more as trace length grew. Larger models and reasoning-tuned models held accuracy longer across steps. Extra context, voting over many tries, and longer thinking were also probed as test-time levers. Much room stays to lift this base skill, the authors find. Readers get a clean ruler for step-faithful reasoning, apart from final answers.
arxiv-2503-23632:
Jianqi Liu wrote a maths work in two thousand twenty-five on vertex operator algebras. Such an algebra codes the rules of a two-space quantum field in maths form. When a small algebra sits inside a big one, a reader wants a set way to build modules of the big one from modules of the small one. That step is called induction.

Liu sets out a finite form of that step. It is built at the level of the finite Zhu algebras tied to each main algebra, not on the full modules. When the pair of algebras meets set terms, the step keeps the known traits of such steps. Those traits are Frobenius reciprocity and a form of Artin's theorem for the linked characters. Liu works the step out in full for the rank-one lattice case, and for a parabolic type part of the rank-two case.
arxiv-2503-23732:
Badr Elmansouri and Mohamed El Otmani wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2025. It proves that a class of reflected backward stochastic differential equations, with a general driver and a possibly jagged barrier, has exactly one solution under broad conditions.

These equations model quantities that evolve backward from a future value while being pushed to stay above an obstacle, a setup used in finance and control. The paper works in a general information flow that carries both smooth Brownian noise and sudden counted jumps. The data need only modest square-integrability, and the driver must obey a monotonicity condition. The authors also tie the solution to an optimal control problem over stopping times. The paper states it is the foundation on which a recent companion paper's results rest.
arxiv-2503-23932:
Ciaran Furey, O. Grace Telford, and colleagues measure winds blowing off the most massive stars in a 2025 astronomy study. Radiation pushes gas outward from hot O-type stars, shaping how they evolve and how they enrich their galaxies. How mass loss depends on a star's makeup is poorly known, especially where heavy elements are scarce.

The team took optical and ultraviolet spectra of eleven such stars in nearby dwarf galaxies poorer in metals than the Small Magellanic Cloud. Atmosphere models and a genetic search routine yielded the stars' properties and wind strengths. Their results test current theories of radiation driven winds at low metal content.
arxiv-2504-00332:
Ahmad Al-Badawi, Faizuddin Ahmed, and İzzet Sakallı present a black hole solution in two thousand twenty-five set in anti-de Sitter space and wrapped in a quintessence field. The solution bridges three known cases: the Ayón-Beato-García hole, the Schwarzschild-Kiselev hole, and the plain Schwarzschild hole. It also folds in nonlinear electrodynamics.

The authors first trace how particles, light and heavy, travel near the hole under the combined effects. They then probe how a massless scalar field ripples around it. Next they compute the black hole's shadow and how its size and shape shift with the field strengths and curvature scale. Finally they derive heat quantities such as Hawking temperature, heat capacity, and Gibbs free energy, tracking how each responds to the parameters.
arxiv-2504-01332:
Evolutionary algorithms that juggle several goals at once often keep an archive of the best trade-off solutions found, trimming it when it grows too large. Zhiji Cui and co-authors ask a simple question in this 2025 paper: when should that trim happen?

Against intuition, trimming after every new solution beat saving everything and trimming once at the end, which often scored worst. The team checked the pattern across three standard trimming rules and analyzed why early trimming helps. Their advice is to invest in good subset selection rather than giant archives, since keeping everything until the end throws away the guidance that trimming provides along the way.
arxiv-2504-02732:
Barbero and co-authors ask why language models pour attention onto the very first token in this 2025 paper. This habit, called an attention sink, affects quantization, security, and streaming systems. Many papers describe when sinks appear, but few explain what they are for.

The authors argue the sink stops information from over-mixing as it flows through the transformer. Their theory connects the sink to known math on signal propagation in deep networks. Experiments then test how context length, model depth, and data packing change sink behavior, matching the theory. The reading reframes the sink as a useful learned tool rather than a glitch, which may guide future model design.
arxiv-2504-03832:
Thorsten Koch and a large team of co-authors launch a benchmarking library for quantum optimization, cast as an intractable decathlon. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that quantum hardware can now host fair tests of heuristic solvers at scale. Optimization is where such tests bite first, since most solvers there are heuristics. Ten problem classes make up the set.

Each class is hard for classic solvers yet tied to real use. Sizes run from under a hundred to vast variable counts. Objective and variable types vary, as do coefficient ranges and density. The library stores instances and score records in a standard form. Classic solver marks are listed for all classes. Quantum baselines for picked classes show the reporting style. The team invites the field to track progress in one shared arena.
arxiv-2504-04732:
Zhenxing Ming and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a car-vision task. The task is to state, from the cameras of the car itself, what fills each bit of space around it and what that material is. Past work refined the inner parts of the system to lift scores. This team adds a twin task to the training: detecting objects in three dimensions as well.

The twin task gives the core features an extra push. It sharpens them for small, fast objects in the scene: bicycles, and people on foot. Those are the ones a self-driving car must not miss. On a known test set, with rain and night counted in, the system reached top scores of its kind. It shone most on the vulnerable road users. The code is to be released.
arxiv-2504-05332:
Markus Penz and Robert van Leeuwen introduce a method to compute a central quantity of density-functional theory on small lattice systems. Their paper came out in 2025. Density-functional theory predicts material properties from electron density alone, and its constrained-search functional is defined by a hard optimization over all quantum states giving a chosen density.

Their method evolves quantum states in imaginary time, a mathematical trick that settles them toward low-energy configurations. As a by-product, it also yields the potential that produces a prescribed density for an energy eigenstate. Beyond computation, the scheme clarifies the mapping between densities and potentials. The authors show it extends to optimizing general quantities under several constraints at once.
arxiv-2504-05432:
Francisco Plaza and Lucila Kraiselburd test gravity models that bend Einstein's theory with new survey data. In f(R) gravity, the curvature term in the action is replaced by a broader function. Fresh baryon acoustic data from the DESI survey gives sharp distance marks from the early cosmos. The team ran sampling chains on all viable forms of the model with that data.

They set the new data's pull against older compilations of the same kind. Cosmic clock data and a large supernova set joined the tests. A formal model comparison then weighed the bent models against the standard cosmos model. For the first time, the bent models won very strong support in that weighing. The authors stress the shift rests on the new data set.
arxiv-2504-07232:
