Zachary Picker asks whether lumps of dark matter could smash the solar system's small bodies. His paper, from twenty twenty-five, treats dark matter as macroscopic chunks. Such stuff-sized objects would cross paths with asteroids, rings, and planets. A hit could shatter a body, knock it off orbit, or leave a crater.

Picker estimates each effect across a wide mass range. The absence of such destruction sets limits on how common the chunks can be. Those limits cover ground earlier searches left open. Asteroid survival, ring stability, and crater counts all contribute evidence. The solar system itself becomes the detector in this framing.
arxiv-2504-07332:
Jean-Marie De Koninck, Nicolas Doyon, and William Verreault study the shortest addition chains that reach a given number, in a mathematics paper from 2025. An addition chain builds a target by adding numbers already in the chain, one sum at a time. The least number of steps needed is a classic hard quantity.

The authors count how many targets in each doubling range can be reached within a small extra allowance of steps. They prove tight upper and lower bounds for that count as the range grows. Their bounds sharpen a result of Erdős about the typical chain length for large numbers. The near-matching bounds leave only a thin gap that shrinks in relative terms.
arxiv-2504-07532:
Tuhin Chakrabarty, Philippe Laban, and Chien-Sheng Wu study how to judge and lift AI writing quality in two thousand twenty-five. AI text now floods fiction, news, and science alike. Models follow prompts well, but raw writing grade is a murkier trait. It is subjective and needs expert eyes to score.

They build a benchmark from five sets of human writing judgments. Top reasoning models barely beat chance on that benchmark. Small reward models trained for the task score far better. At run time, the reward model picks the best of many rewrites. Expert writers favored those picks in most head to head tests.
arxiv-2504-07632:
Long Li, Etienne Mémin, and Bertrand Chapron built a stochastic model in 2025 for the turbulent skin where ocean meets atmosphere. That edge layer, where wind, waves, and currents exchange momentum and heat, is shown crudely in climate models, partly because its randomness is real, not just unresolved. Their coupled Ekman-Stokes model is built inside a location doubt method that treats turbulent swings as a clear random ingredient rather than a fudge factor.

The model weaves established recipes for air-sea fluxes, turbulent thickness, and the Stokes drift that waves impart to currents, on both sides of the surface. Ensemble models were scored against findings from the classic LOTUS field test, and a ranking study priced each part's contribution. Clear doubt in both ocean and atmosphere proved key to reproducing the system's seen variability.
arxiv-2504-08032:
Yilun Ma and colleagues count little red dots, red compact objects that the James Webb Space Telescope found at high redshift. There, they are far more common than ultraviolet-selected quasars. Their count at lower redshift is not sure. The telescope has limited sky coverage and limited reach in blue wavelengths. The team searched from the ground instead. They joined ultra-deep Hyper Suprime-Cam photometry with near-infrared surveys over about three square degrees.

For the brighter little red dots, the count falls from high redshift down through redshift two to four. The team also gives a Magellan telescope spectrum of their first candidate that was followed up, at redshift 2.26. It is a proof of concept for the selection. Like its high-redshift peers, the object shows broad hydrogen-alpha emission. It also shows narrow absorption and very narrow forbidden oxygen lines.
arxiv-2504-08532:
The CMS Collaboration presents a 2025 search for charged-lepton flavour violation in top quark events at the Large Hadron Collider. The Standard Model forbids such flavour mixing among charged leptons, so any sighting would signal new physics. The team sifted 138 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions at 13 tera-electronvolts. Target events hold a muon and a hadronically decaying tau of opposite charge, plus at least three jets, one from a bottom quark.

Machine learning classifiers separated the rare signal shape from background. The data matched Standard Model expectations, so no violation was seen. The team set tight upper limits on the branching fractions for top decays into a muon, a tau, and an up or charm quark, for three operator shapes. The limits sharpen the hunt for physics beyond the Standard Model.
arxiv-2504-09132:
Matthew Webster, Dongheon Lee, and Joonnyong Lee present a network that pulls a clean heartbeat signal from noisy wrist sensor data, in two thousand twenty-five. Such optical sensors mix the pulse with motion and other noise during daily life. Heart rate reads suffer when that noise is strong.

Their autoencoder network learns on its own, from a large public sleep study data set, with no cleaning or selection of the data first. It separates a heartbeat-linked source from the mixed signal, in the spirit of blind source separation. On noisy recordings from nine people in daily activity, the cleaned signal improved heart rate detection clearly. The authors stress the method's hands-off training as a strength.
arxiv-2504-09832:
Ran Ding, Alim Ruzi, Sitian Qian, Andrew Levin, Youpeng Wu, and Qiang Li study quantum entanglement between pairs of Z bosons at a future muon collider, in a 2025 paper. Entanglement is usually tested in tabletop optics. A muon collider would test it at extreme energies. The team focuses on collisions producing two Z bosons. Spin patterns of the pair encode the entanglement. Fixed spin matrices let them define measurable witnesses.

Simulations included backgrounds and detector effects. The measured values favored the entangled picture. Testing against a non-entangled hypothesis reached two standard deviations of significance. That is evidence, though not yet discovery level. The authors frame the work as a thorough feasibility study. It maps what a muon collider could say about quantum foundations. High-energy entanglement tests may one day probe where quantum rules bend. For now, the study sets methods and expectations.
arxiv-2504-10932:
Bo Wang, Lizuo Liu, and Wei Cai improve operator learning for wave problems in this two thousand twenty-five paper. DeepOnet is a neural architecture that learns mappings between functions, such as from a wave equation's coefficient to its solution. Standard networks suffer spectral bias: they learn low frequencies easily and high frequencies poorly. For highly oscillatory functions, that bias cripples accuracy.

The proposed multi-scale DeepOnet inserts multiscale neural networks into both the branch and trunk parts of the original design. That change lets the model capture varied high-frequency components of both the mapping and its output. The test application is the nonlinear map from the Helmholtz equation's coefficient to its solution, central to wave scattering. Numerical results show substantial improvement over ordinary DeepOnet in the high-frequency regime, at a similar number of network parameters.
arxiv-2504-13132:
Zi-Liang Zhang and Bing Zhang propose a new way to pin down the universe's expansion rate using fast radio bursts. Each burst comes with a glowing radio companion that lingers after the flash. A checked relation ties that companion's brightness to how much the burst's signal was twisted in transit. The twist and brightness together carry distance clues.

Older methods used only how much the burst signal spread out, which tangles three unknowns together. The brightness link breaks that tangle. A two-stage sampling analysis first tests the idea on mock data. Then six real companion systems give a first value for the expansion rate, with a wide error bar. The authors sketch how better data and modeling could tighten it. The relation may grow into a fresh probe of the cosmos.
arxiv-2504-13232:
Sayed Pouria Talebi, Clive Cheong Took, and Danilo Mandic use quaternion algebra to model learning on quantum machines. Quaternions are a number system with four parts that fits how quantum bits are handled. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The authors build a model of quantum parts, both their states and their reads, in quaternion form. On that base they frame a learning task for basic quantum units, much like nerve cells in classic models. They then use a modern form of quaternion calculus to build a full training plan. The model stays tractable and lets them state clear rules for when training settles, the authors report.
arxiv-2504-14032:
Haiwen Huang and co-authors published this study in 2025. It sharpens the blurry feature maps that vision foundation models produce. Models like DINOv2 and CLIP see images in coarse patches, which limits tasks needing pixel-level detail. Upsampling those features is the fix, and the team names two keys: the upsampler's design and its training target. Their upsampler, LoftUp, is a transformer that reads image coordinates alongside the coarse features.

For training targets, they build high-grade reference features from class-free masks and self-teaching. The result is sharp features that adapt to varied input sizes. Across downstream tasks, LoftUp beat existing upsamplers by clear margins. Code is public. The work matters for any tool that needs a foundation model to point at exact spots, from segmentation to robot grasping.
arxiv-2504-17632:
Riti Bhandarkar and co-authors measure the true climate cost of charging electric cars in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. EVs cut tailpipe emissions, but charging draws power that can add emissions elsewhere. Common yardsticks use past grid data or ignore how the grid itself grows.

Using a capacity expansion model of the western United States grid, the team tracked how mass EV uptake reshapes power plants and storage. Average emission rates could miss the true impact in either direction. Short-run marginal rates understated the savings, above all when charging times flex. Steering charging by those rates could even raise emissions compared with price signals. The authors urge better control strategies.
arxiv-2504-17732:
Zhanwen Liu and co-authors present a 2025 model that fixes many kinds of image damage with one system. Photos can suffer blur, noise, rain, or low light, and past tools often needed one model per flaw. Prompt-guided tools exist, but their prompts stay coarse. The team's model reads fine detail about the damage and lets that detail steer the repair.

A damage reader pulls fine traits from each image. Those traits become live prompts inside a state space model that rebuilds the image. A second block restores fine local detail that broad repair can lose. On a mixed set with seven damage kinds, the model scored best on two standard quality scales. One tool for all damage types suits phone and archive repair better than a shelf of single fixes.
arxiv-2504-18832:
Manuel Boldrer, Vít Krátký, and Martin Saska field-test drone swarms that watch an area without pause in a 2025 paper. Persistent monitoring means robots keep sweeping a space and catch targets as they appear. Their shared algorithm blends three tools: a synchronization model run in reverse, three-dimensional Lissajous flight curves, and predictive control.

The team flew the method on real aerial robots, up to eleven at once. They define two failure grades. Short glitches, like tracking slips and message delays, form the first. Long outages, like attacks, dead links, or flat batteries, form the second. The system kept monitoring and detecting through both. The authors say the field trials prove the method's strength, resilience, and scale. They present it as ready for real deployments where coverage cannot lapse.
arxiv-2504-19932:
Yang Liu, Rui-Cheng Liu, Wanyu Ma, and Alain Goriely model wrinkling in fiber-stiffened soft tissues in a 2025 paper. Many living tissues gain strength from fibers set in a soft matrix, and the mix of fiber stiffness, direction, and matrix softness shapes the patterns that form when tissue is squeezed. The team studies a film bonded to a deep base, with fibers in the film or the base.

Working in the theory of large elastic strains, they derive rules for when the surface first buckles and an equation for the wrinkle size that follows. For a simple fiber model, the buckling can grow smoothly or snap in suddenly, set by the stiffness ratio between base and film. The results link fiber layout to tissue shape change.
arxiv-2504-20532:
Yue Li, Kassem Kallas, and three co-authors watermark generated speech at three levels of tracing. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, presents TriniMark. Diffusion models now make speech so real that misuse is a live risk. Most past watermarks were built for an older family of generators, and they track content only.

TriniMark ties each clip to its message, its source model, and its user. A light encoder hides the bits in sound features, and a decoder reads them back. A guided fine-tune moves the skill into a diffusion model. The mark must survive edits and noise to be useful. Tests weigh recovery strength against sound quality.
arxiv-2504-21032:
Lior Limonad and co-authors study, in a 2025 paper, how a public agency should pick a language model to write the explanations that come with online government services. Clear explanations build trust and draw people back. The team adapted a known rating scale to compare explanation quality across models in a systematic way.

A tax refund case served as the test bed. Over one hundred survey takers rated rival model-written explanations of refund decisions. The ratings give agencies a method for choosing the model that reads best to citizens. Because surveys are costly, the authors also began testing whether software can predict the human ratings on its own.
arxiv-2504-21232:
Eduard Atonga, Ramy Aboushelbaya, and Peter Norreys propose a new way to hunt gravity waves from boson clouds that die around black holes, a sign of black hole super-radiance. Gravity wave study aids work on the early cosmos, dark matter, and black hole mergers. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The plan uses a light based effect in a boosted mirror cavity to catch waves across a broad band, with good scaling in size and wave rate. The authors show it fits waves from boson decay around black holes across a wide mass range. Waves above a high rate cut off, if coherent, could hint at black holes born in the early cosmos.
arxiv-2504-21432:
Pranav Saxena, Nishant Raghuvanshi, and Neena Goveas built a drone that flies by spoken instruction in a 2025 paper. Their UAV-VLN setup lets an unmanned aerial vehicle navigate unseen settings from free-form natural language commands, end to end. A large text model parses the instruction's high-level goals using common-sense thinking. A vision model detects and locates the objects the words refer to. A cross-modal grounding mechanism aligns the linguistic intent with the visual scene so references resolve unambiguously.

Fusing the two streams, the drone reasons about spatial relations and plans feasible aerial trajectories with minimal task-set supervision. Review spans diverse indoor and outdoor scenarios, testing broad reach to new settings and phrasings. Tongue-guided flight would let functions task drones conversationally, in disaster zones or warehouses, without piloting skill.
arxiv-2504-21632:
Fuma Ito and co-authors tackle, in a 2025 signal processing paper, a hidden cost in image compression: recovering the plus or minus sign of each frequency value from its size alone. Their scheme treats the puzzle as many small yes-no choices. Values are sorted into blocks by frequency band, stacking the image into a three-dimensional array.

A convolutional network then reads that array and calls each sign. Networks suit the job because they pull features from the stacked sizes with ease. In tests, the method recovered signs with high accuracy at a tiny fraction of the usual computing cost. Faster sign recovery could trim the work of decoding compressed images and video.
arxiv-2504-21832:
Mohammad Khajenejad designs a controller for hard-to-model systems that works through a watcher keeping the true state in a range. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The systems at hand change step by step and bend in nonlinear ways. Noise clouds both the state and the readings taken from it.

Rather than steady the system head-on, Khajenejad steadies the watcher, whose state bounds the true one from above and below. Letting the controller shift over time adds give that fixed designs lack. That give can hold the true state in a tighter range. A split-design rule lets the watcher and controller gains be set apart. Tests show the moving design beats a fixed one by a clear margin. The work gives workable math tests that prove the closed loop stays stable.
arxiv-2505-00632:
Kangning Diao, Biwei Dai, and Uros Seljak detect modeling bias on weak lensing maps in two thousand twenty-five. Simulation based inference mines nonlinear scales in sky surveys. Its trust rests on forward models that match the real sky. They recast model checks as out of distribution detection.

Probability density serves as the gauge for that detection task. Continuous time flow models estimate field level density best. They beat feature level rivals and other field level estimators. Scores rest on the area under the receiver curve. The metric also guides model choice and holds across cosmologies.
arxiv-2505-01732:
Marino Romero and Joshua Jeishing Wen wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on a family of polynomials with deep ties to symmetry. Macdonald polynomials sit at a crossroads of algebra and combinatorics, and their wreath versions add a further twist of structure. Many of their key properties are proved by finding operators that act on them in controlled ways.

The authors give an explicit formula for an operator with a special property. Applied to one of these polynomials, it produces a spike concentrated at a character value tied to its partition. That single formula unlocks several results: a duality between two families, formulas for special values, and more. The paper also starts the study of an interpolation version of these polynomials. It derives a counting formula for certain coefficients and gives series solutions to a two-way spectral problem. The approach leans on operators built from quantum algebra machinery.
arxiv-2505-02832:
Andrew King explains a sudden swing in the burst rhythm of a galaxy core, in a paper from 2025. Some small galaxy centers fire off X-ray bursts at near-clockwork gaps, called quasiperiodic eruptions. One source cut its gap from about eighteen minutes to about seven in just two years. King ties the swing to a slow wobble of orbits known as ZLK cycles.

In his picture, a white dwarf circles a black hole while a farther star orbits the pair. The far star makes the dwarf's orbit tilt and stretch in a linked dance. That dance sets both the burst gap and the glow of the infall. He shows the glow should vary in a fixed inverse tie to the gap. The system likely came from a messy infall of several stars. Watching it further should pay off, he argues.
arxiv-2505-04032:
Vazquez Von Bibow and Perotti ran a net form in twenty twenty-five of a wealth swap model where trade takes place on a random web. In the base model, wealth can pile on a tiny few or stay spread, with a sharp turn between the two. They ask how a sparse web of trade links changes that turn.

Their sims and field sums show the turn stays sharp on the web. But wealth piles up in local clumps in place of one world pile. Tax and trade forms shift where those clumps form. The work may guide fair rules for wealth in linked groups.
arxiv-2505-04832:
B J Frei and co-authors simulate plasma turbulence at the edge of a fusion device with a fast spectral code, in work from twenty twenty-five. Edge turbulence sets how heat and particles leak from the hot core. Full kinetic models are accurate but heavy to run.

The code, called GENE-X, uses a spectral method in velocity space to speed the math. On a known test case, it matched grid based results on profiles, fluctuation spectra, flows, and power crossing the edge. The match held as resolution rose. Force balance checks passed with care. Fluid style models missed a key electron driven mode that the kinetic code caught. The authors back the code as a first principles tool.
arxiv-2505-08332:
Johann Fernandes, Archana Pai, and Koustav Chandra work on spotting gravitational waves in a 2025 paper. Searches for these ripples must tell real signals from noise glitches. Standard tools are tuned to expected signal shapes, which can miss stranger events as detectors improve. The team tried a learning-based filter instead.

Their image-based neural network sorts glitches from true events and feeds that judgment into two existing searches. The searches then reach about a third farther in volume over time at a strict false alarm rate. Applied to real recorded data, the method raised the standing of several events, most strikingly the first very heavy black hole merger on record.
arxiv-2505-10832:
Songjun Tu, Jiahao Lin, Qichao Zhang, and a wider team wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It teaches reasoning language models to think only when thinking pays, skipping the long chain of thought for easy questions.

Big reasoning models spell out every step, which wastes time and compute on simple problems. The authors found that slipping a simple ellipsis into the prompt can flip such a model between thinking and answering directly, showing the choice is already latent inside. Their framework, AutoThink, uses several rounds of reinforcement learning with shaped rewards to sharpen that choice. Across five math benchmarks, the tuned models traded accuracy and speed better than rival prompting or pruning tricks. Relative accuracy rose by several points while easy items were answered briskly. The method plugs into any model of the same family.
arxiv-2505-12832:
Ovi wrote a solo study in twenty twenty-five that weighs three ways to train deep nets across groups of graph chips. Each way trades speed, memory use, and the cost of keeping chips in sync. He ran side-by-side tests on a fast chip set and on a cheaper chip set.

One way, which copies the full net to each chip, gave a two-to-three-fold speed gain. A shard way cut top memory by four-to-six-fold but paid more in talk time. A hub way that let chips drift saved time but lost truth in its scores. A fixed hub way lost its speed gain to sync costs.
arxiv-2505-14832:
Wonje Jeung, Sangyeon Yoon, and Albert No grade machine unlearning the way real prompts actually arrive: mixed. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Unlearning should erase chosen knowledge while keeping the rest. Standard tests ask forget and retain questions separately. Real users blend both in one prompt. That blend breaks many current methods.

Their SEPS framework measures separability inside single mixed prompts. Experiments across three benchmarks expose two failure modes. Untargeted methods erase everything once a forget item appears. Targeted methods overfit lone questions and collapse on mixes. The metric gives builders a harder, fairer test. Safer unlearning for deployed models is the stake.
arxiv-2505-15332:
Ria Shekhawat, Hailin Li, Raghavendra Ramachandra, and Sushma Venkatesh test large multimodal models for spotting face morphing attacks, in a 2025 paper. A morph blends two faces into one photo that can fool identity checks, a risk for passport systems. Their study is the first to use such models on real biometric data for this task.

The team used prompts that ask the model to reason step by step, which cut refusals and made decisions clearer to follow. Tests used data from fifty four people in passport style settings. One model was more accurate, in particular against AI generated morphs, while the other gave more consistent explanations. Both models struggled in the hardest cases.
arxiv-2505-19432:
Hao Wu and co-authors present a computing paper from 2025 on long-term Earth forecasts. Smart models can predict weather well for days, but they drift when run for months or years. Small, fast features are the first to blur, and errors then grow out of control.

Their system copies the nested grids of classic weather models. A stable inner core tracks the broad trend at coarse scale. An outer layer adds fine local detail on top of that trend. On a world weather test bed, the system scored at the top for accuracy. It ran a full year of forecasts and multi-year climate runs without drift. It also forecast ocean swirls with skill out to 120 days. The authors say the design could make smart Earth models more trustworthy.
arxiv-2505-19632:
Takook presents a 2025 proposal to turn a mathematical framework from quantum field theory into new quantum computing algorithms. Krein space quantization, built on spaces that allow negative-norm states, has helped tackle hard problems in quantum gravity and gauge theory, including confinement and the mass gap. The paper aims to carry those tools into computation.

The targets are linear systems that are underdetermined or badly conditioned, plus systems with non-unitary evolution and open dynamics, where standard quantum algorithms struggle. The author argues the approach could go beyond workhorse methods like quantum singular value decomposition and dilation tricks. The paper is a program statement rather than a finished algorithm. It sketches a unified framework the author hopes to develop.
arxiv-2505-20232:
Five researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on training medical AI when some kinds of data are missing. Their setting is federated learning, where hospitals train a shared model without sending raw patient data to each other. A scan or record type that one site has may be absent at another, and that gap hurts the model.

Older fixes lean on public data or on fake data made by large models, both of which have limits. The authors offer a small, light tool that rebuilds the missing features from the features a site does have. They test the tool on three data sets, including chest X-ray collections.
arxiv-2505-22032:
Tawfiq Ammari, Anna Gutowska, Jacob Ziff, Casey Randazzo, and Harihan Subramonyam wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It studies two years of tweets from, to, and about the CDC during the COVID-19 pandemic, and what they show about public health talk online.

The agency's posts stayed mostly one-way and drew little back-and-forth. Talk around the virus was split hard by politics. Users often dug up old CDC posts to throw at new guidance that seemed to clash. The team ties the spread of health posts to feeling, media richness, and how much the source is trusted. They offer design moves to help the agency reach unlike groups and fight false claims in a crisis.
arxiv-2505-22432:
Grigorios Zouros, Konstantinos Delimaris, Carsten Rockstuhl, and Georgios Kolezas solve a wave scattering problem for slanted light in two thousand twenty-five. The setup has many long cylinders side by side. Each can twist the field in a gyrotropic way, and each cross-section can take any shape.

Their full-wave method joins three parts. One part writes the field inside the twisted region, one handles non-round shapes at the boundary, and one shifts the solution between cylinders. Checks against exact results and a commercial solver confirm the method. The team then tests a microwave use with ferrite cylinders and shows wide-band forward scattering.
arxiv-2505-23532:
Matthias Meister, Gabriel Müller, and a large team including Nicholas Bigelow report magnetic measurements made with atom interferometers in orbit. The experiments ran in NASA's Cold Atom Lab aboard the International Space Station. Differential setups cancel shared noise, which suits the noisy environment of a space platform.

By running single- and double-loop interferometers, the team compared atoms in magnetically sensitive and insensitive states. That contrast turned the instrument into a magnetometer able to map how the field curves across space. Such precision sensing in orbit could serve navigation and Earth observation. The authors present the campaigns as a step toward dedicated quantum sensing missions in space.
arxiv-2506-00032:
Roman Smirnov revisits how economists should find the function linking inputs to output in a 2025 study. In the late nineteen twenties Cobb and Douglas fit their famous production function to decades of national data. The fit worked, but their method could never rule out a rival function fitting the same data just as well, a gap Smirnov targets.

A data-driven dynamical systems approach treats the economy's path as the trace of an underlying system, and recovers the production function from that dynamics. The method speaks to growth models that still build on the old formula, offering a check on whether its shape is truly forced by evidence.
arxiv-2506-00832:
Kyowoon Lee and co-authors fix the delivery of synthetic speech after the fact in a 2025 paper. Text-to-speech systems now sound natural, but users still need to adjust melody and fix misread words. Older fixes bolt on special modules or retrain the model, and word fixes lean on pronunciation dictionaries that low-resource languages lack.

Their method edits the model's internal activations directly, guided by a counterfactual question: what would this layer have done for the desired output? The edit bends prosody, the rhythm and tune of speech, and corrects misread words while leaving the rest of the voice intact. It works on a pretrained model as it stands, with no extra training. Tests show the fixes land without spoiling overall quality. The door opens to studio-style touch-ups at run time.
arxiv-2506-01132:
L Fossati and co-authors model the atmosphere of an ultra-hot giant planet and compare the model with telescope data. Their 2025 paper studies a Jupiter-like world so hot that standard equilibrium assumptions fail in its upper air. They combine two codes, one for the deep air and one that can drop the equilibrium assumption aloft.

The temperature profile stays flat deep down and high up, climbing steeply between. Departures from equilibrium drive that shape: excited iron levels absorb strongly where the star shines, heating the air, while magnesium levels that would cool it sit underpopulated. The air stays orderly up to very low pressures, beyond which flow physics also matters. Matching ultraviolet and visible spectra tests whether the model captures this extreme world.
arxiv-2506-01732:
Pierre-Carl Langlais and co-authors released Common Corpus, the largest open dataset for training language models that is built only from material free of copyright restrictions or openly licensed. Standard training sets swallow trillions of words of uncertain legal status. This corpus, about two trillion tokens, documents where every part came from and how it was filtered.

The collection spans many languages, from major European ones to rarely represented low-resource languages, plus a large body of code. To prove it works, the team trained two small language models on it and matched the performance of similar-sized rivals trained on ordinary data. They present the corpus as shared infrastructure for open, legally clean AI research and business use.
arxiv-2506-02132:
Michael Li and Nishant Subramani probe how twenty-five language models store word identity and word form inside their layers, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Six tongues supply the tests, from early models like BERT to a large recent Qwen model. Probes read each layer for both traits.

Word form, such as tense or number marks, stayed easy to read at every depth. Word identity shone early, then faded as layers deepened. Models that squeeze mid layers hard lost steering power there even when probes stayed sharp. Form settled early in training while identity kept shifting. Readers see a trade: depth trades word labels for compact forecast skill.
arxiv-2506-02632:
Elena Melnikova and five co-authors use a tunable lens of liquid crystal to probe how firm the twist form of a swirling beam of light is. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such beams, called optical vortices, carry a hole at their core and a twist in their phase. They hold great use in photon work, but no one had set out how to gauge the firmness of their twist. The lens bends light by its inner order, which a voltage can reset. That lets the team reshape the beam's phase live, with no change to the gear. They show the lens can read the twist's state as it is driven. The work gives a way to test these beams for real use.
arxiv-2506-05132:
Manashov and two co-authors study anomalous dimensions at small spins in a 2025 theory paper. In quantum field theory, these numbers set how operator strength changes with scale. For twist-two operators, the numbers blow up at zero or small spin, so they must be re-summed before use. An earlier trick uses a squared mix of the numbers that stays finite at the worst points.

The team works out the small-spin behavior across three models at high loop order. One model has a symmetric scalar field, one uses a complex field, and one mixes fields with fermions. In each case the singular behavior matches what theory expects. They give closed forms for the re-summed numbers. The results give other theorists firm inputs for work where small spin matters.
arxiv-2506-06832:
Clément Hongler and Andrew Emil turn language models into players of formal games built from prediction scores, in a 2025 paper. A language model is, at heart, a probability measure over text. Asking what it means for the model to know that measure leads past plain text generation. Tasks like summarizing, spotting anomalies, hunting for original text, debating, and reverse prompting all become games scored by cross-entropy.

These Xent games can be single-player or multiplayer and are written as small programs. The authors show the game space grows from a few consistency axioms yet holds a wealth of cases. Families of games can then serve as capability benchmarks for models. To tame the endless scope, they suggest exploring the game space with evolution-like dynamics.
arxiv-2506-07732:
Boldorini, Marzano, and Montani trace particle paths around a black hole under a semi classical quantum frame in twenty twenty-five. Polymer quantum mechanics adds Planck scale tweaks to the motion rules. Two cases get the focus: straight falls inward, and circles with their stability. An adjusted energy rule carries the quantum corrections.

A forbidden zone appears around the horizon that falling particles cannot cross. Stable circles also show below the classic innermost stable orbit. Some sit under the horizon itself, on closed time like paths. The results sketch how Planck scale physics could reshape black hole lore.
arxiv-2506-08832:
Frode Hansen and co-authors report a surprise warmth pattern in the nearby universe's cosmic background light, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Photons crossing growing structures should gain or lose heat by the Sachs-Wolfe effects. In the nearest slice of space, under three percent of the way to deep fields, voids came out hot.

Fewer than two in a thousand simulated skies matched that signal. Filaments in the same slice had earlier shown strong cooling, the opposite sign. The size of the effect also dwarfs standard predictions by tenfold. The authors float non-standard dark energy as a possible cause, citing fresh survey hints.
arxiv-2506-09632:
Eva Paraschou and five co-authors draw a bowtie to map who trusts whom when language models enter political life. Biased outputs and misinformation from these systems can corrode democratic processes, yet existing trust models treat trust as a one-way, one-factor affair. Reality ties user context, like ideology, to system-side elements, like features and the scientists behind them.

The bowtie model puts trustor and trustee on its two wings, joined by their relationships at the knot, and extends outward to the sociotechnical ecosystem. A mixed-methods study built around a political discourse analysis tool using ChatGPT explored how user factors shape trust actions. The authors aim to give designers and policymakers a fuller map of trust in such systems.
arxiv-2506-09932:
Marco Federici and four colleagues propose HadaNorm, a way to shrink diffusion transformers, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Diffusion models lead in making images, but they need much memory and compute. That cost blocks their use on small devices with few resources. Post-training quantization cuts the bit width of the matrix math. That shrinks the models after they are trained.

Plain methods of this kind cope poorly with outliers in the data. Stronger cuts call for first reshaping the weights and the activations. HadaNorm is a linear change that does both jobs. It centers channel activations on their mean, and it applies Hadamard transforms. The mix tames outliers and lets the activations be cut much harder. Across the parts of transformer blocks, the authors report lower error than before in each case. Their method beats the best current methods in their tests.
arxiv-2506-10732:
Stefano Frixione, Fabio Maltoni, Davide Pagani, and Marco Zaro present a method to sharpen predictions for lepton scattering, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Precise forecasts matter for future high-energy lepton colliders, where results must be right to within a percent. Some corrections of higher order are usually dropped because full calculation is too hard.

Their method folds in one class of dropped corrections, those from fusing vector bosons, in a way that works for any process. It blends exact fixed-order results with tools that sum up soft radiation, and a subtraction step to avoid double counting. The output stays consistent across the whole event space and keeps mass effects. A companion paper applies the method and argues its edge over rival approaches.
arxiv-2506-13332:
Tian Xue, Jacob Covey, and Matthew Otten adapted a quantum chemistry algorithm in 2025 for machines built from linked modules. Chemistry is a flagship hope for quantum computing, but realistic molecules demand more qubits than one device will hold, so computation must spread across modules joined by slower links. Their distributed version of a selective coupled cluster method plans around that bottleneck.

A packing scheme exploits a near-commutativity in the algorithm's Trotter steps to run module-local work in parallel while scheduling the cross-module operations around the supply of shared entangled pairs. Demonstrated on a chain of hydrogen clusters, the method leans on the molecule's own structure to cut waiting time. Runtime stayed flat even when links between modules ran far slower than operations inside them, while keeping chemical accuracy. In weakly entangled systems the distribution can even come free, checkable by classical algorithms.
arxiv-2506-14932:
Luca Placidi, Anil Misra, Gabriele La Valle, and Casey Rodriguez publish a correction to their own earlier work in a twenty twenty-five paper. The earlier work derived elastic parameters for strain gradient materials from a granular micromechanics model. Such models build a material's stiffness from the motion of grain pairs.

The authors state plainly that key terms in the grain-pair displacement were misidentified when the second gradient of placement was counted. They re-derive the expression, and the fixed terms change the strain energy and the gradient parameters found before. The standard first-gradient elastic tensor is unchanged. Corrected stiffness forms are given for both flat and full three-dimensional cases.
arxiv-2506-16332:
Lukas Gonon, Rodrigo Martínez-Peña, and Juan-Pablo Ortega prove universality for quantum recurrent networks in a 2025 arXiv paper. Quantum reservoir computing uses quantum dynamics to process data over time on today's noisy devices. Feedback versions need fewer parts and can run in real time.

The authors study what these recurrent quantum networks can approximate. Regular state-space systems can be matched without the curse of dimensionality. The qubit count grows only logarithmically as the demanded accuracy tightens. Even linear readouts suffice for universality. The results give practical, theory-backed support for quantum reservoir computing with real-time use.
arxiv-2506-16732:
Fanchen Bu and Kijung Shin exposed a quiet mismatch in how neural solvers for hard combinatorial problems are trained and used. In unsupervised combinatorial optimization, training rewards soft, probabilistic choices that point toward good answers. At test time a derandomization step hardens those choices into final answers. The two stages were designed separately, and the authors noticed lower training loss does not always mean better final answers, even on the training data itself.

They demonstrate the failure cases, then test a repair: fold a smooth, differentiable stand-in for derandomization into training, so the model learns with the end step in view. Alignment between training and testing improved. The authors are candid that the fix also makes training harder, and they frame the work as an opening analysis.
arxiv-2506-17832:
Headlines that learning-based controllers crush classical ones in drone flight may rest on rigged comparisons. Pratik Kunapuli, Jake Welde, Dinesh Jayaraman, and Vijay Kumar re-run the contest carefully for a quadrotor with a fixed arm tracking agile paths. They list three quiet biases that favor learning: uneven access to the goal, to tuning data, and to knowledge of the future path.

After building the best version of each controller under one fair protocol, the gap shrank dramatically. The classical geometric controller held smaller steady errors on gentle tasks. The learned controller reacted better when the flying got wild. Which one wins depends on how agile the job is. The authors release their code and plead for symmetric benchmarks in future comparisons.
arxiv-2506-18432:
Xu and co-authors set a new path to weld learn and talk in 6G nets, called ILAC. 6G nets must blend AI with wave talk for smart apps. Those apps need fast talk and firm learn force at once. A joint frame lets AI hone talk by smart wave work. It lets nets back AI by fast, true data swaps in step. Talk caps, like thin bands and wild paths, curb learn truth.

AI shifts, like model posts and task draws, load talk webs. Those loads call for bend, tale-aware send plans in the nets. A case on cost-to-score tune caps the work text. Tasks, model size picks, and more sit in that case. Large AI tools and hyper codes form the path's two legs. Both legs aim to cut waste in talk and learn.
arxiv-2506-20232:
D Hamm and six co-authors frame plasma image building as one shared Bayesian problem across many known methods. Plasma checks often rebuild glow profiles from a small set of line summed reads. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Years of tweaks have spawned many rebuild methods that share a hidden common shape. In the Bayesian frame, a data fit term meets a prior term that holds beliefs about the profile. Their mix gives a full chance spread for the profile, from which sound rebuilds and error bounds can be drawn. A flow method that chases this spread handles noisy sparse data. The pipeline is shown on soft X-ray images from a Swiss fusion device.
arxiv-2506-20432:
Garai and co-authors revisit whether an ultra-hot giant planet's air really heats up with altitude, in a 2025 paper. Such inversions are expected when light-absorbing gases are present, and one was reported for the planet KELT-7b. But the diagnosis leans heavily on model choices. The team re-measured the planet with two space telescopes, CHEOPS and TESS, plus older data.

They fitted transits and eclipses together, modeled how the spinning star's uneven brightness warps the transit, and ran fresh retrievals of the air's makeup. Albedos came out for both telescopes' color bands. The work tests whether the claimed inversion survives a wider, cleaner dataset. The authors frame it as a cautionary recheck of a headline result.
arxiv-2506-22932:
Zoe Anastasiadou and Andreas Lanitis review how older adults use immersive technology in a 2025 paper. Extended reality, which covers virtual and mixed reality, could help older people in daily life as their share of the population grows. Yet age-related changes in body and mind can make headsets and controls hard to use.

The review first sets out the common physical and mental traits of older users, so builders know what to design for. It then surveys existing apps made for older people and the design patterns they use. Readers get both a picture of current limits and ideas for making such tools more welcoming, simple, and engaging for this group.
arxiv-2506-23432:
Dabiri and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on all-optical relays between low-orbit satellites. Satellite fleets promise global coverage with low delay. Converting signals between light and electric forms at each hop adds delay, though. Their relay stays in the light domain, using a hard limiter to clean noise. They analyze multi-hop links under that design against two standard schemes. The optical relay is sensitive to threshold and beam spread settings. A joint tuning plan adapts both settings in real time as satellites move.

Simulations on a large low-orbit network show the method is viable. Adaptive tuning lowers error rates and delay in their runs. The authors note limits of the optical scheme versus standard relays. They offer design insights for next-generation satellite links.
arxiv-2506-24032:
Sipra Singh defines and analyzes a network choice problem that mixes coverage with profit, in a 2025 paper. A dominating set is a set of nodes such that every node is chosen or next to a chosen one. Each node carries a cost and a profit. The goal is top profit within a fixed budget. Chosen nodes cover their neighbors, so neighbors need not be bought.

The problem proves hard in a strong sense, even on split graphs with two node groups. On star graphs it is hard only in a weaker sense. For tree networks, the author gives an algorithm whose time grows modestly with budget or total profit. Tuning by solution size is unlikely to make the problem easy. Still, two fast methods exist when key graph measures stay small. Variants with fixed set size or minimal sets behave alike.
arxiv-2507-00032:
Grey Kuling and Marinka Zitnik presented KUL-Rec in twenty twenty-five, a biologically inspired system that recommends the next exercise for a learner. Good tutoring picks tasks inside a student's zone of proximal development, which shifts as they learn. Their model couples a fast Hebbian memory with slow replay-based consolidation, echoing how brains stabilize new learning.

Working in an embedding space, one architecture handles both tabular knowledge-tracing logs and open-ended short answers. Across ten public data sets it beat the strongest baseline on ranking quality and recall, with tiny inference cost and a fraction of a graph model's memory. In a thirteen-week graduate course, its personalized quizzes felt easier and more helpful to students. The authors add an audit showing encoder choice affects alignment.
arxiv-2507-00932:
Sara Aghtouman, Godfrey Gumbs, and Mir Hosseini wrote a paper from 2025 on the quantum Hall response of a square lattice with one site in five removed. Such depleted lattices can host unusual topological phases, where current flows along edges in quantized steps. The team modeled electrons hopping to near and next-near neighbors while a magnetic field pierced the sheet. They charted the famous butterfly pattern of energy levels against field strength.

With only near hopping, the pattern kept two exact symmetries and the total topological count across all bands came to zero. Adding diagonal hops broke both symmetries and warped the butterfly. New gaps opened, and the total count could turn nonzero, a sign of unconventional phases. By scanning both hop strengths, they found zones with large single-band counts and wide, stable plateaus. The team offers depletion plus diagonal hopping as a tunable recipe for sturdy topological insulators.
arxiv-2507-02332:
Krishna Kanth Nakka, Xue Jiang, Dmitrii Usynin, and Xuebing Zhou show how steering a language model's inner states can leak private facts. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Models are trained to refuse asks for private traits of people. The team asks if a push on the model's insides can break that guard.

They first find the attention heads that hint at refusal for private asks, using light probes. Then they steer a few of those heads, which makes the model answer in place of refusing. Across four models, most steered replies leak private facts, and over half of them are true. Life events, ties, and past facts spill out. The work shows a real privacy risk in such models.
arxiv-2507-02432:
Jueun Lee and five co-authors test smartwatch buzzes that slow the heart for calm and sleep, in a 2025 study. The watch plays music-like rhythm patterns as gentle pulses on the wrist. The pace adapts in a loop, set a touch slower than the wearer's live heart rate, to coax the body to settle. Twenty volunteers first compared five rhythm patterns at rest.

The best pattern then went into a sleep trial with twenty-eight people. Short sessions raised calm body signals and felt relaxation. Over the full drift into sleep, though, no clear gains showed on sleep measures. The authors share design lessons on pattern choice and timing. They frame touch feedback as a quiet, drug-free aid for winding down, with sleep claims still to prove.
arxiv-2507-02632:
The ATLAS Collaboration measures, in twenty twenty-five, the mass of the top quark using data from the Large Hadron Collider. The top quark is the heaviest known elementary particle. Its pole mass is a precisely defined form of that mass. The team used collisions at a set energy recorded in the collider's second run. They picked events where a top pair was made with one extra jet, and where the tops decayed to an electron and a muon of opposite charge.

They measured how often such events occur across a mass-related variable. A correction method restored the data to a form that theory can match. Two theory calculations were compared, one simpler and one that includes decay effects. Both gave compatible masses. The simpler one gave the sharper value.
arxiv-2507-03832:
Latrille and co-authors model how cosmic rays change the chemistry and ionization of dark clouds, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Cosmic rays ionize cloud gas and steer its chemistry, but tracking their spread through a cloud is costly. Their framework mimics that spread inside a magnetohydrodynamic simulation code.

Attenuation is estimated from the gas column each ray crosses, using the simulation's own weighting. Ionization then feeds chemical post-processing. Both heavy and light species shifted notably, depending on the assumed ray spectrum. A formula links ionization share to observable tracers, and a linear fit gives the rate from local density.
arxiv-2507-05632:
Jianquan Wang wrote a solo mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five on de Finetti theorems for quantum groups. De Finetti theorems say that long random sequences with a strong symmetry must come from a simple mixture of basic patterns. Versions exist for ordinary probability and for the non-commutative world of quantum math.

Earlier work on free quantum groups dealt mostly with infinite sequences. Wang proves finite versions for distributions that stay unchanged under the actions of free easy quantum groups. Finite versions matter because real data are always finite. He also adds refined results for the infinite setting, tying the two together.
arxiv-2507-07532:
Berkant Turan and co-authors present a framework that makes image classifiers both checkable and readable, in a paper from 2025. Games between a prover and a verifier can certify how a model decides, but they had not scaled to complex images. Concept encodings, which turn an image into named ideas, are readable but were tied to weak linear models.

Their framework, called Neural Concept Verifier, joins the two strengths. A discovery model first pulls structured concepts from raw images with little supervision. A prover picks a subset of those concepts. A nonlinear verifier then decides using only that subset, so the proof can be checked. On high-dimensional, logic-heavy data sets, the method beat classic concept models and pixel-based game baselines. It also cut shortcut behavior.
arxiv-2507-08232:
Aditya Srivatsa, Kaushal Maurya, and Ekaterina Kochmar tested in twenty twenty-five whether language models can stand in for real students when developing tests and tutoring systems. Developers increasingly pilot questions on simulated students, but a proxy that answers like a top student misleads design. The team built a yardstick from four hundred eighty-nine items of a national assessment in math and reading, spanning grades four, eight, and twelve.

Using item response theory, they placed eleven leading models on the same ability scale as real student populations. Unguided, strong models outperformed the average student at every grade. Grade-enforcing prompts shifted scores, but no model-prompt pairing matched average students across subjects and grades. The paper gives selection guidelines and warns that realistic student simulation needs new methods.
arxiv-2507-09332: Vasyunin presents a 2025 paper that continues a study of extremal problems for martingale transforms, a topic in probability and harmonic analysis. It repeats neither the introduction nor the references of part one. The formulas cited from that part are put in an addendum with their own numbers. The new work studies two further local foliations, called minor pockets and rectangles. It shows what these look like through examples whose boundary functions are third-degree polynomials. It is a specialist sequel for readers of the first paper.
arxiv-2507-12232:
Tao Chen and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on teaching vision-language models to spot forged faces and explain their verdicts. Past work built question-answer data sets where models name the forgery's type and place. Those sets ignored face quality traits, which often run abnormal in fakes, and training recipes for forgery-aware models were weak. The team widened the data set with richer traits and more varied samples.

Their framework adds prompt learning at several grain levels, from whole-face calls down to fine regions. Results from a classifier and a forgery mask are fed back in as prompts, which sharpens both accuracy and the quality of explanations. A hybrid light-tuning strategy adapts the big model without retraining it whole. Extra loss terms push the model to attend to forgery clues. On text-based judgment and analysis tests, the framework beat past methods.
arxiv-2507-12432:
Andreas Habring and co-authors survey energy based models for inverse imaging problems in this 2025 chapter. Inverse problems rebuild an image from indirect, noisy data. A Bayesian view treats the unknown image as random and asks for its full distribution. Energy based models define that distribution through an energy function.

The chapter starts with rigorous theory on well posedness and stability, in both finite and infinite dimensions. It then explains how to learn such models from data. Sampling methods receive full coverage, from Metropolis-Hastings to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Worked imaging examples verify the properties the theory requires. Readers get both the math and the algorithms needed to use these models in practice.
arxiv-2507-12732:
Fuya Nakamori, Yin Jou Huang, and Fei Cheng study AI agents playing the social deduction game Werewolf in a 2025 paper. In the game, hidden werewolves try to blend in while other players debate and vote. Prior language model agents used fixed or implicit strategies hidden inside their prompts, so they could not adapt as a game unfolded.

The authors propose agents that pick a strategy openly, based on the talk so far and guessed roles of other players. That lets an agent shift tactics when suspicion rises or alliances change. They compare the adaptive agents with baseline agents that use implicit or fixed strategies. The study tests whether open strategy switching improves game performance.
arxiv-2507-14032:
Lam Nguyen, Erika Barcelos, Roger French, and Yinghui Wu present, in twenty twenty-five, KROMA, a framework that matches concepts across ontologies with language models and fetched knowledge. Ontology matching aligns the word sets of data systems. It is a key base for systems to work together. Old systems rely on handcrafted rules or narrow models. KROMA wraps a large language model in a retrieval pipeline. Fetched structural, lexical, and definitional knowledge enriches each matching choice. A similarity-based step and a light refinement step prune candidate concepts first.

That pruning cuts the cost of calling the language model by a lot. Tests on several benchmark data sets show KROMA beating classic matchers and newer language-model approaches. Communication overhead stayed comparable to rivals. The study argues that targeted retrieval plus prompt enrichment makes matching scale.
arxiv-2507-14732:
Vic Vander Linden, Boris De Vos, Kevin Vervoort, Frank Verstraete, and Atsushi Ueda published this physics paper in 2025. It studies the quantum five-state Potts model, a lattice system with a weakly first-order phase transition. Theory describes its critical point with a complex conformal field theory, a framework reached by extending ordinary theory into the complex plane. Testing that picture on a lattice forces the model to become non-Hermitian, which breaks the usual rule that simulations follow the lowest energy.

The team shows that tensor network methods can still handle the system, reaching lattice widths of 28. In their runs, the running couplings trace the spiral flow that theory predicts near the complex fixed point. They also rebuild the full boundary spectrum of the theory from the entanglement pattern of the ground state. The authors argue tensor networks are the right tool for such near-conformal transitions.
arxiv-2507-15032:
Some ultraluminous X-ray sources pulse, a sign that a neutron star is feeding faster than theory once allowed. Finding more pulsators is hard because their signals are faint. Nicolò Oreste Pinciroli Vago and co-authors try a shortcut: teach a clustering algorithm on the XMM-Newton archive of these sources, grouping observations by shared traits. Known pulsating sources then mark which cluster should hide more of them.

The candidate cluster holds 85 sources across 355 observations, and most of them were observed more than once. Only a few traits turn out to matter for sorting an observation into one cluster or the other. A first timing check of the candidates found no new pulses yet. The authors take the list as a map for future observing time: the sources look like known pulsators in many dimensions, but proving it will take deeper data with stronger statistics.
arxiv-2507-16032:
Tsarev and three co-authors study whether exotic cat states can form in a tiny quantum junction despite heat and loss. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses a bosonic Josephson junction, two coupled wells of a Bose-Einstein condensate. A Schroedinger cat state puts the system in two opposed states at once, a prized resource.

At zero temperature, a quantum phase transition births the cat state when the nonlinear strength matches the coupling. The team extends the analysis to finite temperature and weak dissipation. A critical temperature appears, below which the cat can form by quantum tunneling. Their estimates put that threshold well below the condensation point, a hopeful sign for lab tests.
arxiv-2507-16432:
Jean-Baptiste Stiegler, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, studies a family of step-by-step systems that move points on shapes made of straight edges, and asks why they so often collapse. The best known case is the pentagram map.

Signs of collapse show up in most such systems. Stiegler proves it in some cases, and puts forth that it holds near always. He gives a form for the end point the points rush to, in terms of roots of a polynomial whose degree is one more than the space's dims. His path stretches a tool of Glick, read as a trace of a slight loop. He then tests the results on known systems and sets out a new one.
arxiv-2507-18632:
Ye-Chan Kim and four co-authors introduce SIDA in this two thousand twenty-five conference paper. Their topic is zero-shot domain adaptation. That means teaching a vision model to work in a new setting when no real images from that setting are at hand. Older methods lean on text prompts to fake the new style. The team found that text misses fine detail and slows the work down.

SIDA uses made-up images instead. It first builds detailed images like the source set. It then shifts their style toward the target setting and reads style cues from them. The authors say this gives richer cues and faster adaptation. The paper suits readers who build image models that must move to new scenes with no fresh photos.
arxiv-2507-18832:
Ogundare built this risk score in twenty twenty-five for colorectal adenocarcinoma, a common colon cancer. Outcomes vary widely, and stage alone misses the tumor's biology. Immune cells inside a tumor carry prognostic clues. The study mined a large cancer atlas for genes tied to those infiltrating cells.

From one hundred twenty-eight candidate genes, a survival analysis kept two: CCL8 and TYR. Their weighted sum forms the risk score. High-score and low-score patients split into clearly different survival curves. An outside cohort confirmed the split. A chart that adds the score to standard staging sharpened predictions further. The author suggests the score could help guide treatment choices.
arxiv-2507-19032:
Alper Cakan and Vipul Goyal wrote a cryptography paper in two thousand twenty-five on copy-protecting software with quantum states. Copy protection encodes a program into a quantum state so that no one can split it into two working copies. Recent work secured a class of schemes whose secrets can be punctured at chosen points.

The authors widen that class. Their malleable-puncturable schemes only require that a circuit can be built which answers inputs away from the challenge point without helping with the challenge itself. That looser demand captures many more primitives. They show how to copy-protect the whole class under arbitrary challenge distributions.
arxiv-2507-19432:
Sheikh Shadab Towqir, Fei He, Todd Mytkowicz, and Na Meng fix code merge clashes that break builds with a two-path tool, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Their tool first lines up the base and both branch takes. Rules handle the common clash kinds in set ways.

An example path mines the branches for past fixes of like breaks. It lifts and broadens those edits into fresh fixes. On eighty-eight real clashes of twenty-one kinds, the tool solved over a third fully. At least one fix came for most cases. The mix of habit rules and learned cases carries the day. Readers in team coding get a smarter merge hand.
arxiv-2507-19932:
Ken Shiozaki writes a solo physics paper from 2025 on families of quantum spin chains that carry a symmetry. Such chains can sit in distinct topological phases, and the border between two phases holds special structure. Shiozaki builds a discrete framework based on matrix product states that bakes the symmetry action on the parameter space into the math from the start.

From that setup he derives a fixed-point formula for a higher Berry invariant when the symmetry fixes isolated points. The phase border between the Haldane phase and the trivial phase acts like a monopole, a point source of Berry curvature. Layers of defects under smaller symmetry groups are also discussed.
arxiv-2507-21632:
Nadiia Pulatova and a large team of co-authors wrote this astronomy paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on galaxies picked out by their X-ray glow. The sample joins the eROSITA space telescope's X-ray catalog with optical spectra from the Sloan survey.

Nearly thirty-seven hundred galaxies were fitted with stellar population models plus emission line templates. Splitting each line into broad and narrow parts mattered: with narrow fluxes alone, most galaxies shift up into the active nucleus zone of the standard diagnostic diagram. The team confirms that a galaxy's place on that diagram tracks its X-ray to hydrogen-line ratio. They also verify links among X-ray brightness, key line strengths, black hole mass, and stellar velocity spread. The work shows careful line splitting sharpens how we class feeding black holes.
arxiv-2507-21932:
Hadidi and co-authors review ways to split huge energy system models so computers can solve them in parallel. As wind and solar grow, these models swell in size and detail. Solvers often hit their limits on run time and memory. The team first sorts linear energy models by focus, math form, and scope. They then weigh decomposition methods that break one model into linked parts. Many methods help, but none wins in every setting.

A lack of shared test suites makes fair comparison hard. The authors propose rules for future benchmarks and minimum reporting. They also survey the software on offer. The review aims to make parallel energy modeling a more settled craft.
arxiv-2507-22732:
Wittawat Kositwattanarerk proposes a new design for automated crypto trading pools, in a 2025 paper. On decentralized exchanges, each trading pair usually needs its own pool, and savers who fund the pools have to deposit tokens in fixed proportions. Traders hopping between pools pay extra fees at each step.

His design lets savers deposit any amount of any token into one shared pool. The pool keeps each saver's share balanced by value, acting like a personal, self-adjusting portfolio. Because the pool's pricing rule shifts as trades happen, every pair can trade inside the single pool. He warns, however, that the scheme is open to flash loan attacks and needs added defenses before real use.
arxiv-2507-23232:
Sergey Streltsov and Sang-Wook Cheong name a set of stacked stone-like oxides as altermagnets. The work came out in 2025. Altermagnets are a new class of pull-based stuff. They line up in flipped pull rows. Yet they split their bands by spin with no help from swift-spin rules.

The mix needs a core-true frame with shifts in its near parts. It also needs spins in one straight line, set in flipped rows. Side by side, those traits break a joint flip rule. The 6H stones fit that mix. They have stacked forms and, as a rule, flipped-row ground states. The team shows that more than one of them shows spin-split bands. They also probe two more traits. One is a small net pull from spin-path links. One is a large pull born when the stuff is squeezed.
arxiv-2508-00732:
Andrea Sacchi and co-authors study the link between the ultraviolet and X-ray brightness of quasars in data from the eROSITA space telescope, in a 2025 paper. The link is steady enough that astronomers hope to use quasars as distance markers for cosmology. The team works with quasars chosen by their optical light and caught in two eROSITA releases.

To avoid a bias toward X-ray-bright objects, they kept only quasars bright enough in visible and ultraviolet light. The final sets hold 1,248 and 519 sources, reaching back to when the universe was a fraction of its present age. The brightness link showed no clear drift across that span, and its slope matched older compilations. The scatter around the link was small, which suits cosmology, but the samples are still too limited in range and size for firm cosmic measures.
arxiv-2508-00832:
Arimondo Scrivano compares old and new forms of data scrambling in a 2025 study of the quantum era. Codes like RSA keep web traffic and bank data safe today. A future quantum computer could break many of them with a method called Shor's algorithm.

The study weighs the old codes against new ones built to resist quantum attack, such as Kyber, Dilithium, and Falcon. It looks at how safe each one is, how fast it runs, and how hard it is to put in place. It also reviews mixed plans that pair old and new codes during the switch. The author aims to guide builders and policy makers through the move.
arxiv-2508-02932:
Yan and four colleagues present PLoRA in twenty twenty-five, a system that speeds the tuning of large language models. A popular tuning method, called LoRA, adds small trainable parts to a frozen model. It is cheap to run once, but finding the best settings takes many runs. Past work sped up serving many tuned parts, not the search for a good one.

Tests showed that current training wastes much of the hardware's power. PLoRA runs many tuning jobs at once under set limits on chips and model size. It also uses faster core routines for the math. Speed rose more than ten fold in the best cases, and total tuning time fell sharply.
arxiv-2508-03332:
He Xiao and co-authors squeeze small language models harder by spending bits where layers earn them, in a 2025 paper. Big models waste memory on layers that add little, but small models break quickly under crude compression. Their method, LieQ, scores each layer by how much unique information it carries. Layers that concentrate energy during training turn out to be the ones that cannot be cheapened.

That insight yields a geometry-only rule for handing out bit widths under a fixed budget, with no costly retraining or probing. Each layer keeps one uniform width, so standard fast math kernels still apply. Below two bits on average, LieQ shrank the accuracy gap that naive two-bit schemes suffer on two model families. The authors pitch it for edge devices with tight memory.
arxiv-2508-03932:
Viraj Karambelkar and co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper on stellar mergers seen by the Webb telescope. Luminous red novae are dusty eruptions from stars merging after a shared-envelope phase. Four events are observed in mid-infrared light. Their parent stars spanned a wide mass range. Ages since merger run from about eleven hundred to thirty-seven hundred days. Two events also get low-resolution spectra in the same range.

The spectra show strong oxygen-rich molecule features, water vapor among them. That supports a link between merger aftermaths and water fountain sources. Radiative transfer models fit the energy output to map the dust. Astronomers get a dusty, molecular portrait of how merged stars settle. Common-envelope phases shape many binary fates, yet they are barely observed directly. Merger leftovers are the closest fossil record of that hidden phase.
arxiv-2508-04132:
Swati Chaudhary and Takashi Oka found a geometric route coupling light to lattice vibrations in a 2025 paper. In materials whose electrons carry nontrivial quantum geometry, effective theories pick up Chern-Simons-like terms mixing different gauge fields, and for phonons such terms can split chiral vibration modes. The authors show local Berry curvature alone can reshape optical phonon spectra and dynamics even when the material's total Chern number vanishes, demonstrated on a gapped Dirac model.

A previously missed cross-correlation between electromagnetic and pseudo-gauge fields depends on the valley Chern number. It endows phonons with a geometric Born effective charge, coupling them directly to photons. Coherent Raman excitation of phonons becomes a probe of quantum geometry itself.
arxiv-2508-04232:
Chernyak and co-authors measure trace radioactivity in sapphire in this 2025 paper. Sapphire's strength and electrical traits suit it for parts inside sensitive radiation detectors. Even tiny uranium or thorium traces can spoil a detector's quiet background. Checking purity down to parts per trillion has been hard.

The team combined neutron activation with paired gamma-ray counting. Samples are first made briefly radioactive by neutrons, then watched for matched gamma rays. A commercial sapphire sample came in below the tightest limits yet reported for both elements. The test confirms the method reaches the needed sensitivity. Detector builders gain a trusted way to vet sapphire parts.
arxiv-2508-06232:
Manna and Desai wrote in twenty twenty-five about searching for gamma rays from merging galaxies. When galaxies merge, star birth speeds up and fast particles may be boosted. Those particles can produce high-energy gamma rays. The pair studied five well-known merger systems. They used nearly seventeen years of data from the Fermi space telescope, across a wide energy range.

They fit simple power-law spectra and built energy charts for each system. Two systems, NGC 3256 and NGC 660, gave weak hints of a signal. The other three gave no clear detection. The authors say star birth driven by mergers may add some gamma rays. They note theirs is the first targeted search of these five systems.
arxiv-2508-06532:
Fateme Movahedi studies a new graph measure that scores networks by the degrees of linked points, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Graph measures help chemists and others predict traits of a structure from its shape alone. The measure sums a set ratio over every link in the graph.

Movahedi sets sharp bounds that tie the new measure to five classic measures. Those older scores cover unevenness, balance, and link patterns in a graph. For each bound, the paper names the graphs that hit the bound exactly. The work places the new score firmly among the known family of graph scores.
arxiv-2508-08132:
Four researchers make microgrid control both smart and explainable in a paper from 2025. Microgrids mix solar, wind, and batteries to serve a local area. Storms and other rare shocks test their resilience. The team trained a learning agent to manage energy flow, then added a tool that explains each choice in plain local terms.

A case study modeled a microgrid in Ongole, India, during the Layla cyclone. The system kept a very high resilience score and a long projected battery life. Explanations showed renewable output as the strongest driver of decisions. Idle, charging, and discharging modes each had clear stated reasons. The authors say transparency can build trust in automated grid control.
arxiv-2508-09032:
Vision-language-action models steer robots from camera views and text orders, but they often blur where things are and when they moved. The three authors add a visual prompt that carries both: they project traces of key points, drawn from past observations, onto depth maps. The model thus sees the path of motion written into the scene's geometry.

In the SimplerEnv benchmark the method raised the mean number of solved tasks by 4 percent over SpatialVLA and 19 percent over TraceVLA. The gain came with minimal training data, a point the authors stress for real-world robotics, where collecting demonstrations is expensive. A project page hosts the details.
arxiv-2508-09232:
Nick Oh and four co-authors propose a workflow in 2025 for researchers who use social media data in AI work. Such data raises linked duties under privacy law, copyright law, and platform rules, and no single guide covered all three. Their workflow, called PETLP, builds legal checks into each step of handling the data.

The plan treats impact assessments as living documents that grow from planning through to sharing results. Using Reddit as a test case, the authors show that research groups and firms have different rights to take data. They also argue that true removal of identity from such posts is not possible, and they map the gap between making a data set and sharing a trained model.
arxiv-2508-09832:
Linh Nguyen and co-authors test, in a 2025 software paper, whether large language models can sort code review comments into fine-grained kinds without training data. Review comments range from vital catches to trivia, and sorting them shows how useful a review was. Older sorters needed costly hand labeling to learn.

The team asked models to sort comments into seventeen classes. The models beat the best trained system overall. Their edge was largest on the five most useful classes, where the trained system starved for examples. Balance across rare and common classes was the models' strength. The authors pitch the approach as a scalable tool for review analytics.
arxiv-2508-09932:
Liang Zhang and Edith Aurora Graf test four large language models on math tasks made to trip them, and log the step where each slip occurs. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such models now teach and grade math, so their care with facts and steps is a base need. The team built tasks in three fields — sums, algebra, and number theory — from item models set to be hard and error-prone, in place of stock test sets. They grade both the end answer and each step of the work. Four known models are tried. The aim is a clear map of where model math goes wrong, so that school use can rest on proof, not trust.
arxiv-2508-13632:
Yutong Feng and co-authors present a 2025 paper on virtual try-on for any wearable item. Most try-on systems handle clothes only. Shoppers also need jewelry, hats, and accessories in preview. Their system, called OmniTry, works without masks, which suits real use. Extending try-on beyond clothes hits a data wall: paired images of item and worn result are hard to gather.

A two-stage pipeline answers the data problem. Stage one trains on large unpaired portraits to place items mask-free. An inpainting model is repurposed to draw the item at a fitting spot. Stage two fine-tunes on paired images to keep the item's look faithful. Retail tech teams get one frame for all wearables. Mask-free placement removes a fiddly step that breaks consumer apps. The staged data plan is reusable for other image tasks with scarce pairs.
arxiv-2508-14732:
Zijun Huang, Chengdong Liang, Jiadi Yao, and Xiao-Lei Zhang address a nuisance in speaker verification: stretches of silence inside a recording drag down accuracy. Most systems run a voice detector first to cut long silences, but short gaps between words slip through. Their fix, PadAug, works at the raw waveform level during training.

The method simply joins silence segments onto speech segments, teaching the model to stay steady when silence is present. Because it is so simple, it drops into current top architectures unchanged. On a standard voice dataset, adding PadAug to a ResNet34 system cut the equal error rate by five percent in relative terms. The trained systems also held up when test recordings carried varying amounts of silence.
arxiv-2508-15432:
Bidyapati Pradhan and co-authors present SyGra, a graph-based system for making fake training data, in work from 2025. Large language models need vast, clean data for fine-tuning and for learning from ranked answers. Hand-made data is slow and costly to build at scale, so teams turn to data made by models.

SyGra runs a modular pipeline that models complex dialogue flows with little hand work. A two-stage tagging step mixes fixed rules with model grading to score and filter samples. Output fits a flexible schema for both training styles. The authors frame the system as a way to cut prep time in model training.
arxiv-2508-15532:
