John Wallace, Damien Bégué, and Asaf Pe'er present, in twenty twenty-five, a major upgrade to a code that simulates fluid and magnetic fields near black holes. The code is called cuHARM. The upgrade adds full treatment of radiation, light and other rays, and how that radiation pushes back on the fluid. For the ray math, they solve the transfer equation on a grid built along curved paths in space. That lets them track how radiation spreads in each direction at each point.

Such detail matters where the gas is neither clear nor fully opaque. The paper gives the equations, the numeric methods, and standard tests. An example applies the code to radiation-fed inflow onto a black hole. The new module runs on graphics chips for speed.
arxiv-2508-16532:
Ryunosuke Akiba and Francis Nimmo wrote an astronomy paper in 2025 on Eris, a dwarf planet in the outer solar system. Eris is nearly Pluto's size and has a small moon. Recent spin and orbit facts hint that Eris bends and wastes energy inside, which points to inner layers.

The pair modeled Eris's heat history tied to its spin and orbit dance with its moon. To slow Eris's spin as observed, a hidden ocean under the ice works best. Models with an ocean made up most of the successful runs, often nearly all. An ice-only Eris could work only with a warm, thick blanket of ice and odd flow traits. Any ocean would freeze by today unless insulation or antifreeze keeps it liquid.
arxiv-2508-17032:
Maurizio Diaz studies the inner structure of a compressed memory used by large language models. Long inputs make the model's cache of past tokens grow without bound. A method called Cartridges trains a far smaller cache for a text ahead of time. Diaz asks what the trained cache learns, part by part. He tests the claim that its keys act as routers that fetch stored facts.

Tests across tasks and model sizes back the routing claim. Keys can be swapped between tasks with little loss in quality. Most of the learned squeeze sits in the value vectors, not the keys. Diaz also adds a start method that seeds the cache from sampled chunks of text. That start makes training settle faster than past reports showed.
arxiv-2508-19232:
Kaveh Safavigerdini and six colleagues present software that watches carbon nanotubes grow in real time, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Nanotubes are key building blocks in nanotechnology. It is hard to track how they move as they grow. The images come from a scanning electron microscope, and they are hard for a program to read on its own.

Their tool, VFTrack, finds and tracks single nanotube particles in microscope image sequences. It joins feature finders and matchers in one tracking pipeline. A study of 13,540 hand-annotated trajectories picked the best pair, ALIKED with LightGlue. The team splits each move into growth along the tube, drift to the side, and oscillation. From those parts they work out growth rates by area. They also rebuild the shapes of the pillars as those shapes change over time.
arxiv-2508-19932:
Nitish Jaipuria and a team of co-authors present a system against payment scams in twenty twenty-five. Digital payments are fast and handy, but they also draw in fraudsters. Many scams use social engineering and start on platforms far from the payment app itself. Signals from users and transactions alone then miss how a scam truly works.

Their framework, CASE, uses a conversational agent to gather scam reports from users. The agent interviews people who may have been targeted, in a safe and scalable way. That builds a fuller picture of scam methods and patterns. With that picture, scams can be stopped in time more often. Readers see agentic AI used to collect knowledge, not just to flag single payments.
arxiv-2508-20632:
Miao and Wang study, in a 2025 math paper, the fractal size of sets built by iterated function systems whose rules change at each step. When the maps squeeze shapes in a smooth, angle-keeping way, the limit set is a conformal fractal. The authors focus on a spectrum of dimensions that sits between the two classic size measures.

They derive a formula for that spectrum using upper and lower pressure functions from dynamics. Simpler forms for the classic Hausdorff, packing, and box dimensions fall out as special cases. They also handle systems with endless maps at each step, giving a Hausdorff size formula under stated conditions. The work unifies several size notions in one frame.
arxiv-2508-20832:
Haim Bar, Huyen Nguyen, and Joanne Conover build a math model of how stem cells grow and change into other cell types, in a paper from 2025. Stem cells can copy themselves or turn into cells with a set job. That balance drives early growth and later repair of tissue.

The team wants to know how large a stem cell pool must be to build a tissue or colony. Their state model tracks how the stem pool and the changed-cell pool shift over time. Unlike older models, it lets the chances of self-copying and of change vary as time passes. The authors give a method to estimate those chances from data. In computer trials, the method gave good estimates even with small samples.
arxiv-2508-21032:
Decatur and five colleagues offer a faster way to make sets of images from text in twenty twenty-five. Image models that use diffusion are strong but slow and costly to run. When many prompts are much alike, the model repeats much of the same work. The team asked how that shared work could be done just once.

Their method groups prompts by how close their meanings are. Early steps, which set the broad shape of an image, are shared within each group. Later steps still run for each prompt on its own. Tests showed lower cost and, in some cases, better image quality. The method fits into current tools without new training.
arxiv-2508-21632:
Peng Yu, En Xu, Bin Chen, Haibiao Chen, and Yinfei Xu report QZhou-Embedding, a model that turns text into codes that hold its sense, for use in search and match tasks. Their report is from two thousand twenty-five.

The model is built on a known seven-billion-term base that follows commands. The team gives it one frame for many tasks, with set ways to shape data and train. A data pipeline uses a large model to reword, grow, and forge hard near-miss cases. Training runs in two stages: a first pass on search, then a full-task tune. The model tops two known leader boards for such codes, in English and in Chinese, at the time of the report.
arxiv-2508-21732:
João Valente, Atabak Dehban, and Rodrigo Ventura built a tool that generates synthetic training data for teaching vision-language models to read digital measurement devices. Even strong multimodal models fumble this simple task under clutter, occlusions, odd viewpoints, and motion blur. Such conditions are common in head-mounted cameras and augmented reality.

Their tool, CAD2DMD-SET, renders labeled images from 3D CAD models with realistic composition. They also release DMDBench, one thousand annotated real-world images for validation. Fine-tuning three leading models on the synthetic data improved scores substantially; one model's score rose by two hundred percent without degrading other tasks. The tool is planned as open-source.
arxiv-2509-00032: Dominic van der Zypen, working alone, shows in 2025 that two selection principles in topology are not the same. Selection principles are rules that say when covers of a space can be thinned to a smaller cover with a set trait. He builds a space that meets the first rule, written with omega and tau covers, but fails the second, written with omega and gamma covers. The build answers a question posed in a 2003 arXiv note on such principles.
arxiv-2509-00132:
Peiwen Xing, Aske Plaat, and Niki van Stein present CoComposer in 2025, a multi-agent system that writes music in the manner of a human team. AI music tools tend to be short, uneven in quality, and hard to steer. CoComposer splits the classic composition workflow among five agents that collaborate, each with its own task.

An aesthetics system scores the output on four composition criteria. Tests run with three language models: GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, and Gemini Flash. CoComposer beats prior multi-agent music systems on quality and beats a single agent on production complexity. Against a non-language-model tool, MusicLM, it offers better clarity and edit ease, though MusicLM still makes better music. Split roles make AI composition more open to steer.
arxiv-2509-00432:
Guo-Hua Liang, Ai-Guo Mei, Men-Yun Lai, and Shu-Sheng Xu study quantum states in twisted tubes whose cross section varies linearly in 2025. A particle confined in a narrow tube moves mostly along its length, with geometry shaping its energy states. Twist and changing width add effects that a straight, uniform tube lacks.

An extended thin-layer method derives an effective Hamiltonian for tangential motion under general linear transformations. Explicit forms cover rotation, scaling, and shearing. Rotation adds a gauge field coupled to angular momentum, while scaling and shearing create geometric potentials that lift degeneracies in non-circular sections. Square sections split formerly equal energy levels, while circular ones retain them.
arxiv-2509-00532:
Hartosh Singh Bal and Gaurav Bhatnagar give a short proof of two famed results. Ramanujan found both results long ago. One concerns the partition function. That function counts the ways to split a whole number into sums. The other concerns the tau function. Ramanujan built that sequence from an infinite product.

Bal and Bhatnagar show a clean pattern in both cases. Counts in a set pattern are always divisible by five. Tau values in a linked pattern are also divisible by five. Their proof uses one limiting case of Jacobi's triple product. That identity links infinite products and sums. They also use a method Ramanujan used to compute tau values. Students get a direct route to results often proved with heavy tools.
arxiv-2509-00632:
Mario J de Oliveira, writing alone, traces the origins of the Ising model. The Ising model is a landmark model of ferromagnetism. That is the permanent magnetism of materials like iron. Wilhelm Lenz proposed the model in 1920. Ernest Ising then analyzed it in a paper from 1925. Its units take only two states each. Each unit interacts only with its neighbors.

Ising found no ordered magnetic state in a linear chain. That result was correct but frustrating at the time. Rudolf Peierls later showed that order does arise in two dimensions. It thus arises in three dimensions as well. Two spare ingredients explain the model's lasting success. They are the two states and the short-range interaction. The account covers the model's birth up to 1936.
arxiv-2509-00732:
A S Dyatlov leads ten authors in total, with nine co-authors, in simulating an S-band radio-frequency photoinjector test bench at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research. The bench aims to produce high-quality electron beams and later relativistic vortex electrons, electrons carrying quantized orbital angular momentum, a twisting motion.

Dyatlov and his co-authors simulate the photogun at stated gradient and input power, finding stable bunch formation at low charge with weak space-charge effects. Optimizing injection phase and the cathode solenoid yields an emittance-compensated regime, keeping beam spread low. They also model single-electron Laguerre-Gaussian wave packets, finding that acceleration to multi-MeV energies suppresses spreading and preserves the initial angular momentum structure, supporting planned vortex experiments.
arxiv-2509-00832:
Emmanuel Jehanno, with three co-authors, tackles crystal structure prediction. The target is non-polymeric molecules, packed as crystals. Predicting such structures is a prerequisite for designing materials and drugs. They focus on the molecular assembly problem. A set of identical rigid molecules must be packed into a crystal.

Recent methods have grown more sophisticated in technique. Yet the learning objective beneath them remains ill-posed. Many structures can score alike under that objective. The team proposes a better loss function for the task. It captures key geometric properties of molecules. It also ensures the order of molecules does not change the score. A simple regression model then beats prior approaches. It wins on the COD-Cluster17 benchmark, including against flow matching methods.
arxiv-2509-00932:
Andrei Draganescu and L Ridgway Scott prove strong discrete maximum principles for finite element solutions. The setting is linear and semilinear elliptic equations. A maximum principle bounds a solution by its boundary values. Common matrix-based conditions for it often fail in practice. The team introduces a novel technique for those cases.

Their argument extends the strong form from large mesh blocks to the whole domain. A connectivity argument carries the property across the domain. The method applies to discretizations on certain pathological meshes. It also applies to semilinear elliptic equations of this kind. The result widens where users can guarantee sensible bounds. Such bounds matter for the physical fidelity of computed solutions.
arxiv-2509-01432:
Reinforcement learning agents are often tuned separately for reward, safe exploration, and curiosity, as if those aims had little in common. Nikola Milosevic and Nico Scherf present a unified geometric framework that treats all three as one optimization problem. The problem lives on the space of achievable long-term behaviors in an environment.

Inside that frame, classic methods such as policy mirror descent, natural policy gradient, and trust-region algorithms extend naturally to nonlinear utilities and convex constraints. The authors show how the same view captures robustness, safety, exploration, and diversity goals. They also outline open challenges where geometry meets deep reinforcement learning. The paper is a map of how disparate aims in agent learning can be seen as facets of a single geometric question.
arxiv-2509-01532:
Inflation, the early universe's burst of rapid expansion, can be reshaped when gravity departs from Einstein's theory. Miguel Barroso Varela, Orfeu Bertolami, and Andreas Mantziris examine f of R theories, where the gravity action is a general function of curvature, with a non-minimal coupling between matter and curvature. Both positive and negative corrections to standard gravity are considered.

The team builds a robust numerical method that evolves the metric and the inflaton field beyond the usual slow-roll approximation. Stability analysis shows positive corrections are inherently unstable during slow-roll, while negative ones can hold a stable de Sitter attractor. Using the measured strength of primordial fluctuations, they bound the coupling scale. Data from Planck, BICEP and Keck, and a recent telescope release force the effects to sit only slightly above the perturbative level.
arxiv-2509-01632:
Fine-tuning generative models with reinforcement learning has grown central. A recent objective, Relative Trajectory Balance, was introduced for that role in flow networks. Tristan Deleu, Padideh Nouri, Yoshua Bengio, and Doina Precup prove a key fact. This objective is exactly equivalent to Trust-PCL. That is an earlier off-policy method with a penalty that keeps new behavior near old.

The bridge rests on known links between flow networks and maximum-entropy learning. The equivalence places the newer objective inside a broader theory. That theory covers KL-regularized methods, which penalize drift from a reference model. The team revisits an example from the original paper. Older methods reach comparable performance there. Two literatures, they clarify, describe the same mechanism.
arxiv-2509-01932:
N K Kalzhigitov, S Amangeldinova, V O Kurmangaliyeva, and V S Vasilevsky study the lightest hypernuclei, nuclei that hold a lambda hyperon alongside normal matter. A hyperon is a heavier cousin of protons and neutrons. The team treats five such systems as two clusters, pairing the hyperon with a light nucleus. Folding potentials describe how the clusters attract each other.

They give those potentials in both position and oscillator forms to clarify structure. Bound state energies, meaning energies of held together states, are compared across the set. Scattering phase shifts for the hyperon and for neutrons off the same nuclei are also compared. The side by side view shows how the strange particle bond differs from a normal neutron bond.
arxiv-2509-02232:
Liang Xie, Yanting Li, Luyang Tang, and Wei Gao compress geometry for 3D Gaussian splatting point clouds in dynamic scenes. Gaussian splatting renders scenes from clouds of soft three dimensional blobs, but data volume explodes with scene complexity. Storage and transmission strain under that growth on their interactive platform. Their strategy integrates a reference point cloud codec into the platform pipeline.

A hash table caches inter-frame Gaussian transformations for high fidelity delivery within a fixed bandwidth cap. The codec then compresses geometry data precisely on top of that caching. Joint operation preserves fast rendering and high quality synthesis. Bitrate savings land in a solid double digit range on standard test sets. The tradeoff suits storage, transmission, and interaction of volumetric video.
arxiv-2509-02432:
Dylan J. Altschuler and Konstantin Tikhomirov wrote a 2025 paper on online vector balancing. Random sparse vectors arrive one by one. Each one must get a sign at once, with no chance to revise it. The goal is to keep running totals small. Offline versions can see all vectors first.

For binary vectors with few ones, the authors prove a sharp threshold. Every online method is forced to accept some imbalance. That imbalance grows like the double logarithm of the dimension. An efficient method matches that bound with high probability. So the online cost is pinned down exactly. Oddly, the answer does not depend on sparsity in this range. It does not depend on vector norms either. The result splits online from offline performance for the average-case Beck-Fiala problem.
arxiv-2509-02632:
Kay Lehnert wrote a 2025 review, styled as a hitchhiker's guide, translating string theory's swampland programme for cosmologists. The programme sorts effective theories into those that quantum gravity allows and those it forbids, with sharp consequences for cosmic models.

Lehnert explains where headline claims come from: limits on a cosmological constant, trouble for simple inflation models, and black hole decay. Each major conjecture gets a definition, its cosmological implications, and a status report with evidence and counterexamples. Covered topics span dark matter, dark energy, quintessence, and axions, alongside a long catalogue of named conjectures from distance and de Sitter conjectures to the weak gravity conjecture. The goal is to help model builders test their theories against quantum gravity constraints.
arxiv-2509-02832:
Matthew Baker, Hope Dobbelaere, Brennan Fullmer, and Patrik Gajdoš wrote a 2025 combinatorics note on matroid bingo. A matroid is a structure that abstracts independence, as seen in linear algebra and graph theory. The game is played on such a structure.

The authors study natural probability distributions tied to the game. Bingo-style random draws interact with the matroid's independent sets. The paper analyses the distributions that result. The note is short. It focuses on those distributions, not on strategy or optimal play. It adds a probabilistic angle to matroid theory. That field links combinatorics, geometry, and optimisation.
arxiv-2509-02932:
Kazuki Tokuda and 10 co-authors reported 2025 telescope observations of three dense cores in the Taurus cloud, caught near the moment stars begin to form. They used a molecule called ortho-H2D+, a heavy form of a simple ion, which traces cold and very dense gas. The cores were picked to show stages just before and just after a protostar ignites.

A wide view caught the molecule's glow across all three cores over broad regions. A sharper view, though, found compact emission only at the center of one candidate core. The other two gave upper limits, meaning any signal there sits below a stated ceiling. The pattern suggests the tracer stays spread out for most of this brief phase.
arxiv-2509-03032:
Kaicong Huang and 4 co-authors tackled person re-identification in a 2025 computer vision paper. The task is matching photos of the same person across different cameras. Cluttered backgrounds and blocked views make that matching hard, and hand labeling is expensive.

Their framework uses language as well as images, following the lead of models that join the two. Unlike earlier multimodal work, it treats the background as useful evidence rather than pure noise. People, the authors argue, judge a scene partly by pushing distractions aside. Two training branches handle the person and the surroundings, aligning each with matching text while pushing the two apart. Tests on four benchmarks, including ones with heavy blocking, matched or beat leading methods.
arxiv-2509-03132:
Matthias R. Gaberdiel and Ian Le Meur studied a 2025 string theory deformation called the triplet perturbation of the symmetric orbifold. An orbifold glues together many copies of a simpler theory in a symmetric way. The deformation comes from a set of three exactly marginal operators, gentle changes that do not break the theory's basic scale symmetry.

Working order by order in perturbation theory, the authors find the triplet case behaves much like a previously studied singlet case. In particular, the theory stays integrable, meaning its scattering keeps a highly constrained, solvable structure. Symmetries of the setup help them pin down the matching picture in dual supergravity, the gravity-side description of the same physics. The result extends confidence that this family of deformations is under tight control.
arxiv-2509-03232:
Eduard Kuric, Peter Demcak, and Matus Krajcovic re-examined a common shortcut in card sorting research in a 2025 study. Card sorting asks people to group labeled cards by how the topics fit together in their minds, revealing mental models that guide website and menu design. To save effort, researchers often hand each participant a random subset of the cards.

In an experiment with well over a hundred participants, the team compared full decks with random sixty-percent subsets. Similarity patterns between cards came out comparable under both approaches. Category themes, however, could differ, and the subset data varied more, calling for larger samples of roughly twenty-five to thirty-five people. Personality traits and reflective thinking also interacted with sorting behavior. The authors turn these findings into evidence-based guidance for the method.
arxiv-2509-03432:
J. W. Banks and one co-author's 2025 research paper focuses on computing solutions to wave kinetic equations. Those equations track how averaged wave strengths change in nonlinear wave systems. Their test case is a nonlinear Schrödinger model set in two spatial dimensions.

Rather than follow older routes, the authors build the resonant surface from small polynomial pieces. They then evaluate the collision term, which captures wave interactions, with numerical integration. Tests on model problems reach second-order accuracy, meaning errors shrink fast as grids refine. Comparisons with averaged runs of the underlying equation support both the method and the equation itself, for even and uneven wave patterns.
arxiv-2509-03532: Sabir Ahammed and two co-authors wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on the Bohr inequality for a broad class of holomorphic functions. Holomorphic functions are complex-valued functions with well-behaved derivatives. Their functions take values in vectors and live on a unit ball in a finite-dimensional Banach sequence space. Their series are lacunary, meaning many coefficients are missing. The authors also study the related Bohr-Rogosinski inequality for the same class. All results are proved sharp, so the bounds cannot be improved in general.
arxiv-2509-03632:
Miguel F. Martínez and four co-authors devote a 2025 theoretical physics paper to characterising higher-order topological insulators directly from a quantum state. Topological insulators host protected states at their boundaries, and higher-order versions place them at corners or hinges. Normally a Hamiltonian, the energy rulebook of a system, is needed to diagnose such phases.

Their framework instead reads the one-particle density matrix, a compact summary of the state itself. It extends mode-shell correspondence: a mode index counts boundary modes, while a shell index measures bulk topology around them. In one dimension the shell index reproduces the familiar local chiral marker and winding number. Applied to a fourfold-symmetric higher-order insulator with a chiral constraint, a fractional shell index signals an intrinsic phase. Because the method works in real space, it survives when disorder makes the structure amorphous, with no regular lattice at all.
arxiv-2509-03732:
SN 2019hnl, a Type IIP supernova, the kind whose light curve holds a long plateau after explosion, is the subject of a 2025 research paper by Aidan Martas and nineteen co-authors. The ATLAS survey caught this one within about a day of exploding. Its peak brightness, plateau length of roughly 107 days, and early fading rate all look typical for its class.

Optical photometry tracked the brightness while spectroscopy read its chemical fingerprints over time. Late-time nebular spectra, taken when the debris turns transparent, combine with hydrodynamic modelling in three simulation codes to reconstruct the star that died. The progenitor was a red supergiant of about eleven solar masses at birth. It forged a small amount of radioactive nickel in the explosion. Fitting the light curve required reducing the star's hydrogen envelope, evidence it was partially stripped before collapse. That stripping likely built a substantial shell of surrounding material.
arxiv-2509-04032:
Debangan Mishra and four co-authors' 2025 research paper asks how similar a language model's answers are when the same question is asked in different languages. If a model reasons well in English but erratically elsewhere, multilingual users get a lesser system. The study applies a recently proposed model similarity measure to twenty languages and forty-seven subjects in the GlobalMMLU benchmark.

Two patterns stand out. First, consistency across languages grows with a model's size and capability: scale buys cross-lingual stability, not just accuracy. Second, each model agrees with itself across languages more than with other models in the same language, suggesting distinctive internal habits that persist across tongues. The authors argue the measure works as a practical gauge of multilingual reliability, beyond per-language accuracy. It could also guide development: cross-language consistency becomes a measurable, improvable target.
arxiv-2509-04132:
D I Palade, writing alone, studies how ions wander inside tokamak fusion machines in a 2025 physics paper. A tokamak traps hot plasma, meaning ionized gas, in a donut-shaped magnetic field. Small drift-type turbulence stirs that plasma and carries particles outward, which hurts performance. Palade follows the transport from a Lagrangian viewpoint, tracking moving particles rather than fixed points in space. Computer runs with the T3ST code supply the evidence.

Despite uneven, squeezing flows, the particle motion looked close to ergodic, meaning it samples all available states evenly over time. It also stayed steady and time-symmetric in the runs. Broad starting spreads of particles explain those traits, the study finds. Small limits on the starting spread barely changed transport levels.
arxiv-2509-04332:
M Krivos and twenty-six co-authors test powdered screens for catching ultracold neutrons in a 2025 physics paper. Ultracold neutrons drift so slowly that sensitive detectors can count them for precision experiments. The standard screen material, zinc sulfide with silver, glows long after each hit, and its lingering phosphorescence blurs high-rate counting. Two cerium-doped crystals were tried as replacements: YAP and LYSO, both far faster to fade, at tens of nanoseconds.

Both candidates did detect the neutrons. YAP glowed about sixty percent less after two days and counted roughly twenty percent more neutrons than the standard. LYSO lagged on both lingering glow and counts. Faster screens could cut dead time in neutron facilities.
arxiv-2509-04932:
Creating a new view of an object from one photograph is ill-posed because hidden areas could look many ways. Haowang Cui, lead author with four co-authors, propose UniView in a 2025 computer vision paper. Their model borrows prior information from reference images of a similar object during synthesis.

A retrieval system, assisted by a multimodal language model, selects suitable reference images. A plug-and-play adapter then generates reference features for the target views. A decoupled triple attention mechanism aligns those features with the original image details. Experiments on challenging datasets show clear gains over leading methods.
arxiv-2509-05032:
At a magnetic null in the solar corona, heat conduction cools plasma in a pattern set by the earlier heated state. P. J. Cargill, lead author with two co-authors, examine that cooling in a 2025 solar physics paper. They set up an equilibrium balancing thermal conduction against uniform heating, then switch the heating off.

An equation for cooling follows from separation of variables. Remarkably, the cooling equations match the equilibrium equations after a simple change of variables, so the equilibrium determines the cooling phase. For a two-dimensional null, the cooling timescale grows by a modest factor set by flux element areas.
arxiv-2509-05132:
Testing whether a vertex numbering could come from a depth-first search can be done without reading the whole graph. Artur Czumaj, lead author with two co-authors, introduce a property testing model for that question in a 2025 theoretical computer science paper. Their bounded-degree model adds vertex labels that an algorithm may query, though it cannot look vertices up by label.

The model is motivated by processes such as depth-first traversal that assign consecutive numbers to vertices. The authors study which numberings are testable with sublinear queries, where the algorithm accepts valid numberings and rejects ones far from valid with high probability.
arxiv-2509-05332:
Attacking a self-driving car through both its sensors and its messages is made testable by Christos Anagnostopoulos and four co-authors in a 2025 paper. Cars depend on perception and communication systems, and a safe way to probe their weaknesses is a test rig rather than the road.

Their open framework models physical scenes, traffic, and vehicle-to-everything links at high fidelity, synchronised from one settings file. It supports attacks on laser sensor data, forged network messages, and satellite signal spoofing. Links to a common robot software stack ease reuse. When the team attacked a leading 3D object detector with generated scenarios, its performance dropped sharply under realistic conditions.
arxiv-2509-05432:
Generators for the unit group of a Burnside ring are given explicitly by Ziad Ghanem in a solo 2025 algebra paper. The Burnside ring encodes how a finite group acts on sets, and its units, the elements with multiplicative inverses, had no constructive generating description before.

Ghanem proves the units are generated by basic degrees, canonical elements coming from the equivariant degree of the identity map on the group's irreducible representations. Every unit is then the equivariant degree of a linear group isomorphism on a suitable representation. That degree in turn factors as a product of finitely many basic degrees. The result links the ring's multiplicative structure directly to equivariant topology.
arxiv-2509-05632:
A classic model of a particle in a gauge field is quantised in two coordinate systems by Ansha S. Nair and Saurabh Gupta in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. The Friedberg-Lee-Pang-Ren model is a standard test bed for constrained quantisation methods.

Working in the Batalin-Fradkin-Vilkovisky framework, the authors build the nilpotent BRST charges, symmetry generators of the quantised theory, from the constraints and a fermionic gauge-fixing function. They derive the invariant effective action and its symmetries in both polar and Cartesian coordinates. Physical states are shown to be annihilated by the first-class constraints, matching Dirac's formalism. Finite field-dependent BRST symmetries are also established and used to link the gauge-fixed and classical actions.
arxiv-2509-06332:
Language models that ace arithmetic still flounder at a children's number puzzle, report Roussel Rahman and Aashwin Ananda Mishra in a 2025 paper probing the limits of machine numeracy. Their one-hundred-problem challenge escalates through four tiers: basic arithmetic, advanced operations, primality checking, and the Game of 24, where four numbers must combine to make twenty-four.

State-of-the-art agents score high on the first three tiers, which reward executing known algorithms, but fail consistently at the puzzle, which demands heuristic search over a large combination space. The authors read the pattern as sophisticated pattern-matching rather than flexible analysis. Their title calls the models' number sense fragile, with consequences for tasks needing genuinely novel numerical insight.
arxiv-2509-06832:
Particles drifting by a fraction of a lattice step per cycle, without any interactions, are described by Bo Zhu and five co-authors in a 2025 paper on condensed matter. Fractional quantized responses are usually a sign of interacting topological systems. Here the setting is a time-modulated superlattice under a steady slope, a tilt.

Strong tilt drives Landau-Zener tunneling between the lowest energy bands, causing Rabi swings between neighboring bands. The average drift over one cycle then becomes a fraction, set by the ratio of the summed Chern numbers of the involved bands to their count. Adjusting only the lattice period produces drift quantized at one third and one half in the examples. Computer simulations use a realistic setup that lab teams could build. The finding widens the meaning of such fractional responses and of topological materials generally.
arxiv-2509-07132:
Fake speech made by generative AI now threatens speaker checks, voice biometrics, and criminal investigations. Kutub Uddin and 3 co-authors benchmark the detectors built to spot such audio deepfakes, in a 2025 research paper. Their focus is anti-forensic attacks, tricks that hide the traces generative systems leave behind, from simple pitch shifts and added noise to optimized attacks.

The team tests leading detection methods on five deepfake benchmark datasets. They compare raw-audio approaches with spectrogram-based ones, which turn sound into pictures of frequency over time. The tests expose where each detector breaks under attack. By mapping those weak points, the study guides the design of tougher detectors. Such detectors must hold up in real voice security settings, where attackers actively try to fool them.
arxiv-2509-07732:
Shangqi Lu and 1 co-author give fresh theory in 2025 for proximity graphs, the data structures behind fast similarity search. Approximate nearest neighbor search finds near matches to a query point in huge datasets. Graph-based methods lead the field in practice. They connect each point to nearby points, and queries walk the graph. Their foundations were incomplete, though.

The authors build a proximity graph with near-linear construction time. That improves on the quadratic bounds of all past constructions. Query time stays controlled by the data's doubling dimension and aspect ratio. Lower bounds then show a matching limit. Worst-case graphs need at least a set number of edges, up to small factors. Their hard examples are non-geometric. That prompts the question of whether Euclidean space allows smaller graphs. Using geometry, they answer yes. They shrink the graph further for that key case.
arxiv-2509-07832:
Jieao Zhu and 1 co-author design a receiver that listens to many radio bands at once using excited atoms, in a 2025 communications paper. Rydberg atomic receivers use atoms in highly excited states to sense radio signals, and they may beat size limits that bind ordinary antennas. Signals from different users, though, interfere inside the device.

Their answer borrows MIMO, the multi-antenna method used in modern wireless systems, to add spatial separation between signals. A dynamic model of the receiver clarifies how the interference arises physically. Untangling users in space could let one atomic receiver serve several bands cleanly. The design points toward compact, sensitive receivers for crowded future radio spectrum.
arxiv-2509-07932:
Servicing or removing a tumbling satellite starts with knowing its shape and motion, yet the target will not cooperate. Bala Prenith Reddy Gopu and 7 co-authors evaluate 3D reconstruction tools for that job in a 2025 research paper. They built a simulation environment in Isaac Sim. It generates realistic image sequences of tumbling satellites under orbital lighting.

Early tests on static scenes used a leading neural reconstruction method. The resulting meshes matched the original computer-aided design models closely in comparison software. Fine details needed for mission planning were captured. Those results set a baseline for the harder dynamic case, where the target rotates during imaging. Reliable reconstruction of uncooperative objects underpins on-orbit servicing and active debris removal, two growing needs as orbit gets crowded.
arxiv-2509-08132:
A future ten-TeV muon collider could taste flavour physics far above its own energy, argue Alfredo Glioti and 2 co-authors in a 2025 particle physics paper. Heavy new physics that breaks flavour symmetries leaves traces in high-energy collisions of quarks and leptons. At lower energies those traces are suppressed; a muon collider's energy lifts the suppression.

Sensitivity reaches interaction scales well above one hundred TeV in both lepton and quark sectors. The authors catalogue every Standard Model deformation whose four-fermion scattering grows quadratically with energy and project the collider's reach. Electroweak radiation opens extra final states to observe. Studies like this build the physics case for muon colliders while detectors and accelerators are still on drawing boards.
arxiv-2509-08532:
Writing numbers with the smallest possible average digit is subtler than the greedy recipe suggests, shows Carl P. Dettmann in a solo 2025 dynamical systems paper. Beta representations expand numbers in a non-integer base with unrestricted digits, and minimising the average digit is the goal. The problem is equivalent to a one-dimensional switched system obtained from a stabilisable two-dimensional linear system.

For a countable set of bases, the usual greedy expansion is optimal. On an interval of bases, strictly smaller averages are achievable, beating greed. A numerical upper bound and a conditional lower bound cover all bases. Number representations underpin coding and dynamics alike, and this result maps exactly where the obvious algorithm stops being best.
arxiv-2509-08732:
Catherine Wu and 1 co-author study incentives for training an AI twin in a 2025 paper. An AI twin is a digital copy that can write or work in a person's own style. It may help its creator, but over time it may also replace them.

A principal-agent model, where one side hires and the other side works, frames the trade-off. Tasks differ in how easy AI output is to edit and how well non-experts can judge it. Workers may hold back training to keep wage power. The authors argue firms and policy must reward workers if gains are to last.
arxiv-2509-09432:
Muhammad Kashif and 4 co-authors test a quantum method for valuing basket options in 2025, contracts whose payoff depends on several assets at once. Pricing such options on real data is slow and hard with standard tools. Their study centres on quantum amplitude estimation and how its accuracy trades against the computing resources it consumes.

The team varies the count of uncertainty qubits and the count of assets, one at a time, to map that trade-off. Results are checked against classical Monte Carlo runs and Black-Scholes calculations. Readers get a practical picture of where quantum pricing might help, where it strains, and how hybrid workflows should share the work.
arxiv-2509-09732:
Sary Elmansoury and 5 co-authors test, in a 2025 paper, whether breaking image classification into a decision tree helps vision language models. Their framework turns one hard labeling choice into a chain of smaller, readable decisions. They try it on a fine-grained traffic sign task and on the coarser CIFAR-10 image set, where label spaces differ greatly in size.

The models understood the tree structure well, reaching high accuracy at following it, yet tree-based reasoning still scored below plain zero-shot prompting. Adding language model written class names and image descriptions improved both methods. The authors treat the result as a warning that structured reasoning has real limits in visual tasks, even when it looks more transparent.
arxiv-2509-09832:
Hans Jürgen Lüdde and 2 co-authors upgrade a collision model in 2025. The model covers what happens when a highly charged ion strikes a molecule. Their atom-by-atom approach treats the molecule as a set of single targets. Overlap of cross-section areas stops double counting. That scheme worked well for protons at high energy. It also worked for ions with mild charge.

Fast projectiles can hit several atoms in one molecule, one after the next. The new model allows for those repeat hits. It uses mean free paths to judge them. Results match the old model where they should. For strong charges, the predicted ionisation grows past the old value. It stays well below a naive rule, though. That rule would just add each atom's share.
arxiv-2509-10132:
Nour Jamoussi and 3 co-authors propose a cheaper kind of personalization for federated learning in this 2025 paper. In Bayesian federated learning, many users train a shared model without pooling data, and each user also wants the model tuned to their own data. Standard personalization adds heavy sampling or extra training steps.

Their idea is geometric: project the global model toward each user's local model, with a dial that sets the balance between shared and local behavior. They show this projection equals a kind of average point on the space of distributions, which yields closed-form answers. Tests on varied data splits confirm the balance works, with almost no extra computing cost.
arxiv-2509-10232:
Natalie Behague and Patrick Gaudart-Wifling settle a case of the dijoin conjecture in this 2025 combinatorics paper. For an oriented graph, an inversion flips every arrow inside a chosen set of vertices. The inversion number is the smallest count of flips that makes the graph free of directed cycles, and the conjecture says joining two graphs adds their inversion numbers.

The authors prove the conjecture when the first graph has inversion number two and the second has an even one. For an odd second value, they sort out exactly when the claim holds and when it fails. They extend the same ideas to joins of many graphs, which also proves a separate conjecture by Alon and co-authors. Their proofs lean on the notion of tournament minimum rank.
arxiv-2509-10632:
Federico J. Gonzalez and Luis P. Lara identify the equations of a moving system from data, interpretably, in this 2025 control engineering paper. Nonlinear system identification usually forces a choice: flexible black-box models you cannot read, or rigid physical models that may not fit. Their framework splits the difference using characteristic curves, one curve for each nonlinear ingredient such as friction or restoring force.

Each curve gets its own small neural network, keeping the overall equation modular and readable. They test three flavors: a sparse regression version with structural constraints, a polynomial version, and a pure neural version. All handle gentle polynomial systems like the van der Pol oscillator. On harsher systems with stick-slip discontinuities, the neural version wins clearly, capturing complex behavior while the curves themselves remain visible for engineers to inspect.
arxiv-2509-10732:
Hector Giacomini, writing alone, traces how fast a landmark physics book reached Europe in this 2025 note on the history of science. Josiah Willard Gibbs brought out his book on statistical mechanics in 1902. It came out in London and New York at once. The received story says the book spread slowly.

Giacomini asked many libraries what they hold. He also read the Yale archives. The records show copies reached European schools surprisingly fast. The flow began in mid-March 1902. He credits three channels. Yale sent gift copies to leading schools. Gibbs mailed copies to noted scientists himself. The American publisher sent review copies to major journals. The note revises the standard picture of the book's reception.
arxiv-2509-10932:
The same trio, Seongho Joo, Hyukhun Koh, and Kyomin Jung, turn to protecting private examples inside prompts in this 2025 privacy paper. In-context learning lets a language model learn from examples in the prompt with no retraining, but those examples can leak, and differential privacy, the standard protection, usually wrecks the method's usefulness.

Their remedy is help from public data: task-related public examples join the private ones inside a framework that keeps the differential privacy guarantee intact. The resulting algorithm balances protection and utility far better than private in-context learning alone, according to their experiments. It also held up against membership inference attacks, the standard test of whether an attacker can tell if a particular record was used. For organizations sitting on sensitive examples, public data becomes a privacy subsidy.
arxiv-2509-11132:
Choosing a technology stack now has a new wrinkle. So argue Xiaoyu Zhang and seven co-authors in this 2025 software engineering paper. The wrinkle is whether large language models can write good code with the chosen tools.

The team ran the first large study of AI coding proficiency. They tested six language models across many third-party libraries. The count of libraries was one hundred seventy. Libraries doing similar jobs differed sharply in code quality. The gap reached eighty-four percent. Such gaps turn into real debugging costs. If teams simply follow the models, the ecosystem could narrow. A few favored tools would crowd out the rest. The authors urge that AI proficiency join stack selection criteria.
arxiv-2509-11232:
Seongwan Park, Jieun Woo, and Siheon Yang present MIS-LSTM in this 2025 health informatics paper. The system predicts a person's sleep quality and stress level for each day from lifelog data, the steady stream of sensor readings and events that wearables and phones collect.

Continuous sensor streams are chopped into blocks of a few hours and drawn as multi-channel images, while occasional discrete events get their own one-dimensional encoder. An attention module blends the two streams, and a recurrent network reads the sequence of blocks to catch patterns across the day. An uncertainty-aware ensemble then overrules shaky majority votes with confident individual ones. On a 2025 lifelog challenge dataset the full system beat strong recurrent and convolutional baselines, and tests confirmed that four-hour blocks and the multi-channel layout each helped.
arxiv-2509-11532:
Davide La Vecchia and Hang Liu merge two statistical tools to escape a dimensional curse. This 2025 statistics paper treats optimal transport. Transport compares probability distributions with strength and robustness. The robust version's sample cost explodes as dimension grows. Big modern problems get sidelined as a result.

Their framework is E-ROBOT. Entropic smoothing joins robust transport. Schrödinger bridge theory grounds the result. A robust Sinkhorn divergence comes out. One knob sets robustness. Another sets smoothing strength. The headline theorem gives a square-root sample rate at any dimension. The divergence can then serve as a loss in big problems. Demos cover goodness-of-fit tests, centers of corrupted shapes, gradient flows, and image color transfer.
arxiv-2509-12032:
A single antenna that reshapes itself to dodge interference is the hardware behind a 2025 study by Baiyang Liu and nine co-authors on fluid antennas for crowded 6G networks. Their meta fluid antenna can switch among many radiating states through one radio-frequency chain, with no channel knowledge required.

Earlier fluid antenna access used one active position at a time; multi-activation lights up several, multiplying the independent states available for separating users. Simulations under Rayleigh fading show stronger signal-to-interference ratios than rival single-chain designs, and the best state can be picked within microseconds, fast enough for channels that change quickly. Theory, full three-dimensional electromagnetic simulation, and bench experiments all line up behind the claim of channel-free multi-user multiplexing.
arxiv-2509-12432:
Fluids can, in principle, waste energy at infinitely fine scales. That worry is called anomalous dissipation. Claude Bardos and two co-authors give a sufficient condition ruling it out in 2025. Their setting is the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations in a bounded region. The boundary uses Navier conditions, where the fluid slips along the wall under friction.

Earlier arguments leaned on extra assumptions. Some concerned the pressure near the boundary. Others needed a strong solution of the inviscid equations at hand. Their proof avoids both. It draws instead on their recent regularity results for the pressure of weak Euler solutions. The condition clarifies when viscosity alone accounts for all energy loss.
arxiv-2509-12732:
Rishab Parthasarathy and Achintya Bhowmik propose a recurrent neural network system for cancer mutation study in a 2025 paper. Cancer remains a leading cause of death, and pathway study is promising but still relies on hand-derived lab data that is slow to acquire. Their work aims for an efficient end-to-end alternative.

Mutation series were isolated from The Cancer Genome Atlas database and filtered by a first step that selects key mutations by frequency. A recurrent network, a model suited to series, then predicted cancer severity. The system joins those predictions with drug-target databases. From them it forecasts future mutations, with chance built in, and recommends possible treatments. The authors present the system as a way to speed both prediction and treatment suggestion.
arxiv-2509-12832:
Atta ur Rahman, M. Abd-Rabbou and Cong-feng Qiao compare in 2025 a wide range of quantum control styles, from fixed pulses to learning agents that adapt. Tasks include keeping linked states alive, making new links, and guiding transport in a messy walk.

All tests run with colored noise, flaws, and loss in play. Fixed plans did best for making and keeping links in some pulse shapes and even beat learning. A mixed guard-and-pulse plan was most steady for keeping links. Learning agents won when fresh pulse chains had to be found. Pulse shape itself shifted how hard each task was. No one style won all tasks.
arxiv-2509-12932:
V. Guzey reviews in 2025 what photon hits on nuclei in near-miss heavy-ion crashes can teach about the inner parts of nuclei. When ions pass without touching, strong light fields act like photon beams on the other nucleus.

Focus falls on nuclear shadowing, where inner parts screen each other at small scales. Coherent charm output and paired jet output in lead crashes at the LHC are reviewed. Inelastic hits with forward neutrons seen in end detectors are also weighed. The review maps what these crashes can and cannot yet tell about small-scale dynamics in nuclei.
arxiv-2509-13232:
Zhongwen Xu and Zihan Ding replace group baselines in 2025 with a single-stream policy method called SPO. Group methods cut variance but waste work when groups collapse. Sync waits also curb scale in long tool tasks.

SPO keeps one lasting value tracker that adapts with divergence. Gains are scaled across the whole batch, so each sample teaches. No groups means higher throughput and prized sampling for a natural curriculum. On a mid Qwen model, SPO beats the group rival on five hard math sets. Gains stem from baseline and scaling choices, per ablations.
arxiv-2509-13532:
JooYoung Seo, Saairam Venkatesh and three co-authors build Py maidr in 2025, a Python package that encodes tactile, auditory, and conversational forms into Matplotlib and Seaborn plots for shared use. Past accessible tools split sighted makers from blind users in a one-way flow.

A design-for-us stance lets sighted and blind collaborators create and read plots with one tool. One import plus one show call adds accessible layers with minimal code change. Cases span notebooks, reproducible publishing, and reactive dashboards. Benchmarks show small steady overhead versus base plotters. Collaboration replaces hand-off as the accessibility model.
arxiv-2509-13632:
Yi Zhang, Apurav Tambe, and Zhao Pan study droplets held at the corner of a V-shaped fiber in a 2025 paper. A fundamental question in droplet-fiber physics is what maximum droplet volume a fiber can retain. The problem has been studied for horizontal fibers and for apex-shaped bent fibers, but less for V-shaped fibers, despite their demonstrated advantages in applications such as fog harvesting.

The authors investigate how V-shaped fibers retain droplets against gravity. An analytical model predicting the maximum droplet volume is developed from free energy analysis and validated against experimental data from five liquid-fiber pairs. As the V angle increases, the maximum volume first slightly decreases, passes through a broad transition region at intermediate angles, and then increases at larger angles, a pattern captured by their formula.
arxiv-2509-13732:
Hong-Bo Li and three co-authors model ultraluminous X-ray pulsars in a 2025 astrophysics paper. These systems pour out more X-rays than standard limits allow, fed by matter crashing onto a compact star at extreme rates. Whether that star is an ordinary neutron star or a stranger strangeon star, built from a different state of matter, remains unsettled.

Focusing on the strangeon-star picture, the team studies the hot mound piled at the base of the accretion column. Barriers at the star's surface let the mound grow close to a kilometer tall and heat past a billion degrees, hot enough to glow in neutrinos from electron-positron annihilation. At high accretion rates neutrinos become the main cooling channel, though the nearest known system's flux sits far below detection.
arxiv-2509-14132:
Julia Dollis and seven co-authors give virtual patients personalities in a 2025 paper on immersive medical training. Virtual reality simulates physical settings convincingly. Practicing communication, a core clinical skill, needs virtual humans who behave like plausible-feeling people.

Their framework plugs large language models into immersive VR. It creates virtual patients whose traits stay distinct and consistent. Personality sits in a separate module from the clinical facts. Licensed physicians ran simulated sessions in a within-subjects, mixed-methods study. The system proved feasible. It was judged a rewarding, effective enhancement to training. The analysis surfaces design lessons, including a realism-verbosity paradox. Overly talkative patients undermine belief. Challenges must also feel real in the clinic if doctors are to learn from them.
arxiv-2509-14232:
Zhaokai Wang and seven co-authors build GenExam in 2025, an exam that asks image models to draw rather than just answer. A good exam image needs correct facts, sound reasoning and a clean picture at once. Earlier tests covered understanding or loose drawing, but not strict exam style drawing.

GenExam holds a thousand tasks across ten subjects, sorted under a four level scheme. Each task comes with a correct reference image and a detailed scoring list, so judges can check both meaning and looks. The team tested seventeen image and combined models. All found the exam hard, and open models trailed the leading closed models by a wide margin. The results show how far current systems are from joining knowledge, reasoning and drawing in one step.
arxiv-2509-14832:
Stelios Zarifis, Ioannis Kordonis, and Petros Maragos generate future scenarios as trees using diffusion models in a 2025 forecasting paper. Good decisions under uncertainty, in energy markets or finance, need the full spread of possible futures, not just one forecast. Their framework, Diffusion Scenario Tree, builds that spread in a structured form suited to step-by-step control.

The method samples future paths again and again and groups them into a tree by clustering. The tree respects a key rule: each decision can depend only on what has been observed so far. Plugged into model predictive control, the trees were tested on electricity price arbitrage in New York State's day-ahead market. The approach beat the same optimizers fed with trees from conventional models, and it used energy storage more efficiently.
arxiv-2509-15232:
An Pham Ngoc Nguyen, Marija Bezbradica, and Martin Crane study financial contagion between communities of assets rather than single assets in a 2025 finance paper. As markets interlink, shocks in one asset class increasingly spill into others. Most studies trace those spills asset by asset, which can miss the group structure of modern portfolios.

High-frequency data on cryptocurrencies, stocks, and United States exchange-traded funds cover four years of trading. The Louvain algorithm detects asset communities, a vector autoregression model detects contagion, and random matrix theory strips out noise. Three findings emerge, led by this one: the size of contagion stays fairly stable over time, yet contagion density, the share of asset pairs showing spillover, keeps rising. Markets are not necessarily hit harder; they are hit more connectedly.
arxiv-2509-15332:
Krishna Kaipa and Puspendu Pradhan count how lines meet points and planes in a finite space. Their space has a fixed number of points set by a prime power, and it holds a special curve called a twisted cubic. A group of symmetries moves points, lines, and planes around in this space. Earlier work split the lines into groups under this action.

The pair now count, for each part, how many line and point pairs touch each other. They use the fact that points in this space match a set of cubic forms, and lines match bundles of those forms. Their counts finish a detailed map of this small but rich geometry. The work is aimed at readers in finite geometry.
arxiv-2509-15432:
Thong Nguyen leads a team that rethinks how to search scanned documents. The usual way trains special models to match text queries to document images. The team try a simpler path that needs no such training. A vision language model first writes a full text account of each document image. A standard text search model then works on those accounts.

On a known test set, their path scores higher than the best special trained model. It also scales better to large sets and covers more languages. Their study shows current vision models catch fine detail in both words and layout. The result sets a strong no training base line for future search tools.
arxiv-2509-15632:
Gali Eytan, Vincent Desjacques, and Yonadav Barry Ginat compute the drag on bodies moving through gas in space. This drag, called dynamical friction, drains energy and spin from a body on a looping path. The team study oval paths in a smooth, fluid like setting. Their tool splits the drag by wave type and by frequency, then averages over each orbit.

They check their formulas against mock runs of the sound wake the body leaves. For a drag switched on at a set time, calm dissipation sets in within a bounded time. They apply the results to pairs of compact bodies in gas. For unlike mass pairs with mild oval paths, the late growth of oval shape is much delayed. Equal mass pairs differ, since both parts cross sound speed together.
arxiv-2509-15832:
Kenya Otsuka, Yoshihiro Nagano, and Yukiyasu Kamitani rebuild images from brain activity. Such rebuilding turns a person's inner visual experience into a picture others can see. The hard part is scarce data: few paired samples of brain scans and images exist. A translator that maps brain signals to image traits is trained on those pairs, and it bottlenecks any attempt to rebuild sights never seen in training.

The trio analyze two translator types with math: a plain regression and a sparse one that uses few active traits. The plain type suffers a collapse, where its outputs span too few dimensions to generalize. They give a diagnostic that gauges this harm without any brain data. The sparse type, studied in a teacher and student setup, avoids the trap.
arxiv-2509-16132:
Cheap depth sensors may have as few as one pixel, yet each pixel records rich timing data about returning light. Carter Sifferman and six co-authors ask how much scene shape can be rebuilt from a handful of such pixels. Their method first guesses scene traits with a fast predictor, then refines the guess by comparing rendered views with real data.

With as few as fifteen pixels, the method finds the pose of a known object from its plain 3D model. Tests run in both simulated scenes and real captures with built hardware. Early results on other scene types also look promising, which hints at low-cost 3D sensing.
arxiv-2509-16332:
Giving a language model a synthetic personality may change far more than its tone. Stephen Fitz and four co-authors shape model traits along the Big Five personality frame and test the effects on skill and safety checks. Lowering one trait, conscientiousness, sharply cut scores on safety tests that cover harm knowledge, truthfulness, ethics, and flattery.

General skill scores fell as well. The team discuss what this means for safety testing, for steering models after release, and for the risk that bad actors abuse trait control. Their results argue that safety checks should vary personality settings, not just prompts.
arxiv-2509-16832:
Ziyang Xu and co-authors align laser scans with city models in a 2025 mapping paper. Digital twins of cities pair laser point clouds with semantic 3D models. Aligning the two, building by building, is a base step for updates and change checks. Model flaws at a common detail level make that alignment hard.

Their method, L2M-Reg, accounts for model uncertainty while aligning. It gives a building-level answer where older methods struggled. Data and code are shared in public. Cities could keep their digital twins fresh with less hand work. That freshness matters for planning, building, and flood or heat studies.
arxiv-2509-17432:
Giorgio Cartechini and seven co-authors tackle a dosing risk in proton therapy in a 2025 arXiv paper. Pencil beam scanning delivers protons in fine spots, but a breathing patient's motion can smear the dose. The team built a way to predict that interplay effect for lung and esophageal cancer patients who breathe freely during treatment.

Their predictive model, built on synthetic breathing, runs inside the RayStation planning system. An in vivo check uses each patient's real breathing traces and machine log files. Both routes were benchmarked against the FRED Monte Carlo engine, and they agreed closely. Two clinical cases treated without rescanning showed the dose settling after five fractions, under breathing, range, and setup errors. The authors pitch the frame as an automated, clinic-ready check that can run before treatment starts.
arxiv-2509-17632:
The PlantCLEF 2022 challenge gets its overview from Herve Goeau, Pierre Bonnet, and Alexis Joly. The challenge belongs to a long series on automatic plant identification. The stakes are plain: hundreds of thousands of plant species support farming, building, and medicine, and the biodiversity crisis raises the cost of ignorance, while expert naming stays slow.

By 2022, deep learning looked mature enough to aim at global identification in earnest. The data resist with many classes, skewed counts, label errors, duplicates, and photos of mixed quality and content. The 2022 edition steps toward the goal with a multi-image classification task that also uses metadata, across a very large species set. This overview records the task design and the field's results that year. It stands as the reference point against which the 2023 and 2025 editions measure their gains.
arxiv-2509-17932:
Runheng Liu and 4 co-authors spot false claims from a language model with no training at all. Their 2025 paper uses TruthV, a method that reads signals inside the model. Most inner units show no link to truth, the team finds.

A sparse few inner vectors do track truth in a steady way. TruthV pools the picks of those few vectors to judge a text. It needs just a small support set to find them, and adds no new weights. Across model sizes and bench sets, it beat past training-free tools. Truth thus seems to sit in a small, neat part of the net.
arxiv-2509-18132:
Xiuyi Fan argues that medical AI must show both its reasons and its doubt. His 2025 position paper deals with a gap in current tools. They may explain a call, or score how sure it is. Rarely do they do both in a way that fits clinic thought. That split slows trust and uptake in care.

Fan sets out a joint frame, called Explainable Uncertainty Estimation. It maps types of medical doubt to AI doubt ideas. Paths he lists span multi-source doubt sums, plain visual displays, and support tools that show doubt at the point of choice. Guide rules close the paper.
arxiv-2509-18232:
Baudouin Le Charlier presents a working system to store and shrink regular languages in two layers. His 2025 paper deals with regular languages, the sets of strings a finite machine can accept. The first layer uses tidied regular expressions whose set of leftover forms stays finite, so work on them can end.

At the code level, each tidied form gets a plain integer ID. A second layer, the background, groups forms that mean the same language. The shortest form in each group stands for the whole group. Long tests show the frame can hold huge sets in compact form.
arxiv-2509-18332:
Graphene is a one-atom-thick sheet of carbon with unusual electric traits. L. E. Golub studies how two kinds of energy splitting shape its behavior in weak magnetic fields. His 2025 paper builds theory for graphene placed on top of other crystals. Those partner crystals add Rashba splitting and valley-Zeeman splitting, two ways electron spin energies can divide.

Golub works out how weak localization, a small quantum fix to how well the sheet conducts, changes in this setup. He finds the valley-Zeeman split alone does nothing without the Rashba split. With Rashba present, it can flip the sign of the magnetic response. Scattering between the sheet's two valleys can also flip that sign. He gives formulas that hold for any mix of the two splits and scattering rates. The results guide tests on these layered materials.
arxiv-2509-18632:
Language models write plans to help users through complex tasks, and training usually rewards plans users say they like. Nishant Balepur and seven co-authors test whether liked plans actually help in this 2025 paper. Their study, Planorama, had 126 users tackle 300 multi-step questions using model-written plans. Thousands of plan uses and comparisons were recorded.

The gap was clear: what users and models preferred did not predict which plans led to correct answers. Users did about as well with plans they disliked as with plans they liked. Surface traits like brevity swayed preferences but not success. Reward models and agent tests showed the same blind spot. The authors argue that alignment training built on preference alone can drift from real helpfulness. They call for feedback drawn from real task outcomes instead. The paper lays out a plan for that shift.
arxiv-2509-18732:
Hot gas moving in bulk leaves a faint imprint on the cosmic microwave background, called the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect. Amy Wayland, David Alonso, and Adrien La Posta model that signal's stacking spectrum from first principles in this 2025 paper. Stacking analyses cross-match the imprint with rebuilt galaxy momentum fields. Getting the model right matters for unbiased cosmology.

The team evaluates every term in the cross-correlation, including sideways and along-line parts of the velocity field. They add terms that are often dropped: a disconnected cross-term, a non-Gaussian four-point term, and two-halo effects. Satellite galaxies' impact is assessed too. Upcoming microwave experiments should detect several of these terms at four to six sigma. The along-line modes stay negligible in all cases. The paper lists exactly what future analyses must model.
arxiv-2509-18832:
Dirac-type problems ask how dense a graph must be before a given pattern must appear inside it. Allan Lo tackles the step from one copy of a pattern to a full tiling by copies in this 2025 short note. A tiling, called an H-factor, covers every vertex with disjoint copies of the pattern H. Thresholds for tilings are usually harder to pin down than for single copies.

Lo presents a method that turns a threshold for finding one spanning copy into an upper bound for the tiling threshold. He applies it to oriented graphs, where edges carry directions. For large cycles, he proves a sharp-looking degree bound that guarantees a full cycle tiling. The bound improves a result by Wang, Yan, and Zhang. The note is a tool paper: one transfer method, one clean application. Extremal graph theorists are its audience.
arxiv-2509-19532:
Big science tools now make data faster than local computers can chew through it. Flavio Castro and four co-authors ask when sending that data to a distant supercomputer in a live stream beats file-based handling. They build a scoring model that weighs data rate, transfer speed, remote computing power, and file overhead. The score predicts total finish time for each route.

Cases from light sources, particle physics, and fusion work motivate the model. A worked case from a major X-ray laser facility shows streaming cutting end-to-end time by up to ninety-seven percent. File staging adds delays that grow painful for time-sensitive steering of experiments. The framework gives facility teams a principled way to choose. It turns a gut call into a computed one.
arxiv-2509-19832:
Networks of simple agents can solve shortest-path problems by exchanging only local news. Zicheng Huang, Wangzhi Zhou, and Yuanqiu Mo study a biased min-consensus protocol that does so over time. With a well-chosen gain, earlier work promised arrival at the answer inside a preset time window. Noise on the edge weights, though, can blow the gain up without bound.

The authors first bound the errors that noise creates in the estimates. They then design an early stopping rule that avoids the blow-up while still naming the true shortest paths. Simulations confirm the analysis. Distributed path finding runs inside routing, robotics, and sensor webs where no central view exists. A safe stopping rule turns a fragile protocol into a deployable one.
arxiv-2509-20632:
Atoms in highly excited Rydberg states make exquisite radio receivers. Dixith Manchaiah and four co-authors probe the bandwidth and sensitivity of such a sensor in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their device reads signals through electromagnetically induced transparency in a rubidium vapor cell. Bandwidth is normally capped by atom transit times and coupling strength, and widening it was thought to cost sensitivity.

An optical homodyne readout broke that trade-off, preserving sensitivity at a response bandwidth of eight megahertz. The team also received real digital communication signals with the atomic sensor. Error measurements across symbol rates exposed a subtlety: the bandwidth for a pure tone differs from the bandwidth for a modulated signal, because symbols spread in frequency and gather noise. A head-to-head comparison with a conventional radio mixer grounds the claims.
arxiv-2509-20832:
A thin trail of gas stretches across the spiral galaxy NGC 3627 like a jet contrail. Mengke Zhao and Guang-Xing Li report the discovery in a 2025 astronomy paper. The structure was seen in both infrared dust images from the PHANGS-JWST program and gas data from PHANGS-ALMA.

The trail runs about eight kiloparsecs long but only about two hundred parsecs wide, an extreme shape with no Milky Way equal. Its gas moves with supersonic turbulence. The authors argue that a compact object, probably a massive black hole or the core of a dwarf galaxy, flew through the disk and focused gas by gravity. The crossing likely happened recently, within roughly the last twenty million years.
arxiv-2509-20932:
Game theory asks what the best move is, but in real life an almost-best move is often all anyone can compute. Neil Ghani rebuilds that idea from category theory in a solo-authored 2025 paper, first presented at the ACT 2024 conference. The paper proposes a wholly fresh approach to approximate game theory.

Ghani starts with selection functions, abstract tools that pick outcomes from sets of possibilities. On that base he builds a simple, robust model of approximate equilibria. He then develops the algebraic rules that approximation obeys in this setting. Category theory supplies a uniform language for agents, decisions, and near-optimality. The aim is practical as much as theoretical: exact answers may be impossible when inputs are uncertain.
arxiv-2509-21832:
James A. Rossmanith and Preeti Sar build a faster way to simulate gases at the level of particle motion in this 2025 paper. The Boltzmann equation tracks that motion across many scales, but solving it directly is costly. A simplified collision rule, called ES-BGK, keeps the right flow properties at low cost. The authors design a numerical scheme around it for two-dimensional problems.

The scheme splits the gas description into a macro part, much like a fluid, and a micro part that holds the fine detail. That split lets the method use a smaller grid of particle speeds than direct methods need. Heat flow computed from the micro part closes the fluid equations. The team extends an older stable method to two dimensions, the ES-BGK rule, and walls that reflect particles. Tests in one and two dimensions, plus scaling studies on many processors, check the result.
arxiv-2509-22332:
Jonathan Dransfeld, Marvin Künnemann, and Mirza Redzic classify the exact difficulty of a family of graph pattern problems in this 2025 paper. The problems concern dominating patterns: a set of vertices that both dominates the graph, touching every vertex, and forms a specified pattern shape, such as a clique, a matching, or a path. Graph theorists had studied such patterns case by case. Prior work gave algorithms and lower bounds for a few patterns, tight only when the pattern is large.

The authors ask for a complete classification covering every pattern at once. They define a parameter of the pattern that determines the optimal running time, assuming a standard hypothesis from fine-grained complexity. One pattern, the triangle, is the lone exception. The classification leans on a quantity studied since the nineteen eighties for counting pattern occurrences, though the two sometimes differ.
arxiv-2509-22832:
Biyao Zhang and 6 co-authors predict how long large language model training will take across hundreds of graphics chips. Such training is among the heaviest jobs in high-performance computing. End-to-end time depends on transformer parts, parallelism strategy, and network tiers in tangled ways. Learned predictors need costly sampling; analytic ones miss real hardware messiness. Their framework decomposes the model into core compute primitives.

Each key operation gets a light, hardware-aware predictor from small samples. Those pieces combine into an end-to-end system spanning data, model, pipeline, and tensor parallelism. On two large supercomputers, average errors stayed near five and nine percent for models up to twenty billion parameters. The predictor runs on CPUs, so configurations can be tried cheaply.
arxiv-2509-23332:
Domain walls in the two-Higgs doublet model come in flavors, and now they are all classified. Richard A Battye, Steven J Cotterill, and Adam K Thomasson sort the wall solutions of the Z2-symmetric model. Each wall is superconducting, CP-violating, or neither. The class depends on scalar masses and the ratio of vacuum values. Any wall, they show, needs only six of eight field components.

Some parameter regions allow even fewer fields. Superconducting walls can carry stable currents in two spatial dimensions. CP-violating walls break CP locally on the wall itself. That could host out-of-equilibrium CP-violating processes, a setting cosmology cares about.
arxiv-2509-23532:
Numerical integration rules lose their neat error behavior when the function has a kink or a spike. Pei Liu, the sole author, derives an asymptotic error formula for Gauss-Legendre quadrature on such nonsmooth functions. The route uses a contour-integral form of the remainder term. A snag is that standard approximations of Legendre functions fail near the interval, so Liu first swaps in smoother stand-ins with singularities moved off the interval.

The formula gives both the best convergence rate and the leading error coefficient, which depends on where the singularity sits. Users can pick point counts that shrink the leading error, or add the formula as a correction to speed convergence. Tests on power and log singularities confirm the theory.
arxiv-2509-24132:
José Correa and 2 co-authors map every variant between two classic choice problems. In the Prophet Inequality, values arrive in a hostile order and each must be taken or dropped at once, with no return. In Pandora's Box, the chooser picks the order, pays to inspect each value, but may return to any value already seen.

The variants arise by toggling three features: commitment, inspection cost, and control of order. The team sums up what is known for each mix and fills the gaps for mixes not yet studied. They also uncover links to Ski-Rental, a classic online problem. The map gives a single frame for results that were scattered across separate lines of work.
arxiv-2509-24332:
Forecasting how physical systems evolve is hard when the test setting differs from training, as real conditions keep shifting. Siyang Li and 4 co-authors define a two-fold invariance principle for systems governed by partial differential equations. The ingredient operators and the way they compose stay fixed across domains and across time, even as parameters change.

Their method, iMOOE, builds a mixture of operator experts aligned to that invariance, with a frequency-enriched learning objective. On simulated benchmarks and real applications, it led in-distribution scores and, more notably, generalized zero-shot to unseen settings.
