Rivals often still needed test-time samples to adapt, which this design avoids.
arxiv-2509-24432:
Prabhanjan Ananth and 3 co-authors build strong pseudorandom unitaries inside an idealized quantum setting. In the Haar random oracle model, every party can query one perfectly random unitary and its inverse. Pseudorandom unitaries must look random to any efficient test yet be cheap to build, a core tool for quantum cryptography.

Earlier work proved such objects exist only without the inverse, or proved a weaker notion with it. This construction is the first strong version in the full model. The authors also frame it as a viable route to quantum pseudorandomness from random circuits. The result speaks to how pseudorandom objects behave in nature as well.
arxiv-2509-24632:
Zan Li and Jiahui Chen share first credit on this paper from two thousand twenty-five, with a long author list. It presents UniDex, a model-based remake of the inverted index at the heart of search.

Classic indexes match raw terms, which misses sense and ages poorly. UniDex maps both queries and documents to semantic IDs through a part called UniTouch. A second part, UniRank, then ranks by semantic match. The pair swaps hand-built rules for one learned frame, which cuts upkeep. Tests on plant-scale data and live traffic show clear gains. The system now serves the short-video search of Kuaishou at vast scale.
arxiv-2510-00032:
Zeng and colleagues build WaveMind, a conversational foundation model for interpreting EEG brain signals. Tackling a real mismatch that has held back EEG language models. Brain signals simultaneously encode cognitive processes and intrinsic neural states, so aligning them to only one paired modality, images or text. Wastes data and limits generalization, and the team's careful pivot investigation shows the two paired alignment sources are actually complementary in this work.

WaveMind therefore maps EEG and its paired modalities into one unified semantic space, trained with WaveMind-Instruct-338k. The first open cross-task EEG instruction-tuning dataset, assembled from five diverse sources at 338 thousand examples. The resulting model also keeps robust classification accuracy while supporting flexible full open-ended conversation across four downstream tasks. Bridging general-purpose EEG foundation models that generalize and chat models that explain, in a single system for researchers.
arxiv-2510-00132:
Yuxuan Zhang wrote this 2025 theory paper on peaked quantum circuits and the quest to prove quantum advantage. A convincing demo must be feasible, hard for classical computers, and easy to verify. Peaked circuits look random yet concentrate their output on one hidden string. Zhang studies a concrete random way to build such circuits and tests whether they are truly nontrivial.

The construction glues together two random circuits chosen with a postselection rule. Zhang proves the result is provably far from trivial and cannot be compressed. Its circuit complexity grows at least in proportion to the qubit count times the design depth. A second result shows that even estimating the peak is average-case hard for classical methods. Together the results answer an open problem posed by Aaronson in 2022 about random peaked circuits.
arxiv-2510-00332:
Zeshi Dai and colleagues at Surf AI and Princeton University published this 2025 paper introducing CAIA, a benchmark for AI agents under attack. Most benchmarks test agents in calm, controlled settings with honest information. Real financial markets punish errors and reward deception instead. The team uses cryptocurrency markets, where exploits drained billions in a single recent year.

CAIA sets 178 time-anchored tasks that force agents to separate truth from manipulation. Seventeen leading models were tested, both bare and with professional tools attached. Without tools, even frontier models scored between about twelve and twenty-eight percent accuracy. Tools lifted the best model only to about sixty-seven percent, below the eighty percent human baseline. Models kept choosing unreliable web search over authoritative blockchain data sources. The authors argue adversarial robustness must gate any claim of trustworthy autonomy.
arxiv-2510-00632:
Taïbi, a CNRS researcher, states the local Langlands conjecture for connected reductive groups in these 2025 arXiv lecture notes. The conjecture predicts a map from the irreducible representations of a group over a local field to simpler Langlands parameters, with finite fibres called L-packets. Pinning down exactly what that map should be, and what extra structure it must respect, has occupied number theorists for decades. These notes give a careful modern formulation.

Taïbi first recalls parallel features of representations and of parameters, then states the basic and semi-simplified versions of the correspondence. Refined versions describe each L-packet through centralizers of its parameter, handling the quasi-split case directly. The non-quasi-split case needs Kaletha's recent machinery of Galois gerbes, which the notes explain. Shahidi's conjecture on L-functions appears as one of the stated components.
arxiv-2510-00832:
Antipov and Kratsch advance boundaried kernelization in this 2025 arXiv paper on parameterized algorithms. Kernelization means shrinking a hard problem instance to an equivalent one whose size depends only on a parameter. Polynomial kernels are rare because they seem to need strong global structure. Boundaried kernelization instead improves just a local region, separated from the rest by a small boundary, in the spirit of protrusion replacement.

The authors import matroid-based techniques from Kratsch and Wahlström, which identify irrelevant vertices using representative sets. Earlier uses leaned on global connectivity, but they show the local boundary supplies enough structure. That yields randomized polynomial boundaried kernels for s-multiway cut, deletable terminal multiway cut, odd cycle transversal, and vertex cover. They also extend the underlying definitions to annotated graphs with distinguished terminals.
arxiv-2510-00932:
Zaeed, Islam, and Inđić present Opal in this 2025 arXiv paper, a framework that turns performance analytics into LLM-guided code optimization. Profilers and Roofline models can locate GPU bottlenecks, but translating diagnostics into code changes remains manual expert work. Language models know optimization patterns from the literature, yet without hardware context they guess blindly. Opal feeds performance insights, from counters and stall events to Roofline placement, into prompts that an LLM reasons over.

Across sixteen hundred forty experiments on GPU kernels, even a single insight source produced speedups in over ninety-eight percent of cases. Average gains ranged from nineteen to fifty-two percent depending on the source. The prompt template yielded correct code in all but one run, where a vague diagnostic triggered an unsafe suggestion. The authors aim at a multi-agent version that runs the profilers, closing the loop from measurement to synthesis.
arxiv-2510-01032:
Shi and six co-authors explain why meaningless tokens improve language model reasoning, in this 2025 arXiv paper on interpretability. Padding a prompt with long strings of punctuation or separators looks like noise, yet models reason better with the padding than without it. The authors trace the effect inside the network's MLP layers. Meaningless tokens redistribute activations: near-zero activations become rarer, while large-magnitude activations grow more common.

That shift suppresses weak signals and promotes stronger, more informative ones, which expands representational capacity. Building on the mechanism, the team proposes the Activation Redistribution Module, an inference-time tweak that edits activations. It finds near-zero activations after the nonlinearity and pushes them outward, mimicking the padding effect with a few lines of code. Across benchmarks and architectures, ARM improved reasoning performance without changing the input. Gains were modest on base models and larger on reasoning-tuned ones.
arxiv-2510-01132:
Wang and Ammanabrolu write a practitioner's guide to multi-turn agentic reinforcement learning in this 2025 arXiv paper. Training language models as agents that act over many turns is advancing fast, but frameworks and definitions are fragmented. Nobody had systematically mapped which design choices matter across tasks. The authors organize the design space into three pillars, environment, reward, and policy, then test each one empirically in TextWorld, ALFWorld, and SWE-Gym.

On environments, even simple tasks predicted how well an agent generalized to harder ones within a domain. On rewards, dense turn-level feedback sped training, but stability depended heavily on the chosen algorithm. On policy, they compared biased and unbiased policy gradient methods and worked out the best split between supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning under a fixed budget. The findings distill into a concrete training recipe for co-designing all three pillars.
arxiv-2510-01232:
Kim and co-authors X-ray popular language-model benchmarks to learn which abilities each one truly measures. Leaderboard scores claim to grade reasoning or commonsense, yet tasks secretly blend many skills. Without a fingerprint of that blend, gains can reflect shortcuts instead of capability.

Their profiling method combines gradient importance with targeted ablation of model parts. An impact score then rates how much each of ten cognitive abilities drives success. Most benchmarks leaned on several abilities, and same-labeled datasets used different mixtures. Code benchmarks rewarded broad skill, which explains why narrow fine-tuning disappoints there. Three instruction-tuned models supplied the profiling subjects. Irrelevant abilities sometimes dragged performance down, not merely sideways. Ability fingerprints make benchmark shopping an informed decision. Cognitive science grounds the ten abilities in human faculties. Scores become stories about skills again. Diagnosis precedes redesign of the tests.
arxiv-2510-01332:
Hansen and co-authors read the spacing and wobble of compact planetary systems as fossils of their birth in a gas disk. Planets migrating inward usually lock into resonant chains, yet observations show few survivors of that state. A stellar magnetic field sculpting the disk's inner edge changes the story.

Simulations with that sculpted edge produce the observed small fraction of resonant pairs. Architectures settle within a few million years, during the disk's own lifetime. As the gas disperses, diverging pairs cross resonances and pick up exactly the leftover eccentricities astronomers infer. Tides barely alter the outcome under standard assumptions. Transit durations and timing variations supply the observational eccentricities. Magnetic diffusion into the disk softens the inner density cutoff. Resonant chains form and then mostly break, matching the census. Earth and Neptune class planets anchor the tidal assumptions.
arxiv-2510-01432:
Sreedharan and co-authors argue that tutoring systems get better when domain experts hand-craft the knowledge inside them. Education AI often treats expert curation as old-fashioned overhead. Two construction routes show what that curation buys instead.

Expert rules about solving problems, paired with explanation techniques, can generate lessons automatically. An expert-specified curriculum likewise lets adaptive tutors run leaner algorithms while teaching better. A case study on identifying pollinators grounds the argument in a teachable, expert-rich domain. The authors close with outreach, urging both communities to value the collaboration. Explanation methods built for debugging get promoted to lesson authors. Pollinator identification needs exactly the field marks experts know. PreK through workforce learning all stand to gain from curation. Efficient algorithms become possible when the curriculum carries structure. Resources should not drain into projects doomed by missing expert knowledge.
arxiv-2510-01632:
Wang and Oliver partition proteins into flexible substructures and name them from a learned vocabulary, so protein embeddings reflect function-bearing parts. Function lives in coherent blobs of structure, but standard models carve proteins into rigid fixed-radius neighborhoods. Their module, BioBlobs, learns the partition end to end and differentiably.

A seed-and-expand procedure grows connected regions of whatever size the function demands. Quantization maps each blob onto a shared codebook, yielding an interpretable discrete vocabulary. Plugged into standard protein encoders, the representations improved prediction across benchmarks. Mechanistic insight comes along because the vocabulary can be inspected. Three protein-property benchmarks carried the comparative evaluation. Non-overlapping blobs tile each structure exactly once by construction. GVP-based encoders supplied the backbone features being enriched. Source code is public, inviting adoption by other laboratories. Fixed neighborhoods were the quiet rigidity being dissolved.
arxiv-2510-02132:
Cruz-Cruz and Kochanek hunt for the star that exploded as the S147 remnant in this 2025 astronomy paper. The remnant holds a pulsar and a likely runaway companion star, HD 37424. Together they form the only good galactic case of a binary unbound by a core-collapse supernova. Gaia DR3 data let the authors census the stars local to the remnant.

They selected stars in a cylinder around S147 and modeled the most luminous ones individually. The companion star weighs about thirteen and a half solar masses. A neighboring single star is slightly heavier, near fourteen solar masses. Fitting the color-magnitude diagram with population models, both single-star and binary versions, dated the local population. The age distribution favors a progenitor between roughly twenty-one and forty-one solar masses. That is a heavyweight star, consistent with a violent core collapse.
arxiv-2510-02432:
Zhang and co-authors compare how exploding stars reshape a dwarf galaxy at two resolutions. Their astrophysics paper runs the same isolated galaxy in several codes. Supernova feedback regulates star formation and drives gas outflows. Fine detail shows those jobs split into distinct channels. Explosions in thin gas expand far and push outflows. Explosions in dense cradles disrupt only their local patch. The local density around each blast predicts its galaxy wide effect. Two solar-mass resolution codes, LYRA and RIGEL, anchor the study. A coarser code, SMUGGLE, supplies the contrast case.

Galaxy traits differed across the runs at first glance. Those differences traced back to physical and numerical choices. Radiation inclusion, blast energy models, and resolution explained the gaps. Matching those choices brought the runs into good agreement. Simulated galaxies prove robust when setups truly match. Resolution alone can masquerade as new physics.
arxiv-2510-02632:
Ho extends balance equations for special area measures to general three dimensional CR manifolds. His 2025 mathematics paper works in CR geometry. CR structures blend complex and contact geometry. Two special surface area measures anchor the study. Cheng introduced them for such manifolds earlier. Prior work derived their balance equations only in special cases. Constant Webster curvature and vanishing torsion were assumed. Ho removes those crutches for the general manifold. He then studies the measures on concrete model spaces. Disk bundles, the Rossi sphere, and three dimensional tori all appear.

On tori, elliptic generating curves yield clean criteria. A ratio bound guarantees a minimizing surface with zero energy. The intermediate value theorem locates that surface precisely. These tools test curved structures through their minimizers. General equations widen where the measures can be used. Model cases show the theory computing real answers.
arxiv-2510-02732:
Chen and co-authors rebuild moving 3D scenes from single videos by placing control points where motion lives. Their 2025 computer graphics paper improves dynamic Gaussian splatting. One camera view makes 3D motion deeply ambiguous. Sparse control points tame the computation involved. Older methods scatter those points by geometry alone. Static areas then hoard points while movers starve. The new framework scores motion tendency per region. Vision foundation models supply semantic and motion priors. Patch, token, and node links guide the placement. Compression concentrates points in dynamic regions.

Spline trajectories parameterize how each node travels. Optimization stays stable across the sequence. Experiments beat prior state-of-the-art reconstruction quality. Density adapts as the scene's motion demands. Film and telepresence tools need believable dynamic scenes. Smarter allocation spends detail where eyes look. The method turns a fixed budget into better motion.
arxiv-2510-02832:
Imbrogno and co-authors report strange behavior from a black hole in the Coma cluster. The black hole sits in a Seyfert galaxy known as J1257. An automated search of the Chandra archive flagged it in 2020 data. Its X-ray brightness rose and fell in a repeating pattern. Each cycle lasted roughly twenty thousand seconds. The team then checked twenty years of Chandra and XMM-Newton records.

The same pattern showed up again and again across those years. The galaxy also shifted between two clear brightness states. When brighter, its X-rays grew softer. The authors weigh two explanations for the rhythm. It may be a very slow quasi-periodic oscillation. It may instead be a train of quasi-periodic eruptions. Longer steady observations are needed to decide. Either way, J1257 joins a small set of black holes with repeating X-ray pulses.
arxiv-2510-02932:
Datta and Shah exhibit new knots that fool the classic tests of contact geometry. A contact manifold has a field of planes at each point. A Legendrian knot runs tangent to those planes everywhere. Two numbers, named tb and rot, often sort such knots fully. When they do, the knot type is called simple. Chekanov first showed that some knots are not simple. Two unlike knots can share both numbers there.

The authors work inside tight Lens spaces instead. They build fresh families of prime Legendrian and transverse knots. Their test case is the n-twist knot family. More non-isotopic Legendrians of that type live in Lens spaces than in the sphere. The botany of these knots is thus richer there. They also prove connect sum formulas for rational versions of three invariants. Those formulas mark prime knots as the right hunting ground.
arxiv-2510-03032:
de Oliveira and co-authors study the faint glow between galaxies in fossil groups. A fossil group is ruled by one giant elliptical galaxy. Its rivals merged into it long ago, theory says. The leftover starlight strewn through the group is called intracluster light. Its share can reveal how settled the system is. The team measured that share in three fossil groups.

A custom algorithm separated the faint glow from galaxy light. Shares ranged from a few percent up to about fourteen. The share rose toward redder light in two groups. That trend marks stars freed very long ago. It fits systems that are old and truly undisturbed. The third group showed no such trend. Its brightness gap also fails the fossil test now. The authors doubt that it counts as a fossil group yet. The glow itself may serve as an independent fossil test.
arxiv-2510-03332:
Kováčová, Menz, and Patel present a 2025 arXiv paper that extends optimal transport, the math of moving mass at lowest cost. Classic transport keeps mass fixed, so nothing is created or lost along the way. Real problems break that rule, as when a portfolio gains or loses value while it is rebalanced. The authors let mass scale by a factor that depends on where it starts and where it lands.

The team proves that best transport plans exist for this looser problem. They also prove a strong duality result, which ties the problem to a matching price view. In two key regimes, they show that best plans can be carried out by direct maps. For a broad family of costs, they derive a flowing, dynamic form of the problem in the classic style. The framework sits beside unbalanced and entropy based variants and gives finance and economics a cleaner tool.
arxiv-2510-03532:
Liang and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on tracking surgical robot tools with a camera under real operating conditions. Vision guided help, from overlays to automation, needs the tool's exact pose. Cable driven instruments bend and hide parts of themselves, which breaks calibration methods built for stiff, visible robots. Their framework detects two kinds of features, keypoints and shaft edges, through one shared encoding. Projection geometry then turns those detections into a pose in a single fast pass.

Training used large scale synthetic data with projective labels, sparing hand annotation. Across feature detection and pose tests, the method ran fast and reached top accuracy in hard surgical scenes, the authors report. One inference yields both feature types, which trims latency for live control loops. Reliable tool tracking is a quiet prerequisite for safer robotic surgery. It also enables skill scoring and guidance tools that watch how instruments actually move.
arxiv-2510-03832:
Simon wrote this 2025 arXiv paper in combinatorics, on the many ways to peel a point set down to nothing. Take points in the plane, no three on one line, then repeatedly remove a point from the outer hull of the rest. Each removal order is called a peeling sequence. Mathematicians ask how few such sequences a point set can have, given its size.

Earlier work set an upper bound on that minimum using a method by Dumitrescu and Tóth. Simon reuses their method but analyzes it more carefully. The sharper analysis lowers the upper bound on the growth rate of the minimum count. Some point sets must admit far fewer peeling orders than the old bound allowed. Bounds like this map out how structure limits freedom in geometric processes. The result tightens knowledge of a clean and basic counting problem in discrete geometry.
arxiv-2510-03932:
Montoison and Caillau present this 2025 arXiv paper on solving large optimal control problems on graphics processors. Optimal control asks how to steer a system, like a rocket or drone, along the best path. Big versions of these problems are slow on ordinary processors. The authors build a complete workflow in the Julia language that keeps every step on the GPU.

Continuous dynamics are first turned into sparse nonlinear programs with a modeling package. Another package compiles those programs into GPU kernels that compute objectives and derivatives in one pass. A GPU interior-point solver and a sparse linear solver then finish the job without returning to the CPU. Benchmarks on modern NVIDIA cards, including rocket and quadrotor problems, showed large speed-ups over CPU work. Faster control solvers could serve aerospace, quantum control, and biology applications.
arxiv-2510-04032:
Wang and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper benchmarking small language models for emergency department decision support. Emergency rooms are fast, crowded, and high-stakes, and big cloud models are often impractical there for cost and privacy reasons. Small models can run locally on hospital hardware, but it was unclear which ones help doctors best. The authors built a benchmark spanning medical knowledge and general problem solving.

They tested models trained on general text against counterparts fine-tuned on medical corpora. The test sets included medical exam questions and a PubMed abstract task modeled on daily physician work. Surprisingly, the general-domain small models beat the medically fine-tuned ones across the benchmarks. The authors conclude that broad reasoning ability matters more in emergency care than narrow medical specialization. Their benchmark suite gives hospitals a practical way to choose small models for local deployment.
arxiv-2510-04132:
Sobrosa and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper testing whether mean-field theory can be trusted in quasiperiodic moiré systems. Moiré materials host narrow energy bands where electron interactions and quasiperiodicity compete, producing exotic phases. Exact methods are expensive, and mean-field approximations are notoriously unreliable in one dimension. The authors build the mean-field phase diagram of a one-dimensional moiré model with multifractal critical states and check it against exact results.

In the extended regime, they find a charge density wave with exponentially suppressed amplitude, matching the exact wavevector count though missing the transition itself. In the critical regime, mean field predicts a quasifractal charge density wave with a huge number of wavevectors. Time-dependent Hartree-Fock calculations then produced excitation spectra and response functions at the random-phase level. The verdict licenses mean-field methods for two-dimensional quasiperiodic moiré systems, where exact methods cannot reach.
arxiv-2510-04332:
Divyajyoti and a team wrote this 2025 paper on waves from pairs of black holes that crash into each other. Most pairs seen move on near round paths before they merge. Some pairs may move on oval paths, a sign they formed in crowded places. Each hole's spin can tilt, make the pair wobble, and mimic oval motion.

The team made fake waves for oval pairs with no spin, lined-up spin, and tilted spin. They read those waves back with a model that assumes a round path but lets spin wobble. For strongly oval pairs, it got the chirp mass wrong and claimed wobble that was not there. A fit test still backed an oval model over the round one. So analysts need models that treat oval paths and wobbling spins at once, or their results will be biased.
arxiv-2510-04832:
Christopher Bartley and Anton Ragni wrote this 2025 paper on speech recognition for languages close to vanishing. Nearly half of the world languages are endangered, and recognition tools could help revive them. Standard systems demand hours of cut, transcribed speech that these communities rarely have. What they often do have is a spoken dictionary: recordings of words. The authors test whether that resource can seed a recognizer.

Their case study is Manx Gaelic, spoken by two thousand people. Forty minutes of dictionary style speech produced a usable system for Manx. Word error rates landed under fifty percent, rough but serviceable for archives and learners. They then repeated the recipe for Cornish, with six hundred speakers. It worked there, which suggests the method travels across languages. The barrier to entry, in amount and format of data, is far lower than assumed. That finding matters for communities that cannot fund recording projects.
arxiv-2510-05032:
Chris Heunen, Robin Kaarsgaard, and Louis Lemonnier isolate a basic ingredient of computation in this 2025 arXiv paper. Many programs contain controlled commands, which run only when a memory cell holds a certain value. A controlled NOT gate in a quantum circuit is a familiar example. Control is usually tangled up with the rest of the circuit's logic.

The authors write down eight equations that capture control on their own. Adding those equations to a base theory of circuits generates all of its controlled versions. They prove this construction matches a known category construction, the free rig category. Examples cover reversible Boolean circuits and quantum circuits. The split should make circuit optimization and completeness proofs cleaner and more modular.
arxiv-2510-05232:
Martin P. Rey and twenty-six co-authors explain a chemical oddity of the smallest galaxies in this 2025 arXiv paper. Ultra-faint dwarfs show a flat plateau of iron content at the lowest masses. Their average iron metallicity stalls near the same value instead of falling. The team studies the pattern in the new MEGATRON simulations.

The simulated dwarfs match the observed mass-metallicity relation at the present day, plateau included. They trace the plateau to the first stars' pair-instability supernovae. Strong radiation from the young protogalaxy let those explosions occur in halos massive enough to keep their ejecta. The model also predicts a tail of very iron-poor dwarfs, about a fifth of the population. Both features survive wide changes to later star-formation feedback.
arxiv-2510-05432:
Mishra and colleagues present AInstein, a 2025 framework for testing whether large language models can solve research problems. The team drew problem statements from ICLR 2025 conference papers. Each problem was stripped of its solution before testing began. Models then had to work from stored knowledge alone, with no fine-tuning, no search tools, and no outside help.

Solver agents draft answers and improve them through rounds of critique, much like peer review. The authors test on 1,214 papers and grade results for success, match with human methods, and novelty. They find that model quality drives most of the outcome. Models often invent valid approaches instead of copying the human ones. Their skill still breaks down when a problem is framed in a new way. The work gives early evidence on how far such models can go as research partners.
arxiv-2510-05532:
Sartor and Peers present a way to stretch pretrained image generators to new jobs. Diffusion models make strong starting points for graphics work, but they accept only fixed inputs. Many tasks need extra input or output channels, such as material maps for a surface. Their 2025 system, Teamwork, adds those channels without rebuilding the base model.

Teamwork runs several copies of the base model side by side, like teammates. A low-rank adapter variant links the copies, so they coordinate and adapt together. Copies can also switch on or off as a task demands. The authors show the setup on inpainting, material estimation, and image decomposition tasks. Keeping the base model frozen protects the knowledge it gained in pretraining. It also handled neural shading and image synthesis in their tests. The paper appeared at the SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 conference on computer graphics.
arxiv-2510-06032:
Gu generalizes a classic number theory problem in a 2025 mathematics paper. The Erdős distinct subset sums problem asks how small the largest number can be when every subset of a set has a different total. Gu extends the question from single integers to vectors of integers in several dimensions.

The classical approach bounds the answer by studying the variance of a random signed sum. Gu instead uses other statistical quantities, including the average absolute sum and a third-moment measure. The best choice turns out to depend on dimension in a clean pattern. A first-moment method wins in up to four dimensions, and a third-moment method wins in five and six. Beyond six dimensions the older variance method stays best, and the new bounds improve earlier low-dimensional results.
arxiv-2510-06432:
Goyal and Raizes introduce proofs of no intrusion, letting clients verify stored quantum data was never stolen in a 2025 cryptography paper. Detecting theft is classically impossible: a perfect copy leaves no evidence. Quantum mechanics forbids general duplication, reopening the question.

Their protocol lets a classical client remotely test a quantum server. Crucially, the test does not destroy the checked data. No backup copy elsewhere is needed. They construct such proofs for ciphertexts, assuming fully homomorphic encryption. They equip unclonable decryption keys and signature tokens with intrusion tests. Conceptually, almost any unclonable primitive can carry one. The core technique tests coset states non-destructively via classical communication. It is a non-destructive proof of knowledge of a measurement outcome. An intruder who probed the data would disturb it in ways the test can catch. Future quantum cloud services gain a missing burglary alarm.
arxiv-2510-06532:
Chen and eight co-authors build CLAQS, a fully quantum token mixer for text classification, in a 2025 quantum computing paper. Quantum hardware remains qubit- and depth-limited, and quantum training can be unstable. Classical attention is heavy in computation and memory. A compact quantum alternative must respect all three constraints.

CLAQS learns complex-valued mixing and nonlinear transformations in one unified circuit. L1 normalization regulates amplitude scaling, stabilizing optimization. A two-stage architecture separates shared token embeddings from a window-level quantum feed-forward module. Sliding windows with document-level aggregation handle long texts. The system needs only eight data qubits and shallow circuits. Despite that frugality, it scored above ninety-one percent on SST-2 sentiment classification. It outperformed classical Transformer baselines and strong hybrid quantum-classical models on IMDB. Compact quantum mixers are ready for real language tasks.
arxiv-2510-06632:
Yasaman Torabi, Shahram Shirani, and James Reilly improve a clustering method used on signals and images. Their 2025 paper builds on nonnegative matrix factorization, which compresses data into simple building blocks. A flexible variant uses a tunable divergence measure, but stacking it into layers can break convergence. Nobody wants an algorithm that may not settle down.

Their method, Chem-NMF, borrows an idea from chemistry. It treats the search like a reaction crossing energy barriers, guided by Boltzmann probabilities. A bounding factor, acting like a catalyst, steadies each step and reduces overshoot. The authors prove convergence results first, then test the method on real data. Clustering accuracy rose by about five point six percent on biomedical signals. It rose by about eleven percent on face images. The gains suggest the chemistry analogy is more than a metaphor for this algorithm.
arxiv-2510-06832:
Nicholas Crawford and Vesna Iršič Chenoweth study a pursuit game played on graphs. Their 2025 paper concerns Cops and Robbers, where cop pieces chase a robber across a network. The cop number counts the fewest cops that guarantee a capture. That number is known for many classic graph families, but not for partial cubes.

Partial cubes are networks that sit inside hypercubes while preserving distances. They model real structures, including some chemical resonance graphs. The authors prove a general lower bound for the cop number of partial cubes. They also give an upper bound for a subclass of these graphs. One family gets special treatment, the Fibonacci cubes. Those graphs ban consecutive ones in their binary labels. For Fibonacci cubes, the team improves both bounds substantially. Their general lower bound cannot be sharpened for the wider class of median graphs. The results narrow an open gap in pursuit games.
arxiv-2510-06932:
Grégoire Marc, a single author, builds a homotopy theory for a generalized kind of operad. The 2025 paper works in algebraic topology, where operads encode types of algebraic structure. Coloured operads allow several object types, like a ring acting on a module. Marc's version parametrizes the colours through double lax functors, widening the framework.

The main result is a model structure on the category of these generalized simplicial operads. A model structure is the formal package that lets mathematicians do homotopy theory in a category. It declares which maps count as weak equivalences, fibrations, and cofibrations. Marc verifies the package for his setting. In particular, the construction recovers a model structure for the parametrized operads of Nardin and Shah. That earlier framework lacked a homotopy theory. The new result lets researchers compare and deform these algebraic structures with tools. Foundations like this enable many computations.
arxiv-2510-07632:
Zhu, Zhang, and Tang wrote this 2025 artificial intelligence paper on compositional reasoning in multimodal models. Such models must combine objects, attributes, and relations in new arrangements. On standard benchmarks, top models often score near random chance at this skill. The authors argue that the usual scoring methods hide real ability. A model may match images and captions well as a group yet fail pairwise scoring.

They introduce a group matching score that judges the best overall matching within each group. Simply fitting to those matchings lifted scores sharply under the standard metric. One model passed all earlier results, and GPT-4.1 first beat estimated human performance on Winoground. Their Test-Time Matching method then improves models further at test time without outside supervision. It gained across sixteen dataset variants, with the largest relative gain near eighty-six percent on a hard spatial dataset.
arxiv-2510-07932:
Martorell and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on chaos in random recurrent neural networks. A classic model from Sompolinsky and coauthors shows two regimes: silence, or irregular asynchronous chaos. That model balances positive and negative couplings. The authors study a version where the balance is broken. Two extra regimes then appear beside the classic pair.

In one, each unit settles into its own stable activity level and stays there. In the other, activity stays chaotic but circles a nonzero mean, with long-lasting correlations. Using dynamical mean-field theory and heavy simulation, the authors map the full phase diagram. It mirrors the famous Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass with uncanny closeness. The onset of the synchronous-chaotic phase matches the replica-symmetry breaking point. Ergodicity breaking, the spin glass hallmark, has a direct counterpart here. The work unifies two classic models of disordered complexity.
arxiv-2510-08132:
Kawamura and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper teaching vision-language models to forget whole visual domains rather than single object classes. A self-driving system, for example, must not mistake an illustrated car on a billboard for a real one. The authors define Approximate Domain Unlearning: accuracy should collapse on a specified domain while surviving on others. Strong domain generalization entangles domains in feature space, so naive penalties fail.

Their method explicitly disentangles domain distributions and captures domain information instance by instance. Experiments on four multi-domain benchmarks showed it significantly beating strong baselines. One benchmark alone held over one hundred seventy thousand test samples across six domains. The authors present the task itself as a new research direction. Fine-grained forgetting matters for privacy and safety wherever models know more than they should.
arxiv-2510-08432:
Gregory Kahanamoku-Meyer, Seyoon Ragavan, and Katherine Van Kirk combine two tricks to cut the cost of quantum factoring in a 2025 arXiv paper. Pebble games model reversible computing, where steps must be undoable to save memory. Spooky pebbling allows measurements mid-game that leave temporary phase errors, nicknamed ghosts. Parallel pebbling runs many steps at once to save time.

The authors define parallel spooky pebble games and show the two resources multiply in power. A line graph of length l can be pebbled in exactly optimal depth using only logarithmic space. With a highly optimized A-star search written in Julia, they found low-depth schemes for concrete lengths and fixed pebble counts. Applied to Regev's factoring algorithm, the schemes slash arithmetic costs. Factoring a 4096-bit integer needs multiplication depth one hundred ninety-three, far below earlier Regev and Shor variants.
arxiv-2510-08532:
Rishubh Parihar and co-authors add a strength dial to instruction-based image editing in a 2025 arXiv paper. Text instructions tell an editor what to change, but not how much. Users often want a subtle tweak first, then a stronger effect if it looks right. Their model, Kontinuous Kontext, accepts a scalar edit strength alongside the instruction.

A lightweight projector network maps the strength value and instruction into the model's modulation space. Training data was synthesized as image, edit, instruction, and strength quadruplets using existing generative models. A filtering stage then removed low-quality or inconsistent examples. The result is smooth control from no change to a fully realized edit. One unified model handles stylization, attributes, materials, backgrounds, and shapes. No attribute-specific training is required for this fine-grained control.
arxiv-2510-08632:
Cai Zhou and co-authors build diffusion language models that generate text from coarse meaning to fine detail in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their Hierarchical Diffusion Language Models rest on a layered vocabulary. Detailed low-level tokens map onto high-level tokens with coarse meanings, many-to-one. Generation then becomes a climb down the semantic ladder, step by step.

Going forward, each token is replaced on its own by its higher-level, more abstract ancestor. The reverse process predicts progressively more detailed semantics, a next-semantic-scale prediction scheme. The authors derive closed-form formulas for the diffusion training objective, the evidence lower bound. The earlier MDLM model emerges as a special case of their framework. Practical training techniques accompany the theory. Text generation experiments showed steadily lower perplexity, both in validation and in generation, than baselines.
arxiv-2510-08732:
Florian Kranzl and co-authors measure the motion noise of a single trapped ion with spin-locking spectroscopy in a 2025 arXiv paper. Characterizing noise in quantum harmonic oscillators matters for trapped ions, superconducting circuits, and other platforms. Their motional spin-locking method reads the oscillator's noise spectrum directly. A single trapped ion served as the test oscillator in the experiment.

They measured motional noise from two hundred hertz to five kilohertz. The power spectral density resolved noise spanning two orders of magnitude in strength. Coherent modulations of the oscillation frequency could be probed with relative sensitivity at the level of one part in a million, the team reports. Such precision helps diagnose heating and control errors in ion traps. The method transfers to other harmonic oscillator platforms needing fine noise spectra.
arxiv-2510-08832:
Müller and Essick ask how many gravitational wave detections it would take to tell neutron stars from black holes by their squishiness, in this 2025 arXiv paper. As two compact objects spiral together, each one's gravity stretches the other slightly. That tidal stretching leaves a faint mark on the wave, and black holes, which do not stretch, should stand apart. In practice the mark is tiny in any single event and shrinks further for heavier objects.

The pair therefore study whole catalogs of events at once, combining many noisy tidal readings with a statistical method that respects each one's uncertainty. Their simulations show that well over two hundred events are needed before the neutron star share at each mass can be pinned down. Even ruling out that all light objects are black holes takes over a hundred. They conclude that current detectors will not manage it, but planned facilities could.
arxiv-2510-08932:
Zhang and co-authors squeeze more accuracy out of recommendation models after training is over, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Click-through rate models guess whether a user will tap an item, and they power most recommendation feeds. Nearly all research improves them during training, leaving the prediction moment itself untouched. Rare feature combinations are a weak spot there: the model has seen them too seldom to judge them confidently.

Their paradigm, MATT, works with any trained model. It scores each feature combination's trustworthiness by how often that combination occurred, using a layered hashing method to count efficiently. It then runs several prediction paths, sampling detours around low-confidence features, and averages the outcomes into a sturdier final answer. Offline experiments and live A/B tests on real traffic confirmed gains across existing models. The authors frame test time as free value left on the table by costly training runs.
arxiv-2510-09232:
Marwaha, Jorswieck, and Kryszkiewicz squeeze more energy efficiency from massive antenna arrays by letting their amplifiers distort a little, on purpose and under control, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Massive MIMO, many antennas serving users at once, delivers 5G rates at heavy energy cost. Power amplifiers are most efficient near saturation, but there they distort the signal. Earlier studies mostly ignored that distortion and assumed narrowband signals.

The authors model a wideband OFDM downlink with a soft-limiter amplifier and derive a closed-form formula for its signal-to-distortion-and-noise ratio. They define energy efficiency for two amplifier architectures, then give a low-complexity root-finding algorithm that tunes transmit power to maximize it. In simulations the scheme more than doubled efficiency over a fixed back-off baseline, under both low and high path loss. The best point shifts with antenna count, amplifier type, and propagation.
arxiv-2510-09432:
Mats Vroon and Hans Bodlaender study stable cutsets in graph theory in a 2025 arXiv paper. A stable cutset is a collection of vertices, none of them adjacent to another, whose removal splits a connected graph into separate pieces. Deciding whether such a set exists is known to be NP-complete, meaning no fast general algorithm is expected.

The authors give a new exact algorithm that branches on graph configurations and borrows a fast solver for a constraint problem. Its running time improves on what was known before. They also study graphs where every vertex has many neighbours, measured by the minimum degree. Above two thirds of the possible degree, no stable cutset can exist at all. At half density they give a polynomial-time algorithm, and for constant minimum degree they prove the problem stays NP-complete while still offering an improved exact method.
arxiv-2510-09532:
Hung Vuong and five co-authors, among them Richard Friesner, test trial wave functions for a quantum chemistry method in a 2025 arXiv paper. The method, phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo, estimates molecular energies by random sampling, and its accuracy depends on the trial wave function fed into it. Transition metal complexes are a hard test case because their electrons interact in complex ways.

The team first benchmarks ionisation energies for 22 complexes against published high-accuracy values. They then treat six metallocenes with their best protocol and with a standard configuration interaction trial. Coupled-cluster methods are compared too, along with schemes for reaching the complete basis set limit. A mid-cost protocol with a basis correction gave small deviations from experiment. The configuration interaction trial agreed most closely, with errors under two kilocalories per mole, but it scales less well to bigger systems.
arxiv-2510-09732:
P van Oerle, R H Bemthuis, and F A Bukhsh test how much process data a language model needs to explain a business process, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Process models are discovered from event logs, and models are now asked to explain them in text. Feeding large behavioural abstractions, such as directly-follows graphs or Petri nets, can prove expensive.

The authors shrink the input step by step, discovering models from smaller prefixes of one fixed log. A language model writes explanations of each model, and a second model scores them for completeness, for spotting bottlenecks, and for suggested improvements. On synthetic logs, explanation quality held up under moderate reduction, suggesting a trade-off between cost and quality. The authors stress the study is exploratory: the scores come from models, not ground truth, and the data are synthetic. Still, it points toward cheaper assisted process analysis.
arxiv-2510-09932:
Jain and co-authors present Act in this 2025 arXiv paper on compilers for tensor accelerators. Tensor compilers turn deep learning workloads into fast code, but they lean on existing CPU and GPU backends for the final code generation. New neural processing units keep appearing, each needing its own backend.

Act generates compiler backends automatically from a description of an accelerator's instruction set, its ISA. Writing such a backend by hand is slow, expert work that must be redone for every chip. Automating it shortens the path from new hardware to usable software. The authors aim to let tensor compilers target fresh accelerators quickly, instead of waiting for handcrafted support.
arxiv-2510-10232:
Xuening Wu and co-authors present SGM in this 2025 arXiv paper on safe self-modifying AI. Recursive self-modification sits inside AutoML, architecture search, and adaptive optimization, yet no framework ensures these changes are made safely. Gödel machines demand a formal proof of improvement before any rewrite, but hard proofs cannot be had in stochastic, high-dimensional settings.

SGM replaces hard proof with statistical risk control. It allows self-modification only when statistics bound the risk of harm tightly enough. The design aims to keep the spirit of the Gödel machine safeguard while working in the messy settings where modern systems actually adapt. Safe self-improvement is the paper's core concern.
arxiv-2510-10532:
Guoyun Xie and Zhichao Zhang generalize the Fourier transform for signals that live on directed graphs, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Graph signal processing studies data, such as sensor readings, that sit on network nodes. Methods for directed graphs usually rely on fixed matrices. Those rigid structures adapt poorly to complex network shapes. The team builds a more flexible tool from a unified representation matrix that can include classic choices like the Laplacian.

Using singular value decomposition, they build spectral transform pairs from left and right singular vectors. For product graphs, one variant decomposes the full combined matrix. The other decomposes each factor graph on its own, cutting computation sharply while keeping spectral strength. Tests on real datasets showed the method beating fixed matrix approaches at denoising, with gains in signal to noise ratio and bandwidth use.
arxiv-2510-10832:
Baptiste Rabecq, Thomas Lee, and Andy Sun squeeze more capacity out of power lines by letting their limits breathe with the weather, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Grids face rising renewable output and surging load from data centers and electrification, so congestion relief matters. Dynamic line rating adjusts a line's current limit with meteorological conditions. Earlier work imposed preset time varying limits. This team instead embeds the transient heat equation for conductor temperature directly into the optimization.

They derive a closed form solution of the heat equation, turning the dynamics into a finite dimensional problem. A bi level decomposition algorithm based on ADMM, with provable convergence, then solves it at scale. They run the first large scale evaluation of dynamic ratings inside multi period AC optimal power flow. On the 2,000 bus Texas grid, dynamic ratings significantly cut generation cost in congested conditions versus static ratings and ambient adjusted ratings.
arxiv-2510-11132:
The WAVES survey will use the 4MOST telescope to map galaxies over a wide area of sky, but it must first choose which galaxies to observe. G. Kaur and a large collaboration describe the target selection for the Wide subsurvey in this 2025 arXiv astronomy paper. The survey needs samples that are flux-limited and redshift-limited, yet true redshifts are only known after the telescope measures them.

Instead of estimating each galaxy's redshift, the team trains an XGBoost classifier to give the probability that a galaxy lies below the Wide limit. Trained on a spectroscopic sample with nine bands of photometry, the classifier reaches purity and completeness of about 94 to 95 percent across the tested thresholds. Applied to 14 million photometric galaxies, a chosen probability cutoff yields roughly one million target candidates. The probabilities are then combined with other approaches for the final selection.
arxiv-2510-11332:
Spaceability asks whether the points an operator misses still hide a whole endless flat space inside them. Ribeiro returns to work by Kitson and Timoney on that question in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Their setting used Banach spaces, one well known class of spaces, as the domains of the operators. A remark in their 2011 paper asked whether the same result would survive for broader spaces.

Ribeiro shows that it does survive when those domains are Fréchet spaces, a wider class than Banach spaces. He takes one central theorem from the earlier work and proves it again in this broader setting, closely following its spirit. That settles the open remark in the 2011 paper with a yes. He goes further, too. The same hidden-space effect holds for whole families of operators at once, even when the family is too large to count.
arxiv-2510-11732:
Guojian Li and five colleagues improve how computers recognize speaking style from speech. Speaking style covers traits like whether a talker sounds formal, cheerful, or commanding. Earlier systems leaned mostly on the words spoken and used acoustic cues, meaning the sound itself, only lightly. That limited their accuracy. The team's 2025 arXiv paper fuses both information streams in a dual-path design.

One path runs speech recognition first and then judges style, following the order of hearing and understanding. The second path works in parallel and mixes sound and language through a new module built to compare the two streams. Tested against the OSUM baseline model, the design cut the parameter count by nearly nine-tenths. It also raised recognition accuracy by about thirty percent across eight speaking styles. The result is a much smaller model that reads style better.
arxiv-2510-12032:
Jung-Woo Shim and three colleagues refine prompts in stages to starve AI hallucinations. Sloppy prompts, with typos, punctuation slips, misused terms, or missing context, invite plausible nonsense. Their paper, published in Pattern Recognition and posted on arXiv in 2025, introduces Multi-stage Prompt Refinement, a framework that repairs prompts error class by error class.

Each stage deploys a small language model fine-tuned for one repair job. Early stages fix surface mistakes; later stages add clarifying context. A self-reflection mechanism then ranks candidate refinements and keeps the most relevant input. On hallucination benchmarks, answers to refined prompts beat answers to the raw originals more than eighty-five percent of the time. Output accuracy rose alongside. The framework also stacks with post-hoc mitigation methods that check finished answers, so teams need not choose between prevention and cure. The authors describe MPR as lightweight and adaptable across domains.
arxiv-2510-12232:
Dransfeld and co-authors test whether carefully engineered algorithms can solve a hard pattern problem quickly on real inputs, in a 2025 arXiv computer science paper. The Dominating H Pattern problem asks for a part of a graph that matches a fixed pattern H. The chosen part must also dominate the graph, meaning every vertex sits in or next to it. Theory says major speedups on worst case inputs are unlikely without refuting a standard assumption.

The authors implement several approaches and benchmark them on a large and diverse collection of datasets. Baselines include the Glasgow Subgraph Solver, the SAT solver Kissat, and the integer programming solver Gurobi. A direct implementation of the near optimal worst case algorithm merely matched existing solvers. Their tailored branch and bound method, with careful pruning, did far better, reaching gains of up to two orders of magnitude for the test instances.
arxiv-2510-12632:
Lamsahel, El Akri, and Ratnani analyze how reshaping a domain shifts the computed vibration frequencies in an isogeometric simulation, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Isogeometric analysis solves engineering problems using the same spline functions that describe the geometry. For the one dimensional Laplace eigenvalue problem with fixed endpoints, the eigenvalues are the natural frequencies of the system.

Using the theory of generalized locally Toeplitz sequences, the authors study the Galerkin scheme when the domain is reshaped. The same interval is stretched by a smooth change of variables. Under suitable assumptions on that map, they prove a structured pattern emerges in the spread of the discrete frequencies, readable from a symbol analysis. They also establish a uniform discrete version of Weyl's law, the classical count of how many frequencies lie below a threshold. Further estimates follow from the symbol's nearly linear behavior near zero, refining and building on earlier results.
arxiv-2510-12732:
Foley and colleagues teach a fuzzer to aim its mutations at the parts of a JavaScript program most likely to expose engine bugs, in a 2025 arXiv computer security paper. Fuzzing feeds mutated inputs to software to find crashes and vulnerabilities, and JavaScript engines, embedded in browsers and servers, are prime targets. Existing fuzzers choose mutation locations randomly, wasting effort.

Their system, Clutch, frames target selection as a combinatorial bandit problem with a changing number of arms. An attention based deep model reads variable length test case representations to decide where to mutate, and a dropout technique lets it adapt its exploration dynamically. Against three leading fuzzers, Clutch increased the number of valid test cases and the coverage achieved per test case by clear average margins. In volatile and combinatorial bandit benchmarks it also achieved greatly lower regret than leading bandit algorithms, supporting the claim that learned aim beats random mutation.
arxiv-2510-12832:
Brash and colleagues tackle a data gap for low-voltage power networks in this 2025 arXiv paper. Operators planning local grids need realistic demand scenarios, but they rarely see actual flows at the substation level, and standard typical profiles oversimplify how demand behaves. Synthetic profiles often look plausible one by one yet miss how substations rise and fall together.

The team built a conditional diffusion model, a generative method that builds samples by gradually removing noise under given conditions, to synthesize daily active and reactive power profiles. They judged the output by statistical and timing realism and by full power flow modeling of a wider network. The generated profiles proved plausible both individually and as a group, and the model beat naive and leading alternatives at producing coherent scenarios for planning studies.
arxiv-2510-12932:
Stevenson, Möller, and Powell plan how to spot kilonovae with the new Rubin Observatory in this 2025 arXiv paper. A kilonova is the glowing explosion from merging neutron stars, seen together with gravitational waves only once so far. Rubin's wide surveys may catch such events by chance, and those optical sightings could trigger a deep, targeted gravitational-wave search instead of waiting for the reverse.

The authors simulated kilonova light curves for Rubin's first year under its latest observing strategy. At an assumed cosmic rate, alert brokers should see roughly four kilonovae per year bright enough to matter within the gravitational-wave detectors' horizon. Most of them are faint and found a day or two after merger. Using archival survey data they also estimated contamination from other transients at dozens of events per month even under strict selection, so follow-up will demand large telescopes.
arxiv-2510-13032:
Polish and the BICEP collaboration describe an improved absolute polarization calibrator for cosmic microwave background telescopes in this 2025 arXiv paper. Cosmic birefringence is a hypothesized breaking of parity in electromagnetism. It would rotate the polarization of ancient light as it travels. But that rotation looks the same as an error in the instrument's own angle. Only an absolute calibration can separate the two. The source itself rotates during the tests.

The team calibrated the BICEP3 telescope, a ninety-five gigahertz polarimeter hunting for signatures of cosmic inflation. They watched a rotating polarized source with both the telescope and a small test receiver built for exact angle checks. The paper covers recent hardware upgrades and progress on the systematic errors that limited the source before. Their target precision is a few hundredths of a degree. That is fine enough to turn BICEP3 into a sensitive probe of birefringence.
arxiv-2510-13132:
Luo and colleagues select clients for federated learning at the network edge in this 2025 arXiv paper. In mobile edge computing, many devices train shared models without sending data away. But when tasks depend on each other and clients hold different data, choosing which clients participate in each round strongly affects total completion time.

Their framework, CoDa-FL, clusters clients by the Earth Mover's Distance between their local data distributions. That is a measure of how much work it takes to reshape one distribution into another. This lowers computation and communication costs. They derive an explicit relationship between within-cluster distance and the training rounds needed for convergence, simplifying the search for an optimal selection. A directed acyclic graph scheduler manages task dependencies. Numerical experiments showed faster convergence, lower costs, and higher accuracy than existing benchmarks under heterogeneous edge settings.
arxiv-2510-13232:
Kang and co-authors tackle negation failures in vision-language models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such models suffer from affirmative bias, a critical failure in understanding negation. The problem is especially severe in described object detection. They offer two contributions: a dataset and a recipe.

First, they introduce CoVAND, a dataset built with a chain-of-thought and question-answering pipeline that generates high-quality, instance-grounded negation data. Second, they propose NegToMe, a text token merging module that tackles the architectural cause of the bias. It groups negation cues with attributes into coherent phrases, so a phrase like not girl stays distinct from girl alone. Combined with a parameter-efficient LoRA fine-tuning approach, the method significantly improved performance on challenging negation benchmarks. It lowered the false positive rate and boosted NMS-AP by up to 10.8 points on OVDEval, generalizing to leading vision-language models.
arxiv-2510-13432:
Han and co-authors propose CoDS, a method that lets self-driving vehicles share perception despite using different sensors stacks. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies collaborative perception, where nearby vehicles pool what they detect. Most methods assume every vehicle runs the same encoder, which real fleets violate. Aligning features to the host vehicle alone lets domain gaps inject noise.

CoDS attacks the mismatch through domain separation rather than plain alignment. A lightweight resizer first matches neighbour features across space and channel dimensions. A second module then splits features into encoder-specific parts to discard and shared parts to keep. A mutual information loss during training pushes the aligned features to agree. The whole design stays fully convolutional, which keeps inference fast on mobile hardware. Experiments show CoDS eases feature discrepancies and balances detection accuracy against speed well.
arxiv-2510-13632:
Cuervo and co-authors close the understanding gap between text and speech versions of language models. Their 2025 arXiv paper names the problem: speech-adapted models lag their text twins on understanding tasks. They even trail simple pipelines that transcribe speech first. Rival fixes need huge synthetic speech corpora or private datasets nobody can reproduce.

Their analysis blames two causes: forgetting of text skill during adaptation, and misalignment between speech and text. Their method, SALAD, pairs cross-modal distillation with actively chosen synthetic data. Distillation transfers knowledge from the text model into the speech model. Active selection spends the small data budget where it helps most. Applied to three- and seven-billion-parameter models, SALAD matched a strong open model across knowledge and reasoning benchmarks. It trained on over ten times less public speech data than rivals.
arxiv-2510-13732:
Khan, Karthik, and Agnihotri design pilot assignment schemes that cut channel estimation error in distributed massive MIMO. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles pilot contamination, where users sharing the same pilot signal corrupt each other's estimates. Cell-free networks spread many access points around users. Too few orthogonal pilots exist for every user to have a unique one.

Their first scheme works centrally but stays light: it assigns pilots one user at a time. Each choice minimizes the total estimation error across the access points serving everyone. The second scheme is fully distributed and needs no global coordination. Access points use local information only, offering candidate pilots ranked by priority. Each user then picks from its offers, keeping assignments consistent across the network. Simulations beat current state-of-the-art schemes on network throughput, the authors report. Signalling overhead stays low and the method adapts as users move.
arxiv-2510-13832:
Choi, Son, Kim, and Kim prune transformer attention heads using a score that fuses gradient importance with attention entropy. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses the cost of running models with many layers and heads. Gradient-based importance scores alone miss how diverse each head's attention pattern is. A head can look unimportant yet carry unique information.

Their criterion, HIES, combines both signals into one per-head verdict. Pruning by HIES improved model quality by up to 15.2 percent over importance-only pruning in their experiments while more than doubling stability across runs, the authors report. Stability matters because erratic pruning choices make compressed models unpredictable. The method enables substantial compression without sacrificing accuracy, they conclude. Head pruning stays attractive for its simplicity and interpretability among compression options. Code is promised on publication of the work.
arxiv-2510-13932:
Henrik Podéus and colleagues introduce a software toolbox for simulating complex systems that change over time, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their target is hierarchical biological systems, where models at several levels, from organs to whole bodies, must connect and react to inputs such as timed drug doses. Existing Python tools, they argue, handle modular model building and time-dependent inputs poorly.

The toolbox, called SUND, lets users define models with inputs and outputs that plug into each other, so large systems are assembled from smaller reusable parts. It supports time-dependent functions and piecewise constant inputs, which suit dosing experiments. The team demonstrates SUND on a multi-level human glucose-insulin model spanning several time scales and levels of detail. SUND is open source and released through PyPI and GitLab.
arxiv-2510-14032:
Xiaoqian Shen and co-authors present Vgent, a framework that helps video-language models understand and answer questions about long videos, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Long videos overwhelm these models: the number of video tokens exceeds their context window, and long-term order information gets lost. Retrieval-augmented generation, fetching relevant clips before answering, helps but can scramble time order and pull irrelevant material.

Vgent adds two innovations. It represents the video as a structured graph, preserving semantic relationships between clips so retrieval respects content and sequence. It also inserts a reasoning step that uses structured verification to filter retrieval noise and gather relevant information across clips before answering. Evaluated with several open-source video models on three long-video benchmarks, Vgent improved base model performance by three to five percent on one major benchmark. It beat state-of-the-art video retrieval methods by a wider margin.
arxiv-2510-14132:
Rae Corrigan Grove and co-authors extend shadow molecular dynamics, an efficient simulation technique for atomic models with charges, to models that carry dipoles, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Molecular dynamics simulates how atoms move under forces. Polarizable models, where each atom's charge distribution responds to its surroundings, are accurate but expensive. Their charges must be re-solved over and over.

Shadow dynamics avoids that cost by treating the charges as dynamical variables that evolve with the atoms, guided by a shadow energy function. They derive the shadow energies, potentials, and forces for interactions among monopoles and dipoles, the next level of detail, and treat both as dynamical variables. They show the dipole freedom preserves the stability and accuracy seen in monopole-only versions. They also present a variant holding monopoles fixed while dipoles stay flexible. It aims at efficient simulations for machine-learned force fields.
arxiv-2510-14232:
Mehrzad Samadi and co-authors present GenCluster, a framework that won a gold-medal-level score at the International Olympiad in Informatics using an open-weight language model, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Competitive programming is a hard test of reasoning, and proprietary models had reached IOI gold before, but with undisclosed methods; matching them openly remained a challenge.

GenCluster scales test-time compute, the effort spent while answering. It combines solution generation with behavioral clustering, which groups candidate programs by how they behave. Ranking and a round-robin submission strategy follow, all tuned to explore solution spaces under a limited validation budget. Experiments show performance scales with available compute, narrowing the gap between open and closed systems. GenCluster achieved a gold medal at IOI 2025 with the open-weight gpt-oss-120b model, which the authors present as a new benchmark for open evaluation of programming ability.
arxiv-2510-14432:
Kaushik Bal and Shilpa Gupta prove that a class of elliptic and parabolic equations driven by an anisotropic p(u)-Laplacian admits weak solutions, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In these equations the diffusion rate depends on the solution itself and varies by direction. The work needs variable-exponent Sobolev spaces tailored to the setting. Standard results do not apply here.

For the elliptic, steady-state case, the authors show a weak solution exists, using the theory of pseudomonotone operators together with approximation techniques. In the parabolic, time-dependent setting, they obtain a weak solution through a time-stepping scheme combined with the Schauder fixed-point theorem. A priori estimates then yield a limit. The paper extends the footing of diffusion models used for non-Newtonian fluids and image repair.
arxiv-2510-14932:
Sarker and Ndao demonstrate, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a nanostructure whose optical resonance can be tuned in both directions, toward redder and toward bluer light, within one device. Tuning plasmonic resonances, the collective electron oscillations that give metal nanostructures their colors, is central to adjustable optical devices. Getting both redshifts and blueshifts from a single structure had remained elusive.

Their platform is an array of metal-dielectric-metal nanodisks, where a disk couples to its own mirror image in the metal beneath, oriented anti-parallel. The resonance wavelength follows the plasmon ruler relation as dimensions change. The headline result is a record blueshift: changing the nanodisk thickness by only five to ten nanometers shifted the resonance by 457.82 nanometers in the reported measurement, the largest blueshift response shown in a plasmonic architecture. With tunable resonances spanning a wide near-infrared range, the authors target sensing, optical communications, and dynamic displays.
arxiv-2510-15132:
Alex Shtoff offers a simple statistical tool for estimating how likely each outcome is when the list of possible outcomes is huge. His 2025 arXiv paper studies probability mass functions over large supports, where raw sample counts are noisy and the true pattern often has several peaks and a long heavy tail. Smoothing helps, but it can blur key peaks.

Shtoff treats the raw frequency counts as a signal on a line graph. He passes it through a data-driven low-pass filter built from a special matrix tied to the counts. Projecting onto a few of its smoothest directions keeps the broad shape while damping noise, and a short cleanup step restores a valid distribution. The method runs fast and needs little tuning, thanks to an automatic rule for its one main setting. It beat common rivals on heavy-tailed tests, though it can stumble at sharp jumps.
arxiv-2510-15232:
Tiansheng Hu and colleagues from NYU Shanghai, Yale, and partner institutions ask whether language models can be trusted with money questions. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces FinTrust, a benchmark that grades models on trustworthiness in finance, where wrong or unsafe answers carry real risk. The tasks are fine-grained and grounded in practical situations, spanning safety, fairness, and legal duties.

The team assessed eleven models on the benchmark. Proprietary systems such as o4-mini led on most tasks, including safety, while the open model DeepSeek-V3 did better in spots such as industry-level fairness. Every model fell short on the hardest duties, notably fiduciary alignment, acting in a client's best interest, and disclosure, revealing a broad gap in legal awareness. Hu and colleagues offer FinTrust as a yardstick for anyone weighing whether a model is ready for real financial work.
arxiv-2510-15332:
Shamil Asgarli, Dragos Ghioca, and Chi Hoi Yip construct special point sets in finite projective planes, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A blocking set is a set of points that meets every line in the plane. A question from Erdős asked for such sets that meet each line only a few times, which makes them small and hard to build.

Earlier authors built blocking sets by taking unions of algebraic curves. Asgarli and colleagues extend that idea using unions of geometrically irreducible curves, all of one fixed degree. They give new constructions of blocking sets from such unions. They also prove lower bounds on how many curves of that degree any such construction must use. The proofs mix tools from arithmetic geometry, which studies number-theoretic properties of shapes, with combinatorics. Their results sharpen what is known about how cheaply a blocking set can be assembled from curves.
arxiv-2510-16132:
Phalguni Nanda and Zaiwei Chen give the first time-bounded analysis of Q-learning when the learner's own policy keeps changing. Q-learning is a classic method where an agent learns the value of each move from rewards. The worlds it trains in are modeled as Markov decision processes. Most proofs assume fixed sampling rules or heavy exploration, which real on-policy learning does not have.

Under one mild assumption, that some policy can reach every state, they prove the learned values settle near the best ones. The number of samples needed matches the known rate for off-policy learning, though exploration terms cost more. They also bound how good the changing policy itself becomes over time. Their key tool splits the noise from the shifting policy using a Poisson equation, a helper equation from probability theory. That trick may aid other changing-policy methods too.
arxiv-2510-16432:
Zahra Mobini leads five co-authors in a 2025 study on wireless nets with no fixed cell towers. In a cell-free net, many small access points serve users at once. Links back to the core net are thin, so points must work in clusters. Each cluster shares what it knows about the air channels near it.

The team frames two design tasks to lift total data rate in each cluster. One runs fast and sets beams, user links, and power at once. One runs slow and sets links and power on long-term trends. A known maths method, reshaped for the task, solves both hard tasks. Local data only keeps the design lean and fit for real nets.
arxiv-2510-16532:
Ziyong Wu, Renyue Cen, and Romain Teyssier ask how fast giant black holes could grow in a 2025 study. The early cosmos, at the epoch of reionization, holds quasars with huge black holes. Reionization is when first stars and quasars lit up the young cosmos. Their sims show a brief phase of growth past the Eddington cap. That cap is the top feed rate where light push balances pull.

Once a hole hits ten thousand to a hundred thousand sun masses, self-feedback slows it. By a set early age, the jump-start lead is gone. A steady feed at the cap grows holes fastest in the long run. Huge early quasars then need seed holes of that same mass range.
arxiv-2510-16932:
Emily Xiao and five co-authors shrink the cost of teaching chatbots in a 2025 paper. Showing a model many examples works, but long prompts cost money. Their goal is replacing examples with one compact instruction. The instruction should still guide the model just as well.

Their framework, Prompt-MII, learns to write such instructions for new datasets. It trains with feedback scores across thousands of classification datasets. At test time it produces a short prompt on the fly. Quality rose several points on ninety unseen tasks. At the same time, token use fell by a large factor. The method matters wherever models must adapt quickly and cheaply.
arxiv-2510-17032:
Zara Osborn and five co-authors recalculate what dying stars return to space in a 2025 paper. The stars are asymptotic giant branch stars, swollen old stars shedding material. At low metal content, they supply much nitrogen, lead, and dust. Most earlier yield tables treated these stars as single.

The team simulated whole populations of paired stars instead. Their code follows mergers and mass transfers between partners. Paired populations produced far fewer pulsing giant stars than single ones. Ejected carbon fell by about forty percent. Elements built by slow neutron capture fell similarly. Nitrogen totals stayed uncertain because wind loss rates vary. The work warns that chemical histories built on single stars overstate several elements.
arxiv-2510-17132:
Ioannis Tsaknakis and seven co-authors test whether chat models can learn hidden user tastes in this 2025 paper. Users rarely state all they want, say in food picks or trip plans. Key tastes stay unspoken and must be drawn out through talk. The authors build tests to grade that skill in a fair way.

Their tests span a twenty-questions game and two tasks with personal answers. Three roles, user, helper, and judge, score each turn of talk. Scores range from about one third to near full marks by task. Hard tasks, topics, and more hidden traits all change the score. The work shows taste learning is still an open gap for chat tools.
arxiv-2510-17232:
