Jinyu Hu and Chen Wu refine half-life guesses for alpha decay in this 2025 paper. Alpha decay sheds a helium core from a heavy nucleus over time. The authors use a two-wall view of the shed path. They let the core's mass shift with place along that path.

Tests on one hundred ninety-six even nuclei show the shift lifts guess truth. The team then runs the model on cores with one hundred eighteen and one hundred twenty protons. Runs with three mass models point to shell marks at set neutron counts. One mass model shows both marks, while the others show one. The work aids hunts for new super-heavy nuclei and their shells.
arxiv-2510-17532:
Raghu Vamshi Hemadri, with Geetha Krishna Guruju and two co-authors, trains cancer outcome models in a 2025 arXiv paper. Doctors need models that predict survival and also explain their reasoning in plain clinical terms. The team built one system that learns three tasks at once from a large cancer dataset. It classifies survival, estimates survival time, and writes a short rationale for each call.

Three training styles were compared on two model backbones. Step by step prompting lifted accuracy and cut time errors. A reward based method that favors expert like reasoning scored best on both prediction and explanation quality. The work shows that teaching models to reason openly can make cancer predictions more trustworthy.
arxiv-2510-17632: Jean Gasnier constructs record setting curves over small finite fields in a 2025 arXiv paper. A finite field is a number system with finitely many elements. A curve over it has a set of points that can be counted. Gasnier builds new curves with more points than any previously known for fields with four, nine, sixteen, and twenty five elements. Each new curve is built as an unramified abelian cover of a known curve. Such a cover has no branching, and its symmetry group commutes.
arxiv-2510-17732:
Javier Parcet surveys fifteen years of work on Schur multipliers. These are basic linear maps that act on matrix algebras. They connect closely with Fourier multipliers, a core tool in harmonic analysis. That link bridges harmonic analysis and operator algebras, two major fields.

Parcet highlights new bounds for Schatten classes, which measure operator size. Those bounds feed results on group algebras and operator rigidity. Rigidity means some algebraic structures cannot bend into different shapes. He also covers non-Toeplitz multipliers and links to singular operators. The survey began as his invited talk for a major congress.
arxiv-2510-17832:
Henrique de Lima Alexandre and Clodoaldo Aparecido de Moraes Lima create synthetic brain signals for motor imagery tasks. Electroencephalography records brain activity through scalp sensors without surgery. Motor imagery means imagining a movement, which brain-computer interfaces can decode. Real recordings are costly, slow to gather, and vary across people.

Their method trains a diffusion model to rebuild signal channels from noise. Diffusion models learn to turn random noise into realistic data. The team preprocessed real recordings before training the generator. Classifiers then judged the synthetic signals on real task benchmarks. Synthetic data scored above ninety-five percent accuracy and matched real signals closely.
arxiv-2510-17932:
Jiahao Tang, with ten co-authors, tests whether multimodal models can turn charts into working code. Their Chart2Code benchmark is built from real user needs and grows harder in three steps. First a model copies a chart from a picture, then it edits one, and finally it builds a chart from a long dense table.

The set holds just over two thousand tasks across twenty-two chart types. Scoring checks both code correctness and how the drawn chart looks. Results show where today's models break as tasks move from copying to real design work, giving chart tool makers a clear target list.
arxiv-2510-18032:
Zhenyu Bi, with six co-authors, improves multi-agent reasoning by training the talk between agents, not just the agents. Groups of language models often use fixed debate layouts or plain voting, which can silence a correct but outnumbered agent. Their OPTAGENT method builds and reshapes the collaboration graph as work proceeds.

Verbal feedback scores how well agents communicate, and the structure adapts to that signal. Debate quality, the authors argue, is a real driver of the final answer in math and science tasks. Readers who design agent teams get a method that treats conversation itself as the thing worth optimizing.
arxiv-2510-18232:
Yuzheng Hu, with Ryan McKenna and five co-authors, addresses private synthetic text in a 2025 paper. Synthetic text means computer-written text made to stand in for real user text. Differential privacy, meaning a formal promise that one person barely affects the output, should protect users during that process.

Their system first learns key features, then writes new text conditioned on those features. A second step, Anchored RL, uses reinforcement learning, meaning learning from reward scores, while staying close to good examples. That pairing limits reward hacking, where a model games the score instead of improving. Tests show better text quality and stronger control under privacy limits.
arxiv-2510-18632:
Zhangquan Chen and his ten co-authors give vision-language models a way to imagine three-dimensional space while they reason. Models that see only a few flat views struggle with spatial questions, and earlier fixes relied on text maps or two-dimensional clues with limited power. Their framework, 3DThinker, builds an inner three-dimensional picture during reasoning, without receiving any three-dimensional input and without training on labeled three-dimensional data.

Training runs in two stages. First, supervised learning aligns the model's inner three-dimensional representation with the output of a dedicated three-dimensional foundation model. Then the whole reasoning path is refined using only outcome signals, rewarding final answers rather than steps. Across several benchmarks, 3DThinker consistently beat strong baselines, and the authors present it as a route toward unifying three-dimensional representations with general multimodal reasoning.
arxiv-2510-18732:
Matteo Grotti and his four co-authors review neutral atom quantum computers. They ask what these machines can actually do today. Single atoms held in place serve as qubits. Interactions between excited atoms provide the operations. The platform draws growing interest. Its scalability is one reason. Flexible qubit connections are another. It also fits combinatorial optimization problems naturally.

The authors first cover recent hardware progress. They cover ways to map problems onto the atom register. Good mapping raises fidelity and performance. Next they survey use as quantum simulators. Hard problems such as maximum independent set are covered. Many-body physics and molecules for chemistry and drug research follow. Uses that enhance machine learning are reviewed too. The aim is a realistic snapshot of a fast-moving platform.
arxiv-2510-19032:
Abeer Badawi and eight co-authors ask when large language models can be trusted in mental health support, and build large benchmarks to answer it. Judging such models is hard because therapeutic dialogue is emotionally and cognitively complex, and older benchmarks were small or built from synthetic and social media data.

One benchmark gathers ten thousand real-scenario conversations, each with nine model responses, for one hundred thousand pairs. A second compares four strong model judges against human experts across seventy thousand ratings. Together they test both response quality and whether automated judging itself can be trusted.
arxiv-2510-19732:
Gunshi Gupta and four co-authors propose Memo, a transformer architecture that gives embodied agents a working memory without blowing past context limits. Agents acting over long periods drown in visual input, most of it irrelevant, while a transformer's context window fills quickly. Memo teaches the model to compress its experience as it goes.

During training, periodic summarization tokens are interleaved with the inputs, so the model learns to write and later retrieve compact memory summaries. On a gridworld meta-learning benchmark and a photo-realistic indoor navigation task, Memo beat plain long-context transformer baselines while using less compute and storage. It also handled longer contexts at test time and stayed robust when old history had to be truncated.
arxiv-2510-19832:
Ovishake Sen and eight co-authors build a portable brain-computer interface that reads imagined handwriting from scalp EEG and decodes it in real time. Imagined handwriting is a natural route to speech for people with severe motor or speech impairments. But EEG taken from the scalp is noisy and blurry next to implanted electrodes. The team recorded thirty-two channels from fifteen people, cleaned the signals, and pulled out eighty-five features of several kinds.

Their hybrid network, EEdGeNet, pairs a temporal convolutional network with a perceptron over those features. Running on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 edge device, it reached about ninety percent accuracy at under a second per character. Keeping only the ten best features cut the delay to about two hundred milliseconds, with under one percent of accuracy lost.
arxiv-2510-20232:
Khai-Hoan Nguyen-Dang and Nguyen Thai Hung study when a pure number field is alpha-monogenic, asking when the natural order generated by a root equals the full ring of integers of the field. They consider fields built from a root of a polynomial where an integer is raised to a fixed power, assumed irreducible. A short proof using only Dedekind index criterion settles the exact condition.

The order is the full ring exactly when the integer parameter is square-free and an extra valuation condition holds at each prime dividing the degree. The authors then compute the natural density of good parameters in the family, refine the count by arithmetic progressions, and give counts ordered by discriminant for the corresponding fields.
arxiv-2510-20332:
Anna Arias-Duart, Maria Eugenia Cardello, and Atia Cortés examine how data practices during collection shape fairness in artificial intelligence systems for healthcare. Drawing on the AI4HealthyAging project in Spain, their task was to detect bias while clinical data were being gathered for real use cases. They find that biased collection remains a major barrier to clinical adoption.

The authors identify historical, representation, and measurement biases across several cases, showing up in variables such as sex, gender, age, habitat, socioeconomic status, equipment, and labeling. They close with practical recommendations for fairer, more robust clinical problem design and data collection. Their experience is offered as guidance for future projects building healthcare AI systems.
arxiv-2510-20732:
Pier Roberto Pastorino, working alone, classifies special Fano varieties whose Lefschetz defect equals two, focusing on those built by the Casagrande Druel construction. The defect measures how much extra geometric information a variety carries, and cases above two were already understood.

Among nineteen families of Fano three folds with defect two from the Mori Mukai list, fifteen arise from the main construction studied. Pastorino also builds all Fano four folds with Picard number above three and defect two that admit the structure, reaching one hundred forty seven distinct families and completing that classification. A widened construction covers eighteen of the nineteen three fold families, broadening the account further.
arxiv-2510-20932:
Reza Ahmari leads seven co-authors on an experimental study of Trojan attacks against drone navigation models used for autonomous landing in city air travel. A Trojan hides a trigger in training data so the model fails on cue while behaving normally otherwise.

Using the DroNet steering framework, the team plants triggers and measures landing guidance accuracy on clean and triggered inputs. Accuracy falls sharply, from the mid nineties to the low seventies in percent terms, once the trigger appears. The drop shows a concrete safety risk for urban air vehicles and motivates screening of training data and models before deployment in passenger settings.
arxiv-2510-21132:
Tatsuki Murakami leads three co-authors on centi-combs, low noise soliton frequency combs with sub gigahertz repetition rates from crystalline magnesium fluoride resonators. Standard microresonator combs repeat too fast for direct electronic sampling, while mode locked lasers are bulky, leaving a gap in the middle.

Single soliton states are observed at several rates below and above one gigahertz under continuous wave laser drive. Phase noise at the near gigahertz rate beats state of the art microwave generators at the stated offset. These combs bridge lasers and microcombs for real time sampling and optical to microwave conversion in compact instruments.
arxiv-2510-21532:
Mojtaba Nafez and five co-authors harden video anomaly detectors against adversarial attacks. These detectors learn from whole-video labels only, yet must flag the guilty frames, and that weak supervision starves standard defenses. That is because attacks built at the video level arrive too feeble to train against.

Labels the model predicts for itself could enable frame-level defense training, but they are noisy enough to wreck performance. Their answer fabricates clean fake anomalies: a method called Spatiotemporal Region Distortion applies severe distortions to small regions of normal videos while keeping time flow consistent, producing exactly labeled abnormal clips. Mixed with the noisy self-labels, the fakes cut label noise sharply and make adversarial training work. Across benchmarks, robustness jumps well past rival methods on the standard detection score.
arxiv-2510-21632:
Wonki Lee and six co-authors mine giant cosmological simulations for double radio relics, twin glowing arcs that bracket a merging galaxy cluster. These rare features trace the shock waves of the collision and record the merger's history, but real examples are only now growing numerous enough for statistics.

In the TNG-Cluster and TNG300 simulations, pairs show a wide spread of brightness ratios, matching observations. The two arcs in a pair often differ sharply in shock strength and magnetic field, so no single cause explains why one outshines the other. Pairs do hug the collision axis, typically within about thirty degrees, and their separation clocks the time since impact to within roughly two hundred million years. The team predicts smaller clusters will dominate the double relic harvest of upcoming surveys like the Square Kilometre Array.
arxiv-2510-21932:
Sophie Y. Lee, Philipp W. A. Schönhöfer, and Sharon C. Glotzer simulate a tiny swimmer with no brain and no steering wheel: a soft bubble-like vesicle filled with self-propelled rods. Left alone, the rods cluster and line up, pushing the flexible container around and bending its shape as they go.

In the simulations, these composite swimmers, called flexicles, react to their surroundings in surprisingly capable ways. Meeting a wall or obstacle makes the rods re-aim, producing crawling, corner-seeking, wall climbing, and latching onto objects. The rods even split spontaneously into temporary roles, some anchoring while others navigate, and that division of labor steers the whole body. The authors offer flexicles as a programmable platform for microrobots that work through simple physics rather than onboard control.
arxiv-2510-22032:
Jair Koiller writes about a rolling puzzle: a convex body rolling on a flat plane without slipping or twisting, like a rubber ball that also refuses to spin in place. Such rubber rolling under gravity forms a classic nonholonomic system, one whose constraints involve motion itself. For bodies shaped as surfaces of revolution the problem collapses onto a sphere of special vectors.

Koiller revisits an observation by Borisov, Mamaev, and Bizyaev that this revolution case is unusually kind. Its extra conserved quantity has a simple elementary form, unlike ordinary marble rolling, where no such simple integral exists. He connects their finding to newer work showing that reduced systems of this Chaplygin type carry a conformally symplectic structure, a geometric frame that explains why the special case behaves so well.
arxiv-2510-22132:
Xuying Li steers the reasoning of a large language model with learnable thought vectors, internal signals that modulate how the model thinks through a math problem. Rather than prompting from outside, the method tunes these vectors from within, using entropy, a measure of spread in the model's own uncertainty, as the guide. Lower entropy earns reward, encouraging focused reasoning without any external labels.

Tested with the Gemma-2-9B model on the GSM8K grade-school math benchmark, Li reports accuracy just above ninety percent together with a measured controllability score. Finds the thought vectors settle into distinct clusters with consistently tight entropy across control conditions. The work is presented as evidence that a model's reasoning style can be made adjustable through its own internal signals.
arxiv-2510-22232:
Daisuke Hirota explains why cooperative systems stay stuck at mediocre outcomes. The villain is a rational adversary. Its payoff is the gap between the ideal outcome and the actual one. It profits precisely from keeping things fragile. The paper builds a game-theoretic theory of that stagnation. The Prisoner's Dilemma is the starting point.

Blending each player's payoff with a share of the other's creates a fragile cooperation band. Inside the band, mutual cooperation and mutual defection are both stable. A dynamic version adds fluctuating rewards and intervention costs. It sorts behavior into three regimes: immediate destruction, rational stagnation, and abandonment of intervention. An appendix generalizes the payoff and proves stability under reference shifts. Social media algorithms and political trust illustrate the trap.
arxiv-2510-22332:
Mengyu Ye, Jun Suzuki, Tatsuro Inaba, and Tatsuki Kuribayashi ask whether the costly machinery of sparse autoencoders is needed to read a language model's mind. Interpretability research has lately meant training proxy modules, especially sparse autoencoders, to surface clean features, then grading the features. Surprisingly few studies check whether the model's own stored features are already just as readable.

Viewing the feed-forward layers as key-value memories, the team grades the vectors stored there against the autoencoder's features on modern interpretability benchmarks. The verdict is close: the two sit in a similar range, with the autoencoder ahead only minimally in some respects and, in others, the plain feed-forward features surprisingly ahead. The comparison reframes a research fashion: before adding a proxy, measure what the original parameters already explain.
arxiv-2510-22632:
Animated characters should react to obstacles and nearby people, not just follow a preset path. Jose Luis Ponton, Sheldon Andrews, Carlos Andujar, and Nuria Pelechano present Environment-aware Motion Matching in 2025, a real time system for full body character animation.

Earlier motion matching chose motion capture clips by target path, but handled surroundings poorly. Their system extracts shape, pose, and trajectory features from a capture database beforehand. During play, it searches for clips matching user input and current pose while penalizing collisions. Pose and trajectory influence each other both ways, aiming to keep body motion and root movement consistent in crowds.
arxiv-2510-22732:
Web agents based on large language models often fail on new sites. They also take long, wasteful action paths. Jiali Cheng leads a team with nine co-authors. In 2025 they present WebATLAS, an agent that learns from past web tasks.

The agent builds a map of a site by exploring with curiosity. It stores past outcomes as memory. Before it acts, it tests options in a mental rollout. A planner, a simulator, and a critic judge each option. This helps it avoid old mistakes. On a web task test, it reached a success rate well above the prior best mark.
arxiv-2510-22832:
A small reasoning model may adapt its effort to task difficulty. Long H Dang and David Rawlinson extend that model in 2025. The base model is the Hierarchical Reasoning Model. It had only faced static, supervised tasks. Real tasks are dynamic and partly hidden.

Their variant is called HRM-Agent. It trains with reinforcement learning only. Reinforcement learning learns from rewards, not labels. The agent navigates mazes that change over time. Goals must be reached under uncertainty. The team probes its recurrent inference process. Evidence suggests it reuses past computation. That reuse spans earlier time steps. Such reuse suits real world sequential problems.
arxiv-2510-23332:
Ruyi Teng, Dan Wang, Wei Chen, and Yulong Gao study the random return in distributional linear quadratic control, where the whole distribution of outcomes matters, not just the average cost. In this framework the random return has an exact closed form over infinitely many random variables. Prior work approximated it with finitely many variables, called truncation.

The authors analyze a quadratic truncated version and prove positive definiteness, a density result, and log-concavity of the return. Those properties make the truncated model tractable for risk-aware control. The work firms up theory for controllers that care about spread and downside, not only means.
arxiv-2510-23532:
Anirban Das and three co-authors argue that the standard tests for machine reasoning are too easy in a hidden way. Many benchmarks for relational reasoning quietly assume that answers come from chaining links along paths, like following a family tree step by step. Some recent models even have that path-following built into their design, so they shine on the tests yet struggle anywhere else.

To push the field further, the authors introduce NoRA, a new benchmark with several added levels of difficulty. Solving its tasks forces a model to reason beyond composing paths from one relation to the next. The benchmark is meant to reveal which designs — neuro-symbolic systems, transformers, or graph networks — truly learn general reasoning rules. By exposing the shortcut the older tests allowed, NoRA gives researchers a harder, fairer yardstick for progress.
arxiv-2510-23932:
Jayce R. Getz and eight co-authors introduce modulation groups, a new symmetry structure behind certain spaces of test functions in number theory. Conjectures by Braverman and Kazhdan, Ngô, and Sakellaridis have driven the construction of Schwartz spaces for spherical varieties. The authors prove that, under suitable assumptions, each such Schwartz space naturally carries an action of a group they name the modulation group.

The construction broadly generalizes the defining representation of the metaplectic group, a classical object in representation theory. Two cases are worked out in detail: a plain vector space, and the zero locus of a quadric cone in an even number of variables. In both, the modulation group sits close to algebraic groups, and the authors conjecture a general method for tying modulation groups to ind-algebraic groups. The paper ends with adelization and the link between these representations and the Poisson summation conjecture.
arxiv-2510-24032:
Lizhen Qin and Yang Su study a math question about spaces that can cover themselves in a nontrivial way. A space with this trait is called self-covering. They focus on closed shapes whose basic loop group is abelian, meaning loops can be combined in any order without changing the result.

Under mild conditions, the authors prove such shapes fiber over a torus, a doughnut-like surface, in several senses. For shapes above dimension five with a free abelian loop group, they get a fiber bundle over a circle. They also build cases where the result fails without those conditions, showing how much harder the problem gets for other groups.
arxiv-2510-24132:
Tuvi Etzion and two co-authors present new constructions for two related combinatorial designs, mixed Steiner systems and nonuniform group divisible designs. The two differ only in one rule: Steiner systems also require a minimum distance between blocks, while the designs do not. Every mixed Steiner system is thus a design, but not the other way around.

The authors give a construction for mixed Steiner systems based on orthogonal arrays and resolvable Steiner systems. Some new cases depend on whether certain Mersenne or Fermat primes exist. They also derive new parameters for designs from large sets of a generalized design, including many cases with a parameter above three that were not known before.
arxiv-2510-24432:
Seyed Mahdi Basiri Azad and Joschka Boedecker propose a simple way to speed up Q-learning when rewards are rare. In sparse reward settings, agents get little feedback and waste much time exploring blindly. Their method, Fill in the Blanks, uses a handful of successful demonstrations to initialize the agent's value function before online learning begins.

Value estimates are precomputed from the offline demonstrations and used as targets early in training, giving the agent a useful prior over promising actions. The agent then refines those estimates through normal interaction. Experiments on benchmark tasks show much lower exploration burden and better sample efficiency than learning from scratch.
arxiv-2510-24632:
Sebastian Matera, Christian Merdon, and Daniel Runge seek a fast way to solve drift and spread tasks with hard edge rules. Such tasks show up in work on mixed phase chem acts, where the hard part sits just at the edge. Their plan builds a small set of base maps first.

Those base maps come from the main flow rule and do not depend on the hard edge part. So the full hard task shrinks to a much smaller one at the edge alone. The same base set can then be reused for new edge rules. They show the plan on a test case with a fuel gas change at a surface.
arxiv-2510-24932:
Deepon Halder, Alan Saji, Thanmay Jayakumar, Ratish Puduppully, Anoop Kunchukuttan, and Raj Dabre built RiddleBench, a set of hard riddles to test chat models. Known test sets lean on math and set skills, yet miss the loose, multi side thought that riddles need. Riddle work joins logic, space sense, and rule checks in one ask.

The bench holds more than seventeen hundred riddles in English. Top paid models scored just above sixty in a hundred on it. Checks showed deep flaws: models took bad thought from peers as true, and could not fix their own slips due to self trust bias. Their thought was also frail to small shifts in an ask.
arxiv-2510-25132:
Chao Song leads a team with eight co-authors who add substrate sense to enzyme design, so new enzymes can be made for a set target stuff. Past make models are strong at shapes, but weak on bind data and on aim at one substrate. Their set, EnzyBind, holds more than eleven thousand checked enzyme and substrate pairs.

On that base, EnzyControl makes backbones tied to marked core sites and their paired substrates. A lean add part, EnzyAdapter, plugs into a past shape model to make it substrate aware. Two stage training hones the skill to make true, work fit backbones. The aim is enzymes built to order, not just in shape.
arxiv-2510-25332:
Yuhang Hu led seven co-authors in building StreamingCoT. Zhenyu Yang, Shihan Wang, and Shengsheng Qian helped. Bin Wen, Fan Yang, and Tingting Gao followed. Changsheng Xu completes the author team. Their 2025 paper presents a streaming video question dataset. Streaming video needs models that track time well.

Current video question sets have two main limits. Static annotations miss how answers change over time. Missing reasoning steps also hurt model interpretability. StreamingCoT is designed for temporally evolving reasoning tasks. Its framework builds dense descriptions for each second. Similar segments are fused into semantic units. Question sets follow temporal evolution patterns in videos. Reasoning chains come from objects in keyframes. Large language models derive state transition paths. Human checks then verify logical coherence. The dataset supports research on complex temporal reasoning.
arxiv-2510-25532:
Alexandre Sainterme and Fatima Ebrahimi study Hall instabilities in plasma. Their 2025 physics paper examines a differentially rotating cylinder. The plasma model is incompressible Hall magnetohydrodynamics. Non-axisymmetric, flow-driven instabilities are the focus here. Flow shear can supply energy to waves. Both whistler and ion-cyclotron waves extract that energy.

Two distinct branches of global instability result. Non-axisymmetric whistler modes grow significantly faster than ideal modes. The authors discuss the global whistler instability mechanism. Large ion skin depth gives an electron-MHD limit. When magnetic field is azimuthal, special modes appear. Zero axial wave number whistler modes get destabilized. A co-rotation amplifier mechanism drives that destabilization. Hall effects become appreciable at modest skin depths. Distinct global modes emerge in strong Hall regime. Stronger magnetic fields are required there than usual. Hall effect weakens field-line bending stabilization by decoupling. These modes may matter in weakly ionized accretion disks.
arxiv-2510-25732:
Aakriti Shah, Yifan Hu, and Thai Le study what unlearned models remember. Their 2025 paper studies knowledge entanglement in language models. Unlearning is usually tested by fact recovery tests. They ask whether entanglement predicts leakage after unlearning. Structural entanglement links a fact to other knowledge.

Across unlearning methods and domains, patterns emerged. Two fictional and non-fictional domains were tested. Harry Potter and United States senators supplied domains. Four models of varied sizes were tested. One method weakened that relationship but kept it positive. Another method inverted it in every domain tested. Unlearning acts on underlying knowledge form, they conclude. A predictive model values leakage beforehand for auditing.
arxiv-2510-25832:
Mario Reig and Ignacio Ruiz link proton decay searches to the possible size of an extra dimension of space. In one strong form of heterotic string theory, ordinary matter and forces sit at the end of an eleventh dimension. That interval has been suggested as a dark dimension, a large extra dimension where only gravity can travel.

Reig and Ruiz show that limits from proton decay, the hypothetical breaking apart of a proton, press hard on that idea. If protons lasted as long as experiments require, the interval must be extremely small in their setup. The bound they report is on the order of ten to the minus twenty eight meters, far below a micron size.
arxiv-2510-26132:
Nestor O. Perez-Arancibia, working alone, presents body based intelligence as a design principle for advanced tiny robots. Body based intelligence means that body shape, materials, environment interaction, and control are designed together so that smart behavior, especially movement and steering, emerges from the whole system. That contrasts with classic designs that separate sensing, computing, and motion parts into distinct blocks.

Perez-Arancibia shows the idea with robots from his Autonomous Microrobotic Systems Laboratory, including Bee++, RoBeetle, SMALLBug, and WaterStrider among several named platforms. In these machines, clever behavior arises from body dynamics and physical feedback loops, with sensing and motion parts choices built into the body. The paper draws lessons for co design at tiny scales.
arxiv-2510-26632:
Georg Hartl, Conrad Gstöttner, and Markus Schöberl study when a nonlinear control system is differentially flat. A flat system can be fully described through a few special outputs, which makes planning its motion much easier. Testing flatness in general is hard, so tractable sufficient conditions are valuable.

Hartl and his two co-authors introduce a triangular normal form for systems with at least three inputs, built on a multi-chained form. For two specific versions of that structure, they give complete geometric characterisations: exact conditions for when a system can be reshaped into the form by feedback. Those conditions double as sufficient tests for flatness. They also yield step-by-step procedures for computing the flat outputs themselves.
arxiv-2510-26732:
J de Curtò, I de Zarzà, Pablo García, and Jordi Cabot compare the reasoning of foundation models across three kinds of computing platform. The same model may behave differently on a supercomputer, a cloud service, or a university cluster, which would cloud any benchmark. Their test bed spans the MareNostrum 5 supercomputer, Nebius AI Studio, and a university node with eight H200 graphics cards.

The four authors run fifteen models on seventy-nine problems across eight academic domains, in three phases. Early phases set a baseline on nineteen problems and check that results reproduce across platforms. The full run then probes generalisation at scale. Their findings push against simple scaling beliefs: training data quality mattered more than model size. They close with practical guidelines for picking models in education, production, and research settings.
arxiv-2510-26832:
Abha Jha, J Hunter Priniski, Carolyn Steinle, and Fred Morstatter simulate how hashtags evolve in online groups. Networks shape how narratives sway beliefs, and shared tags are a visible trace of that process. The team asks how group talk around narrative media forms beliefs, and how consensus or polarisation emerges.

Jha and her three co-authors build an agent-based framework of networks whose members are large language model agents. They benchmark four leading models against human group behaviour from a prior network experiment and against real Twitter hashtags. Measures of group coherence show the models mimic human-like coherence in cleaned-up settings. In complex or politically sensitive stories, though, weaving in background knowledge and social context seems to need careful, structured prompting.
arxiv-2510-27032:
Grant Merz leads six co-authors in testing a pixel-based way to estimate galaxy distances with the James Webb Space Telescope. Photometric redshifts infer distance from brightness across filters, a key step for studying the early universe. The standard route fits templates to measured brightness, while newer machine learning methods can work straight from image pixels.

The team's tool, DeepDISC, detects and separates sources, then gives probability-based distance estimates directly from near-infrared images. On deep survey data it matches template fitting and beats it when filters are matched fairly. It also skips measured photometry and can catalog tens of thousands of estimates in minutes on one graphics processor. A full catalog for one survey field is released with quality flags.
arxiv-2510-27232:
Liyang He leads eight co-authors in a survey of deep text hashing for fast semantic search. Text hashing compresses documents into short binary codes, so similarity becomes a quick Hamming distance count and storage shrinks greatly. Deep methods learn such codes directly from data with neural networks, beating older data-independent techniques on semantic richness.

The survey sorts current methods by core components: semantic extraction, hash code quality preservation, and other key technologies. A detailed evaluation schema reports results on several popular datasets, followed by practical applications and open-source tools. Closing sections cover key challenges and future directions, including joining deep text hashing with large language models. A companion project page collects resources for researchers entering the field.
arxiv-2510-27332:
Thibaut Francois investigates whether wandering black holes in dwarf galaxies can pair up far from galactic centers. Recent telescope detections of early supermassive black holes renewed interest in black hole growth, while simulations and observations suggest many intermediate-mass black holes sit off-center in dwarfs. In cored dark matter halos, dynamical friction is slow and cores stall sinking, keeping holes off-center for long periods.

Embedding off-center holes in an idealized galactic potential and scanning many orbital configurations, Francois assesses close encounters through Jacobi capture, a gravitational capture mechanism. Captures occur in about thirteen percent of cases. Sustained inside compact stellar systems like stripped nuclei or globular clusters, such captures are a crucial first step toward massive black hole binaries beyond galactic centers.
arxiv-2510-27432:
WonJun Moon, MinSeok Jung, and five other co-authors fix a flaw in video search in this 2025 paper. In partially relevant video retrieval, only part of a video matches the search text. Training treats each text-video pair as a match and all others as misses. That crude rule ignores how much videos and texts vary.

The flaw, which they call semantic collapse, squeezes distinct events in one video into the same corner of the model's map. At the same time, near-twin events in different videos get pushed apart. Their fix has two parts. One keeps the natural closeness among texts that the base model already knows. The other aligns video embeddings, the map points for video clips, across time scales, with token merging that keeps each segment coherent yet distinct. Tests show clear gains in retrieval quality.
arxiv-2510-27532:
Neha Srikanth, Victor Bursztyn, and two other co-authors build a compact map of database questions in this 2025 paper. Text-to-SQL systems turn plain questions into database queries. Judging them by one accuracy score hides where they fail. Their map, SQLSpace, places each example by traits a person can read, built with little human effort.

Three uses show the map's worth. It contrasts top benchmarks side by side, exposing which traits each one really tests. It breaks model performance down by trait, past the single score. And it guides targeted rewrites of questions, steered by a learned guess of success. Patterns invisible in raw examples become plain on the map. That helps builders fix weak spots instead of chasing a lone number.
arxiv-2510-27632:
Riccardo Brioschi and eleven co-authors introduce sketch-guided layout design in 2025. Layout generation builds neat pages, posters, and slides from set parts. Past tools guide that work with detailed written rules, which are slow and hard for users to write. A hand sketch gives a simpler guide: users draw rough boxes to show where parts should go.

Their model joins the sketch with the content parts in one transformer build, a neural design that weighs links among inputs. Hand sketches for training are scarce, so the team made fake sketches at scale. Tests on three public layout sets show the sketch guide works well. Rough drawings could make design tools far easier to steer.
arxiv-2511-00232:
Karol Bołbotowski and Guy Bouchitté compare two ways of measuring distance between probability patterns. One, the Wasserstein distance, tracks the cost of reshaping one pattern into another. The other, the Zolotarev distance, comes from a different mathematical tradition. Sharp comparisons between such measures let researchers swap one for the other without losing precision.

Building on a duality principle the pair proved recently, they extend the Rio inequality to any dimension with the best possible constant. They also give an optimal upper bound for the ratio of the two distances, for centered patterns with fixed spread. The results are compact, exact, and aimed at probability specialists.
arxiv-2511-00332: Olivier Bourget and Angela Vargas-Mancipe analyze the spectrum of a family of first-order finite difference operators with two-component values, acting on sequences over whole numbers. Using the conjugate operator method, they prove limiting absorption principles and rule out singular continuous spectrum for them. Their results cover classes of long-range perturbations that had not been treated before, widening spectral theory for such discrete tools.
arxiv-2511-00732:
Zainab Aizaz, James Knight, and Thomas Nowotny build custom silicon thinking for spiking neural networks, brain-inspired models that promise energy-efficient handling of time-based tasks like keyword spotting. Spiking networks do little arithmetic per byte of memory moved, so graphics processors and tensor accelerators, built for dense arithmetic, suit them poorly. Field-programmable gate arrays fit such memory-bound work far better.

Their FeNN-DMA is a fully programmable RISC-V system-on-chip tailored to spiking simulation on modern UltraScale+ FPGAs. Resource use and energy match fixed-function accelerators, yet the chip supports richer neuron models and network topologies, simulating up to sixteen thousand neurons and two hundred fifty-six million synapses per core. It posts state-of-the-art accuracy on spiking digit, neuromorphic vision, and Braille touch benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-01232:
Yu-Ting Lai and colleagues design and build a surgical robot for operations inside the eye. Robotic systems for cataract and retinal surgery exist, but the authors judge their accuracy, precision, and freedom of motion insufficient, above all for robot tool exchange during a procedure.

The new system targets tooltip accuracy, tracking quality, and a smooth instrument exchange system that keeps the incision small through a remote center of motion. An optical coherence tomography setup measured the tooltip placement accuracy at roughly five hundredths of a millimetre after calibration and coordinate alignment. The team shows the full system on an OCT guided automated cataract lens extraction, using deep learning models of the patient's anatomy built before surgery and real time oversight during it.
arxiv-2511-01432:
Jarosław Mederski and Andrzej Szulkin study a Sobolev-type inequality built around the curl operator, the vector-calculus measure of rotation, in three-dimensional space. They prove that the inequality has an optimizer, a best possible function, and that this optimizer solves a nonlinear curl-curl equation at the critical exponent.

Two cases carry physical weight: one tied to nonlinear Maxwell equations of electromagnetism, the other to zero modes of three-dimensional Dirac operators. Because the curl operator has a huge kernel, standard methods fail, so the proof uses a new variational approach on a Nehari-type constraint. The authors also find symmetric solutions distinct from the known explicit Loss-Yau fields, and recover a compactness result for the classical Sobolev inequality.
arxiv-2511-01532:
Marcin Anholcer, Sylwia Cichacz, and Iztok Peterin study a graph coloring parameter for cubic graphs, networks where every vertex has exactly three neighbors. The coloring is acyclic: adjacent vertices differ, and any two color classes together form a forest, with no cycles. A coloring is maximal in their sense when no vertex can be recolored to drop a color while staying acyclic.

The acyclic b-chromatic number counts the most colors such a stuck coloring can use, framed formally through a recoloring relation and its transitive closure. Pinning down this number for cubic graphs is the paper's aim, a step in understanding how local recoloring rules limit global colorings of regular networks.
arxiv-2511-01632:
Balázs Mészáros, James Knight, Danyal Akarca, and Thomas Nowotny give artificial neurons something real brains have: a position in space. In biology, the distance between neurons sets how long signals take to arrive, coupling space and time. Most artificial networks ignore this; the authors build a spiking network where each synapse's delay is simply the distance between its neurons.

They derive how to adjust neuron positions by gradient descent during learning. Trained on temporal classification tasks, the networks spontaneously organized into local, clustered layouts, and when wiring cost depended on distance, a modular, efficiently wired structure emerged. Functional specialization lined up with the spatial clusters without being imposed, suggesting the space-time coupling itself is a useful inductive bias and a route to more interpretable, efficient hardware.
arxiv-2511-01832:
John Joseph Carrasco and Yaxi Chen find the root of Hawking radiation's warmth in a simpler theory. Hawking showed that a collapsing shell of matter radiates like a hot body. Carrasco and Chen show that spectrum can be derived through the double copy. That is a correspondence translating gravitational calculations into gauge theory ones. Its root here is a non-abelian Yang-Mills process.

Analyzing that gauge theory root, they find the radiation spectrum is thermal in the color charge eigenvalue, not in energy. For the SU(N) theory at large N, the spectrum in charge is a Planck-like factor times the color phase space density, modeled by the Wigner semicircle of random matrix theory. Apparent thermal behavior in energy, on the gravity side, is thus the direct dual of charge thermality in the underlying gauge theory.
arxiv-2511-01932:
Haoming Wang and Wei Gao explain, in words, how a personalized image generator has been personalized. Such models are tuned to individual users' tastes, but users cannot see which aspects changed or by how much; visual examples alone are hard to read. Existing language explanations are too coarse to separate the multiple aspects of personalization or grade their levels.

Their technique, FineXL, produces natural language descriptions of each distinct aspect of personalization together with a quantitative score for its level. Experiments across several personalization scenarios and multiple kinds of image generation models showed FineXL improving the accuracy of explanations by about 56 percent over existing approaches. The work targets trust and control: if a system adapts itself to a user, the user deserves a precise account of the adaptation.
arxiv-2511-02232:
Zhigang Jia, Meiyue Shao, and Yanjun Shao add missing pieces to the numerical machinery for eigenvalue problems over the quaternions. Those form the four-dimensional number system used in areas from signal processing to quantum mechanics. Quaternion matrices that are not Hermitian are the hard case. The standard tool is the quaternion QR algorithm, but computing the eigenvectors themselves, and reordering the eigenvalues into a chosen sequence, had not been fully worked out.

The authors supply methods for both jobs. The reordering method is the key that unlocks aggressive early deflation, a technique that discards finished parts of the problem early and greatly speeds up QR-type methods. They show it now works for the quaternion problem as well. Tests are reported as showing that the proposed methods are both efficient and effective.
arxiv-2511-02632:
Taehyeon Koo and Zijian Guo rethink the synthetic control method, a tool that estimates what a policy change did by building a fake twin from untreated units. Their 2025 paper starts from a weakness: when control units look alike, the twin's recipe is poorly pinned down, and ties can shift after treatment. Results may then rest on shaky weights.

The pair define a new target, the weight-robust treatment effect, drawn from the worst case over all weight sets that fit the past well. That set yields a range of plausible effects, and their target is the point in it nearest zero. They also give a perturbation method for valid confidence intervals, since the estimator's spread is not normal. The tools suit sensitivity checks more broadly.
arxiv-2511-02832:
Yanjie Ze and eight colleagues present TWIST2, a portable system for teaching humanoid robots by remote control. Humanoid research lacks the cheap, rich data pipelines that boosted other robot types. Older teleoperation rigs either split control into pieces or need costly motion capture studios. Their 2025 system keeps full whole-body control without that studio.

A PICO4U headset captures the operator's whole-body motion in real time. A custom two-axis robot neck, costing about 250 dollars, gives the operator a view from the robot's head. With it, the team collected one hundred demonstrations in fifteen minutes at nearly perfect success. On top sits a layered vision policy that drives the whole body from that head view, showing dexterous handling and dynamic kicking.
arxiv-2511-03032:
James Bowden, Sergey Levine, and Jennifer Listgarten speed up the computer design of discrete objects like proteins and circuits. Designers train a generative model to favor candidates with wanted traits, but the search space is combinatorial and huge. Many trait predictors, though, split into loosely linked parts: a protein's active site barely interacts with its far end. Their 2025 algorithm, DADO, exploits exactly that structure.

DADO keeps a soft-factorized search distribution and passes messages along a junction tree that encodes which variables interact. That coordination lets the search respect the predictor's own factorization instead of fighting it. The authors show the method makes distributional optimization more efficient on scientific design tasks. The gain comes from structure that standard optimizers ignore.
arxiv-2511-03532:
Michael Wilson studied the spectrum of a twisted Laplacian tied to smooth SU(2) connections in three dimensions. The submission claimed a sharp falloff rate for curvature. Past that rate, the deep spectrum was said to stay the same as the flat case. A built example at the border rate was offered as proof the bound could not be improved.

Wilson later withdrew the submission after finding substantive errors in the main argument. The notice states that the border example does not establish the claimed threshold. It also states that several compactness and gauge estimates used in the proof are invalid. Those flaws undermine the principal conclusions, so the results should not be cited as standing findings.
arxiv-2511-03832:
Catherine C Blume and Bradley W Hindman calculate how Rossby waves behave deep inside the Sun, where their radial shapes have stayed unknown. Earlier theory either treated the system as nearly flat or assumed a fully radiative or fully convective interior, neither of which fits the real Sun.

Working with Lagrangian pressure changes in a standard solar model, the pair derive cleaner wave equations without the singularities older work hit. The solar interior holds two wave cavities, one in the radiative zone and one in the convection zone. Radiative-zone modes keep nearly constant vorticity through the convection zone, raising the chance they might be seen at the surface.
arxiv-2511-04032:
Divya Pathak, Harshit Kumar, Anuska Roy, Felix George, Mudit Verma, and Pratibha Moogi introduce anomaly detection for trajectories of multi-agent AI systems. Their non-deterministic behaviour breeds silent failures such as drift, cycles, and missing output details. Such failures are hard to spot by eye in long traces.

A building pipeline captures user behaviour, agent non-determinism, and model variation, yielding two labelled benchmark sets of several thousand trajectories in total. Supervised and semi-supervised detectors scored alike, reaching scores up to ninety-eight and ninety-six percent. As a first full study, the work supplies datasets, benchmarks, and guidance for watching agentic systems in use.
arxiv-2511-04132:
Hongbin Zhang, Shihao Gao, Yang Liu, Mingjie Xing, Yanjun Wu, and Chen Zhao explore whether a large language model could serve as a compiler end to end. It would turn source code directly into assembly. Models already assist compiler development, but replacing the compiler itself has barely been tested in a systematic way.

A dedicated dataset and framework, CompilerEval, measure source comprehension and assembly generation across mainstream models. Error analysis, prompt improvements, larger models, and reasoning methods all raised output quality, yet compilation success rates stayed low overall. Cross-platform ability was also checked. The authors stay optimistic and sketch architectures and research directions that might one day make model-based compilation practical.
arxiv-2511-04232:
Jindi Zhong, Ziyuan Guo, Hongxia Wang, and Huanshui Zhang propose a lean learning-based algorithm for visual localization where satellite fixes are denied and computing power is limited. Offline systems in such settings need accuracy and generalization without heavy models, a combination that is hard to reach.

Their algorithm grows out of the optimal control principle. Diagonal information about the Hessian matrix is estimated during training, which improves the resulting neural network and speeds training convergence. Tests on public datasets reached competitive localization accuracy with strong generalization, the authors report. The control-based training angle offers a fresh route for building location models that stay light enough for constrained hardware.
arxiv-2511-04932:
Zhendong Li, Tong Zhao, and Bohan Zhang study how well a class of neural network quantum states can express fermion wave states, when written in second quantization. Such states are a hopeful tool for hard quantum many-body tasks, but their limits for fermions were unclear.

The authors widen the Boltzmann machine form into what they call neuron product states, where each unit links sites across the whole system. They prove such products can match any wave state if the response curves meet mild terms. They also give short proofs for the broad reach of product states of this kind.
arxiv-2511-05232:
Henry Kerr and co-authors study waves of firing that travel through a network of integrate-and-fire neurons, shaped by slow subthreshold oscillations in each cell. Such waves appear in sensory, motor, and cognitive work in the brain.

Their network uses side inhibition, where active cells quiet their neighbors, plus a slow voltage-gated channel that acts in a near-linear way. Unlike field models, the spiking set-up shows single-cell traits at work. The study traces how that slow channel bends wave speed and form, a link from ion channels to whole-tissue patterns in cortex.
arxiv-2511-05632:
A Rostami, K Rezazadeh, and M Rostampour build a relativistic version of MOND, the theory that tweaks gravity to explain galaxy rotation without dark matter. Their route starts from entropic gravity, the idea that gravity emerges from information on a holographic screen. They add temperature-dependent fixes to how energy is shared on that screen.

Solving their equations for a round, static system gives a metric that flattens far away and contains MOND's key acceleration scale. At very low acceleration it reproduces MOND-like behavior with a relativistic base. Tested on rotation data for the galaxy NGC 3198, the model fit far better than baryons-only Newtonian gravity and about as well as a dark matter halo.
arxiv-2511-05732:
Reza Shirazi, Alexander Zech, Peter Pinski, and Vladimir Rybkin benchmark a tool that picks active spaces for quantum chemistry calculations automatically. Methods like CASSCF capture strong electron correlation and can predict how molecules absorb light. Their accuracy and cost hinge on choosing the right set of orbitals, the active space, which is normally expert work.

The Active Space Finder builds sensible orbitals and selects a space using cheaper correlated calculations first. The hard part is balance: one space must serve several electronic states at once. Tested on established sets of small and medium molecules, the tool gave encouraging excitation energies. The authors compare settings and offer practical advice for users.
arxiv-2511-06132:
Yuyang Deng, Fuli Qiao, and Mehrdad Mahdavi study how to train very large models across many small devices. In federated learning, phones and edge clients cannot hold a full modern model. Sub-model training sends each client only a small random piece, but random pieces can converge poorly.

Borrowing from the success of shuffled gradient methods, the authors split the model into fixed parts in advance. The server shuffles those parts among clients each round, then averages the returned updates. They prove a convergence rate for the scheme and show through stability analysis that sub-model training can actually improve generalization. Experiments back up both theoretical claims.
arxiv-2511-06232:
Sushant Mehta and Ishan Gupta build a theory linking two puzzles about large language models: scaling laws and in-context learning. In-context learning lets a model pick up a new task from examples in its prompt, with no retraining. Why that ability appears as models grow has lacked a firm explanation.

Their framework shows in-context performance following power laws in depth, width, context length, and training data, with rates set by task structure. Under stated conditions, transformers carry out gradient-based meta-learning inside a single forward pass. The theory predicts sharp turning points at critical scales and a best split between depth and width, and synthetic experiments matched those predictions closely.
arxiv-2511-06332:
Simran Arora and Mridul Patel test a modified theory of gravity against the Hubble tension, the mismatch between two ways of measuring the universe's expansion rate. Their framework is nonminimal f(Q) gravity, where the nonmetricity scalar couples directly to matter inside a symmetric teleparallel setup. The authors derive the background equations for a representative model.

They fit the model with Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling against cosmic chronometers, baryon acoustic oscillation data, three supernova samples, and cosmic microwave background data. Machine learning regressors checked the predictions from another angle. Across a broad range of parameters, the model partly eased the Hubble tension, marking the framework as promising for late-time cosmology.
arxiv-2511-06432:
Xi Chen settles the long-time fate of solutions to an integrable wave equation, the defocusing Calogero-Moser derivative nonlinear Schrödinger equation. Scattering asks whether solutions eventually behave like free waves as time grows. Chen works with starting data whose Fourier transform lives only on positive frequencies, a broad half-line class.

An explicit formula of Gérard type does the heavy lifting, giving the solution in a form where its distant future can be read off. The scattering term is then described through the distorted Fourier transform tied to the equation's Lax operator. The work stands among the first to use that explicit formula for broad initial data beyond rational cases.
arxiv-2511-06732:
Walter Hartung and colleagues report the first plasma processing trial inside a working accelerator module at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams. Plasma cleaning can restore superconducting cavity performance in place, sparing the huge job of removing a cryomodule for refurbishment. The facility runs hundreds of quarter-wave and half-wave resonators that could benefit.

Earlier tests drove plasma through the fundamental power coupler with promising results, and driving with a higher-order mode promised denser plasma with less mismatch. The January 2024 trial treated quarter-wave resonators inside their cryomodule. Cold tests afterward showed a significant drop in field emission X-rays, the signature the team hoped cleaning would produce.
arxiv-2511-07232:
D Fossion and eleven co-authors probe the spatial reach of the Kondo effect, in which conduction electrons screen a localized spin into a strongly correlated many-body state. How far that screening cloud extends into the surrounding electron reservoirs has been debated for decades. The team built a gallium arsenide quantum dot coupled to an electronic Fabry-Pérot interferometer, which modulates the density of states at the Fermi level in a controlled way.

Oscillations in the Kondo temperature reveal a screening length comparable to the cavity size, evidence the cloud really does extend that far. The authors also vary how asymmetrically the dot couples to its two reservoirs, finding that asymmetry reshapes both the amplitude and the phase of the conductance oscillations. The results expose a subtle interplay between coherent transport through the interferometer and Kondo screening.
arxiv-2511-07332:
Aarash Feizi and sixteen co-authors build the missing training data for AI agents that operate desktop computers. Such agents must ground language instructions in the correct on-screen elements, but while web and mobile grounding data sets abound, desktop resources are scarce. GroundCUA is a large-scale dataset built from expert human demonstrations across eighty-seven applications in twelve categories, with fifty-six thousand screenshots and over three and a half million human-verified annotations.

From the demonstrations the team generates diverse instructions reflecting real tasks, then trains the GroundNext model family on them. At three- and seven-billion-parameter scales, GroundNext set state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks while using less than a tenth of the training data of prior work. Reinforcement learning post-training helped further, and in an agentic OSWorld evaluation the models matched or beat systems trained with far more data.
arxiv-2511-07532:
Grisha Zeltyn, Benny Trakhtenbrot, and Michael Eracleous study black holes that suddenly change their look. Changing-look active galaxies swing between bright and dim spectral states within years, defying slow accretion expectations. What triggers the swings, and whether host galaxies play a role, remains unknown.

Fresh spectra of twenty three such objects come from large telescopes in Chile and Hawaii. Because the same galaxy appears in both states, host traits can be separated from glare. Comparing black hole and host scaling links tests whether these systems follow normal galaxy rules. The sample offers a rare controlled look at feeding black holes.
arxiv-2511-07832:
Phanindra Tallapragada differentiates the operators that turn nonlinear motion into linear prediction. Koopman and Perron-Frobenius operators are now standard tools for flow analysis, robotics, and control. A practical question dogs every use: when the underlying flow changes slightly, how do the operators change?

Flow primitives and infinitesimal generators answer that question without recomputing everything. Small vector field edits, or adding two fields, translate into operator updates through these building blocks. Model changes are routine in control design, so cheap operator updates save heavy computation. The framework also deepens theory linking flows and their linear shadows.
arxiv-2511-08232:
Alkid Baci and colleagues introduce OWLAPY, a Python framework for engineering OWL ontologies, the formal knowledge structures behind the semantic web. Building, editing, and saving OWL 2 ontologies usually means Java based tools, which many Python users find awkward. OWLAPY streamlines creation, modification, and serialization inside Python while staying flexible.

It integrates native Python reasoners and can also call external Java reasoners. Conversions move class expressions between description logics, Manchester syntax, and SPARQL formats. Users can define workflows that use large language models to draft ontologies from plain text. The package is public on GitHub and PyPI, with tens of thousands of downloads.
arxiv-2511-08632:
Alexander Pakpour Tabrizi and six co-authors report a gentler way to shape diamond into nanostructured membranes for quantum sensing. The sensors are nitrogen vacancy centers, atomic defects in diamond whose spins can measure tiny magnetic signals, but they must sit nanometers from the sample to work well.

Standard etching and ion milling damage the crystal below the surface, which destabilizes the charge state and shortens spin coherence for shallow centers. The new fabrication route avoids that damage while still adding photonic structures that boost the light signal. The team shows the optical and spin quality of top shallow sensors survives the process. A pick-and-place transfer then lets the finished membranes join many different sensing targets.
arxiv-2511-08832:
Nikunj Gupta and five co-authors add memory of relationships to multi-agent reinforcement learning, where several agents must cooperate while their partnerships keep shifting. Most existing methods rebuild the interaction graph fresh at every step, throwing away how coordination structures evolved to reach the current state.

The framework, TIGER, links each agent's current interactions to its historical ones in a dynamic temporal graph. A temporal attention encoder then pools information across both structural and time neighborhoods, producing time-aware embeddings that steer cooperative policy learning. On two coordination-heavy benchmarks the method beats value-decomposition and graph-based rivals in both task performance and sample efficiency. Ablation studies separate which design choices matter, showing how structure and timing jointly shape what the agents learn.
arxiv-2511-09232:
Xuanchen Li leads a twelve-author team tackling uneven speech translation quality across languages. Speech large language models translate well for major languages, but they underuse semantic common ground shared across source languages. The result is biased performance that favors high-resource languages.

Their framework, POTSA, aligns speech representations using parallel speech pairs and optimal transport. A bias compensation module first aligns representations coarsely, then token-level constraints on a Q-Former enforce fine-grained consistency. A layer scheduling strategy applies those constraints only where they help semantically. On the FLEURS benchmark, POTSA sets new state-of-the-art results. It gains just over one BLEU point on common languages and nearly three on zero-shot languages. Training used only ten hours of parallel speech per language.
arxiv-2511-09432:
Ege Erdogan and Ana Lucic make sparse autoencoders respect the symmetries of the data they explain. Sparse autoencoders unpack a neural network's dense activations into readable features, fighting the superposition that tangles concepts. But many different feature sets can fit equally well, and rotations common in scientific data make that ambiguity worse.

Extending the linear representation idea to account for symmetry, they build equivariant sparse autoencoders. On synthetic and real science data sets, the equivariant version dodges pitfalls of ordinary ones. Its features prove more useful for downstream tasks even though rebuilds get worse. That inversion warns against using rebuild quality as the main yardstick for interpretability, the authors argue.
arxiv-2511-09632:
Bogdan A. Dobrescu and Max H. Fieg ask whether a hypothetical color-octet scalar particle could explain a bump in CMS data at the Large Hadron Collider. The particle is an electroweak singlet coupling to gluons. It would be pair-produced and decay mostly into quark pairs, appearing as two dijet pairs of equal mass. CMS sees an excess near a dijet mass of about one teraelectronvolt in exactly that channel.

The predicted production rate and signal shape match the observed excess, the authors argue. A complex scalar fits the data better than a real one. They stress the interpretation is testable rather than settled. Additional signatures include trijet-dijet events and top pairs with a dijet resonance. Final states with a Higgs, W, or Z boson plus jets are also predicted.
arxiv-2511-09732:
Perrin E. Ruth and Maria K. Cameron develop theory and algorithms for untangling clusters of cycles in networks that describe materials. In hydrocarbon networks formed during pyrolysis, rings of atoms fuse into dense clusters that resist simple description. A minimum cycle basis is not unique and depends on vertex ordering, while the union of all such bases can explode exponentially.

Their method samples a minimum cycle basis uniformly at random, making the output statistically well-defined with size proportional to the edge count. Equivalence classes partition the relevant cycles, and a postprocessing step yields a dual graph of intersecting cycles. Applied to an amorphous hydrocarbon network, the framework reveals small polyhedral structures. They relate to diamond, and the theory explains exploding cycle counts.
arxiv-2511-09932:
Hanwen Wang, writing alone, studies how data augmentation can make robot visuomotor policies generalize to new scenes. Policies trained by imitation often stumble when object placement and scene conditions change, and existing data-adding pipelines generate data that still lacks diversity. Wang automates data generation around the scene layout factors that most affect how broadly policies work, building a heavily randomized data set from little human demonstration.

The data set spans five manipulator types, two grippers, and six manipulation tasks, randomizing camera pose, lighting, tabletop texture, and table height. Every factor influenced generalization, and any randomization helped, with diverse trajectories best at closing the visual gap. Tests on a low-cost manipulator tested how the randomization supports zero-shot transfer from simulation to the real robot.
arxiv-2511-10032:
Vijay Keswani and six co-authors ask a pointed question for AI alignment: what should a system align to when people's moral preferences keep changing? Alignment pipelines treat human feedback as a fixed target, yet preferences shift through genuine moral learning and through noise such as inattention or bias. The study grounds the problem in kidney allocation, a high-stakes domain where trade-offs are concrete.

Over four hundred participants compared hypothetical transplant patients across three to five sessions. People changed their answer to the same scenario six to twenty percent of the time, and fitted decision models drifted too. Simple AI models trained on the feedback lost predictive accuracy as instability grew and as time passed. The authors argue alignment must separate legitimate moral change from noise.
arxiv-2511-10132:
Théo Leblanc, writing alone, presents Hawkes autoregressive processes, a hybrid model for data that mixes event streams with regularly sampled series. Hawkes models describe events whose rate depends on past events, while autoregressive models describe discrete-time values depending on past values. Real records of one phenomenon often arrive in both forms and at different scales, which motivates a single model containing both dynamics.

Leblanc defines the combined continuous- and discrete-time model and establishes its basic probability theory. Results include the existence of a stationary version, a cluster representation of the process, and stability plus ergodic properties. The paper is foundational rather than empirical: it gives the new model class a rigorous footing for later statistical work on multiscale, heterogeneous data.
arxiv-2511-10332:
Tobias Heibges and six co-authors report the target-of-opportunity campaign of a balloon-borne Cherenkov telescope hunting extremely energetic neutrinos. The EUSO-SPB2 mission launched from Wanaka, New Zealand in May 2023 and ended after thirty-six hours when a balloon leak lost the payload in the Pacific. Its Cherenkov telescope stared just below Earth's limb for light from upward air showers made by decaying tau leptons born from neutrinos above ten PeV.

The campaign targeted astrophysical sources crossing the telescope's field of view during the short flight, any of which might accelerate particles to ultra-high energies. To run it, the team built a Neutrino Target Scheduler, a software tool for planning the observations. The paper documents both the search strategy and the scheduling tool.
arxiv-2511-10432:
Willem Bonnaffé and fourteen co-authors, including the CRUK ICGC Prostate Group, improve how AI systems read whole-slide tissue images in prostate cancer research. Pathologists grade cancer by judging structures such as glands, yet computer pipelines usually chop slides into a plain grid that ignores that architecture. Grid tiles drag in irrelevant tissue and make model decisions hard to interpret.

Their method, histology-informed tiling, first segments glands and uses those gland patches as the model's inputs. It extracted 380,000 glands from 760 slides across two large cohorts. Detection of hidden genetic changes tied to cancer spread improved by ten percent in standard accuracy terms. The gland groupings it found included clusters linked to relapse, mutations, and high Gleason grades, tying the gains to biology a pathologist can inspect.
arxiv-2511-10532:
Jose Berengueres starts from an ergonomic frustration: repetitive strain injury affects roughly one in five computer users. Decades of mouse redesign have not solved it, because every design still demands fine hand motion. He asks whether predictive software can supply the motion instead.

His answer is Preview Accept Discard, a zero-click interaction paradigm. The system predicts the interface elements a user likely wants, shows ranked suggestions to preview, and lets the user cycle through them and accept or discard a choice by key-release timing. In tests with a browser email client and a standardized keyboard prediction task, the paradigm substantially cut hand motion compared with a trackpad. It matched trackpad task times when prediction accuracy rivaled the best spell-checkers.
arxiv-2511-10732:
Sam van Leuven, Kayleigh Mathieson, and Pratik Roy compute superconformal indices, refined counting functions for four-dimensional supersymmetric gauge theories, by a route the standard formulas resist. The usual expression is a set of contour integrals reflecting the protected spectrum at zero coupling, and evaluating it by residues is blocked by non-isolated essential singularities.

Fixing the integral's residual Weyl symmetry removes the block. With that move, the authors evaluate the residue sums for SU(2) theories in terms of basic and elliptic hypergeometric series. They simplify the Macdonald index of the maximally supersymmetric theory using known transformation formulas. The simpler form appears to encode spectral features at nonzero coupling. They extend the method to a general class of SU(2) theories and to the SU(3) Macdonald index in closed form.
arxiv-2511-10932:
Changjian Xie and Cheng Wang offer a new time-step method for computer models of tiny magnets. Such models track how magnet direction evolves under the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, named for its authors. Older methods force a trade between speed and care, so a method that is both fast and exact is of real use.

Their scheme reaches third-order care in time, a step past what current tools provide, and it still runs fast. Tests on a thin strip, a shape like that in real devices, gave the same magnet patterns as trusted methods. It stayed stable across a wide range of damping and avoided false states.
arxiv-2511-11532:
Andrew J. Peterson asks whether a president under scandal coverage shifts his public messaging toward fresh topics, a tactic called strategic diversion, or simply posts provocatively all the time. His test case is Donald Trump's Truth Social output during the 2025 news cycle around the Epstein files.

Computational text analysis shows that when scandal coverage rose by one standard deviation, the pattern of posts moved away from its usual baseline by a clear margin over the following four days. The shift survives timing checks and falsification tests, though the author is careful to say it falls short of formal causal proof. The study offers measured evidence in the debate over media distraction.
arxiv-2511-11632:
Qiuhao Zeng proposes a few-shot learning method that builds each new classifier from shared parts, so knowledge transfers to classes seen only a handful of times. Metric-based meta-learning often overfits the classes used in training because its distance measure is tuned to them.

Classifiers are decomposed into meta-components learned across many training episodes, with an orthogonal regularizer keeping the components diverse so they capture genuinely different shared substructures. A new classifier is then assembled as a combination of those parts. Extensive experiments on standard few-shot benchmarks test whether the assembly generalizes better to unseen classes. Reusable parts, rather than one monolithic metric, are the bet behind the method.
arxiv-2511-11832:
Dmitry Gayfulin and Erez Nesharim carry a classic number theory theme into Laurent series. Continued fraction partial quotients measure how well numbers can be approximated. Hall and Cusick proved splitting results for real numbers. Each real is an integer plus two numbers with bounded partial quotients.

Earlier joint work proved a divergence version of the claim. Each real is a sum of two numbers whose partial quotients diverge. Here, the analogue is proved for Laurent series. Those series play the role of real numbers in function field arithmetic. Moving such theorems across the bridge tests the proofs. It shows which arguments are truly about continued fractions.
arxiv-2511-11932:
J. C. de Albuquerque, J. Carvalho, and Edcarlos D. Silva prove results for a Hartree-Fock type system with log interactions and null mass. It is posed on the whole plane. Whole-space settings remove the compactness that bounded domains give for free. Genuine nontrivial solutions are the goal.

A Nehari-Pohozaev manifold is built for the proof. Existence and smoothness are shown, and long-run behavior is described. Behavior is tracked as the coupling strength varies. For small values, the ground state is a true vector state, with all parts active. For large values, it is semitrivial, with some parts zero. Such precision anchors later numerical and physical work.
arxiv-2511-12032:
Guotao Liang and four co-authors improve masked image generation, the fast technique that predicts many visual tokens in parallel, by giving the model explicit knowledge of how tokens relate. Visual tokens lack clear individual meanings and come in long sequences, so learning their semantic dependencies from data alone is an uphill fight.

Knowledge of token-level dependencies, extracted from the training data, enters as a prior, and three advantageous kinds of knowledge are identified and tested. Richer token representations follow, with fidelity gains over purely self-taught dependencies. Masked generation's speed already suits interactive tools; teaching it the vocabulary's grammar attacks its remaining quality gap against slower autoregressive generators.
arxiv-2511-12232:
Lingfeng Zhang and nine co-authors present SocialNav-Map, a framework that lets a mobile robot move safely among people without training for that specific place. Crowded, changing spaces are hard for robots, and reinforcement learning methods can need thousands of training hours yet still fail in new settings.

The system builds a dynamic occupancy map, a grid that marks where space is free or blocked, and adds predicted human paths as moving obstacles. It predicts those paths in two ways, from past motion and from body orientation. The goal is converted into map coordinates, so the robot can plan ahead and steer clear before a conflict arises.
arxiv-2511-12732:
