Lida Chalangar Jalili Dehkharghani and Li-Hsiang Lin develop statistical methods for modeling human migration when the data cannot be pooled in one place. Migration flows shift over space and time under environmental and social pressures, and varying coefficient mixed models can capture that movement. The obstacle is scale: many random effects, large design matrices, and raw data that distributed sites may not share freely with each other.

Their method passes only summary statistics between sites. Under full communication those statistics recover the estimator that pooled data would give, and under tight limits a one-step version keeps first-order efficiency. A singular value step stabilizes difficult covariance calculations. The supporting theory covers likelihood preservation, convergence, and accuracy, and tests on simulated plus United States migration-flow data recovered dynamic spatial patterns faithfully. The work targets official statistics and health data with the same sharing constraints.
arxiv-2511-13332:
Tanmayee Patra and Biplab Ganguli explain why multi-scroll chaotic attractors grow their wing-like lobes. Workers usually find scrolls by solving the motion equations numerically, which shows the shape but not its geometric cause. The authors argue the cause can be read from Nambu surfaces built from generalized Hamiltonians.

They pair numerical bifurcation diagrams and Lyapunov exponents, which measure chaos, with the geometric Nambu approach. A fixed number of scrolls appears when the Nambu surfaces take a matching layout, and changing parameters reshapes those surfaces in step with the wings. The account links abstract energy-like surfaces to features a reader can see in phase space plots.
arxiv-2511-13432:
Subramanyam Sahoo and Aditi Chhawacharia propose a shared framework for governing language models in democratic societies. Powerful AI now presses on core democratic values, and single-actor oversight cannot cover the full range of risks. Their plan joins public participation, civil society input, and existing global governance ideas.

Three new pieces anchor the framework. First, a seven-part taxonomy sorts these risks from personal harms to system-level threats. Second, an Incident Severity Score adapts to group views and local context. Third, a phased rollout admits that deep institutional change takes time. Together they aim for oversight that is both broad and workable.
arxiv-2511-13732:
Moran Yanuka and 4 co-authors speed up speech generation with speculative decoding that accepts near-miss tokens. A small draft model proposes acoustic tokens and a large model verifies them, but exact matching rejects many tokens that sound the same. That strictness wastes most of the possible speedup for speech language models.

Their Principled Coarse-Graining verifies proposals at the level of acoustic similarity groups drawn from the target model's embedding space. Probability mass is split across the overlapping groups a token belongs to, and sampling runs on the group variable with an exactness promise at that level. On LibriTTS, acceptance and throughput rose over standard and speech-specific rivals while intelligibility and voice likeness held.
arxiv-2511-13832:
Douglas R. Alves, James S. Jenkins, and 30 co-authors report a new planet called TOI-333b. It orbits an F7V star every 3.78 days, inside the so-called Neptune desert, a zone where Neptune-sized planets are almost never found so close to sunlike stars. The planet is a bit over four times Earth's size and about twenty times its mass.

Measurements of lithium in the star suggest the system is younger than a billion years. The planet's makeup is still open: it may be mostly rock with almost no gas envelope, or a rocky world holding a large share of water. Because its host star is unusually hot for this class, the system gives astronomers a rare test case for how such planets form and change.
arxiv-2511-13932:
Rostislav Řepa, Michal Horák, Tomáš Šikola, and one co-author test an idea about how plasmonic antennas concentrate light. These tiny metal structures trap light waves at their surface and boost the local electric field. One hypothesis says a wide antenna acts like a large reservoir of charge, and that this reservoir drives the strong enhancement.

The authors examine whether bigger cross-sections really do deliver bigger field boosts. They find the large reservoir comes with large radiative losses, and those losses dominate. The result is the opposite of the hopeful guess: antennas with a large charge reservoir end up with low field enhancement. The finding redirects design effort for plasmonic antennas.
arxiv-2511-14132:
Kavya Bhand, Payal Khubchandani, and Jyoti Khubchandani propose encryption keys that change themselves in real time. Fixed keys are predictable targets for brute force and theft. Their framework uses a fuzzy inference system that reads live system signals, such as processor load, process count, and timestamp variation, and rates the available entropy under linguistic fuzzy rules.

That rating feeds key generation fused with hardware randomness, and the result is sealed inside a Trusted Platform Module. The sealed key drives AES-GCM encryption, which protects both secrecy and integrity. The authors present the design as a scalable fit for high-assurance, zero-trust, and cloud settings where keys must adapt to conditions.
arxiv-2511-14332:
Gonçalo Martins, Santiago González-Gaitán, João Duarte, and one co-author probe whether mismatched supernova samples fuel the Hubble tension, the stubborn gap between early and late universe expansion rates. The SH0ES project calibrates Type Ia supernovae on one sample and measures distant ones on another. If the two samples differ in color, stretch, or host galaxy traits, the standardization could skew the result.

The authors carve matched subsamples and re-estimate the expansion rate and standardization parameters. The calibration sample indeed underrepresents some host masses and star formation rates, and better matching shifts several parameters, though headline values stay broadly stable. Low and high stretch supernovae still gave persistently different expansion rates.
arxiv-2511-14432:
Marcela Gonçalves dos Santos, Sylvain Hallé, and Fábio Petrillo adapt mutation testing to industrial robots. Mutation testing grades a test suite by seeding small faults and checking whether the tests catch them. Classic fault operators were designed for ordinary code. They were not designed for message-driven robot programs that move and sense the physical world. The authors define robot-specific mutation operators instead.

Their mutants act at the level of high-level reads and writes: movements, gripper actions, and injected sensor noise. In a pick-and-place study the domain operators produced more informative mutants and fewer invalid or equivalent ones than conventional operators. The work points toward stronger test suites and safer, more reliable industrial robotic systems.
arxiv-2511-14532:
Subhajit Ghosh, Kimberly Boddy, and Tien-Tien Yu constrain ultralight scalar dark matter through its effect on cosmic constants. If such dark matter couples to standard particles, the fine structure constant and electron mass would wobble over time. Those shifts would alter light element formation in the early universe. They would also change how the cosmic microwave background formed.

The authors use microwave background data and baryon acoustic oscillation measures to bound the effect. They treat the changed helium abundance in a self consistent way. Allowed dark matter fractions tighten most for very low particle masses. The study links lab style constants to large scale cosmic probes in one framework.
arxiv-2511-14732:
Scott Bogner and five co-authors introduce detail refinement to prepare eigenstates on quantum computers. The idea starts from an eigenstate of a coarse, low detail Hamiltonian prepared by any method. That state is lifted to higher detail and slowly evolved. It becomes the matching eigenstate of a finer Hamiltonian.

Examples cover single particle basis refinement and spatial lattice refinement. Tests include interacting particles in a trap, nuclear states in a Woods-Saxon potential, and a multi species fermion model. In all cases the method proves efficient. Evolution time scales with the inverse energy gap. The bootstrap strategy could ease state preparation, a core bottleneck for quantum simulation.
arxiv-2511-14832:
Marie Hein, Gregor Kasieczka, and four co-authors ask how physicists should pick the best anomaly detector for a given data set. Anomaly hunting can reveal new physics in regions no theory has targeted, but dozens of detectors compete and the winner depends on the data. Their answer is ARGOS, a data-driven score with a firm theoretical base.

ARGOS is tested on weakly supervised, classifier-based detectors, the style most used in particle physics searches. It beats older selection scores, including the standard cross-entropy loss, at picking the most sensitive model. The authors show it working for tuning settings, choosing network designs, and selecting input features, which makes it a practical tool for search teams.
arxiv-2511-14932:
Nicholas Corso and Dong Lai simulate a conducting ball moving through magnetized plasma, a setup behind many space interactions. Planet-moon pairs, star-planet pairs, and close compact binaries all stir plasma this way, and the stirring can radiate. The team runs three-dimensional simulations of an unmagnetized sphere plowing through an ideal plasma flow.

The flow bends field lines into wing-shaped disturbances and pushes back on the sphere with a drag force. That drag mostly follows the classic Alfven wing picture, across flow speeds and plasma pressures. Slower wave wings add a correction that makes the drag depend on conditions in a less simple way, which matters for predicting orbital decay in close systems.
arxiv-2511-15632:
Petrus E. O. G. B. Abreu, Gabriela M. M. Paixão, and eight co-authors release CODE-II, a very large data set of heart tracings for training AI. An electrocardiogram records the heart electrical signal, and AI reading of those tracings needs large, well-labeled collections. CODE-II holds well over two million twelve-lead tracings from over two million adult patients gathered by a telehealth network in Minas Gerais, Brazil.

Each exam follows standard diagnostic criteria and was reviewed by cardiologists, across sixty-six clinically meaningful classes designed with their input. A public subset and a separate multi-reader test set are included. A network pre-trained on CODE-II transferred better to outside benchmarks than models trained on even larger data sets.
arxiv-2511-15832:
Kadja Flore Gali, Hamed Fahandezh Sadi, and eight co-authors show that cloud droplet sizes often barely respond to the size of aerosol particles that seed them. Aerosols govern how droplets activate, and droplet size sets cloud brightness, a strong but poorly constrained influence on Earth energy balance. That chain suggests cloud properties should depend sensitively on aerosol size distributions.

Combining cloud chamber experiments with high-resolution simulations, the team finds microphysical and optical cloud properties are often insensitive to aerosol size. Clear effects appear only under weak convective forcing and high aerosol concentrations. In most conditions, cloud reflectivity can be predicted from aerosol number alone, simplifying how aerosol changes are represented in climate reasoning.
arxiv-2511-16332:
Li-Wen Liao and Andrew Cooper test whether a galaxy's surroundings change its size at fixed mass, using a very large and uniform sample drawn from DESI Legacy Survey imaging. Claims in the literature conflict: environment might reshape galaxies directly, or larger patterns might just reflect assembly history.

The sample holds over half a million galaxies with spectroscopic redshifts and millions more with photometric ones, reaching down to low masses that earlier field studies missed. Splitting galaxies by color and shape, the authors find that red late-type galaxies near clusters are the same size as their twins far away. The apparent environmental trend comes from a changing mix of galaxy types, so individual assembly history, not present surroundings, is the main driver of size.
arxiv-2511-16532:
Fan Yang and five co-authors present a multi-camera system that tracks gymnasts in three dimensions for judging at international championships. Arenas allow few cameras, and lighting, uniforms, and occlusions can leave only two opposing views with valid detections, which breaks ordinary triangulation.

The fix uses gymnastics knowledge: during much of a routine the gymnast's center stays within a known vertical plane. A cascaded association scheme triangulates when cross-view detections suffice and falls back to ray-plane intersection when they do not, producing coplanar candidates that fill gaps in the trajectory. Extensive tests show the method beats existing trackers in hard scenarios. The judging system built on it has already served at recent World Championships, with recognition from the sport's world federation.
arxiv-2511-16632:
Nolan J. Coble, Min Ye, and Nicolas Delfosse address atom loss in long chains of trapped ions, a rare event with outsized damage. Losing one ion destabilizes the whole chain and every qubit it holds. Their fix combines three ingredients.

A quantum error-correcting code is spread across several chains. Special beacon qubits inside each chain detect when a chain has been lost. A decoder is adapted to repair the resulting erasures alongside ordinary circuit faults. Once beacons convert a chain loss into a located erasure, the code can correct it. Circuit-level simulations with a distributed bivariate bicycle code holding twelve logical qubits in seventy-two physical ones verify that the scheme corrects chain losses as designed.
arxiv-2511-16732:
So Chigusa and five co-authors propose hybrid-spin decoupling, a quantum sensing method that rejects magnetic noise while keeping sensitivity to a chosen steady field. Quantum sensors are so sensitive that stray fields become noise, and existing decoupling sequences mostly protect only narrow-band alternating signals.

The trick requires a cluster of spins where the target field and local magnetic fields act differently on each spin. Electron-nuclear spin pairs in diamond nitrogen-vacancy centers meet this condition and serve as the worked example. Against comagnetometers, the standing alternative, the method resists noise over a far wider frequency range, by orders of magnitude. The authors aim it at searches for light dark matter, with gradient sensing, quantum memory, and gyroscopes as further applications.
arxiv-2511-17132:
M. Bellazzini and six co-authors measure the distance to KK 153, a faint, gas-rich dwarf galaxy recently proposed as an unusually small member of its class. Using the Large Binocular Telescope in excellent seeing, they resolved the galaxy's outer regions into individual stars for the first time and reached its red giant branch. The brightness of that branch's tip is a standard distance marker in astronomy.

The new distance, about three million parsecs, is far more precise than the earlier estimate from a galaxy scaling relation, which had suggested a much nearer value. It places KK 153 clearly outside the Local Group. Combined with the galaxy's total brightness, it implies a modest stellar mass, still well above the faintest known gas-rich dwarfs. The authors discuss how cosmic reionization may have shaped its delayed star formation.
arxiv-2511-17232:
Bing Guo and Wanfeng Qi design new interpolation kernels for enlarging images. When an image is magnified, missing pixels must be filled by a kernel that blends known neighbors. The authors construct piecewise rational kernels supported on a small interval around each point: one novel cubic-over-linear kernel and five quartic-over-linear ones. All are symmetric and smooth to first order, with stated approximation orders, and the quartic family contains familiar cubic kernels as special cases.

Numerical tests compare the kernels on standard image quality measures covering peak signal fidelity, structural similarity, and feature similarity. One of the new quartic-over-linear kernels outperformed the widely used cubic interpolation kernel on all three. For software that resizes images routinely, the paper offers drop-in replacements with measurably better fidelity.
arxiv-2511-17332:
Virginia Dignum and Frank Dignum argue that today's agentic AI needs older ideas from the study of autonomous agents. Current systems promise lasting independence, reasoning, and contact with others, yet they often lack clear models of thought, teamwork, and control. The authors point to tools built over decades by the agents research community as the missing base.

Those tools include architectures that track beliefs, desires, and intentions, shared protocols for agent talk, design methods for markets and rules, and models of institutions. Blending them with modern learning systems, the authors argue, could yield agents that are not only capable but also open to inspection, cooperative, and answerable for their acts. The paper is a position piece aimed at both research camps.
arxiv-2511-17432:
Shrikant Kendre and five co-authors introduce SMILE, a metric for grading question-answering systems that tries not to be fooled by wording. Classic metrics score answers by overlapping word sequences, missing meaning; embedding-based metrics capture meaning but drop exact wording and cannot balance sentence-level against keyword-level agreement. Grading by a large language model works but is costly and inconsistent. SMILE combines the three ingredients: sentence-level semantics, keyword-level semantics, and easy keyword matching.

The composite balances lexical precision against semantic relevance, staying computationally light. Across text, image, and video question-answering benchmarks, SMILE's scores correlated strongly with human judgments. The authors present it as a practical middle path for evaluation. Benchmarks need to reward answers that are both correctly worded and genuinely right, without renting a frontier model to judge every response.
arxiv-2511-17532:
Xiaoqian Qi and six co-authors generate synthetic mobile network traffic at several scales at once with a diffusion model called ZoomDiff. Network planners need traffic estimates jointly across base stations, cells, and finer grids, but earlier generators worked at a single spatial or temporal resolution. ZoomDiff maps urban environmental context into traffic at multiple resolutions through a chain of customized denoising refinement diffusion models. Its stages add and remove noise in a way that matches the network's hierarchy.

Each stage of the progressive denoising produces traffic at a distinct resolution, aligning the generation process with the layered structure of real networks. On real-world mobile traffic datasets, ZoomDiff improved on the best baselines by at least about eighteen percent on multi-scale generation tasks. It also proved efficient and generalized across cities, suggesting a practical tool for planning and resource scheduling.
arxiv-2511-17732:
Birendra Dhanasingham, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, and Daniel Gilman explore whether neural methods can reveal dark matter clumps in strong gravitational lens images. Small halos along the line of sight and inside the main lens galaxy bend light in subtle ways that may differ between dark matter theories.

They train a neural estimator to infer lens and clump properties from images at once. Recovery of clump mass patterns proves hard, and two kinds of halo signals trade off against each other. The network also struggles with the pattern measures it targets, pointing to needs in training data and model form.
arxiv-2511-17932:
Yan Xu, Yixing Wang, and Stella Yu tackle building a three dimensional scene from only a few glimpsed views, so a camera can render new angles that were never photographed. They reframe the task as completing a natural video as the camera glides through the scene.

Their zero shot method uses a pretrained video diffusion model to imagine in between views, weighted by an uncertainty measure for spatial coherence. Those imagined frames then supervise a Gaussian splatting reconstruction, and geometry and generation improve each other in a loop. On four standard collections the method beats strong baselines under extreme sparsity, with no scene specific training.
arxiv-2511-18032:
Karl Dilcher and Christophe Vignat derive new infinite series involving central binomial coefficients, the large middle entries of Pascal's triangle, starting from powers of the arcsine function. They apply a general integral transform for power series to the arcsine and its first four positive powers.

Specializing the variable to simple values produces several families of series expansions for pi and some of its powers. They also discuss limit expressions and links with hypergeometric series, the broad family that unifies many classical series. The results add organized new classes to a classical area where such coefficient patterns recur across analysis and number theory.
arxiv-2511-18232:
Mingi Kang proposes a learning system that rebuilds MRI images from data gathered four times faster than usual. Fast scans matter because long sessions limit how many patients a scanner can serve and raise the chance of motion blur. Standard fast methods undersample the raw data and then reconstruct, but a leading approach needs precomputed maps of each receiver coil's sensitivity, which adds a step and a possible error source.

Kang's framework skips the separate maps: one module estimates them from the undersampled data itself, and a U-Net module rebuilds the image, trained end to end. Tests use multi-coil brain scans from ten subjects with eight echoes each. The rebuilt images come out visually smoother than the comparison method, the paper reports.
arxiv-2511-18432:
Serim Han, Jingru Zhang, and Hoseung Song detect shifts in data where each subject is measured more than once. Change point tests flag when a stream's pattern breaks. Most past tests merge repeat measures into a mean, which throws away how each subject varies on its own.

Their graph based test keeps both layers: change inside a subject and change across the group. Math approximations give fast p-values for the joint test score. Proofs show the test and its shift place stay sound as data grow. The method shines when the shift shows in only some subjects, a case mean based tests miss. It suits health and panel data where repeats are the norm.
arxiv-2511-18532:
Affan Khadir and 18 co-authors map the magnetic field inside the galaxy cluster Abell 3581 with background radio sources. A cluster's field twists the polarization of radio waves that pass through it, an effect coded in rotation measures. Past work had about ten sources per cluster, too few for a fine map.

The POSSUM survey's dense source grid yields over a hundred measures for this one cluster. The spread of values falls with radius out to a set reach, in line with a field and gas density that fade outward. Semi analytic field and density models are fit to the inner zone, with best fits pulled from the data. It is the first such dense probe of this cluster's field.
arxiv-2511-19032:
Xiangjie Sui and five co-authors show that image corruption can break a vision language model in ways its top answer hides. A blurred or noisy input may keep the same answer while its support thins, or flip a wrong answer right by luck. Top one accuracy alone cannot see either failure.

Bench-C is a controlled multiple choice testbed built from samples whose calls react to corruption. Nineteen corruption types at five strengths drive the tests. A new Robustness Alignment Score joins confidence and correctness with the direction of uncertainty. Correct and wrong starters are tracked apart, and flips are marked as passing or lasting across strengths. Across thirteen models, mild corruption shows a counter pattern the team report.
arxiv-2511-19132:
Mohammad Abboush, Ahmad Hatahet, and Andreas Rausch look at fault injection, a testing method that adds faults on purpose to check car software safety. Rules under the ISO 26262 standard require such tests during development. The weak point is cost: people must choose each fault type, place, and timing by hand, which grows slow and costly as systems get more complex.

The team instead asks large language models to write the fault test cases from written safety requirements. Several models are compared on sorting requirements and on building usable test cases. The version using GPT-4o performs best on both tasks, suggesting that model-written cases could cut manual work in real-time safety testing.
arxiv-2511-19232:
Christos-Nikolaos Zacharopoulos and Revekka Kyriakoglou hunt for where a causal language model first notices that a sentence has gone wrong in meaning. Their probe is named for the N400, a brain signal that fires on semantic violations. They feed the phi-2 model a curated set of sentences ending in plausible or implausible words. Then they inspect its hidden states layer by layer with two tools, starting with a simple linear decoder trained to spot the violation.

In the lowest third of layers the decoder can barely tell the endings apart, but its accuracy climbs sharply in the middle blocks and peaks just before the top. A second probe tracks the size of the space encoding the violation: it widens early, then collapses after a mid-stack bottleneck. The pattern sketches how a transformer localises a meaning error as depth increases.
arxiv-2511-19732: Sowmitra Das gives a method to build any Clifford operation on n qubits. The starting point is the stabilizer tableau of the inverse operation. The recipe uses extra ancilla qubits prepared in a simple state. It then applies controlled-Pauli gates. Next come measurements in the X basis. Single-qubit Pauli fixes, chosen from the results, finish the job. The gate count equals the weight of the tableau exactly. The depth grows only linearly with the number of qubits. That gives a new normal form for Clifford synthesis.
arxiv-2511-19832:
Aurelio Vivas and Harold Castro introduce nFlows, a runtime system for studying how scientific workflows are scheduled on modern supercomputers. Many such machines use non-uniform memory access, where memory speed depends on which part of the node a task runs on. Most older scheduling methods were built for grids and clouds and ignore this effect.

nFlows can model a workflow, run it on real hardware, simulate it, and check scheduling methods under these memory constraints. It accounts for fast and slow memory types, accelerators, and network cards tied to specific parts of a node. Researchers can use it to design memory-aware schedulers, track data movement, find bottlenecks, and test in-memory execution.
arxiv-2511-20032:
Jianfei Zhao, Feng Zhang, Xin Sun, Chong Feng, and Zhixing Tan present Vision-Guided Attention, a training-free cure for hallucination in multimodal models. Such models often invent objects because their visual attention localizes poorly. The authors notice the models can extract correct visual meaning from image tokens, yet fail to use that strength during later reasoning.

Their method first builds precise visual grounding from the semantic content of the visual tokens, then guides the model's focus toward the right regions. For captioning, the guidance updates during generation by suppressing regions already described. Each token needs only one forward pass, so the delay is negligible, and the method works with fast attention kernels. Benchmarks show top dehallucination results across several models.
arxiv-2511-20432:
Yang, Ji, Möller, and Ayas simulate laser melting of metal without drowning in mesh points. Their 2025 paper models laser powder bed fusion, a 3D printing method. A laser sweeps over metal powder, creating steep moving hot spots. Standard finite element methods need extremely fine meshes there. Costs explode as parts grow more complex. Their fix splits the temperature field in two.

An analytical point-source solution carries the laser's sharp heating. A smooth correction field then enforces the boundary conditions. Isogeometric analysis computes that correction with spline basis functions. Geometry is represented exactly, with no remeshing per scan. Tests near a curved boundary matched refined finite element results. Accuracy held with elements five times the laser spot radius. The finite element rival needed elements under half the spot size. Butterfly-shaped parts scanned cleanly with coarse meshes too. Orders of magnitude fewer degrees of freedom were required overall.
arxiv-2511-20532:
Zhang and a large team teach simulated animal bodies to replay real movements. Their 2025 paper introduces MIMIC-MJX, a framework for motor control modeling. Pose tracking now records animal behavior in rich detail. Trajectories alone, though, hide the muscle commands behind motion. The framework trains neural controllers to drive body models in physics simulation.

The controllers learn to reproduce recorded kinematic trajectories faithfully. Many muscle patterns can produce the same motion, an old redundancy puzzle. Physics grounding narrows that ambiguity toward plausible control. The implementation proved accurate across diverse animal body plans. Training needs only modest amounts of motion data. Simulated behavioral experiments become possible in silico. Researchers can perturb the body or controller and watch outcomes. Whole-brain wiring data could constrain future designs. Motor neuroscience gains a generative modeling tool.
arxiv-2511-20832:
Abdelkarim Kati, Florian Kerschbaum, and Marina Blanton tackle in 2025 a privacy trap in data preparation. Before analysis, missing or wrong values are imputed, filled in, to sharpen results. When data sits split across organisations, say hospitals holding different rows or columns of the same table. Ordinary imputation then exposes the very data private downstream analysis was meant to protect, voiding its guarantees. Their answer is the first optimised protocols for imputation that keep everything private.

The protocols reduce most computation to private set intersection and related primitives, which run fast. Across evaluated datasets, private imputation beat purely local imputation by 20 percent accuracy on average for vertically split data and 5 percent for horizontal splits. In the worst split observed, quality jumped up to 32.7 times vertically and 3.4 times horizontally. The protocols are quick: one imputation over 100,000 records took 2.4 seconds for vertical splits and 8.4 seconds for horizontal ones on a 10-gigabit network.
arxiv-2511-20932:
Vu Phan and Ilie Ugarcovici compute in 2025 how long a bingo game should last, on average. They generalise the classic game: cards are n by n, and each column draws its numbers from m possible values. The standard American card is the case n equals 5 and m equals 15, with its free centre space. A card can win through 2n plus 2 patterns: its rows, its columns, and two diagonals. Inclusion-exclusion over those patterns gives exact formulas for the distribution of the winning call.

Their main theorem: for fixed card size, the expected game length grows in a straight line as m, the column range, increases. Plots for 5 by 5 and 7 by 7 cards confirm two clean straight lines with distinct slopes. The dependence on card size n, by contrast, is nonlinear. The formulas let organisers predict game length for any variant, from classroom bingo to oversized promotional cards.
arxiv-2511-21332:
Mohammad Pouranvari studies in 2025 how loss interacts with localisation in a helical quantum chain. The system: spinless fermions with an Aubry-André quasiperiodic potential, a pattern that never quite repeats, plus long-range hops to partners N sites away, the helical twist. Such potentials trap particles: beyond a threshold strength they stop conducting. Pouranvari adds energy loss and pumping through Lindblad jump operators.

Using third quantisation, a method for open systems, he computes the Liouvillian rapidities, the rates at which disturbances decay. Layouts place the loss everywhere, at one site, at two sites, or as gain-loss pairs on partner sites. Uniform loss keeps a large gap that barely responds to the strength lambda. Sparse loss is fragile: its gap collapses as lambda traps particles away from the lossy sites. Strengthening the helical hop speeds relaxation by improving overlap with them. Level statistics, Poisson versus Wigner-Dyson, back the picture.
arxiv-2511-21832:
Alvarez and colleagues tackle one of the hardest measurements at the Large Hadron Collider: pairs of Higgs bosons decaying into four bottom quarks. This di-Higgs signal is tiny next to overwhelming background from ordinary strong-force processes, and computer simulations of that background are imperfect. Their answer is a Bayesian mixture model that weighs explanations by how well each fits the data.

The model estimates the signal and background amounts and their shapes directly in the region where the signal should appear, using a kinematic score plus per-jet flavour information. On test data with deliberate mismatches, it corrected biased starting guesses and gave calibrated 68 to 95 percent credible intervals for the signal count. It also beat simple cut-and-count counting methods at separating signal from background, measured by ROC and AUC scores.
arxiv-2511-21932:
Chandrasekhar and colleagues use quantum computing to spot intrusions in Internet of Things traffic, where classical detectors struggle with high-dimensional data. Their system first compresses traffic with a quantum autoencoder, a quantum circuit that squeezes data into a compact latent form while keeping the features that distinguish attacks. It then classifies the compressed data with a quantum support vector classifier using a trainable quantum kernel.

Tested on three intrusion datasets, Bot-IoT, IoT23, and KDD99, the combined model scored above 92 percent accuracy in noiseless simulation across all three in the reported results. Surprisingly, moderate depolarizing noise, a type of quantum error, acted like a regularizer and kept accuracy above 95 percent for most datasets under noise in their tests. On real IBM Quantum hardware, accuracy stayed above 83 percent despite calibration errors.
arxiv-2511-22032:
Kimoto, Masuda, Ohe, and colleagues in Japan experiment on the helimagnet MnAu2, a metal whose magnetic moments wind in a spiral, giving the material chirality, that can point two ways. They ask how electric current moves the domain walls between regions of opposite chirality, a question with bearing on low-power memory that stores information in spiral handedness instead of magnetization direction.

They start from a mixed multidomain state prepared in the laboratory. They find the current needed to sweep the sample into a single chirality is much lower than the current needed to flip a uniform state, within certain temperature and field ranges. Which chirality wins depends on whether field and current run parallel or antiparallel. Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert simulations reproduce the behavior, together indicating that domain walls in this helimagnet are highly mobile.
arxiv-2511-22132:
Chaudhuri, Fanelli, Li, and Zatorska, PDE analysts, rigorously justify the anelastic approximation for compressible fluids with degenerate, density-dependent viscosity. When sound waves are much faster than the flow itself, modelers filter them out with anelastic equations. Proving that solutions of the full compressible Navier-Stokes equations actually converge to the reduced system, especially when viscosity vanishes with density, is hard. The team revisits a 2023 result and removes its main crutch.

Using a relative-entropy framework built on kappa-entropy solutions, they prove convergence to the generalized anelastic system for well-prepared initial data in a periodic box. For general ill-prepared data, they prove convergence in the whole space via dispersive estimates for the acoustic waves. Crucially, the analysis works for the standard isentropic pressure law, eliminating the artificial cold-pressure term the earlier proof needed, the first such singular-limit result with degenerate viscosity needing no extra regularization.
arxiv-2511-22532:
Wang, Yu, and Tang add step-by-step reasoning to a driving model. Vision-language-action models steer end-to-end, mapping camera views and instructions to actions, but they reason about numbers and skip the steps traffic demands. Their CoT4AD framework trains the model to reason through a chain: perceive the scene, answer questions about it, predict what will happen, and only then choose an action. This aligns reasoning space with action space.

At driving time the model performs the reasoning implicitly, keeping its numerical estimates consistent and its decisions robust in changing environments. On the nuScenes benchmark and the Bench2Drive benchmark, CoT4AD reached state-of-the-art results in both open-loop testing, comparing trajectories to recorded ones, and closed-loop testing, where the model drives in simulation. The authors note the costs: multi-step reasoning is heavy, and training the planner can be unstable.
arxiv-2511-22732:
Piccirilli and an EMU-Euclid collaboration report the first cross-correlation between a radio survey and the Euclid telescope's galaxy catalogue. Cross-correlating radio-continuum sources with optical and near-infrared galaxies can pin down radio redshifts, suppress systematics, and test cosmological models. The team used EMU Main Survey data from the Australian SKA Pathfinder where it overlaps the 28 square degree Euclid Deep Field South in Euclid's Q1 release.

Building galaxy maps from two independent radio catalogues, using different source finders, and two Euclid photometric redshift samples, they measured the harmonic-space cross-correlation power spectrum. The signal is detected at significance consistently exceeding eight standard deviations across all models and datasets. Results from the two radio catalogues agree within one standard deviation, showing robustness to source-finding choices, and the amplitude matches fiducial cosmology predictions and an analysis using cosmic microwave background lensing. Cross-shot noise contributed negligibly.
arxiv-2511-22832:
Bopardikar, Wang, and Zou teach language models to decide record matches in stages, as a careful human would. Entity matching, deciding whether two records describe the same real-world thing, underpins data cleaning and integration; recent work prompts language models zero-shot or few-shot, usually in one step. The authors decompose the judgement into three explicit reasoning steps.

First the model identifies matched and unmatched tokens between the records, then determines which attributes matter most, and only then predicts match or no match. A second strategy stages a debate, contrasting arguments for and against, to harden the final call. Against multiple baselines on several real-world benchmarks, structured reasoning improved performance in several cases, though not uniformly. Reasoning structure, not just model size or examples, is a lever worth refining for data cleaning, they conclude.
arxiv-2511-23432:
Krolewski and colleagues measure the Hubble constant, the universe's present expansion rate, by a route that avoids standard rulers entirely and stays valid even if early dark energy modified the pre-recombination universe. Starting from today's photon density as an anchor, they chain the baryon-to-photon ratio from Big Bang nucleosynthesis and the baryon-to-matter ratio from galaxy clustering to get the physical matter density. They then divide by the measured matter fraction.

Using DESI DR1 data with the cosmic microwave background's angular acoustic scale and the latest nucleosynthesis constraints, they obtain a Hubble constant of 69.0 kilometers per second per megaparsec, with an uncertainty of 2.5 in the same units, sitting between the local ladder and early-universe values. The method was validated on mock simulations and noiseless theory vectors across both standard and early-dark-energy cosmologies before being applied to the data.
arxiv-2512-00032:
Giuseppe M. Sarda and four co-authors decouple control flow from data access in a RISC-V based GPGPU. The platform, Vortex, offers an open alternative to modeling frameworks built on commercial GPUs. The RISC-V movement for CPUs showed how openness can unlock fresh research directions.

Their redesign separates how instructions flow from how data are fetched inside the GPU. Cleaner separation can improve flexibility and performance studies alike. Open GPU platforms let researchers test ideas that closed hardware keeps out of reach. Fresh research directions are the platform's promise, echoing what open RISC-V designs unlocked for processor research.
arxiv-2512-00132:
How humans perceive color can be described with surprising mathematical depth. Roberto Leporini, Edoardo Provenzi, and Michel Berthier present an operational quantum information framework for studying color perception in a 2025 study. Their line of work builds on axiomatic treatments of color space going back to Schrödinger in 1920.

Later refinements, including Resnikoff's work in 1974, set the stage for recasting color attributes in quantum terms. Berthier, Provenzi, and their collaborators recently proposed that reformulation. An operational framework aims to make the theory testable in experiments, connecting abstract color geometry to what observers actually report seeing. The framework is meant for experiments, giving perception research a shared formal language. The aim is to give labs a shared way to test what the eye sees. The terms are clear ones that all sides can use, check, and trust in their work.
arxiv-2512-00232:
Multidimensional scaling turns tables of distances into maps of points, and the smacof program is a standard tool for it. Jan de Leeuw rewrites that program for square symmetric data in a 2025 study. The new version is one monolithic C program.

The rewrite covers metric and nonmetric versions, weighted and unweighted, in a single codebase. R handles data and parameter setup, input and output, and launches the computation through one call. Statisticians who maintain legacy scaling software gain a cleaner implementation that is easier to build, test, and trust. Smacof has decades of use behind it, so a clean rewrite preserves a trusted method. Square symmetric data appear in similarity studies across the social sciences.
arxiv-2512-00332:
AI assistants that call external tools across several turns can act on the world, which raises safety stakes. Daud Waqas, Aaryamaan Golthi, Erika Hayashida, and Huanzhi Mao study a vulnerability in such agents in 2025, which they call assertion-conditioned compliance. The agents serve business, medical, and financial operations.

Multi-turn pipelines remain hard to deploy in safety-critical industries because model resilience is still uncertain. A provenance-aware vulnerability means the agent's trust depends on where earlier claims in the conversation came from. Exposing how asserted statements can steer tool use helps designers harden assistants before they handle sensitive work. Provenance, knowing where a claim entered the conversation, is the defense the title highlights.
arxiv-2512-00532:
Teaching robots to manipulate objects may start with teaching models to imagine the manipulation first. Pang Ye presents image generation as a visual planner for robotic manipulation in 2025. Generating realistic manipulation videos is framed as a step toward unifying perception, planning, and action.

Video diffusion models need large domain-specific datasets and generalize poorly. Image generation models trained on language-image corpora show strong compositionality, including temporally coherent grid images that can stand in for plans. Using still-image generation as the planner could give embodied agents flexible plans without filming thousands of robot demonstrations. Grid images pack a sequence of poses into one picture a generator can produce at once.
arxiv-2512-00632:
William Swartworth, David Woodruff, and Samson Zhou work on streaming algorithms, where data flows past and cannot all be stored. Their 2025 paper concerns perfect sampling from a stream under a measure called Lp sampling. A sampler should pick an index with chance tied to the size of its entry.

An earlier method from Jayaram and Woodruff set up this kind of sampling for changing streams. Updates can add to or subtract from entries as the stream runs. Swartworth and his coauthors push for much faster updates, with time that grows very slowly as the stream grows. Fast sampling helps systems watch huge data flows in real time.
arxiv-2512-00832:
Cheng Zhang and six coauthors present PanFlow, a 2025 method for generating panoramic video. Panoramic video wraps a full scene around the viewer and feeds virtual reality and other immersive media. Making such video with AI has drawn growing interest, yet control over motion stays weak.

Existing methods often fail when scenes need large, complex movement. PanFlow decouples motion control, handling how things move separately from how they look. That split lets a creator steer movement more directly while the model fills in the scene. Better motion control could make generated panoramas feel less random and more directed.
arxiv-2512-00932:
Erick Duque wrote a 2025 paper on gravity with fermions in the Hamiltonian picture. Fermions are matter particles like electrons, and coupling them to gravity is a step toward quantum gravity. Duque works with the Einstein-Cartan system, where spacetime can twist as well as curve, in its canonical formulation.

The setup includes the cosmological constant, the Barbero-Immirzi parameter, and a non-minimal coupling constant. The result is a set of ten first-class constraints. Those constraints generate gauge transformations that match spacetime diffeomorphisms and local frame rotations when the equations of motion hold. A clean constraint structure is groundwork for quantization.
arxiv-2512-01132:
Luis Rodrigo Arnabal, Santiago Camara, and Cecilia Dassatti trace how global bank shocks reach emerging markets in a 2025 economics paper. When large global banks gain or lose net worth, their lending capacity changes worldwide. The authors ask how those shocks transmit into emerging market economies, from macro outcomes down to micro behavior.

Using an identification strategy based on high-frequency surprises to banks' credit-supply capacity, they find clear effects. Positive shocks appreciate local currencies, lower external borrowing costs, raise capital flows to domestic banks, and lift investment, credit, and real activity. The chain shows how distant bank health shapes local lives.
arxiv-2512-01232:
Donghao Huang, Shila Chew, Anna Dutkiewicz, and Zhaoxia Wang evaluate AI judges for software testing in a 2025 paper. Assessing test coverage at scale is a bottleneck in quality pipelines, since human review of every test is slow. Their framework, LLM-as-a-Judge, grades Gherkin acceptance tests with a rubric and structured JSON outputs.

The study compares many model configurations, including large commercial and open-weight models, across one hundred expert-annotated scripts with repeated runs. It analyzes accuracy, operational reliability, and cost together, which the authors describe as the first comprehensive study of its kind. Production-ready judging could speed up test review in large teams.
arxiv-2512-01332:
Warut Thawinrak counts whole-number points inside a family of shapes. The shapes are generalized permutohedra of type B. They link to mats, groups, and other core math ideas. A prior team found a count for type B from work on delta-matroids.

Thawinrak gives a shorter path to that count. His proof builds on the known frame for type A shapes set out by Postnikov. A short, clear count helps others use the shapes with less fuss. It also ties the type B case more tightly to the type A case that came before it.
arxiv-2512-01532:
Arpan Mukherjee and Mourad Sini justify a time-domain model for sound scattering by bubbles. Clusters of gas bubbles scatter sound in strong ways. The Foldy-Lax frame sums how waves bounce between bubbles. Dispersion, where tone sets speed, is built in through Minnaert resonance.

Their work gives a rigorous functional-analytic base for that frame. The model is cast as a delayed coupled wave system. Firm math lets engineers trust bubble-based lenses and shields. Such tools could steer sound in clinics and oceans with small, cheap parts. Minnaert resonance sets each bubble's ring tone, so a cluster's scatter can be tuned by bubble size in ways the model now predicts soundly.
arxiv-2512-01732:
Yan Huang and co-authors track gradients in distributed learning beyond scaffold methods. Local updates between communication rounds cut network cost. Data gaps across nodes pull local models apart, though. Local gradient noise adds more drift. Both effects move models from the global best.

Their unified spatio-temporal method tracks gradients across space and time. Tracking corrects drift while local steps continue. One frame covers both distributed and federated settings. Less drift means fewer rounds to reach a target, which saves bandwidth for edge and phone fleets. Spatio-temporal tracking reuses stale gradients with care, turning a known source of error into a signal that speeds convergence.
arxiv-2512-01932:
In the early universe, tiny quantum ripples grew into the seeds of galaxies, but somewhere along the way they started behaving classically. Louis Hamaide's 2025 paper studies that quantum-to-classical transition inside a two-field model of cosmic inflation, where one field drives expansion and another acts as an environment.

Hamaide finds a sharp divide based on the starting state. The standard Bunch-Davies vacuum is the only state that can fully recover its quantum purity, a process called recoherence. Every excited starting state keeps a permanent loss of purity instead. The result clarifies how the universe's initial conditions may still echo in what we observe.
arxiv-2512-02432:
Separating a singer's voice from its backing track is a solved problem in the studio dataset and a hard one in the wild, where genres and instruments keep changing. A 2025 paper studies continual learning for singing voice separation, letting users interact with the model and steer it toward better results.

Most earlier systems were frozen after training, however well they scored on their original data. Human-in-the-loop adaptation lets the model adjust when a new track's style drifts from its training. Interactive separation tools could serve remixers, archivists restoring old recordings, and accessibility applications that need the vocal line isolated.
arxiv-2512-02532:
Albert Saiapin and Kim Batselier work on faster stand ins for Gaussian process regression, a flexible but costly method. Tensor network methods offer a fix: they use a huge number of basis functions without a huge computing bill. Turning that trick into a fully probabilistic model raises fresh design problems, though.

Their 2025 study applies the Laplace approximation, a standard way to approximate a probability distribution, to tensor train kernel machines. The setting is system identification, where a model of a process is learned from data. A sound probabilistic version would give not just predictions, but honest uncertainty around them. With sound error bars, teams can trust the twin to guide real tests on new cell types.
arxiv-2512-02932:
Yancheng Zhang, Guangyu Sun, and Chen Chen blend two splatting styles to render new views that are both sharp and geometrically sound. Novel view synthesis rebuilds a scene so it can be seen from fresh angles. Three dimensional Gaussian splatting renders fast with fine appearance but can disagree across views.

Two dimensional splatting enforces multi view consistency at the cost of texture detail. EGGS makes the two exchangeable, seeking balance between geometry and appearance. Balanced rendering serves augmented and virtual reality and self driving simulation, where wrong geometry is as bad as blur. Sharp looks with true shape are the traits that sell a scan. One trait with no mate soon shows its flaw in use.
arxiv-2512-03032:
Konstantinos Chalas, Pasquale Calabrese, and Colin Rylands follow entanglement as it grows from states built of long distance pairs. In a crosscap state, spins at opposite sites of a lattice start locked in Bell pairs. Such states carry maximal bipartite entanglement from the first instant.

Multipodal states generalize that pattern to more partners per spin. The authors study how entanglement evolves after a quench from these states. Highly entangled starting points stress test theories of thermalization, showing how quantum information spreads and scrambles in many body systems. Start states with max links are the stress test of spread laws. A law that holds there will hold for the calm starts labs meet each day.
arxiv-2512-03232:
Nearby galaxy motions can pin down the expansion rate. A. Carr and a large team use DESI first-release data for that aim in this 2025 work. The release already holds relative distance measures for more than a hundred thousand galaxies.

The team's main task is to calibrate the zero-point of two distance relations. Those are the Fundamental Plane and Tully-Fisher relations. Once set, the relations let them measure the Hubble constant. A solid local measure is a key check on values from the early universe. Zero-point care is unglamorous but decisive, since a small offset shifts the final rate.
arxiv-2512-03332:
Earth's magnetic field near the Sun may flip in a local region. Rebecca Booth and a large team model that reversal in three dimensions in this 2025 work. They probe the large-scale Galactic field within a short span of the Sun.

The team uses survey data from the Dominion Radio Astrophysical Observatory in Canada. The survey maps magneto-ionic material across the northern sky. A three-dimensional model shows the geometry of the local field reversal. Knowing field shapes helps trace cosmic rays and starlight polarization across our neighborhood. Radio maps trace ionized gas, letting the team infer field direction across the local sky.
arxiv-2512-03632:
Robert Bird and colleagues model anchors dragging through seabeds to learn how deep they bite before snagging buried cables. Cable burial depth trades safety against the cost of putting cables in, and Britain's standard risk method may misjudge the danger. Their 2025 tool uses the material point method for the huge soil warping.

Jointed anchor rigs, long test pulls, and spin inertia all got upgrades. Spinning scaled anchors in a soil centrifuge, across sand types, checked the model well. The runs exposed flaws in the standard method, which may be too lax on sandy seabeds. Prediction for each real cable route is the practical pay-off.
arxiv-2512-03732:
Remanufacturing restores used products to as-new condition, cutting waste in a circular economy. Zhongxin Hu, Christina Imdahl, and Zümbül Atan ask which business model a manufacturer should choose for that work. Their 2025 preprint, also published in an operations research journal, puts consumer perception at the centre of pricing and production decisions.

Three options are compared: skipping remanufacturing, doing it in-house, or authorising an outside firm under contract. When buyers value restored products highly, in-house work wins on profit and environmental grounds, though restored goods then dominate the market. When perceived value is moderate and an outside partner raises the appeal of new products, authorised remanufacturing earns more but increases total environmental impact. The authors also find two-part contracts handle strict environmental rules better, and they assemble their findings into a step-by-step roadmap for managers.
arxiv-2512-03932:
Image restoration networks learn from ground truth photos, but real-world ground truth is itself imperfect, capped by how the data could be captured. Donghun Ryou and colleagues aim beyond that ceiling in a 2025 computer vision preprint. Their framework improves the reference images first, then trains against the improved versions.

A conditional generator learns frequency masks that blend each original reference with its super-resolved variants, keeping the frequencies that help and dropping the rest. This frequency-domain mixing preserves the scene's meaning while adding perceptual detail, without inventing artefacts that would hurt fidelity. The enhanced references then train a lightweight refinement network that plugs into existing models. Experiments and user studies both favour the approach. Gains come from both halves of the design: better supervision and the refinement step.
arxiv-2512-04132:
Toss two biased coins whose outcomes influence each other, and their joint behaviour needs a bivariate binomial distribution, an object with notoriously clumsy formulas in print. Bart Jacobs gives it a fresh formulation in a 2025 probability preprint, using the language of category theory. The two-coin becomes a single distribution over the four combined results, and dependence between the coins is built in from the start.

Within that clean setup, Jacobs derives its basic properties: mean, variance, and covariance. He covers behaviour under convolution, where independent copies combine. He also treats updating, in the style of Laplace's rule of succession. Expectation maximisation, he shows, can fit mixtures of these distributions to data. The paper concentrates on two coins for clarity. The generalisation to many coins, Jacobs notes, runs in a straightforward manner from the same definitions.
arxiv-2512-05132:
Wenshuo Wang and Fan Zhang name and attack a failure mode they call Scale Anchoring in weather-style forecasting. The setting is zero-shot super-resolution: train a model on coarse data, then ask it to forecast on a fine grid. Success has been judged by errors staying flat across resolutions, but a model standing in for a physics solver should improve as the grid refines. The authors argue low-resolution training caps the frequencies data can represent, so errors stay anchored at the coarse level.

Their remedy, Frequency Representation Learning, works with any architecture. It aligns frequency representations across resolutions and trains for consistency, so on finer grids the model's high-frequency response stays stable instead of collapsing. Errors then fall as resolution rises, and the enhanced models outperform baselines within the tested range, at modest cost. The work reframes what generalization should mean for learned simulators.
arxiv-2512-05232:
Soichiro Fujii and Stephen Lack develop the nerve construction for generalized multicategories, a meeting point of category theory and combinatorics. Starting from any category with a monad — a standard machine for adding structure — they define simplicial objects twisted by that monad. Each generalized category in Burroni's sense then yields such an object as its nerve, much as a plain category's nerve records its chains of arrows.

The nerve turns out to be fully faithful: no information is lost, and the authors pin down exactly which twisted simplicial objects arise this way, by a simple condition. The ambient category carries an enrichment over simplicial sets, which induces the hoped-for two-dimensional structure on the generalized categories themselves. They also study enriched limits and colimits on both sides. They prove that under mild finiteness assumptions, all in sight is locally finitely presentable, the backbone that makes these generalized categories workable.
arxiv-2512-05732:
Ippokratis Pantelidis, Korbinian Randl, and Aron Henriksson test a cheaper way to sort texts into categories with large language models. Prompting with examples works well, but long prompts cost money and time. A framework called CICLe pairs a light traditional classifier with conformal prediction. Together they narrow the list of plausible labels before the big model is asked, so prompts stay short and focused.

Earlier work showed the idea in a single domain. This study evaluates it across many standard classification benchmarks. CICLe beat its own base classifier consistently. It also beat plain few-shot prompting once enough training data existed, and matched it when data was scarce. Prompt shots fell by up to about a third, and prompt length by about a quarter. Smaller models could then compete with larger ones. The gains were largest on tasks with heavy class imbalance, where most sorting work sits.
arxiv-2512-06032:
Ranjan Sapkota, Konstantinos Roumeliotis, and Manoj Karkee explain why expertise in one famous segmentation model does not transfer to its successor. Segment Anything models cut objects out of images. SAM2 works from spatial prompts: a user clicks points, draws boxes, or supplies masks, and gets geometric, video aware segmentation. SAM3 changes the question entirely. It is concept driven: words or examples go in, and everything matching the concept comes out.

The analysis runs through five components. First, the conceptual break and the architectural divergence, in encoders, fusion, and ambiguity handling. Then the datasets, the training recipes that do not carry over, and the evaluation shift from geometric overlap to semantic measures. The message is humility. Mapping where the old intuition breaks helps the community retrain its instincts.
arxiv-2512-06232:
Ellen Su, Solim Legris, Todd Gureckis, and Mengye Ren ask whether AI learns the feel of physics the way a child does, just by watching the world. Children build a strong sense for how objects fall, roll, and bump long before school. Top video models, fed vast amounts of online video, still fail simple tests of that sense, which raises a question about what kind of video they need.

The team trained a video model on SAYCam, a set of head camera clips from three young children at home. The set is tiny next to the data behind top models, but it shows the world as a child sees it. Scores on a physics test barely moved. The authors argue that the fix will not come from more video or better matched video alone; the models themselves likely need new ways to learn how the physical world works.
arxiv-2512-06732:
Aarushi Wagh and Saniya Srivastava build a fairness test that catches bias language models hide in plain sight. Standard bias benchmarks name the sensitive trait outright: a religion, a race, a gender. Real talk rarely does. Bias leaks in through names, cultural cues, and traits that merely hint at the group, and tests that miss those hints leave a blind spot in fairness grading.

Their benchmark, ImplicitBBQ, extends a known question answering bias test by cueing protected traits implicitly across six categories. A leading model that handles the explicit version well lost accuracy on the implicit one, by up to several points in the sharpest category, with drops across most others. The gap means today's models carry implicit biases that explicit tests cannot see. The authors offer the benchmark as a sharper tool for anyone auditing language models for fairness.
arxiv-2512-06932:
Salma Albelali and Moataz Ahmed expose a quiet flaw that can make forecasting research look better than it is. Data leakage happens when sequences are built before the data are split for testing, letting future values sneak into training. Their study measures how much this flaw inflates the scores of LSTM forecasters, and how the choice of validation design changes the damage.

Three common designs are compared under leaky and clean versions of the same experiments. Ten-fold cross-validation suffered most, with error gains large enough to mislead at long forecast steps. Simple two-way and three-way splits stayed much closer to honest results. Window size and lag mattered too: small windows and long lags invited leakage, while larger windows reduced it. The authors urge builders of forecasting pipelines to design against leaks from the start, rather than trusting headline scores that hidden leakage may have padded.
arxiv-2512-07332:
Zhengquan Luo and co-authors let the space inside a knowledge graph bend to fit the graph itself. Knowledge graph embedding places entities in a geometric space so that distances encode facts. Standard methods pick one uniform geometry, flat, spherical, or saddle-shaped, for the whole graph. Real graphs, though, curve sharply in some neighborhoods and lie flat in others, and a single imposed shape distorts the distances everywhere it mismatches.

Their RicciKGE couples the embedding's training to a Ricci flow, a process that smooths a space's curvature over time. Entity positions and the surrounding geometry then evolve together, each adapting to the other. Theory backs the dance: with the coupling kept in bounds, every edge's curvature decays exponentially toward flatness. And the embedding distances converge strictly to a global optimum, the flattening and the learning promoting each other.
arxiv-2512-07532:
Saiyad Ashanujjaman, P. S. Bhupal Dev, Jihong Huang, and Shun Zhou wrote this 2025 particle physics paper. It concerns the type-II seesaw, a model that adds triplet Higgs particles to the standard picture. Direct searches at the Large Hadron Collider have ruled out much of that model's space.

One corner still hides from direct searches. There, charged triplet Higgs particles decay in cascades into their neutral partners and W bosons. The authors ask whether precision measurements can probe that corner indirectly. The known Higgs boson sometimes decays into two photons, and triplet particles can shift that rate. Current measurements agree with the standard model, but their error bars are still wide. Future machines should shrink those errors to well under one percent of the rate. The authors fold in all known constraints and test that forecast. Sub-percent precision, they find, would expose a large share of the hidden region.
arxiv-2512-07832:
Matteo Boglioni, Andrea Sgobbi, Gabriel Tavernini, Francesco Rita, Marius Mosbach, and Tiago Pimentel wrote this 2025 machine learning paper. A model's skill on unfamiliar data decides whether it can be deployed safely. Most studies test that skill on exactly one unfamiliar dataset.

Real deployment throws far more varied shifts at a model than one test set. The authors ask whether results on one shift predict results on another. They track model performance across many test sets during a fine-tuning run. Partial correlation then strips out plain in-domain performance from the comparison. What remains is whether generalization itself travels between test sets. Two model families, OLMo2 and OPT, supply the experimental subjects. No overarching trend appears in their results at all. Whether two test sets correlate positively or negatively depends on the model chosen. Generalization results, in short, do not automatically generalize.
arxiv-2512-07932:
Mohammed Hammam, Cyprian Lewandowski, Vladimir Dobrosavljevic, and Sandeep Joy wrote this 2025 physics paper. Wigner crystals, electrons frozen into a lattice by their own repulsion, are famously fragile. Long-range Coulomb forces frustrate them through a very soft shear mode.

That soft mode is gapless in a perfect, translation-invariant crystal. Disorder changes the story by breaking that clean symmetry. It pushes the soft excitations up in density and energy. The authors show the mechanism at work in explicit microscopic models. Disordered Wigner lattices then survive to far higher temperatures and densities. Disorder looks like a friend to the crystal's stability here. Melting in two dimensions, though, gets smeared out by the same disorder. Solid-like and liquid-like patches coexist across a broad range. Recent microscope experiments have seen exactly that patchwork behavior.  The answer, friend and foe, is both.
arxiv-2512-08032:
Arghavan Sanei, Chaima Amiri, Atefeh Shokrizadeh, and Jinghui Cheng, software engineering researchers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is usability discussion inside open source software projects, where volunteers often favor technical features over ease of use. They ask how argumentation shapes those discussions, and whether the arguments offered are any good.

The authors analyze argument discourse and quality across five open source projects. Usability threads turned out to be largely argument driven, but quality varied, and comments argued more weakly than the opening issue posts. Argument style and quality also changed how participants behaved afterward. The findings give project members practical guidance for building stronger cases for usability. They also speak to research on other distributed online communities where strangers must persuade each other.
arxiv-2512-08132:
Kyriakos Lotidis, Panayotis Mertikopoulos, Nicholas Bambos, and Jose Blanchet, researchers in game theory and learning, posted a long study on arXiv in December 2025. They ask how regularized learning behaves in games when randomness never goes away. With perfect information, play tends to settle at equilibrium. With lasting noise and a steady learning rate, their results say, it generally does not converge at all.

The authors analyze continuous and discrete time versions of learning in continuous games. In strongly monotone games, play can wander from equilibrium again and again, yet always returns nearby within a time they can estimate. Over the long run, play piles up sharply near equilibrium, and they measure how tight that pile up is. If the game is not strongly monotone, every one of these comforts can fail. The paper maps both the power and the limits of regularized learning under real uncertainty.
arxiv-2512-08532:
Oscar Kivinen, a mathematician, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. He defines a family of geometric spaces attached to a complex reductive Lie algebra. They generalize a classical object, the Hilbert scheme, which parametrizes points on the plane, with trigonometric and elliptic versions and companion isospectral varieties.

For these spaces he proves a localization theorem in the style of Gordon and Stafford, connecting their geometry to rational Cherednik algebras at equal parameters. He links the construction to a known correspondence involving affine Springer fibers, and works through concrete examples. He also conjectures that the torus fixed points of these spaces correspond exactly to two sided cells in the finite Weyl group. He proves the claim in types A, B, and C.
arxiv-2512-08732:
Udesh Habaraduwa and Andrei Lixandru use neural ordinary differential equations to simulate how metabolic pathways change over time. Predicting the behavior of living systems is central to health and bioengineering, yet turning rich multiomics data into useful models remains hard. Classic mechanistic models depend on prior knowledge, while data driven models can learn hidden links directly from measurements.

Their framework learns the joint dynamics of proteins and metabolites as a continuous process. It is tested on time series data from engineered bacteria, covering two production pathways. The neural model captures system dynamics far better than standard machine learning pipelines, with error reduced by more than nine tenths in both cases. It also runs inference far faster, by about a thousand fold. The authors present it as a scalable tool for metabolic engineering and discovery.
arxiv-2512-08932:
Schmidt, Thorngren, and Schlaufman study why hot Jupiter planets have larger radii than models predict. Many heating mechanisms have been proposed to explain that inflation. Past work shows such planets reinflate as their host stars brighten, which points to deep heating, yet young hot Jupiters also show delayed cooling that suggests heating closer to the surface.

The authors extend their thermal evolution model with a parameter that allows both deep heating and delayed cooling at once. They fit the model to a uniform, self consistent catalog of hot Jupiter systems inside a hierarchical Bayesian framework. Results show interior cooling rates are reduced dramatically compared with simpler anomalous heating models. The most plausible cause is substantial shallow heating just below the boundary between radiative and convective zones. That heating, from electrical dissipation or temperature transport, would let planets reinflate with much weaker deep heating. Predictions for circulation signals follow.
arxiv-2512-09032:
Finian Ashmead and coauthors study how to compress the relation between galaxy colors and redshift. Spectroscopic redshifts are essential for training and calibration, but they sample the galaxy population in a biased and sparse way. Grid based maps from color to redshift struggle under that bias.

Instead, the team uses a manifold learning method to compress a many band color space into a thin, densely sampled manifold. Redshift and star formation rate vary smoothly and almost independently across that manifold. They compare redshift prediction from a self organizing map, from nearest neighbors, and from nearest neighbors in raw color space. With a representative training set, the compressed method gives smaller scatter and fewer outliers. With a highly biased spectroscopic set, it keeps its performance while other methods degrade badly, especially at high redshift. The physical trends across the manifold support interpolation into poorly sampled regions.
arxiv-2512-09332:
Mahabba El Sahili and Ayman El Zein work on tournaments, a graph theory model in which every pair of players meets once and each match has a winner. A classic theorem of Havet and Thomassé says that any large enough tournament contains every oriented Hamiltonian path. Such a path visits every vertex once, in any prescribed pattern of forward and backward steps.

A recent result strengthened this: in any such tournament, some single arc can be deleted while keeping every oriented Hamiltonian path. El Sahili and El Zein ask the harder stability question: does the property survive deleting an arbitrary arc, not just a well-chosen one? They prove the answer is yes for every arc in any tournament with at least eight vertices, apart from some explicitly described exceptional cases. The paper closes the gap between the chosen-arc result and full stability under arc deletion.
arxiv-2512-09432:
Min Liu and colleagues study pinching-antenna systems, a new wireless idea. Antennas can be pinched onto a waveguide at chosen spots, letting the network reshape its channels flexibly. Their problem is joint localization and channel estimation for the uplink, where many users transmit at once and multipath reflections smear the signals in time.

They first build a multi-user model for the system using orthogonal frequency division multiplexing. A cyclic prefix turns the time-domain smearing into a set of overlapping sinusoids in frequency. Their inference framework then separates users with expectation propagation. It extracts path delays with matching pursuit or a hybrid message-passing method, and refines positions using the geometry those delays imply, feeding improved channels back into the loop. They also derive the Cramer-Rao lower bound, the accuracy limit. Simulations approach that bound, matching cooperative multi-base-station localization with far fewer radio chains.
arxiv-2512-09532:
Vladimir Rovenski develops a classic technique inside Einstein's non-symmetric geometry, a setting Einstein himself explored late in his career. There the main tensor splits into a symmetric part, the usual Riemannian metric, and a non-symmetric part. A connection with torsion comes with it, tied to the tensor by a compatibility condition. Bochner's technique, which turns integral identities into vanishing theorems, had not been set up in this setting.

Guided by a construction from Lie algebroid theory, Rovenski defines the basic objects of Bochner's technique for this geometry and gives a clear example of the Einstein connection it requires. He proves a Weitzenböck-type decomposition formula, which splits a Laplacian into a rough part plus curvature terms. From it he obtains vanishing results about the null spaces of the Bochner and Hodge type Laplacians, showing that under fitting conditions certain harmonic objects cannot exist.
arxiv-2512-09632:
Gustavo R. Ferreira studies Baker domains, regions where the iterates of a transcendental entire function march off to infinity, in a doubly parabolic form. Complex dynamics studies the long-term behavior of iterated functions, and escaping attracting orbits pose a subtle limit case: an attracting fixed point whose pull weakens as it drifts away.

Ferreira shows that if an attracting fixed point escapes to infinity while its multiplier, the number measuring its pull, tends to one. Then the limiting function possesses a doubly parabolic Baker domain, invariant under the function. The converse also holds. Any function with such a domain can be approximated, locally uniformly, by functions in its quasiconformal equivalence class. Those have an attracting fixed point with multiplier tending to one. The two results together characterize these Baker domains as the limits of vanishing attracting cycles, tying an abstract Fatou component to a concrete process.
arxiv-2512-09732:
Anastasios Apsemidis, Dimitris Mavridis, and Nikolaos Demiris develop a network meta-analysis method that compares treatments by the outcome decisions care about: mean survival. Network meta-analysis combines direct and indirect evidence across many trials. It is usually run on stand-ins for mean survival, such as hazard ratios or restricted mean survival times. Those carry their own problems, like assuming proportional hazards or being limited by short follow-up.

Their Bayesian framework targets mean survival. Because observed survival curves end before patients do, the method extends them using techniques that fold in data from death projections. Flexible poly-hazard parametric models and spline-based options provide extensions. A test study compares the statistical efficiency of these options, and the methods are applied to two datasets. The framework is set up for cost-effectiveness work, where costs can be added and the best one picked within a decision setup.
arxiv-2512-09832:
Vittorio Cipriani and four coauthors draw a sharp dividing line for families of countable graphs. Each family they study bans one fixed finite graph from appearing as an induced subgraph, meaning as an exact pattern on a chosen set of vertices. The question is how complicated such a family can be. Their main result is a dichotomy, an either or split, controlled by a single small graph: the path on four vertices.

If the banned graph does not fit inside that four vertex path, the family is as complicated as possible. Its members show the full range of structural and computational behavior, in the sense of effective bi-interpretability. If the banned graph fits inside the path, the family is structurally simple, and every member meets a computable embeddability condition. The same split appears for finite graphs, where isomorphism is either complete for the class or solvable quickly.
