arxiv-2512-10032:
Jan Marco Ruiz de Vargas, Kirtan Padh, and Niki Kilbertus use grouped background knowledge to give causal discovery a head start. Causal discovery algorithms try to recover cause and effect graphs from data alone, and they struggle in high dimensions. Prior knowledge can help, but the usual form, tiers of variables ordered in layers, is rigid. Cluster-DAGs instead group variables into clusters with a graph between the groups. The authors show this format is more flexible than tiered knowledge. They adapt two standard constraint based algorithms to use it, one for fully observed systems and one for partially observed ones.

The modified algorithms, Cluster-PC and Cluster-FCI, begin the search already respecting the cluster structure. On simulated data, both beat their knowledge free baselines. Cluster-DAGs capture the rough groupings scientists often know without knowing exact arrows.
arxiv-2512-10132:
Logan Nye generalizes a classic space saving trick for reconstructing the answer to a dynamic program. Hirschberg's 1975 algorithm recovered a longest common subsequence using linear space instead of quadratic, by recursive midpoint bisection. The puzzle was whether that economy was a quirk of grids. Nye models dynamic programs as deterministic evolution over a directed acyclic graph with a frontier of limited width. Under mild conditions, any such program admits traceback in space growing with frontier width times a log factor.

The construction replaces backward passes with forward only recomputation, organized into a height compressed recursion tree. Its nodes expose small middle frontiers that every optimal path must cross. Near optimal bounds follow for sequence alignment, one dimensional recurrences, and dynamic programs on graphs of bounded pathwidth. Nye also proves a matching style lower bound: in forward single pass models, the width term cannot be avoided.
arxiv-2512-10532:
Gabriel Cipriani Huete and co-authors study how well two parties can find a maximum matching in a graph when the edges are split between them and only one message is allowed. Their setting is semi-robust: the edges of one true maximum matching are scattered at random. But every other edge is placed by an adversary trying to make the task hard.

Against that setup, a strikingly simple protocol does well. Alice just sends Bob the lexicographically first maximum matching of her own edges. And the authors prove this reaches three quarters of the optimal matching in expectation, with an analysis they show is tight. The same protocol gives the same guarantee in the fully robust setting, though an example they construct shows it cannot beat the more involved state-of-the-art method there.
arxiv-2512-10832:
Karel Pärlin and co-authors tune the learning speed of a channel estimator for offset-plagued wireless links. The FO-LMS algorithm estimates a channel while compensating carrier and sampling frequency offsets, given a training signal the receiver knows in advance. It updates its channel and offset estimates by stochastic gradient descent, and the step sizes of those updates decide how fast it learns and whether it stays stable.

Within the stable range, step size is a trade: large steps track a channel quickly but let noise push the estimate around. The authors derive formulas that predict and optimise the tracking and misadjustment errors when the channel's time variation is known. Since that is rarely true in practice, they also propose a scheme that adapts the step sizes from the algorithm's own observed performance. Simulations confirm this and show the variable-step version behaving as designed.
arxiv-2512-11332:
Sara Sameer and colleagues present Pace, a neural network that estimates battery health while respecting battery physics. Batteries in electric vehicles and grid storage need accurate health tracking for safety, cost, and sustainability. Purely data driven models can miss the electrical behaviour that drives ageing.

Pace feeds both raw sensor measurements and physics features drawn from an equivalent circuit model of the battery. Three purpose built components encode time patterns efficiently at several scales, attend to context in chunks, and blend short and long term degradation signals through a two headed output. On a large public dataset it beat the best existing models by clear margins. The team also ran it in real time on a small Raspberry Pi computer, showing the method is practical for on device battery analytics rather than only laboratory use.
arxiv-2512-11432:
Abdelhafed El Khadiri examines a converse question about a classical theorem in smooth analysis, using the Hawaiian earring as a test case. The earring is a famous shape made of infinitely many circles shrinking toward and tangent at one point. René Thom proved that zero sets of sufficiently well behaved ideals of smooth functions contain many smooth points. El Khadiri asks whether the reverse implication holds.

He analyses what blocks such a converse and identifies geometric conditions under which it fails. Any smooth function of two variables vanishing exactly on the Hawaiian earring must be flat at the origin, meaning every derivative vanishes there, a strong degeneracy forced by the infinitely accumulating circles. From this he formulates a criterion about families of smooth arcs tangent at a point with wildly varying curvature. A weakened form of the Łojasiewicz inequality, adapted to this non analytic setting, follows from the analysis.
arxiv-2512-11532:
Chong Tang, Hao Dai, and Jagmohan Chauhan present Parallax, a runtime that speeds up neural networks on phones and edge devices when parts of a model cannot run on the local accelerator. Specialised chips handle most layers, but dynamic control flow and unsupported operations fall back to the main processor. Existing frameworks manage those fallbacks badly, leaving processor cores idle while latency and memory spike.

Parallax first partitions the computation graph to expose work that can run in parallel across branches. A branch aware memory manager uses dedicated arenas and reuses buffers to keep the footprint in check. An adaptive scheduler then runs branches within each device's memory limits, with fine grained control for dynamic models. Across five representative networks and three mobile devices, latency fell by up to nearly half, energy use dropped meaningfully, and memory overhead stayed controlled. No model rewriting or custom operators are required.
arxiv-2512-11732:
Trisha Dawn and Yang Ni build a method to map how gene control networks change across a tissue. New spatial tools read gene activity with location tags, so researchers can ask how wiring varies by region. Most graph models ban loops, yet gene control is full of feedback loops.

Their method, BNP-DCGx, learns directed cyclic graphs that can hold loops while staying stable. A random partition layer splits space into clusters, each with its own graph, and averaging smooths the changes across space. A fast sampling algorithm does the fitting. On human brain cortex data the method found region specific networks with loops and hinted at new cell subtypes.
arxiv-2512-11832:
Jakub Walczak compares three ways to fill gaps in sparse climate station data. The rivals are inverse distance weighting, a plain method that trusts near stations most; ordinary kriging, a stats based standard; and an implicit neural model called MMGN. All three were tuned fairly on validation splits.

Across 100 random sparse samples from the ECA&D database, the plain method won on both accuracy and speed. It posted the lowest errors, with RMSE of 3.00 and MAE of 1.32, and the highest fit score, R squared of 0.68. The gaps were statistically firm with fair to large effect sizes. The result is a useful humbling: tuned simple tools can beat fancy ones on real climate data.
arxiv-2512-11932:
Urjjarani Patel and KVS Shiv Chaitanya apply Thermofield Dynamics to track entanglement in noisy quantum systems. Open systems leak energy and phase to their surroundings, and their master equations are hard to solve for general starting states. Thermofield Dynamics rewrites such an equation as a Schrödinger like one, which is easier to handle.

With a Hartree-Fock approximation, the pair solve two noisy systems in closed form. They then read entanglement and mutual information from the eigenvalues of a covariance matrix. Two mode and single mode squeezed states serve as test cases. The method gives a cleaner route to predicting how fast quantum links decay in real, imperfect hardware.
arxiv-2512-12032:
Eddy de Leon, Joerg Frauendiener, and Christian Klein trace light rays through a spacetime holding two black holes at once. The double Schwarzschild solution is an exact static answer to Einstein equations for two holes. A singular strut, the Weyl strut, holds them apart against their mutual pull.

Ray tracing shows the strut bends light the opposite way from the holes: it defocuses rays while holes focus them. Widely separated holes behave much like a single hole for passing light. Close holes, though, show strongly changed ray patterns thanks to the strut. The study clarifies what an observer would actually see near such an exotic pair, strut shadow and all.
arxiv-2512-12532:
Duc A Tran, Dung Truong, and Duy Le tackle server placement for mobile edge computing in a 2025 paper. Edge servers must sit near users to cut delay, but planners do not know future workloads per cell, and server capacity varies too. Goals pull both ways: process as much work at the edge as possible while keeping communication costs between cells and servers low.

They frame placement and cell assignment as a stochastic bilevel optimization, shown to be strongly NP-hard and new to the literature. Approximating the objective with submodular functions lets greedy algorithms do the heavy lifting. On real world data, their method beat alternatives by as much as 55 percent.
arxiv-2512-12732:
Georgy Ishmaev, Emmanuelle Anceaume, Davide Frey, and Francois Taiani analyze ethical risks in Layer 2 rollups in a 2025 paper. Rollups move blockchain work off the main chain to raise throughput and cut fees, but they hand power back to operators, creating user risk through discretion and information gaps. The authors ask which designs make that risk ethically problematic.

They adapt Ethical Risk Analysis to rollup design, build a taxonomy of decision authority, and test it against a snapshot of 129 projects from L2BEAT plus incidents from 2022 to 2025. Instant upgrades with no exit window appeared in about 86 percent of projects, and proposer controls that can freeze withdrawals in about 50 percent. Incidents clustered around sequencer liveness and inclusion.
arxiv-2512-12932:
Yifan Wu and co-authors ask whether the huge data sets used to pre-train biological foundation models can be trimmed. These models learn from DNA, RNA, or protein sequences, but training can take millions or billions of examples. That cost blocks many labs from repeating or extending the work.

Their pruning method rates how much each example shapes the model, then keeps the most useful ones. On two named models, for RNA and for proteins, the kept sets beat random sets by a wide margin. Even after cutting over 99 percent of the data, results held up well. A kept set could beat a random set ten times its size.
arxiv-2512-13532:
Anshima Singh and David J. Silvester present a sampling method to find stability borders in fluid flow with less computing. Their work builds on a classifier network trained to tell split flow regimes from steady ones. The new step adds adaptivity, so sampling improves as the search goes on.

A classifier maps flow settings to a chance of splitting, and its entropy flags uncertain regions. A model called KRnet then places new samples where that doubt is high, near the border itself. Starting from an even spread, the method finds the border with far fewer Navier-Stokes runs. The authors present it as a base for larger stability studies.
arxiv-2512-13932:
Ming-Yang Zhuang and co-authors report the first clear case of cold gas delivered to a brightest group galaxy by a gas-rich minor merger. Dust and cold gas are common in early-type galaxies, but their origin has been debated for decades. Gas-rich minor mergers were a leading suspect, with little direct evidence in groups and clusters.

With high-resolution JWST imaging, they catch an ongoing merger at redshift 0.25 with a mass ratio near 1 to 56. A heavily obscured, low-mass satellite is being stripped, laying down prominent dust lanes of about 10 kiloparsecs on the central galaxy. Simulations suggest such events involve gas-rich satellites on first infall with eccentric orbits. The result supports minor mergers as a key refueling channel.
arxiv-2512-14132:
Krishnan Suryanarayanan and Harmeet Singh present a 2025 theory of elastic tubes that cannot pass through themselves. They study tubes with a round cross section, using a simpler reduced model rather than tracking every point in three dimensions.

The rule against self penetration becomes part of a variational scheme, a math method that finds shapes by minimizing energy. From it they derive the full governing equations, jump conditions, and boundary conditions. When the rule is active, tube shapes join standard Kirchhoff rod segments to segments of constant Frenet curvature. Three cases show the idea at work: two tubes hanging under their own weight, and one highly twisted tube.
arxiv-2512-14232:
Rawan Alyahya and six coauthors seek a non invasive test for a key gene marker in glioblastoma in a 2025 paper. Methylation of the MGMT promoter affects how well chemotherapy works for this brain cancer, but checking it now needs invasive tumor tissue from a biopsy.

Their method reads MRI scans with deep learning in a multi view approach that uses spatial links between the three scan views. It avoids full 3D models, which are slow and memory heavy. A new tumor slice extraction step beats older methods on several metrics. Compared with state of the art models, their approach works well, and they share a reproducible pipeline to support robust diagnostic tools.
arxiv-2512-14332:
Yannis Belkhiter, Seshu Tirupathi, Giulio Zizzo, and John Kelleher present Step Tagging in a 2025 paper on language reasoning models. Such models can reason longer and more accurately than before, but they waste tokens on excess verification and reflection steps.

Step Tagging is a light sentence classifier that labels each reasoning step by type as the model generates it. A new taxonomy, ReasonType, defines the step kinds to monitor. Watching step counts online gives clear early stopping rules for inference. On three open source reasoning models and benchmarks like MATH500, GSM8K, AIME, GPQA, and MMLU Pro, the method cut token use by 20 to 50 percent. Accuracy stayed comparable to standard generation, with the largest gains on heavy tasks.
arxiv-2512-14532:
Marco Laudato speeds up simulations of odd-shaped particles drifting in slow, viscous flow. Computing exactly how each spheroid or helical particle twists and stresses the fluid is reliable but slow, which blocks studies with many particles. He generated careful reference data with a boundary element solver, checked against classic formulas where those exist.

A neural network then learned to imitate the solver, reading the local flow and particle pose and answering almost instantly. Typical errors stayed under one percent for the stress measure across fresh test cases. Plugged into larger suspension codes, the surrogate makes big studies of particle microstructure and flow behavior practical.
arxiv-2512-14732:
Idan Tankel and four co-authors tackle the extra findings that abdominal CT scans often turn up. Such findings are often benign, yet some carry serious clinical weight and should be reported under set guidelines. Manual review by radiologists is slow and variable.

Their framework, INFORM-CT, joins large language models with foundation vision-language models in a plan-and-execute agentic approach. It aims to make detection, classification, and reporting of these findings faster and more precise. A more consistent pipeline could help radiologists keep follow-up care from slipping through the cracks when a scan reveals something unexpected.
arxiv-2512-15232:
Guillaume Koechlin and six coauthors split a national power grid's total load into the sectors that cause it. Knowing how much homes, services, and industry each draw is key to flexible demand, which helps fit variable renewable power. At regional and national scale, though, end use data is costly and scarce.

Their blind source separation framework works on open high voltage load measurements alone. It uses a constrained form of non negative matrix factorization, where prior knowledge enters as linear constraints on the factors, giving weak supervision. On Italian national load data from 2021 to 2023, the method recovered residential, services, and industrial components. Its monthly sector estimates matched reported statistics. The approach should transfer to other grid scales where direct sector measurements are missing.
arxiv-2512-15532:
Ken O'Hanlon and co authors propose QSCNet, a conditioned UNet for music source separation, in a 2025 paper. Source separation splits a mixed recording into individual instrument stems. Most systems output a fixed list of stems, while conditioned systems take an audio query naming the sound to extract, which suits real collections better.

A prior method, Banquet, used a different network type, and its authors argued UNets should not suit conditioned separation. QSCNet counters that claim by adding conditioning elements to a sparse compressed UNet design. On a couple of separation tasks it beats Banquet by over 1 decibel in signal to noise ratio, while using less than half as many parameters.
arxiv-2512-15632:
Ian Maquignaz presents AllSky, a physically based sky model for image based lighting, in a 2025 paper. Environment maps light rendered outdoor scenes, and recent learned sky models can look good while lighting a scene with wrong tones and shadows. The full dynamic range of outdoor light spans about 22 f-stops, which learned models rarely match.

AllSky is learned directly from physically captured high dynamic range imagery. Users can place the sun and clouds by hand, extending current control. In the author's proposed evaluation, existing learned sky models prove not interchangeable with captured imagery or parametric models. AllSky reaches state of the art sky model performance under that test.
arxiv-2512-15732:
Yijia Chen presents a post mortem of Galaxy Empire, a hybrid deep learning and evolutionary trading system, in a 2025 paper, dated December 5. Combining deep reinforcement learning with evolutionary computation is often called the holy grail of algorithmic trading. This study documents how that promise failed in live high frequency cryptocurrency markets.

A population of 500 autonomous agents paired LSTM and transformer perception with a genetic survival rule. Validation returns topped 300 percent yearly, yet live capital fell by over 70 percent. Chen names three failure modes: overfitting random noise, survivor bias in evolutionary selection, and microstructure friction that cannot be beaten without order flow data. Complexity without an information edge added fragility.
arxiv-2512-15932:
Ping-Rui Tsai and Tzay-Ming Hong propose a dough like model for double slit phenomena in a 2025 paper. The double slit experiment shows interference fringes that express quantum superposition, yet what happens to one particle before and after measurement stays conceptually puzzling. Copenhagen style collapse contrasts sharply with smooth wave evolution.

Their Double Slit Diffraction Surrogate Model, built with deep learning, learns the mapping between wave functions and probability distributions. It explores many propagation paths and selects transmission channels by gradient descent. The authors compare this with a physical analogy: the particle stretches like dough across both slits and reconnects after passing. Monte Carlo simulations reproduce the characteristic interference patterns.
arxiv-2512-16232:
Xin Wang and Zhao-Min Gao design a quantum platform in an arXiv paper from 2025. Giant atoms are artificial atoms that touch a waveguide at several points, so their waves can interfere and cancel out decay. Parametric amplification, which squeezes a field, can strengthen interactions but usually adds noise that speeds up decoherence.

The authors combine the two: giant atoms coupled to a traveling-wave parametric waveguide with a chi-two nonlinearity. Careful interference makes the atom-atom interaction much stronger while shielding it from the squeezed noise. Unlike plain waveguide setups, the atoms show both exchange and pairing interactions, ideal for simulating many-body quantum systems. Turning the squeezing and coupling knobs tunes both interaction strengths smoothly. The proposal offers a scalable test bed for strongly correlated quantum physics.
arxiv-2512-16432:
Nils Foix-Colonier and Sebastien Bourguignon speed up a signal separation task in research shared on arXiv in 2025. Spectral unmixing splits a measured spectrum into pure ingredients and their shares, called abundances. Shares must be nonnegative and sum to one, which makes the problem a convex optimization, and answers tend to be sparse.

Generic solvers waste effort on such problems, so the authors design a dedicated active-set algorithm. Active-set methods guess which ingredients are present and solve only for those, refining the guess as they go. The design extends plain nonnegativity to broader minimum abundance constraints, letting users require a floor share for some ingredients. The paper aims at supervised unmixing with large dictionaries, where a tailored solver should beat off-the-shelf optimization on speed.
arxiv-2512-16632:
Lionel Barnett and coauthors fix a flaw in Granger causality maps for Langevin systems, which are noisy systems that drift and jitter at once. Such maps show, point by point in phase space, how much one part of a system helps predict another.

Older maps sampled the local linear models at set time steps, a slow method that broke down where local motion was unstable, leaving holes. The team derives a direct formula for the causal rate that works even in unstable zones. The job then shrinks to solving Riccati equations, or plain quadratics for a single source. They also show the rate does not change when noise strength is scaled.
arxiv-2512-16832:
Aditya Yadavalli and coauthors measure how meaning splits between the sound of speech and its words. Prosody, the melody of speech, carries much that text drops, and the team asks how much, and about what.

Using large speech and language models, they estimate mutual information between a meaning trait, such as emotion or sarcasm, and each channel, audio or text. On speech from TV and podcasts, audio carried over ten times more information about sarcasm and emotion than text alone, when wider context was withheld. For questionhood, prosody added far less. The work sets up a program to map more meaning types, channels, and languages the same way.
arxiv-2512-16932:
Caili Jia and Yong Lu prove a spectral condition for a graph to hold an even factor, a spanning subgraph where every vertex has a nonzero even degree. A minimum degree of at least two is clearly needed, and the authors ask what stronger sign, read from the graph spectrum, suffices.

Their sign uses the A-alpha spectral radius, a blend of adjacency and degree data that shifts with a parameter alpha. For a connected graph with a given minimum degree, they set a lower bound on that radius that forces an even factor to exist. Spectral tests like this let large graphs be checked from a few computed values.
arxiv-2512-17932:
Yang Xiao wrote this master's project report at Nanyang Technological University on sound sorting that keeps learning on small devices. A phone or earbud that learns new sound classes often forgets old ones, a failure called catastrophic forgetting. Memory and power limits make the fix hard.

The proposed method keeps a diverse set of past examples, picked by how unsure the model is about each one. Tricks like data tweaks and a teaching loss stretch the small memory further. On a spoken command data set the method beat the best rival by 4.2 points of average accuracy while using less memory. It also led on two sound scene data sets.
arxiv-2512-18632:
Ni Ding and three coauthors study data privacy for shared databases in a 2025 paper. They work in the pufferfish privacy framework, which generalizes differential privacy by naming the secrets to protect. Each user in a multi-user system reports a random value, and Laplace noise is added to aggregate query answers. The question is how to size that noise so one person's data stays indistinguishable when they change their value, leave, or are replaced.

Using the Kantorovich method with the Wasserstein metric, the authors derive sufficient conditions for four sets of secret pairs. They find that protection for a person depends only on that person's own statistics. For binary data, the conditions relax further, cutting noise and improving data utility.
arxiv-2512-18832:
Yixia Li and nine co-authors ask whether a large language model can quietly act as a world model, imagining how a text-based environment responds to actions. Agents learn faster with simulated experience, but real environments are limited and hard to scale. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, grades LLM world models on three levels: fidelity and consistency, scalability and robustness, and actual usefulness to agents.

Across five text environments, well-trained world models keep a coherent hidden state and grow predictably with more data and size. They help agents by verifying actions, inventing extra practice trajectories, and warm-starting reinforcement learning. But the gains hinge on how widely the training behavior ranges and how complex the world is. The study draws a clear boundary around when a language model can stand in for reality.
arxiv-2512-19032:
Ran Li, Pan Xiao, Kaushik Dutta, and Youdong Guo automate a slow step in brain imaging: marking which neurons are active in calcium recordings. Their data come from light sheet microscopy and span space plus time, so each record is four-dimensional. Hand marking is slow and does not scale to large studies.

Their Bayesian deep learning method joins a mean summary image with maps of how pixels vary together over time. It outputs a probability map for active neurons and also states its own uncertainty. Scores against reference masks were strong, and repeat runs agreed closely. The method could speed studies that link neuron activity to behavior.
arxiv-2512-19432:
Quyu Kong, Xu Zhang, Zhenyu Yang, and Nolan Gao introduce MobileWorld, a harder benchmark for phone-using AI agents. The dominant AndroidWorld test is saturating, with top agents passing nine tasks in ten. Real phone use is messier: vague instructions, shopping and work apps, and work that hops between apps.

MobileWorld holds two hundred one tasks across twenty apps, built on open-source stand-ins for real services so scoring stays reproducible. Tasks run nearly twice as long as AndroidWorld's on average, and most span several apps. The authors present the set as a production-grade yet checkable yardstick for autonomous mobile agents.
arxiv-2512-19532:
Jea-Hyun Park, Abner Salgado, and Steven Wise propose a gradient method that tolerates sloppy gradients. Their target is a composite objective: a strongly convex energy split into two parts, where one part's gradient is known only roughly. A preconditioner shapes the steps, and a deliberate perturbation steadies the scheme.

The analysis runs in infinite dimensions, matching the function-space nature of real problems. Convergence is linear, up to an error floor set by the gradient inaccuracy. The stationary Cahn-Hilliard equation with variable mobility, under periodic boundaries, serves as the test bed. Numerics confirm the predicted rates and show how mobility steers the computation.
arxiv-2512-19632:
Agricultural AI runs on plant photographs, yet field images are expensive, seasonal, and slow to gather. Da Tan, Michael Beck, Christopher Bidinosti, Robert Gulden, and Christopher Henry test whether diffusion models, the image generators behind much modern synthetic media, can fill that gap for canola and soybean crops.

Three pieces make up their pipeline. A fine-tuned Stable Diffusion model produces realistic text-conditioned plant images that measurably help downstream phenotype classification. A DreamBooth and text-inversion step then translates high-resolution indoor images into outdoor-looking ones, improving weed detection with a YOLOv8 model. Finally, a reward model trained on expert scores steers fine-tuning toward outputs specialists prefer. Together the pieces sketch a data-efficient route to training farm AI.
arxiv-2512-19832:
Mark Díaz and three co-authors report what tech workers say about AI that acts human. The humanlike manner of new AI tools drives their spread at work. Yet scholars warn of risks, like too much trust in machine output. The team ran focus groups to see how workers handle the tension. Thirty workers took part, from six job types. They spanned machine learning, product policy, design, and comms work.

The picture that came out was unsettled. Views split, risks were spotted unevenly, and the word humanlike blurred many unlike things. The authors reply with a map. It links the hazards they found to those blurred notions. They argue workers need clearer concepts and more support from their firms. With those in place, plans to curb the risks stand a chance.
arxiv-2512-20132:
J. Hou and R. N. Cahn lead a thirty-three-author DESI collaboration team looking for a crack in the universe's mirror symmetry. The parity-odd four-point correlation function of galaxies is a unique probe: a nonzero signal would flag fundamental symmetry violation or new physics in large-scale structure. They measure it in the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument's first data release, using the luminous red galaxy sample, with auto- and cross-correlations.

Two covariance strategies, a full analytic matrix on uncompressed data and a hybrid simulation-analytic matrix on compressed data, frame the significance assessment. Raw analysis shows apparent auto-correlation signals up to four sigma, yet the excess is equally consistent with a mismatch between simulated and real statistical fluctuations. The team's verdict: the parity-odd signal is consistent with zero, with sample completeness flagged as a sensitivity limit for future releases.
arxiv-2512-20232:
Onintze Zaballa, Verónica Álvarez, and Santiago Mazuelas forecast electricity demand for many regions or buildings at once. Good forecasts keep power systems reliable and cheap to run, but demand patterns shift and different sites influence each other. Earlier multi-task methods learned offline and could not follow those changes.

Their method rests on vector-valued hidden Markov models and updates its parameters recursively as new data arrives. It produces full probabilistic forecasts, so operators see not just expected demand but also its uncertainty. Tests on data sets with diverse, changing consumption patterns show better accuracy and better uncertainty estimates than existing methods. Grid planners get a tool that adapts instead of going stale.
arxiv-2512-20532:
Anthony Leverrier, Wouter Rozendaal, and Gilles Zémor hunt for small quantum error-correcting codes with provably good bones. Quantum Tanner codes promise linear minimum distance and constant encoding rate asymptotically. Built from left-right Cayley complexes, they admit a lifting description through a base code, which the authors characterize.

They also compute the code dimension exactly when the complex's right degree equals two. Then comes the search: sweeping small groups turns up concrete instances with parameters that pair hundreds of physical qubits with dozens of logical ones and healthy distances. One example packs one hundred forty-four physical qubits, twelve logical qubits, and distance eleven, using weight-nine generators. Small, explicit codes matter for near-term fault tolerance.
arxiv-2512-20732:
Saeed Mohammadzadeh, Erfan Hamdi, Joel Shor, and Emma Lejeune built a test suite called FEM-Bench. It checks whether large language models can write correct code for computational mechanics, the field that models how physical systems respond to forces and deformation. The tasks follow the finite element method taught in a first graduate course.

Thirty-three tasks cover basic but real modeling challenges with clear right answers. Even so, top models did not solve them reliably across five tries each. The strongest function writer finished thirty tasks at least once, while unit test writing lagged well behind. FEM-Bench gives researchers a firm yardstick for scientific coding skill.
arxiv-2512-20932:
Deepit Sapru presents a playbook that turns subscription pricing into a guarded, continuously updated decision system rather than a fixed tier list. The framework joins three forecasts: multivariate demand prediction, price sensitivity estimated for each customer segment, and each segment's propensity to cancel. A constrained optimization then sets prices while enforcing guardrails on customer experience, margin floors, and allowable churn.

Monte Carlo scenario tests map the risk around each price move before it ships. Across varied software-as-a-service portfolios, the method beats static tiers and uniform increases by shifting rises toward segments willing to pay and shielding price-sensitive ones. Built for real-time recalibration through modular interfaces, it also explains its decisions for governance, giving managers a route to dynamic pricing that protects trust.
arxiv-2512-21032:
Mingshu Cai, Osamu Yoshie, and Yuya Ieiri teach night-vision cameras to speak the language of ordinary face recognition. Recognition models are trained on visible-light photos and degrade badly on thermal images. The practical fix is translation: convert the infrared face into a plausible visible one without losing who the person is. Their latent diffusion model does that translation, guided by a multi-attribute classifier that extracts key facial attributes and guards them against the feature loss that plagues cross-modal generation.

A self-attention Mamba module strengthens global modeling across the two modalities and speeds inference noticeably. On two benchmark datasets the system reaches state-of-the-art image quality and identity preservation. For surveillance and security screening after dark, identity that survives the wavelength change is the entire point.
arxiv-2512-21132:
Tobias von Arx, Martin Vechev, and three co-authors automate the making of security exams for code-generating models. Expert-built benchmarks revealed that language models write vulnerable code. But hand-crafting such tests is slow, and static benchmarks decay. They leak into training data, miss new task types, and stop challenging improving models. AutoBaxBuilder instead generates fresh benchmarking tasks from scratch. It pairs a model's code understanding with reliability checks. The result is functional tests and working exploits that probe security end to end.

Its output aligns with an expert-written baseline and survives manual soundness checks. The released AutoBaxBench, built this way, evaluates contemporary models. The economics are stark: new tasks in under two hours for under four dollars. That is a twelvefold cut in human effort, even counting verification. Benchmark builders gain a renewable supply of uncontaminated tests.
arxiv-2512-21432:
Bowei Zhang, E. P. S. Shellard, and James R. Fergusson build a toolkit for testing theories of cosmic inflation against data. Inflation is a proposed burst of rapid growth in the very early universe. Each model predicts a pattern of tiny temperature changes, summarized by a bispectrum built from three-point patterns in the cosmic microwave background.

The toolkit combines two computer codes. Primodal computes a model's bispectrum fast, avoiding slow point-by-point work. Modal then compares it with the bispectrum from the Planck satellite's 2018 data. Scanning a model's parameters, the toolkit keeps the cases that fit and excludes those that do not. As a proof of concept, the authors analyze the IR DBI inflation model and bound its sound speed and other parameters. The work prepares the ground for sharper tests with finer data from the Simons Observatory.
arxiv-2512-22032:
Chatbots powered by large language models answer from text alone, blind to what the user is doing or where they are. Ziyan Zhang and colleagues propose a framework that feeds mobile sensing data into the conversation. Smartphones collect behavioral and environmental signals, abstracted into sixteen contextual scenarios and translated into natural-language prompts.

A structured prompting system then guides the assistant toward replies matched to the user's inferred state. The authors present the integration of passive sensing with language models as a path toward digital health support and more personalized interaction. The framework's contribution is the pipeline itself, from raw phone signals to scenario descriptions an off-the-shelf model can reason about.
arxiv-2512-22332:
Naw Sai studies a mimicry question in 1D quantum scattering: can three delta-function barriers with positive strengths imitate the transmission spectrum of two delta barriers with opposite-sign strengths? The comparison is made across wave numbers below a stated cutoff. Such matching matters because it probes whether a measured spectrum uniquely determines the potential that produced it.

Theory gives a firm negative for exact mimicry: perfectly matched transmission spectra are impossible for physically non-trivial configurations. Numerical tests then map out the minimal set of constraints under which approximate matching becomes practical. The results mark both the achievable accuracy and the hard limits of resonance matching under sign constraints, clarifying spectral non-uniqueness in quantum scattering.
arxiv-2512-22732:
Md Badsha Biswas proposes mining social media to strengthen research on negative pregnancy outcomes, a leading concern behind infant mortality in the United States. Miscarriage, stillbirth, birth defects, and premature birth remain partly understood, and standard datasets are limited. Biswas outlines a natural language processing pipeline for platforms such as Twitter. It finds women publicly sharing pregnancy experiences and sorts them by reported outcome. Full gestation with normal birth weight counts as a positive case.

Social media data are lopsided, noisy, and messy, so the plan leans on robust pre-cleaning and added synthetic data to build usable cohorts. Beyond description, the system is meant to support studies of how specific treatments or prenatal exposures affect maternal and fetal health. The paper presents social media as a viable adjunct resource for pregnancy disease tracking.
arxiv-2512-22932:
Masanori Hanada, Shunji Matsuura, Andreas Schafer, and Jinzhao Sun lay out universal rules for handling gauge symmetry when simulating gauge theories on quantum computers. Gauge theories, the framework behind the strong nuclear force, contain redundant descriptions of the same physics. A simulation must decide how to treat that redundancy. A common belief says physical states must be gauge singlets; the authors show non-singlet representations are equally valid, with different trade-offs.

The principles are shown inside a simulation framework based on the orbifold lattice, producing explicit circuits aimed at quantum chromodynamics. For singlet approaches they give a projection built from Haar averaging with cost and error analysis, plus a Hamiltonian trick that pushes non-singlet states out of the low-energy spectrum. Non-singlet approaches extract gauge-invariant observables from wave packets and excitations. Small classical simulations check errors and yield resource estimates for SU(N) theories.
arxiv-2512-23032:
Kerem Zaman and Shashank Srivastava challenge a popular verdict that chain-of-thought reasoning in language models is usually unfaithful. A recent metric labels a chain of thought unfaithful when it never mentions a hint hidden in the prompt that swayed the answer. Zaman and Srivastava argue that test confuses unfaithfulness with incompleteness: compressing distributed transformer computation into a linear story must lose detail, so silence about a hint is not proof of dishonesty.

On multi-hop reasoning tasks, many chains flagged by the hint metric are judged faithful by other measures, sometimes more than half of them. Giving models larger inference budgets sharply raises hint mention rates, suggesting earlier results partly reflect tight token limits. Causal mediation analysis adds that even unmentioned hints can steer predictions through the written reasoning itself. The authors do not claim every chain is faithful, only that evaluation needs a broader toolkit.
arxiv-2512-23132:
Armstrong Foundjem, Lionel Tidjon, Leuson Da Silva, and Foutse Khomh map the threat landscape facing machine learning systems and propose a multi-agent framework to fight. Foundation models now sit inside finance, healthcare, and critical systems, and the attacks against them, from data poisoning and model extraction to prompt injection and jailbreaking, do not fit classic cybersecurity boxes. The team charted which techniques, vulnerabilities, and lifecycle stages dominate.

They took ninety-three threats from MITRE ATLAS, the AI Incident Database, and the literature, and reviewed hundreds of repositories. A multi-agent retrieval system mined hundreds of articles to build a knowledge-driven threat graph linking attack techniques to weaknesses and stages. The graph surfaced underreported threats, including theft of model APIs and leakage through memorized parameters. It exposed clusters of vulnerabilities in libraries with poor patch spread. The authors conclude that adaptive, ML-specific defenses are essential.
arxiv-2512-23932:
Ioanna Gemou and Evangelos Lamprou combine a language model with a logic solver to diagnose disease in an explainable way. Symbolic AI can reason transparently over medical knowledge, but building the knowledge base by hand is laborious, which has limited adoption. Their framework, McCoy, automates that construction step.

An LLM first translates medical literature into Answer Set Programming code, a declarative logic formalism. Patient data join the generated rules, and an ASP solver derives the diagnosis, so every conclusion can be traced through explicit logical steps rather than a neural network's opaque scores. Preliminary results on small-scale diagnosis tasks show strong performance. The authors present McCoy as a proof of concept that pairing generative models. This are good at extracting knowledge, with solvers, which are good at reasoning with it, yields predictions clinicians can inspect.
arxiv-2512-24632:
Md Nazmus Sakib and four colleagues evaluate a reflection tool for teams that work together. Between meetings, momentum fades and task drift creeps in. Their system, ReflectEd, prompts reflection between checkpoints. Prompts follow theory-driven, progressively structured levels. Scaffolding supports the writers. The study compares two setups: regular reflection and a deeper one with an added transformative activity.

Engagement held steady early in the week under both setups. Deeper reflections grew more actionable over time. Forward-looking planning grew richer there too. The depth cost effort, and sustaining it during busy work was harder. Partner-visible reflections helped coordination. They surfaced differences in focus and supported accountability. The findings trade depth against feasibility. Designers of team tools get a map of that trade.
arxiv-2512-24732:
Li Guo, Hongyu Xiang, and Bin Zhang prove that two Hopf algebras built for multiple zeta values are actually the same structure in disguise. One comes from the quasi-shuffle product, long known to carry a Hopf algebra. The other comes from the shuffle product, only recently given that structure. Quasi-symmetric functions provide the bridge between them.

Their isomorphism is compared with the classic Hoffman, Newman, and Radford isomorphism between shuffle and quasi-shuffle Hopf algebras. Readers in algebra and number theory get a cleaner picture of how two encodings of multiple zeta values relate. Such identifications let results proved in one setting transfer to the other.
arxiv-2512-24832:
Adam Sagmeister and Konrad Swanepoel bound how many touching pairs can occur among equal circles packed in the hyperbolic plane. In flat geometry, a spiral based on triangular tiling is best, and special hyperbolic cases were known for certain diameters tied to triangular tilings. They give upper and lower bounds for every positive diameter.

For diameters above a stated threshold, with one exception, the touching count falls below a spiral construction in the order-seven triangular tiling, which they conjecture is extremal. A lower bound above two per circle is also proved. Discrete geometry readers get a broad picture of penny graphs in curved space.
arxiv-2512-25032:
Jiafeng Chen, Jonathan Roth, and Jann Spiess ask what a random experiment can teach about monotonicity, the condition that a treatment moves all people weakly in the same way. From a standard sampling view, monotonicity is known to be unfalsifiable. From a design-based view, where results are fixed and only assignment is random, the distribution of treatment effects is formally found.

Limits on learning about breaches are then marked, showing identification does not mean easy finding. Statistics and econometrics readers get a precise edge between what experiments can and cannot reveal about effect variety. Monotonicity supports common estimators, so its testability matters broadly.
arxiv-2601-00132:
Alexey Basalaev, writing alone, studies Saito theory through a different algebraic lens. Saito theory starts with a special kind of singularity. It builds a rich geometric structure called a Dubrovin Frobenius manifold. That structure is not unique. It depends on choosing a primitive form, or a good basis.

Basalaev uses Batalin Vilkovisky algebras to study those choices. He gives recursive formulas for two key objects. One is the primitive form that K Saito defined. The other is the R matrix used in Givental theory. The formulas come from computations inside the BV algebra. For geometers, the work turns abstract choices into steps that can be computed.
arxiv-2601-00232:
Atila Poro works with Ehsan Paki, Fahri Alicavus, and Raul Michel on a contact binary star with an extreme mass split. Two stars in such a system share one envelope. Theory sets a floor for how low the mass ratio can go. Some observed systems sit below that floor. Their stability is still debated in the field.

The team reanalyzes one target with fresh tools. Its mass ratio proves the lowest yet known among studied contact binaries. Space telescope light curves anchor the new solution. Six years of period changes show a cyclic trend. A third body likely drives that cycle. Once removed, the true period trend stays unclear. The faint partner looks like a brown dwarf. The third body looks like a small red dwarf. The system reads as unstable, and a merger may follow.
arxiv-2601-00532:
Ping-Yen Shen and Ryan Caverly improve momentum management for NASA's Solar Cruiser, a large solar sail spacecraft pushed by sunlight. A sail cannot fire thrusters to dump built-up angular momentum, so the craft uses an active mass translator and reflectivity control devices to adjust its balance. Those two actuators interact in ways that make control design tricky.

Earlier predictive controllers for the sail assumed the disturbance torques acting on it were known exactly, which real missions cannot guarantee. Shen and Caverly add a Kalman filter that estimates those unmodeled torques in real time and feeds the estimates into the predictive controller. Their dynamics model also includes higher-fidelity effects, making the scheme a more realistic step toward flying large sails.
arxiv-2601-00732:
Michalis Ramp and two co-authors study, in 2026, how to let cars into a city network without jams. Their method holds some cars at the edge and lets them in at a set rate. Each zone makes its own calls, with no central boss. The open question is whether such schemes stay stable when the city's model is off.

City flow is nonlinear, and the link between density, flow, and speed is known only within bounds. The authors bring in passivity theory, a tool about energy-like balance in systems. With it, they derive checks that each zone can run on its own. Schemes that pass the checks stay stable despite the model error. Tests on networks of six zones and of twenty zones back the maths. The work gives city engineers a way to vet entry schemes before use.
arxiv-2601-00932:
Andrea Thomas Nava and four co-authors present, in 2026, a data-driven way to design better products. Their method also says how sure the gains are. Firms log past design tests, then train a network to link design choices to product traits. A slope-climbing search on that network finds choices that should score best.

The new part is a careful doubt gauge for each prediction. It blends a dropout trick, which reruns the network with random parts off, with nested conformal bounds. Those bounds promise a set coverage rate from past data alone. The intervals adapt in width and need no retraining when the rate changes. Tests on five real data sets followed. The method matched the best known scores on design quality. It also gave honest, flexible doubt ranges. That pairing suits costly design work, where a wrong bet wastes real money.
arxiv-2601-01532:
Fanzhe Fu proposes Aletheia, a framework for measuring how deeply a reasoning model believes its own answers. Standard benchmarks test breadth of knowledge, not conviction. Fu extends that line of work to the deliberate, step-by-step reasoning models now in wide use.

The method regularizes and inverts the confusion matrix of the judge scoring the model, yielding an aligned conviction score that also checks that conviction does not erode safety. A synthetic proxy protocol stands in for private data. In a pilot on recent reasoning models, Fu reports that reasoning seems to buffer conviction. Under adversarial pressure, though, the models may overthink defensively. The paper presents itself as a blueprint, not a verdict. Its concepts are proposals with early pilot results. Still, its question, how to measure belief depth, is a live one for AI evaluation.
arxiv-2601-01632:
Mauro Valorani tackles learning computer models of stiff systems, where fast and slow changes mix. Such systems appear in combustion and chemical reactions, and neural models often fail on them in telling ways. Training errors pile up on slow states, fast behavior collapses, and the learned model's vibration pattern can drift from the true one.

Valorani gives three fixes: scaling time steps with stiffness in mind, exciting fast directions with bursts of short local paths, and checking the model's Jacobian with automatic differentiation. On a standard test system, fast vibration errors fell by about tenfold and long runs tracked better. He argues matching the spectrum should be a first-class goal.
arxiv-2601-01732:
Cooling a gas of lithium atoms until it becomes a superfluid is a standard route into exotic quantum physics. The usual method slowly lowers the trap that holds the atoms. That method stalls partway. Bolong Jiao and six co-authors speed things up by tilting the optical trap with a magnetic field gradient once the gas reaches about half its Fermi temperature.

The tilt opens an escape route for the most energetic atoms while leaving the trap's tightness nearly unchanged, so cooling accelerates instead of leveling off. The gas crossed into the superfluid regime and reached a temperature of about sixteen percent of the Fermi temperature in roughly twenty-five milliseconds. The simple trick offers laboratories a faster, robust way to prepare strongly interacting Fermi gases.
arxiv-2601-01832:
Hard optimization problems with expensive evaluations need search methods that spend a fixed budget wisely. SB Danush Vikraman and three co-authors present Yukthi Opus. It is a hybrid metaheuristic. Several search chains mix three mechanisms. Markov chain Monte Carlo explores globally. Greedy local search refines. Simulated annealing with reheating escapes local traps.

A burn-in phase explores first, then a hybrid loop polishes candidates, while a spatial blacklist steers the search away from poor regions already visited. Tests used the Rastrigin and Rosenbrock functions. Traveling salesman problems with up to two hundred cities were also used. The Monte Carlo exploration and greedy refinement drive solution quality. Annealing and multiple chains mainly stabilize results.
arxiv-2601-02032:
Persistent high-pressure systems over Greenland, called blocking, steer weather across the North Atlantic and have grown more frequent in summer. Michele Filippucci, Jacob Maddison, and Simona Bordoni track these events along their paths with a new Python package, blocktrack, applied to ERA5 reanalysis and CMIP6 climate models.

Greenland blocks split into two families: upstream blocks born over northern Canada with strong moisture transport and warm anomalies, and retrograding blocks drifting westward from the Atlantic. The recent rise in blocking, especially in 2012, is driven by the upstream family, which models largely miss. Future projections suggest retrograding blocks decline while upstream blocks may increase, a divergence the authors tie to jet shifts and Arctic amplification.
arxiv-2601-03132:
Mintae Kim studies how to control systems that can only be partly observed, the setting of partially observable Markov decision processes. Optimal decisions formally depend on a belief state, a probability distribution over hidden states, but that object is usually infinite-dimensional and impractical. Kim treats a truncated history of inputs and outputs as a practical stand-in for the belief.

Using the Wasserstein metric, the work derives bounds that tie the information lost by finite memory directly to lost control performance along typical closed-loop trajectories. For linear quadratic Gaussian systems, the belief mismatch can be evaluated in closed form. Experiments confirm the predicted mechanism: mismatch shrinks roughly exponentially as memory grows, and the performance gap scales with it. The result tells engineers how much memory is enough.
arxiv-2601-03332:
Oleksandr Kuznetsov makes Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks fast enough for everyday hardware. These networks replace plain weights with learnable one-dimensional functions, usually splines. That makes them easy to interpret, but slow. Each layer needs many spline evaluations. Standard quantization tools do not help, since they assume matrix multiplication. His method, LUT-KAN, compiles each edge function into a per-segment lookup table, with eight-bit quantization and linear interpolation.

The package comes with an explicit inference contract. It states the boundary conventions and the rules for out-of-bounds inputs, so results can be reproduced. For honest speed claims, spline and lookup evaluation are compared under the same backends. That separates gains from the representation itself from gains due to vectorization or just-in-time effects. The aim is to keep the accuracy of the original networks while removing the CPU bottleneck.
arxiv-2601-03432:
Danny Brahman and Mohammad Mahoor argue that common tests do a poor job of showing what code-trained language models can and cannot do. General benchmarks miss weak spots in code generation, so builders cannot target fixes. Their answer is CodeEval, a benchmark modeled on how programming courses grade students.

CodeEval covers twenty-four distinct aspects of Python across beginner, intermediate, and advanced levels. It includes both class-based and function-based problems, each with clear specifications and full test suites. The pair also released RunCodeEval, an open tool for running the tests. Teachers and model builders can use the results to see exactly which coding skills need work, instead of relying on one overall score.
arxiv-2601-03532:
Andrew Gerard Roberts, Michael Dietze, and Jonathan H. Huggins study how to stay honest about error when a cheap stand-in model replaces a costly one. In Bayesian inverse problems, scientists work backward from data to likely causes, but the true forward model may be too expensive to run many times. A surrogate model speeds things up, yet ignoring its error can make conclusions sound surer than they are.

The authors propose the expected posterior as a general baseline for carrying surrogate uncertainty into the final answer, backed by decision theory arguments. They then examine a popular shortcut, the expected unnormalized posterior, and show where it can break down. The risk grows when surrogate error varies unevenly across the space being searched.
arxiv-2601-03732:
T. A. Petrosyan, writing alone, examines how curvature and topology together shape the quantum vacuum on the Beltrami pseudosphere, a saddle-like surface of constant negative curvature. A charged scalar field lives on this two-plus-one-dimensional space, with a twist condition around its compact direction. The study computes local fingerprints of the vacuum state, namely the average of the field squared and of the energy-momentum tensor.

Parts tied to the uncompactified direction diverge, while the topological parts from the compact direction stay finite and are analyzed numerically and in limiting cases. For a small compact radius, leading terms ignore the field's mass and curvature coupling and grow by a power law. For large radius they decay, except in a special conformal case. Such results inform quantum field theory in curved spaces.
arxiv-2601-03832:
Mei Ian Sam, Tzu-Ling Kuo, and Tai-Yue Li speed up classical simulation of Grover's search algorithm using matrix product states, a compact way to represent quantum states. Grover's algorithm offers a quadratic speedup for unstructured search. Today's noisy quantum devices are too small and error-prone to validate it at scale, so good classical simulators are essential for development and hardware assessment.

Working in the NVIDIA CUDA-Q environment, the team compared iterative and ordinary Grover circuits on statevector and matrix product backends. At twenty-nine qubits, the iterative circuit on the compact backend ran about fifteen times faster than the ordinary circuit and several times faster than the statevector backend. Sampling stayed stable even at a single shot for larger qubit counts. Faster simulation lets researchers test bigger searches before hardware catches up.
arxiv-2601-03932:
Michael Lozovsky, writing alone, studies how uncertain the water content of wet exoplanets really is. Planets between Earth and Neptune in mass often have radii implying volatile material, suggesting water-rich interiors, but no observation directly measures how much water they hold or where it sits. Using an internal structure code named MAGRATHEA, Lozovsky models planets whose water and rock distributions follow miscibility, whether the two actually mix at given pressures and temperatures.

The modeled planets have an iron core beneath a uniform rock-water mixture. In the cooler outer regions, water and rock unmix, forming a pure water shell at the surface. Vapor behavior adds further spread. Because different plausible distributions fit the same mass and radius, the inferred water fraction carries real uncertainty, a caution for headlines calling distant planets ocean worlds.
arxiv-2601-04032:
Max Goldberg, David Nesvorný, and Alessandro Morbidelli propose that Earth-like planets grew from two sources, not one ring alone. The classic ring model matches planet orbits well. It struggles, though, to explain the chemical gradient from Mercury to Mars, where material goes from reduced to more oxidised.

Their model keeps a narrow, heat-processed ring inside one astronomical unit and adds a lighter, spread-out disk beyond it. In N-body simulations, a sweeping resonance driven by gas drag plus Jupiter and Saturn gathers the outer disk inward. That inflow helps form Mars and adds oxidised material to the growing Earth. Leftovers land in the asteroid belt. The most reduced material is never implanted, which matches gaps in the meteorite record.
arxiv-2601-04332:
L. X. Gutiérrez-Guerrero and three co-authors chart how a family of particles and their mirror partners behave as matter heats up, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Working inside a symmetry-preserving contact interaction model of the strong force, they compute screening masses. The masses inferred from spatial correlations — for vector and axial-vector mesons and for the diquarks built from the same quarks.

The study treats light and heavy quarks in one framework and follows both the longitudinal and transverse modes as temperature rises. At zero temperature its numbers match experiment, and at high temperature they approach the free-theory limit. The headline behaviour is convergence: the lightest mesons and their parity partners meet at high temperature, which inside this model signals the restoration of chiral symmetry.
arxiv-2601-04432:
Harshavardhan Kamarthi and six co-authors build a time machine for operational data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Companies that stream video or run networks collect rich per-session quality metrics, and analysts constantly want to replay history differently: test a new anomaly detector, retune an alert, score a new algorithm. Warehouses, samples, and sketches either cost too much for that or cannot replay faithfully.

Their system, AHA, rests on three observations about such workloads. The statistics involved decompose neatly, only a few subpopulations are active among the many attribute combinations, and modern analytics databases aggregate in exploitable ways. On real datasets and production pipelines at a large video analytics company. AHA replayed with full accuracy across downstream tasks at up to eighty-five times lower total ownership cost than conventional methods, counting both computing and storage.
arxiv-2601-04532:
C. Rodriguez and A. Zemlyanova ask whether a crack tip has to be a mathematical explosion, in a 2026 arXiv paper. In ordinary elasticity, stress at a sharp crack tip blows up to infinity, a singularity nobody really believes. Their model gives the crack faces a surface mechanics of their own: surface stresses drawn from an elastic energy that includes stretching, curvature. gradients of stretching along the surface, capturing effects that only appear at very small scales.

Applied to a finite straight crack in an infinite plate under combined opening and shearing loads, with physically motivated conditions at the tips. The complex-variable analysis shows stress and strain stay bounded right up to the tips for nearly all admissible parameters. Together with the authors' earlier tearing-mode result, the theory removes crack-tip singularities under every principal kind of far-away loading — a cleaner foundation for modelling brittle fracture.
arxiv-2601-04632:
Haneul Yoo and three co-authors turn school textbooks into cultural training data for language models, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Models perform unevenly across languages and cultures because their training text leans English and carries its values with it. National social studies curricula, by contrast, are a society's own account of itself, and the authors propose them as a scalable foundation for culture-aware supervision.

Their framework, CuCu, is an automated multi-agent system that transforms a national curriculum into open-ended, culture-specific question-answer pairs for finetuning. Applied to the Korean national social studies curriculum, it produced KCaQA, a dataset of roughly thirty-four thousand such pairs. Analyses and training experiments suggest the dataset genuinely covers culture-specific topics and elicits responses grounded in local sociocultural context, rather than translated generalities — a template other countries' curricula could follow.
arxiv-2601-04832:
Léo Gaspard and Cyril Martins deliver the first full five-orbital dynamical mean-field calculations for layered iridates and rhodates in a 2026 paper. Dynamical mean-field theory, or DMFT, is a leading method for materials with strongly interacting electrons. Full calculations with exact solvers were long too costly for spin-orbit materials, so researchers used simplified one- and three-band models that left out some electron states.

Their hybrid approach includes spin-orbit coupling across all five orbitals. They find correlation effects shift the omitted states mainly through static mean-field corrections rather than dynamic fluctuations. That insight motivates their cheaper hybrid-DMFT scheme. More complete models of these layered materials matter for understanding their unusual magnetism and possible device uses.
arxiv-2601-05032:
Steven Rivetti's 2026 paper, written with 3 co-authors, examines two time effects that jointly trouble systems combining sensing and communication. Integrated sensing and communication, or ISAC, lets one base station serve a user device while also performing radar-like sensing. Channel aging degrades the communication link as the environment slowly changes, while fast changes create Doppler-affected clutter that confuses sensing.

Working with orthogonal frequency division multiplexing waveforms, the authors address a gap: the joint impact of slow aging and fast clutter had been largely overlooked. Their analysis treats both effects in one network model. Understanding their interaction matters for future wireless systems that promise to sense surroundings and carry data on the same hardware and spectrum.
arxiv-2601-05132:
Rafael Torres classifies a family of nonorientable four-dimensional manifolds in a 2026 mathematics paper. Manifolds are spaces that look locally like ordinary space, and classifying them up to homeomorphism, a continuous reshaping, is a central task in topology. Torres starts from a known classification for manifolds whose fundamental group has order two, proved by Hambleton, Kreck, and Teichner.

Through a simple cut-and-paste construction, he extends that classification to a large set of manifolds whose cyclic fundamental group has order twice an odd number. Surgery theory enters only through the earlier results. He also collects open questions, noting the set may cover every such manifold. Classification results organize the zoo of possible four-dimensional shapes into a comprehensible catalogue.
arxiv-2601-05232:
P. Gilda and 13 co-authors describe an application that scores the peacefulness of social media videos in real time in a 2026 paper. Most people now get news from videos on platforms like YouTube and Facebook, not from curated newsrooms. Because language can inflame or calm conflict, the team built a tool measuring hate speech and peace speech aspects of a video's content as the user watches it.

The application draws on supervised machine learning and survey-tagged news language among its approaches. It gives users feedback on their own media diet as they consume it. Such feedback could help viewers notice when their feed is training outrage, a first step toward healthier information habits on conflict-heavy topics.
arxiv-2601-05332:
Gonzalo Herrera's 2026 paper grades how gaps in sky lore blur the hunt for dark matter in deep vaults on Earth. Such hunts wait for a dark grain to strike a core in a shielded tank. What they should see hinges on how fast the dark grains move through our part of the sky. That speed spread is not known with care, and the blur it makes shifts from one dark model to the next, and from one tank stuff to the next.

Herrera takes on each term of the stock set of dark-to-core acts, one by one. He grades the blur with a lore-based score, the KL gap, which tells how far the true speeds could stray from the stock bell curve. Term-by-term grades show which finds stand firm when the sky lore is loose, and which melt.
arxiv-2601-05532:
Benoit Perthame and 2 co-authors present, in a 2026 paper, a new kinetic equation for cells that migrate in response to mechanical forces from their substrate. This effect, called mechanotaxis, had not been captured in earlier kinetic models. It helps explain collective behavior seen in bacterial colonies.

Their equation adds an acceleration term describing how outside signals change the forces between cell and surface. From that starting point they derive a family of larger-scale limit equations. The authors analyze the main properties of those limits, including linear stability and the ability to form patterns. Numerical simulations support the theory, linking single-cell mechanics to colony-scale organization.
arxiv-2601-05732:
Yongyi Yang and Jianyang Gao propose mHC-lite, a 2026 simplification of manifold-constrained hyper-connections for deep neural networks. Hyper-connections mix information across multiple residual streams through learned arrays, speeding convergence. Unconstrained arrays can destabilize training, so an earlier method projected them toward doubly stochastic form with many Sinkhorn-Knopp iterations.

Finite rounds leave an approximation gap, and efficient implementation needs specialized GPU kernels. Yang and Gao instead build doubly stochastic matrices as convex combinations of permutation matrices, guaranteeing the trait exactly by building. Only native matrix operations are required. Tests reportedly matched or beat the earlier method, with higher throughput and none of the instabilities seen before. The code is shared in public, so other teams can run the same tests.
arxiv-2601-05932:
Cheng Chen and 2 co-authors simulate in 2026 how a binary system's orbit changes when its surrounding gas disk settles into a polar alignment, perpendicular to the binary's orbital eccentricity direction. Misaligned circumbinary disks usually end up aligned or counter-aligned around circular binaries. Around eccentric binaries, a polar outcome becomes likely instead.

Using smoothed particle hydrodynamics with steady mass injection, the team covered a range of binary and disk parameters. In every modeled case the binary shrank over time. Shrinkage was faster than with comparable aligned or retrograde disks. For small sink radii, long-lived polar disks around individual stars appeared, fed continuously by the circumbinary disk. Implications span planet formation and merging supermassive black holes.
arxiv-2601-06132:
Do language models see political bias in Western media the same way? Rohitash Chandra and 4 co-authors test that in a 2026 study. Bias in newspapers shapes public opinion and elections, so automated detection matters. The study compares coverage of the Israel-Hamas and Russia-Ukraine wars.

Three models, BERT, Gemini, and DeepSeek, judged left-wing, right-wing, and neutral opinions in the Guardian and the BBC. After the wars broke out, coverage shifted leftward by these measures, but each model gave different results. DeepSeek leaned consistently left in its judgments, while the others stayed nearer the center. The Guardian shifted more on the Israel-Hamas conflict, suggesting event-driven reporting patterns.
arxiv-2601-06232:
Generative AI creates media easily, but users get little control and creators get little protection. Haris Khan and 2 co-authors propose a multi-agent framework for that problem in a 2026 paper. Current tools act as black boxes with no built-in way to guard copyright or trace where content came from.

Five specialized agents divide the work: Director, Generator, Reviewer, Integration, and Protection. Together they keep output aligned with user intent while embedding digital watermark markers that record provenance. Two case studies test the design, one on creative generation with iterative refinement and one on protecting AI art in commercial use. Prior evidence cited suggests better semantic alignment and high watermark recovery, supporting trustworthy creative workflows.
arxiv-2601-06432:
Hui Li reports recent results on hadronic decays of charmed mesons from the BESIII experiment in a 2026 presentation paper. Charmed mesons contain one charm quark, and their decays into lighter hadrons reveal how the strong force binds and reshapes matter. BESIII collides electrons and positrons tuned to produce them copiously.

Seven decay channels receive focus, involving combinations of kaons, pions, and eta mesons from D and Ds mesons. Amplitude analyses of these processes reveal rich internal structures, showing which intermediate states contribute. The paper also reports the phi decay ratio in Ds decays. Such measurements supply fundamental inputs on non-perturbative QCD, the structure of hadronic matter, and searches for CP violation, the matter-antimatter asymmetry effect.
arxiv-2601-07032:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Pranav Kumar and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers classical unattainability of extremality in non-BPS d-brane systems. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. For the worldline theory of an extremal black hole, extremality amounts to vanishing ground state energy.

In light of recent gravity results one would expect much like the ground state degeneracy this fine tuned condition too will not be met. It is unclear though whether this should be a quantum artefact or classical. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07332: A 2026 arXiv preprint by Artem Lopatin and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers polynomial equations over split-octonions. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Over the split-octonion algebra defined over an arbitrary field, we solve all polynomial equations whose coefficients are scalar except for the constant term. As an application, we determine the square and cubic roots of an octonion. Keywords: polynomial equations, octonions, split-octonions, positive characteristic. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07532:
Nathan Green introduces outstandR, an R software package for comparing treatments without head-to-head trials. Indirect treatment comparisons are essential in health technology assessment when direct trials are missing. One drug may have patient-level data while a rival has only published averages. Trial populations often differ in traits that change treatment effects. Green's 2026 preprint describes tools for that gap.

The method family is called population-adjusted indirect comparison. It adjusts for differences in effect modifiers between study populations. The outstandR package puts those methods into R, the standard language for statisticians. Health economists and trial statisticians can use it to compare therapies more fairly. The paper serves as both a method summary and package guide.
arxiv-2601-07732:
Raphael Appenzeller introduces algebraic groups over fields where order still makes sense, in a 2026 preprint. Real closed fields generalize the real numbers while keeping their ordering properties. The paper gives a self-contained introduction to linear algebraic and semialgebraic groups over such fields. It then generalizes key results about semisimple Lie groups to this broader setting. One result characterizes when a torus is maximally split.

Specifically, a torus in a semisimple algebraic group is maximal over the reals exactly when it is maximal over every real closed field. Results of this type let geometers transfer arguments between fields. Semialgebraic groups connect algebra with ordered geometry and model theory. The paper serves readers entering the area as much as specialists. Its self-contained style lowers the cost of learning a niche but growing subject.
arxiv-2601-08032: Jawad Abuhlail and Abdulmushin Alfaraj study separation axioms for a special class of lattices. Their 2026 arXiv paper defines X-top lattices, where a chosen subset carries a Zariski-like topology. Such spaces are T0 but usually far from T2, the Hausdorff property. The authors examine stronger separation levels, including regular, completely regular, and normal spaces. They also apply the results to commutative rings and semirings. The work serves algebraists and topologists who track how much separation a lattice topology can support.
arxiv-2601-08232: Matias Sepulveda-Macias and Erick Burgos Parra link local atomic order to magnetization dynamics in amorphous nanodisks. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies cobalt-iron alloys at three compositions. The soft magnetic behavior of amorphous alloys ties to local topological disorder and magnetic exchange. The authors use a multiscale spin-lattice dynamics approach to probe that link. Their focus is icosahedral short-range order, a favored local packing in these alloys. Understanding how local order shapes dynamics could guide design of soft magnets for sensors and memory devices.
arxiv-2601-08532: L. Pesce and a large team wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a sensor for faint hits in cold silicon. The sensor is a Kinetic Inductance Detector, or KID. Such sensors serve hunts for light dark matter and rare neutrino scatter. They reach low energy floors other sensors miss. In these setups, the KID both feels the hit and soaks up the athermal phonons the hit sheds. The team adds built-in phonon collectors to the design, to raise how strongly the sensor responds.
arxiv-2601-08732:
Vincent Roca and five co-authors build a tool to mark stroke damage on brain scans. Fast, true marks help doctors plan care for a stroke. Deep nets can draw these marks on their own. Most of them use a U-Net shape, a net with a down path and an up path that meet in the middle.

Their tool is called ISLA. It adds close watch at more than one depth in the net. It also uses focus blocks that stress key parts of the scan. The team adds steps to cope with scans from new sites, and they merge the calls of more than one net. A reader in brain health gets a full plan for more sound stroke marks.
arxiv-2601-09032:
Logan Ritchie and four co-authors grade top AI models on long tasks in a fake shop world. Old grades test one reply at a time. Real work needs many steps in a row, with tools, checks, and fix ups. A model that chats well may still fail a long job. The team uses a set of work place tasks in a shop sim from Surge.

Each task runs in a live world that reacts to the model's acts. Scores show a rank of agent skills, from plain to hard tasks. Gaps show where top models still stall. A reader who buys or builds agents gets a rank based on work, not chat. It can guide which tasks are safe to hand to an agent now.
arxiv-2601-09332:
M. Ezziati and eleven co-authors give a Bayes tool to pick far quasars from wide sky surveys. A quasar is a bright core of a far galaxy. Those at the most range show the cosmos in its youth. But they are rare, and they look like two near fakes: cold brown dwarf stars, and mid range old galaxies. A wrong pick wastes scope time.
