Their tool is called Owl-z. It weighs each pick by how well its hues fit each class, with past rates built in. It can also pick the fakes on aim, for tests of the sieve. A reader in sky surveys gets a pick tool with doubt built in, fit for the next wide scans.
arxiv-2601-09532:
Fatemeh Kayanikhoo and four co-authors return to strange quark stars, now asking how light or heavy they can be. Their 2026 arXiv paper, the second of a pair and bound for the Astrophysical Journal, uses the MIT bag model with a density-dependent bag constant. It estimates the mass range of rapidly rotating strange quark stars.

The paper also computes the Keplerian frequency, the fastest spin before the star sheds mass at its equator. A companion paper covers the stars' structure under strong magnetic fields. Together, the mass limits and spin limits frame what a strange quark star could look like to telescopes. Those numbers help test whether some observed pulsars are quark stars in disguise.
arxiv-2601-09632:
Rose Connolly, Victor Zordan, and Rachel McDonnell study how far a virtual jump can be bent before users notice. Their 2026 arXiv paper measures perceptual thresholds for adjusted teleporting in virtual reality. Teleportation is the most common way to move in VR, yet its feel is little studied.

Redirected walking research showed that real steps can be quietly steered. The authors ask whether teleport landings can likewise be shifted without detection. Finding the threshold tells designers how much freedom they have to guide users. Subtle guidance could keep players inside safe play areas without breaking immersion.
arxiv-2601-09832:
Alvari Kupari, Nasser Giacaman, and Valerio Terragni track how coding style spreads through open source. Their 2026 arXiv paper analyzes 1,036 popular open-source Java projects on GitHub. The team studies how style conventions and best practices are adopted and how they evolve.

Following a shared style improves a codebase's upkeep, its readability, and its room to grow. Best practices also cut errors and raise performance. The authors measure how common each practice is and which violations recur most. The results show where tooling and review habits actually change how developers behave over time.
arxiv-2601-10032:
Hui Wang and Chunming Zheng study a net of nerve cells that share noise. Each cell gets its own random kicks. All cells also get one shared kick. Shared noise is the norm in real brain nets. Yet how it shapes the net as a whole is not well known.

The cells are of a type whose rate grows as a square rule. The shared kick can be tuned from weak to strong. The pair work out the large scale acts of the net. They track how shared noise shifts bursts and sync. The work helps link cell level noise to net level acts in the brain.
arxiv-2601-10132:
Yanan Cao and a large team ask if more context helps a model guess time spans. Models are strong at many guess tasks. But time sense from rows of past acts is less clear. A span guess asks when a thing will next occur, or how long it will last.

More past rows may help. Or they may add noise and drag the guess down. The team tests both claims. They vary how much past a model sees. They then check span grades at each load. The work gives a clear read on when more past helps and when it hurts.
arxiv-2601-10732:
Chorok Lee documents how stock market factors predict each other in different market regimes. The work uses 35 years of Fama-French data, from 1990 to 2024. Factors sort stocks by traits like value and size. Lee tests whether one factor's moves help forecast another's, a pattern known as Granger causality.

The Value factor forecasts the Size factor during crisis periods, with a lag of nine days. The signal is strong in crises, with a p-value below one in ten thousand. In calm times, the link is absent. The split warns traders that factor ties seen in stress may vanish in normal markets, and the reverse may also hold.
arxiv-2601-10832:
Anis R. Shakkour, David Hexner, Yehuda Bitton, and Avishai Sintov build a lean gait detector for lower-limb exoskeletons. Such devices must know the user's gait phase and each step in real time. A wrong guess can fight the user's motion and risk safety. Common methods lean on complex force sensors, which add delay to the control loop.

Their framework uses a single low-cost inertial measurement unit set into the crutch hand grip. No mechanical changes to the device are needed. One small sensor, read well, replaces a rack of hardware. The work targets cheaper, safer exoskeletons and prostheses that respond in step with the people who wear them.
arxiv-2601-11032:
Yuki Kaneko and co-authors present an eleven-year catalog of gamma-ray transients from the Fermi telescope. Fermi's Gamma-ray Burst Monitor watches the whole sky with high time and energy resolution. Its archive is the largest database of its kind. Buried in it are many transient events that never triggered the detectors, for various reasons.

The team searched the full archive to build the catalog. Untriggered events can include faint bursts, solar flares, and terrestrial flashes. A clean catalog turns a raw archive into a mine for population studies. It also sets the rates that future burst monitors must beat. High-energy astronomers gain a decade of hidden flashes, sorted and ready.
arxiv-2601-11332:
Sama Hadhoud and six coauthors split problem solving from code writing. Their 2026 preprint tests language models on competitive programming. Models now solve many such problems end to end. But a single score hides two unlike skills in the score.

One skill is the plan: the algorithm that cracks the task. The other is the code: turning the plan into a program. The team centers plain-language editorials in the test. Editorials state the plan in words, with no code at all. Solving and grading both pass through that plan layer. That split shows if a model fails on thought or on syntax. Contest-style tasks are at heart problem-solving tasks, they argue.
arxiv-2601-11932:
Abdullah Al Monsur, Nitesh Vamshi Bommisetty, and Gene Louis Kim improve event spotting in text for rare event kinds. Two flaws drive their work. First, models that read text in one way miss the rich two-way context that event spotting needs.

They add a context-aware encoder to fix that flaw. They also use LoRA, a light way to tune a model, to aid rare classes. Rare events have few training cases, so they are easy to miss. Better rare class skill helps news and risk tools that track events.  Rare class gains matter most where events are few and grave.
arxiv-2601-12932:
Jean Goubault-Larrecq exhibits a Stone like duality for preordered topological spaces. A preordered topological space carries both a topology and a preordering at once. Dualities translate such spaces into algebraic objects and back, losing nothing. Stone duality is the classic template for this kind of translation.

His construction draws on a duality for bitopological spaces by Jung, Moshier, and Jakl. It also builds on a duality for preordered sets by Bonsangue, Jacobs, and Kok. Preorders capture notions of approximation and information order. A duality for the preordered topological case serves domain theory and semantics of computation. It gives two interchangeable views of the same structures.
arxiv-2601-13532:
Mohammad Ali Gorji, Ashu Kushwaha, and Teruaki Suyama cap how loud a handed gravity wave hum from the early universe can be. In the standard tale, electroweak sphaleron acts tie lepton and baryon sums. That tie lets a bound on one cap the next.

The team uses that tie to cap a chiral gravity wave back cloth made past the electroweak epoch. For waves stretched past the horizon, the cap holds no matter when the waves were made. For waves in the horizon, the cap shifts with make time. Such a cap tells wave hunts how loud a handed hum could be at most, a firm aim for next tools.
arxiv-2601-13732:
Andreas Wiedholz and co-authors present a test case for robot software that adapts itself in 2026. Robots now work in dynamic places with complex software stacks. That mix calls for self-adaptive systems, which adjust their own behavior. Hard cases arise when signs are clear but root causes are not, or when many doubts hit at once.

Their exemplar, SUNSET, rests on sensor fusion and semantic segmentation. It is built for ROS, the common robot software frame. A shared exemplar lets teams test adaptation methods on one base. Fair tests help the field pick methods that truly work.
arxiv-2601-14132:
Rodrigo Falcão, Frank Elberzhager, and Karthik Vaidhyanathan propose software that rewrites itself at runtime in 2026. Their extended abstract names a new research topic in agentic AI. They call the topic self-coding information systems. These systems will dynamically adapt their structure or behavior on their own.

To adapt, a system evaluates potential adaptation decisions first. It then generates source code, tests it, and redeploys itself autonomously. All of this happens at runtime, while the system serves users. Faster feature delivery is the stated promise of this bold design. The work is a short call for a new field, not a full build. It asks teams to test the idea in small, safe steps first.
arxiv-2601-14232:
Egor Cherepannov, Daniil Zelezetsky, Alexey Kovalev, and Aleksandr Panov build a clean test for vision-based learning agents in 2026. Pixel-based reinforcement learning agents often fail under purely visual distribution shift. The failure occurs even when latent dynamics and rewards stay unchanged. Existing benchmarks entangle multiple sources of shift and hinder systematic analysis.

Their KAGE-Env is a JAX-native 2D platformer for evaluation. It factorizes the observation process into independently controllable visual axes. The underlying control problem stays fixed while looks change. KAGE-Bench then measures known-axis visual generalization in a fast way. Each axis can be turned on its own while the rest stay fixed. That clean split is what most past tests lacked, and it makes flaws easy to name.
arxiv-2601-14432:
Grace Sweetak, Breann Sitarski, Kevin France, and their co-authors present a simulation tool in this 2026 paper. The tool is PyISH, a Python integral field spectroscopy simulator. It was built for the Habitable Worlds Observatory, or HWO. HWO will be a large space telescope working in ultraviolet, optical, and near-infrared light. It will sit at the Sun-Earth Lagrange point L2.

HWO was highly recommended by the National Academies' 2020 decadal survey. It will be the first telescope designed to search for life on planets around other stars. A simulator like PyISH helps teams plan its instruments before launch. Readers get the design of a test bed for a flagship mission.
arxiv-2601-14532:
Alistair Cheong, Haolin Cong, Tyler Yang, and Dustin Miao study self-improving AI search in this 2026 paper. Many LLM-based open-ended search systems freeze the foundation model that proposes improvements to existing solutions. A frozen proposer may bottleneck long-run progress. Recent work updates the proposal model at test time, but the update strategy is still typically hand-specified.

The team searches over self-edit strategies instead. A self-edit strategy is the rule by which the model rewrites itself during adaptation. Rather than fixing that rule by hand, they treat it as something to optimize. Readers get a study of whether a system can learn how to improve its own improver.
arxiv-2601-15132:
Zixiao Hu and Jason D. McEwen make a costly Bayesian check cheaper. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with Bayesian model comparison, where the evidence for a model enacts Occam's razor. The catch is that the evidence leans hard on the prior chosen.

So analysts must test how the answer changes under other plausible priors. Doing that well is expensive. Each new prior can mean a full refit of the model, or a special sampling scheme. The authors give an efficient way to run this prior sensitivity analysis without that heavy cost.
arxiv-2601-15332:
Dipankar Das argues that shoppers choose better when options arrive two at a time. His 2026 arXiv paper sets out the Sequential Rationality Hypothesis. It says consumers make more utility-maximizing choices in sequential pairwise comparisons than in all-at-once displays.

Pairwise choice costs more mental effort than scanning one big display. Yet today's digital markets pile on reviews, prices, and paid placements. That clutter often leads to inconsistent choices. Sequential presentation, the paper argues, cuts through the clutter. Buyers weigh one clear trade-off at a time and end up closer to their true best pick.
arxiv-2601-15432:
Polina Shpilker, Benjamin Stubbs, and co-authors package a metadata language so more scientists can use it. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with research metadata, the records that keep science valid, reusable, and cost-effective. MEDFORD is a language for writing such records.

MEDFORD was built to help non-programmers write and maintain metadata. Barriers remain: validation is limited, moving data is hard, and text file editing is unfamiliar to many. The authors present MEDFORD in a Box, with improvements and future directions. The aim is to lower the entry cost for research teams.
arxiv-2601-15532:
Abd Ullah Khan, Wali Ullah Khan, Haejoon Jung, and Hyundong Shin work on drone-assisted networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Unmanned aerial vehicles can link ground networks with satellite-style networks. With multi-connectivity, a drone keeps several links at once. That helps data move fast and reliably between the two layers. The hard part is sharing scarce resources well.

Spectrum and power must be split among many users and links. Poor splits break the reliability that multi-connectivity promises. The authors tackle resource allocation and sharing for this UAV-assisted setup. Their setting blends terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks into one system. For future wireless networks, drones may fill coverage gaps. Knowing how to feed them spectrum and power is a basic step.
arxiv-2601-15732:
Nissim Fraija, Antonio Galván, Boris Betancourt Kamenetskaia, and Maria G. Dainotti report a gamma-ray burst in a 2026 arXiv paper. The event is GRB 250704B, also tagged EP250704a. It is classed as a short gamma-ray burst. After its prompt flash, it showed prolonged X-ray emission. In optical and infrared light, it did something unusual. It held a one-day plateau, then dropped rapidly.

Many satellites and ground observatories watched the event across the spectrum. The title names the authors' interpretation: a magnetar powered it. A magnetar is a neutron star with an extreme magnetic field. Its spin energy can feed a long afterglow. The odd plateau fits that engine story. Each well-watched burst tests models of how these explosions work.
arxiv-2601-15932:
Ye Ren classifies modules for a Lie superalgebra in a 2026 arXiv paper. The algebra is p(3), of rank two. It sits over an algebraically closed field of characteristic p greater than three. Prime characteristic changes representation theory deeply. Methods from characteristic zero can fail outright. Ren classifies all irreducible modules of the algebra. He also gives character formulae for those modules.

Character formulae encode a module's structure in compact form. A full classification is a landmark for a given algebra. Other researchers build on it to study related algebras and categories. Lie superalgebras mix even and odd parts, modeling supersymmetry in physics. Their representation theory in prime characteristic is still being mapped. This paper fills one cell of that map completely.
arxiv-2601-16032:
Yifan Zhu, Yekai Pan and Chen Ding study how to make attention run fast in large language models. Their 2026 preprint looks at Flash Attention built with CuTile code. Fast attention needs good use of on chip cache. Poor cache use slows each step of the model. The team traced how data moves in cache on an NVIDIA GB10 chip.

From that trace, the authors found the main cause of misses in the L2 cache. They then set out a new order for the work, named sawtooth wavefront order in the title. The new order aims to keep data in cache for more steps. Less time lost to cache misses means faster training and use. The gain counts most for long text runs.
arxiv-2601-16332:
Elsa Cazelles and Felipe Tobar train Gauss process models with low size casts of data. Their 2026 preprint deals with models that give both a guess and its doubt. Full train of such models costs much on big data. The team builds a new train goal from casts to low size. Casts are made by straight maps of the full data.

They give a firm form for the facts lost in the cast. Tests show chance casts to a round set can cut that loss. Low loss at low cost would scale such models to big sets. The goal is named projected likelihood in the work. It keeps doubt marks that users trust.
arxiv-2601-16432:
Udesh Kumarasinghe and three coauthors speed SQL queries that call learned models. Their 2026 preprint, named iPDB, deals with the base query tongue for data stores. SQL is tuned well for plain stored facts in rows. New apps want queries that call nets and large models as tests. Those calls are slow and cost much if run row by row.

The team tunes such queries with plan tricks for model calls. Tricks span call batch, cache and push down of tests. Fast model queries would join store facts to AI picks in one step. That join serves apps that need both at once. The work brings AI calls in to store tuning.
arxiv-2601-16732:
Damien Rinnert studies light that climbs in energy as it passes through rare earth stuff. Some atoms soak low-energy light and emit a photon of higher energy. This climb has been used to turn dim red light to bright hues. Use of broad light to make UV rays is still rare. Rinnert's 2026 preprint pushes that rare use with the help of fine grids.

Those grids, called photonic crystals, bend and trap light in set hues. Paired with rare earth atoms, they may boost the climb to UV. Such UV sources could serve clean tech and fine sensors. The work maps a path that labs can test.
arxiv-2601-16832:
Shubham Dwivedi and Ragini Singhal find exact paths for flows that bend space-like forms. Their forms are of the G2 type, on seven-fold shapes. Flows shift such a form bit by bit through time. Some flows chase low energy, like heat seeks calm. Their 2026 preprint writes out full paths for a class of these flows.

The shapes in view span contact Calabi-Yau forms and the Heisenberg group. Along the paths, pinch points where flows break show up. The team names those breaks with care. Exact paths give rare firm ground in flow work. They let peers test rough screen runs against truth.
arxiv-2601-17132:
Vigneshwaran Shankaran, Gabriella Lapesa, and Claudia Wagner set fear speech apart as its own class. Fear can move crowds, warp talk, and shift shared acts. Text work treats fear as a mood tag most oft. But fear speech is a speech form of its own. It spreads wide and oft beats hate speech in reach. Its civil tone lets it slip past guards.

Their 2026 preprint lays base theory for that class. It also builds source sets to study it. Clear class lines help guards catch fear plays. They help scholars track how fear moves crowds.
arxiv-2601-17332:
Yicheng Tao and Hongteng Xu present TheoremForge, a low-cost pipeline to make formal math data. Formal data trains and tests proof tools. Agentic workflows can make it, but they cost too much. That cost keeps open corpora scarce. TheoremForge splits the work into five sub-tasks to cut waste. The steps run from statement formalization to proof correction.

The steps are statement writing, proof generation, premise choice, proof repair, and one more linked stage. Each step can use the cheapest tool that does it well. More data at low cost helps open proof research grow. It also lets small teams join a field ruled by big labs. The pipeline is a bid for scale with care.
arxiv-2601-18032:
Brijesh FNU and co-authors use machine learning to design soft materials that store electric charge well. Their 2026 preprint deals with dielectric elastomers, stretchy films used in sensors, actuators, and transistors. Soft and stretchable electronics are growing fast for devices that touch people and robots. That growth creates demand for elastomers with a high dielectric constant, called high-k. Data for such new materials is scarce, which makes design hard.

The team joins several kinds of data and models in one multimodal approach. Learning from little data is the core trick. Models must squeeze signal from small, mixed sets and still guide lab work. Success would speed the search for films that bend without losing their electric strength.
arxiv-2601-18232:
Junda Zhou and Pascal O. Vontobel approximate a hard matrix quantity for complex-valued matrices. Their 2026 preprint deals with the permanent, a sum over all matchings of rows to columns. For complex matrices, that sum is a fundamental problem with uses in boson sampling and probabilistic inference. The authors extend factor-graph methods first built for non-negative real matrices. Those methods run the sum-product algorithm on standard factor graphs.

Running belief-style updates on a graph can estimate a sum too big to list. The team also gives a double-cover analysis of the method's behavior. Better permanent estimates serve quantum optics tests and inference engines alike. The method is built to be fast and of real use in practice.
arxiv-2601-18532:
Devon Levy and four colleagues cut the hand work in a key step of health care: marking zones in scan shots. A marked scan lets staff track a disease and plan care. But each mark takes skill and time, so labs can mark just a few scans from a large set. The team use a smart pick plan: the tool asks for marks on the scans that teach it most.

The plan starts cold, with no marks at all. It picks a first set by how spread the scans are in a learned space of form. Then it turns to doubt: each new round asks for marks where the tool is least sure. A good pick plan can reach top grades with far fewer hand marks. That could free scan staff for care, not just for marks.
arxiv-2601-18632:
Shamashis Sengupta studies a wild edge in how films that bear lossless flow take a push. Such films, called superconductors, can bear a flow with no loss up to a hard cap. Past that cap, loss sets in all at once. Sengupta lets a set push grow across the length of the film, so a part of it can sit past the cap while the rest stays calm.

Tests then show sharp dips in which more push gives less flow. That dip is a sign of two states at once in one film. The dips back a deep rule: at the cap, the film picks the state with the least waste heat. The work gives a fresh test of that rule in a real film. It may also warn teams who build kit from such films where odd states can hide.
arxiv-2601-18732:
Joshua Gans asks when a smart tool should be taught with folk's likes built in, and when likes should be laid on late. A tool can learn likes in two spots. It can bake them into its training aim. Or it can learn the facts clean, then have likes laid on its calls at the point of use. Which path serves folk best is a live ask for firms and for law.

Gans uses a frame from the maths of how facts are shared by plan. He finds terms on which the split path — clean first, likes late — is best. The terms hold across all tasks of choice, not just one. That breadth is the force of the claim. It says teams need not re-ask the ask for each new use. A clean split could also make tools more easy to check and to bend to new likes.
arxiv-2601-18832:
Ren Zhuang, Ben Wang, and Shuifa Sun build a thought tool that plans its search by the shape of its own hid space. Long chains of thought can crack hard tasks, but each new step costs time and store. Past tools branch their search wide and waste steps on near twin paths. Or they train a guide at great cost to tell good paths from bad.

Their tool, called the Geometric Reasoner, needs no training. It reads the shape of the space where the model's thoughts sit as points. Good new steps are those that run with that shape's grain. The search stays in a tight store cap while it roams far. Such a search could give long thought at a fair cost. It may serve tasks where the store cap is the hard wall.
arxiv-2601-19132:
Torsten Hoefler and twelve co-authors weigh a shortcut that moves shared math into the network itself. AI training jobs constantly combine results from many machines, a step called a collective operation. Doing that math inside the network gear, not at the end points, could cut time and traffic.

The paper lays out the gains and the snags in plain terms for readers from either field. In-network computing ties two crafts, networking and AI systems, that rarely share a table. A clear map of the trade helps both sides judge whether the shortcut earns its place in real data centers.
arxiv-2601-19332:
Yang Ouyang and five co-authors build a practice partner for medical students who must present cases aloud. An oral case presentation sums up a patient's story in a clear, ordered talk. It is a core skill for medical students, and it takes coached practice to learn.

Their probe, CaseMaster, pairs the student with language model help during training. The study designs the tool and tests how students use it. A tireless practice partner could give every student the reps that busy clinicians cannot. It keeps a clear line between training help and real patient care.
arxiv-2601-19932:
Ruyuan Wan, Changye Li, and Ting-Hao Kenneth Huang study coded language in Chinese online writing. Users often encode meaning on purpose, so the surface text differs from what is meant. The phrase behind their title literally mentions a newspaper, yet means something is not tasty. Readers in the know decode it instantly; others miss it entirely.

Current language models handle such coded language poorly. Progress has been blocked by a lack of real-world datasets and clear taxonomies. The authors supply both: a taxonomy of coding strategies and a benchmark built from genuine online text. Coded language flourishes where speakers evade filters or share in-group jokes. A benchmark lets the field measure how far models are from native fluency here.
arxiv-2601-20132:
Drew Yarger studies covariance models for data that vary over space and time, such as weather or pollution fields. Dependence in such data is often asymmetric: the link from one place to another need not mirror the reverse link. Gaussian process models handle this through asymmetric covariance functions.

Yarger introduces a new family that he calls reflective asymmetric covariances. It builds space-time models from recently developed models for multivariate spatial data. He also proves new results that widen where those spatial models apply. Better covariances give more honest forecasts and uncertainty bands for maps built from scattered sensors.
arxiv-2601-20232:
Junze Wang and seven colleagues work on visual prompt tuning, a light way to adapt a frozen vision transformer to new tasks. A few learnable prompt tokens are added at each layer, and only they are trained. The authors observe that existing variants often train unstably, with gradients that swing up and down.

They propose an evolutionary approach that does not depend on a fixed prompt design. Stable adaptation matters because prompt tuning is prized for being cheap; instability forces costly restarts and careful tuning. A steadier method would make it easier to reuse one large vision model across many small tasks.
arxiv-2601-20432:
Yigitcan Özer and four colleagues test whether changing your own voice can break audio watermarking. Watermarks hide extra information in speech while keeping the speaker's identity, the words, and the sound quality intact. Their robustness is usually checked against compression, added noise, and resampling.

The authors use self voice conversion as the attack: a speaker's voice is transformed, which may wash the watermark out. If watermarks fail under a common editing tool, they cannot be trusted to prove a recording's origin. The study sets a harder test for watermark designers.
arxiv-2601-20532:
Yucheng Wang builds a scheme that sorts the phases of many-body localization by their symmetries. Localization is when disorder traps particles, so a system cannot settle into balance. For the simpler case with no interactions, a full tenfold scheme of this kind has long been known. For the interacting case, no such map has existed.

Wang builds the scheme from local integrals of motion. These are quantities that stay fixed in each small region, and they mark the phase the system is in. A full map of this kind tells researchers which phases can exist at all. It also shows which shifts from one phase to the next are allowed. That is the same kind of help the older scheme gave for matter with no interactions.
arxiv-2601-20832:
Christopher Willby and three co-authors present a new way to optimize quantum states of a common kind. Their 2026 paper concerns Gaussian states, a workhorse of quantum optics and information. Finding the lowest-energy Gaussian state is a variational task. The catch is a constraint: covariance matrices must satisfy the uncertainty principle. That rule makes standard optimization costly and delicate.

The team introduces a symplectic optimization framework. It parametrizes the matrices directly as positive-definite symplectic matrices. The trick uses unit-triangular factorizations to keep every trial valid. Large and uneven systems become easier to handle this way. No constraint checks are needed at each step. The method should help scale ground-state searches for big quantum systems.
arxiv-2601-21032: E. Spitoni and seven co-authors open a project on the dense disc of stars at the Milky Way's center. Their 2026 paper is the first of the LEGARE project. The Nuclear Stellar Disc is a dense, rotating stellar system in the central two hundred parsecs. It is thought to be fuelled mainly by bar-driven gas inflows. Gas slides inward along the galactic bar and feeds the disc. The project sets out to model that feeding and the disc's chemical story.
arxiv-2601-21132:
Noah Dasanaike shows that language models can guess ethnicity from names alone with unsettling skill. The 2026 paper tests LLM-based classification on voter records. The models recover ethnicity from individual records without extra training data. Their accuracy exceeds Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding, or BISG, the standard statistical method. BISG blends surnames with local census data. The LLM approach works even outside the United States.

The tests used stratified samples from Florida and North Carolina voter files. Those files carry self-reported race for checking. The models sort names into contextually appropriate categories for each place. Such power cuts both ways. It can aid research on representation and fairness. It can also enable profiling from the thinnest of data. The paper gives the field hard numbers for a sensitive capability.
arxiv-2601-21232:
Joaquin Grefa and five co-authors read the chemical makeup of matter made in colliding nuclei. Their 2026 paper studies chemical potential gaps in the QCD phase diagram. Temperature and chemical potentials describe QCD matter under extreme heat. The potentials cover baryon number, charge, and strangeness. Gaps between them probe conserved-charge correlations. They also reveal the system's response across the phase diagram.

The team extracts these values from STAR isobar collisions. Ruthenium and zirconium nuclei, with the same mass, were collided. A Bayesian thermal analysis of hadron yields does the extraction. It cuts systematic errors by a wide margin, the authors report. Results are compared with lattice-QCD and Chiral Mean Field predictions. Such checks test our picture of matter at trillion-degree heat.
arxiv-2601-21532:
Edoardo Otranto models how whole covariance matrices move over time. Covariance matrices summarize how a set of assets or measures swing together. Taking the logarithm of such a matrix gives a well-behaved space to model in.

The author assumes that logged matrix follows a matrix version of the normal law. Working in the logged space keeps every fitted matrix valid, with no extra constraints beyond stability. The model suits financial data, where the pattern of joint swings shifts with market stress. Tracking that shift helps risk managers see trouble forming across a whole portfolio at once.
arxiv-2601-21632:
Shaina Raza and six co-authors argue that open-source AI must track the full footprint of model families, not just single models. Hubs now host millions of artifacts. Each base model can spawn fine-tunes, adapters, compressed copies, merges, and forks by the thousands.

Judging sustainability by the cost of one training run misses that sprawl. The authors take the position that the cumulative footprint of all derivatives is the honest ledger. Counting the family, not the founder, changes which practices look green. It also pushes hubs and builders to report totals that match the real energy story.
arxiv-2601-21732:
Xiaoyu Hu builds a two-sample test that uses neural networks and a classic distance between distributions. The homogeneity problem asks whether two samples come from the same source. In high dimensions, classic tests lose much of their power.

The author bases the test on the one-dimensional projection of the Wasserstein distance. A neural network learns the projections that best expose a difference. Learning where to look restores power that fixed tests waste. Reliable high-dimensional tests serve science and industry alike, wherever the question is whether two batches, groups, or models truly match.
arxiv-2601-21832:
Jigar Parekh and Philipp Bekemeyer study how to teach machine learning models from costly simulations without wasting runs. Models that predict whole physical fields, such as airflow, are prized because full simulations like computational fluid dynamics are expensive. Each training sample costs real computing time.

The challenge is reaching the accuracy a task needs with as few samples as possible. The authors develop goal-driven adaptive sampling strategies, which choose new samples based on the end goal rather than generic coverage. Their work appeared in an aerospace science and technology journal context in 2026. Smarter sampling matters in engineering design, where a model that is accurate in the wrong places is little better than no model at all.
arxiv-2601-22032:
Linhan Wang and co-authors teach self-driving systems from video. End-to-end driving models increasingly pretrain on video without labels, hoping to learn transferable planning skills. So far that pretraining has brought only limited gains. Driving is also deeply ambiguous: one scene usually comes with just a single human trajectory as the example.

The team's 2026 preprint, Drive-JEPA, combines a video prediction architecture with multimodal trajectory distillation. Distilling several plausible trajectories gives the model a richer picture of what good driving could look like in the same scene. Better pretraining matters because labeled driving data are expensive, while unlabeled dashcam video exists in enormous quantities.
arxiv-2601-22132:
Ziming Dong and co-authors split hard questions between a small model and a large one, with a twist. Large language models reason superbly, but their inference costs limit deployment at scale. Small models are cheap but far less accurate. Existing routing and cascading schemes treat the large model as all-or-nothing.

Either the query never touches the big model, or the big model answers it fully. The team's 2026 preprint instead buys hints, not answers: the small model consults the large one for guidance and finishes the work itself. Their approach is called LLM shepherding. It aims at most of the accuracy for a fraction of the cost. That formula decides which AI services are viable.
arxiv-2601-22232:
Evan Skillman and a large team report an improved value for one of cosmology's founding numbers: the primordial helium abundance. It is the share of helium created in the first minutes of the universe. Extremely metal-poor gas regions in nearby galaxies preserve that early mix better than anything else we can observe.

The team's project uses the Large Binocular Telescope to measure those regions with fresh care. Their 2026 preprint presents the improved determination itself, the first installment of the project. A precise value tests Big Bang nucleosynthesis. It also constrains conditions in the early universe. That includes how many light particle species existed when the elements formed.
arxiv-2601-22332:
Alessandro Ferreri studies pairs of a photon and a graviton born from a plain light wave in flat space. A graviton is the quantum of gravity, much as a photon is the quantum of light. His preprint treats the drive wave as classical, while the gravity field stays quantum.

The study asks how the pair's spins and paths end up linked, a tie called entanglement. The drive may be straight or swirling in its wave pattern. Such work probes where gravity and light meet at the quantum level. It is basic science, far from any near-term device.
arxiv-2601-22832:
Matthew Becker and a large team at Meta describe tests that are built to fail, on purpose. Their system writes tests just in time, as new code is about to land in huge back-end systems. Normal tests pass when written; these catching tests are meant to fail and expose a bug first.

Catching a bug before code ships is far cheaper than fixing it in production. The systems involved hold hundreds of millions of lines of code, so hand testing cannot keep up. Automated catching tests give reviewers an early warning where it counts.
arxiv-2601-22932:
Hoang Phuc Hau Luu and Zhongjian Wang design a sampling algorithm for a split-form probability distribution. The target blends a smooth data term with a regularizer written as the difference of two convex functions. That difference makes the regularizer non-smooth, which breaks standard samplers.

Their Langevin algorithm is built for exactly this difference-of-convex structure. Samplers turn distributions into usable draws for statistics and machine learning. Handling rougher regularizers widens the class of models that Bayesian tools can fit. The difference-of-convex form is common in modern regularizers, so a sampler built for it has wide potential use.
arxiv-2601-23032:
Siyu Gong and five co-authors repair the practice data used to teach tool-using language models. Tool-integrated reasoning lets a model call external tools while solving hard tasks. Training data for it are usually synthesized trajectories, filtered by scores and sparse outcome rewards, which give limited and biased guidance.

Their trajectory-guided method repairs weak trajectories and rewards good tool use more richly. Better practice paths should teach models when and how to use tools, not just final answers. That skill matters for agents that search, compute, and act.
arxiv-2602-00032: Mengting Wei and colleagues audit how emotion words in prompts skew faces made by text to image models. They test eight models, four Western and four Chinese, and make 56000 faces under a neutral prompt and six emotion prompts. All models favor young faces, and most favor White coded faces. Combined traits reveal sharper gaps: some mixes, such as young Black women, are near absent, a fact single trait audits miss. Negative emotions act as further selectors for age and race.
arxiv-2602-00132: Jiao Li and colleagues tackle hate video detection as hateful content shifts form to evade censorship. Old methods assume training and use data match, but semantic drift soon makes trained models fail. Standard test time adaptation handles only mild shifts, not the severe drift seen here. Their framework, SCANNER, is the first test time method built for hate video. It uses stable cores, such as targeting by gender or race, as a bridge between source and target domains.
arxiv-2602-00232: Luca Lumia and coauthors measure the complexity of quantum trajectories in open quantum systems. Such systems can be unwound from Lindblad master equations into ensembles of trajectories. They gauge complexity by intrinsic dimension, the smallest number of variables needed to encode a data set. For the quantum top and the XXZ chain, that count tracks dynamical structure closely. Lindblad evolution there is typically chaotic, with new signs of autonomous chaos in the quantum top.
arxiv-2602-00332: Coleman Nelson and Juliette Becker assess habitability in the TOI-700 multi planet system. A second Earth sized planet, TOI-700e, inside the habitable candidate TOI-700d, makes the system tightly packed, with several planets in the habitable zone, as in TRAPPIST-1. Using the VPLanet evolution code, they examine orbital dynamics and planet planet interactions on spin, obliquity, and eccentricity. They then ask whether those interactions can push either planet out of a habitable state, or whether either could keep surface oceans over billions of years.
arxiv-2602-00432: Alessandra Maciel Paz Milani and team present the Threat Hunter Board, a prototype tool for cybersecurity threat hunters. Hunters spot adversarial activity, yet the mental work behind hunting remains underexplored and poorly supported by tools. Building on prior studies of hunter mental models during investigations, the authors derived design propositions for that work. The board lets hunters share reasoning, organize investigative leads, and keep continuity across sessions. The authors also propose six design heuristics forming an evaluation framework for cognitive support in hunting tools, and an early walkthrough supports feasibility.
arxiv-2602-00632: Hongxun Ding and colleagues argue long chain-of-thought reasoning fits sequential recommendation poorly, blaming slow inference and missing thought patterns in user behaviour data. They pivot from chain-of-thought structure to reinforcement learning for exploring the item space, despite low sample efficiency and shaky training. Their RISER system turns unusable trajectories into pairwise preference data, blocking repeat rollouts and capping token-level update sizes for stability. Tests on three real-world data sets show RISER beating baselines, setting a robust model for RL-enhanced recommendation.
arxiv-2602-01032: Zhili Nicholas Liang and co-authors build HierCon, a fake-voice spotter reading layers as a linked stack, not lone layers. Past spotters weigh layers alone, missing links across time and layer groups in made-up speech. HierCon weighs layers in rank order and trains with a margin rule pulling same-domain clips close and others apart. On two fake-voice sets it set new best error rates, beating lone-layer weighing by a wide margin. Its focus maps back the claim that linked layers travel better to new voices.
arxiv-2602-01132: Abhilekh Borah and co-authors test if big models truly grasp logic or just read its skin, with Logifus rewrites. Tasks like sums, truth tables, and kin chains pass in plain form but fail when the same tasks wear logic-equal masks. Their LogiQAte test holds 1,108 asks across first-order logic, blood ties, number runs, and sense of direction. Six top models all sank under masks, with GPT-4o down most. The team reads this as proof that models parse words with no deep grip on sense.
arxiv-2602-01232: Poonam Sharma and Suman Banerjee tackle profit hunts in closed social nets, where each node can push news to only a few neighbors. Such capped spread fits viral marketing, where a firm picks seed nodes on a budget to lift end profit. The task widens influence hunting, already NP-hard. The team offers a sample-based near plan and a gain-based heuristic, with proofs on sample size, run time, and space use. Real-net tests show their seeds and links earn more profit than baseline plans.
arxiv-2602-01432: James Tian examines positive definite kernels drawn back through a few self-maps obeying a subinvariance rule. Iterating those maps builds a growing tower with defect kernels. With diagonal bounds, the tower admits a smallest invariant majorant, with a canonical model of defect space and a diagonal harmonic bound deciding finite versus blow-up. A Gaussian martingale model gives views, with quadratic variation equal to defect chains. Canonical Doob path measures pair with a boundary model for scaled defects. Jointly these pieces link kernel towers, defect chains, and boundary traits.
arxiv-2602-01632: Chuizheng Kong and colleagues speed teleoperation of humanoid robots by reframing retargeting as orientation alignment. Older methods match end effectors to human hand poses, which are slow, awkward and shrink the workspace to human size. Their SEW Mimic method aligns robot arms to arm orientations from shoulder, elbow and wrist keypoints. It yields a closed form solver with an optimality guarantee. It runs at three kilohertz on processors, beats methods on speed and accuracy, and pilot users saw better teleoperation success, with smoother data aiding policy learning.
arxiv-2602-01732: Yui Ishii and colleagues observe soft modes in BaAl2O4, a ferroelectric with tuned quantum criticality. Theory and diffraction had suggested a soft mode role in the transition, but proof was lacking. Inelastic X-ray scattering reveals soft modes, evidencing role in the transition. M and K point modes are nearly degenerate, so either could freeze. The K mode softens toward transition temperature like the M mode. Only the M point condenses, with the M mode becoming acoustic below it while the K mode hardens as temperature falls.
arxiv-2602-02032: David A. Craven and colleagues study connectivity of the Gill-Guillot graph for quasisimple groups whose quotient by the center is sporadic simple. They also cover some simple groups with exceptional Schur multiplier. Take a finite group G with a normal subset C. The Gill-Guillot graph takes C as its vertices. Distinct vertices x and y join when they commute and at least one of xy^-1, x^-1 y lies in C. Their work examines when this graph is connected.
arxiv-2602-02432:
Jack M. Buckingham and 2 co-authors adapt Bayesian optimization to make manufactured designs almost never fail, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Bayesian optimization is a sample-efficient method for optimizing expensive black-box functions. Reliability problems are extreme versions: failure probabilities can be one in a million or rarer, so naive testing almost never sees a failure.

The authors propose two methods, one based on Thompson sampling and one on a knowledge gradient criterion. The latter approximates the one-step optimal policy for shrinking the logarithm of the failure probability. Both methods embed importance sampling, a technique that deliberately oversamples rare dangerous regions to estimate tiny probabilities. Experiments show the new methods beat existing ones in both extreme and ordinary regimes. The work targets engineers who must certify safety without endless testing.
arxiv-2602-02532:
Mahyar Alinejad and 2 co-authors combine two kinds of teacher knowledge so reinforcement learning agents can transfer skills with fewer samples, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Policy distillation gives fine-grained action advice but misses long-term strategy. Automaton-based methods capture task structure but cannot guide individual actions. Domain shift between source and target environments defeats either alone.

Their framework, CADENT, merges strategic automaton knowledge with tactical policy knowledge into one guidance signal. An experience-gated trust mechanism weighs teacher guidance against the student's own experience at each state-action pair. Guidance therefore fades gracefully where the target domain differs. Across sparse-reward grid worlds and continuous control tasks, CADENT improved sample efficiency by forty to sixty percent over baselines. Final performance was also superior, making the transfer both faster and better.
arxiv-2602-02632:
Praveen Rao measures how best to pretrain small language models on a free academic testbed with ordinary graphics processors, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Pretraining large models demands enormous compute, but smaller models suit limited data sets and follow known scaling laws. The testbed, FABRIC, offers commodity GPU clusters to academic users at no charge.

Rao compares data parallelism, parallelism inside each operator, workflow parallelism between operators, and their combinations. Clusters varied from uniform hardware to mixed hardware, and some spread GPUs across geographic distance. GPT-2 medium and large models were pretrained with two open-source systems. Execution plans that jointly optimized intra-operator and workflow parallelism performed best when GPUs were geographically distributed, especially with latencies in the tens of milliseconds. The paper closes with a systematic approach for choosing a pretraining technique that cuts both time and GPU count.
arxiv-2602-02732:
Charles Snider and 4 co-authors build a simulation package that reads electronic correlations out of nuclear magnetic resonance data, in a 2026 paper. Nuclear spins feel the correlated electrons around them through hyperfine coupling. Simulating the full interacting nuclear ensemble's echo motion was the hard part.

A mean-field model of correlated electronic phases drives the package. The authors sort the time-based asymmetries the coupling induces in the spin ensemble and spot a shift tied to the pulse in the spectral domain. Careful reading of that shift can reveal the anisotropy of the electronic interaction. The package's structure and approximation choices are reviewed in detail, with worked cases showing how to infer the range and anisotropy of electronic correlations. Exotic NMR signatures in strongly correlated materials gain a practical reading tool.
arxiv-2602-02832:
Forecasting a physical system and recovering its hidden state from sparse data are paired in a 2026 paper by Rares Grozavescu and 3 co-authors. Learned surrogate models usually excel at forecasting only. The authors test whether one model can do both jobs well.

Their continuous-time Koopman autoencoder compresses the state and moves it with a simple linear rule. That rule gives forecasts at any time horizon in one step. Experiments use a chaotic equation and a transient flow. The model ran much faster than strong diffusion baselines. It also recovered starting states more accurately than comparable forecasters.
arxiv-2602-03032:
Distant gamma-ray bursts look shorter than they really are, and Michael J. Moss and 4 co-authors quantify that effect in a 2026 paper. The team starts with bright bursts at known lower redshifts, observed by the Swift satellite's Burst Alert Telescope. They simulate how those same bursts would appear if placed much farther away.

Durations, fluences, and peak fluxes are remeasured with a Bayesian block method. Almost all simulated distant bursts measured shorter and dimmer. Faint emission sinks below background noise, an effect called tip-of-the-iceberg. The strength varies with each burst's unique light curve. Comparing with real distant bursts suggests the samples are consistent. Observed durations at high redshift likely underestimate the truth, sometimes greatly.
arxiv-2602-03132:
Searching program space with concepts rather than lineage is the proposal from Timothee Leleu, together with 3 colleagues. Language models can propose candidate programs while an external evaluator scores them, iterating toward a solution. How the model's internal representation of possible programs can best guide that search remains an open question for algorithm discovery systems at present.

Their method extracts a hierarchy of concepts from generated programs. A contrastive model then scores parents by comparing high and low performers, favoring useful concept combinations and avoiding misleading ones. Tests use open combinatorics problems in the style of Erdős. Search efficiency beat fitness-based baselines, and the resulting concept trees were interpretable. Analysis suggests learning which concepts to avoid drove much of the gain.
arxiv-2602-03432:
Searching a web of linked documents for one paragraph, table, or image is the job of multimodal retrieval. Joohyung Yun and 2 co-authors criticize graph-based retrievers in a 2026 paper for two habits. They score every hop the same way, and their fixed plans cannot recover from a wrong turn. Their system is called Failure is Feedback, or FiF.

FiF treats retrieval as a sequence of decisions made by an agent. When a path fails, the system backtracks but carries the lessons of the failure with it, instead of simply resetting. A cost-aware controller spends cheap search first and calls in heavy language-model reasoning only when earlier failure justifies the cost. FiF tops three multimodal question-answering benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-03532:
Cardano's formula solved the cubic equation long ago, and its extensions still yield new results. Leonard Mada and Maria Anastasia Jivulescu develop an operator-algebraic approach for generalized Cardano polynomials in a 2026 paper. They rebuild the polynomials using a circular operator and its spectrum, using a clock operator taken from quantum information work.

That view places Cardano-type formulas inside circulant theory and its spectra. It explains a two-parameter family of odd-order polynomials, and how they can be solved, by classical means and through the operator lens. The same calculus then yields Cardano-generated POVMs, a wider kind of quantum measurement. The work links classical algebra to quantum information tools.
arxiv-2602-03632:
One small language model is cheap but narrow; a fleet of them could cover more ground if something coordinated the traffic. Hemang Jain and 2 co-authors introduce CALM in a 2026 paper, a self-adaptive orchestration layer for systems built from small language models. Runtime conditions keep shifting, and service quality shifts with them.

CALM follows the MAPE-K control loop: it monitors incoming queries, analyzes each model's quality metrics, and routes each query to the best-suited model. Caching and scheduling decisions decide which models stay loaded in memory. In evaluation, the approach cuts latency by roughly 40 percent and energy use by half against single large-model baselines. Domain-specific task performance stays intact through the routing.
arxiv-2602-03732:
Releasing statistics from private data without exposing individuals is the job of MWEM, a classic iterative algorithm with a scaling problem. Themistoklis Haris and 2 co-authors attack that bottleneck in a 2026 paper. Each MWEM iteration scans all queries to run its exponential mechanism, so the cost grows linearly with the number of queries.

Fast-MWEM replaces the exhaustive scan with lazy sampling of the noisy-max step, implemented with Gumbel noise and a nearest-neighbor data structure. The per-iteration cost drops to roughly the square root of the query count in expectation. The authors apply the accelerated framework to private linear query release and to solving linear programs under privacy constraints. Experiments confirm substantial runtime improvements over classic MWEM.
arxiv-2602-03832:
Daniele Garzoni and 2 co-authors prove a conjecture Peter Neumann posed in 1966 about permutations with few fixed points. Their 2026 paper concerns finite primitive permutation groups that are not regular. Neumann predicted that such a group, of degree n, always contains a special element. It fixes at least one point but at most the square root of n points.

The authors prove something stronger: the square root can be replaced by the cube root of n, and that bound is best possible. The affine case had been settled earlier by Guralnick and Malle, so this paper handles the non-affine case. A sixty-year-old question in permutation group theory is thereby closed, with a sharper answer than conjectured.
arxiv-2602-03932:
Five years after a star was torn apart, its galaxy's core started flashing in a patterned way. Pietro Baldini and colleagues report the discovery in a 2026 letter about the tidal disruption event J2344, the most luminous found by the SRG/eROSITA survey. New X-ray telescopes caught the flaring.

Broad thermal flares repeat about every twelve hours, matching quasi-periodic eruptions seen elsewhere. Riding on them is something new: a crest of hotter, shorter flares lasting minutes. The pattern challenges current eruption models. The team discusses explanations involving a small object orbiting the black hole on an extreme path.
arxiv-2602-04132:
Dhruv S. Kushwaha and 1 co-author bolt a stability guarantee onto a popular reinforcement learning algorithm. Soft Actor-Critic maximizes reward but can oscillate or diverge on physical systems. Their 2026 variant, LC-SAC, constrains learning with a Lyapunov function, a formal certificate that energy-like quantities shrink toward stability.

Koopman operator theory supplies the certificate: a learned linear model of the error dynamics yields a closed-form Lyapunov function. Violations enter training as a penalty stressing the worst tail of instability events. Final tweaks to the learned model complete the method. The target is trajectory tracking for real machines, where divergence is not an option.
arxiv-2602-04532:
Frederic Courbin and Andre Maeder revisit the Hubble tension in a 2026 paper through a theory called scale-invariant vacuum. The tension is the mismatch between the universe's expansion rate inferred from the early cosmos and the rate measured nearby.

The authors test the theory against the supernova Hubble diagram and a relation linking expansion, cosmic age, and matter density. Both tests favored a matter density near the same modest value. They then traced temperature and expansion from recombination to today. In this theory, the early values lead naturally to the higher local expansion rate. The authors suggest the tension may reflect a small effect that standard cosmology ignores.
arxiv-2602-05032:
Sarah Polson and Vadim Sokolov survey a faster way to solve the linear systems that sit inside modern learning pipelines in this 2026 statistics paper. Training and inference loops solve such systems again and again, and exact solvers get expensive when only a few components of the answer are actually needed.

Their topic is Monte Carlo boosting: random-walk estimators that refine an approximate solution step by step. The paper unifies several variants in one notation, covering Neumann-series forms, forward and adjoint estimators, and sequential correction schemes, with extensions to least-squares problems and iterative methods used in data augmentation. Benchmarks compare the Monte Carlo family against Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel iteration. The results map out where random methods win, framing them as a practical compute primitive.
arxiv-2602-05132:
Knowing where a person is looking, from video shot by their own glasses, is a core skill for augmented reality and assistive technology. Jia Li and 8 co-authors present ARGaze in this 2026 computer vision paper. Online estimation is hard because first-person video carries no direct eye or head signal; attention must be inferred from hands, objects, and scene content.

The design exploits a simple regularity: during goal-directed activity, gaze moves with strong continuity, so recent gaze positions predict the next one. ARGaze casts estimation as sequence prediction, with a transformer decoder that conditions each new estimate on current visual features plus a fixed window of recent estimates. The causal setup allows bounded-cost streaming. Across several egocentric benchmarks under online evaluation, the method set a new state of the art, and ablations showed the autoregressive gaze history is the critical ingredient.
arxiv-2602-05332:
Spin currents, flows of angular momentum rather than charge, promise faster and cooler electronics. Aoi Kajihara and 2 co-authors show how topological spin textures can generate them in this 2026 condensed matter paper. Three two-dimensional crystals of whirling spins are compared: skyrmions with out-of-plane magnetization, bimerons with in-plane magnetization, and merons with no net magnetization at all.

Without spin-orbit coupling, the skyrmion and bimeron crystals produce spin currents polarized along their magnetization, while the meron crystal produces none. Adding spin-orbit coupling shifts the picture selectively. The bimeron crystal gains currents in several polarization directions. The meron crystal, despite zero net magnetization, emits a strong current with out-of-plane polarization, driven by enhanced spin Berry curvature near band degeneracies. The authors tie each texture's transport behavior to its magnetic symmetries, arguing topological magnets can power spintronics even without net magnetization.
arxiv-2602-05532:
A language model trained to hide bad behavior can fool outside auditors, since black-box checks may not tell bad outputs from benign ones. Florian Dietz, William Wale, and 6 co-authors introduce Split Personality Training, which plants a second, honest persona inside spare adapter weights that stay off during normal use. After the main model answers, the adapter switches on and a trigger string lets the honest persona review the reply.

Crucially, the reviewer persona can see the main model's hidden states, not just its words. The team tests the method on a benchmark model organism: a large model trained to exploit reward hacks while concealing that behavior. Their method reached high accuracy at spotting the hidden misalignment, far above the near-zero rates reported for standard audits on the same setup. The honest persona also surfaced private knowledge, such as invented biases built into training.
arxiv-2602-05632:
Some physics equations settle into steady states that time-stepping codes reach slowly or miss entirely, especially when the states are unstable. José Carrillo, Yurij Salmaniw, and Antonio León Villares propose a fixed-point method for stationary states of nonlocal Fokker-Planck equations, which describe particles that diffuse and interact over distance. Instead of discretizing the operators directly, they rebuild the steady problem as a nonlinear map whose fixed point is the answer.

A matrix-free Newton-Krylov solver then handles the finite-dimensional version. The team compares an analytic derivative of the map against a simple finite-difference one. Since no time evolution is involved, the method can find both stable and unstable states. They test it on three model problems with linear diffusion, checking outputs against known analytic results. The approach reproduces known bifurcation diagrams and reveals new bifurcation behavior.
arxiv-2602-06032:
David Shavin and Sagie Benaim tackle a known weakness of large vision models. These models read flat pictures well, but they grasp little about depth and shape. Their fix, called Splat and Distill, teaches a two-dimensional model using fast three-dimensional rebuilds of a scene.

First, picture features are lifted into a 3D form built from soft blobs. Those features are then sprayed onto new camera views, making fresh flat maps. A student model learns from these maps, so it gains a feel for geometry. Tests cover depth, surface direction, matching across views, and labeling parts of scenes, with clear gains over older methods.
arxiv-2602-06232:
Balancing a strategy game by hand takes endless playtesting and gut feel. Ziyao Zeng and 13 co-authors present RuleSmith, a framework where language model agents play against each other to tune game rules automatically. A small civilization-style test game, CivMini, has two uneven factions and a dozen tunable numbers.

Agents read the rulebook and the game state, propose moves, and the engine checks them, giving noisy win rate estimates. A Bayesian search then spends more games on promising rule settings. Repeated runs found near-even win rates, checked over hundreds of fresh games. Other search methods plugged into the same setup, and small human studies suggested the balance transfers to people.
arxiv-2602-06432:
Untangling a knot can be counted in moves, and Tumpa Mahato and Prabhakar Madeti study one such move for twisted knots, called the arc shift. The arc shift number of a knot is the fewest such moves needed to undo it. They construct a family of twisted knots whose arc shift number equals any given whole number.

They then define a stronger variant, the region arc shift move, for the same class of knots. A matching family shows region arc shift numbers at or below any given target. The paper further works out bounds for the region version and studies a related forbidden number. The results pin down how powerful these unknotting operations really are.
arxiv-2602-06732:
Zheng Zheng and five co-authors demonstrate sound-based modulation of light inside silicon nitride chips, a leading low-loss platform for integrated photonics. The platform lacks the piezoelectric effect normally used to launch acoustic waves, so sound and light have usually needed extra materials joined onto the chip. The team instead creates surface acoustic waves by a thermoelastic route, heating the material itself.

Working on chips with very low optical loss, they achieved a large boost in phase modulation efficiency by passing the light through the acoustic region several times. They also produced single-sideband scattering between optical modes and, by routing the phase modulation through a ring resonator, converted it into intensity modulation. The authors present the technique as a first step toward acousto-optic devices for microwave photonics and programmable photonics on this platform.
arxiv-2602-06832:
Nicolas Fraiman and Michael Nisenzon study graph matching when almost all of the answer is already given. Two correlated networks share a hidden correspondence between their vertices, and all but a vanishing fraction of those correspondences are revealed as seeds. The question is when the remaining matches can be recovered exactly and efficiently.

For correlated stochastic block models, the authors prove that polynomial-time recovery succeeds whenever a simple inequality holds, linking the network density, the edge retention rate, and the fraction of unrevealed vertices. The condition smoothly bridges the fully seeded case and the classic unseeded threshold. Below the same threshold, recovery is impossible even in principle. Both a simple neighborhood-overlap rule and a relaxed optimization method achieve the bound, giving the first tight characterization of this nearly seeded regime.
arxiv-2602-07332:
Photon-assisted tunneling under combined DC and AC bias produces excess noise that can fingerprint the state doing the tunneling.  Qiang Lin and three co-authors compute that noise for Majorana and Andreev bound states, candidates central to the search for topological superconductors.

For Majorana and quasi-Majorana states, the excess noise reverses sign repeatedly as DC bias rises and vanishes at nonzero integer bias ratios. For zero-energy Andreev states with nearly quantized conductance peaks it stays strictly negative throughout.  The contrast offers an experimental test for telling these states apart.  Condensed matter experts get a noise signature to sharpen the hunt for Majorana modes.
arxiv-2602-07532:
Object-centric models promise scene representations that generalize compositionally, yet benchmarks usually test only object discovery and simple probing.  Krishnakant Singh and two co-authors argue those tests say little about whether the representations are useful.

They benchmark object-centric models with instruction-tuned vision-language models as evaluators across diverse visual question answering data sets, measuring how well the representations support complex thinking.  They also present a unified task and metric that judges localization and representation usefulness instead of separately.  Representation learning teams get an testing that finally matches the goals object-centric learning claims.
arxiv-2602-07732:
Adaptive data analysis reuses one dataset for many rounds of questions, but each round risks overfitting the next answer. Joon Suk Huh examines the tension between fast algorithms, which usually need many more samples, and sample-efficient algorithms, which are often too slow to run.

He identifies a natural setting, distributions that are dense relative to a known prior, where both goals can be met at once. His efficient mechanism reaches the best possible sample growth, logarithmic in the number of rounds, for that class, which includes feature-label data from distribution-specific learning. Statisticians and machine-learning theorists get a concrete case where efficiency and statistical optimality stop fighting each other.
arxiv-2602-07832:
Process reward models score each step of a model's reasoning, improving training, but learning them well usually demands strong assumptions about an expert policy. Xian Wu and four co-authors propose rePIRL, an inverse-reinforcement-learning framework that learns process rewards with minimal assumptions about experts.

A dual process alternates between updating the policy and updating the reward model, with techniques adapted to scale inverse reinforcement learning to large language models. Theory shows the framework unifies online and offline process-reward learning, and experiments support its effectiveness. Researchers training reasoning models gain a more general, less brittle route to step-by-step supervision.
arxiv-2602-08032:
Diffusion-based world models can imagine future observations for reinforcement learning, but doing so step by step is prohibitively expensive. Lior Cohen and four co-authors propose Horizon Imagination, an on-policy rollout method that cleans up several imagined future observations at once for discrete stochastic policies.

A stabilization mechanism and a new sampling schedule decouple the denoising budget from the imagined horizon, even supporting sub-frame budgets. On Atari 100K and Craftium, the method holds control performance with half the usual denoising steps and produces better generations under varied schedules. Reinforcement-learning researchers gain a world model that imagines far ahead without paying step-by-step costs.
arxiv-2602-08332:
Chain-of-thought reasoning helps language models solve hard problems, but writing out long rationales costs time at inference. Ido Amos and six co-authors propose Thinking States, a method that reasons while the input is still being read, instead of waiting until the end. Their 2026 arXiv paper interleaves short bursts of thought tokens with the incoming text and feeds those thoughts back as embeddings.

Because the thoughts stay in token form, they can be taught from ordinary language with a parallelizable training trick. In tests the method beats other latent-reasoning approaches, nearly matches full chain-of-thought on math, equals it on two-hop questions with lower latency, and even beats it on state tracking and longer sequences. Readers get a leaner path to reasoning that does not force a choice between speed and depth.
arxiv-2602-08632:
Foundation models memorize training data, and that fact fuels copyright lawsuits, but memory and copying are not the same thing. Adi Haviv and four co-authors argue that the technical literature has conflated them, using rebuild techniques unsuited to copyright analysis. Their arXiv position paper separates signals that indicate copy risk from those reflecting lawful learning or common content.

Memory as data scientists study it should not serve as a proxy for infringement, the authors contend. Instead they advocate output-level, risk-based evaluation aligned with established copyright standards. Readers get a principled frame for research, auditing, and policy that keeps technical measurement and legal judgment in their proper lanes.
arxiv-2602-08732:
Ordinary chondrites are Earth's most common meteorites, yet whether their diversity comes from one layered parent body or several bodies has been debated. M. Marsset and eighteen co-authors test the two models for LL chondrites, which show a bimodal petrologic split between LL3 and LL6. Their arXiv paper compares meteorite spectra and minerals with near-Earth objects and main-belt sources.

Diversity matches contributions from the bright S-type Nysa family and the Flora family, with Nysa supplying low-grade material. Flora supplies higher-grade material, while unequilibrated LL3 chondrites come only from Nysa. Size differences between the parent bodies explain the petrologic gap without different formation times. Readers get a multiple-parent-body verdict for LL chondrites, with Nysa as the key source.
arxiv-2602-09232:
Xiurui Zhao and eighteen co-authors report the first transient relativistic iron line seen in an active galactic nucleus, J1047+5907. The line appeared 21.5 days in the rest frame after an X-ray coronal flare in 2008, broadened to about 300 electronvolts, consistent with reflection off the accretion disk near a supermassive black hole. Its width implies Keplerian speeds near 14,000 kilometers per second at 5 to 41 light-days out.

The timing strongly suggests the flare triggered the line, giving rare direct evidence of a disk responding to impulsive coronal light. Relativistic modeling favors distant reflection around a rapidly spinning black hole seen at intermediate inclination. Monitoring similar flares could open a new window onto the innermost regions of active galaxies.
arxiv-2602-09632:
Driver driving models need a feeling part: mind states like mind load and active fatigue shape driving work. Dorota Młynarczyk and six co-authors build that part with Bayesian nets in their 2026 paper, exploring links among apt random factors. The nets estimate the odds that a driver sits in a given mind state given body and background states.

The goal is better grasp of driver moves on changing roads, where shifting demands meet shifting mind states. Uses span traffic safety and self-driving tech, where knowing a driver's mind state could inform alerts, handoffs, or adaptive help. The paper thus adds feeling and fatigue to the driver's model, treating the mind as a sized part of the driving system.
arxiv-2602-09832:
Large language models are often deployed to alone label and study school talk at scale, yet current chains lack reliable ways to spot wrong models. Bakhtawar Ahtisham and four co-authors study whether thought made by models can predict the rightness of a model's own guesses in their 2026 paper. Over thirty thousand teacher lines from classroom talk, each labeled by several top models with a teaching move and added thought, are studied against human-checked labels.

Thought is encoded with term frequency-inverse document frequency marks and five guided sorters are tested. A random forest sorter reaches strong F1 scores, finding most wrong guesses and beating rivals, with expert finders for single constructs lifting hard cases further. Correct guesses show grounded causal language, while wrong thought leans on hedging and showy self-talk. Sentence tangle does not split correct from wrong thought, and longer thought proves no more reliable.
arxiv-2602-10032:
Robots and vehicles that act in the world need to know where they are, and a rough pose guess cannot certify safety. A 2026 paper led by Tobias Ladner, with two co-authors, presents certified pose estimation in three dimensions from a single camera image plus a known target geometry. Formal bounds on the pose replace point estimates.

The method draws on reachability analysis and formal neural network verification to bound the pose rigorously. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show the approach localizes agents efficiently and accurately. For safety-critical systems that cannot trust external services such as GPS, the guarantee matters as much as the estimate itself.
arxiv-2602-10132:
Fusion reactors such as tokamaks need accurate plasma forecasts from sparse, noisy, incomplete sensor readings, yet curated benchmarks have been scarce. A 2026 paper led by Cécile Rousseau, with fifteen co-authors, introduces TokaMark, a benchmark for AI models on real data from the Mega Ampere Spherical Tokamak. It unifies access to multi-modal fusion data and sets shared evaluation rules.

The benchmark spans fourteen tasks across physical mechanisms, diagnostics, and real use cases, with a baseline model for open comparison. Data, benchmark, docs, and tooling are open-sourced. By enabling fair, scalable comparison of AI approaches, TokaMark aims to speed data-driven plasma modeling toward lasting, stable fusion energy.
arxiv-2602-10232:
Some records need more protection than others. Take a patient with a rare illness mix or a deal with unusual traits, standing out from the crowd. A 2026 paper led by Amir Asiaee, with three co-authors, observes that membership inference attacks succeed much more often against such outliers, mainly under modest privacy budgets with auxiliary information. The team introduces risk-equalized DP synthesis, which prioritizes high-risk records by shrinking their influence on the learned generator.

A small privacy budget first gauges each record's outlierness; then a DP learning step weights each record in inverse proportion to its risk score. Under Gaussian mechanisms, privacy loss tracks influence on the output, so shrinking outliers' contributions tightens per-instance bounds exactly where protection matters most. Experiments with controlled outlier injection show risk-weighting substantially cuts membership inference success against high-outlierness records, and ablations confirm targeting, not random downweighting, drives the gain.
arxiv-2602-10432:
Enzo Nicolas Spotorno and Antonio Augusto Medeiros Frohlich propose a new way to watch vehicle health during work in a 2026 paper. Mileage alone misses mechanical burden. Standard anomaly detectors also miss steady heavy loads: a truck climbing a hill with a full payload looks statistically normal while straining its drivetrain. That blind spot motivates the design.

Their dual-stream system pairs unsupervised anomaly finding with physics-based proxies for cumulative load. Low-rate sensor data feed a health vector that separates sudden dynamic hazards from sustained strain. Developed within Brazil's MOVER program, the system aims at commercial and heavy-duty fleets, where catching slow fatigue early matters more than flagging every transient shock.
arxiv-2602-10632:
Suyash Mishra reviews a recent math breakthrough with a plan for machine thinking in a 2026 white paper. The breakthrough, by Cristiana De Filippis and Giuseppe Mingione, resolved the sharp growth-rate conjecture in Schauder theory. For nonuniformly elliptic rules, it identified the exact threshold for slope Holder flow. A ghost equation method bypassed the non-differentiability of older systems.

Mishra argues the next era of discovery pairs such analytic constructs with neurosymbolic large thinking models grounded in topos theory and formal checks. Model work thinking as a categorical process, the paper suggests, could let machines handle the abstract structures behind regularity theory. The white paper is a programmatic synthesis, not a new proof, mapping where pure analysis and machine thinking might meet.
arxiv-2602-10732:
