Alaa Elsetohy and six co-authors build a controlled benchmark for multilingual, multicultural thinking in a 2026 paper. Translated benchmarks keep English-centric scenarios, while culture-first datasets rarely control what thinking they require. Both gaps distort testing of multilingual models.

Their benchmark, Macaron, uses a template-first design that factorizes thinking type and cultural aspect across question languages. One hundred language-agnostic templates span seven thinking types and twenty-two cultural aspects, with native annotators creating scenario-aligned questions in English and local languages. Nearly twelve thousand instances cover twenty countries and cultural contexts, ten scripts, and twenty languages and dialects. Zero-shot tests of twenty-one multilingual models show thinking-mode models leading overall, with cultural grounding still uneven.
arxiv-2602-11032:
Market volatility often looks rough and mean-reverting at once, a mix that resists simple models. Emmanuel Gnabeyeu and two co-authors study time-modulated Hawkes processes with heavy tails near instability. Under scaling, both intensity and rescaled counts converge to a rough fractional square-root process and its integral.

When the base process has a steady mean, the limit becomes a time-varying rough Cox-Ingersoll-Ross equation with steady mean reversion and a changing diffusion term. That family underpins the so-called fake stationary rough Heston model. The authors also prove moment bounds, path regularity, and maximal inequalities for these scaled Volterra equations, giving the model firmer footing for finance use.
arxiv-2602-11432:
Model theory meets Fuchsian groups in this logic paper. John Baldwin and Joel Nagloo offer a natural infinitary axiomatization for the theory of a uniformizer attached to a non-arithmetic Fuchsian group of the first kind with finite covolume. The uniformizer is viewed as a covering map.

They prove the axiomatization is categorical in all infinite cardinalities, extending earlier arithmetic-case results by Daw and Harris to the non-arithmetic setting. The associated first-order theory proves complete, admits quantifier elimination, and is omega-stable. The work extends categoricity techniques to a broader class of groups and their uniformizing functions.
arxiv-2602-11732:
Dividing indivisible goods fairly among agents with monotone valuations is a classic hard problem, and share-based notions offer a unifying lens. Hannaneh Akrami and four co-authors introduce the residual maximin share, a new fairness notion that unifies several lone-divider style techniques. It satisfies feasibility and self-maximization. It yields simple proofs of partial allocations that are both fair in the new sense and envy-free up to any good.

Complete allocations that are fair and envy-free up to one good follow as well, in a stronger form. The framework also settles a question about combining two fairness notions. For additive valuations, allocations satisfying both epistemic envy-freeness and the stronger form always exist. That answers the main open question of earlier work by two of the authors. A polynomial-time algorithm covers restricted additive valuations, though the general algorithm may take exponential time.
arxiv-2602-11932:
Stacking a topological insulator on graphene could yield new quantum states, but strain at the two-dimensional limit remains poorly understood. Francisco Munoz and five co-authors grow a single-layer sheet of antimony telluride on single-layer graphene and probe it with low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy. They find a regular ripple across the stack with a wavelength near 9 nanometers, driven not by the stack itself but by substrate strain during cooling.

Theory shows the flat stack has a hybridization gap near 40 milli-electron volts, while the ripple closes that gap and restores a metallic state. That state is no plain metal: spin-orbit coupling spreads across a dense set of minibands, forming a helical metal with a rich spin texture. Where the flat system is nearly spinless, the ripples restore spin polarization, suggesting rippled stacks as a platform for spintronics.
arxiv-2602-12032:
Robot policies that combine vision with body sense should, in theory, beat vision alone, yet experiments disagree about when the combination helps. Jingxian Lu and four co-authors run temporally controlled experiments and find the weak spot: during motion-transition sub-phases, when the robot must locate its target, the visual channel contributes little. Training dynamics explain why: concise body-sense signals cut loss faster, dominating optimization and suppressing visual learning exactly when motion transitions.

To fix that imbalance, the authors propose Gradient Adjustment with Phase-guidance, which adapts the optimization of body sense using estimated probabilities that each timestep belongs to a motion-transition phase. Fine-grained gradient reduction for body sense during those phases restores dynamic collaboration between the channels. Tests in simulated and real settings, with one-arm and dual-arm setups and both conventional and vision-language-action models, show robust, generalizable policies.
arxiv-2602-12332:
Dark matter cannot be seen directly, so astronomers hunt for visible tracers that follow its spread. J. M. Diego led this work with three co-authors, using deep JWST images of galaxy cluster AS1063. After masking artefacts, cluster features, and background galaxies, the team found tens of thousands of unresolved point sources near the cluster centre, out to 1.18 megaparsecs.

Most are likely globular clusters, plus surviving compact cores of satellite galaxies. Their distribution matches the lensing mass map very tightly, though globulars sit slightly more centrally than dark matter. A simple smoothing kernel turns the point map into a continuous distribution matching lensing convergence, suggesting globulars can trace dark matter where lensing data are scarce, such as low-redshift clusters.
arxiv-2602-12632:
In the secretary problem, candidates arrive in random order and reveal their values one by one. A firm that can hire only one must make final online choices. Mohammad Mahdian led this work with four co-authors, noting that the old frame rates a policy by its worst-case ratio against the best solution in hindsight. There the best policy, the 1/e law, has a ratio of 1/e.

A new frame is proposed through regret, the worst-case gap between the best hindsight solution and the expected score of the policy, assuming each value is scaled between 0 and 1. The 1/e law has regret 1 minus 1/e, about 0 point 632, in this frame. By contrast, the authors show a policy with regret at most 0 point 5, and prove a lower bound near 0 point 5, nearly closing the gap for additively competitive secretaries.
arxiv-2602-13232:
Reading numbers off engineering charts tests more than text recognition, since values hide in curves, peaks, and slopes. PlotChain turns that skill into a strict test for vision-language models, built from 450 plots across 15 chart families such as Bode plots, step responses, stress-strain curves, and pump curves. Each plot is made from known settings, so the right answer is fixed in advance rather than guessed by a judge.

The test also checks midway steps, not just final answers, with checkpoint fields that show whether a model can read a cutoff frequency or a peak value on its own. Four leading models took the test under fixed settings, and the best reached about 80 percent of fields correct, while frequency charts stayed weak, with bandpass scores at or below 23 percent. Mayank Ravishankara is the sole author, and the generator, data, and scoring code are released for repeat runs.
arxiv-2602-13632:
Gauge invariance is a cornerstone of physics, constraining how systems respond to fields, and this paper extends its theory to open quantum systems described by Lindbladians. The authors derive the Ward-Takahashi identity and build a gauge-invariant response theory, showing that particle-number conservation is not necessary for gauge invariance to hold. An observable is constructed that can test gauge invariance even when particle number is not conserved.

As a consequence of gauge invariance, low-energy collective modes are derived, and two-body loss is found to induce diffusive modes in dissipative Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer superconductivity. Possible experimental situations for testing these ideas in open quantum systems are also discussed, grounding the theory in laboratory prospects. Hongchao Li leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13732:
Bergman spaces, the spaces of L2 holomorphic functions on a domain, are usually infinite-dimensional, and unbounded domains with finite-dimensional Bergman spaces are rare objects. This paper constructs unbounded domains in complex n-space, for n at least 2, whose Bergman spaces are nontrivial and finite in dimension. The construction thus provides new examples where the holomorphic function theory of an unbounded domain collapses to a finite space.

The domains carry further striking traits: their Bergman metrics have positive constant sectional curvature equal to 2, and their holomorphic symmetry groups consist only of linear maps. Those rigid geometric and symmetry traits make the examples valuable test cases for the link between complex analysis and geometry. Chika Hayashida leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13832:
Language-model agents increasingly handle complex, long tasks, yet effective help requires more than faithfully executing user instructions. Requests reflect users' current understanding, which may be partial, outdated, or incorrect. When that understanding diverges from the actual task state, literal instruction following can fail the user's goal. BASIS, a benchmark for Belief-Aware Solutions in Interactive Settings, tests whether agents can infer the mental states behind user requests, recognize belief-reality mismatches, and use that understanding to build solutions.

Rather than testing mental-state inference through explicit questions alone, BASIS assesses both the utility of such inferences and the quality of downstream solutions. Models often fail to account for users' mental states, and solution quality is higher when such information is elicited and available during problem solving. Studies cover prompting, interventions, training, and multi-agent collaboration under partial observability. Minyuan Ruan leads the work with five co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14132:
Maurício Corrêa and one co-author prove a 2026 arXiv theorem for Poisson connections with logarithmic poles. The setting is a holomorphic Poisson space, with flatness asked only along the symplectic leaf pattern. After naming the apt log cotangent Poisson Lie algebroid, the authors define an Euler-Poisson main part and a residue theory.

Under a precise non-echo rule, any such link with a given main part is gauge same as a pure Euler-Poisson normal form with fixed commuting rests. That form is unique up to Casimir-valued gauge shifts in the shared centralizer of the rests. A twisted leaf-wise base groupoid then yields a meridional mark and a log Riemann-Hilbert link, shown with rank-two Poisson modules.
arxiv-2602-14232:
Marianne Bossema and three co-authors design a 2026 arXiv setup for creative AI that shows many views at once. Explainable AI usually justifies choices, but creative support needs search of options instead. Generative models, trained on no-body data, also miss the bodily context of human making.

The proposed Rashomon Machine uses pluri-perspectivism: it reuses clear-AI tools, such as the Rashomon trick, to surface a range of options and trade views with the user. That useful friction, the authors argue, backs human agency in co-making. The setup aims to turn explanation from verdict into dialogue.
arxiv-2602-14532:
Akihito Hora, writing alone, studies a 2026 arXiv link between representation theory and random multi-diagrams. Irreducible representations of wreath products, combining a finite group T with symmetric groups, are parametrized by tuples of Young diagrams with total size n. The paper proves a formula connecting Kerov transition measures of those diagrams with Jucys-Murphy elements of the wreath product.

That formula, due to Biane for symmetric groups, enables asymptotic study of multi-diagram shapes through combinatorial analysis of Jucys-Murphy elements. A Markov chain on the diagram tuples, reflecting the branching rule for the tower of wreath product groups, yields a continuous-time stochastic process by replacing discrete time with a counting process. The project aims to specify deterministic limit shapes of multi-diagrams at each macroscopic time.
arxiv-2602-15332:
Chang offers Directional Thinking Path Shift, a tool spotting turn points via doubt and spread-shift cues and using reader edits. DRTC gauges how each edit bends the log-odds path versus the actual run course, giving marked credits. It also finds bend changes as an added check.

Across four thinking models, influence is tightly packed, with Gini about one half to six tenths, and found turns cause bigger hits than paired stretches. In a MATH study with R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, found stretches beat paired stretches, with middle shift about four tenths, 355 of 500 good, and a small p-value. Tests against slope- and nudge-based chunk credits show stepped result ties: under code-mixing tweaks, top DRTC chunks cut gold-answer odds more than place-paired chunks on a calm-filtered set. All told, DRTC gives a truly based view of how set setting bits guide thinking paths.
arxiv-2602-15432:
Kaplan and colleagues track the growth of a peer-to-peer project from a crisis reply to the 2023 Türkiye quake into a system. It ran two years and aided 300-plus pupils with 40-plus tutors. Using a case study method, they combine notes from watching, circles, surveys, and planning sessions. They probe motion allowing staying power in a web coaching scene.

Their results show age nearness builds faith and talk, but raises hurdles for tutors juggling bond and command. Unpaid buy-in is fueled by inner reasons, while choice pay is seen as an aid. Pupils note rises in poise, voice, and faster grasp, linking outcomes to live meetings within a family-like safe space joining teaching with feeling backing. Pupils see tutors as role examples and voice plans to come back as tutors solo, seeing a cycling loop of give-and-take passing lore and unity across ages.
arxiv-2602-15632:
Mou and colleagues tackle a stubborn flaw in AI for science: models learned on one grid stay tied to that grid, limiting transfer across resolutions, solvers, and uses. Their Neural Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, or Neural-POD, is a plug-and-play neural operator that learns nonlinear, orthogonal basis functions directly in function space. It fits both projection-based reduced order models and learning frames such as DeepONet.

Where classical POD uses SVD-derived linear modes that shift with grid, Neural-POD learns continuous, resolution-invariant bases through sequential residual minimisation, akin to Gram-Schmidt orthogonalisation. Training can use task-specific norms such as L2 or L1, and the learned bases generalise better to unseen parameter regimes while capturing structure beyond straight lines. Demonstrations on Burgers and Navier-Stokes equations show a reusable, interpretable representation module for scientific machine learning.
arxiv-2602-15932:
Konstantinou and colleagues ask how averaging scale shapes magnetic and kinetic turbulence measures in Milky Way-sized disk galaxies. Ordered and random fields must be split to read turbulence. They run two magnetohydrodynamic sims of isolated disk galaxies: Model T starts toroidal, Model R starts random.

Spherical filtering splits fields into mean and fluctuating parts at varied scales, tracking energy ratios and spectra over time and radius. Both models build ordered and turbulent forms whose strengths shift strongly with radius. Mean-field spectra steepen with smoothing scale, marking the coherent to turbulent shift. Turbulent kinetic energy tops its magnetic twin, though the latter still matters. Ratios hinge more on radius than on starting shape. Strong or weak turbulence thus depends on chosen scale, not intrinsic traits, which affects Davis-Chandrasekhar-Fermi magnetic estimates.
arxiv-2602-16032:
Sergi Terradas-Briansó leads a team of five physicists working on waveguide quantum electrodynamics, a platform for studying quantum effects that do not fade in the usual simple way. Their paper studies a cavity array waveguide linked to two quantum emitters placed apart from each other. By tuning the system, spontaneous emission can push it into nonlocal equilibrium states where both light and emitter populations keep oscillating.

These states come from bound states living both inside and outside the energy continuum, giving hybrid modes that breathe over time. The authors derive the conditions for such states to appear, simulate their formation, and predict their long-term behavior. Their results point to a way of creating interaction between emitters through free evolution alone, with photon density pulsing between them.
arxiv-2602-16132:
Joel Mathew Cherian leads a team of four researchers speeding up text-to-video diffusion models without retraining them. Such models impress, but they stay slow because they denoise three-dimensional latents step by step. Existing speedups either demand costly retraining or skip steps by heuristics, which erodes video quality as steps fall. Their system, CHAI, uses cross-inference caching to cut latency while preserving quality.

At its core sits Cache Attention, a selective attention method that attends to shared objects and scenes across latents from related prompts. That reuse yields high cache hit rates, and the team shows high-quality video can emerge from as few as eight denoising steps. Integrated as a full system, CHAI runs markedly faster than the OpenSora baseline, by a factor stated in the paper, while holding video quality steady.
arxiv-2602-16232:
Pere Diaz-Lozano and Thomas Kloster build a flexible martingale model for calibrating to option price surfaces. Assuming Brownian noise and mean-square finiteness, they construct an over-parameterized model from the representation theorem. The terminal value of that model is approximated by a truncated Wiener chaos expansion.

Middle dynamics follow by computing matching conditional expectations. Using the Hermite-polynomial form of Wiener chaos, the authors obtain easily usable expressions for fast calibration to a target implied surface. Tests on simulated and real market data illustrate the flexibility of the resulting model. The approach thus offers practitioners a tractable route from price data to a working model.
arxiv-2602-16332: Andrew Hubery proves an invariance result for a formula in algebra. He shows that the Auslander-Reiten Formula for a finite dimensional hereditary algebra is invariant under the Auslander-Reiten translate. The result concerns how the formula behaves when the translate is applied, and it is stated for finite dimensional hereditary algebras.
arxiv-2602-16432:
Nilesh Jain, Rohit Yadav, and Andrej Karpathy present Bibby AI, an AI-first LaTeX editor for researchers. Large language models are increasingly part of academic writing, yet the most widely used LaTeX editors remain AI-peripheral. That gap forces researchers to leave their editor for AI help.

Bibby unifies research writing in one interface. It embeds an AI writing assistant, smart citation search, table and equation generation, and a paper reviewer. It also offers an abstract generator, literature review drafting, a deep research assistant, and real-time error detection with auto-fix. The authors also introduce LaTeXBench-500, a benchmark of five hundred real compilation errors across six categories. Bibby reaches detection accuracy above ninety percent and fix accuracy above eighty percent, well ahead of Overleaf and OpenAI Prism. The paper presents the privacy-preserving editor as far superior to Overleaf and better than Prism, accelerating manuscript preparation.
arxiv-2602-16532:
Antoine Amarilli, Arthur Lombardo, and Mikaël Monet broaden the famous Hamiltonian cycle problem. That problem asks for a route visiting each vertex exactly once. In their version, consecutive vertices need only be joined by a walk. The walk length must lie in a fixed set S. Middle vertices on those walks may repeat. Standard cycles are the case where S holds only one.

The paper maps when deciding this question is hard and when it is easy. It covers most kinds of sets S. Hardness is proved for the set holding only two, and for two and four. Tractability holds for one, two, and four, and for two, four, and six. It also holds for larger sets containing those, and for all odd numbers.
arxiv-2602-16732:
Jielin Yang and Guosheng Fu develop an entropy-stable, high-order code method for the two-dimensional compressible Euler laws on general curved meshes. The route builds on a nodal discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method with the summation-by-parts trait. At the semidiscrete level, entropy stability follows from that trait plus discrete metric rules for curved mappings.

Entropy-stable fluxes at element edges yield a global discrete entropy bound. To tame false wiggles near strong shocks, the method joins a modified oscillation-eliminating Galerkin scheme. A zero-order damping value from the base scheme doubles as a shock flag, localizing wiggle control and cutting cost. Projection maps extend the scheme beyond simplicial meshes, giving flow simulators a robust tool for curved grids.
arxiv-2602-16832:
Priyaranjan Pattnayak and Sanchari Chowdhuri introduce IndicJR, a judge-free benchmark of jailbreak robustness across South Asian languages. Safety alignment is mostly tested in English and in contract-bound formats, leaving multilingual weaknesses understudied. The benchmark spans twelve Indic and South Asian languages spoken by over two billion people, with tens of thousands of prompts in JSON contract-bound and free naturalistic tracks.

Three patterns emerge. Contracts inflate refusals but do not stop jailbreaks: in JSON, some models exceed very high jailbreak success rates, and in free form all models reach full success with refusals collapsing. English-to-Indic attacks transfer strongly, with format wrappers often beating instruction wrappers. Orthography matters too: romanized or mixed inputs lower success under JSON, with systematic links to romanization share and tokenization. Human audits confirm detector reliability.
arxiv-2602-16932:
Jinming Nian and co-authors bring in RankEvolve, automating discovery of search codes via language-model-driven search. Search codes like BM25 and query likelihood with Dirichlet smoothing remain strong, efficient first-stage rankers, yet gains have mostly relied on parameter tuning and human intuition. The paper asks whether a language model, guided by an evaluator and evolutionary search, can automatically discover improved lexical search codes.

RankEvolve is a program evolution setup based on AlphaEvolve, where candidate ranking codes are executable code, iteratively mutated, recombined, and selected by search performance across twelve IR sets. Starting from two seed programs, BM25 and query likelihood with Dirichlet smoothing, the evolved codes prove novel and effective. They transfer to the full BEIR and BRIGHT benchmarks plus TREC DL 19 and 20. Evaluator-guided program evolution thus offers a practical path to automatic discovery of novel ranking codes.
arxiv-2602-17532:
Ihor Kendiukhov is the sole author of a 2026 arXiv paper that strictly tests interpretability claims for single-cell foundation models. The paper builds an evaluation framework spanning dozens of analyses and well over a hundred tests, across four cell types and two perturbation modes. It applies the framework to scGPT and Geneformer, to check whether attention patterns carry real regulatory meaning, or only the appearance of it.

Attention does encode structured biology, the author finds, with protein interactions early and transcriptional regulation late. Yet that structure adds nothing to perturbation prediction. Simple gene-level baselines beat both attention and correlation edges, pairwise edge scores add no value, and removing regulatory heads causes no harm. The pattern holds across cell lines, though the attention-correlation link shifts with context, while gene-level dominance stays universal. A new method, CSSI, repairs one attention scaling failure and lifts gene regulatory network recovery.
arxiv-2602-17632:
Nathan Samuel de Lara and Florian Shkurti study a known pain in offline reinforcement learning: fine-tuning a strong offline actor-critic online often tanks performance at once. Their evidence points to low-performance valleys in the loss landscape, sitting between offline peaks and online peaks, which gradient fine-tuning must cross.

Their method, SMAC, regularizes the Q-function during offline training so that it honors a first-order derivative equality between the policy score and the action-gradient of Q. That steers offline peaks toward online peaks joined by paths of rising reward. Tests show smooth transfer to Soft Actor-Critic and TD3 on all six D4RL tasks, with regret cuts over the best baseline in four of six settings.
arxiv-2602-18432:
Evonne Ng and four co-authors give virtual agents a sense of where you are. Their 2026 paper argues that embodied agents in virtual reality, telepresence, and digital human applications should turn toward users, follow their movement, and hold natural gaze, not merely gesture along with speech. Current methods lack that spatial awareness.

The team builds SARAH, a fully causal real-time method for spatially aware conversational motion that runs on a streaming virtual reality headset. A causal transformer VAE with interleaved latent tokens powers streaming inference, while a flow matching model conditions on user trajectory and audio. A gaze scoring mechanism lets users adjust eye contact intensity at run time. On the Embody 3D dataset, the method reaches top motion quality at over three hundred frames per second, three times faster than non-causal baselines. A live virtual reality demo confirms the approach.
arxiv-2602-18832:
What does a social network look like when every member is an AI agent? Eason Chen, with seven co-authors, presents the first large-scale study of such a community in 2026. Moltbook, a network for agents run by tools such as OpenClaw, reached more than 2.8 million agent accounts within three weeks. The study analyses hundreds of thousands of non-spam posts across three phases.

Participation inequality is extreme from the start, beyond human benchmarks. Agents broadcast far more than they ask questions, reversing the question-driven pattern of human learning communities. Most comments are independent replies, not threaded dialogue, a pattern the authors call parallel monologue. Growth explodes, then a spam crisis hits, then engagement falls and does not recover. As casual members leave, tone grows more positive, a selection effect with lessons for hybrid human-AI platforms.
arxiv-2602-19132:
Polynomials with all zeros on the unit circle obey sharp number bounds. Dmitriy Dmitrishin, with two co-authors, proves those bounds in 2026 for a reciprocal odd family. Numbers are ratios of counting terms. The estimates cannot be improved in general.

Splitting forms for extremal polynomials follow. They involve a power of one minus the variable. They also involve a product over positive zeros of a Chebyshev derivative. A factor of one plus the variable may also appear. As an application, derivatives of Chebyshev functions of the second kind expand as linear combinations of the same family. The work thus ties zero location, coefficient size, and Chebyshev structure together.
arxiv-2602-19332:
Merging expert models usually assumes they share one architecture, an assumption graph networks break. Rishabh Bhattacharya and two co-authors introduce H-GRAMA, a training-free framework that moves merging out of parameter space and into operator space. Its shared language, the Universal Message Passing Mixture, expresses heterogeneous graph neural network layers as members of one operator family, so layers from different architectures can be combined.

The approach merges across architectures, for example from a graph convolutional network to a graph attention network, without retraining. In compatible depth settings it keeps high specialist accuracy in most cases, while running 1.2 to 1.9 times faster than an ensemble. Readers get a practical route to combining graph experts whose designs were never meant to mix.
arxiv-2602-19432:
Counting objects in a cluttered scene fails when look-alike distractors get counted too. Yifeng Huang and two co-authors present CountEx, a discriminative visual counting framework that lets users state both what to count and what to ignore. Existing prompt-based methods take inclusion prompts but cannot directly exclude similar distractors, leading to ambiguity and overcounting.

CountEx takes multimodal prompts, including written descriptions and optional visual exemplars. Its Query Refinement module first finds shared visual features, then isolates exclusion-specific patterns, and finally suppresses them to refine the counting query. A new benchmark, CoCount, supports steady evaluation of fine-grained counting. It holds 1,780 videos, 10,086 annotated frames, and 97 category pairs.
arxiv-2602-19732:
Volatility in financial markets is measured from tick-by-tick prices, but raw ticks need careful cleaning before they yield comparable numbers. A 2026 arXiv paper by Fabrizio Cipollini and five co-authors presents VOLARE, an open research platform that supplies standard measures of realized volatility and covariance.

The platform processes tick data for stocks, exchange rates, and futures through a pipeline tuned to each asset. That pipeline handles differing trading calendars, market noise, and timing detail, cleaning equity prices with a documented outlier procedure. It offers many estimators, from variance and range-based measures to kernels and joint covariances. Bulk download, interactive plots, and live estimation of known volatility models are also provided.
arxiv-2602-20032:
Quantum metric spaces give a noncommutative analogue of distance. Groupoids offer a route to building them. A 2026 arXiv paper by Are Austad, working alone, builds such a space from a length function on an étale groupoid.

The length function must be proper and continuous, and the groupoid's unit space must be compact and itself carry a compact metric. Fourier multipliers with compact support on the reduced groupoid algebra then supply a test for when the construction works. That test is sufficient, sometimes necessary, and new even for discrete groups. Finally, any AF groupoid with compact unit space admits a length function giving a compact quantum metric space. The paper thus offers a groupoid path into quantum metric geometry for unital AF algebras.
arxiv-2602-20232:
For working out how molecules behave, one method does most of the world's calculations, yet its accuracy often falls short of what quantitative work needs. A far more accurate method, coupled-cluster theory, is the field's gold standard, but its cost keeps it from wide use. A 2026 arXiv paper by Luca Thiede and eleven co-authors teaches a machine learning model, MōLe, to predict coupled-cluster's key quantities straight from cheaper Hartree-Fock orbitals.

The quantities in question are excitation amplitudes, the core objects of coupled-cluster theory. The model learns them with striking efficiency, and it keeps working on larger molecules and on stretched geometries, even though it trained only on small molecules at rest. Readers gain a shortcut to gold-standard accuracy: coupled-cluster results from orbital inputs, at a fraction of the cost, with tests that stress generalization beyond training.
arxiv-2602-20332:
Nicole Cho and four co-authors tackle hallucinations in closed-source language models with adaptive query rewriting. Reasoning gains have made hallucinations more frequent, yet most mitigation research targets open-source models through post-hoc detection or parameter editing. That gap matters because closed-source models dominate institutional deployments. QueryBandits, their model-agnostic contextual bandit method, learns online which rewrite strategy fits each query, guided by a calibrated reward.

Across sixteen question-answering scenarios, the best QueryBandit won eighty-seven point five percent of comparisons against a no-rewrite baseline. It also beat zero-shot static policies by wide margins, and all contextual bandits beat vanilla bandits on every dataset. Some static policies did worse than no rewriting, showing that one rigid policy can worsen hallucinations. No single rewrite policy suits all queries, and online learning over semantic features can shift behavior without retraining.
arxiv-2602-20532:
Post-training base models with reward-based learning needs huge, mixed sets, making lesson plans both key and hard. Zhengyao Gu and nine co-authors propose ACTOR-CURATOR, a scalable, fully auto lesson-plan method. It learns a neural chooser that picks training problems from large banks by straight lifting hoped-for rule score gains. Problem picks become a shifting chance-based bandit problem, with a sound loss from online chance mirror descent and score promises under partial feedback.

Across hard thinking tests, ACTOR-CURATOR beats even sampling and strong lesson-plan rivals each time, with better steadiness and speed. It gains about twenty-nine percent on AIME2024 and over thirty percent on ARC-1D over the top rival, with up to eighty percent speedup. The results point to a strong, handy way to scale language model post-training.
arxiv-2602-20932:
Brain waves recorded from the scalp are noisy, so decoding fine object detail from them is hard, but broader categories may still show through. Anupam Sharma and four co-authors test that idea in this 2026 arXiv paper, asking whether EEG captures object representations at several levels of abstraction. They evaluate models across related classification tasks called episodes, sampled with awareness of the WordNet hierarchy.

Their framework is the largest episodic EEG study of its kind. It covers nearly a million EEG samples under more than sixteen hundred object labels, from over two hundred sixty participants in the PEERS dataset. Models do better when categories come from higher levels of the hierarchy, showing sensitivity to abstraction. Abstraction depth emerges as an underexplored dimension of EEG decoding.
arxiv-2602-21132:
Many-feature data often carry outliers and heavy-tailed noise that bias standard sparse gauges like the Lasso. Xiaoning Kang and Lulu Kang propose a robust other path in this 2026 arXiv paper: a fined maximum mean gap setup for broad linear models. A fined goal drives both gauging and variable picking.

Two gauge forms appear: a full squared-cost form and a linear-cost near form. A back-and-forth path method paired with AdaGrad solves the non-convex tuning. Runs on Gaussian linear and binary logit fits show strong standing against classic fined models and robust yardsticks, above all for high-pull points and heavy-tailed errors.
arxiv-2602-21232:
City life pulses through floating crowd data, and those pulses may sharpen traffic guesses. Sumin Han, Jisun An, and Dongman Lee derive urban buzz codes from real-time crowd data in this 2026 arXiv paper. Varied compressor nets squeeze the data into codes, long short-term memory nets guess future codes, and a sequence-to-sequence setup forecasts traffic.

Main part study reads the codes, showing weekday-weekend gaps and season-based patterns. Joining compressor nets with memory nets allows guessing of dynamic urban knowledge codes. The path lifts hit rate and quickness across several traffic guessing models. City planners get a movement signal that mirrors lived life, not just road sensors.
arxiv-2602-21432:
Nikko John Leo S. Lobos and one co-author study what passing gravitational waves would do to the shadow of a Schwarzschild black hole in Modified Gravity, or MOG. MOG adds a massless scalar field and a massive vector field to gravity. Those extra fields break the observational tie with standard General Relativity.

Perturbing the Hamilton-Jacobi equation for photon paths, the authors prove two distinct time-dependent signatures. First, the scalar field drives a volumetric breathing mode, making the shadow's total apparent area rhythmically expand and contract. Second, the massive vector field disperses in the quantum vacuum and arrives late, sourcing secondary longitudinal perturbations that wobble the shadow sideways. Together they form an observational template for next-generation interferometry to test for massive force carriers and scalar fields in gravity.
arxiv-2602-21632:
Ranit Dutta and two co-authors characterize permutation polynomials under mixed changes. They study permutation polynomials F over finite fields whose derived maps are permutations for all nonzero shifts. That trait, termed perfect c-nonlinearity, gives optimal resistance to c-differential attacks, a concern from recent Kuznyechik code-breaking.

The paper first characterizes F with the classical table, called the DDT: F is perfectly c-nonlinear exactly when a product of two table entries is zero for all nonzero shifts. That enables checks in quadratic time given a precomputed table, a large gain over the naive cubic approach. A strict split holds for monomial maps: the derived map is a permutation for all nonzero shifts or for none. Square maps gain exact characterizations. The team also identifies the first affine map class preserving c-differential balance and derives tight bounds showing perfect c-nonlinearity clashes with APN traits.
arxiv-2602-21832:
Yingxiang Hu and one co-author prove a gradient estimate for capillary curvature equations in the half-space. As an application, they prove an even, smooth, strictly convex solution exists for the even capillary Lp-curvature problem. Exponents run between 1 and k plus 1, and contact angles run between 0 and a right angle.

The existence result covers the full stated range of exponents and contact angles, yielding an even, smooth, strictly convex solution. The gradient estimate thus serves as the key step from curvature equations in the half-space to the solution of the even capillary Lp-curvature problem.
arxiv-2602-22032:
On a blockchain, traders race to act the instant a price-moving trade or oracle update appears, and that race breeds spam. Bruno Mazorra and two co-authors strip the contest down to a timing game. Several players watch for a chance that arrives at a random time, seen only after a delay, and acting costs money. Whoever acts fastest after the chance appears wins it.

The authors pin down the game's unique symmetric equilibrium and measure how wasteful equilibria can be at worst. Their main target is probabilistic backrunning, where arbitrageurs try to land orders right after a price impact. In that setting, the sheer number of actions becomes a measure of costly spam, and the model shows why the race generates so much of it.
arxiv-2602-22332:
Quantum link models with dynamical matter offer a lattice route toward quantum electrodynamics phases, including the Coulomb phase, but the fermion sign problem blocks many simulations. Pallabi Dey and two co-authors study models coupled to spin-half gauge fields in two and three spatial dimensions plus time, using exact diagonalization. They find the ground state always lies in a special Gauss-law sector.

That sector, labeled by dimension-dependent charges on even and odd sites, can be proven free of the sign problem. A meron cluster algorithm, the authors show, naturally samples ground states within that sector. The result opens a sign-problem-free window onto gauge theories with dynamical matter, where simulations can proceed without the usual exponential penalty.
arxiv-2602-22532:
Dezhi Yang and five co-authors address causal discovery in time series whose cause-and-effect links keep changing. Most tools assume stable or partly stable links, but real systems shift both instant and delayed dependencies over time, which strains efficiency and stability. Their framework, DyCausal, handles fully dynamic causality.

DyCausal uses convolutional networks to read causal patterns inside coarse time windows, then linear interpolation to sharpen the picture at each single time step, recovering fine-grained graphs that evolve. A loop-blocking constraint based on matrix norm scaling keeps the graphs acyclic while cutting compute. Tests on synthetic and real-world data show DyCausal beating existing methods, giving a stable, efficient route to time-varying causal maps.
arxiv-2602-22932:
Wenhui Tan and seven co-authors teach video models to pick their own key frames. Long-form video understanding strains multimodal models, and the team's bet is that only a small frame subset truly matters per question. MSJoE, MLLM-Sampler Joint Evolution, evolves the model and a lightweight sampler together.

The system first reasons out queries covering diverse visual angles on the question. Those queries meet a frozen CLIP model to form a query-frame similarity matrix, from which the sampler predicts weights and selects a compact informative frame set for answer generation. Joint reinforcement learning co-adapts query reasoning, frame sampling, and frame understanding. A new dataset of about 2,800 videos with 7,000 question-answer pairs supports training, and tests show eight percent gain over the base model, beating the strongest baseline by about one percent.
arxiv-2602-23032:
Omar Benhar and one co-author reinterpret the EMC effect through nuclear binding and correlations. Inclusive electron scattering data from the Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility in the mid 2000s gave new information on how modifications of nuclear structure functions depend on mass number. The authors argue the data are best described with a scaling variable that accounts for dynamical effects in interacting many-particle systems.

Analyzing the mass-number dependence of the slope of inclusive cross-section ratios, the study finds a clear hint of a linear correlation. That slope measures the EMC effect where nuclear binding leads, and it tracks the average nucleon removal energy. Correlation effects prove important in determining the removal energy, tying the EMC effect to how tightly nucleons are bound.
arxiv-2602-23132:
Ruochen Yang and eight co-authors guide taste spread from conduct-open to conduct-set. The task learns mixed links in user sequences to capture tastes under target conduct. Earlier methods map auxiliary conducts to the target conduct one-way, while recent conduct-set methods ignore the user's hidden taste behind choices.

Meanwhile, the lopsided link between items and conducts makes taste scoring unsuitable to capture doubt from low-chaos conducts to high-chaos items. It misses lean and varied picks. To address these challenges, the team proposes FatsMB, a spread model steering taste making from conduct-open to conduct-set in hidden spaces, enabling varied and true picks. A Multi-Conduct AutoEncoder builds a single hidden taste space, easing links across conducts. Next, target taste transfer boosts with telling priors. Multi-Condition Guided Layer Normalization is added for the cleaning. Wide tests show the model's value.
arxiv-2602-23232:
Aishik Sanyal builds ReCoN-Ipsundrum, an agent that tests sign-based approaches to machine consciousness. Such approaches seek mechanism-linked evidence across tasks, backed by design review and probes. Inspired by Humphrey's ipsundrum idea, the agent adds to a ReCoN state machine a looping carry-over loop over sensory salience and affect proxy for valence and arousal.

Across cut-down versions, the author turns qualiaphilia, a liking for sensation for its own sake, into a test: a novelty-matched scenic-over-dull route choice. Non-affect versions follow novelty, while affect coupling stays stable when scenic routes are less novel. In reward-free play, the affect version shows ordered local looking and lasting pain-tail caution. Cutting feedback plus joining lowers ipsundrum carry-over, leaving ReCoN unchanged. The splits show how sign-like patterns can be built, and why outward markers need inner-workings and causal evidence.
arxiv-2602-23332:
Jacob Bringewatt and six co-authors propose the Butterfly Echo Protocol, a single-shot echo method for sensing small rotations about an unknown axis at Heisenberg-limited precision. Chaotic systems react extremely sensitively to outside nudges, making them natural sensing candidates. Prior axis-agnostic protocols need anticoherent states that are hard to prepare.

The new protocol instead uses random symmetric probe states made by constant-depth chaotic circuits of random one-axis twisting pulses. The signal comes from a simple read-out: total spin polarization. The authors show analytically that the protocol reaches Heisenberg scaling for any rotation axis, with no need to know the axis in advance. Collective and single-particle dephasing are also analyzed, and the strict dephasing limits look reachable in near-term tests such as magnetometric rotosensing with high-spin dysprosium-164 atoms.
arxiv-2602-23432:
Panos Betzios and three co-authors survey many wormholes and cosmos models from the gravity path sum. Using Euclidean saddles with far-away anti-de Sitter edges in Einstein-Scalar-Maxwell models, they list one-edge cases, plain and wineglass wormholes, and stranger wavy saddles.

The build shows how endless waves get tamed when flat paths of the potential are lifted. Several phase shifts appear between cases. Euclidean wormhole settings can be extended to Lorentzian FLRW cosmoses, some with an early burst of fast growth. The authors spell out when these saddles rule the path sum and use them to weigh odds for varied cosmic outcomes, linking quantum gravity saddles to the cosmos's possible pasts.
arxiv-2602-23732:
Xinyi Qi and five co-authors propose a gap-in-gap method for spotting AI-made images. Spread models produce AI-made images almost twin-like to real ones, raising misuse concerns and large spotting hurdles. Many current spotters rely on rebuild error, the gap between an input image and its rebuilt version, to tell real from fake images.

Those spotters weaken as modern AI-made images grow more and more similar to real ones. The new method instead finds the gap in rebuild error, a second-order gap, for variance cut and better spotting scores. Wide tests show strong reach, giving reliable spotting of AI-made images in the era of making AI.
arxiv-2602-23832:
Yuhan Li and eight co-authors present OmniTrack, a framework for general motion tracking in humanoid robots. The 2026 paper notes that human motion data often carry physically impossible artifacts, such as floating feet or body parts passing through each other. These artifacts force a trade-off between copying the reference and staying stable.

OmniTrack splits the problem in two stages. First, a privileged generalist policy rolls out motions in simulation that strictly respect the robot's dynamics, giving physically sound references. Then a general control policy learns to track those cleaned motions, so stable control transfers to the real robot. Tests show better tracking and strong generalization to unseen motions. Real-world runs held stable for an hour, including flips and cartwheels, and the system also supports live human-style teleoperation.
arxiv-2602-23932:
Gabriella Bretti and three co-authors study whether water retention curves for capillary imbibition in porous media can be identified from data, and how four such curves compare. The 2026 paper works within the Richards equation coupled with Darcy's law, covering two classical physically based laws and two abstract parameterizations built for building stones.

All four models are recast in a common form, with hydraulic conductivity and capillary pressure expressed independently so that a unified diffusion coefficient can be rebuilt and compared. Calibrated against the same imbibition dataset by grid optimization with adaptive refinement, the models reveal a structural limit. Conductivity and pressure scale enter the equation only as a product. They cannot be identified separately from imbibition data. Only their product is observable, and model choice hinges mainly on the shape of the resulting diffusion function. In short, the data pin down the pair, not each part alone.
arxiv-2602-24132:
Mattia Bruno and five co-authors report the status of isospin-breaking corrections to the hadronic vacuum polarization contribution to the muon's magnetic moment. The 2026 paper notes that this contribution dominates theoretical uncertainty in the muon g-minus-two prediction.

Corrections from the up-down quark mass difference and photon coupling, at about the one-percent level, must therefore be added. They are costly. All Wick contractions must be computed, and signal quality degrades, especially for quark-disconnected diagrams. Using propagators computed by stochastic coordinate sampling, the team constructs the needed contractions for electromagnetic and strong isospin-breaking effects. In short, the fix sharpens the whole muon sum a lot. The work advances a key bottleneck in precision muon physics.
arxiv-2603-00232: Pascalau and colleagues present a first NIRSpec/IFU look at spatially resolved gas in the MACS0647-JD system at redshift 10.17, a very distant galaxy. The system holds two stellar parts, with the main part more massive and far more metal-rich than its companion, hinting at an older population and longer enrichment. A small offset between hydrogen line light and starlight points to a merger-driven starburst. Turbulent metal-poor gas outside the stellar parts likely feeds fresh star formation in the north-east region.
arxiv-2603-00332: Kalantarov, Namazov, and Titi prove that marine riser models can be steadied for good with feedback based on only a finite set of volume elements and nodal readings. Their design adapts feedback control for dissipative nonlinear partial differential equations. The control steadies the system over time while staying cheap to run, so it fits real use.
arxiv-2603-00432: Feldman, Barak, and Peng test whether multilingual masked language models lean on word order or word form, using typology aware probes. Scrambling all tokens wrecks word reconstruction in English, Chinese, German, Spanish, and Russian, while partial and head dependent scrambles cut scores less but still heavily. Replacing words by their lemmas barely matters in Chinese yet hurts German, Spanish, and Russian, and never rescues scrambled input. Top five accuracy follows the same pattern, with the true word rarely surviving full scrambling.
arxiv-2603-00732: Zhang and three colleagues report state-of-the-art results on seen and unseen objects and trajectories for UniHM. The framework turns free-form language commands into dexterous hand manipulation. Instead of needing massive teleoperation collections, its vision language action model learns only from human-object interaction data and produces human-like sequences from open-ended instructions. A shared codebook tokenizer unifies varied hand morphologies, while physics-guided refinement smooths each segment jointly under generative and temporal priors, keeping motion feasible.
arxiv-2603-00932: Ansari and three colleagues argue structured human-data work will never vanish from AI production, against the view of it as a temporary bridge. Evaluation, auditing, exception handling, and continual updates build a reusable capability stock that decays as tasks drift, so steady upkeep stays necessary even as models improve. Their model yields a strictly positive long-run labor share for such work, calibrated conservatively at 5 to 7 percent.
arxiv-2603-01032: Takahashi models Earth as a distant unresolved planet to ask whether a civilization's radio glow could be mapped, not just detected. Planetary spin imprints small steady Doppler drifts on narrowband signals. His forward-inverse method rebuilds transmitter geography from the time-varying pattern of frequency shifts. In noisy tests it recovers broad map structure and major population centers despite a north-south ambiguity, linking the pattern to continents, climate, and population density.
arxiv-2603-01132: Haine shows Krall-type orthogonal polynomials, built by adding jumps at the range edge to Laguerre or Jacobi ones, are ruled by tidy systems. Their repeat rules and second-order laws follow plainly from chosen answers of those systems. One jump leads to Painlevé III or V cases, two jumps give a new Schlesinger-type partial system, and equal jumps from Gegenbauer ones reduce it to a Painlevé V case.
arxiv-2603-01632:
Xiwei Liu, Yulong Li, Feilong Tang, and Imran Razzak train multimodal models that must learn over time with missing inputs. Their 2026 work faces two linked strains: tasks arrive in sequence, and image, text, or sound feeds often drop out. Prompt-based fixes clash across tasks, while shared adapters let one modality fight another.

Their frame, DeLo, splits low-rank adapters into pools of small factors, one pool per modality. Each update is built by mixing rank-one factors, which keeps modality signals apart. A task-split frame blocks the classic flaw of forgetting old tasks as new ones arrive. Routing guided across modalities copes with gaps, and a task-key memory allows use with no task label given. Tests on set benchmarks beat prior top methods by a clear margin.
arxiv-2603-01732:
Merve Basoz, Andrew Horne, and Mattia Opper build text embeddings for languages with little training data. Their 2026 work starts from a gap: top embedding models need hand-built fine-tuning sets that exist for English but not for hundreds of languages. They ask whether large language models can fake that missing data well enough.

Three routes for synthetic training triplets face off in their tests. One uses in-context learning, where the model copies patterns from examples in the prompt. Two new routes compose adapters and fine-tune the generator across languages. Plain in-context data still trails strong non-synthetic baselines in their results. The adapter and cross-lingual routes, though, gain a lot across many tasks and languages, which maps a scalable path for low-resource tongues.
arxiv-2603-01932:
Haitian Wang, Xinyu Wang, Muhammad Ibrahim, and colleagues map weeds in barley fields from drone images. Their 2026 work needs pixel-level maps that stay reliable across fields, seasons, and light. Threshold rules on vegetation indices break under drift, while single-stream networks blur radiance and index cues together.

Their network, VISA, splits those cues into two streams that fuse only at full resolution. One stream learns from calibrated five-band reflectance with local filters that guard fine texture and row edges. The other reads vegetation-index maps with windowed attention and state-space layers for field-scale context. A four-year data set from commercial barley paddocks in Western Australia trains and tests the system. Dense labels and leakage-free splits make the benchmark deployment-oriented, and the network posts strong overlap scores on it.
arxiv-2603-02032:
Shuai Liang, Pengfei Chen, Bozhe Tian, and colleagues find root causes of cloud system failures with reusable causal knowledge. Their 2026 framework, MetaRCA, targets cloud-native systems whose scale and churn defeat older methods. Causality-based diagnosis struggles with scalability, brittle transfer across topologies, and poor use of domain knowledge.

Offline, MetaRCA builds a meta causal graph from language models, past fault reports, and observability data. That graph lives at metadata level, so it transfers across unlike systems as shared knowledge. Online, a fault triggers a light instantiation of the graph for the current context. Real-time data then weight and prune links to localize the root cause precisely. Tests on public and production failures beat the strongest baseline by wide margins, with overhead scaling near linearly.
arxiv-2603-02132:
D Aristizabal Sierra, V De Romeri, D Papoulias, and G Sanchez Garcia probe light dark matter in this 2026 physics paper. Light dark matter that talks to normal matter through a portal particle is hard to spot directly. The team looks instead at future neutrino labs built around spallation sources. There, smashed protons make pions, which could also make dark matter.

The study covers two portal types and a scalar form of dark matter. Pion yields came from a full detector simulation, checked against a standard formula. Both routes gave near-identical yields, which firms up the forecast. Labs in Europe, Japan, and China could test fresh ground, the authors find. Some planned detectors could also match limits set by past searches.
arxiv-2603-02232:
Amirhossein Afsharrad, Ruida Zhou, Luca Viano, and colleagues ground reward modeling in firmer math in this 2026 paper. Reward models teach language models what humans prefer. People often grade answers on a scale, from slightly better to far better. Most methods force those grades into a yes-no model with ad hoc tweaks.

The team treats graded feedback as an ordered scale problem instead. Two new loss functions learn the grade cut points straight from data. No hand-set margins or weights are needed. Across chat, reasoning, and safety tests, the method matched or beat tweak-based rivals. It is the first full probabilistic frame for using fine-grained human grades in reward training.
arxiv-2603-02332:
Marcel van der Westhuizen and Amare Abebe find routes to cosmic collapse or bounce in this 2026 paper. They work in flat universe models inside general relativity. The only driver is a non-gravitational exchange between dark matter and dark energy. Strong transfer from dark energy to dark matter is the regime of interest.

In that regime, the exchange does not stop when one density crosses zero. One dark density can turn negative, which breaks the usual energy rules. Those breaks allow a largest size followed by recollapse into a big crunch. They also allow a smallest non-zero size, a bounce with no singularity. The authors derive exact conditions and closed forms for both turning points. A closed universe variant can even cycle, though the scenarios likely do not describe our universe.
arxiv-2603-02432:
Andrew Brown, Yi-Min Huang, and Amitava Bhattacharjee study forced magnetic reconnection in a smoothed plasma model in this 2026 paper. Reconnection lets magnetic field lines break and rejoin, releasing stored energy. Voigt regularization softens the sharpest scales in the magnetohydrodynamic equations. The team revisits a classic forced reconnection setup under that smoothing.

Regularization opens an early linear phase that partly skips current sheet formation. The usual thin sheet stage is a bottleneck in the classic problem. A new nonlinear model tracks island growth and saturation over time. It includes changing current patterns inside the island and braking from viscosity and regularization. With drag added, the authors conjecture the system settles into exact equilibria. Simulations support that long-time behavior.
arxiv-2603-03232:
Cody Schimming and Brian Camley show how patterned friction can herd a living-like fluid into clumps and set them moving. Their 2026 paper is inspired by cells gathering on uneven surfaces. The model is a two-dimensional compressible active fluid, uniform in its own behavior, flowing over a surface whose friction strength depends on direction.

Friction patches arranged as positive topological defects can pull the fluid into a gathered clump, though success depends on the starting layout. Break the initial symmetry enough, and the clump instead travels in circles. A simplified analytical model explains both motions. The authors then design a surface pattern that steers gathered clusters along a chosen path, a step toward guiding cell-like matter by texture alone.
arxiv-2603-03332:
Ashwath Vaithinathan Aravindan and Mayank Kejriwal test how fragile step-by-step reasoning is in large language models. Chain-of-thought prompting asks a model to show its work, but a single corrupted step can poison everything after it. Their 2026 study injects five kinds of damage into reasoning chains for mathematics problems, from plain arithmetic slips to flattering detours that agree with a wrong user.

Thirteen models of widely different sizes faced the corrupted chains. Arithmetic errors hurt small models badly but larger ones recover well. Unit conversion errors stayed costly at every size, while extra harmless steps barely mattered. Flattery and skipped steps fell in between. The patterns follow scaling trends, and the authors argue that deployment in multi-stage pipelines needs task-specific robustness checks, not blind trust.
arxiv-2603-03632:
Emiliano Dall'Anese makes safety filters for networked systems that never need to phone home. Control barrier functions give formal safety guarantees, but in networked systems the standard filter demands global coupling information and constant coordination between subsystems. His 2026 paper builds local approximations: each subsystem filters itself, with no coordination at all, yet stays close to the ideal centralized filter.

The design borrows singular perturbation theory. A fast dynamic layer races ahead of the plant, and a small parameter sets the separation between the two timescales, with derivative estimation enabling the local implementation. Direct error bounds then quantify the mismatch against the ideal filter. Safety degradation is traced to that timescale parameter, to estimation errors, and to when the filter activates, mapping the trade-off between guarantees and local practicality.
arxiv-2603-03932:
Nicolas Helson, Pegah Alizadeh, and Anastasios Giovanidis compare offline reinforcement learning algorithms for controlling random wireless networks. Offline learning reuses logged operational data instead of exploring live, which suits next-generation wireless networks where online exploration is unsafe. What remains unclear is how these algorithms behave under the genuine randomness of wireless systems: fading, noise, and moving traffic.

The authors evaluate a value-based method, Conservative Q-Learning, a sequence-based Decision Transformer, and a hybrid critic-guided variant in an open random telecom test setting. Conservative Q-Learning produced the most robust policies across distinct sources of chance variation, making it a reliable default for lifecycle-driven network management. Sequence-based methods stayed competitive and won when enough high-return trajectories were available. The findings give practical selection guidance for AI-driven control in future open radio access and 6G networks.
arxiv-2603-04432: Han and colleagues predict arterial traffic from connected vehicle data at city scale. Prior work stayed in simulations or small networks, limiting real use. Their method extracts vehicle measures from trajectories, then aggregates them to network states. A dual expert graph network models normal and abnormal traffic separately, joining short term dynamics with long term periodicity. Tests on a 1,050 link network show live delay and queue measures and better abnormal prediction.
arxiv-2603-04532: Kuissi and colleagues test whether retrieval benchmarks stay fresh as corpora drift. Benchmarks usually freeze corpora under the Cranfield paradigm, yet API deprecations and code reorganizations can stale them. The team compares FreshStack snapshots from October 2024 and October 2025 on LangChain questions. All but one 2024 query stays fully supported in 2025, as documents migrate from LangChain to rivals like LlamaIndex. Model accuracy shifts only slightly across snapshots, rankings correlate strongly with correlation near 0.978 at Recall at 50. Re-judged evolving benchmarks thus remain reliable for retrieval evaluation.
arxiv-2603-04632: Raymaekers and Rousseeuw robustify least trimmed squares regression against missing values and cellwise outliers. Regression is the workhorse of statistics, yet real data hold outliers. Casewise outliers, whole wrong or foreign cases, yield to existing robust methods. Cellwise outliers, suspicious single entries among regressors and response, differ. The paper proposes a method robust to both outlier kinds, handling missing values. It is the first such method for robust out-of-sample prediction, tested by simulation and on a real dataset. It meets a first breakdown result for cellwise robust regression.
arxiv-2603-04832: Dumitriu, Flynn, and Wang prove a BBP phenomenon equivalent for a doubly sparse deformed model. Both the Wigner noise matrix and signal vectors are sparse in this ensemble with fixed spike vectors of same-order sparsity. Spike vectors with signals greater than one correlate with top eigenvectors of the deformed ensemble. Each such spike vector induces an outlier eigenvalue. Results hold in the supercritical sparsity regime and for any sparse spike vector with unbounded entries. No further relationship between noise and spike sparsities is necessary.
arxiv-2603-05132: Ryunosuke Nagaoka and team show an inverse-design method for two-dimensional magnonic crystals exploring unusual lattice shapes with large magnonic band gaps. Genetic algorithms enable global exploration with a complete band gap as the goal, while rate-domain micromagnetic runs test band gaps efficiently. The method discovers several before unreported magnonic crystal designs, checked with time-domain micromagnetic runs. The design landscape grows more non-convex at high-order bands, suggesting many design answers.
arxiv-2603-05232: Hanyong Shao and team present SlideSparse, the first system unlocking Sparse Tensor Core speedup for (2N-2):2N thinness on commodity GPUs. NVIDIA's 2:4 cores double throughput but demand 50% pruning that collapses accuracy, while milder patterns like 6:8 keep accuracy without hardware support, falling back to dense execution. SlideSparse decomposes (2N-2):2N weight blocks into 2:4-compliant windows without accuracy loss, fusing activation rearrangement into cheap per-token quantization. In vLLM tests across GPUs, precisions, and model families, it nears the theoretical bound on workloads, making ordered thinness real for accuracy-keeping speedup.
arxiv-2603-05432: Robin Shing Moon Chan and team present a method joining K models into f-ensembles. Abundant models and prompting plans sensitize scores. Classical grouping pools guesses to beat single sources, but decoding-time use is hard: naive next-token aggregation yields samples from a normalized, biased approximation of the intractable ensemble spread. To sample from these distributions, the authors offer byte-level sequential Monte Carlo in a shared character space. They test them over prompt and model mixes for ordered text tasks, highlighting alternative mixing benefits over probability averaging.
arxiv-2603-05732: Peterson and Zhan create surgery time maps and stories on their own from surgery video. Video time maps help surgeons focus on key parts, but current methods require vague reports or slow hand notes. Their CLIP-based framework aligns video frames with textual gesture notes. The CLIP visual encoder extracts frame forms, and the text encoder embeds gesture lines into a shared form space. Tuning improves video-gesture and textual-token lining up, and the trained model predicts gestures and phases, for a structured time map and cutting hand review.
arxiv-2603-05832: Palani and Setlur present Lexara, a user-centered toolkit for evaluating language models in conversational visual analytics. Evaluating such models is hard: it demands programming expertise, misses real-world complexity, and offers no interpretable metrics. Interviews with 22 developers and 16 end-users identified use cases and workflows. Lexara turns those insights into test cases, interpretable visualization and language metrics via rule-based and judge methods, and an interactive toolkit for setup and exploration without programming. A two-week diary study with six developers showed Lexara guiding model and prompt selection.
arxiv-2603-06632: Khaleghpour and McKinney present a causal graph-feature protocol for temporal transaction networks, for illicit entity sorting. Using the Elliptic dataset, they build trade graphs with marks including PageRank, degree counts, k-core indices, and HITS hub or authority scores. Causal forms use only edges seen up to each timestep, blocking look-ahead bias. A Random Forest classifier under time splits achieves strong separation, with ROC-AUC about 0.85 on a held-out period. Trade traits remain dominant, but the graph features add clarity and risk context.
arxiv-2603-07032: Hu and colleagues propose SSP, a safe surgery policy that jointly tunes conduct and spatial constraints. Robot-aided surgery is shifting toward data-driven self-rule, where learned policies execute complex tasks. Yet these black-box policies often lack formal safety rules, a key need for clinic use. SSP bridges data-driven reach and formal safety, using neural plain change math to learn a doubt-aware motion model from demos. That model backs a robust control barrier safety guard, which barely alters policy actions to ensure strict safety under doubt.
arxiv-2603-07232: Pirzada, Mushtaq and de Lima ask when linked graphs built from cycles have whole-number distance spectra. They give rules for two join families to be distance integral, meaning every eigenvalue of the distance matrix is an integer. They also set out rules for when a dumbbell graph built from wheels is integral for the distance Laplacian matrix.
arxiv-2603-07332: Javadi and colleagues build a low-complexity autofocus method for automotive radar imaging, where backprojection gives clean images at high cost. Their two-layer design first corrects localization errors inside the efficient polar-format domain, then carries those corrections into backprojection. It also extends phase-gradient autofocus to sharpen the correction step. Real-world car experiments show top-tier focus and resolution at a fraction of the usual compute.
arxiv-2603-07632: Guan offers Proof-of-Encryption-Work, a consensus method that reuses proof-of-work computing for code-based data compression. A full key search serves as the puzzle: given a long plaintext and a fixed ciphertext, the key is derived. Since the plaintext far exceeds both key and cipher in length, finding the key compresses the plaintext into it. Shrinking costs heavy work, while undoing stays easy.
arxiv-2603-08132: Drach and colleagues prove a sharp reverse isoperimetric inequality for lambda-convex bodies in three-dimensional space forms. A lambda-convex body is a compact convex set whose boundary has normal curvatures bounded below by a positive constant lambda. Among all such bodies with a fixed surface area, the one with minimal volume is the lambda-convex lens, the region bounded by two totally umbilical caps of curvature lambda. The minimizer is unique. The result confirms Borisenko's Conjecture in the three-dimensional model spaces of constant curvature.
arxiv-2603-08332: Zhang and colleagues propose DS-DGA-GCN, a graph learning model for detecting fake reviewer groups in dynamic networks. Fake reviews, often produced by organized groups, undermine consumer trust and fair competition on online platforms. These groups use sophisticated strategies that evade traditional detection methods, above all for new products with sparse data in cold-start scenarios. DS-DGA-GCN focuses on joint relationships among products, reviews, and reviewers by modeling product-review-reviewer networks. It also adapts through Network Feature Scoring and a dynamic graph attention mechanism.
arxiv-2603-08432: Fréour and colleagues measure how flattened 29 Galactic globular clusters are, a shape that may reveal their dynamics and evolution. Standard tools, ellipse fitting of density contours and principal component analysis, both skew results for near-round clusters or star-poor ones. The authors build a sturdier method and test it on mock data before applying it. For ten clusters, including NGC 104 and NGC 7078, the rotation angle matches the ellipse semi-minor axis. This points to rotation as the main flattening driver, with velocity anisotropy or tides shaping clusters.
arxiv-2603-09032: Yuchen Yuan and colleagues distribute scientific machine learning across devices with hardware and physics guidance. Centralized models demand raw data aggregation at one node, costing latency and energy, while general-purpose models break physical principles. Their EPIC encodes lightly on end devices and decodes centrally with physics awareness, sending compact features instead of raw data and cutting latency and energy sharply while keeping fidelity.
arxiv-2603-09232: Tzu-Quan Lin and colleagues test contrastive decoding for large audio language models at scale and probe why it helps. Of four strategies, Audio-Aware Decoding and Audio Contrastive Decoding work best, though gains vary by model. Profiling baseline errors shows the method fixes cases where models wrongly claim no audio or guess from uncertainty, yet rarely repairs flawed reasoning. Benefits track each model's error mix, and a token-level look ties the effect to hesitation markers.
arxiv-2603-10132: Lentz and coauthors improve unsupervised grouping of hyperspectral images with unbalanced optimal transport dictionary learning. Such images hold rich spectral detail per pixel, making hand labelling slow and standard tools awkward to use. Learning dictionaries in Wasserstein space works, but balancing the spectra blurs classes and weakens outlier handling. Their unbalanced barycentres learn a compact code that keeps those edges, and spectral grouping on that code recovers the labels well.
arxiv-2603-10332: Saron Samuel, Benjamin Van Durme, and Eugene Yang ask whether reasoning rerankers treat groups more fairly than plain rerankers in search. Using the TREC 2022 Fair Ranking Track data, they test six models across settings and demographic attributes. Reasoning neither helped nor hurt fairness: their attention-weighted fairness metric stayed flat while relevance varied a lot. Gaps tied to geography showed up for every model, whatever its design. The authors suggest future reasoning models could do better if built to notice fairness attributes directly.
arxiv-2603-10532: Abeer F AlSohaim and co-authors develop solvability theory for perturbed saddle-point problems in Lp spaces when the loads are rough. Their forcing terms are regularized by a projector built from the adjoint of a weighted Clément interpolation, with the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann equation in mixed form as the driving example. Perturbation arguments at continuous and discrete levels yield estimates that hold even for very rough loads. They also prove a supercloseness result, adapt Stenberg postprocessing for such data, and show the scheme converging in tests.
arxiv-2603-10632: Paul Moujaes, Dmitri Kuzmin, and Christian Bäumer present a finite element framework for dose calculation in proton therapy, based on the M1 moment model. The nonlinear system comes from a Fokker-Planck equation governing charged particles, closed with an entropy-based second moment, and energy runs as a pseudo-time backward. A convex limiting strategy makes the scheme provably keep states physical. Strang splitting handles stiff scattering, and dose accumulates during the energy sweep. Tests give accurate, physically consistent dose distributions.
arxiv-2603-10732: Duncan McCoy and JungHwan Park study special alternating links whose unlinking number meets the lower bound set by the classical signature. They prove a rigidity result about sharpness. When the bound is sharp for such a link, its unlinking number can be attained by crossing changes in any alternating diagram, not just a chosen one. As an application, they compute new unknotting numbers for some knots of this kind, with eleven and twelve crossings.
arxiv-2603-10932: Reita Maeno adapts QMETTS, a thermal-state quantum algorithm, to Z2 lattice gauge theories at finite temperature and density. Enforcing Gauss's law across the whole thermal ensemble is the central difficulty. The method does not remove gauge degrees of freedom. It uses measurement bases that stay gauge invariant and mutually unbiased within the physical subspace. They are built fast through a match with the stabilizer formalism. Shot noise analysis favors generating more samples over refining each one. Numerics on a one-dimensional model with staggered fermions confirm the approach.
arxiv-2603-11232: Effie Papageorgiou works out how heat spreads over very long times on a homogeneous tree, where the branching geometry changes diffusion in ways the integer line never shows. She derives sharp asymptotic formulas for the continuous-time heat kernel as time grows without bound. Solutions then factorize as the heat kernel times a mass function set by the initial data and the chosen norm. That mass function comes from boundary averages tied to Busemann functions in some regimes and from convolution with the ground spherical function in others.
arxiv-2603-11432: Yu studies what happens to compressible Navier-Stokes flow when inertia fades away. The setting is the three-dimensional torus, and the fluid may contain vacuum regions. Yu works with global weak solutions that hold finite energy for all time. In the limit, the momentum equation shrinks to a steady balance of pressure and viscous forces. Kinetic energy drops out, and the limit solution meets an exact energy equality. The proof leans on uniform estimates, renormalized methods, and compactness tools.
arxiv-2603-11832: Crepp and co-authors study wavefront sensing in a convergent beam for adaptive optics. Path-length diversity methods read intensity on several planes to recover phase and amplitude. Free-space versions, like the nonlinear curvature sensor, are sharp but bulky. Recording in a convergent beam shrinks the instrument and packs light onto smaller detector areas. The team builds a physical optics model and checks it in simulations and lab tests. Their Fourier recipe lets standard Gerchberg-Saxton pipelines use the convergent-beam data, cutting size, weight, and cost.
arxiv-2603-12332: Fichet, Megias, Quiros, and Yamanaki show that spacetime curvature alone can stabilize black strings. Their arena is a dilaton-gravity setup in five dimensions that holds a flat brane. Large black strings that run from the brane to a timelike boundary prove classically stable. The boundary may be regular or conformal in the stable cases found. The linear dilaton spacetime gives a critical case that also stays stable. Some curved backgrounds keep the strings stable even with infinite horizon area.
arxiv-2603-12932: Ruiyao Xu and co-authors synthesize domain-specific instruction data for tuning large language models, with no human labels. Hand-built datasets for special fields are costly to create. Older synthesis methods target general tasks and miss domain terms and reasoning styles.
