Model guardrails cause large story erasure. The findings show both promise and limits of LLM-assisted qualitative coding, plus ethical issues in research with at-risk groups.
arxiv-2604-16332: Steele finds that LoRA fine-tuning un-learns contested cases. Items with high annotator disagreement show rising loss during training. That pattern is largely absent under full fine-tuning, and holds across all six models tested, four encoders and two decoder-only models. The finding comes from correlating annotation entropy, from ChaosNLI's 100 labels for each example, with per-example loss-curve area on SNLI and MNLI. Correlations are positive in all 25 conditions tested, stronger for decoder-only models, and survive controls and replication across seeds and datasets.
arxiv-2604-16532: Curl and colleagues argue that attack success rate alone misleads medical imaging robustness tests. The binary metric records only whether an attack succeeds, ignoring strength, image quality and cross-architecture transfer. Their study covers four medical datasets, seven models spanning convolutional and transformer models, and seven attacks at five budgets. It measures success rate plus signal-to-noise ratio, structural similarity and perturbation size. Perceptual and distortion metrics tracked each other closely but barely correlated with success rate, so risk assessment needs multiple metrics.
arxiv-2604-16732: Wills, Blume and Guan develop a coupled-channel framework for spinor dynamics near spin-spatial resonances. Bogoliubov modes of the spin-free Hamiltonian give a basis using a scatter gap. Far from echo, a single wavefunction shows the spin dynamics, the single-mode approximation. Tuning the quadratic Zeeman shift excites modes in two classes, with and without part-hole correlations. Beyond-quadratic-order terms, skipped in standard theories, grow key near echoes. Tested against GP sims, the tool offers a clean echo interpretation.
arxiv-2604-16832: Njungle and colleagues propose DALC-CT, checking constant-time programs through dynamic analysis of low-level execution traces. Timing side channels exploit execution-time variations to recover secrets, and crypto code is highly exposed. Constant-time code must not let execution behavior depend on secret inputs, yet validating that property remains a major challenge. The method measures instruction sequences across input values, flagging any instruction-mix variation between trace pairs. Evaluated on known constant-time and varying-time examples, it detects every issue, offering a lightweight reliable verification path.
arxiv-2604-16932: Mudrik and Charles tackle count data, from word frequencies to neural spike counts, where standard embedding tools wrongly assume smooth continuous geometry. Their p-SNE method measures similarity with Poisson-based distances, recovering weekday patterns in emails, research clusters in OpenReview papers, and drift and stimulus gradients in neural recordings.
arxiv-2604-17132: Qi and four colleagues attack over-refusal, where safety-aligned language models refuse harmless queries. They observe that when models over-refuse, non-refusal tokens remain available in the next-token candidate list, yet the model systematically skips them. Their training-free Adaptive Contrastive Decoding compares output distributions with and without an extreme safety prompt, then adaptively boosts refusal or non-refusal tokens, cutting the refusal ratio for over-refusal queries by 10.35 percent while slightly raising it for malicious queries.
arxiv-2604-17732: Grabchak develops an exact, computationally tractable simulation method for tempered stable laws with infinite variation, the first of its kind, with alpha from 1 up to, but not including, 2. Tempered stable laws modify stable laws so extreme values are damped, giving finite moments for practical modeling. Exact simulation draws samples directly from the target law rather than approximating it, and tractability means the method runs in reasonable time. A small simulation study shows the approach works well.
arxiv-2604-17832: Alladi and Sengupta extend a 1977 duality between largest and smallest prime factors to all higher orders. It proves new results about the Möbius function. They show a sum weighting that function by powers of the count of distinct prime factors vanishes for every order at least two. A refined version covers integers whose smallest prime factor lies in a given residue class. It vanishes for orders at least three, and recasts as a density result equal to one over Euler's totient of the modulus.
arxiv-2604-17932: Kokmotos and two colleagues drive a repulsive Bose-Einstein condensate to implode in simulations, using a direct topological quench. They first create giant vortices by slow phase imprinting, then suddenly reverse the imprint, cancelling the accumulated winding in one step and dropping the condensate to its trivial state. The resulting phase-density mismatch drives rapid inward flow and a strong central density buildup. Later waves break azimuthal symmetry into polygonal shapes set by how the giant vortex was built.
arxiv-2604-18032: Pan Wang and three colleagues present CFSR, a shadow removal framework that treats restoration as a physics-constrained process. It maps observations into an HVI color space to suppress shadow noise and fuses RGB data with depth priors. A dual guided attention mechanism uses DINO features and surface normals to enforce lighting constraints, while a frozen CLIP encoder adds priors for degraded regions. A frequency collaborative module then harmonizes occlusion boundaries with illumination, reaching state-of-the-art results across benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-18332: Das, Macías, Kurtovic, Birnstiel, Viscardi, and Curone study faint dust halos around three young planet-forming disks. Extended emission defies radial drift theory, which predicts dust should spiral inward. Using ALMA observations of Elias 2-24 plus IM Lup and DM Tau, they fit dust properties across wavelengths. Halos hold 20 to 30 percent of total flux. Grain sizes reach up to 2 centimeters in Elias 2-24 and under 4 millimeters in IM Lup and under 9 in DM Tau, easing the disks' mass-budget problem.
arxiv-2604-18432: Nurkanović, Pozharskiy, and Diehl develop real-time look-ahead control methods for hybrid systems with switching contacts. Hybrid control is hard because the tuning problem is nonsmooth and the feedback law jumps. Their three schemes solve one complementarity-constrained quadratic program per sample, yielding piece-by-piece affine stand-ins of the feedback law. Smoothness and slope results bound the gap despite answer jumps, and a robotic handling demo finds contact orders online.
arxiv-2604-18532: De Giacomo and three colleagues study controller building for obligation properties in LTLfp, LTLf stretched to endless traces. They mix safety and guarantee properties, forming the second level of the Manna-Pnueli ladder. They translate into symbolic deterministic weak automata built straight from finite machines for base LTLf cases on trace starts. They inherit Boolean closure and fast shrinking, with the task solvable in linear time once built. Several game-solving methods are tested on examples, showing the approach performs with nearly the same power as LTLf building.
arxiv-2604-18732: Zhao, Netto, and Zhao propose a stiffness-aware decentralized method for dynamic state estimation in power grids run on inverters. These units show fast and slow dynamics through cascading controls, so system models are stiff and old methods need impractically small sampling steps to stay stable. Statistical linearization builds a linear stand-in for the nonlinear dynamics, and matrix-exponential discretization then carries uncertainty forward in closed form in time. The result is stable tracking at lower sampling rates, shown to be fast and true under coarse sampling.
arxiv-2604-19232: Gardi and Zhu review what is known about infrared singularities in multi-leg quantum chromodynamics amplitudes. They explain why the soft anomalous dimension, which governs soft gluon radiation, turns out remarkably simple. They then lay out a new route to computing it from a lightcone expansion of correlators of semi-infinite Wilson lines, using the method of regions. That route has already fixed the three-loop quantity for one massive colored particle with any number of massless ones.
arxiv-2604-19632: Chen and colleagues propose CreatiParser, a generative framework for parsing raster graphic designs into editable layers. Design images consist of layers like text, background, and extras, while most models emit flat raster outputs without explicit layer structures, limiting editing. Current parsing methods rely on multi-stage pipelines combining layout prediction, matting, and inpainting, which suffer error accumulation and limited controllability. It decomposes a design into text, background, and sticker layers, parsing text regions with a vision-language model into a text rendering protocol.
arxiv-2604-19832: Zając and Pracht use the Black-Scholes-Merton framework as a controlled benchmark for testing quantum machine learning methods for option pricing, rather than as an end in itself. They propose a fully quantum approach based on Quantum Neural Networks. It is presented as one of the first such implementations on currently available quantum hardware. The work matters because pricing accuracy and efficiency in a derivatives market worth hundreds of trillions of dollars bear directly on risk management, capital allocation, and regulatory compliance.
arxiv-2604-19932: Upasna and Tavva tackle page migration in hybrid memory systems, where hot data should sit in fast high-bandwidth memory and cold data in slower DRAM or non-volatile memory. Moving pages in a flat address space normally forces costly TLB shootdowns and cache invalidations. Their Duon design stores updated mappings directly in the TLB and page table, removing both overheads. It lifts instructions per cycle by 3.87 percent over leading methods, and works with any existing migration policy.
arxiv-2604-20132: Yu builds world-wide weak answers for the quantum isothermal Euler set on a three-way torus, where pressure rises in step with density. The straight-line pressure law pairs with a log-type inner energy, giving a natural log-type Schrödinger stand-in for the model. A smoothed form of that law, worked through the Madelung change, polar split, and tightness claims, yields the answers. An energy sameness pulls back strong convergence of the fluid factors, and the path fits quantum fluid models with isothermal parts.
arxiv-2604-20432: Stempin and six colleagues build a quantum version of a classical synchronizing automaton, where special input words drive the machine to a fixed state no matter where it starts. Since such resetting looks at odds with quantum unitarity, they add helper qubits encoding the automaton's alphabet, acting through one global unitary step. When the helper register starts in a synchronizing word, the machine lands in a fixed pure state while the register keeps where it began. The team shows how chosen entangled states can be made this way.
arxiv-2604-20532: Saleheen, Wagner, Razzaghi, and Wang review renewable microgrids with keeping power on as the principle. They synthesize work on planning, optimization, flexibility, and assessment. Their synthesis finds that power depends on time-coupled adequacy rather than capacity alone, with Dunkelflaute events, dark windless periods, as a cause of failure. Standard indices fit poorly, squeezing performance into single dimensions and hiding time-based and service-critical risks. The review pulls planning, optimization, and evaluation into a roadmap for keeping power on, while noting gaps in linked scarcity and outage costs.
arxiv-2604-21032: Kim, Mallya, and Angelova bring multi-spectral imagery to generalist multimodal models that were trained on RGB images alone, without retraining them. Their training-free approach adapts non-RGB inputs into the visual space those models understand, then adds field-specific background and step-by-step reasoning prompts. Demonstrated with the Gemini 2.5 model, it delivers strong zero-shot gains on popular remote-sensing benchmarks for land-use classification and environmental monitoring. The result lets geospatial users exploit powerful generalist models for specialized sensor inputs.
arxiv-2604-21232: Xiyin Zeng and four colleagues stop small mistakes from snowballing in vision-language-action systems, where one wrong step can cascade through a multi-step task. Their ReCAPA framework predicts and contrasts deviations at three levels: actions, subgoals, and trajectories, keeping meaning aligned throughout. Predictive correction updates the action generator during training, and two new metrics track how errors spread and fade. It competes on embodied benchmarks and beats strong proprietary and open-source baselines.
arxiv-2604-21332: Masato Arai, Kentarou Mawatari, and Nobuchika Okada probe new physics through entanglement in top-antitop production at future lepton colliders. Within the Standard Model, s-channel photon and Z exchange yields typical spin correlations with real entanglement. They then test three extensions: a neutral scalar mediator, a U(1) B-L model with a new Z-prime boson, and a Randall-Sundrum scenario with Kaluza-Klein gravitons. It falls in the scalar case, while sizable deviations arise in the other two, making entanglement a sensitive probe of new particles.
arxiv-2604-21632: Nevena Lazić and three colleagues study transformers for in-context propositional logic reasoning. Prior work showed models fail on unseen names, partly from copying trouble. Collapse also matters: unseen-token unembeddings collapse to nearly one vector, making unseen variables hard to tell apart when embeddings share settings. This explains active forgetting, which resets embeddings over time. They combine copying tweaks, varied data, and embedding resets, generalizing to unseen tokens. Tests support the claims, and Gemma 3 models show embedding collapse, including 99 unused tokens starting finetuning poorly.
arxiv-2604-22032: Veit presents Kernel Contracts, a rulebook for ML kernel math across varied chips. A matmul on AMD may give a gradient unlike the same matmul on NVIDIA. A contract has eight parts: identifier, scope, precondition, postcondition, tolerance, reference oracle, measurement protocol, and violation signature. The language states twelve contract classes on math, order, build-time, and edge-case faults.
arxiv-2604-22232: Nguyen and four colleagues build a simulator for a quantum key system whose security rests only on breaking a Bell inequality, a test for nonlocal behaviour. Tracing readout noise from the Bell test through error correction, they find a usable key needs noise below 0.89, roughly one sixth of the wider window where a violation still shows. Their result shows certified nonlocality alone overstates how much noise such a link can tolerate.
arxiv-2604-22332: Casuga and Mäntysaari confront the Color Glass Condensate picture of dense gluon matter with HERA collider data at next-to-leading order. They analyse total cross sections and charm production to extract the starting condition for the Balitsky-Kovchegov equation. Their work reaches NLO+NLL accuracy, combining impact factors with the evolution equation. A Bayesian setup then yields the parameter distribution that best fits the data. That posterior lets starting-condition uncertainties flow cleanly into later work.
arxiv-2604-22532: Owusu and Avila Márquez study what standard rules recover when treatment effects spill over between people. Applied teams often use rules with solo response, even when interference is plausible but unseen. For selection, instruments, regression discontinuity, and difference-in-differences, each formula equals an average direct effect plus a bias. Each bias term times an interference part by a gap in others' assignment laws across groups. The bias is zero under generalized assignment independence, untestable from one seen assignment, so the paper builds a sensitivity response.
arxiv-2604-22632: Kvaternik studies accumulation sets and zero entropy dynamics in the Lozi map. For parameters where the fixed point lacks homoclinic points and the period-two orbit attracts, l is the unstable manifold's accumulation set outside itself. A polygon with nested trapping forward images is constructed. This construction characterizes l as the intersection of these iterates. The squared map's non-wandering set then lies in the union of l and the fixed points. Consequently, the Lozi map off l has zero topological entropy, extending Misiurewicz and Štimac's result to broader parameters.
arxiv-2604-22732: Saccani and Tiso stretch the Craig-Bampton part-based method, a modular staple for linear frame motion, to bent-shape parts. They build a quadratic cut-down surface by small-change math, folding fast fixed-joint modes onto slow modes and joint values. Galerkin mapping onto the surface tangent space gives a cut-down model that keeps bent-shape effects with no added degrees of freedom.
arxiv-2604-22932: Hsieh and twelve colleagues analyze main-belt comet 133P/Elst-Pizarro in its 2024 active apparition with JWST and ground-based observations. Water vapor outgassing, measured at two orbital points, nominally falls by about 25 percent between visits, though it is consistent with no change within uncertainties. No carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, or methanol is detected; its hypervolatile depletion matches previously observed main-belt comets. Water production shows no clear link to nucleus size, semi-major axis, or Sun distance among JWST-observed main-belt comets.
arxiv-2604-23132: Xu and five colleagues plan drone routes and bandwidth for low-altitude IoT collection, where interference, shifting data volumes, and obstacles strain standard deep reinforcement learning. Their hierarchical design splits the job: an upper level picks flight paths at coarse time steps, while a lower level assigns bandwidth at finer steps. A hierarchical deep deterministic policy gradient method, TBH-DDPG, solves the joint problem. Simulations show convergence faster by 44.44 percent and far lower computational cost than a non-hierarchical method.
arxiv-2604-23332: Basharat and three colleagues apply machine learning to anomaly detection and threat intel in Zero Trust IoT settings, where guards fall short. They test Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, and Decision Tree models on the KDD Cup 1999 dataset of intrusions and regular traffic. The Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique fixes class imbalance and greatly improves model performance and detection scores. Edge-based machine learning and blockchain are also studied as extra tools for malicious URL and advanced persistent threat detection.
arxiv-2604-23432: Gazzeh and colleagues introduce Sphere-Depth, a benchmark that tests depth estimation from 360-degree images when the camera tilts away from its usual pose. They simulate pose shifts and compare a popular flat-image model against spherical-aware rivals, converting all outputs to real metric depth with a shared calibration protocol. Even purpose-built spherical models degrade sharply under pose change, the experiments show.
arxiv-2604-23632: Li and six colleagues present Hallo-Live, a streaming system that generates a talking avatar's video and speech together in real time from text. Asynchronous dual-stream diffusion plus future-aware attention cuts articulation lag, while preference-guided distillation preserves quality at few steps. It runs at about 20 frames per second with under a second of delay, reaching sixteen times the teacher model's throughput.
arxiv-2604-23732: Cinar and Maleshkova test whether hypoglycaemia classifiers for type 1 diabetes should be tailored by age, using continuous glucose data from children to seniors. They compare a global population model, age-segmented models, and personalised transfer learning for predicting onset up to two hours ahead. The global model matches or beats age-segmented rivals overall, suggesting short-term patterns transfer across ages, though children recall best with an age-specific model.
arxiv-2604-24232: Fava, Ginelli, and Mahault study light-driven structure formation in a minimal model of dry active nematics. Combining small-scale simulations with flow theory, they show the system usually forms a dense, ordered nematic ring at the edge of compact light patterns. That edge structure creates a disordered core whose density is set by itself, not by global particle density. The protected states arise from local alignment plus curvature-driven currents, offering a robust route to edge-made structure and testable predictions.
arxiv-2604-24832: Wang and six colleagues study the trainability of masked diffusion language models via blockwise locality. Masked diffusion models promise an alternative to older models, yet train less well. On linear regression, graph path-finding and Sudoku, random-masking fails to learn linear regression. It shows shaky training on path-finding. It beats rival models on Sudoku. They propose Jigsaw and Scatter, locality-aware models that add left-to-right bias in blocks while keeping refinement. Jigsaw matches rival stability on regression. Scatter keeps diffusion's edge on path-finding.
arxiv-2604-25032: Rampisela studies how fairness in recommender systems is judged offline. Many fairness measures are proposed and used with no check on how robust they are. She asks which outputs score fairest or unfairest, how scores spread in practice and when a score cannot be computed at all, as with division by zero. After theory and tests across user, item, group and individual measures, she offers new measures and rules for picking the right one.
arxiv-2604-25632: Li and ten colleagues study how environment shapes the mass-metallicity relation at redshifts 4 to 10 with JWST data. Combining CEERS and JADES, they compile 225 galaxies with stellar masses, star-formation rates, and gas-phase metallicities. Galaxies in dense regions run more metal-rich at fixed stellar mass by a tenth or two of a dex, with similar slopes across environments. Adding star-formation rate widens the separation, pointing to more efficient chemical enrichment in overdense regions. Star-formation rate density runs higher in overdense regions by a factor of 2 to 3.
arxiv-2604-25932: Adamczyk and eight colleagues test sociodemographic bias in language-model educational counselling. Six models answer questions about 900 student cases, each varied across 14 identifiers plus a control. That yields 243,000 answers. Every model shows measurable bias, partly matching human biases yet distinct in notable ways. Vague prompts amplify disparities nearly threefold. Specific metrics cut them substantially. Bias profiles also differ greatly across models.
arxiv-2604-26032: Addazi, Capozziello, and Meluccio tackle the huge mismatch between observed dark energy and the value quantum theory would naively predict. The gap spans about 120 orders of magnitude. They join two ideas: holographic naturalness, which ties the stability of the cosmological constant to quantum information and entropy, and pre-geometric gravity, in which spacetime itself emerges from symmetry breaking. In their synthesis, a vast de Sitter entropy suppresses decay and explains why the constant stays tiny, while new particles called hairons arise from semiclassical effects.
arxiv-2604-26332: Huang and Leykin fit low-degree algebraic curves to families of periodic orbits in the circular restricted three-body problem. That problem follows a weightless body pulled by two larger primaries, and the curve fits give one-parameter orbit families. The families feed minimal problems for liaison navigation, where craft states are read off from measurements between craft. For typical parameters, the count of solutions matches the degree of a branched covering map, found by both symbolic and numerical means.
arxiv-2604-26432: Kolesnik derived an exact formula for a two-marginal second moment of the symmetric Markov random flight in dimensions three and up. The particle moves at constant speed, changing direction at Poisson-distributed times to uniformly random headings. The formula covers the indexed moment and every analogous two-marginal moment with two squared coordinates. Under standard Kac scaling, it becomes the product of variances of two coordinates of homogeneous Brownian motion.
arxiv-2604-26732: Hermann, Billon, Collet, and Madeo ask how interfaces shape finite mechanical metamaterial structures built to damp shakes. The structures sandwich a metamaterial array between two plain plates, and four arrays cut differently from the same metamaterial at the plate interface act the same when repeated without end. In finite structures, however, plate interfaces and air interfaces strongly affect shake flow, overall results, and local shifts. Tuning interface design can lift a metamaterial from weak to clearly beating standard damping solutions.
arxiv-2604-27032: Crumpacker and Nikolopoulos build a human-in-the-loop flow for tuning language-model inference settings to cut energy use. Picking runtime values usually needs deep app knowledge or slow searches taking days. With human-crafted feedback prompts, chat-based models iteratively find energy-efficient settings faster than classic search, tailoring answers to hardware and other system limits. The enhanced prompt template converged below threshold in fewer prompts than the baseline, with lower final energy per token, and it beat Sobol sampling on speed.
arxiv-2604-27132: Huang and five colleagues propose TRUST, a decentralized framework for checking the reasoning of large reasoning models and multi-agent systems. Central checking fails in four ways: single points of failure, bottlenecks as reasoning grows, hidden audits that erode trust, and exposed traces that risk model theft. TRUST splits chain-of-thought reasoning into five levels for parallel audit, and maps agent interactions onto causal graphs for root-cause attribution.
arxiv-2604-27232: Karabüklü and five colleagues build ASL Minimal Translation Pairs, a benchmark dataset for probing what sign language models actually grasp. Sign models lag spoken-language models, and recent gains in translation and isolated sign recognition leave open how well models capture linguistic phenomena and cues from hands, upper body, and face. The dataset splits American Sign Language phenomena into minimal pairs of translations. A case study applies it to a state-of-the-art ASL-to-English translation model.
arxiv-2604-27332: Guo and three colleagues add jet feedback to simulations of how a supermassive black hole's energy shapes an elliptical galaxy, in the fourth paper of their MACER series. They run three models: jets alone, wind alone, and both together. Jets alone suppress star formation least, because a narrow jet carries little momentum. Together, jet and wind suppress it far more than either alone, as shear between them stirs turbulence that turns the black hole's kinetic energy into heat.
arxiv-2604-27732: Richman and Wüthrich close a gap in claims reserving for non-life insurance by lifting the generalized Cape Cod method to a stochastic model. Chain-ladder and Bornhuetter-Ferguson methods had already been lifted from fixed rules to stochastic models, but the generalized Cape Cod method had not. The note derives a closed-form expression for the method's mean squared prediction error, enabling analysis of claims prediction uncertainty. The result brings the method in line with the other two popular reserving methods.
arxiv-2604-27832: Kaur proves that the Julia set of the transcendental twin of a higher-dimensional polynomial shift-like map of type nu is non-empty. In addition, she provides an example of a shift-like map with a runaway wandering domain. That example cuts against how a polynomial shift map behaves.
arxiv-2604-27932: Liang, Liu, de Vries, and Larson cut vision-language training cost by sampling data with DynamiCS, a cluster method that favors rare ideas. Past efficient training flattens topic mix but can starve rare concepts, while DynamiCS shrinks big clusters and grows small ones, keeping their rank order. It re-samples each epoch, widening cross-epoch variety and making the small-cluster boost workable. Tests show cheaper training plus stronger scores on long-tail ideas.
arxiv-2604-28032: Takagi and Liew study private mean estimation when each user sends one privatised message and the analyser sees only the shuffled pile. They frame design after shuffling as an explicit optimisation using the shuffle index, and prove a lower bound on mean squared error in terms of that index. The bound shows locally optimal mechanisms can fail once shuffled, while their new mechanism is asymptotically optimal at high privacy, nearly matching the central Gaussian mechanism.
arxiv-2604-28132: Salvarese, Chen and Holz tackle finding host galaxies for stellar-mass compact binary mergers, a route to formation histories and the Hubble constant. Only one merger so far has a confident host from light observations. Localisation volumes are large and most events emit no light. Focusing on the brightest galaxies in well-localised volumes, they narrow three events to one, one and four candidates. Those candidates carry a substantial chance of being random, so the authors urge follow-up.
arxiv-2605-00032:
Huifan Zhang, Yun Hu, Caizhi Sheng, Yurui Qu, and Pingqiang Zhou present ROSA, an optical neural network design built on microrings. Computing with light promises speed and low energy, but microring resonator arrays suffer noise from digital-to-analog converters and heat drift. ROSA answers with an optical shift-and-add module and a layer-wise hybrid mapping strategy for placing the network on the hardware.

A noise-aware model links control voltage to weight under converter and thermal variation, and a workload-aware framework sizes the arrays and sets the dataflow layer by layer. The optimized arrays cut the combined energy-delay cost sharply against earlier optical designs, and the shift-and-add module cuts it further. The hybrid mapping also raises accuracy on a standard image task over weight-stationary mapping.
arxiv-2605-00532:
Konstantin Avrachenkov, Lorenzo Gregoris, and Nelly Litvak connect two ranking ideas: PageRank, which ranks web pages, and policy evaluation, which scores a strategy in a Markov decision process. For a fixed policy, they show the value function of a discounted decision process can be read off from a PageRank vector. The vector belongs to a time-reversed version of the same chain, and an explicit rescaling connects the two.

In their correspondence, the discount factor becomes PageRank's teleportation parameter, and the rewards shape the restart distribution. The result extends well beyond the simplest case. Using quasi-stationary distributions and a classical transform, they prove a general decomposition: evaluating any finite decision process splits into PageRank problems on its recurrent and transient parts. Variants cover undiscounted processes with terminal states and rewards that depend on transitions. A numerical example on a sticky random walk shows the approach is efficient.
arxiv-2605-00632:
Massimo Rondelli, Francesco Pivi, and Maurizio Gabbrielli generate three-dimensional objects as Blender code, the scripting language of the popular open modeling tool, with help from retrieval. Asked to write such code directly, leading language models make frequent syntax errors and produce geometrically inconsistent objects. The authors' system, BlenderRAG, grounds each generation in worked examples instead.

The system draws on a curated dataset of five hundred expert-validated examples, each bundling a text description, the code, and a rendered image, spanning fifty object categories. At generation time it retrieves semantically similar examples and feeds them to the model. Across four leading language models, compilation success jumped from about forty percent to seventy, and a standard measure of agreement between text and rendered image nearly doubled. No fine-tuning or special hardware is required, which the authors stress makes the approach deployable immediately.
arxiv-2605-00732:
Kyra H. M. Klos and 4 co-authors generate tiny spin patterns that match a set pattern of topological defects, bridging two scales. A defect pattern is easy to state at large scale, as particles on a map, but what a material does depends on the tiny spins underneath. Their tool extends a Wasserstein generative network with physics-based constraints and Fourier-space data.

The test bed is the flat XY model, whose vortex pairs act as far-reaching defects. Below the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition, the patterns it made matched key measured traits well, from magnetism to spin correlations. Heat uptake exposed a weakness in tracking energy swings. A shape-based analysis of the data revealed subtler differences near the critical point that plain correlation functions miss.
arxiv-2605-00832:
Krisanu Sarkar argues that synthetic images for training vision models should be designed as experiments, not sampled at random. Random sampling hopes to cover a model's failure modes by chance. Sarkar instead borrows the Design of Experiments from statistics, varying scene factors in a controlled fractional plan and treating the downstream model as a black box to be audited.

The audit sorts failures into coverage gaps, where factor levels are underrepresented, and spurious reliance, where a model leans on nuisance features. Targeted synthetic data then addresses each type. In tests, accuracy on a controlled dataset rose from about half to well over three quarters, and segmentation improved after background shortcuts were found and corrected.
arxiv-2605-01032:
Alan L. McCann presents an algebra-based semantics for governed runs, in which rule systems are axiomatized and coterminous with expressibility. The system is mechanized in Rocq across many modules and hundreds of theorems with no admitted lemmas, built on interaction trees and parameterized coinduction methods. A three-axiom rule algebra covering safety, transparency, and properness induces a symmetric monoidal category whose compositions preserve the rules.

An effect system constrains handlers so only rule-preserving handlers can be built in the safe fragment. Programs with no capabilities emit only observation directives. A dual guarantee theorem holds under all composition operators. The capstone shows every expressible program is ruled and every ruled program arises that way, while Turing completeness is preserved.
arxiv-2605-01132:
Mitchell G. Peaks, Mia M. Kaarls, and Crystal Noel present an open-hardware digital-to-analog converter module for low-noise control of ion-trap electrodes. Scalable ion-trap experiments and quantum computing need many DC electrode channels with low noise, sufficient bandwidth, and flexible control, at manageable cost. Design specifications target a modular, scalable platform, with explicit attention to supply-chain management and cost effectiveness for scaling.

The system pairs a Texas Instruments multi-channel converter chip with a Spartan-7 FPGA for signal generation and compute. Characterization of a prototype suggests the design suits a variety of ion-trap physics experiments and quantum computing applications. Readers get a complete module design intended to be reproduced and scaled by other laboratories.
arxiv-2605-01632:
Eleanor Quint builds a whole ensemble of predictors out of one trained network, cheaply, by perturbing it in a disciplined way. Models that tie on familiar data can part ways sharply on shifted data, and that spread is exactly what an uncertainty estimate needs, but training many full models is expensive.

Perturb-and-Correct jitters a hidden layer at random, then fixes the next layer by least squares so the new model still agrees on calibration data. Away from that data it is free to disagree, and the disagreement is the signal. Theory follows the leftover residue after correction, giving a leverage-based bound on what is preserved and a covariance reading of the spread. Tests on robot dynamics and image shift detection show a strong in-versus-out trade, scaling up to a full vision transformer on ImageNet at a share of the deep ensemble cost.
arxiv-2605-01832:
Alberto Riccardi and Lorenzo Maccone tighten the entropic form of Heisenberg's uncertainty rule, the version that bounds the sum of two measurement entropies from below. Entropy bounds beat spread-based ones because they read only outcome odds, not the outcomes themselves, and the floor usually holds regardless of the state measured.

Their new floor beats the textbook Maassen-Uffink bound and, as its parameter approaches a stated limit, becomes asymptotically tight for every pair of observables at once. The construction extends to the Renyi entropy family as well. In a note added after submission, the authors state plainly that they then found the main results already present in earlier work by Rene Schwonnek, who pointed it out to them himself. The paper stands as a clean derivation, with priority openly ceded.
arxiv-2605-01932:
Konstantin Bliokh develops a unified way to describe the intrinsic angular momentum of a relativistic wavepacket. In slow, non-relativistic settings, total angular momentum splits into parts tied to the body itself and parts tied to its path. In relativistic quantum theory, intrinsic spin is usually handled with the Pauli-Lubanski vector, a separate tool.

Bliokh builds an expectation version of that vector from the packet's mean momentum and angular momentum, measured against its energy centre. Unlike the standard version, it has no problem at zero mass. A packet can thus point its intrinsic momentum in any direction relative to its motion, even for massless particles. Examples illustrate the theory.
arxiv-2605-02032:
Ellen Lee and Michael Connelley probe young stars called FU Orionis objects, thought to shine from steady Keplerian disks. Such disks should give a double-peaked line profile in near-infrared spectra, yet that shape is hard to see in most FUor spectra. The authors measure line profiles for fifteen FUors and similar objects with high-resolution data from iSHELL on the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility.

Five targets show double-peaked profiles in the K band that also fit a Keplerian model. For eight targets seen in the J band too, profiles match the K band well, but linewidth does not clearly shrink with wavelength. The paper explains why a double peak can hide, including blending with molecular features.
arxiv-2605-02132:
Aaron Barnoff and Curtis Bright speed up the search for orthogonal Latin squares, a classic hard puzzle in combinatorics. A Latin square fills a grid so each symbol appears once in every row and column. Two squares are orthogonal mates if, when overlaid, no ordered pair repeats. Such pairs exist for all orders except two and six, but finding them can be costly.

SAT solvers are strong at search, yet they lack domain knowledge about Latin squares, such as the Euler-Parker method for building mates. The authors join a SAT solver with that method, run through a Diophantine system solver. The hybrid solver proves effective at finding mates on problems that strain a plain SAT approach.
arxiv-2605-02532:
Koji Matsushita studies conic divisorial ideals in toric rings through matroid theory, a branch of combinatorics about independence. Toric rings are algebras built from geometric data, and their divisor classes carry deep structural information. Matsushita describes the polytope that represents divisor classes tied to conic ideals in matroid terms, giving a combinatorial handle on an algebraic object.

The frame is then applied to a ring built from a signed poset, a subset of a classical root system. For that ring, the divisor class group is computed, and a key symmetry property, being Q-Gorenstein, is characterized in terms of the poset itself. A polytope for its conic ideals is also built. The results recover and extend earlier work on Hibi rings, a well-studied family in this area.
arxiv-2605-02732:
R. X. Zhai recasts a classic trade-off in heat engine design as a problem in plane geometry. Carnot-like engines face a linked limit on power and efficiency: pushing one tends to cut the other. Zhai plots normalized losses from the engine's two branches, and in that plane the curves of constant efficiency become straight lines.

With efficiency contours straight, the best efficiency at fixed power reduces to bounding the slope of an allowed line. When branch losses scale as a power of the process time, the fixed-power condition carves out a two-dimensional region, and the slope problem becomes a linear program. The geometric frame then yields the exact power-efficiency limit for engines with power-law losses. The paper is short and formal, aimed at readers in thermodynamics theory.
arxiv-2605-03432:
Prajyot Pyati, Sapna Sachan, Amulya Kumar Mahto, and Pranjal Phukan present a two-model system that rebuilds full 3D MRI volumes from only an eighth of the usual slices. Long scans strain patients and invite motion artifacts, so cutting acquisition while keeping anatomical detail has direct clinical value.

The first model predicts missing slices with a multi-kernel, texture-aware loss that guards fine detail. A second refinement network then polishes predicted and real slices together as one volume for smooth anatomy. Trained and checked on large brain MRI cohorts, the framework claims accurate, generalizable reconstructions suited to faster scanning.
arxiv-2605-03532:
Stefano Montaldo, Andrea Ratto, and Antonio Sanna prove the existence of certain weakly r-harmonic maps, mappings between shapes that are critical points of an r-energy functional. They construct rotationally symmetric maps from an n-dimensional ball to a sphere. Existence within that family turns out to hold only for specific dimensions.

The authors then show these critical points are unstable, and they note differences between the r-harmonic and ES-r-harmonic cases once r reaches four. Two variants follow: replacing the sphere with a rotationally symmetric ellipsoid yields proper weakly biharmonic maps in dimensions five and up, and triharmonic maps from dimension seven. A warped-product domain variant closes the study.
arxiv-2605-03632:
Robert G. Endres reconsiders a classic puzzle about bacterial chemotaxis, the process by which bacteria such as E. coli swim toward food. Berg and Purcell argued that sensing works near physical limits, yet recent information-theoretic work suggests the cells use only a small fraction of the information in arriving molecules. Endres argues the missing piece is movement strategy.

Using scaling arguments and minimal models, he shows how run-and-tumble motion stays robust to noise through symmetry and time averaging, even when internal information processing is inefficient. Comparing bacterial and eukaryotic chemotaxis sharpens the point. Low information efficiency, he concludes, may reflect an evolved balance of robustness, simplicity, and function rather than poor performance.
arxiv-2605-03832:
Ryan King and four co-authors build a benchmark for moving intensive care prediction models between hospitals. Training clinical models takes data, labeling, and computing power that small hospitals may lack, so transferring a model from a large hospital is attractive. Yet models trained at one site often generalize poorly, because measurement patterns differ across United States regions.

Their benchmark frames regional transfer as domain-incremental continual learning: a model must absorb each new region's data while retaining what the original domain taught it, without catastrophic forgetting. The benchmark tests transportability of intensive care time series models across regions, giving hospitals and researchers a shared yardstick for judging whether a transferred model is safe to adapt locally.
arxiv-2605-04032:
Kuo-Wei Huang derives, from gravity, a set of differential equations, proposed as higher-dimensional versions of the BPZ null-state equations of 2D conformal field theory. The derivation uses the AdS/CFT correspondence, which relates such a theory to gravity in an anti-de Sitter bulk. Huang studies a light scalar field in a black hole background. He uses a near-boundary expansion.

A decoupling effect in the bulk series produces isolated lower-order equations on the boundary. It acts at certain conformal dimensions. The results agree with the four-dimensional equations proposed before. Those equations capture resummed contributions from minimal-twist multi-stress tensors. The gravity-side calculation also yields further equations. They extend beyond the near-lightcone regime where the original proposal applied.
arxiv-2605-04232:
Yichen Tao and three co-authors work on bounding the small rounding errors that build up when computers use floating-point numbers. Worst-case bounds are safe but often far too large to be useful, since the biggest errors are also rare.

Their method gives a probabilistic bound instead: a threshold that the error stays below with a stated level of confidence. They build it by applying concentration results to an existing Taylor-based analysis, after handling a technical obstacle caused by absolute values in that expansion. The aim is bounds that real programs for science and optimization can actually use.
arxiv-2605-04632:
James Dempsey and sixteen co-authors report a pilot absorption survey of cold neutral hydrogen in the Magellanic Clouds and the bridge of gas between them, using the ASKAP radio telescope array. Cold gas is the raw material for future stars, and its distribution across this nearby interacting system was sparsely sampled before.

The survey measures more than three thousand sightlines toward background radio sources, a fifteen-fold increase in coverage. Several hundred candidate cold gas detections emerge. They appear most often toward the Small Magellanic Cloud, and least toward the bridge. In the bridge, the cold gas sits closer to the smaller cloud. It may be forming freshly on a shell's outskirts. The bridge's cold fraction resembles the smaller cloud's.
arxiv-2605-05132:
Kenta Kasai writes a short note comparing two belief propagation decoders for quantum error correction under CSS codes. In such codes, two check matrices constrain the two parts of each Pauli error separately. Writing the posterior as one combined factor graph couples the two parts through a shared prior at each qubit, giving an algorithm he calls joint belief propagation.

Kasai compares this with the four-state version, which labels each qubit by its full Pauli state instead. After relabelling the four local states and summing out the irrelevant part, he shows the two algorithms produce identical posterior weights, messages, and beliefs. The note clarifies that the two formulations are the same decoder in different clothing.
arxiv-2605-05332:
Isabella Khan claims to prove a conjecture by Némethi about a number invariant of 3D spaces called rational homology spheres. The invariant, the Heegaard Floer d-invariant, is defined through a Floer homology group, and Némethi worked it out with lattice homology for one class of plumbed spaces in 2005. He proposed his formula should hold for all negative-definite plumbed rational homology spheres.

Khan uses a match, due to Zemke, between lattice homology and Heegaard Floer homology to carry Némethi's lattice work across to the Floer side. That transfer proves the formula in the full scope he claimed, and expands the earlier partial class. The result closes a twenty-year-old question in low-dimension topology.
arxiv-2605-05432:
Schrödinger bridges describe how a cloud of particles most likely moves between two states. Othmane Mazhar and Huyên Pham study estimating that drift directly from data seen over one time interval. Their estimator plugs kernel averages into the known drift formula, working at the drift level rather than solving the whole bridge problem.

Under stated regularity conditions they prove a uniform error bound and a central limit result. An adaptive rule for choosing the smoothing width satisfies an oracle inequality, and a minimax lower bound shows the rates are nearly best possible. Synthetic experiments check the theory's predictions.
arxiv-2605-05532:
Small, specialized models can beat giant ones at narrow jobs, argue Nicole Lincoln, Nick Whitehouse, Jaron Mar, and Rivindu Perera. Their test case is pulling structured fields out of legal contracts. They pitted Olava Extract, a self-hosted legal model, against five frontier systems on contracts annotated by legal professionals.

Olava Extract posted the best overall scores in the study, with the highest precision as well. Fewer invented or unsupported fields matter in legal work, where errors create review burden and risk. Its running costs were also far lower, falling by roughly four-fifths to nearly all of the frontier models' cost.
arxiv-2605-05632:
Poisoning a retrieval system's knowledge base is a known attack, but almost all testing used the simplest pipeline. Samuel Korn asks whether fancier architectures resist better. He evaluates four designs under controlled single-document poisoning: vanilla retrieval-augmented generation, an agentic variant, a multi-agent debate system, and recursive language models.

The test used 921 question-answer pairs from Natural Questions. Each architecture faced a clean baseline, a naive injection, and an adversarial attack that frames lies to look expert. Comparing outcomes shows how much safety design alone buys, and where each design still breaks.
arxiv-2605-05732:
Teaching a language model new tasks in sequence usually erodes the old ones. Md Anwar Hossen, Fatema Siddika, Juan Pablo Muñoz, Tanya Roosta, and Ali Jannesari propose CRAFT, which adapts without touching the model's weights. Instead it learns small low-rank interventions on hidden representations, one task at a time.

Tasks are first routed to groups of similar tasks by output-distribution divergence. Training against the group's prior state, with a divergence penalty, directly controls forgetting. Interventions then merge into the shared representation using the same signal. Routing, regularization, and merging form one unified continual-learning loop.
arxiv-2605-06032:
Hugo Cazaux, Eyjólfur Ásgeirsson, and Hlynur Stefánsson run a large empirical test of synthetic data for time series forecasting. Synthetic data has reshaped language model training, but forecasters lack clear guidance on when fake series help. Their study covers nine experiment groups and 4,218 runs across five model designs, four synthetic signals, and seven data sets.

The effect hinged sharply on model design. Channel mixing models gained in most trials, while channel independent models were consistently hurt. Averaged over all designs, augmentation hurt in 67 percent of trials. Only one generator, the seasonal trend type, helped reliably. The authors advise gradual schedules, and warn that hard curriculum switching actively degraded accuracy.
arxiv-2605-06432:
Jing Xu, Xuezhi Niu, Didem Gurdur Broo, and Klas Hjort present TouchDrive, a tactile sensing interface for assistive robotic grasping that uses no electronics. Electronic sensing pipelines can make grasping systems complex and less accessible. TouchDrive instead converts contact force directly into pneumatic, meaning air-pressure, feedback through valve switching.

Sensing, signal generation, and feedback sit inside one passive mechanical loop built from a valve, an air tank, a sensing element, and a haptic actuator. Users feel tactile cues and can adjust grasp force for fragile objects. Tests across robotic platforms cover up to 20 objects, including fruit and everyday items.
arxiv-2605-06632:
Yuping Lin and seven co-authors ask whether a behavior taught by supervised fine-tuning can be compressed into a small, causally necessary subnetwork they call a carrier. Fine-tuning spreads new behaviors through a model with no structural control, and post-hoc circuit methods find only correlations, so behaviors cannot be switched selectively at inference time.

Their LCDD method jointly learns routing masks and weights under a utility budget, squeezing a behavior into a sparse carrier. A soft prompt called SFT-Eraser then reverses the behavior by matching activations on carrier channels, without changing weights. Across safety, fixed-response, and style behaviors, carriers preserve the behavior yet allow strong reversal, proving causal necessity.
arxiv-2605-06732:
Nadav Timor, Ravid Shwartz-Ziv, Micah Goldblum, Yann LeCun, and David Harel study training policies inside a learned imagination. Rollouts come from a learned dynamics model, and scores come from a learned reward model, rather than the real environment. Errors in both models distort returns, and the paper asks how to split a sampling budget between them.

Under power-law scaling assumptions they derive the optimal ratio of dynamics to reward samples, and identify small Lipschitz constants as a property that tightens error bounds. They also show noisy rewards leave the policy gradient unbiased when the noise averages to zero, with variance shrinking as rollouts grow. The budgeting choice reduces to a one-dimensional optimization.
arxiv-2605-06932:
Tushin Mallick, Ashish Kundu, and Ramana Kompella present Aquaman, a proxy design that gives legacy clients quantum-resistant session keys today. Attackers already archive encrypted traffic to decrypt later once quantum computers mature, endangering the classical key exchanges anchoring current sessions. Aquaman intercepts key requests at a trusted network's edge, requiring no client setup, and supplies post-quantum power on clients' behalf.

Four modes are described, from proxy-offloaded post-quantum handshakes to hybrid setups and quantum key distribution interfaces. The implemented multi-path mode splits the session key into fragments sent over diverse media like Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and Ethernet, all required for reconstruction. A thousand-run cloud prototype shows latency dominated by transmission, not the splitting overhead.
arxiv-2605-07032:
Montaser Mohammedalamen and three co-authors systematically pull apart reinforcement-learning jailbreak attacks on language models. Such attacks train an attacker over many steps to coax harmful output from a target model. Why the approach works so well had not been studied in a structured way.

The team separates the attack into its reward design, action space, episode length, algorithm, training data, and reward shaping. Their attacker compromised every targeted model and safeguard in the study. Dense rewards and longer episodes emerged as the main drivers of success. That gives defenders a clearer picture of what to harden.
arxiv-2605-07332:
Basanta Mistri, Vishal Ranjan, and Siddharth Dhomkar simulate a promising qubit host: erbium ions inside cerium oxide. Rare-earth crystals emit at telecom wavelengths and store spin information well. Cerium oxide has very few nuclear spins to disturb the qubit and fits silicon technology. The team explores how magnetic field, pulse choices, erbium concentration, and temperature affect coherence.

Near special clock transition points, decoherence from the surrounding spin bath is strongly suppressed. At very dilute doping and sub-Kelvin temperatures, simulated echo coherence approaches one second. Even at liquid helium temperatures, times around ten milliseconds are expected, and standard pulse sequences improve matters further, supporting the material as a quantum memory candidate.
arxiv-2605-07632:
Marcel Binz and seventy-eight co-authors test a popular practice: using large language models as stand-ins for human participants in behavioral research. Whether the models that behave most usefully also behave most humanly was unclear. The team built Psych-201, a dataset designed to measure behavioral alignment between models and people at scale.

Across model families, sizes, and training objectives, they find that post-training, the stage that turns a raw model into a helpful assistant, consistently reduces alignment with human behavior. The gap widens in newer model generations even as the underlying base models improve. A popular fix, giving the model a persona, did not improve predictions for individual people. The processes that make models useful assistants, they conclude, also make them worse human simulators.
arxiv-2605-08032:
Christopher Moore and Frank Marsiglio revisit the Kronig-Penney model, a classic picture of electrons in a crystal. The textbook version places square wells at each atom. Moore and Marsiglio replace them with truncated harmonic oscillator wells, which better resemble real atomic potentials, and still solve the model exactly.

They derive the energy bands and wave functions for the new wells and compare them with the standard case. By writing the governing equation in a tight-binding form, they obtain a direct formula for the tunneling amplitude between sites in terms of the oscillator parameters. The result links a simple teaching model more tightly to real band calculations.
arxiv-2605-08432:
Zhanliang Wang, Jiancong Xiao, Ruochen Jin, Shu Yang, and coauthors build a yardstick for calibration in open-ended question answering. A model's stated confidence should match its real accuracy. That matters most in medicine and law. Open-ended answers defeat the usual metrics, though. Logit scores need restricted formats. Spoken confidence runs overconfident. Sampling methods lean on task-specific extraction rules.

Their Sem-ECE framework samples free-form answers. It groups them into semantic clusters. It measures calibration error against that grouping, with a clear finite-sample target. The semantic step replaces brittle answer matching. Evaluators gain a principled way to audit confidence where models are actually deployed.
arxiv-2605-08732:
Hoang Nguyen, Xiaohao Xu, and Xiaonan Huang replace slow search based planning in learned world models with one fast learned mapping. Vision based world models compress scenes into smooth latent spaces, yet goal planning there usually needs costly iterative search. In a pretrained model whose latent geometry is kept smooth and uniform, they argue planning structure already sits inside the representation itself.

Their goal conditioned inverse dynamics model reads current state, goal state, and time left, then outputs the next action directly. Across navigation, manipulation, and control tests it matches or beats search in nearly all settings at roughly one hundredth of the cost. Structured latent spaces can shift planning from online search to learned inference.
arxiv-2605-08832:
Jonas Weidner, Yeray Martin-Ruisanchez, Daniel Rueckert, Benedikt Wiestler, and Julian Suk recast fluid simulation as inpainting: fill the unknown flow given the parts already fixed. Standard neural surrogates demand explicit geometry and boundary settings, tying them to training conditions and blocking reuse when boundaries shift. Their self supervised approach learns a prior over velocity fields from data alone, then imposes inlets, outlets, or unchanged regions only when solving.

A local neighborhood tokenizer compresses fine three dimensional fields into compact tokens for generative models. On blood flow in brain aneurysms, the method rebuilds full fields from sparse context, beats supervised rivals under shifts, and allows local geometry edits reusing prior context.
arxiv-2605-08932:
J. García-Barceló, Jose Navarro-Madrid, and Alejandro Díaz-Morcillo design bigger hunting chambers for axions, the hypothetical dark matter particles, using hexagonal coaxial cavities tuned near thirty gigahertz. A haloscope's reach grows with sensitive volume, but magnet bores are tight. Moving from one cavity to dual and triple subcavity layouts, they tune resonance by rotating inner hexagonal prisms while preserving strong quality and form factors.

The triple design triples performance over the single cavity baseline. A four subcavity version fits the strict radial limit in theory if wall thicknesses are optimized for frequency stability. Mode splitting, manufacturing tolerance, and heat remain practical hurdles. Dark matter searches gain a scalable one port route into high frequency territory.
arxiv-2605-09232:
Cartmell and Williams survey privacy aware distributed learning for IoT systems, where data stays local and updates travel instead. Keeping data local reduces central collection, but swapping gradients, parameters, and outputs opens new privacy risks. Past surveys describe defences apart, without a shared way to judge them under real attacks and limits.

The authors build a unified threat model covering gradient leakage, inversion attacks, membership inference, and communication based attacks. On that model they base an evaluation framework rating methods on privacy strength and efficiency, including compute, memory, and communication cost. Sample methods include homomorphic encryption, secure multi party computation, differential privacy, Bloom Filter methods, and selective stochastic gradient descent. The analysis finds privacy strength and system efficiency in tension, spanning formal tools, cryptographic approaches, and lightweight probabilistic methods. Bloom Filter codes stand out, gaining privacy through collision induced ambiguity while keeping cost low.
arxiv-2605-09432:
Bentert and four colleagues design algorithms for breeding and scheduling carrier pigeons to meet set communication demand efficiently, minimising the number of pigeons required. It is a lighthearted take on the Carrier Pigeon Internet Protocol. In the pigeon-post link layer, sending a one-hop message to a node calls for a mail pigeon bred and raised at that node. Sending the message loses the pigeon, so each further message needs another pigeon of that node.

While the single-hop variant admits a simple characterisation, both the 2-hop and multihop variants are NP-hard. For those variants, a polynomial-time algorithm built on demand aggregation achieves a 2-approximation on pigeons used. Pigeon-post bandwidth can beat networks using other media, which motivated Internet standards allowing pigeons as link-layer media. The authors hope the pigeon perspective offers funny and instructive insights into network design and ornithology.
arxiv-2605-09732:
Oliveira and Urmian built TreeWidzard, an engine for writing dynamic-programming algorithms that decide graph properties by treewidth and pathwidth. Many hard graph problems, like coloring or finding Hamiltonian cycles, become tractable when graphs are narrow in this width sense. The engine unifies algorithms for basic graph properties and lets users combine them into algorithms for more complex properties.

It also supports width-based automated theorem proving. Given a Boolean combination of properties and a width bound k, the engine can check whether every graph of width at most k satisfies it. The paper walks through implementation step by step, showing how to build and combine algorithms for model checking and proof. TreeWidzard turns width-based reasoning from hand-crafted code into a reusable system.
arxiv-2605-09832:
Shenoy and five colleagues changed how atomic protein models are built from cryo-electron microscopy maps. Knowing a protein's atomic conformational ensemble, its range of shapes, is key to its function, but ensemble models lack high-quality training data. Heterogeneous reconstruction now yields ensembles of density maps for large proteins, yet turning maps into atomic models remains hard.

Instead of the usual two stages, converting maps to structures and then training predictors on them, the team fine-tuned the static structure model Boltz-2 directly on raw cryo-EM maps. Their method, CryoSampler, beat prior model-building accuracy and showed early in-domain generalization, sampling diverse shapes for unseen sequences in the same protein family without cryo-EM data. Raw maps, the paper suggests, can train the next generation of ensemble models.
arxiv-2605-10032:
Acharjee Dip and two colleagues built PlantMarkerBench, a multi-species benchmark for judging plant marker claims from papers. Cell-type marker genes are key to plant biology, yet current tools rely on curated data banks or high-throughput studies without clearly showing backup proof. The benchmark spans four plant species: Arabidopsis, maize, rice, and tomato.

It holds 5,550 sentence cases marked for marker validity, proof type, and support strength. The cases were built in stages combining paper search, species-aware grounding, shaped proof pull-out, and focused human review. The paper defines two tasks: judging whether a test sentence gives valid marker proof, and sorting proof into expression, localization, function, indirect, or negative. Frontier models do well on direct expression but drop on functional, indirect, and weak-support cases, with proof-type mix-ups as the main failure. Open-weight models show more false alarms under doubt.
arxiv-2605-10632:
Claudio Anliker and three colleagues present two attacks on ToA estimation for narrowband ranging. ToA via cross-correlation underpins time-of-flight ranging. In narrowband systems, distance-cutting attacks such as Early-Detect/Late-Commit are notoriously hard to stop. Their 2026 paper presents two attacks reshaping signals to compromise correlation estimation.

The first attack scales the signal with a symbol waveform. The second routes it through a negative group delay filter. Unlike ED/LC, the attacks need no live symbol detection or adaptive compensation; they are symbol-blind. The authors describe plans for both attacks. They discuss group delay filtering for Bluetooth Channel Sounding. Simulating a group delay circuit and an arrival estimator, they show distance cuts of up to 18 meters. The target is Bluetooth Channel Sounding round-trip ranging. They verify feasibility by building a prototype from standard components.
arxiv-2605-10932:
El Mustapha Mansouri and Keigo Arai show that crystal symmetry can build sound-based quantum gates whose errors stay readable to error-correction decoders. Tough processors need control errors that decoders can read, not merely errors that run small.

When both the strain tensor and the lambda-transition operators take one special two-dimensional symmetry shape, the linear strain relation collapses to a scalar dot product. Two phase-locked sound modes driven out of step build a circular strain field for complex lambda-leg control without local microwave fields. Simulations of a nitrogen-vacancy center reach about 99.9 percent fidelity, counting only cases that stay in the gate space, in under two microseconds, with leftover noise filtered by parity into light-visible channels. Solid-state quantum engineers get symmetry-built gates with decoder-friendly errors.
arxiv-2605-11232:
Prathamesh Vasudeo Naik, Naresh Dintakurthi, and Yue Wang rethink LLMOps for fraud and anti-money-laundering work with a compliance-grade LLM serving stack. Fraud and AML serving differs sharply from generic chat: prompts are prefix-heavy, schema-constrained, and evidence-rich, with reusable policy text, risk taxonomies, transaction context, and short structured outputs.

Their workload-aware stack leans on self-hosted open-weight models, Meta Llama and Alibaba Qwen among them. It combines PagedAttention, speculative decoding, multi-adapter serving, Automatic Prefix Caching, sleep/wake lifecycle management, adapter- and prompt-length-aware batching, optional prefill/decode disaggregation, and vLLM-style runtime tuning. A reproducibility track builds prefix-heavy compliance prompts from synthetic AML datasets in the public domain, including IBM AML and SAML-D, without exposing institution-specific data. Compliance engineering teams get a serving stack built for audit-grade fraud and AML workloads.
arxiv-2605-11732: Jiarui Jin and four colleagues split deep research into two cooperating roles instead of one tangled module. In AgentDisCo, a critic agent judges outlines and sharpens search queries. A generator agent fetches fresh results and revises the outlines, and a writer then turns the refined outline into a report. The system matched or beat leading closed systems on three deep research benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-12132: Szilárd Majorosi, Nasr Hafz, and Zsolt Lécz build a high-order real-space solver for particle-in-cell simulations in cylinders. Laser wakefield acceleration relies on simulations, and cylindrical symmetry cuts compute and memory costs, at some accuracy cost. The best prior method solves Maxwell's equations on a Fourier-Bessel basis, as in FBPIC. Their method matches that accuracy in real space with high-order staggered differences and an exponential laser envelope treatment. Tests on laser propagation and wakefield electron injection agree with 3D runs and FBPIC.
arxiv-2605-12232: Kamil Otal constructs set-like sunflower-free subspace families over finite fields. The sunflower problem has analogues: petals in general position over the kernel, or kernel equal to petal intersections. Otal works in the second, set-like setting, noting general-position freeness does not give set-like freeness. He builds large s-sunflower-free k-space families from a tweaked lifting construction, presented as the first systematic construction for this setting. He compares sizes with exact optima for small parameters, from exhaustive search.
arxiv-2605-12432: Tran and Vicente cut the cost of multi-objective optimisation by alternating both the objective and the variable block. Standard multi-gradient methods compute gradients for every variable at every step, which grows expensive at scale. Their framework gives each objective a set number of gradient steps on its own block, exploring the Pareto front while spending less per iteration. The authors prove convergence across convex, non-convex and Polyak-Lojasiewicz settings, recovering single-objective rates. Numerical tests show it beating non-alternating methods.
arxiv-2605-12532: Letteri replaces fixed trading rules with a deliberative team of language-model agents. Standard systems use deterministic heuristics or offline-trained models that cannot adapt to shifting market regimes. His AgenticAITA loop lets Analyst, Risk Manager and Executor agents reason, negotiate and act together, with no offline training or human step. A Z-score trigger gates model inference to statistically odd market conditions, typed JSON contracts govern the chain, and a hard-gate safety layer blocks unsafe actions before execution.
arxiv-2605-12632: Tiwari and four colleagues map tiny interactions of charged anti-de Sitter black holes with quintessence, using Ruppeiner curvature. Its divergence signals phase changes, while its sign tells whether forces attract or repel. Attraction rules at low charge, while repulsion prevails at high charge, unlike usual charged black holes. That strength stays fairly constant through the change, showing how it shapes these black holes.
arxiv-2605-12932: Li, Wang and Yang tackle partial tensor block-diagonalisation: they apply orthonormal matrices to a multiway tensor so its block-diagonal part best captures the whole. Their NPDo method maximises that part and, paired with Gauss-Seidel-style updates, converges to a stationary point while the goal value rises at each step. The method covers Tucker decomposition and approximate dominant tensor SVD as special cases. Small tests show it runs well.
arxiv-2605-13032: Wang, Qiu and Huang tackle out-of-distribution detection for graph neural networks, which falter when node features or graph structure shift. Standard supervised training tends to absorb spurious signals from features or structure. Their TIDE framework splits information into feature-specific, structure-specific and joint parts, keeping only the label-relevant slice of the joint part and filtering spurious parts. The result separates in-distribution from out-of-distribution nodes better, with up to 34% improvement in FPR95 over strong baselines.
arxiv-2605-13332: Johannes Fichte and three colleagues introduce a measure of diversity for extensions in abstract argumentation. In this field, arguments and their conflicts form a graph with arrows. An extension is a set of arguments that jointly meet certain rules. Standard reasoning rarely shows how far apart two accepted viewpoints sit. They measure diversity through symmetric difference, which counts arguments in exactly one of the two sets. They classify how hard it is to decide if diverse extensions exist and to find the largest level.
arxiv-2605-13532: Juho Leinonen, Lisa Zhang and Arto Hellas examine generative AI slide generation from course notes. They test NotebookLM, two general models and two coding assistants. Educators judge whether generated slides are good, and the best slides are used in a real course. Coding assistants produce the most accurate, complete and pedagogically sound slides. Students rate AI slides as similar in quality to instructor slides and cannot reliably tell which are AI-generated. High quality ratings correlate negatively with AI ratings, suggesting students link poor quality with AI origin.
arxiv-2605-13732: R. I. Kamalitdinov and S. V. Sushkov study ripples in the flat Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker model under gravity with non-minimal slope coupling. The coupling term rules early times, driving a primary quasi-de Sitter boom stage needing no fine-tuned curve. The authors derive a full rule set for scalar, vector and tensor ripple modes. They study all modes by hand in two limit cases and build exact number answers for full mode growth.
arxiv-2605-13832: Jȩdrzej Stempin and three colleagues settle an open problem in entanglement theory raised by Yu and colleagues in Nature Communications in 2021. The problem is showing, through an entanglement witness, whether the 14-qubit state Φ_E8 is entangled. Spurred by a method from quantum codes, they combine even spread with moment grids to prove Φ_E8 is entangled. Their path joins and extends earlier methods using the Lovász theta number of the Pauli anti-swaps graph, hinting growth and bend for further uses.
arxiv-2605-13932: Lin and six colleagues address molecular property prediction when test molecules differ sharply from training data. They build SCOPE-Bench, a benchmark that partitions molecular scaffolds in a physicochemical descriptor space, and POMA, a retrieve-compose-adapt framework that selects source domains without target labels. A policy trained on proxy-task error reductions picks the source subset, which then adapts to the target with covariance alignment at whole-molecule and substructure levels.
arxiv-2605-14032: Giustini and six co-authors present StormShield, a fingerprint-based defense against RRC signaling storms in O-RAN 5G networks. In such an attack, a rogue user device floods the base station with signaling, draining its resources and blocking legit devices from connecting. Older defenses mostly just detect attacks, rest on simulations alone, and cannot tell heavy load from attack or handle device motion. The paper first tests whether the attack works on an open-source radio testbed.
arxiv-2605-14132: Glavan and Jaramillo-Garrido study black-hole hair in the linearly coupled scalar-Gauss-Bonnet theory in de Sitter space. Working in the test-field regime, they show scalar hair sourced by black holes grows in both time and space on superhorizon scales. That growth is no special black-hole effect: it follows from the dynamics of a minimally coupled massless scalar field in expanding de Sitter space. It also arises for a point scalar charge, so a scalarized black hole acts like a localized subhorizon source of scalar perturbations.
arxiv-2605-14432: Kariya studies discrimination between one and two incoherent point sources among weak, spaced emitters, using singular learning theory. Alignment lets spatial-mode demultiplexing attain the quantum-optimal Stein exponent. Aligned Gaussian direct imaging and SPADE share a log canonical threshold of one half but differ in multiplicity, giving asymptotics. Fixed nonzero misalignment removes the support mismatch of SPADE, giving the same threshold and multiplicity as imaging. Mode counting about an offset axis reveals a reflection zero branch where the two-source case becomes indistinguishable from the null, with power collapse.
arxiv-2605-14532: Chen, Ishibashi and Ohta test whether quantum-improved charged black holes stay consistent when two couplings vary with radius. The couplings are Newton's constant and the electromagnetic coupling. For Reissner-Nordstrom holes, they claim thermodynamics allows any radial dependence of both, though the chemical potential needs care. Matching the equation approach with the action approach is said to need an extra quantum energy-momentum tensor plus a condition on Newton's coupling.
arxiv-2605-14732: Nangho, Nkwamouo and Woukeng prove density of bivariate polynomials for a weight function. The weight function sits on a simply connected open subset of the plane with piecewise smooth boundary. They also prove compact embedding of a matrix-weighted Sobolev space into a weighted Lebesgue space. As an application, they investigate by a variational method the eigenvalue problem for a degenerate Helmholtz operator. The operator acts on a triangle.
arxiv-2605-14932: Lukas Pirch and six others look at AI agents through the lens of operating systems. These face much the same problems: keeping resources apart, grading rights, and policing talk between parts. Surveying open-source agents, they map a shared design and list attack routes. A case study of four widely used agents finds several defenses failing even against modest attackers. Many flaws, they conclude, yield to classic operating-system techniques, though some agent abilities stay insecure by design.
arxiv-2605-15532: Jaehun Jung, Hyunwoo Kim, Brandon Cui, Ximing Lu, David Acuna, Prithviraj Ammanabrolu, and Yejin Choi flag waste in vision-language model training. Up to 69 percent of prompts in chart and document sets teach nil. Teacher and student already give the same answers on those prompts. Their DeltaPrompts line aims at true student faults. It builds 200,000 fresh high-gap reasoning tasks from old sets as seeds. Tests span distilling, transfer, and tuning. Gains reach 15 percent relative, even over a finely tuned reasoning model.
arxiv-2605-15932: Coelina Robinson and four colleagues present GEMS, an interactive visual tool for human-in-the-loop molecule design toward safe and green chemicals. Sparse green-impact data make machine-learning oracles weak and candidate picks shaky, while plain scores miss expert chemist insight. GEMS lets domain experts guide an evolutionary search firsthand, tuning scores at a high level and steering molecule pools in detail, with no coding or machine-learning know-how needed. A test case designs green antioxidant options, and chats with domain scientists back its value.
arxiv-2605-16032: Huang and Roney-Dougal settle two questions about primitive groups of diagonal type. They determine the size of every base returned by the greedy algorithm, proving Cameron's 1999 conjecture for these groups.
