They also prove the relational complexity of such groups is at least four, that infinitely many attain four, and that it is unbounded across the family. Few exact relational complexity values were known before.
arxiv-2605-16432: Aryan and four colleagues put the supervisor inside the map: the operator, wearing a Meta Quest 3 headset, steers three simulated TurtleBot3 robots. A see-through view lets real objects block the virtual scene, while space-fixed panels report mapping progress on the spot. Each robot builds its own map with a SLAM Toolbox copy, and a ROS 2 back end fuses the grids as they arrive. In trials, agreement between robot map copies reached 94.7 percent across robot pairs, while merged maps covered 17.9 square metres and scans ran at 8.83 Hz.
arxiv-2605-17032: Monroy sets out variational openness to standard settings, where stationarity needs only total cancellation, not separate bulk-boundary ones. Euler-Lagrange and boundary equations appear only when variations test apart. In systems that split apart, bulk and boundary shifts stay testable apart, giving the inner rule and its balance. In regulated systems, shifts form a graph subspace linking bulk and boundary shifts via compatibility, so it becomes an exchange-space balance. A Rayleigh-Ritz test marks where positivity and coercivity fail, shown in a spherical example.
arxiv-2605-17132: Suárez Mantilla and Castañeda Colorado build a high-order ADER-DG solver for compressible gas flow in the ExaHyPE framework. Adaptive mesh refinement sharpens key zones, and a subcell limiter steadies the code near shocks. Tests cover shock tubes, blast waves and vortex sheets. Smooth regions show the expected accuracy, while sharp interfaces stay stable. The code gives a repeatable route to idealized inviscid flow problems.
arxiv-2605-17232: Kelvin Kan and colleagues prove vocabulary-size-independent convergence for discrete diffusion models, whose prior bounds blew up with vocabulary size or failed under masked priors. Working with adjoint equations in observable space, plus coupling, score-marginal cancellation and exit-routing tricks, they bound error in any integral probability metric under a single rate-matrix regularity assumption. The toolkit also guides loss choice and step counts for language, vision and biology models.
arxiv-2605-17932: Sterling Huang and six colleagues test whether LLMLingua-2 prompt compression transfers to diffusion language models, namely LLaDA-8B-Instruct. Prior compression studies focus on autoregressive models. They test GSM8K, DUC2004, and ShareGPT with 250 prompts each at about 50% compression, covering math, reconstruction, and summary. High semantic scores do not ensure stable results: summary stays robust while math reasoning degrades sharply despite close scores. Reconstruction shows similar prompts can omit details needed for stable denoising. Failures stem mainly from gaps, not semantic drift, motivating diffusion-aware compression.
arxiv-2605-18032: Kazuki Kawamura, Satoshi Waki, and Kei Tateno present PROTEA, an interface for offline improvement of workflows. Multi-agent workflows beat single prompts but are hard to debug, since errors propagate downstream. PROTEA runs a workflow, scores outputs with rubrics, and overlays states and rationales on the graph. For systems where only final answers supervise, it generates node expectations backward from final references and compares them with outputs. It offers prompt revisions and reruns the workflow, improving inspection accuracy from 64.3 percent to 83.9 percent and Hit@5 from 0.30 to 0.38.
arxiv-2605-18132: Sihan Ma and two colleagues build the first hands-off source attribution benchmark for modern made 3D assets, covering 22 sample generators under standard, few-shot, and real rules. They find generators leave two stable mark types: cross-view mismatch and shape flaws in geometric statistics and frequency-domain cues. A layered multi-view multi-modal Transformer fuses looks, shape, and wave-domain features within each view and models global links across views. Tests reach 97.22 percent accuracy with full labels and 77.17 percent with only 1 percent training data, under five samples each.
arxiv-2605-18232: Khalid Yusuf Dahir's 2026 paper introduces SomaliWeb v1, the first Somali pre-training corpus with its own tokenizer and a public language-identification benchmark. Somali has about 25 million speakers, yet prior text lived only inside multilingual dumps or small uploads. A six-stage pipeline filters three upstream sources into 819,322 documents holding about 303 million tokens. Audits of existing releases find striking defects, including 17.3 percent byte-exact duplicates in one cleaned release. The new BPE-16K tokenizer emits 40.2 percent fewer tokens than GPT-4's tokenizer on a Somali test set.
arxiv-2605-18732: Matthew Smith and four co-authors test, in a 2026 study, how factual recall scales with size and topic frequency. They evaluate 38 models on over 8,900 references. Recall quality follows a sigmoid in the log-linear mix of parameter count and topic share. Those two variables alone explain 60 percent of variance across 16 dense models. Within families, the share rises to 74 to 94 percent. The pattern fits a superposition account where signal-to-noise gating ties signal to concept frequency and noise floor to capacity.
arxiv-2605-18832: Bo Long and four colleagues give transformers a clear handle on uncertainty through filtering that tracks belief. Every token now carries equal trust, a flaw that bites on cold-start items, uneven signal quality, and attention sinks. In their Bayesian Filtering Transformer, attention becomes precision-weighted kriging, the shortcut link becomes a Kalman update, and the feed-forward block carries that weight onward. A free gauge supplies the seen-data weight. Tests show gains for item suggestions and noisy fine-tuning, largest where uncertainty runs highest.
arxiv-2605-18932: Nikita Klimenko and four colleagues generate floor plans with a language model that writes hypergraph descriptions of rooms and their connections. Trained by supervised fine-tuning, HypergraphFormer encodes spatial relationships and connectivity as text, then renders them as plans. On RPLAN and a new out-of-distribution set, it beats raster and vector methods and uses data more efficiently. Because footprints are decoupled from their subdivisions, the method handles irregular boundaries and stays highly editable for design work.
arxiv-2605-19032: Zachary Yahn and seven colleagues build FaceCloak, a face shield from one photo alone. Scraped shots feed rogue match tools. From that shot it spins a small varied face set. It learns a cloak for weak spots, pushing face code to a far anchor and from a near one. A light pixel mask then fits any shot at good look, beating twenty nine rivals on three sets and ten tools.
arxiv-2605-19132: Giovani D. Lucafó and four colleagues propose CLIC, a heart-diagnosis method that pairs ECG signals with patient context written as text. The ECG is the standard non-invasive test for heart disease, yet most programs use the signal alone, ignoring patient traits and recording context that doctors use each day. Turning context into plain text gives the model an anchor that helps sort complex patterns. Template-based clinical text lifts sorting scores each time, while richer text made by large language models stays close behind.
arxiv-2605-19332: Renee Key and colleagues launch AMPM, a fast microlensing survey in the Large Magellanic Cloud aimed at asteroid-mass primordial black holes. Such black holes, if part of dark matter, would briefly brighten background stars as they pass in front. The team reports five nights of data, its detection pipeline, and how star layout affects efficiency. Second-order effects shift peak sensitivity toward lunar-mass holes, and one candidate caps the galactic share of such black holes at up to 30 percent with high confidence.
arxiv-2605-19632: Alpay and Alakkad define executable boundary contracts for finite sound event traces, aiming at measurement rather than a new temporal logic or leaderboard. A bounded Boolean frame fragment embeds in signal temporal logic after grid projection, while the event layer adds interval matching, duration clauses, fragmentation clauses and restricted vector scoring. Tests span Mini LibriSpeech scenes, MAESTRO soundscapes, frozen timing probes and a DCASE 2024 Task 4 baseline. Standard scores and contract coordinates disagree with clear readings, and the strongest real-corpus finding is that union activity can hide typed boundary failure.
arxiv-2605-19832: Andersson and Elmqvist argue generative AI should serve creative work as an active medium, not merely as a judgeable output. Decision support framing pushes people to evaluate correctness instead of exploring and shaping ideas. They turn to Schön's reflective practice: like a potter with clay, users shape, observe, stir and select their medium in ongoing conversation. Because generative AI tends toward convergence, human disruption and curation sustain creative quality. Their Loom probe, orchestrating simulated narrative agents in creative writing, illustrates the SOSS framework and its design implications.
arxiv-2605-19932: Gu and colleagues give long task agents a small lasting map of the world they keep revisiting. Past tricks save past runs, raw files, or task plans, but none save reusable facts about the world itself. Their PEEK map holds what the world holds, how it is laid out, and which bits proved handy, kept small by a strict size cap.
arxiv-2605-20532: Liubov Kurafeeva and eleven colleagues bridge a gap between edge devices and supercomputers. Edge devices need instant answers from live sensors, yet better models often wait on slow, batch-scheduled simulations. Their RBF design, short for Reverse Backfill, runs light stand-in models at the edge. Improved versions then arrive later from the supercomputer, with spare capacity spent raising accuracy rather than filling schedules.
arxiv-2605-20632: Yun-Peng Li and three colleagues model light from a newborn magnetar left by a binary neutron-star merger. The fast-spinning magnetar drives a relativistic jet powered by magnetic flux, and shocks inflate a pulsar wind nebula between jet and ejecta. Their study tracks the jet-ejecta-nebula system and finds the reverse shock is long-lived in most cases. Emission shifts from thermal ejecta glow to a jet-powered X-ray plateau, then to synchrotron and inverse-Compton light.
arxiv-2605-21132: Jingyi He, Yue Zhou, and colleagues present SurgOnAir, a streaming model that narrates surgery as it unfolds rather than describing clips after the fact. It reads frames in order, emits words as new images arrive, and marks changes of state with special tokens. Trained on their SurgOnAir-11k set, which labels actions, steps, and phases, the model gives layered commentary that tracks the hierarchy of an operation.
arxiv-2605-21332: Michael Kuhlmann and co-authors develop speech quality embeddings to detect and classify flaws in speech signals. Old assessment scores whole utterances or systems, but modern systems produce high-quality speech with flaws that occur only locally. Models trained on utterance-level targets can still yield useful local predictions with suitable architectures and losses. The authors extend such models to frame-level embeddings that cluster by flaw type, using partial mix-up on parallel clean and flawed utterances plus a contrastive loss. Tests show better detection and type ID.
arxiv-2605-21832: Xinhang Yuan and co-authors present FLUID, the first to retire the item ID from a livestreaming ranker. Live rooms air briefly, leaving item IDs unlearned in a cold start that defeats ID-centric ranking. FLUID's multimodal encoder produces hierarchical semantic codes called LUCID. A warmup adds slice-level LUCID beside the ID embedding, then replaces the ID with room-level LUCID. Deployed widely, it gains zero point five five, two point zero five, and zero point zero five percent in watch duration, cold-start room views, and active hours.
arxiv-2605-22432: Kim and colleagues study Muon through the river-valley landscape, where progress runs along a flat river subspace while steep valley walls cause oscillations. Muon's orthogonalisation speeds river progress but amplifies dominant-direction noise. Their AMUSE blends Muon's bulk speed with Schedule-Free averaging for stability. A shifting coefficient starts near the fast Muon sequence. It then shifts toward the stable averaged sequence to damp oscillations. AMUSE needs no schedules and supports anytime training. Across vision and language pretraining, it beats Schedule-Free AdamW and Muon.
arxiv-2605-22632: Bergemann and team argue firm ties fail to launch, not for science reasons. Scholars must publish while companies must protect private models, and no standard contract fixes this tension. Because legal teams alone write contracts, many legal fights are motive problems only scientists can spot. The team offers PBOS, a contract form with a single line: pretraining work is open science; posttraining work (weights trained on private data) is business IP. This line is sound, legally clean, and open to checks. The field should adopt PBOS.
arxiv-2605-22732: Dietrich tests whether acoustic emotion models can stand in for the Pathos dimension of political speech, using one Bundestag speech in 51 segments as a case study. Gemini's valence scores track TRUST Pathos scores strongly, with strong positive Spearman correlation, while an acoustic model's valence shows no link. A further Gemini check of a standard emotional speech database exposes acted speech, cultural bias and category mismatches as benchmark flaws. Dietrich concludes language model multimodal analysis captures political emotion far better than acoustics alone, though acoustics still aid low level arousal.
arxiv-2605-22932: Sharma and fifteen others grow platinum ditelluride films layer by layer, from 1 to 20 monolayers. They track terahertz emission with spin-to-charge conversion across its thickness-driven phase change. Emission is missing in the single-layer semiconducting phase. It switches on near 2 layers at the semimetal transition. It peaks at 10 layers at six times a platinum reference. The pattern points to surface-state and interfacial Rashba channels, not bulk conversion. First-principles calculations confirm this picture.
arxiv-2605-23032: Guo, Wu, and Yiu test whether brain-language model alignment generalizes across languages. They use fMRI from 112 participants in English, Chinese, and French, plus seven language models. Their central finding is that training-language dominance drives alignment, not English itself. A Chinese-dominant model matched to LLaMA-2-7B reversed the gradient. It aligned strongest with Chinese brains and worst with English. Typological distance also covaries with alignment loss. Syntax regions show steeper gradients than lexico-semantic regions, and tokenization fertility explains much of the shift in optimal encoding layer.
arxiv-2605-23632: Klötergens and colleagues present Gaussian Mixture Copula Processes, a copula process for irregular series, rich and keeping its margins right. Earlier copula processes achieve only one: Gaussian copulas stay consistent but only cover elliptical dependence, while attentional copulas like TACTiS-2 are rich but lose margin consistency. GMCP closes the gap by reading mixture copula settings from context, with guaranteed margins, tractable likelihood. Copulas with MargFlow, a flow model for margins, beat trained baselines in forecasting. GMCP proves richer than Gaussian copulas and on par with TACTiS-2.
arxiv-2605-24232: Caja-Lopez, Delgadino, and Kitagawa give stability bounds for best transport maps on curved domains under square cost. Under Holder smoothness, they prove Lipschitz L2 and Holder stability bounds for transport maps. Without the smoothness rule, they obtain a Lipschitz L2 bound for Brenier fields in terms of the L2 distance between loads. Proofs hinge on the Brenier field's linear response along smooth blends, got by using the Monge-Ampere rule. The method also yields a rule for the second change of the Monge-Kantorovich distance.
arxiv-2605-24632: Alfredo Pesoli, Herman Errico, and Lorenzo Cavallaro examine LLM-driven vulnerability discovery through bugonomics, the economics of producing, proving, prioritizing, and fixing defects. Headlines stress capability, but the authors argue the near-term shift is toward broader defender remediation throughput, not more zero-days. Cheaper candidate generation at scale meets scarce maintainer capacity for review, validation, triage, and release work. Drawing on Anthropic's Mythos Preview and Mozilla Firefox work, they show the choke point is taking in and shipping more reports. The effect is acute in open source.
arxiv-2605-24732: Davide Bolognini and Paolo Sentinelli disprove a long-standing conjecture of Simon on the shellability of simplex skeleta. The conjecture held that every simplex skeleton is extendably shellable, meaning any shelling order can be completed. The authors show otherwise. For every dimension three and above, they construct a pure shellable simplicial complex that is not shelling completable. The result draws a sharp line: shellability alone does not guarantee that a partial shelling order can always be extended, settling a question that had stood open for years.
arxiv-2605-24832: Chiyue Wei and co-authors present Optimus, an elastic decoding system for diffusion model serving. Autoregressive decoding wastes GPUs through one-by-one execution, while diffusion models decode several tokens per iteration for speed. Fixed block-size diffusion decoding shifts with load: large blocks use idle GPUs at low load but saturate with wasted computation at high load. Optimus treats decoding granularity as a runtime control, trading GPU use for token efficiency. Chunked decoding enables fine execution without new training, while load-aware scheduling picks chunk sizes from runtime.
arxiv-2605-24932: Yuanye Liu leads X-Edit, a way to fix errors in medical vision transformers without the forgetting that fine-tuning brings. Pretrained vision transformers now aid medical image classification, but patching their failures can erode skills they already hold. X-Edit swaps iterative gradient tuning for a closed-form fix. Causal tracing first pinpoints layers behind a wrong call. Then an orthogonal null-space projection built from a curated anchor set confines the exact update to that null space, so targeted errors get fixed while prior diagnostic knowledge stays put.
arxiv-2605-25432: Mario Ulises González-Rivas and colleagues trace how individual metals drive magnetism in two disordered spinel oxides. Element-specific X-ray magnetic dichroism tracks each metal separately in two magnetic spinels, one mixing five transition metals and one swapping in gallium. Although all species order at the same transition, their moments grow at cation-dependent rates. That pattern follows from differing 3d fillings, which shape each cation's exchange pathways. Dominant cross-sublattice exchange hardens some species fast while frustration slows others, and non-magnetic substitution relieves frustration.
arxiv-2605-25532: Slagter presents a new exact instanton from conformal dilaton gravity, set on a warped spacetime resembling Kerr geometry. Its metric comes from a first-order equation, which opens the link to self-duality, and singularities follow a quintic polynomial. He suggests this quintic is the highest degree for axially symmetric Petrov type D black hole singularities. The solution is a locally conformal Kählerian manifold, and its topology is a three-sphere times a real line modulo two. The horizon comes from the Hopf fibration.
arxiv-2605-25732: Cherubini, Vasta, Recrosi and Gizzi study how collagen fibers in living tissue end up in Von Mises patterns. They show growth plus linear remodeling rules produce generalized bimodal patterns, with no angular mechanical coupling needed. Fibers turn through deposition and removal along preferred directions, a rotation without rotation mechanism. Their results match the patterns seen and point to a direct biological origin for direction stats. Reading fiber density as a probability distribution, they build a Shannon entropy account and derive drift terms for the Fokker-Planck equation.
arxiv-2605-25832: Wang, Xu, Li and Huang present Auto-Robotist, an evolving agent that turns robot search traces into a skill library. Each skill stores an archetype, positive and negative rules, and supporting designs, making memory inspectable. During search the agent retrieves skills to guide edits of elite bodies, keeping a mutation path for exploration. It updates the library by adding, diagnosing and merging. Across seven EvoGym tasks, it improves cold start search and transfers skills to larger spaces, beating genetic algorithms throughout.
arxiv-2605-26132: Lee and Liang ask whether a trained language model can improve itself from bare prompts alone. No outside teacher and no tool feedback are allowed. Their Self-Verified Distillation method starts from seed questions with no known answers, across math, science and coding. The model drafts candidate answers, then filters them in three passes: self-consistency, factual soundness and outright rightness. Survivors form a self-made training set for further training. Only one inference call is needed at test time, the authors report.
arxiv-2605-26232: Bonan Ding and seven colleagues' 2026 framework, UniMVU, fuses video with audio, depth, and auxiliary streams only as instructed, instead of blending every channel equally. Inner gates highlight salient regions inside each stream. Outer gates re-weight whole streams. Both answer to the text instruction, with a fast-to-slow scheme for time-aligned streams. Across six benchmarks, the gated fusion beats static fusion baselines by as much as thirteen and a half CIDEr points. Its gate patterns line up with human judgments of which modality matters.
arxiv-2605-26332: Arian Komaei Koma and three colleagues' 2026 attack, BEAP, targets unlearned image diffusion models without model weights, while evading safety filters. A language model iteratively generates prompts, guided by an embedding-aware search balancing concept presence, picture-text fit, and image quality. Across five unlearning methods, BEAP reaches a macro-averaged attack success rate of ninety-seven point eight percent, beating the white-box baseline by forty-one point six points. Counting failed searches at full budget, it averages thirty-two point one image queries per prompt.
arxiv-2605-26432: Xiong Yin, Wei Kou, and Xurong Chen review muon-catalyzed fusion. Muons replace electrons and shrink atomic orbits a hundredfold, letting deuterium-tritium fusion run near room temperature. Four steps follow: muonic atom formation, muon transfer, resonant molecule formation, and fusion with muon recycling. A kinetic model sizes up cycles per muon, with alpha-sticking, where the muon sticks to helium ash, as the main drag. A four-way scheme mixing dual polarization, dense confinement, muon recovery, and resonant boost might lift cycles per muon from about 150 past 500.
arxiv-2605-26732: Sun and five colleagues tackle wave-field prediction at higher frequencies when high-frequency training data are scarce and costly. Their APEX framework keeps only the amplitude of a coarse lower-frequency prediction as a stable anchor. It then rebuilds the missing wave detail with a flow-matching enhancer guided by a phase prior drawn from Green's functions. On SimpleWave, Helmholtz, and Maxwell benchmarks, APEX beats direct extrapolation and joint generative baselines under limited supervision.
arxiv-2605-27032: Liu and four co-authors present SCKAN, a pancreas segmentation method that learns from few labels, built on Kolmogorov-Arnold networks. Sparse labels and wide shape variation cause a bias problem in existing methods: they lean too much on the few labeled cases. SCKAN mixes two ideas: prototype consistency learning, which forces cross-sample consistency, and consensus fusion, which pools stable consensus and filters sample noise. Tests on two public pancreas datasets show it works well.
arxiv-2605-27132: Hegazy and Gabr test whether quality metrics give unbiased scores for multilevel image thresholding, by correlating thresholding objectives with quality metrics across all thresholds on BSDS500 images. Otsu's between-class variance tracks both SSIM and PSNR closely, while Kapur's entropy correlates more weakly and more variably. Otsu beats Kapur on PSNR for every image and on SSIM for over 91 percent of them, revealing a built-in metric-objective bias. The authors call for more neutral evaluation frameworks and plan to extend the analysis to further criteria and domains.
arxiv-2605-27432: Tianhao Gao, Kai Yang, and Yiyang Li build a federated retrieval system for edge devices that cannot share raw data. Their FD-RAG framework learns adaptive hypergraphs locally, distills them into compact question-answer memories, and answers from memory when coverage suffices. It improves accuracy by about 8 percent while cutting latency more than eightfold against strong baselines.
arxiv-2605-27732: Safa Hameed and colleagues derive weight-based constraints for body model and lead selection in pediatric cardiac device MRI safety simulations. Weight alone separates epicardial from endocardial lead implantation with AUC near nine-tenths, and adding age and height adds nothing. The crossover between approaches sits at 44 kg, far above the commonly cited 10 to 15 kg, with a broad transition zone from 21 to 66 kg.
arxiv-2605-27832: Deshpande and colleagues train language models to be more creative by playing Codenames, a word-association game with objectively checkable wins. Using reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, they tuned three sizes of one model family and tested them on ten tests of creativity and four of reasoning. The largest model gained creativity most steadily, while smaller ones gained reasoning precision instead.
arxiv-2605-28132: Shen and colleagues ask which pretraining better serves spatial intelligence: vision-language models or video generation models. Probing frozen features, they find language-supervised models lead on semantic tagging and grouping, while video models expose geometry and camera motion more readily. A simple fusion of both already excels at geometry and semantics together.
arxiv-2605-28532: Liang Cheng and three colleagues test whether tool-using agents know when a task cannot be done. Their FeasiGen pipeline builds dead-end tasks by finding tools shared across winning runs and masking them, with human checks backing over 94 percent of labels right. They also add metrics for spotting dead-end tasks and stopping early. Across nine models, spotting proves weak, with agents wrongly carrying on up to about 74 percent of the time, while multi-agent designs cut wrong runs under dead-end settings.
arxiv-2605-28932: José Natário and Filipe Nazaré derive how a solid reacts to a weak gravitational wave, starting from relativistic elasticity. Expanding the action to second order in elastic terms and first order in the metric disturbance, they recover Dyson's interaction term from the relativistic theory itself. For a thin rectangular plate with zero Poisson ratio, the equations decouple. They give closed-form displacements and deposited energy for short bursts and steady harmonic waves, and the authors also compute the wave emission of the oscillating plate.
arxiv-2605-29832: Mattia Adamo and Michele Cantarella ask whether workers act the same in experiments and real work. They pair an emoji-counting real-effort experiment with platform records, reported expectations and recalls, and screen-time logs for the same workers. In that window, workers answer expected wage changes as in the experiment but react less to surprises. Once recall error in self-reports is accounted for, behaviour lines up across windows. Recall error thus corrupts self-reported data and reflects inattention shaping effort itself, since surprise wage changes pass unnoticed.
arxiv-2605-29932: Danylo Boiko and Viktoriia Mishkurova forecast brain disease advance by picturing future brain states, not single scores. Their treatment-aware diffusion model starts from screening DaTscan and a year of levodopa dose, tracking drug effects over time with a Transformer encoder. A weighted mask keeps focus on brain zones that matter for the disease. The model holds sharp anatomical edges and beats the baseline, cutting mean squared error about fourteen percent and lifting image likeness about five percent. The result points toward care plans tuned to each patient's course.
arxiv-2605-30032: Prakritish Gogoi, Angela Riva, Émile Cochin and Alex Chin revisit how driven qubit-resonator pairs should be modelled when the two parts mix strongly. Standard Lindblad equations built from separate parts can misstate decay rates, they show, using a microscopic Bloch-Redfield treatment built in the coupled system's own states. With driving on, the fixed and time-varying Redfield forms behave differently as drive strength grows. In structured environments they recover the Purcell filter's suppression of measurement-induced relaxation.
arxiv-2605-30132: Adam Ousherovitch and Yixin Wang tackle task extrapolation to unseen tasks outside the training distribution. Their Relational Task Extrapolator rests on one insight: extrapolation means learning how tasks transform into one another. RTE splits each target into a known anchor plus a transformation, then learns an operator mapping pairs to target predictions. It is tested on parameter, length and compositional extrapolation, and extended to sequence prediction in fine-tuning. Across studies it substantially beats existing approaches on novel tasks, even out-of-range ones.
arxiv-2605-30232: Andy Q Han, David J. Chalmers and Pavel Izmailov show reinforcement learning recruits a pre-existing welfare representation in models: an estimate of how well or badly it is doing. They train models in a maze, extract rewarded and punished vectors, and test them in unrelated settings. The punishment vector behaves like negative welfare, promoting failure tokens and self-reports. The reward vector mirrors it, and the two are antiparallel. The vectors work in pretrained models, so the axis pre-exists training, recruited not created by it.
arxiv-2605-30332: Hadar Davidson, Noam Issachar and Sagie Benaim set out a view of SDE sampling as split energy transfer. Diffusion models exhibit spectral bias, fixing low-end structure early and high-end detail later. They present Colored Noise Sampling (CNS), a training-free solver using a tuned schedule sending added energy toward unresolved bands. By using the model's spectral bias, CNS steers the spread toward the data pattern. Tests show CNS beats ODE and SDE baselines as a direct sampler swap across designs. On ImageNet-256, CNS achieves large unguided FID cuts.
arxiv-2605-30432: Moyi Tian and four co-authors learn models from network dynamics data from many start points, using weak form SINDy. They study a system coupling online and offline social activity, learning models from data with WSINDy. They test learning on data from a mean-field model of an interaction process on networks, checking recovery under varied noise. Results show more trajectories lift accuracy when noise is high, but a few trajectories gain most of the benefit.
arxiv-2605-30532: Ding and Anantharam study true self-avoiding walks as a way to sharpen integral estimates from Markov-chain Monte Carlo sampling. Their walk penalizes transitions by empirical overuse, steering the sampler away from already-visited states and edges. They prove the walk's occupation and transition counts track their stationary targets within a root-log factor, almost surely. For any bounded function, the integral estimator's error then shrinks nearly like one over sample size, far sharper than the usual square-root rate of standard random-walk methods.
arxiv-2605-30632: Dasgupta and colleagues present Rationalize, a framework for shared reasoning between people and AI in data-driven sense-making. People and AI work as paired roles, Explorer-Guide, Investigator-Informant, Teacher-Student, and Judge-Advocate, in one shared reasoning space. Both sides make purposes, questions, evidence, and implications explicit, aligning not just outputs but each side's account of intent and action. The paper links the pairs to two-way alignment and sketches a research agenda for alignment design.
arxiv-2605-30732: Bartusek and colleagues present quantum localization, needing a fixed unique state at the checked point that can be found nowhere else. Under older definitions, security only ensures that some portion of a successful attacker sits where claimed, so a spread-out group of attackers could together fake a prover. The stronger notion closes that gap and extends on its own to checking paths, where quantum data gets followed across space and time. Protocols for both notions rest on quantum anchor states, which broaden coset states.
arxiv-2605-30832: Yao and colleagues address excess thought in reasoning models, where thought chains carry built-in repeats and high compute cost without lifting rightness. Old tactics often rely on token-uniform length fines, giving coarse pressure toward shorter outputs that can suppress useful thought. The authors show waste sits in high-odds segments with low marginal utility. They propose SLAT, a reinforcement learning framework selectively suppressing redundant segments based on this criterion. On standard benchmarks, SLAT establishes a superior accuracy-efficiency frontier, reducing thought length by half while maintaining competitive accuracy.
arxiv-2605-31132: Pandey and colleagues analyse gamma-ray burst 140304A, a distant explosion seen when the universe was young, at redshift 5.282. Combining Swift, Fermi and ground telescopes, they trace its prompt flash and fading afterglow, finding the spectral peak softening over time as in typical long bursts. Flares in gamma-ray, X-ray and optical light line up in time, pointing to synchrotron emission from rapidly accelerated matter.
arxiv-2605-31432: Papi and Bentivogli propose DOA, a training-free policy for long-form simultaneous speech translation. Simultaneous translation generates text while speech unfolds, needing a read-or-write policy. Top systems use encoder-decoder models with cross-attention alignment, but decoder-only speech models rely solely on self-attention. The paper asks whether decoder self-attention holds stable alignment signals. DOA derives a proxy alignment from self-attention. Tests on Phi4-Multimodal and Qwen3-Omni show near-offline quality at low latency, without retraining.
arxiv-2606-00232:
Zhao and co-authors build a fix tool for false facts in mixed-media outputs. A smooth reply can hide claims that the source does not back. Past fix tools read source and draft as one lump. False claims in the draft can then warp how the source is read.

Their tool, TIGER, pulls two graphs apart from the start. One graph maps what the source shows, and one maps what the draft claims. Each claim gets a risk grade based on back-up and clash. High-risk claims are picked for repair, while the base model stays frozen. Math shows total risk should fall in a clean curve. Tests span four paths, from image to text and more. False content drops while task quality holds.
arxiv-2606-00332:
Hernandez and co-authors read the light of young star crowds in a small, poor galaxy. The galaxy, NGC 5253, is a blue dwarf near our own. Its young mass crowds drive winds in the gas round them. The team uses Hubble views in far light past sight to read them.

Seven pointings give age, metal share, mass, and dust marks per crowd. Light-based ages run younger than photo-based ages on the whole. Gas speeds out of the crowds span a wide range. Those speeds track crowd age, mass, and push from blasts in clear links. Blast push shows at the young ages the fits give. No lag shows, though low-metal tales said one should.
arxiv-2606-00532:
Parashar and Bhandarkar sort learned lore cards by task tier for math thought with a frozen model. Prompt lore tools learn text from run feed and stuff it in the prompt. One prompt stuffed with all lore lets stray bits fight key ones. Room in that prompt caps what can be kept as well.

Their tool, KACE, picks both spend and shown lore per task. A tiered self-check plan lets easy tasks quit on two matched tries. The quit tier tags how hard a task was. Cards taught from failed runs sit in a store split by tier and field. Each high tier reads just its own cell of cards. Tests on hard math sets beat self-check and kin lore tools. The store adds clear marks past the tier plan alone.
arxiv-2606-00632:
Li surveys a core plank of grown-up control theory: how to handle a system's best-run aim. Control systems sit at the heart of the third machine age. They crop up in gear, code, use, care, cost, and social fields. Back of all those fields sits one core ask in math terms.

That ask is what control theory, in the strict sense, names. Its charm lies in both know-why and know-how at once. The join of tale and use is where that charm lives. Grown-up control for live use holds more than one base plank. This piece brings in one of them: the best-run plank. It sets that plank in the frame of a named work on the field.
arxiv-2606-00732:
Dey and co-authors build a memory system for long streams in this 2026 paper. Sequence models must learn patterns that stretch far in time as data change. In strict streaming, each item is seen once, with no re-reads. Standard networks hit a wall: their training window or input window caps how far back credit can flow.

Their system, SHARP, splits the job in two. A memory module stores a structured trace of inputs. A second module reads patterns from that memory. In offline 'sleep' phases, stored traces replay at high speed and fold into higher-level memory. The design echoes fast replay in rodents during slow-wave sleep. On the text8 and PG-19 datasets, the authors report, SHARP beats recurrent baselines. It keeps skill on old data while it learns the new stream. Its layered memory grows context span fast, at a cost that grows in a straight line.
arxiv-2606-00832:
Merin and co-authors build a benchmark for AI agents with memory in this 2026 paper. Agents now do complex work with tools and multi-step plans. But most tests judge them in a single session. Real service work spans sessions, where past acts, stated tastes, and prior choices shape what a user needs now.

Their benchmark, Momento, tests agents on tasks that run across sessions. Agents must take real, tool-based steps with knock-on effects. They have to resolve time links and goals that shift as sessions pass. The results expose a main failure mode, the authors report. Agents misjudge the user's current state. They treat old session history as a firm guide to the present. In truth, that history is stale and needs fresh checks. The gap between today's agents and real long-horizon work is wide, they conclude.
arxiv-2606-01132:
Sugiura and co-authors build a Japanese test for chart and table reading in this 2026 paper. Vision language models have raced ahead on English document tests. Non English versions are scarce, so no one knew if the skill crosses languages. Real charts in other tongues are hard to gather at scale. The team turns to government white papers, which are free and rich in charts.

Their benchmark, HakushoBench, draws on 33 Japanese white papers. It holds 2,053 images across more than ten image types. Each question is hand annotated and checked by a second reader. The questions probe whole chart grasp, not local visual cues alone. Open weight models under ten billion parameters reach at most 58.6 percent accuracy in the reported tests. Even the flagship open model trails the leader by 8.1 points in the headline comparison. The set gives Japanese document AI a hard, honest yardstick.
arxiv-2606-01232:
Coleman sharpens a random solver for positive definite linear systems. The solver picks one part at a time to update. Pick chance grows with the size of that part's residual. This family runs from uniform picks to greedy picks. Coleman studies the squared-weight case in depth. He uses a ratio that tracks how spread the residual is. A uniform residual gives a ratio of one. A spiked residual gives a far larger value.

That ratio boosts the per-step progress bound by its square. It costs just linear time to track each step. He extends the proof to async runs on shared memory. Tests back the sharper bound on real hardware. Oddly, clean reads break the method at high thread counts.
arxiv-2606-01532:
Li, Mao, and Teng show transformers can compute fully without position codes. Positional encoding is widely seen as a must for transformers. Without it, the next-token map looks blind to order. All prior universality proofs lean on positional data. They revisit this in the sliding-window regime of long-form reasoning. Generation there runs through a finite moving window. The window itself breaks permutation symmetry, they note. Their HIST model distills that added power precisely.

In HIST, each update uses a small state plus a token histogram. The histogram counts tokens inside the current window. They prove HIST is Turing complete via Post machines. A sliding-window transformer with no position codes can simulate HIST. Window sliding thus captures enough positional signal on its own.
arxiv-2606-01832:
Aurzada and Worf study a time series forced to stay positive. The series is an MA(1) process with uniform shocks. They ask what it looks like under that constraint. The model is cast as a Markov chain. The coupling value lies in a non-expanding range.

The pair prove limit laws for the constrained process. They name the limit as a Doob h-transform. Generating functions are computed for this case. Sharp rates for long survival are drawn from them. Plain formulas give the eigenfunction h as well. The persistence exponent is also made explicit. The limit chain's step rule shows a phase-based form. Such fully solved cases are rare, they note.
arxiv-2606-01932:
Seaton and co-authors make wildlife density models more flexible. Spatial capture-recapture estimates how many animals live where. It rests on a latent map of activity centers. Classic models treat those centers as a Poisson process. Real animals cluster socially or favor hidden habitat traits. That breaks the independence the Poisson form assumes.

Log-Gaussian Cox processes fix that flaw in spatial statistics. But fitting them inside capture-recapture lacked methods until now. The team use penalized regression splines for the center map. Fitting runs through a Laplace-style approximation scheme. The spline form bends to match complex distributions. It avoids forcing a rigid process form on the data. Field studies of animal populations stand to gain.
arxiv-2606-02132:
Chen and co-authors teach agent models when not to use external tools. Agentic reinforcement learning can induce tool abuse. Models overuse tools even for questions they could solve alone. Uniform penalties or hard limits are the usual fixes. Those blunt tools also suppress useful tool exploration.

Their EAPO framework learns selective tool use instead. Tool-free trajectories join each rollout group in training. Difficulty-aware reward shaping penalizes redundant calls selectively. Easy queries draw the strongest penalties for tool use. Confidence-aware token reweighting improves policy learning further. Nine reasoning benchmarks carry the evaluation. Math and knowledge-heavy tasks are both included. Three model families show better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. GRPO is outperformed consistently, the authors report.
arxiv-2606-02532:
Li and co-authors create synthetic microscope images to train defect-finding models. The images come from transmission electron microscopy of irradiated metal alloys. Labeled real data is scarce. Their method uses a mask-conditioned latent diffusion model. It synthesizes realistic images with multi-class defect masks. The masks are labeled automatically, with no manual annotation for generation.

Synthetic pairs augment small real datasets of 10, 50, and 100 labeled images. A Mask R-CNN model trains on the mixed data. It must detect and classify defects. Gains are small but real. The harmonic mean of detection and classification F1 scores rises by up to 0.02. Which task gains more depends on the data split. The authors see targeted generative models as a help for data-scarce microscopy work.
arxiv-2606-02632:
McCormick argues that science with machine learning should hunt structure, not build ever more complex models. Large language models now draft hypotheses and mechanistic stories from observational data. In high-dimensional proxy regimes, that search is underdetermined. Many incompatible mechanisms yield the same observational patterns. Predictive success then proves little about mechanism. Coherent explanations prove little as well.

Language models add a special hazard. They collapse wide classes of rival explanations into one fluent narrative. The paper proposes concrete standards for mechanistic machine learning. The norms would let model-centered workflows support science rather than simulate it. The position reframes what counts as discovery. Fluency is not evidence. Structure that survives the equivalence class is. The paper offers a yardstick for judging future claims of machine-found mechanisms.
arxiv-2606-02932:
Nava-Callejas, Cavecchi, and Page revisit how neutron stars cool after accretion outbursts. In low-mass X-ray binaries, a star gains mass for a time, then cools. Models often add an extra heat source of unknown origin, called shallow heating. It is invoked to match high surface temperatures seen for hundreds of days.

The team asks whether that extra source is needed at all. They use a relativistic code for the star's crust and core. A new boundary condition lets heat from burning accreted hydrogen and helium leak from the envelope into the crust. With this change, seven of eight outburst episodes from seven sources were explained well. No ad hoc shallow heating was required. One source, EXO, matched in shape but still needs added physics for a good fit. The result hints that thermonuclear burning may supply heat that models had assigned to a mystery source.
arxiv-2606-03032:
Wan and co-authors diagnose a failure mode in multi-agent language-model deliberation. Such systems often treat consensus as a sign of success. For deliberative problems, though, what matters is whether facts and viewpoints survive discussion. The authors name the failure the deliberative illusion.

It has two parts. Factual attrition is the steady loss of issue-critical facts. Stance homogenization is the collapse of diverse positions toward consensus. Their framework, DelibTrace, splits each issue into atomic facts, labels the critical ones, and tracks their survival across rounds. Across ethical and news-based deliberation with three model families, discussion erased up to 72 percent of critical facts. The loss misleads: final stances stayed anchored in base-model priors, and one malicious agent could inject misinformation into the shrinking context. The authors call for evaluations that track which facts and disagreements survive. Agents, they warn, can agree more while knowing less.
arxiv-2606-03232:
Verma and co-authors merge graph neural force fields without retraining from scratch. Such force fields give near-quantum accuracy for atomistic simulation at lower cost. Adapting them to new chemical systems takes costly retraining of large base models. The team ports model merging, a trick from vision and language work, to graph networks for the first time.

Their method, GFFMERGE, uses the linear shape of message-passing layers. Merging becomes a convex alignment problem with a closed-form answer. A broad benchmark shows old merging methods, built for vision and language, fail badly on force field tasks. GFFMERGE instead comes close to gold-standard joint training. Tests span molecular, solid-state, and large graph sets. Speedups ran from 5 to 27 times. The closed-form merge alone beat all baselines before any fine-tuning. It also gave a better start for fast, data-light tuning afterward.
arxiv-2606-03432:
Shahzad, Mustaqeem, and Elahi present a hybrid method to detect malware and sort it by family. New malware variants appear at a rapid pace. Sorting finds into families helps teams respond in the right way. Older detection tools often flag malware but cannot name its family. That gap slows down mitigation work.

The method fuses secondary features drawn from each sample. Features include API calls plus n-grams of fixed and variable length. A custom selection step trims the feature set before training. A voting scheme then fuses several learning algorithms into one predictor. Tests use the dataset released by Microsoft for this task. Both binary and multi-class setups are run on that data. The results reach an AUC of 0.989 and accuracy of 99.72 percent. Log loss comes in at 0.01. The authors report the method beats prior approaches on these measures.
arxiv-2606-03532:
Guo and co-authors ask when a teacher model should update during self-distillation. In self on-policy distillation, the student learns from a teacher built from its own past weights. The teacher's update schedule shapes their coupling over time. It had not been studied as a stability factor. A controlled sweep on Qwen3-8B supplies the test bed.

Full freezing of the teacher between updates turns out to be the key trait. Such isolation periods, not teacher age, enable stable learning. A diagnostic frame tracks KL structure, refresh shock, and length-tail risk. It reveals a failure named state-oblivious collapse. Fixed schedules that shine in short runs fail in long ones, when a clock-driven refresh copies a drifting student. The proposed fix gates each refresh on reward gains and length safety. It scores best on four tasks, with zero collapse. No per-task tuning is needed.
arxiv-2606-03632:
Block and Stockar design a finite-horizon controller for traffic flow through variable speed limits. The plant is the first-order Lighthill-Whitham-Richards traffic model. Its fundamental diagram is triangular. Speed limits act inside the domain as a source term in the governing equation. Prior work used infinite-horizon regulators for this task. This study builds the finite-horizon version instead.

A linear quadratic regulator yields a feedback law that varies in space and time. The solution rests on a Riccati partial differential equation. That nonlinear equation is solved analytically by a parametric characteristic method. The Riccati solution depends on time, space, and traffic regime. Sensitivity analysis compares finite and infinite horizons across traffic scenes. Simulations confirm finite-time convergence for the new design. Control performance improves a great deal over the infinite-horizon version. The method suits time-sensitive traffic management best.
arxiv-2606-04032:
Kayyam, Gopal, and Lewis ask if Transformers need three separate projections. Query, key, and value projections sit at the heart of attention. Their single roles and the cost of dropping some were unclear. The team tests three sharing schemes in a systematic way. Two schemes make attention maps symmetric, a flaw they treat with positional codes.

Shared-projection models matched or beat the standard model in many tests. Tests spanned fake tasks, vision sets, and language models up to 1.2B parameters. One scheme cut the KV cache in half with 3.1 percent perplexity loss. Paired with head sharing, cache cuts reached 96.9 percent. That aids on-device inference in practice. The team explains the win by keys and values sharing a similar space.
arxiv-2606-04232:
Kovi Rose and a large collaboration report in 2026 the discovery of a new accreting binary that pulses in X-rays. The team caught it during an outburst and followed it with several telescopes.

Spectroscopy gave an orbital period of about an hour and twenty minutes. The light shows the marks of a cataclysmic variable: a white dwarf pulling matter from a companion star. The X-ray pulses mark the white dwarf's spin, making it an intermediate polar. Polarized light and radio data added checks on the system's geometry. The find adds a rare member to a small class. The authors lay out the follow-up needed to pin down its masses and fields.
arxiv-2606-04932:
Shankar, Li, Dorfman, and Fu simulate how a large Alfvén wave in a plasma breaks down and shares its energy, in a 2026 arXiv plasma physics paper. The parametric decay instability lets an Alfvén wave spawn a backward Alfvén wave and a sound wave. Most prior simulations used periodic boundaries; this team runs fully kinetic one-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations with absorbing boundaries, at low plasma beta.

For the studied parameters, nearly 92 percent of the pump wave's energy goes to the backward child Alfvén wave. Ion and electron heating switch on only once the instability has developed, at rates roughly twice the linear growth rate. Theoretical and numerical growth rates agree qualitatively across plasma and wave parameters.
arxiv-2606-05132:
Ella Chevalier and colleagues report formaldehyde emission from protoplanetary disks in this 2026 arXiv paper, part of the AGE-PRO survey of gas evolution with the ALMA telescope array. Disks of gas and dust around young stars are where planets form, and their organic chemistry helps explain where planetary ingredients come from. Formaldehyde is the most commonly detected organic molecule in these disks.

The team analyzed formaldehyde lines at about 218 and 291 gigahertz in 20 Class II disks in Lupus and Upper Scorpius, spanning ages of one to six million years. They detected the molecule in 9 of the 20 disks, set upper limits for the rest, and measured excitation temperatures and column densities. Adding 13 disks with archival detections, they found line luminosity tracking disk size, disk mass, and stellar mass and luminosity. That pattern fits the molecule forming by hydrogenation of carbon monoxide ice on grain surfaces in extended, massive disks.
arxiv-2606-05532:
Anna Mikeda explains a creativity paradox in this 2026 arXiv paper: AI help makes individuals more creative while making groups less diverse. Study after study finds AI-backed work rated more creative person by person, yet collectively outputs converge toward sameness. Current accounts, cognitive offloading and over-reliance, name symptoms rather than mechanisms. Mikeda offers selective metacognitive adaptation instead.

The claim is that routine AI use shifts mental effort rather than simply shrinking it. Some grow stronger, notably modeling the AI partner and controlling surface features of the work. Others are starved: judging originality and joining ideas. People get real gains, while the neglected ones keep a population's output diverse. Mikeda presents a taxonomy of six capacities organized by phase of the creative process. The framework yields specific testable predictions and design principles for preserving individual satisfaction alongside collective diversity.
arxiv-2606-05632:
Klingner and colleagues compare language models as formal proof writers in a 2026 arXiv paper. The models write proofs in Lean 4, a language a computer can verify line by line. The team aims to guide researchers who want model help on their own projects. Two scoring styles are used: success within a set of tries, and success after rounds of refinement. Tests draw on the miniF2F and miniCTX benchmark sets.

Gemini 3.1 Pro and Claude Opus 4.7 led the field overall. Gemini reached a ninety-two percent success rate on miniF2F with thirty-two refinement rounds. Opus scored eighty-six percent on miniCTX under the same scheme. Cost told a different story, though. NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super and GPT-OSS 120B gave strong accuracy for under a cent per correct proof. The paper maps the trade-off between peak skill and price for working mathematicians.
arxiv-2606-05732:
Kukreja and colleagues simulate a Carrington-class solar storm against today's satellite fleets in a 2026 arXiv paper. Such storms could cost billions of dollars per day. Tens of thousands of new satellites will crowd orbit within five years. Older risk models treat fleets as statistics, not as individual craft. The team built an agent-based model where each satellite acts on its own physics and limits.

The model draws on records for over forty-one thousand satellites and five recent space weather events. In scenario runs, ninety-five percent of low-orbit satellites faced drag at eight times normal levels. Collision risk rose two to three times across the fleet. Monte Carlo runs put direct losses near forty million dollars per affected satellite. The same model issued live maneuver advice with ninety-two percent accuracy. The authors offer it as a planning shield for the next extreme storm.
arxiv-2606-06432:
Shuvadip Ghosh and co-authors propose logic gates that run on heat in this 2026 arXiv paper on quantum devices. Classical computers compute with electric currents switched by logic gates. Quantum circuits also move heat around, usually as a nuisance. The authors instead use heat current itself as the signal, in a pair of coupled quantum dots linked to warm metal reservoirs. Tuning the inputs steers the heat flow above or below a threshold, reading as one or zero.

They show the mapping onto classical gate circuits is one to one: the wiring that builds AND, OR, and NOT from transistors has a thermal counterpart here. Truth tables emerge from tunneling between the dots and their leads. The paper also lays out a concrete nano electronic setup that could realize the gates in the lab.
arxiv-2606-06532:
Haozhe Chi, Yang Jin, and Yadong Mu borrow tricks from video compression to help AI watch long videos in this 2026 arXiv paper. Answering questions about hours of footage requires memory and motion understanding that current agent systems lack. Their GOPAgen exploits the structure already inside video codecs: a Group of Pictures, the codec's repeating frame block, carries motion vectors describing how pixels move between frames, for free.

A dedicated motion agent is trained on those blocks. A tree reasoning algorithm zooms from coarse summaries down to detailed local motion. Structural memory pages bind motion information to captions, and a motion vector database supports retrieval at several scales. The system fetches only the evidence a question needs. On benchmarks including MotionBench and EgoSchema, GOPAgen beat prior approaches. The humble video codec, it turns out, is an untapped ally for machine perception.
arxiv-2606-06732:
Picking which antennas in a sparse array should be active is a puzzle with far too many combinations to try by hand. Kobak, Atiyeh, and Hamza let neural networks do the picking in this 2026 arXiv paper, a companion study to related beamforming work. Their design groups incoming interference by angular sector, the slice of directions it arrives from, and merges nearby sectors that favor the same layout.

That grouping cut the choices down to fifty six representative classes. The team trained a light convolutional network and a deeper ResNet-50 model on four data sets that varied in size and class balance. The deeper model reached classification accuracy as high as ninety seven point three percent. The signal quality of its chosen layouts stayed within one percent of the best possible for most classes. Balancing the training classes helped most when data were scarce.
arxiv-2606-07032:
Retrieval benchmarks can lie when their pictures were already in the model's training data. Yang, Du, Qian, and Xu build an honest test in this 2026 arXiv paper. The task is composed image retrieval: find a target picture from a reference image plus a caption describing the change. Zero shot means no training examples for the task.

Their ZeroSight benchmark draws reference and target frames from the same videos. That keeps pairs visually and semantically consistent. All footage postdates the cutoff of a major model's training data. Earlier data sets, they show, inflate performance badly. Twenty seven methods were retested under the stricter rules. Their own method adds three symmetric consistency checks to spot hard negatives. It plugs into existing systems without training. Scores improved significantly across the board. The authors present the benchmark as a new, less forgiving standard.
arxiv-2606-07132:
The Sun's activity pulses with a roughly two year rhythm that has long puzzled solar physicists. Stefani and co-authors refine a tidal trigger model for it in this 2026 arXiv paper. The rhythm is the quasi-biennial oscillation, seen in coronal holes, cosmic rays, and open magnetic flux. Their suspects are magneto-Rossby waves, slow waves in the Sun's tachocline layer.

These waves have natural periods of a few hundred days. Intriguingly, those periods match the spring tide cycles of Venus, Earth, and Jupiter. Small planetary tides could therefore trigger waves of realistic size. The team optimizes the trigger model's parameters against observations. Earlier work had shown resonance is plausible but left a damping parameter unknown. The paper then turns to the Carrington event, the great solar storm of 1859. A tidal timing framework offers a fresh lens on when such extremes cluster.
arxiv-2606-07232:
Košnik, Polonsky, and Smolkovič use the tau lepton's weak dipole moments as a precision probe for new heavy particles in this 2026 arXiv paper. A dipole moment measures how a particle's magnetism responds to the weak force carried by the Z boson. The tau decays so quickly that its spin direction can be read from its decay products before scrambling. That makes these moments measurable for the tau in a way impossible for lighter leptons.

The authors update the Standard Model prediction, finding a weak magnetic moment near minus 2.1 millionths in the natural units used, with a carefully estimated uncertainty. Combining collider data, including high-mass collision tails at the LHC and the electron's electric dipole moment, they derive current limits on the underlying operators. Future runs at a proposed FCC-ee collider, producing about a trillion Z bosons, would make these moments among the dominant probes of new physics.
arxiv-2606-07632:
Fernandez, Na, Bisk, Samaras, and Strubell argue that counting an AI system's environmental cost needs accounting for its life, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Studies price a training run or inference, missing the pipeline. Life cycle assessment, the industrial ecology method, would fold in embodied costs of making the hardware, operational costs of training and deployment, and downstream impacts. It gives researchers, developers, policymakers, and users a ledger for decisions.

The stakes show in the uncertainty. Projections of data center energy demand vary wildly: some forecasts put AI facilities above 10 percent of national electricity use within years. Annual growth estimates differ several-fold between studies. Narrow accounting cannot resolve which path is real. The authors propose life cycle assessment as the standard, arguing that infrastructure and impact assessment both fail without full-pipeline resource accounting. The paper calls for adopting the method, with the framework sketched rather than an inventory.
arxiv-2606-07732:
Michael J. Bommarito builds the first map of a Windows attack surface in this 2026 arXiv paper. Device drivers answer user programs through I/O control codes, known as IOCTLs. If a driver trusts a length field in the caller's buffer without checking it, an unprivileged program can read or write kernel memory. Scanners for such flaws existed, but nobody had charted the surface itself.

The Windows IOCTL Census recovers the dispatch surface of twenty-seven thousand signed drivers in one deterministic pass over their lifted code, with no symbolic execution. It succeeded for about eighty percent of the corpus across both processor architectures, including the 32-bit drivers other scanners abandon. The dataset holds about three million decoded control codes, eight million functions, and sixteen million call edges. On 64-bit drivers it adds handler reachability and data-flow tracking, and a language model ranks handlers so analysts triage the riskiest first.
arxiv-2606-08032:
Ousmane Amadou Dia re-engineers the standard algorithm for training language models on human feedback, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Proximal policy optimisation, the usual method, tends to collapse the policy onto a narrow set of high-reward behaviours. It explores brittly and drifts from its starting distribution, propped up by clipping rules and penalty schedules.

The replacement, Variational Proximal Policy Optimisation, recasts training as variational inference. A population of particles, arranged as a mixture of experts, is pushed toward high reward by Stein variational gradient descent. That method keeps particles diverse through kernel repulsion. Kernels over expert prototypes and an orthogonalisation loss supply geometric proximal control, reducing reliance on clipping tricks. On a sparse model with thirty-three billion total parameters, it gained about one hundred seventy-nine Elo points on Codeforces-style tasks. It also cut token counts on AIME mathematics problems by about thirty-two percent.
arxiv-2606-08132:
Oğuzhan Ercan fixes a subtle instability in vision transformers: their answers depend on where the grid lines fall, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision transformers chop images into a fixed patch grid. Shift that grid slightly and the token evidence available for a pixel changes, especially near boundaries, so dense predictions can wobble for an arbitrary reason.

Ercan formalises the grid offset, the phase, as a nuisance variable and proposes phase marginalisation: evaluate several grid phases, inverse-align the outputs, and average. The main variant uses four phases and needs no training. Across segmentation, depth, and local matching it improved on the single-grid baseline. In a controlled Cityscapes test with matched compute, it beat the strongest generic shift-based augmentation by about zero point three one mean intersection-over-union points. More phases were not better: sixteen added latency without accuracy. Four is the practical sweet spot.
arxiv-2606-08332:
Mishra, Ballester, and Karatzas propose a cheaper way to train image models without labels, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Self-supervised learning extracts useful features from unlabeled data. But many leading methods demand large batch sizes, memory banks, momentum encoders, or global synchronization. All of these raise cost and training complexity. Their objective, called Semantic Mutual Information, comes from a dependency formula under Gaussian assumptions. It aims for the same feature quality with a lighter mechanism.

Most objectives match large feature correlation matrices. This method instead optimizes a sample-level dependency matrix built from pairwise correlations. The change alters the training dynamics. Strongly dependent semantic pairs get emphasized, while the features stay diverse and avoid collapse onto a few patterns. Experiments on ImageNet with a standard ResNet-50 backbone show competitive results.
arxiv-2606-08432:
Li Jiang, Xu, Ding, and Amy Zhang diagnose a structural flaw in how large models teach smaller ones, in this 2026 arXiv paper. On-policy distillation trains a student model on its own generated rollouts while a teacher supplies dense, per-token supervision. The authors identify a cause of trouble they call prefix failure. Once a student's early tokens go wrong, the dense supervision that follows induces a bimodal teacher mixture, so token-level fixes cannot repair the damage.

Their remedy, Trajectory-Refined Distillation, moves beyond token-level interventions to trajectory-level corrections. The student's rollout is revised under teacher guidance, so problematic prefixes are corrected before distillation begins. This mitigates prefix failure at its source. The refinement also improves exploration by exposing the student to alternative valid derivations under guidance.
arxiv-2606-08732:
Arutkin, Reuveni, and Raphaël compute the drag on objects that wander randomly at a water surface, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Wave resistance is the drag generated by the waves a moving source radiates at a fluid interface, a canonical problem since Havelock's classical calculation for steady motion. Real sources, from swimming microorganisms to drifting sensors, follow stochastic paths rather than straight lines. The authors show that under stochastic motion, the mean drag is controlled by the ensemble-averaged surface profile built from the trajectory's whole history.

The result is a finite resistance below the deterministic radiation threshold, where steady theory predicts no waves and no drag. The authors derive explicit scaling laws for drifted Brownian trajectories, including a universal high-diffusivity decay of the drag. For drifted Lévy flights, random walks with occasional long jumps, they find the mean wave resistance in closed form.
arxiv-2606-08832:
Thorstad examines an argument that advanced artificial intelligence will seek power, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The argument leans on the instrumental convergence thesis. It claims agents with very different final goals will pursue the same intermediate goals, such as self-preservation and resources, because those help almost any aim. In strong form it says capable agents will predictably grab power and disempower humanity. Thorstad asks whether the leading defenses actually establish that strong form.

He argues they do not. Weaker versions of convergence, showing that power-seeking is sometimes useful or likely under special conditions, fall short of what the existential-risk argument needs. The gap matters: the strong thesis carries predictions about what future agents must do, not what they might do. Thorstad closes with consequences for longtermism, AI governance, and the methods used to study agent behavior. The paper tests an influential argument's foundations rather than reporting experiments.
arxiv-2606-08932:
Chen and colleagues test whether language models follow rules with exceptions, or silently drop them, in this 2026 arXiv paper. They name it Silent Scope Omission: a model applies a general rule but skips a nested exception, producing output that looks compliant and is not. Their benchmark, NormBench, holds 2,290 provisions from Chinese laws and policies, United States tax law, the GDPR, and corporate policies, including cross-lingual cases. Each item demands defeasible scope parsing, pinning down which clause overrides which.

Frontier models showed two pathologies. Recursion Decay means performance falls sharply as exceptions nest deeper. The Auditability Trap means models retrieve the text spans yet assemble the wrong control flow from them. Their fix is an intermediate format, Span-Grounded Deontic Trees, anchoring every branch to its source text and demanding explicit exclusion guards. Using it improved whole-tree fidelity and exception recovery, concentrated on exception-heavy cases.
arxiv-2606-09032:
Researchers at Southern University of Science and Technology and Sun Yat-sen University survey an idea: giving AI agents a world simulator, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The text carries no byline, only correspondence addresses at the universities. Agents that browse the web, edit code, or use tools react without a model of how the environment evolves. A text world model predicts, from a state and candidate action, the webpage, terminal output, or reply, for planning.

The survey organizes the field by lifecycle stage. Foundations define text world models by their state representation and grounding domain. Construction splits into two paradigms: a language model as the simulator, or code as the simulator. Applications cover training-time experience synthesis, plus inference-time planning and verification. Evaluation covers grading the world model and using it as a grading environment. The authors consolidate the area and name open challenges, with a public repository.
arxiv-2606-09132:
Chen and colleagues turn vision language models into privacy guards that find and mask sensitive text inside images, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Medical images often carry protected health information burned into the pixels, names and record numbers that must be removed before sharing. De-identification needs two skills: localizing sensitive text precisely, and processing it for privacy. Their framework, VisShield, teaches both through instruction tuning.

The core asset is OPTIC, an instruction-tuning dataset whose prompts guide the model to targeted optical character recognition and bounding boxes around sensitive text. A tailored training strategy adapts the model to privacy tasks, so detected text can be masked. In experiments, VisShield significantly outperformed existing approaches on private information in vision data. The work inverts the usual privacy story: the ability to read text in images that creates leakage risks, documented in the team's companion study, becomes the scrubbing tool.
arxiv-2606-09232:
Meng and colleagues show how stretching a single layer of black phosphorus steers its triple-frequency light, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Third-harmonic generation converts light to 3 times its frequency, a nonlinear process for imaging and photonics. Black phosphorene, a single phosphorus layer, is strongly anisotropic across armchair and zigzag directions. A tight-binding model with Bloch equations gives the response with and without strain.

Unstrained, its dominant susceptibility peaks at 1.8 times ten to the minus seventeen square meters per volt squared, matching experiments. Strain acts as a tuning dial with clear logic. In-plane compression and out-of-plane tension strengthen and redshift the response; in-plane tension and out-of-plane compression suppress and blueshift it. Tuning efficiency orders as out-of-plane, zigzag, armchair. The mechanism is joint modulation of bandgap and Berry connection, the geometric link between states. Biaxial strain adds control, toward reconfigurable infrared devices.
arxiv-2606-09332:
He and colleagues turn a single-lead heartbeat trace from a wearable into a screen for structural heart disease, the physical remodeling behind heart failure, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Echocardiography detects such disease but cannot scale to populations, while single-lead ECG is everywhere through wearables. Their framework, AnyECG-Echo, learns from echocardiography reports as supervision rather than hand labels. It was validated on a geographically independent external cohort of 16,621 patients, with total validation cohorts of 25,222.

The model covers 13 fine-grained subtypes across myocardial, chamber, valvular, and great-vessel disease. Accuracy was high where it matters: area under the curve reached 0.866 to 0.924 for reduced left ventricular systolic function and 0.877 to 0.931 for global heart enlargement. Shapley attributions grounded in electrophysiology, plus outputs that track measured quantities like ejection fraction and wall thickness, make the scores read as digital biomarkers. That combination points to population-scale screening from a wrist sensor.
arxiv-2606-09432:
Karn Tiwari and his colleagues introduce GraMO, a learned simulator for systems of interacting particles, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Simulating many bodies that push and pull on each other is expensive with classical step-by-step solvers, and learned substitutes often accumulate errors over long horizons. Graph neural networks capture who interacts with whom, while state-space models carry memory over time, but earlier work kept the two separate.

GraMO fuses both inside a single latent-space recurrence: a compressed state evolves through graph-based interaction updates and temporal state updates at the same time. The authors evaluated it on N-body systems, human motion capture, and robotics datasets. Averaged across systems, GraMO cut one trajectory error measure by about eighteen percent against the best graph baseline, and another by roughly thirty percent. The largest gains appeared exactly where rivals struggle, in long-horizon prediction.
arxiv-2606-09732:
Vladimir Braun and Hua-Yu Jiang compute small but potent fixes for lattice maps of the proton's inner layout in this 2026 arXiv paper. Generalized parton distributions chart where quarks and gluons sit inside a proton, by share of its push and by side position. Lattice QCD can reach these maps through nonlocal quark links between states of unlike motion. The short-distance expansion turns those links into the maps' moments.

Two kinematic fixes ride on that expansion. One scales with the momentum transfer over the large push component squared. The other scales with the nucleon mass squared over the same base. Both fade as the push grows, but at real lattice settings they loom large. The pair derive them in full, for gauge-safe links. The usable range of momentum transfer widens, which sharpens the three-dimensional proton image.
arxiv-2606-09832:
Meng-Han Lee argues that how an AI agent presents itself is a working part of team design, not mere dress in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multi-agent systems pair many role-holding agents with human operators who must direct and trust them. An agent's identity, its name, tone, and stated role, cues the human's mental script for that role. Lee calls this layer the social affordance layer.

The frame, ASAF, rests on three engines. Identity signaling tells users what to expect before the first exchange. Behavioral priming steers how they engage once work starts. Collaborative governance shapes how oversight is split and checked. A four-tier spectrum grades how firmly identity signals are enforced. A person's bent, toward humanizing or tool-thinking, tempers the effect. Old multi-agent work used roles to bind agents; ASAF flips that lens onto the humans in charge.
arxiv-2606-10032:
Dey maps the behavior of networks of active rotators, simple models of excitable and oscillatory units, in a 2026 arXiv paper on nonlinear dynamics. Each rotator has a phase pushed by a common drive and pulled toward neighbors through Kuramoto coupling, the standard model of synchronization. Local feedback amplitudes are drawn from a zero-mean Gaussian distribution, so some units get positive and others negative feedback.

Using late-time drift measures and the fractions of positively and negatively drifting oscillators, Dey builds regime maps across disorder and coupling strength. At weak coupling, stronger disorder suppresses drift. Stronger coupling can restore positive drift when disorder is not too strong. Analytical limits for the uncoupled and strongly coupled cases explain the map's edges. Finite-size effects and spread-out intrinsic frequencies are also examined, showing mixed-sign feedback alone can reshape the pinning-drifting balance.
arxiv-2606-10232:
Si and his team redesign a small but key part for high-voltage tests in vacuum, in a 2026 arXiv paper on lab hardware.
