Vacuum feedthroughs carry high voltage through a chamber wall, and the electric field on the vacuum side must stay low to avoid breakdown. The authors find commercial feedthroughs as a rule use center conductors that are too small, producing unnecessarily large fields. They study the problem with hand calculations and finite element analysis, mapping how shape piles up the field at conductor surfaces.

They present a simple tuned retrofit for the commercial feedthroughs studied, reducing the vacuum-side field without hurting outgassing traits, a key constraint for vacuum hardware. In such detectors, an oversized field can trigger discharges that damage gear or spoil data. A drop-in geometric fix, checked by simulation and analysis, offers experiment builders a handy upgrade path.
arxiv-2606-10332:
Senjaya studies how a surrounding dark matter halo retunes the ringing and radiation of a rotating black hole, in a 2026 arXiv paper on gravitational physics. He embeds a rotating black hole in a Dehnen-type halo whose inner slope parameter controls how cuspy the dark matter distribution is. The halo deforms both the near-horizon and far-away geometry in a controlled way. It shifts the black hole's quasibound state spectrum, the resonances of fields trapped around it.

Using analytical asymptotic matching, he derives that spectrum: the frequency's real part keeps a hydrogen-like structure but is shifted by an effective halo mass scale. Denser, more extended, and cuspier halos enhance binding energy and lower the critical mass for superradiant instability. They typically suppress the growth rate of the black hole bomb, the explosive amplification such instabilities can drive.
arxiv-2606-10932:
Shinde compresses a state space language model to one-bit weights in this 2026 arXiv paper. Density Field State Space Models pair a binary scaffold with a small int8 low-rank correction. Applied to Mamba-2 with 1.3 billion parameters, the result is a 278 megabyte model, nearly ten times smaller than its full-precision teacher.

It runs 21.4 times faster on GPU at batch one than the reference implementation, and distillation takes only 32 million tokens and six hours on one A100. Probing 445 factual prompts, Shinde finds three processing phases: early layers sort prompts by template, factual links localize to a five-layer window mid-network, and late layers format the output.
arxiv-2606-11232:
Zhang and co-authors ask how language models combine moral signals in a 2026 arXiv paper. Moral benchmarks usually test isolated acts, asking which single value a model prefers. Real judgments are messier: one option bundles several moral goods and harms. The authors built Moral Trolley Arena, a two-stage blind ELO benchmark, borrowing chess-style ratings, to measure composition.

First, the single-scene arena calibrates individual acts across a 229-scenario corpus spanning five moral foundations. Then the composite arena combines calibrated acts into two-act items, measuring preferences in ten frontier models from nine providers. Composite judgments were largely predicted by component act strength, but the relationship is compressed rather than additive: combined options count for less than the sum of their parts. Models also showed non-additive intensity anchoring and bounded residuals, and their preference surfaces converged across providers. Moral audits should test composition rules, not just isolated rankings.
arxiv-2606-11632:
Jun He and Deying Yu tackle a control problem created by autonomous software agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agents powered by language models can now propose high-stakes changes to production systems, such as scaling resources or rotating credentials. Ordinary access controls check who asks, not whether a non-deterministic agent's proposal is justified, and audit logs only record actions after they happen.

Their design, the Sovereign Assurance Boundary, intercepts each proposal at what they call an assurance airlock. The proposal is compiled into a typed execution contract, bound to a cryptographic digest of the supporting evidence and a policy version, then routed by how serious its consequences are. Passing emits a signed certificate, valid only for a set identity, time window and revocation state. A separate broker rechecks revocation and drift before running anything. A prototype in the Go language handled 2,500 admission attempts in feasibility tests.
arxiv-2606-11932:
Sachin Sarode, Chetan Patil and Vinayak Joshi generalise prime ideals inside abstract lattices in this 2026 arXiv paper on algebra. Multiplicative lattices abstract the ideal structure of rings into an ordered system with a multiplication. Prime and primary elements are the lattice analogues of prime and primary ideals, cornerstones of commutative algebra.

The authors study versions relativised to a multiplicatively closed set S, called S-prime and S-primary elements, and define weaker variants of both. Their main results characterise these notions and connect the abstract theory back to rings. Specifically, the weakly S-prime ideals of a commutative ring correspond exactly to weakly S-prime elements of its ideal lattice. Product lattices are also analysed: an element is weakly S-primary exactly when one component is S-primary and the others are suitably dominated. The paper thus extends a web of generalisations into the lattice framework.
arxiv-2606-12132:
Zang and co-authors show that a slice of a quantum ground state can expose its hidden order, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Topologically ordered materials hide their nature in long-range entanglement and host anyons, exotic particles with fractional traits. The team shows the reduced density matrix itself, the state of one region at the cut, forms a one-dimensional mixed-state phase.

For the toric code, a model topological phase, that boundary state shows strong-to-weak symmetry breaking, a symmetry holding in one sense and failing in another. Freed anyons appear as short-range links of charge and domain walls. In gapped spin liquids, spinons, fractional spin particles, leave a sharp cusp in a disorder measure at exactly half a turn of rotation. The signature needs only one ground-state wave function, confirmed analytically and numerically on a kagome-lattice state.
arxiv-2606-12232:
Frković and co-authors recheck a popular self-correction trick for a new kind of language model, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Masked diffusion models write text by unmasking hidden words in any order, many at once, instead of typing left to right. Once a word is revealed it normally cannot change, so early mistakes stick. Remasking methods let the model re-hide low-confidence words and try again, with no extra training. One such method, WINO, reported encouraging early gains.

Under standard settings with shorter blocks, WINO adds little to nothing over plain confidence-based unmasking. With looser, non-greedy decoding, remasking softens errors from the extra randomness. The cost is worse diversity collapse: outputs grow more alike. Benefits therefore depend heavily on the exact setting. The authors argue this family of methods needs broader, more honest evaluation before its promise can be trusted.
arxiv-2606-12332:
He and co-authors score conversations by how much the answerer's uncertainty shrank, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Judging multi-turn dialogue is hard because quality accumulates across turns, not inside single replies. For information-seeking chats, they define semantic progress: the buildup of new, relevant, non-redundant information. Formally, progress is question-conditioned uncertainty reduction. Their metric estimates it in embedding space, where answers become points and spread measures doubt.

A Gaussian formulation gives closed-form updates as each turn arrives. The score is monotone, splits additively across turns, and discounts redundant evidence automatically. Unlike LLM-as-judge methods, it needs no model generation at scoring time and is reproducible. It even runs on CPUs with lightweight embedding models. On MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena, and UltraFeedback it agrees with human judgments competitively. On two of those it aligns better than several judges. Semantic progress alone carries signal about dialogue quality.
arxiv-2606-12732:
Binder and colleagues analyse X-ray observations of 85 Sun-like stars to chart how their emission changes with age, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sun-like FGK stars emit X-rays from an atmosphere called the corona, heated by magnetic activity that fades as rotation slows with age. That radiation can strip atmospheres from orbiting planets. The sample spans ages from 0.2 to 12 billion years, with 37 stars over 4 billion years old.

Using XMM-Newton and Chandra data, the team measures luminosities, variability, and plasma temperatures. Quiet spectra are described by 3 plasma components at 0.1, 0.4, and 0.8 of a kiloelectronvolt. The share of flux from gas hotter than 7 million kelvin rises with surface flux, reaching 50 percent for the most active stars. Converted to the ROSAT band, luminosities follow the decay with age, falling as age to the power minus one point five. Several outlier stars look too active, suggesting age errors, inclination, or hidden companions.
arxiv-2606-13432:
Liu and colleagues present OmniDirector in this 2026 arXiv paper, a system for cloning camera motion in generated video. Filmmakers want scenes to follow the camera work of a reference, including edits across shots. Methods either used camera descriptions that struggle with multi-shot sequences, or relied on paired training data that is scarce. The authors encode camera motion as grid motion videos, a representation of camera parameters that can combine trajectories. This format plugs into video generation models.

OmniDirector is a framework trained on a million-scale collection of camera grid and video pairs. It coordinates characters, actions, and cameras, giving director-level control inside multimodal diffusion transformers. A hierarchical design supports multi-shot motion that defeated approaches. The authors position the system toward generated video that respects cinematography, where camera language is as deliberate as the action in front of the lens.
arxiv-2606-13732:
Qiao and co-authors show that a supposed cure for model collapse can actually speed it up. Model collapse happens when models trained again and again on synthetic data lose rare cases and produce ever blander output. Data selection, filtering synthetic samples against real reference data, is widely trusted as a safeguard. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies what happens when each checker sees only a small, biased slice of the real data, as in hospital groups or banks that cannot pool records.

Selection then keeps samples matching the local slice and prunes globally important rare modes. The authors prove this siloed selection hastens collapse and drives diversity down following a power law. Experiments on skewed data confirm local references fail this way. As a first fix, they build shared Wasserstein proxy references combining several silos without moving raw data, and diversity loss shrinks.
arxiv-2606-13832:
Silva studies why AI defenders for computer networks can look strong in training yet be unsafe to deploy. Multi-agent reinforcement learning lets several software agents learn to answer attacks together. Reward-only training can raise security scores while breaking operational limits a security center must respect, such as downtime budgets. His 2026 arXiv paper builds safety contracts into the learning, alongside graph attention networks that encode the network's host and subnet layout.

Tests used CAGE Challenge 4, a standard cyber defense benchmark. Every unconstrained method broke the downtime budget in one hundred percent of episodes, with mean costs between three hundred eleven and four hundred thirty against a budget of fifty. Adding Lagrangian budget control cut violations to zero point three percent and mean cost from three hundred fifty-five point four to fifteen point five. The fuller ACD3-GAT system traded some compliance for other strengths.
arxiv-2606-13932:
Takook bridges quantum field theory in an expanding universe and a famous number-theory function. The completed Riemann xi-function encodes the zeta function, whose zeros drive the Riemann hypothesis. His 2026 arXiv paper starts from scalar fields in de Sitter spacetime, the geometry of an expanding cosmos. Their two-point correlation is written with Legendre functions through harmonic analysis.

Applying the Mehler-Fock transform yields an integral form of the xi-function where the Legendre kernel appears naturally. Takook then defines a retarded propagator, a response function respecting cause and effect, whose spectral weight is the xi-function itself. Krein space quantization, which allows sign-indefinite spectral measures, hosts this construction. On the critical line, xi gains a geometric, spectral reading. Its zero spacing links to a mass-time scaling in de Sitter geometry. The framework joins curved-spacetime quantum theory, harmonic analysis, and number theory.
arxiv-2606-14332:
Marinucci, Liguori, Semenzato, and Wandelt squeeze more cosmology out of galaxy maps by weighting each location before counting patterns. Marked statistics transform the density field with a local mark, a weight set by environment, so its power spectrum captures higher-order information otherwise expensive to model. The risk is leaving the trusted regime of perturbation theory. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds the framework within the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, supplying a validity regime and small-scale counterterms.

Optimizing the mark and marginalizing over counterterms shrank forecast error bars: by up to 2.3 times for the matter density, up to 8.3 times for the fluctuation amplitude sigma-8, and up to 2.5 times for the Hubble parameter, depending on redshift and smoothing. The optimized mark has a simple form, interpreted physically via its response to the underlying density field. Marked statistics thus offer a cheap route to information beyond standard two-point analyses.
arxiv-2606-14432:
Pierre–Cyril Aubin–Frankowski, Sodini, and Stefanelli extend a classic variational principle in a 2026 arXiv paper on analysis in metric spaces. The Brezis-Ekeland-Nayroles principle recasts certain evolution problems as a search for a curve that makes a functional zero. Here the setting is curves of maximal slope, paths that descend a functional as steeply as possible, in spaces where only distances are defined.

Building on a variational description of the local slope of a functional, the authors carry the null-minimization principle into this time-continuous metric setting. They then check that the resulting global-in-time functionals actually admit minimizers, so the principle is not vacuous. The work gives researchers studying gradient flows in rough spaces a firmer foundation for proving that steepest-descent curves exist.
arxiv-2606-15032:
Yu and coauthors argue that world models for embodied agents should be judged by decision quality in a 2026 position paper. The term world model now covers video predictors, latent simulators, and planning models alike. Papers often claim decision-making value while showing only pretty generated video. The authors survey recent evaluation practice to expose that mismatch.

They organize evidence on a ladder from visual plausibility up to policy optimization utility. Their framework stresses action fidelity under intervention, closed-loop rollout validity, and reward prediction. Policy-ranking agreement, improvement lift, and uncertainty calibration also belong in the core set. The diagnosis is that generative world model research re-encountered a known lesson from model-based reinforcement learning. Predictive accuracy is a poor proxy for control usefulness, a fact that older literature already established. The paper closes with a benchmark protocol, including a minimal reporting set for real-robot settings.
arxiv-2606-15532:
Zhu and colleagues introduce EIBench in 2026, a simulator-based benchmark for the emotional intelligence of large language models in multi-turn conversation. Static tests miss the point: managing emotion is interactive, and a good model should improve a user's emotional state over several turns. The benchmark holds over two thousand scenarios across support, defense, repair, and charm.

In each scenario a simulator plays the user, updates an emotion-relation state after every turn, and scores the final state. Testing fifteen models shows a split: they handle support and rapport well but struggle to hold boundaries under pressure. The team then trains with Centered Turn-Credit GRPO, reusing the per-turn updates as dense feedback for reinforcement learning. It lifts Qwen3-8B from minus twenty-two to plus twenty-two points on EIBench, with gains on outside emotion benchmarks. Simulator-tracked states thus serve as exam and as training signal.
arxiv-2606-15632:
Su and colleagues tackle open-world video segmentation in 2026, where a system must discover objects and track identities through long videos with moving cameras. Existing methods target short clips and fixed label sets, and standard scoring forces a rigid one-to-one matching that penalizes valid predictions at the wrong granularity. The team offers a system, Savvy, and a fairer evaluation suite, OGA.

Savvy combines mask discovery, deferred admission of tracks, and track consolidation to keep identities stable. OGA relaxes matching to many-to-one while policing temporal breaks, and adds identity persistence and concentration diagnostics. On VIPSeg, scoring underestimates open-world methods, while the protocol recovers much of the suppressed performance. On the long-horizon benchmarks ScanNet and HM3D, Savvy beats baselines across classical and proposed metrics. Together they break a circle: no fair scoring without a real system, and no credit for real behaviour without it.
arxiv-2606-15732:
Jia and Zhang study flat gauging of continuous symmetries in two-dimensional conformal field theory in 2026, using the compact boson, a free field on a circle. Gauging here means summing only over flat gauge-field configurations. They build the torus partition function with general momentum and winding backgrounds, including non-invertible cases.

Flat gauging either symmetry decompactifies the theory into the non-compact free boson, the leftover backgrounds merging into a real symmetry through a mixed anomaly. At the self-dual radius, gauging a diagonal SO(3) symmetry reproduces the continuous orbifold, outside the usual moduli space. Continuous non-invertible gaugings need a prescription for zero-measure fixed loci. Finally, the symmetry topological theory becomes a non-compact BF theory whose boundary states encode the Narain moduli space and T-duality. The work sharpens how generalised symmetries act on the best-understood conformal theory.
arxiv-2606-15832:
Sokolov, Condat, and Richtárik propose SILAGE in 2026, an optimization algorithm for training on data split into many blocks. Risk minimization often has a nested form, with samples grouped into blocks such as pooled data silos. Variance-reduced methods reach strong accuracy for nonconvex objectives, but scale badly here. Some need periodic full-gradient refreshes over every sample, which is expensive.

Other single-loop methods avoid refreshes but store a control value per sample, an impractical memory load. SILAGE exploits the double-sum structure to escape both traps. It needs no periodic global refreshes, evaluating at most one local group gradient per iteration. Its storage stays at block level rather than growing per sample. Breaking this trade-off matters for out-of-core learning and stratified datasets too large for full passes.
arxiv-2606-15932:
Zhao and colleagues survey multimodal code intelligence in 2026, systems that generate, edit, and reason with code from visual inputs. Text-to-code is mature, but many real tasks specify intent visually, through screenshots, charts, or interactive states, where correctness depends on layout, semantics, and behaviour after execution. The survey organises the field by the role code plays: rendered artifact, editable structure, reasoning trace, or tool interface.

Benchmarks and methods group into four domains: user interfaces, scientific visualisation, structured graphics, and frontier agentic frameworks. Across the literature, how similar outputs look proves useful but incomplete evidence of correctness; semantics and interaction must be checked too. The authors argue for four verification-centred directions: multi-signal validation, multi-state checks, cross-task transfer tests, and agent traces that can be verified. Code, in their framing, should be judged by the evidence it exposes after rendering and execution.
arxiv-2606-16032:
Bakhshan and colleagues present a 2026 framework for designing milling settings backwards from a wanted surface finish. Milling cuts metal with a rotating tool, and surface roughness, meaning how uneven the cut face is, strongly affects friction, wear, and fatigue life. Shops normally find good settings by trial and error. The authors instead train models on simulated data and search them for settings that should deliver a target roughness.

Inside, a deep neural network and a random forest learn how cutting speed, feed rate, insert count, insert radius, and run-out errors shape average roughness and maximum surface height. Bayesian optimization then works around the many-to-one problem, where many settings give the same finish, and returns top candidate setups. Both models stay below five percent average relative error against reference results. Reliable inverse design could cut wasted test cuts and help shops plan jobs before machining begins.
arxiv-2606-16232:
Hong and colleagues present PolyMerge in 2026, a way to make photorealistic 3D scene models light enough for safe drone navigation. Radiance field reconstructions, including 3D Gaussian Splatting, model scenes with high fidelity, but are too heavy for onboard path planning on small robots. PolyMerge converts such a model into convex polytopes instead.

The polytopes' union provably over-approximates every obstacle in the original model, so safety margins are guaranteed, not estimated. Designers can tune the polytope count to trade conservativeness against compute cost. The representation plugs into control barrier functions, which plan collision-free paths with formal safety conditions. Simulation and hardware tests use a Crazyflie drone with severe onboard limits. The drone computes and follows safe trajectories in real time, outperforming baselines in speed while keeping the safety guarantee, per the report.
arxiv-2606-16332:
Chen and Chen characterize in 2026 how large language model inference should use the matrix units now built into modern CPUs. Arm's Scalable Matrix Extension offers high-throughput matrix work inside the processor. Yet inference stages differ sharply: prefill, decode, attention, and KV-cache handling vary in arithmetic intensity and memory layout needs. Treating the matrix unit as a universal replacement for ordinary cores disappoints, the authors show through a roofline-based study.

Their engine, SMEPilot, chooses whether to run on CPU cores alone, the matrix unit alone, or both cooperatively. It partitions matrix work at tile granularity, overlaps matrix stages on the unit with vector stages on cores during attention, and keeps packed tensor layouts instead of rebuilding them. Tests span Llama-3.2-3B and two Qwen3 models across phone, PC, and server platforms. The reported speedups come from applying the matrix unit selectively, where its throughput is amortized best.
arxiv-2606-16632:
Yu and colleagues study atom interferometers in a 2026 quantum physics paper. A Kasevich-Chu interferometer splits and recombines matter waves to measure gravity with great precision. Its sensitivity is limited by a standard quantum limit, and by the Doppler effect, since moving atoms shift the light they absorb. The authors ask whether squeezing the atoms' motion can beat those limits.

They add a motional squeezing state, which trades uncertainty between position and momentum, as the input. A full framework computes quantum and classical Fisher information, measures of how much data reveal a parameter, for two readout protocols. Optimizing the controls shows population measurement can reach four times the semi-classical sensitivity limit. For joint population and position readout, quantum gain and Doppler suppression compete, with an optimal squeezing level in one regime. The scheme suits mobile gravimeters where spin entanglement would decay quickly.
arxiv-2606-16932:
Dobney leads a team demonstrating quantum state learning from photon pairs in a 2026 experimental physics paper. Tomography normally recovers a mixture's density matrix, but not which pure states were mixed or in what proportions. A protocol by Agarwal and colleagues breaks that limit when qubits arrive in identical pairs.

The experiment uses photons and their polarization. Single photons are measured by tomography, then paired up afterward using arrival-time records. From the pair statistics the team reconstructs a two-photon state and splits it uniquely into the two pure polarization states and their weights. Various state choices and mixing ratios are learned successfully. Roughly ten thousand detected pairs suffice for fidelities near the top of the scale. The method can even tell apart two preparations of the same mixed state whose pure components differ by less than five degrees, a distinction invisible to ordinary tomography.
arxiv-2606-17232:
Li and Wang present a 2026 arXiv paper on mediation analysis when the mediator and the outcome are never measured on the same people. Mediation splits an exposure's effect into a path through an intermediate variable and other paths. When one study records the mediator and another records the outcome, the usual way of identifying those effects breaks down completely.

The authors build a data fusion framework that restores identification by joining the two incomplete sources through shared instrumental variables. The method allows unmeasured confounding under a no-interaction condition and handles shifts across sources under a latent alignment condition. Two strategies are given, for known valid instruments and for instruments that must be learned from data. The resulting estimates stay valid under several failures at once, and one is as sharp as theory allows, with an application to dementia genetics.
arxiv-2606-17532:
Xiang, Jeon, and Sakai present a 2026 arXiv paper on how the charge pattern of electrons in an aperiodic system can change phase without any symmetry breaking. Their test bed is a generalised Aubry-André model, a one-dimensional system with a wavy potential that never quite repeats. Charge patterns there are sorted by hyperuniformity, a measure of how strongly long-range density fluctuations are suppressed compared with a random arrangement of the same average density.

Across filling fractions and potential shapes, the many-body charge pattern was always hyperuniform in their calculations. Its hyperuniformity class, though, tracked the localisation of states near the Fermi energy, ignoring high-energy states entirely. A change of class marks a genuine phase transition between two uneven many-body states. The authors show that transition is third order, a subtle kind rarely pinned down so cleanly.
arxiv-2606-17732:
Lüderssen, Neumann, and Peng present a 2026 arXiv paper on counting four-cycles in graphs that arrive as streams of edges, too large to store. Four-cycles gauge cohesion in bipartite networks and user-item data, and they matter in social graphs too. The authors target sparse, low-degeneracy streams and build samplers that estimate the count within a small factor. They use far less space than earlier methods needed for the same accuracy on such inputs.

A two-pass algorithm sampling subgraphs matches the space lower bound for constant-degeneracy graphs. A one-pass variant stays accurate when four-cycles are spread evenly rather than concentrated on single nodes, edges, or wedges, as in many real networks. On test streams the two-pass method beat the state of the art, using much less space for the same accuracy. Both methods handle non-bipartite graphs well, unlike several recent rivals.
arxiv-2606-17832:
Kim and colleagues ask whether the beliefs of large language models stay coherent as they answer, in a 2026 machine learning paper. A coherent reasoner should obey the martingale property, where expected future beliefs match current ones, and earlier tests in synthetic settings found violations. The team revisits the question in ordinary multiple-choice question answering, where exact answer distributions can be computed.

Their method, prompted predictive resampling, has a model answer the same question again and again so its belief path can be tracked. Early answers drift, breaking coherence, but after enough rounds the beliefs settle into a stable distribution on their own. A seed-answer prompt speeds that settling, and a self-consistency training loss bakes it into the model. Across benchmarks, drift fell and calibration improved while accuracy held.
arxiv-2606-18332:
Bonaca, Conroy, and colleagues from the Via collaboration lay out the science case, instrument, and survey plan for the Via Project in a 2026 overview paper. Via is a forthcoming all-sky spectroscopic survey built to measure stellar radial velocities with stability near one hundred meters per second for millions of faint stars across the whole sky.

No existing or planned facility, the team argues, pairs that precision with Via's depth, multiplexing, and full-sky reach. The survey is timed to work alongside wide-field facilities such as the Vera Rubin Observatory, feeding on their imaging discoveries. Its goals sit where dark matter physics, galaxy formation, and time-domain astronomy meet, from tracing faint stellar streams that record past mergers to watching stars wobble under unseen companions. The paper describes the instrument design, the survey strategy, and the organizational structure behind a project spanning several major observatories and universities.
arxiv-2606-18832:
Abeyrathna and the team recast algorithmic recourse so the person denied a loan or benefit can demand not just a flipped decision, but a confident one. The work is a 2026 explainable AI paper. Standard counterfactual answers find the smallest change that crosses the model's decision boundary. Yet counterfactuals that barely cross are fragile under noise, and hard to justify.

Their scheme TRUST lets users specify a target prediction confidence. It searches for minimal changes meeting it, for principled comparison of options along cost, confidence, and robustness. It is built with a Probabilistic Tsetlin Machine, whose clause-based structure exposes whether a decision rests on robustly or fragily fired rules. Bayesian optimization handles the search. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets showed target-confidence counterfactuals are more robust and readable than boundary-based ones. They hit perfect robustness on multiple benchmarks, while keeping recourse cost low.
arxiv-2606-19132:
Pollack studies small values of Carmichael's lambda function in a 2026 number theory paper. The lambda function gives the exponent of the multiplicative group modulo n, the least power that sends every coprime base to one. The paper counts how many integers up to x have lambda below a threshold y, across a wide middle range for y where the count is neither trivial nor complete.

Pollack proves an upper bound for the logarithm of that count relative to x. The bound is asymptotically sharp if a plausible hypothesis on powersmooth shifted primes holds. As an application, he obtains a new upper bound on odd integers where the order of two modulo n is much smaller than the square root scale. Such counts matter because small lambda values signal unusual multiplicative structure. They also connect to factoring and primality questions.
arxiv-2606-19432:
Plestid and Quílez Lasanta construct well-defined partial-wave amplitudes for theories with long-range interactions in 2026. Theories with massless particles carry forward-scattering singularities. Those singularities make standard fixed-order partial-wave amplitudes ill-defined. That blocks systematically improvable unitarity bounds, a classic tool that once constrained the Higgs mass.

The authors build the amplitudes inside a modified perturbation theory that keeps long-range effects. Off-shell Coulomb modes play a central role. A universal description of the forward scattering region emerges. It renders the amplitudes independent of the renormalization scale. The resulting partial waves become well-defined single-scale objects, free of spurious dependence on the infrared regulator. The paper also gives a practical method to compute them order by order. Clean partial waves restore unitarity bounds as a sharp instrument for theories where massless exchange is not a nuisance but the physics itself.
arxiv-2606-19732:
Erick Arguello Cruz and Grigory Tarnopolsky realise the Yang-Lee phase transition in four quantum models in 2026. Yang-Lee criticality began with zeros of the classical Ising partition function. The deformation used here keeps parity-time symmetry intact.

The four hosts are an antiferromagnetic Ising chain, the massive Schwinger model, the Blume-Capel model, and a three-state quantum clock model. State-operator correspondence locates the Yang-Lee critical point in each. Scaling dimensions of the lowest operators match exact two-dimensional Yang-Lee results perfectly. Bosonization handles the Schwinger model; a Polyakov-Hubbard transformation handles the rest. Every critical point is described by a massless boson with an imaginary cubic interaction. In the clock model that field couples to a massive boson, and both states appear in the spectrum. The two-point function grows with distance, as theory expects.
arxiv-2606-19932:
Jindi Lv and eight colleagues present STORM in 2026, a spatial-aware way to trim tokens in visual Mamba models without wrecking accuracy. Mamba handles long visual sequences cheaply, but cutting tokens from structure-enhanced variants causes a sharp performance collapse. Existing trimming ignores the two-dimensional layout that the selective scan depends on. STORM instead reduces whole spatial units under local constraints, keeping the grid and neighbourhood structure intact.

As a plug-in needing no training, STORM upgrades existing trimming pipelines with explicit spatial awareness. Across several vision Mamba backbones it reaches the best training-free pruning accuracy reported. On VMamba it recovers up to sixty-three points of top-1 accuracy over prior methods, and on PlainMamba it loses only about one point. Faster vision models become usable where token trimming previously destroyed them.
arxiv-2606-20332:
José Kuruc, Juan Ruiz-Álvarez, Bo Wang, and Dionisio Yáñez sharpen Shepard interpolation so it stops smearing jumps in data. Their 2026 paper adapts ideas from radial basis function work to the Shepard framework, a classic weighted-average method that never oscillates but blurs discontinuities. The fix makes the shape parameter data-dependent. Local smoothness indicators detect where the data jumps: squared second differences on grids, and least-squares Laplacian estimates for scattered points.

Near a detected jump, the kernels tighten toward a local delta function, so values stop leaking across it. The authors establish the method's theory and prove the smearing reduction is achievable. Numerical experiments in one and two dimensions confirm the scheme sharply reduces blur at jumps while keeping Shepard's oscillation-free character elsewhere. Shock-like data is exactly where classical interpolation fails most visibly.
arxiv-2606-20532:
Nityanand Mathur and six colleagues trace how individual words in a style caption steer synthesized speech. Their 2026 paper addresses style-captioned text-to-speech, where natural language controls voice characteristics but the mechanism stays opaque. Knowing which caption tokens matter is critical for diagnosing failures and improving controllability.

The team adapts the DAAM attribution framework to speech diffusion models for the first time, applying it to CapSpeech-TTS. Per-token heatmaps are extracted across 25 layers and 24 ODE steps, over 3,600 caption-transcript combinations. Style tokens show lower temporal variance than content tokens, style attention correlates with pitch and energy, and conditioning peaks in early steps and deep layers. Attribution maps turn expressive TTS from a black box into something engineers can debug.
arxiv-2606-20632:
Luyang Zhang and three colleagues ask what shapes how language models talk to each other in 2026, testing whether model family or post-training recipe matters more. Multi-model systems rely on models behaving differently when they debate, judge, or coordinate. Earlier offline work advised picking one model per family for diversity, because models tend to favor their own family in isolation. Whether that label predicts live interaction had not been tested.

Zhang and colleagues build a corpus of 940,000 conversation chains across eleven checkpoints, plus a controlled Llama study with 1.6 million chains from one base model. On hedging, their main measure of cautious wording, a reasoning-tuned Llama shifts by 18 percent depending on its partner, more than any cross-family gap. Checks with Qwen and closed systems suggest the pattern is broader. The lesson is practical: how a model was post-trained can outweigh which family it came from.
arxiv-2606-20832:
Veronica Saz Ulibarrena and Simon Portegies Zwart introduce ReLaTS in 2026, a reinforcement learning method that sets coupling time steps in astrophysical simulations. Such simulations split multi-scale systems into subsystems. Each part uses its own integration scheme. The parts are coupled on a fixed timescale set by hand. A poor choice wastes computing time or loses accuracy. ReLaTS learns to choose that step dynamically.

Tests use star clusters that contain a planetary system. The number of stars and planets is varied. The method finds a step that balances speed and accuracy without expert knowledge. The trained network works apart from the coupled N-body codes. Performance stays stable across setups. One weakness appears for bodies with tiny masses. Their energy share is so small that the network can miss their error contribution. Adaptive coupling could still make large gravity simulations cheaper and less dependent on manual tuning.
arxiv-2606-21032:
Bai-Shan Hu reviews ab initio nuclear theory in a solo 2026 paper, covering heavy nuclei and dark matter scattering on nuclei. Ab initio methods compute nuclei from the underlying nuclear force and currents, with quantified uncertainty. Recent breakthroughs extend such calculations to lead-208, a heavy nucleus long out of reach. Medium-mass systems with complex deformation and weakly bound nuclei near the driplines are also covered.

Nuclear responses for dark matter direct detection are summarized. Dark matter experiments scatter particles off nuclei. Interpreting a signal, or a null result, needs nuclear form factors. First-principles calculations reduce those uncertainties substantially. Robust interpretation matters for searches beyond the Standard Model. As detectors grow more sensitive, nuclear theory error can dominate the error budget, so progress in computation directly sharpens what experiments can claim.
arxiv-2606-21332:
George Koutsoumbas, Andri Machattou, and Eleftherios Papantonopoulos study a hairy black hole in 2026, an extension of the GHS-GM solution that adds a dilaton field and a magnetic monopole field. Hair here means extra fields beyond mass, charge, and spin. They ask whether such a black hole is stable, both against heat-driven change and against small disturbances that ring through it as quasinormal modes.

Thermal behavior turns on the dilaton's scalar charge: as that charge decreases, the system grows more thermally stable. Raising the black hole's charge lowers both the ringing frequency and the decay rate of the quasinormal modes. Overtone modes die out faster than the fundamental mode, and no mode grows instead of decaying, so the system shows no instability. The results map how extra fields reshape black hole stability.
arxiv-2606-21432:
Christophe Meessen builds a minimal spiking neural network in 2026 whose activity organizes into soliton-like waves, packets that travel without spreading and vanish when they collide head-on. His neuron model runs in discrete time and combines weighted spike-timing-dependent plasticity, which adjusts synapses by spike order, with divisive normalization and threshold adaptation that keep activity in range. Each element uses only locally available information, keeping the design biologically plausible.

Pairs of excitatory and inhibitory neurons fill a two-dimensional recurrent sheet, driven by periodic local stimulation. Stable waves emerge only when excitatory links reach farther than inhibitory ones and inhibition starts stronger. Plasticity engraves the travel direction into the weights, so the network teaches itself one-way propagation. Colliding waves leave a boundary that encodes the relative timing of two sources, a hint at spatial memory.
arxiv-2606-21632:
Jaehong Kwon and David B. Graves fine-tune a universal machine-learned potential for plasma-surface simulation in 2026. Molecular dynamics of oxygen plasma striking WS2, a layered two-dimensional material, needs a potential that is accurate, fast, and fluent across many elements and bond types. They start from Meta FAIR's pretrained UMA model and run an iterative loop: maximally diverse structure sampling, density-functional labeling, and retraining on energies, forces, and stresses.

Even before fine-tuning, the stock model already reproduces the target observables, the chemisorbed sulfur and oxygen coverage under 15 eV oxygen-ion bombardment. Fine-tuning then cuts errors to 4.5 meV per atom in energy and 0.076 eV per angstrom in force. The recipe shows how foundation potentials can be adapted to plasma processing questions at production scale.
arxiv-2606-22132:
Rovenchak and Husiev examine, in 2026, the thermodynamic stability of virus-host interaction networks for humans, mice, and chickens. In these networks, nodes are viruses and host molecules, and directed weighted edges record their interactions. The authors compute topological measures alongside heat-style quantities derived from the spectra of the network adjacency matrices.

Stability is tested under two node-removal scenarios. One deletes the most influential nodes in a targeted attack, and the other removes nodes at random. The spectral functions show transition-like behaviour as removal proceeds. Structural measures shift in step at the same points. The authors read this as evidence that a heat-style framework can usefully describe the robustness of virus-host networks. It also offers a route to judge how such networks respond to strong perturbations.
arxiv-2606-22432:
Sourabh Paul and ten colleagues report the first clustering measurement from the MeerKLASS radio survey in this 2026 astronomy paper. The survey, taken with South Africa's MeerKAT telescope, images the sky at 816 megahertz. Its first data release covers about eight hundred square degrees of sky.

The authors measure the angular two-point correlation function, which counts how much more likely pairs of sources are to appear at each separation than chance allows. They detect a clear positive clustering signal across separations from a fiftieth of a degree up to ten degrees. The signal stays stable when the depth mask and flux threshold change within reason. Fitting standard cosmology templates gives an effective bias, the factor by which sources trace dark matter, near two under one redshift prior. A second prior gives a lower value, showing the redshift distribution is the dominant modelling uncertainty.
arxiv-2606-22532:
Sayanjit Banerjee, Sanatan Digal, and Sumit Shaw study colliding domain walls in this 2026 theoretical physics paper. The setting is SU(N) gauge theory, the framework behind the strong nuclear force. Its centre symmetry allows domain walls, thin sheets separating regions in different centre phases, labelled by the group Z_N.

Using Polyakov-loop effective models, the team simulate how the walls meet and merge. String junctions turn out to drive the dynamics. In the three-colour theory, two non-planar walls merge into one by creating a vortex-antivortex pair. In the four-colour theory, slow collisions form a single wall with no vortices at all. Faster collisions either bounce the walls back or scatter them into a new pair through vortex formation. In three spatial dimensions the vortex pairs generalize to string loops. The results give topological strings a direct dynamical role in how wall networks evolve.
arxiv-2606-22632:
Andreas Kosmas Kakolyris and nine colleagues, including Onur Mutlu, propose defences against a new memory chip flaw in this 2026 paper. ColumnDisturb disturbs DRAM columns rather than rows when nearby memory is accessed repeatedly. Unlike RowHammer, it can flip bits across three consecutive subarrays, widening the blast radius.

Their mitigation family, ColumnKeeper, comes in two variants. The deterministic one keeps two counters per subarray, tracking activations that hit odd and even columns. When a counter reaches its threshold, one row in that subarray is refreshed, resetting the danger. The probabilistic variant refreshes one row in each of the three subarrays with a set probability when the middle one fires, giving configurable guarantees at low area cost. Both track the next row to refresh with a small table for each subarray. The authors report strong security guarantees with low performance and energy overheads for that design.
arxiv-2606-22932:
Dikshant Kukreja and colleagues rethink how neural networks store gradients during training in a 2026 paper. A gradient records how each weight should change to reduce error. Standard training computes every gradient, saves them all in memory, then updates the weights afterward. At that handover moment, every layer gradient sits in memory at once. That peak sets how large a model a machine can train. The team names its system FORGE.

Kukreja and colleagues fuse the weight update into the backward pass itself. Each small tile of gradient is used the moment it is computed, held only in fast on-chip registers. Nothing about the math changes, only the timing. In full precision the fused update is provably identical to the standard one. In the lower precision formats used in practice, the difference stays small and bounded, while memory use drops.
arxiv-2606-23132:
Jaehyuk Jang and colleagues defend vision-language models against adversarial images at test time in a 2026 paper. These models recognize images in a zero-shot way, matching pictures to text labels. Tiny crafted perturbations can flip their answers. Existing test-time defenses adjust prompts or pixels, an indirect and costly route that never repairs the damaged visual representation itself. Their method, T-VSS, works directly in visual feature space. It builds a compact, sample-specific subspace from feature differences across several views of the attacked image.

Jang and colleagues learn one shared correction inside that subspace, guided by reliability-weighted entropy minimization. Confining the fix to the compact geometry steers features toward stable, discriminative predictions. Full-space noisy updates are avoided. Across fine-grained, ImageNet, and out-of-distribution benchmarks, T-VSS improved adversarial robustness. It kept clean accuracy competitive and ran more efficiently than earlier test-time defenses.
arxiv-2606-23232:
Mateo Cámara and colleagues test whether speakers stretch words at the end of a turn in a 2026 linguistics paper. Smooth turn-taking needs listeners to predict when turns end, within a few hundred milliseconds. A final lengthening of speech before a boundary is one candidate cue. The team asks three questions: are final words longer, is the effect prosody rather than word choice, and where inside the word does the stretch sit. They analyze four corpora in English and Spanish.

Cámara and colleagues compare tens of thousands of final words against far more mid-sentence words from over five hundred speakers. Final words were clearly longer on average. The effect survived matched-word, within-speaker tests, ruling out word choice as the cause. The extra length sat mainly in the last syllable. Final lengthening thus stands as a robust, localized cue to handing over the floor.
arxiv-2606-23332:
Mads Østergaard and colleagues introduce own-voice cancellation for far-field speech devices in a 2026 paper. When a device streams enhanced audio back to its user, delay makes the user hear their own voice late, a disturbing artifact. Own-voice cancellation removes the enrolled user's voice from a noisy multi-speaker mix while keeping everyone else. It is framed as the mirror image of target speaker extraction. Their time-domain model conditions on a short enrollment recording and adds only two milliseconds of algorithmic delay.

Østergaard and colleagues benchmark a TD-SpeakerBeam model against a lighter design built from Mamba blocks, with MinGRU units mixing over time. Swapping the auxiliary network for a linear recurrent encoder improved signal quality and predicted speech quality while cutting compute. The results establish own-voice cancellation as a practical, low-latency goal for far-field speech enhancement.
arxiv-2606-23432:
M. W. G. Winkel and colleagues study detachment dynamics in an advanced tokamak divertor in a 2026 fusion paper. The divertor is the exhaust region of a tokamak, and detachment is a desirable state where the plasma cools before striking the wall plates. The X-Point Target design adds a second X-point inside the divertor volume. Working on the TCV tokamak, the team compares its dynamic response against a standard single-null divertor. They use system identification with multi-sine perturbations, wiggling fueling, impurity seeding, and heating power while watching the detached state respond, in both simple and heated scenarios.

Winkel and colleagues demonstrate an inherent disturbance rejection at the second X-point, across all perturbation types. Upstream of that point, the two designs respond much alike. The passive buffering could help exhaust control greatly. It also makes the detached state harder to monitor close to the second X-point.
arxiv-2606-23932:
Colletti and Holzinger prove that the two standard versions of a workhorse reinforcement learning algorithm are secretly the same algorithm in disguise, in a 2026 paper on machine learning theory. Proximal Policy Optimization, PPO, trains agents by keeping each policy update close to the last. Textbooks present two forms as rivals: PPO-Clip, which clips the ratio between new and old policies, and a version penalizing the Kullback Leibler divergence between them. Years of experiments compare them as different methods.

The clipped objective's gradient, they show, is reproduced exactly by a KL penalized objective whose coefficient varies per sample. The identity holds at every step of training. On five MuJoCo benchmarks the two losses draw indistinguishable learning curves. Clipping is thus revealed as an implicit per sample penalty, a shape the authors propose as the dial for generalizing PPO.
arxiv-2606-24132:
Baycroft, Faria, and Delisle add Gaia space telescope models to kima, an open-source code for fitting orbits. Gaia's next data release should reveal tens of thousands of exoplanets. It should also pin down three-dimensional orbits for binary stars and even black holes. Many finds will need close follow-up that pairs Gaia's epoch astrometry, positions measured across time, with radial velocity data from ground telescopes.

Two new models inside kima handle Gaia data alone, or jointly with radial velocities. Diffusive nested sampling explores the parameter space. It also computes evidences for comparing rival models and estimates orbital parameters. Tests on real and simulated data reproduce published and expected values, which validates the tool. Baycroft's team also probes whether the Gaia model can split genuine orbits from scan-angle artefacts, a known trap in Gaia work. The software paper is dated 2026.
arxiv-2606-24232:
Kim and colleagues conjure a photorealistic, animatable head avatar from one portrait photograph. A single image hides most of a head's three-dimensional shape. So inferring geometry and appearance well enough for a drivable avatar is severely underdetermined. Their 2026 pipeline, FiCA, developed with Meta's Codec Avatars Lab, leans on human-centric vision foundation models plus a diffusion model, to fill the gaps plausibly.

The diffusion model learns to map partial observations to a complete, authentic three-dimensional mesh. A feed-forward refinement network then sharpens fidelity and identity preservation. That removes any need for per-person test-time optimisation, which slows rival systems. Finally a universal prior decoder converts the mesh into a set of 3D Gaussians, the splat-based representation behind crisp real-time rendering. Kim's team positions the result as instant avatar creation: one photo in, a lifelike codec avatar out, ready to be driven.
arxiv-2606-24332:
Zeni and colleagues let a neural network choose which determinants matter in near-exact quantum chemistry work. Selected configuration interaction builds a compact variational space, determinant by determinant. It reaches near-exact energies only if its heuristics spot the key determinants among huge candidate pools. Their 2026 framework recasts that judgement as a yes-no call. A neural classifier joins the loop through active learning.

At each step, a random subset of candidates is labelled by a temporary exact solve. The model learns from those labels, and its calls select the rest worth keeping. Tests on a diatomic molecule's ground-state energy cover classical and quantum-classical forms of the method. The classical form matches standard accuracy at roughly a fivefold cut in memory and per-step cost. The quantum-classical form converges in far fewer steps. Zeni's team offers model-assisted selection as a light compressor for variational spaces.
arxiv-2606-24432:
Clark, Pratten, and Schmidt confront theory predictions for black hole flybys with full numerical simulations, for the first time. When two black holes scatter rather than merge, their deflection encodes strong field gravity. Post-Minkowskian theory, an expansion treating gravity step by step, predicts it order by order. The 2026 letter extracts azimuthal and polar scattering angles from numerical relativity simulations, with generic, freely oriented spins, and relates them to the theory's spin kick observable.

Euler angles for unbound motion are introduced, and tied in geometry to the scattering angles. The simulations then expose something the perturbative results miss. A strong field precession turning point structure appears, including a polar angle sign change with no counterpart in the post-Minkowskian predictions. Clark's team targets better waveform models for oval, precessing binaries, the systems gravitational wave detectors increasingly see. It shows exactly where high order theory stops describing nature.
arxiv-2606-24532:
François Brunault, David Lilienfeldt, and Yusuke Nemoto construct explicit elements in algebraic K theory for Fermat curves. A Fermat curve is given by the equation x to the N plus y to the N equals one. The authors work in the group K four for every N from three upward. Their construction, uniform in N, uses polylogarithmic complexes and a map of de Jeu. The work tests Beilinson's conjectures linking such groups to L function values.

Brunault and colleagues prove their elements are nontrivial. They show the images under Beilinson's regulator map are nonzero. They give explicit formulas for the regulator integrals, involving special values of Zagier's trilogarithm function. One corollary gives the growth rate: a constant times zeta of three times N squared. The team further rewrites the regulators with hypergeometric functions, extending Otsubo's work, and checks the conjectures numerically for three values of N.
arxiv-2606-24732:
Addison Day and Jonathan Kujawa introduce interpolating Schur algebras, a one parameter family generalising a classic object of representation theory. Schur algebras have linked the theories of symmetric and general linear groups for over a century, through Schur Weyl duality. They are also the prototype quasi hereditary algebra. The new family adds one parameter, t. At nonnegative integer values of t, the classical Schur algebra reappears as a canonical quotient.

Day and Kujawa pin down when the new algebras are semisimple. They show the algebras are based quasi hereditary. Their module categories are highest weight categories. More precisely, each can be identified with a subcategory of parabolic category O for the general linear Lie algebra. The construction mirrors Deligne's interpolation work for the symmetric group. Classical Schur theory thus becomes one slice of a broader landscape. The work is pure proof based algebra.
arxiv-2606-24832:
Sander Beckers, a philosopher of causation, argues that a prominent new account of actual causation collapses distinctions its own authors rely on. Andreas and Günther have published seven definitions of actual causation across seven papers. They sort those definitions into three rival types: factual difference making, counterfactual difference making, and regularity based accounts. Their newest definition is presented as the factual kind. It is also offered as superior to rival accounts.

Beckers shows the newest definition in fact instantiates all three types at once. The threefold classification, he argues, marks distinctions without a difference. He then compares the new account directly with the authors' six earlier ones. Several crucial examples drive the comparison. On his reading, the results falsify both selling points claimed for the new account. Worse, the analysis undermines all seven accounts together. The preprint is a critique, not a new definition of its own.
arxiv-2606-25032:
Aswini Bala, Sachin Jain, and Vibhor Singh build a BCFW style recursion for cosmological correlators. BCFW recursion rebuilds scattering amplitudes algebraically from lower point data, avoiding integrals. Whether curved space admits anything similar was unclear. Their key step is a bridge transformation on the Grassmannian that leaves each constraint intact. The result is algebraic, with no spectral or radial integrals. At four points, for gluons, the bridge yields poles only in the two factorisation channels.

Two kinds of singularity sort themselves out. The total energy singularity comes from the three point building blocks. The shifted energy one appears only once the two recursion channels are combined. The bridge lifts to the supersymmetric setting, where a scalar correlator seeds the gluon one. Geometrically, the stripped four gluon correlator turns out to be the canonical form of a rectangle. Both edge types sit inside one positive geometry.
arxiv-2606-25432:
Long answers cost money: every extra token a vision language model writes is compute someone pays for. The DatologyAI Team argues in 2026 that brevity, not just smaller models, is the missing efficiency lever, and that training data curation can deliver it. Models trained on concise, correct examples learn to answer in fewer tokens. The team applied its curation pipeline to a large public vision language dataset and compared the result against standard training data and open frontier models.

Priced in compute per correct answer, the curated models gained a thirty five fold advantage over the most verbose comparable model while staying within about a point of its accuracy. Against the same data left uncurated, matched length accuracy rose by over seventeen points, growing with model size. Verbose reasoning, by contrast, bought no accuracy at any scale tested.
arxiv-2606-26032:
Somdeb Bandopadhyay works on moment closures for kinetic theory, where particle detail is compressed into averages. Closures at odd truncation order misbehave in a known way. The standard Gramian closure hugs the realizability boundary too tightly. Hyperbolicity, the property that keeps wave speeds real, comes out weak. Maxwellian equilibrium is not preserved.

Decomposition unlocks the analysis. Every odd-order closure splits into a boundary term plus a positive margin. The margin is the Schur complement of the Hankel moment matrix. An exact polynomial identity ties the margin to flux Jacobian eigenvalues. Hyperbolicity becomes a root-splitting question. A one-parameter family interpolates between two known closures. Its geometric end runs a few percent more accurate on bimodal tests. Its arithmetic end, the Morin-McDonald closure, gives the sturdiest profile. All members share an equilibrium Jacobian with a smaller spectral radius than Grad's closure, allowing larger time steps.
arxiv-2606-26332:
Dingshan Deng, Uma Gorti, Ilaria Pascucci, and Maxime Ruaud weigh planet-forming disks with a self-consistent model grid. A disk's gas mass decides how giant planets can grow and migrate, yet gas hides from direct view. Their DiskMINT engine couples disk structure, radiation transfer, and a reduced carbon monoxide chemistry in one framework. The GARDEN grid spans disk size, star mass, disk mass, and dust-to-gas ratio, and emits synthetic telescope observables for each point.

Machine learning reads the observations back. A regression model infers disk mass, dust ratio, and size from dust glow and a rare CO line. Applied to thirty-four archived ALMA disks, the masses agree well with dynamical and hydrogen-deuteride estimates. Rival chemical models needed heavy element depletion to fit the same data. Grain-surface chemistry in DiskMINT, converting CO to carbon dioxide ice, explains the gap instead. Little extra processing is needed.
arxiv-2606-26432:
Yingshuo Wang and four colleagues fix a clash between powerful prediction models and economic common sense in discrete-choice models, which estimate how people pick among options such as travel modes. Tabular foundation models, large pre-trained systems for table data, predict choices well but can say demand rises when price rises, or assign chances to options that do not exist. Planners cannot use numbers that break basic logic.

Their two-stage adapter places the foundation model's predicted probabilities inside a classic logit model's utility, a numerical score for each option's appeal. First the structural coefficients are fitted with sign rules enforced, then frozen while a small neural correction learns from the model predictions. The authors prove the blend keeps the logit's value-of-time formula exact. Tests gained accuracy over the plain logit while keeping cost behaviour sensible on every case.
arxiv-2606-26832:
The CMS Collaboration, the team behind a huge particle detector, reports the most precise such count ever made at a collider of this kind. Luminosity measures how many particle collisions a collider actually delivers. Knowing it precisely is essential: claimed discoveries rest on comparing counted events against expected rates. The measurement covers proton smashing at the Large Hadron Collider.

Several independent detector monitors were calibrated with special beam-separation scans. Their long-term stability was checked against production rates of Z bosons, a well-known reference process. Doubt sources were mapped and shrunk one by one. The combined precision reached well under one percent for the full data set. Crossing that threshold sharpens every test of the Standard Model from this data. It also sets the baseline for the coming high-output era.
arxiv-2606-27032:
Jesper Klicks, Sander Vržina, and Vincent François-Lavet show that what a learning agent is told about the market decides how well it trades energy. Their test bed is pumped-storage arbitrage: buy power cheap, store it as water, sell dear. A fixed Double DQN agent was used throughout. Only the state features changed between runs.

Three feature families were compared: absolute prices and calendar data, relative prices against recent history, and forecasts. Absolute features shone in validation but collapsed on later test data and across dozens of other market zones. Relative and forecast features alone also lagged a simple rolling heuristic abroad. Combinations were far stronger. Absolute plus relative features topped the home test and travelled best across zones. The lesson: representation, not algorithm tweaks, drove success.
arxiv-2606-27132:
Nozaki and Fujita connect two standard languages for electron flow through tiny devices. The GKSL master equation tracks an open quantum system leaking into its surroundings, suiting weak coupling and step-by-step tunnelling. The Landauer formula instead describes smooth coherent transmission between two electrodes. Their model places separate electron orbitals between left and right electrodes. Each electrode carries its own Fermi filling pattern, which sets how electron states fill by energy in this derivation from 2026.

Within the master equation framework, the authors derive a general current formula for that setup. Coupling between different orbitals is included, not just single-level flow. They then pin down the exact conditions under which the general formula collapses to the Landauer result. Energy-linked and energy-free electrode fillings are treated as separate cases. Earlier links needed high temperature, large chemical potential, and wide-band limits together.
arxiv-2606-27332:
Oztas and colleagues move objects inside a single photo by bending the position codes of a diffusion transformer. Shifting an object demands more than cut and paste: hidden regions must be invented, shadows and reflections must follow. Their RoPEMover method works directly on rotary positional embeddings, the structured spatial field inside the model. Extending those embeddings with depth lets the system place objects in front of or behind others. In the 2026 image editing paper, scene-aware updates ride along with the move.

Training mixes synthetic data with a small set of real images through light fine-tuning. Object identity survives large displacements in the results. Newly revealed regions fill in plausibly, and lighting effects update consistently. Standard object motion benchmarks show state-of-the-art scores across all reported metrics. The same machinery supports object removal and insertion as bonus edits. Geometry-first control proves stronger than appearance-only tricks.
arxiv-2606-27432:
de Souza and Bunk read the shape of a spectral line the way one reads a path, not a list of summary numbers. Standard summaries cannot distinguish broad wings, shoulders, double peaks, or layered emission and absorption. Borrowing from rough path theory, each profile becomes a trajectory across a velocity-flux plane, swept from blue to red. A compact set of low-order measures then captures signed area, blue-red imbalance, shape complexity, and the ordering of emission against absorption in this astrophysics paper from 2026.

Synthetic profiles show the measures separating shapes that share the same width and moment summaries. Applied to integral-field spectroscopy of galaxies, the measures are computed pixel by pixel and clustered. The resulting classes form coherent regions of similar line shape. Stacked spectra within each region recover large-scale velocity patterns matching reference velocity fields, although no velocity information was given to the clustering.
arxiv-2606-27632:
Safety failures in deployed language models often come from attacks, not accidents. Users may plan multi-step tricks to evade a model's rules. General-purpose training mostly ignores this adversarial side of safety. Measured safety then overstates real robustness. The Yuvion Team at the Alibaba Security AGI Lab built Yuvion LLM in 2026 to face that problem directly.

Training treats adversarial robustness and agentic skill as first-class goals. The pipeline starts with adversarially aware data construction. Knowledge-enhanced continued pretraining follows. Policy-grounded safety post-training comes next, mixing risk-aware fine-tuning with reinforcement learning. Tool use and multi-step reasoning get their own safety-aware training. The team also built RiskEval, a set of ninety-three benchmarks in four categories. Across them, Yuvion shows clear safety advantages and strong robustness under attack. The eight-billion-parameter version beat most larger baselines on several safety tasks, the team reports.
arxiv-2606-27732:
Diffusion language models unmask tokens in parallel, which is fast. Their design forces a dilemma, though. Bidirectional attention gives quality but blocks the key-value caching that makes serving cheap. Causal attention allows caching but loses all right-side context, hurting quality. Yuhang Chen and thirteen colleagues propose Bifocal diffusion models in 2026 to escape the dilemma. The context design is asymmetric, like bifocal lenses.

Their model, R2LM, pairs two mechanisms. Standard causal attention supplies precise left context with full cache compatibility. A lightweight reverse Mamba sidecar supplies compressed right-side context without breaking cacheability. Experiments continued pretraining of Qwen3-1.7B on sixty billion tokens. Throughput ran from about twofold to nearly thirteenfold higher than bidirectional diffusion models in batch serving. Speedups over autoregressive baselines ranged from about twofold to threefold. Quality beat the causal baseline on most benchmarks. It also surpassed the bidirectional diffusion model on average.
arxiv-2606-27832:
Adversarial detection asks whether a batch of inputs hides attacks. It is a two-sample test against clean reference data. The false-alarm rate must stay controlled. Zhijian Zhou and colleagues note a weakness of the standard tool in 2026. The usual test misses how attack inputs actually differ. Such inputs show abnormal feature spread. They are also unstable under small perturbations.

Their detector, USAD, measures those two patterns directly. One statistic captures global spread differences between clean and attack features. The other captures local instability. It adds Gaussian noise and watches the features move. Adding the two statistics gives the final detector. Against various attacks, USAD beats baseline detection methods. The conclusion stresses a general lesson. Detection statistics should encode how attack inputs behave. Generic distribution distance is not enough. High detection power with few samples is reported, and false alarms stay under theoretical control.
arxiv-2606-27932:
Daniele Angelini tackles a testing problem in fractional processes in 2026. Self-similarity is hard to test from one observed series under long-range dependence. The classical test breaks down there. Its limit collapses when the Hurst exponent passes one half. Angelini builds an adaptive framework on the Grünwald–Letnikov fractional derivative. The filter removes the low-frequency memory spike. It keeps the scaling structure the test needs.

The resulting Hurst estimator is proved consistent. Tests back the method. The method is then tried on real market data. For log-realised volatility, the estimates favour rough volatility. The exponents sit well below the Brownian threshold of one half. For log-prices, the method separates persistent, anti-persistent, and efficient market states. The key idea is a clean split. Memory is filtered out while scaling survives, so the test recovers a standard short-memory regime.
arxiv-2606-28132:
Modern JVM software mixes Java, Kotlin, Groovy, and Scala in one codebase. They must reconcile subtle semantic differences across those language boundaries. Errors there cause critical miscompilations, yet testing tools only cover single-language work. Xiaotian Ma and four colleagues present CrossLangFuzzer in 2026, the first framework for differential testing of cross-language JVM work. Test programs are synthesised from the Kotlin compiler's unified intermediate representation. Seven mutation operators diversify them.

Five major JVM compilers were tested at their latest versions. CrossLangFuzzer uncovered thirty-two confirmed bugs. Fifteen sit in Kotlin, four in Groovy, seven in Scala 3, two in Scala 2, and four in Java. The testing compares outputs across tools to expose disagreements. Cross-language programs stress interactions that single-language fuzzers never generate. The bug tally shows the gap was real. Compiler interoperability, the paper argues, needs its own testing discipline.
arxiv-2606-28332:
Yige Li and seven colleagues built MedHarm, a benchmark that stress-tests language models on dangerous medical questions. Models now answer health questions daily, yet their behavior on high-risk prompts, where a helpful tone could cause real harm, was barely measured. MedHarm holds eleven hundred grounded queries across ten safety-critical categories, from toxicology to fetal harm.

Li's team evaluated fifteen language models plus four guardrail systems. Passing ordinary alignment checks did not guarantee medical safety: aligned models still produced unsafe, actionable answers. Medical fine-tuning sometimes made harmful answers more specific and therefore worse. Guardrails blocked some failures but also refused clumsily and offered weak safe alternatives. Domain-specific stress testing, they conclude, is essential before deploying models in safety-critical medicine.
arxiv-2606-28632:
Tailan S. Sarubi, Moisés Alves, Santiago Zamora, Vinícius F. Alves, A. de Oliveira Junior, and Rafael Chaves study a broadcast twist on quantum messaging tests. In their prepare and broadcast scenario, a sender prepares a system that is then broadcast, copied in a limited sense, to several receivers who measure their shares. Whether the resulting correlations need quantum resources is the question.

The team builds a hierarchy of classical, quantum, and nonsignalling models for the scenario, maps their correlation sets, and derives Bell-like inequalities plus computer-based certification methods. With shared randomness and just one measurement per party, the hierarchy is proven to collapse to a single set: nothing nonclassical can show. Allow several measurements, though, and the scenario activates nonclassicality, exposing quantum behavior in resources that look fully classical in standard prepare-and-measure and Bell tests.
arxiv-2606-29032:
Garcia-Martinez, Ladra, Leite da Cunha and Lopes study compatible Lie algebras, structures carrying two Lie brackets that satisfy a mixing condition. Lie algebras encode infinitesimal symmetry, and their classical theory rests on famous theorems by Lie, Weyl and Levi. The authors test whether those pillars survive when a second compatible bracket is added.

Several do not: they produce counterexamples to the paired versions of all three theorems. On the constructive side, they classify the two-dimensional cases up to isomorphism. Their representation results include families of indecomposable representations that are not semisimple, meaning they cannot be split into simple pieces. The solvable two-dimensional cases have wild representation type, the most complex classification behaviour. They classify all irreducible finite-dimensional line representations, and prove a Clebsch-Gordan formula for splitting tensor products of those representations.
arxiv-2606-29232:
Tushar asks whether a vision-language model's skill measured on synthetic medical images predicts its skill on real scans, before any real labels are available. The question matters because real labels are exactly what medical imaging lacks. His answer is a mechanism. On synthetic digital twins of lung CT scans, competence driven by the donor, the transplanted nodule itself, survives the move to real hosts. Competence driven by the host anatomy need not.

He tests this on three lung-CT tasks spanning that axis, across five public models, four guidance conditions and seven real-world datasets. The prediction held in every case: judgements of nodule presence and size transferred almost perfectly, while lobe identification did not. The split survived leave-source-out calibration checks. A training-free council system, calibrated only on synthetic scans, matched the best fixed model exactly where transfer was predicted, confirming the diagnostic's practical use.
arxiv-2606-29432:
Laha and van Loock improve fusion gates, measurements that join two photonic qudits into an entangled pair. A qudit is a quantum unit with more than two levels; here each one is a single photon spread across several rails. Passive linear-optical fusion succeeds with a known probability, and all failures land in one structured part of the logical space, the diagonal subspace.

Adding identical single-mode squeezers before photon-number-resolving detection recovers part of that failure sector. Squeezing is a quantum operation that reshapes a light mode's noise. Photon-number parity keeps the good fusion signatures intact, while certain all-even patterns act like genuine Bell projectors. The authors derive the exact measurement description and a closed formula for the gain. For four rails, ideal success rises from three quarters to nearly four fifths. The cost is more squeezing operations and a wider photon-number range at detection.
arxiv-2606-29632:
Arora and four colleagues make language-model-based audio-visual speech recognition robust to noise. Such systems read both sound and lip movements, which helps when audio is corrupted. Recent versions connect pretrained audio-visual encoders to a large language model and score well in clean conditions. Their weakness is the language model backbone itself, which has no mechanism for staying stable under noisy input.

Their model, VIB-AVSR, inserts Variational Information Bottleneck layers at targeted positions inside the language model backbone. The information bottleneck principle squeezes representations down to what matters, discarding noise-driven detail. Those layers regularize the representations, meaning they keep them steady when conditions worsen. The result is reduced performance degradation across several signal-to-noise levels and noise types. No architectural overhaul and no additional training data are required. The code is released publicly.
arxiv-2606-29832:
Hu, Duan, and Zhang set up the first theory linking machine unlearning with continual learning. Unlearning removes the influence of specific data from a trained model for privacy, while continual learning keeps updating the model on new tasks in sequence.

The authors formulate the goal as minimising post-unlearning excess risk, which splits into the continual learning risk and an unlearning loss, exposing a forgetting-retention trade-off.
