They adapt two certified unlearning methods to this setting. The gradient-based one is weaker at cutting unlearning loss but needs almost no extra storage, while the Hessian-based one is stronger. This motivates a hybrid strategy that keeps storage low and performance high, and experiments back the theory.
arxiv-2606-30332:
Qin Guo, Hao Luo, Dongxu Yue, Weixuan Jin, Xiao Fu, Fan Wang, and Dan Xu unify image generation and dense prediction inside one diffusion transformer. Controllable generation makes pictures obeying depth or normal maps. Dense prediction estimates those maps from pictures. The two tasks are usually trained as separate models. Their framework, UniGP, trains both jointly on shared foundations.

UniGP builds on the MMDiT architecture without task-specific designs or losses. A copied image branch models dense outputs beyond plain color images. A unified dataset strategy mixes heterogeneous training data together. The model learns the joint distribution of image and geometry pairs. It can generate, predict, and do both jointly. Experiments show it surpassing earlier unified approaches overall. It performs on par with specialized single-task methods too. Joint training helps both directions: generation gains structural alignment. Perception gains detail from the generative priors.
arxiv-2606-30932:
Yufei Wu and Zhen Yan describe how a large job marketplace personalised a policy whose benefits pull in opposite directions. The policy sets free-value thresholds, how much complimentary service each job listing receives, across millions of employers and job seekers. Helping employers can hurt seeker engagement, and the effects differ by job segment. Worse, marketplace interference forces cluster-level randomisation, so experiments offer only a few discrete policy levels, ruling out standard uplift methods built for continuous treatments.

Their framework ranks segments with separate ensemble models for the target metric and the guardrail, cutting guardrail risk by over 10% at equal target gains against single-objective approaches. An extrapolation method extends effect estimates to untested policy levels under monotonicity assumptions they validate empirically. Post-launch production data confirmed both the extrapolation accuracy and guardrail compliance.
arxiv-2606-31032:
Hamidah Oderinwale, David Atkinson, Rachel Hong, Art Abal and Ben Laufer use language models to compare software licences at scale. Licences are legal instruments chosen and written with little structure, so basic questions lack answers: is this licence more permissive than that one, or are their terms simply incomparable? The question matters for platforms like GitHub, Hugging Face and the Python Package Index, where stacked components each carry their own licence. The team build two comparison methods. One asks models pairwise questions to assemble a partial ordering by permissiveness. The other draws on existing licence taxonomies, treating selection as a combination of shared provisions.

Their analysis recovers interpretable attributes that track with stricter licences. Tracing restrictiveness this way, and decomposing licences into provisions, offers a systematic handle on relationships across the growing licence ecosystem, with legal implications for open source.
arxiv-2606-31332:
Li and seven colleagues present CryoACE, a system that builds atomic protein models from cryo-electron microscopy density maps on its own. Turning a fuzzy density map into an exact atomic graph is hard because models must stay chemically valid and proteins bend into many shapes. Older solvers give one static answer or rely on slow heuristic search.

CryoACE samples density features right at atom positions and recycles them to refine the structure step by step, skipping costly voxel convolutions. A training-free guidance step uses predicted local resolution to settle regions that move. On a new high-quality dataset it beats prior baselines on static tests. On the complex EMPIAR-10345 data it reveals atomic-level moving shapes with no pre-built model, a first for this kind of tool.
arxiv-2606-31432:
Gong and two colleagues present BiRG-LoRA, a rank-gated adapter method for medical question answering. Medical questions span drugs, diagnosis, public health, and nursing, and each kind may need a different low-rank update, while plain recall items should barely touch the base model. One fixed adapter cannot serve all of them well.

BiRG-LoRA keeps one LoRA module per layer but lets each question choose a sparse set of rank atoms. A biaxial gate mixes semantic evidence with specialty and clinical-operation priors, and a scalar coefficient sets the update strength. On a matched Qwen3-8B protocol it posts the best macro-average across CMB, CMExam, MedQA, and MedMCQA among trainable rivals. It also beats a mixture rival while using about 28 percent fewer trainable parameters.
arxiv-2606-31532:
Li and two colleagues build a forecasting framework for staff absenteeism that predicts ahead instead of describing the present. Most absence models map features at one time to a label at the same time, which repeats what already happened and throws away the sequence in each worker's attendance history. High-demand employers need warning before an absence lands.

Their time-series classification design splits past attendance sequences from future absence labels, so prediction is genuinely forward-looking. A reproducible simulated dataset, calibrated to a public benchmark, stands in for unavailable real records. Under severe class imbalance, performance hinges mainly on the focal loss weight, and a plain setting of it reaches strong specificity and balanced accuracy. The analysis shows how imbalance handling, not model size, decides success here.
arxiv-2606-31732:
Zheng and seven colleagues tackle visual-to-code generation, where a model turns charts, vector graphics or webpages into code that redraws them. Standard fine-tuning leaves small errors in colors, positions and labels. Reinforcement learning could help, but its rewards are often too coarse and its search can stall before any valid code appears.

Their framework, UniCoder, adds two fixes. A helper model parses generated code into discrete attributes such as hex colors, giving dense element-level rewards. A second trick injects correct example trajectories into weak rollout groups, guiding exploration. On four benchmarks the resulting 8-billion-parameter model beats open-source rivals and matches proprietary systems, the authors report.
arxiv-2606-31932:
Fiechter and Richardson propose a way for vibropolaritonic chemistry to work, given the puzzling finding that a tuned optical cavity can change reaction rates. Placing molecules between mirrors set to a vibrational resonance modifies chemical properties, yet a decade of work has not settled why. Any real account must be both resonant and collective, growing with the number of coupled molecules.

Vibrational strong coupling modifies the London dispersion interaction between molecules, the attraction arising from fleeting charge shifts, they show. Mixed quantum-classical dynamics then gives a resonant rate boost for two coupled molecules across all solvent friction regimes. The dispersion changes persist as molecule numbers grow. Whether rates also change in the collective lab limit stays open, beyond their method's reach.
arxiv-2608-00332:
Anari, Rashidi, and Rajabi test fast population leakage in astronomical masers. A three-level Maxwell-Bloch model drives their study. An inverted transition may amplify as a maser or burst as superradiance. Its upper level may also decay through a much faster second pathway. That shared-upper-level layout occurs in methanol and OH masers.

They focus on the mixed case: the observed transition is inverted, the fast path is not. Rapid decay through the rival path does not by itself suppress amplification, they find. The response rests on the shared population reservoir and starting coherence. Relaxation and dephasing timescales also matter. A methanol flare case at 6.7 GHz benchmarks the model. Its burst stays compatible with transient superradiance once leakage is included.
asclepius-latin-1532:
The Asclepius is the one full Hermetic book that the Latin West kept through the Middle Ages. It was ascribed to Hermes Trismegistus and said to be the work, in Latin, of Apuleius of Madaura. The edition here is the Basel printing of 1532. The dialogue itself dates from the second to fourth century.

Hermes teaches Asclepius about God, the world, and man, the being who stands between earth and heaven. The famous lament for Egypt foretells a day when the gods will leave and the temples stand empty. Augustine quoted that passage against the pagans. The talk of statues breathed alive by rites made the book a byword for bold Hermetic claims.
austin-province-jurisprudence-1832:
John Austin published The Province of Jurisprudence Determined in 1832. Austin, a former soldier turned law professor in London, set out to define what law is and where its study should stop. The book grew from his lectures at the new University of London.

Law, Austin argued, is the command of a sovereign, backed by the threat of punishment. That command theory cut law loose from morals: a rule can be law and still be wicked. Critics have fought the theory ever since, but it founded legal positivism, the school that studies law as it is, not as it ought to be. Austin's dry book shaped how the English-speaking world teaches law's first questions.
ballads-pg2732:
William Makepeace Thackeray wrote ballads all through his career, and this volume gathers them between one pair of covers. The contents run from the Chronicle of the Drum and the Ballad of Bouillabaisse to Mahogany Tree, Pocahontas, and the comic Policeman X songs. Imitations of Beranger and Horace sit beside Irish pieces in the Lyra Hibernica section.

Thackeray's verse here is lighter than his novels and often kinder. Little Billee retells a sailor's mishap as a music-hall turn, while The End of the Play looks back over a life's performance. Some pieces are parodies, some are drinking songs, and a few are quietly sad. The collection shows the novelist at play, in short forms he could finish between chapters.
berkeley-alciphron-1732:
Alciphron: or, The Minute Philosopher, from 1732, is George Berkeley's defense of Christian belief in dialogue form. Seven dialogues stage a debate between Berkeley's speakers and the freethinkers of the age. His targets, named in the evidence of the work itself, include Collins, Mandeville, and Shaftesbury, the wits who made unbelief fashionable.

Berkeley answers them on their own ground, with wit, learning, and close reasoning about language and morals. The minute philosophers of his title are men who magnify small doubts into systems. Alciphron is the fullest statement of Berkeley the churchman and controversialist. It shows the philosopher of vision turned defender of faith, in his most polished prose.
berossus-chaldaean-fragments-cory-1832:
Berossus, a priest of Babylon, wrote the Babyloniaca in Greek around 280 BCE to tell the Greeks the true history of his own land. His three books are lost, but later writers quoted pieces of them. Isaac Preston Cory printed those fragments in 1832, and he added kindred scraps from Abydenus, Megasthenes, and Alexander Polyhistor.

The fragments give the Babylonian story in Babylonian terms: the making of the world, the great flood, and the long lists of kings from before it. They run on through Nebuchadnezzar and the fall of Babylon to Persia. Berossus stays our key native source for the king lists and dates of Mesopotamia.
cia-0000009032:
How specialists compared prisoner-of-war photographs gets a full technical treatment in a March 1969 CIA paper. The authors lay out method for matching faces across poor images and long gaps in time. Their audience was other analysts doing the same work on live cases.

Good method protected the whole identification program from error. The paper likely covers features, measurements, and how to state confidence honestly. Readers today can watch a forensic routine being standardized in wartime. That routine later decided hundreds of individual case files. The document is thus a manual behind the search, not a report of one man.
cia-0000009532:
One American air force officer was killed and another captured in a single incident, a November 1972 report observes. The two fates, side by side, show how chance split crews who flew together. The report came during the war's final bombing season.

Paired outcomes forced officials to open two kinds of files at once: a death record and a prisoner case. Witnesses to the same event could serve both inquiries. The entry's plain wording carries that double weight without comment. It shows the accounting working at the level of one aircraft, one day, two very different men.
cia-0000009932:
Sightings of American prisoners moving through Laos lead an October 1971 item, followed by North Vietnamese and Pathet Lao regulations, cut off in the title. Transit sightings and written rules make an odd but useful pair. One shows the system in motion; the other shows it on paper.

Regulations told analysts what should happen to a captured man at each stage. Sightings showed what actually happened on the road. Comparing the two exposed the system's real workings. This file preserves both halves of that comparison, the moving prisoners and their captors' rulebook, in a single dated item.
cia-0000011832:
Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania were the three new states of East Africa, and a CIA paper from February 1967 surveys them together. Each had won freedom from British rule within the past few years. Their founding leaders, Kenyatta, Obote, and Nyerere, were setting very different courses for their young nations.

The paper compares the stability and direction of the three governments. It weighs their economies, their armies, and their leanings in the Cold War contest for Africa. Written with cautious optimism, the survey shows the independence generation in its first years, before coups and crises changed the region's path.
cia-0000013232:
Evacuation, escape attempts, illness, and detention fill a CIA paper from November 1970. Its subject is the human reality of the prison system. The paper follows American prisoners through the system's hardest passages. Men were marched between camps as fronts shifted around them. Some tried to escape into jungle that offered little mercy. Others sickened on short rations and endured cells built to break them slowly.

The paper catalogues that suffering in the file's calm hand. It may be the most human document in this whole accounting. For readers, it records what captivity cost, item by item, from the files of the side that waited.
cia-0000015332: A letter to Robert Palmer from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated March 3, 1961. Strong answers Palmer's inquiry of February 21, per the title. By 1961 the saucer mail was a known chore with a known form. Each new writer got the same fair hearing and the same short answer. The Palmer reply is now kept in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015432: Money for the great official study of UFOs came through an Air Force contract with the University of Colorado, recorded January 2, 1967. Under that contract the university would study saucer reports and issue a final judgment. Edward Condon led the work in Colorado. The CIA kept the funding record, a reminder that the agency tracked the study from its first formal step.
cia-0000020332: A plot to assassinate President Castillo Armas, said to be planned by Captain Fernando Romero, fills a CIA record dated July 1, 1955. The title names Romero, so an older summary blaming communists is not followed here. Castillo Armas then ruled Guatemala, a state watched closely from Washington. Plot reports of this kind were logged whether or not they proved true.
cia-0000022332: Soviet broadcasts of the Powers trial are kept in a CIA record dated in 1960. Radio carried the Moscow courtroom to Soviet homes and, through monitoring, to Washington. Broadcast text let analysts study exactly what the Soviet public was told. The trial was theater as well as law, and this entry holds the script as listeners heard it then.
cia-0000022532: Results of a photo comparison, case number blank in the released title, fill a CIA record dated in 1971. The missing number was cut or left empty before release. Photo comparison matched faces in enemy pictures against missing Americans, case by case. A result without its number is half a record, yet the finding itself was still worth keeping on file.
cia-0000028332: Honduras, its major towns and other important features, is surveyed in a CIA item dated in 1982. Town by town surveys were basic reference work, the gazetteer side of intelligence. Honduras in 1982 was becoming a base for the contra war against Nicaragua next door. A plain features list from that year quietly served a fast growing military interest.
cia-0000037532: An untitled CIA document dated September 2, 1971 mentions a source, whose name is deleted, who was shown photographs of missing men. The source's identity is blacked out in the released copy, so the file turns on what such a source could say about the photographs. Showing pictures to a source was a standard step in the MIA and POW work, since one recognition could settle a case. The redactions leave the method visible and the person hidden.
cia-0000045232:
Rivera y Damas warned that the kidnapping might hurt dialogue, in a CIA record dated August 1, 1985. Dialogue meant the slow talks aimed at ending the war itself. One crime, he feared, could poison a much larger peace.

Inside, the archbishop's caution about the talks is preserved. He had spent years building the bridges such talks would need. A kidnapping strained every one of those bridges at once. The file holds his warning from the case's opening days. It was spoken by the man who kept the idea of dialogue alive in that war.
cia-0000045932: A press release announced a joint United States and Vietnam search for missing American servicemen. A CIA item dated July 4, 1991, kept the text. Joint field work was a new step: former enemies digging side by side at crash and burial sites. The release marks the point where the accounting effort became open, shared work.
cia-0000049032: A CIA item from 1982 discusses whether Koos Koster matches a photograph of a man handing over money. Koster was a Dutch journalist killed in El Salvador that same year, which gave the comparison its charge. The item survives in the Truth Commission files, where photographs were evidence like any other record.
cia-0000049132: An Argentine doctor died in El Salvador in 1989, and a CIA item from that year preserves the report, kept with the Truth Commission records. Foreigners who came to help, as doctors, priests, or journalists, kept dying in other people's war. Each such death drew cables, questions, and a file that outlived the news.
cia-0000102932: Involvement of the MVD in the use of forced labor, plus treatment of political prisoners, form the two numbered topics of declassified CIA document 0000102932, dated August 3, 1982. The ministry is named by initials. Readers get a short double-topic record tying an institution to the labor system, filed among the cluster's project reports.
cia-0000112332: State Center for Study of Ufo's Established is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112332, dated March 1, 1990. The title reports a new state center for the study of UFOs. Established is the heading's word for its founding, in the title itself. The brief record shares its date with a companion UFO item on sightings near Moscow.
cia-0000112832: Juan Tria - Espionage is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112832, dated October 1, 1945. The title pairs a name and a charge in three words: Juan Tria, espionage. No place or act is stated in the heading itself. The brief record is a name and charge file from the autumn of 1945 in the wartime files.
cia-0000119732: Filed in the Eastern Europe series in September 1956, this CIA report covers the situation in Hungary. The regional roundup placed Budapest's growing crisis inside the wider unrest of the Soviet bloc that autumn. Regional framing mattered because trouble in one satellite state tended to echo in the others, a pattern the series was built to catch early.
cia-0000120632: An August 1962 CIA memorandum records a meeting with the President about Cuba. It was written two months before the missile crisis brought the two superpowers to the brink. Kennedy's White House was already deep in Cuba planning, and the paper preserves what was said while the stakes were still hidden.
cia-0000124332: A January 1960 CIA document holds information on American prisoners of war who had not been repatriated, the word information misspelled in the heading. Years after the Korean fighting ended, some Americans had still not come home. The paper preserves what the agency knew of their cases. Non-repatriates were the hardest cases of the war's aftermath, men whose fate turned on politics in Beijing rather than on any list the armistice had produced.
cia-0000126932: Filed around January 1983, this untitled CIA document is a list of names and memberships. No title or purpose was recorded with it in the file. Rosters of this kind were raw material for counterintelligence work, and the paper preserves the list as it was filed. Bare rosters frustrate readers by design of their filing, yet names and memberships together form the raw graph from which network studies of groups are built.
cia-0000132232: Situation report 549, from January 1991, gives the status of the oil spill along with political developments, the heading breaking off. The spill was spreading along the Gulf coast as a deliberate act of war. The report tracks both the slick and the politics around it. Pairing the spill with politics in one heading captures the crisis exactly: the oil was at once an environmental disaster and a lever in the bargaining.
cia-0000132432: Cuban arms purchases fill a CIA document dated January 2, 1960. The new revolutionary government was shopping for weapons in several markets. Washington watched each shipment and each rumor of one with close care. Arms deals would soon become the hard currency of Cuba's new Soviet ties. The short document tracks the purchases known to analysts at the start of that year.
cia-0000132632: Events in Cuba are surveyed in a CIA paper dated June 1, 1960. By the middle of that year the word developments had come to mean seizures of firms, deals with Moscow, and a break with Washington drawing near. The file was growing too fast for colorful titles by then. The short paper gathers the latest events as analysts recorded them.
cia-0000135732: This Spanish-language document from the 2506 Brigade files carries an estimated date of 1 January 1961. The brigade of anti-Castro exiles was in CIA-run training that winter. The catalog title flags the estimated date and gives no subject. Like its companions in this series, the item is preserved in Spanish as a primary source. Its description here rests on the record: brigade, language, estimated date, and declassified release.
cia-0000135832:
A Study of Assassination is a short CIA training text tied to the Guatemala operation, with an estimated date of January 1954. It was written for PBSUCCESS, the covert plan against President Jacobo Arbenz, and the record lists the agency itself, not a single author, as its creator. Few papers in the whole file carry a plainer title, or a darker one.

Inside, the study treats killing a chosen leader as planned work, weighing how a target should be picked and how the act should be done and hidden. Long kept secret, the paper later became the best known and most condemned text of the Guatemala operation. Readers still cite it when they ask how far the agency was willing to go in 1954.
cia-0000135932: A cable of 1 January 1954 survives in the declassified CIA files, dealing with follow-up on the public reply to a white paper. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136232: The record dated 3 May 1954 is a declassified CIA situation report about daily operations situation report number 3, the countdown series running in May 1954. Guatemala in these years meant PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against President Jacobo Arbenz and the government he led. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136632: Dated 3 February 1961, a Spanish text from the declassified files of Brigade 2506, the CIA-trained Cuban exile force. The brigade was about ten weeks from its landing at the Bay of Pigs. The catalog gives this document no subject heading. Preserved in Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, it is a dated piece of the brigade's paperwork from its final training stretch.
cia-0000136932: Loads of arms are landing at Toncontin field, a source in Tegucigalpa reports in April 1954. He says it is common knowledge there. Planes land and stay only minutes. They unload fast, then take off again. A second source doubts the tale. It fits nothing he knows, he says. He asks how the first man reached his findings. Did anyone read insignia through overpainting? No. The report went to Playdon at once on receipt.
cia-0000137332: Communist bloc approaches to Cuba continue, this NSC briefing states. It is dated 24 July 1960. A memorandum for the record transmits the paper. A trade pact was concluded with Communist China on 23 July. It marks a strong Chinese effort at recognition from Cuba. It also shows Peking's willingness to back an anti-American move. Considerable material support stands behind it. The memorandum is a routing vehicle. It carried the briefing into the file a year before the Bay of Pigs.
cia-03153732:
Disarmament opens a long Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 12 October 1957. Japan's UN delegate believes neither the Western nor the Soviet proposal can win two-thirds support. Japan's own plan, an immediate test suspension with resumed talks on inspection, might then pass. Sweden's Unden urges the West to accept a simple ban. The missing controls are noted against both plans.

The Supreme Soviet may meet in December. Yugoslavia reportedly recognises East Germany within the week. Tito is warned to curtail liberalisation. Unrest continues in North Vietnam. Syria expects more Soviet aircraft this year: fifteen MIG-17 fighters, IL-28 bombers, and transports, with crews to train in the USSR. Jordan, Sudan's cotton crisis, Pakistan's fallen premier Suhrawardy, and the French army's political role fill the rest.
cia-03155132:
Burma opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 24 August 1956, with a strong note to Chou En-lai. Premier Ba Swe rejects calling part of the frontier undetermined. The line drawn in 1941 by Nationalist China and Britain should stand, he insists, with a joint commission to mark it. Chinese troops remain in the disputed ground. Chou's planned goodwill visit is read as placation without concessions.

Soviet army demobilisation measures follow. Moscow had announced a cut of 1.2 million men by May 1957, and Marshal Zhukov has reportedly ordered steps to carry it out. Krishna Menon's role in the Suez controversy is examined next. Egyptian terrorist activities may be stepped up. Turkey's finance minister resigns. Algerian rebels reportedly have enough small arms. The Arab-Israeli situation closes the issue in its standing section.
cia-03156032:
Summit diplomacy opens the Central Intelligence Bulletin dated 7 April 1959. Senior Soviet foreign ministry officials showed Ambassador Thompson obvious pleasure at the agreed foreign ministers' conference. Their almost pleading stress on a summit is read two ways. Khrushchev pressures his officials to arrange one, and they know the danger his Berlin move created. Deputy Minister Zorin admits confusion over American aims since Dulles fell ill.

Two Soviet long-range submarines have finished four-month voyages toward Cape Horn, their longest cruises yet. East German workers are reported increasingly refractory, dooming Ulbricht's living-standard promises. Mao tells visiting Japanese he will retire as government chairman. China may be sending MIG-17s to Indonesia. Himalayan states fear Tibet's fall threatens them too. France hints at unilateral action inside NATO if America sells arms to Morocco.
cia-03156632:
The Taiwan Strait crisis fills the Central Intelligence Bulletin dated 19 September 1958. Nationalist claims for 18 September list five Communist MIGs downed and a torpedo boat sunk, against one vessel damaged by artillery. Peiping issues its sixth warning against American warship intrusions. The Watch Committee concludes the Communists can now attack the offshore islands with little warning, though no invasion lift for Kinmen has been seen.

Peiping also tries applying a twelve-mile limit off Hong Kong, forcing a British patrol craft off course. Soviet preparations for a new nuclear test series near completion. Moscow radio prepares opinion for resuming tests if Western tests continue. Yugoslavia may see its Peiping ties severed. The USSR will supply Indonesia twenty million dollars in rice. EOKA resumes violence in Cyprus. An Algerian government-in-exile is expected at Cairo.
cia-03185132:
Korea opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 8 August 1956. President Rhee is considering martial law, waiting only for further violence. He believes every recent disturbance is Communist-inspired. The security bureau, the comment warns, feeds him fabricated data to keep him convinced. A peaceful assembly demonstration of 27 July was misreported to him as an overthrow attempt.

Police and Home Ministry influence grows at the moderates' expense. Disorders may follow the 8 August local elections, and Rhee would likely act then. An Ecuadoran garrison at Portoviejo rose on 6 August, perhaps to block president-elect Ponce Enriquez's inauguration. Reports conflict, but the revolt looks localised. A West German diplomat calls Allied talk of cutting conventional forces an impossible position for Bonn. India finds a new formula for the Bombay linguistic state dispute. The Arab-Israeli situation follows.
cia-06820732:
International Issues journal, number RP AII 77-003, is dated 16 March 1977 and marked Secret. It is prepared by the International Issues Division, Office of Regional and Political Analysis. Contents list two articles: Nuclear Politics in Brazil from page 1, and Trends in Terrorist Skyjacking from page 17.

The Brazil article assesses likely reaction to American pressure over the 1975 West German-Brazilian nuclear accord. Washington sought to block parts of that deal, the article states. Brazil's forceful refusal to consider any change suggested the American goal, stopping Brazil gaining a complete nuclear fuel cycle, would be exceedingly hard to reach. Even success would probably cost US-Brazilian relations dearly, it argues. Later pages warn of doubt among investors and of harm to Brazil's export-led development strategy if access to the American market shrank.
cory-ancient-fragments-1832:
Isaac Preston Cory gathered surviving fragments of lost pagan writers into one English volume in 1832. Phoenician, Chaldean, Egyptian, Persian, and other traditions all appear in his collection. It was the first English sourcebook of its kind.

Readers met the Chaldean Oracles and Orphic fragments in English here. Cory translated scraps preserved inside later Greek and Latin authors. Nineteenth-century occultists devoured the volume and quoted it for decades. His pioneering collection channeled ancient fragments into the modern imagination. Some translations have aged, and later editions improved many texts. As the doorway through which these fragments reached English readers, it matters.
doe-osti-3683717-sierra-sd-verification-:
Sandia report SAND2026-25636, printed August 18, 2026, is the verification test manual for Sierra/SD, version 5.32. The Sierra Structural Dynamics Development Team prepared it. Sierra/SD models how structures bend, shake, and take shock loads. Sandia uses such models to help manage the nuclear stockpile. Users must trust the code's math before its answers can certify parts for hard settings.

The manual lays out the verification plan and then details each test case. Cases cover model reduction methods, beam-to-beam contact, and many element types. Tables compare element results across mesh shapes, from hexagons to wedges and shells. Mesh refinement studies check that answers sharpen as the grid gets finer. Each test states its setup, its expected result, and how the run is judged. Together, the cases guard the code's maths and number methods as new features land.
doe-osti-3683719-sierra-sd-its2sierra-us:
Sandia report SAND2026-25632, printed August 17, 2026, is the user's manual for Its2Sierra, version 5.32. The Sierra Structural Dynamics Development Team prepared it. The Integrated Tiger Series, or ITS, builds a database of energy deposition data. Stored in an Exodus file, that data does not fit Sierra Mechanics analysis directly. Its2Sierra maps the data onto a Sierra mesh so engineers can use it.

Sections cover how to run the tool, its input file syntax, and what comes out. Output keeps the final time step's data from the input Sierra mesh. Only the energy deposition variable is mapped today. Theory sections list the element types the tool supports. Three mapping methods are explained: a blockwise method, a nearest neighbour method, and a distance-weighted blend. A short part deals with keeping total energy the same through the move. Release notes reach back to version 5.22.
doe-osti-3683720-sierra-sd-user-s-guide-:
Sandia report SAND2026-25634, printed August 17, 2026, is the user's guide for NasGen, version 5.32. The Sierra Structural Dynamics Development Team prepared it. NasGen moves structural models out of the Nastran bulk data format. It writes both an Exodus mesh file and a text input file. Those outputs feed Sierra Structural Dynamics and Sierra Solid Mechanics runs. Many Sandia tools use the Exodus format, so the bridge sees wide use.

The guide states what the translator can and cannot do. Numbering rules for nodes, elements, blocks, nodesets, and sidesets come first. A table then maps each Nastran element type to its Sierra match. Sidesets, which carry pressure loads, grow from set pressure cards. Only the face-normal part of pressure is carried over today. One trick is shown for forcing a needed sideset: add an unused pressure card. Users are warned to check the output file for correct boundary settings.
doe-osti-3683721-sierra-sd-user-s-manual:
Sandia report SAND2026-25667, printed August 26, 2026, is the user's manual for Sierra/SD, version 5.32. The Sierra Structural Dynamics Development Team prepared it. Sierra/SD runs structural dynamics finite element analysis in parallel across many processors. Its models serve modal, vibration, static, and shock studies of weapons systems. High-fidelity, checked models are the point of the code.

The manual guides users through the full input file. Release notes trace changes from version 5.26 through 5.32, plus how features are retired. Early chapters cover how to run the code and split a mesh across processors. Later chapters detail each solution type, output choice, element type, and parameter. Materials get their own long section, with stiffness tables by material type. Appendices give worked examples and notes on running on parallel platforms. At over a million characters, the hosted text is a full reference, not a short guide.
europmc-pmc10016932:
Umakanthan and colleagues review what was known about COVID-19 in a 2020 paper, covering its origin, spread, diagnosis, and care. Coronaviruses had already caused two major outbreaks in two decades. The new disease, first seen in late 2019, was spreading across the world as they wrote.

The authors explain where the virus likely came from and how it passes between people. They survey the tests used to confirm infection and the care given to patients. The paper stands as a compact record of early knowledge, written while the pandemic was still young.
europmc-pmc10183032:
Zhao and colleagues review the role of gut microbes in cancer therapy in a 2023 paper, from molecular mechanisms to clinical use. Fast DNA sequencing has revealed how deeply the gut's microbial community affects cancer growth and treatment response. Patients with similar tumors can respond very differently to the same drug, and gut microbes seem to be one reason.

The review explains how microbes shape immunity and drug metabolism. It gathers evidence on diet, probiotics, and stool transfer as ways to aid therapy. It also notes the care needed, since cancer patients are fragile.
europmc-pmc10451032:
Hu and co-authors tested in 2023 how changes in a virus enzyme could defeat a key Covid drug. The drug, nirmatrelvir, blocks the main protease of SARS-CoV-2, a tool the virus uses to build itself. New variants raised fears that the drug might fail. The team built and checked 102 changed forms of the enzyme.

Twenty-two changes at five spots kept the enzyme strong yet shrugged off the drug. Hu mapped the shapes of six of these forms with X-ray methods. Live virus tests then proved the resistance in full virus. Some drug-proof forms grew more weakly, a small comfort. The team flags these spots for close watch in clinics.
europmc-pmc10564932:
Huangfu and co-authors reviewed the IL-17 family of immune signals in 2023. The family holds six members, named IL-17A through IL-17F. Their matching receptors have all been found in recent years. These signals stir swelling during infection and immune disease. They also help the body fight germs.

That dual role makes the family hard to pin down. Huangfu traces the signal chain each member sets off in cells. The chain guards tissue, drives repair, and can feed cancer growth. Two disease cases get close study: lupus, an immune attack on the body, and spread of tumours. The review closes with drug and test gains for immune disease and cancer.
europmc-pmc10687432:
Basak and co-authors reviewed tumour-linked macrophages in 2023 and why immune therapy often fails. Macrophages form the bulk of immune cells inside a tumour. They come in two broad kinds: M1, which fights cancer, and M2, which shields it. Tumours tilt the mix toward M2 to secure their growth.

That tilt speeds blood vessel growth, spread, and immune shutdown, Basak reports. It also helps seed cancer stem cells, which can restart a tumour after care. The stem cells return the favour with escape tricks of their own. Weak grasp of this crosstalk helps explain stalled immune drugs. The review backs plans that strike cancer cells, stem cells, and macrophages at once.
europmc-pmc10873332:
Quintard and a large team built a chip system that grows tiny organs with working blood vessels in this 2024 paper. Organoids are small 3D cell clusters that mimic organs in the lab. They need blood vessels to survive long term, yet adding vessels on chips has stayed hard. Most devices also fail to copy the flow patterns found in the body.

Their platform grew vessel networks around cell balls and vessel organoids for up to 30 days. The networks linked up and carried flow into the tissues, the team reports. Tissues on the chip grew, matured, and worked better than those grown without flow. The system was tested on support cells and insulin-making cell clusters. The authors present it as a base for more lifelike organ models in drug testing.
europmc-pmc11093732:
Pachitariu, Sridhar, Pennington, and Stringer present a new version of a brain signal sorting tool in this 2024 paper. Electrodes in the brain record mixed electrical spikes from many nerve cells at once. Spike sorting is the computing task of assigning each spike to one cell. It is hard because recordings drift and the fields of nearby cells overlap.

Their tool, Kilosort4, adds clustering methods inspired by graph maths, the study of linked networks. To test it fairly, they built simulations from densely sampled real recordings with realistic noise and drift. Kilosort4 beat rival tools in all tested conditions, they report. It correctly found even faint cells and tiny cells under heavy drift. Earlier versions also beat most rivals. The framework is developed openly for the field to use.
europmc-pmc11126432:
Jeblick and colleagues test whether ChatGPT can rewrite radiology reports in plain words in this 2024 case study. Radiology reports are written for doctors, and patients often cannot parse them. Large language models, AI systems trained on vast text, might simplify them. The team asked whether the simplified versions stay correct and safe.

A radiologist wrote three fictitious reports, and ChatGPT rewrote each for a child, as prompted. Fifteen radiologists then rated the rewrites for correctness, completeness, and risk of harm. Most raters judged the rewrites correct, complete, and not harmful. Still, raters flagged some wrong statements, missed facts, and risky passages. The authors see large potential for patient-centred care. They also stress that the tool needs further adaptation to medicine before routine use.
europmc-pmc11461632:
Hu and colleagues review how metabolism regulates the immune system in health and disease in this 2024 paper. Immune cells run on metabolic pathways such as glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation, and fatty acid oxidation, meaning burning sugar, burning fuel with oxygen, and burning fat. Which pathway dominates shapes what an immune cell does. The concept linking the two fields is called immunometabolism.

Introduced over a decade ago, the concept has widened from chronic low-grade inflammation to metabolic reprogramming across diseases. In cancer, autoimmune disease, and metabolic disease, reprogrammed immune cells turn pro-inflammatory or anti-inflammatory. Those shifts then drive disease development, the authors trace. The review summarises the mechanisms pathway by pathway. It closes with interventions that target immune metabolism, from diet-level measures to drugs under study.
europmc-pmc11485232:
Vorontsov and a large team present the largest AI foundation model for pathology to date in this 2024 paper. Foundation models are large AI systems trained on broad data and then adapted to tasks. Pathology AI aims to support clinical decisions and precision medicine, but it must model very diverse tissue patterns. Their model is called Virchow.

Virchow enabled pan-cancer detection across nine common and seven rare cancers, the authors report. Detection reached a specimen-level score of 0.95 on the standard curve measure. Built on Virchow, a detector trained with less labelled data matched clinical-grade tissue-specific models already in production. On some rare cancer variants it outperformed them. The authors also evaluate biomarker prediction and cell identification. They argue the gains show the value of scale where labelled data are scarce.
europmc-pmc11486532:
Ru, Li, Chen, Wu, Min, and Wang review iron balance and iron-driven cell death in human disease in this 2024 paper. Iron is an essential mineral used across body processes, and keeping its levels steady is crucial. Both overload and deficiency cause disorders. Ferroptosis is a cell death that depends on iron and features extensive peroxidation of membrane lipids.

Unlike classic unprogrammed deaths, ferroptosis is tied to disrupted iron metabolism, lipid peroxidation, and antioxidant imbalance, the authors explain. It is regulated at the levels of transcription, translation, and protein modification. Over the past decade it has been linked to cancers, metabolic and autoimmune diseases, brain diseases, heart diseases, and muscle diseases. Ferroptosis proteins are attractive drug targets for incurable diseases. Some such regulators showed benefit in clinical trials.
europmc-pmc1240132:
Blount and co-authors measured plastic chemical traces in urine in 2000. Phthalates are chemicals used widely in plastics and goods. Their breakdown products appear in urine after exposure. Animal work links some of them to reproductive harm.

A new selective method measured seven breakdown products directly. Samples came from 289 adults as a reference group. Three products showed the highest levels overall. Women of childbearing age had higher levels of one key product. Blount gives baseline values for judging exposure in the wider public. It appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2000.
europmc-pmc1280332:
Sioutas, Delfino, and Singh tackled exposure measurement for ultrafine particles in 2005. Health studies had used particle mass as the exposure yardstick. Ultrafine particles behave very differently from larger ones. Their counts and surface area run orders of magnitude higher per mass.

They also carry more oxidant gases, organics, and metals per unit mass. Lab tests show far higher redox activity than larger particles. That chemistry supports a distinct health role. Exposure science for ultrafines is complex, the authors warn. Studies must measure number and surface, not mass alone. A companion paper covers the health evidence in depth.
europmc-pmc1483832:
Two pools of water sat side by side in a Minnesota mine, yet held unlike microbe worlds. Edwards and co-authors read their DNA in 2006 using pyrosequencing, a fast and cheap gene reading method. The two spots in the Soudan Mine differed in chemistry and water flow.

Gene reads showed the microbes ran distinct chemistry on what each pool offered. Paths for carbon use, iron capture, nitrogen uptake, and breathing set the two groups apart. Both groups also differed wholly from any microbe set read before. Edwards argues the method will speed the study of microbe life in the wild.
europmc-pmc1637132:
New neurons born in the adult brain may end up just like those born in youth. Laplagne and co-authors tested that in 2006 in the mouse hippocampus, a region that keeps making neurons for life. They labeled neurons born at each stage with different glow tags.

Recordings from neighbor neurons of different ages showed near-identical wiring. Both received the same balance of excitatory input from the cortex and inhibitory input from local cells. Adult-born neurons fired action potentials like development-born ones. Laplagne proposes the two cohorts form one homogeneous population, a key premise for understanding adult neurogenesis.
europmc-pmc1865532:
Phuc, Alphey and co-authors modeled and built in 2007 a genetic way to crash mosquito populations late in life. Releasing sterile insects can shrink pest numbers, but in species where crowding limits survival, killing larvae early just frees resources for the rest. Death timed late in development should beat that compensation.

Math models confirmed that killing late in development works considerably better than killing early. No natural strain had the needed traits, so the team engineered one as proof of principle. Their Aedes aegypti strain, the mosquito that spreads dengue and yellow fever, carries a dominant lethal gene that can be repressed during rearing. Released males would pass the lethal trait to wild offspring, which die late rather than as young larvae. The approach stays species-specific and leaves no chemical residue.
europmc-pmc1950232:
Sandi and Pinelo-Nava reviewed in 2007 how stress bends memory, in both helpful and harmful directions. Reports in the field scatter widely: stress can sharpen memory, blunt it, or leave it unchanged. Single-factor explanations had failed to sort out that diversity.

The authors organize the literature by five factors. Those are the source of the stress, its length, and its strength. The last two are its timing against the learning phase, and the kind of learning tested. High stress, whether it comes from the task itself or from outside conditions, tends to strengthen simple Pavlovian conditioning, the learned link between a cue and an outcome. The same high stress tends to harm spatial and explicit learning, which instead follows an inverted U against task-driven stress. All five factors, they conclude, are needed for a model that fits the whole pattern.
europmc-pmc1961632:
Mei, Stewart and co-authors tested in 2007 whether engineered stem cells can prevent acute lung injury in mice. The human form, the acute respiratory distress syndrome, floods the lungs when the air-blood barrier breaks down, and no specific treatment exists. Mesenchymal stem cells calm inflammation, and the gene angiopoietin 1 protects vessel walls.

Thirty minutes after bacterial toxin was placed in the windpipe, mice received stem cells by vein, either plain or carrying the human angiopoietin 1 gene. Treated mice showed far less lung inflammation. Cell counts in lung wash fluid fell by about half, and the neutrophil counts that mark acute injury fell by about three fifths. Inflammatory cytokine levels dropped in both the wash fluid and the lung tissue itself. The gene-armed cells combined cell therapy with a vessel-protecting payload.
europmc-pmc2124932:
Joseph Erlanger and E. G. Festerling, of the University of Wisconsin and Washington University in St. Louis, took up the breathing waves of blood pressure in 1912. Lewis had lately called the teaching a widespread misunderstanding.

The literature, they find, does not support one wave type. Workers studying the same species recorded opposite results, and most human findings disagree with the textbook pattern. Their second aim is a method: continuous blood pressure records in man, using the cuff instrument's oscillations read against steady outside pressures. Figures show how the swings shrink and change shape as pressure falls, and how the foot of each oscillation splits or merges. Readers get both a correction to a textbook claim and a tool for watching pressure breathe, beat by beat.
europmc-pmc2125232:
E. B. Krumbhaar and J. H. Musser closed their spleen series in 1914 by testing the organ's supposed rule over red cell making and breaking. Three checks come first. Blood entering the spleen and blood leaving it show no real differences in their counts. Free hemoglobin, reported by Banti and Furno in the splenic vein, could not be confirmed. Spleen extracts show no definite power to break red cells in a dish.

Then comes the surprise. Extracts of liver, kidney, and red cells do nothing of the kind. That supports Danilewsky's idea that the spleen sends the bone marrow a go-ahead signal for red cell formation. Feeding raw spleen to spleenless dogs, though, does not clearly prevent their anemia. Readers get an organ acquitted of destruction and tentatively credited with encouragement.
europmc-pmc2125332:
Samuel Goldschmidt and Richard M. Pearce of the University of Pennsylvania's research medicine department tracked metabolism in four dogs in 1915, before spleen removal and from three days to three months after. Nitrogen balance, fat use, and iron output were the measures, against claims (Richet's among them) that the spleen steers such things.

The fourth dog developed a definitely progressive anemia of moderate severity, with slight weight loss, a slightly disturbed nitrogen balance, and a marked rise in iron elimination. The authors lay that dog's troubles on the anemia itself, not the missing spleen. Their verdict: the spleen has no important influence on metabolism. Readers get a major organ's metabolic reputation retired on four dogs' ledgers.
europmc-pmc2128332:
Theobald Smith and Ralph B. Little measured what colostrum, the first milk after birth, means for a newborn calf's survival. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1922. High death rates in the first week of life, from scours and joint and navel infections, framed the question. The calves were split at birth into fed and unfed groups.

All ten calves allowed colostrum after birth survived. Of twelve denied it, eight died and one was killed while dying. A calf killed on the twenty-seventh day carried mixed bacteria in its organs, with hardened kidneys and a diseased joint. Of the last two survivors, one had passing joint trouble and the other a nasal infection. The contrast leaves little room for doubt: something in the first milk arms the calf against the gut germs waiting in its first days.
europmc-pmc2131132:
Richard H. P. Sia showed that a trace of the pneumococcus's soluble substance disarms the defense against that type alone. His paper is the sixth in a growth inhibition series, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1926. The test was a mixture of serum and leucocytes that ordinarily destroys harmless pneumococci in large numbers.

Add a trace of the substance of the matching type, and even a few harmless pneumococci grow freely in the mixture. The action is highly specific: Type II substance helps only Type II germs, Type III substance only Type III. Broth filtrates of young cultures do the same work, tying the chemical to the substance first seen in filtrates. The germ carries a shield cut to its own pattern, a soluble cloak that blinds the defense to the type that shed it. Type specificity, elsewhere a diagnostic gift, appears here as a weapon.
europmc-pmc2131532:
Walther Goebel and Oswald Avery studied the self-digestion of pneumococcus in a 1929 paper at The Rockefeller Institute. Left to themselves, pneumococci break down and dissolve, a process called autolysis. The pair used chemical measures to learn what inside the cell does the breaking, tracking nitrogen and fatty products as the germs dissolved.

Autolysis came with both protein splitting and fat splitting. Protein breakdown raised the amino and non-coagulable nitrogen; fat breakdown freed fatty acids that dissolve in ether. Extracts holding the cell's active enzymes made heat-killed germs dissolve the same way. A bile salt in excess blocked the protein enzyme but not the fat enzyme. Cold germs dissolved in the bile salt without either breakdown, a separate action.
europmc-pmc2131632:
Duran-Reynals studied organ extracts and vaccine virus in a 1929 paper in The Journal of Experimental Medicine. Tissue from rabbits immune to vaccinia was mixed with two strains of vaccine virus, and extracts of normal organs were tested the same way. The question was whether body tissues can weaken the virus, or, strangely, make it stronger.

Brain and testicle tissue from immune rabbits fixed or inactivated both virus strains. Extracts of normal testicles, by contrast, raised the infectivity of both strains to an extraordinary degree. The extracts seem to act on the host's cells, not the virus: virus injected into a vein settled most readily in skin prepared with testicle extract days before. Rabbits with such boosted lesions also showed general symptoms.
europmc-pmc2140732:
Crozier and Stier, at Rutgers University, measured the frog's throat breathing rhythm against temperature in a 1925 paper. Frogs pulse their throat in a steady respiratory rhythm. Around one mid temperature, many frog processes change their temperature behavior, and the pair tested whether this rhythm shares that critical zone.

The rhythm's frequency carries a single critical thermal increment across the range. Near the critical temperature irregularities appear, though they fade as the animals settle to room conditions. The controlling process seems to sit at a synapse, a nerve junction, and belongs with the respiratory group of reactions. Its temperature characteristic sets it sharply apart from reactions known to be catalyzed by hydrogen ions.
europmc-pmc2141032:
Before asking whether clotted blood pigment can be unclotted, M. L. Anson and A. E. Mirsky first need hemoglobin that is fully clotted. Their 1929 paper, from the Rockefeller Institute, opens a series on protein coagulation and its reversal by setting out several ways to prepare completely denatured hemoglobin.

The methods are given with the evidence that each one fully changes the protein. Hemoglobin, they show, behaves as a typical coagulable protein, much like the better-known examples. That groundwork matters because coagulation was long treated as a one-way change. By fixing exactly what the clotted starting material is, the paper prepares the ground for the pair's later claims that the process can in fact be reversed.
europmc-pmc2242832:
Couderc and a large team built a mouse model in 2008 for chikungunya, a mosquito-borne virus causing fever, rash and joint pain. Severe cases involving the brain had appeared in newborns and vulnerable adults, but the basis of severity was unknown. Adult normal mice resisted infection. Newborn mice proved susceptible, with severity depending on age. Mice with partly or fully disabled type-I interferon signalling, a first-line antiviral system, developed mild or severe disease respectively.

In mild infection the virus first multiplied in the liver, then targeted muscle, joint and skin fibroblasts, matching human biopsy findings. In severe infection it also reached the brain, specifically the choroid plexuses and meninges, the brain's fluid and lining tissues. Symptoms thus match the tissues the virus attacks. Youth and weak interferon signalling are identified as risk factors.
europmc-pmc2292732:
In 2008 Heinemann and co-authors pooled results from trials of drug treatment for advanced pancreatic cancer. The standard drug was gemcitabine, used on its own. Their question was whether adding a second cell-killing drug helped patients live longer.

They combined 15 trials with 4,465 patients in a meta-analysis, a study that merges earlier studies. Adding a second drug gave a small survival gain overall, with a hazard ratio of 0.91, and the gain was clearest for platinum drugs and for fluoropyrimidines. Patients who were fit at the start gained the most, with a hazard ratio of 0.76, while frail patients gained nothing. Combinations with irinotecan, exatecan, or pemetrexed showed no benefit.
europmc-pmc2573032:
Dudbridge and Gusnanto tackled a practical puzzle in 2008. It concerns genome-wide association studies. How strong must a signal be to count as real, when a million markers are tested at once? Theory had suggested thresholds, but nobody had checked them against real data. The team used genotypes collected by the Wellcome Trust Case-Control Consortium, a landmark British study collection.

They thinned the markers to increasing densities. Using permutation, shuffling the data to build a null picture, they found the cut-off giving a 5 percent family-wise error rate. Extrapolating to infinite density gave a genome-wide threshold near 7.2 times ten to the minus eight. A shortcut based on eigenvalues underestimated the true number of tests tenfold. The authors conclude permutation is still needed, but thresholds can be standardised per population.
europmc-pmc2603332:
Steel, Lowen, Mubareka, and Palese tested in 2009 which versions of an influenza protein let the virus pass between mammals. Since 2003 over 380 human H5N1 cases had been reported, often fatal, yet person-to-person spread stayed rare, and the barrier was unknown. Viruses from human cases often carried changes at positions 627 or 701 of the PB2 protein. The team engineered those changes into two virus backgrounds. They then tested transmission in guinea pigs.

Swapping the mammalian residue at 627 for the bird version reduced transmission in both the H3N2 and H5N1 backgrounds. Adding the asparagine change at 701 alongside it largely restored transmission, compensating for the loss. The authors identify PB2 positions 627 and 701 as determinants of transmission between mammalian hosts across diverse influenza viruses.
europmc-pmc2606032:
van Engelsdorp, Hayes, Underwood, and Pettis surveyed American beekeepers in 2008 to measure honey bee colony losses over the winter of 2007 to 2008. A new ailment, Colony Collapse Disorder, was emptying hives entirely, leaving no dead bees behind. Earlier estimates had skipped winter losses, so the team surveyed operations covering over 19 percent of the nation's estimated 2.44 million colonies.

Total losses reached 35.8 percent of colonies, up from the year before, implying somewhere between three quarters of a million and a million colonies died that winter. Operations reporting colonies that vanished without dead bees lost 40.8 percent of their colonies. Operations without that symptom lost 17.1 percent. Sixty percent of all dead colonies showed the empty-hive pattern. Large operations were hit more, hinting at a contagious factor. Almond pollination made no difference.
europmc-pmc2639432:
Tautenhahn and co-authors described in 2008 a computer method that finds chemical signals in complex lab data more reliably. The data come from a machine pairing that separates mixtures and then weighs each part, a standard tool for studying small molecules in living things. Each compound leaves a two-dimensional signal, and software must first spot those signals correctly.

Their method, called centWave, first gathers rough signal regions from the raw data. It then applies a wave-based filter that sharpens each signal's peak and edges. The team tested it on diluted plant extracts with known contents. centWave found more of the true signals and made fewer false calls than two older tools. It also split apart signals that sat close together or partly overlapped, a common source of error.
europmc-pmc2667632:
Logozzi and colleagues reported in 2009 that the blood of melanoma patients carries far more tiny tumor-linked parcels than the blood of healthy people. The parcels, called exosomes, are shed by normal and cancer cells alike. Melanoma that has spread is incurable, and doctors lack a simple blood marker to track it.

The team built a lab test that catches exosomes using two common parcel proteins, then counts a second set marked with caveolin-1, a protein tied to tumors. In mice carrying human melanoma, parcel levels rose with tumor size. In 90 patients and 58 healthy donors, both parcel types were much higher in patients. The caveolin-1 test caught about 68 percent of patients, the better of the two. Tuning this blood test, the authors suggest, could give a needle-free way to screen and follow the disease.
europmc-pmc2673032:
Dong, Manfredini, and Dimopoulos showed in 2009 that the bacteria living in a mosquito's gut help it fight off malaria. The malaria parasite must cross the mosquito's midgut wall, its narrowest bottleneck, before it can reach a human host. Gut bacteria were known to lower infection rates, but the mechanism was a mystery.

Mosquitoes raised germ-free caught the human malaria parasite far more easily than normal ones. Feeding bacteria back along with the parasite cut infections below normal levels. Gene readings showed the gut flora keeps a set of immune genes switched partway on, a standing guard that includes several parasite-fighting factors. Some of those factors only worked when the flora was present. The mosquito's microbes, the authors conclude, tune its basal immunity, its always-on first defense, against the parasite.
europmc-pmc2683932:
Sabuncu and colleagues, led in reporting by Guillemot's group, evaluated in 2009 a nationwide French campaign to cut needless antibiotic use. France had faced rising drug-resistant pneumococci, the germ behind many chest and ear infections, fed by heavy prescribing. The campaign, run from 2002, urged doctors and the public to save antibiotics for when they truly help.

The evaluation found a significant drop in community antibiotic use over the five years to 2007. The fall was sharpest in prescriptions for children, the group most often given antibiotics for viral colds that the drugs cannot cure. Cutting use matters because resistance follows consumption: the more a germ meets a drug, the faster resistant strains spread. France's result, the authors argue, shows a coordinated national push, repeated each winter, can change prescribing habits at population scale.
europmc-pmc2688132:
Taccone and colleagues analyzed in 2009 how cancer patients fare in European intensive care units, using a 198-unit study across 24 countries. Cancer patients reach intensive care more often than they once did, through both the disease and its harsh treatments, yet solid outcome data were thin. Of 3,147 patients in the parent study, 473 had cancer.

Most had solid tumors; the rest had blood cancers, and that group was sickest, with the most sepsis, lung failure, and kidney failure. Their hospital death rate, 58 percent, was the highest of any group. Averaged together, though, cancer patients died at the same 27 percent rate as patients without cancer. The picture flipped when organs failed in threes: over 75 percent of cancer patients with more than three failing organs died, against about half of other patients. Cancer alone, the authors conclude, should not bar a patient from intensive care.
europmc-pmc2700132:
Merlin, Weston, and Tooher reported in 2009 the revision of Australia's official levels of evidence, the ladder used to grade medical studies. The 1999 ladder ranked study designs by how well they dodge bias, which suited treatment questions. But guidelines and technology assessments also judge tests, prognosis, causes, and screening, where the old ladder fit badly.

A working party kept the four familiar levels, one through four, and stretched each to cover the other question types. A commissioned review of grading systems worldwide and the available empirical evidence guided where each design lands for diagnosis, prognosis, cause, and screening. The revision went through wide public consultation and two long pilot rounds with the agencies that use it daily. Consistency was the goal: the same ladder, with the same meaning, whatever the clinical question.
europmc-pmc2797632:
Vieira-Silva and Rocha showed in 2010 that how fast a microbe can grow leaves a readable stamp on its genome. They compared traits across two hundred fourteen kinds of bacteria and archaea, single-celled life forms. Fast growers carry more gene copies, arrange their chromosomes in set ways, and favor certain code words in their genes.

All these traits tracked together, and code word bias predicted top growth speed better than any other trait, even ribosome gene counts. The authors built a predictor that works on short DNA fragments from mixed samples. Gut samples favored fast growers, a toxic mine film favored slow ones, soil held all speeds, and baby gut microbes grew faster than adult ones.
europmc-pmc2810332:
Gamboa and colleagues found in 2010 that many malaria parasites in Peru's Amazon region are invisible to the rapid tests clinics rely on. Most rapid tests hunt a parasite protein called HRP2. In Iquitos, eight of nine blood samples that clearly held parasites under the microscope tested negative or barely positive.

Gene checks showed those samples lacked the genes that make HRP2 and its sister protein, or their neighbors. Looking back over one hundred forty-eight samples from across the region, about four in ten lacked the first gene and seven in ten lacked the second. The authors warn that HRP2-based tests will miss many cases there, and other test types should be used instead.
europmc-pmc2864732:
Chevin, Lande, and Mace worked in 2010 toward a theory that predicts when a population can track a steadily changing environment and when it will die out. Species face faster change than most have evolved with, driven largely by human activity. A population can cope by adjusting during life, called plasticity, or by evolving across generations.

Their framework joins those coping routes with population growth math to find a critical speed of change. Below that speed a population holds on, and above it decline runs away toward extinction. Plastic responses help most when change is moderate and predictable, but they can also shield genes from selection and slow true adaptation. The authors show how each piece can be measured in real populations, making the theory testable in the field.
europmc-pmc2882432:
MacKay, Smith, Dobbie, and Pell studied in 2010 whether being born even slightly early raises a child's need for special educational support. Earlier work had tied preterm birth to such needs, but the risk across the whole range of pregnancy length was unmapped. Linking birth records to school records gave them over four hundred thousand Scottish schoolchildren to analyze.

Need for special education rose step by step as birth came earlier, with no safe threshold where risk suddenly began. The gradient extended well into the range usually called full term. Children born at thirty-seven to thirty-nine weeks carried a small but real extra risk over those born at forty. Even modest shifts matter at population scale, the authors note, when timing of planned deliveries is decided.
europmc-pmc2896632:
Jancík, Drábek, Radzioch, and Hajdúch reviewed in 2010 the clinical weight of KRAS, one of the most common cancer genes. KRAS makes a small switch protein that relays growth signals from the surface of the cell to the nucleus, flipping between on and off states. Mutations jam the switch on, driving uncontrolled division in pancreatic, colon, lung, and other cancers.

Jammed KRAS also blunts treatment: tumors carrying the mutation resist chemotherapy and shrug off a major class of targeted antibody drugs aimed at a surface growth receptor. Testing tumors for KRAS status therefore guides which therapies are worth giving and sharpens prognosis. The review covers how the gene is regulated, where its mutations cluster, and the strategies being tried to drug a protein long called undruggable.
europmc-pmc2902432:
Vanier reviewed in 2010 Niemann-Pick disease type C, a rare disorder in which cells cannot move cholesterol and related fats properly. It affects roughly one in one hundred twenty thousand births. The illness mixes body and brain signs: newborns may show liver jaundice, infants enlarged spleen or liver, and brain symptoms that define severity arrive at almost any age.

The most characteristic sign is failure of up-and-down eye movement. Clumsiness, slurred speech, swallowing trouble, and progressive dementia follow, with seizures and sudden muscle-weakness attacks in many patients. Faults in either of two genes cause it, one accounting for ninety-five percent of families. In brain tissue the stored fats are mainly gangliosides, a puzzle the review weighs alongside emerging therapies.
europmc-pmc2910032:
Seidler and co-authors mapped in 2010 how the blood's patrolling monocytes change across healthy adult life. Monocytes come in classical and non-classical subsets with different patrol routes and jobs, and mouse work hints they shift with age. Blood from one hundred eighty-one volunteers aged eighteen to eighty-eight was profiled for subset counts, surface markers, and the chemokines that call monocytes into tissue.

Total monocyte counts stayed flat with age, but the non-classical subset grew steadily in older volunteers. Those extra cells carried less of a key display molecule and less of a vessel-patrolling receptor, which may blunt their work. A calling signal, MCP-1, also rose with age in blood, while lab-grown macrophages from old and young donors released cytokines alike. Aging remodels the patrol force rather than shrinking it.
europmc-pmc2936532:
Bustos and colleagues studied how the plant Arabidopsis answers phosphate starvation in a 2010 gene study. The transcription factor PHR1 was already known to matter, and the team asked how much of the whole response it commands alongside its partner PHL1.

Comparing normal plants with mutants lacking PHR1, PHL1, or both, they found the pair controls most genes switched on or off during starvation. Switched-on genes often carried the PHR1 binding motif in their promoters, while switched-off genes did not, suggesting indirect control of repression. Mutating that motif in two test genes broke their starvation response.
europmc-pmc2950132:
Johnson and co-authors estimated which pneumococcal types cause severe disease in young children worldwide in a 2010 project summary. The bacterium leads among causes of pneumonia, blood infection, and meningitis in children under five, killing hundreds of thousands yearly.

Vaccines protect only against the types they contain, and three versions with widening coverage were reaching use around that time. The project gathered type-specific disease data globally and by region to show how much illness each vaccine could prevent. Such counts guide which vaccine each country should adopt and help track whether non-vaccine types grow after rollout, especially in poorer nations.
europmc-pmc2982832:
Maricic, Whitten, and Pääbo described a cheap way to fish out complete mitochondrial genomes from mixed DNA in a 2010 methods study. Enrichment tools usually need pricey commercial kits and suit short targets poorly.

Their trick uses tailor-made long copying products as bait to capture whole mitochondrial genomes, several kilobases long. In one run they captured forty-six genomes in parallel and read them on a single lane of a high-throughput sequencer. Because the approach is simple and economical, it fits population genetics, forensics, and ancient DNA work where many mitochondrial genomes are wanted at once.
europmc-pmc3019132:
Gupta and Lis systematically reviewed whether low blood albumin before treatment predicts shorter cancer survival in a 2010 article. Albumin, a blood protein tied to nutrition, is cheap to measure, and interest in malnutrition as a survival factor was growing.

Searching fifteen years of studies across cancer types, they found a strikingly consistent pattern. In gut cancers, nearly every study linked higher albumin with longer survival after full adjustment. Similar findings recurred elsewhere. Because the test is routine and inexpensive, the authors present pretreatment albumin as a practical, if rough, guide to outlook.
europmc-pmc3179432:
Wan-Seob Cho and colleagues traced severe lung injury from zinc oxide nanoparticles in rats in a 2011 paper in Particle and Fibre Toxicology. The particles are produced in bulk for sunscreens, paints, and coatings, so accidental breathing is a realistic risk. Two doses were placed into rat lungs, with checks over the following month.

Injury progressed rather than fading: allergy-type cells flooded in, airway lining and mucus cells multiplied, and scarring fibrosis spread around the airways, with allergy antibody levels rising. The particles dissolve quickly in acid, exactly the condition inside the cell compartments that swallow them, and dissolved zinc alone reproduced the same lung damage. In cultured scavenger cells the particles burst those compartments and killed the cells. The authors blame rapid acid dissolution as the core mechanism.
europmc-pmc3279232:
Kyung-Mi Song, Seonghwan Lee, and Changill Ban reviewed aptamers, short molecules that fold to grip chosen targets, in this 2012 article in Sensors. Aptamers are pitched as rivals to antibodies, matching their targeting ability while adding heat stability, low production cost, and broad design freedom. The review explains how they are made and what they are good for.

Aptamers are fished out of vast random libraries by in vitro selection. The authors detail the main selection setups. They range from membrane filtration and affinity columns to magnetic beads and capillary electrophoresis. On the application side, aptamers serve disease diagnosis and the detection of small molecules, read out by electrochemical, color, optical, or mass-sensitive instruments that exploit their stability and easy modification. The authors present them as core components for future medical and analytical devices.
europmc-pmc3284432:
Ruqaiyyah Siddiqui and Naveed Ahmed Khan reviewed the biology and disease-causing behavior of Acanthamoeba in this 2012 article in Parasites and Vectors. This free-living protist, found widely in the environment, can cause a blinding infection of the cornea and a fatal inflammation of the brain. The review draws together what makes it dangerous.

Contributing factors span the microbe's own biology and genetic diversity, its spread through soil and water, and the susceptibility of the host. The authors highlight possible treatments and preventive measures alongside the risk factors. They also note the organism's second career as a laboratory model. It serves studies of cell differentiation, movement, engulfing behavior, bacterial pathogenesis, and evolution. And it acts as a Trojan horse, sheltering other microbes inside itself, from viruses and bacteria to yeasts.
europmc-pmc3292132:
Yoo and Lee reviewed devices that measure blood sugar for people with diabetes, in an article published in 2010. Keeping blood sugar near normal lowers the harm diabetes does over time, so patients need to check levels often. Over fifty years, inventors moved from lab tests toward small meters patients can use at home and sensors worn on the body.

The review explains how the sensors work, how well they perform, and where each kind fits in daily care. It covers finger stick meters, continuous monitors, and experimental systems that need no blood at all. The authors say real progress has been made, but accuracy and reliability still fall short, and patients need steady training to use the devices well.
europmc-pmc3338532:
Tran and colleagues reviewed whether certain hospital procedures raise the risk of passing respiratory infections to health workers, in a 2012 paper. Procedures that stir up fine sprays of fluid, such as placing a breathing tube, are suspected of spreading germs from patient to staff. The SARS outbreaks, where many workers fell ill, made the question urgent.

Searching two decades of literature, the team found ten usable studies, all on SARS. Placing a breathing tube in the windpipe carried the most consistent added risk across studies. Noninvasive breathing support, cutting an opening in the windpipe, and hand ventilation before tube placement also raised risk. Many other suspected procedures, including suctioning, scoping the airways, and chest compressions, showed no clear link. The authors stress that the evidence is thin and confined to one disease.
europmc-pmc3351032:
Powe and colleagues tested which form of vitamin D in the blood actually tracks with bone health. Clinicians usually measure total 25-hydroxyvitamin D, yet most of it circulates bound to a carrier protein, and the free or bioavailable fraction may be the part tissues can use.

In 49 healthy young adults, the researchers measured total, free, and bioavailable vitamin D alongside bone mineral density. The free and bioavailable fractions correlated with density, while the total level did not show the same relationship. The result challenges routine reliance on total vitamin D and suggests binding protein levels help explain differences between population groups.
europmc-pmc3367632:
Voss and colleagues reported in 2005 on a drug-resistant staph germ found among Dutch pig farmers. Their study began after a baby girl awaiting chest surgery tested positive for MRSA, a strain that resists standard drugs. Her parents, who raised pigs, carried the same germ, which pointed the team toward farms.

Screening twenty-six farmers in the region, the team found six carried MRSA in the nose or throat. That rate was far above the very low level seen in Dutch hospital patients.
