Lab typing showed one clone, called t108, spread most widely among farmers and their surroundings. The findings warned that livestock work could seed resistant infections in the wider community.
europmc-pmc3385432:
Perera and colleagues followed New York City children in 2012 to test whether air pollution before birth shapes behavior at school age. The pollutants, called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, pour from fossil fuel burning and traffic. Mothers wore personal air monitors during pregnancy, and their blood was checked for pollution-linked DNA marks.

At age six or seven, more than two hundred fifty children took a standard behavior checklist. Those with high prenatal exposure, by either measure, showed more symptoms of anxiety and depression and more attention problems. The mothers were nonsmokers from two city communities, which sharpens the result. Ordinary city air, the authors conclude, can affect young minds.
europmc-pmc3397132:
Corbeil, Williams, and Labute warned in 2012 that how a test dataset is prepared can swing the reported success of drug-docking software. Docking programs try to fit candidate molecules into protein pockets. The team ran their MOE software on the standard Astex test set with a new scoring function.

For most targets the top-ranked fit landed close to the known X-ray structure, and nearly all targets had a good fit among the top thirty tries. The failures traced mostly to water molecules missing from the source data. A small energy-scale slip in preparation moved success rates by more than a fifth. Clean, complete datasets, they argue, matter as much as clever software.
europmc-pmc3420432:
Téllez-Zenteno and Hernández-Ronquillo reviewed in 2012 what is known about the epidemiology of temporal lobe epilepsy, the most common partial epilepsy sent for surgery. Partial epilepsies make up about three fifths of adult cases, and this type often resists drugs. Yet counting it demands brain scans, electrical recordings, and careful reading of seizures, so population data stay scarce.

Most knowledge comes from specialist referral centers or is inferred from broader epilepsy studies. Silent scar tissue found by chance in healthy people, plus mild benign forms, hint the true numbers are underestimated. The review walks through definitions, published rates, and the traps in studying them. It closes with recommendations for cleaner future studies.
europmc-pmc3460232:
Falcone Ferreyra, Rius, and Casati reviewed flavonoids in 2012, the plant pigments and protectants with a long list of jobs. How plants build them is now well mapped, along with the trio of regulator families that switch the pathway on and off. That knowledge has let engineers retune the pathway for valued products.

In the plant, flavonoids shield against ultraviolet light and pathogen attack, help roots invite the bacteria that feed them nitrogen, and keep pollen fertile. The review covers those functions and the engineering record, from tweaking flowers and crops to rebuilding the pathway inside microbes for bulk production of prized compounds. Industry interest runs from nutrition to materials, and the authors chart where genetic control is heading.
europmc-pmc3491832:
Joining a useful protein to an antibody's Fc tail can make a drug last longer and hit harder, and Daniel M. Czajkowsky, Jun Hu, Zhifeng Shao, and Richard J. Pleass review this Fc-fusion field in 2012. The first example, a CD4 fusion blocking HIV entry into T cells, dates to 1989.

Several Fc-fusion products have since reached the market for a range of diseases. Newer work pushes into vaccines and intravenous immunoglobulin therapy, and outside medicine into affinity reagents for microarray devices. The review gathers strategies to raise efficacy and safety for each use, with extra attention to younger, less-charted applications. Fc domains, the authors show, have become a general engineering platform.
europmc-pmc3494832:
Broca's area in the left frontal lobe has hosted a long argument: is it a specialist language region or a general-purpose one? Evelina Fedorenko, John Duncan, and Nancy Kanwisher answer with single-subject brain scans in 2012, mapping each person's region precisely rather than averaging brains.

Both sides turn out to be right. Inside Broca's area, one set of subregions responds quite specifically to language. Beside and around them sits another set engaged broadly across many tasks and kinds of content. The two systems lie side by side, which explains why group-average studies kept blurring them into one mixed picture. Specialization and generality, the study shows, can share one named brain area.
europmc-pmc3511432:
Genome scans have named ten new risk genes for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, and Celeste M. Karch and six colleagues ask what those genes are doing in the brain in 2012. They measure gene expression and risk variants in parietal lobe tissue from Alzheimer's cases and age-matched cognitively normal controls.

Expression of ABCA7, CD33, and CR1 tracks the clinical dementia rating: higher levels accompany worse decline. CD33, CLU, and CR1 expression also separates disease from control brains. BIN1 behaves differently, with higher expression tied to later onset. MS4A6A levels track tangle and plaque scores. The risk genes cluster around cholesterol handling, synaptic function, and immune response, the authors note.
europmc-pmc3570532:
Andreas Roetzer, Stefan Niemann, and colleagues compared two ways of tracing a tuberculosis outbreak in PLoS Medicine in 2013. Health teams type the bacteria from each patient to decide which cases are linked. The standard typing methods read only small parts of the genome, so unrelated strains can look alike. Whole genome sequencing reads nearly everything, and the team set the two approaches against each other over years of one outbreak.

Old-style typing did group some strains together falsely, the comparison showed. Sequencing split those cases apart and matched the links found by shoe-leather contact tracing far better. Cases that contact work had connected turned out to share near-identical genomes, while look-alike strains from typing proved distant. For outbreak teams, the result argues that full sequencing gives a truer transmission map and fewer false leads.
europmc-pmc3619132:
György Haskó and Bruce Cronstein reviewed adenosine as the immune system's own brake fluid in Frontiers in Immunology in 2013. Adenosine is a small molecule released when the energy currency ATP breaks down, which happens wherever tissue is stressed. Nearly thirty years earlier it was first shown to quiet neutrophils, the first-responder white cells. Since then its receptors have emerged as feedback regulators that keep inflammation from overshooting, and this review takes stock of that system cell by cell.

Effects on neutrophils and on monocytes and macrophages get the deepest treatment: adhesion, engulfing, and signal release all shift under adenosine's four receptor types. A clinical thread runs alongside, since methotrexate, the anchor drug for rheumatoid arthritis, works in large part by raising adenosine where it matters. Understanding that pathway, the authors argue, explains both the drug's power and its limits, and points to receptor-targeted anti-inflammatory drugs.
europmc-pmc3681632:
Screening cuts cervical cancer deaths, Peirson, Fitzpatrick-Lewis, Ciliska and Warren conclude in a 2013 systematic review and meta-analysis in Systematic Reviews. The review fed a Canadian task force update of its screening guideline. Searches from 1995 to 2012 across three data banks yielded 27 papers on 24 studies, plus five older studies from a United States review. Women aged 15 to 70 were screened by cell tests or virus DNA tests in the studies covered.

One Indian trial found even a single lifetime screen cut death risk from this cancer by about a third against no screening. Cohort and case-control proof agreed: cell screening roughly halved or better the risk of invasive cancer. Proof could not pin down best start and stop ages or screening gaps. Data did support screening women aged 30 and over, with gaps of up to five years.
europmc-pmc3700032:
Rudan and colleagues estimated the burden of childhood pneumonia for 192 countries in 2010, giving national figures for cases, severe illness, deaths, risk factors, and the pathogens responsible. Their model spread global and regional totals across countries using five main risk factors, including malnutrition, low birth weight, and solid fuel use.

In low- and middle-income countries, incidence ran near a fifth of an episode per child each year, and roughly one case in nine became severe. The estimates draw on systematic reviews of the major causes, including pneumococcus, Hib, RSV, and influenza. The authors intend the country-level numbers for policymakers planning pneumonia control.
europmc-pmc3700832:
Chen, Ou, and Hollis systematically reviewed what happens when cancer services routinely collect patient-reported outcome measures, questionnaires in which patients score their own symptoms and wellbeing. They re-examined earlier reviews and graded twenty-seven studies published between 2000 and 2011.

Well-implemented collection clearly improved communication between patients and clinicians, and patient satisfaction. Evidence also grew that it helps monitor treatment response and surface problems nobody had spotted. But evidence was weak or absent for changes in patient care, better health outcomes, or gains in how services perform. The reviewers support routine collection while warning that its deeper benefits remain unproven.
europmc-pmc3733432:
James Krinsley and a large international team reported a cohort study in Critical Care in 2013 on blood sugar control in very ill patients. High blood sugar, low blood sugar, and wide swings in blood sugar have each been tied to higher death risk. The team asked whether having diabetes changes those links.

They studied 44,964 patients in 23 intensive care units across nine countries, using data gathered from 2001 to 2012. For patients without diabetes, mid-range average blood sugar was safest, and low blood sugar and wide swings each raised death risk. For patients with diabetes, the safest average range sat higher, and very tight control was tied to more deaths. Faults in more than one sugar domain stacked up, above all for patients without diabetes.
europmc-pmc3762332:
Shaohui Hu and a large group of co-authors reported a study in eLife in 2013 that overturns a standard view of DNA methylation. Methylation at gene start regions was generally thought to block transcription factors, the proteins that switch genes on, and so silence genes. The team used protein microarrays to survey the whole human transcription factor family.

Many purified factors turned out to bind DNA only, or better, when a CpG site was methylated. Some factors bound different DNA sequences depending on methylation. Focusing on one factor, KLF4, the team separated its methylated and unmethylated binding by mutation, and confirmed both modes in human embryonic stem cells. The authors say methylation-dependent binding is widespread and reframes how methylation controls genes.
europmc-pmc3860432:
Howard J. Edenberg wrote a solo review on alcohol genes in Alcohol Research & Health in 2007. Two enzymes do most of the work of breaking down alcohol in the body. The first turns alcohol into a toxic middle product, and the second clears that product away. Both come in gene variants that change their speed.

Fast first-step variants flood the body with the toxic product, which makes drinking unpleasant. A near-dead second-step variant does the same by blocking cleanup. Both types protect against alcoholism, and they are more common in some ethnic groups than others. The review also notes that non-coding gene variants may tune risk in ways still being mapped. Genes thus shape drinking habits in part through simple chemistry.
europmc-pmc3915232:
David Z. I. Cherney and colleagues test a diabetes drug's effects on artery stiffness in Cardiovascular Diabetology in 2014. Their subjects were forty adults with type 1 diabetes and normal blood pressure. The drug, empagliflozin, blocks sugar reabsorption in the kidneys and had already lowered blood pressure and blood sugar in this condition, raising hopes it might also ease stiff arteries.

Each patient was tested with blood sugar held low and then high, before and after eight weeks on the drug. Artery stiffness measures fell under both sugar conditions, and systolic pressure dipped slightly when sugar was normal. Heart rate variability and adrenaline-related chemicals did not change. The authors suggest the benefit comes from the drug's wider actions, including sugar and weight loss.
europmc-pmc3948032:
Ami R. Zota, Antonia M. Calafat, and Tracey J. Woodruff track how Americans' exposure to phthalates changed over a decade, in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2014. Phthalates are plastic additives found almost everywhere; three of them were being phased out over health concerns and replaced by substitutes, but whether body levels followed was unknown. The team combined urine measurements of eleven phthalate breakdown products from 11,071 people in the national health survey, 2001 to 2010.

Breakdown products of the phased-out chemicals fell sharply, by between 17 and 42 percent over the decade. But products of replacement phthalates climbed, one by more than 200 percent. Children carried higher levels than adults for several compounds, though the gap narrowed. Regulation and industry substitution, the authors note, are reshaping exposure rather than removing it.
europmc-pmc3988532:
Chuan Hua He and colleagues identify the receptor for a disease-linked protein. Their paper appeared in Cell Reports in 2013. The protein is chitinase 3-like 1, or Chi3l1. It belongs to an ancient enzyme family. Its levels go wrong in inflammation, infection, and cancer. It boosts bacterial killing in the body. Yet it also protects tissue by restraining cell death and scarring. No receptor for it was known until this work.

The team shows that Chi3l1 docks onto a specific receptor. The receptor is interleukin-13 receptor alpha 2. The two form a three-part complex with interleukin-13 itself. Through that receptor, Chi3l1 switches on several signaling chains in macrophages. It steers a long list of responses. Oxidant injury, cell death, and inflammasome activation are on the list. Antibacterial defense, melanoma spread, and scarring signals are too. Naming the receptor turns a puzzling protein into a druggable axis.
europmc-pmc3989032:
T. J. D. Knight-Jones and J. Rushton assess the cost of foot and mouth disease in Preventive Veterinary Medicine in 2013. The disease kills few animals, yet it strikes huge numbers of livestock. Its total impact, they argue, is vast, and it falls in two broad parts.

Direct losses come from lower output and changed herd make-up. Indirect losses come from control costs, lost access to markets, and limits on better breeds and methods. Losses in regions where the disease is settled run to billions of dollars a year, and outbreaks in free zones cost billions more. The poorest livestock keepers suffer most, so the authors call for shared public spending and stronger vet services in poor countries.
europmc-pmc4003832:
Dimitry A. Chistiakov, Igor A. Sobenin, Victor V. Revin, Alexander N. Orekhov, and Yuri V. Bobryshev review how mitochondria age, in BioMed Research International in 2014. Mitochondria are the cell's power units, and they bear their own small set of DNA. With age, that DNA picks up faults and harm from reactive oxygen, a by-product of the power-making process itself.

Aged mitochondria make less energy and leak more reactive oxygen, while their defences weaken. The making of new mitochondria slows, and the clean-up process that removes worn units fades. Faulty quality control adds to the decline, and more cells in old tissue die by a self-kill program that mitochondria help drive. Eating less and regular exercise can delay this ageing and soften age-linked traits in people. The review ties these strands into one account of how power-unit decline feeds whole-body ageing.
europmc-pmc4010932:
Kei Arimatsu and ten co-authors test whether a gum disease germ can disturb the gut and the body, in Scientific Reports in 2014. Gum disease has been tied to diabetes, artery disease, and fatty liver, but direct proof of a route was missing. The team guessed that swallowed oral germs upset the gut's microbe mix, letting toxins leak into the blood.

Mice were fed Porphyromonas gingivalis, a lead gum disease germ, by mouth. Their gut microbe mix shifted, with one large group rising in share. The mice also showed insulin resistance and broader body inflammation. Blood toxin levels tended to rise, and genes for the gut wall's sealing proteins fell in the small intestine. A leakier gut fits the toxin rise. The authors offer this chain, from mouth germ to gut shift to body-wide effects, as a new frame for how gum disease links to other illness.
europmc-pmc4060032:
Jonathan B. Puritz, Christopher M. Hollenbeck, and John R. Gold presented dDocent, a free software pipeline for population genetics. Their paper appeared in PeerJ in 2014. The pipeline handles RADseq data, a method that reads DNA at many cut sites to find genetic differences across a population.

dDocent was built for non-model organisms, species without a finished reference genome, including ones with very high genetic variation. It trims reads, builds loci from scratch, maps reads, and calls single-letter and insertion differences. Tested on double-digest data from three marine fishes, it found more shared variants, across more individuals and at higher coverage, than the older Stacks pipeline. A full online manual accompanies the tool.
europmc-pmc4071332:
Irene Gallego Romero, Athma A. Pai, Jenny Tung, and Yoav Gilad measured how RNA decay distorts gene activity readings from RNA sequencing. Their study appeared in BMC Biology in 2014. Old or poorly stored samples are often the only option, for instance in fieldwork, but whether decay biases results was disputed.

The team let tissue samples decay for set times before extracting RNA, covering the full range of a standard quality score. Decay shifted measured activity for many genes, and standard corrections failed to remove the effect. Degraded samples also yielded slightly less complex libraries. Fitting the quality score directly in a statistical model corrected most of the distortion, letting meaningful signals be recovered when quality and the study factor are unrelated.
europmc-pmc4096432:
Robert A. Laird, Jayce Gilbert, Peter Kent, and Jennifer L. Keating compared spine and pelvis movement in people with and without low back pain. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders in 2014. Clinicians routinely check posture and movement, assuming faulty movement can be spotted and corrected to ease pain.

Searching eight databases to January 2014, they found forty-three eligible studies using skin-surface measures. On average, people with back pain showed no difference in standing spinal curve, but they did show reduced lumbar range of motion, poorer position sense, and slower movement than pain-free people. Whether these traits precede the pain or follow from it is unknown. The findings give clinicians a firmer picture of what actually differs.
europmc-pmc4097832:
Marcos Malumbres, writing alone, reviewed cyclin-dependent kinases, a family of enzymes that run cell division and adjust gene transcription. His review appeared in Genome Biology in 2014. Each kinase in the family only works when paired with a partner protein called a cyclin.

In mammals the family has expanded into three subfamilies tied to the cell cycle and five tied to transcription. Most members bind just one or a few cyclins, a sign of specialised jobs. Malumbres stresses that the two roles often combine in a single family member, blurring the traditional split. Loss of control over these enzymes marks several diseases, including cancer. Drugs blocking specific members have produced encouraging results in clinical trials.
europmc-pmc4113732:
Matthias Eder, Klaus Kopka, and colleagues reported preclinical and production details for a radioactive tracer that images prostate cancer. Their paper appeared in Pharmaceuticals in 2014. The tracer targets PSMA, a protein on prostate cancer cells, and had already shown promise in first human scans.

The molecule pairs a PSMA-blocking unit with a chelator, HBED-CC, that grips the radioactive gallium label. Swapping in a standard chelator had wrecked image quality, proving HBED-CC itself helps the tracer bind its target. The chelator also labels fast at room temperature and holds the metal stably. The paper explains these chemistry advantages and adds new preclinical data plus practical aspects of making the tracer as a radiopharmaceutical for clinics.
europmc-pmc4140132:
Manzoor Ahmad Gatoo and a team of peers reviewed how the traits of nano stuff shape its power to harm. Their review came out in BioMed Research International in 2014. Nano goods are now part of daily life. That spread makes it a must to know what they do to living things and to the world around us.

For plain bulk stuff, what it is made of rules its harm. At the nano scale, more traits take charge. Size and shape count. So do the build of its core, its skin area, its charge, its rough or smooth skin, and how long it lasts. Two goods with the same make-up can act in far apart ways once made this small. The team works through each trait and its role in the harms on record. It urges full checks before a stuff is judged safe.
europmc-pmc4275032:
Jessica L Lister and Alexander R Horswill review how Staphylococcus aureus biofilms break apart and spread. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology in 2014. This bacterium is a major cause of hospital and community infections, and its biofilms on implants and tissue resist drugs and immune attack.

When cells leave a biofilm they can seed new sites and make an infection worse. The review sets out the known escape routes: enzymes that cut the biofilm matrix, signals that switch cells to a free state, and newer broad mechanisms found in recent work. Knowing the escape routes matters because blocking or forcing dispersal could change how chronic infections are treated.
europmc-pmc4276632:
Jean-Philippe Chaput, Valerie Carson, Casey E Gray, Mark S Tremblay, and Rachel Davey argue that health rules for children should cover the whole day, not just hard exercise. Their paper appeared in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health in 2014. Guidelines of the time stressed strong activity and, more lately, sitting time, but left out light activity and sleep.

Light movement such as walking brings real gains, and sleep shapes how the other behaviors affect health. The authors show that the parts of the day trade off against each other, since hours spent on one cannot be spent on another. They call for guidance built on all movement behaviors across the full twenty four hours.
europmc-pmc4287932:
Tuan Zea Tan and six co-authors built a single score for how far a cancer has shifted toward a mobile, invasive state. Their study appeared in EMBO Molecular Medicine in 2014. This shift, called epithelial-mesenchymal transition, is thought to help cancers spread, yet each cancer type had its own gene signature and no shared measure existed.

The team derived a universal scoring method from gene patterns across ovarian, breast, bladder, lung, colorectal, and gastric cancers. Scores lined up with known signatures and separated cell lines and tumors along one spectrum. High scores tracked with worse disease free survival in ovarian and colorectal cancers, and with distinct drug responses. The score gives cancer research a common yardstick for a key process.
europmc-pmc4308932:
Cosimo Chelazzi, Gianluca Villa, Paola Mancinelli, A Raffaele De Gaudio, and Chiara Adembri review the glycocalyx, the sugar rich coat on blood vessel walls, and how sepsis strips it away. Their review appeared in Critical Care in 2015. The coat helps keep fluid inside vessels, and its loss lets fluid leak into tissue, a hallmark of severe infection.

In sepsis, inflammatory signals and white blood cells attack the glycocalyx everywhere at once, which helps explain organ failure far from the infection site, in kidneys, lungs, and liver. Fragments of the coat in blood can mark how bad the damage is. The review also covers early ideas for protecting or restoring the layer during treatment.
europmc-pmc4356432:
Hamish Smith reviewed depression in people with cancer in Oncology Letters in 2015. Depression affects more than one in ten cancer patients, he notes, and a cancer diagnosis brings heavy stress that can pass from normal sadness into a major disorder. His review covers causes, effects, screening, and treatment, with stress on the body systems behind the mood change, not just the mental strain.

Smith links depression in cancer to tissue damage, immune signals, and the long stress response, which ties the immune and hormone systems together. Some cancer treatments themselves may also trigger low mood. He surveys screening tools, talk-based care, and drug care, and warns that drug choice must fit with chemo side effects and drug clashes. Better detection and care, he argues, would raise quality of life and lower deaths.
europmc-pmc4376132:
Stoyan Stoyanov led a team that built a rating scale for health apps. The report ran in JMIR mHealth and uHealth in 2015. His co-authors were Leanne Hides, David Kavanagh, and three more. Health apps were booming at the time. Yet nothing rated their quality beyond user star ratings. The team searched papers and web sources from 2000 to 2013. They gathered all quality criteria they could find. An expert panel then sorted them into a scale.

The search yielded 372 criteria. These fell into four quality areas. The areas were engagement, function, looks, and information. A fifth scale covered personal judgment. The final tool has 23 items. The team tested it on wellbeing apps picked from iTunes. Raters agreed well with each other. The scores also hung together well. The scale gives reviewers one shared tool.
europmc-pmc4383932:
Gloria Giraldo-Calderón and co-authors, with the VectorBase consortium, updated a resource for disease vector genomes in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. VectorBase, a United States-funded bioinformatics center, serves researchers who study invertebrate carriers of human disease, such as mosquitoes. In its 11th year it hosted genomes of 35 organisms, including some non-vectors kept for comparison. Data span genome assemblies, gene annotation, expression, population variation, and insecticide resistance traits.

New features include Web Apollo, which lets the community edit gene annotations together in the browser, and Galaxy, which supports user-built analysis workflows. The center also runs hands-on workshops and online tutorials for its users. All data are free on the project website. Better vector genomes feed directly into control work against the diseases these animals carry.
europmc-pmc4404432:
Emma Scotter, Han-Jou Chen, and Christopher Shaw reviewed the protein TDP-43 in ALS and related dementia, in Neurotherapeutics in 2015. Drug options for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis are scarce. Nearly all ALS cases, and a major class of frontotemporal dementia, share clumps of the protein TDP-43 in nerve cells, which makes it an attractive shared target. The review traces how disease starts: stressors tied to stress granule formation, plus mutations in RNA-handling and protein-disposal genes, push TDP-43 out of place.

From there the protein misfolds, gathers into aggregates, and gains phosphate and ubiquitin tags. The authors weigh treatments at each step, from antisense drugs that lower genetic risk to small molecules that boost cell cleanup systems. Their verdict: stopping TDP-43 misfolding, or clearing it faster, is the most important target for treating both diseases.
europmc-pmc4412032:
Zachery Lewis and co-authors showed how a mother's milk-sugar genetics shape her baby's gut bacteria, in Microbiome in 2015. A gene called FUT2 decides whether a mother is a secretor, adding fucosylated sugars to her milk. Some Bifidobacterium species, common and welcome in infant guts, eat exactly those sugars. The team compared gut communities of breastfed infants of secretor and non-secretor mothers, with emphasis on which bifidobacteria settled and how fast.

Infants of secretor mothers gained bifidobacteria earlier and more often. In their guts, the Bifidobacterium longum group tracked with total bifidobacterial share, and more of their isolated bacteria consumed the key milk sugar. Infants of non-secretors were delayed in building this community. Milk chemistry set by one maternal gene thus steers the first gut ecosystem a child assembles.
europmc-pmc4421932:
Xi-Nian Zuo, Michael Milham, and a very large group of collaborators shared a brain imaging resource in Scientific Data in 2014. Their Consortium for Reliability and Reproducibility gathered resting-state brain scans so that measures of brain networks could be tested for steadiness. Without such checks, claims about differences between people rest on shaky ground.

The shared set holds scans from typical volunteers at sites around the world, gathered with varied machines, designs, and scan quality. Users can test how methods, motion, and other flaws change network measures, and can compare results across sites. By making repeat scanning a basic standard, the resource aims to make functional connectomics, the mapping of linked brain activity, more trustworthy.
europmc-pmc4448532:
Richard Kelwick, Ines Desanlis, Grant Wheeler, and Dylan Edwards reviewed the ADAMTS enzyme family in Genome Biology in 2015. These enzymes are released by cells and cut proteins in the matrix that surrounds them, using a zinc atom at their core. Humans have nineteen family members, and they shape tissues as the body forms, remodels, inflames, and heals.

The review sorts the family by what each member cuts. Some trim the building protein collagen. Some cut the gel-like proteoglycans of cartilage. One cuts a blood clotting factor, and several remain orphans with unknown targets. Faults in single members cause inherited disorders, while wrong levels of others appear in arthritis, cancer, and heart and vessel disease. Two members stand out as drug targets for arthritis. The article maps structure, control, and disease links for the whole family.
europmc-pmc4476132:
Francesco Asnicar, George Weingart, Timothy Tickle, Curtis Huttenhower, Nicola Segata, and Jaume Bacardit presented GraPhlAn, a drawing tool for family trees of microbes, in PeerJ in 2015. Genomic and mixed-sample sequencing now produces trees with thousands of species, each carrying rich extra data such as abundance, traits, or host information. Plotting all of that clearly, in a compact figure fit for publication, had become a bottleneck.

GraPhlAn draws circular tree diagrams and rings of annotation around them, combining a phylogeny with community abundance, physiology, or environmental data in one picture. It runs from the command line for use inside analysis pipelines, locally or through an online Galaxy version. Example figures cover taxonomic surveys of microbial communities, metabolic functions, and biomarker discovery. The open-source tool aims to make huge microbial data sets legible at a glance.
europmc-pmc4521932:
Jörn Diedrichsen, Ewa Zotow, and Izumi Sugihara present a flat map of the cerebellum in PLoS ONE in 2015. The cerebellum, at the back of the brain, is folded so tightly that standard volume displays hide much of its surface. Scans averaged across people have lacked a surface view like the ones long used for the cortex.

Their method builds white- and grey-matter surfaces from the averaged anatomy itself, rather than from each person's brain. Scan data are projected onto those surfaces, then unfolded into a flatmap sized to match the true grey-matter area. The whole surface shows at once, with front-to-back and side-to-side order readable. Example maps show rest networks and task activity, and the tools are freely shared.
europmc-pmc4557132:
M. Geoffrey Hayes leads a twelve-author team hunting genes behind polycystic ovary syndrome, in Nature Communications in 2015. The syndrome is common, strongly heritable, and mixes excess male hormones, irregular ovulation, and blood sugar trouble. Its root cause stays unknown, though hormone imbalance and insulin resistance are suspects.

The team scanned genomes of women of European ancestry with the strictest form of the syndrome, the type carrying the highest metabolic risk. Three regions reached firm significance: two new ones, on chromosomes 8 and 11, and one on chromosome 9 already found in Chinese patients. The chromosome 11 hit sits by the FSHB gene, which makes a hormone that drives egg development, and it also tracked hormone levels, pointing at brain hormone control.
europmc-pmc4569432:
Sachiko Miyake leads a twelve-author team comparing gut microbes in multiple sclerosis, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease of brain and spinal cord whose cause remains murky. Animal studies hinted that gut microbes help trigger it. The team sequenced bacterial genes from stool of 20 Japanese patients with the relapsing-remitting form.

Forty healthy Japanese subjects served as the main comparison, and 18 more gave repeat samples over months to gauge normal drift. Patients showed a moderate imbalance in gut community structure. The striking feature was a loss of species from two Clostridia clusters, groups known for calming gut immunity. The pattern supports a gut link worth testing as a treatment angle.
europmc-pmc4575032:
Ole S. Søgaard leads a twelve-author team testing a drug that wakes dormant HIV, in PLoS Pathogens in 2015. Antiretroviral therapy suppresses HIV but cannot cure it, because the virus hides silently inside resting cells. A cure strategy proposes forcing that hidden virus awake so it can be cleared, while therapy holds the line.

Six adults with fully suppressed HIV received romidepsin, a cancer drug that loosens DNA packing, once weekly for three weeks. Within hours of each dose, a marker of the drug's action on cell proteins rose up to 7.7-fold. Viral gene activity climbed significantly, and virus appeared in the blood plasma of five of six patients, at low but measurable levels. The trial is proof of concept that latency can be reversed in people.
europmc-pmc4600732:
Zhipeng Meng, together with colleagues, released a 2015 study filling a gap in the Hippo pathway, a signal chain that controls organ size and tissue balance. The chain ends with LATS kinases switching off the growth promoters YAP and TAZ. The textbook view held that MST kinases switch LATS on, yet evidence suggested others could too. The work appeared in Cell.

Deleting LATS, but not MST, stopped YAP and TAZ control, which confirmed the gap. The team found that MAP4K family kinases switch LATS on directly, working in parallel with MST. Only when both sets were deleted did the pathway fail across many signals. The Hippo pathway is thus wider than once drawn, with backup activators that matter for growth control and cancer research.
europmc-pmc4644232:
In 2015, Rebecca A. Schwab and colleagues published a study on how the Fanconi anemia pathway protects the genome when DNA copying and gene reading collide. This pathway counteracts copying stress, and its failure causes bone marrow failure and cancer risk. How its proteins limit that stress was unclear. The work appeared in Molecular Cell.

Clashes between the copying machinery and transcription activate the pathway. Stopping transcription, or removing DNA-RNA hybrid loops left by transcription, eased fork stalls and damage in cells lacking the pathway. Simple aldehydes, which harm patients, raised those hybrids. One protein's motor activity, from FANCM, was required to clear the loops. The findings tie everyday transcription traffic to the disease's cancer risk.
europmc-pmc4668832:
Arie H. Havelaar and colleagues published the World Health Organization foodborne disease estimates for 2010, covering thirty-one hazards in food. A WHO group built the counts of illness, death, and lost healthy years by region.

The full load came to thirty-three million lost healthy years, on a par with HIV/AIDS, malaria, or tuberculosis. Germs that cause diarrhoea, above all norovirus and Campylobacter, made the most people ill. One Salmonella type led the deaths, with typhoid, a pork tapeworm, and hepatitis A virus close behind. Children under five bore forty percent of the load while making up just nine percent of the world's people. Africa bore the worst load of any region. The counts give food safety work a firm base.
europmc-pmc4703832:
Jigang Wang, Chong-Jing Zhang, Wan Ni Chia, and a large team probed how the malaria drug artemisinin works, in Nature Communications in 2015. Artemisinin and its relatives are the strongest anti-malaria drugs known, yet their killing mechanism stayed partly mysterious for decades. The team attached a chemical tag to the drug, fished out everything it bound inside the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum, and identified the catch by protein analysis.

The drug bound 124 parasite proteins, many of them essential, a spread so wide it wrecks the parasite's chemistry wholesale. A fluorescent version of the tagged drug settled a second dispute: haem, not free iron, mainly switches the drug on. That haem comes from the parasite's own production early in its cycle and from digested blood later. The results support one unified model of the drug's action and its deadly aim at this parasite.
europmc-pmc4772032:
David O. Kennedy, writing alone in Nutrients in 2016, reviews the eight B vitamins and their work in the brain. Research and public advice have centered on three of them, folate, B12, and B6, because of their role in handling homocysteine. The other five have drawn far less study, though all eight act as helpers in the cell's core chemistry.

Kennedy argues the group must be read as a team. Together they drive energy making, DNA building and repair, chemical marking of genes, and the making of brain messengers. Survey data show shortfalls in one or more B vitamins are common even in rich countries. He makes the case that taking the full set, at levels above current official targets, is the rational way to guard brain health where diet falls short.
europmc-pmc4773932:
Thomas G. Weiser leads a large author team in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 2016 counting how much surgery the world performs. Their target year is 2012, with a comparison back to 2004. Sound counts matter because surgery treats injury, blocked birth, infection, and heart disease, yet supply is uneven across countries.

Only 66 of 194 member states reported real data, so the team filled gaps by modeling from health spending. They estimate about 313 million operations in 2012, up from about 226 million in 2004. The poorest states, holding over a third of the world's people, got only a small share of that care. In those states nearly a third of all surgery was cesarean birth, against a tiny share in rich states.
europmc-pmc4779832:
Jixiang Zhang and six colleagues review reactive oxygen species as cell signals in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity in 2016. These reactive forms of oxygen were long cast only as damage agents, the sparks behind rust-like harm in tissue. Work since then shows cells also use them as messengers that set growth, change, and death in motion.

The review covers how the messengers form and how the cell keeps their level in bounds. It then traces their grip on the main signal paths of the cell, on ion channels that pass calcium, and on the protein-recycling machinery. The two-way traffic gets stress: signals shape the messengers as much as the messengers shape signals. Links to artery disease, diabetes, cancer, and aging run through the account.
europmc-pmc4804632:
Yasuyuki Kakihana and four co-authors review heart failure during sepsis in the Journal of Intensive Care in 2016. In sepsis, the immune reply to infection overshoots and organs fail; the heart is one of them, pumping weakly and relaxing poorly. The review gathers what drives that weakness and what care can do about it.

Signals from invading germs, immune messengers, and nitric oxide all depress the heart muscle. Worse, dying cells spill their own alarm molecules, which fire the same pathways and deepen the injury in a loop. Care rests on breaking the loop early: antibiotics and source control to cut the germ signals, plus fluids and pressure-raising and pump-helping drugs to rest the heart. The authors warn that too much fluid or too long on stimulant drugs can backfire.
europmc-pmc4833332:
Berrak Ugur, Kuchuan Chen, and Hugo J. Bellen make the case for the fruit fly in Disease Models & Mechanisms in 2016. Fly organs look nothing like human ones, yet the molecules that run them are largely shared, and about two-thirds of human disease genes have a working fly counterpart. That likeness, the authors argue, is underexploited for studying how disease mutations act.

The review, published with a poster, sets out the parallels organ by organ: brain, heart, liver, and kidney stand-ins in the fly. It catalogs the tests built to probe gene function in each, and gives cases where fly work answered a human disease question. Cheap, fast, and genetically pliable, the fly offers a first-pass laboratory for mechanisms that would take years in mammals.
europmc-pmc4838832:
Benjamin Lacar and a large team used RNA sequencing of single cell nuclei to study active neurons, in Nature Communications in 2016. Single-cell methods can sort brain cell types, but whole cells are hard to pull from adult brain. The team tested whether nuclei alone keep the gene-activity marks left by experience, such as the fast-response genes Fos, Arc, and Egr1.

Nuclear sequencing matched whole-cell patterns well, including those activity genes. Applied to mouse dentate granule cells, the method showed broad gene changes in neurons switched on by experience. The work gives brain researchers a workable route to read the state of single active neurons and compare how cells respond to the same event.
europmc-pmc4870732:
Jeremy Pasquier and co-authors built PhyloFish in BMC Genomics in 2016, a database on gene change after whole genome doubling in fish. Ray-finned fish hold about 30,000 species, near half of all vertebrates. Their line doubled its whole genome about 350 million years ago, with later doublings in salmon, carp, and other groups. Such doublings often spark new forms.

PhyloFish gathers expressed gene sets for 23 ray-finned fish species, all collected and processed the same way. Users can trace which gene copies survived each doubling and where each gene is active. A uniform set across many species makes fair comparison possible, a base for studying how doubled genomes evolve.
europmc-pmc4880932:
Benjamin K. Chan and co-authors showed in Scientific Reports in 2016 that a virus of bacteria can force a drug-resistant germ back to drug sensitivity. They isolated a phage, OMKO1, that infects Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a hard hospital pathogen. The phage docks onto OprM, the outer gate of the germ's drug pumps, the very pumps that throw out antibiotics.

To dodge the phage, the germ must change that gate, which cripples its pumps. Phage resistance thus costs drug resistance, an evolutionary trade-off. Picking a phage that targets a resistance tool flips the arms race: whichever way the germ evolves, it loses something vital. The trick sketches a smarter way to treat stubborn infections.
europmc-pmc4900032:
Lidwine B. Mokkink and co-authors described the COSMIN initiative in 2016, a set of tools for picking health measurement instruments. Trials and clinics must choose questionnaires and tests, and poor picks waste whole studies. COSMIN, built by an international team, defines measurement traits such as validity and reliability in one shared taxonomy.

Its tools include a checklist to grade studies of measurement quality, a search filter for finding such studies, review protocols, and a database of past reviews. A further guide helps trial designers pick core outcome sets. An update then underway sharpened rules for content validity. Shared standards make instrument choice a checkable craft rather than habit.
europmc-pmc4931332:
Xiaoli Zhang and a large team of co-authors identify a lysosome channel that senses harmful oxygen molecules and triggers cell cleanup. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Lysosomes are the cell's recycling centers, and they host sensors that start autophagy, the process that clears damaged parts. The team studied a channel called TRPML1, coded by the gene MCOLN1, which lets calcium out of the lysosome.

Reactive oxygen species opened the channel directly. Calcium release then switched on a factor, TFEB, that orders more autophagy and more lysosomes. The path did not need mTOR, the known nutrient sensor. When the channel was blocked or removed, cells failed to clear damaged mitochondria and excess reactive molecules built up. The authors describe the channel as a stress sensor that runs a feedback loop to limit oxidative harm.
europmc-pmc4993332:
Brandon M. Hall leads a team tracking macrophages that carry senescence markers as mice age. Their study appeared in Aging in 2016. Senescent cells, worn cells that stop dividing, are blamed for age linked inflammation and are targets of anti-aging therapy. When the team implanted senescent human cells into mice, immune cells cleared them fast unless the cells were shielded in alginate beads. Studying what the beads attracted revealed an odd cell type.

The attracted cells were macrophages wearing the same markers used to flag senescent cells, including the p16(Ink4a) gene and a signature enzyme activity. Such cells also build up naturally as mice age. Giving young mice senescent cells induced the same macrophage state. The authors warn that common senescence markers can mark macrophages instead, which complicates counts of senescent cells in aging tissue.
europmc-pmc4996332:
Beata Tick and four co-authors pool twin studies to estimate how heritable autism spectrum disorders are. Their meta-analysis appeared in the Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry in 2016. Twin studies had split on how much of autism risk is genetic versus shared environment. One recent study claimed a large shared environment effect. The team gathered every twin study of autism to date. They re-analyzed the best recruited ones with shared methods, and tested trait scores in a large population twin sample.

Identical twin correlations came out near unity in the pooled work, a sign of strong genetic influence. The authors reject the claim that shared environment explains most of the variance. They do not rule out non-genetic effects altogether. Their warning is about method: a single study should not outweigh a consistent literature. They present the pooled estimate as the safer base for counseling and research.
europmc-pmc5005332:
Iko T. Koevoets, Jan Henk Venema, J. Theo M. Elzenga, and Christa Testerink review root shape under stress in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2016. Roots change their branching, depth, and growth direction when conditions turn harsh. Crop breeding has mostly judged the shoot, since roots are hard to watch, so this link between root shape and stress survival is the review's focus.

The authors walk through root responses to low nutrients, drought, salt, flooding, and heat or cold, in both Arabidopsis and crop plants. For each stress they set out the cell and gene steps behind the shape change. They then weigh studies that tie a root response to real survival gains. Their case is that proof of useful root change can help breeders add root traits to crop selection for tougher harvests.
europmc-pmc5068732:
Jamie J. Kirkham and eleven co-authors present a reporting standard for core outcome set studies in PLoS Medicine in 2016. A core outcome set is the agreed minimum outcomes every trial in a field should measure, and over two hundred existed, yet their reports were often unclear. Without complete reporting, the sets cannot do their job of making research comparable and relevant. The COS-STAR statement was built to fix that.

An international group of developers, methodologists, editors, users, and patient representatives drafted items, then ran a two-round survey of nearly two hundred stakeholders and a consensus meeting. The result is an eighteen-item checklist covering the introduction, methods, results, and discussion of any core outcome set report. The authors admit the process lacked voices from low- and middle-income countries, where the sets matter as much, and the guideline may need to grow to fit those settings.
europmc-pmc5118932:
D. Lee Taylor and seven co-authors, with D. Cullen also named in the text's byline, improved a DNA method for counting fungi in Applied and Environmental Microbiology in 2016. Sequencing a marker gene can survey fungi in soil or roots, but biased primers give skewed counts of who is there and how many.

The team designed new primers for the fungal marker region and a matching Illumina sequencing routine. In test mixes of eight fungi at known, widely varied amounts, they recovered all members. Counts matched expectations closely. Still, some fungi were consistently over- or under-counted, likely due to gene copy number. On real soils, their results agreed closely with older cloning methods, and non-fungal DNA stayed under half a percent.
europmc-pmc5158132:
Gido M. van de Ven, Stéphanie Trouche, Colin G. McNamara, Kevin Allen, and David Dupret studied memory replay in the mouse hippocampus in Neuron in 2016. Groups of neurons that fire together during exploration are thought to store a place memory, and replaying them during rest, inside sharp wave-ripple events, is thought to lock the memory in.

Recording assemblies formed in new and familiar spaces, they found that reinstatement of the new-space pattern tracked its offline replay. Blocking ripples with precisely timed light pulses broke that reinstatement. Replay mattered only for assemblies that had gradually strengthened during exploration; patterns formed fully within minutes did not need it. The hippocampus, they conclude, can hold two kinds of representation side by side with different consolidation rules.
europmc-pmc521732:
Juleen R. Zierath and John A. Hawley wrote a primer on skeletal muscle fiber types in PLoS Biology in 2004. Muscle is not uniform: its fibers come in types that differ in how fast they contract and how they make energy. Muscle also adapts remarkably to training, loading, diet, and temperature, and people differ widely in how much theirs can adapt.

The piece explains how fiber types are classified and how each type's contractile and metabolic traits shape performance, from endurance to strength. In most mammals, skeletal muscle makes up about 55 percent of body mass and drives movement, heat production in the cold, and much of daily metabolism. Fiber mix also relates to disease states such as obesity and insulin resistance. The authors argue that pinning down the signals that set fiber type could reveal new genes and pathways in common diseases.
europmc-pmc5222932:
The Japan Esophageal Society published part one of the eleventh edition of its esophageal cancer classification in the journal Esophagus in 2017. The classification lays down general rules for describing cancer of the esophagus so that clinical, surgical, and pathology records share one language. President Hisahiro Matsubara of Chiba University chaired the English edition committee.

The rules cover the primary tumour first: its number, size, position around the wall, location, visible type, and depth of invasion. Later sections standardize how to record spread to lymph nodes and distant organs, cancer stage, and multiple primary cancers. Surgical sections govern handling of removed tissue, margins, and the grading of node spread and leftover tumour. Separate rules treat pathology findings, tissue typing, vessel invasion, and the judged effect of radiation or drug treatment, plus findings from endoscopic removal.
europmc-pmc5310132:
M. Fata Moradali, Shirin Ghods, and Bernd H. A. Rehm reviewed the germ Pseudomonas aeruginosa in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology in 2017. The germ preys on people with weak immune defenses. It is a top cause of death in cystic fibrosis and a common source of hospital infections. Its skill at survival and drug resistance makes its infections hard to clear.

The review maps the tools the germ uses to adapt. Cell to cell signals, called quorum sensing, and small inner messengers switch the germ between free swimming and settled film life. Control proteins time gene use so the germ can react fast to stress. The germ also resists many drug classes by more than one route. The authors trace how these systems shift across the stages of infection, from first hold to long stay.
europmc-pmc5379932:
Matthew Stephens offered a new deal for false discovery rates in Biostatistics in 2017. Big studies test thousands of claims at once, from genes to brain spots. Many flagged hits are false, and the false discovery rate gauges that share. Standard tools sum up each test in one number and treat all effects as alike, which wastes what the data hold.

His method takes two numbers per test: the size of the effect and its error bar. It also bakes in a plain prior hunch, that true effects bunch at zero with one hump. That hunch makes the math a simple, sturdy fit and sharpens the calls when it holds. The output adds ranges for the true effect of each hit, not just a yes or no. Labs can then rank hits by real size, not by noise.
europmc-pmc5489032:
Narayanan and Jones present a review in Chemical Science on sulfonyl fluorides in chemical biology. Sulfonyl fluorides are reactive groups that bind proteins in a lasting, covalent way. Such probes help map enzyme active sites and find drug targets. Most older probes targeted only cysteine residues. Sulfonyl fluorides reach a far wider set of residues.

They can capture serine, threonine, tyrosine, lysine, cysteine, and histidine sites. The review is organized by which residue each probe attacks. Classic reagents such as PMSF and AEBSF get full coverage. Newer custom probes for single enzymes also feature. The authors close with fresh uses in drug discovery.
europmc-pmc5522532:
Bayliss and co-authors report a cohort study in The Lancet on joint replacement revision risk. Hip and knee replacements relieve end-stage arthritis well. Patients still need honest odds on needing a second operation. Those odds hinge on age at the first surgery. The team mined UK primary care records for over 117,000 patients.

Implants lasted 20 years in about 85 to 90 percent of cases, they report. Patients over 70 faced only about a 5 percent lifetime revision risk. Men in their early 50s faced up to 35 percent. Women of that age ran notably lower risk. The figures challenge the drift toward ever-younger surgery.
europmc-pmc5530532:
Ghosh and co-authors present a review in the Journal of Biomedical Science on free fatty acids and blood vessel lining damage. Blood levels of these fats run high in obesity and type 2 diabetes. The vessel lining, or endothelium, is an early casualty. Its failure opens the road to atherosclerosis and heart disease. The authors gather clinical and lab evidence on the link.

Fatty acids blunt insulin signaling inside lining cells, they report. Nitric oxide output falls, so vessels relax poorly. Oxidative stress and inflammation rise at the same time. Some lining cells die off under the assault. Blocking these pathways could protect vessels early, they suggest.
europmc-pmc5548832:
Capaldo, Powell, and Kalman present a review in the Journal of Molecular Medicine. Their subject is the barrier that lines the colon. That barrier keeps gut microbes apart from the body. Its failure is a central feature of inflammatory bowel diseases.

Two layers do much of the sealing work. Mucus coats the surface and traps bacteria before they reach cells. Tight junctions then close the gaps between the cells themselves. The review explains how these layers act together. It also shows how inflammation weakens both layers in bowel disease. Readers learn why barrier loss can feed a cycle of leak and swelling.
europmc-pmc5673632:
Bonaz, Sinniger, and Pellissier present a review in Frontiers in Immunology. It examines the vagus nerve in gut inflammation. The vagus is the longest nerve in the body. It forms a core part of the parasympathetic system. About four fifths of its fibers carry signals toward the brain. It links brain and gut in both directions.

The nerve plays a dual anti-inflammatory role. Incoming fibers trigger hormone release through a stress axis. Outgoing fibers drive a cholinergic pathway that calms immune cells. Together with the splenic nerve, it curbs TNF release by macrophages. The review focuses on inflammatory bowel diseases. Target routes include drugs, nutrition, exercise, and nerve stimulation.
europmc-pmc5682332:
Carta and co-authors reassess palmitic acid, a common saturated fatty acid. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Physiology. Palmitic acid makes up a large share of body fat. It comes from food or body synthesis. The authors argue its bad reputation hides key roles. Tissue levels stay tightly controlled.

The acid supports membrane structure in cells. It enables protein palmitoylation and lung surfactant action. Problems start when control breaks down. Excess calories and sugars boost new fat synthesis. Sedentary habits add to the strain. Tissue palmitic acid then accumulates. That buildup links to blood lipid problems. Inflammation and ectopic fat follow. The authors stress dietary balance with unsaturated fats.
europmc-pmc5722032:
Hartwig and co-authors explain how to avoid common pitfalls in a genetic causal method. Their guide covers two-sample Mendelian randomization. The method uses genetic variants as stand-ins for a risk factor or exposure. It draws on summary results from two separate groups of people.

Such studies rose from none in 2011 to 42 percent of the field by 2016. The approach is powerful, but it rests on strict assumptions. Variants must link to the exposure and reach the outcome only through it. Sample overlap between the two groups can bias results. Weak instruments pose a further risk. The authors show how careful design can dodge these downsides.
europmc-pmc5723032:
Ostrowitzki and co-authors report a phase III trial of gantenerumab in prodromal Alzheimer's disease. Gantenerumab is an antibody that binds clumped amyloid-beta and helps clear its plaques. The SCarlet RoAD trial tested whether this early treatment could slow decline.

The trial was randomized, double-blind, and placebo controlled over two years. Of 3,089 people screened, 797 took part and got shots every four weeks. Doses were 105 or 225 milligrams, or a placebo shot. The trial stopped early for futility, with no gain on the main score. Brain imaging side effects rose with dose and with the APOE ε4 gene form. Later checks hinted that higher doses may be needed for a real effect.
europmc-pmc5766532:
Wei and co-authors compare ways of filling gaps in mass spectrometry metabolomics data. Missing readings are common in such data, and the fix chosen can change later results. Their study tests eight imputation methods across four datasets.

The methods ranged from simple fills, such as zero or the mean, to random forest, k-nearest neighbours, and a left-censored regression approach. The team scored accuracy and checked effects on sample patterns and single-variable tests. They report random forest worked best for values missing at random, while the left-censored method suited values missing because readings were too low. They also built a free web tool that applies their strategy.
europmc-pmc5803132:
Aldridge and co-authors review illness and death among excluded groups. They study homeless people, prisoners, sex workers, and people with drug disorders. All groups live in rich nations, yet face deep poverty and stigma.

Their review covers 337 studies found in major medical databases. Death rates ran far above the general public's rates. Standard rates were near twelvefold for women and eightfold for men. Infections, heart disease, and mental illness were all common. Injury and poisoning drove many early deaths. Readers get stark proof of extreme health gaps and a call for joint action.
europmc-pmc5815332:
Piwowar and co-authors measure how much research is free to read. Open access lets anyone read papers without paying. No large, current count of it existed. The team built oaDOI, a service that checks access status.

The service covers 67 million articles with DOIs. Three samples of 100,000 papers each test different pools. At least 28 percent of all literature is open access. For the newest year studied, 2015, the share hit 45 percent. Much free material lacks an open license, a class they call Bronze. Open papers drew 18 percent more citations. Readers get a firm baseline for access policy.
europmc-pmc5823932:
Kageyama and co-authors review mixed-anion materials, a rising class of solids. Oxides ruled materials chemistry for a century. Solids that mix two anions, like oxyfluorides, open fresh ground. Their paired anions can yield traits no oxide shows.

The review tracks progress in making and measuring these compounds. New synthesis routes shape both local and overall structure. Modern probes can tell the anions' states apart. Mixed anions aid catalysts, energy devices, and electronics. The authors also flag the hurdles to wider use. Readers get a field guide to a platform that expands what solid materials can do.
europmc-pmc5826932:
Yang and co-authors show how molecular packing drives lasting glow in organic crystals. Some pure organic solids phosphoresce at room temperature. Such metal-free glow is rare and prized for devices and imaging. What packing rules favor it was unclear.

The team built seven variants on one glowing scaffold. Strong pi-pi stacking in the solid state favored persistent glow. One variant, CS-CF3, switched its glow with light as its packing changed. Another, CS-F, glowed long enough for imaging in living mice. No excitation was needed during that imaging. Readers get design rules for a scarce class of light materials.
europmc-pmc5954232:
Granja and co-authors review factors that decide success or failure of eHealth interventions. Their systematic review appeared in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. eHealth promises better cost, quality, and reach in care. Yet a gap sits between research hopes and clinical reality. The team searched PubMed for studies of tools in real use. They kept papers that reported success or failure factors.

Of 903 articles found, 221 met the inclusion rules. The team sorted the factors into 27 categories. Quality of healthcare was cited most often for success. Costs were cited most often for failure. Workflow drew the most papers overall, with workload its top barrier.
europmc-pmc6041332:
Brenner and co-authors boost organ drug delivery by hitchhiking on red blood cells. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Nanocarriers usually end up trapped in the liver. Little dose reaches organs like lung or brain. Targeting tags have helped only modestly so far.

The method sticks nanocarriers onto red blood cells. As cells squeeze through capillaries, carriers transfer off. They land in the first organ downstream of injection. Lung uptake rose about forty-fold for liposomes. Brain delivery passed ten percent of the dose. The team tested mice, pigs, and human lungs outside the body. No clear toxicity to blood cells or organs appeared. Readers get a platform that could serve many diseases.
europmc-pmc6048132:
Feig and co-authors build soft conductive gels that mimic body tissue. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Electrodes that match tissue softness could interface better. Dry conductors are far stiffer than brain or skin. Conductive hydrogels are soft but often conduct poorly.

The design weaves two gel networks together. One network is the conducting polymer PEDOT:PSS. It gels at very low loading levels. Conductivity reached a record for such stretchy gels. The second network sets the mechanical feel. Stiffness could be tuned across three orders of magnitude. Stretch stayed above one hundred percent throughout. Conductivity stayed high across that range too. Readers get a material suited to bioelectronic interfaces.
europmc-pmc6054932:
Weber and co-authors review lab testing of materials that touch blood. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology. Devices like stents, valves, and catheters meet blood directly. A bad reaction can trigger clots or inflammation. Testing must happen before clinical use.

Rules in an international standard guide the testing. Materials sit with fresh human blood in lab models. Models can be still, shaken, or flowing. Teams then measure cell damage and counts. Platelet, clotting, and complement activation are checked. Surfaces are inspected for stuck cells and proteins. Clot and fibrin formation on surfaces is scored. Readers get a full checklist for judging blood safety of new materials.
europmc-pmc6124632:
Bowden and co-authors present a methods article in International Journal of Epidemiology on Mendelian randomization studies. These studies use gene variants to test cause and effect. Results are often shown on a scatter plot. That plot can mislead when some estimates are far less precise than others.

The authors propose a radial plot instead. It makes outliers and strong data points easier to spot. It also removes the need to recode gene data. The plot leads to a new form of radial regression. They show the method on blood pressure and heart disease data. One outlying variant explained a clash between two common estimates.
europmc-pmc6145832:
Yang and co-authors report a phase III clinical trial in Journal of Clinical Oncology on esophageal cancer treatment. The trial, called NEOCRTEC5010, tested chemoradiotherapy given before surgery. The cancer was locally advanced squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus. Whether the added treatment helps was still controversial.

From 2007 to 2014, 451 patients were randomly assigned to chemoradiotherapy plus surgery or surgery alone. The combined group also received the drugs vinorelbine and cisplatin with radiation. The combined treatment raised both overall survival and disease-free survival. Side effects were tracked as well. The trial supports the combined approach for patients whose tumors can still be removed.
europmc-pmc6173832:
Khan and co-authors present a research article in Diabetology and Metabolic Syndrome on a simple index for insulin resistance. Insulin resistance is the hallmark of metabolic syndrome, a cluster of risk factors. Measuring it directly is hard in routine practice. The TyG index, built from fasting triglycerides and glucose, has been proposed instead.

The team studied 227 subjects and compared TyG with other markers. These included body measures, blood fats, and the HOMA-IR index. TyG matched or beat the other markers in its links with several body and blood measures. Sex differences in many values were also noted. The authors support TyG as a practical screening tool, while noting data from their region had been lacking.
europmc-pmc6212432:
Deng and co-authors studied two signal systems in osteoarthritis. Osteoarthritis wears down joint cartilage. It is a top cause of pain in older people. The study used a mouse model of the disease. It appeared in Nature Communications.

One system centres on proteins called YAP and TAZ. The other is the NF-kB pathway, which drives inflammation. The team report that each system blocks the other. Turning YAP on kept cartilage intact in mice. Deleting YAP in cartilage cells sped up damage. Inflammatory signals trigger YAP breakdown through a kinase called TAK1. YAP in turn binds TAK1 and calms NF-kB. The work points to new drug targets.
europmc-pmc6265732:
Chakrabarti, Guha, and Majumder review health active peptides hidden inside food proteins. Their review appeared in Nutrients. Such peptides sit locked in the parent protein until digestion or processing frees them. Once free, they can affect blood pressure, immunity, and other body functions. Many sequences have been found in the past few decades. Trade use has still lagged behind the science.

Making the peptides at scale is one barrier. Many are broken down in the gut before they can act. Uptake rates vary from person to person. Proof from well run human trials is also thin. The review covers production methods old and new. It weighs gut survival and uptake evidence with care. Rules for health claims are also mapped. The authors see strong promise if those gaps close.
europmc-pmc6278532:
Zininga, Ramatsui, and Shonhai review heat shock proteins as immune modulators. Their review appeared in Molecules. Heat shock proteins help other proteins fold into shape. Stress raises their levels inside cells. Some are also released outside cells under stress. Out there they act as danger signals to the immune system.

Effects can run in both directions. Some heat shock proteins stir inflammation, while others calm it. Dose and species decide which way the effect goes. Cancer cells that release more of them can be flagged for killing. Their sameness across species also links them to autoimmune disease. The review maps the pathways each main protein uses. It also asks why reports clash between labs. Method differences may explain many of the conflicts.
europmc-pmc6280432:
Escapa and co-authors present an expanded database for microbes of the nose and mouth. Their paper appeared in mSystems. The resource is the expanded Human Oral Microbiome Database, or eHOMD. It covers the whole aerodigestive tract. That tract runs from the nose and sinuses through the throat to the lower airways. Naming microbes at species level is key for clinical use.

The database groups gene marker sequences at a strict identity level. It gives names even to microbes never grown in a lab. Reference genomes support deeper sequencing studies. Links connect out to other major databases. Nostril data added new insight for this release. Groups such as Corynebacterium feature in the nose findings. The open resource serves basic and clinical researchers alike. It helps turn raw sequences into named species.
europmc-pmc6356332:
Khan and Mukhtar review tea polyphenols and their effects on human health. Their review appeared in Nutrients. Tea is the world's most widely used beverage. It has been drunk in Asia for centuries. Its active parts are mostly polyphenols. Green tea is richest in a group called catechins.

One catechin, EGCG, is the most studied of them. Cell and animal studies show wide benefits. Cancer, diabetes, and heart disease are the main targets. Tea type depends on how leaves are fermented. Green, black, and oolong teas differ that way. Leaf, season, and climate shift the chemistry too. The authors gather the evidence for tea as preventive aid. Human trial proof is still thinner than lab proof.
europmc-pmc6357032:
Abotaleb and co-authors review flavonoids as cancer agents that trigger cell death. Their review appeared in Cancers. Cancer is the second leading cause of death worldwide. Standard treatments often hurt and face growing resistance. Restoring apoptosis, the cells' suicide program, is a key strategy. Plant compounds draw interest as gentler options.

Flavonoids are common plant pigments with low side effects. They are cheap and widely available in food. Many show strong killing power against cancer cells. They push those cells into apoptosis through several routes. The review gathers which flavonoids work on which cancers. It explains the death pathways each one engages. The authors see them as partners for standard therapy. More trials are needed before clinic use.
europmc-pmc6370632:
Yin and co-authors present a review in Frontiers in Immunology on plant polysaccharides and immune control. More than 300 natural polysaccharides are known, and plant types draw interest as low-toxicity immune modulators. The review centers on their effects on macrophages, the immune system's front-line eating cells.

Plant polysaccharides can switch macrophages on and raise their output of reactive oxygen, cytokines, and chemokines. Effects depend on structure, including sugar makeup, bond types, and molecular weight. The authors gather findings across many plant species and receptors. They present these compounds as a promising source of new immune medicines with fewer side effects than microbial or synthetic options.
europmc-pmc6373132:
Nathwani and co-authors present a systematic review in Antimicrobial Resistance and Infection Control. They assessed the clinical and economic value of hospital antimicrobial stewardship programs. Such programs promote careful antibiotic use to fight drug resistance, but hospitals need proof they pay off.

The review covered 146 studies, mostly from North America, Europe, and Asia. Most studies found shorter hospital stays and lower antibiotic spending after programs began. US studies saved an average of 732 dollars per patient, driven mainly by reduced stays. Programs with therapy review and antibiotic limits saved the most. The authors call for stronger data from lower-income countries, where evidence is scarce.
europmc-pmc6407232:
Huang and co-authors review a platelet receptor in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology. The receptor, integrin alphaIIb beta3, sits in large numbers on platelets. It plays a central role in blood clotting and in artery blockages.

At rest the receptor is switched off and binds weakly. Signals from inside the cell flip it into a sticky, high-grip state. Binding then sends signals back inward that build the clot. The review explains both signal directions and their controls. It also covers drugs that target the receptor and the receptor's part in cancer spread.
europmc-pmc6432532:
Dong and Lv review collagen scaffolds in tissue engineering, from how the material is prepared to where it is already used. Collagen, the main structural protein of animal tissues, offers low immune reaction, natural pores, and safe breakdown in the body. Its weakness is mechanical strength, which limits some applications.

Cross-linking by chemical or physical means, blending with natural or synthetic polymers, and adding inorganic materials all stiffen the scaffold. Growth factors can also be loaded to boost biological activity. Applications covered include nerve, bone, cartilage, tendon, ligament, blood vessel, and skin repair. The closing sections weigh prospects and the problems still blocking wider clinical use.
europmc-pmc6437932:
Niu and co-authors show that FTO, an enzyme that strips m6A marks from RNA, drives breast cancer growth by silencing the protective gene BNIP3. FTO levels ran high in human breast tumors, and patients with more of it survived less often. Experiments used three breast cancer cell lines plus 36 primary tumors and 12 neighboring tissues.

Sequencing of marked RNA pinpointed BNIP3, a gene that promotes cell death, as FTO's target. FTO removed marks from BNIP3 messenger RNA and triggered its decay, freeing cancer cells to multiply, form colonies, and spread in animals. Restoring BNIP3 largely cancelled those effects. Blocking FTO is proposed as a new treatment strategy.
europmc-pmc6441232:
Guilhaumou and co-authors present joint French advice on how to dose beta-lactam antibiotics in very ill patients, issued by two national expert bodies. Beta-lactams are the ICU's most used antibiotics, but severe illness scrambles how the body handles drugs and invites underdosing. A panel of 18 experts worked from studies published since January 2000 and graded the proof with a set scale.

Few strong trials used death as the main endpoint, so all 21 points of advice are classed as optional. The core target: keep the free drug level at four to eight times the level that just stops the germ, for the whole time between doses. The advice sorts care into four areas and ends in a one-page flow chart that sums up dosing, timing, and drug checks.
europmc-pmc6510332:
Baker, Thomson, Weill and Holt review what genome sequencing shows about drug-resistant bacteria. Their review appeared in Science. Whole-genome sequencing tracks how resistance emerges and spreads in space and time. Some resistant pathogens now cause infections that cannot be treated.

The authors explain three routes to resistance. Bacteria may lack the drug target by nature. They may gain resistance through mutations passed to their offspring. Or they may pick up genes from other bacteria. Case studies cover MRSA, hospital superbugs, community infections, and foodborne spread. The authors argue that evolution here is partly predictable. That foresight can guide surveillance and smarter use of current drugs.
europmc-pmc6518732:
Qin, Yan, Zhang and Zhang review the protein STAT3 as a drug target in triple negative breast cancer, writing in the Journal of Experimental & Clinical Cancer Research. This subtype lacks the three receptors most breast cancer drugs aim at, so options are few and deaths are high.

STAT3 is switched on in these tumors and stays on. It drives growth, spread, drug resistance, immune evasion and stem-like renewal by setting the levels of many genes. Small-molecule blockers of STAT3 have shown strong anticancer effects in cell and animal models of the disease. The review surveys current ways to hit STAT3, and proposes fresh routes toward more precise blockers for prevention and treatment.
europmc-pmc6530332:
Peixoto and co-authors review how changed sugar coatings on proteins help drive cancer, writing in Frontiers in Oncology. Nearly all cell surface proteins carry glycan chains, and tumors rewrite them. The changes are shaped by the tumor's surroundings, and in turn reshape what the cancer does.

The review tracks glycans through the classic hallmarks of cancer: growth signals, death resistance, altered energy use, new blood vessels, invasion and immune escape. Stromal cells around the tumor trade signals with cancer cells through these sugars. The same altered sugars create fresh surface marks that could serve as biomarkers or drug targets. The authors urge that glycans join genes and proteins in precision medicine models.
europmc-pmc6540032:
Shin and co-authors review the molecular mechanics of skin aging in the dermis, writing in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. The dermis is mostly scaffold: collagen and elastic fibers made and kept by fibroblast cells. With age, collagen breaks into fragments and thins out, and skin wrinkles and sags.

Reactive oxygen drives much of the loss. It boosts enzymes that chew collagen and blunts a growth signal that orders more. A weakened scaffold then grips fibroblasts poorly, so they falter and make still less collagen, in a downward spiral. Elastic fibers thin in sheltered skin but pile up in sun-damaged skin.
