The review closes with antiaging tools — creams such as retinoids, laser and energy devices, and fillers — judged by how well they undo these changes.
europmc-pmc6547132:
Hanseeuw and co-authors track the two hallmark proteins of Alzheimer's disease in healthy older adults, writing in JAMA Neurology. Amyloid and tau build up in the brain years before symptoms start. The team followed 60 adults with normal thinking at entry, scanning each brain repeatedly for both proteins and testing cognition over time.

The speed of tau build-up in the lower temporal cortex matched the speed of cognitive decline. Amyloid build-up came first and predicted the later tau rise. That chain — early amyloid, then tau, then weaker cognition seven years on — explained the link between first scans and final scores. The authors say amyloid scans spot the disease early, while repeat tau scans best track its advance.
europmc-pmc6565732:
White and co-authors put a number on nature's weekly dose, writing in Scientific Reports. Time outdoors is linked to better health, but nobody had mapped how much is enough. The team analyzed survey data from 19,806 adults in England, weighted to represent the nation, and charted self-reported health and wellbeing against minutes spent in nature over the prior week.

A clear threshold appeared at 120 minutes. People reaching two hours were significantly more likely to report good health and high wellbeing than people with no nature contact. Gains rose toward 200 to 300 minutes, then leveled off. One long visit worked as well as several short ones, and the pattern held for older adults and people with long-term illness alike.
europmc-pmc6646332:
Antunes and co-authors show that a gut microbe product protects mice against RSV. Their study appears in Nature Communications. Severe RSV infection is a leading threat to infants. The team fed mice a high-fibre diet before infection. Those mice lost less weight and carried less virus. Lung inflammation also ran lower. The protection depended on gut microbes and acetate. Giving acetate alone reproduced the benefit.

Acetate switched on interferon-beta responses in the lung. It raised interferon-stimulated gene expression there. The receptor GPR43 on lung epithelial cells was required. Mice lacking GPR43 lost the protection entirely. Type 1 interferon signalling proved essential as well. The findings link diet, microbes, and antiviral defence.
europmc-pmc6658332:
Olingy and co-authors review monocyte diversity and its functions in cancer. Their review appears in the Journal of Leukocyte Biology. Monocytes were once viewed as one uniform cell type. They actually split into distinct subsets. Classical, intermediate, and nonclassical groups are now standard. In cancer these subsets pull in opposite directions. Some kill tumour cells and rally lymphocytes. Others feed blood vessel growth and matrix remodelling. Monocytes also seed tumour-associated macrophages and dendritic cells.

Which signals dominate decides the net effect. The review covers subset behaviour during steady state first. It then details their cancer progression roles. Closing sections describe monocyte-targeted treatment strategies. Better subset control could sharpen immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc6658832:
Köhl and co-authors explain why the mode of action of microbial biocontrol agents matters beyond efficacy. Their review appears in Frontiers in Plant Science. Growers spray living microbes to suppress crop diseases. These agents work through several distinct routes. Some prime the plant's own resistance. Others starve pathogens by competing for nutrients and space. Direct attackers parasitise the pathogen itself. Still others secrete antimicrobial compounds on the spot.

Lab production of a compound proves little, they warn. In vitro output often fails to match field antagonism. Screening on simple media biases selection badly. Risk assessment needs the same rethink. Treating these microbes like single-molecule fungicides misfits their biology. Registration rules should follow the mode of action.
europmc-pmc6677832:
Tang and co-authors identify a long non-coding RNA that fuels colorectal cancer metabolism. Their study appears in Nature Communications. The RNA, GLCC1, rises sharply under glucose starvation. It helps cancer cells survive and keep growing. Mechanistically, GLCC1 binds the HSP90 chaperone directly. That contact shields c-Myc from ubiquitin tagging. Stabilised c-Myc then reprograms its target genes. The glycolysis enzyme LDHA is a key target. Through this cascade the RNA boosts glycolytic flux.

Clinical data matched the laboratory picture. High GLCC1 tracked tumour formation and larger size. It also predicted poor patient prognosis. The authors call GLCC1 oncogenic on all three levels. They propose its pathway as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc6780632:
Khalifa and co-authors review marine natural products as a source of new anticancer drugs. Cancer caused about 10 million deaths in 2018, from roughly 18 million new cases. Fresh drugs with new modes of action are urgently needed. The sea holds vast reservoirs of bioactive chemicals. Algae, bacteria, fungi, sponges, and soft corals all produce unusual compounds.

The review first surveys anticancer effects seen in cell and animal studies. Compounds from seaweed, for instance, killed neuroblastoma and colon cancer cells at low doses. It then explains how these products trigger programmed cell death and other killing routes. Chemical diversity is a recurring theme. Therapeutic strategies, current uses, and limits close the survey.
europmc-pmc6815032:
Davis and Patel analyse PD-L1 testing in the Journal for ImmunoTherapy of Cancer. Drugs called checkpoint inhibitors free the immune system to attack cancer. They help only some patients. Tumours that make PD-L1, a brake protein, were expected to respond best, so its level became an early test for who should get the drugs.

The authors reviewed the trials behind all 45 United States FDA approvals of these drugs. PD-L1 level predicted benefit in only 28.9 percent of the approvals. In the rest it was not predictive or was never tested. Studies also scored the protein in unlike ways. The pair urge caution in leaning on this single marker.
europmc-pmc6889432:
Koveitypour and co-authors review the signalling pathways behind colorectal cancer, in Cell and Bioscience. This cancer is the fourth leading cause of cancer death worldwide. Its growth is driven by mutations in a handful of communication pathways inside cells. Each pathway normally controls division, death, and tissue upkeep. Broken in the right way, each can push a cell toward cancer.

The review takes the main offenders in turn: the MAPK cascade below the EGF receptor, Notch, PI3K/AKT, TGF-beta, and Wnt. Wnt signalling, which maintains the gut's stem cell compartments, gets detailed treatment. For each pathway the authors list the mutations found in tumours. They close with drugs aimed at each route.
europmc-pmc6902032:
Malireddi and co-authors review master switches of cell death, in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology. Cells can die by several distinct programmes: quiet apoptosis, and the inflammatory routes pyroptosis and necroptosis. Each was long studied as a sealed system. Recent work shows they are wired together, with shared triggers and cross-talk. The authors gather that evidence around two regulators.

ZBP1 senses viral material, above all from influenza, and can fire all three death routes at once. TAK1 acts as a brake that keeps the same machinery in check. The combined pattern has been named PAN-optosis. Understanding these master controls, the authors argue, may explain tissue damage in infection better than any single pathway.
europmc-pmc6914932:
Guan reviews how inflammatory bowel disease develops and why it persists. His review appeared in the Journal of Immunology Research. The disease causes repeated bouts of intestinal inflammation. It includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Cases rose sharply during the last century. Newly industrialized countries now report fast growth.

Guan works through the main causes in turn. Genes shape risk, as do gut microbes and the wider environment. Faulty innate and adaptive immune responses drive much of the damage. He stresses how these factors interact. Recent findings, he argues, point toward new markers that could predict disease course. They may also guide fresh therapies.
europmc-pmc6959232:
Rubenstein and co-authors build a single-cell map of human skeletal muscle. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. Muscle is a mixed tissue: fibres drive movement, while many smaller cell types shape immunity, metabolism, and thinking. Studies of whole tissue blur those separate voices together.

The team sequenced single muscle fibres and single smaller cells from a human thigh muscle, plus mouse muscles. They found 11 human mononuclear cell types, including two subtypes of fibro-adipogenic progenitors, the cells that can make fat or scar tissue. One subtype, marked by the gene FBN1, was new, and mice had a match. The signatures let the team re-read older exercise studies at cell-type level, revealing shifts tied to age, sex, and training.
europmc-pmc6974432:
Kennis and co-authors test whether body markers can predict depression before it strikes or returns. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in Molecular Psychiatry. Leading theories blame changes in brain circuits, gut factors, immunity, growth factors, transmitters, hormones, or oxidative stress. Prospective proof was scattered.

Their search screened 67,464 articles and kept 75 forward-looking studies. Hormone studies were the largest group, with 39. Brain volume and immune marker analyses showed no significant prediction. Only cortisol stood out, with an odds ratio of 1.294 for onset or relapse. That effect vanished when studies starting with already ill participants were removed. Other markers were too varied to pool. Evidence for the leading theories, the authors conclude, remains thin.
europmc-pmc7017232:
Degirmenci, Wang, and Hu review a key cancer signalling pathway in the journal Cells. The RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK cascade carries signals that control cell growth, survival, and differentiation. Mutations in its genes drive about one-third of human cancers. Blocking the pathway is therefore a major goal of cancer drug design.

The review traces the cascade from its discovery to recent work on RAF control. RAF activity turns on shape changes, self-blocking, pairing, and phosphate tags. A central problem is paradoxical activation, where a RAF-blocking drug can switch the pathway on instead. The authors weigh what this means for treatment. They focus on how new findings could yield drugs that shut the pathway down without that rebound.
europmc-pmc7045432:
Jin and co-authors untangle an RNA control circuit in lung cancer in Molecular Cancer. ALKBH5 is an enzyme that erases m6A marks from RNA. YAP is a growth driver switched on in many cancers. How ALKBH5 might govern YAP in non-small cell lung cancer, and with what effect on tumours, had not been worked out.

YAP levels moved opposite to ALKBH5 across the cell systems tested. ALKBH5 stripped m6A marks from YAP RNA, changing how reader proteins handled it. One reader, YTHDF3, bound the RNA; YTHDF1 then promoted its translation while YTHDF2 pushed its decay through the AGO2 system. ALKBH5 also acted through a microRNA route involving miR-107 and LATS2 to restrain YAP activity. The net effect: ALKBH5 slowed tumour growth and metastasis. The circuit suggests restoring this eraser could rein in aggressive lung cancers.
europmc-pmc7145632:
Mitchell and co-authors report the 2020 state of MGnify, the EMBL-EBI platform for analysing microbiome sequence data, in Nucleic Acids Research. The free service assembles, analyses, and archives data from microbial communities sampled in environments from oceans to guts. Its public analysed datasets more than doubled in two years.

A new pipeline system, version 5.0, tailors the analysis to the input data and records each workflow formally, aiding reuse and reproducibility. Assembled datasets grew six-fold, and the protein database built from them passed 1 billion sequences. Added features include pathway predictions for assembled contigs and a viewer for inspecting them closely.
europmc-pmc7187532:
Wu and co-authors present CircAtlas, a large database of circular RNAs. Their article appeared in Genome Biology. Circular RNAs are ring-shaped RNA molecules made by cells. Most older databases held few species or tissue types. That limited work on which circles matter most. The team built a broader resource from many transcriptomes. It spans six vertebrate species and 19 normal tissues.

CircAtlas holds more than one million circular RNAs. The count comes from 1,070 RNA sequencing samples. Over 81 percent of entries have full-length sequences assembled. The database profiles how each circle is expressed across tissues. It also scores conservation across species. Co-expression and regulatory networks help rank candidates. The authors offer the resource as a tool for picking promising circles for study. Access is free through the project website.
europmc-pmc7205032:
Ahmed and co-authors analyze Twitter talk linking 5G technology to COVID-19. Their study appeared in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. The conspiracy claim spread widely online early in the pandemic. It even led to arson attacks on 5G towers in the United Kingdom. Understanding what drives such claims is key to fighting misinformation.

The team mapped the network of accounts sharing the theory. They sampled 233 tweets from a dataset of 2,328 for close reading. About a third of sampled tweets endorsed the 5G link. Another third denounced it, and the rest were general commentary. YouTube ranked among the most shared domains. The authors draw lessons for spotting and countering health misinformation quickly.
europmc-pmc7239332:
Dbouk and Drikakis simulate how far cough droplets travel through the air. Their study appeared in Physics of Fluids. They used advanced fluid dynamics that track droplets as they disperse, evaporate, and break up. Air humidity, turbulence, and droplet interactions all enter the model. A mild human cough was simulated at 20 degrees Celsius and 50 percent humidity.

Saliva droplets carrying disease traveled farther than expected. Wind speed changed the safe distance between people. Small droplets lingered and drifted rather than dropping quickly. The results question fixed social distance rules that ignore weather. Ventilation and outdoor conditions matter for airborne spread, they argue. The work speaks to how guidelines should treat coughs in shared air. It also models a process that experiments struggle to measure directly.
europmc-pmc7266132:
Adelman and co-authors review how the gut microbiome shapes sepsis, a life-threatening overreaction to infection. Their review appeared in Critical Care. Healthy gut microbes support immune balance and protect the gut barrier. When the microbial community is disturbed, the risk of sepsis changes.

Before sepsis begins, altered gut microbes can let harmful bacteria expand, prime the immune system for an oversized inflammatory response, and cut production of helpful short-chain fatty acids. Once sepsis sets in, the disruption deepens and organ damage becomes more likely. Early evidence hints that probiotics and related treatments may help some patients, though safety worries limit their use. The authors lay out a research agenda, since most proof so far comes from animal studies.
europmc-pmc7272632:
Kanaan and co-authors show that when the protein tau gathers into liquid droplets, it can twist into harmful shapes. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Tau is best known for building up in Alzheimer's disease and related disorders. Like several disease proteins, it can separate out of solution into droplets, a process called liquid-liquid phase separation.

At normal protein levels in lifelike buffers, tau formed dynamic droplets. Disease-linked changes, including the P301L mutation and a disease-associated phosphate pattern, made droplets form more easily and move more slowly. Left longer in this state, tau adopted toxic shapes and clumped into small oligomers rather than fibers. The P301L form produced the most oligomers. Droplet formation, the authors suggest, may be an early step toward disease.
europmc-pmc7338432:
Shanahan and co-authors follow young adults through the COVID-19 pandemic in Psychological Medicine, using a cohort first measured before the outbreak. Few studies could compare the same people before and during lockdown. Here 768 participants were assessed at age 20 and again at age 22, during the pandemic.

Perceived stress and anger rose on average, while internalizing symptoms such as anxiety and low mood did not. Distress before the pandemic was the strongest predictor of distress during it. Economic and lifestyle disruption, hopelessness, and older social stressors such as bullying also mattered. Fear of illness itself mattered less. Keeping a routine, staying active, and reframing problems in a positive light all linked to lower distress.
europmc-pmc7347232:
Zimin and Salzberg present a software paper in PLoS Computational Biology. It introduces POLCA, a tool that polishes genome assemblies. Long-read sequencing gives long, joined-up assemblies but with many errors. Short, cheap reads can fix those errors after assembly.

POLCA aligns short reads to an assembly and calls variants from the match. Spots where reads point to a likely error get corrected. The authors test it on simulated data and on real bacterial and human genomes. They report that POLCA matched or beat two widely used tools, Pilon and Racon, on accuracy. It also ran much faster and used little memory. The tool ships with the MaSuRCA assembler. Readers get a fast option for cleaning up long-read assemblies.
europmc-pmc7351732:
Dong and co-authors review how the cancer gene MYC rewires cell metabolism, in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. MYC is a master switch for cell growth, and it runs out of control in up to 70 percent of human cancers. Fast growth forces cancer cells to reorganize how they make energy and building blocks.

Oncogenic MYC touches nearly every part of that rewiring, from sugar use to the making of fats and DNA parts. That very dependence is a weakness, since tumor cells may rely on MYC-driven pathways more than healthy cells do. Blocking those pathways could yield new drugs. Readers get a map of where metabolism and a famous cancer gene meet, and where treatments might strike.
europmc-pmc7402632:
Hadjadj and co-authors profile immune responses in severe COVID-19 patients in Science. Interferons are central antiviral signals, and their failure was suspected in the worst cases. The team studied immune cells from the blood of patients across severity grades.

Severe and critical patients showed impaired type I interferon activity: no detectable interferon-beta in blood at any grade, and weak interferon-alpha production in the sickest, tied to slower virus clearance. At the same time, inflammatory signals ran hot, with excess tumor necrosis factor and IL-6 driving an NF-kB fueled response, and blood viral load stayed high. A double failure, too little alarm and too much inflammation, marks severe disease. The contrast with lung-local interferon effects frames a timing problem for therapy.
europmc-pmc7464532:
Zielińska and co-authors review polymeric nanoparticles, from making them to their safety. These particles span 1 to 1000 nm in size. Drugs can sit inside their polymer core or stick to the surface.

The term covers both nanocapsules and nanospheres, which differ in build. Such particles can carry drugs straight to diseased tissue. That skill gives them strong promise for many diseases. The review covers the main production methods and ways to characterize the particles. It explains how well drugs attach to the core and how they release in lab tests. Safety gets close focus, for both people and the environment. Toxic effects on nature are weighed beside medical gains.
europmc-pmc7504732:
Jiménez-Gómez and Cecilia review chitosan, a natural polymer drawn from chitin. Chitin is among Earth's most plentiful biopolymers, but it barely dissolves. Removing some acetyl groups yields chitosan, which dissolves in acid.

Chitosan can take many shapes and carry many added groups. Those traits let makers tune its surface for a set task. It breaks down in the body, sticks to tissue, and shows bioactivity. Uses in medicine span skin, bone, and tissue engineering, wound healing, and artificial organs. It can trap dyes and organic compounds from water. It can split mixtures and serve as a catalyst base. The review covers its structure, ways to modify it, and its wide range of uses.
europmc-pmc7523332:
Lin and co-authors profile single cells from pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. They study both primary tumors and metastatic lesions. Solid tumors hold cancer cells plus many support and immune cells.

The team used single-cell RNA sequencing on patient samples. Clustering and a tool called SuperCT sorted the cell types. Cancer cells varied a lot between patients. Stromal cells looked more alike across patients. Immune cells were mostly macrophages and tired lymphocytes. Cell mix helped define tumor subtypes. Marker levels for some cell types also linked to patient survival. The work gives a detailed cell map for this hard cancer.
europmc-pmc7574532:
Clift and co-authors develop the QCOVID risk algorithm for COVID-19 hospital admission and death. The model was built and tested in English adults. It aims to rank risk at population scale.

Data came from 1205 general practices in England. Records linked to test results, hospital data and death registries. The derivation set held 6.08 million adults. A validation set held 2.17 million adults. Deaths in the derivation cohort numbered 4384 people. Predictors included age, ethnicity, deprivation and body mass index. Many existing health conditions also entered the model. The algorithm calibrated well in validation tests. Top risk groups captured most early deaths in follow-up.
europmc-pmc7794332:
Behary and co-authors study how gut microbes shape immune responses in fatty liver disease and liver cancer. The patients had non-alcoholic fatty liver disease with cirrhosis. Some had developed hepatocellular carcinoma, and some had not. The team used metagenomic and metabolomic profiling. They also tested bacterial extracts on immune cells outside the body.

Gut imbalance marked the cirrhosis group. Shifts in microbe makeup and function came with cancer onset. Microbe genes in the cancer group favored short-chain fatty acid output. Metabolite tests confirmed that pattern. Extracts from the cancer group pushed T cells toward a suppressive state. Regulatory T cells grew while CD8+ T cells weakened. Extracts from control groups did not do this.
europmc-pmc7870932:
Samur and co-authors trace how one myeloma patient beat CAR T therapy by losing its target. BCMA-directed CAR T cells give deep responses in myeloma. Relapse after treatment is common, though. Its causes were ill-defined. The team followed one patient over time.

Single-cell gene checks compared samples before and after relapse. A cancer clone lost both copies of the BCMA gene. One copy was deleted outright. The other carried a stop-making mutation. Without BCMA, the second cell dose could not expand. Blood levels of loose BCMA vanished as well. The case warns teams to test the target gene at relapse. Loss of the bullseye can defeat the whole therapy.
europmc-pmc7904932:
Gharahkhani and co-authors report a genome-wide meta-analysis of primary open-angle glaucoma. The disease is a common inherited cause of blindness. Finding its risk loci can reveal how the damage starts. The team pooled genome scans from many studies and ancestries to search at a far larger scale.

The analysis covered 34,179 cases and 349,321 controls. It found 44 risk loci that had not been reported before. It also confirmed 83 loci already known, for the total named in the title. Most loci acted in the same way across European, Asian, and African ancestries. Combining ancestries sharpened the search for the causal variants. The authors name genes that may drive the disease. Some are already targeted by known drug compounds, which could seed new glaucoma treatments.
europmc-pmc7911532:
Sharma and co-authors present a review of COVID-19 covering its origins, spread, detection, control, and prevention. Three major coronavirus outbreaks have hit since 2002: SARS, MERS, and COVID-19. Bats serve as the main animal reservoir for these viruses. The newest virus jumped to humans and spread across the globe.

By 8 October 2020, the virus had infected over 36.5 million people. It had reached 213 other countries and territories from its start in China. Spread through people without symptoms made it hard to contain. The review gathers up-to-date facts on how the virus evolves and transmits. It covers test methods and the control steps in use at the time. Readers get a single, broad briefing on a fast-moving crisis, written while the outcome was still open.
europmc-pmc7916132:
Hu and Ecker present a review of MMP-13 as a target for treating osteoarthritis. The disease wears down joint cartilage and inflames nearby tissue. MMP-13 is the main enzyme that cuts type II collagen, the core protein of cartilage. That role makes it an attractive point of attack for new drugs.

No current treatment can restore cartilage that has been lost. The review explains how MMP-13 is switched on and off at the gene and protein levels. It traces the enzyme's part in starting and advancing joint damage. Past attempts to block MMP-13 are surveyed, along with their setbacks. The authors argue the target still deserves work. A safe, selective blocker could slow a very common disease. The review gathers the case for fresh inhibitor design.
europmc-pmc7940032:
Meek presents a historical study of the beginnings of physiology in America. Physiology was the first of the experimental medical sciences, he argues. The rise of the organised laboratory was thus a turning point for all medicine. In Europe, that laboratory first appeared at Breslau in 1824 under Purkinje. America followed some fifty years later, at Boston and Baltimore in the 1870s.

Before laboratories, American students of the living body were scattered. Some were lone practitioners in remote settlements. Others were professors who taught anatomy or therapeutics and speculated on function as a side line. A rare student might run an experiment now and then. Meek divides the story into pre- and post-laboratory days. He traces how a fringe pursuit became a founded science. The paper honours the seminar of W. S. Miller at Wisconsin.
europmc-pmc7983032:
Türei and co-authors present a resource called OmniPath that joins knowledge of signals inside and between cells. Omics studies read thousands of molecules at once. Reading them well takes maps of how proteins interact. Maps of cell-to-cell talk were scarce and scattered, and they were not linked to the signals inside cells. This work closes that gap in one place.

The team combined over 100 resources on protein interactions and roles. They added data on protein complexes, jobs, places, and disease links. The resource covers humans, with mouse and rat reached by matching kin. Access comes through a web service, a plug-in, and packages in R and Python. Workflows and tutorials guide users through cell-talk analysis. Trial uses on SARS-CoV-2 infection and bowel disease show the range. The authors aim to serve both bench and computer scientists.
europmc-pmc8051032:
Panigrahi and O'Malley review what enhancers do, and what nobody yet understands about them. Enhancers are DNA stretches far from the genes they control. They set when, where, and how strongly genes switch on. That control builds the many cell types of a body from one genome. Enhancers are widely believed to touch their target promoters physically. The full mechanics of that touch remain unsettled.

The pair gather recent findings into emerging concepts of enhancer action. Which proteins take part is still an open roster. How contact turns into activation lacks a final answer. The review lays out the leading models side by side. It then lists the questions the field must settle. Each unknown is framed as a testable problem. Gene regulation's most familiar actors remain partly mysterious.
europmc-pmc8063132:
Villar and co-authors compare pregnancy outcomes with and without COVID-19 in a multinational cohort. The INTERCOVID study enrolled women at 43 hospitals in 18 countries. For each woman diagnosed with COVID-19, two women without the diagnosis joined at the same site. Enrollment ran for 8 months from March 2020. The final groups held 706 women with the diagnosis and 1,424 without it.

Women with COVID-19 faced higher rates of pregnancy-induced hypertension, at a relative risk of 1.46 in the adjusted comparison. Preeclampsia and eclampsia rose higher still, at a relative risk of 1.76 across the cohort. Infections needing antibiotics were far more common as well. Admission to intensive care carried a relative risk of 5.04 for the infected group. Their babies also faced more morbidity. The study gave clinics firm numbers for counseling pregnant patients.
europmc-pmc8076232:
Shorstova and co-authors chart a route to clinical success for BET inhibitors in cancer. BET proteins switch on the gene networks that drive many tumors. They dock onto chromatin through two bromodomains apiece. Blocking those docks can shut the networks down. A decade of work has produced potent blockers of one or both domains.

The review lays out BET biology first. It then tracks how inhibitor design has advanced across generations. Candidate biomarkers that predict response get close attention. Resistance routes are mapped as carefully as the successes. Combination therapy forms the core strategy on offer. Pairing BET blockers with other drugs may deepen and prolong control. The authors frame three needs as the roadmap ahead. Know the mechanism, find the markers, and build the synergies.
europmc-pmc8081532:
Riera and co-authors review how the COVID-19 pandemic delayed and disrupted cancer care worldwide. People with cancer faced a double risk. The virus itself threatened them more than most. At the same time, strained health systems cut the services they depend on. The team ran a systematic search across major databases. Sixty-two studies met their inclusion rules.

None of the 62 studies reached high methodological quality. The review sorted the harm into 38 categories of delay and disruption. Shrinking service capacity drove most of them. Cancer surgeries fell, radiotherapy slipped, and clinic visits were delayed or cancelled. Facilities reported disruption rates up to 77.5% in the worst-hit reports. Supply chains and staff availability suffered almost as much. The authors urge standard ways to measure such harm.
europmc-pmc8096432:
Beghini and co-authors present bioBakery 3, a rebuilt suite for profiling microbial communities. Shotgun metagenomics can name microbes, list their genes, and split strains apart. Reference genomes have grown vast, and the tools must keep pace. The suite joins updated versions of its three core methods. Each was tuned against the largest reference set yet built.

MetaPhlAn 3 sharpens species-level naming from sequence reads. HUMAnN 3 improves the read on gene function and activity. Applied to colorectal cancer, the suite handled 1,262 metagenomes. For bowel disease, it took 1,635 metagenomes plus 817 metatranscriptomes in stride. Fresh disease-microbe links surfaced in both tests. Strain tools then profiled 4,077 further samples. They resolved the family tree of one gut microbe known from just 15 isolates before. Open code and cloud workflows complete the package.
europmc-pmc8158032:
Rao and co-authors test a gut bacterium as a treatment for fatty liver disease in mice. Akkermansia muciniphila has shown promise against obesity and diabetes. The team fed mice a high-fat, high-cholesterol diet to induce the liver disease.

The authors report that the bacterium reversed liver fat build-up, inflammation, and injury. Benefits lasted after long-term withdrawal, though antibiotics weakened them slightly. Treatment raised mitochondrial oxidation and bile acid metabolism along the gut-liver axis. It also eased oxidative stress. The proposed path runs through L-aspartate metabolism. The results point to the gut-liver axis as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc8187432:
Wang and co-authors present MOGONET, a method that merges multi-omics data for patient sorting. Single data types give only part of the picture of a disease. Their graph network learns from each omics type and from links across types.

The method used mRNA, DNA methylation, and microRNA data together. The authors report that it beat other leading integration methods on several tasks. It also flagged biomarkers tied to the classes it found. Graph learning lets patient similarity guide the sorting. The tool aims at sharper diagnosis from combined molecular data.
europmc-pmc8218332:
Liu and co-authors test how well sera neutralise the Delta-family variants of SARS-CoV-2. These variants spread fast and drove a severe wave of infection across India. The lead variant was named a variant of concern in the United Kingdom soon after it emerged.

The team used monoclonal antibodies plus vaccine and convalescent sera in lab tests. Both variants in the family were harder to neutralise than the early strains of the virus. Structural work mapped where antibodies bind the spike protein. The study also charts the antigenic space of the variants then in circulation. Reduced neutralisation did not mean absent protection, and existing vaccines still showed activity against them.
europmc-pmc8234032:
Subhan and co-authors survey tumour targeting through the EPR effect in cancer treatment. Most cancer drugs lack tumour selectivity, a core weakness. Nanodrugs given by vein behave in a way that helps.

They are too large to slip through tight walls of normal vessels. They also escape quick clearance by the kidney. Tumour vessels leak, and tumours drain poorly. So nanodrugs build up in tumour tissue over time. Levels can reach several times those in plasma. The review traces progress and prospects for this route since its first report in mouse tumours.
europmc-pmc8266832:
Huang and Zhou review DNA damage repair in cancer, from history to targeted therapy. Genomic instability marks many cancers as damage piles up. Radiotherapy and chemotherapy exploit that weakness.

Both treatments also injure normal tissue, a heavy cost. Targeted therapy aims at cancers that lack set repair functions. Knowing each repair pathway's wider role guides that aim. The review traces how the field's ideas developed. It sets out the main repair routes and their machinery. Clinical uses, above all in repair-weak tumours, close the survey. Repair faults are framed as the cancer's exploitable flaw.
europmc-pmc8707132:
Gao and co-authors pool studies on factors tied to sarcopenia, the loss of muscle with age, in older adults who live at home. The team searched major databases for observational studies up to August 2021. Two reviewers screened and rated each study on their own. Data were pooled with standard statistical models.

The pool held 68 studies with 98,502 cases. Older age, being single or widowed, and limits in daily tasks raised the odds. Being underweight carried an odds ratio of 3.78. Smoking, low activity, and poor nutrition also raised risk. Long and short sleep both linked to higher odds. The results map who faces the most risk.
europmc-pmc8786632:
Su and co-authors identify early factors that anticipate post-acute sequelae of COVID-19, the long symptoms after infection. The team followed 309 patients from diagnosis to recovery two to three months later. Deep multi-omic profiling was joined with clinical data and patient reports. The aim was risk factors visible at first diagnosis.

Four factors stood out at that early point. They were type 2 diabetes, virus RNA in blood, Epstein-Barr virus in blood, and certain auto-antibodies. Immune patterns sorted patients into four groups with distinct paths. Gut symptom patients showed unique T cell shifts during recovery. The authors argue early measurement can guide care for chronic outcomes.
europmc-pmc8791832:
Kagawa and co-authors show that human stem cells can form blastoids, models of the blastocyst that mimic implantation. One week after fertilization, embryos implant in the uterus. That step needs a hollow ball of cells with three founding lineages. The team grew such models from naive pluripotent stem cells.

A special medium and three blocked pathways drove the process. More than 70 percent of attempts formed blastoids. Over 97 percent held all three lineage types in the right order and timing. The models formed a first body axis on their own. They also attached to hormone-treated uterine cells in the right direction. The model is scalable and avoids embryo use.
europmc-pmc8890532:
Zhang and co-authors review mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and their role in keeping the body in balance. Mitochondria are the main source of these reactive molecules. They were long treated as pure hazards to health. Newer evidence gives them a second face. At the right levels, they carry signals through the cell. They help the body adapt and defend itself under stress.

The review explains how these molecules are made and cleared. It traces how they are transformed inside the cell. It then maps their jobs in normal physiology. Cell growth, cell specialization, aging, and cell death all feature. Stem cells and low-oxygen adaptation get attention too. The authors argue that dose and place decide the verdict. The same molecule can protect or harm.
europmc-pmc8912932:
COVID-19 Excess Mortality Collaborators estimate how many deaths the pandemic truly caused through 2021. Official counts miss many pandemic deaths. Excess mortality offers a fuller measure. It compares observed deaths with expected deaths. The team covered 191 countries and territories. Reports came from 74 countries plus many subnational units. Six models estimated the expected baseline. An ensemble combined them by past accuracy.

Where death records were missing, a statistical model filled the gaps. It leaned on pandemic and health-system covariates. Prediction used repeated draws to size uncertainty. Late registration and heat waves were stripped from the data. The result is a global excess estimate with intervals. National and regional breakdowns accompany it. The authors frame excess deaths as the honest ledger. Public health decisions, they argue, need that ledger.
europmc-pmc8967832:
Kim and co-authors show that gels from real gut tissue can replace Matrigel for growing organoids. Matrigel is the standard scaffold for organoid culture. It comes from mouse tumors, though. Batches vary, costs run high, and safety questions linger. The team decellularized stomach and intestine tissue instead. The remaining matrix formed hydrogels. Gastric and intestinal organoids were grown inside them. Growth and function were compared head to head.

Organoids in tissue gels matched or beat those in Matrigel. They also survived long-term subculture. Transplantation worked from the new gels. The gels mimic the organoids' home tissue closely. Protein analysis revealed tissue-specific matrix profiles. Age of the source tissue shaped results too. The authors propose these gels for disease modeling. Drug development and tissue regeneration are the wider aims.
europmc-pmc8995832:
De Vos and co-authors review how gut microbes steer health through concrete chemical routes. The gut community is now seen as a key health regulator. Its shifts link to obesity, diabetes, fatty liver, and bowel disease. Cancer joins the list as well. New lab tools keep exposing the traffic between microbes and organs. Metabolite studies lead that work. The review judges the evidence with a critical eye. It asks which links look truly causal.

Known actors come first. Short-chain fatty acids and bile acids are the classics. One compound, trimethylamine N-oxide, gets its own fame. Newer actors widen the cast. Cannabis-like body lipids and plant-derived compounds appear. Receptors that receive these signals are mapped. Each route suggests a therapy angle. Some are already in development. The authors set the base for microbe-based treatments.
europmc-pmc9033932:
Peng and co-authors review efforts to target TGF-beta signaling in fibrosis and cancer. This cytokine guides development, tissue repair, and immune balance, but in excess it drives scarring and tumor growth. It pushes cells to change state, lays down matrix, and reshapes the tissue around tumors. Drugs against the pathway look promising, yet risk harm across the body.

The review explains the pathway's dual role, helpful early and harmful late in disease. It then surveys therapies in clinical use and trials. The authors argue that smarter targeting is needed to gain the benefits without systemic toxicity.
europmc-pmc9052532:
Lu and co-authors review how gut microbes shape responses to cancer immunotherapy. Evidence from lab and clinic studies shows the gut community can raise or blunt the effect of checkpoint inhibitors. Microbes reprogram the tumor surroundings by engaging innate and adaptive immune cells. Their metabolites also travel beyond the gut and tune the body-wide response.

The review covers microbial signs that predict benefit or side effects. It then surveys strategies to harness the effect, from fecal transplants to probiotics and engineered microbes. The authors argue that these tools could sharpen precision care in cancer.
europmc-pmc9280632:
Gao and co-authors review how the states of tumor-associated macrophages shape cancer immunotherapy. Macrophages can polarize into M1 forms that fight tumors or M2 forms that help them. In tumors, the M2-like form dominates and aids vessel growth, immune suppression, and spread. That makes these cells a hot target for new treatments.

The review first explains polarization and its effects in the tumor setting. It then covers how M2-like cells blunt checkpoint blockade and CAR-T cell therapy. Signaling paths that set macrophage state are mapped next. The authors discuss ways to flip cells back to the M1 state. Turning tumor helpers into tumor fighters is the central hope.
europmc-pmc9281132:
Zhao and co-authors review Wnt signaling as a driver and drug target in colorectal cancer. The Wnt network guides embryo growth and cell fate, and its canonical branch is a known colon cancer driver. Beta-catenin sits at the center of that branch. Its control and breakdown are key events in tumor growth.

The review lays out the three Wnt branches and their biochemistry. It links the pathway to cell growth, stemness, cell death, metabolism, and spread. Drugs, plant compounds, and molecular blockers aimed at the pathway are surveyed. Some Wnt blockers are already used in the clinic for this cancer. The authors argue that better pathway drugs could treat colorectal cancer well. Clear targets now exist at many steps of the cascade.
europmc-pmc9402432:
Mishima and co-authors report that vitamin K can block ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron and lipid damage. Ferroptosis plays a part in organ injury and in some cancers that resist treatment. The team asked what other cell systems guard against it.

They found that the fully reduced forms of vitamin K act as strong radical traps. These forms stop lipid damage before membranes break. An enzyme called FSP1 makes the reduced form from vitamin K. That same step explains how vitamin K works as an antidote to warfarin poisoning. The authors frame this as a non-canonical vitamin K cycle. It sits apart from the known clotting role of the vitamin.
europmc-pmc9408932:
Aibar-Almazán and co-authors survey the current state of diagnosis and care for osteoporosis. The disease thins bone and raises fracture risk. It hits mostly women after menopause and older adults. Bone loss outpaces bone growth, yet early signs are often silent.

The review starts with the basics of bone biology. It then covers checks such as bone densitometry and dual X-ray scans. Fracture risk scoring is covered too. Care options split into drug and non-drug paths. Drugs that slow bone loss lead the drug side. Newer cell therapies and bioactive hydrogels are also reviewed. On the non-drug side, the authors stress exercise, diet, and quitting smoking and heavy drinking.
europmc-pmc9481132:
Yoon and co-authors review brain lipidomics, the large-scale study of lipids in the brain. Lipids build cell membranes and carry signals between cells. They also store energy and keep cell balance. Faulty lipid patterns are tied to nerve cell loss and other brain diseases.

The authors first set out the main brain lipid classes. Cholesterol, glycerophospholipids, and sphingolipids each get a section. They then trace lipid changes in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Huntington's disease and schizophrenia are covered too. A methods part surveys mass spectrometry tools for lipid work. It also covers joint analysis with other omics data. The closing part looks at pairing lipidomics with artificial intelligence. Such pairing may aid early diagnosis of brain disease.
europmc-pmc9869432:
Li presents miniprot, a new tool that aligns protein sequences to a complete genome. Such alignment is key to annotating genes in non-model organisms. Older tools for this task were built over 10 years ago. They are slow beside today's genome and protein data growth.

Miniprot uses recent methods such as k-mer sketching and vectorized dynamic programming. The author reports it runs tens of times faster than existing tools. Accuracy on real data stayed comparable in the tests reported. The tool can help teams annotate new genomes at scale. Its code is shared through a public GitHub page given in the article.
fielding-old-debauchees-1732:
The Old Debauchees, a farce of Fielding's early stage years, was first played in 1732. It is also known as The Miser Punished in some printings of his plays. Young Fielding was then the busiest comic playwright in London, turning out pieces at speed.

The plot turns on rakes, guardians, and young lovers outwitting age and greed, in the brisk manner of the Drury Lane farce. Songs, disguises, and sharp talk keep the short piece moving. Fielding's stage career ended when the Licensing Act of 1737 shut his theatre down, pushing him toward the novel. This farce preserves the sparkle of the playwright he first was.
fort-wild-talents-1932:
Fort's last book asks what strange powers sleep in man himself. Wild Talents, printed in 1932, takes up latent gifts, poltergeist girls, and crime worked by occult means. It closes the four-volume pile of data the learned would not touch.

He tells of folk who start fires by a look, of killers traced by dreams, and of talents that flare and die. His claim is that man has wild powers, bred down and feared out of him by church and school. The book is Fort's last word on the damned. It points his whole work at the reader's own skin.
frus-1861-d132:
Writing on 22 June 1861, William H. Seward addressed William Dayton, his envoy in Paris. The letter is document 132 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward wrote to Paris and to Brussels on the same June day. The twin letters show a chief working a whole front in one sitting. For Dayton, the note was fresh proof that France stood high in Washington's mind that summer. A whole front worked in one sitting shows the scale of Seward's daily labor. One sitting's work, spread across a map, shows a chief at full stretch.
frus-1861-d232:
Dated 2 April 1861, a report from Mr. Murphy went to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 232 in the President's message volume for 1861. It belongs to the month the Civil War began, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d32:
Henry Sanford wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 30 July 1861, the same day Seward wrote to him. The dispatch is document 32 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Letters crossing in the mail were a fact of life in the age of steam. Neither man could know the other's latest word for weeks. The matched dates here let readers see two ends of one link, each writing in the dark about the other. Crossed letters fill this file, a sign of how far apart the two desks truly were.
frus-1862-d132:
Seward's incoming mail for 22 August 1862 held a dispatch from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 132 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d232:
On 4 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Stuart, acting head of the British legation, in a letter printed as Document 232 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Lee's army was crossing the Potomac into Maryland as Seward wrote, carrying the war onto Union soil. European governments watched the invasion as a test of Southern strength. If the South won in Maryland, Britain might move toward backing it. Seward's letters in this window worked against that reading, and this one is part of the file that shows the effort. Both offices kept up the formal courtesies even when their governments were near quarreling.
frus-1862-d32:
Seward's incoming mail for 13 March 1862 held a dispatch from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 32 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The letter comes from the winter of the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d332:
On 8 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton a dispatch printed as Document 332 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister to France, posted in Paris.

Seward wrote while the French truce proposal waited on the British cabinet, the hinge of the fall. His guidance to Dayton in October mixed patience with plain warnings about what foreign action would mean. Letters like this one kept the Paris envoy aligned with the simultaneous effort in London, where the decision would be made. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d432:
Gabriel García Tassara wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 July 1862, a week after receiving Seward's last note. The letter is Document 432 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Resident ministers wrote often, and on small matters as well as great ones: a seized ship, a consul's complaint, a point of form. Each note from Tassara also told Seward, between the lines, how Madrid viewed the war that month. In July 1862 that view mattered, because Spain's ports in Cuba sat astride Confederate trade routes. The exchange preserved here is the working surface of a relationship both sides wanted kept calm.
frus-1862-d532:
A second reply of 7 June 1862 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Roest van Limburg at the Netherlands legation. It is Document 532 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's printed record.

Two questions, two letters: that was the Department's rule, and the Dutch file of that week obeys it strictly. Seward's paired replies matched Van Limburg's paired notes point for point. The business between the governments concerned Dutch trade and shipping. It concerned their rights and treatment in wartime. The Netherlands wanted no part of that war, except as a carrier. The exchange shows formal diplomacy at its most procedural, and its very dryness is what makes it a faithful picture of the work.
frus-1862-d632:
Edward Joy Morris reported from Constantinople to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 July 1862. The dispatch is Document 632 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Morris wrote as the Seven Days ended in Virginia, news that would take the summer to reach and be weighed in the Levant. His own subjects were the standing ones of the post: trade, protection, and the treatment of Americans under Ottoman rule. The independence of his file is its lesson. While the war consumed Washington, the republic's older foreign business went forward on its own momentum. It did so in places the war barely touched. Ministers like Morris were that momentum in person.
frus-1863p1-d132:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 27 March 1863. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 132 in part one of the 1863 volume.

A three-letter day closed the legation's March mail in a rush. Adams had the cabinet, the press, and the shipyards to cover, and he gave each its sheet. This one opens the set of 27 March. The run of his spring letters is the record of a watch kept without pause, and this dispatch is a fair piece of it.
frus-1863p1-d232:
The Secretary of State, William H. Seward, wrote to his minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 11 July 1863. The letter is document 232 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d32:
Three letters from London bear the date 16 January 1863; this one came from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Two more Adams letters in the volume share the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 32 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Three sheets in one day is a heavy day at any legation. Adams sorted his London news into parts: the cabinet, the press, and the Southern agents who worked the city. This dispatch is one of the three. It shows the scale of the post's work in a month when the war's meaning abroad was in flux.
frus-1863p1-d332: On 5 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 332 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d432:
28 March 1863 is the date on a letter from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d532:
On 25 May 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington wrote to Secretary William H. Seward. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d632:
From Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington: a letter dated 20 October 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d132: Stephen Early wrote again on November 16, 1943 to Hull, Stimson, Knox, and the Secret Service chief, in a letter that is Document 132 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. It repeats the address list of his note of the day before, a sign of standing summit business passing through his office. The record gives the names and the date. The letter's business is stated in the printed Foreign Relations text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d232:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 390/1 aboard the Iowa on 18 November 1943, on future operations in the Southeast Asia Command. It answers a paper from the British side and guards the Combined Chiefs of Staff's right to decide more than grand strategy alone.

The American chiefs hold that the combined body should choose among courses of action, and fix their order and timing, for Southeast Asia. Since the United States cannot supply what Operation First Culverin would need, they agree that Operation Buccaneer should be mounted as early as possible. They also ask the Southeast Asia commander to study further land, sea, and air moves to pin down Japanese forces in south Burma.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d32: Alexander Kirk, the American ambassador in Egypt, wrote to the Secretary of State on September 10, 1943, and his dispatch is Document 32 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Kirk's post in Cairo put him at the hub of Middle East reporting, and his cables home fed Washington's picture of the region. Two months later his city would host the Cairo Conference itself. The record names no topic for this dispatch.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d332: President Roosevelt sent Ambassador Alexander Kirk a one-line memorandum at Cairo on 26 November 1943. It asks Kirk to have Wadsworth, the American consul general at Beirut, come down to Cairo when Roosevelt returns there, which he expects to be about Thursday or Friday. The editors date those days to 2 or 3 December, during the second Cairo stay after Tehran. The brief note is signed only with the President's initials.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d432: Harry Hopkins sent Ambassador Steinhardt an urgent telegram from Cairo on 3 December 1943 about the greeting party for President Inönü of Turkey. Major John Boettiger is accompanying the President's plane to Adana that day, to extend Roosevelt's greetings to Inönü on his arrival and to travel back with him. Randolph Churchill is flying on a similar mission in the Prime Minister's plane. Hopkins adds a small point of ceremony and tactics in one line: the President would be pleased to have Inönü ride in the American plane.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d532:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt in Ankara wrote on December 24, 1943 to Paul H. Alling, chief of the State Department's Division of Near Eastern Affairs. Writing to a division chief meant writing to the desk that ran Turkish policy day by day. The State Department printed the letter in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Steinhardt's channel to Alling was where embassy reporting met Washington policymaking on Turkey and the Near East. Three weeks after the Cairo meeting with President İnönü, the Turkish question remained open and delicate. For readers, the letter shows diplomacy at the working level: an ambassador and a desk chief keeping a difficult account in order.
frus-1944-quebec-d132:
Myron Taylor, the president's personal representative at Vatican City, sent this urgent, strictly confidential telegram on September 1, 1944. It is addressed to Roosevelt and Hull, and it concerns Italy rather than the Vatican. Taylor wanted the president briefed by a man on the ground before the reported conference with Churchill.

Taylor urged a frank talk with General William O'Dwyer, who ran the economic section of the Allied Control Commission for Italy. O'Dwyer could explain Italy's relief needs and the plans to meet them, Taylor said. He asked that Hull or Leo Crowley telegraph O'Dwyer at once, ordering him to Washington for consultation without delay.
frus-1944-quebec-d232:
General Deane reported fast movement from Moscow on September 13, 1944. Marshall's Octagon 10 arrived just as air force headquarters signaled the Warsaw project was scheduled for that very day. Deane and the two ambassadors saw Molotov, who arranged approval from the Red Army General Staff. General Spaatz was informed, and the mission was rescheduled for September 14.

Deane doubted that representatives needed to come to Moscow at all. Planning details, he argued, were better worked out in London; all Moscow needed to supply was Soviet approval, which the two missions could seek. The editors' note adds that bad weather later postponed the relief mission to September 18.
frus-1944-quebec-d32:
A second message from Harry Hopkins to Prime Minister Churchill is dated August 28, 1944. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume, next to its companions of the same date.

Hopkins divided his business among separate messages, a habit he shared with Churchill. His late-August letters to London prepared the Quebec meeting from the American side: who would come, what would be discussed, and what the President hoped to settle. For readers, this message is one panel of a day's concentrated staff work, valuable because it shows how much of a summit happens before the leaders arrive.
frus-1945-50-intel-d132:
Vandenberg wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 3 January 1947. The director of central intelligence opened the year with a letter to the board's senior secretary. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

January 1947 was the CIG's last season under the old charter: within months, Congress would debate the law that made the Central Intelligence Agency. Vandenberg's letter to Byrnes belongs to the director's campaign for that stronger future. Readers who have followed him since July can see the arc complete. He went from pressing the FBI over a hemisphere to pressing the cabinet for an agency. The volume ends its main run with the campaign still rising.
frus-1945-50-intel-d232: "Memorandum for the Record" bears the date 8 April 1948. It is document 232 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was in its first year, and the Council was taking up covert action for the first time. The form is a note to the file: no request and no order.
frus-1945-50-intel-d32:
Robert Lovett, assistant secretary of war for air, wrote to General Bissell, the Army's intelligence chief, on 23 October 1945. Lovett was one of the War Department's most able civilians. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Air power had its own intelligence needs, from target folders to reading enemy air strength, and Lovett watched them closely. His letter to Bissell shows the air arm stating its interest inside the Army's house. The name Lovett returns in the volume at the head of a committee on intelligence. Readers who note his early papers will see why he was chosen. Able men gravitated to this question in 1945, sensing it would shape the next war's opening days.
frus-1945-50-intel-d332:
Formal minutes cover a meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board, held on 20 November 1947. It survives in print as document 332 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The shift from the old group to the CIA was fresh. The Council was still learning how to run its side of the work.

A set of minutes does one job well. It fixes what a body took up and what it settled, in the order the items came up. Such pages are often the only proof of when a choice was made, and by whom. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d432:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 1, in the form issued on 19 January 1950, is document 432 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Directive No. 1 was the base rule of the whole series, so a new version mattered. Reissuing it in 1950 let the Council restate the CIA's core duties in light of hard use. Readers get the closest thing the system had to a founding charter, revised by experience. Later chiefs worked under versions of this first rule for the rest of the Cold War. Restating the base rule let each agency test its own habits against it once more.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d132:
Preventing a third world war is the single aim of this Treasury paper of 19 January 1945. Titled “Long Range Program for Germany,” it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume among the papers prepared as the Big Three meeting neared. No author is named on the document itself.

Germany, it argues, must be rendered weak in politics, arms, and wealth, and kept weak for many years. Any program that builds Germany up as a bulwark against Russia and communism will lead, in time, to a third world war. The paper admits no plan can promise peace. Its standard is therefore the opposite of a minimum program: see how far we can go now to make another German war impossible.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d232:
A Foreign Office man's fears about Iran fill this cable of 2 November 1944 from London. Waldemar Gallman, counselor of the American embassy, reports the talk to the Secretary of State. The cable is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

The British government, the official said, is gravely concerned at the Russian attitude in the oil deadlock. If Iran gives in, the concession would be one large step toward folding northern Iran into the Russian orbit for good. The Soviet request, he added, was unlimited in scope. Unlike the British or Americans, the Russians never named the royalties they would pay. He went on to list other Soviet moves, from bought newspapers carrying Moscow's line to pressure inside the joint censorship committee in Iran.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d32: Harriman wrote again on 27 December 1944, his second report to Roosevelt in two days from Moscow. Preserved as document 32 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta, it extends his late December run of messages. The cluster of reports shows the ambassador working hard to prepare the president before the American delegation left for the Mediterranean.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d332:
Staying at Yalta instead of going back to Malta was the liveliest item before the Joint Chiefs on February 5, 1945. A British proposal suggested a change of plan. The Combined Chiefs would finish their open work at Yalta — called Magneto in the code names — and drop the return to Malta, called Cricket. Admiral Leahy put the idea open for debate.

General Marshall called the change agreeable, the next best thing to his own wish. He would rather have sent the American shipping men to Yalta instead. The minutes show war planning bent around planes, ships, and where tired staffs could sleep.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d432:
Late at night on February 9, 1945, the foreign ministers fought over Poland again, and Bohlen's minutes catch the heat. Molotov announced they had met to discuss formulas. Eden interrupted with news: a strong cable from the War Cabinet rejected the earlier basis of discussion. Unless something like his text of three days before could be had, London would approve no formula.

Eden handed over a revised formula. A lively argument followed over whether it was a new text or just a change to the American one. Molotov objected to treating it as new. The minutes show allies bargaining past 10 p.m., with London's cabinet pulling one way and Moscow the other.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d132:
The Joint Chiefs' secretary listed Secretary of War Henry Stimson's traveling party in a memorandum dated July 8, 1945. The memo to his British counterpart is document 132 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It gives the party's route and arrival time so the British could track the flight.

Stimson's group will reach Gibraltar about 8 a.m. on July 14. With him travel Assistant Secretary John McCloy, special assistant Harvey Bundy, the Surgeon General, and a row of colonels and support staff, eleven people in all. Two aircraft, a C-54 and a C-47, will carry them on to Babelsberg, though their numbers are not yet known. Stimson's presence at Potsdam mattered far beyond protocol: he carried the secret of the atomic bomb project, whose first test came on July 16, the day before the conference opened.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d232:
Edward Page recorded Molotov questioning China's seat in a memorandum dated July 11, 1945. The extract is document 232 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It covers the second half of Harriman's call on Molotov about the Berlin agenda.

Molotov noted that the American letter proposed China taking part in the Council of Foreign Ministers that would study the peace machinery question. He seemed to doubt the wisdom of it. Many subjects are new to the Chinese, he said, since they had not joined talks on European matters and were not members of the European Advisory Commission. Harriman had no information beyond his letter. He reasoned that Germany's war had worldwide reach. He reasoned that Far Eastern countries hold interests in Europe. And he reasoned that China, as a permanent member of the Security Council, should be kept close to European questions.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d32: Churchill's reply, sent May 23, 1945, is two lines long. Thank you for your Number 46. I shall be delighted to see Mr. Davies as soon as he arrives. The telegram welcomed the President's envoy to London ahead of the three-power conference. Davies, a former ambassador to Moscow known for his sympathy toward the Soviet Union, was Truman's chosen sounding board with Churchill. The brief text survives in the Leahy Papers.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d332:
Army planners on the Joint Strategic Survey Committee weighed dismemberment of Germany in an undated memorandum, and advised against it. Cutting Germany into several states, they wrote, would not fully break the aggressive nationalism of the past century. New small states in central Europe would instead widen the field for rivalry among the great powers.

From a long-range military and political view, the committee called substantial dismemberment undesirable. It raised no objection, though, to fair border changes sought by Denmark, the Netherlands, and Belgium. The extract reached President Truman through Admiral Leahy, though the Joint Chiefs had not approved the committee's views as their own.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d432:
Coal once more links Washington and London in a State Department aide-mémoire to the British Embassy dated July 11, 1945. The Department had considered the British aide-mémoire on the messages exchanged between the President and the Prime Minister about raising German coal production. It now proposes steps to meet the points London raised.

The suggested directive has been revised in three ways. Each commander-in-chief is to seek agreement in the Control Council on a coal program for Germany as a whole. The zone commanders are to act together on the measures needed to meet western Germany's coal export target. And other British suggestions are taken into account. An enclosure gives the proposed directive text.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d532:
A Berlin air link nears in Harriman's cable from Moscow of June 30, 1945. Vyshinsky had told him the day before that Soviet planes were now flying daily between Moscow and Berlin. As soon as the American army took over Tempelhof airdrome, a connection could be made. American transport planes would then fly regularly to Berlin from the west. Passengers and mail could move on to Moscow.

Members of the Reparations Commission, Harriman notes, have already been accorded Soviet air facilities from Berlin, connecting with an American plane. Vyshinsky suggested the technical and administrative details could be worked out promptly. General Deane has telegraphed Eisenhower's staff to approach the Russians in Berlin, and the Department may soon drop the slow Tehran courier service.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d632:
Secretary of War Stimson answered the Secretary of State on U.S. forces in Iran on June 19, 1945. His secret letter is document 632 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The State Department had asked for the War Department's views.

Stimson reports that the Persian Gulf Command's supply work wound down through the year. Its main mission was declared complete on June 1, 1945. Troops not needed have been leaving since January, and the rest of the service troops will follow as fast as the military picture allows. Some U.S. troops, though, must stay in Iran for an open-ended span. He puts that span at not less than the war against Japan plus six months. Those staying include caretaking troops at U.S. sites across Iran and the men who support them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1032:
The European Advisory Commission sent this report to the four occupying governments on July 26, 1945. It follows the Crimea Conference decision to invite France to join the occupation of Germany. The commission had studied how to draw the French zone. It now passes on an agreement amending the September 1944 protocol on zones and on Greater Berlin.

The report notes that two articles of the new agreement replace parts of the November 1944 amendments. It does not try to draw the French area inside Berlin itself. Given the city's ruined state, that line should be settled by the Control Council in Berlin. The French share there must come from the American and British areas.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1132:
Carnwath of the United Maritime Executive Board's London branch joined the War Shipping Administration's regional chief Monroe in this message of 21 July 1945. Their note went to shipping chief Land and his aide Morse. The board was the joint body that steered Allied merchant shipping.

Merchant fleets had to be re-routed as one war ended and the other went on. Ships were wanted for Pacific duty, for troops coming home, and for food for freed Europe. A joint message from the London end of that system shows the chiefs lining up their plans. It is the supply line of the alliance, caught mid-shift.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1232:
Sato cabled Togo on 24 July 1945, after a short gap in the exchange. The Moscow bid was stalling in plain view. Soviet officials kept the envoy at arm's length while their own armies readied in the east, a fact hidden from Tokyo.

The report continues Sato's grim brief: soundings taken, doors still shut, hints that Tokyo's terms would not move Moscow. Two days later the Allies would issue their surrender terms from Potsdam. This cable lands just before that blow. It shows Japan's last channel to a softer peace closing, reported by the man who had to watch it close.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1332:
George Allen, deputy director of the office for Near Eastern and African affairs, wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on 25 July 1945. The note was sent while the Potsdam Conference was under way in July and August 1945. It was the last wartime summit of the American, British, and Soviet leaders. Allen's office handled American policy across the Middle East and Africa.

Readers get a staff-level paper from inside the department, written far from the summit table at Potsdam. Papers of this kind show how regional desks in Washington kept feeding views and facts to the men making choices in Germany. The note also shows the Near East holding a firm place on the wartime agenda even as the talks centered on Europe and Japan.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1432:
A fourth Soviet text dated 29 July 1945 continues the cluster of late submissions at Potsdam. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

By the fourth text, readers should be watching for the themes Moscow returned to again and again. Repetition in drafting is a signal of what a side values most. This paper adds weight to that signal. Set in the full run, it helps explain the shape of the final settlement. The points pressed hardest and latest were the ones the other leaders had to answer. In the protocol they granted, split, or refused them outright.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-132:
Bohlen's minutes cover a Potsdam meeting held on July 29, 1945. Charles Bohlen, interpreter and Russian specialist, wrote several of the key American records at the conference. His set for this date entered the second Potsdam volume. The conference had four days left, and the pace of decision was rising.

Minutes by Bohlen blend record with insight. He knew the Soviet players and their stock phrases well. Readers benefit from that knowledge in the way points are framed. The text also fixes the meeting in the closing sequence of the talks. It helps readers see how positions hardened as the end neared.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-32:
Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 20, 1945, record a morning session on basic objectives, strategy, and policies.
