The top secret extracts are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Potsdam papers. General Marshall brought forward proposals by Lord Leathers to amend the joint strategy paper, C. C. S. 877.

Admiral Leahy read the proposed changes aloud and compared them with the paper. He also read a shipping paragraph that General Somervell wished to add. Marshall thought Lord Leathers would accept Somervell's text as part of the objectives. He suggested it might sit better as a commentary on them than as part of the text itself. Admiral King objected on a deeper ground. Leathers' paper, he said, in fact changed national policy, and the Joint Chiefs could not consider it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d732:
Henry Stimson, Secretary of War, wrote directly to President Truman on July 16, 1945, in document 732. The letter predates the conference's opening session by a day. Stimson had the President's ear on the gravest matters of the war. His letters carried a weight few cabinet papers could match. This one entered the second Potsdam volume.

A Stimson letter to Truman is a summit inside the summit. The old secretary wrote with candor built over years of trust. Readers meet the private channel through which huge choices were framed. The document shows the President's inner circle at work before the formal talks began. It sets the human scale of the week.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d832:
The Acting Secretary wrote to Byrnes on August 1, 1945, the day the Potsdam Conference closed. Document 832 is Grew's letter on the summit's final day. The Washington-Potsdam channel ran to the very end. The letter was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

A closing-day letter from the deputy has a handover feel. The travelers would soon be home; the files would follow. Readers see Grew preparing that return. The document ends the volume's great correspondence on its natural note. The partnership that carried the Department through the summit signs off in working order.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d932:
American staff drew up this undated table of food and raw material surpluses in the Soviet zone, Berlin excluded. The figures come from 1936. They measure goods shipped out beyond goods received, in thousands of metric tons. The table supported talks on swapping eastern surpluses for western goods.

Brown coal leads by far, at 3,492. Potatoes follow at 1,113, then wheat at 883 and sugar at 450. The table also lists rye, barley, oats, flour, and milk and cream. Among raw goods, potash fertilizer reached 1,182 and clay products 1,256. Pit props, used in mines, came to 448.
frus-1964-68v03-d132: Secretary McNamara's memorandum to President Johnson of September 1, 1965, asks leave to send still more troops to Vietnam. Westmoreland seeks six more combat battalions past the 28 announced on July 28. With air and support units, the new lift totals 85,000 men. The whole in-country force would pass 200,000. McNamara backs the request in full. He also advises that no word be given out now. Deployments should be stated only as units reach the field. The short memo marks the build-up's quiet doubling, by paper rather than by speech.
frus-1964-68v26-d232:
A memorandum from Secretary of Defense McNamara to President Johnson judges the worth of U.S. military aid to Indonesia. It is document 232 in Volume XXVI of the 1964-1968 Foreign Relations series. McNamara writes after General Suharto took the powers of the presidency. He credits the aid program with shaping the army that crushed the Communist Party. He notes that key officers in the new regime trained in the United States.

The memo gives figures: total aid of $63.2 million from 1950 through 1965, with most spent after 1959. It covers arms, trucks, radios, and civic action gear. McNamara argues that keeping training alive in bleak years paid off.
frus-1964-68v32:
Volume XXXII of the 1964-1968 series groups four Caribbean and South American cases. The Dominican Republic takes the largest share, with 222 documents. Cuba follows, then Haiti, then Guyana. The Dominican chapters cover civil war and U.S. intervention in 1965. The Cuba chapters track exile raids, trade controls, and talks on hijackings and migration.

Haiti's chapter deals with the Duvalier regime. Guyana's covers the move to independence and border claims. The records mix embassy cables with memos on covert action. They show Washington guarding against new Communist gains in the region. Each case turns on how far the United States should step in.
gao-gaoreports-b-295932:
GAO ruled in file B-295932 on March 18, 2005, in the protest brought by White Sands Concessions, Inc. The National Park Service had issued a prospectus for a concession contract to run a gift shop and snack bar. The site was the visitor center at White Sands National Monument in New Mexico. GAO dismissed the protest. A concession of this kind does not involve the delivery of goods or services of more than minimal value to the government. It thus falls outside GAO's bid protest jurisdiction.

The point is jurisdictional, not a judgment on the prospectus terms. Some federal deals simply sit outside the protest system.
gao-gaoreports-b-310732:
PMC Solutions, Inc. lost its protest. GAO ruled in B-310732 on January 22, 2008. The U.S. Commission on Civil Rights sought Lean Six Sigma aid. The award went to Booz Allen Hamilton, Inc. Ten firms bid for the work. PMC fought the score of its tech plan. The score turned on its named expert and its past role as a sub. PMC also held a much lower price.

GAO denied the protest. The score was fair and fit the stated points. The pick weighed plus and minus points of both bids. The winner's tech edge was judged worth the price gap. Best value can pay more for a top plan when the file backs the call.
gao-gaoreports-b-311332:
Corcel Corporation lost its protests — GAO decision B-311332, dated June 13, 2008. The Agency for International Development sought pipe and parts for West Bank towns. The pipe would bring clean water to more than 100,000 homes. Corcel bid on valves in the call. The agency killed the valve part once bids were in. It bought valves through a held deal for a like good.

GAO denied the protests. The specs in the call fell short of the need. That flaw gave a strong cause to kill the call. The side buy was for a type of good not at stake in the dead call. Both acts held up.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-632:
Tracking health hazards during deployments in Iraq is the subject of GAO-05-632, dated July 14, 2005. Lessons from the 1991 Gulf War pushed the defense department to log air, water, and soil risks for troops. For Iraq, the services did gather such data, but each used its own methods for air and soil checks. Skill levels among the staff varied too. Not all finished reports reached the central archive, and headquarters kept no full list of reports due each quarter. It could not tell how many were missing.

Reports did help commanders act on quick risks. Long-term health follow-up is weaker. GAO urged tighter, shared rules, and the department is revising its policy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1132:
Questioned costs on Iraq contracts are tallied in GAO-06-1132, a report issued on September 25, 2006. Contractors supply billions of dollars in goods and services for the Iraq effort. Many were told to start work before key contract terms were set. The Defense Contract Audit Agency reviewed many of these deals and flagged costs it saw as questioned or unsupported. Congress directed GAO to report on those audit findings for Iraq and Afghanistan work.

GAO focused on Iraq and picked 18 audit reports. Together they cover about 50 percent of the audit agency's questioned and unsupported costs. GAO measured how the Department of Defense answered the findings. It checked what action officials took and how much money was withheld from contractors. The report tests whether audit work leads to real recovery of weak claims. DOD gave no comments on the draft.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-132:
Plum Island, the nation's animal disease lab off New York, is reviewed in GAO-06-132, issued on December 19, 2005. The livestock industry adds over $100 billion a year to the economy. A foreign animal disease outbreak could cause severe losses. The Agriculture Department ran Plum Island until June 2003. The Homeland Security Act then moved it to the Department of Homeland Security. Agriculture staff still work there under a joint agreement.

GAO found the two agencies coordinate current research and testing work well. Priorities have shifted some since the transfer, and long-term plans for joint work are still under review. Space on the island is scarce. GAO urged DHS, with USDA, to move work that does not need the island's unique features to other centers. Both agencies broadly agreed with the report. DHS said it had largely met the recommendation already.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-232:
Air Force plans to blend its active, Guard, and reserve arms are reviewed in GAO-06-232, dated January 31, 2006. The Future Total Force concept aims to get more from the whole force. The Air National Guard ran its own Vanguard initiative to guard its role in the new force. GAO traced how the service built its 20-year force plan. It asked who had a say and how the Guard's plan fit in. It also judged the management tools guiding the hunt for new Guard missions.

A full management framework is missing, GAO found. The title says the effort needs one to guide it. Without shared goals, measures, and clear roles, the blend of forces may drift. Force choices made now will bind the service for decades. The report presses the Air Force to lead the change as one team, not three camps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-332:
AIDS money and the formulas that steer it are questioned in GAO-06-332, published February 28, 2006. Two programs anchor the federal fight against HIV/AIDS. The CARE Act funds care; a housing program funds shelter for people with AIDS. Both split money by counts of AIDS cases alone. Counts of HIV cases must join the formulas by fiscal 2007. GAO asked how the money divides among services. It measured how unevenly funds land across grantees. It traced how formula rules create those gaps.

Changes are needed, GAO concluded. A formula frozen on AIDS cases can miss where the epidemic now lives. Places with many HIV cases but fewer AIDS cases may draw less than their need. Hold-harmless clauses and other tweaks shape the outcome further. The report gives Congress a distributional map before the mandated change lands. Fairness here is arithmetic with human stakes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-732:
Block grants for city development are reviewed in GAO-06-732, issued on July 28, 2006. The Community Development Block Grant program funds housing, jobs, and neighborhood projects. Congress appropriated about $4.2 billion for it in fiscal year 2006. The Department of Housing and Urban Development sends the money to cities and urban counties. Local leaders prize the program's flexibility to fit local needs.

GAO found that recipients funded a wide variety of activities. But the department lacked central data showing compliance with legal spending limits. Its monitoring used a risk-based approach, yet it had no plan to replace monitoring staff as they left. Field staff also had too small a role in redesigning the program's data system. GAO urged stronger oversight to match the flexibility.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-832:
Hispanic hiring in the federal workforce is analyzed in GAO-06-832. GAO released it on August 17, 2006. Hispanics have long held a smaller share of federal jobs than of the civilian labor force. A skilled, inclusive workforce matters for agency performance. GAO modeled the factors that shape that gap. GAO also reviewed the oversight roles of the equal employment and personnel agencies.

GAO found that two measurable factors had the greatest effect. Citizenship rules bar many noncitizen Hispanics from federal jobs, and education levels shape who qualifies. After accounting for citizenship, Hispanics were nearly as likely as others to hold federal work, relative to the nonfederal workforce. GAO said added insight into these drivers could sharpen agency outreach. The report moves the debate from raw shares to root causes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-332:
Job training raises pay for many disability beneficiaries, yet few earn enough to leave the rolls. GAO tracked long-term results in GAO-07-332, issued March 30, 2007. State rehab agencies served about 1.2 million people a year. Federal funds for the program reached $2.6 billion in 2005. GAO followed over 303,500 beneficiaries who finished services in fiscal years 2000 to 2003. It compared earnings before and after.

About 40 percent earned more in the year after services, GAO found. Another 32 percent had no earnings at all. The rest, 28 percent, earned less than before. Among those who left services in fiscal year 2000, 33 percent kept some earnings through 2004. Gains rarely reached the level that ends cash benefits. Health coverage fears and transport gaps hold some back. GAO probed which traits and agency methods link to better outcomes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-432:
Lost and misused gear at the space agency is the charge in GAO-07-432, a GAO report dated June 25, 2007. The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) reports $35 billion in property, plant, and equipment. For years, reviews found that NASA kept poor control of that stock. This report, the first in a planned series, tests whether its safeguards work.

GAO read agency rules, gathered loss reports from every center, and visited two sites. It found a culture that did not hold staff to account for losses. Weak controls left gear open to theft and misuse. Some gear costs never reached the books at all. GAO gave the NASA chief eight steps to tighten control. It warned that new software alone would not fix a culture problem.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-32:
In GAO-08-32, a report dated October 12, 2007, GAO assesses how industry trends strain the federal financial regulatory structure. Large firms now offer many products across markets, raising doubts about whether the current system of regulators fits. The study was required by the Financial Services Regulatory Relief Act of 2006.

GAO found that regulators and firms struggle to measure the costs and benefits of regulation. Compliance costs are hard to separate from other business costs, and benefits such as consumer protection resist dollar measures. Forum participants and regulators agreed that better measurement would aid accountability. GAO made no new recommendations, but said its earlier options for reform remain relevant.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-432:
Unspent money in expired grant accounts is examined in GAO report GAO-08-432, released August 29, 2008. GAO studied the Payment Management System, the largest civilian grant payment system, run by the Department of Health and Human Services. The system handles payments for about 70 percent of federal grants.

During calendar year 2006, about $1 billion sat undisbursed in expired grant accounts in that system. For accounts that still held money, the leftover funds averaged about 26 percent of the original grant amounts. The open accounts spanned thousands of grantees and over 325 federal programs. Past audits tie the problem to weak grant closeout work. GAO recommended that agencies track and report these balances each year. The Office of Management and Budget backed the intent but did not commit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-732:
Palau, a Pacific island nation, gets U.S. aid under a 1994 pact set for review in fiscal year 2009. GAO-08-732, dated June 10, 2008, totals the aid, checks how well Palau accounts for it, and weighs the islands' path to paying their own way.

U.S. aid for fiscal years 1995 to 2009 should top $852 million. Direct pact aid makes up 48 percent, and a new road finished in 2007 makes up 17 percent. Palau's yearly audits have grown more timely and sound. Still, weak bookkeeping skills leave control gaps. GAO urged the Interior Department to help Palau build finance skills.
geschichte-der-alchemie-1832:
A history of alchemy in German, printed in 1832, fills this thick volume. Its author was a doctor of philosophy and professor at Kassel, and the book came out at Halle. The scan's old German type is hard to read in places. The work treats alchemy as a case to be tried: it had lost in the first court, the author jokes, but might yet plead new grounds.

The history traces the hunt for the stone and the tincture from old times through the Middle Ages and into the age of print. Lives of adepts, their books, and their claims are set in order and judged. By 1832 real chemistry had split from alchemy, and this book looks back with both scorn and care. It stands as an early try at a full history of a dead science, in the language of that science's homeland.
in-the-wilderness-pg3132:
Charles Dudley Warner's Adirondack sketches fill this small volume, eight pieces written from his summers in the north woods. The contents promise sport of an unheroic kind: How I Killed a Bear, Lost in the Woods, A Fight with a Trout, and A-Hunting of the Deer. The first essay opens with a correction of the public record about his bear.

Warner met the bear while both were out blackberrying, he insists, armed himself with a six-quart pail and a borrowed Sharps rifle. He confesses early that he is no sportsman, and proves it with the story of a robin and a shotgun. Old Phelps, the guide, gets a character study, and Camping Out and What Some People Call Pleasure mock the tourist's idea of roughing it. The humour is dry, self-deprecating, and exact.
irving-alhambra-1832:
Washington Irving lived for a time inside the Alhambra, the old Moorish palace at Granada in Spain. Out of that stay came Tales of the Alhambra, published in 1832. The book mixes travel sketches of the palace and its city with legends told by local guides and servants.

Irving describes ruined courts, towers, and fountains, then retells the tales tied to them. Readers meet enchanted Moorish kings, hidden treasure, and lovers parted by fate. His warm, curious tone made Spain look romantic and storied to English readers. For many years it stayed the best-known American travel book about Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-eliez: Aaron ben Eliezer Lipman, rabbi of Zempelburg in West Prussia, is treated in this Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. He flourished toward the middle of the seventeenth century and was an intimate friend of Shabbethai Hurwitz, rabbi of Prague. His Korban Aharon, the Offering of Aaron, was first published at Amsterdam in 1646. It summarizes in alphabetical order the decisions that Moses Isserles laid down in his ritual work Torat Hatat. Aaron also wrote an acrostic meditation beginning, My eye droppeth tears, O my God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-cohen-of-b: Abba Cohen of Bardela was a scholar of the last tannaitic age, about the start of the third century. The few legal rulings from him deal with rabbinical civil law. Some of his readings of Scripture are also kept, in Sifre on Deuteronomy and in Genesis Rabbah. One warns of the day of judgment. If Balaam was shamed by his own ass, and Joseph silenced his older brothers, the passage asks, how will man stand before the all-knowing Lord?
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abelson-judah-b: Judah ben Isaac Abelson was a merchant who gave the greater part of his time to study. He lived toward the end of the eighteenth century at Sherwenty, in Lithuania. His zeal for the Talmud was so great that, by his grandson's account, for twenty years he did not take off his clothes to sleep. He wrote a method of the Mishnah, and openings to two of its Orders, under the title "Zikron Yehudah." Only parts of that work were printed, at Wilna in 1851 and in 1860.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abital-332: Abital was a wife of David during his time at Hebron. She bore him his fifth son, Shephatiah. The entry cites Second Samuel iii. 4 and First Chronicles iii. 3 for that fact. It gives no account of her family, her later life, or any act of her own. Her place in the record rests on the marriage and on Shephatiah's birth at Hebron.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-mor:
Egyptian rabbi Abraham ben Mordecai ha-Levi worked at the end of the seventeenth century. In 1691 he edited his father's responsa, Darke No'am, at Venice. He added a treatise of his own on circumcision, which drew strong pushback from rabbis of his day.

His own responsa set, Ginnat Weradim, or Garden of Roses, follows the order of the four Turim. His treatise on divorce bears the title Yaïr Netib, or Illuminator of the Path. His son-in-law Hayyim ben Moses Tavila, a physician in ordinary to the sultan, published both of those works at Constantinople in 1716-18.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-emile-4:
Émile Abraham was a French playwright born at Paris in 1833. He gave himself wholly to the stage, as a writer of plays, as a theater critic, and as editor of a theater column in the Petit Journal. Later he served as general secretary of two Paris theaters.

His comedies and vaudevilles run from Chapitre V. in 1863 to La Charité Chrétienne in 1885. He often wrote with partners such as Jules Prével. He also made librettos for operettas, from 1862 onward. Under the name Adrien Laroque he published a yearly book of theater lives, Acteurs et Actrices de Paris.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-achmetha-732: Achmetha is the Old Testament name for a Persian city. Ezra vi. 2 uses it for the place Greeks called Ecbatana. In Old Persian the name is Hagmatana. The modern form is Hamadan. When the Median realm rose in the seventh century B.C., Ecbatana was its chief city. Later it served as a summer home for Persian kings. Herodotus tells of walls with towers of many colors. The royal records of Ezra were likely kept inside the inner wall.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-admah-red-or-re: Admah was a town in the family list of Canaan, in Genesis x. 19. Its king was Shinab, as Genesis xiv. 2 and 8 tell. The town was wiped out with Sodom and Gomorrah. It is not named in the tale of that fall. Later texts name it in that link. Deuteronomy xxix. 23 and Hosea xi. 8 both do so. The hosted text is a few lines. It gives the king, the two verse links, and the shared fate, and it gives no site or size for Admah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-932: Aha was the brother of Abba. He was also the father of Jeremiah, son of Abba. He lived in the third century. He was a contemporary of Abba Arika. The entry keeps one striking judgment by Arika. In all history, Arika said, no man was so penitent as King Josiah. After Josiah came Aha himself. Nothing else about him is recorded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-iii-a:
Alexander III., Alexandrovich, was emperor of Russia. He was born at St. Petersburg on March 10, 1845. He died at Livadia on November 1, 1894. He took the throne on March 14, 1881, the day after his father's murder. Instead of reforms, he chose reaction. His old teacher Pobiedonostzev counseled him, and he ruled with absolutism.

His reign was marked by the pogroms of 1881. Riots broke out at Elizabethgrad on April 27 and 28, and at Kiev on May 8 to 11. In six months they spread to 160 more places in the south. Thousands of Jewish homes were wrecked, and many people were killed or hurt. Officials largely failed to protect the victims. The czar told a Jewish deputation that anarchists, not race hatred, were to blame. Yet on September 3, 1881, his minister's circular blamed the Jews for exploiting the Slavs. A great emigration wave followed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alt-ofen-hungar:
Alt-Ofen is an old Hungarian city now part of Budapest. It forms the third district of that capital. Word of its Jews starts in the twelfth century. The first firm date is the year 1217. In that year a query on warm springs reached a Vienna sage. The query came from the Jews of Ofen.

Turkish rule held the town till 1686. A few Jews came back when that rule ended. Kind rule by the Zichy lords drew more Jews in. In 1727 just 22 families lived there. By 1735 the count had grown to 43 families. Land for a synagogue and a burial ground was bought. The long entry tracks schools, rabbis, and trade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amram-ben-isaac:
Amram ben Isaac ibn Shalbib served as an envoy of Alfonso VI. Alfonso ruled Leon and Castile in the eleventh century. Jews then held high posts in Christian Spain. The king said his realm could not do without them. In 1085 Amram went to Seville on his behalf. His host was the prince Almutamid.

Tales of that mission clash from source to source. All agree that Amram died on the mission. One tale says he was nailed to a stake. One says the prince brained him with an inkstand. Fear of revenge drove a fateful call for help. That call brought the Almoravides into Spain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anhalt-1532:
Anhalt was an old principality of Germany, later a state of the German empire. It had once been split into four duchies, Bernburg, Dessau, Kothen, and Zerbst. Its former capital, Zerbst, stands on a branch of the Elbe, about ten miles northwest of Dessau.

Jews were allowed to live there before 1440, and a Jews' Street is said to date from the fifteenth century. A pact of 1460 split the income from Jews between prince and town. The entry notes that Jews held no real estate there and lived in small, shifting numbers. It then follows later settlements at Bernburg and Dessau town by town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apharsachites-1: Apharsachites were a tribe living in Samaria in the days of Ezra. The book of Ezra, in chapters 4, 5, and 6, shows them objecting to the Jews' building of the Temple. They carried their complaint to King Darius. Asnapper had moved them into Samaria, Ezra says. Who they were has never been fully settled. The entry suggests the word may have been misunderstood all along. It may name certain officials rather than a people at all, and it points to the entry Apharsites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-archevites-1732: Archevites were a people whom Asnapper brought from Erech, or Uruk, a political and religious center of Babylonia, and settled in Samaria. Ezra, chapter 4, verse 9, shows them writing to King Artaxerxes about the building of the Temple at Jerusalem. Their letter had the work on it stopped. Erech itself is named in Genesis, chapter 10, verse 10, the entry adds. It gives no numbers, leaders, or later fate for the Archevites in Samaria.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-articles-of-fai:
Judaism, unlike Christianity or Islam, holds no fixed articles of faith backed by a ruling church body. Many thinkers tried to sum up its core beliefs in set phrases and order. None won binding force, since no supreme authority stood behind them. Such lists entered prayer and teaching, yet their weight came only from the fame and learning of their authors. None matches the standing of the great Christian creeds or of Islam's Kalimah.

Why this gap exists is the entry's main question. Ancient nations, it notes with Leibnitz, had rites, sacrifices, and priesthoods but no dogmatic theology. Judaism grew in that older pattern, centered on practice and covenant rather than on confessed formulas. The long account then weighs the best-known Jewish attempts at a creed and the limits each one met.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asser-carel-203:
Carel Asser was a Dutch jurist and scholar. He was born at The Hague on June 1, 1843, and died at Leyden on Dec. 10, 1898. His father Louis was a district court judge at The Hague. Carel studied at the gymnasium there and at the University of Leyden. He took his doctor's degree at the age of twenty-three.

Asser served as a judge of the district court at The Hague from 1878 to 1892. He then became professor of civil law at Leyden. The government also named him to a commission on revising the national statutes. His dissertation on telegraphy, from 1866, won a gold medal. He left an unfinished handbook on Dutch civil law, and he was known as a musician as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-augsburg-2132:
Augsburg is the capital of Swabia and Neuburg in Bavaria. By tradition it holds one of the oldest Jewish communities in Germany. Papers first name the city in 1259, though single Jews of Augsburg appear earlier. By 1276 the congregation had a synagogue and a cemetery. Its Jews lent money and traded in meat and wine under set limits.

The entry then follows a hard cycle. The rich community was pledged, taxed, and squeezed by emperors and counts. In 1348, during the Black Death, its Jews were massacred, and the emperor pardoned the killers. In 1385 King Wenzel canceled all debts owed to Jews. In 1440 some 300 Jews were driven out, and their gravestones were built into a city hall. From that time no Jews could live in Augsburg. Visitors could stay a day and a night at most, under guard, a rule set in 1540.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azulai-azulay-2:
Azulai is the name of a family that came from Spanish exiles. After the expulsion of the Jews from Spain in 1492, the family settled at Fez, in Morocco. One of its members derived the name from the first letters of a verse in Leviticus. The entry doubts that guess and points to a place name in Morocco or Spain instead.

The entry then gives a family tree and long notices of its chief men. Abraham Azulai, born at Fez about 1570, fled unrest in Morocco and settled at Hebron. There he wrote on the Zohar. Plague drove him to Gaza in 1619, where he wrote his famed cabalistic book "Ḥesed le-Abraham." It was printed at Amsterdam in 1685, long after his death at Hebron in 1643. The longest notice goes to Ḥayyim Joseph David Azulai, a scholar of sharp critical mind who still held, the entry notes, some striking superstitions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baer-issachar-b: Issachar b. Elhanan Baer was a rabbi at Eibenschütz, born at Frankfort-on-the-Oder in the second half of the seventeenth century. He wrote a set of cabalistic sermons and comments called "Arba' Ḥarashim" (Four Skilful Artificers). The entry names its four parts, on Judah, on the kings of Israel, on the prophets, and on the priests. It notes that only the first two volumes were printed, at Frankfort-on-the-Oder in 1710.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bampi-issachar-: Issachar Dob Baer Bampi was a scholar and giver born at Minsk, Russia, in 1823. He died there on March 10, 1888. For the last thirty years of his life he lectured daily on a chapter of the Bible in his own synagogue. His special work was tracing Jewish customs to their sources in the two Talmuds and the Midrashim. That work, "Meḳor Minhagim," stayed in manuscript, with extracts printed in 1888. He stood on good terms with Orthodox Talmudists and with the Maskilim alike, and helped many Hebrew writers into print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barlow-thomas-2:
Thomas Barlow, bishop of Lincoln, was born in Westmoreland in 1607 and died on October 8, 1691. Educated at Queen's College, Oxford, he became keeper of the Bodleian Library in 1654. He was later provost of his college and Lady-Margaret professor, and bishop in 1675. Among his many theological writings stands "The Case of Lawfulness of the Toleration of the Jews." It seems composed about 1654, when Manasseh ben Israel had raised the readmission of the Jews to England.

Barlow favored readmission, the entry says, less from tolerance than because public opinion and Cromwell leaned that way. He argued the state could gain money from the Jews, and the Church might gain their conversion. For their government he proposed rules near the medieval canon law. They might profess but not propagate their religion, repair old synagogues but build none new, and wear distinct dress. His nickname, "The Trimmer," fits the occasion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beelzebub-or-be:
Beelzebub, also spelled Beelzebul, is named in the New Testament as chief of the demons. Pharisees charge that Jesus casts out demons by that prince's power. Jesus replies that a kingdom split against itself cannot stand, and asks by whom their own sons cast demons out.

The entry traces the name to Baal Zebub, god of Ekron, whose oracle a sick king once consulted. It reads the name as Lord of Flies and links flies to plague and evil spirits in old lore. A German folk devil in fly shape ends the survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belmont-2832:
Belmont is a Jewish family of Alzey, in Rhein-Hessen, that takes its name from Isaac Simon at the end of the eighteenth century. His line runs back to town leaders of the Jews there. The banker August Belmont of New York descends from this house.

The family ranked as the most important Jewish house in Alzey. A gift of 30,000 florins from Isaac Simon became a fund in 1790 for church costs and dowries for poor girls. The entry guesses the line stems from the Belmonte family of Amsterdam by way of the Rhine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benedictus-coen: Coenraad Benedictus worked as a mohel and surgeon at Surinam, in Dutch Guiana, about 1830. Nothing is known of his life beyond one rare book. At Paramaribo in 1830 he brought out a tract on the rite of circumcision, set as questions and answers for men training as a mohel. The Hebrew quotes in it were filled in by his own hand. The entry notes there was most likely no Hebrew type to be had in Paramaribo at that time, which adds to the book's rarity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstamm-leopo:
Leopold Bernard Bernstamm, a Russian sculptor, was born at Riga on April 20, 1859. He entered a Riga studio at thirteen and the Imperial Academy at St. Petersburg at fourteen, winning its highest prizes. Busts of famed Russians in 1883 made his name as a portrait sculptor.

After study at Rome and Florence, he settled in Paris in 1885 and grew famous for busts of leading Frenchmen, from Renan to Zola. A silver medal came at the Exposition of 1889. In 1896 the czar called him to make busts from life of the emperor and empress.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beturia-paulina: Paulina Beturia was a Roman proselyte to Judaism. She lived about the year 50. She was also known by the name Sarah. Her Latin epitaph gives her age at death. She died at eighty-six years and six months. For sixteen years she lived as a Jewess. She held the title mother of the synagogues. That covered the Campesian and Volumnian communities in Rome. Talmudic sources name a learned proselyte Beluryah. She taught her slaves to convert too. The entry suggests she may be Beturia herself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blumenthal-hein:
Heinrich Blumenthal was a German maker and giver born at Darmstadt on March 12, 1824. He died there on March 27, 1901. Trained as a mechanic in Vienna, Nuremberg, and Paris, he came home to build farm tools.

His Darmstadt works grew into a large maker of steam threshing machines. He backed farm laws, led farm groups, and sent help to Hessian troops in war. He led the city Jewish community for more than two decades. His sway with the Grand Duke helped Hesse stand against anti-Jewish agitation. For his services he got the title of Kommerzienrath. He also held the Hessian Ludwig cross and the Prussian Order of the Crown.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brandenburg-363:
Brandenburg is a province of Prussia. Papers of the thirteenth century name Jews living in the mark and trading there. A host charge brought persecution at Pritzwalk in 1287.

Margrave Ludwig gave letters of protection to many towns' Jews from 1334 onward. Flagellant attacks still struck Berlin, Stendal, and Spandau in 1349. Under later rulers Jews were jailed, burned, and expelled in turn. In 1671 fifty Jewish families from Wiener-Neustadt won leave to settle for twenty years. Frederick the Great used the Jews as he pleased, the entry says. Their number in the mark reached 18,394 by 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brody-heinrich-:
Heinrich Brody was an Austrian rabbi born on May 21, 1868, at Ungvár, Hungary. He was a descendant of Abraham Broda. He studied at Tolcsva, Presburg, Berlin's seminary, and the University of Berlin.

Brody served as secretary of the literary society Mekize Nirdamim. In 1896 he founded a journal for Hebrew bibliography and co-edits it still. By 1902 he was rabbi of the congregation of Nachod, Bohemia. He takes great interest in the Zionist movement, the entry notes. His works edit Hebrew poets such as Yehuda ha-Levi and Moses ibn Ezra. Under a pen name he also asked whether Zionism conflicts with Jewish religion in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-burgdorf-3832: Burgdorf was a town in the canton of Bern, Switzerland, with a few Jewish residents in the fourteenth century. In 1347 a Jew named Simon lent forty pounds of pennies to the cathedral provost Ulrich. On Feb. 16, 1349, the debt laden Eberhard von Kiburg drove all Jews out of Burgdorf by night. He claimed their wrongdoing as his reason and seized their goods. In 1900 a few Jews still lived there, but they formed no congregation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calendar-histor:
Calendar history, for the Jewish year, falls into three periods in this entry. The Biblical period rested on watching the sun and moon alone. The Talmudic period mixed watching with reckoning. The post Talmudic period used reckoning only. Festival dates drove the study: a Deuteronomy command to keep the month of Abib forced care with the sun's place.

The entry names the old Hebrew terms for this science, ending with the secret of intercalation. It surveys the Babylonian year of twelve thirty day months, with added months when priests judged them needed. Later parts follow Jewish practice through the Middle Ages. A closing list names calendar writers from Talmudic times to the eighteenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cardoso-isaac-f:
Isaac Cardoso, born Fernando to Marano parents at Celorico, Portugal, before 1615, became a physician, philosopher, and polemic writer. He studied at Salamanca and rose to chief physician at Madrid. There he printed works on Vesuvius, on the color green, and on cold water's uses. Fleeing Spain and its Inquisition, he went to Venice with his brother Miguel. Both openly took up Judaism, and Fernando became Isaac.

At Verona, where he lived honored until his death after 1680, he printed a free philosophy in seven books in 1673. It attacks the Cabala and the false Messiah Shabbethai Zebi, though his own brother backed that cause. His last great work lists the Jews' excellences in ten chapters, then answers ten slanders against them, blood charge among them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caslari-3532:
Caslari was a family name taken from Caylar, a village in the department of Hérault, France. A notable Jewish community lived at Caylar in the Middle Ages. After the royal edict of Sept. 17, 1394, its Jews moved to Provence and the Comtat-Venaissin. Some appear at Tarascon in 1459 and 1487, and at Avignon in 1480.

Scholars kept the family name in repute into the late sixteenth century. David Caslari, a physician at Narbonne, gained privileges from the archbishop in 1284 and rendered Galen into Hebrew. En Bongodah Caslari and his son exchanged poems with Solomon Bonfed about 1400. Mossé du Caylar served as a warden at Avignon in 1480. Ẓemaḥ ben Jedidiah copied a manuscript of Ibn Ezra in 1525. Ẓemaḥ ben Moises was rabbi at Carpentras about 1583.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-castro-de-famil:
De Castro is a family of Spanish and Portuguese origin. After the Inquisition was set up, members moved to Bordeaux, Bayonne, Hamburg, and cities in the Netherlands, and later to the United States. Descendants are found in Turkey, Egypt, Holland, Germany, England, and Italy. Some branches kept the plain name, while others added names such as Sarmento, Osorio, or Orobio.

A long roll of members follows, with dates and posts. It names parnassim at Amsterdam, physicians at Verona and Amsterdam, and the noted printer David de Castro-Tartas. Rodrigo de Castro and Jacob de Castro-Sarmento receive their own entries elsewhere. Only the Dutch branch, the entry says, allows a firm pedigree. One early figure, Abraham de Castro, served as master of the mint in Cairo under Sultan Sulaiman. His yearly gifts of 3,000 gold florins won him wide influence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chileab-4332: Chileab was a son of David, born to him at Hebron. His mother was Abigail, whom David married after the death of her husband Nabal, the Carmelite, as II Samuel iii. 3 reports. The parallel account in I Chronicles iii. 1 gives his name as Daniel. Greek versions give still other forms at both places. The entry says the original name cannot be restored, though Daniel lies much nearer than Chileab. A Talmud passage gives a fanciful reading of the name, tied to his shaming Mephibosheth in the Law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohn-solomon-45: Solomon Cohn, a German rabbi, was born at Zulz, Prussian Silesia, on March 24, 1822. He died in Breslau on Sept. 22, 1902. He was a grandson of Meshullam Solomon Cohn of Furth. After a short stay at the Presburg yeshibah he studied at Breslau, taking a doctorate in Oriental languages and philosophy. Calls took him to Oppeln in 1847, then Maestricht and Schwerin. Berlin followed in 1876. He retired to Breslau in 1894. From 1878 to 1894 he lectured on homiletics at Berlin's Orthodox rabbinical seminary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-covo-or-covos-4:
Covo, or Covos, is a Jewish family of Salonica, Turkey, with a branch at Widdin, Bulgaria. The name points to Covo, near Milan, Italy, as its first home. Several rabbis bore the name. Asher Covo served as chief rabbi of Salonica for twenty-six years. Born in 1799, he died in 1874. The sultan decorated him for his service to the community.

Other entries follow in turn. Elias Covo, who died at Salonica in 1689, left forty-three responsa, printed at Constantinople in 1739. Isaac Covo became Sephardic Ḥakam-bashi of Jerusalem in July, 1848. Jacob Hananiah Covo, born at Salonica in 1825, rose from orphanhood to its chief rabbinate. Each man gets dated facts and book titles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-czarnikau-4832: Czarnikau is a town in the district of Bromberg, in the province of Posen, Germany. Its Jewish community probably dates to the start of the seventeenth century. Numbers peaked in 1855-64 at 1,200 persons. The count was 470 in 1815 and 600 in 1900. A new synagogue of 1878 replaced the old one of 1759. The community built its own schoolhouse in 1842. It also ran a Hebrew religious school under the rabbi. Named rabbis and societies fill out the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-of-arles-:
Maestro David of Arles was rabbi of Avignon in the sixteenth century. He stood at the center of a legal dispute that stirred the rabbis of Provence, Italy, and Palestine. Two brothers, Isaac and Jacob Gard, had allowed a marriage that was really forbidden, misled by a misprint in a rabbinical code.

David and his son-in-law led the protest against that ruling, backed by scholars in Bologna and Rome. When argument failed, they appealed to Joseph Caro, the highest authority. Caro and his college upheld David twice, in 1560 and in 1562, and excommunicated Isaac Gard, whose brother had meanwhile died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dittel-leopold-:
Leopold Ritter von Dittel was an Austrian surgeon born at Fulneck, Moravia, on May 15, 1815. He took his medical degree at Vienna in 1840. After spa practice in Hungary he trained further under Skoda, Rokitansky, and Hebra. He died at Vienna on July 28, 1898.

Dittel rose to surgeon-in-chief of the Allgemeine Krankenhaus in 1861 and founded the university's surgical-anatomical institute in 1864. His fame rested on urinology. In 1894 he reported on 800 operations for stone that he had performed. The entry credits him with a drug carrier for the urethra and with better endoscopic diagnosis of bladder tumors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-edinburgh-5432:
Edinburgh, capital of Scotland, drew Jews early in the nineteenth century. They seem to have come there before other Scottish towns. A first regular synagogue opened in 1816 with twenty families. It sat in a lane off Nicholson street.

The congregation later moved to Richmond Court, then to Park Place in 1868. Its present Graham street synagogue rose in 1897. A second congregation formed in the Dalry quarter by 1880, among waterproof-clothing workers. The first minister, Moses Joel, served forty-six years until 1862. The city also ran three Jewish charities and a Hebrew school at the Graham street synagogue. The entry counts about 2,000 Jews in the city in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-b-durda: Eleazar ben Durdaia is famed as a great penitent. His early life was given to vice, which leads men to death. At last he turned his thoughts to his end. He begged the parts of nature to plead for his pardon. Each refused, since all created things must pass away. He saw then that his fate rested on himself alone. He prayed and wept until he died in that act. A voice from heaven, the tale adds, declared him sure of bliss.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-ben-zee: Eliezer ben Zeeb Wolf was a preacher and Talmud writer. He lived at the end of the eighteenth century. The entry names two books by his hand. The first holds sermons and came out at Poryck in 1786. The second bears the title Dammeseq Eliezer. It mixes notes on Talmud with moral sermons. A reading of a block of psalms stands in it too. Other comments and homilies fill out the volume. It came out at the same town in 1790.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-emet-we-yazzib-: Emet we-Yazzib is a prayer said each morning in the rite. Its first words mean true and firm in Hebrew. It comes right after the Shema in the service. It closes with the blessing for Redemption in its turn. Priests said it in the Temple hall in old days. It has kept its place in the rite ever since. A rule guards the seam between Shema and this prayer. No break may fall between God's name and the word true.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-era-4732:
Era means a span of years counted from a fixed event, and the entry surveys the eras Jews have used. The Bible dates some events from the Flood, the Exodus, and the Babylonian Exile. After the return from exile, Jews dated by the reigns of Persian kings. The entry also explains the fifty-year jubilee cycle set out in Leviticus.

The Seleucid era, counted from the battle of Gaza in 312 B.C., became the era of contracts in Jewish documents. Two eras are called truly Jewish: one counted from the Destruction of the Temple, one from the Creation of the world. The Creation era, fixed at October 7, 3761 B.C., became the common Jewish way of dating. The entry traces when each system arose and how scribes used them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-erlanger-camill:
Camille Erlanger was a French composer born at Paris on May 25, 1863. He studied at the Conservatoire and won the first Prix de Rome in 1888 in the class of Leo Delibes. That same year he composed St. Julien l'Hospitalier at Rome. The work placed him at once among the noted composers of his day. He later served as choirmaster of a Jewish temple in Paris.

His stage works include Velleda and La Chasse Fantastique, a symphonic piece drawn from St. Julien. Kermaria reached the Opera Comique in January 1897. Le Juif Polonais, based on a novel by Erckmann-Chatrian, played the same house. He also wrote Bar-Kokeba with Catulle Mendes and La Glu, based on a novel by Richepin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-exchequer-of-th:
The Exchequer of the Jews was a branch of England's Court of Exchequer that handled Jewish taxes and lawsuits from 1200 to 1290. It grew, the entry says, from the estate of Aaron of Lincoln, which needed its own clerks. Riots at Richard I's accession showed the risk when no record of Jewish debts was kept. Richard ordered duplicate records in 1194.

Four justices of the Jews ran the court, two of them Jews in the first record of 1200. The chief rabbi sat with them on points of Jewish law. The court judged debt cases between Jews and Christians and claimed sole right to do so. It also set the Jews' payments to the king: reliefs, fines, and tallages. Period checks of the debt chests, called scrutinies, fill the entry's later pages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fassel-hirsch-b:
Hirsch Bar Fassel was an Austrian rabbi and author born at Boskowitz, Moravia, on August 21, 1802. He died at Nagy-Kanizsa, Hungary, on December 27, 1883. He trained under Moses Sofer at Presburg, then tried trade and disliked it. In 1836 he took the rabbinate of Prossnitz, over the state rabbi's protest, and the government upheld him.

Fassel preached in German and brought in some reforms, a pioneer of modern culture in Moravia. Breslau chose him in 1845 to serve beside Abraham Geiger and calm its conservatives, but he declined. In 1851 he moved to Nagy-Kanizsa and stayed until death. His Mozene Zedek is a handbook of practical law for rabbis, leaning toward mild rulings. Reform, he wrote, must rest on rabbinism or decay into mere denial.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fire-6132:
Fire in daily and sacred life is the subject here. Hebrew has several words for it, and one priestly term for a burnt offering. Fuel was wood, charcoal, thorns, and dung. Fire could be made by rubbing sticks. It could also be struck from flint with steel. At home, fire cooked food, baked bread, and gave warmth. No fire for home use could be lit on the Sabbath.

Fire served in metal work and in war. Idols and cities were burned, and some crimes were punished by burning. The altar fire was kept burning at all times. Later sections treat fire in figure and tale. Rabbinic lore tells when fire was made and names six kinds. Sabbath rules on fuel and stoves close the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-forgery-6232:
Forgery is the false making or changing of a writing, meant to defraud. To count, the writing must be one that could carry legal force if genuine. Mosaic law says little about documents. It punishes deceit in selling and false weights, but it makes no rule against forgery. The rabbis therefore built rules for drawing up legal papers. Their aim was to make forgery impossible. Yet they set no fixed punishment for it.

A deed or note had to be written on stuff that would show any erasure at once. A gap of two lines before the witnesses' names voided the paper. Words in the last line had no force, being kept for a summary. Mistakes had to be noted at the end, above the signatures. Sums were written in words, never in letters with number values. A plea of forgery reduced the claim to an oral one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frauenstadt-chr:
Christian Martin Julius Frauenstädt was a German student of philosophy. He was born at Bojanowo, in Posen, on April 17, 1813. He died at Berlin on January 13, 1879. He was schooled at his uncle's house at Neisse and embraced Christianity in 1833. At Berlin he studied first theology and then philosophy. There he came to know Schopenhauer and became his follower. From 1848 he lived in Berlin.

Frauenstädt wrote much on theology and philosophy in his early years. Later books treat beauty, the sway of science over poetry and faith, and materialism. One book of 1856 was written against Büchner. Schopenhauer made him his literary executor, charged with editing his works. He printed letters and papers from the master's desk. He also made a dictionary of Schopenhauer's thought. In 1873-74 he brought out the full works in six volumes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-furst-alexander: Alexander Furst, a German physician born at Braunsberg on April 15, 1844, died in Berlin on May 25, 1898. He studied medicine at Konigsberg and took his degree at Berlin in 1867. After hospital work near Berlin and at Danzig, he practiced at Memel from 1869. He served as an army doctor in the Franco-Prussian war. At Memel he helped found a small hospital. He first found leprosy in East Prussia, and state steps against eye disease owed much to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gavison-meir-65: Meir Gavison, an Egyptian scholar of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, was one of the rabbis at Cairo in the days of Jacob Castro. The short entry says he was widely known as a great Talmudist. One volume of his legal replies was seen in Egypt by Azulai. His replies are also named by Abraham ha-Levi in Ginnat Weradim. No birth or death dates and no other books are given for him in this entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gerstmann-adolf: Adolf Joseph Gerstmann, a German author born on July 31, 1855, at Ostrowo in Prussia, moved to Berlin as an infant. He studied thought and letters at gymnasium and university there. In 1879 he joined the Kleine Journal as literary editor. In 1888 he began teaching dramatic art at the Berliner Theater. He ranks as a power on the history of the stage. His plays and comedies treat Prussians in Paris and folk life at Hohenselchow.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-godliness-6732:
Godliness means being godlike in character and conduct, in conscious response to man's divine origin and destiny. Since man is made in God's likeness, Judaism holds that every person can reach godliness; no original sin has damaged that faculty. The godly man, set against the proud and violent ungodly, delights in the Torah and follows Micah's rule: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly with God.

Charity stands at the center of the teaching. God clothed the naked, comforted mourners, and buried the dead, so the godly imitate Him in personal kindness. Quiet giving ranks above showy giving, and the entry adds that slander, pride, and shaming others cannot live with godliness, while forgiving enemies can.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gottstein-adolf: Adolf Gottstein was a German physician. He was born at Breslau on Nov. 2, 1857. He studied at Breslau, Strasburg, and Leipsic. He took his medical degree at Leipsic in 1881. That same year he became assistant at Breslau's city hospital. He left that post in 1883. Berlin became his base, and he was still practicing there in 1902. His journal essays dealt mainly with bacteriology and epidemiology. His books were "Epidemiologische Studien über Diphtherie und Scharlach" (1895) and "Allgemeine Epidemiologie" (1897). The entry is a brief professional notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-haggai-book-of-:
The Book of Haggai is one of the minor prophetical books, and it holds four addresses. The first, dated the first day of the sixth month of 520 B.C., speaks to Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest. It rebukes people who build fine houses for themselves while God's house lies waste, and it lays drought and want on that neglect.

The second address heartens the dispirited: the new house will outshine the old, and peace will reign in it. The third uses priestly rulings on purity to explain the people's want. The fourth, to Zerubbabel alone, foretells thrones overturned and Zerubbabel made God's signet. The entry also judges his plain, prose-like style and the good state of his text.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hamburger-jacob:
Jacob Hamburger, born at Loslau, Silesia, on Nov. 10, 1826, was a German rabbi and author. He studied at Ratibor, at the yeshibot of Hotzenplotz, Presburg, and Nikolsburg, and at the University of Breslau. In 1852 he was called as rabbi to Neustadt-bei-Pinne. In 1859 he went to Mecklenburg-Strelitz as Landesrabbiner, a post he still holds in 1903.

His "Geist der Hagada" of 1859 gathers haggadic sayings from the Talmuds and Midrashim. It was meant as the first of a series that never went on. In 1862 he began his "Realencyclopädie des Judenthums." Three volumes have appeared: Bible, Talmud, and a supplement, with a second edition in 1896. The entry calls the work, as one man's labor, a striking monument of industry and learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanover-7232:
Hanover is the capital of the Prussian province of the same name. Jews lived there by the first half of the fourteenth century. At first they were well treated. The municipal law of 1303 even barred offence against them in word or deed. After the Black Death, the mood turned. The Jews were accused of poisoning wells. They were banished in 1350. They were expelled again in 1371. Yet a privilege of 1375 let the city readmit them. The city could also keep their taxes.

The entry follows the cycle for centuries. An eight-year admission came in 1499, at 150 gulden a year. A synagogue rose in the Neustadt. It was torn down in 1613. Court preachers preached conversion sermons there. Princes admitted wealthy families against the Landtag's votes. The entry closes with the community's later institutions. It also names its scholars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hatsek-ignaz-73: Ignaz Hatsek, born at Olmutz on April 7, 1828, was a Hungarian mapmaker and engraver. He was schooled in both public and Jewish schools in his home town. In 1848 and 1849 he served as a lieutenant in the Honved artillery. From 1851 he worked as mapmaker for the state survey office of Hungary. He held that post for forty-three years and left it in 1894. His maps include railroad maps of Austria-Hungary and atlases of Hungary's counties. He later lived in Budapest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-helkath-hazzuri: Helkath Hazzurim is the name of a place in the Second Book of Samuel. There the men of Joab and the men of Abner fought a set combat. All on both sides were slain. The passage suggests the name means the field of the sword-edges. The Greek version reads it as the field of those who lay in wait. Several modern critics accept that reading. Another scholar reads it as the field of the adversaries. The entry is short and stays with the name itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herzenstein-gri: Grigori Markovich Herzenstein, born in St. Petersburg in 1851, was a Russian physician. He graduated from the Medico-Surgical Academy there in 1874. From 1887 he taught medical geography and statistics as an adjunct professor. His main work was his 1885 thesis on syphilis in Russia. Other writings covered health order in war, the bodies of Russian recruits, and the health of Jews in 1884. He also edited that field for a medical reference work. He died in St. Petersburg in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-gaston-7: Gaston Hirsch, born at Metz in 1830, was a French dramatic author. The entry lists his chief plays by title, running from an early prejudice play to works dated up to 1903. Several carry music by named composers, the latest by Massenet in 1903. Other dated plays fall in 1879, 1883, 1884, 1885, 1886, and 1890. He also wrote four prose works, two of them travel books dated 1862 and two later novels dated 1887 and 1889. One illustrated reference work is the only source cited.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-huna-bar-abbin-:
Huna bar Abbin ha-Kohen, also called Nehunya, was a Palestinian teacher of the first half of the fourth century. He studied under Jeremiah and reports sayings in his name. He held a high place in the Tiberias school under Jose and argued points of law with him.

Huna spent time in Babylonia and knew its teachers' rulings well. He tells of rabbis hiding in a grotto under Roman pressure, telling day from night by lamplight while they weighed a leap month. He traded in asafetida and knew some medicine. Though born to a priestly family, he refused tithes. His sermons burn with love of the land and anger at Rome.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-vives-al-lo: Joseph ben Joshua ibn Vives al-Lorqui was a Spanish physician who died before 1372. He was the father of Joshua ben Joseph ibn Vives al-Lorqui. The whole entry gives just two works. He revised Tibbon's translation of Maimonides' Millot Higgayon and dedicated the revision to his pupil Ezra ben Solomon ibn Gatigno. He also wrote the Sefer Yesodot. No birth date, place of practice, or other life detail is given in this very short notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaacs-samuel-h: Samuel Hillel Isaacs was an American calendar maker born in 1825 at Raczek, Poland. He studied under Judah Bacharach and Moses Leib of Kutna, then emigrated to New York, arriving June 30, 1847. In 1886 and 1887 he was principal of the Talmud Torah in New York. He wrote for the American Jewish press and for a Jerusalem monthly. His chief work was calendar-making: he compiled an "Artificial Perpetual Calendar" and a "Civil and Ecclesiastical Perpetual Calendar," printed at New York in 1891.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israels-joseph-:
Joseph Israels was a Dutch genre painter born at Groningen on June 27, 1824. His mother wanted him for the rabbinate. His father, a banker, planned a counting-room career instead, and the boy sketched in the margins of the great ledgers he had to keep. At last his father gave way, and he took up art.

He studied at Groningen, then at Amsterdam under Cornelis Kruseman, then in Paris under Picot, Horace Vernet, and Paul Delaroche. Millet's first Paris showing in 1848 struck him early. Back in Amsterdam he tried history painting, with a William the Silent scene in 1855, and found little success. He then turned to the peasants who came in on market days and to the fisherfolk of the seaside villages. Those plain scenes of Dutch life made his fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ha-levi-h: Jacob ha-Levi, called he-Hasid, was a French rabbi and cabalist of the thirteenth century who lived at Marvège. It was said that by prayer and invocation he could draw decisions on religious questions down from heaven, given to him in dreams. Those dream rulings were gathered as "She'elot u-Teshubot min ha-Shamayim," Questions and Answers from Heaven. They were printed at Leghorn in 1818, inside the responsa of David ibn Zimra. Some of his rulings also appear in the "Shibbole ha-Leket."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jastrow-marcus-:
Marcus Jastrow, called Mordecai, was an American rabbi and scholar born on June 5, 1829, at Rogasen in Prussian Poland. He studied at Posen and Berlin and took a doctorate at Halle in 1855. In 1858 he became rabbi at Warsaw, where he backed the Polish national cause with sermons and public acts.

That stand brought arrest in November 1861, weeks in the Warsaw citadel, and expulsion across the frontier in February 1862. The entry follows his later career in Germany and America and his fame as a scholar. He died on Oct. 13, 1903, at Germantown, Pennsylvania, remembered above all for his great dictionary work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jewish-colonial:
Jewish Colonial Trust was set up as the money tool of the Zionist movement. The idea was put forward at the First Zionist Congress at Basel in 1897, and real steps began at Cologne in May 1898. The trust was meant to hold Zionist funds for the movement's aims and at the same time to work as a bank on sound trade lines, teaching self-reliance rather than giving charity.

Its stated aims center on Palestine and Syria: growth of the Jewish colonies there, land buying on a firm legal base, loans and advances for settlement, and banks in the colonies. The main office was set in London, with capital of two million pounds in one-pound shares that buyers could take up by small first payments.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-john-albert-jan:
John Albert, also called Jan Albrecht, was king of Poland from 1492 to 1501. He took the throne the year his brother Alexander became grand duke of Lithuania. Teachers in his youth had filled him with hatred of the Jews, and though he first confirmed the rights his father Casimir had granted them, he soon turned to harsh measures.

In 1496 he backed a statute that cut Jewish rights. After a great fire at Cracow in 1494, when mobs looted Jewish houses, he ordered the city's Jews to move to the suburb of Kazimierz and live apart. That town kept its own Jewish life for centuries. Yet he also let Jews driven from Lithuania in 1495 settle in Polish towns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-of-dreux: Joseph of Dreux was a French Talmudist of the first half of the thirteenth century. His name appears in a British Museum manuscript of notes on the Pentateuch. Gross took him to be a son of Solomon of Dreux. On that view he is also the Bible commentator whose place name was misspelled in another manuscript. Gross adds that this Joseph ben Solomon wrote letters to Isaac ben Abraham of Dreux. The entry is short and leans wholly on Gross's Gallia Judaica for its facts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jost-liebmann-8: Liebmann Jost was court Jew and court jeweler to Elector Frederick III of Brandenburg, later King Frederick I of Prussia. He was also an elder of the Jewish congregation of Berlin, and he died in 1701. He followed Israel Aaron in the court post and married Aaron's widow. His wealth let him keep his own synagogue, with his nephew as its rabbi. His feud with Marcus Magnus, the crown prince's court Jew, split the congregation in two. Among his many descendants were the composer Meyerbeer and his brothers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judas-the-galil:
Judas the Galilean led a popular revolt against Rome when the first census was taken in Judea, in the year 6 or 7. Born at Gamala, he joined with Zadok, a Pharisee, to head the Zealots in resisting the count. He proclaimed a Jewish state that owned God alone as king and His laws as supreme.

Judas died in the rising and his followers scattered, but his spirit lived on in them. Two of his sons were later crucified by Tiberius Alexander. A third son, Menahem, led the Sicarii for a time before the high-priestly party killed him. Graetz and Schuerer take this Judas to be the same man as Judas son of Hezekiah, who had seized Sepphoris in an earlier revolt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kasmunah-someti: Ḳasmunah, sometimes called Xemone, was a Jewish poet of Andalusia. She lived in the twelfth or thirteenth century and wrote in Arabic. Al-Maḳḳari lists her among the Arab poets of Spain. Her father Ishmael was a poet too. He took great pains with her schooling. He would start a strophe and call on her to finish it. Only two of her verses have come down to us.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kohn-tobias-943: Tobias Kohn, an American merchant and silk maker born at Prague in Bohemia, died at Hartford, Connecticut, in 1898. He left for America after the revolution of 1848-49, bringing part of his braid machinery with him. After a start in New York he settled in Hartford, where by 1858 his braid works filled a whole block. In 1859 he wove the first piece of silk goods made by a loom in the United States. Patents followed between 1865 and 1868, and his methods helped plant the silk industry at Paterson.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lapapa-aaron-b-: Aaron ben Isaac Lapapa, an Oriental rabbi and Talmudist who died in 1674, served first at Manissa in Turkey. At an advanced age he was called to Smyrna as a civil judge. In 1665, at the height of the Shabbethai Ẓebi fever there, he was one of few rabbis with the nerve to oppose the false prophet and ban him. The movement answered by deposing Lapapa and driving him from the city. After Shabbethai turned to Islam, Lapapa seems to have been restored. His responsa appeared at Smyrna in 1674.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leipziger-henry:
Henry Marcus Leipziger, an American educator, was born at Manchester, England, on Dec. 29, 1853. He came to New York in 1865. He earned degrees from the College of the City of New York and from Columbia, taking his Ph.D. in 1878.

Leipziger taught in New York public schools from 1873 to 1881. He later served as assistant superintendent of schools and as supervisor of lectures for the city. He pushed manual and trade training in public schools, and urged Jews to take up skilled trades. From 1884 to 1891 he directed the Hebrew Technical Institute in New York. His book "The New Education" came out in 1888.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-simhah-ary: Simhah Aryeh ben Ephraim Fischel Levi was a Russian Hebraist and author of the nineteenth century. He was born at Hrubieszow, in the government of Warsaw. He wrote a double commentary on Job, with a preface and two poems, printed at Lemberg in 1833. A year later came "Dibre Purim," an epic poem centered on Ahasuerus and Esther. He also began a Hebrew dictionary on new lines, called "Memalle." Only the first letter came out, at Warsaw in 1839. Benjacob attacked that work sharply in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lewita-gustaw-9: Gustaw Lewita, a Polish pianist, was born at Plock, Poland, in 1855. He died at Paris in February 1889. He graduated with honors from the Vienna Conservatorium and went to Paris. There he joined the orchestra of the Pas de Loup concerts. In 1882 he was called to a professorship at the Warsaw Conservatorium. In 1885 he played at the court of the Archduke Charles in Vienna. He then toured America, giving concerts in its chief cities and before the Emperor of Brazil.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-literature-mode:
Modern Hebrew literature, dated here from 1743 to 1904, is set apart from older rabbinic writing. The entry gives it two aims: freeing the language by a return to Bible models, and using a plainer Hebrew to help free Jews from ghetto limits. Both aims meet in the word Haskalah.

Italy led an early shift, but Moses Hayyim Luzzatto's drama from 1743 is called the first work of the new literature. Pupils in Amsterdam and writers in Germany followed. Under Mendelssohn, groups spread new ideas through Bible translation and through a Hebrew journal founded in 1785. The survey continues to the death of Smolenskin in 1885 and beyond.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-low-a-maurice-1:
A. Maurice Low gets a short biographical entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, written by Cyrus Adler. Low was an Anglo-American writer born in London on July 14, 1860. He trained at King's College School and later in Austria before turning to journalism. From 1888 he reported from Washington for the Boston Globe.

The entry follows his rise as a link between British and American readers. In 1896 he became Washington correspondent for the London Daily Chronicle, the first such post an English paper had created. He edited the American section of the National Review and wrote for leading magazines on both sides of the Atlantic. The entry also notes his 1901 novel, The Supreme Surrender, showing how a period reference recorded a working journalist at mid-career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ma-aserot-tithe:
Ma'aserot, meaning tithes, names a tractate of the Mishnah described in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It is the seventh tractate in the order Zera'im, on seeds and farming law. A Tosefta and a Palestinian Gemara accompany it. The subject is the tithe of farm produce owed to the Levites.

The article sets this tithe apart from its cousins. The second tithe had to be eaten by its owner in Jerusalem. The poor man's tithe came every third year. This tractate covers the first tithe, the Levite's share. Its five chapters ask what food counts as tithable and when the duty begins. They cover workers who eat from the crop they gather, and sales to people suspected of skipping the tithe. The entry serves readers who want the shape of a legal text without reading all its cases.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marriage-10432:
Marriage in the Bible and in early Hebrew life fills a long Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Solomon Schechter, Joseph Jacobs, and Julius H. Greenstone were among its writers. The article does not start with rules. It first asks what marriage looked like in the world of the Old Testament.

The first sections find no clear trace of kinship traced through the mother. They describe polygyny, marriage to more than one wife, as the common pattern. Only rich men, chiefs, and kings kept large households, the article notes. It names Gideon, David, and Solomon as cases. Later biblical law then set limits and guarded the rights of less favored wives, slave wives, and their children.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meat-tax-10532:
The meat-tax, a duty on kosher meat that Jewish communities once levied on themselves, is described for Austria in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Gotthard Deutsch. Communal taxes on meat were nothing new; what changed in the eighteenth century was the collector. Governments discovered the tax and took it over, using its revenue to support schools. In Bohemia it stood in for the old toleration-tax, abolished in 1782.

The machinery was petty and painful. The duty ran about two kreutzer on a pound of meat and ten on a goose. Butchers had to hand over a receipt with every pound, and the slaughterer could not kill a fowl until the customer produced one. Worse, the tax was farmed out to contractors whose agents, almost always Jews themselves, exacted payment with merciless rigor, while evasion drew heavy fines. Kulke's novels, the article says, show the human cost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-ben-mac:
Menahem ben Machir was an eleventh-century German liturgist of Ratisbon. Cyrus Adler and M. Seligsohn catalogue him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He stood close to the founding generation of Ashkenazic scholarship. His grandfather was a nephew of Gershom ben Judah, and he himself was cousin to Isaac ben Judah, Rashi's teacher; Rashi's "Pardes" quotes him. He also lived through the massacres of 1096 in Germany. He commemorated them in penitential hymns.

The entry then lists his output, poem by poem. It names hymns for the Esther fast and for Yom Kippur afternoon. It names one for the seventeenth of Tammuz and a lament for the Ninth of Ab. It names five morning poems, hoshanas, and pieces for Tabernacles and Simhat Torah. Nearly all are alphabetical in arrangement. All bear his signature. So a whole year's liturgy can be followed through one man's hand.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-milhau-joseph-b:
Joseph ben Moses Milhau, called Joseph Moscat, was a French scholar and liturgical poet. He lived at Carpentras in the later eighteenth century. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. His known book, Oẓerot Yosef, was printed at Leghorn in 1783. It comments on Rashi and Elijah Mizraḥi on the Pentateuch.

A poem of his was recited at a circumcision ceremony at Avignon, Zunz reported. The Avignon prayer-book holds more of his liturgical pieces. But the entry ends in doubt. Zunz elsewhere gave those poems to a Joseph of Milhau. That Joseph sat on the rabbinical college in 1751. He was apparently an earlier, different man of the same name and town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-molitor-joseph-:
Joseph Franz Molitor, born at Ober Ursel on June 8, 1779, was the German Christian philosopher who gave his life to the Cabala, as Isidore Singer and S. J. Levinson write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He began with Kant, Fichte, and Schelling, publishing on the philosophy of history. A teaching post at Prince von Dalberg's institute for the improvement of Judaism turned him toward Hebrew.

He learned Hebrew and Aramaic, read Talmud, and in 1813, under the Jewish cabalist Metz, caught his insight into the Cabala and devoted himself to the Zohar for good. The fruit was his Philosophie der Geschichte, whose volumes of 1824, 1834, and 1839 move from tradition in general to a compendium of the Cabala itself. He died at Frankfurt in 1860.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mortgage-or-hyp:
Mortgage, or hypothec, in Jewish law is the subject of this Jewish Encyclopedia article by Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz. A hypothec is a written security for a debt placed on property. Unlike a pledge, it does not hand possession of the property to the creditor.

The article traces the word from the Greek hypotheke into Mishnah Hebrew, where it was reshaped as apoteke. It explains why land suits a mortgage but an ox or other chattel does not: a chattel has no voice to warn later buyers. It then works through hard cases, such as a flooded field, a sale of mortgaged land, and a mortgaged slave set free. The piece preserves rabbinic property law as scholars stated it in 1906.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-nathan-be: Moses Nathan ben Judah was a liturgical poet of the fourteenth century. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach give him a three-line entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He may be the same man as the Catalonian parnas Moses Nathan, who was still living in 1354. His liturgical poems found a lasting place: they were taken into the prayer books of Avignon and of Africa.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-murviedro-11232:
Murviedro, a city in the old kingdom of Valencia, held a Jewish community with special privileges. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on it. In 1327 the community was given ground for a cemetery. Its leading man in the late thirteenth century was Yusuf ibn Shaprut.

Yusuf was freed of taxes, rented the city's baths, received real estate from the king, and became bayle. In the Unionist rebellion of 1348 the Jews were plundered and many killed. Yet in the general slaughter of 1391 Murviedro was the only place in Valencia where the Jews were spared. By 1431 the shrunken community could pay only a small tax.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ne-ilah-11432:
Ne'ilah is the last of five services on the Day of Atonement. Gotthard Deutsch, Cyrus Adler, and Francis L. Cohen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name means the closing of the gates. Rabbis argued whether those gates were the Temple's or heaven's. Both great rituals pray as if heaven's gates close.

The oldest part is a confession, What are we? It asks what human life is worth at all. In Ne'ilah the word seal replaces inscribe in prayers. That shift runs from Rosh haShanah up to this hour. Late hymns stretched the service until night fell. It ends with seven cries of The Lord is God. Kaddish and a shofar blast close the fast day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-niederlander-ab:
Abraham ben Ephraim Niederländer was an Austrian mathematician. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the sixteenth century, at Prague. He was scribe to Judah Löw ben Bezaleel, the MaHaRaL. He is also known simply as Abraham Schreiber.

His mathematical work is called Berit Abraham. It was printed at Prague in the year 1609. It rests largely on Elijah Mizrahi's writings before it. Non-Jewish writings also fed into its making. The book is divided into five full sections. It gathers problems under the title Mozne Zedek. That title means, in Hebrew, the scales of justice. The entry is short, but the book's plan is clear.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nuremberg-11632:
Nuremberg was the chief trade city of Bavaria, in Germany. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote its long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived there by the start of the twelfth century. A stone from 1129 bears the name of Elijah ben Simon. Later stones date from 1273 and 1308.

The entry tells a hard tale of blame, tax, and loss. Jews were charged with harm to the host, a holy wafer. In 1298 a mob killed 698 Jews there. Whole kin groups died in that attack. Kings then set tight rules on trade, dress, and baths. Jews could not sell meat to Christians in their shops. Such rules pushed many Jews toward money lending for work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-jacqu:
Jacques Oppenheim was a Dutch man of law at Groningen. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Groningen on March 3, 1849. He read at the high school and university there. He took his law degree in the year 1872.

Jacques taught at the high school of his town at first. In 1873 he became clerk to the town of Groningen. In 1885 he was made a teacher of law there. In 1893 he was called to a chair at Leyden. That chair was in the field of public law. He held deep care for the Jewish flock of his land. Twice the state named him to groups that framed new laws. He wrote a chief work on Dutch town law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-passigli-ugo-11:
