Ugo Passigli was an Italian physician born in Siena in 1867. He studied medicine in Florence and joined its health department. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Passigli wrote often for science and literary journals.

Many of his pamphlets deal with medicine in the Hebrew Bible. One studied circumcision as a guard against disease. Others covered ancient food rules and child care. He wrote on skin disease and on birth care among the ancient Hebrews. A later work traced old methods of fighting infection.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pergamus-bergam:
Pergamus, now Bergama, is a city of Asia Minor near Smyrna. Isidore Singer, Abraham Galante, and M. Franco wrote the entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its known Jewish settlement dates to the eighteenth century. The community kept a synagogue and a small school.

The settlers came from Constantinople, Salonica, and north Africa. Trade once lay mostly in Jewish hands there. By 1904 most families had fallen on hard times. Gambling and new rivals hurt them badly. Most earned their bread at the weekly fair. About five hundred Jews lived among eighteen thousand people.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pichon-pitchon-: Joseph Pichon was a rabbinical author in Ottoman Turkey. Isidore Singer and M. Franco wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived there at the end of the seventeenth century. He wrote one known work, Minhage ha-Bedikah be-Ir Saloniki. Its subject is the inspection of slaughtered meat. It set out how Salonica made its meat kasher in the slaughter-house. Nothing more of his life is recorded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-polak-gabriel-j:
Gabriel Jacob Polak was a Talmudist and book scholar who lived from 1803 to 1869. Isidore Singer and Moses Löb Bamberger wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He spent his life at Amsterdam, where he led a school. His name rests on careful Hebrew books and lists of books.

Polak made a Dutch and Hebrew almanac for the year 1844. He also made a Dutch-Hebrew dictionary and a set of Hebrew poems. His essays came out in 1851 under the title Ben Gorni. He wrote on the accents in Job and the Psalms. His list of two private libraries still helps book scholars today. His editions of prayer rites won praise for their care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prayer-books-12:
Prayer-books, meaning the gathered prayers of the Jewish year, are treated by Cyrus Adler and Judah David Eisenstein. Their article appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. One book holds prayers for weekdays and Sabbaths. It holds prayers for holy days and fast days too. Jews call such a book the Siddur.

The first known book of this kind came from Babylon. Amram Gaon made it in the years 846 to 864. He led the school of Matah Mehasya there. His book, the Seder Rab Amram, spread very wide. Rashi and other great names used and cited it. All later prayer-books rest on his work, the writers say.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-puchowitzer-jud:
Judah Löb Puchowitzer was a Russian rabbi, mystic, and author. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the last quarter of the seventeenth century. He served as rabbi at Pinsk for a time. In his old age he moved to the Holy Land.

Puchowitzer settled at Jerusalem for his last years. He charged his son Elijah to print his books. One book holds seventeen sermons, printed in 1681. One treats morals and strict living in thirty-two parts. A third gathers words of the wise on right living. His books show a rabbi of both law and Cabala.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ragstatt-friedr:
Friedrich von Weila Ragstatt was born in Germany in 1648. Gotthard Deutsch and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His Jewish name was probably Weil. In 1671 he became a Christian at Cleves.

The article says Ragstatt then worked as a pastor in a Dutch village. It lists eight works written between 1671 and 1689. His first book tried to prove the messianic mission of Jesus. It also argued against Jewish critics, above all Lipmann of Mülhausen. Other works cover sermons, baptism talks, and Psalm 2. The entry records a convert who wrote against his former faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reeve-ada-12632:
Ada Reeve was an English actress born in London about 1870. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Her parents both worked in the theater. Her father acted in stock companies for many years.

The article says she first appeared at age six. That debut was a pantomime at the Pavilion Theatre. As a child she played servant girls and even old women. At twelve she sang as a serio-comic performer. A song called What Do I Care made her a hit. In 1895 she played at the Criterion in London. She later led in Florodora at the Lyric Theatre. She also appeared in San Toy at Daly's. The entry follows a child performer to West End success.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ribeiro-joao-pi:
João Pinto Ribeiro was a Portuguese scholar who kept the royal archives. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He worked at Torre do Tombo in Lisbon. He died there on August 11, 1649.

The article centers on one long work in his name. Its Spanish title asks a sharp policy question. Should Portugal expel reconciled New Christians from its kingdoms? The work defends the Maranos against such expulsion. It remains in manuscript, the writers note. Its long Spanish title states the question plainly for modern readers. Two Portuguese bibliographies support the short entry fully.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosen-joseph-b-:
Joseph b. Isaac Rosen was a Russian rabbi born at Horodok, near Pinsk, in the early nineteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote his 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Though set for business, he taught himself and rose fast as a scholar.

Rosen served as head of the rabbinical court in his home town until 1864. He then acted as rabbi at Telz, and from 1873 led the community at Slonim. He held that post until his death in 1885. His books include comments on the Shulhan Aruk and a volume of Sabbath sermons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rufus-tineius-w:
Tineius Rufus was governor of Judea when the Bar Kokba war broke out. Isidore Singer and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The war was the great Jewish revolt against Rome under Hadrian.

Rufus took a leading part in the fighting against the rebels. He could not withstand their first onslaught, though, and help was sent. Syria's governor, then Rome's best general Julius Severus, took over the war. After the revolt fell, Rufus is said to have cleared Judea of its Jews. The plowing up of the Temple Mount is laid to his deed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saloman-siegfri:
Siegfried Saloman was a Danish violinist and composer born at Tondern on October 2, 1816. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was a brother of the painter Geskel and the physician Nota.

At twelve Saloman played in public at a Copenhagen concert with success. A scholarship let him study in Dessau and Dresden from 1838. His operas include Tordenskjold i Dynekilen and Diamantkorset, both staged widely. The latter, in German dress, scored marked success at Berlin and Leipsic. He married the Swedish singer Henriette Nissen and toured Europe with her.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schuster-arthur:
Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Arthur Schuster. He was an English physicist. Schuster was born at Frankfort-on-the-Main on September 12, 1851. He studied at Frankfort, at Owens College in Manchester, and at Heidelberg. He took his doctorate in 1873. Spectrum analysis drew his early interest.

In 1875 Schuster led the expedition to Siam to watch a solar eclipse. He joined a similar expedition to Egypt in 1882. The Royal Society gave him its medal for his researches. He became a fellow of that society in 1893. Since 1885 he has been professor of physics at Owens College. Many of his papers appear in the society's Transactions. He also writes often for scientific journals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shein-pavel-vas:
Pavel Vasilyevich Shein was a Russian ethnographer born in 1826 and trained at Moscow University. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. After converting to Protestantism, he taught Russian at Tula. He later taught at Tolstoy's school at Yasnaya Polyana.

Shein loved his country's language and customs above all. Though crippled, he traveled to countless villages and hamlets. There he collected songs and stories straight from peasants. His chief work, printed at St. Petersburg in 1890, covers White Russian family life. It presents that life through rites and songs. The Academy of Sciences backed the book. He died at Riga in 1900, and the entry honors a collector of folk memory.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sichel-nathanee:
Nathaneel Sichel was a German painter born at Mainz on January 8, 1843. Isidore Singer wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He studied at Munich's Royal Academy of Art from 1859. His teachers there included the painter Julius Schrader.

In 1863 Sichel's Joseph Explains Pharaoh's Dreams won a scholarship. The prize let him spend two years working in Rome. He first passed a year painting in Paris. His portrait shown at the Salon of 1865 drew notice. In Rome he painted grand historical scenes. They treated Mary Stuart, Don Carlos, and Francesca da Rimini. Back in Germany from 1869, he turned to portraits. Eastern and romantic figures fill his later list of works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simhah-of-rome-:
Simhah of Rome was a scholar and rabbi of the Roman community in the late thirteenth century. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His community sent him out with an open letter. His task was to find Maimonides' commentary on the Mishnah. He was to bring a copy back to Rome.

He searched through Provence and Catalonia without success. At Barcelona, Solomon ben Adret gave him a new letter of help. At last he found parts of the work at Huesca. Scholars then translated the Arabic original into Hebrew in 1296 to 1298. Simhah carried it home through many dangers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sotah-faithless:
Sotah is a treatise on the wife suspected of unfaithfulness. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It appears in the Mishnah, Tosefta, and both Talmuds. It defines the rite set out in Numbers chapter five. In most editions it is the sixth treatise of Nashim.

It has nine chapters and sixty-seven paragraphs in all. Chapter one tells how a husband shows jealousy and warns his wife. It tells how the suspected wife is brought to Jerusalem. Chapter two tells how the offering of jealousy is prepared. The priest pours holy water and adds earth to it. Later chapters weigh when a woman may refuse the bitter water.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-karoline-:
Karoline Stern was a German opera singer born at Mayence on April 10, 1800. Isidore Singer and Regina Neisser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about her in 1906. Her father, a noted violinist, was her first teacher. She later studied under Heidelhof. The date of her death is not known.

Stern made her stage debut at Treves in 1816. At Düsseldorf she met the Heine family. Young Heinrich Heine praised her in his verse. In 1819 she became lead soprano at the Stuttgart court theater. Later engagements took her to Munich, Augsburg, and Würzburg. She retired from the stage in 1841. Her greatest triumphs came in operas by Mozart, Weber, and Rossini. She sang in concerts successfully until 1855.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-susskind-suezki:
Süsskind of Trimberg was a German minnesinger of the thirteenth century. Isidore Singer and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He took his name from Trimberg in Franconia, near Würzburg. Little is known of his life beyond his poems. He may have worked as a physician.

Six of Süsskind's poems survive in the Manesse collection. They show he ranked high among poets of his day. He sang of the worth of the virtuous woman. For knights he drew the ideal nobleman in verse. His best-known piece is the Fable of the Wolf. In it he laments the scant support of the rich. He vows to quit poetry and live henceforth as a Jew. The entry preserves a rare Jewish voice in German court song.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tanhum-bar-jere:
Tanhum bar Jeremiah was a Palestinian amora of the fourth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He studied under Mani the Elder. His record survives in a handful of sources. One anecdote shows the limits on a pupil's authority.

At Hefer in Galilee, Tanhum once ruled on a religious question. Others objected that his teacher lived within twelve miles. A pupil could not rule independently so near his master. Only one legal decision of his is extant. It concerns the liturgy, recorded in the Jerusalem Talmud. Several of his sermonic sentences do survive. They appear in Genesis and Lamentations midrashim. One comments on a psalm of David. The brief entry keeps a minor sage from vanishing entirely.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tokahah-admonit:
Tokahah is the name for Moses' warnings of punishment for disobedience. Wilhelm Bacher and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The warnings stand in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. Blessings for obedience come first in both chapters. The Mishnah calls the warnings simply curses.

Custom forbids splitting the tokahah when it is read aloud. One reader takes the whole chapter on fast days and Sabbaths. Each reading must start and end with a cheerful verse. Ashkenazim do not call the reader up by name. In some towns the passage fell to men who could not understand it. That slight led rabbis to read it themselves. The phrase became a byword for a scolding.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trusts-and-trus:
Trusts in Jewish law never grew as wide as in Anglo-American law. Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Guardians for orphans are treated under other headings. A trustee could also hold property for a married woman. Such a man was called the third man, in Hebrew.

The Mishnah sets minimum support a husband owes through a trustee. A key case puts money with a trustee for a daughter. She trusts her husband and wants the fund released. R. Meir says the trustee must still invest it in land. R. Jose lets an adult woman sell as she wishes. Later authorities rule the law follows R. Meir. Divorce bills held by trustees raise further disputes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vali-valle-mose:
Moses David Vali, also spelled Valle, was an Italian rabbi and doctor at Padua. He died there in 1777. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry about him. Vali was known as a scholar of Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition. He gave lectures to a Padua study group.

One young listener was Moses Hayyim Luzzatto, later a famous writer. Luzzatto began his study of Kabbalah under Vali. At age twenty five, Vali wrote an Italian work arguing against Christianity. He also wrote eight large Hebrew volumes, mostly a commentary on the whole Bible. Those volumes were never printed, and they survive in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-volterra-meshul:
Meshullam ben Menahem Volterra was an Italian jeweler who traveled east. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in Florence in the fifteenth century. His father traded in precious stones and grew very rich. Meshullam may have written a book on jewelry.

In 1481 he sailed for the Orient by way of Rhodes. He reached Alexandria, then Cairo, buying gems. On July 29 he arrived in Jerusalem. Sickness struck him there and again in Crete. A shipwreck cost him his precious stones. He reached Venice in October, and his travel account survives in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weill-alexandre:
Alexandre Weill was a French writer born Abraham Weill. He was born at Schirhoffen, Alsace, on May 10, 1811. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died at Paris on October 18, 1898. His parents planned a rabbinical path for him. He studied Talmud at Frankfort toward that end.

In 1837 Weill gave up the rabbinate for Paris. A letter from Heinrich Heine opened salon doors. He wrote for many leading French journals. His village tales of 1847 made his name. Heine wrote a preface for that book. Weill may have pioneered the rustic tale in France. Meyerbeer and Victor Hugo admired his work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wilmersdorffer-:
Max Wilmersdörffer was a Bavarian financier and philanthropist. Gotthard Deutsch wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Bayreuth on April 8, 1824. He died at Munich on December 26, 1903. As a youth he entered his uncle's Munich bank. He married his uncle's daughter in time.

Saxony named Wilmersdörffer its consul general. Bavaria and Saxony both decorated him with orders. In 1888 he became a knight of the Bavarian Crown. He knew German classics deeply and mastered coin lore. He patronized art and many charities in Munich. A strict Jew, he led Munich's congregation in 1864. He served as its president for two years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wunderbar-reube:
Reuben Joseph Wunderbar (1812-1868) was a Russian teacher and author on Jewish life. Herman Rosenthal and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Mitau, he learned from a private teacher at home. At eighteen he went into the trade of his father.

He wed in 1834 and lost his funds soon after. He then lived by private lessons for a time. His tract for Jews who moved to farm colonies drew note. Max Lilienthal read it and gave him a school post. That post was at the Riga school under his charge. In 1848 Wunderbar went back to Mitau for good. There he taught faith and read Hebrew for the state. He filled the rabbi role at times till his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zacuto-abraham-:
Abraham ben Samuel Zacuto (born about 1450) was a Spanish star scholar and scribe of the past. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broyde wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Salamanca, he won wide fame for his star craft. He taught at the school of that town and at Saragossa.

When Spain cast out its Jews, he went to Lisbon. The king made him court star man and past scribe there. The king asked his view on the great sea trip to come. That trip was the voyage of Vasco da Gama to India. Zacuto backed the plan and urged the king to sail. The ships bore his new astrolabe of iron, not wood. Fresh laws then forced him to flee that land in turn. He was seized twice on his flight to safe shores.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zelazowska-cath:
Catherine Zelazowska (1460-1540) was a Polish woman who took the Jewish faith. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was the widow of a town chief of Cracow. In her day the church of Poland split in more than one sect.

The Bible drove that split in the minds of many folk. She took the path of a great lord's girl in that age. She left her old faith and embraced Judaism in full. The bishop of Cracow judged her case in his court. He gave the word that she be burned for that act. She was eighty years of age at that hard hour. She went to her death with joy, the entry says in brief.
knowlton-fruits-of-philosophy-1832:
Charles Knowlton, a doctor, wrote Fruits of Philosophy, first issued in 1832. Its subtitle calls it the private companion of adult people. This fourth edition, with additions, was printed in Philadelphia in 1839.

The book gave married adults plain information about birth control. Such advice was bold and risky to publish at that time. Knowlton put his motto on the title page: knowledge is wealth. The work remains a key early American text on contraception, kept here in its own plain early printing. Its plain medical tone set it apart from rumor and quack advice. Later birth control writers treated Knowlton as an early pioneer.
laplace-mecanique-celeste-bowditch-vol-2:
Bowditch's English Mecanique Celeste reached its second volume in 1832, again with his full commentary. Pierre-Simon Laplace devoted books three to five to the shapes and motions of heavenly bodies. Their topics include the figures that spinning planets take. Tides and the rotation of the Earth also receive full treatment.

Laplace works out how gravity shapes seas and worlds alike. Bowditch guides English readers through each hard passage step by step. The volume forms the middle of a four part translation. It shows French math astronomy at its peak strength. Students of the era learned the field from these pages. The commentary alone earned lasting praise.
manetho-fragments-cory-1832:
Manetho, an Egyptian priest, wrote the Aegyptiaca in Greek around 280 BCE to set out the true line of Egypt's kings. His book is lost, but church writers and chronologers quoted its lists. Isaac Preston Cory printed the fragments in 1832, with kindred Egyptian scraps from other hands.

The lists run from gods and demigods through thirty dynasties of human kings, the frame on which all dating of pharaonic Egypt still rests. Manetho gave the dynasties the names and order that scholars use today. These dry lines of kings are among the most used pages in Egypt's study. Cory's gathering keeps them in one place.
morrell-narrative-four-voyages-1832:
Benjamin Morrell sailed on four long trade and seal trips in the 1820s. His Narrative of Four Voyages came out in 1832. The tales range wide, from the Pacific to the far south seas. One claim in the book still sparks debate to this day.

Morrell said he found a coast he called New South Greenland in the far south. Later sailors could not find that land where he placed it. Some call him a liar, while others think he erred in his charts. The book stays at the heart of talks on early Antarctic finds.
openalex-w1997401532:
Aminael Sanchez-Rodriguez, Hanne Tytgat, Joris Winderickx and colleagues studied sugar-adding enzymes in bacteria. Their paper appeared in BMC Genomics in 2014. These enzymes, called glycosyltransferases, help build the sugars on bacterial surfaces. The team asked how to predict which sugar each enzyme acts on.

They built a computer workflow that combined gene sequence checks with a network method. The network linked enzymes to likely substrate groups. They tested the workflow on a well known gut bacterium strain. They then applied it to a probiotic strain. The workflow predicted many enzymes there. Some had not been reported before. The method helps labs plan tests of bacterial surface sugars.
openalex-w2102671432:
Serguei Chatrchyan and colleagues in the CMS Collaboration searched for the Higgs boson made alongside a W or Z boson. Their paper appeared in Physical Review D in 2014. In this channel, the Higgs decays to bottom quarks. That decay is common but hard to spot. Partner bosons help tag the rare events.

The search used LHC data from two energy runs. Six related signal channels were analysed together. An excess of events appeared above background. Its size matched standard model expectations well. The excess centred near the known Higgs mass. Its strength was about twice the noise level. The result supports the standard model Higgs picture.
openalex-w2103574532:
Celia Maria Ferreira Gontijo and Maria Norma Melo reviewed visceral leishmaniasis in Brazil. Their paper appeared in the Brazilian Journal of Epidemiology in 2004. The disease is widespread and common there. It can turn severe and fatal, especially with malnutrition. Its spread into cities raised new concern.

The authors analysed biological and social drivers of expansion. Urban growth over twenty years changed the disease pattern. Sand fly vectors adapted to city edges. Dogs serve as urban reservoirs of the parasite. Diagnosis and treatment tools remain imperfect. Past control efforts failed to stop transmission. New epidemics still occur despite campaigns. Better tests and drugs are advancing, they note.
openalex-w2113108732:
Steven Goodreau, Nicole Bohme Carnegie, Eric Vittinghoff and colleagues modelled what drives HIV spread among men who have sex with men. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2012. They compared the United States and Peru. Prevention choices depend on where transmissions truly occur. Guesswork can waste scarce programme funds.

Their computer models simulated sexual partnership networks. Men differed by age, behaviour and treatment history. The models split infections by partnership type. Main and casual partnerships were tracked separately. Most infections traced to partners in the chronic stage. Early-stage partners caused a smaller share. Undiagnosed and untreated partners both drove many infections. Testing and treatment gaps matter greatly, they conclude.
openalex-w2114838732:
Nikolaos Fyllas, Sandra Patino, Timothy Baker and colleagues compared leaf traits across the Amazon Basin. Their paper appeared in Biogeosciences in 2009. Leaves reveal how trees cope with local conditions. Traits vary with ancestry, soil and climate. A basin-wide dataset allowed the three to be separated.

The team measured over a thousand individual trees. Sixty-two plots spanned the whole basin. Every tree was identified to species. Leaf weight, carbon signals and nutrients were recorded. Leaf traits differed between the basin's east and west. Soil fertility explained part of that split. Climate and family history explained more. The data feed models of forest carbon uptake.
openalex-w2472132332:
William Joseph Gutowski, Filippo Giorgi, and Bertrand Timbal wrote this 2016 paper with a large international team of climate scientists. It appeared in Geoscientific Model Development. The paper explains CORDEX, the Coordinated Regional Downscaling Experiment, and its role inside CMIP6, the latest round of global climate model comparisons. Global models give broad climate pictures, but planners need detail for single regions.

CORDEX sets shared rules so groups worldwide can shrink global model output into finer regional projections. Its regional challenges focus the work, and flagship pilot studies test new downscaling ideas. A planned CORDEX-CORE effort would produce a uniform set of high-resolution projections for regions everywhere. These products help researchers study uncertainty in the projections. They also feed information into vulnerability, impact, and adaptation planning.
openalex-w2600399632:
Rachel Hoesly, Steven J. Smith, and Leyang Feng, with colleagues, present this emissions dataset paper, published in Geoscientific Model Development in 2018. It introduces CEDS, the Community Emissions Data System. The dataset gives yearly human-caused emissions of reactive gases and aerosols from 1750 to 2014. Knowing these historical trends is essential for models of air quality and climate.

CEDS improves on older inventories by applying one consistent, repeatable method to every substance. It blends energy data with national and regional inventories and updated emission factors. Results come by country and sector, plus monthly grids for map-based models. The estimates run slightly higher than earlier global inventories, the authors note. Recent years carry the most uncertainty, especially where national inventories are scarce. The team plans refinements, uncertainty estimates, and open-source release of the system.
openalex-w2741543132:
Jorge Ovalle, Roberto Casadio, R. da Rocha, and A. Sotomayor wrote this 2018 theory paper in the European Physical Journal C. It works within Einstein's general relativity on models of dense stars. Simple star models assume pressure pushes equally in all directions, called isotropic. Real sources may push unevenly, and the authors seek a systematic way to include that.

Their tool is gravitational decoupling, carried out through the minimal geometric deformation approach. Starting from one acceptable isotropic solution, the method generates whole families of anisotropic ones. The new solutions inherit the physical acceptability of their parent model. The authors study the surface matching to the outer Schwarzschild spacetime in detail. This gives theorists a recipe book for building realistic star models. Such models matter for understanding neutron stars and testing gravity in extreme conditions.
openalex-w2802815532:
Ditte Demontis, Raymond Kenney Walters, and Joanna Martin lead a huge consortium reporting ADHD risk genes in Nature Genetics. The hosted sample is the group's 2017 preprint of that paper. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder affects about five percent of school-age children. It is highly heritable, yet no single gene variant had been firmly tied to it.

The team meta-analyzed genome data from over twenty thousand ADHD cases and thirty-five thousand controls. Twelve separate genome regions crossed the strict significance threshold for the first time. The linked regions cluster near genes active in the brain and intolerant of damaging mutations. Signals also enriched in evolutionarily constrained stretches of DNA. Extra analyses in a self-reported sample supported the clinical findings. The study finally gives ADHD genetics solid ground to build biological explanations on.
openalex-w2906214132:
Millicent R. Smith, Idupulapati Madhusudana Rao, and Andrew M. Merchant reviewed source-sink relations in crops in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2018. Farm yields rarely reach their biological potential; the difference is the yield gap. Closing it matters because raising potential alone cannot meet future food demand. Inside the plant, the gap is governed by sources and sinks: leaves making sugars, organs consuming them.

The review examines how this supply-demand balance shapes yield and nutritional quality. Yield metrics like harvest index summarize the plant's allocation choices. Yet the processes steering that index remain poorly understood, the authors note. Stress sensitivity, input costs, and grain quality all complicate the simple gap picture. Better source-sink understanding could target breeding and management precisely. The paper synthesizes physiology into an agenda for food security research.
openalex-w2914300732:
José Bellosta von Colbe, J. R. Ares, Jussara Barale, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in the International Journal of Hydrogen Energy. It covers metal hydrides, materials that can hold hydrogen in solid form, and their use for storing and compressing hydrogen gas.

The review traces hydride research from the late 1970s to the present day. It notes their role in rechargeable nickel-metal hydride batteries since the early 1990s. It also describes systems built in the 2010s for emergency and backup power. The authors weigh the current state of the field and what may come next for storage and compression.
openalex-w2914637832:
Linda Reiling, Michelle Boyle, Michael White, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2019. It concerns malaria caused by the parasite Plasmodium falciparum, which still sickens and kills many people worldwide. The team studied children and asked which parasite parts are targeted by a helpful type of antibody.

Some antibodies can attach to merozoites, the parasite form that invades red blood cells, and recruit complement proteins that block parasite growth. This response appears in both natural infection and vaccine-induced protection, but its exact targets were not known. Naming those targets could help scientists choose and rank parts of the parasite for future malaria vaccines.
openalex-w2925056832:
Nick Holmes, Dena Spatz, Steffen Oppel, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2019. It asks which islands matter most for saving highly threatened vertebrates from invasive mammals. Rats, cats, and other introduced mammals are a leading cause of island wildlife losses.

Drawing on the Threatened Island Biodiversity database, the authors rank islands where removing invasive mammals would help the most threatened species. Their aim is to guide conservation groups and funders toward eradications with the largest global benefit. Island eradications are costly and hard, so choosing the right islands first is central to the paper's argument. The work turns a global species database into a practical priority list.
openalex-w2995385432:
Esteban Beltrán-Gracia, Adolfo López-Camacho, Inocencio Higuera-Ciapara, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Cancer Nanotechnology. It tracks clinical progress in liposomal medicines, drugs packed inside tiny fat bubbles called liposomes. The goal of such packaging is stronger drug action with less harm to healthy tissue.

The authors review the lipid building blocks and how each choice affects a formula's stability, travel through the body, and delivery. Many liposomal products are already on the market. Trials have shown them beating the plain drug in blood cancer, hepatitis A, pain care, and several solid cancers. The review concludes that liposomal forms are gentler and better behaved than the same drugs given alone.
openalex-w2999600532:
Dirk Thielen, Karl-Ludwig Schuchmann, Paolo Ramoni-Perazzi, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2020. It asks where the Pantanal, the world's largest wetland, is heading as the climate changes. The study region is the Brazilian part of the Upper Paraguay River Basin.

The team analyzed rainfall patterns and extremes over space and time, alongside sea surface temperature records. Their results point to more frequent heavy rain extremes in the highlands. At the same time, warming seas in the North Atlantic and North Pacific are linked to severe, long droughts in the lowland wetland. Because the sea signals lead the rains, the links improve forecasting of both flood and drought.
openalex-w3043102132:
Shadab Alam, Marie Aubert, Santiago Avila, and colleagues published this capstone paper in Physical Review D in 2021. It reports cosmological results from the completed extended Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey, part of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. The survey capped two decades of sky spectroscopy at Apache Point Observatory.

Baryon oscillations are echoes of sound waves in the early universe, frozen into how galaxies are spaced. Measuring them across cosmic time traces how the universe expanded and how structure grew. The authors place their results within the standard flat model of the cosmos, alongside supernova and microwave background evidence. Combining galaxy surveys with those probes breaks ties that each method suffers alone, sharpening the cosmic picture.
openalex-w3110969532:
Françoise Contreras, Elif Baykal, and Ghulam Abid wrote this review in Frontiers in Psychology in 2020. It examines e-leadership and teleworking in the time of COVID-19 and beyond. Working from home grew at great speed during the pandemic, changing work methods almost overnight.

Telework frees staff from fixed place and hours, but it succeeds only with the right support. Technology, social backing, and above all leadership practiced through screens decide whether it works. The authors analyze how e-leadership, teleworking, and virtual teams fit together. They close with propositions for further study, since remote work is set to outlast the crisis that forced it. The review maps what is known and where research should go next.
openalex-w4220744632:
María Elena Velázquez-Meza, Miguel Galarde-López, Berta Carrillo-Quiroz, and Celia Alpuche-Aranda review antimicrobial resistance through a One Health lens, in Veterinary World in 2022. Antimicrobial resistance means germs no longer respond to the drugs meant to kill them. It threatens people, animals, and the environment at once. One Health treats those three as a single connected system.

The authors blame careless, heavy use of antimicrobials in farming, livestock, and human medicine. Poor infection control, farm waste, pollution, and travel then spread resistant bacteria widely. Bacteria also swap resistance genes under drug pressure, speeding the problem. The review analyses the actors involved and argues that only joint action across sectors can slow resistance.
openalex-w4283722432:
K. G. Arun, Enis Belgacem, Enrico Barausse, and colleagues present a white paper on fundamental physics with LISA, in Living Reviews in Relativity in 2022. LISA, the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, will listen for gravitational waves from space. In the extreme gravity near black holes, gravity is both strong and fast-changing. That regime is where Einstein's theory faces its hardest tests.

The paper, from the LISA Consortium's Fundamental Physics Working Group, maps where LISA data could give key input. Topics include tests of general relativity with compact objects such as black holes and neutron stars. The authors set out open questions and the research paths most likely to answer them. Their aim is to ready the field before the first observations arrive.
openalex-w4367369432:
Chor-Wing Sing, Tzu-Chieh Lin, Sharon Bartholomew, and colleagues chart the global pattern of hip fractures. Their study appeared in the Journal of Bone and Mineral Research in 2023. Hip fracture is a major result of weak bones and a heavy burden on patients, families, and hospitals. More than ten million hip fractures occur worldwide each year. Many could be prevented with the right public health action. Patterns by place, age, and year reveal where prevention and care are working.

The study tracks long-run trends in fracture rates across many countries. It also follows what treatment patients received after fracture and how death rates changed. Rates vary sharply between regions and over time. Such maps help health systems target screening, fall prevention, and surgery where the need is greatest.
openalex-w4410981132:
Toshiaki Akashi, Kanako Kumamaru, Akihiko Wada, and colleagues describe the Japan-Medical Image Database, known as J-MID. Their paper appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2025. Radiology has been digital for nearly two decades. Artificial intelligence handles images especially well.

That combination makes large shared image collections valuable. J-MID gathers medical images as big data for data science research. Researchers can train and test AI tools on real clinical scans. Shared data also lets small teams do studies once limited to big centres. The authors explain how the database supports this work. Well-built image banks speed up reliable AI for diagnosis while keeping research grounded in real practice.
openalex-w7204464632:
Camila Castro Deorristt and co-authors in Brazil released a Portuguese-language review in 2026 on necrotizing enterocolitis, a devastating intestinal emergency of newborn intensive care. The disease strikes mainly extremely preterm and very low birth weight babies. Searching two sources for 2014 to 2024 studies, the team kept five papers. Focusing on babies born before thirty-two weeks and under fifteen hundred grams, their risk factors, and the earliest medical signs.

The disease has many causes at once, the review finds. Severe anemia, a high maternal neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, multiparity, lower gestational age and birth weight, and prenatal antibiotic exposure were linked factors. Warning signs included abnormal gastric residue, abdominal distension, bluish abdominal coloring, and visible intestinal loops. A risk score showed promise but cannot diagnose alone, and nursing vigilance is key.
openalex-w7204886632:
Girlaynne Michellyne Farias Santos and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva released a Portuguese-language review in Brazil in 2026. It covers special education in Brazil and how effective it has been, mainly in regular public schools. Including people with special needs in every social environment has been a problem for decades, despite national and global legal instruments guaranteeing the right. Special education enrollments in regular schools grow yearly.

Progress on equality, equity, and recognition of human dignity has come drop by drop, the authors find. Basic problems persist: teacher training, structural investment and teaching resources, and overcrowded classrooms. Against speeches of a fully inclusive society, the reality in regular classrooms, they conclude, still has a long road to travel.
openalex-w7205015932:
Paulo Dionisio Muniz Goncalves and three colleagues ask how far the internal culture of the Amazonas military police shapes the force its officers use. Their 2026 article covers the Brazilian state of Amazonas in 2023 and 2024, a setting of high violence, organized crime, and hard geography. The study is qualitative, built from published research and official documents on police culture, graded force, and human rights.

The authors describe a lasting tension between respecting rights and getting results on the street. Yet official figures for 2024 show falls in both intentional violent deaths and deaths caused by police action, with drops larger than the national average. They conclude that updated doctrine, steady training centered on human rights, and stronger internal oversight are what align police work with democratic law.
openalex-w7207773232:
Guilherme Milagres Viana, Daniel Rodrigues de Lima, and Karen Cecilia Dias Amorim study the film Oppenheimer as a teaching resource for science classes. Christopher Nolan's film tells the story of the Manhattan Project and the making of the atomic bomb. The authors watched the full film, logged its key episodes, and read them through the lens of science-technology-society studies and socioscientific questions, alongside historical documents and scholarship on nuclear science.

A film like this, they argue, lets students see science as a human practice shaped by politics, war, and moral choice, not a set of neutral facts. It opens discussion of ties between science, technology, state power, and a scientist's responsibility for consequences. Their condition is clear: the film works only with teacher guidance and historical context, never as a replacement for scientific and historical sources.

Michel Haddad and Dener Martins dos Santos test if rubble can help build roads. Waste from builds and tear-downs is one of the bulkiest parts of town trash. To dump it costs the wild world dear. The pair took lots of this waste in Brazil and ground it to fine grit. They ran the trade's set tests on it: pack, strength to bear loads, and swell. The aim was to judge it as a base stuff for bendy roads.

The ground waste met the base marks the rule sets for some road coats. Its damp and swell scores also sat in ranges fit for road mixes. Reuse, the pair close, can cut both dump harm and the cost of fresh stuff. It can aid works for the poor as a side gain. The study gives road men test scores in place of good hopes.
openalex-w7212133632:
Aryane Alves Parriao Ribeiro leads a team on obstetric violence, the harm women can face in care around birth. The harm shows in cold or rough care, in steps taken with no need, and in scorn for a woman's own choices. The team ran a full search of health databases in March 2025. A large first pool shrank to a small core of five studies that fit the bar.

Nurses, the review finds, stand in a hard spot in this fight. They lack room to act on their own call. Their sites resist change, their loads are heavy, and their training has gaps. Yet nurses also hold a key role in stopping the harm. The authors call for steady training on the job. They also call for stronger public rules and a real voice for nurses in the birth room.
openalex-w7212225632:
Manoel Henrique Alves and Fabiano Perin Gasparin study the fine print that runs Brazil's public solar plants. A solar park is easy to praise at its launch. Its long life rests on the less seen work of care and repair. The pair read bids, deals, and terms from the state bid portal. They asked who must do what, how work is tracked, and how risk and wear are planned for.

The deals, they find, vary a great deal from place to place. Most lean on lists of tasks, with care split in bits and few hard marks of good work. The best deals join watch by screen, set checks, and spare parts in one plan. Sound rule, they argue, needs clear posts, a clear trail of facts, and proof that work hit its mark. That is what keeps a plant sound for its full life.

Vaneide Pereira de Oliveira and Mariana Fernandes Ramos dos Santos review the load borne by mothers of children with atypical growth. Such mothers face care that does not end, a stream of expert visits, and a home life reshaped round the child. The strain can run deep. The pair read past work through one lens: a talk-based care that sorts how thoughts, moods, and acts link up.

These mothers, the work shows, can feel stress, guilt, and deep tiredness. Their web of help can wear thin at the same time. A held space to talk can aid them, the authors hold. It gives room to name pain and to see one's own thoughts with more calm. But they are firm on the limit: talk alone has not been shown to lift the load. It is a prop, not a cure.
openalex-w7213276332:
Maryane Francisca Araujo de Freitas Cavalcante leads a team on cancer care for autistic grown-ups in Brazil's state health net. Some work can seed cancer: dust, fumes, and rays on the job. For an autistic adult with such a past, the road to care is rough. The team read health rules for work and for the disabled, and past work on fair earth and the social roots of health.

Three veils, they find, hide these adults at once. The wards clang and glare, which grates on their senses. Talk in forms they cannot parse blocks their voice. And no log of job harms means the link to work is lost, so rights lapse too. Care paths break, and help comes late. Their call: write the mind's range into work-health rules, use plain paths of care, and log each job's harms from the start.
openalex-w7213973132:
Márcia Henrique Pachêco examines the family-school relationship in Brazil. Her single-author 2026 article rests on library research into scientific and academic production. Family and school form students in distinct yet complementary ways, across intellectual, social, cultural, and emotional growth.

Steady interaction between families and schooling professionals helps track the school path, she finds. It also surfaces educational needs early and builds firmer relationships among all involved. Weak communication, and poorly drawn boundaries between each party's duties, can break that joint work. Bringing family and school closer is thus a condition for better practice. Formation becomes more democratic, participative, and alert to diverse pupil needs.
openalex-w7214596932:
José Roberto Coelho, Niceas Arcoverde Gusmão Neto, and Ana Célia Querino wrote a 2026 article that treats recycling as a question of human dignity, not only of waste. Their bibliographic and documentary study focuses on Brazil's waste pickers, the workers who collect, sort, and recover recyclable materials. These workers keep large amounts of material out of dumps and feed the circular economy.

Despite that role, pickers still face informal work, unsafe conditions, unstable income, and little social recognition. Open dumps and poor waste disposal deepen social and regional inequality. The authors argue for stronger picker cooperatives, environmental education, public participation, and technology adopted in ways that include workers rather than replacing them. Valuing recycling, they conclude, means recognizing pickers as rights holders and essential agents of a fairer, cleaner waste system.
openalex-w7214673932:
Letícia Costa Leopoldino led a 2026 epidemiological study of self-harm among Brazilian adolescents before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic. The team analyzed more than seventy-eight thousand official self-harm notifications from seven Brazilian states between 2018 and 2022, testing which demographic, contextual, and violence-related factors predicted repetition and which methods were used.

Cases mainly involved girls, white adolescents, city residents, and young people exposed to domestic violence. Poisoning and sharp objects were the most frequent methods, and nearly half of cases were repeated acts. During the pandemic, total notifications fell but more lethal methods rose, especially hanging. Repetition was more common among boys, adolescents with disabilities or mental disorders, and those exposed to several forms of violence. The models tied exposure to interpersonal violence strongly to the methods chosen.
openalex-w7214789632:
Geisy Natiele Borges Ribeiro led an eleven-author 2026 integrative review on testing eyesight in primary care and the need for glasses or other optical correction in adults. Searching four databases in three languages for studies from 2021 to 2026, the team kept thirteen. Uncorrected refractive error, they note, remains the main cause of distance vision impairment worldwide.

Uncorrected presbyopia, the age-related loss of near focus, accounts for most near vision impairment. Measuring visual sharpness is cheap and feasible in primary care, though less accurate than a full eye examination, and direct evidence that screening symptom-free adults helps is still insufficient. The authors conclude that eyesight testing should be guided by complaints and risk, linked to services that actually deliver correction, rather than used alone as universal screening.
openalex-w7220899332:
Vanessa da Silva Azevedo led a nine-author 2026 time series study of childhood vaccination coverage in Amazonas, Brazil, between 2013 and 2022, read against the bioethical principle of beneficence, doing good. Using national health data for four vaccines, the pentavalent, polio, pneumococcal, and measles-mumps-rubella first dose, the team made forty coverage observations across ten years and checked them against the ninety-five percent target.

Only seven of the forty observations reached or passed the target, while the rest stayed below. The best year was 2015, near full coverage on average, and the worst 2021, far lower, with partial recovery in 2022. From 2017 onward, none of the four vaccines reached the target in any year. Childhood coverage performed insufficiently across the decade, the authors conclude. So strategies must widen immunization's individual and collective benefits if the principle of beneficence is to be more than an aspiration in Amazonas.
openalex-w7221113332:
Ana Rita Gonçalves Santos de Oliveira led an eight-author scoping review, published in 2026, on parents who care for neurodivergent preschool children — and on how those parents care for themselves. Daily care can reorganize a family's routine and press on caregivers physically, emotionally, and socially.

Eleven studies from 2013 to 2025 were sorted into three themes: family life and the child's care, therapeutic interventions and development, and autonomy, independence, and support networks. Caregivers reported strong needs for information and backing. The authors conclude that promoting the child's health must include the adults who carry the daily work. Parental self-care, on their account, is part of family-centered care, not a luxury beside it.
opera-nvova-molto-utile-e-piaceuole-oue-: Opera nuova, printed in 1532, is an Italian book of four dialogues. Angelo de Forte wrote it. His title page calls him a most excellent doctor of arts and gilded physician. The hosted sample shows only the copy's opening leaves, though. Repeated copyright pages from the Early European Books collection come first. A garbled dedication starts after them. No dialogue text appears in the sample. This note rests on the title page alone. It claims nothing about the dialogues' subjects.
phrenology-or-the-doctrine-of-the-mental: The sample provided here shows only a Yale library bequest page and the title page of Spurzheim's Phrenology, or The Doctrine of the Mental Phenomena, with no text pages visible. The title page names G. Spurzheim and plans the work in two volumes, the first being the physiological part, with plates. It calls itself the first American edition, greatly improved by the author from the third London edition, published at Boston by Marsh, Capen and Lyon in 1832.
plos-pbio-0020132:
Philipp Khaitovich, Gunter Weiss, Michael Lachmann, and their group proposed a neutral model of transcriptome change in PLOS Biology in 2004. The transcriptome is the full set of gene messages a tissue makes. The authors ask how much of its change over evolution is driven by selection, and how much is mere drift.

A neutral model gives the null case: change with no selection at all. Only data that beat that baseline need a stronger story. The team found much of the pattern fits drift well. That does not make selection rare, but it sets the bar for claiming it. The paper is a useful guard against over-reading gene data from any two species.
plos-pbio-0020332:
Shelly Beer, Anders Zetterberg, Rebecca A. Ihrie, and their team tested a cancer gene's timing in PLOS Biology in 2004. MYC is a powerful growth gene that can drive tumors when stuck on. The team switched it on in different tissues and at different stages of growth in mice.

The same gene took very different times to cause tumors depending on context. Some settings resisted for long spans, while others fell fast. That gap, called latency, shows cancer is not just about which gene breaks. The state of the cell counts as much. Results like this help explain why one mutation can be deadly in one organ and quiet in another.
plos-pbio-0020432:
Christiane E. Wobus, Stephanie M. Karst, Larissa B. Thackray, and their team grew norovirus in the lab in PLOS Biology in 2004. Noroviruses cause most cases of viral stomach flu, yet they long refused to grow in cell culture, which stalled research. The team's mouse norovirus system broke that barrier.

Grown in culture, the virus favored immune cells: dendritic cells and macrophages. That tropism, its taste for certain cells, shapes how infection starts in the gut. A working culture system lets labs test antivirals and study the virus life cycle at last. The mouse virus now serves as the stand-in for its human kin, which still resist culture.
plos-pone-0000032:
Marina Bacac, Paolo Provero, Nathalie Mayran, and co-authors found a survival signal hiding around tumors in a 2006 study. The stroma is the supporting tissue that surrounds a tumor, and it responds when cancer invades. The team measured that stromal response in mice as tumors spread into it.

A gene pattern in the responding stroma predicted how long prostate and breast cancer patients survived. In other words, tissue that is not itself cancer still carries a forecast of the patient's fate. Doctors usually grade the tumor alone; this work argues the neighborhood matters too. Such signatures could one day help decide which patients need aggressive treatment and which can safely be spared it.
plos-pone-0000132:
Ximena J. Nelson and Robert R. Jackson published this ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It features a predator from East Africa that, as the title says, chooses malaria vectors as its preferred prey. Malaria vectors are the mosquitoes that carry the malaria parasite to people.

A predator that hunts those mosquitoes by choice is a natural ally in malaria control. The authors document this preference and what it means for the food web around it. The work drew attention because most predators eat mosquitoes only by chance; a specialist hunter raises the prospect of biological control of a deadly disease.
plos-pone-0000232:
Nooshin Tabatabaei-Zavareh, Anastasia Vlasova, Chelsea Pamela Greenwood, and colleagues published this stem cell paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Natural killer cells are frontline immune defenders, and making them in the lab from embryonic stem cells could supply therapies. The authors characterize the developmental pathway those cells follow as they grow from stem cells in vitro.

Knowing each step of natural killer cell development lets researchers steer and check the process. The paper maps that path in the dish. It supports efforts to grow immune cells on demand, a goal for cancer therapy where a patient's own cells are in short supply.
plos-pone-0000332:
Erik Cobo, Albert Selva-O'Callagham, Josep-Maria Ribera, and colleagues published this randomized trial in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks whether statistical reviewers improve reporting in biomedical articles. Manuscripts were randomly assigned review with or without a statistician's input, and the quality of reporting was compared.

Poor statistical reporting wastes research and misleads doctors. The trial gives rare experimental evidence on an editorial practice usually adopted on faith. Its result speaks to journal editors deciding whether statistical review is worth its cost and delay. Good reporting is not a small thing: doctors act on what papers say. Weak numbers can mislead care, so proof of what helps is worth having.
plos-pone-0000432:
Jonas Dahlberg and colleagues linked a common gene variant to salt handling in the body, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The gene is NEDD4L, which helps control sodium channels in the kidney. The team tested whether a polymorphism in it goes with increased salt sensitivity. They also checked two hormone-related markers, P-renin and Nt-proANP, which moved in opposite directions.

Salt sensitivity, where blood pressure rises sharply with dietary salt, varies from person to person and runs in families. A gene that explains part of that spread could help identify who most needs to cut salt. The study connects a kidney sodium channel regulator to everyday cardiovascular risk.
plos-pone-0000532:
Andrés Muñoz-Alarcón and colleagues compared fly and human versions of a disease of the cell's scaffolding, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Lamins are proteins that line the nucleus and give it structure. Human mutations in them cause laminopathies. That family of disorders affects muscle, fat, and aging. The team characterized lamin mutation phenotypes in Drosophila and compared them to the human diseases.

A fly that shows the same cellular defects as a human patient becomes a fast, cheap model for testing treatments. Comparing phenotypes across species also shows which parts of lamin function are ancient. The study validates the fly as a stand-in for a group of rare but revealing human disorders.
plos-pone-0000632:
Hassan Khan, Ather M. Taqui, Muhammad Rizwanulhaq Khawaja and colleagues compared two ways of teaching medical students, in PLOS ONE in 2007. One group learned by problem-based learning, working through cases. The other followed a conventional lecture-based curriculum. The subject under test was health research: what students knew about it and how they felt about doing it.

The authors argue that medical curricula in developing countries should stress research training. Students who can judge and do research strengthen a whole health system. By comparing knowledge and attitudes side by side, the study gives curriculum planners direct evidence about which approach builds research-minded doctors.
plos-pone-0000732:
Wei Hou, John Stephen F. Yap, Song Wu and colleagues tackled the fine-mapping of trait genes in breeding experiments, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Mapping quantitative trait loci, or QTL, aims ultimately at cloning the actual genes behind farm and medical traits. Yet only a small portion, at most about one percent of detected QTL, had been characterized at the molecular level.

Their method haplotypes a quantitative trait using a high-density map in experimental crosses. Haplotyping reads the pattern of inherited blocks, not single markers. Denser, smarter mapping could raise that one-percent success rate. Breeders and medical geneticists share the same bottleneck, so a better method serves both fields.
plos-pone-0000832:
Harald Staiger, Fausto Machicao, Norbert Stefan and co-authors tied new diabetes risk genes to how well the pancreas makes insulin. Type 2 diabetes sets in when the body resists insulin and the beta cells that make it wear out. Diet, low activity, and a web of inherited traits all play a part. Genome scans had just found new risk spots, but not what they do.

The team's title states the link: variants in those new risk spots set beta-cell function. In other words, the risk acts through the insulin-making cells themselves, not just through insulin resistance. Knowing where each risk gene does its harm tells drug makers where to aim. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2007.
plos-pone-0000932:
Raquel Ferreira, Claudio Lazzari, Marcelo Lorenzo and colleagues asked how blood sucking bugs find veins under the skin, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Some of these insects slide their mouthparts straight into a vessel and feed from inside it. How they locate the vessel was largely unknown, and less than five percent of skin holds vessels at all.

The team tested whether the bugs read skin surface temperature as a guide. Warm patches could betray the blood flowing below. Knowing how a blood feeder aims matters beyond curiosity. These bugs spread serious diseases, and each step in feeding is a possible place to block them.
plos-pone-0001032:
Jae Hyang Lim, Hirofumi Jono, Tomoaki Koga and colleagues studied a protein that brakes inflammation from a common airway germ, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae causes respiratory infections in adults and children. The inflammation it triggers runs largely through NF-kappaB, a master switch for immune genes.

The tumor suppressor CYLD acts as a negative regulator of that switch. The team examined its role in middle ear and lung inflammation in mice infected with the germ. A natural brake, understood well, suggests how harmful inflammation might be eased without silencing defense. Ear infections in children are a major target.
plos-pone-0001132:
White blood cells must crawl out of the bloodstream and into tissue to fight infection. Jürgen Schymeinsky and co-authors traced one step of that journey in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They focused on Syk, a signaling protein found mainly in blood cells, and on a second protein, PI3K-delta.

The authors show that Syk controls the movement of PI3K-delta to the leading edge of a migrating white blood cell. That placement helps the cell build a lamellipodium, the flat front extension it uses to move. The pathway they map connects the cell's grip on blood vessel walls to its crawling machinery.
plos-pone-0001232:
Glycans, the sugar chains decorating proteins, are built step by step by many enzymes, and finding which gene makes which enzyme is slow work. Harumi Yamamoto and colleagues present a screening method in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They call it CIRES, for correlation index-based responsible-enzyme gene screening, and it uses DNA microarray data.

The logic is that an enzyme gene's activity should track the appearance of the glycan it builds. By correlating expression patterns, the method nominates candidate genes for a given step in glycan biosynthesis. Faster gene hunting matters for understanding diseases of abnormal glycosylation.
plos-pone-0001332:
Common painkillers, the NSAIDs, work mainly by blocking cyclooxygenase enzymes, but they have other targets too. Asher Peretz and colleagues explored one such target in new diphenylamine compounds, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Two NSAIDs, diclofenac and meclofenamate, had recently been shown to also affect potassium channels called M-channels.

The authors describe derivatives in which the function switches: cyclooxygenase inhibition fades and M-channel modulation takes over. M-channels calm neuronal excitability, so such compounds interest researchers in pain and epilepsy. The study is medicinal chemistry: reshaping a known drug scaffold toward a new target.
plos-pone-0001532:
Robyn Kim, Aaron Seitz, and Ladan Shams wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on learning with more than one sense. Most learning studies use sight or sound alone. Yet the senses work as a team in daily life, even at early steps. The team tested whether matched sight and sound cues help visual learning more than mixed ones.

Matched cues did boost how well people learned the visual task. The gain shows the senses aid each other when their signals agree. Training that pairs senses with care could speed skill gains. The result also shapes models of how the brain merges sense data.
plos-pone-0001632:
Martine Muleris, Alexandra Chalastanis, Nicolas Meyer, and their co-authors studied unstable chromosomes in bowel cancer for a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. In many tumors, cells gain or lose whole chromosomes or swap pieces of them, a fault called chromosomal instability. It can arise when normal chromosomes are sorted wrongly at cell division, or when chromosome structure is rearranged.

The team focused on tumors that stay near the normal chromosome number, called near-diploid colorectal cancers. They asked which chromosomes each kind of fault tends to hit. The full text gives the chromosome counts and structural changes they found, and the link they report between number changes and structure changes. Knowing which faults come first may help explain how these cancers grow and change.
plos-pone-0001732:
Thilan Wickramarachchi, Yengkhom S. Devi, Asif Mohmmed, and their co-authors identified a new malaria parasite protein in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Plasmodium falciparum causes the deadliest malaria. Its merozoite stage invades red blood cells, and proteins on the merozoite surface or released from its apical organelles are leading vaccine candidates.

The team characterized a novel merozoite apical protein, PfAARP, rich in the amino acid asparagine, and tied it to red cell binding and invasion. The full text gives the gene, the protein's location, and the binding tests. Each new invasion protein is a possible vaccine piece, since blocking invasion stops the parasite's blood stage, the phase that makes people sick.
plos-pone-0001832:
Elisabeth Fonteneau and Heather K. J. van der Lely measured brain responses in language-impaired children in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Specific language impairment, or SLI, affects over 7 percent of children. It is studied as a window onto the biological foundations of language and its evolutionary origins.

Recording electrical brain responses to language stimuli, the team found grammar-specific deficits in the children with SLI. The full text gives the response patterns for grammar versus other language features. A deficit confined to grammar supports the idea that grammar rests on its own brain machinery. That machinery is separate from general intelligence or vocabulary, which shapes how these children should be taught.
plos-pone-0001932:
Pekka Kaitaniemi wrote a theory study in PLOS ONE in 2008 on a neglected number in a common growth law. Allometric equations link a trait to body size with the form Y equals b times X to the power a. They are used across biology, from trees to animals, to scale one measure against another.

Most work focuses on the power a, while the constant b is treated as a mere scaling fix with no meaning. Kaitaniemi shows how real biological facts can be read out of b itself. If he is right, old data sets hold untapped facts, since b has been reported for decades and largely ignored.
plos-pone-0002032:
Matthias Habjan and co-authors showed how some viruses trim their genomes to hide from immunity, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Fast interferon release is the core of innate defense against viruses. Two sensors, RIG-I and MDA5, detect viral RNA by traits such as triple-phosphate ends or double strands, and set off that alarm.

Negative-strand RNA viruses carry genomes whose ends can bear those alarm traits. As the title states, processing the genome's five-prime ends is a strategy these viruses use to avoid RIG-I and the interferon call. Naming the dodge helps design viruses and vaccines that cannot hide.
plos-pone-0002132:
Roger Bate and co-authors bought malaria drugs from pharmacies across Africa and tested what was in them, for a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The team worked in the major cities of six African countries, in the part of the world where malaria hits hardest. They collected a range of antimalarial drugs from private drug shops in city and near-city areas.

Using thin-layer chromatography, a simple lab test that separates the parts of a mixture, they checked drug quality. Fake or weak malaria drugs cost lives, since patients trust pills that may hold too little of the active drug. The study gives hard data on a trade that thrives where checks are rare.
plos-pone-0002232:
Melissa Andrew, Arnold Mitnitski, and Kenneth Rockwood measured how social weakness relates to frailty and death in older people, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Social vulnerability covers things like living alone, low contact with others, and poor support. It is tied to the health of elderly people, but how to measure it, and how it relates to physical frailty, was disputed.

The authors built a social vulnerability index by counting deficits, the same approach used for frailty indexes. They then compared the two measures and their links to mortality. The study gives geriatric care a firmer way to count social risk alongside bodily risk.
plos-pone-0002332:
Selene Báez and Scott Collins tracked what happens when shrubs invade a desert grassland in New Mexico, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Climate change is shifting species ranges worldwide. As invading species enter a community, they alter who interacts with whom, which can reduce the stability that guards biodiversity. Arid lands are seeing this change fast.

In the northern Chihuahuan Desert, the team found shrub invasion decreases plant diversity and alters community stability. Fewer species and a shakier community make the ecosystem less able to absorb drought and other shocks. Their long look at one desert site gives measured weight to a pattern reported across dry regions.
plos-pone-0002432:
Research by Rao and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Srinivas Rao, Wing-Pui Kong, Chih-Jen Wei, and others. Its subject is multivalent HA DNA Vaccination Protects against Highly Pathogenic H5N1 Avian Influenza Infection in Chickens and Mice. Sustained outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 in avian species increase the risk of reassortment and adaptation to humans.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002532:
Hsiao and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Edward C. Hsiao, Yuko Yoshinaga, Trieu D. Nguyen, and others. Its subject is marking Embryonic Stem Cells with a 2A Self-Cleaving Peptide: A NKX2-5 Emerald GFP BAC Reporter. Fluorescent reporters are useful for assaying gene expression in living cells and for identifying and isolating pure cell populations from heterogeneous cultures.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002632:
Work by David Cohen and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was are child and adolescent responses to placebo higher in major depression than in anxiety disorders? a systematic review of Placebo-Controlled trials. The catalog record names David Cohen first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. In a previous report. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002732:
Work by Margarida Cunha-Rodrigues and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was Genistein-Supplemented diet decreases malaria liver infection in mice and constitutes a potential prophylactic strategy. Authorship is credited in the record to Margarida Cunha-Rodrigues and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. In tropical regions millions of people still live at risk of malaria infection. The authors add a further point. Indeed the emergence of resistance to chloroquine and other drugs in use in these areas reinforces the need to implement alternative prophylactic strategies. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. The full text can be read in the library, and this summary adds nothing beyond the record and abstract held for the entry.
plos-pone-0002832:
Work by Elina Mäntylä and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was from plants to birds: higher avian predation rates in trees responding to insect herbivory. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Elina Mäntylä, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. An understanding of the evolution of potential signals from plants to the predators of their herbivores may provide exciting examples of co-evolution among multiple. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002932:
Matt Finer, Clinton Jenkins, Stuart Pimm and co-authors mapped oil and gas threats in the western Amazon in 2008. That region is the richest part of the Amazon basin for wildlife and home to many indigenous groups. Some of the world's last uncontacted peoples live there in voluntary isolation.

Unlike the eastern Brazilian Amazon, the west was still largely intact at the time. The PLOS ONE paper sets out where energy projects press on wilderness, biodiversity, and indigenous peoples. Conservation planners get a region-wide picture of risk at a moment when choices could still protect large areas.
plos-pone-0003032:
Lorenzo Moroni, Doreen Hamann, Luca Paoluzzi and co-authors built scaffolds for joint tissue repair in 2008. Scaffolds for osteochondral engineering, covering bone plus cartilage, must be mechanically stable. They must also signal cells to regrow both tissues and offer a fully connected pore network for cell movement and growth.

Their approach converges technologies, combining polymer and ceramic composites toward that end, as the title phrases it. Published in PLOS ONE, regenerating articular tissue matters for joint injury and arthritis, where cartilage heals poorly on its own. Scaffold design is a main bottleneck. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003132:
Antonio G. Pacheco, Betina Durovni, Solange C. Cavalcante and colleagues study AIDS and tuberculosis together in Rio de Janeiro in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Brazil has offered free combined antiretroviral therapy to all since 1997, which sets the scene for the study. The team used past surveillance records at the population level.

They tracked how often tuberculosis, AIDS, AIDS deaths and combined AIDS-TB infection occurred in the city. Readers get a population view of two linked epidemics under free HIV treatment. The work helps judge where TB control in people with HIV still falls short.
plos-pone-0003232:
Yuki Sugiura, Shuichi Shimma, Yoshiyuki Konishi and colleagues apply imaging mass spectrometry to brain fats in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Gangliosides are particularly abundant in the central nervous system and are thought to play important roles in memory formation, nerve growth, synaptic transmission and other neural functions. Although several molecular species of gangliosides had been characterized, their exact distribution was less clear.

The authors visualize age-dependent accumulation of C20-ganglioside species in the mouse hippocampus, a memory region. Readers see chemistry mapped in place and across age. Spatial maps like this can link specific molecules to the brain regions they may affect.
plos-pone-0003332:
Carolina Rezával, Jimena Berni, Ezequiel Axel Gorostiza and colleagues screen for degeneration genes in flies in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Drosophila is a proven model to study the molecular basis of neurodegenerative diseases. The team carried out a misexpression screen to find genes involved in neurodegeneration. They examined locomotor behaviour in young and aged flies. They thought a progressive loss of function would appear with age.

Their screen uncovers a role for the gene Enabled in progressive neurodegeneration. Readers get a gene lead found by behaviour first, then biology. Fly screens remain a fast way to name genes for study in human brain disease.
plos-pone-0003432:
Mathieu Tilquin and co-authors followed a mosquito control microbe in nature in this 2008 study. Chemical sprays harm the environment and human health, so growers seek safer options. One option is Bti, a bacterium whose spores kill mosquito larvae. The team checked how long Bti lasts in real mosquito habitats.

Bti stayed present in those habitats for a long time after spraying. Long persistence can be good, since it keeps killing larvae. It also raises questions about effects on other small life. The study gives spray programs real field data on staying power.
plos-pone-0003532:
Christelle Tougard and co-authors traced how common voles spread across Europe in this 2008 paper. Ice age climate cycles repeatedly reshaped where species could live. Temperate animals survived in refuges, then spread out again. Europe's colonization stories had been sketched in general terms.

The team combined molecular evidence with the fossil record. Together they gave a finer picture of vole colonization routes. Genetic lines and dated bones checked each other's stories. The result shows how climate swings redrew the map of biodiversity. Voles breed fast and range widely, which makes them good trackers of past change.
plos-pone-0003632:
Marcos Seoane, Pablo Iglesias, Teresa Gonzalez, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It examines what happens when cells lose the retinoblastoma protein, a key brake on growth. The team focused on how that loss changes the cell's response to DNA damage.

Healthy cells often answer damage by entering senescence, a halted state that blocks tumors. With retinoblastoma lost, that damage response shifts in ways that favor tumor growth instead. The study shows how one lost safeguard can weaken the whole defense that keeps early lesions from becoming cancer.
plos-pone-0003732:
Christine L. Huffard, Roy L. Caldwell, Ned DeLoach, and colleagues published this marine study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Tracking wild animals over time often requires marking them, which can harm rare species. For the octopus Wunderpus photogenicus, the authors tested a gentler idea based on looks.

They found each octopus wears a body color pattern that is individually unique. Photographs alone can therefore tell one animal from another. This photo identification opens long-term studies of lifespan and movement in a shy species prized by divers and hard to follow.
plos-pone-0003832:
