Valeria I. Petkova and H. Henrik Ehrsson published this psychology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Writers and artists have long imagined swapping bodies with another person. Science had not investigated the experience. It touches a basic question: why do we feel ownership of the body we inhabit?

The authors created a perceptual illusion of body swapping in volunteers. Participants felt they inhabited another person's body rather than their own. The experiment probes how the brain decides which body is mine, a process at the root of the sense of self.
plos-pone-0003932:
Benjamin L. Kidder, Jim Yang, and Stephen Palmer mapped where two gene switches bind in stem cells in 2008. Embryonic stem cells keep their flexible state through networks of such switches. Stat3 and c-Myc are both needed for mouse stem cells to self-renew. C-Myc also belongs to the set that can reprogram adult cells.

Their PLOS ONE article charts promoter sites that Stat3 and c-Myc occupy genome-wide. Promoters are the DNA stretches that start gene activity. Knowing shared targets shows how the two switches hold cells in the stem state. The map aids work on growing stem cells for research and therapy.
plos-pone-0004032:
Nitish Agrawal and Ruma Banerjee studied an enzyme linked to high homocysteine in 2008. Cystathionine beta-synthase, or CBS, starts the path that clears homocysteine. Mutations in CBS cause the most common severe inherited high homocysteine. The team used a yeast screen to find CBS partners.

Their PLOS ONE article identifies human Polycomb 2 protein as a SUMO ligase for CBS. Adding SUMO tags changes how other proteins behave. Substrate build-up had been shown to inhibit that tagging. Their finding ties protein tagging to sulfur amino acid handling. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004132:
Tomáš Kučera and colleagues published this study of blood vessel origins in PLOS ONE in 2009. Animals with two-sided bodies share a common ancestor that already had a blood system. Yet invertebrates have no endothelial cells, the lining cells that form vertebrate vessels, so early tubes must have formed without them.

The paper asks how those first vessel tubes opened a hollow space, called a lumen, inside. The authors argue that the hollow formed at the basal surfaces of cells, the sides facing away from the tube's centre. Their account offers a possible route by which the earliest blood vessels in animal history took shape.
plos-pone-0004232:
Melha Mellata, Jeffrey Touchman, and Roy Curtiss published this plasmid study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Avian pathogenic E. coli causes a complex of diseases in birds, and its close relatives sicken people. Large plasmids, rings of extra DNA, are often tied to the virulence of these bacteria, yet they remain poorly characterised.

The team present the full sequence of plasmid pAPEC-1 from strain chi7122, a reference avian pathogen. They compare it with related plasmids to see which genes it carries. The sequence gives researchers a parts list for the tools this bacterium uses to cause disease.
plos-pone-0004332:
Alison Morse and colleagues published this pine genome study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gymnosperms, the seed plant lineage that includes pines, carry some of the largest and most complex genomes known, yet the elements involved are poorly understood. Gymny is a previously undescribed family of retrotransposons, jumping genes, in Pinus that is related to Athila elements of flowering plants.

The team used Gymny and other repeats to trace the evolution of genome size and complexity in pines. Genomes grow, in large part, by the copying of such elements. Pines show that process written very large.
plos-pone-0004432:
Hydrogen made by bacteria is a possible clean fuel, and Zhanmin Fan, Ling Yuan, and Ranjini Chatterjee worked to boost output from the gut bacterium E. coli in PLOS ONE in 2009. Left to itself, E. coli makes some hydrogen when it grows without oxygen. It does so by breaking down a compound called formate, using an enzyme system built for that task.

The team reworked the bacterium's gene controls to push more of its sugar feed toward hydrogen. They changed the regulators that govern the relevant genes. The result, as the title states, was increased hydrogen production from glucose. Work like this matters because it tests whether cheap, farmed microbes can make fuel gas at a useful scale.
plos-pone-0004532:
Laser scans and three-dimensional models give better estimates of how much dinosaurs weighed, show Karl Bates, Phillip Manning, David Hodgetts, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Estimates of body mass are most reliable when a skeleton is complete enough to rebuild the body around it. Digital models are cheaper and faster than physical ones, and can be changed endlessly.

The team used laser imaging to capture skeletons, then built 3D computer models to estimate mass properties, including total mass and balance. How heavy a dinosaur was shapes everything else we infer: how it moved, how much it ate, how fast it could run. A transparent, adjustable method lets other researchers test the numbers instead of trusting a single artist's reconstruction.
plos-pone-0004632:
Squeezing a tumor slows its growth and can kill its cells, show Gang Cheng, Janet Tse, Rakesh Jain, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Compressive mechanical stress produced during growth in a confining matrix limits the size of tumor spheroids, balls of cancer cells grown in gel. Little was known about the dynamics of stress accumulation, how stress affects cancer cell phenotype, or the molecular pathways involved.

The team embedded single cancer cells in matrices and watched spheroids grow against resistance. Mechanical stress controlled spheroid size and morphology by suppressing proliferation and inducing apoptosis, cell death, as the title reports. Solid tumors are physical objects under pressure, not just genetic ones. This work helps explain growth patterns that pure genetics cannot.
plos-pone-0004732:
Chunjiang He and colleagues took a genome wide view of cancer specific message variants, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genes can be cut and joined in varied ways to make distinct proteins. That process shapes growth and disease, yet its role in human tumor growth was not well known.

The team built a search base and used a subtractive scan across the full set of messages. They sought variants found in tumors but not in normal tissue. A clean list of tumor only variants can yield new markers. It may also reveal weak points that drugs can target in cancer cells.
plos-pone-0004832:
Jon Oyer and colleagues showed that aberrant epigenetic silencing is triggered by transient reduction in gene output, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Aberrant silencing plays a major role in cancer by inactivating tumor suppressor genes. Endpoints are known, namely promoter DNA methylation and altered histone modifications, but triggers of silencing were not known. Leaving a gap in knowledge how stable repression first becomes established in a normal cell.

Brief output dips can lock genes off long term. That step explains how temporary events cause lasting change. Preventing the lock in may be possible. The finding reframes cancer epigenetics.
plos-pone-0004932:
Ewing tumors are cancers of bone and soft tissue. They strike mostly young people. A fused protein called EWS-FLI1 drives them. It forms when two genes wrongly join. Noëlle Guillon and colleagues reported a genome-wide search in PLOS ONE in 2009. They mapped where this fusion protein binds in living tumor cells.

Earlier hunts looked only near gene promoters. This search found EWS-FLI1 binding long repeats of the letters GGAA. Such stretches can act like switches for nearby genes. Those landing spots may be the levers the fusion protein pulls. Pulling them switches genes on and drives the cancer.
plos-pone-0005032:
Musicians rarely slip, but their brains still watch for errors. When can an error be detected? Clemens Maidhof and colleagues recorded brain waves from performing musicians. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They looked for event-related potentials before errors happened. Earlier studies had focused on signals after wrong responses.

Error-related signals appeared before the wrong note sounded. The brain monitors performance in real time, ahead of the fingers. That fast monitoring may allow last-second corrections. It may also explain the feeling of knowing a mistake is coming. The finding shows our inner critic works quickly. It operates even in experts whose movements are highly trained.
plos-pone-0005132:
Some bacteria swap sulfur for oxygen in their DNA backbone. The trait is called phosphorothioation. It was first noticed over twenty years ago in Streptomyces. Hong-Yu Ou and colleagues built a database for it in PLOS ONE in 2009. The database is called dndDB. The name comes from the dnd gene cluster that governs the trait.

Similar clusters are widespread among bacteria. The database collects the genes and chemistry behind them. It maps a weird DNA modification across species. Researchers chasing sulfur-armored genomes gain a reference. Such modifications can protect DNA or mark it as self. They may also matter for biotechnology. A shared database keeps discoveries organized and comparable.
plos-pone-0005232:
Proteins that hold sister chromosomes together are vital for healthy development. Faults in them cause Cornelia de Lange syndrome, with effects across many body systems. Zhang and colleagues varied the dose of one regulator, PDS5, in PLOS ONE in 2009 to see how development responds.

PDS5 helps control chromosome cohesion and has two forms in vertebrates. Changing its amount disturbed mammalian development in their tests. The results show how sensitive embryos are to the dose of cohesion factors, which informs care and research for the group of disorders called cohesinopathies. For parents of children with this syndrome, work of this kind brings the dose needs of the growing body into clear view at last.
plos-pone-0005332:
Several long-term lung diseases share an overactive immune response, with many inflammatory signals and proteases in the lung. Zhang and colleagues proposed a modeling-derived hypothesis for that chronicity in PLOS ONE in 2009, covering diseases such as cystic fibrosis and chronic bronchitis.

In their model, hyperactive IRAK and TRAF6 signaling desensitizes pathogen recognition. A dulled alarm would let germs persist while inflammation keeps raging, a seeming paradox the model resolves. A clear, testable hypothesis like this gives lung researchers a new target list. Lung diseases that drag on for years cost health and wealth, so a model that can be put to the test in mice. In cells is the right next step for this bold claim.
plos-pone-0005432:
Mihaela Balasu and colleagues mapped a meeting point between two proteins in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. One protein, ERK2, carries growth signals inside cells and is kept under tight control by partner proteins. No one had yet captured a clear picture of ERK2 joined with those partners.

The authors studied how ERK2 joins with PTP-SL, a major partner that holds its activity in check. They mapped the surface where the two proteins touch and how that contact works. Knowing that shared surface helps explain how growth signals are switched off and could guide new drug design.
plos-pone-0005532:
Masami Tanaka and co-authors reported a blood marker for acute leukaemia in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. MicroRNAs are short RNA strands that tune how genes are used. Their levels go wrong in many cancers, and some act like cancer drivers while others act as brakes.

The team found that one microRNA, miR-92, drops in the blood plasma of patients with acute leukaemia. A blood test for it could help doctors spot the disease and follow its course. Blood-based markers spare patients some painful bone marrow tests. A marker that falls and rises with the disease could also show early whether treatment is working.
plos-pone-0005632:
Amy Hurford warned about GPS errors in animal tracking data in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Collars and tags that record position by satellite are now standard tools for studying animal movement. Each recorded position carries some error, though.

Hurford showed that the error alone can create fake sharp turns in the path and strong false biases in direction. Models that ignore the error will describe the noise, not the animal. Her warning pushes ecologists to clean movement data before drawing conclusions about behaviour. The warning applies to birds, fish, and mammals alike, since all tracking studies share the same error source.
plos-pone-0005732:
Sunghee Choi and co-authors found in 2009 that common stomach-acid drugs also calm allergic responses. These drugs, proton pump inhibitors, block acid pumps in the stomach. A protein called TCTP, released by immune cells, helps drive allergy symptoms.

The team showed the acid drugs cut the release of TCTP from cells. Less TCTP outside cells means a weaker allergic signal. A drug already taken by millions might thus have a second use against allergy. The finding also hints that cell acid control and immune signaling are linked in ways worth mapping further.
plos-pone-0005832:
Stefania Trazzi and co-authors dissected in 2009 the tail end of a protein that helps build the centromere, the hub that pulls chromosomes apart. CENP-C is a core part of working centromeres in mammals. It carries distinct regions that bind DNA and partner proteins.

The team focused on its C-terminal domain and found it carries several critical jobs. Without them, centromeres fail to form properly and cell division goes wrong. Division errors are a root of miscarriage and cancer alike. Pinning jobs to one domain helps the field assemble the centromere's parts list in working order.
plos-pone-0005932:
Some plant genes must stay silent, or their stray messages can harm the cell. Todd Blevins, Olga Pontes, Craig Pikaard and colleagues studied one such case in the plant Arabidopsis in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper looks at odd transcripts from 5S ribosomal DNA, a set of repeated genes held in dark, packed chromatin.

Two separate guards keep those stray messages down: small RNAs from the repeats, and DDM1, a factor that keeps the DNA packing in place. Each works on its own, the team reports. The study shows how plants layer their defenses to keep a restless gene family quiet, a task every complex genome must solve.
plos-pone-0006032:
Flu shots must be rebuilt each year as the virus drifts, and older adults gain the least from them. Ted Ross, Kutub Mahmood, Corey Crevar and colleagues tested a different build in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper describes a trivalent vaccine made of virus-like particles, empty shells that look like flu but carry no genes, aimed at three seasonal strains.

Mice and ferrets given the shells raised protective immune responses, the title reports. Particles that teach without infecting could be made faster and more safely than grown virus. The platform is also flexible, so it could be tuned as strains change. The work backs a promising route toward stronger flu cover for those at greatest risk.
plos-pone-0006132:
A rare fish's genes can be spread by lending them to a common fish's body. Sullip Majhi, Ricardo Hattori, Masashi Yokota and colleagues advanced that surrogacy in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper transplants germ cells into the gonads of sexually competent adult fish, an approach for rapid propagation of endangered and valuable germlines.

Germ cell transplantation also serves basic study of how germ cells grow and mature. Using adults that can breed at once, rather than waiting for young recipients to mature, speeds every use. For species near extinction, speed is the point: a germline banked in a living surrogate can rebuild a population while habitat work proceeds.
plos-pone-0006232:
Breaking genes at random is a classic way to learn what each gene does. Jorge Vidal and colleagues built a better random mutagenesis tool for Clostridium perfringens in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The toxin-making bacterium causes food poisoning and gas gangrene, but older mutagenesis systems worked poorly in it.

Their EZ-Tn5 based system jumped a marker into random spots of the genome. With it they found a previously unknown locus that controls toxin production. A new control point offers fresh angles on how the bacterium causes disease. The tool itself will serve other studies of this stubborn pathogen.
plos-pone-0006332:
Strep throat bacteria leave immune fingerprints that may misfire in some children with tics. Mauro Bombaci and colleagues screened blood sera from tic patients against a protein array of Group A Streptococcus antigens in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The bacterium also causes severe invasive disease and complications where host antibodies attack the body.

Patients showed a broad and enhanced immune response against the strep antigens. That pattern supports a role for post-strep immunity in tic disorders. Protein arrays let many antigens be tested from tiny blood samples. The study sharpens the hunt for the specific targets involved.
plos-pone-0006432:
Marie Billaud and colleagues examined how blood vessel walls talk to each other in PLOS ONE in 2009. The inner lining of a vessel, the endothelium, helps control how the smooth muscle around it tightens or relaxes. That control shapes blood flow in health and disease. Yet the two-way talk between lining cells and muscle cells was far from fully mapped.

The authors show that muscle cells also shape the lining's control of vessel response. Signals pass through tiny links between the two cell types. Reactive oxygen species, active oxygen-based molecules, carry part of the message. The result gives a fuller picture of how vessels tune themselves.
plos-pone-0006532:
Raymond Schuch and Vincent Fischetti explored the hidden life of the anthrax bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ecological and genetic factors governing anthrax reservoirs in the environment are obscure. A central tenet about the bacterium's life outside hosts rested on limited and often contradictory data. The authors reconsider how Bacillus anthracis persists in soil between outbreaks.

They highlight bacteriophage-mediated ecological adaptations: viruses of bacteria shaping the anthrax agent's survival. Phages can change what a bacterium does without changing its own genes permanently. This view may explain how anthrax lingers for decades in some places. It opens new questions for biodefense and ecology alike.
plos-pone-0006632:
Ahmed Hajri and co-authors put forward a fresh idea about how bacteria pick their hosts in PLOS ONE in 2009. Why a germ infects one host and not another is still poorly known for plant and animal pathogens. In plant germs, host range is often quite narrow. The team advance what they call a repertoire-for-repertoire idea. Type three effectors are proteins that bacteria inject into host cells to bend them.

They propose that the full sets of these effectors on each side are prime candidates for what sets host range. If the sets must match, that match could decide who gets infected. A clear, testable idea like this helps plan the next round of plant disease work.
plos-pone-0006732:
Mahamadou S. Sissoko and colleagues tested a malaria drug combination against a parasitic worm disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. The disease is schistosomiasis caused by Schistosoma haematobium. It infects the urinary tract of many children in Africa. The standard treatment is praziquantel. The test drug paired artesunate with sulfamethoxypyrazine and pyrimethamine, at malaria doses.

School-aged children with the infection received one treatment or the other. The team then compared how well each cleared the parasite. A malaria drug that also cures schistosomiasis would be valuable where both diseases overlap. Mass treatment campaigns could then tackle two diseases together. The trial gives direct evidence on whether that shortcut works.
plos-pone-0006832:
Hossein Khiabanian and his team set the ages of flu cases side by side for two flu types in PLOS ONE in 2009. Two types of influenza A have gone round each year since 1977. They are called H3N2 and H1N1. Each year, both make part of the land sick. The team asked if the two types hit the same age groups.

They did not. The age spread of cases set the two types apart. Gaps like that can mirror who met the germs in past years. They can also guide who gets flu shots first. Side-by-side age data turn plain case counts into clues.
plos-pone-0006932:
Yi-Chieh Nancy Du, David Klimstra, and Harold Varmus used engineered mice to study pancreatic cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. A basic question was unsettled at the time. Do different pancreatic tumors start from different target cells, or from shared precursors? The team switched on an oncogene called PyMT in chosen cell types.

In insulin-producing beta cells, PyMT caused irreversible overgrowth called hyperplasia. In pancreatic progenitor cells, it produced acinar cell carcinomas that depended on the oncogene. The contrast shows that the starting cell shapes the tumor that follows. That insight guides how researchers model and classify pancreatic cancers.
plos-pone-0007032:
Jonathan Bohbot and Joseph Dickens characterized a mosquito smell receptor in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some odor molecules come in mirror-image forms called enantiomers. The forms share the same chemistry but opposite handedness. In insect communication, one form can be active while its mirror is not.

Working with the yellow fever mosquito Aedes aegypti, the pair studied one receptor closely. That receptor could tell mirror-image odors apart. Such selective receptors help mosquitoes find humans and mates by smell. Knowing them may aid new repellents or traps for a major disease carrier.
plos-pone-0007132:
Il-Man Kim and Matthew Wolf built a switchable heart disease model in flies in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dilated cardiomyopathy enlarges the heart chamber and weakens its squeeze. Fruit flies can model the condition, as earlier gene studies showed. The team went further, making the disease inducible and reversible in individual adult flies.

They examined the same fly's heart repeatedly as disease turned on and off. Watching one heart through the whole cycle removes guesswork between animals. A reversible model lets researchers test when damage can still be undone. That timing question is central to heart failure care.
plos-pone-0007232:
Janine Scholefield, L. Jacquie Greenberg, Marc S. Weinberg, and colleagues designed a gene-silencing treatment for a brain disorder in 2009. Spinocerebellar ataxia type 7 is caused by an expanded repeat in DNA. The repeated section makes a faulty protein that drives progressive neurodegeneration, and no treatment existed.

The authors design RNA interference hairpins that silence only the mutant form of ataxin-7. Sparing the normal copy is essential for safety. They report correction of a disease phenotype in their model. Their work tests a precise strategy for other repeat-expansion disorders as well.
plos-pone-0007332:
Bart van de Sluis, Arjan J. Groot, Jeroen Vermeulen, and colleagues studied a regulator of the low-oxygen response in 2009. The protein COMMD1 is linked to copper balance, immune signaling, and sodium transport. The authors had identified COMMD1 as a new player in signaling by HIF-1, the master low-oxygen transcription factor.

Mouse embryos lacking Commd1 showed increased HIF activity. The authors report COMMD1 promotes breakdown of HIF-1 alpha without needing the usual oxygen-dependent pathway. The breakdown involves heat shock proteins HSP90 and HSP70. Their work adds a backup route for controlling oxygen responses in cells.
plos-pone-0007432:
Ilmari Kurki, Tarja Peromaa, and Aapo Hyvärinen published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on why we judge brightness the way we do. Two patches can give the same reading on a light meter yet look clearly different. Perceived brightness depends on the spatial pattern of an image, not only on light levels. The usual assumption blamed the borders between light and dark areas.

The team used a method called classification images to reveal which features drive brightness judgments. Volunteers judged many noisy images, and the patterns behind their answers were extracted statistically. The results show that brightness perception rests on more than border analysis alone. Richer image structure shapes what people see. The findings refine how vision scientists model one of the most basic acts of seeing.
plos-pone-0007532:
Terry Smith and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the parasite that causes African sleeping sickness. Trypanosoma brucei coats itself in a dense layer of variant surface glycoprotein. That coat shields it from destruction by the host's complement system. The team blocked production of the coat using RNA interference. They then watched what happened inside the parasite.

Blocking coat synthesis triggered a general arrest in translation initiation. The parasite stopped starting new proteins across the board. The coat is so essential that the cell will not build without it. That coupling is a striking piece of quality control. It also suggests a vulnerability: attack the coat supply and the whole factory halts. The study reframes the parasite's famous disguise as a load-bearing wall.
plos-pone-0007632:
Jean-Fred Fontaine and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on improving gene-based diagnosis of thyroid lesions. Microarray tests measure the activity of many genes at once. Markers found this way for thyroid cancers had offered limited accuracy. The authors blamed the coarse categories usually used: too few classes of lesions were analyzed at once. They re-ran the analysis with more lesion classes included simultaneously.

With finer classes, the diagnostic markers became more relevant. Separating look-alike lesions lets each one's true signature emerge. A sharper test can spare patients needless surgery for benign growths. It can also catch cancers that coarse tests blur. The lesson reaches beyond the thyroid: category design shapes what gene tests can see. Sometimes the fix for a weak marker is a better question.
plos-pone-0007732:
Mourad Ferhat and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns Legionella pneumophila, the bacterium behind Legionnaires' disease. People catch it by breathing in contaminated mist. In nature, the bacterium lives inside free-living amoebas.

The authors studied a protein called TolC in the bacterium's outer membrane. TolC plays a major role in resistance to many drugs. It also matters in the early steps of invading a host. A single pump-like protein thus helps the germ both survive treatment and start infection. Blocking it could weaken the pathogen on two fronts.
plos-pone-0007832:
Erik van Lunteren and Michelle Moyer published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It profiles gene activity in the breathing muscle of diabetic rats. Diabetes weakens the diaphragm, the main muscle of breathing. Known causes include changed sugar and fat use, oxidative stress and altered membrane behavior.

The authors asked how much of that damage involves changed gene expression. They measured which genes turn up or down in the type 1 diabetes rat diaphragm. The profile shows the muscle's decline written in its genes. It may reveal new points where treatment could protect breathing in diabetes.
plos-pone-0007932:
Sandro Santagata and colleagues tested a marker for rare eye and brain tumors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The marker is CRX, a protein that helps keep retina and pineal cells true to their type. Tumors from those tissues are hard to sort by looks alone.

Staining tumor samples for CRX showed the protein marks cancers of retinal and pineal origin well. A clear stain can help pathologists name a tumor when other signs are mixed. Naming the tumor right guides care, so a trusty marker has real value for these uncommon cancers.
plos-pone-0008032:
James Jones and Marcel Salathe measured public fear in the first days of a new flu in PLOS ONE in 2009. A swine-origin H1N1 virus had just begun to spread worldwide, and news coverage was intense. Health teams needed to know how scared people were and what they were doing about it.

Surveys taken early caught anxiety levels and the steps people took, from hand washing to shunning crowds. Fear can help or harm in an outbreak: it drives care, but also panic buying and stigma. The early snapshot gives planners a base for wording advice that calms without dulling caution.
plos-pone-0008132:
Paolo Carrega and colleagues tested whether a patient's own killer cells can kill their own melanoma in PLOS ONE in 2009. Natural killer cells are built to destroy tumor cells, but most proof came from cells of strangers. A patient's own cells meeting their own tumor is the test that matters for therapy.

Some patients' killer cells did destroy their melanoma; others barely scratched it. The gap tracked with HLA types, the identity tags on cells, and with a group of killer cells called unlicensed. Knowing who carries able killers could guide cell therapy to those it can help.
plos-pone-0008232:
Dale Hedges and colleagues reported exome sequencing of a human family in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The exome is the small part of the genome that codes for proteins. Reading it requires capturing just those regions from a sample. New capture arrays had recently made that comprehensive capture possible. Efficient use of next-generation sequencing depended on such tools.

The team sequenced a multigenerational pedigree, a family tree spanning several generations. Family data help separate real inherited variants from noise. Their work showed exome sequencing could serve human genetics research in practice. It was an early step toward routine exome studies.
plos-pone-0008332:
Ludmil B. Alexandrov, Stoyana Alexandrova, and Anny Usheva modeled cells in altered gravity in PLOS ONE in 2009. How living systems respond to hostile environments is important but hard to study. Living systems are overwhelmingly complex for standard differential equations. Gravity changes are one such hostile factor for cultured cells. The team chose computer modeling as another way forward.

Their model describes gravity-related adaptation in cell cultures. Simulation can explore conditions that are costly to test in orbit or clinostats. Predictions from the model can then guide real experiments. The work applies computing to a problem in space biology.
plos-pone-0008432:
Warren Pilbrough, Trent Munro, and Peter Gray wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on CHO cells used to make drugs. CHO cells are lab cells from hamsters. Drug firms grow them to make proteins used as medicine. Picking a good cell line takes much time and money. Cells from the same clone can still make very unlike amounts of protein.

The authors study that spread within a clone. They ask why sister cells differ so much in what they make. Their findings bear on how firms screen and pick cell lines. More stable lines would make drug production faster and cheaper.
plos-pone-0008532:
Zhi-Xiang Xu and co-authors test a plant compound on cancer cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Avicin D belongs to the avicins, a family of plant triterpenoids. Avicins potently inhibit tumor cell growth. They also show antioxidant, anti-mutagenic, and anti-inflammatory actions. Prior work used Jurkat cells, a leukemia cell line. The team ask how Avicin D triggers apoptosis, the programmed death of cells.

They find Avicin D recruits Fas, a death receptor, into lipid rafts. Lipid rafts are ordered patches in the cell membrane. Downstream signaling molecules gather there too, starting the death cascade. That recruitment explains how a plant compound can kill tumor cells.
plos-pone-0008632:
Fengxia Liu and co-authors compare rice gene expression under stress in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Rice feeds more than half the world's population. Two major Asian subspecies are japonica and indica. They show significant phenotypic variation in stress responses. The molecular mechanisms behind that variation were unclear. The team profile gene expression in Nipponbare, a japonica variety, and 93-11, an indica variety, during oxidative stress.

Their profiles decipher which genes drive the differing responses. Some genes switch on in one subspecies but not the other. Those differences may explain why varieties tolerate stress unequally. Breeders can use the candidates to improve stress tolerance in rice.
plos-pone-0008732:
David Vandorpe, Chang Xu, Boris Shmukler, and colleagues studied why sickle red cells dry out. Their work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Red cells carrying sickle hemoglobin deform when oxygen runs low. Low oxygen opens an unknown leak that lets calcium flood in. Calcium then triggers potassium loss, and water follows. Dried cells stiffen and block small vessels.

The team characterized the leak in human and mouse sickle cells. Carbon monoxide and a spider-toxin peptide both dampened the current. Naming what controls the leak gives drug makers a target. Blocking it might keep sickle cells hydrated and flexible.
plos-pone-0008832:
Tomas Drgon, Ping-Wu Zhang, Catherine Johnson, and colleagues double-checked a genome-wide hunt for addiction genes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Addiction risk is largely inherited but spread across many genes. Each gene contributes only a small share. Genome-wide scans without templates offer one way to find them. A second analytic style offered an independent check.

Results that replicated across both approaches carry more trust. The comparison also exposes where methods disagree and why. Addiction genetics needs such cross-checks before claims harden. The work steadies a field prone to false leads.
plos-pone-0008932:
Jacob Nabe-Nielsen and co-authors modelled what happens to wild animals when people reshape the land, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Roads, farms, and towns split wild habitat into smaller pieces. Managers need to know whether a population can survive such changes for decades. Real experiments on whole landscapes are almost impossible to run.

The team built computer landscapes and let virtual animals live, breed, and die in them. They then altered the land and watched which populations held on or faded out. Small changes in movement or breeding success could decide survival over the long run. The model gives planners a way to test land changes before making them.
plos-pone-0009032:
Maureen Donlin and co-authors asked whether the hepatitis C virus's own genes shape treatment success, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hepatitis C comes in six major genotypes. Patients with genotype 1 answer interferon therapy worse than others. African American patients respond only about half as often as Caucasian American patients.

The team compared whole viral genomes from patients of both groups. Differences scattered across the virus, not just in known hotspots, mattered. Viral genetics helped explain who cleared the virus on interferon. Reading the virus's genome could one day guide treatment choices for each patient.
plos-pone-0009132:
Orit Uziel and co-authors shortened cancer cells' chromosome caps to make drugs bite harder, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Telomeres cap the ends of chromosomes and shrink as cells divide. Telomerase rebuilds them, and most cancers switch it back on to keep growing. Blocking this enzyme makes tumours shrink and sensitises them to many drugs.

The team asked whether the shortening itself does the sensitising work. Cells with shortened telomeres died more readily under chosen cytotoxic agents. The effect held in lab dishes and in tumours in animals alike. Pairing a telomere attack with standard chemotherapy could strengthen both treatments.
plos-pone-0009232:
Christian Denecke and co-authors published this transplant study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Older patients are a fast-growing group on organ waiting lists. Age changes the immune system, and that changes how a transplant is attacked or tolerated. The team compared T cell behavior in young and old mice.

Using both normal and transgenic mouse transplant models, they tested effector and regulatory T cells. Grafts lasted longer in older recipients. The reason was weaker attack from effector T cells, while regulatory T cells still did their calming job. That imbalance suggests older patients might need gentler anti-rejection treatment than younger ones.
plos-pone-0009332:
Jack Nguyen and co-authors published this flu drug study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The 2009 H1N1 flu spread worldwide and was declared the first pandemic of the century. At the same time, flu strains were growing resistant to single drugs. A resistant virus can render a whole medicine cabinet useless.

The team tested three flu drugs together: amantadine, ribavirin, and oseltamivir. In lab dishes, the triple mix was highly active against drug-resistant strains. The drugs also boosted each other, an effect called synergy. Combining drugs makes resistance harder, because the virus must escape all three at once.
plos-pone-0009432:
Rajesh Singh and co-authors wrote in PLOS ONE in 2010 about a surface protein of the germ that causes pneumonia. The protein is called PspA. Helper T cells, a type of immune cell, must spot parts of it for a vaccine to work well. The team mapped which small parts of PspA these cells can see.

They measured how strongly each part sticks to the immune markers that present it to T cells. Strong sticking matched a stronger T cell response. That link helps vaccine makers pick the parts most likely to train the immune system. It is a step toward a protein based shot against this lung infection.
plos-pone-0009532:
Theodore Sarafian and colleagues studied support cells of the brain in dishes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Astrocytes feed and guard nerve cells. A signal protein called STAT3 helps direct astrocyte behavior. The team blocked STAT3 signaling in astrocytes grown in the lab. They then checked the cells' mitochondria, which supply energy, and their levels of oxidative stress.

With STAT3 disrupted, mitochondria worked less well. Oxidative stress, a form of chemical wear, rose in the cells. So one signal switch helps keep the energy system of support cells sound. When support cells fail, nerve cells suffer too, which makes the link relevant to brain disease.
plos-pone-0009632:
Danika Bannasch and co-authors searched dog DNA for the roots of the flat face in PLOS ONE in 2010. Breeds such as pugs and bulldogs have short, broad skulls, a trait called brachycephaly. Because the trait is fixed within breeds, standard mapping inside one breed cannot find its genes. The team mapped across breeds instead, comparing flat faced and normal faced dogs. Shared stretches of DNA among flat faced breeds point to the cause.

The approach located genomic regions tied to the trait. Dogs' extreme variety makes them a strong model for skull genetics. Findings here may also inform human cranial disorders, since the same genes often shape faces in both species.
plos-pone-0009732:
Bile ducts carry bile from the liver, and their shape depends on how cells divide. Junnian Zhou and colleagues studied a protein that guides that growth in rat liver cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The protein, epimorphin, regulates duct formation through mitosis orientation. Mitosis orientation is the angle at which a cell splits into two. The work used rat liver epithelial stem-like cells, cells that can help rebuild liver tissue. How cells angle their divisions, the study shows, shapes the growing duct. Liver development depends on such fine control.
plos-pone-0009832:
Tumors grow among support cells called fibroblasts, and the two talk to each other. Christina Stuelten and colleagues tested whether even brief contact with fibroblasts changes tumor cells. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Malignancy means how aggressive and invasive a tumor is. The contact was transient, yet it raised the malignancy of breast tumor cells. The effect ran through TGF-beta, a signal molecule tumors often exploit. The model was a xenograft, human-style tumor growth tested in mice. Brief encounters with support cells, it seems, can leave lasting marks on cancer.
plos-pone-0009932:
California's Sierra Nevada stores winter snow that feeds rivers all summer. Sarah Null, Joshua Viers, and Jeffrey Mount modeled how climate warming changes that water supply. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The range is the state's main natural water tower.

Hydrologic response is how streams and runoff react to weather shifts. Watershed sensitivity measures how strongly each river basin feels warming. Warmer air turns snow to rain and melts the pack earlier. The results help water managers plan for a less reliable snowpack. Snowmelt timing decides summer water for farms and cities.
plos-pone-0010032:
The authors were Kaitlin Bratlie, Tram Dang, Stephen Lyle, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study sped up safety checks for medical materials. Many new materials fail because living tissue reacts badly to them. New synthesis methods create candidates faster than old tests can judge them.

The team used glowing imaging in live mice to judge tissue response quickly. Fluorescence let them watch reactions in the body rather than waiting for slow lab tests. A fast screen like that can weed out poor materials early and focus effort on safer ones.
plos-pone-0010132:
The authors were Ken Noguchi, Daniel Riggins, Khalid Eldahan, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study covered E. coli and an enzyme system called hydrogenase-3. Fermenting bacteria like E. coli make hydrogen gas, a possible biofuel source. Making hydrogen uses up protons, so it links closely to how cells handle acid.

The team showed hydrogenase-3 helps E. coli resist acid when no oxygen is present. That role makes sense, since consuming protons should ease acid stress inside the cell. The finding connects clean fuel research with basic bacterial survival biology. The enzyme thus serves the cell in two ways at once.
plos-pone-0010232:
The authors were Gabriele Lohmann, Daniel Margulies, Annette Horstmann, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper gave brain imaging a new analysis tool. Resting state scans record the brain with no task at all. Such data need methods that do not assume a pattern of activation in advance, unlike classic task-based brain scan analysis.

Their method, eigenvector centrality mapping, finds the most connected hubs in brain networks. It needs no prior model and no adjustable settings to run. Hub maps can reveal how brain regions organize at rest, in health and in disease.
plos-pone-0010332:
Robert Brown, David Kaczka and Wayne Mitzner studied dog airways and lung tissue in PLOS ONE in 2010. Airways stay open partly because the soft tissue around them tugs outward. That support is often left out of talks about asthma. Yet drugs that make airway muscle tighten also make the lung tissue stiffer. A stiffer lung might actually help hold airways open.

The team measured how tissue stiffness changed airway size as lungs filled with air. Their question was practical as well as basic. If stiffening defends the airway, then some drug effects may cut both ways. Asthma research often focuses on the airway wall alone. This study argues the surrounding tissue deserves equal attention.
plos-pone-0010432:
Qiang Wang and co-workers studied a protein that helps blue-green bacteria handle low iron in PLOS ONE in 2010. These bacteria harvest sunlight with large antenna complexes. Iron shortage and other stresses reshape that machinery. Under stress, the team spotted two extra-large complexes beyond the normal trimer form. A protein called IsiA appeared in this picture. They tested whether IsiA is needed to build the large complexes.

Without IsiA, the super-sized complexes did not form properly. The protein also helped the cells switch energy flow efficiently between states. Such flexibility keeps photosynthesis working when conditions worsen. These bacteria shape oceans and once gave Earth its oxygen. Understanding their stress tricks matters for ecology and bioenergy alike.
plos-pone-0010532:
Deborah Kelly and colleagues published a study of the Notch receptor's outer structure in PLOS ONE in 2010; the article was later retracted. Notch passes fate decisions between neighboring cells during development. When Notch signaling fails in humans, diseases and birth defects follow. Knowing the receptor's shape should reveal how it works. The team used electron microscopy to picture its outer domain and how two copies pair.

Readers should note the retraction prominently attached to this record. A retracted paper remains in the scholarly record as a caution, not as reliable evidence. Its methods and claims failed later scrutiny. The entry is preserved so the history of the claim, and its withdrawal, stays visible. It should not be cited as sound support for Notch structure.
plos-pone-0010632:
Marjolein Meijerink and colleagues hunted the genes that let a probiotic bacterium steer immune cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lactobacillus plantarum is a friendly gut microbe used in fermented foods. Different strains calm or stir immune cells in very different ways.

The team compared strain genomes and matched the differences to immune responses. Dendritic cells, which teach the immune system what to attack, reacted differently to each strain. Certain gene regions lined up with stronger or weaker reactions. Knowing which genes drive the effect could help makers choose probiotic strains on purpose, not by trial and error.
plos-pone-0010732:
Anna de Breij and colleagues probed why one hospital germ succeeds so well, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Acinetobacter baumannii resists many drugs and has infected wounded soldiers and intensive care patients worldwide. Two candidate edges were biofilm growth, where germs coat surfaces, and direct dealings with human cells.

Clinical and non-clinical strains were compared on both traits. Biofilm strength and cell interaction varied by strain but did not cleanly explain which strains caused outbreaks. The germ's success likely rests on several traits at once, led by drug resistance itself. Infection control, the authors imply, must lean on hygiene and antibiotic care, not one trick.
plos-pone-0010832:
Anne-Sophie de Preux Charles, Valérie Verdier, Jennifer Zenker and co-authors published this diabetes study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Nerve damage is a common and painful effect of type 1 diabetes, yet the gene changes behind its start are poorly known. The team used Akita mice, which develop diabetes from a faulty insulin gene, to watch the earliest stage of nerve injury.

They tracked weight, blood sugar, and nerve signal speed during the first months of life to pin down when damage begins. Then they profiled gene activity in two nerve compartments, the dorsal root ganglia and the inner nerve tissue, before and just after symptoms appeared. Gene programs proved surprisingly steady as disease began. That resistance itself is a clue, suggesting early nerve damage may hinge on a few targeted changes rather than a broad gene shutdown.
plos-pone-0010932:
Jihong Li, Kazuaki Miyamoto, Sameera Sayeed and co-authors published this food poisoning study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The bacterium Clostridium perfringens makes an enterotoxin, CPE, that causes several gut diseases in people and possibly animals. The toxin gene sits in different DNA neighborhoods depending on the strain type, and the arrangement in types C and D was unknown.

Standard tests built for type A strains failed on type C and D isolates, an early sign their gene neighborhoods differ. The team cloned and sequenced the region around the toxin gene in selected isolates, then built a test to survey more. All seven type C isolates surveyed shared one arrangement. Li and colleagues map a toxin gene's address book, useful for tracing outbreak strains and judging which animals and foods carry risk.
plos-pone-0011032:
Anne-Laure Todeschini, Laure Teysset, Valérie Delmarre and co-authors published this fruit fly epigenetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. In flies, a jumping gene inserted near the chromosome ends can silence matching genes elsewhere in the genome, an effect passed through mothers and called trans-silencing. The team dissected which molecular machinery carries that inherited silencing signal.

Mutations in two genes of the piRNA pathway, the small-RNA system that polices jumping genes in the germline, strongly weakened the silencing. Silencing also tracked with accumulation of small RNAs from the target gene, and depended on HP1, a protein of tightly packed chromatin. Todeschini and colleagues connect a classic epigenetic puzzle to the piRNA pathway. Their work shows how mothers can hand offspring a ready-made defense, written in small RNAs rather than DNA.
plos-pone-0011132:
Marji, O'Donoghue, McClintock and colleagues studied a rapid aging illness in PLOS ONE in 2010. Children with this syndrome, called progeria, age far too fast due to a faulty form of a nuclear protein. The team traced how that fault disrupts a growth control signal in cells.

They found the faulty signaling could be reversed by blocking an enzyme that adds a fatty tag to proteins. That reversal points to a drug path already explored for this rare disease. Even a partial fix in cells brings hope for treatment. The work also informs research on normal aging, since the same protein is involved there.
plos-pone-0011232:
Barbosa proposed a network measure in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some puzzle like problems, such as coloring a map so neighbors differ, are far easier on certain networks than others. The author named that helpful quality conduciveness and tested it on coloring and independent set problems.

The measure aims to predict when a hard problem will yield to solvers quickly. That could save computing time by matching methods to networks in advance. It offers algorithm designers a new lens on why instances differ so much in difficulty. The idea links network shape to the phase changes known in optimization problems.
plos-pone-0011332:
Sonia del Rincón and colleagues set out in 2010 to build a better way to watch proteins being changed after they are made. Cells add small chemical tags to proteins, and those tags alter where a protein goes and what it does. Reading many tagging reactions at once, across the whole set of proteins, had been hard to do well.

The team built and tested a method that uses protein chips, with many proteins fixed in tiny spots on a slide. Samples run over the chip reveal which tagging activities are present and how strong they are. A reliable chip method lets researchers compare healthy and sick cells side by side. It can speed the search for tag patterns that mark disease or predict how a patient will respond to treatment.
plos-pone-0011432:
Marin Schweizer and co-authors reviewed hospital records in 2010 to test a routine habit in severe infection care. When Staphylococcus aureus enters the blood, doctors start antibiotics at once, before lab results name the exact strain, a practice called empiric therapy. The assumption is that an early, best-guess drug saves lives compared with waiting.

In their retrospective cohort, patients who got empiric therapy did not show lower death rates in the hospital than those who did not. That sobering result does not prove early treatment is useless, but it challenges a reflex habit in one of medicine's nastiest bloodstream infections. Hospitals reading the study are pushed to check their own data and to ask which patients, if any, truly gain from the early guess.
plos-pone-0011632:
Robert Pool and colleagues checked the reliability of trial data in the MDP301 vaginal microbicide trial, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Such HIV prevention trials depend on honest reports of gel use and sexual behaviour. No gold standard exists, so reports are usually taken on trust.

The team applied the Microbicides Development Programme's mixed methods model, cross-checking different data sources against each other. Their assessment shows where self-reports hold up and where they drift. Trialists can use the verdict to correct results and to design future studies that catch reporting errors before they distort conclusions.
plos-pone-0011732:
Shan-xue Jin and Larry Feig traced a memory pathway in the rat hippocampus, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Long-term potentiation, a lasting strengthening of synapses, is a leading model of how learning is stored. Receptors called NMDA receptors are major contributors, and a version containing the NR2A subunit had been the focus of most prior work.

Jin and Feig showed that potentiation driven by those receptors in the CA1 region runs through Ras-GRF2 and the Erk MAP kinase relay. Detailing this route from synapse to lasting change refines the molecular account of how memories may form.
plos-pone-0011932:
Joaquín Muñoz and colleagues traced in 2010 the history of a brine shrimp that reproduces without males. Artemia parthenogenetica is an obligate parthenogen, meaning females produce daughters without fertilization. Studying where such lineages come from bears on a big question: why sexual reproduction persists at all.

The team assessed the lineage's geographic origin, genetic diversity, and spread across its range. A clone-like animal that has traveled widely is a natural experiment in how far asexual life can go. Its history shows both the reach and the limits of skipping sex, since the lineage's diversity records every mutation it has gathered since its birth.
plos-pone-0012032:
Joern Kuhbier and co-workers tested in 2010 whether spider silk can serve as a scaffold for growing tissue. Tissue engineering needs matrices for cells to live on, and silk's strength and fineness make it a candidate. Silkworm silk can provoke immune reactions, pushing interest toward spider silk instead.

The team seeded NIH/3T3 fibroblasts, standard connective tissue cells, onto miniature weaving frames holding spider silk, then studied how the cells interacted with the fibers. Whether cells attach, spread, and thrive on silk decides if the material has a future in implants. Hand-built frames let the team test real woven silk rather than silk dissolved into films.
plos-pone-0012132:
Mathew Cox, Murray Cairns, Kaushal Gandhi, and co-authors studied small RNAs in the blood of people with multiple sclerosis, in PLOS ONE in 2010. This disease turns the immune system against the nerves, yet what loosens the immune system's normal controls is still unclear. Small RNAs called microRNAs act as dimmers on genes, and two of them were known to restrain genes that switch T cells on.

In blood from patients, those two microRNAs were present at lower levels than in healthy people. Looser dimmers could let T cell activation genes run hotter, fitting the disease's immune attack. The finding names candidate markers in an easy-to-sample tissue and new suspects in the search for what drives the illness.
plos-pone-0012232:
Christine Waasdorp Hurtado, Lucy Golden-Mason, Megan Brocato, and co-authors studied newborns of mothers with hepatitis C, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most childhood hepatitis C comes from infection around birth, yet strikingly few exposed babies actually catch the virus, while most infected adults stay infected for life. Something in the newborn's first defenses seems to hold the virus off more often than chance would allow.

The team examined the built-in, fast arm of immunity in placentas and cord blood from infected mothers and their infants. Finding what protects most babies could point to vaccine ideas or treatments for everyone. It is a case where the exception, resistance, teaches more than the rule.
plos-pone-0012332:
Maria Wilbe, Martine Lund Ziener, Anita Aronsson, and co-authors linked immune genes to a claw disease of dogs, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Symmetrical lupoid onychodystrophy destroys the claws of otherwise healthy dogs, and its pattern suggests the immune system attacking the claw bed by mistake. The team typed the dog version of the immune identity genes, the DLA class II set, in ninety-eight affected Gordon setters and compared them with controls.

Certain alleles of those genes tracked with higher risk of the disease. A genetic risk map lets breeders lower the disease's frequency over generations without losing the breed's other traits. It also confirms the autoimmune theory, pointing treatment toward immune-calming approaches.
plos-pone-0012432:
Steven Boyden and Louis Kunkel scanned the genomes of long-lived families for shared DNA regions, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. About a quarter of human lifespan runs in families, and genes may matter most for the rare people who pass ninety in good health. Siblings of centenarians live far longer than average, a strong hint of protective genes.

Using dense genome-wide linkage in families with exceptional longevity, the team found several new regions tied to long life. Each region is a haystack with candidate genes inside. Finding true longevity genes could reveal how some bodies resist age diseases and suggest ways to extend healthy years for everyone.
plos-pone-0012532:
Piotr Grabarczyk, Viola Nähse, Martin Delin and colleagues raised a gene regulator in cancer cells and tested drug response, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Bcl11b is a transcription factor found in T cells, neurons, and skin, and its locus is often disturbed in blood cancers. What extra Bcl11b does to a cell's drug sensitivity was unknown.

Cells with more Bcl11b resisted chemotherapy and piled up in the G1 phase of the cell cycle, the waiting stage before DNA copying. Slow-cycling cells often survive drugs aimed at dividing ones. The finding warns that this regulator's level could mark tumors likely to shrug off standard treatment.
plos-pone-0012632:
Sjoholm, Backlund and co-authors linked a clock gene to the fastest form of bipolar disorder. People with bipolar disorder often have broken sleep and daily rhythms. The gene CRY2 helps run the body's inner clock, and its activity in blood cells was known to change with mood state.

Their 2010 study compared patients whose moods cycle rapidly with others, looking for CRY2 differences. A link would tie rapid cycling to the clock machinery itself, not just to symptoms. That could guide treatments that steady daily rhythms, such as light and sleep routines.
plos-pone-0012732:
Henry, Blank, Hoose and co-authors separated two jobs of the cell's protein stress response in yeast. When proteins fold badly in the cell's workshop, the unfolded protein response raises the alarm. Their 2010 study used baker's yeast to test whether that response is needed for cells to enter division.

They found it is not required for the move into DNA copying, but it is required to keep chromosomes intact. Splitting those roles clarifies what the alarm is really for. Chromosome care links this basic pathway to cancer and ageing research.
plos-pone-0012832:
Osterblom, Sumaila, Bodin and co-authors argued that illegal fishing fleets move to wherever enforcement is weakest. Illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing drains fish stocks and harms sea ecosystems. Their 2010 paper frames this as a governance problem that shifts across regions rather than a fixed map of bad actors.

As some regions tighten control, effort slides toward places with a lower governance score. Chasing that slide needs joint action across countries, not port-by-port fixes. The paper gives managers a dynamic picture of the problem instead of a static one.
plos-pone-0328432:
Sergio Delle Monache and a team in Italy studied how the eye follows a falling object that briefly vanishes, in 2026 work. Catching relies on the brain predicting motion under gravity, and the team asked whether doing a hand task at the same time changes that prediction.

Volunteers tracked targets that fell truly or with altered gravity, against plain or realistic scenes, while some also reached to intercept. Eye movements showed a blend of fresh visual input and gravity based prediction, and the mix shifted with task and scene. The results help explain how people time catches when sight is briefly blocked.
plos-pone-0335832:
Selin Kankaya and co-authors compared gene silencing marks in stomach cancer and in stomach inflammation tied to a common bacterium. The tumour suppressor gene in question is often switched off by methylation, a chemical tag, during cancer development. Whether the tag appears early, in Helicobacter-related gastritis, was unclear. Their 2026 study sampled tumours, inflamed tissue with and without the bacterium, and healthy lining.

Methylation ran far higher in cancer than in uninfected gastritis or healthy tissue. Strikingly, infected gastritis matched cancer levels and exceeded uninfected gastritis. The tag separated cancer from non-cancer fairly well, but poorly from infected gastritis. Protein levels did not differ across groups. Kankaya and colleagues caution the mark alone cannot flag cancer where infection is common.
plos-pone-0339732:
Mustafa Tunc runs flume experiments on how sand and gravel beds in straight channels reshape under flowing water. Two features matter for engineers: how deep the flow digs local holes and how high it piles dune crests. Working with three grain sizes, Tunc measured bed shapes across flow rates and built prediction formulas from the results.

Stronger flow raised both digging depth and dune height in every case. Fine grains shifted easily into regular dunes, while the coarsest grains armored the bed and held it stable; middle grains formed a mixed pattern of holes and bars. The formulas predicted both measures with high accuracy. Tunc presents them for designing channels and structures that must survive moving riverbeds.
plos-pone-0341532:
Mohan and Biro, in a 2026 experiment, watch how pairs of people invent shared conventions, the unwritten rules a group settles on to coordinate. Their task copies a color-matching game first used with baboons. Partners had to agree, through play, on which color should win when two colors met.

Pairs got different amounts of help: some could see a partner's screen, and some were told how the task worked. More upfront knowledge slowed the birth of a shared rule, rather than speeding it. Pairs kept their rule even when they could see each other's screens and a simpler trick was open to them. When a seasoned player was paired with a newcomer, a rule formed fast, but the newcomer's rule was not a copy of the veteran's. Know-how passed between partners, the authors argue, more readily than the content of the rule itself.
plos-pone-0343832:
Zehua Liu and colleagues present in 2026 a self service drone photo system built for visitors at cultural sites. Their aim was to remove the need for a licensed pilot on each order and to cut waits that once ran to days. The system splits work into small linked services that handle orders, drone choice, flight control, and video making.

In tests with many simulated users, core responses stayed fast and errors stayed very low. Cost per order fell sharply and delivery shrank to well under an hour. Fault tests caused no full outage. The authors offer the design as a model for other low altitude visitor services.
plos-pone-0344932:
Macy Garrood and colleagues present a method for putting whole fixed human brains into deep freeze for the long term. It is an alternative to storing them in jars of fluid. Fluid storage slowly degrades some molecules researchers care about. Their 2026 protocol gradually loads brains with cryoprotectants. It ends in a strong ethylene glycol and sucrose bath, then stores them below zero.

Patience is the catch. Scans showed the protectant needs roughly nine months to fully penetrate a whole brain. An early validation run froze too soon, leaving ice crystal damage in white matter. With the longer soak, microscopy showed cells and fine structure preserved. Brain banks weighing decades-long archives now have a tested freezing recipe.
plos-pone-0345032:
Naveed Sattar and colleagues re-analysed major obesity trials to see how often a weekly injection hits three health targets at once. Tirzepatide had already produced large weight losses in the SURMOUNT programme, in people with and without diabetes. Their 2026 post-hoc analysis counted patients reaching weight, blood pressure, and cholesterol goals together.

About a third of treated patients hit all three targets at the main weight-loss threshold, against only a small share on placebo. Results were similar when the weight bar was raised. Sattar and colleagues argue the combined endpoint matters because heart risk travels in clusters. Meeting weight, pressure, and cholesterol goals together marks fuller benefit than weight loss alone.
plos-pone-0346432:
Remya Ampadi Ramachandran and co-workers train machine learning models to predict how fast animals clear a drug from the body, a key number for setting doses. Direct clearance data are missing for many drug and species pairs. Their 2026 study mines published studies for drug, dose, species, and route details, then races nine models on the assembled data in several slices.

Simple regression, a small neural network, and a forest model led the pack overall. Accuracy jumped higher still when models focused on single animal groups such as hoofed stock or pets. Separate handling of skewed data through resampling kept rare cases from being swamped. Veterinarians and researchers could estimate dosing gaps before running costly animal studies.
plos-pone-0346532:
Chen and colleagues built a risk score for sepsis from routine blood gas tests in a 2026 study. Sepsis kills many intensive care patients, and existing scores need many inputs. Records came from two large American intensive care databases, one used to build the score and both used to check it.

The score joins three blood gas measures: oxygen, acid balance, and lactate. It predicted death within twenty-eight days on its own, and high-risk patients were clearly sicker. A chart form of the score beat older scales in their tests. Because blood gases are already drawn in every intensive care unit, the score asks for no new tests.
plos-pone-0346732:
Kanokphol Supasirimontri, Vilai Kuptniratsaikul, and Metita Wiwitkul tested five fast screens for muscle loss. The patients were older adults in stroke rehab wards. The state is called sarcopenia: low muscle mass plus weak grip. Missing it slows recovery. Full tests take time and gear. The team checked all five screens on one hundred fourteen patients in 2026.

Half the patients had the condition. A tape measure around the calf worked best. Cutoffs sat just above thirty centimeters, with a slightly lower mark for women. A short survey plus the tape also did well. The three survey-only tools were much weaker. The team backs the tape as the ward's first screen.
plos-pone-0347032:
Baochen Su and colleagues surveyed nearly two thousand Chinese university students confined to campus during COVID-19 closures, asking what protected their quality of life. Mental component scores sagged well below physical ones. Their 2026 analysis weighed psychological distress, daily habits, and career planning against standard health-related quality of life measures.

Low distress was the strongest shield for both body and mind scores. Regular exercise and a steady study routine helped substantially, and students with clear career plans fared better physically and mentally. Having a romantic partner, oddly, cut both ways. The authors urge universities in future crises to bundle mental health support, lifestyle guidance, and career services together.
plos-pone-0347932:
Patricia Orlandi Barth and co-workers evaluate a home-built machine reader that measures antibiotic test discs in a working microbiology lab. Such tests show which drugs still kill a patient's germs, and reading the clear zones by ruler is slow and varies by reader. Their 2026 study compares the reader with manual measures across five hundred tests and thousands of zones.

The two methods agreed on the drug call in nearly ninety-seven of a hundred cases. Serious errors were rare, and zone sizes tracked each other closely. Automating this reading could standardize results between staff and speed up answers for doctors choosing antibiotics. The trial shows a locally built tool can hold its own in daily lab work.
plos-pone-0348132:
Parviz Shahmirzalou and Hassan Ebrahimpour Sadagheyani read three years of bite logs in Khoy County, Iran. Bites count there chiefly through rabies, a near sure death once signs start. The logs span from the spring of 2021 to the spring of 2024. The team asked who gets bit, by what beast, and in which months.

Rates ran high each year, at times near five hundred per lakh of folk. Dogs made nine in ten bites, most in sudden strikes. Warm months saw the most bites. The team's forecast sees the same peak next year. They urge more teaching for at-risk groups and fast shots post-bite.
plos-pone-0348232:
Aryalakshmi Sreemohan and colleagues examined nearly fifteen hundred hospitalised dengue patients at an Indian tertiary centre between 2021 and 2024, asking who dies and how the liver shapes the odds. Dengue attacks the liver in most admitted patients. The team graded liver involvement, hunted for death predictors, and checked whether existing prognostic scores work in this infection.

About five percent died. Severe dengue, intensive care admission, a high inflammation ratio, and above all low blood albumin predicted death. Surprisingly, patients with fatty liver survived better than those with healthy livers, while decompensated cirrhosis fared worst. A simple albumin-based grade separated risk well. Machine grouping found four patient types with very different death rates.
plos-pone-0348432:
Zhonghan Wu and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One surgical study of a curved guide tool nicknamed the Gold Wrist. The tool helps place the guidewire when nailing a broken hip. The patients were obese, with weak bones, which makes the operation risky. Five hundred such patients at one center were split evenly. Half had surgery with the new guide, and half with standard tools.

The guided group had shorter operations and smaller cuts. Their inflammation markers were lower. Their early hip function scores were better. Internal complications, like clots, lung embolism, and infection, were far fewer. Hospital costs were lower too, as was the estimated carbon footprint. Computer modeling confirmed the device is sound. The authors present it as a practical aid for a high-risk operation.
plos-pone-0348632:
Qiyue Song and three co-workers asked what makes fans of metaverse music apps post their own work. These apps mix songs with virtual worlds you can roam. The survey reached four hundred thirty-five users in China. It split the pull of the apps into two paths: a social path and a lost-in-the-moment path.

Warmth and the sense of real people near by fed the social path. Dressing an avatar, tales, and rich sights and sounds fed the flow path. Both paths made the apps feel more dear, and that dear feel drove posting. Trust in the tech boosted just the social path. App makers can use that split.
plos-pone-0349032:
Youngju Lee and colleagues scanned the brains of forty shoppers deciding whether to buy shoes, to find out why free shipping feels so good. The total price never changed; only the split between the shoe price and the delivery fee moved. Participants rated their wish to buy while a scanner watched which brain areas woke up for each price arrangement.

Free shipping won clearly, and the brain showed why: choosing it lit up a region tied to positive emotion, especially when compared against even the smallest fee. It was as if zero delivery carries a special emotional charge beyond saving money. As fees grew, that emotional glow faded and cooler calculating regions took over. The authors say sellers are not imagining it; the pull of free shipping is wired into how the deciding brain responds.
plos-pone-0349132:
Yuping Yan and colleagues propose an algorithm that adjusts how often electrical substation equipment gets serviced, based on the equipment's actual condition rather than a fixed calendar. Substations keep power grids stable, and servicing too late risks failures while servicing too early wastes money. Sensors across the substation feed live condition data into their system.

The method weighs the cost of planned maintenance against the cost of a failure, then solves for the service interval that balances the two. Scheduling limits, such as how daily plans and start times interact, act as constraints. The result is a maintenance cycle that shifts as equipment ages or weakens, a step toward smarter grid upkeep.
plos-pone-0349232:
Rathi Ravindrarajah and colleagues evaluated a digital self-help service for people with type two diabetes in Greater Manchester during the pandemic. The service, MyWay Diabetes, gives patients online access to their records and learning tools. The team compared about five hundred users with a matched group of non-users over two years of follow-up.

Users showed a clear drop in long-term blood sugar compared with non-users, plus small gains in blood pressure and cholesterol. A long-range model then weighed health gains against costs and found the service good value, possibly even saving money once medicines were counted. The authors say digital support of this kind can help clinics care for more patients between visits.
plos-pone-0349432:
Jie Guo, Renjing Liu, and Jinsheng Xing address two headaches in federated learning, where many devices train a shared model without handing over their data. Sending model updates back and forth eats bandwidth, and ordinary encryption can fail when several parties collude. Their scheme trims unneeded parts of the model automatically, guided by accuracy feedback, and encrypts updates with several keys at once.

With multiple keys, the central server can combine encrypted updates without ever decrypting them, and the design resists collusion by nearly all parties. Tests on two standard image datasets showed the trimming sharply cut both local computing and the volume sent each round. The authors aim the approach at phones and edge devices with little spare power or bandwidth.
plos-pone-0349632:
How happy citizens feel with public services varies sharply across Peru's coast, mountains, and jungle. Miluska Odely Rodriguez-Saavedra and colleagues analyzed a 2024 national household survey covering nearly thirty-four thousand people and twenty-one public services, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Scores differed significantly across the eight geographic domains, though the overall gap was modest in size. City and countryside answers diverged as well. A statistical grouping step explored whether services cluster into a few underlying dimensions of satisfaction. The authors say national averages hide regional discontent, and improvement plans should be drawn region by region rather than from Lima alone.
plos-pone-0349732:
Agnes Karingo Karume and colleagues describe a trial plan, with no results yet, for adding mental health care into routine pregnancy clinics in Kenya. Low mood and anxiety around birth are common, yet trained specialists are scarce. Twenty clinics in western Kenya will be split by chance into two arms. Close to three thousand pregnant women will take part.

Clinics in the main arm will screen every woman, offer talk support from trained lay helpers for mild to moderate cases, and use video psychiatry for severe cases or poor response. Other clinics will screen and refer as usual. The team will compare health gains, service reach, and how well the model fits daily clinic work.
plos-pone-0349932:
Ismaila Ajayi Yusuf and co-authors pooled trials of a new class of blood pressure drugs in 2026. The drugs block the making of aldosterone, a hormone that raises pressure, and no trial had yet pitched them against each other directly.

Seven randomised trials with nearly three thousand patients were combined in a network analysis. All the drugs lowered systolic pressure clearly against dummy pills, with one agent showing the largest drop. Effects differed between hard to control and truly resistant cases. The ranking gives doctors an early map of a promising class, while head to head trials are still missing.
plos-pone-0350032:
Kristina M Kokorelias and Annie Robitaille published a 2026 protocol for mapping what helps and hinders putting childcare services inside long-term care homes. Such homes struggle to hire and keep staff, many of whom juggle young children, and on-site childcare could steady the workforce while giving residents time with children. No synthesis of the implementation evidence existed.

As a protocol, the document lays out the planned review: searches across five databases plus grey literature, duplicate screening, and a thematic sorting of barriers and supports using an established implementation framework. Care home and childcare staff will help interpret the findings. The authors expect the map to expose evidence gaps and guide homes considering the model.
plos-pone-0350132:
Haiming Liang and co-authors searched for uric acid related genes in diabetic retinopathy in 2026. The eye disease is a leading cause of blindness in diabetes, and uric acid, the gout chemical, seems to play a part in its course.

Public gene data were screened by several methods, and two candidate genes stood out with higher levels in patient blood samples. Pathway checks tied them to distinct signalling and protein handling routes. Immune cell patterns in the samples also shifted, and the genes related in opposite ways to natural killer cells. Two genes will not explain a complex disease, but they offer testable leads for early detection.
plos-pone-0350232:
Katarzyna Hildt-Ciupinska, Karolina Pawlowska-Cyprysiak, and Zofia Mockallo surveyed nine hundred and twenty seven working women in Poland, aged eighteen to sixty five, on health habits, well being, and work ability. Online forms used standard well being and work ability indexes plus a positive health behaviour scale scored out of one hundred and two points.

Average behaviour scores sat in the middle, near sixty points. Health care effort rose with age, and office workers scored above physical and mixed workers. Better health habits linked clearly with higher well being and stronger work ability. Workplace health teaching, the authors argue, is a practical lever employers control directly.
plos-pone-0350332:
Amlak Abaza and co-authors modelled solid oxide fuel cells in 2026, using a nature inspired search method to fit the model's unknown values. These fuel cells convert fuel to power cleanly for vehicles and buildings, but accurate models need careful tuning.

The search method, modelled on predator and prey behaviour, was paired with a switching strategy that changes tactics by phase. The stack model was tested at four temperatures, with some runs kept for validation. Against several known methods the new pairing fit experimental curves closely. Better fitting matters because engineers design and control real stacks from these models, not from prototypes alone.
plos-pone-0350732:
Self-driving cars must spot rare dangers: fallen trees, loose barrels, scattered debris. Afeera Bint-e Tanveer and colleagues trained a compact vision model, YOLOv8-n, for exactly these roadside surprises, in this 2026 PLOS One study aimed at cheaper on-board hardware.

Images from several open collections were merged and cleaned into one training set.
