Extra training images with changed brightness, tilts, and partial blocking taught the model to cope with bad light and clutter. On a mid-range graphics card it read sixty-eight images per second with high precision and recall. The authors say such lean models suit cars that cannot carry data-center hardware.
plos-pone-0350932:
Yuxing Wang and colleagues stretched frozen loess, a wind blown soil, to test how added plastic fibres change its strength in the cold. Frozen ground strength guides building in cold regions and frost heave forecasts. Custom gear pulled samples with varied fibre doses, freezing levels, and pull speeds, while microscopes revealed the soil inner structure.

Fibres turned clean breaks into slow, cracked stretching and raised load capacity greatly. A dose near three tenths of one percent worked best, lifting strength by over seventy percent. Colder samples grew stronger fast, and faster pulling also raised strength. Too many fibres clumped and weakened the soil. A light fibre dose, properly mixed, toughens frozen ground for foundations and slopes.
plos-pone-0351132:
South China Sea knowledge lies scattered across many sources. Historical, legal, and political texts span centuries. Ruinan Zhao, Zhifan Han, and Huiling Liu used a large language model to join them. They built a knowledge graph from the sources. A knowledge graph stores facts as linked triples. Computers can search and reason over it.

The pipeline works in three stages. It extracts facts, standardizes names, and verifies links. The finished graph holds nearly sixty thousand entities. It stores over six hundred fifty thousand fact triples. Users can answer questions across eras. Hidden multi-step connections also surface. The authors offer the method for other tangled domains.
plos-pone-0351232:
Christiane Al-Haddad and colleagues used a scan that maps tiny eye blood vessels to compare children with lazy eye, their fellow eye, and healthy controls. Lazy eye, or amblyopia, affects vision in one eye in childhood. Seventy eight children took part, half with lazy eye split evenly between crossing and focus mismatch causes, with average age near ten.

Lazy eyes showed higher vessel and flow density in outer and full centre zones than control eyes. The dark centre spot with no vessels was smaller in lazy eyes than in fellow eyes. Disc measures mostly matched controls. Vessel growth may overcompensate in lazy eyes, a clue that the condition reaches beyond the brain visual centres.
plos-pone-0351332:
Adrianne Katrina Nelson led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of deaths inside Los Angeles County jails from 2008 to 2023. Linking custody and death records for the biggest jail system in America, they examined how long people had been confined before dying, and how overdose and COVID-19 figured in.

Deaths used to come early in confinement; during the pandemic and opioid crisis they shifted much later, and long stays plus restrictive pandemic rules tracked with higher mortality. Nelson calls for shorter incarceration, drug treatment access, and stronger health safeguards.
plos-pone-0351632:
Cynthia Osei and co-authors studied three hundred sixty-five people with high blood pressure at a university hospital in Kumasi, Ghana, tracing how family life affects their health. Taking medicine faithfully is known to improve quality of life, but relatives who remind, cook, pay, and encourage may be part of why. Questionnaires measured adherence, family support, and quality of life for each patient.

Patients who stuck to their medicine reported better quality of life, and family support carried part of that effect: support helped adherence, and adherence helped life feel better. The chain means clinics gain by treating the family as part of the prescription. In settings where relatives already share care work, inviting them into blood pressure management is a cheap lever with real payoff, provided the patient's own wishes lead.
plos-pone-0351832:
Farm soil near mines can quietly gather toxic metals, and Ying Hu and co-authors sampled fields around the Baiyun Mountain mining area in Nanyang, China. Their 2026 PLOS One study tested more than four hundred surface samples for nine metals and elements, including silver, copper, lead, and arsenic.

Zinc, molybdenum, and mercury stood well above the natural background for the province. A risk model rated the overall ecological danger, and a source-fitting model split the pollution among likely origins such as mining, farming, and rock itself. Mapping where each metal concentrates helps local officials decide which fields need watching or cleanup first.
plos-pone-0351932:
Xiaolin Tang and seven colleagues build a smarter safety check for intravenous nutrition bags prepared for newborns, in this 2026 hospital study. Ready-to-use nutrition for fragile infants must contain exactly what the prescription says; small errors matter at small body weights. Their system computes each bag's expected weight from drug densities held in the hospital computer, then compares it with a precision scale reading, replacing a slower method based on leftover liquid.

Across several hundred bags prepared by seven technicians, the weighing method proved precise and stable between operators, with nearly all error rates inside the preset limits. It also worked almost twice as fast per bag and caught several faulty infusions the older method missed. The authors recommend the system for pharmacy compounding centers preparing neonatal nutrition.
plos-pone-0352032:
Naja and colleagues surveyed young children's eating in the United Arab Emirates in a 2026 study. More than four hundred children aged four to nine were measured and their diets recalled in detail across three emirates. Sorting foods into broad patterns can show habits that single food counts would miss.

Two patterns stood out: a healthy one rich in fruit, vegetables, olive oil, and whole grains, and a Western one heavy in fast food, salty snacks, sweets, and sweet drinks. Children scoring high on the healthy pattern had lower weight-for-age scores. About one in five children was overweight or at risk, which makes the contrast useful for building food programs that fit local culture.
plos-pone-0352132:
Saima Hirani and colleagues present a protocol, published in 2026, for the first review mapping research on postpartum mental health among racialized mothers in Canada. Nearly a quarter of Canadian mothers report depression or anxiety symptoms after birth. The authors note that mothers from racialized communities can face added stigma and discrimination. They can also face care that does not fit their culture.

The planned review will search four major databases plus grey literature for Canadian studies and programs. It will screen them in duplicate. It will chart themes rather than pooling statistics. Programs and interventions will be catalogued alongside research findings. The resulting map is meant to guide culturally responsive services. It should also show researchers exactly where evidence about these mothers is missing.
plos-pone-0352332:
Debbie Gach and seven co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One study of long-term health after COVID-19 in the Netherlands. They compared patients who had the post COVID-19 condition, the lingering illness often called long COVID, with patients who did not. More than a year after infection, people from three hospitals took wide-ranging checks. The checks covered quality of life, lungs, body chemistry, strength, thinking, mood, and social life.

Those with the lingering condition felt clearly worse. They reported poorer quality of life, more fatigue, more anxiety, and poorer sleep. They also scored lower on breathing-muscle strength and exercise capacity. Yet most lab and scan tests showed no gap between the groups. Formal thinking tests showed no gap either. The authors stress this mismatch. Patients feel far worse than standard tests can explain, which makes care and recognition harder.
plos-pone-0352932:
Yuxuan He and seven co-authors examine how the burden of anxiety disorders differs between middle-income and high-income countries in this 2026 PLOS ONE analysis. Drawing on a major global health database, they tracked cases, prevalence, and years of healthy life lost from 1990 through 2023. They also projected trends forward to 2035 and weighed the role of violence-related risks.

Anxiety remained heavy and unevenly spread, with clear gaps by income group, sex, and age. Partner violence, bullying, and childhood sexual violence each accounted for part of the harm. The team urges mental health plans shaped to income level and aimed at preventing violence, especially where services are scarce.
plos-pone-0353032:
Toshiko Mori and six colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study of a urine marker that may catch diabetic kidney disease earlier than standard tests. The usual measures mainly reflect damage to the kidney's filters and can miss early injury to its tubules, including patients whose urine protein looks normal. In more than two hundred Japanese outpatients with type 2 diabetes, the team measured modified fragments of the protein fetuin-A in urine.

Higher levels of the marker were independently tied to worse kidney risk categories, roughly quadrupling the odds of being in a higher-risk group. It was already raised in a substantial share of patients whose standard tests looked reassuring, unlike a comparison tubular marker that only rose late. The authors propose it as a complement to existing tests for earlier risk sorting.
plos-pone-0353232:
Olga Gorodetskaya and co-authors asked whether landing tenure changes when academics have children. Research usually runs the other way, asking how parenthood dents careers. Their 2026 study used a large original survey of Italian academics and tracked moves into first and second parenthood over time.

Job stability did open the door to parenthood. Tenure raised the chance of a first child for men, and for women who won it before their mid-thirties. Among childless women, tenure also raised short-term plans for a child. Tenure showed no link with second births for either sex. Gorodetskaya and colleagues say secure posts shape family timing, not only family shaping careers.
plos-pone-0353932:
Lisa Van Wilder and five colleagues publish the protocol for a Belgian study of whether structured support helps teenagers with chronic illness move safely into adult care, in 2026. The transfer from pediatric to adult services is a known cliff edge where young patients drop out and health suffers. Their program, co-designed with patients, offers four structured consultations over more than a year, building readiness, autonomy, and continuity.

Two university hospitals will run a pretest-posttest comparison enrolling seventeen- and eighteen-year-olds with type 1 diabetes, asthma, or obesity into the program or usual care. Readiness is the main outcome, with empowerment, medication adherence, quality of life, and mental health also tracked, plus a cost-effectiveness analysis and a close look at how faithfully the program is delivered. The authors aim to inform both a refined program and a future large-scale trial.
plos-pone-0354032:
Xavier Sánchez and four colleagues survey medical trainees in Ecuador about the link between a positive mental attitude and depression, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Seven hundred students and residents at a private university completed a standard depression screening scale and a questionnaire on health habits, covering diet, exercise, rest, and outlook. Nearly half screened positive for significant depressive symptoms.

Of all the habit domains, only positive mental attitude — a hopeful, constructive way of framing events — stayed linked to lower odds of depression once the others were accounted for. Women, younger trainees, and those with other illnesses fared worse. The authors argue medical schools should teach positive-psychology skills, not just clinical ones.
plos-pone-0354132:
Yasmine Wazzani and five colleagues published this 2026 field study of mint plants and the microbes living around their roots. Three closely related mint types grew side by side in the same soil, letting the team compare root-zone bacteria and fungi against soil chemistry and each plant's essential oil blend.

Each mint hosted a distinct microbial community, tied to both its oil chemistry and the surrounding soil. Root fungi that help plants feed were also measured. Wazzani's results show that even near-identical crops shape their own underground partners, a factor growers of medicinal herbs may learn to manage.
plos-pone-0354232:
Malou Masereel and six colleagues published this 2026 study protocol for treating adults with avoidant and restrictive food intake disorder, a pattern of severely limited eating not driven by body image. No proven treatment exists yet. Their plan, run across eleven Dutch centers, gives about a hundred and twenty patients weekly therapy built on gradual exposure to feared foods.

Severity interviews anchor the checks before treatment, after it, and months later, while session notes track fear and expectations. Because there is no comparison group, Masereel presents the trial as groundwork for later controlled studies and sharper therapy design.
plos-pone-0354732:
Rainer Mere and three colleagues published this 2026 scoping review of the theory frameworks behind process evaluations of community mental health programs. Such evaluations explain how programs work, not just whether. Searching three databases, they found eighty-three studies using fifty-four different primary theoretical frameworks, which they sorted into a family tree by outlook and purpose.

Framework use has shifted over two decades from community-engaged approaches toward tidy, systematized ones. Mere warns that the tidy turn may silence community voices, and offers the typology to help evaluators pick suitable frameworks deliberately.
plos-pone-0355232:
Nurlan Smagulov and five colleagues examine what years of teaching do to the body and mind, in a 2026 study of female secondary school teachers in Karaganda, Kazakhstan. Teaching is known to be draining, but researchers rarely separate the effects of simply growing older from the effects of a long career. The team measured heart rhythms, blood pressure, fitness, mood, anxiety, and attention in just over one hundred teachers.

Age and years of service were so closely tied that teasing them apart proved difficult. Still, career length was linked to a wider set of measures than age alone, including physical work capacity and emotional reactivity alongside blood pressure and self-rated well-being. The findings suggest that a long teaching career leaves its own mark beyond aging, a point schools could use when planning health support.
plos-pone-0355332:
Samaneh Abolli is first author on a 2026 PLOS ONE water treatment study using iron nanoparticle reactors to remove dissolved organic carbon. This carbon measure signals water quality; too much causes taste and odor problems and feeds bacterial regrowth. Two small reactors ran in sequence through chemical, biological, and bio-electrochemical phases.

One reactor held activated carbon coated with iron oxide nanoparticles made in the lab; the other held plain carbon. The iron version cut carbon levels more and stayed stable in the final powered phase, while the plain reactor faded and even released carbon. Flow analysis suggested the iron coating also regulated microbe growth on the carbon. Longer gains held under electric current.
plos-pone-0355732:
Holly Edward and colleagues gather in 2026 expert views across Canada on a new guide role for physiotherapists in acute cancer care. A physiotherapist navigator would assess patients early, sort who needs what, and steer care. Two survey rounds plus a final meeting shaped the role, with set thresholds for agreement among health workers who treat cancer patients.

Agreement was reached on four parts: process, assessment, sorting decisions, and duties. Feedback lengthened appointments, spaced follow-ups, allowed self referral, and added objective tests. Respondents rated the role's usefulness very highly. A future trial will test whether the agreed design helps patients in real clinics.
plos-pone-0355832:
Lucas Pietan and colleagues hunted for genes behind the loss of smell and taste that many COVID-19 patients report. These symptoms can linger, and their biology is still partly unclear. Their 2026 study applied machine learning to genome data from two American patient cohorts of different sizes.

The team built a pipeline that ranks genes and variants by how well they separate patients with sensory loss. Best models sorted patients moderately well on held-out data. The shortlist mixed new candidates with known factors tied to immune response, nerve signalling, and calcium signalling. Pietan and colleagues say the results support earlier ideas about how the virus disturbs smell and taste, and they offer targets for follow-up.
plos-pone-0355932:
Teshome Kabeta Dadi and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on what shapes rural Ethiopian women's say over farm and household decisions. Autonomy is tangled: age, schooling, wealth, religion, and cultural norms all pull at once, and effects differ between groups of women. Using survey data from nine rural districts, the team fitted a statistical tree model splitting women into segments by marital status and household headship, finding which factors matter in each.

Among married women in male-led households, autonomy rose with age, wealth, and joining social groups, and varied with religion and views of cultural gender norms. Unmarried women in male-led households showed the same pattern. In female-led households, fewer factors mattered: age and religious affiliation carried the signal. Programs, they advise, should work the levers that actually move each segment, cultural norms and social groups included, rather than treating rural women as one audience.
plos-pone-0356632:
Maria Lamarca leads a team of eight asking whether men and women benefit equally from a psychological therapy for psychosis, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Metacognitive training teaches patients to spot the thinking shortcuts that feed delusions and suspicion. Sex shapes how schizophrenia begins and presents, so a fair question is whether one therapy fits both. The team pooled harmonized records from an international consortium, covering five hundred seventy-three patients treated in real clinics and studies.

Symptoms of every kind, positive, negative, and general, fell significantly after training across the whole group. Crucially, sex did not moderate the change: men and women improved comparably in every symptom domain, even though their starting profiles differed. With no control group, the data cannot prove the training itself caused the gains. But as far as equity goes, the therapy appears to travel across sexes without adjustment, a useful reassurance for routine services.
plos-pone-0357032:
Ahmed Saad AL Zomia and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE charting three decades of blindness and visual impairment across the six Gulf countries, with forecasts to 2030. Using Global Burden of Disease data, prevalence and disability burden were modeled with time-series methods, country by country and by sex.

Most countries improved. Prevalence edged down in Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, barely moved in Kuwait, and stayed broadly stable in Oman and Qatar. Disability burden fell across the region, though Saudi Arabia carried the heaviest load. Women bore higher prevalence than men almost everywhere, the Emirates being the exception. Forecasts point to continued declines in most countries through 2030, but a moderate rise in Oman. Gender-sensitive eye care and stronger infrastructure are urged: the Gulf's gains are real but uneven, and Oman needs attention before its trend turns.
plos-pone-0357232:
Amani Abdallah Hepautwa leads a team of five baking waste into better bricks, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The recipe starts with burnt red soil and a swelling clay additive. Into it goes biochar, made by roasting coffee grounds or tobacco waste at three temperatures. The biochar replaces five to twenty percent of the mix. The team fired the bricks and measured strength three ways, resistance to water and chemical attack, and the microscopic structure behind the numbers.

Everything mattered: the waste type, the roasting temperature, and the dose all significantly shifted performance. One recipe won outright, coffee biochar roasted at the middle temperature and used at ten percent. It delivered the best balance of compressive, tensile, and bending strength in the study. The work gives brick makers in agricultural regions a tested way to convert two troublesome waste streams into a building material that outperforms the plain article.
plos-pone-0357832:
Talyson Aparício Gomes and coauthors published a 2026 qualitative study in PLOS ONE on patients who effectively live in a hospital, a tropical diseases referral center in Manaus, in the Brazilian Amazon. Some stays stretch past six months not because treatment continues, but because there is nowhere to discharge to. The team interviewed ten professionals working at the hospital and eight relatives of long-stay patients.

Five themes emerged, led by social hospitalization and institutional dependence. The cases overlapped heavily: chronic conditions, often HIV, fragile family ties, and deep poverty. Stigma around HIV and families' inability to afford home care blocked discharge, so the hospital became housing, community, and safety net at once. Caregivers' lives bent around the routine, and clinicians described obstacles no treatment plan could fix. Without intermediate care institutions and real policy, they conclude, tertiary hospitals will keep serving as the address of last resort.
plos-pone-0358132:
Kaothar Lambe and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on malaria in sub-Saharan Africa. It follows Plasmodium falciparum histidine-rich protein 2, a protein that many rapid malaria tests detect. The authors study its spatial and genetic dynamics, how the protein's gene varies across places and over populations.

Changes or deletions in this gene can make rapid tests miss infections, a serious threat where those tests are the main diagnostic. Mapping the gene's geography shows where test failure risk is highest. Malaria control programs across Africa rely on this surveillance to decide when to switch diagnostic tools.
plos-pone-0358232:
Vincent C T Hanlon led a team of eight authors testing an idea about a crop pest's genes, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Potato cyst nematodes devastate potato crops, and their HYP1 gene varies a lot between individuals. One theory held that the variation arises from programmed changes in body cells during development.

Hanlon's team tested that theory and found it does not explain the diversity at HYP1. Ruling out a mechanism is real progress: it narrows the hunt for where the variation truly comes from. Pest control may one day target this gene's variability, since it may help the worm evade plant defenses. Knowing what does not cause it saves other teams years of work in the wrong direction.
plos-pone-0358332:
Masaru Shirasuna and Yuto Yoshida compare how trivia champions and large language models read a quiz question, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Human experts often buzz in with the answer after only a few words, working from far less knowledge than a model holds. The authors had both the experts and language models rate the importance of every word in Japanese quiz questions, using the models themselves as judging tools.

Experts spread their attention widely, treating many words as useful clues even when each looked weakly tied to the answer on its own. Their importance scores also piled up faster as a question unfolded. The models, by contrast, concentrated on fewer, more obviously connected words. The authors read the pattern as a hint about human intelligence under time pressure: experts may weave many faint signals together rather than waiting for one decisive hint.
plos-pone-0359232: Kim and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a balloon used to reopen narrowed heart arteries. The balloon carries a drug coating and a fine surface pattern of tiny structures. In pigs with re-narrowed stents, the title reports stronger early biological effect from the patterned balloon. Re-narrowing after stenting is a stubborn problem, so coating design draws wide interest.
plos-pone-0359632: Lim and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE survey study on advance care planning. Such planning lets people state the care they want if they become too ill to decide. The team asked patients how they feel about it and what shapes whether talks happen. A questionnaire design captured views at one point in time. The answers can help clinics start these talks sooner and more gently.
plos-pone-0360432:
Yirui Jiang and colleagues proposed in 2026 a method for sorting city patrol cases by how urgent they are. Patrol and municipal hotline systems receive a flood of reports, from broken streetlights to active hazards, and staff must decide what to handle first. Their method uses a graph neural network, a model that learns from cases and the connections between them, trained with self-supervised clustering so it needs few hand labeled examples.

Sorting by urgency sounds clerical, but it decides how fast real dangers get attention in a big city. An automated first pass, checked by humans, can keep urgent cases from waiting behind routine ones. The study belongs to a wider effort to bring machine learning into everyday city administration.
pmc-10659732:
Wenwen Li and co-authors probe how a classic herbal brew fights artery clogging in two thousand twenty-three. Erchen decoction is a traditional formula used against atherosclerosis, the fat-lined artery disease behind most heart ills. Its inner workings were unknown.

Databases of herbal chemistry and drug targets supplied the brew's parts and their protein targets. Disease target lists came from three gene banks. The overlap, mapped as a web of drug, part, target, and disease, ran to one hundred twenty-seven active parts acting on over two hundred targets and one hundred fifty pathways. Six core parts stood out, led by quercetin. Docking tests checked that the top parts fit their top targets.
pmc-10674732:
Rachel Loney and co-authors report seven near-twin bacteria viruses from desert soil that form a brand-new family branch, in this 2023 paper. Phages outnumber everything alive, yet most remain undescribed. The team pulled the seven from southwest United States soil, sequenced them, and compared their genomes. They infect Bacillus subtilis and match each other closely in gene content.

One oddity stands out: their tail fiber and wall-cutting genes seem borrowed from different sources than the rest of the genome. Such gene swapping is a known phage habit. Host range tests suggest the mix helps them attack hosts with different cell walls. The authors read the group as a snapshot of phages adapting on the fly. They name it a novel subcluster within its wider family.
pmc-10691032:
Jiachen Wang and co-authors described a vaccine strategy in Weifang City, China, in two thousand twenty-three. The vaccine protects children against pneumococcal disease, which world health bodies rank as a top vaccine target. In China it is not in the national program, and cost keeps coverage low.

From June two thousand twenty-one, Weifang offered one free dose to registered children aged six months to two years. An insurance model later extended a free dose to older children. Officials negotiated prices with several makers and weighed safety, access, and schedules first. Full-course coverage rose from well under one percent to about six point six percent, still below rich-country levels. The authors urge wider financing routes.
pmc-10693032:
Hachem Saddiki leads a team on air pollution, pregnancy, and the placenta. Their study from twenty twenty-three uses a cohort in the Northeast US. Air dirt in pregnancy links to harm for mother and baby.

The placenta runs the womb world and shapes later life. Dirt can reach it and change its DNA mark patterns. The team asked if dirt shifts the mix of cell types there. Fine particle levels were mapped day by day at fine scale. DNA marks were used to infer cell type shares. Links split by baby sex in their checks.
pmc-10694932:
Taesung Joo, Tae Gi Kim, and Sang Woong Moon report a case where an eye illness hid a blood cancer. The eye illness swells the optic disc and forms a star of deposits in the central retina. Its causes split into germs, other illness, and unknown roots, so checks must be wide. A woman aged fifty-four came in with blurred sight in both eyes.

Eye checks showed disc swelling, fluid, and deposits that fit the eye illness. Blood tests showed no germ or swelling signs, but counts hinted at bone marrow failure. That lead brought a diagnosis of multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells. The authors warn that blood cancers can show first in the eye and should stay in mind during workups.
pmc-10696032:
Muhammad Junaid and colleagues published a dataset study in 2023. They mapped brain cells that connect to stress circuits. The hypothalamus controls survival and balance behaviors. Its wiring involves many steps between brain cells. A modified virus traced connections backward across synapses. Single-cell gene reading identified the upstream neurons. Mice engineered for stress hormone circuits were used. Over one thousand five hundred cells were profiled. A huge reference atlas validated the cell identities.

Label transfer matched new cells against the atlas. The method confirmed the dataset was technically sound. Diverse hypothalamic cell types appeared in the data. The resource deepens maps of stress-related circuits. Other researchers can reuse the validated dataset freely. Better circuit maps may guide future behavior research.
pmc-10697032:
Mina Boshra, Feras Ghazawi, and Carmen Liy-Wong published a 2023 case report on mouth sores in a teen after COVID-19. The condition is a reactive eruption where infection triggers raw inflammation of the mouth lining, with little skin involvement. It has lately been tied to the COVID-19 virus.

Reports in children and teens are rare, so proven treatments are few. Standard care leans on strong immune-suppressing drugs, like steroids and cyclosporine. The case follows one PCR-positive teen and the care that worked. A short review of past reports sits beside the case. Each new case widens the menu of options for a rare and painful illness.
pmc-10697832: Muna Sharma and co-authors report a bladder fistula case in a 2023 paper, opening with the condition's background. A vesicovaginal fistula is an abnormal channel between bladder and vagina, leaking urine without pause. In developing countries it follows mainly from obstructed labor. In rich countries the usual causes are radiotherapy and cancer. Shame around leaking and painful urination keeps many patients from seeking care. They present late, often with advanced complications. The case pairs the fistula with massive bladder stones.
pmc-10699032:
Alena Kalyakulina and a large team present the first chemical-tag study of DNA in the Yakut people of far northern Siberia, in a twenty twenty-three paper. Yakuts live with severe winters, with January means below minus forty degrees in their capital. The team read DNA tags in blood from Yakut residents and compared them with people from central Russia. They looked for tag patterns tied to climate adaptation and to aging.

Some tag regions differed by place and touched water use, digestion, and hormone control. Yakut participants also showed faster epigenetic aging than the central Russia group. In both places, men aged faster than women on this measure. The study opens a line on how harsh climates shape the aging body.
pmc-10701432: Daisuke Noshiro and Nobuo Noda present a protocol for fixing lipid nanorods onto two-dimensional crystals of the protein tamavidin 2, for use in high-speed atomic force microscopy, in work published in 2023. The protocol covers making the protein, forming the lipid nanorods, and growing the protein crystal layer on mica. The anchored rods then serve as a stage for watching specific proteins in action under the microscope.
pmc-10701932:
Maciej Szymanski and co-authors study clusters of transfer RNA genes in the plant Arabidopsis thaliana, in this 2023 paper. Most tRNA genes sit scattered across the genome, but some bunch into clusters. One small cluster on chromosome 5 holds four cysteine tRNA genes in repeating units, next to a broken copy. The team compared that region across many plant strains.

The cluster's overall layout stayed the same across strains, yet the count of repeats varied a lot. A jumping gene element sat inside the cluster, a rare feature. Two more tiny cysteine gene pairs turned up elsewhere in the genome. Gene activity reads showed most copies are switched on. Comparing five related species let the authors sketch how these clusters diverged over time.
pmc-10702032:
Weihang Gao and four co-authors review gold nanoparticles as a candidate osteoporosis therapy that could build bone and slow its breakdown simultaneously. Current drugs each do one job or the other and carry side effects and costs. Gold particles, biocompatible and optically distinctive, have been shown to push bone-forming cells to mature, restrain the bone-eating cells, and divert fat stem cells away from becoming fat.

The review covers how the particles are synthesized and how size, shape, and surface chemistry steer their effects in cell and animal studies. It weighs drawbacks honestly alongside the promise. Several research directions are flagged as most likely to move the particles toward clinical reality.
pmc-10704632:
Yan Zhang and six co-authors published a 2023 study of how nano-textured implant surfaces change cell behavior through calcium signals. The team grew titanium nanotubes on implant metal and watched living cells with calcium imaging. On the nanotube surface, cells boosted a key calcium entry route from internal stores, and the channel parts that form it linked up more strongly. A custom holder let them track cell movement on the opaque surface without losing the field of view.

Cells on nanotubes migrated faster and more vigorously. The shift tracked with more adhesion proteins, higher activity of a calcium-driven cutting enzyme, and more of a channel component. The authors say this calcium route is a fresh design target for implant surfaces that cells colonize well.
pmc-10704732:
Shang Liu and nine colleagues published a 2023 study on the family tree of a key cotton variety. The variety, called CRI12, anchors a common breeding style in China that builds new types from proven parents. Gene-based breeding is the other main path, and the limits of the parent-based path were unclear.

The team read the full DNA of CRI12 and 20 of its relatives using long-read methods. They found 13,138 structural changes across the family. Good DNA chunks from parent plants proved unstable as they passed down, a flaw of the strategy. They also flagged 623 useful segments tied to many farm traits. The work may guide a shift in how cotton is bred.
pmc-10704832:
Dagninet Alelign and Aschalew Kidanewold test street food in Arba Minch town, southern Ethiopia, for germs that shrug off strong drugs. They collected 100 vended food items in early 2023 and grew bacteria from the family that lives in the gut, checking each strain against a panel of medicines.

They found 112 strains across six genera, with Escherichia coli the most common. About 15 percent made enzymes that defeat a whole class of penicillin-like drugs. About 9 percent defeated carbapenems, a last-line group. Every strain of the second kind also made the first kind of enzyme. Most enzyme-making strains resisted several drug classes at once. The authors warn that street food can carry drug-resistant infections and urge routine checks of vended food and steady tracking of resistance trends.
pmc-10708132:
Chulpan Allagulova and colleagues prime wheat seeds with a nitric oxide donor and watch the seedlings weather drought, in this study from twenty twenty-three. Pre-sowing treatment with sodium nitroprusside, which releases the signaling gas, was tested against dehydration imposed by polyethylene glycol.

Primed seeds germinated better and grew stronger in good conditions, and held up under drought: water content and transpiration stayed steadier, membranes leaked less, and damage markers fell. Hormone assays explained part of it: the treatment raised growth hormones, auxin and especially cytokinins, and damped the wild swings drought causes in all three hormones measured. A drought-protection gene, the dehydrin TADHN, switched on harder in primed plants. The authors present seed nitric oxide priming as a cheap chemical rehearsal for dry spells.
pmc-10708732:
Athina Tsanousa and colleagues detect room occupancy by fusing the readings of ordinary environmental sensors on a live construction site. Smart building systems sense temperature, dust, and air quality for energy efficiency, but combined cleverly, the same sensors can infer whether people are present, aiding security and safety. The study evaluates sensor fusion strategies on data from a building under construction.

The authors compare several late fusion methods, which combine each sensor stream's calls, against early fusion feeding ensemble classifiers. They also test a novel weighted fusion method built for lopsided samples, key because empty periods dominate occupancy data. The dataset collected from the site's sensors is released in public. Occupancy from such sensors is in effect free information: no cameras, no wearables, no new hardware.
pmc-10712032:
Pegah Sicahni and co-authors link insulin-raising diets and lifestyles to colorectal cancer odds in Iran, in a 2023 study. Two index scores grade how strongly a person's diet, and diet plus lifestyle, push insulin up. The team compared 71 cancer patients with 142 controls at Tehran hospitals. Food questionnaires covering 168 items fed the scores, along with weight and activity data.

People in the top third of the diet score had about triple the odds of cancer compared with the bottom third. The lifestyle score's top third carried nearly five times the odds. The gaps persisted after adjusting for other factors. The authors conclude that eating and living in ways that keep insulin low may help hold this cancer at bay.
pmc-10713332:
Jun Takada and six co-authors report freeing a narrowed gullet without a balloon in this two thousand twenty-three case report. Removing wide surface cancers from the esophagus can leave a tight scar ring. Steroid shots prevent some, but not all. Balloon stretching is the usual fix, yet it once tore this patient's wall. The team chose a different route: radial incision and cutting through the scope.

Their patient was a seventy-six-year-old man whose cancer removal spanned most of the gullet's width. The cutting method opened the stricture while sparing the weak spot. Cases like this map options when the standard tool is dangerous. Endoscopists who treat post-surgery strictures are the readers. The report stresses care around old perforation sites.
pmc-10715232:
Paulo Roberto de Brito-Marques and Janaina Brito-Marques describe an unusual language disorder case, in a report published in two thousand twenty-three. Primary progressive aphasia erodes language as brain networks degenerate, usually on the left side. Crossed aphasia means the damage sits on the same side as the dominant hand.

Their patient was a sixty-year-old left-handed man whose symptoms began at fifty-two. Brain SPECT imaging showed left-sided asymmetry despite his left-handedness. A full battery covered handedness, memory, and executive tests. Assessment found severe cognitive deficits consistent with the non-fluent aphasia variant. The case is instructive because handedness usually predicts language dominance. Exceptions like this refine how clinicians interpret scans in left-handed patients.
pmc-10716132:
Qiao Yu, Brian Yueshuai He, Jiaqi Ma, and Yifang Zhu wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It maps electric vehicle adoption across California neighborhoods and finds cleaner air arriving unevenly: wealthy areas buy the cars, while disadvantaged areas breathe a shared but incomplete benefit.

Census-tract data from 2015 to 2020 show per-person zero-emission vehicle ownership nearly four times higher outside state-designated disadvantaged communities. Minority residents owned fewer such vehicles everywhere. Traffic and air dispersion models for greater Los Angeles found disadvantaged residents actually gained larger pollution cuts in 2020, thanks to clean cars passing through. Yet their total exposure stayed higher. Projecting to 2035, when new sales go fully electric, narrows the gap. The authors say trucks and targeted policy must carry the rest.
pmc-10723032:
Rui Ren, Kuangnan Fang, Qingzhao Zhang, and Shuangge Ma release an R software package for studying dense genetic marker data, in a 2023 paper. Such data pack thousands of markers per person, and the sheer count defeats standard analysis, especially when gene-environment interplay matters. A newer strategy treats the markers as samples of one smooth genetic function, sidestepping the size problem. Until now, no friendly software package carried those methods.

Their package, FunctanSNP, bundles tools to fit the models, pick out what matters, and draw the results. The authors tested it on simulated and real data and report it holds up reliably. The package is freely available through the CRAN archive. They present it as a practical way for geneticists to use functional methods on SNP and similar dense data.
pmc-10726132:
Arslan Pannu and three co-authors test a glow-based method to find tiny glands during neck surgery, in this twenty twenty-three study. The parathyroid glands are small, easy to miss, and vital for calcium balance. A near-infrared light trick makes them glow on their own, helping surgeons spot and spare them.

The study covered patients having first-time surgery for overactive parathyroid glands across three years. In a share of cases the glow method was used, and the team compared cure rates and surgery times with cases done without it. They also mapped glow patterns in the thyroid and the glands, and in single- versus multi-gland disease.
pmc-10726232:
Walter Hanel and Narendranath Epperla wrote a commentary in twenty twenty-three for Blood Advances on a phase two trial in mantle cell lymphoma. The trial, by Karmali and colleagues, gave patients the drug ibrutinib for up to four years after their first round of chemotherapy. Ibrutinib blocks a protein that helps these cancer cells grow.

The trial's five-year results were strong: eighty-nine percent of patients had no disease growth, and ninety-one percent were still alive. Patients who had a stem cell transplant did even better. The commentary notes these results compare well with older trials using a different drug for upkeep care. The authors still urge care, since the comparisons cross between trials rather than testing the drugs head to head.
pmc-10728732:
Gioia Cappelletti and co-authors asked whether the virus behind COVID-19 can infect the motor neurons that drive muscles. Many patients report nerve and muscle symptoms during and after infection, yet these specific cells had not been tested. The team grew motor neurons from human stem cells in the lab and exposed them to the virus.

The cells carried all the known entry receptors for the virus, two of them in large amounts. The virus infected the neurons and multiplied without visibly killing them, and fluid from the infected cells could infect fresh test cells. Infection also switched many genes tied to cell survival, defense, and inflammation. The authors say this may help explain the neuromuscular problems seen in COVID-19 and long COVID.
pmc-10735332:
Jungwon Min and seven co-authors tested whether slow breathing that swings heart rate can lower a brain risk protein in blood, in a study published in 2023. The protein rises with age, and most of it comes from platelets. Blood flow stimulates the vessel wall cells that calm platelets. A ten-second breathing cycle swings heart rate most. More than a hundred healthy adults trained each day for four weeks, half to raise the swings and half to reduce them.

Both forms of the protein shifted strongly with training. The shifts tied to the swing size during practice, not to resting readings. In older adults, a vessel wall cell marker rose in the raise group and fell in the reduce group. Changes in that marker ran against the protein changes. The authors read the effect as flow driven: wall cells, stirred by the swings, calm platelets and cut the protein.
pmc-10736732:
Evan Plys, Christopher Lyons, and Ana-Maria Vranceanu describe a community-engaged research project in US nursing facilities in a 2023 paper. Older adults who go to a skilled nursing facility for rehab after a hospital stay often carry heavy physical, mental, and social needs. Stress around the move home can lead to poor transitions and repeat hospital stays, above all for families with little money.

The project, called BRISK, set out to build, with the community, a paired psychological program for patients and their care partners. It would run during the shift from facility to home. The paper tells how the team found facility partners, weighing chains and physician groups, and formed a community advisory board. It also covers the practical and regulatory hurdles of recruiting patient and partner pairs. The case offers a model for research done with, not just in, care settings.
pmc-10736832:
Tina Kilaberia, Yuanyuan Hu, Edward Ratner, and Janice Bell study social isolation in older adults during COVID-19 in two thousand twenty-three. Older adults were hit hard by the virus and by rules that kept people apart. The team used written surveys plus phone and video interviews. They compared adults with health problems to those without them.

Half of those with health problems put off routine care. Many felt cut off when they could not go to church. Church was the biggest event in their week. Those with health problems also felt stress from both the virus rules and social unrest. The authors say faith support may guard against isolation in a crisis.
pmc-10736932:
Cal Halvorsen, a solo author, presents a talk summary from 2023 on building a career with impact. Halvorsen works in social work research. A mentor's blunt question guides the work: so what? In plain terms, why does the research matter, to whom, and what will change?

The talk traces a path that blends campus research with public work. Past jobs at a think tank and an advocacy group in Washington shaped that path. Examples include joint projects with local, state, and national groups, where terms were set to serve both sides. Writing spans open-access journals, opinion pieces, and plain reports for the public. The talk ends with tips on meeting tenure norms while keeping the public mission. The aim is research that changes real lives.
pmc-10737332:
Karyn Esser wrote this conference paper, published in 2023, summarizing a study of how the body's daily clocks weaken with age across many tissues. Each cell runs a circadian program that times gene activity for health and repair.

The team profiled rhythmic gene activity in six tissues of mice, brain, lung, heart, kidney, muscle, and adrenal gland, across three age groups. Aging generally cut the number of genes that rise and fall on schedule, a sign of fading clock control. The losses differed by tissue, and the rhythmic genes left were rich in aging hallmarks. In brain and muscle, the timing of peak activity collapsed toward one part of the day. Looking at fixed times instead revealed separate, non-rhythmic age changes. The work maps how timekeeping and aging intertwine organ by organ.
pmc-10738532:
Lillian Agyemang and Louanne Bakk study, in twenty twenty-three, dental care use among older adults on Medicare in the United States. Oral health gaps in this group are understudied. Medicare and Medicaid dental cover is thin, and poor oral care can lead to tooth loss, low self-esteem, poor diet, and heart harm. The team used a twenty eighteen wave of a national aging study. The sample held more than eight thousand people aged sixty-five and older on Medicare.

Dental visits linked to race, ethnic group, health, schooling, and age. Black and Hispanic older adults saw a dentist far less in two years than White peers. Use also fell with older age, worse health, and less schooling.
pmc-10738632:
Kristin Merss, Laura Block, and Stephen Kwas published a review in 2023 on words used for older prisoners. How researchers name people can shape self-image, trust in care, and use of health services. A long-running movement urges person-first words that avoid stigma.

The team did a fast review of studies on older adults moving through the prison system. Nineteen studies met their rules. They then checked the words each study used for its subjects. Person-first terms were common, but most studies also used harsh labels like prisoner, offender, or ex-convict. Most subjects were people already out of prison. The authors urge journals and researchers to keep person-first words for this group as well.
pmc-10738732:
Paavani Jain, Nancy Schoenborn, and Thomas Cudjoe report early lessons from engaging older adults and caregivers as stakeholders in an artificial intelligence research collaboratory. AI tools for aging often miss their users' real needs. As the stakeholder core of the Johns Hopkins collaboratory, the team formed a council to advise pilot projects over time.

All five clinicians approached agreed to serve, as did ten of twenty older adults and caregivers. Outreach used clinic relationships, plain-language materials, and personal approaches to homebound and disabled adults. Many council members needed email and computer support. Others declined because of heavy caregiving or health demands, despite strong interest. The authors urge flexible engagement plans for high-needs participants.
pmc-10738832:
Tracy Christianson and five co-authors studied how pandemic visit rules affected families of long-term care residents in British Columbia, in a paper from twenty twenty-three. Family help is tied to good quality of life for residents. Strict rules during the outbreak cut families off from their loved ones in care homes.

The team used surveys, interviews, and small arts-based group talks with family members. Six linked themes came out, covering quality of life, quality of care, mental health, and how homes shared news and set rules. Families who felt well treated by staff were more content with care. The paper ends with family ideas for fairer rules in future outbreaks.
pmc-10739032:
Amanda Sesker and four co-authors trace a twenty-year chain from life purpose to thinking skills, in a 2023 study. A sense of purpose has long been tied to healthier aging. The team asked whether the way people cope with stress carries part of that benefit.

They used a national study that measured purpose in the late 1990s, coping style a decade later, and thinking in a third wave nearly twenty years after the start. People high in purpose later favored practical, problem-focused coping and shunned emotion-focused coping. Both styles partly explained purpose's link to later memory and overall thinking. Emotion-focused coping carried about a seventh of the total effect. The results suggest coping habits are one path by which purpose protects the aging mind.
pmc-10739432:
Michael Pervratil, Dorota Kossowska-Kuhn, and Neil Charness compared how well older adults find their way, in twenty twenty-three. One group had cognitive impairment and the other was healthy. Finding one's way is a complex skill of several parts, and it helps in daily life. Skill is expected to fall with normal aging, and impairment may deepen the loss.

The impaired group was drawn from three sites in the eastern United States. They took tests of how they find their way, by tasks and by self-rating. Their scores were set against a community group aged sixty to ninety. The impaired group did much worse on a test of spatial orientation. They rated themselves worse on a general wayfinding scale. Yet the groups did not differ in help felt needed, or how often they felt lost. The authors discuss what this split means for measurement.
pmc-10740532:
Min Kyoung Shin and co-authors identify a new spider toxin peptide with dual activity in this 2023 paper. Antibiotic resistance drives the search for new antimicrobial agents. Animal venoms hold many functional peptides worth mining. Computer screening of a spider venom gland transcriptome found the candidate, named Lycotoxin-Pa2a.

Lab tests matched or beat a known bee peptide against several pathogenic bacteria. The peptide breaks both bacterial membranes and raises reactive oxygen species inside cells. It also calmed inflammation in their assays. Human primary cells and mouse cells showed no major toxicity at working doses. A predicted lack of red blood cell damage held up as well. Venom mining offers leads that differ from standard antibiotics.
pmc-10741232:
Nesrine Merabet and co-authors test, in a 2023 study, whether variants in the hunger hormone's genes sway prostate cancer risk. Ghrelin and its receptor had been tied to several cancers, but single-variant studies disagreed. The team genotyped six marker variants across the two genes in one hundred twenty patients and ninety-five healthy controls, then looked at single markers, combinations, and gene-gene interplay together.

Taken one by one, none of the six markers associated with the disease. One genotype did stand out as more common in patients, and an interaction analysis found a two-variant combination that predicted case status with high accuracy in this sample. The authors read their own result with care: markers may only point at regions where a functional variant hides. They offer the findings as leads for larger studies, and as a caution against reading single markers as causes.
pmc-10741932:
Romuald Tematio Fouedjou and co-authors review the Cordyline plant group, its folk uses, its chemistry, and its effects in lab tests, in a 2023 paper. People have long used these plants for bloody cough, dysentery, and high fever. The group holds about 26 accepted species spread around the world. The team searched the literature for reports on traditional use, plant chemistry, and biological activity.

They gathered 98 pure compounds reported from eight species, most of them sugar-linked compounds from a few chemical families. Extracts and some pure compounds showed antioxidant effects, slowed cell growth, killed microbes, or lowered blood fats in lab tests. Many species have never been studied in depth. The authors present the group as a promising source of new active compounds for drug research.
pmc-10742632:
Antonella Meloni, Laura Pistoia, and ten colleagues link low vitamin D to higher iron loading of the heart in transfusion-dependent thalassemia, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-three. In beta-thalassemia major, years of transfusions load organs with iron, and cardiac iron is the dangerous kind.

The study examined two hundred seventy-eight patients with MRI scans that measure cardiac and liver iron, heart function, and scar tissue. Vitamin D was deficient in about thirty-nine percent of patients and insufficient in another third. Patients with deficient vitamin D had significantly more myocardial iron overload than those with sufficient or borderline levels. Parathyroid hormone levels were assessed alongside. The association does not prove that low vitamin D causes iron uptake, but it flags a correctable factor in a high-risk group. Heart failure from iron remains this disease's killer, so every contributing factor matters.
pmc-10742732:
Telesca and Czechowski probe in twenty twenty-three how nonlinearity in a random-walk style model shapes the gaps between extreme events. Two versions of a standard noise model differ in what stays fixed as a bend parameter grows. Extremes were marked by percentile thresholds, and the team measured the order and surprise in the timing and length of extreme runs using two classic information tools.

In the first model, both measures fell steadily as the bend grew, tying order to the model's shape. The second model showed the same trend more weakly, even though its overall distribution never changed. Higher thresholds raised both measures in either model. The authors say such tools can fingerprint how extremes behave in generated series.
pmc-10743232:
Shweta Gautam, Lubomir Lapcik, Barbora Lapcikova, David Repka, and Lilianna Szyk-Warszyńska wrote a study in twenty twenty-three on edible films made of polysaccharides and loaded with bioactive substances. The films are meant for food packaging. Plastic wrap leaves waste that lasts for ages, so researchers seek films that rot away and still guard food. Their films use sodium carboxymethyl cellulose, a polymer drawn from plants, set with citric acid.

The team checked the films for traits that count in packaging: how thick, how clear, how much water they hold, how fast they take up water, and how well they block it. The rich cellulose mix and citric acid gave strong water handling and barrier traits. Crosslinks and bioactive parts did not notably weaken the films. Such films could wrap food while giving off compounds that keep it fresh, cutting both plastic waste and spoilage.
pmc-10745932:
Esimbekova and three colleagues review enzymes locked inside starch and gelatin gels in twenty twenty-three. Trapping enzymes in soft gels keeps them stable through storage and rough handling. The natural polymers are cheap and break down safely. The review sums the gel traits that suit this use.

The authors' own gel based enzyme products are assessed for activity and shelf life. Their sensitivity as sensing parts in inhibition assays is weighed. Such sensors flag poisons by how much they slow the enzyme. The gels serve as the sensing heart of those tests. The work maps a green route to hardy enzyme tools.
pmc-10747232:
Yu and co-authors test how ginkgo biloba extract changes gut microbes in a mouse model of Alzheimer disease. Alzheimer disease is a complex brain disorder with no simple cure. Drugs that act on the brain-gut axis have shown promise in easing its symptoms in past work.

Ginkgo extract is widely used in care for heart and brain vessel disease. The team fed the extract to Alzheimer model mice and tracked gut flora and microbe-made chemicals. Shifts in both suggest the extract works partly through the gut. The study adds detail on how a plant extract may aid the diseased brain.
pmc-10747532:
Yuxuan Lu and co-authors review gels made from proteins that change their behavior when triggered, in a paper published in 2023. Protein gels suit the body well: they are friendly to tissue, break down safely, and can carry active cargo. The challenge is copying how real tissue matrices answer changes around them.

By combining engineered proteins with parts that respond to physical, chemical, or biological cues, researchers have built smart gels whose stiffness and activity can be switched by gentle triggers. The review lays out the design rules and making methods behind them. It then surveys their uses in treating disease, delivering drugs, and growing replacement tissue. The authors close with the field's open problems and likely next steps.
pmc-10748332:
Laura Mihaela Isop and co-authors review a common diabetes drug for possible use in brain-wasting diseases, in work from two thousand twenty-three. The drug is cheap and widely used, and animal work hints it may shield the brain. Demand for care in Alzheimer and Parkinson disease keeps rising.

The review traces how the drug works, from a key energy switch to gut and microbe effects. Targets inside cell power units and waste sacs are still being pinned down. Animal results look promising, but human trial results stay mixed and unclear. The authors call for trials designed around the drug's true targets.
pmc-10752532:
Pétra Vande Zande and co-authors published this study in 2023. It uses baker's yeast to study how gene networks absorb shocks. When one gene's output drops, a sibling gene often rises to cover the loss. That cover can be passive, or active, needing a real change in the sibling. The team studied TDH3, a yeast gene, and its sibling TDH2.

As TDH3 output fell, TDH2 rose in step, dose for dose. The rise needed two shared switch proteins that both genes answer to. A third, more distant sibling used a different route. Other sugar-burning genes under the same switches shifted in a like pattern. The authors read this as one wide balancing response, run by shared regulators, not a patch for one gene alone.
pmc-10763832:
Hassan Abed and six co-authors review how psychiatric drugs can harm oral health, in a review published in two thousand twenty-three. People with mental illness face more mouth disease, from dry mouth to tooth decay, and need more dental care. The causes mix the illness itself, drug side effects, and hard access to care. The team searched three databases and drew on forty-eight papers.

The review covers the most common mental illnesses in Saudi Arabia, among them schizophrenia, obsessive-compulsive disorder, bipolar disorder, and dementia. It sets out how anti-psychotic drugs dry the mouth and raise decay risk. The authors press for regular dental visits, clear patient teaching on self-care, and closer work between dental and mental health teams.
pmc-10764232:
Gi Dae Kim tested a plant-derived compound on liver cancer cells in two thousand twenty-three. Harmine hydrochloride dissolves easily in water. Tissues absorb it readily as well. Liver cancer remains common worldwide. New natural drugs could soften chemotherapy side effects. The study used one human liver cancer cell line.

Growth, migration, and invasion all fell with dosing. Cells arrested before the division phase. Death proteins rose, while a survival protein fell. Harmful oxygen species increased inside treated cells. Mitochondria faltered under that oxidative stress. Two signaling pathways shifted in opposing directions. The compound shows clear anticancer potential in dishes.
pmc-10795832:
Sailaja Battula and colleagues anchor the immune cytokine IL-12 to aluminium hydroxide so it stays inside tumours and fights cancer longer. Their 2023 study tackles toxicity and rapid clearance that have limited this potent immune activator.

Given systemically, IL-12 causes toxicity, while unanchored tumour injections clear within hours. The engineered complex formed a depot retained locally for weeks in mouse tumours, shown by imaging. One or two injections produced single-agent antitumour activity across diverse tumour models, including checkpoint-resistant ones. Treatment also shrank non-injected lesions, especially combined with checkpoint blockade. Tumour tissue showed prolonged immune signals and recruitment of T and natural killer cells.
pmc-10800432:
Yanna Zhou, Chunhai Xiao, and Yiting Yang built a prediction model for pre-eclampsia, a dangerous blood pressure condition in pregnancy. Their study, published in twenty twenty-four, compared pregnant patients who developed the condition with those who had normal pregnancies at the same Shanghai hospital. They recorded body weight before pregnancy and measured four blood markers tied to the placenta, cell stress, and metabolism. Statistical screening picked the factors that independently tracked with the condition, and the team turned them into a scoring chart.

Combined, the five factors predicted the condition far better than any single marker, with strong sensitivity and specificity in their sample. Checks of the chart showed predicted risks close to actual outcomes, and analysis suggested the model would help decisions across a wide range of risk levels. The authors offer it as an aid for earlier warning in prenatal care.
pmc-10800832:
Mingxi Li and five co-authors profile gut bacteria taken from captive giant pandas in a study whose head reports 2023. Escherichia coli can cause diarrhea in pandas. The team tested one hundred strains from panda feces for drug resistance, type groups, and virulence genes, and typed them by a standard gene method.

Most strains resisted several common antibiotics, though two drugs still worked well. The strains carried many resistance genes, and some resistance patterns varied with the panda's age or sex. Twelve O type groups were found among the typed strains. The results inform care and drug choice in panda breeding centers.
pmc-10824932:
Daniel Neuhoff, Günter Neumann, and Markus Weinmann propose field trial standards for plant growth promoting microbes, in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. Such products sell widely as soil improvers and bio-stimulants, promising greener farming. Unlike registered pest products, they need no proven field efficacy in the European Union, only safety.

The paper drafts design, data, and reporting rules to close that gap. A literature check found most trials well designed but thin on sites and crop types. Site and soil weather details were often missing. Following the standards should sharpen what trial results really prove, the authors argue.
pmc-10876032:
Francesco Galassi, Elena Varotto, and Mariano Martini trace the history of pertussis. Their review deals with whooping cough across the ages. It was once an ancient scourge and still burdens health today.

Early mentions come from medieval Afghanistan records. A famed Paris outbreak was described by a French physician. The path toward an effective vaccine is traced here. Family trees of the germ are matched to history. Recent public health challenges from the disease are noted. The piece joins old records with gene based evidence. Its arc runs from old plagues to present day.
pmc-10895032:
Fei Chen and nine colleagues build a scoring chart to predict whether papillary thyroid cancer has already spread to the lymph nodes in the center of the neck. That spread worsens the outlook, but surgeons disagree on removing those nodes ahead of time as a safeguard. The team studied 691 patients treated between 2018 and 2021, pairing clinical features with ultrasound scoring.

Five factors on their own predicted spread: male sex, age over fifty-five, clinically positive nodes, a tumor at least one centimeter wide, and high ultrasound suspicion scores. The chart told cases apart fairly well and matched real outcomes closely. An analysis of its use suggested it would help in practice. The authors offer this tool, which needs no surgery, to help surgeons size neck surgery to each patient's risk.
pmc-11535432:
Emanuele Fornasier and ten co-authors published a structural biology study in twenty twenty-four on how the coronavirus main protease's two halves talk to each other. The enzyme works as a paired dimer with two distant cutting sites, and pairing is essential to viral replication. The team watched it handle three natural peptide substrates.

Crystal structures showed the free enzyme symmetric but the working complexes lopsided: binding at one site reshaped the other. Two arginines proved key to the symmetry switch. Activity assays revealed positive cooperativity of the kinetic kind, faster processing rather than tighter binding. The authors suggest the virus uses this internal signaling to time and place its protein cutting. Drug designers gain a subtler target than the active site alone.
pmc-11535532:
Fang, Wang, Marie, and Sun wrote a review in twenty twenty-four on tiny flaws in layered crystals that can sense the world. These flaws hold spin, a quantum trait, and can be read with light. Placed in atom-thin layered materials, they could measure fields and heat with fine precision. The review covers gains from pairing light-readable flaws with thin layers. It also lists the main hurdles, such as making flaws on demand at exact spots.

The authors map where more work is needed, from flaw choice to layer thickness effects. They sketch uses in magnet studies, chip research, and biology. One sketch joins fluid chips with sensing flaws for DNA reading. They expect flaw craft to push these sensors into wide use.
pmc-11536532:
Behnaz Shokri, Hamid Mohebbi, and Javad Mehrabani test vitamin D and intense interval exercise against fatty liver in rats, in a twenty twenty-four study. Forty male rats drank fructose water, which drives new fat making in the liver. Groups added interval running, vitamin D shots, or both for twelve weeks, beside control groups. The team then measured liver fat, blood sugar, and the protein switches of fat making.

Both the exercise and the vitamin raised two guard proteins that brake fat making. They also lowered the main fat-making switches and liver fat stores. The pairing followed the same pattern. The authors say lifestyle steps can undo much of the fructose effect, at least in rats.
pmc-11536932:
William Chen, Leili Abkar, and Madjid Mohseni published a water testing study in two thousand twenty-four on faster microbe checks for distribution systems. ATP tests read living-cell energy molecules in minutes, far quicker than growing colonies. Worries about chlorine neutralisers and waiting times had slowed adoption.

Samples came from two Canadian utilities. In these low-activity waters, ATP and colony counts did not correlate, yet both methods reached the same pass-fail conclusion for ninety-five percent of samples. ATP tracked free chlorine better in one system. Adding the standard chlorine quencher changed nothing, and results held across four to twenty-four hour waits. The authors back ATP as a reliable monitoring swap.
pmc-11572532:
Conghui Huang and Rebecca Lee Smith model coronavirus spread in Illinois primary and middle schools. Schools ran with mask rules and weekly testing from spring 2021 to spring 2022. Their model splits students and staff and tracks spread inside and outside school walls. It was tuned to watch data from 116 school districts in the state.

Spread from outside school ran far above spread inside school for both groups. Middle school students and staff faced higher outside rates than primary students. Wider weekly testing cut infections in the model runs. Adult mask habits in the area showed no clear link while a state mask rule held. The authors note testing costs grow with volume and urge cost checks.
pmc-11577232:
Peter Mukwevho and Naushad Emmambux study why heat-treated Bambara groundnut flour makes thin pastes, in a food science paper from 2024. Bambara groundnut is a hardy African legume. Heating its seeds was known to lower the paste thickness of the flour, which limits its food uses.

Past work blamed heat-changed protein that wraps the starch and hides it from water. The team used the enzyme trypsin to cut the protein in the flour. Microscope views then showed free starch grains and no protein signal. Paste thickness more than doubled after this treatment in one sample set, while the cooking temperature held steady. Heat also reshaped the protein's inner structure, raising sheet forms and cutting helix forms. The authors confirm protein change as the main cause.
pmc-11577532:
Smitesh Padte and co-authors present a 2024 review on whether diabetes raises death risk in pulmonary hypertension. In this disease, pressure in the lung arteries climbs and strains the heart. Diabetes is common in these patients, but its effect on survival was unclear.

The team searched four databases and screened over fifteen hundred papers. Fourteen cohort studies fit their rules and entered the pooled analysis. Together they covered 116,455 patients, of whom 41,228 had diabetes. The review set out to combine the survival results across all fourteen studies. Work of this kind helps doctors weigh diabetes care as part of treatment for a serious lung and heart condition.
pmc-11578932:
Laura Matarredona and co-authors report a 2024 study of salt-loving microbes called haloarchaea and how much stress they can take. These microbes need at least ten percent salt to grow and can live in water that is more than a third salt. Firms already use them in some industrial work. The team asks how well nine kinds cope with toxic metals and other harsh settings.

All nine kinds grew despite metals such as chromium, nickel, cobalt, and arsenic in their medium. One kind stood out: it grew in lithium salt at levels high enough to replace table salt entirely. Another kind soaked up large amounts of lithium inside its cells. The authors say such toughness could help clean polluted water and serve in extreme industrial jobs.
pmc-11583632:
Zhang and co-authors review complicated grief after perinatal loss, the death of a baby around birth. Such loss is a severe stressor that triggers sharp grief in most parents. For some, acute grief deepens over time into a chronic, disabling state called complicated grief.

Despite its weight, no full review had gathered this literature before. The team searched six major databases, from PubMed to Web of Science, for studies on the topic. Their synthesis covers how often complicated grief occurs, who is at risk, and what helps. The work aims to guide care for bereaved parents.
pmc-11585632:
Felix Ritzkowsky and a large team bring optical-frequency electronics onto a chip. Their twenty twenty-four article deals with petahertz electronics, circuits driven by light waves themselves. Attosecond science showed electrons can be steered within one light cycle, but past setups needed huge laser pulses and lab rigs.

The team links many tiny plasmonic antennas into one network on a chip. Driven together, the antennas yield enough charge to detect the carrier-envelope phase of a light pulse in a single shot, at rates of tens of thousands per second. Past designs starved for charge. The authors frame this as a flexible base for future light-speed field sampling and logic.
pmc-11596132:
Ana Glavina and co-authors test the stress cord in folks with primary Sjögren's ill, a dry-mouth and dry-eye auto-immune state. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Past work split on if this cord runs low or high in such folks. Spit cortisol was read in seventeen sick folks and seventeen matched well folks by a lab test.

Sick folks' spit cortisol ran near ten times the well group's, with a clean split past a set cut line. Sick folks also scored far higher on stress, worry, and low mood forms. Mouth health scores ran worse too. The team read the cord as on a short high run in this ill.
pmc-11600232:
Nine researchers led by Miriam Vélez-Bermúdez asked whether a smoother, concierge-style kidney transplant workup improves how patients view their care. The standard workup is long and heavy, above all for Black patients, who report more unfair treatment and mistrust. The study followed eight hundred twenty Black and white adults at one city center.

Patients filled surveys before and after the guided workup, which cut steps and support gaps. The team compared reported unfair treatment, perceived racism, mistrust, and trust in doctors across race and time. The work tests whether easing the process itself can mend strained views of the health system among those waiting for a kidney.
pmc-11603032:
Roszak and co-authors show code tools can design new join acts in vast counts. New act types grow the reach of forms chem hands can build. They can also make old forms at less cost in one step. Join acts, MCRs, build hard forms from more than one start in one pot. For a full age, such acts were found, not made, by hands. Their count stays capped at just a few score in print.

Code taught act paths and stuff rules can design such acts. It does so on its own, in vast counts, in the work runs. Pace marks let the tool guess yields for the new acts. Those guesses flag acts with skill for green aid acts too. Tests on more than one act mode back the tool's calls. Forms made span a wide range of end shapes.
pmc-11603232:
Deng and seven co-authors surveyed the fish of China's Danjiang River in twenty twenty-four by reading DNA that fish shed into the water. This method, called eDNA metabarcoding, can name many species from a water sample without catching a single fish.

The survey found fifty-nine species across eight orders and forty families. Carp-like fish and perch-like fish dominated, and one goby species made up nearly a fifth of the signal. The team also picked up eight rare species and two foreign invaders. Compared with old records from cage catches, the DNA method found far more kinds of fish. Water temperature, acidity, and a measure of chemical reactivity shaped where each community lived. The authors say the method could become a standard tool for river surveys, once local DNA reference libraries improve.
pmc-11603332:
Daodong Chen, Tao Liu, Kunyang Du, and Zhenjun Zhu compare, in a 2024 study, two routes for fusing slipped lumbar vertebrae. Both operations thread a spacer between the bones, one approaching at an angle from the side, the other from the back at a slant. The team reviewed 133 patients treated over three years and tracked pain, daily function, spinal alignment, fusion, and recovery speed.

Both operations eased pain and disability well. The side route gave better lasting pain relief and straighter correction of the spine's curves. Fusion rates were nearly equal, near ninety-seven percent, but the side route's spacers sank less often. Its patients also stood up sooner and left hospital earlier. The authors judge the side approach the better option for this kind of fusion, on the strength of alignment, comfort, and recovery.
pmc-11606032:
Ronan Mullins and co-authors present a 2024 veterinary study on checking spinal screw paths in dogs. Spinal stabilization surgery drills tracts into vertebrae for implants. A tract that breaks the canal wall endangers the spinal cord. Surgeons feel for breaches with a ball-tipped probe. The authors test how reliable that feel is in large-breed dog cadavers. Fifty-six spine segments receive drilled tracts of five types, from intact to full wall breach. Printed guides standardize the drilling.

Two investigators probe each tract twice, two weeks apart, without knowing its type. Scans afterward grade the true state. Sensitivity and specificity scores judge the probe. Veterinary surgeons get hard numbers on a hand skill usually trusted by habit. A probe that misses full breaches needs backup imaging in live cases. Cadaver models let the test run every breach type safely, which live patients never could.
pmc-11608232:
Baeksun Kim and Heh-In Im show that even brief nicotine dependence leaves delayed behavioral and molecular damage in mice, in a two thousand twenty-four neuroscience paper. Withdrawal from acute dependence is known to bite quickly; its long tail had not been explored.

After acute dependence, mice failed a passive avoidance test while anxiety and general learning stayed intact. In the dorsal striatum, F-actin rose abnormally, dendritic spine density fell, and neural population activity dimmed. The microRNA miR-27b dropped throughout the protracted phase, releasing its grip on the membrane gene Marcks, which rose in turn.
