The authors link acute nicotine exposure to lasting striatal dysfunction with a defined molecular signature.
pmc-11608432:
Malai and co-authors show how dwarf grapevines can be grown indoors under LED light in a water-based system. Indoor farms are growing fast, but they need more high-value crops suited to tight, controlled spaces. Dwarf vines, called microvines, fruit early and stay small, which fits that need. The team set out to build methods for copying a new seedless table grape type. They then grew the young vines to first flowering and fruit.

The work covers each step from cuttings to harvest in a fully indoor setup. It tracks how well the clonal copies took root and grew. The case study offers a template for adding grapes to indoor farm crop lists.
pmc-11609132:
Ioannis Liampas and a team of co-authors asked if brain shrink in the front and side lobes ties to mind signs in older adults with no dementia. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, used a large national Alzheimer's data set. Adults of age fifty and up with a read on that shrink were in the pool. They split the pool by thought state: clear minds and mild impairment were read apart. Mind and mood signs came from a set carer form.

Stats models weighed the odds of each of eleven signs next to the shrink mark. Psychotic signs were grouped as one. Readers in brain aging learn which signs walk with this shrink before dementia sets in. That can sharpen who gets a scan or a closer watch.
pmc-11612432:
Xin Wang and five co-authors build a network that sorts mangrove species from drone photos. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Mangroves guard coasts and store carbon, but species differ in their roles, and telling them apart from the air is hard.

Crowded canopies, look-alike shapes, and scarce labeled data all fight accuracy. Costly special sensors help but block wide use. The new network, UrmsNet, works with ordinary drone images. One part sharpens fine features cheaply. Another pays selective attention across scales to separate similar species. A third fuses surface detail with deep meaning so edges and small trees stay crisp. The authors aim for accuracy close to special sensors at routine monitoring cost.
pmc-11615132:
Francisco Javier Giménez and co-authors describe a new methane-making microbe in a 2024 paper. Safe burial of radioactive waste in Belgium's Boom Clay needs a clear picture of the microbes that live deep in the clay. Such microbes make methane, which shapes the local chemistry.

The team isolated a strain from clay pore water and studied its genes and growth. The strain is a new species, named Methanosarcina hadiensis. Its round cells are wrapped in a slime-like layer. It grows on methyl compounds or hydrogen to make methane, but not on acetate under the tested conditions. Its traits place it between two known groups of its genus.
pmc-11615332:
Maximiliano Anzibar Fialho and a team of co-authors scan the brains of mice modeling a nerve disease, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is classed as a disease of outer nerves. The Trembler-J mouse copies one severe human form.

Using working ultrasound, the team watched blood flow in the touch cortex during whisker stimulation. Sick mice showed weaker responses and a smaller active area than healthy mice. Links between brain regions also shifted in the sick group. The authors argue the disease reaches the central nervous system, not just the limbs.
pmc-11617332:
Randall and co-authors chart how children's respiratory infections swung across the COVID years in this 2024 study. Lockdowns famously suppressed common viruses, and the rebound after reopening was unclear. The team reviewed every respiratory test at a large children's hospital from 2018 to 2023.

Before 2020 the lab ran a median of 1,080 tests a week with positivity near 4 percent. In 2020 volume halved to 486 a week and positivity fell to 1.74 percent. After schools reopened in 2021, tests recovered partly and positivity returned to 4.07 percent. The panel covers flu, RSV, and many lesser viruses. The record gives a baseline for judging future seasonal surges.
pmc-11621432:
Hye Ran Shin, SuJin Song, and Sun Yung Ly build and test a survey tool that estimates vitamin D intake from food among Korean women, in a paper from 2024. Vitamin D supports bone health and may help against chronic disease. Intake data for Koreans were scarce, which made status hard to judge.

The tool asks how often thirty-one foods rich in the vitamin are eaten, drawn from eight food groups common in Korea. Just over one hundred and fifty women took part. Their intake was tracked with a twelve-day food record across four seasons and with the new survey twice, about ten months apart. The survey gave slightly higher intake values than the record. Repeat surveys agreed well, and checks supported the tool's validity.
pmc-11622432:
Peter Calverley comments on how doctors grade the severity of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, in a 2024 editorial. Grading guides treatment, and for decades it has rested on a breathing test with set cut points. The scheme used worldwide sorts patients by how far their lung capacity has fallen.

Calverley traces this habit back to the long history of classifying disease by measurable traits. He weighs a newer staging idea, hinted at by the STAR in his title, against the charge of merely reshuffling the same groups. Lung capacity remains the strongest single predictor of death, he notes. Any new scheme must prove it adds real insight beyond that number. The piece is a caution against relabeling without better prediction.
pmc-11625432:
Jinrui Ji and colleagues test whether two blood inflammation scores can flag dangerous heart artery plaques. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses light-based artery imaging. Vulnerable plaques rupture and cause heart attacks without warning. Finding them before rupture is a cardiology priority.

Over five hundred acute syndrome patients underwent artery imaging. Plaque type was classified by optical coherence tomography directly. Both inflammation scores ran higher in the dangerous plaque group. A standard inflammation protein also ran higher there. Statistical modelling built a combined prediction approach. Accuracy curves judged the scores' diagnostic value. Cheap blood scores could triage who needs invasive imaging.
pmc-11628432:
Anja Cannon, Caitlon Jacoby, and Allyson Hughes published a literature review in 2024. They examine links between diabetes and serious mental illness. Three conditions are covered: schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and OCD. Living with both diabetes and mental illness is hard. Care teams also struggle to coordinate treatment well. The review covers rates, shared risks, and care implications. Recent studies show strong metabolic links overall. Many psychiatric drugs promote weight gain and metabolic disease.

Evidence on two-way effects remains limited for these conditions. Most prior work studied depression and anxiety instead. Treatment gaps and service gaps appear repeatedly. Patients may fall between separate care systems. The authors call for integrated research and practice. Screening for diabetes in psychiatric care seems important. Joint clinics could reduce the burden described.
pmc-11629532:
Roqaia Radwan, Wafaa El-kholy, Afaf Elsaed, and Ahmad Darwish study leukemia risk factors in Egyptian children in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia grows aggressively, in part by evading cell death. Two signaling proteins may shape that risk: one that promotes cell death and one that promotes growth.

The team compared one hundred child patients with one hundred healthy controls. A gene variant in the death-promoting protein was tied to higher risk of the disease. Patients also had much lower blood levels of the growth factor than controls, counter to its usual role. That factor sorted patients from controls with very high accuracy in their tests. The authors call for larger, more diverse studies to confirm the findings.
pmc-11636632:
Steffen Koschmieder wrote this review of new treatments for myelofibrosis in two thousand twenty-four. Myelofibrosis is a blood cancer in which scar tissue fills the bone marrow. It brings a swollen spleen, heavy symptoms, and risk of clots, bleeding, infection, or shift to acute leukemia. Care today is matched to risk scores. High-risk patients may be checked for a stem cell transplant, the only cure so far.

Lower-risk patients with symptoms often get JAK inhibitors or other drugs. Yet no drug has brought lasting full remission for many patients. The review sums up lab and trial work on fresh options. These include new drug pairs built around JAK inhibitors and new single drugs. It gives clinicians a clear map of where treatment may head next.
pmc-11638532:
Chiara Frascarelli and co-authors published a 2024 study on teaching a computer to read breast cancer slides for signs of a key gene's damage. The gene, TP53, guards against cancer and is often broken in aggressive breast tumors. Standard tests for its status can be finicky and vary between observers. The team asked whether deep learning could read the status straight from routine stained slides.

A pre-trained network was taught to find tumor areas and predict the gene's status from the images. Its maps matched the tumor regions well. Predictions were checked against staining tests and gene sequencing. The model flagged abnormal protein patterns across ninety-two percent of the tumor area, close to the ninety percent found by staining. The authors call this a proof of concept. Software reading of slides could speed biomarker testing and steady its quality, though real-world validation is still needed.
pmc-11640032:
Peng and a large team of colleagues find a cow gene that mutes lung fight in TB germ tests in this twenty twenty-four study. A germ kin of the human TB germ lives in cows and can live long in their cells. How it dodges the cell's fight was not fully known till now.

Inside, a gene with a nitric link was cut out of cow lung skin cells by gene snips. Cells with no such gene let far fewer germs live and died less by their hand. Their fight scents and gas marks rose in step with the gene's loss. Gene reads showed whole fight paths lit up in the cut cells. The team casts the gene as a brake the germ leans on to live.
pmc-11640332:
Juan García-García, Miguel García-García, Juan Mauricio, and colleagues profile proteins inside yeast biocapsules in this two thousand twenty-four food science paper. Yeast biocapsules are spheres of yeast cells attached to the threads of a fungus, a new way to hold cells still for brews such as beer and wine. Holding cells still promises better control, product quality, and process gains. The authors used gel proteomics to compare protein levels in trapped versus free yeast.

The trapped cells' proteins centered on DNA repair, cell cycle control, protein synthesis, and translation. Free cells instead showed mainly glycolysis proteins. The contrast suggests the trapped yeast mounts a defense response against its fungal partner, coordinated across DNA, RNA, and protein levels. The authors frame the study as opening work on yeast-fungus trapping: stress responses, binding polymers, and biocapsule proteomics, with possible new uses.
pmc-11640532:
Lina Ma and co-authors scanned the genomes of 256 Chinese Tan sheep to find DNA variants behind three traits. These are wool length at birth, birth weight, and head color. The breed is prized for lambskin and curly white wool. Whole-genome sequencing yielded over twenty-three million variants. The search tied 208 variants to wool length, over a thousand to birth weight, mostly on one chromosome, and as many to head color.

Candidate genes emerged for each trait, including a pigmentation gene for head color. A follow-up test in 102 sheep confirmed five variants in that gene, with black-headed animals usually carrying one copy of each form. The authors say the results lay groundwork for breeding programs. Marker-assisted selection could speed improvement of the breed. The study adds to knowledge of the breed's genetic structure. Each trait has named suspects for functional follow-up.
pmc-11641732:
Dina Hamed and co-authors report a 2024 study of frozen shoulder. The condition brings pain and a stiff shoulder that barely moves. The team asks whether body chemistry links to pain and function in these patients. Blood markers cover liver enzymes and thyroid function. The study held 32 patients, 22 women and 10 men, seen at one point in time.

Each patient had clinic checks and blood tests on the same plan. A standard index scored shoulder pain and disability. The team ran links and combined models between markers and scores. If chemistry tracks pain, doctors may gain extra clues beyond the shoulder exam. Metabolic health is already tied to frozen shoulder risk in other work. The small, one-time design limits strong claims. Still, the study maps which markers deserve a larger, longer test in this patient group.
pmc-11641832:
Mateusz Werłos and six co-authors tested a modified light-sensitive dye for cancer therapy that uses light to kill tumors, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Adding a simple amino acid unit to the dye was the single change under study. The base dye family absorbs deep-red light, which can reach further into tissue.

The modified dye absorbs even deeper-red light and stays stable enough to work. Under light it makes both of the reactive oxygen forms that damage cancer cells. The added units also help it enter a breast cancer cell line that often pumps drugs out. In animal tests, it gathered in tumor vessels before light treatment. The authors see it as a strong candidate for targeted therapy.
pmc-11642032:
Sajan, Griepp, and Isaacson compare imaging and radiation dose across two angiography systems in twenty twenty-four. The procedure treats an enlarged prostate by blocking its arteries. Cone beam CT helps guide the work. Use of that scan and total radiation may depend on the machine.

One hundred twenty patients treated by one specialist were reviewed. Cone beam CT was used in thirty-one percent of cases on the first system. On the second system it was used in eighty-five percent. Total radiation dose was far higher on the first system. Fluoroscopy time did not differ between systems. The authors conclude the equipment choice strongly shapes imaging use and exposure. Lower exposure also protects staff.
pmc-11642432:
Aída Moreno-Juste, Beatriz Poblador-Plou, Clara Laguna-Berna, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It maps the crowd of other diseases that travel with chronic liver disease, using health records for nearly seven thousand patients in a Spanish cohort.

Patients averaged sixty-two years of age, and women made up about sixty-three percent. Each carried an average of thirteen chronic conditions. High blood pressure, blood fat disorders, diabetes, obesity, and muscle and joint diseases led the list. Of one hundred ten conditions checked, seventy-five were statistically tied to liver disease. Chronic pancreatitis stood out with odds over forty times higher. Factor analysis found three recurring multimorbidity patterns, similar in men and women. The authors say liver care that ignores the entourage will misjudge both patients and budgets.
pmc-11642532:
Joana Mota Gomes and eight colleagues extract useful compounds from banana leaves and weave them into fabric, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Banana leaves are agricultural residue, rich in phenolics and antioxidants. Hemp knitwear is a natural textile that can carry them well. The team joins the two in one line of work.

Three extraction methods were set side by side. They were the conventional way, ultrasound-assisted, and pressurized-liquid extraction. Water and two strengths of hydroethanolic solvent were tested in turn. Phenolic content and antioxidant activity were gauged with standard assays. Ultrasound and pressurized methods raised phenolic yields by a lot. The extracts were then padded onto cationized hemp fabric. Functionalized textiles of this kind aim at gains for the skin, or at antimicrobial wear. The work ties the picks made at the extraction step head-on to how the end product performs.
pmc-11643932:
Osamu Shimomura leads a team on a hidden catalyst for urethane making. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with DABCO inside zirconium phosphate layers. The mix was tested with a standard isocyanate and butanol.

At room temperature the catalyst showed no activity. At higher heat it became strongly active. Viscosity rose fast at that heat in half an hour. Release of the amine from the layers was tracked. Butanol proved key to freeing the amine guest. The other liquid showed no such release signs. Two end group monomers were also tested.
pmc-11645432:
Kiyoshi Shikino and six co-authors surveyed residency program directors across Japan about overtime limits for young doctors, in this 2024 study. New rules cap resident overtime in tiers, and directors must balance training depth against rest. The survey went to 701 teaching hospitals, and 254 replied.

Most directors favored about forty extra hours a month as the right balance between skill building and mental well-being. Only a quarter picked that figure outright, but the average landed there too. The authors note a gap between what directors judge wise and what current rosters actually demand. They offer the results to policymakers weighing training quality against doctor health, in Japan and beyond.
pmc-11647932:
Manato Ohsawa and twelve colleagues published a 2024 review on a bacterium, Fusobacterium nucleatum, and its influence on cancer treatment. The bacterium, normally found in the mouth, tends to clump and form biofilms, protective communities that shield microbes from drugs and the immune system.

Biofilm-forming microbes inside tumors can blunt the effectiveness of cancer treatments, including radiotherapy. Esophageal cancer still kills a large share of its patients despite combined surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation. The review examines how this bacterium affects those treatments and discusses its future potential role in esophageal cancer, whether as a target to attack, a marker of prognosis, or both. Understanding tumor microbes may open a new lever in cancer care.
pmc-11648132:
Huanhuan Chen, Nawaz Haider Bashir, Lei Zhu, Tong-Xing Zhao, Tao Xu, Yong Gao, and Yong-Kang Sima sequence the chloroplast genome of a rare protected plant, in a 2024 study. The plant is a Schisandra species with large fruit. It recently joined China's national protection list. The team used a high-throughput sequencing platform. The full chloroplast genome ran about one hundred forty-four thousand letters. Its structure followed the classic four-part layout.

Two single-copy regions are split by a pair of repeats. Overall, the letters G and C made up forty percent. Annotation found one hundred twenty-eight genes. Most code for proteins, with the rest for RNA parts. Family analysis placed the species near a known relative. The authors offer the genome for conservation work. It can guide identification and breeding decisions.
pmc-11648932:
Michael Stubna, Aditi Shukla, and David Bartel show that a cellular enzyme widely destabilises small regulatory RNAs in the roundworm. Their 2025 study examines a degradation pathway in which special transcripts trigger destruction of the RNA's protein partner.

Twenty-two small RNAs proved sensitive to losing the worm version of the enzyme, implying they undergo this targeted degradation. Effects varied by life stage, peaking in young larvae by pool share and in germline-free adults by count. Sensitive RNAs included a well-known family and many of the worm's least stable RNAs generally. Excess family members accumulating without the enzyme repressed their target messages more strongly. Changing one RNA's tail region sharply reduced its sensitivity, unlike an earlier family example.
pmc-11649332:
David Voegeli and co-authors (2024) ran a randomized trial of a new wound dressing for chronic ulcers. The dressing is a silicone foam shaped by 3DFit technology to fit the wound bed. In an open trial across several centers, 102 patients with leaking, uninfected chronic ulcers were split evenly between the new foam and standard care, a filler plus a cover dressing. The patients had venous leg ulcers or diabetic foot ulcers, and care ran for four weeks.

Wound shrinkage was similar in both groups, about 54 percent with the new foam and 43 percent with standard care, a gap too small to rule out chance. Total costs, though, were clearly lower with the single foam, about a third less than the two-dressing routine over the four weeks. The authors conclude the foam heals as well as standard care for ulcers up to two centimeters deep while costing less.
pmc-11650332:
Yunho Jung and twelve colleagues published a randomised trial in two thousand twenty-four on bowel cleansing before colonoscopy. A clean bowel is essential for spotting polyps. Sulfate tablets offer an alternative to drinking two litres of the standard solution.

Two hundred eleven healthy adults at thirteen Korean hospitals took either the tablets or the standard drink, in split doses. Overall success rates were nearly equal on two scoring scales. The tablet group scored higher on total cleanliness and on top-grade cleaning in every bowel segment. Patients rated the tablets better on taste, ease, and amount, and more would repeat the same prep. Side effects and lab changes matched between groups.
pmc-11653032:
Arsi Ikäheimonen and colleagues published a 2024 study using smartphone data to track depression. Diagnosis and follow-up usually rely on interviews and questionnaires. Phones quietly record behavior all day. Such data might reveal symptom patterns. The team followed patients and healthy volunteers for up to a year.

The patient group covered several depressive disorders. Phone behavior data were collected continuously. Researchers tested whether the data could flag depression. They also checked whether it tracked symptom changes. Reliable phone markers could support care between clinic visits. The study adds evidence on both promise and limits.
pmc-11653832:
Maria Antonietta Gambacorta and nine co-authors set out a study plan for rectal cancer that has come back after past radiation. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Such returns have a poor outlook. Past work shows rays plus surgery raise the odds of a clean cut-out, but many cases cannot be cut at all.

The RETRY study, run across Italian centres, tests chemo with rays in all forms on hand. Forms span classic rays, proton and carbon beams, and tight high-dose rays. Surgery follows when it can. Those who cannot be cut get a higher-dose carbon plan. The main aim is local control at three years, with life, life quality, and clean cut rates as side aims.
pmc-11654332:
Yap and co-authors weigh carglumic acid for long-term care of two rare acid buildup disorders. Propionic and methylmalonic acidurias stem from faults in one metabolic path. Both can trigger high ammonia through a side fault in the urea cycle.

Carglumic acid copies a natural activator of the urea cycle's first step. It is approved to treat high ammonia in both disorders and is well tolerated. Its short-term use in acute episodes is well proven. This expert review searched PubMed for chronic use proof. It also weighs diet, ammonia scavengers, transplant, and gene therapy in long-term care.
pmc-11655532:
Liangbo Zhao and a large team of co-authors name a fresh driver of colon cancer growth, in a study published in twenty twenty-four. Colon cancer ranks among the most common cancers and the top causes of cancer death. Its inner workings stay partly unclear, so new targets are needed.

Scanning genes that run hot in tumors flagged one called CPNE7. It ran high in colon tumors, and patients with more of it fared worse. Raising it made cancer cells grow and spread faster in dishes and in animals; lowering it did the reverse. The protein works by teaming with a partner to switch on a second gene. Blocking that team-up, with a gene-silencing tool or a small drug, slowed tumors in animals. The chain offers a new target.
pmc-11656732:
Kincaid and three co-authors trace how breathed-in prions reach the brain in hamsters in this twenty twenty-four study. Prions are bent proteins that seed grave brain ills in beasts and folks. Breath-in is a far more sure catch route than food, yet why was not known.

Inside, nose-linked nerve hubs were checked for prion loads week by week past a dose. Loads showed first in the face-feel nerve hub and its brain stem path. Loads also lit in cord hubs that serve the gut nerve net far down the line. The smell nerve hub stayed clean for months past the dose date. The team names the face nerve as the new direct road to the brain.
pmc-11657232:
Qianting Deng and six co-authors review gamma waves in the brain and efforts to tune them, in a 2024 paper. Gamma waves are fast rhythms that help brain regions work together in sight, movement, memory, and feeling. When these rhythms falter, several brain disorders seem to follow.

The review lists ways to nudge the brain into gamma rhythm, from light and sound pulses to magnetic and electric stimulation applied through the scalp. It then weighs links between faulty gamma activity and illnesses such as Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, stroke, schizophrenia, and autism. Early evidence hints that rhythm tuning may protect the brain, though results are mixed. The authors call gamma tuning a promising but unsettled path for treatment research.
pmc-11657432:
Fei Li, Yanjun Luo, Xin Li, Yan Dai, and Qingping Xiang pool studies on whether metabolic syndrome raises glaucoma risk, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Nine studies with over two million people fed the pool. The syndrome bundles pressure, sugar, fat, and waist risks.

The pooled odds ran about a third higher for glaucoma with the syndrome. High pressure and high sugar parts carried the tie, while waist and fat parts did not. Study style, age, sex, and eye type did not bend the result. The authors urge eye checks for people with the syndrome. Cause still needs proof. Readers get a firm link with its drivers named.
pmc-11657632:
Lin Yao and co-authors ask, in a 2024 study, whether gaining too much weight in pregnancy raises the chance of catching the Omicron variant of COVID-19. They studied pregnant women treated at a hospital in China during December 2022, when the variant spread widely. Women who caught the virus were compared with those who did not.

The study covered 369 women, of whom 113 were infected. Weight gain above the level set by a United States medical guideline was linked to a higher chance of infection, and the link held after other traits were taken into account. The pattern was clearest in women whose weight had been in the normal range before pregnancy, where high gain more than doubled the odds. The authors name high gain as an independent risk factor in that group.
pmc-11658132:
Min Shen and co-authors look back at hospital records in a 2024 study of lung tuberculosis in Tibetan teens who live at high altitude. Teen cases at such heights are often missed or reported late. The study, done at Linzhi People's Hospital in China, sets out the signs, test results, and chest images seen in these young patients.

The team compared sixty-three teens with one hundred ninety-two adults, all newly found to have the disease. Classic signs of the illness were much less common in the teen group. Sputum samples were tested with a gene-based assay for the germ that causes the disease. The comparison brings out ways teen cases differ from adult ones, which can help doctors in high areas spot the illness sooner in young people.
pmc-11659332:
Ozgur Mete and a panel of experts issue consensus advice in 2024 on biomarker testing for thyroid cancer. Gene tests on inherited and tumor DNA now guide targeted treatment, but testing practice varies and patients are missed. The panel reviewed world guidelines and the evidence for tests that can change care.

Algorithms are given for the main thyroid cancer types, from medullary to the most aggressive anaplastic form. The advice stays neutral about which drug to use, so it fits many health systems and budgets. Gaps in testing access are discussed, with stress on team based care. The aim is steady, fair application of biomarker testing in practice.
pmc-11662632:
Jialin Gu, Hongqun Zhang, Kang Qian, Xunwen Ye, and Guolin Wu map world research on excess weight in women with certain cancers, in a 2024 analysis. The cancers are those of the female organs and the breast. Obesity is a major public health concern tied to these diseases. The team searched a large citation database. They covered work from 2013 to late 2024. Software tools charted output, citations, and partnerships.

Nearly fifteen hundred papers were analyzed. Output has grown steadily over the decade. The United States leads in both papers and citations. China and Italy follow. Two journals anchor the field. Hot topics include body mass index and cancer risk. Survival, physical activity, and fat tissue inflammation also rank high. Newer themes involve cell vesicles and tumor support cells. The authors urge work on how obesity drives these cancers at the molecular level.
pmc-11671932:
Shaida Ouladan and Elias Orouji present a 2024 commentary on new ways to slice colorectal cancer into subtypes. Classic consensus subtypes lean on gene activity alone. Two newer schemes add deeper layers: one sorts tumors by their enhancer landscapes, the other by pathway behavior rather than single genes. The commentary walks through how the schemes overlap and clash.

The enhancer scheme splits one classic subtype into groups with sharply different survival. The pathway scheme found three groups, the worst marked by fewer stem cells and more mature cells. Both split the same classic subtype in telling ways. The authors argue layered genomics should sharpen prognosis and treatment choice.
pmc-11672432:
Sung Young Lee, Ji-Hyun Nam, Jung Wook Kim, Soo Hyun Kim, and Jung Sik Yoo track a stealthy form of drug-resistant gut bacteria in Korea, in a 2024 study. These enterococci carry resistance genes yet still test sensitive to the drug vancomycin. If missed, they can switch on resistance during treatment. The team examined over three thousand bloodstream isolates gathered from 2017 to 2022 through a national surveillance system.

Nearly six percent of the isolates were of this variable type. Two species made up the count. While full resistance cases have fallen since 2020, the variable type is rising. Only one resistance gene variant appeared in Korea. Most isolates belonged to one hospital-linked family group. Three sequence types dominated. The authors urge labs to test both drug response and genes. Watching these strains closely matters, since each one is a step from open resistance.
pmc-11672632:
Kuanfeng Zhu and co-authors study how seminal plasma affects freezing of boar sperm in this 2024 paper. Frozen sperm is key to pig breeding programs. Some boars freeze well and others poorly. The fluid part of semen may carry factors that explain that gap. The team compared plasma from high and low freezability boars.

Semen came from 30 boars, with 11 high and 11 low freezers chosen after repeated tests. Six reproductive hormones showed no clear link to freezing success. Protein and metabolite profiling found clear differences between the two plasma types. Plasma from good freezers was then used directly as a freezing base to test protection. The findings point to plasma components that could improve standard freezing media.
pmc-11673432:
Moussa and colleagues published in twenty twenty-four a study making silver nanoparticles with a sage plant extract. Green synthesis avoids harsh chemicals by using plant chemistry instead. The team used common sage extract to form the particles under tuned conditions. A battery of instruments confirmed particle size, shape, and surface charge. They then tested antioxidant power with standard radical assays. Antibacterial tests covered eleven strains plus bacteria from industrial wastewater.

The particles showed strong antioxidant activity in both assays. They stopped bacterial growth at far lower doses than the extract alone. That held for resistant strains and for wastewater isolates too. The extract itself also showed useful activity in both roles. The authors propose uses in medicine and in sustainable wastewater treatment. Dual action makes the particles attractive for both fields.
pmc-11673532:
Jun Hirose and co-authors published a 2024 study of delivering gene editing into living animals with fat-based nanoparticles. Editing genes inside the body could fix single-gene diseases, but delivery is the bottleneck. The team used a knock-in method that does not need a matching DNA template, and it beat the classic template-based route in liver cells. They tuned the particle recipe and dosing route for the task.

Shipped through a vein, the particles inserted a marker gene into mouse liver DNA in about 2 to 3 percent of cells. Repeating the dose roughly doubled that share, suggesting the edits add up over treatments. The authors present the result as a foundation for nanoparticle knock-in therapy. Human use would need higher rates and careful safety work.
pmc-11674532:
Abdulaziz Alodhialah, Ashwaq Almutairi, and Mohammed Almutairi studied why older adults in Saudi Arabia skip cancer screening. Screening catches cancer early and lifts survival, yet many older people face blocks. The team surveyed one hundred adults aged sixty and up in Riyadh and held talks with twenty of them.

Three barrier groups stood out. Getting there was hard, with transport and service gaps. Fear and worry about a cancer finding held others back. Family support was thin, and social stigma played a part too. The authors call for fixes that join all three fronts, and they draw lessons for cancer nurses who guide older patients to screening.
pmc-11674632:
Chia-Ming Wu led a large team tracing a deadly pattern in bowel cancer in a 2024 paper. Spread of the cancer is the usual reason for poor outlook, yet some non-spread patients also die early. A transcription factor and a long non-coding RNA team up in tumors and mark worse survival regardless of spread. The team screened their shared target genes and focused on two growth genes downstream.

Tumors with high levels of the pair plus high cell-cycle gene but low signaling gene did worst, with survival dropping steeply by year three. The opposite mix did better. The authors suggest drugs blocking that cell-cycle path for the poor-outlook group.
pmc-11675232:
Hanxuan Zhou presents a 2024 paper on a quantum teleportation scheme for four participants. Teleportation moves a quantum state using shared entanglement plus ordinary messages. Here Alice and Bob each send two-qubit states while Charlie sends a three-qubit state, all in a cycle, supervised by David, who guards security.

The channel uses eleven entangled states, and the protocol runs on special measurements and corrective operations. Analysis shows the transfer can succeed with probability one hundred percent in the ideal case. Real channels are noisy, so Zhou checks four noise types, from bit flips to full depolarizing. Fidelity then depends only on the starting state's shape and the noise rate. A comparison with earlier schemes argues this one is more efficient.
pmc-11675632:
Cameron Foreman and his team studied how to test random number generators in two thousand twenty-four. Such tools are hard to build and hard to check, yet they are key for safe codes. Tests based on chance patterns are the main way to judge their output.

The team ran deep tests on three generators, from a simple chip design to a quantum device. They then cleaned up each output with tools that pull purer chance from weak chance, and tested again. A test suite they built can run in quick or deep modes. The work lets users compare clean-up methods side by side and pick what works best.
pmc-11676332:
Pagani, Tasca, De Vincenti, and Fedi report using heat ablation to stop bleeding from a ruptured liver tumor, in a case report from twenty twenty-four. Spontaneous rupture of liver cancer is rare but can kill quickly. Best management is still debated among specialists. Their patient is a seventy-four-year-old man with cirrhosis in hemorrhagic shock.

Scans confirm the rupture, and emergency surgery follows. Standard hemostasis fails in the operating room. Given instability, poor liver reserve, and multifocal tumor, the team turns to ultrasound-guided ablation. Heat seals the bleeding site successfully. The patient recovers in intensive care and returns to the ward in two days. The authors back ablation for unstable cases.
pmc-11676432:
Mirela Văduva leads a team that reviews iron oxide carbon nanocomposites. Their review from twenty twenty-four deals with biomedical uses. The mixes pair magnetite with carbon nanotubes or graphene forms.

They show promise for tissue repair and cancer heat therapy. The magnetic part makes heat under alternating fields. They can also carry drugs to target sites. Spread in body fluids and clumping block wider use. Wet co precipitation is the most common build route. Sizes and shapes of the mixes are surveyed. Synthesis routes are compared in the text here.
pmc-11677132:
Reza Yarahmadi and his team weigh the spread found in the wild in plant goods and scent oils in groups of common myrtle in Iran. Their 2024 study takes leaf tests from twelve groups in their home ground, for use in drugs and farm work.

Leaves picked in twenty twenty-three were tested for all phenols, for flavonoids, for strength to fight air harm, and for scent oil share and mix. Phenol grades and strength to fight air harm swung a lot from group to group. One check group showed the most phenols and flavonoids, while two more groups showed the most strength to fight air harm. Scent oil share ran wide, with two groups at the top. Gas tests found twenty-nine clear oil parts, with more than one big part shared by groups.
pmc-11678232:
Bin Wang and Xu Meng design a branched molecule that kills bacteria while staying gentle on body cells, in a study from 2024. Their molecule joins two known parts: a four-arm branched core called PAMAM and a bacteria-killing chain called PHMB. The joined form is named PAPB in the study.

Tests showed that PAPB killed both main classes of bacteria well. Joining the two parts gave a stronger joint effect than either part alone. The branched core also lowered the harm to mouse cells used in the lab tests. The authors present the design as a route to safer antibacterial materials for medical use.
pmc-11680332:
Lei Wang and co-authors published a study in 2024 on a pig virus test. The virus harms pig herds around the world and has no vaccine on the market. A fast, cheap blood test would help farms and vets track its spread. The team built such a test around a shell protein of the virus.

Their test runs on a fully automated machine and uses light to read the result. In trials, it caught about ninety-seven in a hundred true cases and cleared most healthy samples. It did not react to two kindred pig viruses or to other common pig germs. Results matched a shop-bought kit in about ninety-five in a hundred cases. A survey with the new test showed the virus is still wide-spread in South China.
pmc-11683232:
Ying Lin and co-authors present a lab protocol for spotting Notch1 signaling in blood vessel tissue, in this 2024 paper. Notch signaling steers vessel development, new vessel growth, and steady upkeep. Seeing its components in fixed tissue takes a sensitive staining method. Their recipe uses tyramide signal amplification, a booster step that brightens weak signals.

The protocol tailors each stage: antigen retrieval tuned for vessel samples, blocking solutions, and a linked enzyme complex that deposits the tyramide dye. Wash steps are optimized to cut background noise. The authors aim the method at vascular samples where Notch parts are scarce and easy to miss. Full usage details point back to the group's earlier study. The recipe gives vessel researchers a repeatable way to map Notch activity.
pmc-11683632:
Pradeep Kumar Gollapudi, Kranthi Kumar Gollapudi, and Nimmagadda Padmaja devised a fast lab method to gauge nitrate and nitrite in water in twenty twenty-four. Both ions matter for the safety of natural waters, and gauging them together is a routine need. The team built the method with a quality-by-design plan, testing choices in a set order rather than by trial and error.

The method runs on a liquid chromatography rig with a fluorophenyl column and a steady, single-mix solvent flow. Detection uses ultraviolet light, and each run takes a five-microliter sample. Checks under global guidelines showed the method was sound on setup fit, sensitivity, exactness, and straight-line response. The authors say the method is highly sensitive and fit for gauging both ions in many kinds of natural water samples.
pmc-11688032:
Cheng Li, Yong Luo, Yan Jiang, Xumiao Wu, and Qi Li build a prediction tool for breast screening in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Mammography misses cancers in women with dense breasts, and added ultrasound catches more but flags many harmless masses, causing needless biopsies. The authors aimed to predict which masses found by ultrasound after a clear mammogram are malignant, raising its hit rate. Past data on four hundred twenty-five masses, eighty of them malignant, were split into training and test sets.

A selection method picked the five predictors for the nomogram. The model split cases strongly, with area under the curve near zero point nine one in training and zero point eight eight in the test set. Fit checks showed good match. The nomogram aims to keep ultrasound's gains in finding cancers while cutting the biopsy load from false alarms.
pmc-11688232:
Li and co-authors compare seven body measures for spotting insulin resistance in Chinese adults. Insulin resistance underlies many metabolic diseases, so early flags matter. The study gathered history, body measures, and blood samples at three hospitals in China. Measures ranged from body mass index to waist ratios and shape indexes. Two candidates, waist-to-height ratio and body roundness index, are simple to take. Resistance was judged with a standard model based on fasting values.

The team tested how well each measure sorts people by risk. Age and sex were factored into the comparison. Simple tape-based measures can reach people clinics miss. The authors name the strongest of the simple tools for screening use.
pmc-11689832:
Teresa Liu-Ambrose and six co-authors report a year-long trial of strength training for people with a form of memory loss caused by poor blood flow in the brain. The work, from two thousand twenty-four, tests if lifting and pushing work can help thought.

Ninety-one older adults took part. Half did strength training twice a week, and half did balance and tone work. All had small vessel disease and mild loss, but not dementia. At one year, the training group scored better on a broad test of thought. The gain was clear in women but not in men. The authors say this training should be part of care for this group.
pmc-11690932:
Debra Dobbs and Hongdao Meng introduce a set of four studies on dementia care in a 2024 symposium paper. About six point seven million people in the United States live with dementia, and the count will grow as the population ages. Family members and front-line care workers give most of the care, across homes, centers, and hospice.

Each study tests a support plan in a distinct setting. One taught palliative care in assisted living homes to boost advance care planning. One used a virtual dementia tour to train clinicians in the veterans' health system. One tried group digital games in adult day centers. One tested online pain support for hospice caregivers at home. The session weighs how far each plan could spread.
pmc-11691032:
Hannah Wilks and co-authors test how setting, mood, and tiredness affect scores on phone-based thinking tests in older adults at risk of Alzheimer disease. Remote tests help researchers track the subtle changes that come before dementia, but daily life may sway the results. The team follows 288 adults, with an average age of 75, recruited from a research center. Each person takes short tests on a phone app up to 28 times over one week, in real-life settings.

Memory and processing speed both scored worse when other people were present, when the test happened away from home, and after quiet, seated activity. Mood and tiredness showed no clear link to scores. The setting effects grew stronger in people who already had very mild dementia symptoms, above all for processing speed. The authors warn that studies using remote tests should record where and how each test was taken.
pmc-11691532:
Deborah Dadson and Karlene Ball ask whether chronic disease changes how cognitive training affects mobility in older adults, in work published in 2024. Mobility loss ties to disease, inactivity, and fear of falls. Cognitive training has been shown to improve gait and daily function, offering an option for adults who cannot exercise much.

The analysis used a large trial of over twenty-eight hundred community-dwelling adults aged sixty-five and up. Training types covered reasoning, memory, and processing speed. Life-space mobility was modelled against training, with diabetes, cancer, and heart disease as moderators. Speed-of-processing training, education, and heart disease each predicted mobility. Reasoning and memory training did not. The authors highlight processing speed as the active ingredient for everyday function.
pmc-11692032:
Taylor Fein, Muhammad Thalil, and Soomi Lee study how short sleep and exercise together relate to heart rhythm variation, in two thousand twenty-four. Variation in the time between heartbeats is a sign of heart health. Both sleep and exercise are tied to it on their own, but their joint effect was less clear.

Their sample held close to four hundred middle-aged American adults with sleep tracking and heart measures. Neither short sleep nor low exercise alone showed a clear link. Together, though, they mattered: short sleepers who exercised little had lower variation than short sleepers who exercised enough. Among good sleepers, exercise made no such difference. The authors suggest exercise may blunt the harm of short sleep.
pmc-11692632:
Rebecca Koszalinski and six co-authors test whether older adults accept smartwatches for health tracking. Their 2024 pilot ran in an independent living community in the southeastern United States. Wearables can flag health changes cheaply, but older users often disengage. The team asked whether the barrier is skill, interest, or bias.

Twenty-seven residents agreed to join. All who started wore the watches for one to five days. Engagement stayed high across months of data collection in 2023. Comments praised the look, comfort, and the data shown. A few flagged the watch's size and weight. Several wanted the clock kept right to manage their own time. Interest, it seems, was never the problem.
pmc-11696632:
Zakeri and four co-authors build a fast search index for whole kin gene sets in this twenty twenty-four paper. Such sets hold the full gene range of a species, not one lone code. Fast search in them helps sort the tiny reads that pour from gene decks.

Inside, the tool rests on a packed index form that grows with runs of like signs, not raw size. It can run deep match checks that past tools ran far more slowly in tests. Speed comes from fewer cache slips and from fetch tricks that hide wait time. The team casts it as a fit for live calls, like quick pick of which reads to keep at a deck.
pmc-11698932:
Tahar Kernif and co-authors present a 2024 review on whether ticks can carry a family of single-celled parasites. Members of the Trypanosomatidae cause serious disease in people and animals, and their DNA keeps turning up inside ticks. Finding DNA is not the same as spreading disease, so the vector question stayed open.

The team searched three databases for studies from 1912 to mid-2023, keeping ninety-four papers for review and eighty-six for pooled analysis. About 15.5 percent of ticks tested positive, with rates varying by year, method, and region. Most positive ticks came from four genera. Lab experiments showed both soft and hard ticks can potentially pass the parasites on. The authors weigh what that means for surveillance.
pmc-11706732:
Darshika Amarakoon and co-authors identify a possible cancer driver in 2024 in colon cancer cells. The gene in question, TRAPδ, helps move new proteins into a cell's processing hub. Its role in disease had not been studied before.

When the team dialed the gene down in colon cancer cell lines, the cells' survival dropped sharply. Some lines stalled at set points in their growth cycle, and one line died off in large numbers. In cells with the gene dialed down for good, growth in dishes and in soft gel also fell. The authors conclude the gene acts like an oncogene in these cells, meaning it helps the cancer grow, and it may be a target for future drugs.
pmc-11709332:
Alessia Sciortino and four co-authors test antibodies that target only the toxic forms of the tau protein in very old mice bred to model Alzheimer's disease. Their study came out in 2025. Most animal studies treat young mice, missing the inflammation and cell aging that shape the human disease.

The mice, nearly two years old, received a single injection of the antibody or a control. Treatment changed the extent of both tau and amyloid deposits in memory-related brain regions. It also shifted markers of age-related inflammation and cell senescence, suggesting toxic tau interacts with aging itself. Behavior was tested a week after injection. The authors argue that selective tau immunotherapy might help even at late disease stages.
pmc-11709632:
Ranjie Xu and Yanru Ji present a 2025 conference abstract on a lab-grown brain model for sporadic Alzheimer's disease. Most animal models copy the rare inherited form, and drugs that work in them often fail in people. The team built human stem cell organoids that hold neurons, immune cells, support cells, and blood vessels together.

To mimic the common sporadic form, the team dosed the organoids with extracts from donated Alzheimer's brains. The extracts seeded amyloid plaques, tau tangles, and inflammation inside the tissue. The authors offer the model as a human-based test bed for screening drugs, including antibody treatments like lecanemab.
pmc-11709732:
David Facal and seven co-authors present early results from a Spanish aging study on what predicts language change in middle and later life. Their paper came out in 2025. Naming and fluency tests can foreshadow dementia, but the drivers of change are poorly mapped.

About a hundred participants, spanning healthy aging, subjective decline, and mild impairment, were tested twice, eighteen months apart. Groups differed in language level but not in how much language changed over the interval. Only the naming model held together statistically, and within it grip strength was the significant predictor. The authors treat this as a first pass: a short window may hide real change. They argue for judging reserve, body function, and brain measures together.
pmc-11710132:
Yuanpu Chiu lays out a 2025 conference abstract on blood vessel failure in new mouse models of Alzheimer's disease. The disease involves amyloid, tau, and poor vessel function, and the blood-brain barrier normally shields the brain from harm in the blood. Chiu plans to track how that shield breaks down in early-onset and late-onset models from a national consortium.

The plan follows the mice at three ages each, with healthy mice as controls. A fine-scale gene mapping method will chart changes in the vessel system. Early expectations include immune responses that rise with amyloid and later tau changes. The results should guide vessel-focused treatment ideas.
pmc-11712332:
Fengpei Yuan and co-authors build AI simulations of dementia care in a 2025 study. Caregiving talks are complex, and training helpers is slow and costly. The team used a large language model to create agents that play both the person with dementia and the helper during daily tasks such as grocery shopping.

A reinforcement learning frame then coached the helper agents toward better, more personal strategies. In test scenes the coached helpers beat naive helpers at guiding the tasks. The agents copied the verbal and nonverbal flow of real care talks well, the authors say. They call for richer scenes and real-world data to sharpen the model. The goal is training and planning support that lifts life for patients and caregivers alike.
pmc-11713632:
Tangban Cynthia Nyen and Ajibade Testimony Prescillia report this animal study, published in two thousand twenty-five, on omega-3 oil and brain harm from aluminium. Aluminium chloride is a toxin that can hurt memory and raise stress inside brain cells.

The pair fed forty female Wistar rats in four groups for twenty-eight days. One group got the toxin, one got omega-3 oil, one got both, and one got plain water. Toxin-fed rats did worse on memory tests and showed more cell stress in the hippocampus, the brain's memory hub. Their brain tissue showed dying cells and more signs of cell death. Rats that also got omega-3 oil were shielded from much of this harm. The authors credit the oil's boost to the rats' own defense system.
pmc-11715632:
Diana Bocancea and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on whether an active life builds cognitive reserve. Reserve is the mind's power to keep working well even as the brain shrinks with disease.

The team used a large Amsterdam memory clinic cohort of more than four thousand people with many diagnoses. Each person reported past and present mental activity, like reading and puzzles, plus current physical activity. People further along the Alzheimer's path who scored high on both kinds of activity thought better at the start. Yet activity did not slow their later decline at a given level of brain shrinkage. The authors read the pattern as a sign of reserve at work in the moment. They note that proof of a shield against decline needs more than a snapshot.
pmc-11727032:
Jose Castillo, Michael Nhien Le, Khadija Soufi, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It reviews one hospital's choices for children with a borderline spine fracture score, where guidelines run out and doctors must judge case by case.

The score, TLICS, rates thoracolumbar fractures; a four sits exactly between brace and operating room. Adult data dominate the literature, leaving children's care unsettled. The team reviewed eleven young patients treated from 2015 to 2023. Four wore a brace alone, mostly for fractures of the rear column. Others went to surgery. The authors compare how each managed group fared. Their single-center experience is offered as practical evidence for a decision that pediatric spine teams face without consensus, balancing stability, growth, and the risks of operating on a child's back.
pmc-11727532:
Siladji and six co-authors add algae to caseless sausage and measure effects on quality and taste, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Algae promise functional benefits as meat ingredients, but type and dose matter. Three algae, Chlorella, sea spaghetti, and wakame, enter standard sausage recipes at varied levels. Protein, fat, moisture, texture, color, and taste are all assessed.

Protein and fat barely change with algae addition. Sea spaghetti and wakame cut moisture and cooking loss, while all algae raise salt. Texture softens with two algae but firms with wakame. Wakame darkens color most and scores lowest on taste panels. Other algae at chosen doses stay close to control quality. Careful selection is key for viable products.
pmc-11728132:
Po-Han Su and co-authors compare, in a 2024 study, how well one bunion operation works on moderate versus severe deformities. The surgery pairs a V-shaped bone cut with a soft-tissue procedure. It is a classic choice for mild cases, and surgeons have lately stretched it to worse ones. The team reviewed 99 feet from 94 patients, grading success by X-ray measures and by whether two small bones under the big toe returned to place.

Both groups improved clearly on X-ray measures after surgery. The small sesamoid bones, though, settled back into place more reliably in the moderate group. Severe cases also relapsed more often, though the gap was not statistically firm. The authors conclude the operation serves moderate bunions well. For severe ones, they urge surgeons to insist on full sesamoid correction and to expect more recurrences.
pmc-11731932:
Dina Dalimunthe leads a team on dry skin in kidney patients on dialysis. Their study from twenty twenty-four is set at a hospital in Indonesia. Dry skin is very common in chronic kidney disease.

It brings itch that harms sleep and mood for many. The team measured skin moisture with a hand checker tool. Blood urea levels were taken from vein samples. A skin life quality form scored how folks felt. Links among moisture, urea, and life quality were the ask. Exact causes of the dryness stay unknown.  Dialysis had run for at least three months in each case.
pmc-11769932:
Yadong Li and ten co-authors build an AI model that separates sugar beet plants from weeds in field images, in a paper whose text dates to 2024. Spotting weeds exactly is a first step toward machines that clear them without blanket spraying. Fields are messy, with changing light and overlapping leaves, so the task is harder than it looks.

The model pairs a proven image network shape with a transformer encoder that reads both fine detail and the whole scene. An attention block in the second half helps it weigh edges and textures. On a sugar beet dataset the model beat the base design on both overlap and pixel accuracy scores. The authors present it as a step toward faster, more exact automated weeding.
pmc-11771832:
Jumana Hussain Timraz and seven co-authors review how social media shapes beauty ideals and cosmetic surgery, in a paper published in twenty twenty-four. The work focuses on Saudi Arabia, where social media use is high and growing among the young. The team searched studies from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-four.

The review finds that filtered images, celebrity backing, and before-and-after photos push people toward procedures. Surgeons' own marketing adds to the demand for both surgery and milder treatments. The authors weigh the mental cost of beauty standards no one can meet, and the ethics of advertising in this trade. They also ask whether the platforms serve clinics' profits or pile pressure on doctors to match raised hopes. More varied study groups are needed, they say.
pmc-11774732:
Hongkun Xu and colleagues pooled long COVID data in cancer patients in two thousand twenty-five. Lingering symptoms after infection burden many survivors. Cancer patients may face special risk. Thirteen studies with thousands of patients qualified. Reviewers appraised study quality with a standard checklist. Prevalence was pooled across the studies statistically.

Roughly a quarter of patients reported long COVID overall. Rates fell as follow-up lengthened over the year. About one in eight still reported symptoms at twelve months. Fatigue was the most common complaint. Breathing symptoms and muscle pain followed. Risk factor analysis accompanied the prevalence work. Cancer clinics should plan long symptom follow-up.
pmc-11795932:
Jo Weeks, Anna Cuthbert, and Zarko Alfirevic ask what happens to review conclusions when untrustworthy trials are removed. Their study was published in twenty twenty-three. Worry is growing that many trials inside respected Cochrane reviews cannot be trusted.

The team applied a trustworthiness screening tool to eighteen Cochrane reviews covering pregnancy nutrition, three hundred and seventy-four trials in all. The tool checks governance, baseline data, feasibility, and plausibility. Trial authors were contacted when answers were missing. Each study ended included, excluded as retracted, or held in doubt. The exercise measures how much of the evidence base survives scrutiny, and what that does to clinical guidance.
pmc-11816032:
Siddi and co-authors track two gut bacteria through the pig meat chain in Sardinia. Salmonella and Yersinia enterocolitica can move from farms to pork eaten by people. The team sampled the farm environment at six pig farms. The same pigs were then sampled at slaughter, from tonsils, lymph nodes, colon contents, and carcass surfaces. All isolates faced drug resistance tests and full genome reads.

Yersinia turned up on two of the six farms, while farm environment samples held no Salmonella. Carcass checks also counted general bacteria as a hygiene measure. Gene data showed how closely isolates from farm and slaughter matched. The study maps where control steps in the chain matter most.
pmc-11841432:
Shihao Li, Lina Zhang, and Haiyang Zhang present a 2024 study building a telomere-related gene signature for osteosarcoma prognosis. Bone cancer in the young invades and spreads aggressively. Telomere biology shapes cancer growth, so its genes might forecast outcomes.

Public tumour data sets fed survival models that selected ten telomere-related genes. The combined signature split patients by risk well. Immune settings and cell talk patterns differed between risk groups. Lab assays in cells checked growth, migration, and invasion. A telomere lens may help doctors judge which osteosarcomas need the hardest follow-up.
pmc-11851832:
Enes Şahin and six co-authors test whether deep learning can find liver cancer in CT scans, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. Liver cancer is often found late, which drives its high death toll, so earlier and more exact detection is a pressing need.

The team trained a YOLO model, a fast image-spotting system, on one thousand two hundred and ninety CT images from one hundred and twenty-two patients. Images were split for training, checking, and final tests. The model scored high marks: overall accuracy above ninety-five in each hundred, with strong scores for both catching cancers and avoiding false alarms. The authors say such a tool could beat older reading methods and help doctors find the cancer sooner.
pmc-11888632: Al-Bayati presents case reports from twenty twenty-four on two severe drug reaction syndromes with mouth signs. Both are rare, severe allergy-like reactions to drugs; one strips skin and mucosa, and the other brings fever, rash, blood changes, and organ strain. The report details presentation, tests, rival diagnoses, and treatment for the cases, stressing that prompt diagnosis and hospital care are essential.
pmc-11891132:
Patience Atuhaire and co-authors published this cohort study in 2024. Babies born to mothers with HIV face higher infection risks, but hard data on confirmed bloodstream infections in such infants is scarce in poorer countries. The team worked in Kampala, Uganda, inside a large vaccine study cohort. Any infant under three months with signs of infection gave blood for culture. Of 4,492 cultures taken overall, 460 came from HIV-exposed babies.

Nine exposed infants, about two percent, had positive cultures. The germs found included Escherichia coli bacteria and group B streptococcus, the target of the parent vaccine study. Worryingly, these organisms resisted the standard antibiotics used for suspected sepsis. Exposed babies also died at higher rates than unexposed ones, 15.8 against 11.2 percent, despite mothers receiving HIV treatment. The authors call for research into why that mortality gap persists. Rising drug resistance in this setting adds urgency.
pmc-11927532:
Yun Zhang and co-authors probe how a protein that aids artery plaque growth reshapes cell chemistry, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. The protein is a known promoter of the artery disease. Mice prone to plaques had the protein silenced in their immune cells, and both gene and chemical profiles were read.

Thousands of genes and chemical products shifted after silencing. Two pathways stood out at both levels: building blocks for DNA and a carbon-shuffling pathway key to cell growth. Key genes in those paths moved in telling directions. Treated cells grew slower and stalled at a cell-cycle gate. Sugar and fat handling also changed.
pmc-12534732:
Abtahi, Shakeri, and Tajbakhsh describe anesthesia care for an infant with PHACES syndrome in this case report. The syndrome bundles a facial birthmark with brain, artery, heart, eye, and chest defects. Many of those features complicate anesthesia directly.

The patient was a 2.5-month-old girl weighing 2,100 grams. She needed laser therapy for an eye condition of prematurity. The team induced and maintained anesthesia with sevoflurane gas. A size 1 laryngeal mask managed her airway instead of a breathing tube. No complications arose during or after the procedure, and she went home the next day. The authors stress tailoring perioperative care to each child's particular defect pattern.
pmc-12663232:
Zeev Kalyuzhner and colleagues read shapes from the back of the head in 2025, using scattered laser light instead of electrodes. When a person views a shape, activity in the visual cortex changes blood flow and tissue properties, which alter how laser speckle patterns reflect. The team captured those patterns with a fast camera and trained deep neural networks to classify which shape the viewer was seeing: rectangle, triangle, mixed shapes, or a blank screen.

The classifier recalled rectangles almost perfectly and triangles with high accuracy in single-shape trials. With several shapes shown at once, performance stayed robust, though circular stimuli produced subtler signals and resisted consistent classification. The appeal is a non-invasive, low-cost, portable window on visual cortex activity. If the method matures, it could support brain-computer interfaces or visual monitoring without implants or bulky scanners.
pmc-12663532:
Anne Talkington and Anthony Kearsley build math models to tune immune checkpoint blockade for cancer. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Cancer cells bind brakes on T cells to mute attack, and blockade drugs free those brakes. Yet many cancers shrug off such drugs. The pair test blockade tweaks in a whole-tumor model and a cell-level model.

The whole-tumor model shows a tip point where rest or calm fates grow more like and growth fates less like. The cell model is an agent frame where each cell acts by set rules. It lets blockade plans be tried in fake before lab work. The team offers it as a guide for drug design.
pmc-12665032:
Arushi Gupta and four co-authors count salt-part ills in sick kids at an Indian ICU with thin purse. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Near five hundred thirty kids aged one month to past teen were read from twenty twenty-three to spring twenty twenty-four for five salt parts in blood. More than one thousand off marks were taped.

Low calcium led, then low potassium salt and low sodium salt. All low-calcium kids bore nerve signs. Low potassium salt tied to nerve, gland, and heart signs, and to deaths most. Death hit six percent of kids, tied most to the potassium and calcium marks.
pmc-12679132:
Jiang-Bo Li and Wei Rong write an editorial on how low mood and nerve control flaws cut lung function in patients with chronic lung disease, called COPD. Low mood and COPD occur together at high rates, and each worsens the other. The piece came out in twenty twenty-five.

Low mood links to worse lung function through lower heart rate spread, higher swelling signals, and stress hormone flaws, the authors argue. Drug care alone cannot fully offset these harms. Mood drugs, talk care such as mind training, Chinese medicine, and life changes like yoga or walking can help both mood and lung function. Doctors must weigh gains and risks for each patient when they pick mood drugs.
pmc-12690132:
Ramin Kazemi and colleagues modeled geopolymer concrete emissions with AI in two thousand twenty-five. Geopolymer concrete replaces ordinary cement with industrial slag. Its production still releases carbon dioxide. Many mix variables influence that footprint. Repeated lab testing for each mix is impractical. The team trained a hybrid neural model instead.

An optimization method tuned the network's learning. Twenty-five mix and curing variables fed the model. Most predictions landed within five percent of actual values. That beat a plain neural network clearly. Sensitivity analysis named the strongest drivers. One additive raised footprint most, while coarse aggregate lowered it. Mix designers can now estimate emissions upfront.
pmc-12692232:
Mengxue Zhang and co-authors report plant research from two thousand twenty-five on a rice gene that affects leaf color and starch. The gene makes a motor protein that moves along tiny tracks inside cells. Such motors help with cell division, transport, and the inner frame of the cell.

The team located the gene, cloned it, and studied what changes when it is broken. In the mutant rice, a sugar-moving protein ended up in the wrong places in the cell. Starch built up too much inside the leaf's green parts, their inner structure broke down, and the leaves turned yellowish. The results add to knowledge of this motor family and of how leaf color is controlled in rice.
pmc-12692632:
Jia-Hao Hu and three colleagues published an animal science study in two thousand twenty-five on why cloned buffalo give different amounts of milk. Cloned animals share the same genes, so milk differences must come from other controls. The team looked at chemical tags on DNA and at gene activity in the udder.

Low-yield clones had fewer DNA tags across the udder tissue than high-yield clones. Genes with differing tags clustered in growth, hormone, and immune pathways. High yielders switched on genes for fat making and cell growth. Low yielders favoured immune stress and protein breakdown genes. Joining both data layers flagged a small set of hub genes. The authors call the map a first draft that needs more testing.
pmc-12693332:
He and eleven co-authors build a one-click tool that grades heart scars from scans in this twenty twenty-five paper. Heart scans are a key test, yet their reads take long and lean on rare pros. Scar size and depth from those reads guide much of heart care.

Inside, one scan pass takes both bright and dark blood shots of the heart. Deep nets trained on those shots cut heart parts and scar zones on their own. Scar bulk, span, and depth come out as grades in a bull's-eye chart. A full care note with those grades is built by the tool as well. The team casts it as a fast, fair path for wards with few pros.
pmc-12699732:
Kristin Koller-Schlaud, Johannes Meixner, and eight colleagues lay out the protocol for the VeRDoC study, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. It maps psychiatric patients onto research dimensions and follows what happens to them. The framework is the Research Domain Criteria, a scheme from the United States National Institute of Mental Health that cuts across diagnoses.

Instead of sorting patients by label, the VeRDoC study measures six domains: positive and negative valence systems, cognition, social processes, arousal, and more. It enrolls both psychiatric patients and healthy controls, prospectively rather than after the fact. The question is whether these dimension scores predict clinical outcomes and care-related outcomes like service use. Earlier hints came from retrospective data. If dimensions forecast real-world trajectories, assessment and triage could follow measured traits rather than labels alone. A pre-registered protocol also guards against flexible analysis.
pmc-12703032:
Mahmood Showail and Renad Aljuhani published a 2025 survey study on willingness to donate corneas in western Saudi Arabia. Corneal transplants restore sight, but donated tissue is scarce against a rising burden of corneal blindness. The team measured public knowledge and attitudes, and what tips people toward or away from donating.

An electronic questionnaire spread through social media between October 2021 and January 2022. Of the respondents, about twenty-four percent said they were willing to donate their corneas after death. Over half, fifty-three percent, remained undecided. Statistical modeling sorted which factors accompany each stance, knowledge and beliefs among them. The undecided majority is the story: a large persuadable middle whose choices could ease the shortage. The authors argue awareness campaigns should aim at that middle, addressing specific misconceptions. Organ donation research often counts the willing; this study maps the hesitant.
pmc-12705732:
Chen and co-authors present a 2025 study of disordered metasurfaces at the brink where their parts start to fuse. Such sheets, films of tiny shapes, steer light by their layout. Past work used lone shapes or half-melted films. At the brink, called critical packing, a good share of shapes touch and merge. The team made such sheets and watched the scattered light flip its pattern at the brink.

A wave-mode census ties the flip to a jump in the states light can take. Both the mirror beam and the spray change, unlike in plain metal films. The spray can shift color or turn white by design. Glare-cut screens are one use in view. The brink itself becomes a design dial.
pmc-12707632:
Ren and colleagues published in twenty twenty-five a study of an iron-storage gene in a frog species facing bacterial infection. Ferritin keeps iron stable in cells and joins immune defense. The team cloned the full heavy-chain ferritin gene from Rana dybowskii, a brown frog. Computer analysis showed the gene codes a protein of one hundred seventy-seven amino acids. Its sequence matched a common frog relative most closely. They then infected frogs with a water bacterium to model inflammation.

Infection caused strong oxidative damage in frog tissues. Antioxidant enzyme activities shifted markedly after the challenge. The ferritin gene was active in all tissues examined. Its expression rose significantly after infection, and protein levels followed in liver and muscle. The authors propose the gene helps the frog's anti-infection response. The work widens knowledge of amphibian immune mechanisms.
pmc-12708732:
Atsushi Matsuoka and a large team map a rare split-form lung cancer cell by cell to find cure aims. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. This cancer mixes skin-like and flesh-like parts in one growth, and its base was scant known. Place maps and lone-cell gene reads were run on tumor cuts, with drug gene flaws checked too.

Flaws in MET and ALK genes showed among the cases. The MET gene and its protein lit in the skin-like part alone, even in flaw cases. Cells on a mid path, part skin and part flesh, held build-mat change marks. The team flag those mid cells as a fresh cure aim.
pmc-12713232:
Michele Guida and co-authors show that how much of a tumor carries a mutation predicts melanoma treatment results, in a 2025 study. Drugs blocking the BRAF pathway help many patients with spread disease. No marker predicts who benefits most. The team reviewed two hundred sixty-four patients on first-line targeted therapy. Tumor samples were sequenced with panels. Only samples rich in tumor cells were kept. The mutation's allele share was tested against outcomes.

Patients above a cutoff near forty-four percent progressed sooner. Their median time without progression was ten months versus thirteen. Survival showed the same split at a higher cutoff. Adjusting the share for tumor purity strengthened the signal. The adjusted score independently predicted progression, with nearly fourfold risk at high values. The authors propose the measure as a cheap biomarker. It comes free from sequencing already done. Validation in new cohorts should follow.
pmc-12714732:
Zhou and Lu study how income segregation people actually experience relates to travel, in work from twenty twenty-five. Income segregation is a barrier to social inclusion and equity. It is shaped by travel behavior and by local living models that keep daily life inside one neighborhood.

The team quantified experienced segregation using a huge dataset of mobility records, over a billion of them. They asked how the link between segregation and travel varies with neighborhood social and urban context. Results can show whether fifteen minute city style planning deepens or softens the income mixing that daily movement creates.
pmc-12716032:
Iwona Poziomkowska-Gęsicka and four co-authors report on wasp venom therapy for people with severe sting allergy, using records from a Polish registry, in a 2025 study. Stings by wasps of the Vespula group are a top cause of life-threatening allergy attacks in adults. Venom therapy, a series of shots with tiny venom doses, is the one way to prevent later attacks. The team reviewed records for one hundred thirteen patients treated in the West Pomerania region.

A fast build-up schedule, called ultra-rush, proved safe and saved time for patients and staff. Full-blown attacks during therapy were rare and were well controlled. Problems arose more often when therapy began at a lower starting dose, which forced more shots. Age and a blood marker level also tracked with worse problems. The authors back the fast schedule for most patients.
pmc-12716232: Efrat Neter, Refael Youngmann, and Naama Gruper compared two kinds of health literacy in 2025. One kind covers skill with online health tools and sources. The other covers knowledge about mental health. The team tested whether the two skills move together. Overall scores showed no clear link between them. Only weak links appeared between specific sub-skills. The authors read the gap through self-judgment. People may rate their own ability higher than their real performance. Skill in one health domain should not be assumed in the other.
pmc-12716832:
Qi Zou leads a fourteen-author team measuring phone-tracked social media time against depression in young adults, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Self-reported screen time is unreliable, weakening earlier research. Objective measurement was this study's remedy.

Students at six universities were enrolled in two thousand twenty-two. Their phones' own system monitoring logged social media duration. Depression symptoms were scored on a standard self-rating scale. Statistical models, including flexible dose-response curves, linked heavier use to symptoms. Sleep quality was tested as the pathway in between. Emerging adulthood, the late-teens-to-twenties transition, is when both social media habits and depression risk peak. The mediation result suggests sleep interventions might blunt the association.
pmc-12717232:
Zhang and co-authors tie fat burn in sacs to drug hold in lung growth. Sacs shed by growth cells bear drug hold from cell to cell. How that spread works in lung growth had stayed thin. Sacs from hold-fast cells boosted kin cells' life on the drug. The drug in view is gefitinib, a front care for such growth. In sum, 157 shared high parts sat in sacs and parent cells.
