Those parts split hold-fast sets from soft sets in the count. Of the shared parts, 69 are tools that drive cell work. Most of those tools crowd fat burn paths in the pool. One tool, ACC1, showed the top fold rise of the set. Soft cells that took hold sacs raised ACC1 in their turn. Blocks and gene cuts proved ACC1 backs cell life on the drug.
pmc-12717732:
Adrien Maillot and a large team of co-authors study poisonings from new psychoactive substances on Reunion Island in this 2025 paper. These designer drugs are hard to detect with routine tests, and their toxicity is unpredictable. Suspected cases had been seen for years on the island, but lab proof was scarce.

Records came from four public hospitals between August 2022 and March 2024. Cases were found mainly in emergency and intensive care units. Blood and urine samples were tested with high resolution mass spectrometry. Confirmed drugs were grouped by drug class. Clinical features and outcomes were pulled from medical records. The study gives the island its first firm picture of which substances are causing harm.
pmc-12721732:
Akihiro Nishiyama and six co-authors present a 2025 case report on a jaw nerve injured by a root canal treatment. Calcium hydroxide, a standard filling aid, had overfilled a lower molar and reached the nerve running through the jaw. The patient lost feeling, and months of watching brought no recovery. Surgeons then repaired the nerve with an artificial conduit, a small tube that guides regrowth.

Tissue examination found leftover filling material inside the nerve bundle, including barium sulfate, an ingredient added so the paste shows on X-rays. The authors blame two harms: chemical burning from the paste's strong alkalinity and physical pressure from the residue. Six months after repair, feeling had returned to a functional grade. They urge dentists to handle injectable pastes with care near the nerve canal. When feeling does not return on its own, they advise considering surgical repair.
pmc-12722632:
Jiefeng Huang and colleagues tested a metabolite for skin flap survival in 2025. Random-pattern flaps rebuild tissue after damage. Poor blood flow often kills flap edges. Necrosis follows that blood starvation. Gene sequencing in mice flagged metabolism trouble. Glutamine pathways looked disrupted in flaps.

One metabolite, alpha-ketoglutarate, was given as treatment. Flap viability improved with that treatment. Blood perfusion rose inside the flap. A growth factor for vessels rose too. Signalling ran through one known pathway. New vessel growth explained the benefit. Surgical reconstruction may gain a helper. Flap surgery outcomes could improve widely.
pmc-12722732:
Shiwei Lin and Xiaofang Chen published a 2025 study of a blood score and death risk in people with overactive bladder. The score corrects the blood's acid balance measure for the patient's albumin level. It flags acid-base and electrolyte disturbances, and it has predicted outcomes well in other chronic diseases.

The team drew more than six thousand patients from a United States health survey that ran from 2005 to 2018. Over an average follow-up of nearly eighty months, more than a thousand participants died of any cause, and more than three hundred died of cardiovascular disease. Each one-step rise in the score accompanied a rise in both death risks, after adjustment for other traits. Those in the top third of scores faced a far higher risk than those in the bottom third. The team proposes the inexpensive blood score as a flag for patients who need close monitoring.
pmc-12729432:
Paolo Cornale and three co-authors review how a warming climate affects farm animals in the Alps, in this twenty twenty-five paper. Alpine farms tend to run on low inputs and open pasture. That style supports wildlife, rural income, and old traditions, but it also leaves herds exposed to weather shifts.

The review gathers what is known about heat stress, feed and water change, and disease risk for mountain livestock. It weighs how these pressures bear on animal welfare in high pastures. For farmers and policy makers, the paper pulls scattered findings into one guide for adapting alpine herding to a hotter future.
pmc-12729532:
Luís Loureiro, Cândida Loureiro, and José Santos studied how resilience, life satisfaction, and well-being connect in Portuguese teenagers, in a paper published in 2025. Five hundred eighty-nine students aged ten to eighteen, from the country's central region, completed three standard questionnaires. The team tested whether satisfaction with life carries part of resilience's benefit.

Resilience and the joint well-being measures moved together very strongly. The model fit that claim: teenagers with more resilience felt more satisfied with life, and that satisfaction in turn aided positive mental health, while resilience also helped directly. About a third of the spread in well-being was explained by the model. The authors argue schools should build both resilience and life satisfaction as shields for mental health.
pmc-12731132:
Yongshuai Jiang and seven co-authors study a protein that seems to shield cervical cancer from the immune system. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. The protein, called PRMT5, marks other proteins with chemical tags and is higher in cervical tumor tissue than in healthy tissue.

High PRMT5 levels in patient data went with fewer immune cells inside tumors and worse outcomes. In mice, tumors lacking PRMT5 grew much more slowly. That benefit largely vanished in mice missing killer T cells, which shows the effect runs through those cells. Gene reads found that blocking PRMT5 raised output of a signal that calls T cells in. The work names a drug target that could let more immune cells reach the tumor.
pmc-12731632:
Wang and coauthors ask how breast cancer subtypes and immunity shape outlook. Triple-negative breast cancer lacks three common drug targets. All such patients get drug care after surgery in most plans. Yet their outcomes vary a lot from case to case.

The team reviewed 111 patients treated from 2002 to 2014. A 50-gene test split tumors into four intrinsic subtypes. A risk score split patients into high, mid, and low groups. A 17-gene panel split immunity into strong and weak. Both splits tracked with survival in the data. Joint use may refine care plans for patients.
pmc-12732332:
Olga Pomares and co-authors study variants in the leptin gene in children in this 2025 paper. Leptin is a hormone that helps control appetite and body weight. Two common variants were tested for links to body mass, leptin levels, and blood lipids. The sample was population based and large.

The study covered 1,270 children aged six to eight years, before puberty. Both variants linked to leptin levels after adjusting for sex. Neither linked to body mass index in this group. In girls, both variants linked to levels of a protective blood protein. One variant also linked to HDL cholesterol. Those lipid links held even after accounting for leptin itself, which is why the title calls them leptin independent.
pmc-12732532:
Quan Wang and six co-authors map a family of jumping genes in beetles in this 2025 study. The genes, called PiggyBac transposons, cut themselves out of DNA and paste in elsewhere. They are prized as lab tools and they reshape genomes over time. Beetles form the richest order of animals, yet their PiggyBac story was poorly known.

The team mined one hundred thirty-six beetle genomes for the gene family's key part. They found the elements in sixty-two species, sorted into six branches. Most copies looked fresh, a sign the elements still jump today. Three beetle species held copies with strong promise as genetic tools. The study sketches how this gene family spread and stayed active across beetle evolution.
pmc-12732632:
Yezhou Yu and co-authors study what extra amounts of a muscle protein do to cell stress paths in two thousand twenty-five. The protein, carbonic anhydrase 3, is a weak enzyme but carries surface sulfur sites that react under oxidative stress. It has been tied to cell protection and to a partner that guides cell recycling.

Three cell lines were loaded with extra protein and read by gene and protein scans. Path sets tied to protein making and RNA handling were dialed down, as were sets linked to brain decay diseases. Under low oxygen, immune signal sets also fell. Pull-down tests found fresh binding partners, among them heat shock proteins and a ribosome part.
pmc-12733332:
Jacek Michalski and co-authors examined how two kinds of nitrogen links shape the form of two new pyridine compounds, in twenty twenty-five. Azo and hydrazo compounds find wide use in foods, drugs, cosmetics, and electronics, which drives work on new ones. One compound here carries a hydrazo bridge and the other its azo twin. The team read their structures with a battery of light-based tools and with crystal diffraction.

Crystals of the two compounds grew in unlike symmetry classes, each with one molecule in its basic unit. The diffraction results were set against quantum chemical calculations, and the two agreed well. The paper works through the traits of the hydrazo bridge and its azo counterpart in fine detail. Such groundwork on shape and spectra helps chemists design new compounds of these families with set traits.
pmc-12733532:
Gloria Roberti and co-authors review whether the cupping of the optic disc in glaucoma can partly reverse when eye pressure is lowered, in work published in 2025. Cupping is the hollowed shape the disc takes as glaucoma damages it. Reversal has been seen in children and adults after successful pressure control.

Lab models show a strong link between pressure drops and disc shape recovery. Children show the greatest reversal because their eye tissues stretch more. Adults show smaller but measurable changes after sustained pressure lowering. Modern imaging, including laser scanning and cross-section scans, confirms the shape changes track the pressure drop. The authors stress the reversal reflects tissue remodelling, not regrowth of nerve cells. It remains a useful sign that pressure control is working.
pmc-12733732:
Vincenza Gragnaniello and a team of co-authors follow newborns flagged for a rare metabolic condition in northeast Italy, in two thousand twenty-five. The condition ranges from no symptoms at all to dangerous crises. Its place on screening panels is debated, since screening finds many infants who may never fall ill.

Over a decade, more than three hundred thousand newborns were screened and nine cases were confirmed. Most children stayed well on yearly checks, with an emergency plan for illnesses. One child had a crisis during an illness and was treated promptly. Parents felt a strong early burden that faded over time, and all backed the screening program.
pmc-12733832:
Brunna Boaventura, Harold Koenig, and Fatima Cody Stanford present a review from twenty twenty-five that frames obesity care round flourishing, not weight alone. Weight is a real clinical mark, they grant. Yet it misses the full shape of health for a person with obesity. Flourishing spans six fields: joy and life satisfaction, mind and body health, meaning, virtue, close ties, and material steadiness.

Care built on those fields adds grit, bonds, and purpose to the usual marks. It fits tailored, team based care. Weight stigma makes the whole person view a must, not a luxury, they argue. The shift needs buy-in from care, school, research, and policy hands.
pmc-12736532:
Silva and six co-authors print composites of polylactic acid with cellulose using a display-based printer, in a study from twenty twenty-five. The acid plastic is biodegradable with good strength, while cellulose adds stiffness. Blends with one to ten percent cellulose are compared to pure plastic. Tests cover heat, strength, structure, and water uptake.

Cellulose raises hardness, pull strength, and stiffness across the blends. Fracture surfaces grow rougher and less uniform than pure plastic. Heat stability shifts with cellulose dose, with some blends degrading faster. Water uptake also rises with more cellulose, a limit for humid use. A moderate three percent dose gives the best balance overall.
pmc-12737032:
Maczák and co-authors show how the math behind wrist activity trackers shapes sleep study results. These devices record wrist motion fast, then compress it into activity counts. Each maker compresses the data in a different way, which can shift results.

The team applied several makers' methods to raw motion data they gathered themselves. They checked rhythm measures and sleep-wake scoring under each method. They also tested whether rhythm scores could come straight from raw motion. Every approach was strongly swayed by the maker's method. The effects traced back to set choices in filtering and compression steps.
pmc-12741332:
Tamara Rodrigues dos Santos and colleagues describe the methods of a study of nutrition, health, and food security among Indigenous peoples in Alagoas, Brazil. Their 2025 article explains how the ENSSAIA survey was designed and carried out.

Conducted from twenty twenty-two to twenty twenty-three, the cross-sectional household survey covered all eleven Indigenous ethnic groups in the state. Fourteen of twenty-nine villages were randomly selected, and about fourteen hundred families were assessed. Data covered environment, income, public services, food security, and health across age groups. Measurements included body size, blood markers, diet, chronic diseases, and alcohol and tobacco use. The methods paper supports later findings papers.
pmc-12742132:
Naeem Mubarak and co-authors ask, in a 2025 study, what must change in Pakistan's Doctor of Pharmacy curriculum. Pharmacy work has moved toward the clinic and the patient, while curricula often lag in lecture-hall mode. The team interviewed forty-nine senior experts, drawn from every province and from abroad, and let the themes emerge from the transcripts rather than imposing them.

Six themes organize the verdict. Experts described the current curriculum's gaps, named the changes they judge unavoidable, and detailed subject-level fixes: more clinical pharmacy, integrated teaching, electives, learning alongside other health professions, and mandatory hospital placements. Simulation and research work both earned a place. The group also mapped the first steps, the barriers, and the expected payoff. The authors deliver the study as a consensus brief for the policymakers and deans who must act together.
pmc-12745732:
Blade Olson and six co-authors published an immunology study in twenty twenty-five on manufacturing tiny vesicles that present antigens to T cells. Immune cells naturally release such vesicles, which can start, expand, or quiet immune responses. Making them artificially could yield cell-free immunotherapies, but production had been cumbersome.

The team engineered ordinary cells to build and shed the vesicles. A peptide-MHC construct carried an added tail piece that recruits the cell's ESCRT machinery, which buds vesicles off the surface. The trick worked across several constructs. Purified vesicles triggered interferon release only from T cells matching their displayed antigen, showing selective stimulation.
pmc-12746632:
Maher Hajjaj and eight colleagues asked whether cleaning a tooth's post space before cementing a fiber post actually strengthens the bond. Fiber posts rebuild root-treated teeth, but leftover smear layer and debris can weaken cement grip. Ninety-one extracted human premolars were root treated and prepared. Seven cleaning methods were compared, from saline control to acids, antiseptics, air abrasion, and a commercial cleaner. Posts were cemented with self-adhesive resin cement.

Each tooth yielded two root slices, giving twenty-six specimens per group. After heat-cycling that simulates aging, a push-out test measured bond strength. Failure modes were inspected under a microscope. The twenty twenty-five study ranks everyday cleaning options by measured grip. Dentists gain evidence for a step often decided by habit alone.
pmc-12748932:
Withanage and co-authors describe liver injury caused by kava, a traditional Pacific drink now used more widely in the West. A 46-year-old man came to hospital with three weeks of fatigue and pain under the right ribs. Blood tests showed very high liver enzymes, with ALT at 1,546 and AST at 920. He had taken 10 grams of kava daily for five weeks to aid sleep. He stopped two weeks before the visit as his blood results worsened.

Tests for viruses and immune causes came back normal, and a liver scan was clear. A biopsy showed spots of dead liver cells and other signs of drug injury. A standard scoring tool gave a score of 7, supporting kava as the cause.
pmc-12749332:
Wang and nine co-authors build an early diagnostic model for pulmonary hypertension from aging-related genes, in a study from twenty twenty-five. The disease raises lung artery pressure toward heart failure silently. Cell aging in vessels is implicated in its development. Multiple data sets are mined for aging-linked gene differences.

Three machine learning methods converge on six hub genes. A nomogram built on them discriminates with excellent accuracy. Three genes verify as lowered in patients and cell models. Immune and oxidative stress pathways enrich around the genes. A candidate compound docks strongly to all three targets.
pmc-12752332:
Areni Altun and ten co-authors study how migrant mothers use online mental health resources around childbirth. Websites now carry much of this support, but their reach among migrant women is unclear. The team ran group talks and interviews with women from Chinese, Arabic, and Indian language backgrounds. They asked about five digital resources and what helped or blocked use.

Women valued content in their first language, but poor translations, hidden language choices, and hard navigation put them off. Videos and podcasts beat heavy text, above all with images that felt true to their lives. Many women found the resources late in pregnancy. The paper shows how design and timing decide who these tools serve.
pmc-12752832:
Made Artika and co-authors review how labs pull RNA out of viruses for sharp testing, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. RNA viruses drive most new outbreaks, and PCR checks live or die on clean extraction. Poor yield can hide a case and stall tracing.

Three main routes, solvent, column, and bead based, are weighed with newer auto platforms. Fit with PCR and gene reading, cost, and scale all enter the trade-offs. Sample travel, storage, and RNA decay get full play, above all where cold chains are thin. Field kits that join extraction to detection are rising. Readers get a field guide to the quiet first step of virus hunts.
pmc-12753132:
Yanwen Liu and colleagues review how well machine learning predicts knee osteoarthritis progression. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in twenty twenty-five. Forecasting joint decline could guide earlier, targeted prevention. Published model results vary widely by data and design.

Searches covered four major databases up to late twenty twenty-five. Two reviewers screened studies and judged bias risk independently. Models were compared across datasets, inputs, and progression definitions. Deep learning entries were weighed against traditional statistical methods. The pooled results summarise where prediction already works well. Gaps in study quality also stand out from the bias checks. Clinicians gain a sober map of precision prevention claims.
pmc-12753432: Shiyi Qin, Shimeng Guo, Xinmiao Tan, Ke Li, and Jiayu Huang review the case that gut microbes help drive polycystic ovary syndrome, in a 2025 paper. The syndrome is among the commonest hormone disorders in women of childbearing age, yet its root cause stays obscure. Genes, environment, diet, and lifestyle all seem to play parts. The review gathers the fast-growing evidence tying the gut community and its chemical products to the syndrome's features, presenting the gut as a promising new front for treatment.
pmc-12753632:
Jiayang Zhang and co-authors compare, in twenty twenty-five, how six tea types and four tea compounds affect the body clock. Clock disruption links to sleep and metabolic disorders, and fixes are few. Teas are widely drunk and rich in active compounds. The team tested oolong, dark, green, black, yellow, and white teas in mice and cells with shifted clocks. They also tested theanine, theophylline, a green tea catechin called EGCG, and tea polyphenols. White tea sped re-adjustment to advances in the light schedule. Dark and black teas helped with delays.

Dark tea most strongly shifted core clock genes across tissues. In cells, polyphenols, theophylline, and EGCG lengthened clock periods and aided adaptation to long cycles. Effects were distinct and context-dependent, the authors conclude, which points to tea as a natural aid against jet lag.
pmc-12754032:
Yi Zhang, Ying He, Qiang Liu, and Hongwu Deng test cell-death markers as cancer prognostic signs in a 2025 paper. The markers come from a fiery form of cell death and were measured in blood from over a hundred patients with metastatic breast cancer who had not yet had chemo or radiation. Patients were followed for two years and split by survival. Three death markers were compared with standard tumor markers.

High levels of one marker and low levels of another each tracked with shorter survival. The second marker proved a protective factor in adjusted analysis, and the first an independent risk factor. The authors say the pair adds prognostic value.
pmc-12756132:
Adnan Agha, Javed Yasin, and Fayez AlShamsi published a study in 2025 on spotting sepsis from routine blood counts. Sepsis is a body-wide response to infection that can kill fast, so early flags matter. New counters report extra inflammation measures from the same blood draw.

The study compared fifty-three intensive care patients with proven sepsis to 104 healthy clinic visitors. A model mixing three of the extra measures sorted the groups with high accuracy in this sample. Self-checks by resampling kept the score high. The authors warn the design flatters the score: sick ward patients against healthy visitors is an easy split. In an emergency room mix, they expect far lower accuracy. They call the work a first step needing real-world trials.
pmc-12756432:
Zhongjun Jiang and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-five study of a gene called TRIP13 in kidney cancer. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma is becoming more common. The gene relates to mitophagy, a cleanup process that removes worn mitochondria.

The team mined tumour data for cleanup-related genes tied to survival. TRIP13 stood out as a risk marker linked to immune response. Lab and animal tests showed it speeds cancer cell growth and movement. Blocking it may slow the disease. Readers get a candidate predictor for patient outlook and a possible drug target in kidney cancer.
pmc-12756832:
Nayara Gomes dos Santos and colleagues explain why alcohol oxidation at electrodes oscillates in neutral solutions, when such swings were thought to need acid. Oxidizing small alcohols feeds direct alcohol fuel cells and can supply protons and electrons for hydrogen production. The team studied methanol, ethylene glycol, and glycerol in unbuffered neutral salt solution. They used voltammetry and constant-current and constant-potential methods.

Math modeling gauged the near-surface pH during polarization. It swung hard, dropping by up to six and a half pH units in a depletion layer millimeters thick. The reaction itself acidifies its own microenvironment, making the acidic state the swings require, right there. When mass transport was eased, surface pH stayed near the bulk value, and both low-potential work and the swings disappeared. At an electrode, what matters is thin-film chemistry.
pmc-12756932:
Carolina Silva, Tiago Sousa, Marisa Pinho, and six colleagues track blood fats as dog gum disease worsens in this two thousand twenty-five pilot study. Periodontal disease is among the most diagnosed conditions in dogs, and fatty acids steer inflammation both ways. Comparing whole-blood fatty acid profiles across twenty-nine Portuguese Podengo dogs, ten healthy, ten with gingivitis, nine with periodontitis, the team used gas chromatography-mass spectrometry to look for stage-linked shifts.

Two fatty acids, arachidonic acid and an omega-3 docosapentaenoic acid, ran significantly higher in periodontitis than in healthy controls, while arachidic acid was lower in gingivitis. Total saturated fatty acids dropped in periodontitis as total polyunsaturated fatty acids rose in both disease groups, and omega-6 polyunsaturates were significantly higher in periodontitis. The authors read the pattern as the systemic fingerprint of periodontal inflammation, suggesting blood lipid profiles shift measurably as oral disease progresses in dogs.
pmc-12775032:
Zijian Zeng and colleagues review the PD-1 and PD-L1 immune brake across liver diseases. Their review from twenty twenty-five spans infection, fatty liver, autoimmunity, and cancer. The liver naturally tolerates much immune activity daily. This checkpoint pathway helps keep that tolerance in balance.

When signalling goes wrong, disease follows in several forms. Viruses exploit the brake to persist in hepatitis. Fatty liver and autoimmune attacks also involve the pathway. In liver cancer, tumours use it to hide from immunity. The review details control at gene, protein, and environment levels. Checkpoint drugs already transform some liver cancer care. Knowing the pathway helps predict benefits and harms.
pmc-12775532:
Derya Çokal, Wolfram Hinzen, and six co-authors studied how speech hangs together, in work published in twenty twenty-five. They worked with Turkish speakers in four groups: people with a first bout of psychosis, youth at high risk, kin of patients, and healthy peers. Three sides of speech were tracked: how speakers name and track things, how close word meanings stay, and how easy speech is to predict.

People with a first bout used fewer clear naming phrases and more bare ones. Unclear references were more common in all three risk groups than in healthy peers. The high-risk and first-bout groups also kept word meanings closer than expected. The team links naming habits to both meaning and flow in speech.
pmc-12780032:
Asad Ullah and colleagues put a vision transformer in a phone app that spots lumpy skin disease in cattle. Their study from twenty twenty-five targets a costly contagious virus. Early detection limits herd outbreaks and losses. Transformer models were barely tried in veterinary imaging.

Eight thousand cattle images trained the classifier. Standard preparation steps cleaned and varied the images. Accuracy, precision, and recall all landed near ninety-eight percent. The transformer beat several established comparison approaches. A mobile app carries the model to the field. Farmers and vets can screen animals on the spot. Rapid triage supports quarantine decisions during outbreaks.
pmc-12782332:
Premnapa Sisopa, Supaporn Lamlertthon, Ruchadaporn Kaomongkolgit, Pratthana Chomchalao, and Waree Tiyaboonchai tested Thai plant extracts and oils against the yeast Candida albicans, in this 2025 study. The yeast causes oral thrush and clings to dentures in biofilms that resist drugs. The team measured how well natural products stop biofilm growth, kill settled biofilms, block sticking to denture plastic, and halt the yeast's shape change.

Cinnamon bark oil came out strongest on nearly every test, followed by lemongrass and clove oils and two plant extracts. One extract cut sticking to denture acrylic by more than eighty percent. Several agents also stopped the yeast from sprouting germ tubes, a step in its attack. The authors propose these natural products as alternative antifungal options for mouth infections.
pmc-12783232:
Kunal Nandy and his team tell of ends of big pancreas knife work in sick folk with scarred livers at one site. Their 2025 study looks back at past cases. It also sifts past work in print on this high-risk pair.

The knife work tends to bring a big load of ills in its wake, and a scarred liver adds more risk. Twenty-four sick folk with scarred livers had knife work twixt twenty thirteen and twenty twenty-four. A math check linked death to a past of pancreas burn prior to knife work. It also linked death to blocked tubes, bile duct ills, low clot cell counts, and off-track clot tests. Sick folk with big vein force in the gut, low clot cells, and poor clot tests faced high risk of death. The finds help pick which such folk face the most grave risk.
pmc-12784732:
Larisa Maria Badau and co-authors review, in twenty twenty-five, whether body mass index predicts outcomes for a common breast cancer treated with CDK4/6 inhibitors. These drugs, plus hormone therapy, are standard for hormone-positive, HER2-negative metastatic disease. Body fat affects hormones and the drugs' targets, so BMI might matter. The team searched two databases for studies from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-five. They kept real-world studies and cohorts that linked BMI or body composition to survival on these drugs. Fourteen of sixty-nine records qualified.

Findings were mixed. Four studies found better survival at higher BMI; most found no clear link. Scan-based measures, such as visceral fat and muscle area, predicted prognosis more reliably than BMI alone, the review concludes.
pmc-12787432:
Eliana Berrio-Mesa and co-authors present a 2025 journal article auditing a factory that densifies recycled foam in Medellín, Colombia. Expanded polystyrene packaging waste is bulky and rarely recycled. The plant melts and compacts it into densified stock. Over six months of operating data, the team balanced every material and energy flow and priced the whole line.

The process yielded about seventy-eight percent product, losing mostly solid residue and water. Over half the energy leaked away, chiefly as heat at the melting stage. Even so, the books balanced over a twelve-year horizon, and the carbon footprint fell by about two thirds against disposal. The authors call the route viable and green.
pmc-12788432:
Polisetty Siva Krishna and five colleagues compare four ways of preparing tooth enamel for orthodontic brackets when an adhesion booster is used. Strong bracket bonding decides treatment success, but the standard acid etch can cost enamel and irritate tissue. Eighty extracted premolars were split among acid etching, sandblasting, sandblasting plus acid, and laser etching, all finished with the booster.

Laser etching gave the highest bond strength, essentially tied with sandblasting plus acid. Both clearly beat acid alone, while sandblasting alone was weakest. Leftover adhesive patterns did not differ among groups. The authors conclude the booster improves all methods, and laser or combined preparation offers the strongest hold in the laboratory.
pmc-12804732:
Richard Pan and co-authors edit DNA methylation inside living mice, in work from 2025. Methylation is a chemical tag that helps switch genes off and on. Editing it with care can reveal what it does, but delivery hurdles kept most edits in lab dishes. The team bred two mouse lines with switchable editors, one that adds tags and one that strips them.

Tagging one gene's start zone in the liver cut its output and lowered harmful blood cholesterol. Stripping tags from a second gene woke it on the quiet X chromosome and eased a cell size flaw in brain cells. Wide scans showed few off-target shifts.
pmc-12808732:
Flynn, Vahedifard, and Schaaf hand over a checked set of cases where river water topped earthen levees in the United States, for risk work, in work from twenty twenty-five. Earthen levees are the chief flood guard on Earth, and water over the top is their chief way to fail. Fine field facts on such cases were thin and split before this set. It pulls together four hundred eighty-seven river cases.

Facts come from Corps reports, shots from the air, water data stores, and words from folks who saw the floods. Each case logs water load, soil, shape and size, upkeep, and the size of the breach. Cross-checks across sources keep the set in line. Breach traits track with soil type, water depth, how long water sat over the top, and levee shape. Risk, design, and flood teams gain hard facts to tune their models.
pmc-12812732:
Zhang, Xia, and Zhang hunt for aging linked genes in a scarring lung disease and test drug matches in twenty twenty-five. The disease, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, stiffens lungs with scar tissue and has no clear cause. Aging is a prime suspect, as old cells pile up and repair goes wrong. The team merged three gene data sets from patients and controls.

Nineteen aging linked genes stood out from the changed set. Two genes sat at the hub of the gene webs they built. Two known compounds docked well onto those hub genes in computer tests. Checks in a fourth data set and in scarred mouse lungs backed the gene findings. The work links cell aging to lung scarring.
pmc-12813032:
Llor and co-authors survey antibiotic use for chest and airway infections in Spanish nursing homes. Staff in 34 homes across five areas recorded cases from February to April 2023. They noted symptoms, diagnoses, and which drugs were given in each case.

Among 533 cases, the common cold and acute bronchitis were the top diagnoses. Yet antibiotics were given in 77.5 percent of cases, most often amoxicillin-clavulanate at 34 percent. Of 328 prescriptions that could be judged, 63.1 percent were deemed not needed. The team also modeled what drove both use and poor use of these drugs.
pmc-12817732:
Six researchers report a brain tumor study from two thousand twenty-five on why some tumors resist immune therapy. The tumor is glioma, a highly malignant brain cancer. Its surroundings shut down immune attack, and that trait tracks with poor outcomes for patients.

The team studied a gene switch called NFE2L2, which runs high in glioma tissue. High levels went with more immune cells of a type that shields the tumor. Raising the switch in cells made tumor cells move and invade more. In mice built to lack the switch, the picture changed. The work ties the switch to drug resistance against a common immune therapy.
pmc-12819932:
Zhang and co-authors look for blood markers that warn of thinking problems after chest surgery in older adults. This disorder, called PND, is common after such surgery and leads to poor outcomes. No good treatment exists once it is late, so early signs matter.

The study followed 60 older patients having chest surgery at one site. Blood was drawn just before anesthesia and again after the breathing tube came out. Five markers were measured, among them adiponectin and BDNF. Three markers were lower in patients with PND and acted as protective factors when higher.
pmc-12822832:
Kimia Khonakdar and co-authors review whether videos and multimedia calm patients before spinal anesthesia in a 2025 systematic review. Neuraxial anesthesia numbs the lower body through the spine, and fear of the needle and the unknown raises stress and can shake blood pressure. A short video before the procedure is a cheap, kind intervention, if it works.

Following standard review guidelines, the team searched four databases for trials comparing multimedia education against usual verbal briefing. Ten studies qualified. They compared anxiety, satisfaction, and stability of vital signs across the arms. Pooling small trials is the only way to hear a quiet effect over noise. The review gives anesthetists an evidence base for pressing play, and shows where the record is still thin.
pmc-12825232:
Luo, Zhang, Zhang, and Peng report in twenty twenty-five a trauma patient whose common antibiotic quietly caused a trio of side effects after surgery. The broad-range drug had run for over two weeks before his chest operation for broken ribs. From the second day after surgery he spiked fevers only in a fixed late-evening window, with normal temperatures by day, while his white cell count and potassium both sagged.

Stopping the drug ended the fevers at once, and the blood values drifted back to normal. The authors note drug fever is easy to miss among post-surgery complications that also cause fever. When the pattern fits, they urge teams to suspect the antibiotic early, even while hunting surgical causes.
pmc-12826632:
Alfred Doku and colleagues published an evaluation study in 2025 on cardiac arrest training in Ghana. The Ghana Heart Initiative has trained health workers since its launch. Staying current on life support guidelines is essential for those workers. The study measured knowledge and skills right after training courses.

Hundreds of professionals took basic or advanced life support courses. A subset completed questionnaires immediately after their training. Instructors also scored hands-on skills against American guidelines. About three quarters of basic trainees showed adequate knowledge. The report covers courses run across several years. It aims to show where Ghanaian emergency training stands and where it should improve.
pmc-12829232:
Xiao-Juan Zhang and her six co-authors, publishing in 2025, review outcomes for newborns operated on for critical heart defects at one Chinese hospital. Over three years, 234 babies had corrective surgery with a heart-lung machine, at an average age of twelve days. Most had the blue, oxygen-poor form of disease. The team recorded operation times, recovery measures, and survival.

The babies averaged about twenty-five days in hospital and three and a half days on a ventilator. Two hundred twenty-two went home recovered. Twelve died, a survival rate near 95 percent. Most operations were full corrections done electively; a small share were emergencies or staged procedures. The authors describe a maturing system: as surgical and bypass techniques improve, success rates climb and the menu of options for these fragile newborns widens.
pmc-12829332:
Sen Yang and co-authors map what weakens front-line health services and what can rebuild them, in a review published in two thousand twenty-five. The team searched three databases for work from two thousand fourteen to two thousand twenty-four and kept seventy-six papers. Themes were drawn across mixed health systems.

Staff shortages, uneven resource spread, split policy, and weak health data tools topped the problem list. Unequal access to care also ran through the results. Fixes stressed local staff training, smart use of new tech, fair service models, and team work across fields. Readers who run clinics get context-aware paths toward care for all, with stress on poor settings.
pmc-12829432:
Karishma Harrilal-Maharaj reviews how gender bias delays diagnosis in young women. Her narrative review from twenty twenty-five spans several specialties. Young women's serious symptoms are often blamed on stress. Visual changes, chest pain, and fatigue get dismissed as benign.

Longer diagnostic waits appear for several named conditions. Multiple sclerosis, heart syndromes, lupus, and chronic pain all feature. Male-centred research history leaves female symptom patterns under-taught. Clinician shortcuts sort women's complaints into anxiety categories disproportionately. Scandinavian systems with equity frameworks show narrower gaps. Structured safeguards, not goodwill alone, close the delay gap. The review assembles scattered evidence into one indictment.
pmc-12830032:
Rodney Cheng-En Hsieh and a large team of co-authors compared proton beam therapy alone against proton therapy paired with modern drugs for advanced liver cancer, in this 2025 study. Records covered 137 patients with stage B or C disease treated in Taiwan between 2020 and 2023. Sixty-four had protons alone, forty-four added immunotherapy, and twenty-nine added a kinase-blocking drug.

Two years out, about seventy-seven percent of the immunotherapy group were alive, against roughly half in the other two groups. Their cancer also took longer to advance and to spread, while severe side effects stayed no more common. Local control was strong in all groups. The authors urge prospective trials, but read the pairing as the stronger recipe.
pmc-12831632:
Yoshinobu Masumoto, Shigeo Fukunishi, Takuya Nakai, and Toshiya Tachibana compared two ways of measuring hip implant angle during surgery, in a study published in 2025. In hip replacement, the tilt of the stem placed in the thigh bone affects how long the implant lasts and how well the joint works. Surgeons can judge it with a handheld guide or with a CT-based navigation system.

In eighty-three patients, both tools were used during the same operations, then checked against scans taken afterward. The handheld guide missed the final angle by about eight degrees on average. The navigation system missed by about three degrees, a clearly smaller error. The authors conclude that navigation gives the truer reading while the hip is being built.
pmc-12836932:
Ma, Chen, Hu, and Fan compare two nails for hip fractures in older patients, in work from twenty twenty-five. The break is an unstable fracture between the top parts of the thigh bone. Internal nails must hold the bone while it heals, and the best design is debated.

The team built computer models of both nail types fixed in the standard fracture pattern. They also ran bench tests on physical models. Measures covered stress peaks, movement, stiffness, and the gap at the break. Comparing a newer anatomical nail with a widely used anti rotation nail can guide surgeons to the implant that best fits this fracture in older bone.
pmc-12838432:
Leiming Zhang leads a ten-author team comparing body measurement indexes as predictors of multiple cardiometabolic diseases, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Having several metabolic conditions at once is increasingly common in older adults. Simple tape-measure indexes might flag risk cheaply.

Data came from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, spanning two thousand eleven to two thousand eighteen. Seven indexes competed, from body mass index to waist-to-height ratio and newer roundness measures. Propensity matching balanced age and gender. Regression models and dose-response curves compared predictive performance. The authors aim to tell clinicians which single measurement best anticipates cardiometabolic multimorbidity in middle-aged and older Chinese adults.
pmc-12842932:
Kinga Lis, writing alone, reviews allergy to vitamin B1 and gives a worked plan for desensitizing a patient, in a twenty twenty-five paper. The vitamin is vital for energy use and nerve health, and lack of it causes grave disease. Supplements are given by mouth or by injection when need is high. Allergic reactions are rare and seem tied mostly to fast, large vein doses.

The reaction likely follows the classic fast allergy path, with the vitamin acting as a small trigger. No firm lab test exists, so diagnosis rests on the history. The paper sets out the causes and signs, then shows a step-by-step plan that lets a needed patient take the vitamin safely.
pmc-12844732:
Sangita Jana, Akshit Malhotra, Honey Mittal, and six colleagues coat materials with a bacteria-killing film in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Polypropylene meshes and sutures used in hernia repair invite bacterial colonization and biofilms, and antibiotic resistance limits countermeasures. The team synthesized zinc oxide nanorods and embedded them in a cellulose derivative coating for meshes and sutures. They tested hydrophilicity, ion release, durability over six months, and safety in mice.

The nanorods killed up to ninety-nine point nine nine nine percent of Klebsiella pneumoniae. Coated meshes turned more water-loving, contact angles dropping about forty-one degrees, and blocked bacterial adhesion by sixty to over ninety-nine percent across four species, including Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus. Coated sutures cut adhesion by sixty-seven to ninety-six percent. Antibiofilm activity survived six months of storage. The authors present the coating as durable, contact-killing protection for implants.
pmc-12845432:
Ji Hye Hwang and You-Kyoung Choi (2025) reviewed animal studies of herbal and natural products for diarrhea caused by antibiotics. Antibiotics disturb gut microbes, weaken the gut lining, and stir inflammation, which drives the diarrhea. Probiotics help only so far under that pressure. The reviewers gathered 27 controlled animal studies from five databases. They tracked microbe diversity, gut chemical output, lining strength, and immune signals. Twenty-one studies tested herbal products alone and six tested them with probiotics.

Herbal treatments restored microbe diversity and raised helpful gut chemicals across studies. They strengthened the proteins that seal the gut wall and lowered inflammatory signals. Combinations with probiotics repaired more at once, and the few head-to-head studies favored the mix over either part alone. The authors note weak spots: few studies compared all options directly. They call for tighter animal work and human trials before clinics adopt these remedies.
pmc-12846232:
Marie Mailly and Jerome R Lechien present a 2025 scoping review of a throat disorder that blocks burping. In retrograde cricopharyngeal dysfunction, the upper food-pipe sphincter will not relax backward, trapping gas. The review pulls together what is known about causes and mechanisms, from family patterns to pressure-test findings.

Family history appeared in over a quarter of patients, and most cases began in childhood. Reflux was common, and throat-muscle motion faults showed in most pressure studies. A fizzy-drink test helped unclear cases. Oddly, most patients stayed well long past the expected life of botulinum toxin shots, hinting the throat relearns the move. The authors ask for epidemiology and child studies.
pmc-12847832:
Keneth Okello and colleagues reviewed sickle cell admissions in Uganda in 2025. Sickle cell anaemia burdens sub-Saharan Africa heavily. Most affected people worldwide live there. Records came from Gulu regional referral hospital. Hospitalised children were the study focus. Presenting features and outcomes were charted.

Most children left hospital with favourable outcomes. Deaths stayed below many regional reports. Rates elsewhere run higher in published work. One drug gap stood out clearly. Hydroxyurea use stayed limited for these children. Access barriers likely explain that gap. The authors urge stronger sickle cell policies. Wider drug availability is a priority.
pmc-12852532:
Ming Yan Zhong, Xin Chang Zou, and Pei Huang Chen build explainable machine models to call survival in women after bladder surgery. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Bladder cancer strikes men more, but women face worse odds and later stage at find. A sharp call on survival after the bladder is cut out is thus key.

They draw thousands of cases from a national registry, plus a small hospital set for outside checks. Screening picks seven drivers, among them stage, age, tumour size, and chemo. Five learning methods are trained on them. A boosted tree model wins at one, three, and five year calls, and a Shapley read names which drivers push each call. Checks of fit and net gain back the tool.
pmc-12860132:
Mehmet Güler and co-authors wrote a randomized trial from 2025 testing core stabilization exercise against standard physiotherapy for chronic low back pain with no clear cause. Such pain often comes with a shrunken, fat-streaked deep back muscle, the lumbar multifidus, which steadies the spine. Thirty-six patients trained for eight weeks, half supervised then home-based. Scans measured the muscle's size and fat, alongside pain, disability, and trunk stability scores.

Both groups improved on pain and function. The core group gained more muscle, chiefly at the lower lumbar levels, and shed more fat within it. Their activity pain fell by over four points against under two in the standard group. Disability dropped three times as far, and stability scores ended higher. The authors conclude targeted core work rebuilds the muscle in ways standard care does not.
pmc-12864832:
Muhammad Umar and five colleagues simulate blood flow through a narrowed artery and rank the settings that shape it, in a twenty twenty-five study. Their flat computer model treats blood as a special fluid under a magnetic field set across the flow. Narrowed arteries change pressure and wall stress in ways that matter for heart health. A decision method called TOPSIS ranked the setting mixes from best to worst.

One magnetic strength measure let the team control where flow splits from the wall. Wall stress rose with the magnetic measure and with a fluid stiffness factor. Heat transfer rose with several flow settings. The rankings stayed firm under checks, and the authors offer the model for planning diagnosis and care.
pmc-12872932:
Seven authors wrote a review, published in two thousand twenty-five, on designing lab-grown tumor models with the help of fluid simulation. The models are organ-on-chip systems: small devices where cells grow under flowing fluid. Their focus is glioblastoma, a fast and deadly brain cancer whose local environment helps it resist treatment.

Chip models beat flat cell cultures, but most are still built by trial and error. Flow, chemical gradients, and push on the cells are hard to control that way. The authors map the main design limits to fixes drawn from fluid simulation. They set out a step-by-step workflow for building and checking chip models of this tumor.
pmc-12879432:
Cuiyun Zhang and a large team of co-authors measured cancer risk from faulty DNA-repair genes in Chinese ovarian cancer patients, in this 2025 study. Broken repair genes are known risk factors, but exact risk figures for Han Chinese patients were missing. The team sequenced forty-five repair genes in 666 patients from Henan.

Harmful variants in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes tied strongly to the most common cancer subtype and to family history. Risk was also clearly raised for three further genes, RAD51D, RAD51C, and MSH2. Most patients had advanced disease, and the median age at onset was fifty-three. The authors say these first population-specific risk figures can guide screening and prevention plans shaped for China's own genetic profile.
pmc-12929432:
Izabela Mamede and co-authors present a study published in 2025 on long non-coding RNAs in the response to an Ebola vaccine. These RNAs do not build proteins but steer gene activity, and their part in vaccine immunity was unmapped. The team reanalyzed gene sequencing data from three groups given the licensed Ebola vaccine.

Several long non-coding RNAs switched on consistently after vaccination, including two named LEF1-AS1 and DOCK8-AS1. Their levels tracked with antibody strength and with genes of early defense and T cell development. One of them appears tied specifically to the Ebola vaccine when compared with other vaccines. The findings suggest these quiet RNAs help conduct the immune response and could mark how well vaccination took.
pmc-12948632:
Bhakti Banerjee and four colleagues test whether light sensors on the kidney and thumb can warn of kidney stress during heart surgery, in a twenty twenty-five study. Heart surgery on a bypass machine often strains the kidneys, and a blood marker called creatinine shows the harm late. The team fitted fifty-five adults with sensors that read oxygen in kidney and thumb muscle tissue during surgery.

A drop of more than twenty percent in kidney oxygen strongly predicted later creatinine rises. A fifteen percent drop in muscle oxygen also predicted well. The two readings tracked each other. The authors say live oxygen reads at the bedside could flag at-risk kidneys hours before blood tests do.
pmc-12950232:
A large team led by Sandra Vranic tested whether surface tweaks make silica nanoparticles safer. These tiny particles are used widely in industry, and changing their surface coat is a hoped-for route to safer design. The team compared plain particles with two coated kinds, in mouse lungs and in immune cells in dishes.

Plain particles raised lung weight in mice, while coated ones did not. One coated kind drew more immune cells into lung fluid at the high dose, and the plain kind cut them. Cell tests probed which death paths the particles trigger, using blocker drugs. The work maps how surface choice shapes lung response, step one toward safer particles.
pmc-13084832:
Simin Chen and co-authors sequenced the chloroplast genome of Trevesia palmata, a striking Southeast Asian tree in the ivy family nicknamed the snowflake aralia. The team assembled the full genome and placed the species among twenty-three relatives by comparing their chloroplast DNA.

The genome runs about one hundred fifty-six thousand base pairs with the classic four-part structure: two single-copy regions split by a pair of mirrored repeats. It holds one hundred thirty-three genes, most of them protein-coding, plus transfer and ribosomal RNA genes. The family tree puts the species closest to Brassaiopsis and Eleutherococcus. The authors offer the genome as a base for identifying Trevesia species and tracing their evolution.
pmc-13086532:
Wei Siang Lee and co-authors report a first known case of catatonia following taxane chemotherapy, in this 2026 case report. A seventy-five-year-old woman with schizophrenia in remission received docetaxel for breast cancer and slid into the rigid, withdrawn state. Her score on a standard catatonia scale reached twenty-three.

A test dose of lorazepam brought a clear response, and steady oral doses resolved the episode quickly. A mild relapse later settled with a dose increase. The authors weigh how the drug's known effects on the brain might have combined with her other risks. They stress that catatonia after chemotherapy is easy to miss, and that early recognition matters because treatment works fast.
pmc-13113632:
Ponsit Sathapondecha and seven co-authors wrote a gene study in 2026 on drug-proof traits in a germ found in shrimp. Shewanella algae can hold drug-proof genes that put food safety and health at risk. One strain from wild black tiger shrimp stock was read in full, base by base.

Its genome, five point two one megabases long, held two hundred five drug-proof genes. One was an exact match for a fluoroquinolone proof gene. Tests showed proof against ampicillin and colistin, though the strong colistin gene set was not there. In a scan of one hundred twenty-five genomes, one change in one gene was tied to strong colistin proof. The team flags shrimp waters as drug-proof pools that call for close watch.
pmc-13134932: Josef Finsterer argues, in a letter from twenty twenty-five, that immunoglobulins for Guillain-Barré syndrome should be blamed for a false-positive hepatitis test only when all other causes are ruled out. False positives can also stem from cross-reacting antibodies of other infections or autoimmune diseases. A recent hepatitis B vaccination, rheumatoid factor, and biotin can interfere too. Faulty reagents and poor methods add technical causes, and some chronic diseases play a part. In the study at hand, he sees a purpura condition as the likelier culprit.
pmc-13135532:
Sarah Marwieser and six co-authors study repeat ruptures after hand tendon repair in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Flexor tendons bend the fingers, and a torn repair is a serious setback. It can limit work, daily life, and sport. The team reviewed patients treated at one center from two thousand ten to two thousand twenty-two. The group held two hundred ninety-two patients with over four hundred complete tendon injuries.

They gathered injury type, location, timing, surgical method, and rehab plan for each case. Statistical analysis then flagged which factors track with a second rupture. Such knowledge can refine both surgery and aftercare. Hand surgeons and therapists can use it to warn high-risk patients. The study is a look back at records, not a trial.
pmc-13139232:
Kirsch, Drossard, Schriek, and Hübner compare two ways to treat a painful sinus condition near the tailbone in teens, in a study from 2026. The classic fix cuts the tissue out in open surgery. A newer method works through a small scope, but its special gear has slowed uptake. Their variant uses standard urology tools and a saltwater rinse.

The study covered 113 young patients treated over a decade. The scope group stayed in hospital about two and a half days less than the open group. Surgery time and return rates were near the same in both groups. Scope patients reported good looks of the scar and little pain. Many were back at school right after discharge. The authors say the cheaper kit can spread the gentler method to more hospitals.
pmc-13145732:
Philippine van Wijngaarden and five colleagues pooled studies on what can go wrong during treatment of a burst brain aneurysm. Two routes exist: threading tools through vessels, or open brain surgery. Reports of each route's risks vary widely. The team set out to give each complication a firm rate.

They gathered one hundred fifty-two studies covering nearly seventy thousand patients. For the vessel route, blocked blood flow and clot events were the most common problems, each near six or seven percent. For surgery, tearing of the aneurysm during the operation topped the list, near fifteen percent. Blocked flow followed at about twelve percent. The rates varied a lot between studies. Still, the pooled picture gives patients and doctors a clearer base for weighing the two routes.
pmc-13146032:
Morgan Hayden, Naama Raquib, Suheil Ponnambath, Divya Singh, and Nazia Zaman present a stroke case built around a rare artery variant. In some people, one small artery feeds both sides of a deep brain hub, the thalamus. A blockage there can cause coma, odd eye movements, and confusion. Standard scans often miss the tiny blocked vessel.

The patient, aged seventy, arrived drowsy and hard to rouse within the treatment window. First scans of the head and its vessels looked normal. An urgent MRI showed matching damage on both sides of the thalamus, the mark of this variant. The team gave clot-busting treatment in time and moved the patient to a stroke unit. The authors stress keeping this rare cause in mind when scans look clean.
pmc-13148332:
Mohammad Saad and co-authors compare two imaging signals in 2026 from a tumor-targeting dye used in cancer scans. The agent pairs an antibody that seeks a growth receptor on tumors with a dye that both glows and makes sound waves under light. Glow imaging is sharp but shallow, while sound-based imaging reaches deeper with lower sensitivity.

In mice with tumors, the glow signal rose steadily over a day. The sound signal peaked early, at about three hours, then faded. The team traced the fade to clumps of the agent that boost the sound signal at first, then break apart as tumor cells swallow the agent. The lesson is timing: each method has its best window.
pmc-13148532:
Rita Helleren and colleagues count the savings of home IV antibiotics with a digital pump. Their cost study from twenty twenty-six reviews a Norwegian hospital programme. Outpatient therapy frees beds and pleases patients generally. Norway adopted it slowly because its preferred antibiotics need several daily doses.

One hundred seventy patients received home treatment over five years. Costs covered pumps, drugs, staff time, travel, and patient time. The same courses as inpatients formed the cost comparison. Sensitivity checks tested how sturdy the savings were. Continuous pumps solve the multi-dose problem elegantly. Home therapy also shifts some work onto families. Honest costing helps hospitals argue for programme funding.
pmc-13155132:
Faraz Khodakarami, Mohammad Atai, Zahra Shahidi, and Fariba Motevasselian test how polymer weight shapes a dental cement's grip, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Glass ionomer cement bonds to dentin through poly(alkenoic acid). The team made three acid grades: heavy, light, and a half-and-half blend.

Twenty-four molars carried tiny cement posts from each mix, then endured five thousand hot-cold cycles. The blended acid beat both the heavy grade and the standard control on bond strength. Mixed breaks were the most common failure type. Tuning the blend, the authors conclude, is a cheap way to firm up the bond.
pmc-13157632:
Kakarla Chalam, Lourdes Ceja, and Anny Cheng report a rare eye complication of syphilis in this 2026 case report. Syphilis is returning as a cause of eye inflammation. A forty-seven-year-old woman came in with worsening blur in both eyes. Scans showed widespread retinal vessel inflammation and a blocked branch artery in one eye.

Blood tests confirmed active syphilis. Intravenous penicillin plus anti-inflammatory drops calmed the inflammation. Her right eye recovered fully, while the left kept mild damage from the blocked vessel. The authors stress that layered eye imaging pins down such cases. Fast penicillin treatment after firm testing can save sight.
pmc-13158132:
Mohammad Mahdi Narimani, Mohadeseh Motamed-Jahromi, and Maryam Radmehr compare two non-drug treatments for dialysis headache in a 2026 trial report. Headaches are common during hemodialysis, and drugs carry risks for these patients. The team tested acupressure and eucalyptus scent against routine care.

The trial ran at a dialysis center in Tehran in 2023 with 33 patients in three groups of eleven. One group received pressure at set points on the hand, face, and neck. Another breathed in eucalyptus scent, while the control group had routine care alone. Headache severity was measured before and after, and the groups were compared with standard tests.
pmc-13171832:
Zhefu Zhang and co-authors explore resilience in new medical students in a 2026 study. Their students attend a medical vocational college in China, where the first year brings sharp academic and social strain. The authors used a qualitative method that studies lived experience closely. Twenty-four freshmen were chosen on purpose and interviewed in depth in early 2025.

Nine subthemes grouped into three arcs. First, challenges eroded resilience as students struggled to adapt to college life, study loads, and self-management. Next, support rebuilt it, from family, peers, and the students' own growth. Last, new ways of thinking held the gains in place. The authors suggest teachers use thought-restructuring and hands-on learning to steady resilience. They frame resilience as a cycle of loss, recovery, and upkeep, not a fixed trait.
pmc-13177832:
Imene Salah-Mabed and co-authors compare an algorithm-driven eye exam against an expert's manual refraction, in this 2026 study. Subjective refraction, the familiar which-lens-is-clearer routine, depends on examiner skill. The automated system tested here runs the exam by algorithm and prints its own report. The trial enrolled 107 adults at a Paris foundation with a wide spread of vision errors.

Results from the two methods were converted into three power components for fair comparison. Mean gaps were near zero, with one component off by a small, clinically trivial amount. Agreement ranges were tighter than the usual spread between two human examiners. The expert judged the system's reports accurate in every case. The authors conclude the automated exam matches expert work.
pmc-13183132:
Kaiyuan Zheng and co-authors compare two ways of doing hip replacement surgery in a 2026 study drawn from two hospitals in China. Both groups used an approach from the back of the hip. In one group the surgeon preserved the piriformis, a small muscle at the back of the hip joint; in the other the muscle was handled the standard way. The study covered 420 patients treated between 2019 and 2024 for worn hip joints or death of the thigh bone head.

Patients were checked at one week, one month, three months, and twelve months after surgery. Hip function scores started alike in both groups and stayed alike at one year, with both groups scoring in the mid-nineties on the Harris Hip Score. The paper sets out whether sparing the muscle changes recovery or the risk of the new joint slipping out of place.
pmc-13187532:
Yunfan He and co-authors trace how deer antler peptides speed bone healing through the nerves in a 2026 study. Antler is a self-regrowing mammalian organ, and its peptides carry many activities. Fractured mice given the peptides by mouth healed faster, with stronger callus. Chemical scans found over three hundred active peptides in the mix.

The chain runs through a signaling lipid, PGE2, which rose at the fracture site. It switched on a receptor in sensory nerves, which in turn lit a brain signal and eased sympathetic tone. That shift pushed skeletal stem cells to build bone. In mice lacking the nerve receptor, the whole benefit vanished. Gait, scans, and strength tests backed the story. The authors present the nerve-to-bone axis as the mechanism, and the peptides as a candidate fracture therapy drawn from a traditional remedy.
pmc-13196932:
Mohammad Al-Shalalfeh leads a team of seven authors surveying University of Jordan students on neck pain, and find it is already the majority experience. Five hundred seven students, sampled proportionally across the university's twenty faculties through face-to-face interviews, reported their study devices, posture, duration, and pain intensity. Students with known musculoskeletal disease or prior neck trauma were excluded.

Over half, about fifty-two percent, reported neck pain within the previous week; the neck itself was the commonest site and the left shoulder the least. Regression models probed which device habits and postures associate with pain. The authors frame student study ergonomics as a prevention target before habits harden into working life.
pmc-13198132:
Goodwin and seven co-authors report sequential progression of alternating bundle branch block to complete heart block, in a case report from twenty twenty-six. Alternating block shows right and left bundle failure on consecutive tracings. A seventy-four-year-old man with hypertension and prior infarction presents with fatigue and syncope. His first tracing shows first-degree block plus alternating bundle block.

During admission he faints again with unstable complete heart block. Emergency pacing resuscitates him, followed by permanent pacemaker implantation. Alternating block signals severe infra-Hisian disease with rapid progression risk. Guidelines give pacing a class one indication with or without symptoms. Early recognition is essential for timely device placement.
pmc-13200132:
Christer Ruff and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-six imaging study measuring edge sharpening in fast, deep-learning rebuilt eye scans. Accelerated magnetic resonance scans save time but the rebuilding may alter edges. Eye socket imaging depends on crisp tissue boundaries.

Twenty-five patients had both standard and accelerated versions of the same sequences. Two blinded specialists rated quality, sharpness, and lesion confidence. Computer metrics measured sharpness and blur after edge detection. The learning-based scans won on edge and overall sharpness in key sequences. The study reassures clinics that faster eye imaging need not blur what matters.
pmc-13201932:
Treatment for anemia relies on an expensive hormone, and a 2026 virtual study authored by Md Nahid Hasan searches microbe chemistry for cheaper substitutes. The research article screens microbe metabolites for compounds that could switch on the erythropoietin receptor, mimicking the hormone that drives red blood cell production.

The team screened ninety compounds and studied sixteen in detail using molecular docking, drug-property prediction, and safety profiling. Abyssomicin W emerged as the strongest option, binding the receptor well and showing favorable forecast absorption and safety. Long simulations showed its complex with the receptor stayed stable, though the authors stress that lab experiments must come next.
pmc-13202932:
Gottvall, Isaac, Nankinga, Solimena, and Carlsson published this study in twenty twenty-six on health care for forced migrants. It focuses on migrants who fled persecution over their sexual orientation or gender identity. The team asked migrants and health workers what good care and good research look like for this group after arrival in a new country.

The team interviewed seventeen migrants and twenty service providers. Open doors and open minds emerged as the core theme for quality care. People stressed easy access, kind and informed staff, and strict privacy, given past trauma and shame. For research, they asked for real representation and care for overlapping forms of disadvantage. The authors urge services to adapt to these needs.
pmc-13203532:
Ziyan Tang and six co-authors combine two molecular tools into one fast stomach-bug test in a 2026 paper. The bacterium they target is tied to chronic stomach inflammation, ulcers, and stomach cancer, so quick detection matters. Their one-pot assay first copies a key gene many times, then uses a programmable enzyme system to flag it. Every part of the reaction, from mix ratios to temperature, was tuned step by step.

The finished test detects about ten times fewer copies than standard methods and finishes within an hour. On dozens of cultured samples it matched the culture verdict every time, with no false calls either way. The team pitches it for clinics with limited resources.
pmc-13204932:
Shamatova and four co-authors showed in twenty twenty-six that sodium channels, the tiny gates that carry electric signals in nerves, also steer how certain stem cells move. The cells came from the lining of the uterus and are widely used in tissue repair research.

Tests found nearly every known sodium channel part present in these cells, and electric recordings confirmed the channels open and close as expected. A blocker drug and an opener drug both changed the cells' behavior. In flat dishes, the two drugs slowed the cells' crawl into a scratch wound. In three-dimensional balls of cells, the same drugs sped up how fast cells spread outward. The flip shows the channels' role depends on the setting the cells grow in. The authors say this matters for designing stem cell therapies that rely on movement.
pmc-13205432:
Xiaoqiang Zhang, Pengfei Chen, and Xueheng Zhang design an image scrambling method built on a new chaotic map and a three-dimensional twist. Their study appeared in 2026. Pictures sent over networks leak easily, so encryption must be fast and strong. Their map beats classic chaotic systems on wildness and range. The algorithm lifts the flat image into three dimensions, scrambles and diffuses it there, applies a further mixing step, then folds it back down.

Encrypted images showed flat histograms, passed randomness checks, and carried information entropy above 7.9992. Standard attack measures hit the values expected of strong ciphers. A typical photo encrypts in about seven tenths of a second. The authors pitch the scheme for real-time secure image sharing.
pmc-13206632:
Eunjeong Park and Ki Han Kwon surveyed Korean adults about "inner beauty" foods in a 2026 study. These are swallowed products sold to improve skin, hair, and general wellness rather than to treat disease. The team asked 502 adults who had used such products about their reasons, shopping channels, and preferred formats.

Skin health was the top reason, named by nearly half, and it mattered most to younger and female buyers. Older adults more often cited weight control or hair and nail health. Online shops dominated, especially among buyers in their twenties. The survey shows a market split by age and motive, which sellers can use to match products and formats to the right customers.
pmc-13207032:
Rachel Dombrower, Alyssa McKenzie, Andrew Tucker, and Johnathan Atwell review nausea care after surgery in a 2026 paper. Nausea and vomiting after surgery remain a common, preventable problem. They matter even more inside Enhanced Recovery After Surgery pathways, which aim for smooth recovery.

The review gathers current evidence on prevention within these pathways. It covers risk scoring tools such as the Apfel score, drug combinations, and choices of anesthesia that spare opioids. It also reviews non-drug steps, such as fluid care and early movement. The authors stress matching prevention to each patient's own risk.
pmc-13207332:
Formula makers now add living microbes and milk sugars to mimic breast milk, and a 2026 narrative review led by Salvatore Scirè Calabrisotto weighs that evidence. The article reviews infant formulas supplemented with prebiotics, probiotics, postbiotics, synbiotics, and human milk oligosaccharides, focusing on gut, immune, and hormone growth in early life.

The authors find these formulas generally safe and supportive of normal growth, including for some infants with clinical conditions. Effects were most consistent in the gut itself: friendlier microbe profiles, better stools, and a stronger intestinal barrier in the studies surveyed. Evidence for body-wide immune, metabolic, and brain outcomes stayed promising but uneven, so long-term trials are still needed.
pmc-13207532:
Eliza Dobruchowska-Kesikowska, Mateusz Wityk, and Natalia Dowgiallo-Gornowicz poll how sleep-drug care for weight-loss knife work is run by sleep-drug docs in Poland. It checks how world guide lines for care round knife work turn into day-to-day work.

Seventy-one sleep-drug docs gave takes on thirteen closed asks sent through shared sites in late twenty twenty-five. A plain Macintosh tool to see the throat was the top tool to place a breath tube. A screen throat tool was used by a large small group. Most docs used plus air force as a norm, in lots of cases set right for body weight. Pain care with lots of drugs was the norm, led by paracetamol and dexamethasone. Asks took in blood force marks to put off knife work and to treat low force in work. Work split on those points.
pmc-13207932:
Shu Wang and eight co-authors track deep brain stimulation for a side effect of Parkinson's care over three years. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The side effect is dyskinesia, or unwanted moves brought on by the main drug. A device placed in a brain hub can calm those moves, but its long-run effect was not well known.

They follow a large group at a Beijing hospital from before surgery to one and three years after. Scores for unwanted moves drop a great deal at one year and stay much better at three, though some gain fades. Motor scores and life quality follow the same arc. A two-phase form of the side effect bodes ill, while strong drug response bodes well.
pmc-13208232:
Vladimir Churnosov, Maria Churnosova, and eight colleagues test whether inherited variants near a hormone gene shift a woman's risk of endometrial hyperplasia, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-six. In this condition the womb lining overgrows, a precursor state that can precede cancer, and sex hormone levels are part of the story.

The study compared five hundred twenty women with the condition against nine hundred seventy-three controls. The team genotyped nine variants already tied by genome-wide studies to sex hormone levels. Two variants in the FSHB gene, which helps produce follicle-stimulating hormone, tracked with lower risk, roughly halving the odds for some forms. A combined haplotype of the two also reached significance. Genetics will not replace the microscope for diagnosis. But risk variants point at the hormonal levers that drive the overgrowth, and at women who might warrant closer watching.
pmc-13208432:
Li Tian and co-authors design a membrane for vanadium flow batteries that lets protons pass while blocking vanadium ions, in a paper from 2026. Such batteries store energy for the grid, and the membrane is a key part. It must conduct well yet keep the two battery fluids from mixing.

The team grafted water-repelling side chains onto the membrane material. That pushed the material to separate into phases, forming wide, linked channels for protons even though the membrane holds few charge sites. Resistance was low and vanadium crossing was very slow. The balance between passing protons and blocking vanadium beat a widely used commercial membrane by a wide margin. In battery tests, energy efficiency was higher and loss per cycle was lower.
pmc-13210032:
Maryam Safarnavadeh, Leili Salehi, and Marjan Havaei published a 2026 study that adapts a questionnaire on attitudes toward labor pain relief for use in Persian. Labor pain is a nearly certain part of childbirth. How a woman views relief of that pain shapes her choices during birth. The questionnaire had to be adapted to the language and the culture, and its quality had to be proven.

The work ran in four steps. The questionnaire was translated into Persian and back, then adjusted. Its face and content quality were checked, and its structure was tested with a strict statistical tool. More than three hundred pregnant women in the capital took part. All six questions were kept. The structure check fit well, with two dimensions to the questionnaire. Willingness to seek relief can be read from the score: the higher it runs, the stronger the willingness.
pmc-13210132:
Zhiwen Tu and colleagues tested stem cell vesicles against bone loss in 2026. After menopause, bone thins as marrow cells age and inflame. Tiny packets shed by dying stem cells may calm that process. The team compared those packets with the better-known exosome packets. Tests ran in mice lacking ovaries and in aged human marrow cells. Small RNA reads compared the cargo of both packet types. The team tracked inflammatory output and bone-forming ability.

The dying-cell packets eased bone loss more than exosomes. They also cut aging-related inflammatory signals more strongly. Their cargo held a rich cluster of small regulatory RNAs. Those RNAs target two growth control proteins. Treated cells showed lower levels of both proteins. Two inflammatory signaling routes also quieted down. Marrow inflammation eased, and bone-forming capacity held up. The authors propose the packets as a cell-free therapy lead.
pmc-13210432:
Shen leads a large team reviewing traditional Chinese medicine for glioma, in work from twenty twenty-six. Glioma is the most common and aggressive primary brain tumor. The blood brain barrier, tumor variety, and drug resistance make it hard to treat, with poor outlook.

Plant derived active ingredients act on many targets at once, a trait the authors value. They can trigger tumor cell death and boost other therapies. The review covers mechanisms, delivery systems that cross the brain barrier, and progress toward clinic use. It aims to show where this traditional source may add real options to modern brain tumor care.
pmc-13210532:
Marcia Martins and four co-authors test new compounds against skin inflammation in a 2026 study. Long lasting skin inflammation often comes with itch, driven by a receptor that responds to a pain related signal molecule. The team designed variants of a natural compound family and screened them first by computer docking against that receptor.

Several variants bound as well as or better than a known blocker drug in the computer tests. In lab cells, the best compounds cut a key inflammation signal by about half without harming cells. The effect came with lower levels of the enzyme that makes that signal. Safety predictions were mostly favorable, though breakdown in the environment looked limited.
