pmc-13211632:
Anette Furevik and fourteen co-authors report a farm-scale trial of a new salmon vaccine. The vaccine targets a variant bacterium that causes winter ulcer disease in farmed Atlantic salmon. About eight million fish at eighteen sites in Norway took part. At each site, one group got the standard shots plus the new vaccine, and the other got the standard shots alone. The fish were watched from vaccination to harvest.

Deaths right after vaccination were low and alike in both groups, though local reactions ran slightly higher with the new vaccine. At three sea sites where the disease broke out, vaccinated fish died far less and fewer were downgraded at slaughter. The trial backs the vaccine under real farm conditions.
pmc-13212632:
Yuki Tada and colleagues report in 2026 a better way to locate brain responses to touch using scalp electrical recordings. Pinpointing where a signal arises inside the head depends heavily on the head model used, and standard models first split MRI scans into tissue types.

Sixteen healthy volunteers received small shocks to arm nerves and individual fingers while a 65-channel cap recorded responses. A personalised model that skips tissue segmentation placed sources closer to reference points from earlier studies, improving accuracy by up to a few millimetres. Finger responses also lined up in the expected thumb-to-little-finger order. Refined modelling, the authors note, cuts systematic error without new scanners.
pmc-13213132:
Timothy O. Ogunbode reviews alone in 2026 Nigeria's progress toward the global goal of clean water and sanitation for all between 2016 and 2024. Millions of Nigerians still lack reliable services, so tracking the gap guides where money and reform should go.

Drawing on government reports, national statistics, and publications from international agencies, the review finds progress that is real but uneven. Rural districts and conflict-affected regions lag badly, held back by thin infrastructure spending and weak governance. Comparisons with other African countries sharpen the picture. Ogunbode recommends stronger governance, clearer policy, enforced rules, and heavier investment aimed at underserved regions before the 2030 deadline arrives.
pmc-13213232:
Susanto and seven co-authors shrank moringa extracts into nanoparticles against breast cancer in this study from twenty twenty-six. Moringa leaves carry compounds with reported anticancer activity. Packaging them with silver or chitosan at nanoscale may sharpen the effect. The team treated breast cancer cells and normal cells in culture with both versions.

Both nanomaterials slowed the cancer cells' growth. Gene checks showed the Wnt growth pathway switched down, including its cyclin partner. A proliferation marker and two spread-related genes also fell. The materials are made by green synthesis routes. The authors nominate both as candidate breast cancer drugs. The evidence so far is confined to cell cultures.
pmc-13214932:
Douglas Jaxon Vadner and Sidney Smith report a skin cancer treated without surgery in a 2026 case paper. The cancer is extramammary Paget disease, a rare gland-type skin cancer that often spreads past its visible edge along skin structures. Surgery is the standard fix, but it can do real harm in sensitive areas like the scrotum, above all in older patients.

Their patient was a man of eighty-eight with the disease across the scrotum and perineum. Scans showed no deeper cancer. Given the size of the patch, its place, and his wish to skip surgery, shallow radiation was chosen. The dose was delivered in seventeen sessions, with the beam energy picked to reach the depth where stray cells hide. The authors argue that planning by depth makes radiation a sound option for selected patients like him.
pmc-13215432:
Kristina Sundqvist and Martina Martinez report a 2026 qualitative study of how workplace managers view alcohol prevention. Managers shape workplace culture, so their choices decide whether prevention policies turn into daily practice.

The authors interviewed 44 managers and sorted their answers into four themes covering social events, drinking norms, formal structures, and a health-promoting work environment. Managers described limiting servings at work events, offering alcohol-free options, and raising alcohol openly in conversation. Policies, training, and human resources support gave these efforts a formal base. The authors conclude that prevention works best when it is folded into wider well-being efforts.
pmc-13215532:
Andrew J. Nasr and co-authors report a 2026 study of how rotator cuff muscles respond to a short bout of low-intensity resistance exercise. They compared shoulders with rotator cuff tears against healthy shoulders using ultrasound-based stiffness measures.

Twenty participants performed thirty isometric contractions at a fifth of their maximum effort, with imaging before and after. In torn shoulders, the supraspinatus grew less stiff under passive conditions after exercise, a change the authors read as poorer adaptation. Muscle cross-section grew in both groups during active testing, and strength fell in everyone. The findings suggest torn muscles recover differently and may need longer rest after rehabilitation exercise.
pmc-13215632:
Syed Ali Haider and co-authors report a 2026 pilot randomized trial of AI-generated avatar videos for teaching postoperative care. Written discharge instructions are often poorly understood, and video is costly to produce by hand.

Thirty-eight health care workers, standing in for future patients, received ten postoperative topics either as a text handout or as avatar-led video. Quiz scores were similar in both groups, yet the video group spent longer with the material and rated it clearer, more engaging, and better for remembering. Feedback praised the format while suggesting the avatar itself needs refinement. The authors call for trials in real patient groups with varied health literacy.
pmc-13216132:
Aart Zwaan and co-authors present a 2026 study of what decides whether a patch of Central African landscape becomes forest or savanna. Fire feedbacks are the usual explanation for these mosaics, and the authors test whether the shape of the land itself does more work.

They identified mosaic landscapes from satellite tree cover data and extracted terrain measures from elevation models. Machine learning models predicted the vegetation state of patches with an average accuracy of 0.75 in the study's scoring, and local elevation relative to the surroundings was the strongest single predictor. Which terrain features mattered varied between landscapes. The authors conclude that mosaics are more predictable, and less prone to sudden wholesale flips, than the fire-only story suggests.
pmc-13217432:
Alihan Oral and co-authors present a 2026 retrospective study of thyroid hormones and fatty liver disease in people whose thyroid tests all sit inside the normal range. The patients were living liver donor candidates, which gave the team the rare advantage of biopsy-proven liver status.

The comparison set 227 people with confirmed fatty liver against 145 without. The fatty liver group showed the expected metabolic burden, with higher liver enzymes, blood fats, insulin resistance, and body mass. Free T3 and free T4 levels differed significantly between the groups, and both hormones related negatively to the stage of liver fat accumulation. The authors conclude that thyroid hormone levels at the lower end of normal may mark risk for steatosis even when the thyroid reads as healthy.
pmc-13218132:
Gudrun Agusta Sigurdardottir and the LightCOM team describe a 2026 protocol testing the feasibility of a weight-neutral intervention in Denmark. Weight stigma and self-directed weight bias are linked to poorer mental, social, and physical health. Weight-neutral programs skip weight loss and instead prioritize well-being and habits people can sustain, but their workability in practice is untested.

The single-arm study enrolls 56 adults with a body mass index of 30 or higher in the Capital Region of Denmark. Over six months, participants attend a preparatory session and eleven group sessions led by trained practitioners. Sessions center on intuitive eating, body acceptance, and self-compassion, with optional support-network events and size-inclusive yoga. The question is whether participants complete follow-up, judged against preset traffic-light criteria for a larger trial. The study gathers questionnaires, blood samples, hair cortisol, and activity tracking, plus interviews about acceptability.
pmc-13218532:
Job Agba Opue and co-authors, including Fucai Lin, apply abstract algebra to supply-chain resilience in a 2026 theory paper. Supply chains are systems where a disruption can cascade through suppliers, transport corridors, and synchronized demand. Most current models simulate or optimize; this one asks what the mathematics of irreversible change can reveal about collapse and rebound.

The framework represents each disruption or intervention as a transformation acting on a finite set of states. The set of those transformations forms a semigroup, an algebraic structure built for processes that cannot be undone. Within the structure the authors derive rules for synchronizing collapse, for stable states, and for spotting backups, together with algorithms that prune spare backup options. Cases span manufacturing, agriculture, and e-commerce logistics. The payoff is clarity: semigroup properties translate into measurable resilience indicators, giving managers tools for judging shock-containment strategies before a crisis forces it.
pmc-13222632:
Linhui Zou and co-authors review nanozymes for burn wound healing, in a 2026 article. Burn care must juggle infection control, inflammation, regeneration, and scarring over a long course, while antibiotic resistance and sepsis risks grow. Nanozymes mimic several natural enzymes at once and resist breakdown, making them attractive dressing ingredients.

Variants covered imitate oxidases, peroxidases, and protective enzymes that disarm reactive oxygen. Combined actions can kill bacteria, cool oxidative stress and inflammation, grow new blood vessels, and limit scarring. The review also maps pathophysiology of burn wounds stage by stage. Remaining limits and design directions close the piece, aimed at a next generation of burn treatments.
pmc-13224032:
Daniela Prates Chiarelli, Lee Lynd, Luana Bergamo, and Daniel Olson test if genes lent from kin germs can ease a jam in one germ's sugar path. Their study is from two thousand twenty-six.

The host germ eats plant waste and is bred to make fuel. Bred strains that make much fuel turn less of their feed sugar into it, a hint the sugar path jams. The team lent it three step genes from two heat germs, plus a wide set of forms of a fourth. Some lent forms proved live and brisk in the host. The host's own pace at one step is low next to trade germs. The work names where the path lags.
pmc-13226232:
Tengfei Hui and colleagues run a 2026 laboratory experiment on whether natural sounds from forest parks can relieve stress in university students. Thirty-two students, screened with a standard perceived-stress scale, listened to eleven recordings of animal sounds gathered from forest parks in Henan. Brain-wave recordings and surveys captured both body and mind responses during listening.

Biological sounds generally raised feelings of security and relaxation and eased fatigue, with stronger benefits in the most stressed students. A cricket and two bird species produced the most positive effects, while a crow and one katydid species scored negatively. Survey ratings tracked brain responses closely, supporting deliberate soundscape design in parks aimed at stressed young visitors.
pmc-13228932:
Zhiqiang Wang and a large Chinese team analyse a 2026 real-world safety dataset for fruquintinib, a targeted drug that blocks blood-vessel growth signals in metastatic colorectal cancer. Trial results had established its benefit, but routine practice mixes it with chemotherapy and immunotherapy in ways trials did not. The phase IV dataset covered 2,798 patients treated between 2019 and 2022, split by regimen.

About two thirds took the drug alone, while the rest combined it with chemotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors, or both. Side effects of any kind were least frequent on monotherapy and most frequent when chemotherapy joined the mix, and severe events followed the same ordering. Exposure lasted longest on the triple combination. The authors judge combination use acceptably safe overall.
pmc-13229532:
Michael R Dueno and colleagues review in 2026 whether anti-seizure medicines can ease stopping long-term benzodiazepine use. Withdrawal during tapering can be severe, and many people resume the drug. The review searched PubMed and checked reference lists for studies of these medicines used as add-on support.

Twenty-one articles met the criteria, covering trials, observational work, and case reports. Carbamazepine beat placebo at three months in one comparison, with more patients free of benzodiazepines. Oxcarbazepine helped rapid detox in a small study without a control group. Results for valproate, pregabalin, and gabapentin were mixed. Overall evidence stays limited, so the authors call for larger trials.
pmc-13230032:
Hui Li and Jiasheng Zhu test if set-text ways to learn much-used English words lift the skill to write in teen learners. Their 2026 study is like a trial but not a full one. It tracks forty-seven grade-eleven youth for sixteen weeks.

Youth moved from guided hunts in a large set of American English texts to hunts they ran on their own. A frame held them up as they made that move. Four write tests and polls tracked their path prior to the step and in the wake of it. Mean write scores rose by more than a third. That rise was firm in math terms and had a large size. Wealth of word use, right pairs of words, range of clause forms, and flow each rose by near half. Drive scores rose a lot. The finds back set-text word work to grow skill in writing.
pmc-13230232:
Irina Valentin offers in 2026 a framework for how identity rebuilds after major life disruption. She argues that feeling, symbols, and the body must develop together for a stable sense of self. Big changes such as migration, parenthood, job loss, or trauma can force that rebuilding at any age.

The framework names three levels, moving from emotional validation toward a joined, lived identity. A central idea is semiotic overextension, where a neat story about the self forms before daily habits and bodily regulation catch up. Digital tools and artificial intelligence can speed up the symbolic side further. Clinicians are warned not to mistake fluent self-talk for real functional change.
pmc-13230932:
Yang Gao and colleagues build in 2026 tiny DNA frames that compute inside living cells and release treatment only on the right signal. Each tetrahedron reads three small RNA markers at once and can carry out seven kinds of logic rules. A drug-carrying RNA stays locked until the chosen rule is satisfied.

One version used a majority rule across three markers linked to breast cancer cells. It silenced a survival gene called survivin only in cells showing the target pattern, sparing other cell types. Tumors shrank strongly in dish and animal tests, with little off-target harm reported. Reading several markers at once sharpens the line between cancer and healthy tissue for future smart medicines.
pmc-13233132:
Roberto Salvatori, Gary L Gallia, and Calixto-Hope G Lucas published a 2026 case report linking a missing tumor suppressor protein to a growth hormone tumor. The retinoblastoma protein normally brakes cell growth, and mice lacking its gene reliably develop pituitary tumors. Whether the same holds in people has been unclear.

Their patient developed eye cancer at age one from an inherited RB1 gene variant and was diagnosed at twenty with a somatotropinoma, a pituitary tumor that releases growth hormone. Staining of the tumor showed its cells had lost the retinoblastoma protein entirely. The case suggests the protein also guards the human pituitary, and it gives doctors a reason to watch RB1 carriers for pituitary growths.
pmc-13233332:
A large research team led by Julian R Buissant des Amorie reports a two thousand twenty-six study of early colorectal cancer. The paper asks when cancer cells gain the ability linked to spread, called oncofetal plasticity. Such cell states were once thought to appear only late in tumour growth.

Using organoid models, genome sequencing, and single-cell maps of the tumour surroundings, the team found these states at the earliest stages. They appeared widely, even in early cancers that had not spread. Fibroblasts resembling normal submucosal support cells seemed to trigger the change at invasive fronts. The findings suggest spread requires extra steps beyond this early plasticity, such as escaping immune attack.
pmc-13233632:
Angela Spartz and colleagues published a 2026 study on how breast cancer cells escape blood vessels to seed metastases, helped by fibroblasts that travel with them. Earlier work showed these circulating cancer-associated fibroblasts boost lung metastases when clustered with triple-negative breast cancer cells in mice. The team asked whether the fibroblasts help cancer cells cross vessel walls in the first hours after arrival.

In lung tissue assays, more cancer cells exited vessels within a day when clustered with fibroblasts, and the clusters stuck better to vessel-lining cells in dishes. Gene profiling pointed to PLAU, which makes the enzyme uPA, switching on in clustered cancer cells. Silencing PLAU reduced both vessel binding and escape. The findings nominate uPA as a lever against early metastatic seeding.
pmc-13233832:
Sanskar Thakur and colleagues published a 2026 imaging study on detecting endometrial cancer without cutting tissue. Cancer of the uterine lining is the most common cancer of the female reproductive tract, yet diagnosis still depends on invasive sampling that can miss disease. The team built a thin catheter using optical coherence tomography, a light-based scanning method, and imaged 57 intact wombs removed in surgery.

The specimens spanned normal lining, benign conditions, high-risk precancer, and cancer. Computer features drawn from the images separated the groups well: a similarity-based visualization reached about ninety-four percent sensitivity and eighty-seven percent specificity, while a cross-checked classifier scored slightly lower on both. The authors call the approach an optical biopsy and argue it deserves testing in living patients.
pmc-13234132:
Ling Huang and colleagues published a 2026 correction to their Scientific Reports study of repeated low-level red light therapy for short-sightedness in guinea pigs. The original experiment used form deprivation to induce myopia, then tested whether different light powers slowed it, tracking eye length, choroid thickness, and choroidal blood flow. In the first figure, one treatment group was mislabeled: the animals receiving two milliwatts of light were printed as receiving twelve milliwatts.

The correction fixes that label and reproduces the original figure with its legend so readers can see the experimental flow. It also supplies funding information that the original article omitted, crediting a Natural Science Foundation of Shandong Province grant. The notice states the original article has been corrected, and no results or conclusions were changed.
pmc-13236732:
Meng and colleagues trace how the brain's immune cells calm inflammation after a bleed around the brain. A subarachnoid haemorrhage often triggers a second wave of injury driven by inflammation. Their focus is the crosstalk between microglia, the brain's own immune cells, and astrocytes, the star-shaped support cells that can turn harmful or helpful.

The team follows a signalling route centred on a vitamin A receptor and two partner factors. Through it, microglia steer astrocytes toward their calmer form, easing inflammation. Naming the route gives drug hunters a target: boost this natural calming signal, and the second wave of damage after such bleeds might shrink.
pmc-13238532:
Tham and colleagues map the weight management services of the East of England before wiring them into doctors' computers. Obesity drives much ill health in England and strains budgets. Behavioural weight services work, yet reach too few people, since referrals depend on patients and doctors finding the right local offer among many.

Electronic signposting would use health records and digital messages to connect patients with fitting services automatically. Before building it, the team mapped who provides what across the region. A clear map of the current maze is the groundwork: the digital tool must point to real services, with real places, or it will send people nowhere.
pmc-13239632:
Sangini Tolia and colleagues report a 2026 study of group support for weight loss at a community gastroenterology clinic. Ninety-four patients with obesity joined a six-month programme pairing lifestyle change with regular support group sessions for shared experience and education.

Attendance proved decisive in the results. Patients who came to at least three quarters of sessions lost significantly more weight than those who attended less often. Frequent attenders were also far more likely to reach the clinically meaningful mark of losing a tenth of their body weight. The authors argue that keeping people engaged in the group is what makes lifestyle advice stick.
pmc-13239832:
Tina Yi Jin Hsieh and co-authors present RescueGPT, an automated reader of ambulance notes, in a 2026 proof-of-concept study. Safety reviewers normally hunt harmful care events by hand in emergency medical records, a slow process that cannot scale to national data, especially for rare cases like child cardiac arrests outside hospital.

The system converts free-text notes into structured prompts guided by an established paediatric safety framework, then asks a large language model to flag events across six care domains. Testing on forty-two cases showed strong accuracy for common details such as rhythm, age, and weight. Rare events with messy documentation, like wrong airway equipment size, proved harder to catch.
pmc-13240432:
Jorge Luis Medina-Lopez and co-authors test a bedside ultrasound measure for predicting kidney injury in severe preeclampsia in a 2026 study. The renal resistive index reflects resistance to blood flow inside the kidney, and a quick scan at admission might flag which dangerously hypertensive pregnant patients are heading for kidney failure.

Twenty-two intensive care patients were scanned on arrival, and nine developed kidney injury by standard criteria. Those patients had clearly higher index values on average. The measure separated the groups well in accuracy testing, with strong performance at a chosen threshold. Its link with measured filtration rate trended in the expected direction without reaching significance in this small group.
pmc-13241532:
Abubakr Shafique and co-authors report a 2026 study of reliability in AI image retrieval for pathology. Retrieval tools find look-alike tissue images to support diagnosis, yet scanner differences can bias the underlying models. Their dataset used the same slides scanned on two different machines.

Because the images were aligned to the same tissue spots, the team could isolate scanner effects on model output. Several large vision models were compared. Transformer-based systems, including three named pathology models, performed best and generalized most steadily across scanners. The authors frame scanner bias as a fairness and trust issue for clinical AI. Their paired dataset offers a clean way to test robustness before deployment.
pmc-13242332:
Alotaibi and colleagues in Riyadh packed the flavonoid rutin three ways to rescue its poor water solubility. Free rutin faced rutin nanocrystals and elastic spanlastics head-to-head. Human breast cancer cells supplied the test bed. Radical-scavenging assays gauged antioxidant power alongside cancer cell kill.

Spanlastics came out smallest, most uniform, and most stable in suspension overall. They quenched test radicals best and killed MCF-7 cells hardest. Apoptosis markers rose sharply and the cell cycle stalled in its first gap phase. The authors recommend follow-up animal studies of the winning vesicle formulation.
pmc-13243332:
Simon Martina-Perez tackles a puzzle in the study of active matter, the swarms and flocks formed by self-moving agents. The paper appeared in the Bulletin of Mathematical Biology in 2026. Imaging now yields dense tracks of cells, animals, and synthetic particles, and front-back or sideways patterns in those tracks are often read as proof of directional interactions. Martina-Perez shows that this reading can fool us.

The paper derives a linear equation that connects measurable velocity correlations between pairs of agents to the hidden interaction rule behind them. Analysis and simulations show that striped dipole and quadrupole patterns can arise even when every agent interacts through a plain, direction-blind attraction-repulsion rule. Adding a weak tendency to align velocities suppresses the dipole pattern. The work ends with practical guidance for experimenters who want to tell true directional forces from patterns that emerge on their own.
pmc-13244832:
Masatomi Shimizu and colleagues test whether diets rich in seed oil fats raise DNA damage in mice in 2026. Fats called PUFAs are needed by the body but break down easily into harmful products. One aging theory holds that PUFA-rich membranes shorten life through this damage.

Young male mice ate high-fat diets built on coconut oil or soybean oil for 12 weeks. The coconut group made stand-in fats and showed no lack of essential fats. That group also carried less DNA damage, less mitochondrial DNA harm, and fewer protein marks from fat breakdown. The soybean group showed the heavier load. The results back the idea that dietary fat type shapes inner damage.
pmc-13245432:
Koustuv Saha and co-authors compare AI answers with human answers to mental health posts in 2026 work. Online communities give peer support around the clock, and chatbots now promise the same at larger scale. Whether machine words match the feel of peer support was untested.

The team drew on more than 24,000 posts and about 139,000 human replies from 55 Reddit communities. Three leading chatbots answered the same posts for comparison. Machine replies ran longer, read more smoothly, and sounded more orderly. Human replies carried more varied words and personal stories. The authors favor blends that keep human warmth while using machine speed.
pmc-13247132:
Jomehzadeh and Fakari checked whether a reserve antibiotic is losing ground in Abadan, southwestern Iran, in this 2026 Health Science Reports study. Fosfomycin is an older drug increasingly used against E. coli strains producing extended-spectrum beta-lactamases, enzymes that defeat many standard antibiotics. The team collected ninety clinical isolates in 2020 and 2021, testing drug susceptibility and screening for resistance genes.

About a third of isolates produced the resistance enzymes, and over half of those carried the main CTX-M gene. Outright fosfomycin resistance was still uncommon, in roughly one isolate in eighteen, but warning genes circulated: half of the enzyme producers carried a glpT change and a minority carried fosA3. The authors urge continued local surveillance to protect a valuable fallback drug.
pmc-13247532:
Lim, Peluso, and Downs report a hard lesson about cancer immunotherapy in this 2026 JCEM Case Reports article. Their patient had autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1, an inherited failure of immune tolerance caused by a faulty AIRE gene. She received checkpoint inhibitor drugs for a squamous cell cancer of the hard palate, treatment that releases the immune system's brakes and can provoke autoimmune attacks even in ordinary patients.

She developed three such attacks at once: immune hepatitis, thyroiditis, and new diabetes. Doctors treated her with immune suppressants, thyroid hormone, and insulin. The authors use the case to argue for careful screening for hidden autoimmunity before checkpoint therapy, proposing a two-hit model: weak central tolerance plus released immune brakes invites multiple, severe autoimmune complications.
pmc-13248432:
Protti and an international team reviewed breathing machine settings during heart-lung bypass support, published in 2026. Patients on veno-arterial ECMO, which pumps blood outside the body, usually also receive mechanical ventilation. Whether vent settings help or hinder the heart's recovery was unclear, so the team gathered every study they could find through mid 2025.

Only twelve studies qualified from more than five thousand records. Gentler pressures and slower breathing rates were linked with better survival in several reports. Moderate air pressure at the end of each breath seemed to protect lungs without straining the heart. The authors stress how thin and uneven the evidence remains.
pmc-13248732: Tirth Uprety and co-authors published this genome announcement in 2026. It reports near-complete genome sequences for three equine herpesviruses, types 1, 3, and 4, collected in the United States. The team combined short reads from Illumina machines with long reads from Oxford Nanopore machines, a hybrid approach that yields higher-quality assemblies than either alone. The authors say the new sequences should sharpen understanding of how these horse viruses vary and evolve in the United States.
pmc-13249532:
Edie Sperling and Mohammed Elsalanty describe a patient who has two rare ear conditions at once, a pairing not reported before. Their case report was published in twenty twenty-six.

The patient was a forty-three-year-old woman. In her right ear she had Ménière's disease, an inner ear disorder with attacks of spinning, fullness, ringing, and shifting hearing loss. She also had red ear syndrome, with spells of redness, pain, and burning of the outer ear. The two share some features, which complicates diagnosis. The authors propose links between them, including atypical migraine, nerve control faults, vessel leakiness, and hormone factors. The case may alert ear doctors to look for the second condition.
pmc-13250032:
Clara Barros and co-authors review a brain chemical signal in this 2026 article on chronic pain. Long-term pain is now seen as more than sore tissue: it involves lasting inflammation in the nervous system, overactive support cells, and changed wiring.

The review centres on adenosine, a calming chemical made in the body, and one of its four receptors, called A2A. That receptor shapes how support cells and nerve cells talk to each other, and how excitable pain circuits become. The authors weigh evidence that tuning this receptor could ease neuroinflammation linked to chronic pain, while noting how mixed its effects can be across cell types.
pmc-13250232:
Najibi and colleagues test whether high blood pressure and ringing in the ears travel together in rural Iran. Their 2026 BMJ Open study uses the Fasa adult cohort, covering nearly ten thousand people aged thirty-five to seventy. Earlier studies hinted at a link but left open how severity and control of blood pressure matter.

About one in five participants had hypertension, and about one in fourteen reported tinnitus. People with hypertension had clearly higher odds of tinnitus, and the odds rose with worse and poorly controlled pressure. Even well-controlled hypertension carried somewhat raised odds compared with normal pressure readings. The authors suggest doctors screen for tinnitus in all blood pressure patients and call for work on the vessel mechanisms behind the link.
pmc-13250332:
Romain Lefranc and colleagues report a striking bladder cancer case in this 2026 paper. A 59-year-old man had bladder cancer that had already spread, a stage with a poor outlook, and he received a modern two-drug treatment as his first therapy.

After ten rounds of treatment, scans showed the cancer had fully vanished and stayed gone. Surgeons then removed the bladder and prostate as a settling step, and lab checks confirmed no cancer remained at all. The authors argue that such follow-up surgery may be worth weighing for the few spread-stage patients whose cancer responds deeply and lastingly to drug treatment.
pmc-13251232:
Wilhelmus Grooten and a team of eleven researchers reflect on a double layer of evidence work in this 2026 commentary. At Sweden's Karolinska Institutet, they ran two systematic reviews of systematic reviews on exercise therapy for long-term back and neck pain.

Reviews of reviews help readers keep up, since dozens of new reviews appear daily, and merging them can clarify how certain the evidence is. But the method stacks weaknesses: each layer depends on the quality of the studies beneath it, and reviews often disagree. The team weighs these strengths and limits for muscle and joint health, and concludes the approach still adds real value.
pmc-13251432:
Sepideh Khazaie and a large team study the body clock of the nervous system in sleep apnea in this 2026 paper. Participants had both pauses in breathing during sleep and bursts of irregular heartbeat, and the team tracked how heart rhythm control shifted across day and night.

Data came from 109 people wearing heart recorders for one to three weeks, plus sleep studies before and after three months of CPAP, a mask therapy that holds airways open. Breathing severity linked most strongly to nerve balance measures while awake. After CPAP, several rhythm measures changed during both waking and sleep, in different directions. The authors see daily patterning as a clue to lasting heart strain.
pmc-13253132:
Lyndal Hulse and colleagues evaluate two rapid molecular platforms for detecting Hendra virus in horses in a 2026 study. Hendra is a lethal virus endemic to eastern Australia that spreads from bats to horses and can kill people who handle sick animals. A trustworthy field test would let veterinarians act before laboratory confirmation arrives.

The team compared a standard real-time PCR test with an isothermal amplification method designed for simpler field use. The PCR test proved far more sensitive, detecting a single copy of viral material per microliter against a thousand copies for the rival method, so the weaker platform was dropped early. Statistical modeling estimated the PCR test's accuracy on field-style samples prepared with a quick extraction-free method. The authors judge PCR with rapid sample preparation a feasible first-line field tool for ruling Hendra in or out.
pmc-13254232:
David Tesina and co-authors report a hidden cancer return found during surgery in a 2026 case report. A patient thought to be in full remission had delayed breast reconstruction with a DIEP flap, which uses the patient's own belly tissue. Pre-surgery imaging and blood markers showed no cancer.

Tissue tests on the removed mastectomy scar unexpectedly found a local breast cancer recurrence. The team then had to lift the fresh flap and cut out the tumor again just 23 days later. The authors call this the first such case and urge routine tissue checks of mastectomy scars.
pmc-13255032:
Daniel R. Cuesta-Aguirre and colleagues report a 2026 ancient DNA study from northeastern Iberia, covering the Iron Age into early Roman times. The team sampled newborn burials found beneath houses at three sites, dating from 775 BCE to 50 CE. Infant burials under floors were a regional custom, making them a window into local families.

Genome-wide data came from 22 of the 54 babies, with mitochondrial lineages for nine more. The results show strong continuity with local Bronze Age populations, alongside slowly growing Mediterranean-related ancestry. That pattern held fairly steady until Roman expansion brought extra inputs and a more mixed population. The authors link the genetic story to the region's long cultural continuity despite major political change.
pmc-13255732:
Ye Pyae Naing and Seon-Ho Kim report a 2026 study of heat stress in Holstein dairy cows in Korea, comparing the dry period with early lactation. Fourteen cows were observed during hot August weather, when heat load peaks. Blood and rumen fluid samples showed how metabolism, digestion, and microbes responded at each stage.

Cows in early lactation carried lower energy-related substances in blood but higher markers of energy use and stress. Their blood cell patterns suggested a different immune posture as well. Rumen fermentation in the early-lactation group produced more of certain energy-yielding acids, and microbial communities shifted. The authors conclude that freshly calved cows face the greater metabolic strain under heat, so cooling and feeding strategies should prioritize that stage.
pmc-13257232:
Lizhi Niu and co-authors review in 2026 how feed choices shape poultry meat quality. Buyers now judge chicken by color, tenderness, flavor, and nutrition, not just weight. Diet is the most flexible lever producers control during a short growing cycle.

Protein and amino acids, fats, minerals, and vitamins are each covered, along with plant extracts and functional additives. Mechanisms run through muscle metabolism, oxidation balance, and tissue microstructure. Adjusting fat sources can enrich helpful fatty acids, while antioxidants protect flavor during storage. The review joins visible traits to molecular pathways so choices rest on cause, not habit. Poultry scientists and feed makers share the audience. Precision feeding, tailored to breed and stage, is presented as the direction for higher-value meat.
pmc-13257532:
Hongqiao Yan and colleagues pull cracked pipeline steel tubes apart to watch strain gather in a 2026 experiment. X46 steel tubes carried pre-made cracks of varied size, depth, and angle, while cameras tracked full-field deformation. Sound material balanced strength and stretch well in baseline tests.

Uncracked tubes deformed evenly, then localized, then necked before failure. Cracked tubes localized at crack tips from early on, and the hot zone grew with pulling. Larger cracks sharpened tip strain and widened the strained region. Through-wall cracks forced earlier instability than surface cracks, while small surface flaws barely changed the failure path. Diagonal cracks at forty-five degrees produced the worst cross-shaped pattern. Pipeline inspectors gain a ranking of which flaw shapes demand fastest attention in thin walls.
pmc-13257732:
Eleonora Casalini leads a 2026 safety study of ultrasound-guided lung needle sampling in patients aged eighty and older. One hundred forty-one patients at one Italian hospital underwent the bronchoscopy procedure under moderate sedation without an anesthetist present, across seven years of records. Complications, sampling success, and diagnosis rates were tallied.

About one in nine patients had a complication, and nearly all events were mild. Two patients needed hospital care for major problems. Sampling succeeded in almost every case, specimens were adequate nearly as often, and a diagnosis followed in most patients. More than half the diagnoses were cancers, and most of those patients went on to active treatment. Geriatric pulmonology teams gain reassurance: age past eighty alone should not bar this key diagnostic step when sedation is handled carefully.
pmc-13258432:
Hye Jin Jee and colleagues test a two-herb extract for sleep promotion in mice in a 2026 study. St. John's wort and lemon balm were combined and given in a drug-induced sleep model, with receptor blockers used to trace the mechanism. Brain activity mapping and gene expression in the cortex added cellular evidence.

Treated mice fell asleep faster and slept longer. The effect ran through adenosine and melatonin receptor pathways, with two marker compounds splitting the labor between them. Wake-driving neuron groups quieted, while a sleep-promoting brain area activated more strongly. Receptor gene levels rose in the cortex after treatment. Sleep researchers gain a candidate botanical with a defined mechanism, rare in this market. Human insomnia claims must await clinical trials, since mouse sleep architecture differs from ours.
pmc-13258732:
Dominika Myśliwczyk and colleagues systematically review weight drug treatment for children and teens with obesity in a 2026 article. The drugs mimic a gut hormone that controls appetite and blood sugar. Fifteen studies covering nearly fifteen hundred young patients met the review criteria.

Drugs studied ranged from daily injections to newer weekly options. Reported body mass reductions varied widely, with one weekly drug showing the largest drops. Lifestyle support differed greatly between studies, from brief advice to full family programs. That uneven reporting blocked any firm verdict on how much lifestyle help adds. Clinicians get a careful summary of benefits so far plus the reporting gaps future trials must fix.
pmc-13258832:
Nghia Thi Hieu Phan and colleagues bioprint wound scaffolds with jelly from umbilical cord tissue in a 2026 study. A two stage salt hardening process let a gelatin alginate ink carry the delicate cord extract. Printed grids kept sharp shape and target pore sizes.

Both plain and enriched scaffolds proved safe for skin support cells in culture. Enriched scaffolds held more cell coverage over two weeks. In mouse burn wounds, enriched scaffolds produced smoother new skin coverage by day fourteen. Print accuracy stayed high despite the added biological material. Wound care researchers gain a printing method that protects fragile healing ingredients.
pmc-13260432:
Manluan Sun and colleagues profiled in 2026 how a chemical tag called lysine acetylation shifts with diet in a model mycobacterium. The work uses Mycobacterium smegmatis, a fast-growing relative of the tuberculosis bacterium, grown in a lean medium and a rich one. Mass spectrometry catalogued which proteins carried the tag in each condition.

Hundreds of proteins were tagged in only one condition, and many more changed their tagging between media. The affected pathways covered central carbon use, energy cycles, and RNA breakdown. In lean medium, tagging of one key enzyme likely slowed it, steering carbon toward a bypass route that saves resources. In rich medium, tagging pointed the flow the other way. The authors argue the tag acts as a dual switch, redirecting fuel use while also slowing RNA decay so signal molecules can build up.
pmc-13260532:

pmc-13264332:

pmc-13264832:

pmc-13279032:
Bader Khayat, Omar M. Alabbasi, and Ghadi Aljohani published a 2026 case report on an eye implant made from donor tissue. The patient was a man in his mid fifties. One eye had severe regular astigmatism. His corrected vision had declined. Other correction options were limited.

Surgeons placed ring segments of donor cornea inside his cornea. Such segments usually treat a cone-shaped cornea disease. One year later, scans showed much lower astigmatism. The cornea looked more regular and stayed stable. No complications appeared. The case suggests a tissue-preserving option for selected patients.
pmc-13279932: Prakash Gyawali and colleagues issue a 2026 author correction to their 2025 Scientific Reports study that used near infrared spectroscopy, a light based scan, to predict the warming impact of biomass fuels. The methods text held a flawed set of steps for computing greenhouse gas output and total warming impact. The notice prints the fixed steps, with per gas factors and heat values in the right units. It adds a climate carbon effect value from the AR6 report that the first version left out. The scan model itself stands.
pmc-13280332:
Maud Reynier and colleagues present a 2026 survey of surgeon views on planning software in shoulder replacement. Preoperative planning software lets surgeons view patient anatomy in three dimensions and tune implant position before the cut. Wide uptake rests on surgeon satisfaction and felt utility, not just accuracy. Data on those views were limited. The survey covers users of one planning tool, Blueprint, in shoulder arthroplasty.

A web questionnaire went by email to one thousand one hundred orthopaedic surgeons in late 2024. Items read overall satisfaction, usage patterns and accord with set statements. Likelihood of future use and of recommending the tool to others were key outcomes. Willingness to back it as a training tool for fellows, junior surgeons in specialty training, was also asked. Surgeon felt worth decides if planning tech earns a daily place in practice.
pmc-13280532:
Patricia da Cunha Brito and team give a 2026 practical guide to care around surgery for primary aldosteronism, written for hormone doctors. The condition is the most common hormone cause of secondary high blood pressure, yet it stays underdiagnosed. Excess aldosterone, a salt hormone, causes major heart and kidney harm. About one third of patients have one sided disease. For them, adrenalectomy, removal of one adrenal gland, beats drug care for long term outcomes.

Before surgery, goals hold blood pressure below a set mark and potassium levels in range. Salt hormone blockers, called MRAs, should start in all patients, with dose titration to ensure blockade. A dedicated pre surgery hormone consult is key to review expected outcomes, kidney function decline, cortisol co secretion and adrenal insufficiency risk. Post surgery concerns are covered as well.
pmc-13280932:
Dorie E Apollonio and colleagues surveyed online tobacco sellers in a 2026 study. Ads by sellers are a big cost for the tobacco trade and shape what people buy. The team searched the web from March to July 2022 with terms like buy vapes. They kept English sites that sold vape products and shipped within the United States. Ninety-seven sellers met their rules, and the team logged what each site showed.

About six in ten sites asked visitors to confirm their age before browsing. Vapes, both single-use and refillable, were the goods sold most. More than a third of sellers also sold cannabis goods. A like share sold other goods, from pipes to drug-laced sweets. Flavored goods were pushed hard across the sites. The authors say such sales may clash with federal aims to curb tobacco use.
pmc-13281332:
Laura Valido and colleagues trained heart ward nurses with a fake heart pump patient in a 2026 study. The Berlin Heart is a pump that helps a child's heart while it waits for a transplant. Their program grew fast, and many bedside nurses had little practice with the device. The team built a lifelike simulator of a child on the pump. Staff took classes and then drilled on the simulator. Eighty-two staff members took part in all.

Surveys before and after showed staff felt far more ready to care for such a child. Scores on a short knowledge test also rose. Six to eight weeks later, the gains still held. The authors say pairing classes with hands-on drills can lock in rare skills. They offer the plan as a model for other wards that face fast growth in complex care.
pmc-13281532:
Max Franck and colleagues published a 2026 materials study growing ultrathin hexagonal boron nitride films directly on silicon. This layered insulator protects graphene electronics and emits deep ultraviolet light, yet it is usually grown on metal and transferred, leaving contamination chip fabs cannot tolerate. Their vapor deposition process feeds a precursor, borazine, onto silicon wafers cut on the standard (001) face, avoiding reactive nitrogen species that would form a silicon nitride layer at the interface.

The films came out at seven layers thick, give or take one, with near-perfect stoichiometry and a surface roughness of 1.1 nanometers. Spectroscopic ellipsometry, validated here for routine thickness checking, returned a refractive index of 2.17 and an optical bandgap of 5.89 electron volts. The authors argue direct growth on CMOS-compatible silicon removes the transfer bottleneck and could let boron nitride join standard fabrication lines.
pmc-13281632:
Esben Østergaard Eriksen and colleagues proposed a sharper meaning for herd health management in a 2026 review. Farm vets once treated one sick animal at a time. Their work now centers on the health of whole herds. Yet the term for that work is used in clashing ways in print. The review pulls the strands together into one definition. Herd health work is cast as a loop that never ends.

In the loop, teams plan, act, and check choices that keep herd health high. Health means normal body function and freedom from disease across the farm. The aims must serve the farmer's goals for output, animal welfare, and outside effects, like drug use. Choices sit at three levels, from long plans to daily acts. Mid-level steps size up the herd, set goals, spot risks, plan changes, and track results. The authors offer the frame to align research and farm practice.
pmc-13281732:
Merel H de Heer and colleagues studied personal learning paths in doctor training in a 2026 paper. The setting was the Dutch national program for women's health doctors in training. Alongside fixed goals, the program lets each trainee set open personal goals. No set test hangs over those goals. The team interviewed twelve trainees and read their portfolios. They asked what drew trainees in and what helped or blocked them.

All twelve used their personal path, though depth varied. Drive came from interest, values, hard cases, role models, and chances at work. Three supports mattered. The formal place of the path in the program made it feel allowed. Time and varied work helped trainees spot goals that meant something. Program heads helped most when they coached, not just checked boxes, though some did little. The authors call the blend structured freedom.
pmc-13281932:
Clara Vazquez and colleagues published a 2026 case description of an 8-year-old boy with double-chambered right ventricle, where a muscular band splits the chamber in two. Referred for a heart murmur, he showed blue discoloration, breathlessness on exertion, and blood oxygen of 80 percent at rest. Ultrasound revealed the band dividing the chamber into inflow and apical parts. A narrow passage between them carried pressure gradients near 47 millimeters of mercury, plus a second tortuous channel.

A hole between the atria shunted blood right to left, explaining the low oxygen. Imaging through the esophagus confirmed the band and twisting channel, while CT built a three-dimensional picture that ruled out a missing tip of the ventricle. The pulmonary valve was also narrowed. The authors present the multi-imaging workup as the lesson: each modality caught anatomy the others blurred, and together they map the obstruction well enough to plan correction.
pmc-13282132:
Ryusuke Sumiya and co-authors wrote a 2026 surgical technique article on robotic lung surgery in patients whose chest shape is deformed. Deformities such as a sunken chest narrow the working space. They also complicate where the robot ports, the entry points for its arms, should go. The authors present two patients with lung cancer who had right-sided anatomical resection, meaning a defined lobe or segment was removed.

In the first case, a forty-one-year-old woman had a lower lobe removed with the standard port layout. The protruding spine blocked the view and trapped the retracting arm. In the second, a thirty-eight-year-old man had upper segments removed after ports were shifted toward the front of the chest. That change made the operation more comfortable despite closer port spacing. The authors advise placing the camera line in front of the spine in such chests.
pmc-13282332:
Lorenzo Maggi and co-authors report a 2026 study on adding a surgical robot to a knee replacement team already skilled in computer navigation. Total knee arthroplasty replaces a worn knee joint. Robots promise precision but often slow surgery while teams learn. One centre reviewed two hundred thirty-six first-time knee replacements by a single high-volume team, comparing navigation alone with an open-platform robot added to the same workflow.

Early robot cases took longer, with a median of eighty-four minutes. After a learning curve of fifty-eight cases, times settled to seventy-seven minutes, comparable with navigation's eighty-one. In the steady phase, the robot's active cutting step was actually faster than manual navigated cutting. Planning time inside surgery was offset by faster resection. They conclude that a well-prepared navigation team can adopt this robot without a lasting time penalty.
pmc-13282432:
Ludwig Federico Garello and co-authors present a 2026 study scoring the methods quality of heart imaging radiomics research, and testing whether an AI chatbot can help score it. Radiomics turns scans into many numeric features for prediction models. Two scoring systems rate how well such studies are designed and reported. Human readers with mixed expertise scored studies published up to February 2025.

Of seven hundred eighty-one records screened, one hundred fifty-four studies were included. One scoring system rated quality as good overall, while the other gave much lower scores. Both exposed common flaws: little outside validation, few prospective designs, and scarce open data. Human readers agreed well with each other on one system and moderately on the other. The chatbot's agreement with humans was moderate to good on one system but poor to moderate on the other.
pmc-13282732:
Xiaoyun Liu and co-authors present a 2026 study on how repeated use of diamond milling burs affects the accuracy of machine-made dental crowns. The crowns were milled from polymer-infiltrated ceramic, a hybrid material, on two different milling systems. As burs wear, crown fit and surface quality can suffer. The team made one hundred twenty-one premolar crowns and checked bur wear after every five fabrications.

Accuracy differed by region and machine. One system made truer inner surfaces, the other truer outer surfaces. Wear pushed the two machines into opposite error modes: one increasingly over-milled, cutting too much, while the other under-milled but degraded more slowly. Surface roughness also diverged, rising sharply in one system after the fifty-fifth crown. The authors conclude that bur replacement schedules must be system-specific, since each machine's degradation harms crown quality in its own way.
pmc-13283132:
Cancer biomarkers hiding in gut microbes are charted across the literature by Joao Daniel de Souza Menezes and colleagues, writing in 2026. Microbes may predict drug response, side effects, and disease course. The review maps proof and gaps for use in precise cancer care.

Five databases were searched with a clear plan and standard reporting rules. Adult patients on chemo, immune drugs, or combined plans were the focus. Certain microbes predicted immune drug response well in some studies. Probiotics cut gut lining harm in one cited result. Models based on microbes often beat standard clinical markers. The authors note wide method gaps that block routine clinical use for now.
pmc-13283632:
Kelsie Richardson and colleagues studied in 2026 how birth control pill use interacts with concussion in teenage girls. Female athletes face higher concussion risk than males, and hormone control from the pill has been floated as a possible shield after injury, though proof is thin. The team enrolled fifty girls with a recent concussion and sixty-nine uninjured controls.

Pill use was self-reported on a standard questionnaire, and both groups answered mood, mobility, and fatigue scales. Concussion status drove the clearest gaps: the concussion group rated low mood, mobility, and fatigue worse than controls, whatever their pill use. Pill users reported worse mobility on their own. No combined interaction between concussion and pill use appeared in the reported tests.
pmc-13284732:
Liying Wen and colleagues surveyed nearly five thousand students in Inner Mongolia in 2026 on school climate and aggression. Perceived school climate means how safe, fair, and supportive school feels to a student. The sample spanned primary, middle, and high schools, and students rated climate, friendship quality, resilience, and aggressive behaviour on standard scales. The team tested whether friendships carry the climate effect and whether resilience changes it.

Climate, friendship quality, and resilience all correlated positively with each other, while aggression correlated negatively with all three. Friendship quality did carry part of the climate-to-aggression link, though modestly. Resilience also softened the effects of both climate and friendship quality on aggression. The authors weave setting, relationships, and personal strength into one framework for schools.
pmc-13285032:
Laiba Shahab, Syed Huzaifa Khan, and Javeria Kashaf Zain write to a journal in 2026. They question a study of people with high blood pressure. That study linked a body-shape score to calcium build-up in the aorta, the body's main artery. The three writers accept that the question is worth asking. They doubt that the math backs the claims.

One flaw, they say, is that the score went into the models with the same waist and weight measures used to build it. That mix can skew the results. A curve test that finds no curve does not prove a straight line, they add. A past group used the same data and found a U shape. They also judge the score too weak to sort risk well.
pmc-13285132:
Ali El Safadi and co-authors present a 2026 case report and literature review on a tube and ovary abscess after frozen embryo transfer. Such pelvic infection is rare after fertility care and is usually tied to egg collection, not transfer. A 41-year-old woman with endometriosis grew the abscess two weeks after a hormone-prepared transfer done under sterile terms with preventive antibiotics.

She arrived with pelvic pain and fever, and imaging showed a multi-chamber abscess on the right side. Since she was stable, doctors chose antibiotics alone, given by vein then by mouth. The abscess cleared fully with no drainage or surgery. The authors warn that even low-risk transfers need watchful follow-up.
pmc-13285932:
Smita Agarwal, Lily Yu-Li Chang, and Erin Thornell check a new toric lens in routine cataract care in a 2026 real-world study. The Clareon PanOptix Toric lens fixes focus at several ranges while also correcting astigmatism, but only if it stays on axis after surgery. The team tracked lens twist and vision in patients treated outside a strict trial setting.

The lens went into 40 eyes from 22 patients who had both eyes done by standard surgery. Mean twist at twelve weeks stayed small, and most eyes sat within five degrees of the target axis. Vision without glasses tested sharp at distance, middle, and near ranges, and patient scores for near tasks rose after surgery. Contrast and depth sense held near normal levels, though the share of eyes meeting the strict alignment bar fell a bit short of the set standard.
pmc-13286132: Mamothena Carol Mothupi and colleagues issued a short 2026 correction to their study of a composite index for maternal health care in South Africa. The notice is brief and fixes labels only: two figures had their vertical axes named with older index labels, and both should read as the C3MH index instead. The corrected figures show index scores by district across five years and sub-index scores for 2016. No data, results, or conclusions change.
pmc-13287032:
Tao Zhang and co-authors review the two-way conversation between DNA methylation, a chemical gene-silencing mark, and the gut's innate immune defenses in inflammatory bowel disease. Their 2026 article covers Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, chronic relapsing conditions where barrier failure, immune overreaction, and epigenetic change intertwine.

Methylation patterns can lock immune and barrier genes into pro-inflammatory settings, helping explain why inflammation persists and returns. Running the other way, inflammatory signals, oxidative stress, and key pathways can rewrite methylation, forming a feedback loop the authors name an interaction axis. They propose the axis as a frame for biomarker hunting and combined epigenetic-immune treatments, while calling for single-cell and long-term studies to pin down timing and cell types.
pmc-13287232:
Hanan A M Hassanien and colleagues added mealworm powder to lamb feed in 2026 and followed 18 young Ossimi lambs for 120 days. One group ate a standard ration, one received powder from larvae, and one received powder from whole insects, each at a small daily dose.

Both insect groups gained slightly more weight, though the edge was not statistically firm. Digestion of protein improved in the whole-insect group, and digestion of dry matter and carbohydrates rose in both insect groups. Blood protein patterns shifted without signs of harm. Returns looked numerically better for insect-fed groups. The authors suggest mealworm feed deserves larger trials in growing lambs.
pmc-13287432:
Lucas Lima Najar and Marleide da Mota Gomes built a questionnaire in 2026 asking adults with epilepsy what they believe triggers their seizures, then gave it an early quality check. One hundred patients at two public hospitals in Rio de Janeiro took part.

An opening set of twelve questions was trimmed during testing. Four questions drew too many blank answers to score well, leaving a seven-question core. That core behaved mostly as one scale, with consistency just below common cut-offs. The authors judge it fit for group research, not for judging single patients. Larger multi-site samples must confirm the structure before clinics rely on it.
pmc-13287532:
Patients on breathing machines through a face mask often develop pressure sores on the nose, sometimes bad enough to stop treatment. Raffaele Scala and co-authors set out a trial protocol comparing three protective dressings against that damage. The trial will run in fifteen intensive care units in Italy and Spain.

Patients with acute breathing failure who need mask ventilation for over a day will be assigned by chance to one of three brands of protective pad or to standard care. Staff will grade any skin lesions, pain, and comfort with standard scales. The main measure is how long patients stay free of skin injury. Costs and the odds of ventilation succeeding are also tracked. The authors aim for evidence sturdy enough to write into guidelines.
pmc-13287732:
Istvan Papp and co-authors re-examined overnight sleep recordings in 2026. The set held 32 controls and 26 adults living with nightmare disorder. They looked beyond the dream sleep stage, where nightmares were long assumed to live. A shared analysis pipeline measured how two brain wave patterns pair up during deep non-dream sleep.

Pairing between slow waves and spindle bursts at the front of the head ran weaker in the nightmare group. Another pairing type stayed normal, so the balance between them shifted. A further wave event also appeared less often across the first six hours. The authors argue that nightmare disorder reshapes quiet sleep structure too, and ask for confirmatory studies.
pmc-13288532:
Jia Fan and co-authors compare two ways of running intrauterine insemination in a 2026 retrospective cohort study from China. They followed 1,451 couples through a first insemination cycle using the husband's sperm, contrasting natural cycles with cycles where the ovaries were stimulated, and sorting results by the reason for infertility.

Of the cycles, 833 were natural and 618 were stimulated. Couples with an ovulatory disorder fared better than those with normal ovulation on pregnancy and live birth, though preterm birth was also more common in that group. Among patients ovulating normally, natural cycles trended ahead for endometriosis, tubal, and male-factor cases, while stimulated cycles trended ahead for unexplained infertility, without firm statistical support.
pmc-13288832:
Zhiyu Lu and colleagues build an mRNA vaccine for syphilis in 2026. Their work is an animal study. The target is TP0435, a surface lipoprotein. The bug is Treponema pallidum. The mRNA rode in lipid particles. Early checks showed stability and no acute harm.

In mice, a five-microgram dose worked well. Antibodies rose strongly. Cell immunity leaned to the Th1 type. Memory CD4 cells grew in number. In rabbits, both vaccines slowed lesions. Bacterial loads also fell. The mRNA type fully blocked ulcers. Loads stayed lower at lesion sites. Spread through the body was limited. Tissue showed fewer neutrophils and more defenders.
pmc-13289132:
J P Sevilla and colleagues weigh the full cost of new infectious diseases in 2026. Their study ranks 15 high-priority diseases. It spans 223 nations and territories. Past years run from 2000 to 2022. Future years run from 2025 to 2034.

Health loss was turned into money terms. Hospital costs, direct and indirect, were added. Pandemics bore the largest loads by far. Among the rest, dengue and cholera led worldwide. West Nile virus led inside the US. Dengue led in US territories. Fair-weighted loads topped raw loads fivefold. The Americas and Africa bore the heaviest per-person loads. Results can guide research spending.
pmc-13289232:
Lina Hult led a 2026 population study on uneven heart muscle contraction in middle-aged adults in Sweden. The measure, left ventricular mechanical dispersion, tracks how evenly the main pumping chamber squeezes. Uneven squeezing is known in heart disease and links to dangerous rhythms, but its place in the general public was unclear.

Heart ultrasound with speckle tracking was done in 3997 people aged 50 to 64 from the Swedish Cardiopulmonary Bioimage Study. A healthy subgroup set the upper normal limit at 53 ms for this timing measure. About 11.8 percent of the full group sat above that limit overall. Those people were older, more often male, and had higher body mass, blood pressure issues, and heart mass. Age, body mass, heart mass, and heart rate each linked to the measure on their own.
pmc-13289332:
Idalina Maria Santos Vieira Lisboa Bordalo and coauthors offer a 2026 systematic review of codes used to describe how children function. The International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, called ICF, sorts functioning into body, activity, and environment domains. The authors asked which codes researchers reach for most when studying children from birth to age 18.

Four databases were searched through September 2024, and two reviewers screened and rated studies on their own. Only eight studies qualified, holding 29 core sets and 1665 coded instances in total. Activity and participation codes led, followed by environment codes such as support, services, and policies. Body structure codes were rare. The pattern shows a shift toward daily life and context, not just body problems.
pmc-13289532:
Filipe Dantas-Torres and Ben J. Mans compiled a 2026 world checklist of ticks, blood-feeding parasites that spread disease to animals and people. Tick naming has shifted for decades as species were added, merged, dropped, or restored, and genus groupings were revised with new gene evidence. Older world lists no longer match current science, so a fresh census was needed.

The list counts 1033 valid species, including 21 fossil species known only from remains. Four families are recognized, led by Ixodidae with 800 species, then Argasidae, Nuttalliellidae, and the single-species Khimairidae family. An updated genus classification accompanies the species list. Vets, doctors, and ecologists gain a shared naming base for tracking tick-borne threats.
pmc-13289632:
Xue Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 record review comparing two dual therapies to clear Helicobacter pylori stomach infection. That germ drives ulcers and stomach cancer risk, and first-line cure rates matter as resistance grows. One pairing used vonoprazan with doxycycline, the other used vonoprazan with high-dose amoxicillin, both built around strong acid blocking.

Records covered 357 patients treated at three hospitals in Ningxia and nearby areas from December 2024 to December 2025. Groups held 180 and 177 patients, with cure checked by breath test four weeks after therapy ended. Cure rates by initial assignment fell below the usual 80 percent bar for first-line care in both groups. Rates among those finishing therapy ran higher, near nine in ten.
pmc-13289932:
Wei-Gang Gong and colleagues chart a 2026 first map of m7G methylation marks on RNA in early ischemic stroke brain tissue. Ischemic stroke kills and disables worldwide, and saving the at-risk rim around dead tissue, called penumbra, is the core of acute care. How that rim slips into dead core at molecular level was poorly known, and RNA methylation may steer the slide.

Mice with a blocked middle brain artery had penumbra tissue profiled for methylation across all RNA messages. Changed marks clustered in messages tied to MAPK signaling when marks rose, and to axon guidance when marks fell in the data. The landscape offers fresh targets for protecting threatened brain tissue.
pmc-13290932:
Two lifelong viruses collide in pregnancy and infancy, Swetha Pinninti and colleagues review in 2026. Their subject is cytomegalovirus among children living with HIV or born to mothers who have it, and whether the pairing worsens outcomes beyond either infection alone.

Congenital CMV is the commonest viral infection present at birth and the top cause of sensorineural hearing loss in children. Co-infection with HIV raises the chance a baby is born with CMV, though what that means for long-term health is still largely undetermined. In the treatment era, outright CMV disease has grown rare in HIV care, yet the review argues the viruses' interplay can still shape childhood health quietly. Pinninti and colleagues call for close long-term follow-up of these children while outcome studies catch up.
pmc-13291032:
Gene editing aimed at the glue that lets drug-resistant bacteria form biofilms is reported in a 2026 study by Aysegul Ates, Sohret Aydemir, and Safak Ermertcan. A clinical isolate of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus served as the target, with three biofilm-linked genes, icaA, icaD, and bap, chosen for editing with CRISPR-Cas9 tools.

Guide molecules were built into plasmids, edits were confirmed by sequencing, and gene activity fell across all three targets after editing. Biofilm growth dropped sharply in each mutant strain, most strongly where icaA was hit. Drug levels needed to stop growth also fell steeply for oxacillin and ciprofloxacin, though every strain still counted as resistant under standard clinical cutoffs, a limit the authors state plainly.
pmc-13291132:
Tuberculosis and diabetes together are targeted in mice by Rashmi Arora and colleagues in 2026. Diabetes weakens defense against tuberculosis. The infection in turn unsettles blood sugar. Shared cell switches offer one route against both.

Mice were made diabetic, then exposed to tuberculosis germs. Lung immune cells were screened for receptor changes. Three receptors stood out in the combined illness. A triple treatment targeted those three receptors. Treated mice held weight better than sick controls. Blood sugar ran lower under treatment. Infection measures also improved with the pairing. One therapy for two linked diseases is the hope.
pmc-13291732:
David Kerr and colleagues compare a digital diabetes platform with usual care in a 2026 retrospective study. The Dario platform logs blood glucose automatically and nudges behavior change. Users were matched against nonusers in United States health and lab datasets from 2017 to 2021. Matching produced 568 users and 1,699 nonusers with similar starting profiles. The main outcome was change in HbA1c, a blood sugar average.

HbA1c fell further in platform users, by an extra 0.23 percentage points on average. The advantage held at twelve months in sensitivity checks and appeared in every subgroup split by starting HbA1c level. At six months, forty-seven percent of users cut HbA1c by at least one full point. Only about thirty-seven percent of nonusers reached that mark. The authors read the results as real-world support for digital tools, while noting that motivated users may still differ from matched controls.
pmc-13292332:
Maximilian Hellkamp and a large team attack a 2026 problem in rectal cancer: tumors that shrug off chemoradiotherapy before surgery. They built a panel of patient-derived cancer cell lines and profiled which ones resisted treatment. Resistant lines turned out to burn more energy, running both glycolysis and mitochondrial ATP production at higher levels.

Drug screening showed the resistant cells dodged most compounds but leaned hard on two sugar gateways, the glucose transporter GLUT1 and the lactate transporter MCT1. Blocking those routes re-sensitized the cells to radiation, with GLUT1 inhibition working most robustly across models. Patient data agreed: high GLUT1 matched poor response to pre-surgery treatment in their cohort and public datasets. The authors propose metabolism blockers plus metabolic profiling to sort patients before therapy.
pmc-13292432:
Huan Yang, Michael Brines, and Ulf Andersson advance a 2026 perspective reframing how to fight HMGB1, a protein that fuels inflammation and pain once outside cells. Drugs meant to neutralize it have disappointed in the clinic. The authors argue the real problem is access: whether HMGB1 can assemble into harmful complexes, engage receptors like RAGE, slip into cells, and deliver inflammatory cargo inside.

Their model plugs HMGB1 into the inflammatory reflex, the vagus nerve circuit that restrains immune activity. Acetylcholine, acting through alpha7 nicotinic receptors, limits both HMGB1 release and the uptake of HMGB1-carrying complexes. Vagus nerve stimulation thus becomes a bioelectronic way to lock the gate upstream, not just mute cytokines downstream. The authors stress the model reorganizes known biology rather than replacing it.
pmc-13292532:
Monica Oldani and co-authors untangle a 2026 conversation between fat cells and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, cancers that strike more often with visceral obesity. Using BON-1 and QGP-1 tumor lines with lab-grown adipocytes in shared-media systems, they watched each side change the other. Tumor cells pushed fat cells toward a cancer-associated state, draining their lipids and silencing fat genes.

Interleukin-1 beta from the tumor cells drove that conversion. The reprogrammed fat cells answered by releasing the chemokine CXCL12, which fed back to boost tumor growth and further interleukin release. Blocking the loop at either end worked: the CXCR4 blocker AMD3100 and the IL-1 beta drug canakinumab each calmed secretion, spared the fat cells, and slowed tumor proliferation. The authors nominate the axis as a drug target for these rare tumors.
pmc-13293432:
Yu-Tsung Lin and colleagues link, in a 2026 study, low blood albumin before a spine procedure to higher long-term death risk. The procedure, vertebroplasty, cements a crushed vertebra, and albumin marks nutrition and general frailty in older patients.

Records covered 145 patients treated at one center from May 2013 to June 2020 for compression fractures, after set exclusions. Follow-up averaged a few years. Patients with albumin below the cutoff the authors used died at over three times the rate of others, even after many health factors were counted. Better nutrition care may matter for survival after this fracture fix.
pmc-13293632:
Cinta Lleixà and a large European team study, in a 2026 paper, whether set immune gene types raise the chance of autoimmune nodopathies. These are nerve illnesses driven by antibodies against Caspr1 or CNTN1 proteins. Such gene links could explain why only some people develop these rare conditions.

Gene typing covered 44 patients from 19 hospitals, plus 50 patients with a related nerve illness but no such antibodies. One gene variant, DRB1*11, appeared far more often in the CNTN1 group than in comparison groups. Another, DRB1*03:01, stood out in the Caspr1 group with even stronger gaps. Each antibody type thus carries a distinct gene signal.
pmc-13293732:
Xiaoting Zhang leads a 2026 multicenter cohort study on whether newborn breathing distress raises wheezing risk at preschool age in very preterm babies. Wheezing burdens clinics heavily in young children, and early lung injury may set the stage for later airway trouble.

Study highlights report wheezing in 11.3% of preschoolers who had the distress syndrome, versus 5.6% of other preterm children in the cohort. After other factors were counted, the syndrome still stood as an independent risk for later wheezing. The authors urge targeted breathing follow-up for these children. Preventive watch in preschool years may catch problems while they are still mild.
pmc-13293932:
Jing Hu and colleagues build a cancer immunotherapy from a fungal compound, in a 2026 study targeting the immune cells that shield tumors. Tumor-associated macrophages are the most common suppressive cells inside tumors, and efforts to remove them have largely disappointed. The team instead generated fungal metabolites with help from added precursor chemicals and screened them for compounds that could reprogram these macrophages rather than kill them.

One compound, IM502, blocked a signaling enzyme and flipped the macrophages' internal switches toward an attack mode. Treated tumors gained more and better natural killer and T cells, and the compound restored T cell growth in samples from human colorectal cancer. It shrank established tumors and spread across several cancer types in animals and worked even where a standard immunotherapy had failed. The platform offers a new source of immune drugs.
pmc-13294332: Hai Wang and coauthors are named on a 2026 retraction note. The note pulls their 2021 Nature Communications article on carbon nano-onions made to hit two targets against cancer drug resistance. A joint probe by three universities found flaws in two figures. The editor states that trust in the article is lost. Two authors disagree with the retraction. Most others did not reply to the publisher. The item is only a retraction notice, with no new data or new analysis of any kind.
pmc-13294432:
Ganesh Kumar, Nisha Sharma, and Younis Ahmad Hajam build a plant gum hydrogel to release a cancer drug slowly in a 2026 study. Oxidized fenugreek gum plus chitosan formed the base, with catechin plant extract locked in by Schiff base links. Five imaging and heat methods verified structure, and antioxidant plus blood safety tests ran alongside drug release trials with methotrexate.

Catechin loading reached 53.23% encapsulation in the reported figure. The gel swelled most at stomach-like acidity and released 75.19% of drug over 24 hours in simulated gastric fluid, following a diffusion-erosion pattern. Blood tests showed no clotting or bursting problems, and catechin boosted antioxidant power.
pmc-13294632:
Xiangbei Chen and co-authors present a 2026 study linking a newer form of cell death, disulfidptosis, to preeclampsia. Preeclampsia affects only pregnancy and has become more common in recent decades. How disulfidptosis-related genes behave in the condition had not been clear.

Gene data from the GSE75010 set were grouped by clustering, then network analysis and machine learning singled out five central genes: SASH1, CST6, CCBL1, FSTL3, and SPAG4.
