A model built from those genes performed well in outside datasets and in laboratory checks on samples. The authors note possible overfitting and a small laboratory sample, so wider testing is still needed.
pmc-13295032: Fouzia Perveen, Muhammad Farooq, and co-authors published a correction in 2026 to their study of making levulinic acid from waste corncobs with a tungsten oxide grafted catalyst. The notice is a correction only. It clarifies that several figures in the original article and its supplement were reproduced from an earlier paper by the same group, published under a Creative Commons license. It also replaces an incorrect gas chromatography figure and states the corrected library reference and the retention time for levulinic acid.
pmc-13295732:
Federica Massaro and colleagues test three antimicrobial peptides from Antarctic fish against germs that plague fish farms, in a 2026 study. Farmed fish suffer bacterial and viral disease, and heavy antibiotic use feeds resistance. The peptides, named Trematocine, Chionodracine, and Cnd-m3, come from fish that live in icy seas. The team checked their killing power, their harm to fish cells, and their pull on the immune system.

Cnd-m3 was the best antibacterial of the three, killing and halting several strains, among them Lactococcus garvieae. Tests showed it breaches the germ's outer membrane and then reaches its inner nucleic parts. Trematocine led against viruses, acting on two enveloped kinds. Both leaders showed low harm to a sea bass cell line and to fish red blood cells in the checks run.
pmc-13295832:
Meghan Nelson and colleagues sequence genomes in early childhood lupus in a 2026 study. Lupus starting before age ten is rare and severe, and its genetic roots differ from adult disease. Whole genome reading covered 37 young patients to hunt large-effect rare variants.

Over a third of the group carried at least one rare harmful variant in genes already tied to single-gene lupus forms. Fresh suspects surfaced in cell power and interferon pathways among the thousands of rare variants found. A combined genetic risk score tied to higher odds of kidney involvement but not to earlier onset. Larger studies must confirm which variants truly drive the disease.
pmc-13296032:
Cristian Zaha and colleagues pilot, in 2026, heat-camera checks after back surgery in dogs with slipped discs. Fifteen dogs had a standard operation to relieve spinal cord pressure, and skin temperature over the surgical area was recorded before surgery and twice afterwards.

Temperatures and heat patterns changed clearly across the week after surgery, with no wound complications seen in any dog. The authors suggest infrared imaging, which is quick and touch-free, could complement hands-on checks of healing after this surgery. The small pilot supports wider testing of the method in veterinary care.
pmc-13296132:
Wei Song and Jingxin Wang study why being cyberbullied ties to distress in vocational college students in China, in a 2026 survey. From 4,290 sound replies, 1,419 students told of at least one bout of cyberbullying, and the team focused on 1,107 who were victims only, never bullies themselves. Students rated victimization, relative deprivation, moral disengagement, and distress symptoms.

Being bullied tied straight to more distress. Indirect paths also held: through feeling deprived next to peers, through moral disengagement, and through the two in a chain, deprivation first. The authors read the chain as one way hurt turns inward for these students. Since all data came at one time by self-report, they urge care in calling the paths causes.
pmc-13296332:
Shiue-Lin Li and colleagues report a 2026 trial that draws power from farm wastewater in southern Taiwan with fuel cells run by microbes. The farm waste is rich in nitrogen and plant matter, which holds back its biogas system, so the team sought a second way to gain energy. Two fuel cells of about one litre each ran on the raw waste for more than seventy days.

Both cells cleared more than four fifths of the waste load in their best weeks and gave a steady power output. A side test compared ways to prepare the starting microbes. Waste solids trained without carbon gave no clear current, while solids trained with carbon powder gave a strong peak. The team advises study of the microbe mix next to lift performance further.
pmc-13297232:
Jakub S. Gąsior introduces a special issue on fundamental movement skills in children and adolescents in a 2026 overview article. Running, throwing, catching, and balance skills are the building blocks for sport and daily activity. They do not appear on their own, the article stresses, but need teaching and practice.

Six papers cover assessment tools, links with physical literacy, and intervention results. One major review reports a worrying global decline in skill acquisition. The overview frames the problem through a triad of physical illiteracy, too little daily activity, and low strength in children. Terminology muddles, missing school-ready standards, and unknown best practice doses remain open gaps.
pmc-13297332:
Wen-Kan Feng, Kun-Long Hung, and Ting-Hao Wang report an adolescent boy whose muscle disease was first read as one condition and proved to be another, in a 2026 case report. Over several years the boy grew weaker in his shoulders and hips and lost muscle bulk, a pattern that pointed to limb-girdle muscular dystrophy. Full gene sequencing told a different story.

The scan found a single altered copy of CHRNB1, a gene for a receptor part at the junction where nerves meet muscle. That finding fits postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome, a rare inherited fault in nerve-to-muscle signalling present from birth. Treatment aimed at that fault brought clear improvement. The case shows why gene testing matters when weakness does not fit the first label.
pmc-13297732:
Bushra Afzal and colleagues compare two scan methods that watch leg blood flow recover after artery blockage in young and old mice, in a 2026 study. Peripheral artery disease often stays silent, so non-invasive tracking matters. The femoral artery was sealed in mice aged two months and eighteen months, and both groups were scanned over two weeks.

Sound-based imaging showed oxygen in the starved limb dropping right after surgery, then recovering faster in young mice. Light-speckle imaging told the same story for flow itself. Tissue checks confirmed damage and showed richer new vessel growth and cell division in the young. Neither method needs injected dyes, which suits repeated checks of therapy.
pmc-13298532:
Po-Tsen Liu and co-authors present three women whose lung cancer carried EGFR changes whose tumours developed a rare resistance change, in a 2026 case series. After progression on targeted therapy, RNA testing found an intragenic rearrangement inside the ROS1 gene. Such changes can escape narrower gene tests, so broader testing mattered here.

Combining targeted drugs against both alterations produced long-term survival in one patient, while another suffered serious side effects. When combined therapy proved intolerable, standard chemotherapy remained an effective fallback. The authors argue treatment must be individualised for this rearrangement, and they call for functional studies confirming exactly how the change drives drug failure.
pmc-13299232:
A compound from a traditional medicinal plant eased colitis in mice by switching on the cell's self-cleaning machinery, report Zhongxing Miao and co-authors in a 2026 study. They tested oridonin in inflamed macrophages in dishes and in mice given a chemical that damages the colon lining.

In cells, oridonin lowered inflammatory cytokines and raised the calming signal interleukin-10. In mice it blunted weight loss and disease scores, preserved colon length, and restored barrier proteins. The mechanism ran through quieting the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, which lifted autophagy markers and cleared the p62 backlog. Blocking autophagy pharmacologically confirmed the pathway's role in the benefit.
pmc-13299732:
Blow fly pupae keep a hidden diary of their age, and Jiani Yang with co-authors learned to read it in a 2026 forensic study. Phormia regina spends nearly half its development inside the puparium, so pinning down pupal age sharpens estimates of time since death at crime scenes.

At 25 °C the team documented shifting internal anatomy, pigment changes, and steady weight loss, then sequenced the full transcriptome to find genes switching on and off by stage. Candidate age markers with consistent timing were confirmed by targeted PCR. Combining appearance and gene signals, the authors say, makes fly-based postmortem interval estimates more trustworthy for casework.
pmc-13300232:
Amin Thwairan and co-authors report early experience, published in 2026, with a transportable extracorporeal membrane oxygenation system called VitalFlow. Such machines support failing hearts or lungs, and a pre-assembled console aims to cut setup delays during emergencies. The retrospective review covered the first fifteen deployments at a high-volume German cardiac surgery center between November 2025 and March 2026, twelve supporting the circulation and three supporting breathing only.

Median time to full flow was thirty-three minutes, and support lasted a median of eight days. Sixty percent of patients survived to hospital discharge, and every survivor had a favorable neurological outcome. No major bleeding or stroke occurred, while limb ischemia in four patients was the main complication, with two needing fasciotomy. The authors support wider multicenter evaluation of the platform.
pmc-13300932:
Match demands in Portuguese football do not simply rise with league rank, Diogo Tereso and colleagues show in a 2026 load-monitoring study. Ninety-six senior players aged 19 to 36, spread across five competitive levels, wore GPS trackers and heart-rate bands during play. External load captured the work done; internal load captured the body's answer to it.

Outside measures separated the levels clearly, yet not in ladder order: third- and fourth-division players logged the most reactive, high-intensity actions, while second-division players showed a steadier profile. Internal load barely distinguished the groups, with average heart rate in the second half the lone exception. Coaches, the authors suggest, should plan by measured load, not division label.
pmc-13301432:
The right side of the heart may betray who will relapse into atrial fibrillation, Aristi Boulmpou and colleagues report in a 2026 prospective echo study. Seventy-three patients with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, scanned while in normal rhythm, were followed for twelve months. A wide battery of chamber measures and coupling ratios was screened against recurrence.

Thirty-one patients, 42.5 percent of the group, saw the arrhythmia return. Usual left atrial size and strain measures failed to predict it. A right ventricular fractional area change at or below 42.5 percent stood out as an independent predictor after adjustment. A new left atrial efficiency ratio also leaned toward significance, hinting that mechanical mismatch marks risky hearts.
pmc-13301532:
Reading the grain of a kidney scan might one day spare patients a biopsy needle, Marcin Majos and colleagues test in a 2026 imaging study. They compared MRI texture patterns from healthy volunteers with those from chronic kidney disease patients who also had biopsy results, splitting the sick group by tissue activity. Both 1.5-tesla and 3-tesla scanners fed the analysis.

The final algorithm, drawing on three image types, separated sick from healthy kidneys with sensitivity reaching the high eighties and specificity into the low nineties. Texture features from T1 and T2 images also tracked filtration rate closely. Scanner type did not break the method, which the authors read as a step toward universal, needle-free kidney assessment.
pmc-13302332:
A Carecci and co-authors compare, in a 2026 prospective study, a two-lead resynchronization defibrillator against the conventional three-lead system. The newer DX design senses the upper chamber through a floating sensor on the defibrillator lead itself, cutting the hardware inside veins. Fewer leads should mean fewer infections and failures over time.

The study enrolled 210 patients who qualified for resynchronization and did not need upper-chamber pacing. After nearly four years of follow-up, both groups shared the same freedom from the combined outcome of heart-related death, heart failure admission, or new fibrillation. Heart shrinkage and therapy delivery also matched. Upper-chamber sensing actually read stronger with the new system, and lead problems were rare in both arms.
pmc-13303132:
A tilted head buys back some depth vision for children born with a weak eye muscle, Yufei Wei and colleagues measure in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Twenty patients with congenital superior oblique palsy who hold a compensatory head posture faced three stereo tests, both in their habitual tilt and straightened, against twenty matched controls. Fundus photos supplied the fovea-disc angle between the two eyes.

Patients' depth perception lagged far behind controls on every test. The tilt genuinely helped near vision, yet distance stereopsis stayed impaired in eighty-five percent of patients regardless. Larger fovea-disc angles accompanied worse scores at both distances. The authors propose that angle as an imaging marker of binocular dysfunction.
pmc-13305132:
Adriano Souza Santos Monteiro leads a 2026 case report of urinary infections that kept returning for eight years despite treatment. The culprit, Klebsiella pneumoniae, is the second most common cause of such infections and increasingly resists many drugs.

One patient endured 18 community-caught episodes, and every sample grew bacteria that made enzymes breaking key antibiotics. Ten samples studied in depth shared the same capsule type and germ family line, though resistance genes varied between episodes. Matching fingerprints point to relapse of one stubborn strain rather than fresh infections, urging care with first-choice antibiotics.
pmc-13305832:
Marek Misiak and co-authors review evidence in 2026 on whether anti-inflammatory drugs change the chance of developing colorectal cancer. Chronic inflammation, acting through the COX-2 enzyme and prostaglandin E2, can help tumours grow and spread. The team searched PubMed and gathered 119 articles on aspirin, related painkillers, and selective COX-2 blockers.

Aspirin carries the strongest record, with long-term use linked to lower cancer incidence and mortality. Benefit looked greatest in tumours with PIK3CA gene changes, and effects varied with tumour site and molecular features. The review closes by urging personalised decisions that weigh preventive gain against side-effect risk. Genetic profiling, the authors suggest, should guide who receives these drugs for prevention.
pmc-13306132:
Branislav Jovanovic asked whether wobbly early weight predicts weaker later loss in a 2026 analysis of the CALERIE diet study. Participants without obesity followed a plan cutting energy intake by a quarter over two years.

For 143 people, week-to-week variation across the first twelve weeks was measured from repeated weights. Greater early wobble linked to less extra loss by month six in adjusted models, with a reported coefficient of −0.38 in the main result. The time interaction was not clear, though checks hinted the pattern may run longer, supporting steadier early routines during dieting.
pmc-13306332:
Exequiel Porta and co-authors review in 2026 small-molecule drug prospects against the structural and accessory proteins of SARS-CoV-2. Most approved antivirals aim at the copying machinery, yet other viral proteins control entry, assembly, exit, and immune evasion. The review judges each target by how realistic a drug programme looks.

Membrane, envelope, and nucleocapsid proteins, plus the accessory protein ORF3a, earn the strongest confidence, backed by emerging chemical evidence. Spike and several host-facing accessory proteins are rated earlier-stage, needing firmer proof that candidate molecules act on target. Many candidates face hard problems because their targets sit in membranes or work through protein contacts. The authors frame these targets as partners for existing antivirals in future combinations, rather than replacements.
pmc-13306832:
Zhida Zhai and colleagues published an engineering paper in 2026. They tackle tuning for nuclear magnetic resonance probes. The probe sends radio pulses and receives weak signals. It must be tuned and matched precisely for sensitivity. Hand tuning by repeated search is slow. Each trial needs hardware measurement and waiting. New in-place uses make slow tuning even harder.

The team proposes a learning method informed by physics. Their model predicts the right component settings directly. It learns from only a few real machine measurements. A physics-based penalty keeps predictions sensible and stable. Tests cover wide bands and several resonance frequencies. The approach aims for fast, accurate, automatic setup. Faster setup could support continuous, efficient NMR testing.
pmc-13307732:
Lucas Monteiro Delgado and co-authors pool in 2026 studies of chest nerve surgery for severe sweating, to test whether sparing the T2 ganglion cuts the main side effect, new sweating elsewhere. Their search to July 2025 found 11 studies with 3090 patients in total across the two surgical choices.

Sparing T2 linked to far less new sweating overall, with an odds ratio of 0.38 in the pooled results here. Severe new sweating also fell, and the edge held in both trial types and at short and long follow up. No sign of publication bias turned up. The authors advise that surgeons skip T2 when they can, while fresh forward looking studies confirm the gain.
pmc-13308732:
Nuo Zhang and co-authors weigh in 2026 the world burden of ovarian cancer from 1990 to 2021 and hunt its cause factors with gene based tests. They used Global Burden of Disease 2021 data for 204 lands plus large gene study sums for 12 candidate exposures.

Deaths and years lost rose in raw counts, while age set rates for both fell over the span in most tallies. High body mass bucked that trend, with all its rates still climbing year by year. Gene tests tied hip size, belly fat, waist size, drink rate, child body mass, and life long smoking to higher risk. Schooling and some foods tied to lower risk in the same tests.
pmc-13309132:
Atsushi Shima, Satoshi Yoshikawa, and Takeshi Ueda describe in 2026 a case of livedo reticularis, a lacy skin pattern, caused by amantadine in a woman aged 80 years. She had vascular parkinsonism, dementia, and face movement quirks, and she had taken the drug at 100 milligrams a day for six years.

The pattern sat on her ears and lower legs, a rare ear site that no past report had named for this drug. Stopping the drug cleared the ears in three days, while a restart for worse movement brought the pattern back in 11 days. Blood tests ruled out a clot linked cause in her case. Full stop of the drug cleared all marks by six months.
pmc-13309432:
Elizabeth J Wilk and co-authors make the case in 2026 for using artificial intelligence to help read genetic test results. Gene testing has grown cheaper, yet many results come back unclear, which can worry patients or falsely reassure them. Reading each unclear result by hand takes scarce expert time.

Software tools can gather scattered evidence, rank which unclear results matter most, and speed the path to a firm diagnosis. Final calls still need real biological proof, which software cannot supply. New scoring rules for variant reading will also raise the amount of evidence to weigh. The authors urge clinics to build these tools into each step, from patient traits to final ranking.
pmc-13309532:
Mateusz Garbulowski and co-authors map how RNA-binding proteins steer gene activity in liver cancer in a 2026 study. These proteins grip RNA and shape which messages a cell uses, so their networks can reveal cancer drivers and drug leads. Work centered on the HepG2 liver cancer cell line.

Gene networks were built from knockdown data by several methods, then merged into one agreed network. Binding data from two lab assays checked key links and sites in that network. Grouping the network into modules and screening known drugs against it suggested fresh treatment options. The authors present the map as a base for testing which protein links matter most in this cancer.
pmc-13309632:
Moonki Hong and co-authors compare two drug plans for lung cancer after targeted pills fail in a 2026 study. The cancers carried gene changes in EGFR, ALK, or ROS1 and had grown despite matched targeted drugs. One plan joined two immune and vessel drugs with chemotherapy, while the other used standard chemotherapy alone.

Records from several centers covered 114 patients treated between 2016 and 2023. The four-drug plan shrank tumors in half of judged patients, against 35 percent for chemotherapy alone in the reported data. Time without growth was longer on the four-drug plan, while total survival did not differ clearly. The authors suggest the four-drug plan as an option after targeted failure.
pmc-13310032:
Raffaele Giancotti and co-authors present DataAtlas, a tool that writes data dictionaries on its own, in a 2026 article. Shared data sets often ship with thin or uneven notes, which blocks reuse and second-pass analysis. A data dictionary explains each table and variable in plain terms.

The open-source system pairs hard structural profiling with language-model inference to draft clear descriptions. Column facts, summary statistics, and sample values feed each draft. Trials on three varied clinical data sets pitted drafts against official notes in blinded comparisons, expert review, and downstream tasks. Drafts were often preferred where official notes were thin, with low rates of invented content. The authors also used the tool to flag errors in existing notes.
pmc-13310932:
Han Phan reports phase 1b results for a muscle drug in Becker muscular dystrophy in a 2026 study. The drug sevasemten tempers fast muscle contraction to cut injury that leads to swelling, scarring, and muscle loss. Animal work hinted at protection without loss of strength, so long term safety in adults was tested.

Twelve ambulatory adults aged 18 to 55 years took daily doses in rising steps over two years. All side effects were mild or moderate, with no serious events or dropouts due to harm. Blood markers of muscle injury fell within four weeks and stayed low. Function scores were tracked as a secondary check.
pmc-13311132:
Leonardo M. Caisachana Guevara and colleagues test conflict adaptation in a cleaned face word Stroop task in a 2026 study. People adjust control after clashes, easing the next clash, and brain scans often use this effect. Cleaner task versions that strip learning tricks may shrink the effect, so its strength and stability were checked for scan use.

Five experiments varied task rules and gaps between trials. A classic Stroop clash appeared in every test. The sequence benefit was strong in a gender sorting task but appeared only under select settings in the cleaned version, with wide person to person spread. Careful design buys clarity at a cost in effect size.
pmc-13311232:
Yue-Hao Gao and six co-authors review ways to edit plant genes without leaving foreign DNA behind. Their review was published in twenty twenty-six. Classic editing can lodge stray fragments in the genome and raises drift and off-target worries.

Transgene-free methods deliver the editing tools briefly or as ready-made protein-RNA bundles, or as RNA alone. The review covers direct bundle delivery, RNA delivery systems, and base editors that swap single letters. It also covers prime editing, which uses a template-guided enzyme to write small changes. Crops made this way can count as non-genetically modified in some rules. The authors map the principles and the hurdles for breeding programs.
pmc-13311332:
Giovanna Lopez and co-authors study who stays engaged with Los Angeles County's TelePrEP program in a 2026 cohort analysis. The phone-based service, launched in May 2023, widens access to HIV prevention drugs.

Records covered 412 clients from May 2023 through May 2025. Most were male, nearly half were Hispanic or Latino, and most were aged 18 to 39. Over half left the program, mostly over trouble keeping to the drug schedule. Finishing three or more quarterly visits showed no clear tie to gender, age, background, or insurance. The authors back stronger early support to keep clients in care.
pmc-13311832:
Bryn Crandles and colleagues report a 2026 EEG study on brain network balance in schizophrenia during quiet, no-response tasks. The measure at stake is small-world propensity, which blends cluster and path efficiency.

Networks were built from 42 patients and 42 matched controls across three passive tasks. Patients varied less in the measure from task to task than controls did. The authors link the flatness to faulty default mode network behavior. The measure and its variation also tracked symptom scores on the PANSS scale. A steadier network, paradoxically, may mark a brain less able to shift states.
pmc-13311932:
Zayel Z Frijmersum and colleagues examine a 2026 Dutch cohort on sick leave around childbirth and later workforce participation. The study follows women who claimed maternity benefits in 2020 or 2021.

The cohort held 261,171 women. Sick leave during pregnancy tied to higher odds of staying in the workforce, while sick leave within two years after birth tied to lower odds. Pregnancy sick leave also strongly predicted later sick leave, with odds over threefold. Job sector, contract type, area, and age shaped both leave length and staying in work. Timing of leave, the authors argue, changes what support should follow.
pmc-13312132:
Mohammed Turky and Paul MH. Dummer write a 2026 commentary on trust in conversational artificial intelligence used in endodontics, the branch of dentistry focused on the tooth root and pulp. AI tools already help read dental images and predict treatment outcomes, and attention has turned to whether their reasoning can be explained and checked.

The authors argue that large language models raise a sharper problem than explainability alone. Fluent, confident answers may rest on sources no one can trace, yet users may trust them more as traditional institutions lose credibility, a pattern they frame as a trust paradox. Unlike social media, where rival claims from named sources can be compared, chatbot output arrives as one polished voice. The piece asks how evidence-based dental practice should handle such tools.
pmc-13312532:
Daniel Fong and his team tune lab make of gut enzymes from the bite fly that spreads dengue, with low start dose and very cold growth. Their 2026 study takes on enzymes from Aedes aegypti that fight clean make in germ cells.

These enzymes need bonds of a kind for firm form, so plain germ cells with a low-charge core failed first. Bred cells with a high-charge core let the enzymes form in a clean way. Rich food and cold states helped too. Tests with low start dose at ten degrees slowed the make of the proteins. Slow make stopped a rushed build that leads to clumps that will not melt. Five fly enzymes were checked. They took in two trypsins and more than one serine enzyme. The span of growth swayed clean form for each enzyme too.
pmc-13312632:
Jian Liao and co-authors report a study of very ill patients with severe liver scarring. The catalog lists the work under 2026. They test a simple blood ratio taken when a patient enters intensive care. The ratio joins a waste marker in blood with a blood protein level. The question is whether a high ratio is linked to death in the next weeks and months.

The team used a large hospital database and split patients at a cutoff score. Patients above the cutoff were compared with those below it. Models that adjust for other risks still showed a link with death at 28 days and at 180 days. Survival curves show the gap plainly. If the link holds in more tests, the cheap score could help staff judge risk early and plan care with care.
pmc-13314732:
Alejandro Acuña-Pacheco and colleagues report a rare bladder growth in a 2026 case study. Villous adenomas of the bladder are uncommon surface tumors that can turn malignant and look much like their gut kin, which makes them hard to sort from bladder cancers.

Their patient was a 63-year-old woman with heart and metabolic disease who came in with blocked urine flow and blood in the urine. Scans showed a bladder mass and hints of a channel to the bowel, though none was proven. A scope found a frond-like lesion of 6 cm at the bladder trigone, as measured in the report, and it was cut out fully through the urethra. Tissue and stain tests, positive for CK-20 and CDX-2, proved the adenoma, and the patient did well after, by the account given.
pmc-13314832:
Robson dos Santos Soares and co-workers scan the genomes of Beauveria fungi for the gene clusters behind their pest-killing power, in a study from 2026. These fungi are sprayed worldwide as living pest control, yet the gene variety under their virulence was unmapped.

The team compared 322 high-quality genomes from the genus, counting one new isolate from soil in southern Brazil, as the report states. That isolate, AS272, spans 32.9 Mb with 9778 predicted genes and near-full completeness at a score of 96.7 percent as given in the report. Gene families were broadly shared, but AS272 grew its kit mostly by swelling old families, above all transporter genes of a big pump family. Tying chemical-making clusters to killing power can guide picking strains for farm use.
pmc-13315532:
Yan Ma and colleagues tested two amino acid supplements in 2026 in broilers stressed by a bacterial toxin. In total, 384 day-old yellow-feathered broilers were split into four groups. Groups got plain feed, toxin alone, or feed plus 1 percent L-citrulline or 1 percent L-arginine. Toxin injections came late in the 27-day trial.

Growth over the first 21 days did not differ between groups. Both supplements raised antioxidant capacity and antibody levels, with measures such as superoxide dismutase, IgG, and IgM higher than in the toxin-only group. The team also tracked gut wall shape, barrier function, and microbes to judge protection of the jejunum.
pmc-13315632:
Antoni Colom and a large team asked in 2026 whether walkable neighborhoods soften the link between poor areas and body fat in older adults. They used baseline data from 1,286 city dwellers aged 55 to 75 years, all with metabolic syndrome plus overweight or obesity, in six Andalusian cities in Spain.

Area poverty came from the 2011 Spanish Deprivation Index, and walkability combined population density, street crossing density, and access to daily services. Body measures included waist size, the ratio of waist to hip, and a body shape index, all directly measured. Two-level models tested whether walkability changed the poverty and fat link, a question for fair city planning.
pmc-13316032:
Chia-Yu Chang and colleagues develop, in a 2026 study, frozen starter cells from human stem cells for Parkinson's disease. Midbrain brain-cell starter cells have shown safety and efficacy in phase I grafting trials, but yield, stemness loss speed, and post-graft neurite growth needed improvement. The team refined a neural induction protocol and applied n-butylidenephthalide, which selectively reduced stemness gene expression and enhanced neurite growth during maturing.

With these techniques, 71 percent of stem cells matured into dopamine neurons, showing burst dopamine secretion and phasic firing activity with external stimuli. Frozen starter cells grafted into immune-weak mice produced no tumor or neural tumor within 24 weeks. In sick rats, starter cells survived and matured into neurons in the recipient striatum within eight weeks, leading to significant functional recovery. The authors present the process as enabling off-the-shelf starter cells with accelerated stemness loss and early functional restoration.
pmc-13316232:
Hui-Fang Hung, Peng-Peng Zhu, and Craig Blackstone show in 2026 that the centrosome linker protein CEP68 also works in the cell nucleus during stress. Beyond holding centrosomes together, CEP68 appears at the Golgi and in the nucleus, where it partners with stress response proteins.

During oxidative stress CEP68 tunes a key phosphorylation step and stress granule formation. In the nucleus it builds liquid-like droplets beside nuclear speckles and shifts their protein dynamics. The heat shock protein HSP27 binds CEP68, more strongly under stress, and each controls the other's placement, with disease variants altering that bond.
pmc-13316632:
Maximilian Scheer and a German neurosurgery team reviewed, in a 2026 study, a scan trap after glioma surgery. A bright spot was not returning cancer but a foreign body granuloma, a lump of inflammation around surgical materials. Mistaking the two can trigger needless treatment.

Among 211 glioma patients, 38 had repeat surgery for suspected return, and 11 of them showed no tumor at all under the microscope. Foreign material appeared in three of those cases, and standard scan rules had called every one progressive disease. A diffusion measure trended lower in the no-tumor group without proving the split. The authors urge team review before acting on scans alone.
pmc-13317432:
Anna Donnan, Samuel M M Prudence, and Sarah A Kessans review, in a 2026 article, how fungi can manufacture antimicrobial peptides, nature's own germ-killing molecules that germs struggle to resist. Harvesting or chemically building these peptides is costly and wasteful, so living factories are attractive.

Yeasts such as Pichia pastoris grow fast, ferment cheaply, secrete products for easy harvest, and add the chemical finishing touches many peptides need. The review details tricks to raise yield and strength: stronger gene switches, tuned code words, better secretion tags, helper fusions, and chained or hybrid peptide designs. Case studies show what already works. The authors position fungal brewing as a realistic route to affordable new antimicrobials.
pmc-13318732:
Pingwen Lan, Zhi Fang, and Bi Wu offer a 2026 critical review of bio-inductive scaffolds for rotator cuff repair. Large tears often fail to regrow the graded tendon-to-bone junction. Collagen scaffolds aim to invite host cells in and rebuild tendon-like tissue. The review weighs evidence from 2004 to 2026.

Trials and meta-analyses show scaffolds improve tendon integrity on imaging. Retear rates fall in selected patients. Yet patient-felt gains often miss accepted thresholds for meaningful benefit. Recovery also depends on tear age, muscle fat, tendon quality, and rehabilitation. The authors warn against routine use in low-risk tears, given cost. They favour selective use and compare body-own graft options such as biceps tendon and fascia lata.
pmc-13319032:
Xiangting Li and colleagues present a 2026 study of a rapid field test for Potato virus S, a widespread threat to potato crops. Lab PCR testing is slow for on-site screening. The team built a lateral-flow strip using a new probe. A porous framework shell holds a fluorescent dye inside and gold particles outside.

The strip gives both colour and fluorescence readouts within fifteen minutes. It barely reacted to two related potato viruses in specificity checks. Detection limits reached 31.2 pg/mL by colour and 7.6 pg/mL by fluorescence in their testing. That beats a standard gold strip by more than tenfold. Virus in field-collected potato leaves was detected successfully. The authors say the platform can adapt to other plant viruses with swapped antibodies.
pmc-13320332:
Laura Gimeno and co-authors compare two British generations on illness and work loss in mid life in a 2026 study. Rising health linked work loss worries policy makers, yet whether illness pushes people out of work more strongly now than a generation ago was unknown. Two birth cohorts, born in 1958 and 1970, were tracked from health checks at age 42 to work status in their early fifties.

The older cohort held 9761 people and the younger held 7336 people in the counts used. Long standing illness at age 42 raised later work loss risk by about five to six points in both cohorts, and mental distress raised it by about four points in each. Near all illness links held steady across generations, so prevention and job support for sick workers remain key.
pmc-13321032:
Kai Liu and co-authors use cell death markers to judge a hormone drug after womb polyp surgery in a 2026 study. Endometrial polyps are common benign growths, and removal by hysteroscopy is standard care, yet polyps return in 30 to 50 percent of cases in cited work. The oral progestin dydrogesterone is often given after surgery.

Two markers of inflammatory cell death, GSDMD-N and Caspase-1, were raised in polyp tissue, and using both improved diagnosis. The markers also tracked with sex hormone levels. A prospective cohort ran from February 2023 to April 2024. It followed marker change after surgery in treated and untreated patients. It then matched those shifts to recurrence, testing whether the drug acts through that cell death path.
pmc-13321132:
Kearns and colleagues study young adults who live with RUNX1 familial platelet disorder, an inherited blood condition. A faulty RUNX1 gene causes easy bruising and slow clotting. It also raises the lifetime risk of blood cancers such as acute myeloid leukemia.

Twenty-two adults aged eighteen to thirty-nine shared survey answers and open comments. Half scored above the usual range for anxiety. About three in five had seen a mental health worker. Nearly two in three reported signs of traumatic stress. Many named the long wait for possible cancer as the hardest part. The team urges wider access to counselling, peer groups, and gene advice.
pmc-13321632:
Sarita Thawanaphong and co-authors wrote a study from 2026 on hidden airway sweeping defects behind some severe asthma flare-ups. Severe asthma with heavy white-cell influx often hides bacterial infection. The team suspected the tiny hairs that sweep mucus out of airways, since broken sweeping traps germs. They ran gene tests for a known sweeping disorder in fifty-two patients with frequent infections or intense sputum white cells.

Three in five carried gene variants tied to that disorder. In those tested, the hairs beat far slower than normal. Slower beating tracked with worse lung function and heavier sputum white cells. A nasal gas that runs low in the disorder was low in most of those measured. Sputum care guided by these findings let doctors cut steroid doses hard across the group. Most patients with variants avoided starting costly biologic drugs. Lung function improved modestly on the new plan.
pmc-13322832:
Mikhail Kostinov leads a vaccine study in 14-year-olds, published in 2026, on booster shots for diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis. The open study enrolled 121 healthy teens who received Td-M, Tdap or Tdap-M, with blood antibody tests before the shot and one month after.

At the start all teens were protected against tetanus, while a small share lacked protection against diphtheria or pertussis. Boosters raised diphtheria antibodies strongly in all groups and tetanus antibodies most in the Td-M group. Pertussis antibodies, by contrast, showed no overall rise and varied widely between teens. Side effects stayed mild for all three vaccines, and the authors treat Tdap-M as holding pertussis levels more steady.
pmc-13322932:
Chunwei Hou leads a review team comparing blood flow restriction exercise with general rehabilitation for kneecap pain, in a 2026 pooled review of trials. Their search to February 2026 found 13 studies, with 11 randomised trials and 508 participants pooled.

Restriction training cut pain during tasks such as single-leg squats and step-downs right away, and the relief still showed 45 minutes after exercise in the pooled results. Over longer follow-up it gave a modest edge for overall pain and knee extensor strength. Self-reported knee function did not differ between groups, and evidence on thigh muscle size stayed thin. The authors present the method as a useful add-on rather than a full replacement.
pmc-13323132:
Rong Cheng and co-authors track exercise and symptoms in real time among hospital patients with COPD, in a 2026 study using phone-based momentary checks. Their group held 168 middle-aged patients who rated breathlessness, irritability and exercise activity three times daily for seven days.

Breathlessness and irritability each predicted less active exercise on the same tracking window, while confidence in managing the disease predicted more activity. Confidence also softened the drag that irritability placed on activity. Multilevel models captured these within-person swings. The authors urge ward teams to watch symptoms as they shift, and to build patient confidence into lung rehabilitation so bad mood days do less harm.
pmc-13325032:
Behshad Pournasr and Stephen Duncan model inherited methylmalonic acidemia in lab-grown human liver cells in a 2026 study. The recessive disorder raises methylmalonic acid in the body, and faults in the MMUT gene are its most common cause.

The pair used gene editing to knock out MMUT function in human induced pluripotent stem cells, then grew those cells into hepatocytes. The edited liver cells copied core features of the disease, giving researchers a human model that animal work cannot fully match. Because the healthy and mutant lines share the same background, any difference traces to the gene change alone. The model opens a clean test bed for studying the disorder and screening future treatments.
pmc-13326032:
Mengdie Xia and co-authors target the protein PCSK9 inside artery wall muscle cells to slow abdominal aortic aneurysm in a 2026 study. The ballooning vessel can burst with deadly effect, and no drug yet slows its growth.

PCSK9 ran high in human aneurysm tissue and in two mouse models. Forcing extra PCSK9 in muscle cells widened the aorta, shredded elastic fibers, and triggered ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death. Cell tests traced the death to ferritin being eaten by autophagy, which frees iron. A cell-penetrating peptide called Cadd4 destroyed PCSK9 and restored the iron store protein. In mice, Cadd4 shrank dilation and preserved wall structure.
pmc-13326132:
Zhanao Meng and a large team of co-authors test a scan method for liver scarring. Their 2026 study tackles a flaw in standard tests for chronic liver disease. Common blood and scan markers mix two signals: scarring and inflammation. That blend blurs diagnosis. The team set out to separate the two signals cleanly.

They rechecked ninety-nine patients whose disease was confirmed by tissue samples. A common blood score, FIB-4, turned out to track inflammation rather than scarring. Two scan measures, including their dual-phase map, tracked scarring alone. A two-step plan pairing the map with the blood score screened well for advanced scarring. The authors note the group was small, so wider tests must confirm the plan.
pmc-13326432:
Xiaohan Hu and ten co-authors study fat burning in brain tumors in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Gliomas are aggressive cancers of the brain. Their growth leans on rewired metabolism, including how they handle fats. The team found that a surface protein called B7-H3, known from immune research, also drives fat breakdown in these tumors. It partners with another protein, cMet, to switch on a signaling chain.

That chain raises the activity of a key fat-splitting enzyme. Faster fat burning then fuels the tumor's spread. The authors checked the protein's levels in public data and in patient samples. Lab and animal tests confirmed its effect on tumor behavior. Blocking this axis could become a treatment angle for glioma.
pmc-13326532:
Louise Hambücken, Denis Baurain, and Luc Cornet studied how thylakoid layers first evolved in cyanobacteria. Their 2026 study notes that they host the light reactions of oxygen-making photosynthesis, yet the earliest splitting-off lineage, Gloeobacterales, lacks them. It makes food from light in the cytoplasmic membrane, an old state. Using gene-tree checks across diverse blue-green algae, including basal lineages, plus AlphaFold3 shape modeling, the team traced membrane dynamics and photosystem II assembly proteins.

Two candidate membrane-moving proteins emerged, including the SPFH family member Slr1106, thought to have arrived by lateral gene transfer. Analysis of 36 light-system II building factors showed changes in late-stage building, notably in manganese balance. Shape changes in the YidC mover may have eased move of electron transfer components from cell fluid to inner layers. The authors present these innovations as key steps toward thylakoid emergence.
pmc-13326632:
Meraj Neyazi and colleagues teach deep learning to flag future heart failure from a single ECG lead in a 2026 study. Finding high-risk people early is the bottleneck for prevention at population scale.

Their AI-HF tool trained on 31,740 UK Biobank participants and was checked in two German cohorts of 3,025 and 1,342 people. Five-year accuracy scores reached C-indices of 0.693 in the training population and up to 0.791 in one validation cohort. Each standard step up in the score raised risk by 1.43 to 1.67 fold across cohorts. Adding body measures helped only slightly. Wearable-grade signals may carry the screen.
pmc-13327932:
John C Grotberg, Francesco Romanò, and James B Grotberg build a fluid equation for lung edema in a 2026 modeling study. Fluid flooding the air sacs blocks gas exchange, and how cleared fluid reaches the lymph channels had puzzled physiologists since 1896. Their two-dimensional model of a tissue strip joins blood flow, tissue flow, and the air-side liquid layer.

About 80 percent of the strip carries straight cross-flow, letting them write simple pressure and flow formulas that clinicians can use. Against textbook habit, the air-side membrane's leakiness, not the capillary's, sets the cross-flow rate. Their edema equation for the blood pressure that triggers flooding matches clinical data and could tailor breathing support pressures.
pmc-13330332:
Four researchers pool evidence on steroid treatment for ventilated lung patients in a review from 2026. The patients have severe flare-ups of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and need breathing support. Steroids help many flare-up patients, but ventilated ones were often excluded from trials. The team searched three databases for trials and observational studies up to April 2025.

Six studies with about sixteen hundred patients were found. Steroids did not clearly lower intensive care deaths. In randomized trials only, they shortened time on a ventilator by about a day. High blood sugar episodes were more common with steroids. Other outcomes, like intensive care stay, showed no clear difference. The authors say the benefit case for this subgroup stays unproven.
pmc-13330932:
Tripti Gupta and Matthew R. Carazo give general cardiologists a practical guide to adult congenital heart disease in a 2026 review. Adults born with heart defects form a growing group needing lifelong expert care, yet many drop from follow-up or surface only in adulthood with chest pain, breathlessness, or palpitations.

Four narrowing problems anchor the guide: pulmonic stenosis, branch pulmonary stenosis, aortic coarctation, and subaortic stenosis. For each, the authors lay out body mechanics, key signs, imaging findings, and triggers for intervention. Worked adult cases show how common complaints can hide a congenital cause. Spotting such lesions early in general clinics can speed expert referral, the authors argue.
pmc-13332732:
Jie Zhang and colleagues designed new oxazolidinone antibiotics in 2026 work aimed at keeping linezolid's killing power while dropping its risky side effect. Linezolid blocks bacterial protein building and works against tough Gram-positive germs and tuberculosis, but it also inhibits human monoamine oxidase A, which limits its use.

Guided by how linezolid sits differently in the bacterial ribosome and in the human enzyme, the team docked candidate molecules in silico. They favoured strong ribosome binding and weak enzyme binding, then made and tested the best designs. Compound 3a beat linezolid against Staphylococcus aureus, its resistant MRSA form, S. epidermidis, and Enterococcus faecalis, with inhibitory levels around 0.5 to 1 μg/mL, while inhibiting the human enzyme far less. It also hit tuberculosis bacteria hard and showed low harm to human cells. The authors present 3a as a lead for a safer next generation.
pmc-13333332:
Dennis Christoph Harrer and colleagues show in 2026 laboratory work that turning down a single enzyme makes engineered CAR T cells fight tumors harder. When CAR T cells activate, they raise CD39, which chews up ATP and, through CD73, builds adenosine, a chemical that quiets T cells, forming a self-brake.

Cells engineered with low CD39 kept more of their killing machinery, releasing more granzyme and perforin and degranulating more strongly across repeated stimulations than standard CAR T cells. Their mitochondria worked better and their sugar burning ran higher. In mice carrying human gastric cancer, the low-CD39 cells controlled tumors better than conventional ones. Turning down CD38, a related exhaustion-linked molecule, gave no such gain under the same stress conditions. The authors suggest CD39 lowering may work best inside combination strategies that also target other metabolic or checkpoint brakes.
pmc-13333632:
Erica Hargety Kimei and co-authors describe a 2026 deep learning model that forecasts greenhouse gas levels from dairy cattle housing. Farm-level forecasts of nitrous oxide, methane, and carbon dioxide can guide climate planning for livestock systems.

The model joins remote sensing data with ground sensor readings and predicts hourly gas levels one step ahead from a 24-hour lookback window. A dual-output gated recurrent unit estimates both the expected value and the spread of each forecast, so uncertainty comes with every prediction. Testing showed stable accuracy across time periods and well-calibrated prediction intervals, with coverage between 93.6 and 94.8 percent on held-out data. Rainfall, vegetation index, humidity, and temperature ranked among the strongest inputs.
pmc-13335932:
Zhiheng Miao and colleagues study 2026 precisely printing perovskite nanocrystals in glass via TE synergy. Perovskite nanocrystals (PNCs) set in glass exhibit strong stability and light traits, yet patterned spread of PNCs in glass remains a challenge. Precise spread control of CsPbBr3 PNCs in glass was achieved through TE treatment. Upon TE fields, the structure and element spread in the hit region of the glass undergo reshuffle.

Cs movement and buildup in the glass are the primary reasons for forming of CsPbBr3 PNCs, tied to temperature, electric field strength, and duration. By tuning temperature, electric field strength, and duration during TE processing, the depth and thickness of the glowing layer of CsPbBr3 PNCs can be exactly controlled at the micron scale. Furthermore, by using patterned electrodes, a steady patterned spread of CsPbBr3 PNCs in glass was achieved.
pmc-13336132:
Yang Zhu and colleagues study 2026 Pt single-atom nano-enzyme wrapped in nano-islands for bone death repair. Too much buildup of harmful oxygen species impairs bone regrowth and new vessel growth in steroid-induced bone death of the femoral head. Current anti-rust treatments remain limited by low enzyme-like power and short life.

Single-atom nano-enzymes, with well-defined shapes and maximal atomic efficiency, show great potential for treating harmful oxygen species-induced diseases by copying natural enzymes. However, strong binding between metal sites and electron-giving middle steps creates high energy hurdles, capping their enzyme-like powers. Pt is set into CeO2-x to form CeO2-x/Pt nano-enzyme, which enhanced enzyme-like power via an island-sea combined effect. Using unique charge-transfer shapes and trapping effect of nano-islands, this nano-enzyme shows superior enzyme powers than CeO2.
pmc-13336232:
Raphael Cuencas Budini and co-authors tested ivermectin in a rat model of kidney ischemia-reperfusion injury in a 2026 experimental study. The drug drew wide off-label interest during the pandemic, making its kidney safety under stress a fair question.

Twenty adult male Wistar rats were randomized to sham surgery, ischemia alone, sham plus ivermectin, or ischemia plus ivermectin. The drug was given orally at 10 mg per kilogram daily for five days, and kidney pedicles were clamped for 30 minutes in the ischemia groups. Ivermectin-treated animals showed higher kidney-to-body weight ratios, higher serum creatinine, and more oxidative stress markers in urine. The authors conclude ivermectin acted nephrotoxically in this setting, worsening renal function rather than protecting it.
pmc-13336432:
Liding Zhang and colleagues present 2026 machine learning-enhanced fine immuno-CRISPR array facilitating early diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease by detecting multiple plasma markers. Early and accurate diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease remains a significant challenge due to the many-factor and shifting nature of its disease process. Although plasma markers such as amyloid-β (Aβ) and phospho-tau (p-tau) have shown promise as diagnosis clues. Current single-marker detection tools lack the needed sharpness and trueness for early-stage diagnosis.

The authors present a fine CRISPR-based multi-protein detection array capable of at once detecting six core AD markers, including Aβ40, Aβ42, p-tau181, p-tau217, p-tau231, and p-tau396,404. By integrating immune pair-based multi RPA with place-coded CRISPR-Cas12a finding. The array reaches a finding limit of 1 fg/mL, which is 10 000-fold more sensitive than standard ELISA.
pmc-13336832:
Kai Wang and Kai Jiang developed a two layer piezoelectric scaffold in 2026 to repair diabetic bone defects, where bone and blood vessel regrowth fall out of step. Poor mitochondrial function underlies that failure, and the team copied the layered structure of the periosteum, the membrane covering bone. Their Janus scaffold pairs a zinc doped electrospun membrane with a hydrogel carrying resveratrol microspheres.

Body movement alone powers the scaffold, which sends electrical cues and releases resveratrol to steer vessel growth and cell energy use. In diabetic animals with skull defects, treated bone volume reached 21.1 percent against 8.5 percent in controls. The platform offers a self powered route to rebuild bone and its blood supply together.
pmc-13337432:
Qing Jiang and co-authors chart protein modification networks in diabetic kidney disease in a 2026 review. This complication scars the kidneys of a large share of people with diabetes and current care cannot reliably stop it. Beyond sugar damage, chemical tags added to proteins after they are built dynamically steer their function under diabetic stress.

The review dissects six tag systems: phosphorylation, acetylation, ubiquitination, glycosylation, methylation, and SUMOylation. Their tangled dysregulation links body-wide metabolic disturbance to lasting kidney injury. Emerging therapies aim to tune these tags directly. The authors frame tag-targeting as a shift from broad symptom control toward precise molecular intervention that could finally slow progression of this disease.
pmc-13337632:
Ya Han and co-authors ask what controls straw breakdown in cold northern soils in a 2026 field study. Returning straw to fields should build soil carbon, but results vary. Litterbags of maize straw were buried at 15 and 30 cm depths for 17 months at two sites, Nenjiang and Harbin, with different accumulated warmth.

Site and time governed how much straw remained; burial depth mattered little. Carbohydrate-type carbon steadily fell away while lignin-like fractions grew relatively richer, and Harbin's warmer conditions decomposed straw further. Straw chemistry, especially nitrogen content and carbon makeup, steered the bacterial and fungal communities more than soil or climate factors did. The title's claim is plain: straw quality itself is the master control in these mollisols.
pmc-13337732:
Rakesh Aithal and colleagues review how regulators judge copycat antibody drugs in a 2026 article. Monoclonal antibodies target single antigens and have changed care for many diseases, but high prices limit access. As patents expire, similar versions called biosimilars could widen access if quality is proven.

Approval in the United States and European Union rests on close comparison with the original product. Quality features and lab methods for that comparison are the focus here. Strong lab, function, and body-handling evidence may let regulators waive large efficacy trials in some cases. That shift could cut development time and cost while keeping safety and quality standards high.
pmc-13337832:
Antara Dhenki and colleagues answered critics of lung ultrasound protocols in a 2026 author response, defending a wider 12 zone scanning approach in critical care. Critics argued that more zones cannot overcome ultrasound's blindness to deep lung disease. The authors agree on that limit, noting the 12 zone negative predictive value for consolidation was 0.61, below the rule out power of high resolution CT.

Even so, agreement with CT rose from moderate to substantial, with kappa moving from 0.52 to 0.81, a gain that matters when transporting unstable patients for CT carries risk. The response also addresses the 24 hour scanning window for follow up. The authors present wider scanning as closing a diagnostic gap, not replacing CT for deep pathology.
pmc-13338832:
Yixiao Huang and colleagues compare two skin conditions that often appear together in a 2026 review. Symmetrical acral keratoderma forms brown, thick patches on wrists and hands, mostly in young men. Ichthyosis vulgaris causes lifelong dry, scaly skin from early childhood.

Literature in English and Chinese from three databases was compared side by side. Heat and humidity worsen the acral condition, while cold dry winters worsen ichthyosis. Both involve filaggrin gene faults at different spots as reported. Patch shape and placement also differ clearly. The review concludes the two are distinct disorders that can overlap, rather than one causing the other.
pmc-13339032:
Lanling Tian and colleagues sequence full mitochondrial genomes for two flea subspecies in a 2026 study. Fleas spread disease germs between mammals, and mitochondrial DNA aids species identification and family trees. Both subspecies of Neopsylla had no complete sequences before.

Illumina sequencing, assembly, and gene labeling produced both genomes. Data from 35 other flea types enabled comparison across 37 species in total as reported. All showed strong AT bias, and all 13 protein genes evolved under purifying selection. One gene varied most while another stayed most conserved. Family trees from both methods agreed closely, placing the new subspecies firmly.
pmc-13339132:
Bembe C. Mackintosh and colleagues tackle trapped charge in lead-free solar materials in a 2026 study. Metal chalcohalides promise safer solar absorbers, yet charges often localize within picoseconds and stop moving. Swapping the metal in a mixed family was tested as a cure.

Lead and tin versions of the same framework took different crystal symmetries. Only the lead form showed the rapid trapping in the reported light tests, while the tin form kept conductivity for nanoseconds. Higher symmetry and electron behavior explain the gap as analyzed. The contrast gives a chemical rule for picking solar materials that keep charges mobile.
pmc-13339732:
Jason M Nagata and colleagues follow parenting around media and later teen screen use in a 2026 cohort study. Data came from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study, with practices recorded at year 3 and outcomes at year 4. A total of 7,947 adolescents averaged 12.9 years old as reported.

Using screens as reward or punishment and bedroom screen access each predicted more screen and phone time later. Parents modeling heavy use and screens at meals also predicted more teen use. Watching and limiting teen use predicted less time instead. Problematic social and phone habits followed the same household patterns, guiding family media advice.
pmc-13341532:
Severe obesity plus inflammation marks the deadliest mix after a type of heart attack, in a 2026 cohort study by Yuqing Li and colleagues. The analysis covered 7,815 critically ill NSTEMI patients across one Chinese and two American cohorts, with external validation built in.

In the discovery cohort, severe obesity (BMI ≥ 35) carried a hazard ratio of 1.69 for in-hospital death and 1.68 over ten years, while overweight patients fared better than normal-weight ones. In-hospital death hit 8.36% in severe obesity versus 1.55% in the overweight group. Adding C-reactive protein at 2 mg/L or more sharpened the high-risk picture further.
pmc-13341632:
Forest fungi both store and release soil carbon, in a 2026 review by Yun-Xiao Han and colleagues on ectomycorrhizal fungi. These partners of tree roots dominate many forest biomes and channel large shares of photosynthetic carbon below ground.

The review weighs carbon arriving as fungal necromass and protected in aggregates against losses from enzyme-driven priming of soil organic matter. It examines the debated Gadgil effect, mineral binding pathways, and controls like nitrogen deposition, climate change, and forest management. Measurement disputes, from isotope dilution to biomarker conversion, get candid treatment. The net balance under global change remains the field's open question.
pmc-13341732:
Breathlessness deserves a brain-aware rethink, argue Gianvito Lagravinese and research partners in a 2026 perspective on pulmonary rehabilitation in COPD. Dyspnea is not one sensation but at least three: air hunger, breathing effort, and chest tightness, each with distinct triggers and emotional weight.

The authors model conscious breathlessness as an interplay of motor drive, sensory feedback, and interoceptive inference, explaining why symptoms often diverge from lung function readings. Respiratory biofeedback might help not only by reshaping breathing patterns but by restoring perceived control. Neurofeedback, they caution, is a plausible future tool rather than a proven treatment, and their pilot data only loosely support the mechanism.
pmc-13343232:
Jingjing Ye and co-authors chart how the edible mushroom Volvariella volvacea builds its hardy survival spores, in a 2026 study joining microscopy with genome and gene activity data. These thick-walled chlamydospores carry the fungus through heat, drought, and hunger, but their control system stayed murky compared with model fungi.

Across four growth stages, spores moved from swollen threads to early buds to mature forms with reinforced walls. Storage making, energy switching, and wall remodeling switched on in coordination. Two Velvet family genes, VvVel1 and VvLaeA, showed stage-tied patterns that mark them as likely regulators. The framework gives breeders a base for tougher, stress-resistant mushroom strains.
pmc-13343832:
Claire E. Kaple and co-authors test a cheaper way to hunt stool for drug-resistant gut bacteria in 2026. Fidaxomicin is a favored treatment for Clostridioides difficile infection, and rare strains shrug it off, but current surveillance culture methods cost heavy labor and supplies.

The team spiked standard selective agar with a small fidaxomicin dose so only less-sensitive strains could grow. All 126 positive stool samples were plated both ways, and the spiked plates caught every one of the eight reduced-sensitivity isolates, matching the standard method exactly. Other stool microbes broke through often, yet their colonies looked clearly different. Wider surveillance for creeping resistance could now run at far lower cost.
pmc-13344232:
Sheree L. Boulet and a large team test a patient-centered planning program for postpartum visit attendance in a 2026 randomized trial. Patients with diabetes, blood pressure disorders, or obesity face high risk after birth yet often skip follow-up. In all, 320 patients at a city safety-net system were split between standard care and added planning support.

The added arm received prenatal teaching and built a personal postpartum plan with staff. Attendance at a full visit between 4 and 12 weeks landed at 52.8 percent with the program versus 55.3 percent without, no real difference. Among experienced mothers, though, more contact visits with coordinators tracked with far higher attendance, hinting that steady engagement, not one plan, moves the needle.
pmc-13344432:
Tania Cardona and colleagues systematically reviewed in 2026 what caregivers think of mental health services for children and young people across the World Health Organization European Region. Rising need has made responsive, high-quality care urgent, and caregiver views are central to judging whether services truly meet families.

The review searched five databases for qualitative studies published between 2010 and late 2023, registering its plan in advance and excluding work on neurodevelopmental disorders, inpatient care, and general practice. Eighteen papers covering 754 caregivers, mostly from Western Europe and especially the United Kingdom, were grouped into three main themes. The synthesis aims to feed practical quality standards that reflect what families actually experience, not only what clinics intend.
pmc-13345832:
Yitian Lang and co-authors weigh value for money of a potent antibody-drug conjugate against standard second-line care for advanced stomach cancer in 2026. The analysis sits inside China's health system and compares trastuzumab deruxtecan with ramucirumab plus paclitaxel for HER2-positive metastatic disease, using trial survival data in a partitioned model.

Base results put the added cost near 607,789 yuan per quality-adjusted life year gained, with only a 4.3 percent chance of counting as cost-effective, while the rival regimen scored 95.7 percent. Capping later treatment costs leveled the field and flipped the verdict, and pre-progression results alone favored the new drug. Price and follow-on care, the authors show, decide the answer.
pmc-13345932:
Yutong Ma, Wenjuan Xiong, and Yanming Xie mine real-world hospital records for how a Chinese herbal granule is used against prostatitis in 2026. Electronic records covered 1,922 patients given Compound Jinqiancao Granules across 20 top-tier hospitals, and network and association tools traced who got it and what traveled alongside.

Most patients were 46 to 65 years old, urology admitted the bulk, and stays ran 8 to 14 days with prostatitis as the lead diagnosis. Western partners included finasteride, diuretics, antibiotics, and steroids, while companion Chinese formulas followed syndrome patterns, pairing damp-heat cases with Kushen injection. Use matched the label overall, though without a control group nothing here can prove the granules work.
pmc-13346332:
Zhenhua Huang, Maohua Ding, Yue Ma, and Xiaoguang Tong demonstrate, in a 2026 technique paper, a backup patch for sealing the skull base after endoscopic surgery through the nose. Such surgery can open a leak of spinal fluid, and the standard repair borrows a flap of the nose's central partition, prized for its blood supply. When tumor or earlier surgery ruins that partition or its vessels, the standard flap is off the table.

Their alternative harvests the lateral nasal wall instead, a flap fed by a dependable artery at the back of the side wall. The paper walks through the harvest step by step, in the how-I-do-it genre, with the anatomy that makes the flap reliable. Coverage rivals the standard flap's, they report. The authors offer the technique as the reserve parachute every skull base team should know before they need it.
pmc-13347332:
Faisal Alissa and colleagues present a chelant-free way to clear gypsum scale from industrial pipes, in a study from 2026. Gypsum blocks flow in oil, power, and water plants, while standard removers such as EDTA linger in the environment and can move heavy metals. So the team paired potassium carbonate with a plant-based dispersing polymer.

Carbonate treatment converted up to 96 percent of the scale under mild conditions in the reported tests, mainly into a slow-changing mineral form called vaterite. A tuned dose of the polymer kept converted grains suspended with little loss of conversion, avoiding fresh blockages downstream. Cost and waste gains are claimed for this combined route to flow control.
pmc-13348032:
Georgi M. Trifonov and co-authors wrote in 2026 about how mRNA display can find peptide substrates for enzymes. Display tools screen vast peptide sets. Their use for binding ligands is well known. Their use for enzymes that change peptides has lagged. Yet work in this area has sped up in the last five years.

Surveying published work through December 2025, the authors traced trends in mRNA- and cDNA-display studies of enzyme substrate likes. They noted which enzymes, libraries, and readouts worked best. The write-up serves as a primer for newcomers. It also maps open asks, from library design to data reading, for a method that could speed enzyme craft and drug discovery.
pmc-13348132:
Nicola Churchill, Thuy-Tien Le, and Roch A Nianogo chart dementia policy spread and death trends across the United States, in a descriptive study from 2026. State policy records from 2008 to 2020 were set beside national death data from 1999 to 2022, since dementia ranked sixth among killers of older adults in 2022 and about 7.2 million older Americans lived with Alzheimer disease in 2025 by the cited count.

Every state adopted a dementia policy by 2020, with Iowa and Kentucky first in 2008, the biggest wave in 2013, and four states last in the reported order. Death rates rose steadily throughout, which may reflect better recording or policies needing more time to bite.
pmc-13348432:
Leila Najd-Hassan-Bonab and colleagues test European heart risk gene scores in an Iranian cohort split by sex, in a study from 2026. Data from a Tehran genetic study followed 4,594 adults free of heart disease for a median of 15 years, during which 991 heart events occurred. Three set scores plus combined versions were judged beyond standard clinical factors.

The 241-variant score held up in both sexes, with top-quarter women at a hazard ratio of 1.70 and men at 1.54 against the bottom quarter in the reported models. Scores built on European data can still rank Iranian risk, yet local tuning is needed before clinic use, the authors imply through added-value checks.
pmc-13348632:
Muhammad Musa and five colleagues enlist a fungus living inside maize to help the plant endure poisoned soil, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Lead and cobalt contamination puts a tighter and tighter curb on farming. Fungi that dwell in plant tissues can make growth hormones. They can also shore up the defenses of the plant they live in.

The endophyte Paecilomyces lilacinus produced phytohormones even under metal stress, its culture filtrate showed. In the maize, the fungus modulated metabolism as it grew. It shaped both enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidant systems in the plant. Good antioxidant management caps the harm that metals do to cells. Such fungal partners hold out a gentle way to help. It stands in place of soil removal or chemical treatment of the land. How long they last in the field is the open question for all endophyte remedies.
pmc-13349832:
Artem Oganesyan and co-authors pooled trial results in a 2026 meta-analysis on two PD-1 blocking drugs, pembrolizumab and nivolumab, used as first treatment for classical Hodgkin lymphoma. They searched PubMed, EBSCO Host, and CENTRAL for clinical trials.

Nine trials with 880 previously untreated patients were combined, with median age 34 years and median follow-up of about 31 months. The pooled outcomes covered complete and overall response rates, two-year survival and progression-free survival, and severe side effects. PD-1 blockers were first approved for lymphoma that had returned or resisted treatment. Weighing their first-line results together helps doctors judge whether they should move earlier in care.
pmc-13349932:
Tiansheng Su and colleagues studied a simple blood ratio and stroke in a 2026 analysis of United States survey data. The data ran from 1999 to 2018. The ratio divides uric acid by HDL cholesterol. It combines markers of metabolism and inflammation.

Adults with higher ratios had higher odds of having had a stroke. Those in the top quarter showed about 37 percent higher prevalence than the lowest quarter. The pattern rose in a roughly straight line. The ratio also separated people with and without past stroke fairly well. Support came from a separate dataset of imaging-confirmed bleeding strokes. The authors caution the measure describes current status, not future risk.
pmc-13350032:
Kun Zhu and co-authors pooled trial evidence in a 2026 meta-analysis on hesperidin, a citrus compound, for people who are overweight or obese. Sixteen randomised trials with 845 participants were gathered from five databases.

Outcomes covered inflammation signals such as C-reactive protein, oxidative stress measures, and blood vessel function, each checked for study quality and evidence strength. Pooling used the difference in averages for most measures. Excess weight keeps the body in a state of low-grade inflammation and chemical stress, and a food-derived compound that eases both would be a cheap aid. The synthesis judges how consistent that promise looks across trials.
pmc-13350232:
Ting Li and colleagues presented a brain-signal identity system in 2026 for brain-computer interfaces. Recognising people from electroencephalogram traces is hard because signals drift over time, differ between sessions, and new users must be added without wrecking old accuracy.

Their network, DyAMNet, mixes microstate analysis of brain activity with attention, adversarial training that strips out dataset quirks, and contrastive learning that pulls each person's pattern together. Across three public datasets it reached 87.2 percent accuracy, and kept 84.0 percent when grown step by step to 60 users. Tolerating artefacts and drift matters if brain-based login is ever to leave the lab.
pmc-13350332:
Yuyu Deng and co-authors reviewed microRNA control of hair regrowth in a 2026 article. Restarting hair growth means waking follicle stem cells, keeping the dermal papilla's instructive power, and calming the immune setting around the follicle.

Tiny microRNAs tune all three, switching growth phases on through Wnt and hedgehog signals and off through other pathways, while also setting inflammation thresholds in immune-driven hair loss such as alopecia areata. Getting such molecules into follicles is the practical hurdle, so delivery methods get close attention. The authors map where microRNA therapies could plausibly restore hair and what still blocks clinical use.
pmc-13350632:
Elaine Yuen Phin Lee and co-authors tested in 2026 whether deep-learning rebuild lifts multiplexed sensitivity encoding diffusion-weighted MRI of the female pelvis, where artefacts often spoil image quality. Diffusion imaging helps characterise pelvic lesions. Yet motion and susceptibility artefacts curb its trustworthiness.

Patients booked for pelvic MRI with two-shot MUSE diffusion imaging were enrolled prospectively, with a subset also getting paired four-shot scans. Two radiologists rated overall quality, artefacts, lesion visibility, and sharpness on a five-point scale, with and with no deep-learning rebuild, while signal, contrast, and apparent diffusion coefficients were weighed quantitatively. The rebuild lifted quality with no distortion of quantitative measures, backing its use in pelvic MRI.
pmc-13352632:
Omio Rani Das leads a 2026 zeolite study showing that acid sites locked inside tiny sodalite cages drive much of zeolite Y activity. Those cages have windows of only 0.26 nm, too small for fuel molecules to enter, so their acid sites were long counted as useless. Catalysts were made across acid densities, up to the theoretical maximum reported for the first time.

With supercage acid held fixed and sodalite acid varied, cracking of isooctane at high heat tracked the hidden sites. Isotope exchange with bulky molecules and spectroscopy backed the count. Computer models suggest protons rotate out of sodalite cages into big pores through framework flexing. Standard activity scores may thus miss a dominant site pool.
pmc-13352732:
Qianyi Yao and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six study on protecting the gut from radiation injury. Radiation therapy often harms the intestinal lining and limits dosing. A cannabis-related receptor on gut cells might shield it, but its local role was undefined.

Mice lacking the receptor suffered far worse gut injury after radiation. Screening found a new dual-target compound that activates the receptor. Cell studies traced protection through a signaling loop involving a growth regulator and a developmental gene. Damage routes including oxidative stress were also mapped. The work nominates a drug lead for radiotherapy support.
pmc-13352932:
Chengzhang Zhang led a 2026 review of tertiary lymphoid parts, clusters of immune cells that form in tissues outside the usual lymph organs during disease. Similar in group to lymph nodes, these parts mature from loose cell gatherings into organised sites with germ centres. They appear in chronic swelling, autoimmunity, and cancer, where they can shape local immune replies.

The review explains how chemokine signals, lymphotoxin pathways, stromal cells, energy change, and microbes jointly guide their making. It describes their cell mix, spatial layout, and functions, and weighs their influence on disease course and care response. Readers gain a structured opening to a fast-moving area of immunology with direct relevance to cancer care.
pmc-13353132:
Zuercher and colleagues surveyed United States middle and high school students in 2026 on how the way breakfast is served affects whether they eat it. School breakfast supports learning, yet far fewer students take it than lunch. The survey covered 1,097 students across eight states and compared standard before-school service with options such as breakfast in the classroom, a second-chance serving after first period, and grab-and-go lines.

Two thirds of students had only the standard option. Classroom breakfast came with nearly four times the odds of taking part and lower odds of time-related barriers, and second-chance breakfast roughly doubled the odds. Grab-and-go helped modestly, chiefly among high school students. Results held whether or not the state offered free meals to all. The authors say serving breakfast after the bell is a practical way to reach more students and support health and learning.
pmc-13354132:
Donald Alverson leads a 2026 equine case of phage therapy for a stubborn, drug-resistant surgical wound infection. An American Quarter Horse mare aged 14 years developed deep infection after emergency belly surgery for a twisted, displaced large colon.
