Cultures grew Escherichia coli and Enterococcus faecium, later joined by multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa, narrowing drug choices.

A tailored lytic phage mix was applied to the wound daily for 35 days, adjusted each day by fresh culture results. Target germ counts fell sharply and healing advanced steadily, while microbial mixes shifted without recolonisation by leftovers. At discharge the wound area had shrunk by over 85 percent and the body wall closed without hernia signs.
pmc-13355032:
Nhung Thi Doan and co-authors present 2026 draft genome data for a fungus that lives inside a medicinal plant in Vietnam. The fungus, Fusarium proliferatum strain TQN5T, was taken from the root of Dysosma versipellis in Tuyen Quang. Long-read sequencing was used to build and check the genome.

The draft spans about 47.7 million bases in 443 pieces, with a quality score near 96 percent. It holds more than 14,000 predicted genes plus many transfer and ribosomal RNA genes. The team also found 60 gene clusters for making active compounds, a resource for later work on how this fungus makes useful chemicals.
pmc-13355532:
Jing Li and co-authors review in 2026 brain imaging proof that faulty cell powerhouses and brain inflammation play a role in mental illness. The two problems are linked and may drive illness together, across disorders from schizophrenia and depression to autism and substance use. The review covers scans that track cell energy use and scans that track immune activity in the brain.

Three shared patterns stand out across disorders: weak energy use, changed immune cell states, and harm to the brain's wiring insulation. Few studies, though, have imaged both targets in the same people, so their direct link is unproven. The authors urge paired imaging to sharpen diagnosis and care.
pmc-13355732:
Sara M Hussein and co-authors ran a 2026 trial of a long-acting numbing drug in breast reduction surgery, using each patient as her own control. One breast got standard numbing drug alone, and the other got an added long-acting form, assigned at random. Thirty-two women rated pain twice a day for three days after surgery.

Pain was lower on the long-acting side on days one and two, with the biggest gap on the first morning, at about eight-tenths of a point. By day three, both sides felt the same, and no harms occurred. The authors call the gain modest and say a larger trial is needed to judge if the drug is worth its cost.
pmc-13356632:
Giorgia Rutigliani and co-authors critically review in 2026 the science linking highly processed foods and drinks to body weight. Governments are weighing guidance based on processing level to fight obesity, but the term itself has no agreed definition, and rival definitions predict distinct risks. Most proof comes from observational studies, which the authors judge weak and mixed.

Ward feeding trials were small and short, with no appetite change and only brief shifts in intake. Community trials often failed to change diets as planned, and none saw weight gain on the high processed arm. The authors argue that guidance based only on processing is not now in the public's interest.
pmc-13358332:
Christina Roberts and co-authors examine a hard question in a 2026 study from England. Some people with a learning disability have a formal note saying doctors should not try to restart their heart if it stops. Yet in some cases, staff still tried. The team studied reviews of 21 such deaths to learn what went wrong.

Using records from a national review program for deaths of people with a learning disability, they traced common themes. The cases point to rushed, chaotic moments, poor sharing of the note, and staff unsure of their duty. The work aims to help hospitals honor these choices and treat this group with more care and respect.
pmc-13358532:
Hong Hu and co-authors present a 2026 lab study on lung squamous cell carcinoma, a major cause of cancer death with few targeted drugs. They studied a protein called GNL3L, which helps control when cells divide. The team tested how this protein links with a second protein, LMNB1, and drives tumor growth.

Using patient tissue, gene data, and tests in cells and mice, they found the pair switches on a pathway called NF-kappa B. That signal helps tumors grow and resist a type of cell death driven by iron, called ferroptosis. Blocking this chain could open a new line of attack on a cancer that badly needs one.
pmc-13358832:
Ziyun Wu and co-authors review a microscope-on-a-probe technique for lung spots in a 2026 paper. Small lesions deep in the lung are hard to diagnose even with modern guided scopes: doctors may miss the exact spot or take tissue that tells little. Confocal laser endomicroscopy sends a tiny microscope to the lesion and shows living tissue up close, in real time.

The review gathers studies through 2025 and compares the images this method gives of healthy and diseased tissue, using natural glow and added dyes. Knowing these patterns could help doctors confirm they are on target before taking tissue, raising the yield of each procedure.
pmc-13361232:
Bernhard Zapletal and co-authors studied the safety of a breathing-tube procedure in very sick heart patients in a 2026 paper. The procedure opens the windpipe through the neck to help patients breathe long term. Many of these patients are on strong blood thinners for heart support machines or artificial valves, and stopping the drugs carries its own risks. The team reviewed all cases in a heart intensive care unit from 2016 to 2024.

They compared bleeding problems between patients kept on full-dose thinners and those on low preventive doses. The main question was whether the procedure stays safe when thinning is not paused. Bleeding is the chief fear with this bedside operation. Firm safety data help ICU teams weigh two dangers against each other instead of guessing.
pmc-13361432:
Jan Krekora and co-authors review a family of proteins that sense fuel use in the failing diabetic heart in a 2026 paper. Heart failure with diabetes forms a distinct pattern, marked by poor sugar use in heart muscle and weak cell power plants. The proteins, called sirtuins, depend on a helper molecule named NAD+ to work. They coordinate how the heart burns fuel and answers stress.

In animal and cell studies, sirtuin loss, often from drained NAD+, made heart metabolism stiff and wasteful. Restoring NAD+ or sirtuin action improved power plant efficiency and coordination. Human tissue and blood marker studies back the story, though mostly by association, not proof of cause. The review weighs sirtuins as drug targets for a common and deadly pairing of diseases.
pmc-13362032:
Junwei Zhang and six colleagues replace the opaque metal tube used in keyhole disc surgery with a transparent one, and measure the difference in sixty-five patients. The standard metal channel blinds the surgeon to tissue behind its wall during endoscopic removal of prolapsed lumbar discs, risking nerve injury and missed fragments.

The transparent channel delivered a near-complete field of view by image-quality metrics, cut average operating time by about fourteen minutes, and slashed nerve-monitoring alerts from eleven to two. Pain and disability outcomes matched the conventional approach. The authors frame a humble materials innovation as a direct safety and efficiency gain.
pmc-13364332:
Tursun Mamat and co-workers build a 2026 two level plan to route self driving carts that must visit many stops in busy store rooms. One layer uses a swarm search to tune the plan. The next grows two path trees that meet in the middle.

Smart sampling cuts wasted search in tight aisles, and a light watch loop tweaks settings as the plan grows. A last step smooths sharp turns. Tests show a good mix of speed, safe gaps from shelves, and smooth runs. The plan fits fleets that move goods all day in tight halls.
pmc-13364732:
Won-Gun Yun and co-workers test in 2026 if a machine guess of early cancer return can pick who gains from drug care after gallbladder cancer surgery. Drug care helps some such patients, yet gains shift by case. The team split 395 past patients by a learned risk score for quick return.

Low risk patients lived much the same with or with no drug care. High risk patients on drug care lived five years at a clear higher rate than those on watch alone. The split could spare low risk patients cost and harm from care they do not need.
pmc-13365532:
Ziyuan Wu and others harnessed the glycolysis-TCA cycle axis to boost newborn defence against illness, in 2026. Preterm infants are highly susceptible to sickness that can progress to sepsis, yet care beyond drugs are limited. Food and host energy use modulate defence, but how they interact in newborn defence was poorly known.

In a birth cohort of seven hundred children, elevated plasma tricarboxylic acid cycle metabolites were linked to illness results, and mechanistic work showed those metabolites modulate early-life immune replies. The glycolysis-TCA axis emerged as a lever for host defence. Neonatal teams gain a energy plan that could complement drugs for at risk preterm infants.
pmc-13365832:
Mudit Raj Sade and others built an tuned confidence-driven plan for fusing lidar and visual data in drone landing testing, in 2026. Self-run landing needs finding a safe spot, and lidar alone can mislead: a flat water surface looks safe in three sizes but is not landable. Image data reveal texture and stuff that lidar misses.

The plan fuses lidar structure with visual texture and material understanding. Lidar detects slope, uneven faces, and obstacles such as rocks, trees, poles, and buildings. Each source is weighted by confidence in real time. The joined testing avoids single-sensor traps. Drone builders gain a landing system that reasons about both geometry and surface identity.
pmc-13366532:
Susan Ziolkowski and co-workers warn in 2026 that a fat share score can call thin muscle folks fat by fault. The score, from bone scans, splits fat by whole weight, so low muscle lifts it. A fat mass score that frees the count from muscle exists as a kin tool.

In near fifteen thousand US adults, the share score calls more than three fourths fat, far past all kin tools. Of folks with thin muscle, near two thirds get a fat tag by it, yet near none by weight score. The team backs the free score for care and study.
pmc-13373532:
Lalevee and co-authors trial a boot that triggers fake ankle sprains during walking. Chronic ankle instability shows in repeat sprains, but safe lab tests were lacking. Thirty-two feet split into instability and control groups. Boots on a treadmill fired a sudden ankle roll at random steps. Peak roll speed was read right at foot contact.

Roll speed averaged 213.5 degrees per second in the instability group. Controls averaged 177.0 degrees per second. A ratio to prior steps split the groups even more sharply. Survey scores on ankle function were gathered for contrast. The authors say the device sorts unstable ankles from healthy ones.
pmc-13376732:
Nur Syamimi Makbul and colleagues measure breastfeeding duration in wild Bornean orangutans with stool proteomics in a 2026 study. Orangutans live slowly, with long gaps between births and low infant mortality, and milk may drive that pattern, yet milk intake is hard to measure and weaning age estimates conflicted. Milk-specific proteins in twenty stool samples from five young orangutans in Danum Valley, Sabah, were tracked.

Orangutans consistently drank milk for at least six and a half years, among the longest breastfeeding periods in mammals. Milk intake tracked with higher immune defence and probiotic bacterial proteins. Mothers did not conceive again during breastfeeding. The work confirms long, continuous nursing as a core part of orangutan slow life history and shows stool proteomics can reveal hidden feeding patterns in wild animals.
pmc-13377132:
Konstantinos Stratakis and co-authors ask if hard exercise is its own thing for mind health in a 2026 review. Most past work lumps all moves as one dose, by time or by a yes-no on sport. Hard bouts tax the body, feel, and day in ways light moves do not.

The review puts proof from trials and watch work next to how the body may act. Signs for sad mood are the most grown of the lot. Mixed past finds may stem from loose word use for hard, the team says. If hard moves are their own dose, guides should name them as such, not hide them in one sum.
pmc-13377832:
Yiqian Zhou and co-authors tied food protein to joint ills in a 2026 study in the United Kingdom. Food logs from a day's recall set each folk's protein take, by type and by food. Four joint ills were tracked through ward logs for more than 12 years.

More than 23,000 new stiff knee and hip cases came, plus far less of three kin ills. High whole protein went with less gout risk. Plant protein went with less risk of two ills, while beast protein went with more of one. Blood fire marks sat in the chain in part. Food guides for joints can use this split.
pmc-13380232:
Ebony N Gary and a large team report a 2026 study on delivering long-acting diabetes and weight drugs as DNA instead of repeated injections. Current drugs that copy gut hormones have changed care for obesity and type 2 diabetes, but making them is costly and patients must keep taking them. DNA instructions can make the body produce a treatment for a long time.

The team built DNA carrying designs for long-lasting versions of two gut hormones, joined to part of an antibody to extend their life. Given once to obese mice with a mild electric pulse device, the DNA drove lasting production. Treated mice ate less, lost weight, and kept blood sugar lower.
pmc-13380832:
Chaimae Bekhakh and co-authors present a 2026 case of a rare blood-cell tumour in the breast that mimicked ordinary breast cancer. The tumour, called myeloid sarcoma, is made of immature white blood cell precursors growing outside the bone marrow. It usually accompanies leukaemia, and breast involvement is exceedingly rare.

Their patient was a 39-year-old woman with masses in both breasts that looked malignant on scans. Tissue tests showed immature cells spreading through the breast, and marker tests pointed to a myeloid origin rather than breast cancer. One marker more typical of another cell family was also present, adding to the diagnostic trap. Gene testing found a specific fusion, helping to confirm the diagnosis.
pmc-13381032:
Kyra Salinkas, Sabeen Wazir, Madeline Keen, and Lance Albin describe a 2026 case where a small bowel polyp caused the bowel to telescope into itself in a young woman with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. That inherited condition causes polyps in the gut and dark spots on the lips and hands, and raises the risk of this emergency. She also carried a gene change for a second inherited condition.

The 29-year-old arrived with stabbing pain in her lower back and nausea. She had needed bowel surgery as a teenager for the same problem. Scans suggested the telescoping had returned. Surgeons removed about twenty centimetres of small bowel, and tissue tests confirmed the polyp type behind it.
pmc-13382032:
Caitlin McCartney and co-authors wrote a 2026 scoping review of genetic tests sold directly to the public that promise personalised diet advice. Consumer demand for control over health care is driving the market. The review maps which genes the tests use and what diet advice follows, to support informed choices.

An internet search found 104 companies offering 204 nutrition-related testing panels. The average price was a little over two hundred United States dollars, and most companies were registered in North America. Only just over half of the companies publicly disclosed which genes they test. That lack of openness is a central finding for regulators, clinicians, and buyers alike.
pmc-13382732:
Stefan Elde and co-authors report direct views of two MitraClip devices inside a human heart removed at transplant in 2026. The heart came from a 64-year-old man who had the clips placed two years earlier for severe mitral valve leakage. Views from the lower chamber, rarely seen during the usual procedure, form the core of the report.

Inside, the clip arms sat deep in both valve leaflets and were covered by firm fibrous tissue. The cords that anchor the valve ran around the fused area without breaking, though their angles and tension had shifted. Readers gain a clear picture of how the device heals into the valve and why effects on nearby parts may shape long-term results.
pmc-13383432:
Lin Huang's team designed a self-fueling particle drug to wipe out cancer stem cell-enriched tumors, in a 2026 study. Such tumors resist drugs through cholesterol-driven defenses against ferroptosis, a form of iron-dependent cell death. The team's particle loads cholesterol oxidase into hollow porous zinc-copper sulfide, targeted with hyaluronic acid.

Cholesterol loss dismantles protective lipid rafts and releases a molecular brake on fat damage, while copper and zinc chemistry plus hydrogen sulfide amplify a lethal fat-damage storm and relieve hypoxia. Lab and animal studies showed potent anti-tumor and anti-spread effects through stem cell killing. The strategy pairs membrane attack with cell chemistry attack in one particle.
pmc-13383532:
Anna Michalik's team found a stable feeding team-up across a cryptic hopper species complex, in a 2026 study. Sap-feeding hoppers rely on obligate bacterial partners for amino acids missing from phloem, but whether those partnerships persist across hidden host diversity was unclear. The team sampled hoppers identified as Verdanus abdominalis from Poland, Sweden, and Austria.

Host genes revealed several far-apart lines, yet gut microbes varied little across groups. The ancient symbionts Sulcia and Nasuia held on throughout, backed by gene sequencing and metagenomics. The staying power suggests symbiont loyalty outlives host splitting, a useful anchor for hopper ecology and pest research.
pmc-13384332:
David Ramzy and co-authors report a fatal infection striking 26 years after spleen removal in a 2026 case report. A 36-year-old woman arrived with flu-like illness and confusion, then slid fast into septic shock. Her spleen had been removed decades earlier for an immune platelet disorder, leaving her exposed to certain bacteria.

Blood tests found pneumococcus, and her care required breathing support, dialysis, and strong drugs to hold blood pressure. Widespread clotting and limb blood loss followed, and she died within 48 hours of arrival. The authors stress lifelong vaccination, patient education, and fast antibiotics for people living without a spleen.
pmc-13384432:
Raluca Jumatate and colleagues link right heart muscle stretch function to walking capacity in lung hypertension in a 2026 imaging study. Forty-nine patients with pre-capillary disease had walk tests, blood markers, catheter measures, and both ultrasound and MRI heart scans, mostly within one day. Right heart function was clearly impaired across the group.

Walk distance tied to several lengthwise function measures in adjusted models, no matter which scan supplied them. A blood marker of heart strain reflected filling pressures more than muscle function after adjustment. The authors conclude that resting lengthwise function helps explain exercise limits in this disease.
pmc-13385432:
Sara K. M. Jörgensen and colleagues test how running, diet, and selenium shape new neuron growth in the mouse hypothalamus in 2026 work. That brain region helps govern body energy balance, and its stem cells can birth new neurons in adults. Mice ran voluntarily for short or long spans, on normal or high-fat food.

Long running raised new neuron growth on normal food, while short running rescued growth that high-fat food had suppressed in one niche. The rescue faded with long running, a region-specific twist unlike the memory center pattern. Selenium copied the short-run effect and woke stem cells, which hints it acts like an exercise signal here.
pmc-13385832:
Brandon Hubbard's team traced kidney insulin resistance to a single receptor site, in a 2026 mouse study. Poor suppression of glucose output drives organ damage in insulin resistance and diabetes, and the kidney cortex role was underappreciated. High-fat diet raised membrane DAGs, PKC-epsilon movement, and insulin receptor T1160 tagging while blunting insulin-stimulated pyruvate burning and signaling.

In high-fat mice, kidney glucose output rose 6.5-fold and supplied 60 percent of total glucose output under high insulin. Excess kidney glucose came equally from glycerol and mitochondrial sources, chiefly pyruvate. Signaling and flux defects vanished in IRK T1150A knockin mice except glycerol-derived glucose output, pinpointing the DAG-PKC-receptor axis.
pmc-13385932:
Manuel Liaci and colleagues reveal, atom by atom, how the signal peptidase complex recognizes the tags that route newly made proteins. The complex cleaves signal peptides from roughly a tenth of the human proteome. Signal peptides share a tripartite structure, three regions defined by general chemistry rather than strict sequence, yet the enzyme processes this diversity with exquisite specificity.

The team presents a cryo-electron microscopy map, at near-atomic resolution, of one human complex paralog bound to a model signal peptide. The peptide's end region sits in a hydrophobic groove near the active site; a narrow gate marks the transition to its helical middle region, which lodges in a transmembrane window. Substrate engagement stabilizes helices of the catalytic subunit that frame the peptide. Simulations confirm the network, and modeling supports the binding mode across real signal peptides.
pmc-13386632:
Kumbha and colleagues investigate risk factors for mucormycosis, a rare but often fatal fungal invasion, among people with diabetes in Bathinda, Punjab, in a 2026 case-control study. A surge at the regional AIIMS hospital in November 2023 prompted the inquiry. The study compared 36 confirmed diabetic cases with 102 diabetic controls from the same hospital's endocrine clinic. It interviewed both about recent stress events such as hospitalization, surgery, dental work, or trauma, plus rural exposures including cattle handling and household water storage practices.

Cases were mostly men, 81 percent, with a median age of 54 years, and the infection attacked the nose, eye, and brain region in 78 percent of cases. Adjusted analysis found acute stress events raised the odds of disease, with an odds ratio of 3.2. Cattle handling carried an odds ratio of 4.9, and storing drinking water in earthen pots 3.7. Kumbha recommends safer cattle handling, hygienic water storage, and clinician awareness in rural diabetic populations.
pmc-13386932:
Junwang Liu's team built and validated a frailty classification model for older maintenance hemodialysis patients, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Frailty is common in older dialysis patients, yet a practical classification tool for this group was lacking. The team screened factors in 510 cases from three Fujian hospitals using univariate analysis, LASSO regression, and random forest. The resulting logistic model and web calculator use five variables: albumin, walking-aid use, sleep condition, pain score, and psychological resilience.

It told frail from non-frail patients well, with area under the curve near 92 percent in training, test, and validation sets alike. Calibration and clinical applicability also looked good. The tool lets clinicians spot frailty in older dialysis patients and supports routine screening in dialysis care.
pmc-13390132:
Gaofeng Zhang's team pooled eleven studies covering 1,697 patients to compare early versus delayed minimally invasive drainage in necrotizing pancreatitis, a severe pancreatic complication. Guidelines debate timing, so the team searched major databases through November 2025 and joint randomised trials and cohort studies.

Early drainage, within four weeks, carried clearly higher mortality and more than double the need for later debridement, though the mortality finding proved unstable. Hospital stay, intensive-care stay, and overall complications did not differ clearly. The authors conclude that delaying drainage past four weeks should be the priority where feasible.
pmc-13390332:
Sara K. Nutley's team tracked hoarding symptoms over five years in 1,275 adults enrolled in the online Brain Health Registry, the first prospective study of hoarding's course. Hoarding is usually described as chronic and progressive, yet its actual trajectories and drivers were little known.

Latent-class modelling found three paths: lasting severe symptoms in about sixteen percent, lasting mild or subclinical symptoms in about seventy-five percent, and rapid improvement in about nine percent. The data-driven paths diverged from four theory-driven trajectories, and demographic and medical traits distinguished membership, challenging the assumption that hoarding only worsens.
pmc-13390432:
Anaísa Coelho's team refined the e-uptake pathway of Sideroxydans lithotrophicus ES-1, a fresh-water germ that gathers energy from outside-cell e-transfer. The Mto pathway's shape and give were poorly understood, so the team mapped the single-heme proteins MtoD and PmcA plus the four-heme protein ImoA.

PmcA, but not MtoD, linked with ImoA and with MtoA, marking PmcA as ImoA's living redox partner on heat and binding evidence. MtoD's high redox power made transfer to ImoA poor. It hints MtoD instead feeds a high-power acceptor such as a final enzyme, changing the proposed e-transfer model.
pmc-13390732:
Yusra Wahab and colleagues hunt, in 2026, for plasmid-borne colistin resistance in drug-resistant bacteria taken from patients with weak immunity. Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic revived as carbapenem resistance spread, and the mobile mcr gene now threatens that final defence.

Over twelve months at Lahore General Hospital and the University of Health Sciences in Lahore, the team collected one hundred multidrug-resistant Gram-negative rods from patient samples. Each isolate was checked for visible colistin resistance and for the mcr-1 gene. Infection specialists gain a local prevalence figure for a resistance gene that can jump between bacteria on plasmids, a finding with direct weight for protecting immunocompromised wards.
pmc-13392132:
Pei Jiang Low's team showed quantum logic in a single twenty-five-level trapped-ion qudit, using barium-137 ions to push beyond binary qubits. Scaling quantum computers is hard, and exploiting an ion's full internal levels promises greater algorithmic power per particle.

The team achieved high-fidelity preparation and readout of up to twenty-five levels. They probed superpositions of up to twenty-four states to chart how errors scale with dimension, and ran a three-qubit Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm plus a four-qubit Toffoli gate in one ion. Large-dimensional qudits thus look promising for hardware-efficient quantum computing.
pmc-13392432:
Xiaoting Ling's team built split-second flashing charge-field sorting to profile the charge landscape of bio droplets at near single-droplet detail. Charge patterns inside droplets regulate stability and function, yet exact electrical marks had been elusive.

Applied to droplets of the human DNA sensor cGAS with DNA, the rig found two zeta-charge groups from same components under same conditions, a surprise. Minus-charged droplets proved only open to the exo-enzyme TREX1, while positive ones were spared or boosted, and harmful cGAS forms disrupted this charge control, linking droplet bio-physics to inborn immune regulation.
pmc-13392632:
Valeria Solórzano-Araque and eight colleagues built a detailed exposure model for air pollution in Medellín, Colombia, a city folded into a steep tropical valley where movement data are scarce. Their framework links a chemical transport model of the air to a travel survey covering more than one hundred eighty thousand trips. Samples of airborne particles were also checked for metals and carbon content linked to harm.

Simulations mapped pollution at one-kilometre detail for 2019, then weighted each group's exposure by time spent in each place. Central and southern districts, home to about sixty percent of residents and crossed by main highways, showed peak-hour particle levels above health guideline values. Clustering flagged those zones as the highest risk, and the authors direct follow-up health studies and clean-air action there first.
pmc-13393232:
Adrian Arrieta and nine colleagues traced how daily body clocks and outside signals jointly control two muscle genes in growing heart cells. Titin-cap and myosin light chain 2 help build the sarcomere, the heart's contractile unit, and earlier data flagged both as clock-influenced. Working mainly in newborn rat heart cells, the team applied adrenaline-like drugs, varied cell crowding, and cut oxygen to mimic postnatal cues.

Crowding shifted clock timing, while low oxygen shrank cells yet switched Titin-cap on through the master clock protein Bmal1. Removing Titin-cap worsened oxygen-starved shrinkage and blunted partner gene responses. The authors conclude the two genes read environmental cues through the clock in distinct ways during early heart growth.
pmc-13394032:
Toru Beppu and colleagues review functional liver volumetry for major liver surgery in a 2026 paper. Knowing how much working liver will remain after hepatectomy is crucial for safety, yet standard CT volume measures anatomy, not function, especially in diseased livers or after preoperative therapy.

The review centers on technetium-labeled galactosyl albumin scintigraphy fused with SPECT and CT, which maps regional liver function together with volume. It shows stronger prediction of post-hepatectomy liver failure than volume alone. Surgeons gain a guide to choosing the safest resection extent for each patient.
pmc-13394332:
Deborah Carrick and co-authors report a 2026 study on how much contrast dye to give during belly CT scans. Their team compared a fixed dose of 100 millilitres with a dose based on body weight. They matched 90 scans from each group by age, sex, weight, and scan settings. They also measured how bright key organs and blood vessels looked on the images.

Weight-based dosing gave more even brightness across patients of different sizes. Yet even brightness did not always mean images that looked equally good to readers. Lighter patients seemed to need stronger enhancement than heavier patients for the same judged quality. The authors argue that dose plans need more fine tuning beyond weight alone.
pmc-13395432:
Alberto Nogales and co-authors test, in 2026, whether step-by-step AI reasoning grades student medical records better. Teachers of medicine face heavy loads of written case records, here in Spanish. Two AI models graded records with a scoring guide, using either one sample answer or chain-of-thought prompts that show each step. Faculty checks followed the machine scores.

One model, Claude, reached top accuracy near eighty-six percent with plain prompts. Its step-by-step mode led on most other measures, such as catching faults. Expert review found many gaps were in fact machine wins, lifting final accuracy higher. The present illness section caused the most clashes. The authors say such tools can also audit the guides themselves.
pmc-13395832:
Mythili Ilango and colleagues chart, in 2026, why Australian children's vision falls short at each age. Five Sydney study groups covered ages three to seventeen, each with full eye exams. Poor unaided sight was set at worse than a standard chart line. The team also tracked new cases as children grew between studies.

Poor sight grew more common with age, from a small share at preschool to near a fifth at seventeen. Lazy eye drove much of the loss in the youngest groups. Short sight took over later, causing most cases by age twelve. The authors back preschool screening for lazy eye. They also urge glasses promotion for teens with short sight.
pmc-13396332:
Chenguang Zhang and co-authors linked nutrition risk scores with signs of immune shutdown in 60 patients with community-acquired pneumonia, in a 2026 study. Two proteins, PD-1 and CTLA-4, act as brakes on T cells, and high levels can mark an immune system too tired to fight infection.

Blood tests measured those brakes on several T-cell types, and charts supplied severity and nutrition scores. The braking proteins showed no firm link to severe pneumonia or death within 28 days. Higher levels on CD4 T cells did track with worse severity index scores, and patients flagged at risk of malnutrition by the NRS-2002 screen showed their own pattern.
pmc-13396432:
Xinsheng Xiao and co-authors heated aromatic tree seeds four different ways before cold-pressing them, to see which preparation gives the best oil, in a 2026 food study. The oil comes from Litsea cubeba kernels and is valued for its scent compounds and protective antioxidants.

Stir-frying, roasting, infrared, and microwave pretreatments left the oil's fatty acid makeup essentially unchanged. Other qualities moved a lot. Infrared treatment gave the highest yield at about 17.19 percent and the richest phenol content, along with strong activity against test radicals. Flavor compounds also differed by method, with the infrared oil led by its own key aroma set, a result processors can use when tuning taste.
pmc-13396732:
Hui and co-authors compare, in 2026, how successive Omicron sub-lineages of SARS-CoV-2 behave in human tissues, finding the newer BA286 and JN1 lines have shifted toward the gut. Using bronchial and lung explants, airway organoids, proximal-intestine enteroids, and colon cells, they measured replication and entry routes from BA1 through JN1 while background immunity was absent, isolating intrinsic viral traits.

In respiratory tissues, XBB15 and EG51 out-replicated BA286 and JN1, showing stronger airway fitness. EG51 additionally used dual entry pathways with greater lung cell replication. The picture reversed in proximal intestinal enteroids, where BA286 and JN1 replicated more efficiently than EG51, dependent on ACE2 and the TMPRSS2 entry protease. Blocking that protease cut JN1 replication to 57 percent of control in cell tests, versus 5 percent for the original virus. JN1 also provoked limited inflammatory cytokine release in gut tissue, suggesting quiet intestinal infection with fecal transmission potential.
pmc-13396832:
Jennifer A. Rybak and co-authors probe how two cell-surface receptors that cancer drugs target interact, and what breaks their partnership, in a 2026 cell study. EGFR drives growth in many tumors, and a second receptor, EphA2, often rises when EGFR drugs stop working, making their link a clue to resistance.

Using glowing tags and a proximity test that lights up only when two proteins sit close, the team watched the pair at the cell membrane. When EGFR was pulled inside the cell, a process called endocytosis, its binding to EphA2 at the surface fell. The finding suggests the cell's own recycling habits tune a resistance pathway that drug makers hope to block.
pmc-13396932:
Paul Köhli and co-authors ask whether calcium built up in the belly aorta can serve as a warning sign for weak bone in spine surgery patients. Their 2026 study, a German Spine Society prize paper, covers 139 people undergoing lumbar fusion, where screws must grip bone that may be quietly poor.

Calcification was scored on side-view spine X-rays, and bone density was measured by quantitative CT. Small bone samples from the pelvis were scanned for fine architecture and probed for the quality of the matrix between cells. Vessel calcium already tracks with low density and fractures; this work tests whether it also signals the deeper traits that decide whether fusion hardware holds.
pmc-13397132:
Bethany Harding and others count tubule and microbranch shifts in human dentine in a 2026 three-dimensional study. Microbranches form fluid-filled webs that join dentine tubules, but their shape and web build were poorly caught in flat views.

Serial block-face scanning electron microscopy built 3D volumes showing microbranches winding in twists through dentine between tubules, varying in crowding by spot, with more branches where tubules were sparser. Microbranches raised tissue pore space a lot, while widths mostly ranged 140 to 210 nanometers no matter the zone. Dentists gain a 3D map of fluid paths behind tooth ache.
pmc-13397632:
Yi Xiong and others bare the genomic basis of local adaptation in Siberian wildrye in a 2026 study. Grasping how this native Eurasian alpine grass adapts locally matters for ecology, evolution, and forage breeding.

Population reads grouped 316 accessions into Xinjiang, northern China, and Qinghai-Xizang Plateau clusters, with selection sweeps pinning climate-adaptation genes and six gene swap events among thirteen subgroups. Population histories swung widely in recent times. The paper links genome shifts to the climates each lineage endures, giving breeders gene leads for forage grasses in harsh alpine zones.
pmc-13397732:
Åsa Thelaus and fellow authors check whether a video-based score can steer treatment when clubfoot returns in children who already walk. Their 2026 study covers 55 children aged 4 to 15, with 85 affected feet filmed for review. Care for relapsed clubfoot varies widely between centres, and the value of scoring systems in this age group was unclear.

Four senior children's bone surgeons from different countries scored each video with the Pirani Böhm Sinclair scale and named their chosen management. Higher scores sharply cut the odds of advising watchful waiting, with a score near 10 marking the swing toward active treatment. Yet even at set scores, surgeons picked quite different operations, showing the score guides but does not settle decisions.
pmc-13398132:
Lu Yang and co-authors flip a materials rule by making a normally brittle alloy phase bend instead of crack. Intermetallic phases usually harden alloys but start cracks at their edges, trading toughness away for strength.

Chemical complexity within the B2 phase, plus ready dislocations and patchy composition, lets it keep gliding and multiplying its line defects under strain. The laminated layout spreads deformation and redirects stress away from interfaces. At room temperature the alloy reached a yield strength of 1.24 GPa in the tests reported, pairing that strength with the ductility such phases rarely allow.
pmc-13398832:
Lijun Zhu and Bin Song write a 2026 letter questioning a study that linked two blood markers to bone health in older patients with type 2 diabetes. The study under discussion, by Wang and colleagues, tied serum CTRP3 and cystatin C to bone turnover markers and bone density in patients who also had osteoporosis. Fresh markers for early bone loss in diabetes would be welcome, the writers grant.

Two cautions follow: a one-time snapshot design cannot show which came first, and kidney trouble could drive both the marker and the bone changes. Key confounders such as vitamin D, activity and true body makeup also went unmeasured. Until follow-up studies track the markers over time, the pair should be read as companions of bone loss, not proven predictors.
pmc-13399132:
Guo and co-authors examine, in 2026, what the binding protein IGFBP4 does in human fat precursor cells, using knockdowns across adipocyte models including LipPD1 preadipocytes taken from an infant lipoma patient. Silencing it slowed preadipocyte growth and reduced the IGF1 receptor and its activated downstream signal, phosphorylated AKT, while leaving fat-cell maturation untouched.

When protein synthesis was blocked, the downregulation persisted unless a proteasome inhibitor was co-applied, pointing to proteasomal disposal as the mechanism rather than lysosomal routing. They nominate it as a therapeutic target for growth and metabolic disorders of IGF1R dysfunction.
pmc-13399232:
Seok Woo Shin and co-authors gathered the existing systematic reviews comparing balanced crystalloid fluids with plain saline in critically ill patients, for a 2026 overview. Both fluids are given into a vein to restore circulation, yet saline can push the blood toward acidity and may strain the kidneys. Guidelines already lean toward balanced fluids, though the evidence is thin and trial results have conflicted.

Quality checks with the AMSTAR-2 tool found critical weaknesses in 13 of the 14; only one was free of such flaws. Pooling across reviews pointed to a small advantage for balanced fluids, clearest in patients with sepsis and those without traumatic brain injury. The authors present the overview as a map of where the evidence is strong and where it rests on weak reviews.
pmc-13399532:
Kasey Stickler and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a high school quarterback whose neck injury turned out to be a clay shoveler's fracture. The injury is a break of the small bony knob at the back of a lower neck vertebra, named for clay workers who snapped the same bone shoveling. It happens when muscle or ligament force avulses the spinous process, and it is known for being stable rather than dangerous. The 18-year-old arrived at a sports medicine clinic four days after the game.

Examination found tenderness precisely over the seventh cervical spinous process, with strength, sensation, and motion all preserved. X-rays confirmed an isolated C7 spinous process fracture. Treatment stayed conservative: a rigid collar, rest, and anti-inflammatory drugs, with the collar weaned gradually in coordination with neurosurgery. The case reminds clinicians to consider this fracture in athletes with pinpoint neck tenderness after contact.
pmc-13399832:
Katherine Koch and colleagues mapped dance-related injuries among children and teens treated in United States emergency departments. Their 2026 epidemiologic study uses the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System from 2019 to 2023, covering an estimated 93,062 dance injury visits. Dance is popular among young people, yet injury patterns by age and sex had not been fully charted.

Knees and ankles were the most injured regions, sprains and strains the most common diagnoses, and floor impacts plus ankle rolling the leading mechanisms. Younger children more often hurt knees and ankles through sprains and noncontact moves, while teens more often fractured bones. Girls more often sustained knee and ankle sprains, while boys more often sustained head injuries and fractures. The paper helps coaches and clinicians target prevention by age and sex.
pmc-13399932:
Arthur Cavalcante Lopes and colleagues tested the FIB-4 score as a liver fibrosis screen in people living with HIV who also have diabetes or prediabetes. The work is a 2026 study from a tropical medicine center in Belém, Brazil. The team enrolled 100 patients on continuous antiretroviral therapy between March and November 2025 and combined the score with ultrasound imaging and metabolic measurements.

FIB-4 came back altered in 32 of the 100 participants, with no difference between men and women. Ultrasound showed mild fatty liver in 47.0 percent and clinically significant steatosis in 11.0 percent. The score's weakness showed in classification: it did not adequately pick out the significant steatosis cases. The authors recommend FIB-4 for what it does well, ruling out advanced fibrosis, while pairing it with metabolic assessment. Anyone at or above a score of 1.3 should go for elastography rather than trusting the index alone.
pmc-13400132:
Rushikesh S Patil and colleagues reviewed whether structured exercise can rebuild muscle and function in people whose cirrhosis has decompensated and wasted their muscles, in this 2026 review. Searching five databases for work from 2012 to 2026, the team gathered ten studies of exercise, rehabilitation, and nutrition programs in this population. They appraised their quality with standard risk-of-bias tools.

The programs that worked combined methods: aerobic training, resistance work, balance practice, and home-based rehab, sometimes with branched-chain amino acid supplements. Across the studies, patients gained muscle strength, walked and performed daily tasks better, improved aerobic capacity and body composition, and reported better quality of life. These helped preserve muscle mass and liver function. The authors conclude that integrated exercise is safe and effective even in advanced disease, and they position combined rehab and nutrition as core cirrhosis care.
pmc-13400232:
Amanda Rushing and colleagues report rerouting brain blood flow and relining the aorta in a man whose aortic arch curves the wrong way, in a 2026 case report. Every endovascular device on the market assumes a left-sided arch, so the team improvised. Surgical cerebral debranching came first, building bypasses to keep the brain supplied. Then a thoracic branch endoprosthesis landed in zone 1 of the arch.

The branched graft deployed just beyond the left common carotid origin, with a stent extended into the right common carotid artery. Imaging afterward showed the aneurysm excluded, with the carotid stent and the cerebral bypasses all patent. The patient carried serious cardiac baggage, including an ejection fraction of 25 percent and a defibrillator, which made avoiding open arch surgery especially valuable. pmc-13400432:

Following participants for a median of over thirteen years, the team recorded 180 new cases of hair loss and close to three thousand new cases of dermatitis. People with depression at the start faced notably higher risk of both conditions later. Genetic scores and blood inflammation markers were also examined for their roles. The authors caution that hair loss case numbers were small, so those estimates need care.
pmc-13400732:
Feini Huang and a large team quantify, in 2026, how vegetation upwind shapes soil moisture downwind across South America. Air carries moisture from land surfaces over long distances, linking distant ecosystems. How much upwind plants contribute to downwind soil wetness had not been measured at continental scale.

Combining air trajectory data with deep learning, their model beat a local-only version, with upwind information supplying about two thirds of predictive power and vegetation about fifteen percent of it. Effects were stronger over farmland and followed major air transport corridors. In humid forests, canopy loss meant drier soils downwind. In semi-arid zones, some greening helped, but more greening eventually reversed the benefit.
pmc-13400832:
Mehtap Er Kemal, Mehmet Kemal and Hasan Temiz create, in 2026, hybrid cheeses blending cow milk with soybean drink to hunt for natural blood pressure and diabetes related peptides. As milk and soy proteins break down during ripening, small fragments can block enzymes tied to hypertension and blood sugar control. The team varied the soy share and the fermenting culture.

Profiling found 102 peptide sequences, about a quarter from soy, several never before reported in cheese. The strongest enzyme-blocking activity appeared in the highest soy cheese fermented with one particular culture. Computer docking suggested selected peptides fit the target enzymes well, though that is supporting evidence only. The work frames hybrid cheese as a sustainable route to functional foods.
pmc-13400932:
Andrew S Bi and co-authors demonstrate, in 2026, a hybrid surgical technique for rebuilding the elbow ulnar collateral ligament, the structure throwers famously tear. Many overhead athletes injure this ligament, and repair works only when tissue quality is decent. Chronic tears, mid-substance damage and older age often rule repair out.

The method combines a graft taken from the patients own forearm tendon with a suture brace that reinforces it, aiming for strength matching the natural ligament while preserving normal elbow motion. The video walks through graft harvest, drilling the graft tunnels, brace placement and graft fixation. The procedure ends by moving the ulnar nerve, for patients with nerve irritation. Prior outcome studies of the approach are summarized.
pmc-13401532:

BRAF drugs clearly work in melanoma, but their wider role was once doubted. The team searched four databases for studies from 2010 to 2025. Trials and cohort studies of BRAF inhibitors qualified. In total, 36 studies with 3,141 patients entered.

The studies spanned more than 14 tumor types, mostly in phase II basket trials. Outcomes covered response rates and several survival measures. Benefit proved broad but varied by tissue of origin. The review tempers tumor-agnostic hopes with tissue-level facts.
pmc-13401632:
Jamir Pitton Rissardo and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on how environmental toxins contribute to neurodegeneration in Parkinson's disease. Mitochondrial failure, oxidative stress, inflammation, and poor protein clearance emerge as shared routes to dopamine cell vulnerability. pmc-13401932:
Songlin Wang and co-authors reviewed the evolution of targeted treatment for gastric cancer in a 2026 article, tracing the field from antibody drugs through RNA interference to nanotherapy. pmc-13402232:

Following Cochrane and PRISMA-P guidance, they analyzed definitions, antecedents, and consequences of self-care across disciplines and population groups. An independent coder handled 20 percent of eligible records, and a quarter of the corpus was double-rated to verify the category system.

The analysis confirmed that self-care keeps being renewed and recast, with professional groups studied far more than ordinary people grouped by age. For the general population, they describe self-care as intentional and purpose-driven at its core. It spans purposes from managing health to enhancing overall well-being, and braids together actions, abilities, and social and thinking processes. Discrepancies between judges were resolved to full agreement. The authors recommend a systemic view and policies built on the concept's antecedents.
pmc-13402332:
Mihiro Dejima and co-authors examine an ovarian yolk sac tumor in a 59-year-old woman, a setting where this germ cell cancer almost never appears and usually ends badly. Full genomic profiling found changes in ARID1A, CTNNB1, NFE2L2, and PIK3CA, a set more typical of ovarian clear cell and endometrioid cancers. That reading matters for care, since such tumors may answer to treatments aimed at clear cell carcinoma instead.
pmc-13402932:

pmc-13403032:

pmc-13403632:

Their lens is Kant's duty-based ethics, set against laws in Brazil and abroad. Research leans ever more on detailed records, including records of people who have died.

Brazilian rules, they find, leave the post-death use of such data unclear. Other countries tie use more closely to wishes voiced while a person lived. The authors propose a legal consent tool signed during life. Such a tool would let patients set terms for later use and guard their dignity.
pmc-13403732:

pmc-13404132:

pmc-13405232:

Orphan drug uses drew requirements more often than standard ones. Completion rates and label changes complete the picture, giving policymakers evidence on whether post-approval oversight delivers.
pmc-13405632:

Periodontitis slowly destroys the tissues holding teeth, and painless fluid tests could catch it earlier. Standard gum measures were worse in the disease group, as expected. Salivary periostin was roughly double in patients, at 1,234.5 against 596.32 in the reported units, and gum fluid TGF-beta1 was also higher. Samples were tested with ELISA kits, a standard lab method. The authors weigh both fluids as monitoring tools, noting the study covers only early disease stages.
pmc-13406332:

Corn, corn flour and protein samples tested the platform's tolerance of real food matrices.
pmc-13407732:

pmc-13407832:

pmc-13408132:
