pmc-13408832:
Hunter Gaudio and colleagues benchmark six commercial language models in 2026 on a task with real diagnostic stakes: nominating gene panels from cell-free RNA in blood. Such panels could flag disease from a blood draw, yet almost no published biomarkers survive to approval. Three paired clinical puzzles were used, distinguishing Kawasaki disease from a related inflammatory syndrome, active tuberculosis from other respiratory illness, and chronic fatigue syndrome from healthy inactivity.

Asked to nominate genes from the literature, the models recovered sensible immune pathways and their panels beat random ones everywhere, even matching standard statistical selection in the tuberculosis cohort. Asked to build complete classifiers from raw data alone, results became uneven: one model neared conventional performance on the first puzzle, while scores fell on the other two. The study maps where language models already help biomarker hunting and where they still falter.
pmc-13409032:
Benny Aprisa Surya Perdana and colleagues swab dogs passing through an Indonesian animal quarantine station in 2026, hunting for bacteria armed against frontline antibiotics. Companion animals can carry extended-spectrum beta-lactamase genes, which disarm whole antibiotic families, and travelling dogs can move them between regions. Rectal swabs from one hundred thirteen dogs at Surabaya's Juanda station were cultured during a three-month window in 2025.

Three quarters of the dogs carried Escherichia coli, as expected for gut flora. Three isolates, a small share, carried the resistance genes under study, mostly a pairing of two gene families, and a third gene family was absent entirely. Low prevalence is reassuring, the authors argue, but not a reason for complacency: even rare carriers can seed spread between animals, people, and environments. They recommend prudent antibiotic use and One Health surveillance at transport checkpoints.
pmc-13409332:
Katsuyuki Dainaka and colleagues report in 2026 a small mechanical trick. It salvaged a difficult bile duct procedure in a patient whose anatomy had been rebuilt by stomach surgery and then distorted by returning cancer. The man, jaundiced from a recurrent tumour's stricture, had a Billroth II reconstruction that left the bile duct opening facing the wrong way for the scope, even with balloon-assisted deep access.

An S-O clip was fixed to a mucosal fold above the opening and its loop anchored to the opposite bowel wall, pulling the tissue into a frontal, stable view. With the axis steadied, a standard catheter and guidewire entered the duct, the opening was cut, and a plastic stent placed, all without complications. Similar traction methods exist, the authors note. Tumour distortion is precisely where they feared traction would fail. That makes the success worth recording.
pmc-13411432:
Kátia Avena and colleagues argue in 2026 that basic science in medical training is not being cut, it is quietly fading from view. Integrated courses, digital tools, and uneven resources dilute step-by-step mechanistic thinking, the habit of tracing disease from molecule to symptom. That habit, they contend, remains the spine of good doctoring.

Reform fads come and go, yet the authors ask schools to protect three things: clear conceptual progression, visible space for science, and transfer into clinic. Active learning, digital aids, and AI can help when anchored by trained faculty and firm standards. Without that anchoring, shiny tools deepen the inequality between rich and poor schools.
pmc-13411732:
Yifan Yu and co-workers find in 2026 that a sugar coating keeps an immune-damping protein alive on liver cancer cells, wearing out the killer T cells that attack them. The protein, B7-H3, abounds in hepatocellular carcinoma. Fine mapping pinned its survival on one sugar attachment point.

With the sugar in place, a recycling route returns the protein to the cell surface instead of destroying it. Blocking the sugar, by drug or by mutating the attachment point, sent the protein to cellular incinerators and revived killer T cell attack. In mice, either block strengthened standard immunotherapy antibodies. The sugar-recycling axis thus ranks as a druggable weakness in the tumor's immune shield.
pmc-13413232:
F. Costabile and co-authors explore in 2026 whether long-term exposure to ultrafine air particles tracks heart disease across rich countries. These particles are far smaller than the fine dust regulators usually measure and can burrow deep into the lungs, yet harmonized exposure records only recently became available. Using a new global dataset, the ecological study estimated population-weighted exposure from 2010 to 2019 in high-income countries and set it beside national heart disease statistics.

Patterns linking higher ultrafine exposure to more disability and lost life years recurred across the outcomes checked. The authors stress these are country-level associations, not proof about individuals, and they should not be extended beyond wealthy nations. They still argue the signal justifies monitoring ultrafines even where standard dust limits are met.
pmc-13413832:
Mei Zhang and colleagues trace in 2026 how a Weigela japonica flower changes dress over four days of blooming, from yellow through orange to purple-red at its base. Chemists measured three pigment families across four stages while gene sequencing watched the petal's factories switch on and off. Network analysis then hunted the regulator genes whose activity moved with pigment build-up.

Carotenoids crested during the orange stage, while the red-purple anthocyanins and their flavonoid cousins surged only at the end. Gene activity followed a relay: early enzymes ran first, mid-pathway genes peaked through the middle stages, and the final colour enzymes peaked last in their sequencing. Three hub regulators, MYB44, bHLH92, and ERF3, tracked the closing colour surge. The authors propose a stepwise timetable model, awaiting direct proof.
pmc-13415632:
Jennifer Armstrong, Shannon Morley, and Jennifer Utter build short dietitian led videos to teach irritable bowel syndrome self care, reporting in 2026 from Brisbane, Australia. Referrals at their hospital outpaced dietitian capacity, leaving long waits. Four short videos were made with the gastroenterology team from best practice guidance.

Patients and clinicians alike called the videos clear and educational. Every patient surveyed would recommend them to family or friends with the condition, and most planned dietary changes. About 45 percent felt they might no longer need a face to face dietitian visit. Video first teaching could free scarce appointments for complex cases.
pmc-13415832:
Viktor Gavrilyuk and co-authors improve a compound that blocks ALOX15, an enzyme that oxidizes fatty acids and figures in inflammation and ferroptosis, in 2026. The lead compound blocks the enzyme's linoleic acid activity through an allosteric route, meaning it binds away from the active site. Three chemical changes were tried on pure rabbit enzyme.

Swapping the rigid indole core for a phenylpyrrole weakened potency somewhat. Adding water loving groups improved solubility greatly yet cut potency more than tenfold. Replacing one chemical group with a sulfonamide sharpened selectivity: strong against human and rabbit ALOX15, weak against the related human ALOX15B and mouse enzyme.
pmc-13416232:
Eszter Kustos-Tóth and co-authors test whether correcting chronic low blood sodium raises levels of BDNF, a growth factor important for memory and cognition. Their 2026 pilot analysis reuses data from a randomised crossover trial in nine patients whose bodies retain too much water, a condition called SIAD.

Patients received the diabetes drug empagliflozin and a placebo for four weeks each, in random order. Median sodium rose from 131 to 134 units on the drug and stayed low on placebo. Larger sodium increases were significantly tied to larger BDNF increases, even after adjusting for treatment, sex, age, and antidepressant use. The link was stronger during empagliflozin treatment, and patients whose sodium normalised gained slightly more BDNF. Cognitive test scores, however, did not differ between phases, and the authors call for larger studies.
pmc-13416432:
Ying Lin, Jackson G. Lu, and Michele J. Gelfand examine how social class shapes negotiation at work, in a 2026 research summary. Negotiation decides pay, assignments, and promotions, so reluctance to negotiate can compound into lasting inequality. Their program studies both willingness to start negotiations and the social cost of trying.

Lower class individuals initiate negotiations less often than higher class peers. When they do negotiate, they meet stronger social backlash for the same behavior. The pattern helps explain pay and advancement gaps that persist even with equal credentials. Negotiation is framed as both a barrier and a possible lever for mobility.
pmc-13417232:
Rifayee and collaborators used computer simulations to study the enzyme KDM6B. The enzyme normally removes methyl tags from histone proteins. It can also strip larger alkyl groups from lysine, one of the building blocks of those proteins. Their team combined molecular dynamics, which tracks how molecules move, with quantum-level calculations on the enzyme at work.

The simulations showed KDM6B oxidizing the alkyl groups step by step. It produced an alcohol first, then an aldehyde, and finally a carboxylic acid. Two amino acids, numbered N344 and Y239 in the enzyme chain, formed a network. That network guided each bulky group toward the reactive iron center. Swapping either residue in simulated mutants changed that access, confirming their guiding role. The authors argue these findings could help engineers design related enzymes. Such enzymes could reshape drug-like peptides with chosen selectivity.
pmc-13419032:
Juan Pablo Salica and colleagues set out a treatment plan for alkali burns of the cornea built around an enzyme switched on by the injury itself. Alkali damage sparks a self-feeding loop of swelling, tissue breakdown, and stray blood vessel growth that often beats standard care. The enzyme in focus, transglutaminase-2, rises after injury and could serve as an anchor point on the damaged surface.

The review joins enzyme biology with the known effects of a protective protein that calms tissue-eating enzymes. Fusing an anchor part to that protective protein would park the drug where damage is worst. Earlier animal work from the group backs the targeting idea with direct tests. Steroids and vessel-blocking drugs remain the base of care, and the fused protein would add a guided strike on top.
pmc-13420532:
Tiseo, Galfo, and Falcone survey in 2026 the global spread of MRSA, the form of Staphylococcus aureus bacteria that resists standard antibiotics. It remains a leading cause of deadly bloodstream infection worldwide.

The review finds that overall prevalence has fallen over the past decade, mainly in high-income countries. Yet the pattern differs sharply by region and by setting, from acute hospitals to long-term care homes to the wider community. Successful bacterial lineages and changing resistance genes keep the organism circulating. The authors discuss nasal screening as both a prevention measure and a guide for careful antibiotic use. They note that newer anti-MRSA drugs with good safety profiles have recently expanded treatment choices.
pmc-13421232:
Gouvea Silva and colleagues report a 2026 study of robotic surgery training inside Brazil's public health system.  At one public hospital, eight trainee surgeons operated on eighty patients between March 2025 and January 2026 under a standard training curriculum, while the team recorded patient details, operation data, and costs.

Most patients were men, with a mean age near 51 years. Groin hernia repairs made up about half the cases, followed by gallbladder removals at about four in ten, with other procedures making up the rest. Funding came in parts from the public system, private partners, and the robot provider. The series shows a training model can run inside public care.
pmc-13421332:
Dyke Ferber leads a large team introducing MIRA in a 2026 paper, a self-directed artificial intelligence agent built to manage patient cases inside an electronic health record. Unlike chat tools that answer single questions, MIRA works inside a sealed record system. Its access to patient data is governed, and it may start only defined actions.

In tests on real patient cases, the agent took histories and ordered lab, imaging and microbiology tests. It read the results, built a list of possible diagnoses, and drafted treatment plans. Those plans covered prescriptions, surgery bookings and admission decisions. It beat the doctors on diagnostic accuracy in these tests. Its choices followed guidelines and kept medication use safe. The authors present the study as early proof that agents built into the record can handle whole cases, within strict safety limits.
pmc-13422332:
Max Duong Phu leads an ten-author team linking, in a 2026 study, the embryonic heart's rhythm to male hormone signalling. Birth defects of the heart are the commonest congenital malformation. In sex-chromosome syndromes, where androgens run low, up to half of babies are affected. Yet the androgen receptor's role in early heart building was unreported.

Blocking the receptor in zebrafish embryos, three different ways, produced swollen, slow and irregular hearts. The likely culprit was an excess of adrenomedullin, a vessel-relaxing peptide that surged when the receptor was silenced. Cell work in mouse cultures supported the chain, and the authors connect it to the proepicardium, a cell cluster that mingles with the heart's conduction system. The pathway reframes how hormone shortages may shape heart disease present at birth.
pmc-13422932:
Mounter and colleagues map in 2026 what is known about fitness and physical activity in adults with fibromyalgia, the chronic condition marked by widespread pain and fatigue. They focused on quality of life and on muscle-strengthening activity.

The scoping review, searching databases to March 2025, included 79 articles. Compared with healthy adults, people with fibromyalgia showed weaker muscles, lower cardiovascular fitness, and poorer agility, balance, flexibility, activity levels, and quality of life. Studies measured quality of life with a wide, inconsistent mix of questionnaires, which limits comparison. Progressive resistance training stood out as a promising way to improve quality of life, though program designs varied widely. The reviewers found that what helps or blocks people from starting strengthening activity remains barely studied.
pmc-13423932:
Pagliarani and co-authors report an unusual zoo case in this 2026 paper. A captive white-cheeked turaco, a fruit-eating African forest bird, had disseminated mycobacteriosis. The cause was a species almost never seen in animals. The adult bird arrived with persistent breathing difficulty that antimicrobials could not fix and was euthanized on welfare grounds.

Autopsy found granulomas, the walled-off inflammatory nodules typical of mycobacterial disease, in the lungs and spleen, packed with chains of slender acid-fast bacteria about two micrometers long. Culture and gene sequencing of two marker genes identified Mycobacterium shimoidei. The slow-growing species was first found in a Japanese patient in 1975. It had previously been reported in a non-human host only once, in a goldfish. The authors stress molecular testing for atypical mycobacteria in zoo collections and better surveillance, given possible public health spillover.
pmc-13424032:
Agnes Grill and seven colleagues report long-term outcomes for babies whose mothers' waters broke before 23 weeks of pregnancy. The data are meant to ground the hard counselling families face at the edge of viability. Their retrospective cohort covers infants given active care at one centre between 2009 and 2022, with development checked at two to three years of corrected age.

Of 109 infants, 33 died before discharge. Among survivors with follow-up, average scores sat lowest for language. Cerebral palsy affected 11.1%, and 72.6% survived without moderate or severe impairment. Serious newborn complications, rather than how long the waters had been broken, drove worse outcomes. Birth timing and female sex favoured better results in early models.
pmc-13424332:
Ayumi Takaoka and ten colleagues review outcomes of robot-assisted rectal cancer surgery combined with removal of neighbouring invaded organs, among the most demanding operations in the field. At one high-volume centre, forty-five consecutive patients with locally advanced cancers had the combined procedure between April 2021 and June 2025.

Serious complications, grade III or worse, struck four patients, about 9 in every 100. Pathology confirmed deep invasion in nearly half the cases, and clear margins were achieved in about 87%. Over a median follow-up of twenty-three months, patients with completely clear margins enjoyed far better three-year freedom from recurrence. The figure was about 75%, against about 33% for involved or uncertain margins. The team calls the robotic approach safe with acceptable midterm results.
pmc-13424732:
Shanshan Li and five colleagues pool the trials of group reminiscence therapy, structured sessions where older people share memories together, for nursing home residents whose thinking is intact or mildly impaired. Ten databases were searched to September 2025 for randomised and quasi-experimental studies, with quality graded by standard risk-of-bias tools.

Nineteen studies covering 925 residents qualified. Group reminiscence clearly eased depression and fear of death, and it lifted life satisfaction, self-esteem, and happiness, with effects that were large by the standards of such research. Loneliness, surprisingly, did not fall significantly, its pooled estimate straddling zero. Effects varied with how sessions were run, and the authors supply the subgroup detail for programme designers.
pmc-13424932:
Keen, Hassoulas, and Richardson reviewed in 2026 whether oestrogen-based add-ons help antipsychotic drugs in women with psychosis around and after menopause. Oestrogen is thought to shield the brain against psychosis, and its fall at menopause opens a window for symptoms to start. The team searched major databases for trials giving hormone therapy or selective oestrogen receptor modulators, drugs that mimic oestrogen in some tissues, alongside standard antipsychotics in women over 40.

Keen found ten studies, nine of them on raloxifene and only one on hormone therapy itself. Six of the nine trials reported significant gains: four cut total scores on the standard symptom scale, and two improved only the positive symptom domain, such as delusions and hallucinations. Quality checks flagged publication bias, uneven reporting, and varied designs. The authors call raloxifene promising as an add-on, but they want stronger trials before hormone-informed protocols enter routine care.
pmc-13425032: Shraddha Uprety, Pratichya Thapa, Prakriti Lamichhane, and Sunil Jaiswal report a rare tumor variant in a case report from 2026. The tumor, a glomangioma, usually appears on the fingers, but this case arose elsewhere on the body, which is called extradigital. Such tumors often lack the classic signs doctors expect and can be mistaken for other lumps, so suspicion plus a tissue biopsy are needed for a firm diagnosis.
pmc-13425632:
The European Food Safety Authority, known as EFSA, reports its peer review of the risk assessment for Trichoderma asperellum strain T34, a living fungus used as a pesticide. Sweden and Italy prepared the first assessments for the renewal of its European approval.

The review covers the fungus's planned use against plant disease on ornamentals and on crops such as tomato, sweet pepper, cucumber, and melon. EFSA lists the reliable end points, meaning the measured values regulators can trust for risk judgements. It also lists missing information and data gaps that the rules require before approval can rest on firm ground. During the process, the applicant dropped support for one product form while keeping the active substance itself under review.
pmc-13425732:
Wei Zhang and colleagues built a new sponge-like material to pull indole, a toxic ring-shaped pollutant, out of industrial wastewater. The material joins a layered mineral with a porous metal-organic framework, a scaffold of metal and carbon parts full of tiny holes.

Tests showed the combined material had more surface area and more grabbing sites than either part alone. It removed about 93 percent of indole within two hours under neutral conditions in the lab tests. Pulling power came from electric attraction on the surface and from flat ring parts stacking together. The material still removed over 82 percent after five reuse cycles, pointing to use in coke-plant wastewater treatment.
pmc-13425932:
Dan Shao and colleagues test echinatin, a plant compound with anti-inflammatory action, against mastitis, the udder infection that cuts milk yield and harms dairy animals. Antibiotics work but carry side effects, so safer plant-based options are sought.

In cow mammary cells stressed with bacterial toxin, echinatin lowered key inflammatory signals, including tumour necrosis factor, interleukin 1 beta, interleukin 6, and interleukin 17A, plus mediators called COX2 and iNOS. A mouse model of mastitis extends the test to living tissue. Farmers and vets get a candidate that may calm udder inflammation with less drug burden.
pmc-13426332:
Campbell and colleagues review in 2026 whether root traits explain why some introduced plants invade, noting that invasion science has mostly studied stems and leaves. Their mini-review gathers studies across settings that differ in disturbance and soil nutrients, then proposes a framework linking root traits, environment, and invasion success.

No single root trait predicted invasion on its own. Patterns shifted with context: in calm, nutrient-rich sites, invaders often carried more root mass for fast resource capture. In disturbed, nutrient-poor sites, invaders grew finer roots with greater length per gram than natives. Their framework predicts rapid root turnover or clonal regrowth where disturbance and nutrients are both high, and microbe partnerships or conservation strategies where nutrients are scarce. The authors say roots may sharpen invasion risk forecasts.
pmc-13426432:
Chen and colleagues compared in 2026 the smoke-free laws of 23 Chinese cities that meet world tobacco treaty standards, asking how much the legal vehicle behind each law matters. China has no national smoke-free law, so cities acted alone through three kinds of regulation: dedicated tobacco control rules, patriotic health rules, and civility promotion rules. Together the cities shield about 178 million people, far below the national target.

Two coders scored the full texts. Dedicated tobacco rules were far longer and covered nearly every topic, from fines for smokers and venue owners to complaint hotlines and youth sales bans. Seven of nine coverage areas differed sharply by vehicle. The authors argue that only a comprehensive national law can carry protection to the target of eighty percent of the population.
pmc-13427732:
Gadallah and colleagues ran a prospective study in 2026 on predicting when patients can come off non-invasive ventilation, breathing support through a mask, in a respiratory intensive care unit. They followed 150 adults with acute respiratory failure treated between April 2024 and March 2025, recording blood gases, lab values, and two severity scores. Ninety-nine patients weaned successfully and fifty-one failed.

Failure clustered in older patients and in those with a failing right heart, low hemoglobin, or low albumin, a protein that signals poor nutrition. Two scores predicted failure well: a combined bedside score reached about eighty-two percent accuracy, and a general severity score about seventy-six percent. Earlier repeated episodes on a ventilator through a tube also independently raised the risk. The authors suggest adding the bedside score to weaning protocols so failing patients are spotted before they deteriorate.
pmc-13427832:
Antao Ming and colleagues tested whether uneven foot temperatures in people with diabetes can warn of heart rhythm trouble and blood clot events. They re-analysed a foot study that used heat cameras and sensor insoles to track the soles over time.

The follow-up covered 239 patients for a median of about 67 months, with surveys capturing irregular heartbeat, strokes, lung clots, and leg artery disease. Patients whose sole readings showed downward temperature shifts had higher event rates than those without such shifts. One high-variability group carried far higher odds of the combined events after adjustment for other risks. Heat images with uneven sides marked the sharpest split, at about 49 percent events versus about 6 percent.
pmc-13428032:
Azzam and colleagues report a 2026 case of a 14-year-old boy with scrotal pain and swelling. The problem was first treated as epididymitis, a common infection, but it proved to be a rare cancer. A full month of intensive antibiotics, including intravenous meropenem, brought no improvement, which prompted deeper imaging.

Ultrasound showed a mixed solid mass beside the testicle with rich blood flow, and MRI measured it at roughly nine centimeters across. Staging scans found enlarged lymph nodes but no distant spread. Surgeons removed the testicle and cord through a groin incision, and tissue tests confirmed embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, a muscle-type cancer, with marker stains proving muscle origin. He was referred for standard children's cancer chemotherapy. The authors warn that scrotal masses ignoring proper antibiotics demand urgent suspicion of malignancy.
pmc-13428432:
Benedikt Schoser sets out, in a 2026 position statement, clear numeric bounds for judging when Pompe disease treatment stops holding steady. Pompe disease slowly weakens muscles, including breathing muscles, because cells cannot clear stored sugar properly. Enzyme replacement therapy changed its course, and three such drugs now compete. Drawing on major trials, extensions, registries, and real-world cohorts, the statement defines a corridor of stability for treated patients.

Breathing capacity that drifts within a small yearly band counts as stable, while a confirmed fall beyond a set threshold should trigger review. Walking distance works the same way, with a margin of about 25 meters around the best result. Chemical markers and strength tests fill out the picture. Clinicians gain shared alarm lines for escalating, switching, or reassessing therapy instead of judging by feel.
pmc-13428732:
Seifert and colleagues traced prescribing trends from 2007 to 2024 for 1,902 psychiatric inpatients in German-speaking countries. All were treated for depressive episodes of bipolar disorder, and the data came from a drug safety monitoring program. Nearly every patient, over ninety-eight percent, received psychotropic drugs, and most received several at once.

Antipsychotics were the most used class and grew from about seventy to about eighty-one percent of patients, driven by newer second-generation drugs such as quetiapine and aripiprazole. Antidepressant use fell from about seventy-eight to sixty-eight percent, and antiepileptic use dropped steeply, while lithium held steady at about a third of patients. The average drug count per patient fell slightly, yet two thirds still took three or more psychotropics, and double antipsychotic combinations doubled. The authors see a persistent gap from guidelines.
pmc-13429132:
Min Zhang, Hairong Lin, and Yanmei Huang search, in a 2026 study, for asthma markers tied to a chemical edit made to RNA letters. The edit, called ac4C, may help drive inflammatory diseases. Starting from public gene data on adult asthma, the team overlapped disease-linked genes with edit-related genes. Genetic methods that mimic a natural experiment then tested which candidates might cause, rather than merely follow, asthma.

Five genes survived every filter and became the marker set. Three looked protective and two looked risk-raising in the genetic analysis. A scoring chart built from the five separated asthma samples from controls acceptably well. One marker tracked closely with two immune cell types in lung tissue. Drug screening even suggested a compound that touches several markers at once. Lab checks of gene activity backed the computing, giving asthma researchers fresh targets.
pmc-13429632:
Megan A. Brickner and colleagues record, in a 2026 study, dopamine signals in the rat amygdala, the brain hub that tags experiences with emotional weight. Dopamine's role there was murky next to its fame in reward circuits elsewhere. The team watched dopamine release in living rats across several learning tasks. Cues ranged from reward and threat to safety and neutral signals, and their emotional intensity varied by design.

Dopamine rose with how intense a cue felt, not with its reward value or how strongly it had been learned. Reward cues actually evoked smaller signals as training went on, the reverse of classic reward teaching signals. Threat and safety cues produced the largest, longest responses. When rats juggled several associations at once, the signal rescaled to mark relative importance. The authors cast amygdala dopamine as a salience reporter, telling the brain what deserves attention.
pmc-13431132:
Shrestha and colleagues identify an unexpected courier of fat into the liver in this 2026 study. Fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction is a leading cause of chronic liver illness. But how neutrophils contribute to early fat buildup was poorly understood. Neutrophils are front-line immune cells. The team found neutrophils soak up fatty acids from their surroundings through two transporter proteins and store them as triglycerides rather than burning them.

These lipid-laden neutrophils then shipped their cargo to liver cells inside extracellular vesicles, tiny released parcels also carrying fat-regulating microRNAs, increasing the liver cells' fat stores. Transferring such neutrophils or their vesicles into mice raised liver fat, and neutrophils from patients with fatty liver disease showed the same lipid-loaded pattern, as did their blood vesicles. A distinct lipid-handling neutrophil subgroup appeared in single-cell data.
pmc-13431432:
Yang and colleagues built a prediction model in 2026 for anastomotic leak after esophagus removal. A leak is a dangerous failure of the surgical join, and the patients studied had first received combined chemotherapy and immunotherapy. The study covered locally advanced esophageal squamous cell cancer at two centers.

Among 550 patients, leaks occurred in about one in ten in both the 350-person training group and the 200-person validation group, and most leaks were at the neck join. The final model combined changes in three blood indexes of inflammation and nutrition with low body mass index and poorer daily functioning. It separated patients who leaked from those who did not with good accuracy in training and acceptable accuracy in outside validation.
pmc-13431732:
Akseli Kehusmaa and a large team brought out a new score in 2026 that grades how ragged the deep edge of a bowel cancer runs, then tied that grade to gene traits. Ragged edges have long spelled worse outlook, yet older grades proved hard to repeat between readers. The new score counts how much of a hot spot at the deepest push point is support tissue and fat.

Two patient groups, each near a thousand strong, anchored the checks. High scores went with later stage disease, tumor buds, vessel spread, and a thinner guard of two immune cell types. High scores also forecast higher death rates from the cancer itself, apart from other risks. Gene work tied ragged growth to sound repair machinery plus faults in two known cancer genes. Silencing two loud genes in a lab cell line cut its push through barriers.
pmc-13432032:
Renee Fiolet and colleagues explore how community health nurses put trauma-informed care into practice in general health settings in Victoria, Australia. The study targets care for people affected by sexual assault or domestic violence, where trauma-informed practice is urged but its everyday shape is vague.

A focus group of four nurses plus one individual interview, all with nurses delivering trauma-informed care in general services, were analysed by reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes showed nurses turning theory into practice, starting with recognising what trauma can look like in patients. The small study gives managers essential ingredients for training and support, rather than a slogan.
pmc-13433332:
Atif and colleagues studied how married adolescents in rural Pakistan lived through a life skills program. Their spouses and families took part too. The program offered planned social and emotional support. In this setting 30 percent of women marry before age 18. Through interview-based work, they looked at emotional and relationship challenges inside very young marriages. They also asked what the program changed.

People said they had been told to live happily without being told how. That was the gap the training aimed to close for these young couples. The program built communication, empathy, and emotional bounce-back among the married adolescents who took part. Bringing in husbands and other key family members spread the gains beyond the wives. Relatives' grasp of the wives' emotional needs grew as well. The authors argue life skills and mental health parts belong inside adolescent and maternal health services in places like rural Pakistan.
pmc-13433732:
Jia Hu and colleagues show how an enzyme, B3GNT7, guards the gut barrier during acute pancreatitis by sugar-coating the mucus protein MUC2. That protein keeps the gut lining in balance, and its mature form falls when Golgi damage strikes goblet cells in pancreatitis.

Two mouse models of acute pancreatitis, induced by caerulein with lipopolysaccharide or by L-arginine, showed Golgi stress markers shifting as mature MUC2 dropped. Gene-activity work found B3gnt7, a Golgi sugar-transfer enzyme rich in goblet cells, turned down in sick mice, and its levels ran opposite to pancreas and colon damage scores. Patients with pancreatitis also showed markedly lower gut B3GNT7, marking a barrier pathway worth protecting.
pmc-13434332:
Helve and colleagues charted non-fatal heart attacks and strokes after kidney transplantation in Finland across three decades, covering all 4,942 first-time recipients transplanted between 1990 and 2019. They asked whether cardiovascular risk truly fell for transplant patients, or merely mirrored improvements in the general population over the same years.

A total of 811 non-fatal cardiovascular events occurred during a median follow-up of 7.4 years after transplantation in the registry data. Adjusted long-term risk was significantly lower for patients transplanted in the 2000s and 2010s than in the 1990s, at hazard ratios of 0.75 for the 2000s and 0.78 for the 2010s. Against the general population, the excess heart attack rate shrank from a standardized incidence ratio of 4.61 down to 1.65 between the earliest and latest periods. Stroke excess fell similarly, from 3.62 in the earliest period to 1.13 in the latest, showing transplant patients gained faster than everyone else.
pmc-13434532:
Yolanda Martí-Mateos and colleagues show in 2026 that a stress guard inside liver cells also guards against liver cancer in old mice. Animals lacking the guard protein OMA1 grew more liver tumors and died sooner. A stress pathway stayed switched on without the guard, causing early liver harm.

Chronic swelling and scar tissue followed the early harm. Tired immune cells built up in the liver and let tumors grow. Liver cells alone lacking the guard were enough to trigger the chain. Moving immune cells between mice confirmed the liver itself drove the immune wear. Drug plans that target this guard need care.
pmc-13434632:
Rashad Al-Gaashani's team took on farm waste in Qatar in 2026, where about two million tons a year are made and under a fifth is reused. They turned mixed green waste and woody waste into biochar, a charcoal-like product. Each waste was heated at four temperatures and four dwell times, then yield, carbon, ash, surface area, and heat behavior were measured. The aim was a solid base for using biochar in the dry region's linked food, water, and energy systems.

Woody waste gave the best solid yield at low heat and, at high heat, built far more surface area than green waste, with a more stable carbon frame. Green waste lagged on both counts. Readers get a careful comparison that points woody farm waste toward soil and filter uses, while green waste needs more work to match it.
pmc-13435432:
Dehdab and colleagues test two large language models, ChatGPT-5 and Qwen3, as stand ins for a multidisciplinary tumor board deciding care for gastrointestinal stromal tumors. These rare gut tumors need tailored calls that mix scans, genetics, surgery, and drugs, and expert boards are scarce in many regions. Their 2026 study feeds 99 real board cases to each model with a structured prompt, then has two blinded experts score replies across five domains.

Both models matched expert board calls closely, scoring about nine tenths of the ideal on average, with no clear gap between them. Perfect matches landed in about half the cases for each model. Diagnostic suggestions, what workup to order next, scored lowest for both, likely because board notes hide the context behind such calls. Reviewer agreement was near perfect. Language models could assist tumor boards, the authors conclude, but expert oversight stays essential.
pmc-13435632:
Machado and colleagues present a 2026 analysis of Brazilian health policy from 2016 to 2022, spanning the Temer and Bolsonaro governments and the COVID-19 pandemic. The study reads federal policy through historical institutionalism, treating the period as a critical juncture, a moment when choices lock in lasting change. Documents, news, and academic literature feed the analysis of Brazil's universal health system, the SUS.

The authors find immediate, severe effects: squeezed sector funding, setbacks in specific programs, weakened institutions, and organized resistance defending the system. The pandemic response unfolded inside that prior weakening, which shaped its failures and its pockets of resilience. Framing six years as one juncture matters for what comes next: systems do not simply bounce back after such periods, because budgets, staff, and norms were all rewritten while the emergency ran.
pmc-13436732:
Feiyang Liu and coauthors update a pooled review of water exercise for stroke balance in 2026. Twenty nine trials with 1,075 stroke patients now feed the math, up from a thinner base rated very low before. Five databases were searched to July 2025 under standard review rules.

Water exercise lifted the main balance scale with a moderate effect size. A reach test also favored water work with a large effect. Walking gains are part of the update scope as well. Bias checks, funnel plots, and evidence grading temper the claims. Pool therapy looks like a real option where pools and staff exist.
pmc-13439532:
Qiaoxing Liang and colleagues pick single bacterial cells out of teeming gut communities and grow only the chosen ones, reporting a precision culturing method in 2026. Standard growing methods favour abundant microbes and take weeks, so rare species get missed. Their system reads each cell's shape and light-scattering fingerprint without labels. Machine learning names the species from those cues, and a laser transfer step lifts chosen cells into culture one by one.

Applied to faecal and vaginal material, the method cultured wanted species while excluding others, long before colonies would appear. Light fingerprints also measured some cell contents directly. Genomes from single-cell cultures showed that short antibiotic courses boosted both old resistance and fresh mutations in gut residents, with like changes across species. The authors offer the tool for close study of microbe variation cell by cell.
pmc-13442932:
Omer Abdullah and Peter LeWitt revisit carbon monoxide as a hidden cause of Parkinson-like illness in a 2026 paper. The gas can scar the brain widely, yet in some people it picks out twin deep zones called the globi pallidi. A 1972 case anchors the tale: a 48-year-old man with repeat gas hits and blackouts later grew stiff, slow movement that answered levodopa.

Twin-zone change on scans now serves as a strong clue for gas-tied cases. Long low-level contact in daily life may also raise risk, the authors note. Oddly, fresh work hints that tiny gas doses might shield the brain from the true disease. That hint needs careful, safe tests before any use. The paper urges doctors to ask about gas contact when stiff movement shows odd scan marks.
pmc-13443632:
Jing Fu and colleagues introduce a 2026 mathematical model of blood flow through the branching vascular tree, a problem complicated by varied vessel shapes, branching, and winding paths. Their multi-fractal model blends varied fractal dimensions with scaling laws, yielding formulas for flow in single vessels, vessel trees, and bundles of trees, plus a permeability expression for the whole system.

Four case studies checked the model against experiments with maximum relative error under 5 percent. Sensitivity tests confirmed intuition: wider vessels and larger diameter ratios raised flow, while longer vessels lowered it, mapping how resistance tracks diameter and length. Clinicians and modelers gain a computational tool for studying vascular disease, with patient-specific validation still ahead.
pmc-13443932:
Liulei Wu and coauthors report a 2026 cross-sectional study seeking ultrasound markers that flag respiratory sarcopenia early in healthy adults. The team measured handgrip strength, breathing pressures, and both diaphragms by ultrasound in 149 adults, tracking thickness, thickening ratio, excursion, and dynamic indices.

Two left-right measures together best foretold inspiratory strength, while one right-sided thickening measure alone best foretold expiratory strength and one thickness measure alone best foretold grip strength. Bilateral differences proved clear throughout, warning against one-sided shortcuts. The panel offers clinics a practical, objective screen, though patient cohorts must confirm the cutoffs.
pmc-13445532:
Fatima Ali and colleagues model what could follow if two copy versions of biologic drugs for psoriasis join the World Health Organization list of essential medicines, in a 2026 economics study. Psoriasis affects at least sixty million people, yet costly biologics stay out of reach in poorer lands. The model covers adults whose disease resists standard systemic drugs.

The target group holds close to nine million adults worldwide. Over five years, wide access in the model yields a health gain the authors put in the millions of quality-adjusted life years, at a cost in the hundreds of billions of dollars. They flag the figures as upper bounds, since the model grants full access and steady benefit to all. Even so, the scale frames the access debate.
pmc-13445632:
Meng and colleagues test whether flexible body plans fuel species richness in daddy long-legs spiders. Their 2026 paper examines the family Pholcidae, roughly 2,000 described species, combining large-scale genomic and taxonomic sampling with comparative methods. The team measured evolutionary flexibility, the variance in traits such as body size and leg proportions, alongside speciation rates, trait change rates, and habitat shift rates.

Lineages with greater trait flexibility speciated faster, evolved their traits faster, and held more species. In species-rich lineages, leg length scaled almost isometrically with body size, suggesting stabilising selection holding proportions steady. Species-poor lineages showed positive allometry instead, a sign of directional selection. Trait change and microhabitat shifts also rose together. The authors argue environmental variety promotes flexibility, while extremes such as dwarfism or gigantism can trap a lineage in a dead end.
pmc-13445932:
Shihua Zhang and coauthors review a 2026 roundup of exosome-carried long non-coding RNAs in bone reshaping, a talk channel with healing promise. The review pulls together evidence on how these RNAs steer bone builders, bone eaters, stem cells, and gristle cells through signal networks in defects, breaks, thin bones, and worn joints.

RNAs that guide bone-forming stem cell maturing, bone-eating work, vessel coupling, and spread show promise as barely cutting markers for spotting, risk sorting, and treatment watch. They offer natural, buildable carriers for bone-aimed, low-poison-risk therapy. The field still needs carrying and safety checks before medical use.
pmc-13446332:
Benjamin Stodt and colleagues test whether virtual reality can stand in for a real room when studying how listeners pick out one voice among rivals, in a 2026 brain study. Volunteers did the same task in a real lab and in a virtual one, with sound alone or sound plus sight, while scalp electrodes logged brain waves. Voices came from spots set side to side, in depth, or both.

Answers ran slower and less true in the virtual room, with sound alone, and in depth-only trials, which points to slower build-up of proof in the mind. Early brain replies stayed steady across settings, while later waves bent with room, cues, and layout in matching ways in both worlds. The authors back virtual rooms as a true test bed.
pmc-13446632:
De Geus and six co-authors test a decision aid for parents of infants with reflux symptoms, in work from twenty twenty-six. Regurgitation and heavy crying are common in infants and usually need no medicine. Parents often feel uncertain and seek treatment anyway.

Acid suppressive drugs are frequently requested but rarely needed. The study evaluated whether a decision aid reduced caregiver preference for such medication in referred infants. Decision certainty was also measured. Supporting parents to choose watchful waiting safely can cut unnecessary prescribing, sparing infants drug exposure and families cost, without missing the few true cases.
pmc-13447232:
Michał Witkowski and co-authors review gut microbe disruption in kidney disease tied to metabolic problems in 2026. Obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure increasingly damage kidneys worldwide. Gut microbes and the chemicals they make may feed that damage through inflammation and a leaky gut barrier, forming a gut and kidney axis.

Helpful products such as short-chain fatty acids are weighed against harmful ones made from protein and fat breakdown, which can build up as kidneys fail. Proposed harms include insulin resistance, vessel lining damage, fat toxicity and scarring signals in kidney tissue. Diets, probiotics, some diabetes drugs and stool transfer are discussed as possible levers. The review is candid that animal work dominates, measuring microbe chemicals is hard, and cause in humans remains unsettled.
pmc-13448032:
Lener and colleagues tested in 2026 whether a 20-point score called MSI-20, built to forecast death in spinal infection, holds up in a large outside cohort. Spinal infection is uncommon but deadly, and treatment choices in frail patients are hard. A simple score could guide talks with patients and planning of surgery, if it travels well between hospitals.

The team scored 1,122 adults treated at six major centers over more than a decade. About one in six patients died. The score sorted risk fairly, and deaths rose steadily with the score, reaching near half among patients with the highest marks. Performance was similar across all six centers, and no extra admission measure beat the score's own parts. The authors present MSI-20 as a dependable aid for counseling and team discussion, not a stand-alone verdict.
pmc-13448232:
Hyunjin Kim and colleagues profile blood immunity in a chronic nerve disease where immune attack strips insulation from peripheral nerves in 2026 work. Responses to current immune therapies in this condition, called CIDP, are often incomplete, and its immune basis contrasts with multiple sclerosis despite surface similarities. Single-cell gene reading plus protein and cell-sorting checks offered a layered view.

Blood from twenty patients and twenty matched healthy controls was analysed, with multiple sclerosis data as a cross-disease reference. CIDP blood showed stronger type I interferon and inflammasome programmes than sclerosis blood. B cells were fewer yet transcriptionally primed for germinal centre activity, a training ground for antibody production. Killer T cells carried stronger cytotoxic and scaffolding programmes. A coordinated axis joining B cell dysregulation to killer T cell activation is proposed.
pmc-13449232:
Cang-Dian Huang and colleagues examine in 2026 when tube feeding should start after surgery for a perforated stomach ulcer in elderly patients. Their retrospective study covered 142 patients who had surgical repair between May 2017 and May 2025. A clustering method first split patients into favorable and adverse outcome groups, and machine learning then traced how risk moved with each day feeding was delayed.

The adverse group, 38 patients, suffered far more abdominal infections and leaks, and stayed in hospital a median 22.5 days against 9.5. Each single day of delay in starting enteral nutrition raised adverse outcome risk by about 3.55 percent. Risk shifted to a higher level around postoperative day six, which also proved the best decision cutoff in the team's tree model. The authors argue feeding plans should treat the first week as a window that closes quickly.
pmc-13449732:
Zihan Yan, Xiaorong Hou, and Fuquan Zhang trace in 2026 how focused radiation is moving from the margins of liver cancer care toward partnership with immunotherapy. Hepatocellular carcinoma is the third deadliest cancer worldwide, and radiation long played a minor role for lack of top-tier evidence. The turning point they describe is the NRG/RTOG 1112 trial, the first phase three test of stereotactic body radiotherapy added to sorafenib in locally advanced disease.

Adding the radiation stretched progression-free survival from 5.5 months to 9.2 months, a hazard ratio of 0.55, and overall survival improved after adjustment, at 0.72, with severe side effects no worse than drug alone. The reviewers are candid about limits: the trial closed early at reduced power, and its drug-only arm no longer matches today's immunotherapy-based standard. Still, they argue that precise radiation, unmasking tumors to the immune system, makes combinations with checkpoint inhibitors the field's compelling frontier.
pmc-13450232:
Guihua Fang and co-authors show in 2026 that a fatty acid can ferry a vessel-blocking drug from the eye's surface to its back wall. Injections are the price of reaching that wall. New vessel growth at the fundus drives blindness in wet macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy. The drug axitinib fights that growth but barely dissolves in water, and eye drops wash away before crossing the cornea and sclera. The team loaded it into nanoparticles spiked with oleic acid.

At two percent oleic acid, the particles raised the drug's solubility 2,125-fold. Rat studies showed tear retention was not sacrificed. Tissue tests found the acid boosting corneal passage and scleral holding in proportion to its dose. In animals the formulation reached the posterior segment better and carried more drug there. In a laser-induced vessel-growth model it suppressed new vessels more than particles without the acid, with good tolerance.
pmc-13452232:
Deyi Yang and co-authors brew in 2026 a sweet rice wine with green tea powder folded into the ferment. Classic sweet rice wine runs high in sugar and alcohol, which puts off health-minded drinkers. The team tracked scent compounds, microbe work, and enzyme swings as the tea wine brewed, set against the classic.

Scent scans found 135 volatile compounds, with 37 key ones; two gave clove and honey notes from amino acid paths. The tea wine showed stronger antioxidant power in dishes and curbed pressure, sugar, and fat rises in bench tests. It also landed lower in alcohol and sugar. The authors pitch tea powder as a flavor and function lift for rice wine.
pmc-13452832:
Andrea N. Riner and others audited tumor board documentation at a US cancer center in 2026, finding wide gaps in frequency and quality. Multidisciplinary tumor boards generate consensus recommendations for cancer care, yet no documentation standards exist, and missing notes could affect outcomes. The team reviewed patients discussed at six tumor boards from January to June 2024.

Among 991 patients, with median age sixty-three, documentation was present in only 51.7 percent of records, ranging from 5.5 percent for breast to 97.0 percent for colorectal boards. Among documented notes, 44.7 percent were unstructured with variable content, though nearly all recorded consensus recommendations. Documentation patterns varied by disease site and patient traits. Cancer centers gain a baseline for standardizing tumor board notes.
pmc-13453032:
Paulo Vitor França Lemos, Julian Marcel Kunert, Marie-Luise Trutschel, and Karsten Mäder test small starch rods that could be implanted after surgery to release a steroid drug where it is needed. The drug, dexamethasone, calms swelling and pain at the site instead of flooding the whole body. Their 2026 study pressed the rods at two widths, 600 and 1000 micrometres, from approved pharmacy ingredients.

The rods drank water fast in the first hour and swelled about 30 percent without falling apart. Rods carrying cyclodextrin, a sugar ring that helps drugs dissolve, began to wear away within a day. Width ruled the release pace: the thin rods freed about 80 percent of the plain drug within ten days. The team presents starch as a cleaner base than common plastics, since it breaks down without acid byproducts.
pmc-13453732:
Dong-Xia Liao and five co-authors hunt for the factors that turn radiation skin damage severe in patients treated for a cancer behind the nose. Their 2026 study reviews 287 patients treated between August 2020 and August 2025, grading skin damage on a standard scale. Severe damage, grade three or worse, hit 86 patients, or 30.0 percent of the group.

Mild damage began at a mean of 24.8 days, while severe damage began at 37.6 days. Older age, smoking history, higher dose, and a larger treated area each raised the odds of severe damage. Two blood signs of body wide swelling also raised the odds, while higher albumin, a nutrition marker, lowered them. The authors suggest that flagging these traits early could guide skin care and dose planning for the patients most at risk.
pmc-13454232:
Zhengwei Heng and five co-authors ask how desert patchiness shapes the chemistry of short lived spring plants and the microbes at their roots. Their 2026 study covers four ephemeral species from two plant families across sandy, salty, and gravel deserts. Whole plant chemistry, from leaf and root together, is set against the root zone microbe community in each habitat.

Chemistry looked broadly alike across species, yet its variety split by family and by habitat in species specific ways. Microbe communities stayed alike at the broad phylum level, as if the harsh setting filters who can live there, while their networks varied with host and habitat together. Network complexity came loose from stability under stress. Modeling showed soil factors reach plant chemistry mainly through microbe variety and network traits, at least for within site diversity.
pmc-13454432:
Michael F. Royer and seven colleagues report, in 2026, what clients of a medically tailored grocery program actually want in their food boxes. Such programs send healthy groceries to people with diet-linked illness, under the wider Food is Medicine idea. The team asked 13 clients to rate items and share thoughts through a phone app as they received food.

Vegetables, fruits, and protein foods earned the warmest ratings. Clients praised fresh produce and protein picks in their notes. Complaints focused on packaged produce and items they had not asked for. The authors argue that programs should let clients help design the boxes, since unwanted food goes uneaten. Matching boxes to taste, they say, should raise how much of the food clients actually consume and benefit from.
pmc-13454632:
Elham Tohfegar and Alireza Habibi tuned magnet whole-cell epoxidation in 2026, to make epoxy fatty acids from soap-stock waste. Soap stock past degumming holds unsaturated free fatty acids that can be epoxidised, but mixing oil and water reactants is hard. The team used iron-oxide-loaded Candida catenulata whole cells as a living catalyst in snake and spiral microfluidic tubes under a magnet field.

Magnet cell motion stirred the unlike reactants well and gave high yields in short hold times. Cell stir rate under the magnet field swayed epoxidation a lot. Tune-up over flow rate, cell load, and magnet rate found best settings at zero point two two nine millilitres per minute, one hundred weight-per-volume, and two point five hertz. Yield hit forty-seven point six seven percent after one point five three minutes. Chem teams gain a fast magnet tube route to bio epoxides.
pmc-13454832:
Mahendro Prasetyo Kusumo and three colleagues test, in a 2026 community study, a fingertip light sensor that screens blood sugar without a needle. The device, GlucoNeo Check, reads blood flow patterns through the skin. The team checked its accuracy in 660 participants, building 3,300 paired readings against standard measures, and interviewed 31 users about the experience.

Readings landed within a few percent of reference values on average, with a mean error near 3.6 percent. A standard safety grid placed nearly all readings in the harmless zones, none in the dangerous ones. Sorting accuracy reached about 89 percent. Users praised the device's comfort, ease, and clear display across four themes. The authors judge it fit for community diabetes screening, while calling for stronger clinical validation before it guides treatment choices.
pmc-13455632:
Jiahuan Zhou and seven colleagues demonstrate, in a 2026 study, a gentler way to revive worn lithium cobalt oxide, the cathode inside many phones and laptops. Direct recycling stalls on surface damage: tangled defects and a stiff, unfriendly skin block lithium movement. Most fixes only top up lost ingredients. This team instead retuned the surface's electronic state with a tailored lithium aluminum compound.

A ligand in the compound coupled to high-valence cobalt sites and loosened the cobalt-oxygen grip at the surface. Loosened defect bonds let inactive cobalt wash away and healed oxygen gaps, while lithium and aluminum rebuilt the layered frame. The revived material stored charge near commercial levels and kept about 87 percent of its capacity after 200 cycles. The authors present electronic softening as a general route for closed-loop cathode recycling.
pmc-13457332:
Luigi Del Debbio's 2026 lecture notes tackle inverse problems, the task of recovering a whole function from a limited set of measurements, in particle physics. Two examples anchor the lectures. Physicists must extract parton distribution functions, which describe how momentum is shared inside the proton, from scattering data or from lattice QCD calculations. They must also pull spectral functions out of lattice correlation data. Both jobs are ill-posed: finite data cannot pin down an infinite-dimensional answer without added assumptions.

Del Debbio frames the work probabilistically: every assumption sits openly in a prior, and results emerge as posterior probabilities with honest error bars. Three strategies get detailed treatment: the Backus-Gilbert method, Gaussian processes, and neural-network fits. Readers see how bigger datasets, more precise data, and different priors each move the answer. The lectures suit graduate students needing rigorous uncertainty estimates in precision phenomenology.
pmc-13457832:
Huijuan Jiang and colleagues examined a gene called EGFL6 in esophageal carcinoma, a cancer of the food pipe, to see whether it tracks with patient outcomes. Their 2026 study mined public cancer databases, including The Cancer Genome Atlas, hunting for basement-membrane genes switched on abnormally in these tumors. EGFL6, already known as a cancer-promoting gene in other tumor types, emerged as strongly overexpressed in esophageal tumors.

Higher EGFL6 levels were tied to shorter disease-specific survival and shorter time before the cancer progressed again in patient records. The analysis connected the gene with immune cell patterns inside tumors and with methylation changes on its DNA. Lab work completed the picture: esophageal cancer cells with active EGFL6 proliferated and invaded more aggressively and moved through the cell cycle faster. That supports the gene as a prognostic marker and possible drug target.
pmc-13458532:
Saeideh Abdolahpour and colleagues map fuel-use types in preterm versus term newborns in a 2026 study. Preterm infants show fuel systems not yet ready, yet variety inside the preterm group remains little studied. Targeted fuel scans on dried blood spots from 448 preterm infants at 32 to 36 weeks and 351 term infants at 37 to 40 weeks used tandem mass scans. They compared amino acids, fat carriers and pathways.

Preterm infants showed higher tyrosine, leucine and isoleucine, arginine and a long fat carrier, with lower glutamate. A multi-factor look found three clusters tied to birth age and redox signals. Pathway work flagged urea cycle, ammonia reuse, purine fuel use and cell-power fat burning, with C18:1-OH as a key marker of cell-power unreadiness. The authors present fuel-use scans as a step toward exact newborn risk sorting, pending long-term checks.
pmc-13458932:
Deng and colleagues review whether cholesterol-lowering PCSK9 inhibitor drugs also calm inflammation in this 2026 article. PCSK9 is a protein that raises blood cholesterol, and blocking it is now standard for high-risk patients. The review gathers evidence on the protein's inflammatory roles. These run through pathways including the NLRP3 inflammasome and the Toll-like receptor 4 signaling axis. It also covers what the inhibitors achieve beyond cholesterol.

Clinical studies show the inhibitors barely move standard blood markers of inflammation such as C-reactive protein, the authors find. Their benefits instead appear in steadier atherosclerotic plaques and altered immune gene activity, suggesting the anti-inflammatory action does not show up in conventional tests. The authors recommend sharper risk tools combining multiple biomarkers and molecular profiling to target treatment at the right patients.
pmc-13459232:
Najaf Ahmadi Aghziarat and co-authors charted twelve years of injury deaths in West Azerbaijan province, Iran, and calculated the years of life those deaths stole. Their 2026 registry study drew on the national death registration system for 2013 through 2024, computing death rates and years of life lost, then forecasting monthly deaths with a time-series model. Injuries are a leading cause of preventable early death, and provincial patterns can differ sharply from national ones.

The registry recorded 20,003 injury deaths over the period, 76 percent of them men and most in urban areas. Annual deaths rose 37.94 percent, from 1,389 in 2013, reaching 1,916 by 2024, with traffic crashes the top cause throughout. Suicide deaths surged 141.50 percent across the period, the fastest-growing category found. Total years of life lost reached 473,700, concentrated in the fifteen-to-twenty-nine age group, and forecasts see monthly deaths fluctuating between 120 and 182.
pmc-13459632:
Yobelis Quintero and six co-authors present a 2026 study that rechecked stored respiratory samples from Panama's 2016 flu surveillance program. Many samples that year had no cause found by the standard test panel. The team searched a set of these samples for common coronaviruses and for enterovirus D68, a virus that can cause severe breathing illness.

They tested 127 swab samples with a sensitive gene-based method. Enterovirus D68 turned up in seventeen samples, while each of two coronaviruses appeared in three. Some samples carried two viruses at once. Most positive patients were in hospital, and over half were children under five. The work confirms these viruses circulated in Panama in 2016 and argues they belong in routine testing panels.
pmc-13460232:
Yafei Xie and colleagues traced in 2026 three decades of change in Asia's burden of tracheal, bronchus, and lung cancer using Global Burden of Disease estimates. Asia carries nearly sixty percent of the world total for these cancers. Data from 1990 to 2021 covered new cases, prevalence, deaths, and lost healthy years, analyzed with trend, decomposition, and forecasting models.

Total cases roughly doubled and deaths nearly tripled across the period, with age-standardized incidence climbing by about a fifth. Men carried more burden than women on every measure, though female rates rose significantly while male rates eased. East Asia, China, Japan, and India led the region. Population growth drove most of the rise, followed by aging, and the peak burden age shifted five years later.
pmc-13460832:
Theodora Wingert and co-authors measured in 2026 how often children's hearts falter during cardiac MRI scans performed under anesthesia. Children with congenital heart disease are fragile even without surgical stimulation, yet event rates in the scanner were undefined. Their single-center review covered 330 anesthetized scans from 2013 to 2025, counting an event as sustained low blood pressure for age, use of pressure-raising drugs, or a severe cardiac incident.

Events occurred in nearly thirty percent of cases, driven mainly by low blood pressure, with about ten percent needing vasopressor drugs and no severe events at all. Risk rose with age and was several-fold higher for children scanned from neonatal or pediatric intensive care units. Thirty-day mortality was under two percent. The authors press for sharper risk sorting before these scans.
pmc-13461332:
Sergey Budaev and colleagues argue that stress is best understood as a failure of prediction, viewed through computational complexity. Living things act as forecasting systems, bracing for near-future demands; stress begins when challenges outrun what they can anticipate.

When prediction and control fail, the authors propose, the body discounts its failing feedback controllers rather than fighting on with them. Uncertainty, unpredictability, and uncontrollability are the conditions that most often push systems past their limits. That retreat should shrink the control program and simplify behaviour, giving a measurable fingerprint of mounting stress. Simpler behaviour in animals under strain matches this picture, the review of prior work suggests. Budaev lists software tools for measuring such complexity, offering stress researchers a new yardstick to test.
pmc-13461932:
Vincenzo Aiello leads a 2026 review of food compounds that may help prevent or soften insulin resistance, a state where the body answers the hormone insulin poorly. Blood sugar stays high, and the body makes extra insulin to compensate. The state sits behind obesity, abnormal blood fats, and type 2 diabetes, and is very common worldwide. Patterns rich in whole grains, fruit, vegetables, beans, and unsaturated fats are tied to better sugar control.

The review weighs active compounds in foods, including polyphenols and flavonoids from plants, dietary fiber, and omega-3 fats from fish. These compounds may act through several routes: easing oxygen-based cell stress, calming long-term inflammation, shifting gut microbes, and tuning cell signals that handle sugar and fat. The authors frame food strategies as tools for prevention and care. They argue the public health payoff could be large, given how widely insulin resistance spreads.
pmc-13462432:
Zelia K Chiu leads a 2026 study of endophthalmitis, a severe infection inside the eye, covering twenty-five years at Victoria's main eye hospital. The study gathered every case in the state, since the hospital is the referral center. 1,423 eyes from 1,408 patients were included. The average age was 71, and most arrived with vision at hand movement only.

Cataract surgery caused the largest yearly share of cases until 2009, after which eye injections overtook it. Infection rates after cataract surgery fell sharply, dropping after preventive antibiotic use began. Rates after injections stayed low and flat. About two thirds of cases grew a germ in the lab, most often gram-positive bacteria. Final vision split two ways: many eyes ended with very poor sight, while a third recovered to near-driving standard or better. Infections starting in the cornea fared worst, while cases after cataract surgery or injections fared better.
pmc-13463432:
Almulla and colleagues wrote an editorial in 2026 opening a research collection on the biology of chronic fatigue, including myalgic encephalomyelitis, also called chronic fatigue syndrome. The condition still has no proven diagnostic marker and no cure, and post-COVID fatigue has widened the gap between need and understanding. The collection spans ion channels, muscle function, brain structure, breathing control, long-term outcomes, and possible treatments.

Almulla highlights one firm cellular finding: two separate labs, using patch-clamp recording in natural killer immune cells, both found reduced activity of a channel called TRPM3 in patients. That channel helps manage calcium signals, so the result links ion transport with immune cell behaviour. The editors stress the channel test is a research tool, not yet a clinic test, and its accuracy against other fatigue causes is unproven. The collection's value, they say, is replacing broad description with measurable signals.
pmc-13463632:
Madleen Orumaa and four co-authors track two diseases tied to human papillomavirus types 6 and 11 in Norway. Genital warts and a throat growth disease both trace to these virus types, and a vaccine can prevent them. The team read national registry data from 2010 through 2023.

Wart rates in women aged fifteen to twenty-nine fell from 1120.0 to 280.6 cases per hundred thousand people across the period. The throat disease fell in step, from 3.7 to 0.6 per hundred thousand. Both drops ran near ten percent a year after the four-type vaccine arrived in 2009. The parallel fall gives strong population-level proof that vaccination cut spread of these virus types.
pmc-13464032:
Sicong Tu and four co-authors ask whether a brain excitability test can sort ALS patients by their brain chemistry. ALS, or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, slowly kills motor neurons, and excess glutamate may drive the harm. The team paired magnetic brain stimulation with spectroscopy scans that read chemical levels in the motor cortex.

Patients split by the stimulation test showed sharply different chemistry. The excitable group held lower levels of NAA, a marker of healthy neurons, and higher glutamate-linked ratios on both brain sides. The calmer group kept near-normal chemistry at first testing. Two pilot patients followed for years showed steady chemistry in limb-led disease and drifting chemistry in classic disease, which backs the sorting idea.
pmc-13464332:
Yuwu Chen and colleagues traced in 2026 how cigarette tar turns artery lining into a target for killer-like T cells, worsening atherosclerosis. Smoking is the top driver of artery plaque growth, yet its immune mechanics were murky. Mice lacking a cholesterol-clearing gene inhaled tar, while artery lining cells faced tar in dishes, and single-cell gene reading mapped the immune shift.

Tar raised a granzyme-armed CD4 T cell subset that damages lining cells, while lining cell share fell. Tar pushed lining cells to display MHC class II flags through a CIITA-PRMT5 methylation switch, inviting T cell attack, and blocking either partner eased plaque. The chain names two druggable links between smoke and artery injury, beyond quitting alone.
pmc-13464432:
Lenzinger and many colleagues examine how cells release tiny parcels called small extracellular vesicles in this 2026 study. Cells use these membrane bubbles to send molecular messages, but how they are secreted was only partly understood. The team had previously found an unusual route. They nicknamed it the torn bag mechanism. In it, a larger sac is released and then spills the small vesicles outside the cell.

Checking more mouse organs, they confirmed the sac-based route operates everywhere they looked in calm, steady conditions. Under stress, however, such as membrane stress from a calcium-raising chemical or starvation, cells switched on the classic route: fusing internal compartments with the surface to release vesicles directly. Silencing specific genes separated the two routes, showing the steady route needs an autophagy gene while the stress route needs a different trafficking protein.
pmc-13465332:
Khushboo Yadav and six co-authors review Madhuca longifolia, the mahua tree, as a food weapon against the triple burden of malnutrition. Underfeeding, overfeeding, and hidden nutrient gaps now coexist in many regions. Their 2026 framework segments each scan into air, signal, and noise zones by itself, then computes three whole-image quality metrics that no operator can bias by region choice.

Across skin scan datasets, the new metrics characterized quality more consistently than the conventional region-based scores under the conditions tested. The scores also tracked both the physical settings used to acquire scans and human viewers' own quality judgments. Because the pipeline is fully automatic, competing enhancement algorithms can finally face the same yardstick. Babaee presents the metrics as a reproducibility fix for a fragmented field.
pmc-13490532:
Gui and team predicted how easily fluids flow through underground rock from seismic data, using a Gaussian process model fed with on its own built traits. The Gaussian process also reports its own doubt for each forecast, a rarity among machine-learning regressors. pmc-13491632:
Chengqing Yang and five colleagues report in 2026 an unusual case of lung tuberculosis that looked like cancer spread on scans. A fifty-nine-year-old man recovering from esophageal cancer surgery and radiotherapy developed four months of cough and two weeks of fever. CT imaging showed many round cystic cavities scattered through both lungs, a pattern rarely linked to tuberculosis.

Doctors started anti-tuberculosis treatment, and the cavities collapsed into solid nodules, which raised fresh suspicion of metastases from his earlier cancer. A biopsy instead showed granulomatous inflammation, the tissue pattern typical of tuberculosis. Eight months into treatment the lesions had nearly vanished. The authors present the case as the first systematic record of cystic tuberculosis lesions turning into nodules during therapy.
pmc-13491732:
Anne-Line Strange Laursen leads a twenty-author team testing in 2026 why alpha-synuclein protein piles up inside support cells called oligodendroglia in multiple system atrophy, a rare and fatal brain disease. Clumps in those cells define the illness, yet why the protein gathers there was unknown. The team bred mice that produce extra human alpha-synuclein only in oligodendroglia.

The engineered mice carried the protein in the right cells without forming clumps on their own. When researchers injected pre-made protein fibrils into the brain, clumps inside oligodendroglia grew more over six to nine months than in normal mice. Seeds grown from patients with the disease also spread more widely in the engineered mice. Extra protein inside the cells, the authors conclude, lowers the barrier to clump formation.
pmc-13491932:
Takahiro Kato and five colleagues check in 2026 whether the drug interaction warnings printed in Japanese package inserts are a safe first screen for intensive care patients on injectable medicines. No gold standard exists for spotting harmful drug pairs. The team tested insert-based screening against the Lexi-Interact database across 345 intensive care admissions, at three points in each stay.
