Sensitivity and specificity were also solid, although the inserts overcalled many pairs the database rated minor, which dragged down positive predictive value. Agreement on severity grades was only moderate. Most interactions found by the database alone were mid-level warnings, so the authors endorse inserts for screening with database backup for interpretation.
pmc-13492332:
Vögeli and co-authors describe a 2026 case in which doctors used focal pulsed field ablation near the opening of the coronary sinus. The technique kills small patches of heart tissue with electrical pulses. The spot is awkward because a lead from the patient's existing resynchronization device sat very close by. That device helps the heart's lower chambers beat together. Ablating there risked damaging the lead or disturbing the device, so the team checked the system carefully before and after the procedure.

The ablation ended the patient's atrial tachycardia, the fast abnormal rhythm being treated, and the nearby lead kept working normally throughout. The authors note that different ablation systems interact with implanted devices in different ways, so one safe case cannot guarantee safety for other equipment. They recommend device checks before and after every such procedure to catch delayed problems.
pmc-13492432:
Yuta Taomoto and four colleagues contrast in 2026 two patients whose new atrial leadless pacemakers briefly failed to capture the heart at slow rates. Leadless devices avoid wires and pockets, and screw-in atrial models have widened their use for faulty sinus nodes. Shortly after implantation both patients showed a rate-dependent rise in the energy needed to trigger a beat, a quirk known from older wired systems.

One patient's thresholds settled on their own while the device stayed put, rewarding watchful waiting. The other's elevation persisted, and imaging revealed a subtle shift in device position as the likely culprit. The authors draw a practical line: when the device is stable, patience is reasonable, while continuing capture failure should trigger imaging to check for drift before assuming the problem will pass.
pmc-13492832:
Chongder and colleagues report a 2026 controlled study of a school mental health program for young adolescents in Bhubaneswar, India. Puberty brings hormonal and social pressures that can disturb behavior. Ninety-two students aged nine to fifteen took part; the program group received five structured sessions on mental health and coping, while the control group received none. A thirty-item behavior scale measured change.

Before the program, over four in five students in both groups showed maladaptive behavior. Afterward, adaptive behavior reached about three quarters in the program group, while the control group barely moved. The between-group gap was statistically strong. Behavior also linked to age, gender, pubertal stage, schooling level, and family type. Five sessions is a light dose for such a shift, which argues for building structured mental health teaching into normal school curricula.
pmc-13494032:
Stefano Giampiccolo and others propose a more honest way to measure doubt when neural change-rate models face new states. In 2026, the study shows that standard groups of neural and universal change-rate models grow too sure outside training data, because models started apart tend to act alike. Reliable doubt matters for changing systems in biology and beyond.

The new group method on purpose varies rebuilt arrow fields in chosen state-space regions while keeping fit on training data. Tests on Lotka-Volterra, damped swing system, and Lorenz benchmarks, plus a cell death model with partial sight and noise, show better trust over standard groups. Builders gain a method that flags where guesses should not be trusted.
pmc-13494232:
Lee and colleagues test whether celery-family vegetables can protect the gut against a Western diet's damage. The apiaceous family includes celery and parsnip, and earlier hints suggested anti-inflammatory powers. In the 2026 experiment, mice ate a total Western diet, modelled on typical American eating. About a fifth or two fifths of it was replaced by fresh apiaceous vegetables, while a chemical called DSS inflamed their colons to mimic colitis.

The vegetables blunted nearly every sign of disease. Weight loss recovered by well over two fifths, colon shortening by more than half, and the overall disease score fell by a similar share. Inflammatory messenger levels in blood dropped by between a third and three quarters, and invading immune cells in the colon lining fell sharply. The authors say the family deserves testing as dietary protection for people eating Western-style diets.
pmc-13494632:
Kevin Whelan calls, in a 2026 article, for better design, conduct, and reporting in human trials of probiotics, the live microbes taken for health gain. Proof from pooled reviews shows probiotics help in set cases, from gut infection in early-born infants to colds and lung infections in the very ill. Yet many trials in those reviews carry high or unclear risk of bias from weak design or poor reporting.

That gap, Whelan argues, holds back clinical advice and daily use, since surveys show health workers vary widely in trust and use. He points readers to new recommendations named PRODARE, published in the same journal issue, which set out how probiotic trials should be planned and written up. The piece frames the puzzle plainly: the field has many trials, yet their uneven quality blurs what clinicians can safely take from them.
pmc-13495232:
Muhammad Saljuqi and colleagues survey, in a 2026 study, injuries among male futsal players in Herat, Afghanistan. Futsal's sharp sprints, turns, and contact raise injury risk, yet proof from poor or post-conflict settings is scarce. The team questioned 229 league players from the top two local divisions about their build, habits, training, and career injury history.

Nine in ten players reported at least one injury from futsal. The ankle led, then the knee, and ankle sprain was the most common single injury. Most injuries struck in matches, blamed chiefly on opponent contact and poor venues. Injury history ran higher in players aged twenty-five to thirty-four, in better-off players, in evening trainers, and where venues were only sometimes fit. The authors, giving the first such picture for Herat, urge prevention work aimed at match play and playing surfaces.
pmc-13495432:
Yue Peng and colleagues read, in a 2026 study, how rice seeds rewire their genes when germinating in the cold. Direct-seeded rice needs seeds that sprout evenly in chilly soil, and a gene-editing step called alternative splicing, which remixes gene messages, was suspected to help. The team sequenced RNA from seeds of a standard rice line after a day of cold during sprouting.

Over twelve thousand genes changed activity, clustering in daily rhythm, hormone signaling, and metabolism. A like number of splicing shifts hit nearly five thousand genes, most often by skipping a segment or keeping an extra one. The spliced genes leaned toward fat and terpene chemistry, fitting cold adjustment. The authors name several candidate regulators, among them kinases, a phosphatase, and three switch factors, and offer the set as breeding material for cold-tough rice.
pmc-13498432:
Majed N Alanizy and colleagues survey in 2026 how phone and social media habits relate to mental well-being among adults in Saudi Arabia. Heavy daily use is common there, and past work has tied excess use to low mood, anxiety, and poor sleep. Far less was known about links with positive well-being, which the team measured with a short World Health Organization index.

Between January and March 2026, a total of 1,248 adults answered an anonymous online survey on habits, lifestyle, and well-being. Average well-being scores fell steadily as daily phone time rose, and poor well-being was far more common among the heaviest users. After adjustment for other factors, using a phone more than six hours a day still more than doubled the odds of poor well-being.
pmc-13499732:
Heidi Monkman and colleagues study in 2026 how long touch deposits, the invisible skin cells left by a fingertip, survive on everyday surfaces, a question that guides forensic sampling. A fluorescent dye that lights up cell material can reveal such deposits, yet spraying it may disturb the very cells investigators need. The team first tuned the spray method across several distances, judging glow strength against how far cells scattered beyond the original mark.

With the tuned method they tracked deposits on glass, plastic, melamine, aluminium, leather, and cotton for up to a year. Cell survival fell over time and varied sharply by surface, with cotton and leather holding cells worst, and repeat spraying helped keep deposits visible. DNA recovered ran well below what cell counts predicted, a caution the authors offer caseworkers choosing where to sample first.
pmc-13500532:
Sara L Cantoreggi and co-authors compare in 2026 laboratory methods for telling whether malaria that returns after treatment is the same infection rekindling or a fresh mosquito-borne infection. The distinction decides whether a drug truly failed. Samples came from a 2018 drug efficacy study in Rwanda. The team tuned a fingerprinting assay for four microsatellite markers, tested its sensitivity on laboratory parasite mixtures, then reanalysed patient samples with classic length markers and with deep sequencing of variation-rich genes.

Two microsatellite markers proved most sensitive at detecting minority parasite clones hiding among others. Classification rules disagreed in a telling pattern, since the World Health Organization algorithm counted the fewest relapses, a two-of-three rule counted the most, and a Bayesian method landed between them. Deep sequencing gave the most consistent answers regardless of rule, making it the authors' favoured route, with chance-based methods advised after wider validation.
pmc-13500732:
晓煌 杨 and others test whether PET/CT energy tests predict lives in recurrent tongue cancer treated without surgery. In 2026, the look-back study covers ninety-three patients treated at a Hunan cancer hospital from 2017 to 2024. It tests pre-treatment glucose uptake, energy tumour volume, and total lesion glycolysis, then tracks progression-free and overall lives over a median thirty-eight months.

Post-recurrence radiotherapy protected progression-free lives in main analysis, while total energy tumour volume and post-recurrence radiotherapy independently predicted overall lives. Treatment response protected overall lives but not progression-free lives in time-dependent analysis. Models showed only modest discrimination, so the authors present energy volume and radiotherapy as useful but limited prognostic markers.
pmc-13500932:
Iwasaki and colleagues wrote a 2026 editorial on the rollout of artificial intelligence in gastrointestinal endoscopy. They argue it risks widening health inequities unless the field asks which tools serve which unmet needs. Commenting on the World Endoscopy Organization's response to the World Health Organization's artificial intelligence initiative, they praise its equity framing but push further.

Iwasaki notes innovation's ten-ninety gap, in which a tenth of research spending targets the diseases causing most suffering. They warn artificial intelligence could amplify it because its gains concentrate where data and infrastructure already exist. In wealthy systems the tools refine existing services. In much of the world the service is absent: a survey across four eastern African countries found six of eighty-seven physicians performing a bile duct procedure. Tools built for rich-world diseases would thus miss twice, the authors argue, on both margin and disease choice.
pmc-13501132:
Abshire and Maquat pinned down when the exon junction complex begins assembling on the splicing machine, in a 2026 study of human cells. The complex is a protein marker stamped onto RNA during splicing. The complex governs RNA export, translation, and quality control, but published accounts disagreed about the order in which its core and alternative parts arrive.

Abshire fished out complex proteins from cell extracts and catalogued their partners by mass spectrometry. They cross-checked the patterns against known three-dimensional structures of the spliceosome at successive stages, backed by protein blotting of nuclear fractions. The core trio and one alternative factor, RNPS1, were already attached to fully assembled but inactive spliceosomes, while the other alternative factor, CASC3, joined later on activated machines. The staged timeline resolves conflicting models and maps which version of the complex is present to shepherd the RNA at each step of its processing.
pmc-13501732:
Noa Klein and Dorit Shweiki report a 2026 analysis of why tumour mutational burden differs between women and men with stomach cancer. That burden predicts response to checkpoint immunotherapy, so its biology matters. Working with the TCGA stomach cancer collection and independent targeted sequencing cohorts, the pair stratified tumours by sex. They layered in gene expression, promoter methylation, and regression modelling centred on MLH1, a DNA mismatch repair gene often silenced by methylation.

Female tumours carried significantly higher autosomal mutation burdens, with the gap widest in older women. Burden rose as MLH1 expression fell and its promoter methylation climbed, and female tumours showed higher MLH1 methylation. Once those MLH1 measures entered the models, the sex association faded, suggesting the epigenetic silencing explains much of the gap. Subtype checks pointed to a larger share of repair-deficient tumours among women. Outside cohorts echoed the direction without reaching significance.
pmc-13501832:
Anastasia Marquette leads a six-author team with a 2026 cross-sectional analysis of cannabis use by gender in Canada and the United States. Data came from the International Cannabis Policy Study's yearly national surveys between 2018 and 2023. The pooled sample held 281,533 respondents aged 16 to 65, including 2,445 transgender respondents and 783 gender-diverse people. Weighted models compared use patterns, effects, and comfort using cannabis in social settings across groups.

Daily use clustered near 14 percent among cisgender men, transgender men, and gender-diverse respondents, and near 12 percent among cisgender and transgender women. Feeling very addicted was reported by about 12 percent of cisgender men, transgender men, and transgender women alike. Yet transgender women and gender-diverse respondents were far less likely to say so than cisgender men. Gender-diverse people reported stronger positive personal effects, and cisgender women were least comfortable using socially.
pmc-13503732:
Sukriye Turkoglu Kayaci and four colleagues test how well chatbots answer exam questions on children's dentistry, in a 2026 study. The questions came from the past ten years of the national dental specialty exam in Türkiye. Scores show how close the tools come to trained dentists on this narrow field.

The team gave 119 questions to 11 recent large language models, some in more than one mode. Gemini 2.5 Pro led with a score just over 92 percent, with GPT-5 close behind. Some models fell below 60 percent. Fast models tended to score low, while slow modes that reason step by step scored higher but took up to 68 seconds per reply. The authors urge care before such tools enter exam prep or testing.
pmc-13503932:
Dongling Wu and others design energy-aware approximate multipliers for internet-of-things edge devices. In 2026, the work puts forward a lively power-saving straight map multiplier that monitors runtime energy and adjusts approximation level, plus an improved variant adding dynamic operand truncation. Static approximate multipliers cannot adapt when harvested energy fluctuates.

Dynamic adaptation added fifteen to twenty-five percent energy cut over static competitors, while preserving acceptable rightness. A solar-powered ESP32-C3 sensor node showed forty-seven percent energy cut with negligible rightness loss. Edge systems gain flexible computation under tight energy budgets.
pmc-13505032:
Audrey Moyo leads a team reviewing how heart health and common mental disorders relate in adults up to age fifty, in a 2026 systematic review. Depression and anxiety are widespread in younger adults, and heart risk habits form early. Each condition may feed the other, but the paired evidence had not been pulled together.

Eleven studies with more than seven hundred thousand people met the rules, most from the United States. Seven studies found better heart health scores went with fewer depression and anxiety symptoms. Four found the reverse path: mental disorders went with poorer heart health. Most studies were snapshots in time, so the authors call the two-way claim a reasoned inference, not a proof. They back joined screening and lifestyle support in primary care.
pmc-13505132:
Jace Li and co-authors analysed eating-disorder discussion on Twitter, focusing on the community known as EDTWT. They gathered 48,341 tweets from 18,587 users posted between January 2022 and February 2025. Their aims were to map posting habits, feelings, and themes, and to build tools that sort such posts automatically.

A small share of users produced nearly half the posts, and activity peaked late on Friday nights. About a quarter of tweets used clinical keywords, covering body image, restricted eating, and recovery. Topic modelling found ten themes, including calorie tracking and Spanish- and Polish-language subgroups. An ensemble classifier sorted posts with strong accuracy, beating a biomedical language model on rare categories. The authors say such tools could support platform moderation and earlier help for users at risk.
pmc-13505432:
Faustine Girardet and co-authors reviewed a decade of nocardiosis cases in southern France, from 2014 to 2024, hunting for factors that predict death within a year. Nocardia bacteria live in soil and water and mainly strike people with weakened immunity, such as transplant recipients, or with chronic lung disease. Infection can stay in the skin, settle in the lungs, or spread through the body.

Advanced disease, meaning spread, chest involvement, cavities in the lung, or brain involvement, also raised that risk. pmc-13506132:

Fifty-three children each received both versions on molars in sessions a week apart, with neither the children nor the scorers knowing which was which. Pain was scored by watching children's reactions and by their own face-scale ratings.

Shiri Varnamkhasti found buffered lidocaine produced lower distress scores about a sixth lower, and a faster onset of numbness than the standard mix. The pain children reported on the faces scale did not differ between versions, and pulse rate rose alike after both shots, showing no blood-flow effect. Cutting distress still makes buffered anesthetic a strategy in children's dentistry.
pmc-13506532:
Ting Li, Li-Juan Wang, Chang Zhang, Yu-Wei Liu, Yan-Ping Qiu, and Guo Liang wrote a 2026 paper on how Chinese schoolchildren spend their days and how that links to mental health. The team sorted children into pattern groups, such as high sitting with short sleep. Patterns with more movement and longer sleep went with better mental health scores. The results support school and family routines that protect activity and sleep together.
pmc-13507132:

Removal tests, where parts of the method are dropped in turn, showed the full pairing beat rival methods and a deep learning baseline. Streaming updates suit on-site smart monitoring chips.
pmc-13507332:
Guoxing Zhang leads a 2026 team that maps metabolism in place inside bone marrow biopsies from patients spanning the plasma cell disorder spectrum, from the harmless precursor MGUS to full multiple myeloma. Ultra-precise imaging mass spectrometry charted metabolite patterns across archived biopsy tissue, paired with marrow fluid chemistry.

Myeloma niches showed raised 3-hydroxykynurenine, a tryptophan breakdown product, plus busier nucleotide and lipid activity tied to growth. Some solitary tumor cases already carried myeloma-like niches invisible in fluid alone. Shared signatures linked tissue and fluid compartments. Spatial chemistry could sharpen risk sorting before symptoms appear.
pmc-13507832:
Ryan Kaya and nine co-authors test a headset-based way to measure balance loss in Parkinson's disease. Falls strike close to half of patients each year, yet clinic balance tests are often too easy and scored by eye. The team filmed patients and healthy adults in three stances of rising difficulty using an augmented reality headset. Custom software read body pose from the video.

The headset measures matched lab-grade motion capture for sway and side-to-side range. Patients swayed more and lost balance sooner than controls. A model built from the headset data predicted who would lose balance. The paper points to a clinic-ready tool for a risk that now goes unmeasured.
pmc-13508132:
Kertesz and colleagues showed that activating a taste receptor found in lung blood vessels protects those vessels from damage by the coronavirus spike protein, in a 2026 laboratory study. Acute lung injury from viral attack on the vessel lining is a major driver of death in COVID-19.

The activator also increased surface levels of ACE2, the virus's entry protein, and binding tests showed it strengthened the pairing between the receptor and ACE2. The authors propose the receptor anchors ACE2 at the surface, preventing the internalization that triggers injury signaling, and nominate receptor activation as a strategy for virus-induced lung damage.
pmc-13508332:

Twenty-nine of thirty-four invited women took part. The score landed high, at 4.67 out of 5, and satisfaction scored highest of all. Follow-up care and environment rated strongly. Openness and the doctor-patient link scored lowest, though still high. Those two areas mark where the service could improve first. The authors offer the tool as a barometer fetal therapy centers could adopt and refine.
pmc-13509532:
Surguchov wrote a 2026 review on a membrane protein linking diabetes and Alzheimer's disease. Type 2 diabetes raises the risk of Alzheimer's, a link long noticed but poorly explained. It also shapes how the amyloid precursor protein gets processed in cells. Restoring it in lab models eased amyloid harm and thinking decline. Surguchov frames it as a hub joining metabolism, vessels, and brain decay. Most backing evidence still comes from preclinical models, he notes.
pmc-13510832:

Drawing on general legal sources, European law, and the regulation itself, the authors sort the word's uses and ask whether it makes a clause binding and enforceable. They also weigh what follows when a duty set by shall goes unmet. The piece is framed as an authorized opinion rather than a research study or formal legal advice. Its goal is practical: keeping drafters, firms, and officials from misreading duty as choice.
pmc-13511232:

Alzheimer's mixes brain decay with immune disorder, and cause is hard to separate from effect. The team compared gene activity in patient cohorts, then checked the findings in two outside groups. A selection algorithm narrowed the field to key genes. A genetics method that mimics a trial tested causality.

One gene, named in the title, was consistently raised in patients and tied to disease risk. Immune mapping and cell tests backed its role in inflammation. A marker with causal evidence beats a mere correlate for drug hunting. The work serves Alzheimer's researchers chasing immune targets.
pmc-13511432:

Exercise therapy had the deepest evidence and reliably improved pain, function, and shoulder movement. Plasma injections helped pain and function in several studies, though recipes varied widely between centers. Shockwave therapy also improved pain and recovery in a number of reports. High-power laser work looked promising in a few studies, while low-level laser evidence stayed unclear. Taping and electrolysis showed possible gains on thin evidence. The authors keep exercise as the cornerstone of care.
pmc-13512732:
Adamov and co-authors compare ancient and modern Y chromosomes to reconstruct Tuvan ancestry in southern Siberia. Their 2026 paper analyses paternal markers in samples from Scytho-Siberian populations of over two thousand years ago and in 633 modern Tuvan men of various clans. None of those three appears in the ancient material. Network analysis supports broad continuity for two branches, Q-YP1102 and R1a-Y39884, both of Siberian origin. Yet the dominant modern branch clusters are young, the main one dating to roughly 670 years ago. The authors conclude recent expansions reshaped a partly continuous paternal inheritance.
pmc-13513132:
Mariola Rychlik-Sych and three colleagues wrote a study in twenty twenty-six on the PON1 gene and the clogging of the heart's arteries. Two common variants in the gene, Q192R and L55M, change how well the enzyme works.

The team looked back at two hundred eighty-two Polish patients who had all had imaging of their heart arteries. They grouped the two variants into haplotypes, the sets passed down together on one chromosome. Two sets, 192R-55L and 192R-55M, went with higher risk of clogging bad enough to call for a stent or bypass surgery. A third set, 192Q-55L, went with a risk fifty-three percent lower. Such gene profiles could one day sharpen how doctors judge heart risk.
pmc-13515132:
Şerife Altun Demircan leads a nine-author team describing ocular syphilis at a Turkish referral centre in a 2026 retrospective review. Syphilis is resurging worldwide, and infection reaching the eye can appear at any stage with varied signs. The team reviewed twenty-one adults treated between 2018 and 2023, covering thirty eyes, and charted symptoms, eye findings, blood and spinal fluid tests, and outcomes.

Most patients were men, with a median age of forty-four, and blurred vision was the leading complaint. Inflammation inside the eye, mostly at the back, and optic nerve inflammation were the most common findings. Five patients had a negative standard blood test despite positive specific tests, and half of those who had a spinal tap showed normal fluid. All received treatment aimed at neurosyphilis, and vision improved or held steady in every eye. The team warns against ruling the disease out on one test alone.
pmc-13515332:
Hugo Frías heads a sixteen-author team tracking gut microbes in wild guinea-pig relatives, Cavia tschudii, during their first three weeks in captivity, in a 2026 study. Moving wild animals into managed care changes diet and surroundings at once, and the gut community might swing in response. Faecal samples collected over twenty-one days, on a standard alfalfa diet, were profiled by gene sequencing to watch diversity and composition.

Little moved. Diversity measures, community structure, and the leading groups held steady across the sampling points. Two bacterial groups, Bacteroidota and Firmicutes, together made up more than eighty-five percent of the community throughout. Minor groups kept low, stable shares, and no parasite infections were found. Frías's team offers the findings as a baseline for conservation and possible domestication work, while noting the study's exploratory scale.
pmc-13515532:
Huckvale and colleagues report a 2026 method that predicts which metabolic pathways a molecule belongs to, expanding the maps researchers use to interpret metabolomics data. The team trained a multitask neural network to predict these links across three databases: KEGG, MetaCyc, and Reactome.

They tested the added predictions on 990 real datasets from a public metabolomics repository. Using both known and predicted links, the median number of enriched pathways detected per dataset rose about eightfold compared with database links alone. Enriched pathways are those with more changed molecules than chance would suggest. The authors say this fuller coverage should help scientists draw clearer biological meaning from metabolomics experiments.
pmc-13515832:
Shengsheng Wei and four colleagues design a graphene-based acceleration sensor for extreme impacts in a 2026 simulation study. The team refined the structure in four steps, from a plain beam to a beam carrying masses and grooves that focus stress.

Adding a central mass multiplied the peak strain more than fifteen-fold over the plain beam. Stress grooves added roughly another thirty percent. Symmetric masses gave a further small gain while cutting cross-axis response, which pollutes readings. The final design kept its natural frequency above two hundred kilohertz and its stress inside safe limits. A readout model then turned strain into voltage, giving a full sensor-level forecast for the design.
pmc-13516432:
Diana Laura Gonzalez-Tolentino leads a ten-author team profiling proteins across the road from cervical precancer to cancer in a 2026 study. Nearly all cervical cancers follow lasting infection with high-risk HPV, above all type 16. The team compared biopsies of HPV16-positive low-grade lesions and full squamous cell cancers against healthy HPV-negative cervix tissue, using high-end mass spectrometry to count thousands of proteins.

Over sixteen hundred proteins shifted in the low-grade lesions, clustering around cell grip and matrix structure. A similar count shifted in cancers, clustering around chemistry and transport work. Proteins raised in early lesions leaned toward metabolism and immune and stress responses. Those raised in cancer leaned toward cell division, DNA damage handling, and protein disposal. Two proteins, S100A10 and thymidine phosphorylase, stood out across stages and matched public gene data.
pmc-13517532:
Guangling Li and six colleagues hunt for a microbe that eats a stubborn weedkiller in a 2026 study. Diflufenican lingers in farm soil for weeks and can scorch later crops. From wheat-field soil long dosed with the herbicide, enrichment culture fished out a bacterium, strain 88-1, that uses the chemical as food. Gene and trait tests named it Enterobacter hormaechei, a species happy with or without oxygen.

Performance hinged on conditions. Warmth near thirty degrees, mildly alkaline water, and a strong starting dose of cells suited it best. Under the best setup the strain cleared about fifty-five percent of the herbicide in five days, with breakdown starting within the first day. The main leftover product was a single named amide compound. Li's team offers strain 88-1 as a candidate for cleaning treated soils, turning a pollution problem into a microbial workforce.
pmc-13518832:
Hyeongwoo Kim and colleagues introduce in 2026 a deep learning system that redesigns drug molecules by swapping one chemical fragment for a similar-acting one, a trick chemists call bioisosteric replacement. Done well, it improves a drug's traits while keeping its grip on the target.

Older computer methods needed experts to pick the swap site or could tune only one trait at a time. Their model, DeepBioisostere, chooses the site and the replacement itself, aiming at several goals at once, such as drug-likeness and ease of synthesis. Trained on real assay data, it proposed swaps that kept biological activity, including some never seen in its training set. The authors show it working through lead-optimization exercises typical of early drug discovery.
pmc-13519032:
Kyuseon Jang and a large team show in 2026 that seasoning the grain boundaries of a thermoelectric material can stop it rotting in damp air. Yttrium telluride, Y2Te3, promises waste-heat conversion, yet water sneaks along the seams between its crystals, oxidizing the inside into breakdown products. Microscope and atom probe work traced that seep path at first hand.

Adding just 1 atomic percent of bismuth changed the story, because bismuth drifts to the seams and alters their chemistry. Math showed why bismuth gathers there and how the local electronic setting then resists attack. Jang's team proposes seam chemistry design as a general shield for next-generation thermoelectrics, with no extra coatings needed.
pmc-13519332:
Adam Andruska and co-authors present a study dated 2026 on spotting a dangerous subtype of pulmonary arterial hypertension. In this subtype, the tiny veins and capillaries of the lung are involved, not just the arteries. Standard drugs can trigger serious complications in these patients, and many die while waiting for a lung transplant.

No registry tracks this rare group, so the team pooled data from published case studies. They tested which clinical traits best separate the subtype from ordinary disease. The strongest traits were combined into a likelihood score. That score was then checked against thirty-seven cases confirmed by tissue examination. An early, accurate flag could change drug choices and speed transplant referral.
pmc-13519432:
Vikas Rangare and colleagues asked whether an early heart-injury blood marker can flag which sepsis patients in intensive care face the worst odds. Published in 2026, the prospective study followed 170 adults admitted with sepsis to an intensive care unit at a district hospital in Chhindwara, India, from late 2024 into early 2026. Troponin I, a protein released when heart muscle is hurt, was measured within a day of admission.

Roughly two thirds of patients showed raised troponin, and those patients died far more often than those with normal levels, while also needing more organ support. Statistical modeling kept troponin as an independent predictor of death even after accounting for other factors. The authors back early troponin testing to sort high-risk patients for closer watch and targeted care. Readers get a cheap, fast triage aid with clear limits, since one center and one marker cannot settle every case.
pmc-13520232:
Morteza Solati Kooshkqazi, Mahnaz Rakhshan, Hojatollah Roosta, and Fatemeh Shirazi test a structured breathing routine in 2026 for patients recovering from coronary bypass surgery. Pain and anxiety after chest surgery slow recovery, and drug-free relief is prized. Seventy-six patients were randomized, with 73 finishing, to standard respiratory care alone or plus the Active Cycle of Breathing Technique.

The breathing group received four 10-minute sessions across two days, cycling calm breathing, chest expansion, and coughing practice. After baseline adjustment, their pain scores ran lower from the second session onward, anxiety was lower after every session, and blood oxygen saturation was higher throughout. The authors urge sham-controlled trials before firm adoption.
pmc-13520332:
Jianguang Li and colleagues report in 2026 a modified carbon material that cleans organic impurities from hydrogen peroxide destined for chip making. Even tiny amounts of leftover carbon compounds can spoil semiconductor devices, so peroxide for electronics must be very pure.

Treating activated carbon with sodium metaborate added surface groups that grab impurities by chemical bonding. The best version removed over 96 percent of organic impurities and left residue low enough to meet the electronic-grade standard. Model fits pointed to surface chemistry as the step that controls speed. Industry readers gain a practical sorbent design tested at two peroxide strengths.
pmc-13521332:
Lara Unger and colleagues evaluate in 2026 heart MRI mapping for amyloid cardiomyopathy, a stiff-heart disease from protein deposits, in older heart failure patients with thickened walls and raised blood markers. All patients also received bone scans and protein screens for comparison.

The group numbered 112 patients with median age 81 years, while amyloid disease was confirmed in 38 patients. Deposit patients showed heavier hearts, weaker pumping and higher mapping values. One mapping measure sorted disease well, while a combined rule using two measures settled diagnosis in half the group and could have avoided contrast dye in one third. Staged use may cut extra testing.
pmc-13522132:
Nasim Binesh and Ahmad Syah review the ethics of AI in hospitality and tourism, a field where the work is thin and scattered. Hotels, airlines, and attractions now use AI to price rooms, sort guests, staff shifts, and shape offers. The review searched three databases and kept 32 studies. Their findings were sorted into nine themes, with gaps and open questions named for each.

The authors read the field through epistemology, the study of how beliefs are formed and justified. AI systems in service act on beliefs: a guest's inferred tastes, a risk score, a ranking. When those beliefs are unjustified, harm follows. From this lens they build two tools. One is a risk ladder that classes AI uses from unacceptable to minimal risk. The other walks the AI life cycle, from problem framing to feedback, and marks the safeguard each stage needs.
pmc-13522332:
Fatemeh Maghool and colleagues examine in 2026 a long non-coding RNA called MAGI2-AS3 across cancers, with focused attention on colorectal cancer where levels consistently fall. Data spanned bulk tumour atlases, healthy tissue sets and single-cell sequencing.

The RNA concentrated in stromal and myeloid cells rather than tumour cells themselves. Links covered shape-change programmes, immune tuning and cytokine signalling. Diagnostic sorting in colorectal cancer looked strong, yet higher levels inside tumours paradoxically tracked with poorer survival and an inflamed but suppressive environment with weaker checkpoint response. Lab checks in ten paired tissue samples confirmed the expression pattern.
pmc-13522532:
Liia R Valeeva and collaborators compare bacteria-fighting compounds released by different lines of a model moss in a 2026 study. Mosses are gaining attention as sources of useful natural compounds. Four natural isolates of the fire moss Ceratodon purpureus were compared, and released compounds from two lab lines were partly cleaned and profiled by broad chemical analysis.

The isolates differed a lot in which bacteria-fighting compounds they produced. One line released a far more mixed set, including amines, fatty acids, lactones, quinones, and terpenoids, while shares of compounds with nitrogen, phosphorus, or sulfur stayed similar across lines. Several compound classes with possible bioactivity were predicted in both lines. The study shows that even within one moss species, released chemistry varies a lot by isolate.
pmc-13522732:
Stefania Vacaru and co-authors test how early bonds may shape adult stress response, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. One hundred ten young adults took a test of secure base knowledge from childhood bonds. Heart and skin measures were tracked while they worked, as signs of two stress systems.

Three stress profiles came out of the combined measures. Adults with stronger secure base scores were less likely to fall in the flat, low-response profile. Two other profiles did not differ on that score. A side finding linked sex and scores inside one profile. The work backs a link between early bonds and later stress tuning.
pmc-13523332:
Xile Zhang and co-authors relate blood inflammation markers to stroke severity and recovery in a 2026 study. Two hundred twenty-five patients with acute ischemic stroke and forty-six healthy people provided clinical data and blood counts, from which six combined inflammation indices were calculated. Standard scales scored neurological deficit and disability at admission, discharge, and one and three months.

Several indices were elevated at admission and tracked the severity of deficits in the acute phase. One ratio, lymphocytes to monocytes, independently linked to larger infarct size and worse functional outcome, while some other indices pointed in the opposite direction, which the authors flag as complex and unresolved. Prognostic value peaked at different times for different markers. The panel may aid early risk grouping and personalized treatment after stroke.
pmc-13523532:
Lian-Yu Sui and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, an imaging model to predict whether targeted drugs will work for lung cancer that has spread to the brain. Patients had non-small cell lung cancer with EGFR mutations and received EGFR-blocking drugs. The team combined clinical features with radiomics, numerical features extracted from contrast-enhanced MRI scans.

Data from 338 patients across three centers were analyzed, with features taken from inside tumors and from rings of tissue around them. Seven machine learning algorithms were compared, and random forest performed best. A combined clinical and radiomic model beat either alone in the test set, reaching an area under the curve near 0.76, with similar performance in external validation. The authors propose the model for forecasting one-year treatment benefit.
pmc-13523832:
Samuel George Oxley leads a very large team in the 2026 PRESCORES cross-sectional study of quality of life after risk-reducing hysterectomy in women with Lynch syndrome. Removing the uterus lowers endometrial cancer risk, yet effects on daily quality of life had not been studied. The team invited over four thousand UK women without prior gynecological cancer.

Analysis included 1,120 participants, of whom 529 had undergone the surgery, with a median age of 55 against 39 for those who had not. Adjusted quality-of-life utility scores were slightly lower after surgery, a difference that did not reach statistical significance overall. Premenopausal women showed a clearer reduction, while postmenopausal women resembled the comparison group. Cancer worry was also assessed, and multiple sensitivity checks tested the robustness of the findings.
pmc-13524132:
Karnik, Kumar, and Patil reported in 2026 a case of plasma cell gingivitis with lip inflammation in an 18-year-old girl. This rare gum disorder, rich in plasma cells, can look like plaque-driven gum overgrowth, blood disease, or even a plasma cell tumor. She had a year of growing gum swelling and upper lip swelling, with red, firm gums that bled when probed.

Karnik's blood screening showed anaemia but no sign of leukaemia or body-wide infection. A biopsy found gum tissue packed with mature plasma cells and no abnormal features that would suggest cancer. Standard gum therapy and steroid creams helped too little, so surgeons removed the overgrown gum tissue. A month after surgery, both the gum enlargement and the lip swelling had shrunk back. The authors stress biopsy plus blood screening when lasting gum growth comes with lip swelling, since look-alike causes can be serious.
pmc-13525932:
Begonya Nafria and others investigate, in a 2026 study, the expertise of European clinical trial units in running cross-border pediatric trials for rare diseases. Children with rare conditions often must travel abroad for trials, since expertise concentrates in few sites. Language barriers, consent adaptation, and logistics limit that access, and current rules offer few fixes.

Three online surveys went to trial units through European research networks, covering general expertise, good practice with international patients, and documented discrimination linked with native language requirements. Forty-three units from 17 countries replied, spanning children's, general, and university hospitals. International patients did travel to these units for participation. The authors map where experience sits and which practices support families, aiming to improve both scientific feasibility and equity of access.
pmc-13526032:
Young Jun Kang, writing alone in 2026, finds a switch that restrains the calming side of macrophages, the immune cells that can either attack or calm tissue. The protein 4-1BBL was already known to sustain pro-inflammatory responses, yet its role in the other program was unclear. Such switches matter for diseases where inflammation fails to resolve.

Removing or blocking 4-1BBL in mouse macrophages boosted anti-inflammatory cytokines and markers. The protein dampens a signaling chain downstream of the IL-4 receptor, and its absence raised fat-burning, oxygen-based energy production in mitochondria, with metabolic gene expression. Gene checks confirmed a shift toward calm, oxidative programs. Blocking the protein also boosted anti-inflammatory responses in human monocytes, leading Kang to propose it as a target for helping inflammation resolve.
pmc-13526232:
Joshi and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the two main families of dental implants, conventional and basal, and how clinicians should choose between them. Conventional implants root into the spongy jawbone crest, come in many designs with treated surfaces that encourage bone bonding, and often need staged work with delayed loading. Basal implants instead grip the dense cortical bone, the jaw's hard shell, in a single piece with a polished surface.

Anchoring in cortical bone lets basal implants load at once without bone grafting, suiting patients with severe bone loss or medical compromise. They demand expert handling, though, and can look less natural for single front teeth. Conventional designs remain the flexible standard where bone is adequate. The authors frame the two as complementary tools rather than rivals, and close with decision guidance and future directions for a field still refining materials and technique.
pmc-13527132:
Amanullah Baloch and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, lip-reading systems for Urdu alphabets, a capability that can help deaf users, noisy settings, and silent password entry. Urdu lacked a suitable dataset, and adapting an established model called LipNet proved difficult. The team created a new dataset of Urdu alphabet lip movements.

Three neural network designs were compared: a LipNet-based two-dimensional model, a hybrid model mixing two- and three-dimensional processing, and a plain three-dimensional baseline. All were helped by data augmentation and tested in varied environments on familiar and unseen speakers. The LipNet-based model reached about eighty-two percent accuracy on unknown data, leading on precision, recall, and F1 as well. The hybrid model generalized best among the others, reaching about sixty-nine percent on unfamiliar data.
pmc-13528032:
Ambra Bisio and six colleagues test whether adding muscle vibration to virtual reality improves movement copying in a 2026 study. Twenty-three healthy young adults watched an avatar bend and straighten a forearm in a headset. Some trials added 80-hertz tendon vibration. That buzz creates a false feeling of movement matching the avatar.

Copying was tested during the buzz and after it ended. After-effects favored the combined method: speed errors were lower than with vision alone. During the buzz itself, errors grew instead. Trajectory error showed the same split pattern. Participants also felt more ownership and agency over the virtual arm with vibration. The authors suggest the boost in body feeling helps later copying. Timing matters, since copying while buzzing hurt accuracy.
pmc-13528132:
Emin Celalettin Ün measures nerves before a rite of passage for dental students in a 2026 study. Seventy-four fourth-year students in Türkiye faced their first real-patient tooth extraction. Just before the session they filled in a standard anxiety scale. The same scale's trait part was taken during a calm lecture. Forty-nine students were women and twenty-five were men.

Momentary anxiety averaged about 53.5, clearly above the scale midpoint. Everyday trait anxiety averaged about 40, a normal level. The gap between the two was huge. Most students, about eighty-one percent, showed moderate moment anxiety. About eighteen percent scored high. Women and men did not differ. Ün argues the spike comes from the situation, not the person. Staged practice and calm preparation could ease the first pull, he suggests.
pmc-13529632:
Renata Sigrist and ten colleagues move production of a plant-helping compound into a new host microbe in a 2026 study. The compounds, pteridic acids, help crops face drought and salt. The natural maker produces almost none, under a tenth of a milligram per liter. The team copied its sixty-eight thousand letter gene cluster. They pasted it into related Streptomyces hosts with precise gene tools.

At first the hosts made a cousin compound instead. Swapping in a strong always-on promoter woke the right pathway. Computer models of cell metabolism then tuned the growth broth. Fed-batch brewing reached about 1.7 to 2.8 milligrams per liter by host strain. That beats the native maker more than twentyfold. The authors call it the first working platform for these acids. Field-grade supply is the long goal.
pmc-13530232:
Abdulaziz A M Abahussain leads a 2026 check of a simplified math model for dry reforming of methane, a reaction that turns two greenhouse gases into useful synthesis gas. Many shortcut models get tuned to data and never face a true prediction test. This team ran one published model exactly as written, with no refitting.

A simulated plug-flow reactor traced conversion from low to high temperatures. The model matched measured trends well at moderate and high conversion yet drifted off course at low temperatures. Energy analysis suggested the high barrier reflects several surface steps acting together rather than one single slow step.
pmc-13530832:
Poulson and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 63, a systematic review and meta-analysis of mid- to long-term results for the FDA-approved MACI implant. In MACI, a patient's own cartilage cells are grown and returned on a collagen membrane to fill large knee cartilage defects. Most long-term data used non-approved scaffolds, dating the evidence.

Nine studies with 500 patients and 504 defects, followed at least five years, qualified. Defects clustered on the thigh bone knuckles and averaged three and a half square centimeters in area in this pooled analysis of the approved product. Every standard knee score improved significantly by the five-year mark and the gains held. The pooled failure rate was about nine percent, reoperation about fourteen percent, and conversion to a total knee replacement only about one percent across the studies.
pmc-13532132:
Moritz Jahn and colleagues added organic groups to molybdenum sulfide agents to tune light-driven hydrogen output. Published in 2026, the study built routes for adding organic nitrogen-donor ligands to thiomolybdates, molecular agents that split water to hydrogen without noble metals. The noble metal works well but costs too much for large-scale green hydrogen, so cheap earth-based options matter.

Light and modeling studies explained how the new ligands shift hydrogen-making activity, toughness, and the prospects for fixing them to supports. The work sets up design rules for this new agent family, aiming at versions that link to light traps or photocathodes. Readers get a basis for solar hydrogen systems that are molecularly defined and tunable, with device testing still ahead.
pmc-13532332:
Lahiru Malalasekara and Jorge C Escalante-Semerena report in 2026 that Salmonella germs release cobamides, a group that includes forms like vitamin B12. Only some germs and archaea can make these compounds from scratch, yet many life forms need them. How germs release them was not well known before this work.

In lab tests the Salmonella strain made cobamides without oxygen and released them into the fluid around the cells. Small colonies formed without oxygen kept making them after air was added. The authors suggest release may help the germ shift life mode and may feed nearby germs that need cobamides.
pmc-13532932:
Sofoklis Mavrantonis and colleagues compare in 2026 two surgery orders for bowel cancer that has spread to the liver at the same time. Surgeons can remove the bowel tumour first or the liver tumours first, and past proof was mixed. The review pooled 15 studies with 8,611 patients from 2010 to 2025.

Bowel-first surgery linked to higher one-year survival and higher disease-free rates at one, three, and five years. Major problems, deaths within 90 days, and failure to reach the second operation were alike. The authors urge caution because no randomised trials were in the pool.
pmc-13534432:
Vamis Kamil and colleagues characterise in 2026 Shigella flexneri germs from child patients in Ahvaz, Iran. The germ causes dysentery and harms many children under five in lower-income settings, while drug resistance keeps rising. From 500 stool samples the team recovered 49 isolates for drug tests, gene checks, and typing.

All isolates resisted four common drugs, and most produced enzymes that break down key antibiotics. Typing split the isolates into 22 types with wide genetic variety, suggesting resistance spreads by gene transfer rather than one clone. Readers gain local data to guide treatment and tracking.
pmc-13534732:
JunZhe Feng and colleagues propose in 2026 a fine-grained retrieval system for knowledge-based visual question answering. Standard retrieval pulls whole passages or whole images, which mismatch the small visual details many questions need. Their framework aligns tiny image patches with matching text fragments through added training signals.

A shared loss joins the searcher and a language-model reranker, with generation scores feeding back to guide search. On two image datasets the method beat leading rivals on top-rank recall by clear margins. Question answering accuracy rose and made-up answers fell notably versus standard systems.
pmc-13535032:
Senamile Ngobese, Olalekan Ayo-Yusuf, and Catherine Egbe studied South African adults about smokeless tobacco, which is used there far beyond leisure. In KwaZulu-Natal, snuff and similar products serve in ancestral communication, healer initiation, rituals, and traditional healing. The team spoke with twenty-five users, split between traditional practitioners and trainees and people using the products for daily reasons.

Other users cited stress relief, a belief it helps their health, sexual enhancement, being cheaper than smoking, and social influence. Modes of use ranged across oral, nasal, and ritual use. The users named health, social, and money harms, yet some traditional users believed ancestral protection shields ritual use from harm. The authors urge control programs that engage healers and respect cultural meanings while facing the risks.
pmc-13535232:
Junichi Inaba and colleagues show a potato pathogen rewires plant fat handling to feed itself. Their study from twenty twenty-six infects tomato plants with phytoplasma. These bacteria live only inside plant sap channels. How they steal nutrients from hosts was largely unknown.

Infection switched on the plant cell recycling system, autophagy. Fat droplets moved toward the bacteria inside cells. Membrane fats fell while storage fats rose in infected tissue. Microscopy showed droplets sitting close to pathogen cells. Blocking autophagy stopped droplet breakdown and distorted cell structure. The pathogen appears to farm host fats for its growth. Crop protection might target that supply line.
pmc-13536632:
Liang Ma and colleagues study in 2026 how the TT-TG distance, a knee alignment measure, relates to leg rotation and straightness in recurrent kneecap dislocation. Records covered 99 patients with repeat dislocations, using standing leg films and knee scans. Groove shape, rotation angles, and coronal alignment were measured for each patient.

The distance rose with shin-to-thigh rotation overall, but not with side-to-side straightness of the leg. The link was clearest when the distance stayed below the common surgical threshold. Surgeons should read the measure together with rotation and groove shape when planning tailored treatment.
pmc-13536832:
Yalin Zhang and colleagues measure joined-up high blood pressure care in Chengdu community health centers in a 2026 survey. Good control needs coordination across services, yet joined care varies widely. All centers in the city were invited between late 2021 and early 2022, and 110 took part. A rainbow model tool scored six dimensions from person focus to technical skill, with models testing what drives higher scores.

Person and community focus scored highest, while organizational joining scored lowest by a clear margin. Better integration tracked with staff schooling, emergency services, special outpatient management, and hospital alliance membership in the reported models. Eye services and wearable device use tracked the other way. The authors urge stronger staff training, facilities, and cross-organization teamwork.
pmc-13537232:
David Zimmerman, Benjamin de Bivort, and Aravinthan Samuel study how a fruit fly larva merges smells from both sides of its body, in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Smell neurons on each side report only to the same side of the brain. Yet the animal must make single, coherent choices. The team used calcium imaging, targeted stimulation, connectome maps, and light-based control to trace the circuit. They focused on the mushroom body, a learning center in the fly brain.

They found that smell entry cells stay strictly one-sided. In contrast, modulatory input cells pool signals from both sides evenly. Some output cells still kept a trace of which side the smell came from. Activating those cells on one side steered the larva's turning. The study shows how a small brain balances separate sensing with unified action.
pmc-13537332:
Nathalia Novaretti and colleagues reviewed the safety of ketamine taken by mouth. Published in 2026, the planned review pooled 18 random placebo-controlled trials in adults, children, and healthy volunteers. Oral ketamine draws growing off-label use for hard-to-treat low mood, long-term pain, and child procedure calming, yet no standard oral form exists.

In low-mood trials with 427 people, side effects ran mostly mild and short-lived. Child trials before procedures, with 239 children, showed brief nerve effects without major safety worries. Pain and lab trials with 372 people showed mostly mild events, with spaced-out feelings at higher doses. Compared with controls, ketamine brought more dizzy spells, sleepiness, and spaced-out feelings, while serious harms stayed rare. The authors call the short-term safety picture good but the proof weak and long-term safety still open.
pmc-13537432:
Matheus Lokadjaja and co-authors map research on large language models in mental health, in a scoping review dated 2026. Chat-style models are being tried for diagnosis, outlook forecasts, and decision support across psychiatry. With models and tweaks multiplying, the field needed a census.

The team screened over three thousand papers from three databases, covering work from early 2023 to late 2025. Two reviewers sorted the pile independently, with a third settling disputes. Forty-one papers made the final cut. For each, the review records the model used, the task, the data, and how the model was adapted. The synthesis shows where effort clusters and where proof is still missing, guiding groups that want to build or judge mental health tools.
pmc-13538332:
Xinyu Liu and co-authors build a neuron-like gene signature for papillary thyroid cancer in a 2026 study mixing bulk and single-cell gene data. Cancer cells can borrow nerve-like traits to advance, yet relevant channel genes in this cancer were unclear. Bulk data from 521 patients supplied an eight-gene model for spread to neck lymph nodes. Single-cell data from seven tumors then traced which cells actually carry the signals.

The eight-gene model predicted node spread with fair accuracy. Single-cell checks showed one gene, GABRB2, concentrated in malignant thyroid cells at rates far above immune cells, supporting tumor-born nerve mimicry rather than background noise. High-risk patients showed a more suppressed immune pattern with shifted cell entry. The authors suggest channel targeting as a possible future lever, pending lab validation.
pmc-13538732:
Corrao, Cosentino, and Federici offer a critical reading in this 2026 commentary of SURPASS-CVOT, the cardiovascular outcomes trial of tirzepatide, the dual-action diabetes and obesity drug. The trial compared tirzepatide against dulaglutide, itself a proven heart-protective drug, and found non-inferiority on the composite of cardiovascular death, heart attack, and stroke, with a hazard ratio of 0.92 in the report discussed.

The commentators question that verdict: the pre-set non-inferiority margin of 1.05 was wide relative to the comparator's known benefit, under a stricter margin the claim would fail, and an outright win narrowly missed at p equals 0.09 in the trial. Other signals favored tirzepatide, including all-cause mortality at a hazard ratio of 0.84 against dulaglutide. Their argument reframes the question from whether the drug protects the heart to where its distinctive biology, spanning weight, kidney, and metabolic effects, actually acts.
pmc-13539432:
The European Food Safety Authority publishes its peer review conclusions on a fungal pesticide, Beauveria bassiana strain R444. The fungus is proposed as an insecticide for tomatoes and as a mite killer for stone fruits. Denmark acted as the initial assessing country, and the authority reviewed that work under European pesticide law.

The document reports the reliable endpoints regulators should use in risk assessment. It lists information still missing under the regulatory framework and flags issues that could not be finalized. It also considers whether the substance belongs on the list of active substances for which residue limits need not be set. The review is a regulatory decision document rather than a research study.
pmc-13539932:
Hilary Takunda Takawira offers a 2026 methods study showing demographers an alternative when the usual Cox survival model breaks its core assumption. The example is timing of a first birth, drawn from the 2015 Zimbabwe Demographic and Health Survey covering 9,955 women.

Checks confirmed that the proportional hazards assumption failed, so several parametric models were fitted with and without a term for unmeasured regional differences. A log-logistic model with that frailty term fitted best and handled a hazard that rises then falls. Higher schooling and later cohabitation delayed first birth in its estimates, while marriage and contraceptive use pointed the other way.
pmc-13540932:
Mingkai Shu and five colleagues investigate, in a 2026 multicentre study, why a leukaemia subgroup that mimics acute promyelocytic leukaemia bleeds so dangerously early in treatment. Blood vessel lining injury is their prime suspect, measured by an index called EASIX built from routine laboratory values.

Across three Chinese institutions, the look-alike group numbered 344 patients beside true promyelocytic cases and other leukaemias. EASIX scores in the look-alike group matched the true disease and far exceeded other leukaemias, and the index tracked closely with a direct vessel injury marker. High EASIX, overt clotting failure, and one cell marker independently predicted major bleeding, forming a new risk ladder the authors validated in a second cohort.
pmc-13542032:
Pumo Cai and colleagues spray a pest control bacterium in a 2026 study. The setting is a tea plantation. The bacterium is Bacillus thuringiensis, sprayed at two frequencies. The question is what the spray does to soil health. Soil sits beneath the tea bushes. Such sprays are a garden staple, yet soil effects were little studied.

Three sprays over three weeks helped the soil most. Organic matter rose, and so did available nitrogen and potassium. Several enzyme activities rose too. Helpful bacteria grew richer, and pathogen fungi fell sharply. Six sprays pushed two enzymes highest. That heavier regime fed the soil less and weakened its microbe network.
pmc-13542132:
Yi-Neng Zhou and co-authors trace how infection and low oxygen push cancer cells into chromosome chaos in a 2026 study. Aneuploidy, a wrong chromosome count, is common in cancers and helps them resist drugs. The team found a control chain centered on CDC20, a protein that times cell division. An enzyme called PHD1 marks CDC20 for keeping, while a second protein, TRIM21, marks unmarked CDC20 for destruction.

Low oxygen and low fuel both stall PHD1, leaving more CDC20 unmarked. Infection switches TRIM21 on. Both paths cut CDC20 levels, so its targets pile up. One target locks sister chromosomes together too long, scrambling their count. Another blocks cell death, aiding drug resistance. In cells and mouse tumors, saving CDC20 cut the chaos and restored drug response. The authors name the chain a drug target.
pmc-13542232:
Somaya Albhaisi and Brian P Lee published a 2026 commentary on a blood marker that could sharpen how fatty liver disease is sorted into types. Modern labels split the condition by cause: metabolic disease alone, metabolic disease combined with alcohol, or alcohol alone. That sorting still leans on what patients say they drink. The commentary examines a prospective cohort study by Torp and colleagues, which tested phosphatidylethanol, a direct alcohol marker in blood, against self-reports.

Among roughly 3,000 participants, about two in five people with heavy drinking histories had understated their intake when checked against the marker. The writers argue that an objective blood test can correct such misclassification and place patients in the right category. Correct placement matters because treatment and risk advice differ by cause, so the commentary supports wider use of the marker in liver clinics.
pmc-13543532:
Andrew Panyin Vormawor and colleagues published a 2026 household survey of urinary incontinence not caused by fistula among adult women in Bantama, a district of Kumasi, Ghana. The condition is common but understudied in sub-Saharan Africa despite its toll on daily life. Trained teams interviewed 374 women aged twenty to sixty-nine, chosen by cluster sampling, using a structured questionnaire with a validated health survey covering symptoms and quality of life.

Nearly one in three women, 32.9 percent, reported leakage, most of them once a week or less, though more frequent leakage interfered more with daily activities. Incontinence clustered with older age, obesity, more births, menopause, hysterectomy, and heavier babies at delivery, but not with education level. Urge-type leakage hit emotional and social quality of life hardest. A hidden, common, and treatable burden, the authors argue, deserves routine enquiry in women's primary care.
pmc-13543632:
Hu and colleagues feed sheep leaves from Eucommia ulmoides, a tree prized in Chinese medicine, to see whether a functional roughage can grow animals better by retuning their gut microbes. Twenty-one ewes were split into three groups eating no leaves, a twentieth of their dry feed as leaves, or a tenth. The team tracked growth, intake, and the rumen's microbial activity using gene-expression sequencing of the community.

The middle dose won: sheep on the five percent diet gained more weight, ate more, and converted feed more efficiently than both the control and high-dose groups in the trial's results. Their rumens hosted more butyrate-producing bacteria, including a genus called Coprobacillus, and microbial genes for carbohydrate and amino acid processing ran hotter, suggesting better nutrient extraction. Doubling the dose erased the advantage, a more-is-not-better pattern.
pmc-13544832:
Le and colleagues present a 2026 report of two kidney transplant cases saved by a new way to flush the graft without removing it. Blood clots in the graft's artery or vein during surgery can kill the organ; the standard fix is taking it out and flushing it on a side table. At Viet Duc University Hospital in Vietnam, the team perfused the kidney in place instead.

Both patients, women aged 20 and 58, had clots treated by in situ perfusion during the operation. Blood flow and graft function were restored, and neither patient had complications afterward. Skipping removal saves time, staff, and supplies, and avoids extra handling of a fresh graft. Two cases cannot prove a technique, but a faster rescue for a rare emergency is worth reporting for other transplant teams to test.
pmc-13545032:
Jesús Vera and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of integrated sports vision training, programmes that combine several visual, cognitive, and movement drills rather than exercising one skill alone. The question was whether such batteries transfer to sport-specific tasks, measured by response time and accuracy. Four databases were searched to October 2025 under standard review rules; seventeen studies entered the review and fourteen the pooled analysis, with quality graded on a standard checklist.

Trained athletes improved markedly on both outcomes: pooled effects were large for response time and accuracy alike, and sensitivity checks kept the direction and significance intact. Results varied a great deal between studies, especially for timing outcomes, which the authors report openly. Because the training mimics real sporting demands more closely than isolated drills, they argue, transfer to performance is plausible, while optimal design and long-term retention remain open research questions.
pmc-13545232:
Menikae Heenkenda and co-authors probe how two breast cancer risk factors shape breast tissue, in work published in 2026. Dense breasts and estrogen exposure both raise risk, but the biology is murky. The team drew fluid from the breasts of sixty-one women and counted hundreds of proteins tied to swelling, in breast tissue and in fat.

Dense tissue showed a protein mark of immune activity, fat shifts, and cell stress. Estrogen-exposed tissue showed a unlike mark rich in swelling signals, vessel growth, and tissue reshaping. Both states may let tumors grow, but by unlike paths. The authors say guard plans may need to target each path on its own.
pmc-13547332:
Fen Yuan and colleagues read the genome of a plant that partly lives off woody hosts. Published in 2026, the study mapped Taxillus sutchuenensis, a green guest prized in nature study and medicine. Green guests add layers of twists over non-green kin, yet only one Loranthaceae genome was on record.

Long reads, RNA reads, and chromosome-linking data built a 406-million-letter genome across nine chromosome groups, with a scaffold span near 46 million letters. The build covered 93.6 percent of a standard gene set with a high quality score, and 21,795 protein-coding genes were found, with nearly 95 percent given a known role. Repeats covered just over half the genome, mostly jumping LTR bits. The genome opens study of parasite change over time, gene function, and host-tapping tricks.
pmc-13547932:
Sang Zhou, Chengrong Zheng, Weiwei Li, and Zhitao Jin chart, in a 2026 study, at what ages calcium appears in the heart arteries and chest aorta of Chinese adults. Routine chest scans taken for other reasons often catch these deposits, and guidelines tie statin advice to a person's calcium rank for their age. Local age and sex thresholds were missing. The team read over forty-two thousand community participants' scans.

Heart artery calcium reached a quarter of men at forty-eight and of women at fifty-eight. Half and three-quarter marks followed the same ten-year gap. Aortic calcium rose steeply with age in both sexes. Heart-only deposits were commoner in men, aorta-only in women, and combined deposits dominated with age. The authors give exact ages when a positive finding should prompt statin talks, and ages below which a clean scan spells a good outlook.
pmc-13548132:
Samira Sadigh Batha, Nazanin Nasr, and Nasser Kaviani report full dental treatment for a small child with the most severe form of von Willebrand disease, an inherited bleeding disorder. In type 3 of the disease, a key clotting factor is nearly absent, so even dental work can bleed dangerously. The patient, a 4-year-old boy, had pain in an upper front baby tooth.

Working with a blood specialist, the team gave clotting factor concentrate before and after surgery and did the whole repair under general anesthesia in one session. They treated baby molars with pulpotomy and steel crowns and fixed the front teeth with pulpectomy and tooth-colored fillings. The case shows that, with careful planning across specialties and factor cover timed around the operation, even extensive dental rehabilitation can be done safely in such children.
pmc-13548532:
Huachen Liu and colleagues characterize a feeding-control signal in the sea cucumber Apostichopus japonicus, in a 2026 study of neuropeptide evolution. Signals of the cholecystokinin family tell many animals to stop eating, but how they act in sea cucumbers was unknown. The team identified the sea cucumber version of the signal, the two peptides it produces, and the receptor those peptides switch on.

Both peptides raised calcium signaling inside cells and tightened longitudinal muscle strips in the dish. One peptide also kept the rear section of the gut contracted, an effect not seen elsewhere in the gut. Injected over time, the peptides cut food intake and quieted genes for orexin, an appetite-promoting signal, in the nerve ring and gut. Unlike mammals, which slow the stomach outlet, sea cucumbers appear to hold back gut emptying at the rear, a contrast the authors link to farming uses.
pmc-13548632:
Jiuling Shen and colleagues automate the planning of needle paths for internal radiation treatment of cervical cancer, in a 2026 methods study. In brachytherapy, needles placed through a template deliver radiation from inside the tumor, and hand planning takes hours while risking collisions. Their greedy algorithm first generates candidate paths from safe entry zones, then picks needles one by one using a coverage radius tested at three widths, keeping paths clear of the central applicator.

Plans for twenty patients all met clinical standards. Tumor coverage matched manual planning closely, doses to bladder, rectum, and bowel were no worse, and needle counts fell from an average above five to just over four. Total planning time dropped from two to three hours to about eight minutes. The authors present the tool as a fast, consistent starting point for a laborious task.
pmc-13549132:
Homan and colleagues built in 2026 a multi-step pipeline to find targets on liver cancer cells for imaging and targeted radiation drugs. No approved drug of this kind yet picks out hepatocellular carcinoma, the main form of liver cancer. The team mined gene activity data from 371 tumors and single cells from 34 cases. They filtered for proteins sitting on the cell surface. The best candidates were then checked in tissue samples and lab cell lines.

Homan confirmed five lead proteins with strong tumor enrichment and little signal in normal organs. A panel of four markers together covered nearly nine in ten patient tumors. Antibody tracers aimed at the chosen targets lit up tumors in mice on PET scans, a type of whole-body imaging, and signal strength matched the lab staining. The authors call this a blueprint for imaging agents and later radiopharmaceutical therapy in liver cancer.
pmc-13550632:
Yogesh Patil, with four colleagues, published a 2026 design for a vehicle system that manages headlights and honking together. Glare from high beams and needless horn use harm night safety and add urban noise, while most adaptive lighting controls one lamp in isolation. The proposed module pairs a programmable logic controller, a rugged industrial controller, with camera-based artificial intelligence.

Ladder logic with 33 rungs switches beams and modulates the horn using speed, steering, and stability inputs. The vision part spots approaching vehicles and quiet zones, and can override the controller. Simulations and hardware-in-the-loop tests reported beam switching accuracy above 99 percent and response times under 60 milliseconds, which the authors offer as a practical intelligent vehicle design.
pmc-13551032:
Xincheng Wu, Saori Uematsu, Yan Wu, and Shu-Bing Qian study how ribosomes skip a step when building proteins in a 2026 paper. Certain viruses carry a short 2A sequence that makes the ribosome fail to join two protein pieces, releasing two separate proteins instead. The skip happens at a conserved three letter motif, but the details were murky.

Using precise reporters and ribosome profiling, the team found the ribosome pauses at the motif's last codon, and that pause acts as a decision point: longer dwell means less skipping. Loosening the growing protein chain nearby boosted skipping, while water hating stretches further back suppressed it, an effect fixable with flexible inserts. The chain outside the ribosome talks back to its catalytic center.
pmc-13551832:
Chia-Jen Tsai, with seven colleagues, published a 2026 study of lymph node counts in pancreatic cancer surgery. Guidelines urge surgeons to take at least fifteen nodes. That count aids staging, yet its survival value was unsure. Taiwan registry and insurance data held 885 patients. All had curative surgery between 2013 and 2019. The team modeled survival with checks for bias.

The median node count was fifteen. Just over half the patients met the guideline count. In the whole group, survival at one and three years did not differ by count. One subgroup did gain: patients with head tumors of set stages who had the standard Whipple operation. They lived longer with higher counts. The team qualifies the guideline by tumor site and operation type.
pmc-13553532:
Su and Pei study early vitamins plus caffeine in preterm infants, in work from twenty twenty-six. Babies born before thirty-two weeks risk a chronic lung disease called bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Caffeine citrate is a standard early treatment to support breathing.

The single center retrospective study used a seventy-two hour landmark design. More than a hundred infants admitted over two years were included. The question was whether adding vitamin A and D drops early to caffeine was associated with less lung disease and better short term respiratory outcomes. Landmark timing avoids counting treatment that starts after outcomes are already set.
pmc-13554332:
Haowei Chen leads a five-author team training a neural network to predict lasting leg damage after deep vein clots in a 2026 study. The syndrome, called postthrombotic, strikes between a fifth and a half of clot patients despite blood thinners. Standard models assume straight-line links and miss tangled patterns in clinic data. Records from 212 patients at one vascular centre trained the network.

Sixty-seven patients developed the syndrome within six months of their clot. The network predicted cases with accuracy above eighty percent on fresh test data. Its balance of catching cases and clearing healthy patients also ran high. The authors pitch the tool for early action and tailored care, while calling for multi-centre data to prove it travels well.
pmc-13555332:
Li and five co-authors study mindful parenting and child social skill in Chinese families, in work from twenty twenty-six. Mindful parenting means calm, aware, non judging care. It links to child emotional growth, but the path to peer competence was not well mapped.

More than five hundred kindergarten families took surveys. Parents rated their mindful parenting, the parent child bond, and child peer competence. Children emotion control was tested as a bridge in the link. The parent child bond was tested as a factor that changes the strength of the path. Results in a Chinese cultural setting can guide family programs that fit local norms.
pmc-13555932:
