Zeyu Zhang leads a five-author team profiling oxyphil cells in overactive parathyroid glands from kidney patients in a 2026 study. These cells sit beside the hormone-making chief cells, yet their role in the disease stayed murky. Gene maps from more than ninety thousand cells, plus spatial mapping of one gland, pinpointed the oxyphil group with high confidence. Six diseased and three normal glands supplied the material.

Oxyphil cells carried an unusually high share of mitochondrial gene activity. A transcription factor driving power-plant building explained that trait. The cells also showed low levels of the vitamin D receptor, making them resist the active vitamin. A second factor switched that receptor on, easing the resistance. The authors nominate it as a drug target.
pmc-13556032:
Hamad Khan and twelve colleagues ran a three-year field trial, reported in 2026, on how sowing date and soil warmth shape cotton growth in Henan Province, China. The cultivar CCRI 134 was sown on six dates from mid April to mid May in a randomised block design at Anyang on the North China Plain. Sensors tracked soil temperature at several depths, and the team recorded heat accumulation and final seed cotton yield across the 2022 to 2024 seasons.

The best sowing date moved with the weather of each year, yet very late sowing lost yield every time when set against the stronger dates. Shallow soil layers swung most with sowing date, while deep layers stayed steadier. Sowing between 18 April and 6 May balanced heat capture and yield most reliably. Growers get both a planting window and a case for watching soil temperature below the surface.
pmc-13558432:
Yuta Yamamoto and ten colleagues compare bypass with standard surgery for non-strangulated adhesive small bowel block. Bypass value for this condition was unclear. Their 2026 study covers 55 patients failing conservative care. Fifteen received bypass surgery, while 40 had standard surgery to free or remove bowel.

Albumin and nutrition matched between groups at 12 months after surgery. No bypass patient had repeat blockage, against 13 of 40, or about 33 percent, in the standard group. Recurrence-free survival ran longer with bypass. Bypass surgery may thus cut repeat blockage and offers a good option for this problem.
pmc-13560132:
Malin Hultberg, Elena Surra, and Oksana Golovko test a fungus in 2026 as a way to clean drug traces out of wastewater. Drug leftovers pass through normal treatment plants and end up in rivers and lakes. The fungus is the oyster mushroom, grown as small pellets from its spawn.

In lab-made wastewater, living pellets cut the level of most test drugs within hours. In real plant outflow, total drug levels fell by about half or more within a day. The team also weighed the full cost to nature of the process. Burning the used fungus for energy scored better than burying it. The authors say more work is needed on what the broken-down drugs turn into.
pmc-13560332:
Tao and colleagues built an MRI deep learning model in 2026 to help diagnose obstructive sleep apnea, guided by mouse experiments on the thalamus. The apnea condition is widely missed, and its repeated oxygen dips may alter the thalamus, a relay station in the brain. Mice exposed to intermittent low oxygen showed strong thalamic activation, strongest in one small nucleus, which justified focusing the human model on both thalami.

The team segmented the thalamus in brain scans from 760 adults across two centers and trained a dual-branch three-dimensional network with a transformer stage to fuse the two sides. The model scored high discrimination in training, validation, and an outside test center, and clearly beat single-side models. The authors present the biology-first design, where animal findings choose the imaging target, as a template for translational imaging tools that carry their reasoning with them.
pmc-13561832:
Yanchen Dong and three co-authors present a 2026 case study of radial nerve palsy with several rare causes at once. This nerve controls much of the arm and hand, and when it fails without injury, one cause is usually to blame. Here, three rare causes were present in the same patient.

The causes were a cyst in the elbow joint, an hourglass-like pinching of the nerve, and harm done during past medical care. Because the signs overlapped, finding each cause took care. The authors walk through how the case was diagnosed and treated, then review past reports. Their aim is to give clinicians a guide for sorting out such tangled cases.
pmc-13562432:
Jun Yang and co-authors review how lung cancer adapts to the brain once it spreads there, and how care can fight back, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Spread cells trade signals with brain tissue, reshaping the blood barrier and local immune and nerve cells. That trade aids growth, escape, and drug failure.

Care has gained focused radiation, targeted drugs, immune drugs, and drug-linked antibodies. Lasting control in the skull still lags, thanks to uneven barriers and hidden leftover disease. Lab models and resistance paths are mapped beside the care gains. Readers get a frame that ties brain-only spread biology to next treatment plans.
pmc-13562632:
Mobin Golabzaei and two colleagues sharpen stock-price forecasts by letting a finance-trained language model read the market's mood. Word-list sentiment tools miss the context of financial chatter, so the 2026 framework uses FinGPT, a large language model tuned on market text, to score posts from Twitter. Those mood scores join price history and standard technical indicators as model inputs. Four deep learning designs were compared, including a new hybrid that pairs attention-based memory layers with convolutional ones.

Trials covered eight large stocks listed in New York. Adding the language-model sentiment improved every architecture's accuracy. The hybrid won overall, catching both long swings and quick moves. On AMD stock it posted the lowest error, an MSE of 46.06, with a fit score of 0.624 quoted by the authors. They argue that behaviour-aware inputs make machine forecasts more realistic for investors.
pmc-13563732:
Ahmadi and colleagues published in twenty twenty-six a comparison of respiratory viruses among Iranian pilgrims at two mass gatherings in twenty twenty-five. The Hajj and the Arbaeen walk draw huge crowds where infections spread easily. The team swabbed one hundred ten symptomatic pilgrims returning from the events. Sixty came from the Hajj and fifty from the Arbaeen walk. Molecular tests screened their samples for respiratory viruses. Rhinovirus, the common cold virus, was most frequent in both groups.

Covid virus rates differed sharply between the gatherings. Only about two percent of Hajj pilgrims tested positive for it. Nearly a third of Arbaeen pilgrims carried it instead. Mixed infections appeared in some Arbaeen cases as well. Other flu and cold viruses showed up at low levels. No MERS virus was found among Hajj pilgrims. The authors urge continued surveillance at such gatherings.
pmc-13565132:
Ozan Başkurt and seven co-authors tested whether inherited variants in the progesterone receptor gene track with tumor features in brain gliomas in a 2026 paper. Progesterone signaling is suspected in these tumors, but what varies its strength was unclear. The team studied 66 patients with confirmed diffuse gliomas.

They assayed three receptor variants in tumor DNA alongside receptor levels, growth markers, and standard tumor traits. Receptor gene activity ran lower in high-grade tumors, though protein levels did not differ by grade. One variant's form tracked with higher receptor expression and a lower growth index. Effects shifted with sex and grade, hence the paper's context-dependent framing. The authors present the variants as one piece of glioma biology, not a stand-alone test.
pmc-13565932:
Oana-Maria Mișcă and a large team of co-authors tested four add-on treatments meant to shield rabbit tendons from an antibiotic known to damage them, in this 2026 pilot study. Twenty-one rabbits took levofloxacin for a week, with one leg treated and the other as a spare comparison in most groups. Add-ons ranged from platelet-rich plasma to vitamin E with selenium.

Three months on, tissue scores were low and flat across all groups, controls included. Ultrasound thickening in one vitamin group could not be tied to the treatment with confidence. The authors are frank: the model caused only mild damage, so the study cannot tell weak protection from a weak challenge. They frame the work as groundwork for a bigger trial.
pmc-13567332:
Nine authors present a study dated two thousand twenty-six on food habits and mental health among Brazilian teenagers. They used two rounds of a national school health survey, from two thousand fifteen and two thousand nineteen. The students were aged thirteen to seventeen and attended school.

For each survey year, the team derived two eating patterns from the answers students gave. They then checked how those patterns linked to a combined score of poor mental health signs, with the worst-off group as the outcome. The two survey years were analyzed apart, and the links were adjusted for other factors. Nationwide evidence of this kind has been scarce for Brazil.
pmc-13568432:
Lei Zhao and co-authors review, in twenty twenty-six, dissolvable polymers and composites for the oil and gas industry. These materials make tools such as fracturing plugs. A plug must hold under extreme heat and pressure deep in a well, then dissolve fast in well fluids so production can flow. Medical and consumer dissolvable plastics lack the heat strength, toughness, and low cost needed here. Over two decades, joint work between universities and industry has yielded new polymers suited to the task.

The review covers material design, how the materials break down, how they are made, and field uses. Named families include glycolic acid polymers, polyurethanes, and epoxies. It closes with future opportunities for the field.
pmc-13569432:
Rakesh Arul and five colleagues published this 2026 physics study reporting a synchronised state of light-emitting molecules at room temperature. The molecules sit inside plasmonic nanocavities, arrays of gold particles separated by tiny gaps. Synchronisation usually collapses at this scale because energy leaks away almost instantly. The system embeds methylene blue dye molecules in spacer cages packed between the gold particles. It pumps them with a laser that is not tuned to resonance.

As pumping rose, neighbouring dipoles began swinging in step. Measurements showed coherence spreading across the array, with it forming in ten femtoseconds. Yet the emission showed no narrowing and no beaming, the signs of a laser. Photon coherence stayed very short. The order lives in the molecules themselves, coupled through the cavities' near fields. The authors present the self-assembled platform as a testbed for synchronisation and quantum tools.
pmc-13570132:
Heribert Playa-Albinyana and colleagues grow, in a 2026 study, three-dimensional balls of chronic lymphocytic leukemia cells taken from patients, together with each patient's own T cells, with no artificial scaffold. The mixed cells organize themselves into disc-shaped spheroids that stay alive and dividing for up to six days.

Cancer B cells made up about ninety percent of each spheroid, with T cells showing a realistic spread of active and exhausted states. Standard drugs including ibrutinib and venetoclax produced measurable responses, validating the system for screening. Because the model preserves the conversation between cancer and immune cells, it offers drug testers a closer stand-in for the patient's own tumor environment.
pmc-13571332:
Sameh Madanieh and co-authors report, in a 2026 case, a 77-year-old man with atrial fibrillation and heart failure who developed a slow ventricular rhythm and repeated fainting. He had recently started cilostazol for poor leg circulation. His blood digoxin level looked normal, yet the sample had been drawn more than thirty hours after the last dose, outside the valid window.

Stopping digoxin cleared the rhythm problem completely. The authors explain that cilostazol blocks the pump that clears digoxin through the kidney and separately boosts heart cell calcium, a pairing that can poison a patient at normal-looking levels. Prescribers pairing these common drugs in older patients are urged to monitor proactively.
pmc-13571932:
Yuan, Xiu, and Peng review azithromycin resistance in gonorrhoea bacteria in twenty twenty-six. The bacterium is a major cause of sexually transmitted infection worldwide. Health bodies class it as a high priority threat due to drug resistance. A two drug regimen that once worked is now at risk.

Resistance to azithromycin has risen fast around the world in five years. It arises through mutations in a ribosomal gene and through a pump that expels the drug. These mechanisms vary a lot between strains and places. That variety makes molecular tests for routine surveillance hard to design. The authors review recent genomic and epidemiological data on the problem. They urge surveillance and tests tailored to local genetic patterns.
pmc-13572432:
Raghav Krishna, with four colleagues, presents a 2026 design for low-power signal filters that run on random bit streams. Small edge devices, such as wearables and sensors, need filters to clean signals like heart traces and voice. Standard parts for this work use multipliers that burn most of the power budget.

The design steers how the random streams line up with each other, which cuts a bias that plagues this style of computing. Tests used heart-like, speech-like, and vibration signals in software runs. Error stayed below 1 percent, and signal quality reached 23 to 49 decibels across the signal types. Switching activity fell up to ten fold next to a 16-bit standard design. Steering alone cut bias from 3.8 percent to below 0.5 percent. The authors see a path to cheaper, cooler sensor chips.
pmc-13573432:
Faith Eshofonie and Ezra Gayawan report a 2026 mapping study of missed childhood vaccines in Nigeria. The DPT vaccine guards against three diseases, yet many children never start or finish the course. National averages hide where the gaps sit, so the team mapped them by state and year.

Household survey data from 2003 to 2024 fed Bayesian spatial models. Missed doses clustered hard in the north compared with the south across the whole span. Dropout between doses shrank over time, which shows better follow-through once a child starts. Still, each later dose missed more children than the one before. Maps flagged states such as Kebbi, Sokoto, and Zamfara where the chance of zero-dose rates above ten percent stays high. The authors urge targeted local fixes.
pmc-13573632:
Sachin and three colleagues published an electrochemistry study in two thousand twenty-six on cheaper hydrogen production. Splitting water wastes much energy on the oxygen side. Swapping that step for oxidising useful organic chemicals can cut the energy bill and yield valuable products at the same time.

Their catalyst pairs ruthenium with manganese oxide, made by a fast urea-assisted method that spreads the metal evenly. In ethylene glycol oxidation it reached high currents at low voltages and turned the alcohol mainly into glycolate with about ninety-two percent efficiency. A full cell using the catalyst on both sides produced hydrogen at about ninety-three percent efficiency and held up well. The authors pitch it for biomass-linked electrolysis.
pmc-13574332:
Vinayak Anand Kumar and co-authors worked with international students in Germany to design a digital tool that prepares patients for primary care visits. Students reported feeling misunderstood, anxious, and poorly informed during appointments, with system barriers adding to the trouble. Many already took notes to structure their visits. Across four workshops, twelve students helped adapt an existing preparedness tool, guided by a behavior change framework built on capability, opportunity, and motivation.

Feedback on the existing tool was mixed: its purpose was welcome, but long structured lessons felt too slow. Students preferred a concise, interactive design with communication prompts and help booking appointments. Germany's digital health system lags peer countries, the authors note, so tools built for one setting may travel badly. Their study shows how cocreation with target users surfaces design choices outsiders would miss.
pmc-13574732:
Woo Hyeon Lim, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 benchmark of AI report writers for chest X-rays in an emergency department. Vision-language models can draft radiology reports, which could ease a global shortage of radiologists. Quality, though, swings between models, and invented findings are a real risk.

The study covered 478 adults who had a chest X-ray and a CT scan on the same day for fever or breathing symptoms. Five models drafted reports, and three chest radiologists graded all drafts blind, against the human reports. One model beat the humans on a disagreement score and on acceptability, with invention rates at human level. The other four lagged, with far more invented findings. Clarity often favoured the machines. The authors back careful, model-by-model adoption.
pmc-13575132:
David Kuratko leads a 2026 modelling study on how skull properties distort EEG readings in rats. EEG source finding depends on a forward model, a calculation of how brain signals reach the scalp. Skull traits such as uneven tissue, directional conduction, and thickness may shift those signals.

The team tested five simple head models plus a realistic one, checking results with four simulation tools and a physical phantom. Seams in the skull changed readings mainly at nearby electrodes. Thicker skull lowered signals at top electrodes yet raised them at the sides. Directional conduction had the largest effect, up to 60 percent, for sources near electrodes at extreme settings. Effects shrank at realistic values and for deeper sources.
pmc-13575232:
Chuanlong Ma and colleagues built SpaDC, a tool that reads the DNA code behind spatial maps of open chromatin. Spatial ATAC sequencing maps where chromatin is open in whole tissue, but its data are noisy, patchy, and vast, and most tools ignore the code motifs that drive control. SpaDC, a graph-based neural network, fuses place, open spots, and code, and uses triplet learning to merge data sets while wiping out batch quirks.

Tests showed top scores on spatial zone detection, noise cleanup, and gene-control network inference. Applied to mouse embryo brain, it found known brain parts and signals; on newborn mouse brain multi-omics data, it found zone-only control parts and networks. The authors present SpaDC as a stronger, code-aware route into tissue layout and chromatin order.
pmc-13576132:
Guo Li leads a 2026 study presenting a tool that edits the chemical marks on mitochondrial DNA without changing its code. Mitochondria, the cell's energy units, carry their own small genome. Adding methyl marks at set spots can quiet mitochondrial genes, a possible route to study ageing and disease.

Their editor steers DNA-binding modules fused to methylating enzymes into mitochondria. At one target site, methylation passed 53 percent and the linked gene's output fell by about 95 percent in human cells. In mice, marking an ageing-linked site in the brain rose by 11.76 percentage points, lowered the target gene there, and shifted two blood markers tied to brain disease. Off-target activity stayed low in the checks run. The authors offer the tool for probing mitochondrial ageing.
pmc-13578032:
Matthias Aschenbrenner, Lou van den Dries, and Joris van der Hoeven publish a correction to their 2025 paper on relative differential closure in Hardy fields. Hardy fields belong to mathematical logic and deal with ordered fields carrying a derivation. While preparing a book version of a source preprint, they found a mistake in a corollary that their paper had used as a key lemma.

The correction restates that lemma in a weaker form, dropping one claim about the H-couple built from the field's universal exponential extension. The authors then show the weaker version still carries the main proof. They generalise an earlier result to H-couples over a general ordered field, and prove a new lemma about such couples. They also rewrite the closing step of the affected proof in full. Readers of the original paper need this note to use its results safely.
pmc-13578332:
Widad Kebsa and colleagues profile propolis from Algeria and test whether a month of daily doses harms rats, in a 2026 study. Propolis is the resin bees gather from plants, long used in folk remedies, yet safety data for the Algerian kind were thin. Lab work first mapped the extract, which proved rich in plant defense compounds, with two flavonoids leading the list.

Dish tests showed strong power against damaging oxygen forms. In rats dosed daily for thirty days, the extract guarded cell powerhouses, kept stress markers low, and left liver and kidney tissue looking normal. Computer models of the main compounds predicted safe handling by the body and snug fits onto protective protein targets. The authors read the month long course as well tolerated at the dose used.
pmc-13578432:
Yongzeng Liu and colleagues build a digital twin to run a water pumping station on less power without risking harm, in a 2026 study. Pump stations juggle three aims that pull apart: save energy, keep pressure surges low, and spare the machines. Their case is a first stage station on a Yellow River diversion line in Shanxi, China.

The twin mirrors the station from past records, machine specs, and live sensor feeds. A tuned genetic search then weighs trade-offs among the three aims. The chosen plan cut energy use and surge peaks by clear margins and stretched machine life. Simulation errors stayed small, and answers came back in under half a second. Field trials backed the setup as steady and safe.
pmc-13581532:
Hongfu Chen and co-authors published this cohort study in 2026. Patients with bleeding inside the brain face a dilemma: blood thinners prevent dangerous clots in the veins, but might worsen the bleeding. Timing is the open question. Using an intensive care database, the team compared patients who started preventive blood thinners within forty-eight hours against those who did not. Their design fixed patient status at a two-day landmark and statistically balanced the groups.

The analysis covered 2,380 patients. Death in hospital occurred in 10.8 percent of the early group and 17.4 percent of the rest. After adjustment, early prevention carried twenty-eight percent lower odds of death. Rates of vein clots did not differ significantly. Most checks of the analysis pointed the same way. The authors note that missing brain-scan details could bias the result. Even so, the findings support starting prevention early rather than waiting.
pmc-13582232:
Shotaro Miyamoto and a large team of co-authors track a body water ratio against kidney decline in diabetic kidney disease, in a 2026 study from a Japanese clinic. Forty adults with type 2 diabetes gave three hundred fifty five visit records over about four and a half years. A body composition zap test split water inside and outside cells, and the outside share was set against each year's slide in kidney filtering power.

A higher outside water share, both at the start and averaged over time, went with a faster slide. Urine protein gave the same warning. Patients on a modern kidney friendly drug class carried lower water ratios, and stacking several protective drugs deepened the drop. The authors read hidden fluid overload as a quiet engine of decline that this drug class may ease.
pmc-13582532:
Philip Starks argues that odd acts by parasite-infected wasps need not mean the parasite pulls the strings, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Infected paper wasps leave nests, group before winter sleep, and later join set nests, a chain often told as a zombie tale. Starks urges a passive model as the base case to beat.

Old trials with a sterile nylon implant, which cannot signal at all, still cut energy use and drove nest leaving. Seal strength around the implant did not track the change. True control claims should face tests that split infection, insult, secretions, and host variants. Readers get a sterner bar for manipulation claims in animal behavior.
pmc-13582732:
David Alexander Christian Messerer and colleagues set error rates for hands-on skills side by side with error rates for frame skills in a big peer-marked clinic exam. Third-year med students at Ulm University did 2,076 exam tasks scored on a twenty-item tick list. Hands-on items dealt with exam moves, while frame items dealt with clean hands, talk, and notes.

Error rates were low but patchy in both sets, with a mid rate of ten percent for hands-on skills and zero percent for frame skills, though frame errors swung wide by task. Short tick-list exams can thus bare hid gaps in clean hands and notes. Schools should teach these frame skills as strictly as they teach the exam moves.
pmc-13583432:
Lauren Roe, Joseph Zmuda, and Iva Miljkovic reviewed fat inside muscle as a sign of ageing in 2026. Fat infiltrating skeletal muscle, called myosteatosis, is linked on its own to metabolic problems and weaker muscle in later life. Whether it marks ageing itself, or merely follows disease and inactivity, was the question guiding their summary of population studies using non-invasive imaging.

Studies of community-dwelling middle-aged and older adults showed age-related rises in muscle fat across well-described groups. Biological pathways that might drive the rise are reviewed. The authors judge the evidence consistent with muscle fat as an independent marker of ageing, and ask for standard imaging and long-term studies in diverse groups.
pmc-13583632:
Shweta Talhar and seven colleagues examine how fetal hemoglobin levels shape disease severity in forty patients with homozygous sickle cell disease. Fetal hemoglobin, the form dominant before birth, is known to soften sickle cell symptoms, but its exact relationships with blood counts and clinical course needed documentation in this cohort.

Fetal hemoglobin fell with age and tracked almost perfectly with total hemoglobin and red cell counts. Higher levels meant lower clinical severity scores, and in modeling it was the only independent predictor of severity. The authors support using fetal hemoglobin as a biomarker for how sick these patients will be, reinforcing therapies that raise it.
pmc-13584132:
Mark McCauley and John Solaro review proof that harmful sarcomere signaling helps trigger atrial fibrillation. Fresh therapies are needed since the roots of this rhythm flaw stay murky, above all in atrial cardiomyopathy. The review came out in twenty twenty-six.

That heart muscle illness can persist even after ablation care, which points to deeper drivers. The authors argue that changes at the atrial sarcomere, the muscle's force unit, form one shared path for both inherited and acquired forms. Such changes may spark fibrosis, inflammation, hormone strain, and rhythm flaws. New findings on atrial sarcomere control get full treatment.
pmc-13587332:
Tadesse Fikre Lema, writing alone, measures pre-cancerous changes of the cervix among women in Adama, Ethiopia. Such changes grow on the cervix surface under long infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus and can turn into cancer if missed. His 2026 study screened 383 women in the spring of 2023 with a vinegar-based visual check and a structured interview, then modeled which factors traveled with the changes.

One woman in eight showed a pre-cancerous lesion, a rate the author calls high next to a past northern Ethiopian figure. Four factors stood out on their own: bleeding after sex, the age at first sex, the number of lifetime partners, and HIV status. The author calls for public teaching on these risk factors and for awareness drives that push women toward screening before symptoms appear.
pmc-13587532:
Aude Mondeilh and colleagues study how Traveller communities in southwest France lived through the COVID-19 pandemic. Travellers, mostly French citizens living in caravans or settled halting sites, faced crowding and poor services long before the virus arrived. Their 2026 study mixed questionnaires with deep interviews in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region, asking about illness, prevention habits, and trust in the official response.

Among 406 people, about half reported a likely infection, and close to one in ten of those had been hospitalized. Only three in ten had taken a COVID vaccine, against a national rate near eighty-five percent. Vaccination rose with age, stable housing, past routine shots, clear official information, and trust in the government. Interviews told of sites where distancing was near impossible and of fear that frayed social life. The authors urge pandemic plans built with such communities, not just for them.
pmc-13588832:
Gulsum Ozen and eight colleagues track forty years of childhood type 1 diabetes to see when the seasons matter. Type 1 diabetes begins when the immune system destroys insulin-making cells, and cases have long seemed to bunch in colder months. Their 2026 study reviewed 2,954 patients diagnosed between 1981 and 2024, comparing onset season against age, birth season, sex, and other autoimmune diseases.

Diabetes starting early in childhood showed no seasonal swing, pointing to genes and immunity as the drivers. Later-onset cases peaked in autumn and winter and were more common in children born in spring and summer. Where several autoimmune disorders piled up in one child, the seasonal pattern vanished, as if strong internal autoimmunity drowned out environmental triggers. The authors call for screening plans tuned to age and immune load.
pmc-13592232:
Shuo Sun and seven colleagues build a microwave absorbing sponge from wood carbon laced with silica aerogel. Wood's aligned cells survive charring, giving the sponge a built in direction sense that earlier biomass absorbers rarely exploited. The team measured how the material handles microwaves along the grain, across the rays, and around the trunk. Each direction behaved quite differently.

One direction swallowed microwaves across a very wide band at under five millimeters thick, covering two whole radar bands. Another reached the deepest single absorption reading. The sponge also insulates heat well and springs back under squashing, unevenly by direction. Sun and the team present wood's natural grain as a design lever for light stealth materials that also keep heat in or out.
pmc-13593732:
Isabel Müller and colleagues studied what cigarette smoke extract does to TRPV4, a channel protein that helps airway lining cells sense their surroundings, in human bronchial cells grown at an air interface. Their 2026 experiments used a twenty-eight day smoke exposure on cells matured into a layered, ciliated lining resembling the real bronchial wall.

Smoke exposure switched on seven smoke-related genes yet stripped TRPV4 from the cell surface near the cilia, and calcium flow through the channel stopped. The wall's barrier strength held up, so the loss was specific rather than general damage. A partner protein called OS-9, which normally shields TRPV4 from destruction, also fell. Adding extra OS-9 rescued the channel levels, pointing to a fresh mechanism of smoke toxicity and a possible route toward new COPD treatments.
pmc-13594532:
Alqheedan checks how ready Saudi Arabia is to govern AI in health care under a One Health lens. AI is entering diagnosis, disease tracking, and health data work faster than rules can keep up. Risks include unsafe triage advice, weak data sharing, and staff who cannot oversee the tools well.

Saudi bodies such as the data and AI authority and the food and drug authority have built much groundwork. Yet binding AI-specific health rules are still missing, the analysis finds. The study benchmarks Saudi policy against global models to show what steps would turn broad principles into firm rules.
pmc-13595932:
Maria McClave, Samantha Marzi, and Ekaterina Heldwein compare ways to screen pairs of antiviral antibodies for how they interact, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Antibody pairs are used as virus treatments, but judging whether a pair helps, harms, or just adds up lacks a standard method. The team studied antibodies against a herpesvirus protein using three screening designs.

The classic grid assay rated most pairs as merely additive or opposed. Apparent teamwork showed mainly at very high doses. A drug-screen tool adapted for antibodies gave different verdicts. A third method, which varies the dose ratio, caught dose-dependent effects the others missed. The authors warn that claims of antibody teamwork depend heavily on the test design.
pmc-13599132:
Swain and Fricke study how listeners recognize spoken words in Spanish across dialects. Past work suggests listeners blend social and language cues when hearing speech, storing fine sound detail tied to speakers. Studies also showed gaps between instant word recognition and longer-term effects, with most work done in English.

Their study moves the question to Spanish varieties, which are far less studied. It tests when top-down effects, where knowledge guides hearing, emerge during word recognition. Even words meant as neutral controls showed such effects. The results extend cross-dialect speech science beyond its English base.
pmc-13600932:
Kapil Devkota and colleagues introduced Raygun in this 2026 paper, a generative artificial intelligence tool that shrinks, stretches, and rewrites natural proteins while keeping their function. Protein design tools often change one building block at a time, so large edits have stayed out of reach.

Raygun encodes each protein as a fixed-size pattern of probabilities drawn from a protein language model, so proteins of any length can be compared directly. Two settings control how many swaps and length changes it makes. It cut many proteins by a tenth to a quarter, sometimes by half. In cell tests, shortened fluorescent proteins and a tagging enzyme still worked, and an expanded growth factor bound its target more tightly than the natural version.
pmc-13601232:
Hriday Chandra Shil and colleagues surveyed employees in Bangladesh about how artificial intelligence tools in human resources affect their work lives. AI now helps firms recruit, train, judge, and keep staff, yet employee-level effects in emerging economies are little studied. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the team surveyed full-time staff at dozens of firms that use AI in human resources, in two waves five weeks apart. Early answers covered the AI practices, trust in the technology, and privacy worries, while later answers covered satisfaction, engagement, performance, well-being, and plans to quit.

AI human resource practices tracked with higher satisfaction, engagement, performance, and well-being, and with lower intent to quit. Feeling that one fits the firm and feeling empowered each carried part of the effect. Trust strengthened the links, while privacy concern weakened but did not erase them.
pmc-13601632:
Sharma and co-authors found a 2026 immune brake in which type I interferons shut down the inflammatory sensor NLRP1. That sensor can trigger PANoptosis, a fiery form of cell death, and its mutations cause inflammatory disease. How the sensor is normally restrained was poorly understood before this work.

A bacterial molecule called LPS, a classic immune activator, paradoxically blocked NLRP1 driven death in mouse and human immune cells. Sharma traced the block to a signalling chain needing the adapters TRIF and IRF3 but not MyD88, ending in interferon production. Adding interferon alpha or beta directly also stopped the death programme in their cell experiments. The interferons lowered production of the NLRP1 sensor itself, suggesting a therapy angle for diseases it drives.
pmc-13602532:
Jose H. Marco-Salvador leads a six-author team reporting a 2026 trial of skills training for family members of people who have attempted suicide. Caregivers often carry guilt, depression, hopelessness, and burnout, and earlier work suggested both psychoeducation and dialectical behavior therapy could help. No study had compared the two head to head. The team randomized 108 caregivers of patients diagnosed with suicidal behavior disorder to one of the two programs.

Both approaches eased caregiver burden by about the same amount. DBT pulled ahead on three other outcomes: family confidence, validating behaviors that accept feelings as valid, and stress. Analysis used mixed-effects models, counting everyone as assigned. DBT-based skills training is a truly effective option for these families, the authors conclude, not merely a match for the standard program. They present it as an option for wider use in suicide prevention.
pmc-13603232:
Catherine Gallagher and Nena Messina examine grief in women prisoners whose child has died, in a conceptual paper from 2026. Women in prison carry high loads of loss and trauma, and their suicide risk is elevated. A child's death inside such a setting is a deep loss that research has largely passed over.

Prison rules strip away privacy, family contact, mourning rituals, and support, the very things that shape healthy grief. The authors use two coping frameworks to show how confinement bends the grieving process. What looks like moving on may only be the institution's routine, not true recovery. Blocked facts, banned rituals, and punishment for grief behavior can freeze the story a mother tells about her loss. Support paths, such as family ties, are also mapped.
pmc-13603632:
Xiangcheng Lei and colleagues test how magnesium ion dose steers the many cell types that rebuild bone. Magnesium-releasing implants are popular in bone repair, yet the concentration that helps one cell type may not suit another. Biomaterial designers lack agreed ranges. The team exposed bone regeneration cells to graded magnesium levels and measured behavior changes with dose, hunting for effective windows for each cell kind.

Bone defects from trauma, large segment loss, or osteoporosis often heal slowly and incompletely, the authors note, and simply pushing bone formation is not enough. Blood vessel growth, nerve involvement, and immune conditions all shape repair. Their concentration-response results offer preliminary in-vitro guidance for magnesium-releasing materials with controlled ion output. The goal is implants whose release is tuned to each cell type's biology rather than set by guesswork.
pmc-13604332:
Yui Uekusa and ten co-authors tested how a signaling protein drives swelling in joint lining cells from knee osteoarthritis patients, in twenty twenty-six. The protein, interleukin-24, is found in the joint lining and has been tied to pain severity in women with the disease. The team took lining cells from patients having knee replacement and dosed them with the protein.

Gene reads found dozens of genes switched on at six and twenty-four hours, clustering in swelling pathways. The protein raised output of several swelling signals in a dose- and time-linked way. Two blocker drugs, aimed at pathways named STAT3 and p38 MAPK, were used to test which routes carry the signal. The work marks interleukin-24 as a direct driver of swelling in these cells, which may open new treatment angles for the disease.
pmc-13605032:
Orlando Meneses Quelal, David Pilamunga Hurtado, and Marco Burbano Pulles review AI food fraud detection in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Food fraud, from watered oils to swapped species, may cost billions yearly worldwide. Labs increasingly pair smart algorithms with instruments to catch it. The authors ask a sharper question: does detection become prevention in the real supply chain? They screened recent literature and kept eighty-three records.

Most work stops at showing a model can spot fraud in the lab. Field use faces cost, speed, and trust barriers the papers rarely face. The review names the structural blocks between demo and deployment. Food safety agencies and industry labs are the readers. The gap framing could redirect research money.
pmc-13605932:
Kailin Li and co-authors report food research from two thousand twenty-six on a new gel added to bread. The gel mixes fine powder from bamboo shoot shells with a seaweed-based thickener. Bread quality depends on its inner structure and on how water and flavor compounds move inside it.

The team added the gel at several levels and measured texture, color, taste, and storage changes. The gel formed a denser, more stretchy network than the thickener alone. Bread with the gel was softer, lost water more slowly, and kept its spring for longer in storage. A level of ten percent worked best for structure. The results offer a use for a bamboo waste product.
pmc-13607232:
Giannousi and co-authors test manganese nanoparticles that keep insulin from clumping in this 2026 study. Insulin can fold into amyloid fibers, a problem for diabetes therapy and drug handling. The team coated several manganese compounds with polyol layers to make them compatible.

They used a fresh insulin aspart product and an aged insulin glargine product already holding aggregates. Every particle delayed the start of fiber growth in the fresh system. One stretched the lag from about 21 hours to over 105 hours. In the aged system, small negatively charged particles restarted a lag and slowed further clumping. The best dispersed particles also acted as antioxidant nanozymes, cutting amyloid signal to about 40 percent.
pmc-13610032:
Yukinori Nagakura, Fumiko Yamaki, Hiroshi Saimaru, Kou Hiroya, and Koji Ichinose study how attendance mode relates to learning in a pharmacy exam course in work dated two thousand twenty-six. The four-month course used a flexible format: students could attend in person, live online, or mix the two. All groups got the same content and tests.

Students who came in person gained more over the course than online or mixed peers. Their pass rate on the national pharmacist exam was also higher, though that gap did not reach a clear level. Since students picked their own mode, keen students may cluster in person. The authors note that gains during a course may not carry to the final exam without support after it ends.
pmc-13612332:
Xinning Ren leads an eight-author team reviewing a delivery trick borrowed from herbal brewing itself. When Chinese medicinal herbs are decocted, their ingredients assemble into nanoscale aggregates. For ischemic stroke, where the blood-brain barrier blocks nearly all drugs, these natural assemblies could carry medicine straight to damaged brain tissue. The review maps the penumbra's chemistry and its carriers.

The injured region is acidic, rich in reactive oxygen species, and loaded with matrix metalloproteinases. Each signal can trigger the aggregates to fall apart and release their cargo on site. The authors detail four barrier-crossing mechanisms, from sugar-mediated self-targeting to co-assembly with aromatic herbs. Preclinical studies of key ingredients and herb pairs follow. Bottlenecks get an honest hearing: batch consistency, safety, and scale-up all lag. The review closes with directions for turning a decoction phenomenon into precision stroke therapy.
pmc-13612432:
Migraines that ride the menstrual cycle are common and hard to treat, and Kun Hong led a team that lays out a trial of press-needle therapy timed to the cycle. Seventy-six women aged eighteen to forty-five will be split at random between the needle treatment and a standard pain drug, naproxen. The needles, tiny and left in place at set points, are applied in rounds before and after each period, over three cycles.

The main yardstick is the change in days per cycle with at least moderate headache pain. Secondary measures cover pain strength, life quality, rescue drug use, and heart rhythm signs, with blood markers and brain scans as extras. The protocol is a pilot: its numbers will size a later, larger trial.
pmc-13613532:
Giuseppe Panuccio and co-authors pool, in a 2026 review, studies on using imaging from inside the artery to guide stent work in hardened heart arteries. Calcium makes such work hard, and it is unclear which guidance method serves best. The team compared ultrasound guidance, light-based guidance, and plain X-ray guidance across ten studies.

More than four thousand patients were included in the pooled data. Both imaging methods cut major heart events by roughly a third or more versus X-ray guidance alone. Stent clotting was also far lower with either imaging method. The two imaging tools did not differ clearly from each other. The authors back routine imaging guidance for calcified lesions.
pmc-13613632:
Shaobo Cao and ten co-authors hunt left fat-linked signs that guess heart hits past leg artery fix in limb artery ill. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Such folks stay at high heart risk past fix, and plain fat reads lose their edge when fat drugs run wide. One hundred sixty-five folks had blood protein and waste reads drawn at fix.

A fat-linked gene web split folks in two kinds with split fate: one kind's heart-hit free span ran far short. A tight score of one protein and four waste parts split the kinds and tied to hits on its own. The score read hits with strong truth at past a year.
pmc-13614832:
Jiayu Yan and co-authors present a review dated 2026 on incretin hormones in women's diseases. Incretins are gut hormones, chiefly GLP-1 and GIP, best known for controlling blood sugar. Obesity, a global health problem, is closely tied to several gynecological disorders, including polycystic ovary syndrome and womb cancer.

The authors searched three databases for work from 1995 onward. Evidence shows the hormones also tune inflammation, cell recycling, immune responses, and gut-brain signaling. Drugs that mimic GLP-1 are already common in diabetes and weight care. The review weighs what they might offer for ovary, womb, and related conditions. It sums up mechanisms and treatment promise across the field, based on original studies and major reviews.
pmc-13614932:
Raphaël Charron and coauthors report a 2026 study of how Escherichia coli living in surface films adapts to disinfectants used daily in food plants, and whether that adaptation also blunts antibiotics. The team grew the bacteria as biofilms, the slimy layers that cling to equipment, and exposed them for a month to four disinfectant agents. They then checked for resistant variants and traced the genetic and protein changes behind any shift in drug response.

Two agents raised the rise of variants resistant to rifampicin, an antibiotic. Variants picked by one agent, a diamine disinfectant, repeatedly carried changes in genes that build the outer coat molecule lipopolysaccharide, with a more negative cell surface and lower membrane leakiness. Protein work showed the cells rerouted coat-building sugars toward colanic acid, a slime component, which thickened the film and raised tolerance.
pmc-13616332:
Zhuorui Wen leads a team coaxing high performance out of violet phosphorene. This layered form of phosphorus is tipped for future electronics. Adding tellurium atoms cuts the resistance where metal contacts meet the sheet. Two-dimensional materials promise tiny devices, yet phosphorene transistors usually need protective, air-free handling, and their measured charge speed falls far below the true value because contacts choke the flow.

Tellurium doping kept the violet crystal structure intact, with tellurium taking one specific phosphorus seat, as X-ray analysis of grown crystals showed. Devices could then be measured in open air and delivered high charge mobility. Relieving the contact bottleneck, rather than changing the sheet itself, shows how much of a new material's promise hides in its wiring, a lesson for every flat crystal now in development.
pmc-13616632:
Alessandra Buja and co-authors published this cancer registry study in 2026. It asks how other cancers already present when melanoma is found affect a patient's outlook and costs. Using the cancer registry of Italy's Veneto region, the team identified melanoma cases from 2019 and 2021. They then flagged patients who had another primary cancer in the five years before the melanoma diagnosis.

Of 2,978 melanoma patients, 134, or about 4.5 percent, had such an earlier cancer. The most common sites were the prostate, breast, colon, and kidney. The study set up survival comparisons between patients with and without earlier cancers, using standard survival models. It also tracked three years of health care costs from the health system's point of view. The work speaks to how cancer services should plan for patients who arrive with a double disease burden.
pmc-13617032:
Sara Lettieri and fourteen co-authors present a 2026 study on monthly cell therapy for failing lung transplants. Chronic lung allograft dysfunction is the main cause of late illness and death after lung transplant, with few treatment options. Mesenchymal stromal cells can calm immune attack and support repair. The team gave monthly infusions of donor bone marrow cells to six patients whose disease had resisted standard care.

The patients received 251 infusions in all, with follow-up up to fifty-eight months. All six were alive at two years, and no infusion-related toxicity appeared. Infection rates did not rise clearly, though the group was too small to rule out risk. Lung function kept declining but at a slower rate after treatment began. The authors judge long-term monthly dosing feasible and safe. They stress the lung findings are exploratory and need larger trials.
pmc-13617232:
Steph Sloan, Jane Sadler, and Sharleen Woods evaluate a new outcome measurement tool piloted by dietitians in a community eating disorder service. Dietitians are central to eating disorder treatment, yet their impact is seldom recorded in a structured way. The six-month pilot in 2024 combined tool data from one hundred two patients with interviews of the dietitians using it.

Restrictive eating patterns and malnutrition were the most common concerns, and improving nutritional status was the most frequent goal. Outcome status was recorded for only a little over half of patients, and among those, just under half fully met their recorded outcome. Dietitians backed routine monitoring for showing their professional value, but time pressure and poor fit with digital systems blocked fuller use. The authors recommend clearer outcome definitions and better electronic integration to cut clinician burden.
pmc-13617332:
Xiaofeng Zeng and three co-authors review new blood markers for death risk in heart failure in a paper from 2026. Standard markers capture only part of the risk, since death in heart failure grows out of many body systems at once, above all in older patients. The review groups markers by the pathway they reflect, from heart strain and scarring to vessel aging and kidney reserve.

Aging itself shifts marker levels through low-grade inflammation, stiff vessels, and slower clearance, so cut points need care. The authors propose a pathway-based frame for reading several markers together. They stress that the frame is a concept to be tested, not a proven clinical tool.
pmc-13617832:
Fardowso Mohamed Harbi and three colleagues argue that Somalia's sudden aid cuts have become a primary health-care crisis in their own right. Somalia's health system leans heavily on outside financing while drought, displacement, outbreaks, and malnutrition keep needs climbing. The authors contend that funding volatility itself acts as a driver of health system failure, not merely a budget problem in the background.

They cite 2025 service suspensions across eight hospitals, forty primary facilities, and sixteen mobile teams in twenty-one districts. The suspensions affected roughly three hundred fifty thousand people, alongside closure of more than three hundred nutrition centers. Such shocks destabilize staffing, medicine supplies, referrals, surveillance, and continuity of care, hitting children and displaced communities hardest. Their prescriptions include protecting essential primary care, strengthening government stewardship, and arranging steady transition financing before shocks harden into lasting crises.
pmc-13619932:
Junbao Zhang and co-authors published this lung study in 2026. Lung nodules found on scans may be early, mild growths or true invasive cancer, and telling them apart before surgery is hard. The team built an AI system that joins CT image traits with clinical facts. They gathered 1,179 nodules with known outcomes from one center.

Image traits came from a frozen vision model, then a trained probe summed each nodule's slices. A fusion step let image and clinic data weigh each other before the call. Across held-out folds, the system scored well, with accuracy near eighty-one percent. It beat a clinic-only model and a standard score, though not image-only builds by a clear edge. The authors require tests at other centers before clinic use.
pmc-13620832:
May Abiad and eight colleagues used a national hospital database to give low-lying placenta its own risk profile, separate from the more dangerous placenta previa. New diagnostic codes introduced in 2017 finally let researchers split the two conditions, where the placenta sits low in the womb or covers the cervix outright. Their analysis covered more than five point six million single-baby deliveries from 2017 to 2019.

Bleeding struck about a fifth of low-lying placenta deliveries, against a small fraction with normal placement, and severe maternal complications more than doubled. Transfusion and womb removal also ran higher, stays lasted a day longer, and bills grew. Adjusted models kept the risks clearly raised, though previa still doubled them again. The authors say a low-lying placenta should no longer be filed as a minor variant: delivery planning needs to respect its real hemorrhage risk.
pmc-13621332:
Nico Bruder, Jan Meis, Maximilian Pilz, and Meinhard Kieser wrote a practical guide to designing adaptive two-stage clinical trials that squeeze the most from limited patients. Adaptive trials can resize themselves at an interim look, which protects both resources and conclusions. Choosing the best design settings means minimizing something like expected enrollment while holding error rates firm, yet older guidance covered mostly normal-shaped data or binary outcomes handled by brute force.

The guide shows how standard test statistics behave close enough to normal curves that the same optimization machinery extends to yes-or-no outcomes and time-to-event outcomes. Worked results show tuned designs cutting expected sample sizes and raising the power left after the interim look, compared with standard sequential plans. A warning section flags traps in two-sided testing. The authors aim the guidance squarely at rare disease research, where every patient counts.
pmc-13623932:
Yuan and eight co-authors test a simple blood ratio in heart failure, in work from twenty twenty-six. The ratio joins two routine tests: alkaline phosphatase and albumin. The team asked if it links to death within ninety days of hospital admission.

Records came from a heart failure database in Zigong, China, with about two thousand patients. Most had the data needed to compute the ratio and a known outcome. Only a small number of deaths were recorded, which limits certainty. Models adjusted for age, sex, and key heart and kidney measures. The authors favor using the ratio as a continuous measure, not a single cut off.
pmc-13624132:
Rongquan Chen, Zhijin Hu, Yan Lin, Xiaoying Wu, Binlian Liu, and Wenqing Zhang compare breathing tubes in keyhole heart surgery in a paper from 2026. Double-lumen tubes allow one-lung ventilation but can injure airways and lungs. The study reviewed one hundred seventy-six adults at one center. One group used a single-lumen tube with brief, controlled lung collapse when exposure demanded it. The other used the double-lumen standard throughout.

Lung complications hit twenty-nine percent of the single-lumen group versus fifty-six percent of the other. Infections and lung collapse were both less common. Airway problems also fell, and ventilation and intensive care times were shorter. Setup before incision was faster too. The authors call for prospective trials to confirm the advantage.
pmc-13626232:
Elizabeth F Smith, Callan Lavery, and Shannon J Simpson examine the young lungs of adults born far too early. Up to half of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease begins with poor lung growth. The illness, called COPD, is a long-term breathing condition. Being born before thirty-seven weeks is now a recognized cause in the 2023 global guideline update. Extremely early birth has been tied to many-fold higher odds of a COPD label in young adults, yet the early warning states remain uncounted in this group.

Their study describes those states, pre-COPD, where symptoms or scans warn before breathing tests fail, and PRISm, where one key measure drops while its ratio stays normal. Both flag people headed for trouble who might gain from close follow-up. Counting them in a well-described cohort of very preterm survivors fills a blank in lifelong lung care.
pmc-13627032:
Quanyou Miao and seven co-authors built a model to predict early return of liver cancer after surgery, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The cancer often comes back within two years of tumor removal, which limits lasting control. Their model uses scans taken before surgery plus routine lab and clinical factors.

Data came from two hospitals in China, one to build the model and one to test it. More than half the patients saw the cancer return early. Six factors stayed in the final model, including tumor size, spread into nearby vessels, and a blood marker level. The model scored well at the second hospital, though its raw risk levels ran high for low-risk patients.
pmc-13627132:
Jaysson T Brooks and nine colleagues, publishing in 2026, test whether children can have spine screws guided without a radiation-heavy CT scan. Their method converts an MRI into a synthetic CT that navigation machines can read. Twenty young patients had posterior spinal fusions this way. These were the first such cases in the United States in 2025. Radiation was compared with matched groups treated by freehand fluoroscopy or by a true CT paired with the same navigation.

Children averaged about fourteen years old, and 335 screws were placed. The synthetic route exposed patients to under a fifth of the radiation of the true CT route, a cut of over eighty percent, while fluoroscopy still checked key levels. For growing bodies that will be scanned for life, trading CT for MRI guidance is a meaningful saving.
pmc-13627432:
Alba Sanchez-Gil and co-authors lay out a trial plan to help family caregivers of people with dementia, in work from twenty twenty-six. Caregivers face long physical and mental strain that can wear down strength and raise anxiety. Past work tested exercise and relaxation apart, but few plans join the two.

The trial will enroll sixty-two caregivers and split them by chance into two groups. One group gets strength training plus muscle relaxation for ten weeks. The other gets relaxation alone. The main check is leg strength and balance at ten weeks, with grip, anxiety, burden, and safety also tracked. A later check comes at three months. Results should show if the joint plan works and is safe.
pmc-13628032:
Chaudhary and six co-authors surveyed in twenty twenty-six women in Louisiana on health apps for use in pregnancy. Such apps can aid care before and after birth, but what drives their use is not clear. They ran a ten-minute web survey with near six hundred women in the state.

Most who were asked said they were apt to load such an app, and many felt sure on a healthy weight in pregnancy. Two known apps were the most used so far. Stress and mind health, plus which foods are safe, ranked as top needs. Trait and price picks were also mapped in the survey.
pmc-13629932:
Batoul Hojeij and sixteen colleagues set out the protocol for the PDPID study, an international effort to catch psoriatic arthritis flares early using phones and smartwatches. Psoriatic arthritis flares arrive unpredictably and erode quality of life, while their triggers remain poorly understood.

Over twelve months across four countries, patients will attend regular clinic visits plus extra visits when flares strike, pressing a flare button in a study app at any time. The app gathers questionnaires, photo and video tests, and passive sensor data, while clinics collect saliva DNA, gut microbiome samples, hair cortisol, and inflammation markers alongside weather and pollution exposure. Machine learning models will fuse these streams to detect and predict flares.
pmc-13630232:
Elizabeth Opiyo Onyango and four colleagues examined how COVID-19 control rules landed on women who sell food in Kisumu, Kenya. These women trade informally, outside formal shops. Fieldwork in 2024 blended key informant and deep interviews. Four focus groups joined them. A review of four policy documents rounded out the study.

Vendors had been shut out of choices made by technical experts and national officials. The resulting rules ignored their layered identities and daily realities. Uneven enforcement deepened their exposure as women. They faced harassment, extortion, and assault while keeping city households fed. The authors urge city and national authorities to build standing consultation channels. Vendors should shape emergency policy through them. They present the framework as a portable tool for equity-focused health research.
pmc-13630432:
Ashraf Soliman and five colleagues review unexplained short stature in the genomic era. Their study appeared in 2026. The label covers short children whose standard workup finds no cause. The authors argue it should be a working label, not a final diagnosis. Modern testing keeps moving these children into defined genetic disorders.

Test yield climbs steeply with test power. It runs from single-gene checks through chromosome arrays and panels to full exome sequencing. The strongest route solves roughly a third of cases. Recurring culprits include genes shaping the growth plate and the growth hormone path. Brain imaging findings are usually unhelpful. Growth hormone response depends on the gene fault. Some defects respond robustly and others modestly. Careful trait mapping anchors their advice. So does honest handling of unclear variants.
pmc-13631132:
Eduardo José Carcausto Huamaní and two colleagues adapted a lifestyle questionnaire for Peruvian adults with type 2 diabetes. They checked whether its scores can be trusted. Their study appeared in 2026. The tool, IMEVID, spans diet, activity, emotions, and self-management. The team worried a single total score could blur distinct behaviours.

One hundred eighty adults completed the adapted version. Expert judges strongly endorsed its content. Overall reliability was acceptable, though single domains varied. Modelling rejected a single underlying dimension. It supported the first seven-domain structure instead. The authors recommend reporting domain scores side by side. They caution that ceiling effects and the modest sample make the structural findings early ones. Larger validation should come first.
pmc-13631932:
Krista Whitley and six colleagues modeled where extra spending could cut mothers' deaths most in the Philippines. National figures have improved, yet women in poor, rural, and conflict-affected regions still die far more often around childbirth. The team used a United Nations equity tool to compare regions against the national benchmark. They then costed three packages of care through the year 2030.

One package upgrades emergency obstetric and newborn care in local facilities. Another guarantees steady supplies of key medicines, including drugs that stop bleeding and treat dangerous seizures. The third widens access to modern contraception for teenagers, poor households, and women with many children. Together the packages could prevent roughly one thousand to twenty-five hundred maternal deaths. Contraception came out cheapest for each year of healthy life gained.
pmc-13632832:
Joshua Kayiwa and colleagues reviewed how fast Uganda spotted and answered a cross-border outbreak of Bundibugyo virus disease in 2026. The disease is a form of Ebola with no licensed vaccine or drug. Uganda and its neighbor the Democratic Republic of the Congo declared linked outbreaks in May 2026. The reviewers used a framework that allows seven days to detect an outbreak, one day to notify, and seven days to finish early response steps.

By early July, Uganda had recorded twenty confirmed cases, most imported, with a fatality rate well below earlier outbreaks of this virus. The country beat all three timing targets, detecting the outbreak in six days and finishing early actions in two. Slow clinical suspicion, patchy cross-border data sharing, and late community engagement still caused friction. Strong leadership and coordination were the most praised supports. The review names what to fix before the next emergency.
pmc-13633832:
Ajay Ramesh leads a team with a hidden retrocaval ureter case. Their case from twenty twenty-six deals with a man of seventy. He had long term right loin pain that came and went.

Scans showed a swollen kidney and a tight junction that blocked flow. That block masked a second flaw: the ureter ran behind a vein. Both flaws in one non doubled system is very rare. Signs on scans hinted at the hidden vein course. Robot surgery found the ureter behind the big vein. Cutting that segment did not free the kidney, they report.
pmc-13636132:
Thomas Hummel and eleven colleagues report five-year results, in a study written in German, on varicose vein surgery done to one standard. The operation ties off and strips the great saphenous vein where it meets the deep vein in the groin. Veins returning at that junction are costly and common in vein practice. Six German vein centers enrolled four hundred five patients covering five hundred nineteen legs, all treated with one standardized technique.

Just over half the patients returned for the five-year check. Visible varicose veins had come back in a small share of legs. True groin recurrences were rare; only two mattered. Most returns traced to leaky perforating veins elsewhere, not the groin work. The authors credit fine details of the standard: tying tiny side branches near the junction and closing a fascial layer as a barrier. Five years out, they call the results excellent.
pmc-13642532:
Yadong Yue led a 2026 photonics study that splits chirality from topology in Janus bound states in the continuum, gaining a control knob for one-way devices. Janus bound states carry different topological charges on their two sides, but in earlier designs chirality stayed tied to those charges, limiting freedom. The team built a bilayer photonic crystal combining a symmetric slab with a magneto-optical slab. It broke time-reversal symmetry with a magnetic field.

When symmetry broke, matched bound states in the magneto-optical slab split into opposite chiral modes. Handedness was steered by the field's direction and strength. Simulations showed charges and chiral modes varying on their own in far-field light patterns and in the motion of chiral points as slab separation changed. Device designers get a route to twist-dependent parts and uneven light-matter effects, where topology and handedness can be tuned separately.
pmc-13643332:
Chryso Lambride and three colleagues present a computer modeling study of cerebral autoregulation, the brain's ability to hold its blood flow steady as pressure swings. How local vessel responses combine across whole networks to protect the brain, and what fails after stroke, stayed unclear.

Simulations on realistic microvascular networks showed regulation is a team effort led by surface arteries, which buffer pressure for wide territories. Denser arterial networks resisted pressure shocks better. After stroke, faulty vessel reactivity, more than collateral routes, drove harmful overperfusion during reopening. Keeping vessel muscle tone intact emerges as a possible way to limit reperfusion injury.
pmc-13644032:
Ling Shi and nine colleagues present a 2026 UK Biobank study testing the obesity paradox in stroke, the claim that heavier patients somehow fare better. Earlier work leaned only on body mass index, so this team added waist, ratio, and body fat measures.

Among 502,128 participants, stroke incidence and death were lowest in the lean-normal BMI band and rose on both sides. Other fat measures tracked stroke risk in steadier straight lines. Within stroke patients, no measure tied obesity to stroke-specific death after adjustment, which argues against a true paradox. The authors note that stroke severity and care details were missing.
pmc-13646332:
Mohamed and co-authors published a 2026 randomized trial testing whether feijoa fruit powder helps prevent type 2 diabetes. Low-energy diets already cut weight and improve risk markers, and the polyphenol-rich powder might add benefit. Ninety-seven adults with overweight and prediabetes took either the powder or a placebo daily for six months. The first two months paired the doses with a strict diet, followed by four months of advice to hold the loss.

Both groups lost weight on the diet, then slowly regained some. The powder made no difference to weight or fasting blood sugar over the six months. One signal stood out: systolic blood pressure fell more in the powder group, with a gap at months four and six. The authors suggest the fruit's compounds may help blood vessels, and call the result a lead for further study.
pmc-13647132:
Qi Ai, Wen Chen, and Qinhui Tuo review a gut protein called RELMβ that can protect the intestine yet also shows up in diseases far beyond it. The protein is made by goblet cells lining the gut, and its level answers to microbes, gene programs, and immune signals. Lab studies show it can puncture the membranes of susceptible bacteria. Mouse work ties it to keeping microbes at a safe distance from the gut wall and to fighting worms.

Beyond the gut, the protein has been linked with lung vessel remodeling, fatty liver disease, artery hardening, aneurysm, and some cancers. The authors stress that causal proof comes mostly from rodents, while human evidence is thinner. They propose a framework that weighs where the protein is made, how it assembles, and what partners surround it. That lens, they argue, can explain why one protein helps in one tissue and harms in another.
pmc-13648132:
Breathing illness after a lithium hydroxide dust leak at a battery plant is documented by Lee and colleagues. Reactive airways dysfunction syndrome is an acute form of irritant-induced asthma. It follows a single heavy exposure to an irritant, yet no prior case series had linked it to lithium hydroxide dust. The team evaluated sixteen workers with symptoms after a connector failure spilled tens of kilograms of powder at a Korean cathode facility in March 2024.

Most workers reported cough and sputum. Over half had symptoms worsening at night or early morning, while bronchial challenge testing was positive in three of ten tested workers. By standard criteria, one case counted as definite, four as probable, six as possible, and five as unlikely. Lee and colleagues argue that lithium hydroxide's alkalinity injures airways, and clinicians should consider this syndrome after alkaline dust exposure even when tests look normal.
pmc-13648232:
Hanzhong Zheng and six colleagues estimate how much biodiversity loss could be avoided if consumers actually followed their stated intentions to eat more plant-based meals. Earlier assessments often assumed ideal diets, which can overstate gains, so this team surveyed consumers in the Netherlands, Britain, and the United States.

Over half of respondents had no intention to cut meat or dairy at all. Among those planning swaps, the biodiversity footprint of main-meal meat could fall by up to about a third, but averaged across everyone the reduction was far smaller. Dairy alternatives showed a mixed picture, especially in the United States. The authors conclude that closing the intention gap remains a major challenge.
pmc-13648532:
Saija M. Niemi and two colleagues test how past sights bias present orientation judgements, asking whether a short-term pull toward recent stimuli builds into a longer-term pull toward the average. Perception researchers call the first effect serial dependence and the second central tendency bias, and some models treat them as one mechanism.

Volunteers judged orientations drawn either from a full circle or from a restricted slice. They showed a bias away from cardinal directions and a pull toward the previous stimulus in both settings, yet no central tendency appeared. Instead, judgements leaned away from the centre of the restricted range. The authors argue the two biases need separate explanations and that stimulus geometry matters.
pmc-13649232:
Tuğba Atak and Tuba Betül Karadeniz ask acne patients how they use AI tools for health help. Acne scars the skin and weighs on the mind, so fast phone advice tempts many. The study covered 123 adults with acne and web access, plus a doctor's skin check for each.

Near half had asked an AI tool for health help before they saw a doctor. Speed of access drove most of that use. Still, two in three said a doctor must check any AI advice first. Over half feared wrong calls, and near half balked at sharing photos. Skin severity did not drive use at all. The authors want AI kept as a watched aid, not a doctor swap.
pmc-13649432:
Alexandra Vrabie and colleagues followed 147 patients with lupus kidney disease at one centre to find what best predicts long-term outcomes. Care has improved, yet kidney failure and death remain too common in this group. They tracked response at 6 and 12 months and a combined bad outcome of doubled blood waste levels, kidney failure, or death.

Older age, high urine protein at the start, and low blood haemoglobin each raised the risk. The strongest shield was cutting urine protein below a set level by month 12, which about half of patients reached. A score built from these facts sorted risk well, and adding the 12-month result made it sharper. The score still needs outside checks.
pmc-13649732:
Sewon Oh and five colleagues share an open bank of clips that can trigger misophonia, in a 2026 paper. In this state, plain sounds like chewing or tapping spark rage and dread far past their size. Labs had no shared, true-to-life sets to test with, which held the field back.

The bank holds over 1,400 clips, each five seconds long, in twelve trigger classes drawn from past proof. It ranges past mouth sounds to chirps, taps, and more. Each clip pairs sight with sound, so labs can test how the seen scene bends the heard blow. The authors hope the set speeds lab work, cross-site checks, and machine tools that flag triggers.
pmc-13650432:
Arij El Haddouchi and nine colleagues review what genes and gene regulation contribute to endurance performance, the capacity that separates elite distance athletes. Endurance is plainly many-gene and many-factor, shaped by inheritance interacting with training, so the review gathers candidate gene studies, genome-wide scans, and pooled analyses.

More than forty gene variants have been tied to endurance traits, and a handful recur across studies, touching oxygen transport, energy production in mitochondria, fuel metabolism, and muscle fiber makeup. One iron-related variant stood out as a strong predictor. Training also rewrites gene activity through chemical DNA marks and small regulatory RNAs that respond to exercise. Fewer than a small subset of the hundreds of variants linked to athlete status replicate consistently, which pushes the authors toward combined multi-layer studies and training plans tailored to the individual.
pmc-13650532:
Ramzi Hazboun and six colleagues review why serious chest and mediastinal conditions are diagnosed late in young adults. Doctors often rate young patients as low risk, and vague symptoms, thinking traps, and system delays combine to postpone recognition of diseases that punish waiting.

Five conditions illustrate different delay patterns. They are a torn esophagus, hidden diaphragm injuries after trauma, germ cell tumors of the mediastinum, airway tumors mistaken for asthma, and Hodgkin lymphoma appearing as a chest mass. That lymphoma mimics other tumors and needs tissue sampling to prove. Hours of delay matter most for perforations and mechanical emergencies, where contamination and deterioration advance, while slow tumors mainly suffer added complexity and burden. The authors name anchoring and premature closure among the thinking traps, plus limited imaging access and slow referrals. They note that much evidence comes from wider adult groups rather than young cohorts.
pmc-13651032:
Luisa Pucci Bueno Borges led a 2026 veterinary study comparing three laparoscopic liver biopsy tools in buffaloes, where no standardized instrument comparison existed. Liver biopsy guides diagnosis of hepatobiliary disease in ruminants, and laparoscopy offers direct viewing with less trauma, yet cattle protocols may not transfer to buffalo anatomy. The team performed biopsies on five healthy female buffaloes through a right intercostal approach, taking sequential samples with Babcock forceps, laparoscopic biopsy forceps, and a 14-gauge tru-cut needle.

The tru-cut needle gave adequate-quality samples in every case, against 80 percent for laparoscopic forceps and 60 percent for Babcock forceps. Sufficiency matched that pattern, edge detachment was lowest with the needle, and crush artifact appeared in none of the needle samples but in 60 percent of forceps samples. Veterinarians get a clear instrument recommendation for buffaloes, tempered by the tiny sample and fixed sampling order, which limit generalization to sick animals.
pmc-13652532:
Roberto Dias de Oliveira and two colleagues write an editorial on nursing inside the Brazilian prison system. Prisons across Latin America suffer chronic overcrowding and poor sanitation, and Brazil holds one of the largest prison populations in the world. Within those walls, nurses are often the only health workers present, carrying the duty to turn a constitutional right to health into real care for people deprived of liberty.

That duty runs into structural, organizational, and security barriers every day, from scarce supplies to custody rules that override clinical judgment. The authors argue that strengthening prison nursing is urgent and basic, not optional. Their reflection speaks to health managers and policymakers who decide staffing and resources. It frames prison health as a test of whether the right to care applies to everyone or only to those outside the gates.
pmc-13664432:
Márk Matus and seven co-authors test a brain scan marker for surgical risk in a study from two thousand twenty-six. During carotid surgery, clamping the artery can starve the brain of oxygen. Usual risk checks lean on anatomy and predict poorly.

Fifty-eight patients had white matter disease graded on pre-surgery MRI and brain oxygen watched during clamping.
