Worse white matter scores on the opposite side predicted deeper oxygen drops in the first two minutes, even after age and other factors were counted. The model explained only a small share of the variation. The authors say small vessel disease dulls the brain's tolerance of brief ischemia. A simple scan grade could sharpen consent and monitoring plans.
pmc-13666832:
Matteo Bizzotto led a 2026 study of how infection before birth reshapes offspring brain development through type I interferon signaling and the microglial receptor TREM2. Immune activation before birth raises risk of brain development disorders, yet the chain from the mother's signal to the offspring synapse was unclear. The team used a mouse model in which a viral mimic, poly(I:C), triggers immunity before birth, then tracked gene activity, synapses, and microglia in young offspring.

It rose, nerve gene paths and excitatory synapse balance were disrupted, and offspring microglia showed lower TREM2, weaker eating of debris, and a muted immune response. A muted immune pattern also appeared in schizophrenia tissue after death. Blocking that signaling before birth restored synaptic defects and TREM2 function. Researchers get a treatment lead: watching interferon responses before birth and fixing faulty chains in newborns might lessen brain development harm.
pmc-13671032:
Adam DeCosta, Rebecca Barrick, and Julia Kardon study a tail piece that steers the unfoldase ClpX in mitochondria. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. ClpX is a force motor that pulls proteins open so they can be cut or switched on. Its form in mitochondria holds an extra insert on the face that meets substrates, which the bacterial form lacks.

The insert proves key to draw in and switch on ALAS, the first enzyme of heme build, in yeast. In the human pair, it is not needed for guided disposal of ALAS, but it helps grip a plain test substrate. Small tweaks split its grip role from its push on the motor's fuel burn. The insert can thus both fetch a substrate and speed its run through the motor.
pmc-13677632:
Marco Battistelli and co-authors looked for what drives neck pain in people with age-related neck spine wear but no deformity, in a study published in 2026. One hundred thirty patients at two Italian university hospitals were assessed before surgery. Records combined pain scores, mental health and personality surveys, and a battery of spine alignment measures from standing X-rays.

Only one alignment measure, the curve between the top two neck bones, stayed clearly tied to severe pain after full comparison. Several mood-related scales also separated patients with moderate-to-severe pain from the rest, and two of them tracked pain scores directly. The alignment measure itself moved opposite to pain in the correlation checks. The authors argue neck pain in this group is a mind-and-posture story, not a simple wear story.
pmc-13679732:
Tu and four co-authors review ways to make tiny light-driven motors run on mild light in this twenty twenty-six paper. These motors turn light into a one-way spin at the scale of single molecules. Most past motors need harsh UV light, which can harm cells and soft goods and limits real use.

Inside, the review sorts the main design tricks that shift motor action into plain light and near heat-ray bands. Mild light lets motors work in safer and more useful settings, from smart cloth to care for the body. The authors also list what still blocks wide use. They close with paths toward motors that are faster, stronger, and able to do more than one job.
pmc-13680832:
Ryan Finnel and co-authors (2026) studied two DNA enhancers that control the gene Sox17 in early mouse development. The gene guides a group of starter cells that can become either pancreas or bile system tissue. The team found two enhancers far from the gene and deleted each one with CRISPR editing. Deleting either enhancer lowered the gene's activity for a time. That delay kept the starter cells undecided longer, shrinking the pancreas and enlarging the gallbladder.

Deleting both enhancers lowered activity further and delayed both fates, shrinking both organs. Crossing the deletions onto a background with no working copy of the gene exposed sharp sensitivity in the bile system. Outcomes ranged from a small gallbladder to a missing one and blocked bile ducts. The authors conclude the two enhancers add their effects, and that the starter cells read the gene's dose carefully. Different organs need different thresholds at different times.
pmc-13686932:
Olivia Venezia and co-authors show that fused mRNAs make working proteins in mammalian immunity. Most mRNAs were thought to come from one gene locus each. Whether distant genes could splice into joint messages stayed unclear. Their pipeline pairs long-read RNA reads with checks to find such fusions in macrophages.

Inflammation pulls far genes close in the nucleus, which sets up the fusions. One fusion joins a pore-forming protein gene with a second gene read out of frame. Its protein speeds pore opening and boosts release of a key alarm signal. Mice lacking it survived sepsis better but fought bacteria worse. Extra copies flipped both effects, showing a balance role in defense.
pmc-13689332:
Ravi Sonani and co-authors wrote a 2026 paper on two workhorse enzymes that unexpectedly form long chains. Enzymes sometimes join into polymers to switch their activity on or off. Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team found that two enzymes used daily in labs, alkaline phosphatase and proteinase K, can link into filaments no one had planned.

Their atomic models show how the units stack. What the chaining does for the living cell is still unknown. The find also shows off the microscope method: it can reveal detailed structures of assemblies that were never purified, even ones hiding as contaminants in a sample. The paper invites a second look at other common enzymes for the same surprise.
pmc-13689832:
Nils Mutschler and Johann Maierl map the root and build of the arm nerve web in the alpaca. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Six beasts aged one day to past teen were cut and read. In five, the web formed from the low three neck roots; in one, a chest root joined too.

Roots ran through neck muscles, the low neck one lone, then joined to trunks and two cords. Shoulder nerves bore the mid root most. The mid arm nerve drew from all three roots by a loop join. Few roots may tie to the long neck bones, the team say. Cuts and blocks gain.
pmc-4779832:
Zhang, Wang, Vikash, and their colleagues reviewed reactive oxygen species signaling in 2016. Reactive oxygen species, or ROS, are reactive molecules made in cells. It has long been known that a rise in ROS can modify signaling proteins and change what cells do.

The review traces how ROS-mediated signaling works in healthy cells and how it can go wrong. Excess ROS is tied to diseases such as atherosclerosis, diabetes, unchecked growth, and degeneration of nerves, plus inflammation. Cells also use controlled ROS as messengers, so the balance matters. Understanding that balance guides antioxidant and signaling research.
pmc-7402632:
Jérémie Hadjadj and colleagues reported in 2020 that patients with severe COVID-19 share a telling immune weakness. Interferons are the body's first alarm proteins against viruses, and type I interferons switch on a battery of antiviral genes. In these severely ill patients, that alarm was unusually faint, while inflammation elsewhere in the body ran high.

The team measured interferon activity and inflammatory signals in patients across levels of illness severity. The pairing they found, weak antiviral defense beside strong inflammation, helps explain why the virus can gain ground while the body's response still damages tissue. Their report pointed toward treatments that might restore the early alarm or calm the late inflammation, and it shaped how doctors thought about timing immune therapies.
pmc-8096432:
Francesco Beghini and colleagues introduced bioBakery 3 in 2021, a set of tools for profiling microbial communities in depth. Shotgun metagenomics reads all the DNA in a sample, letting researchers ask which microbes are present and what they can do. The new version extends profiling beyond species lists to the functions microbes carry and even to individual strains.

The authors describe how the tools integrate taxonomic, functional, and strain level views of the same community. They show the system working across varied sample types and studies. Distinguishing strains matters because two microbes of one species can behave very differently, and the update brought that finer resolution into a widely used workflow.
pmc-8995832:
Willem de Vos, Herbert Tilg, and colleagues reviewed in 2022 the mechanisms by which the gut microbiome shapes human health. The community of microbes in the gut is now counted among the key regulators of the body's condition. Nearly every body site carries its own microbes, each in conversation with the organs nearby.

Drawing on newer molecular tools, the authors explain how gut microbes influence immunity, metabolism, and even the brain, and how those influences can turn harmful. They survey the pathways involved, from the chemicals microbes produce to their effects on the gut wall. The review offers a mechanism level account for readers who want more than the claim that the microbiome matters.
regardie-tree-of-life-1932:
Israel Regardie set out the whole theory of magic in The Tree of Life, printed in 1932. His ladder is the Kabbalah's Tree, with its ten spheres and its paths between them. Regardie was Crowley's former secretary and a deep student of the Golden Dawn.

He shows how rite, symbol, and god-forms map onto the Tree, and how the student climbs it. The book is a system, calm and ordered, where Crowley's own could be wild. It laid the ground for Regardie's later Golden Dawn work. Many still call it the clearest statement of his magic thought.
roy-translation-veds-1832:
Rammohun Roy opened Hindu scripture to English readers in his Translation of Several Principal Books, Passages, and Texts of the Veds. The second edition of 1832 gathers his renderings of Upanishadic and Vedantic passages. Roy, a Bengali scholar writing in two worlds, argued that the oldest texts teach one God, not many idols.

His translations armed India's reformers and startled Britain's scholars at once. The book stands as a founding document of Hindu reform and of the Bengal Renaissance that followed. Roy's English versions were the first by an Indian hand, which gives them their landmark place.
shahnameh-atkinson-1832:
James Atkinson Englished Ferdowsi's Shahnameh in 1832, the first English translation of Persia's national epic. The Oriental Translation Fund issued his rendering, abridged in a mix of prose and verse. Kings and heroes of ancient Iran parade through its pages, from the first rulers to the fall of the Sassanian throne.

Rostam's feats, Sohrab's tragic duel, and the long grief of empires fill the Shah Nameh's vast span. Ferdowsi spent decades singing Persia's past back to itself after conquest. Atkinson's shortened version, for all its cuts, first let English readers feel the epic's scale and sorrow.
sismondi-italian-republics-1832:
J. C. L. de Sismondi wrote his History of the Italian Republics in 1832. The Swiss historian treats the medieval city-states of Italy in one sweep. Venice, Florence, Genoa, and Milan lead his tale of free towns.

Communes rise, fight, trade, and craft laws in his brisk narrative. Sismondi praises their liberty as a light in a dark age. Tyrants seize some cities while others guard their councils with pride. His book taught Europe to admire the communes of the Middle Ages. Readers meet banking, art, and war born in the same busy streets. The work remains a classic hymn to town freedom.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5032:
Theodore Roosevelt gives eight yearly addresses, from December 3, 1901, to December 8, 1908, parted by three stars. The first opens under the shadow of a great loss. On the sixth of September, President McKinley was shot by an anarchist at the Pan-American Exposition at Buffalo, and died in that city on the fourteenth. Of the last seven elected presidents, Roosevelt notes, McKinley is the third to be murdered.

That bare fact, he holds, should wake grave alarm in all loyal citizens. The case has a darker shade than those before it: Lincoln fell to the fierce passions of four years of civil war, and Garfield to the spite of a thwarted office seeker. McKinley was killed by a warped criminal of the band that hates all governments, good and bad alike, and hates free rule even under the most just laws.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: No. 32 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It, dated June 17, 1897, is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a premium offer. The offer is the bicycle offer that stands in two earlier numbers. A reader who sends one hundred regular subscriptions may choose any wheel in the market. He buys from any dealer he chooses, and the publisher pays. Six-month subscriptions count as one half, and three-month ones as one quarter.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
In Ormsby's translation, Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes moves on to Volume 2, Part 32. Chapter forty-six tells of the terrible bell and cat fright Don Quixote got during the enamoured Altisidora's wooing. The knight goes to bed wrapped in reflections raised by her music.

Those thoughts, like fleas, will not let him sleep or rest, and the broken stitches of his stockings help to keep him awake. Morning comes at last on swift hours. Cervantes builds a night of comic torment out of love songs, torn hose, and a fright with bells and cats waiting in the dark.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, July 18, 1829, No. 381, illustrates Apsley House, the Duke of Wellington's mansion at Hyde Park Corner. Town mansions of the nobility, the article says, are generally beneath architectural criticism. An educated foreigner, told of a nobleman rich as a principality, is shown a plain brick house of forty or fifty feet. In the last three years, improvement has spread from public buildings to private mansions.

Apsley House's renovation, encasing it in a fine stone front, earns foremost notice. Benjamin Wyatt designed the Palladian work: a rusticated basement, a pediment on four Corinthian columns, and a bold cornice with pilasters at the angles. Only the door and window cases seem rather too small to the critic. A bronzed palisade continues the classical taste of the Hyde Park entrance gates opposite. Readers see the Iron Duke's house dressed to match his reputation.

Wingfield Manor-House in Derbyshire fills No. 576 of The Mirror, dated November 17, 1832. A writer in the Quarterly Review, quoted here, ranks it among the richest surviving embattled mansions of Henry VII's and Henry VIII's time. That period, between castle and palace, is called the best age of English architecture.

Camden credited the building, around 1440, to Ralph, Lord Cromwell, treasurer of England under Henry VI. Stone bags, or purses, carved over the gateway back the claim, since they pun on the treasurer's office. The manor once held two parks of nearly 1,100 acres, surveyed in 1655 and later divided into farms. Its plan of two square courts is laid out in detail.
tob-0132:
Svatmarama, a yogi of the fifteenth century, compiled the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, the classic manual of hatha yoga. After Patanjali's Sutras, no yoga text has guided more practice. The Sanskrit work teaches the way of force: training the body to steady the breath and mind.

Chapters treat postures, breath control, locks and seals of the body, and the rising of kundalini, the coiled energy at the spine's base. Svatmarama promises health, calm, and at last absorption in the divine. Teachers still quote his lists of asanas. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-10032:
Virgil, Rome's best-known poet, began his career with the Eclogues, ten short pastoral poems. Shepherds sing, compete in song, and talk of love, loss, and land taken from its owners. Mackail's translation is the version named for this entry.

Most poems stage a song contest or a talk between herdsmen in a green, idealized countryside. The fourth eclogue stands out: it foretells a child whose birth will bring a golden age, a passage Christians later read as a prophecy of Christ. These poems set the rules for pastoral poetry, and writers imitated them for well over a thousand years.
tob-13532:
Johann Weyer, a physician who had served at courts in Germany, published De Praestigiis Daemonum in 1563. Its title means On the Tricks of Demons. Weyer wrote against the witch trials then spreading through Europe, at real risk to himself.

He argues that so-called witchcraft is largely illusion, fraud, and sickness of mind, above all in old women charged with crimes they could not do. The true deceivers, he says, are demons who fool judges into burning the innocent. The book first broke the logic of the persecution in print and armed later critics of the trials.
tob-4032:
François Rabelais told of the giants Gargantua and his son Pantagruel in a five-book comic epic, presented complete in the Urquhart and Motteux translation. The giants eat, drink, learn, travel, and philosophize through a France of monks, lawyers, and pedants. Every pomposity meets earthy laughter, often at enormous length and volume.

Beneath the bawdiness lies a humanist manifesto for education, tolerance, and appetite for life. Its most famous invention, the Abbey of Theleme, runs on a single rule: Do What Thou Wilt. Urquhart and Motteux, translating a century later, matched Rabelais's verbal excess with their own. The result is English literature's happiest monument to learned laughter.
tob-4132:
Volume four of Mead's Echoes from the Gnosis presents the Hymn of Jesus, drawn from the apocryphal Acts of John. On the night before the Passion, Jesus leads his disciples in a round dance, singing a hymn full of riddling lines. Mead translates and comments on the strange, lovely text.

I would be saved, and I would save, the voice sings; I would be loosed, and I would loose. Early Christian esotericism seldom survives in so pure a form. Verified from the 1919 edition, the small volume lets readers watch a Gnostic-leaning community at prayer, with its Lord dancing at the center.
tob-4166-2832:
Andrew Lang, a Scottish scholar and storyteller, opened Myth, Ritual and Religion in 1887 with a challenge. Rival scholars claimed all myths were coded tales of the sun. Lang answered that so-called savage myths keep the earliest thought of mankind, and must be read on their own terms.

Volume one lays out his method, comparing Greek tales with the stories of peoples in Australia, Africa, and America. He finds the same puzzles about death, dreams, and ghosts everywhere. The writing is lively and combative, full of learning worn lightly. Anthropology's first great debate over myth begins in these pages.
tob-4214-10732:
Studies in Pessimism collects Schopenhauer's darkest short pieces in Saunders's translation. On the suffering of the world, he argues that pain is positive and real, while pleasure is only the brief absence of pain. Human striving, on his view, swings between want and boredom.

Other essays weigh the vanity of existence, suicide, and the short span of life. The tone is bleak, yet many readers find the honesty oddly freeing: lower the claims, and life disappoints less. Schopenhauer's wit keeps the gloom from turning dull. For a pure dose of his outlook in a small compass, no other selection serves better.
un-ga-res-32:
Early in 1946 the UN General Assembly took up the case of Spain, then ruled by General Franco. Resolution 32 recalls two wartime pledges. At San Francisco, states set up with Axis help were barred. At Potsdam, the big three powers vowed not to back Spain's entry to the UN. The Assembly backs both pledges in full.

Members are urged to act in the letter and spirit of those pledges in all future dealings with Spain. The text stops short of a break in ties. But it marks Franco's Spain as a state born of fascist aid. As such, it is unfit for a UN seat while his regime lasts.
un-ga-res-a-69-32:
An arms race in outer space must be stopped before it starts, says Resolution A/69/32, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the shared gain of all mankind in the study and use of space for peaceful ends. It voices grave concern at the chance of weapons spreading to orbit, and recalls the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bars mass-kill arms from space.

The rules now in force, the Assembly holds, do not by themselves bar a space arms race. The legal frame must be made stronger and more firm. A draft treaty on the point, laid before the Conference on Disarmament, is welcomed as a step in that work.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 32, adopted on 9 February 1946 at the twenty-sixth plenary meeting, dealt with Spain and its standing at the new United Nations. The Assembly recalled the San Francisco ruling. Under it, the Charter's membership terms could not fit states whose regimes had been set up with help from the armed forces of countries that fought the United Nations. That held while those regimes lasted.

The text also recalled the Potsdam statement that the leading Allied governments would not back membership for the sitting Spanish government, founded with Axis support. The Assembly backed both statements and urged members to guide their dealings with Spain by their letter and spirit.

Resolution 69/32 of the General Assembly, 'No first placement of weapons in outer space,' urges an early start to work on a treaty banning weapons in orbit. It welcomes the draft treaty against placing weapons in outer space or using force against space objects. The draft was tabled by China and the Russian Federation at the Conference on Disarmament in 2008. It was updated in 2014. Pending a treaty, the Assembly encourages all states, especially space-faring nations, to pledge not to be the first to place weapons in space.
un-sc-res-1032:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was renewed by the Security Council on 19 December 1995. The Secretary-General's report of 10 December advised keeping the United Nations Peace-keeping Force in Cyprus. The island's government agreed it should stay past 31 December 1995. No progress had been made toward a final political solution, the Council noted with concern.

The Council extended UNFICYP's mandate to 30 June 1996. Military authorities on both sides were told to keep the buffer zone free of incidents and to cooperate fully with the force. The Secretary-General was asked to keep the force's structure and size under review for possible change. The Council backed the force's advice on living conditions for Greek Cypriots and Maronites in the north and Turkish Cypriots in the south. It also voiced concern at growing military spending and the failure to extend the 1989 unmanning deal along the whole buffer zone.
un-sc-res-1132:
The Security Council turned to Sierra Leone in Resolution 1132, adopted on 8 October 1997. A military junta had seized power in a coup on 25 May 1997. It refused to step aside for the elected government. Violence spread, aid was blocked, and hunger deepened across the country.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands that the junta give up power at once. It bans the sale of oil, fuel, and arms to Sierra Leone. Junta members and their adult families face a travel ban. West African states may stop ships at sea to enforce the bans. A sanctions committee will track compliance and grant narrow aid exceptions. The bans end when the elected government returns.
un-sc-res-132: Claims about foreign troops inside Laos reached the Council in 1959. On 7 September 1959 it set up a sub-committee to look into them. Argentina, Italy, Japan, and Tunisia supplied the members. The group had to study the statements made before the Council. It could gather more statements and papers. It could also run inquiries of its own. A report was due as soon as possible. The vote was ten to one, with the Soviet Union against. The step let the Council test the claims without yet judging them.
un-sc-res-1332: Readers meet Resolution 1332 here as a Security Council record, catalogued with a date of 2000. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1432:
Angola's peace held through the summer of 2002, and sanctions stayed paused. On 15 August 2002 the Security Council added ninety days to a suspension of measures on UNITA. The limits came from resolution 1127 of 1997. They had first been paused that May. The April memorandum between the government and UNITA had ended the fighting. The Council wanted to encourage the peace process further.

Before the new period ended, the Council could review the measures again. It would weigh all facts, including word from Angola's government. The review would test how well the peace accords were being used. Suspension was a reward with a clock on it. Full lifting of the sanctions came later that year.
un-sc-res-1532:
Former Liberian president Charles Taylor is the target of Resolution 1532, passed in March 2004. Taylor had gone into exile in Nigeria after Liberia's civil war, but the Council feared his money and allies could restart the fighting. The members voted to freeze his assets.

The freeze reaches Taylor, his family, and close associates, and it covers funds held in other countries. States must stop those people from moving or spending the money, with narrow limits for basic needs. The text is a clear case of the Council using money as a tool to guard a peace deal.
un-sc-res-1632: From 2005, Resolution 1632 records a decision of the fifteen-member Security Council in official wording. The source is English Wikisource's transcription of the UN record. Inside, the members first align on the facts as they state them, then vote the response. The untouched text is the primary evidence of that response, and it is kept whole.
un-sc-res-1732: From 2006, Resolution 1732 records a formal decision of the Security Council, preserved in official-record form. The transcription here is English Wikisource's. Inside, the members build their case in the preamble before acting in the operative part, a rhythm as regular as a court's. The whole performance is kept, so the reasoning survives with the result.
un-sc-res-1832:
UNIFIL's mandate was extended for a further year on 27 August 2008. Lebanon's prime minister had written on 18 August asking for one more year without change. The Secretary-General advised the same on 21 August. The Council praised the force and its commander, and it restated its pledge to carry out resolution 1701 (2006) in full. Lebanon's state of affairs still threatened regional peace, it found.

The Council extended UNIFIL's present mandate until 31 August 2009. It praised the force's positive role. Its deployment beside the Lebanese Armed Forces had built a new strategic setting in the south, the Council said. Joint work between the force and the Lebanese army was welcomed and urged to grow. All parties were called to respect the halt to hostilities and the Blue Line along its whole length. They also had to work fully with the United Nations and guard UNIFIL staff.
un-sc-res-1932: Kept under number 1932, a Security Council resolution survives in official-record form through English Wikisource. The act's preamble and operative paragraphs divide the labor of governing between them: one explains, the other obliges. The entry preserves the division intact, giving readers the complete instrument rather than an account of its effects.
un-sc-res-232: Dated 1960 in the catalog, Resolution 232 records formal action by the United Nations Security Council. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-32: Fighting on the island of Java drew the Security Council back in Resolution 32, passed on 26 August 1947. Armed work by Dutch forces on the soil of the Republic of Indonesia still ran on. The vote calls both the Netherlands and the Republic back to the Council's call of 1 August 1947. That call had ordered a cease-fire and a peaceful fix to their fight. Both sides are told to hew to it in strict form.
un-sc-res-332:
An Israeli raid on Beirut in April 1973 brought Lebanon's protest to the Council. On 21 April 1973 the Council voiced deep concern at all acts of violence. It grieved the loss of innocent life in the recent attacks. Lebanon and Israel had both spoken. Truce records showed a pattern of broken resolutions. The Council's anger in the text runs in both directions, but its formal blame lands on one side.

The Council condemns Israel's repeated military attacks on Lebanon. Those attacks broke Lebanon's sovereignty and the Charter. They also broke the armistice deal between the two states. Israel had to stop all such attacks at once. The warning closed a tense debate on cross-border raids.
un-sc-res-432:
Walvis Bay's place inside Namibia was declared by the Security Council in July 1978. The Council recalled resolution 385 (1976) and its own resolution 431 (1978), adopted the same day as this text. The General Assembly had declared in November 1977 that Walvis Bay is an integral part of Namibia. South Africa held the port enclave apart from the rest of the territory it occupied.

The Council declared that Namibia's territorial integrity and unity must be assured by bringing Walvis Bay back within its territory. It promised full support for the steps needed to win the port's early return. Until that day, South Africa must not use Walvis Bay in any way that harmed Namibia's independence or the health of its economy. The Council stayed seized of the matter until the bay was fully reintegrated. The port stayed in South African hands until 1994.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1032, adopted unanimously on 19 December 1995, keeps the UN force in Cyprus into 1996. The Secretary-General's December report had recommended extending UNFICYP, and Cyprus agreed the force was still needed beyond the year's end. The Council noted with concern that no progress had been made toward a final political settlement, nor on widening a 1989 agreement to unman sensitive posts along the buffer zone.

The mandate was extended to 30 June 1996. Military authorities on both sides were told to prevent incidents along the buffer zone and cooperate fully with the force. The Secretary-General was asked to review the force's structure and strength with an eye to restructuring it.

Sierra Leone's military junta is sanctioned in Resolution 1132, adopted on 8 October 1997. The junta that seized power on 25 May 1997 had refused to restore the democratically elected government, violence and humanitarian conditions were worsening, and ECOWAS had agreed sanctions at Abuja.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands the junta relinquish power immediately and make way for constitutional order. It imposes a travel ban on junta members and adult family members, as designated by a new sanctions Committee, and an embargo on petroleum products and arms to Sierra Leone. The Committee may authorize exceptions case by case, including petroleum imports for the elected government and for humanitarian or ECOMOG needs. Acting also under Chapter VIII, the Council authorizes ECOWAS to enforce the embargo, including by halting inward shipping to inspect and verify cargoes, and requires thirty-day ECOWAS reports. The measures end when the junta complies.

A claim of invasion in Laos sent a Council fact team to Asia in 1959. On 7 September, it adopted Resolution 132. Ten members voted yes and one voted no. The Soviet Union was the lone no. Laos, neutral under the 1954 Geneva deal, charged that North Vietnamese troops fought on its soil. The Council heard claims it could not check from New York.

The text names a four-member sub-panel to look into it. Argentina, Italy, Japan, and Tunisia hold the seats. The panel must study the claims made before the Council. It may take fresh statements and papers as well. Any inquiries it finds needful are in its remit. Its report is due as soon as can be. No clear proof of invasion came back from the trip.

Congo's peacekeeping mission, MONUC, is kept in place by this text of 14 December 2000. The Lusaka Ceasefire Agreement was still largely unimplemented and fighting went on. At the same time, new deals on pulling forces apart had just been reached at Maputo and Harare, and the Council wanted observers ready to check them.

MONUC's mandate now ran to 15 June 2001, and the Council backed sending more military observers once conditions allowed. Those observers would verify that the parties kept the ceasefire and carried out the agreed pullbacks. All parties were called on to stop fighting, honour the chain of peace deals, and cooperate fully with the mission.

Angola's long civil war had just ended when Resolution 1432 passed unanimously on 15 August 2002. The government and the UNITA rebels had signed a ceasefire addendum on 4 April 2002. UNITA soldiers were being demobilized. On 2 August the movement disbanded its military wing. It was turning toward politics.

To help the peace hold, the Council suspended some sanctions on UNITA. The travel bans dated from 1997. They were lifted for another ninety days under Chapter VII. Free movement would let UNITA members join the peace process. It would also aid national reconciliation. Members said they might review the measures before the ninety days ran out.

Liberia's former president and his circle have their wealth frozen in this text of 12 March 2004. The Council found that Charles Taylor and his associates had drained Liberia's resources and hidden funds and property abroad. From exile, he still controlled much of that money and could use it to stir up trouble in Liberia and the region.

Acting under Chapter VII, all states are ordered to freeze funds and assets owned or controlled by Taylor. The freeze also covers his immediate family, senior officials of his former regime, and close allies named by the sanctions committee. The freeze is meant to keep that money from wrecking Liberia's recovery, with the aim that the assets eventually be returned for the benefit of its people.

The Group of Experts watching the arms embargo on Côte d'Ivoire is extended until 15 December 2005 in this text of 18 October 2005. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council noted that the situation in the country still threatened peace in the region. The group was asked to send a brief written update through the sanctions committee before its term ended, ahead of a fuller report.

Its own sanctions working group is closed down on 21 December 2006. The Informal Working Group on General Issues of Sanctions had been asked to develop general recommendations for making United Nations sanctions work better. The Council decided the group had fulfilled that mandate. It took note with interest of the best practices and methods in the group's report and asked its own subsidiary bodies to take note of them as well.

Resolution 1832, adopted on 27 August 2008, extends the UN force in southern Lebanon for another year, unchanged. Lebanon's prime minister had written on 18 August asking for a one-year renewal without amendment, and the Secretary-General recommended granting it. The Council praised UNIFIL's active role and the dedication of its personnel and commander since the force was strengthened after the 2006 war.

The present mandate was extended until 31 August 2009. The Council restated its commitment to carrying out resolution 1701 in full, the text that ended the 2006 fighting and promised a permanent ceasefire and long-term settlement. It also underlined that UNIFIL must have every means and piece of equipment its mandate requires.

The war crimes court for Rwanda faced a familiar problem in June 2010: it could not finish its work on time. Resolution 1932, adopted on 29 June 2010, deals with that court, which was set up after the genocide of 1994. Its president warned that experienced staff were leaving before the trials ended.

The Council extended the terms of the court's appeals judges until the end of 2012. Trial judges, both permanent and temporary, would serve until the end of 2011, or until their cases finished. The court could also bring back a former judge as a temporary judge if no judge on its roster was free. States were pressed to help arrest the fugitives who were still at large. The point was to let the last trials finish properly.

A year of appeals had failed to end the rebellion in Southern Rhodesia. On 16 December 1966 the Council adopted Resolution 232, which turned the pressure into binding sanctions. The white minority regime still held power after its one-sided declaration of independence from Britain. British measures had not brought the rebellion to an end.

The Council ruled that the situation was a threat to international peace and security. All member states had to block imports of key Rhodesian goods. The list included asbestos, iron ore, chrome, sugar, tobacco, copper, meat, and hides. Arms, aircraft, and vehicles had to be kept from the regime. States were also told to give the illegal government no financial or economic aid. These were the first binding sanctions of this kind in United Nations history.

Fighting continued in Indonesia in the summer of 1947 between Dutch forces and the Republic of Indonesia. Resolution 32, adopted on 26 August 1947, is a short reminder to both sides. It recalls Resolution 27 of that year, with its cease-fire order and call for a peaceful settlement. The Netherlands and the Republic of Indonesia were called on to stick strictly to the Council's recommendation of 1 August 1947. Nothing new was added; the point was to hold both governments to the earlier order.

Israeli commandos raided Beirut in April 1973, killing Palestinian leaders. Lebanon brought its outrage to the Council. Members grieved the civilian deaths caused by cross-border violence. Resolution 332 was adopted on 21 April 1973. Eleven members voted yes. China, Guinea, the Soviet Union, and the United States abstained.

The Council condemned every act of violence that harms innocent people. It then condemned Israel's repeated military attacks on Lebanon by name. Those attacks broke the Charter, the 1949 armistice, and past ceasefire orders. Israel was told to stop all such attacks at once. The text balances two angers: at raids on Lebanon, and at the wider cycle of killings endangering civilians and air travel.

Walvis Bay belongs to Namibia, Resolution 432 declares; it was adopted unanimously on 28 July 1978. Walvis Bay was a deep-water port enclave on Namibia's coast that South Africa administered as its own, separate from the territory around it. The General Assembly had already called the port an integral part of Namibia in 1977.

The Council declared that Namibia's territorial integrity and unity must be secured by bringing Walvis Bay back within its territory. It promised full support for steps toward that early reintegration. Until it happened, South Africa was told not to use the bay in any way that harmed Namibia's independence or economic viability. The port was in fact handed over in 1994, four years after independence.

Kazakhstan was the largest republic to leave the Soviet Union in land terms. Its independence came in December 1991. An application for UN membership followed quickly. Resolution 732, adopted without a vote on 23 January 1992, took up the request at the Council's 3034th meeting.

Members advised the General Assembly to admit the Republic of Kazakhstan. The Assembly acted in March 1992. The new state inherited Soviet nuclear weapons on its soil. That fact gave its arrival unusual weight in security debates. Kazakhstan later gave those weapons up. Its admission formed part of the broad post-Soviet intake that reshaped the UN in early 1992.
un-un-res-sixth-report-of-the-secretary-:
Late 2000 in Sierra Leone is covered by the sixth report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Mission there, document S/2000/832. UNAMSIL had survived its spring hostage crisis and was being rebuilt with more troops and a firmer mandate. A fresh ceasefire was being tested on the ground.

The report describes patrols, disarmament steps, and the slow return of state control to rebel-held areas. It also deals with the diamond trade that funded the war. The text shows a mission moving, with care, from survival toward real peace work.
uslaw-usc-t2-s132: Section 132 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers the departments of the Library of Congress. It sits in Chapter 5 of that title, on the Library of Congress. The rule is a single sentence. It states that the Library of Congress is to be set out in two departments. One is a general library and the other is a law library. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4132:
Section 4132 of Title 2 of the United States Code recasts the Senate recording and photo studios. It sits in Chapter 41 of that title, on congressional officers, in the part on those studios. Part (a) winds up an older body. The body known before 1 April 1991 as the Senate Recording and Photographic Studios is abolished. In its stead two bodies are set up.

The two new bodies are the Senate Recording Studio and the Senate Photographic Studio. The heading of the section also covers rules and fees for photographs and photo services of the new studios. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s632:
Section 632 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers the yearly adoption of a concurrent resolution on the budget. It sits in Chapter 17A of that title, on the congressional budget process. Part (a) states the content of such a resolution. On or before 15 April of each year, Congress is to complete action on the resolution. It covers the fiscal year that begins on 1 October of that year.

The resolution is to set out fit levels for that fiscal year. It is also to set levels for at least each of the four years that ensue, as the text goes on to state. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
wolff-psychologia-empirica-1732:
Christian Wolff, the great system builder of the German Enlightenment, published his Psychologia Empirica at Frankfurt in 1732. The Latin title adds that the science is handled by the scientific method, step by ordered step. The first edition is the text here, and no public-domain English translation of the work exists.

Wolff treats the soul as a field for exact study: its powers of knowing and desiring, measured and defined. His empirical psychology sorts what experience shows before reason builds its higher system upon it. The book's methodical order shaped how German universities taught the mind for a century. Kant grew up in Wolff's shadow and spent his career escaping and honoring it at once.
